A Ruling for a Shochet: Not to Eat Meat.
Some time ago the shochet in Golonóg signed a written ban undertaking not to slaughter any cattle from Dąbrowa. Later it turned out that the same shochet keeps only very barely to the ban to which he had given his signature, and has again caused damage to the Dąbrowa kehilla through his secret slaughtering.
In connection with this the Jewish kehilla in Dąbrowa, in the person of its president Mr. Najfeld, summoned the shochet to the Będzin rabbinate for having transgressed the ban.
The ruling issued by the Będzin rabbinate says that the shochet must give 200 zł., must not eat any meat or fish for 2 weeks, and if he transgresses the ban once more he will be removed from his post as shochet.
—o—
The Number of Licences for Peddlers Reduced.
Yesterday the presidents of the Będzin and Sosnowiec merchants' associations, Messrs. Rubinlicht and Klajner, intervened at the Katowice voivodeship office concerning the question of licences for peddlers for the year 1934.
The official in charge of the question was of the opinion that the number of licences for this year should be reduced substantially. Thanks to the intervention it was achieved that the number of licences will be smaller by 10 per cent.
—o—
What's Heard in Zawiercie?
The Well-Known Surgeon Dr. Jakub Lewinsztajn Has Died.
Last week the surgeon beloved by everyone, Prof. Dr. Jakub Lewensztajn, died in Warsaw. The town of Zawiercie has lost in him one of its best public activists. Several years ago the doctor donated to the municipality a plot for a park. At his expense the wall around the Krymiłów [probably Kromołów] cemetery was built. The deceased was brought to Krymiłów, where he was buried in his family grave.
—o—
A Festive Academy.
On Saturday night a festive academy was held in the „Arlekin“ hall, organised by „Betar“ in connection with the 10th anniversary of its existence. After the greetings, stud. L. Rozenberg set out[?] in his lecture the aims and tasks of the organisation.
Then the second part was performed, in which Mr. Mańczyk[?] and stud. Rozenberg distinguished themselves. With their recitations and parodies.
—o—
Suicides.
On New Year's Eve (Sylvester night) the student Lakata and Miss R. committed suicide here. The latter was successfully saved from death.
Z. Zelinger.

Cast Us Not Off in Old Age

[Będzin — charity and institutions.] (On the continued campaign to complete the new building of the Będzin "Moshav Zkenim" [old-age home]).
Some months ago — as is known — the foundation stone was laid for enlarging the building of the Będzin "Moshav Zkenim".
With heavy hearts the board of the institution approached the beginning, but the belief that the campaign would find the warmest response among Będzin's Jewish public drove it to begin the construction work.
And so indeed it was. The sympathy of the Jews of Będzin for the institution is very great.
To their credit it must be stressed that not only was there not a single person who wished to refuse to give for the building, but when the delegates of "Linat Cholim" came about the campaign, they were received as is fitting, with a friendly countenance, and thanks to this the construction work was in full swing.
But a strong force of nature compelled the work [?] to be interrupted: the severe frosts, which prevailed for several weeks, caused the old men and women not yet to be housed in the large new rooms.
Now, when the work can already be continued, the collection campaign is being stepped up again, so that in the coming weeks the building may already become the home of the old men and women.
There is still a sufficient number of people who have as yet no share in this good deed, and it is to them that we turn with our warm appeal:
— Do not forget the prayer that everyone says on the Days of Awe — "Cast us not off in the time of old age"...
Give the aged people the possibility of living out their last years in tranquillity, in airy rooms, under proper care; receive our delegates, men and women, with a friendly countenance and help in building the old-age home.
Respectfully,
The board of "Linat Cholim", Będzin.
A "Brilliant" Feat by a Young Man from Wolbrom

[Wolbrom — family life.] A "dispute" between America and Poland over a young wife from Wolbrom.
In 1931 Miss Bala W. of Wolbrom married an uncle of hers in Danzig. The couple's economic situation was not good [?]; the antisemitic deeds of the Germans in Danzig also tormented the young man badly, and he emigrated to America.
The young wife could not remain in Danzig, and she returned to her parents in Wolbrom.
Month after month passed; Mrs. W. waited for a letter from her "faithful" [?] husband, but it was as if he had vanished into water — no news of him at all.
At first the young woman's grief was very great, but little by little she too began to forget her husband — and needless to say, a young man from Wolbrom fell in love with her, and she was, after all, one of the lucky ones; and without waiting long she stood with him — with the lover, that is — under the wedding canopy according to the Law of Moses and Israel.
She would long since have forgotten her first husband, were it not for the sudden "bombshell". The first husband informed her in a letter that she should prepare for the journey, since he was sending her a ship's ticket and travel expenses.
To this letter the Wolbrom husband wrote back to America that he no longer had any wife to claim in Wolbrom and that Bala already belonged to another.
The American uncle, learning that his "goods" in Wolbrom did not belong to him, turned to the American consul in Warsaw, who at his request informed Mrs. Bala that she had the right to travel to America.
The Wolbrom husband, seeing that his position was threatened, hit upon a "brilliant" invention that would establish that Bala belonged to him and no longer thought of going to America.
He called a photographer into his flat and told him: "Mr. Photographer, turn to the wall for a while." And when the couple was under the quilt, he called out to the photographer:
— "Now do the job!"...
And the photographer took a picture of which no one could say that they were not man and wife...
The husband quickly got out of bed, crying: "Now let them see who Bala's husband is!"...
The photograph was sent to the American consul, so that he might be convinced that Bala's real husband is in Wolbrom and not in America.
Greets the New Year with His Christian Sweetheart and Catches Blows from His Jewish "So-and-So"

[Sosnowiec — scandals.] In a Sosnowiec restaurant a stormy scene took place on Sunday night.
To a table at which a Jewish young man of about 35 was sitting in the company of a young Christian woman, a Jewish woman suddenly ran up and, with the cry "Take that, you scoundrel!" [Polish podlec], grabbed a bottle and brought it down on the young man's head.
There was an uproar; the waiters threw themselves on the woman and took her away to a separate room.
There the woman calmed down a little and told the following:
The gentleman whom she had "honoured" with the bottle over the head is her own husband — he is a commercial representative of an Upper Silesian firm.
A short time ago he fell in love with a Christian woman and carried on [?] a romance with her, and he abandoned his own wife with the 2 children and now lives elsewhere.
On Sunday she learned that the unfaithful husband had gone to a restaurant to greet the New Year in the company of his sweetheart. The woman therefore decided to take revenge on him and make a scandal for him.
Having told this, the woman left the restaurant.

The First Wife Found a Bride for Her Former Husband

[Będzin — a true story; everyday life.]
Things that happen...
Modrzejowska Street in Będzin is buzzing ("going on wheels"): from mouth to mouth passes the sensation that took place there.
The prologue of the story begins in the year 1914, after the outbreak of the World War. Together with other reservists, Mr. R., a resident of Modrzejowska Street, also went off to the Russian army, leaving behind a wife and children.
Since Mr. R. left, no news whatsoever was received from him, so that it was more than certain that he had perished in the war.
A year went by, two — how long can one sit alone? The widow found herself a match, and a respectable one at that, and she married.
After some time the Będzin woman learned that her first husband was alive and that he had married in a small town in the Kielce province. Well, what can be done? He with a second wife — she with a second husband. But the Angel of Death disturbed the "idyll" and took away the second wife of her first husband.
And when his wife died, he remembered that a number of years ago he had left a wife and children in Będzin — so he came back and wanted to "make peace". To his great regret, however, he found his wife in Będzin already a married woman.
"Don't worry, my husband," the first wife comforted him, "I'll find you a suitable match, and as they say: '[—]' (an undeciphered saying) [?]..." The first wife found him a match "fit for God and for people", and at the wedding, which was celebrated last week in Będzin, the first wife was "the right hand", conducting herself like a close in-law, as long as her former husband would be satisfied with the match she had made for him...

Begging and the kehilla representation — Operating on the modus of "philanthropy"

Operating on the modus of "philanthropy".
Not long ago we had occasion to witness a fact that could have upset anyone who read about it, anyone who saw it.
It came to light that a begging couple in Sosnowiec had a little child die, and that they made little of it; they informed neither the Chevra Kadisha nor the Jewish kehilla, they left it lying as though nothing at all had happened, and even — as is the way of the world — went off begging, leaving the dead child with a second one, a living one. It did not bother them in the least, just as if nothing at all had happened. In the evening — after "work" — they came home, lit the stove, ate supper, went to bed, and the next morning went back to their daily occupation, once again leaving the room locked with the living and the dead child.
Once, in earlier years, such an occurrence would have stirred up a whole town, and people would certainly have reacted to it as they should; but those former times are long gone, and today nobody has a head for dealing with such matters.
True, people heard about it, read about it, talked it over — some with bitterness, some with mockery and disgust — and there it stayed; it went no further. After all, each one has "his own" troubled head. Everyone chases the bullet [?] to earn his daily needs, for as a rule those who get upset over such matters are the ordinary people, those who work hard until they get hold of their hard-earned groszy; whereas the great ones, the sharp [?] minds, the intelligentsia, those who really ought to have dealt with such a matter — they don't lift a finger [literally: don't put their hands into cold water], they stand at a distance and take no interest at all in what goes on there, in the lower strata of the Jewish masses.
It pains the heart when one dwells on the fact described above, and it pains even more because there is nobody to react properly, so that similar bitter occurrences should not repeat themselves again and again — occurrences by which we are only degraded in the eyes of the authorities, in the eyes of non-Jews. Moreover, one may be sure that if we do not react to such loathsome crimes, they will become more and more widespread and bring shame upon us.
It is no longer a secret that in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia many hundreds and possibly thousands of families make their living from this "profession" — young people who could have worked and earned, but who for various reasons stretched out their hands for the crust of beggar's bread. They no longer want to work, even if they were given any employment whatsoever — all the more so when they collect each day as much cash as they need to live on.
Zagłębie and Upper Silesia are a very good place for them, so that every day they are busy in another town, and "working" the district usually takes a month.
What becomes of these people once they take up this occupation can be seen from the fact mentioned above, which clearly proves that they are turned into non-humans, into beasts; the worst immoral deeds occur among them, they live among themselves like the wildest tribes, and when they come into their ghetto [?], when they are in their own places, no one is ashamed before the other to commit the most terrible acts; the most loathsome and barbaric things are everyday phenomena with them.
Besides, one must not forget that this camp is steadily growing. There are reasons enough and more, first of all the bitter situation that we call the crisis period. People have nothing to do, they grow desperate, they wander about without employment until they sink to the level of stretching out their hand, so that first of all there is something to buy a piece of bread with. Thus this element is drawn in one by one, until one loses all shame, and then it seems to them that begging is an occupation, a profession, to which they have a right, like all other people who live in God's little world.
And the bitterest thing of all is that young people are joining, and the young ones have children whom they already bring up in their ways, and so beggars sons of beggars grow up as a matter of course. That is the most terrible and most painful thing; to our shame we must say that among no other people in the world are beggars "manufactured" in such a way as happens among us. Young people loading themselves onto the shoulders of an entire people merely because they become lazy — that is unheard of and impermissible, and the end of it is that because of this those suffer who need to be supported, those who truly ought to be maintained by the people.
There are people of the common folk who have worked all their lives: one was a water-carrier and another a labourer, one a craftsman and another grabbed at whatever came along; and these people have become unable to work in their old age and have no relatives able to support them — so why should such worn-out people not deserve to be supported by the people? Why should they not be maintained in a dignified way by, let us say, a Jewish kehilla administration? It is not enough that we give such a person a grosz when he drags himself from door to door while he hasn't even the strength for it.
Would it not have been wiser to support, in a dignified way, this element which has earned merit, rather than let such a camp grow, which brings us shame and because of which we are degraded in people's eyes?
If the middle class takes no interest in the question — whether because they cannot or because they will not; if the matter is foreign to our notables; if the intelligentsia does not want to know about it; then [?] — for the honour of the Jewish people this ought to have been dealt with; if the question, which becomes more serious and at the same time more loathsome from day to day, has found no one to take up [?] its solution — should the Jewish kehilla as such not have been permitted to deal with it?
Who, who but the Jewish kehilla, the Jewish representation, must not allow Jewish honour to be degraded; and the professional beggars, the young camp of outcasts, who commit all sorts of crimes under the mask of begging, must be separated from the Jewish camp. On no account may such a matter remain unsolved.
We have had enough disgrace from this gang, so that one must react properly in this field, especially when the undesirable category keeps growing. It is high time for the question to be dealt with properly at the kehilla meetings.
From our kehilla representatives we have had nothing to this day; they have created nothing productive or useful, therefore they should [?] at least take up the solution of this question, and if they managed to solve it properly, that would be one of their finest merits, one of the highest achievements, for in this way they would bring a little order and light into this field, which is so burdensome to every decent person, to every Jewish citizen.
The Jewish people is accustomed to giving charity without measure, without valuation and without system. In the worst conditions, in the hardest times, we feel our people's sufferings; we always give beyond our strength and means; one Jew does not let another fall, so that not for nothing have we been crowned with the name "merciful sons of the merciful". But in today's bitter times we are not able to give charity without a system, especially when, because of this, those elements suffer who really ought to be supported with a generous hand.
It is not out of the question that among this camp of young beggars there are people with broken hearts, ruined merchants and manufacturers, people who were themselves givers, and they are certainly treated no better than all sorts of individuals. But is that any wonder? Is the average Jew able to investigate and study who really ought to be treated more decently and who not? Is that an occupation for busy people, who are often more alms-givers than merchants? If a merchant is sometimes exasperated and does not give — and precisely to the one who does need to receive — that is no wonder. After all, one loses one's equilibrium and stops being patient.
This field must not be allowed to branch out any further; our representatives must set about solving the question seriously and energetically — a question that is simply crying out for a little order to be introduced.
Here, once and for all, a Caesarean section must be performed, and that which is undesirable, that which is dangerous, that which degrades us at every step, must be uprooted.
If our whole life could be transformed in the course of the last years, if we could adapt ourselves to incomprehensible phenomena, then surely we must bring something new and desirable into this field.
The watchword must be: support what is necessary with every possible means, introduce a system and order in this field; on the other hand ignore, despise and uproot without mercy that which is harmful, that which brings degradation upon us. Not only must we not give a single grosz to what is harmful, but with all our strength it must be torn out by the root. For [not only] do we lack the strength to support what we ought not to have, but it also hinders us from conducting the desired planned, productive work.
Let the kehilla representations take note of all this and begin to deal with it intensively, until the desired fruits are achieved.
The History of the Będzin Kehilla in the Second Half of the 19th Century

Moshe Feinkind. — Based on archival records. *)
I.
The Będzin kehilla is a very old one. It already existed in the 16th century, possessing its own cemetery, which not every congregation of Jews could have at that time.
The Będzin kehilla was also highly respected. This is explained by the fact that it had a representative in the Council of Four Lands, and not every kehilla had the right to be represented among the 23 elected members of the Council.
This Będzin delegate was called R' Israel ben Shmuel (Shmuelevich).
We also find that a Jewish merchant of Będzin, known by the name R' Moshe Bendiner, was present in the year 1695 at the Leipzig fair (Messe).
In the year 1675[?] there belonged to the Będzin kehilla 268 men and 281 women; together they were 549 souls, of whom 219 men and 227 women lived in the town of Będzin itself. The rest — in the surrounding area.
The statistics were compiled for the sake of the "head tax" that Jews had to pay to the state treasury, and since in recent times it came to [—] about three gulden for each Jewish head, the Jews had to declare a considerably smaller number of inhabitants. In fact Będzin had a much larger Jewish population than the official statistics show.
Since in Poland's historical times [the town] belonged to the Bishop of Kraków, the Jews had to pay him separately[?] a certain sum for living and trading in the town.
The draconian clerical law "de non tolerandis Judaeis" (not to tolerate Jews) did not, it seems, apply to Będzin, but the Jews were only allowed to live there on certain streets; on the Old Market and two side alleys was the Jewish "ghetto", in which all the Jewish poverty was squeezed and crammed together, and the "Jewish Street" too is a part of this Będzin "ghetto".
Afterwards, however, when Poland after the Congress of Vienna (1815) passed into Russian hands, a law was issued in the year 1823 according to which no foreign [newly arrived] Jews might settle in Będzin without the permission of the central government authority, because the town lay within the 21-verst belt from the border.
This law remained in force until the year 1862. In that year Alexander the Second abolished altogether all the decrees and restrictions concerning the residence and trade of Jews in the towns of Congress Poland.
And being severely restricted in legal residence in the town — since it was not so easy to obtain from the Warsaw central authority, with the consent of the Namiestnik, such a permit for an average Jew, not even for the rabbi of the town, who was only granted, by way of exception, a concession to live in Będzin for as long as he would be rabbi there — the Jews settled in the area around the town, [in places] lying farther than 21 versts from the German or Austrian border.
Because of this harsh law, the villages of Sielce[?], Modrzejów[?], Sławków, Łagisza, Strzemieszyce, Gzichów, Siewierz etc. belonged at that time to the Będzin kehilla. And with all that, the entire Jewish population in Będzin amounted in the year 1856 to 2440 souls, and only 1718 Christians.
And from the 1850s of the last century — from which time I have succeeded in finding the kehilla records in the Piotrków State Archive — I will sketch here the events and experiences as far as the framework of a newspaper article permits.
2.
The town of Będzin belonged at that time to the Olkusz district (powiat), Radom province (guberniya), and only when in Poland 10 whole guberniyas were created instead of 5 (1867) and Piotrków also became a provincial town, did Będzin become a district attached to the Piotrków guberniya.
According to the records concerning the kehilla in Będzin, which are in the Piotrków State Archive, in the year 1834 the rabbi of Sieradz, R' Yohanan David Langfus[?], was elected as rabbi of Będzin [—], for whom an annual pension of 180 roubles was fixed, besides a free apartment and other rabbinical income.
Rabbi Langfus received the concession only at the end of 1858, with the well-known clause that as long as he would be rabbi here, he had the right, by way of exception, to live in Będzin.
The entire kehilla budget for the year 1854 amounted to 672 roubles.
Part of the budget was covered by the income from the mikveh and from other sources, such as, for example, from house number 120 on Jews' Street (Juden-Gasse), which had been bequeathed as a perpetual legacy for the benefit of the kehilla by the Będzin butcher Hershel Kushanovski, who at the same time also donated his Torah scroll to the synagogue (December 1848) on condition that his yahrzeit be observed. The rest of the budget was levied on the householders in the district.
In the year 1855 the whole etat [kehilla tax] amounted to 495 roubles. Of 374 registered, only 289 householders paid the etat. The remaining people were disqualified as poor.
The poverty of the Będzin Jews was great at that time, for in the "middle year"[?], i.e. 1856, only 359 householders were registered, of whom 202 were the payers of the etat of a sum of 495 roubles; and in 1855 one person appears who paid a whole 30 roubles of etat, and the largest number paid only 50 kopecks. The same person no longer appears in 1856 in the etat list. The highest etat sum is only 10 roubles and the rest down to 20 kopecks. The entire etat then amounted to 422 roubles.

The Year That Has Gone

[Leading article — the year in review; world, economy and politics.]
The times when people used to take leave of the old year carefree and with stormy joy and go out to meet the new one belong already, it seems, to legend. Unrest, fear, insecurity, helplessness — these are the feelings with which one crosses the threshold of the new year; but never have these feelings been so strong, so pronounced and so justified as this year.
The consequences of the World War, the „curse of the monstrous evil deed“ that was committed over four endlessly long and boundlessly criminal years, have perhaps never until now been felt so strongly, have never ripened into such a heavy vengeance, as in the year just past. On the surface, it seems, all is calm; formally peace reigns everywhere. And even in distant Manchuria, where human blood is being shed, there reigns, in the conception of the world leaders, a state of peace. Yet in the hardest years of the war man was perhaps not so worried, so anxious about the morrow, not so full of insecurity, so lost in his deeds and hopes, as he is today, in a time of full peace. A heavy expectation of unknown events, of unforeseen disasters, weighs upon the soul of the individual and of whole societies and nations alike.
The past year showed with the greatest clarity and vividness[?] that from a criminal sowing no blessing comes forth, that a peace built on the graves of millions of people is no peace, that a prosperity that sought to be erected on the ruins of countries is no prosperity.
The gravest and deepest result of the war, the economic crisis, which long ago turned into a chronic disease of mankind, took on in the past year such dimensions, such an enormous scale, that people everywhere already speak openly of an economic catastrophe. There is no country that has not been gripped by the crisis. Even a country like America, which was regarded as a land of especially great economic power and financial might, is also beginning to feel the economic convulsions in which all the other countries writhe. Overproduction, unemployment, financial difficulties and currency chaos have become the fate of all countries without exception — the small and the large, the industrial and the agrarian, the old well-established ones and the new ones that arose only as a result of the turmoil of the war.
The year 1933 helped to an enormous degree to shatter various illusions about might and power. It turned out that there are no sufficiently firm systems, no sufficiently strong economic organisms that could withstand the destructive onslaught of the crisis. The year showed that the strength of the mighty currencies is just as illusory as that of the weak ones, that the rock-solid banks in America are not rock-solid at all.
And standing at the edge of the abyss, knowing that they are heading for a catastrophe whose like has never been, the rulers of the nations cannot come to an agreement on common means to avert the unavoidable. Instead every state tries to save itself on its own and at its own risk; every country acts exactly as if it existed alone in the world, completely isolated, exactly as if it were not the clearest truth that under today's system there are no sealed-off countries, that one organism is most closely bound to and dependent on the other. Measures are being taken!
A strange picture was presented in the past year by the responsible leaders of the world, the famous politicians. The picture would truly have been a very merry one, had it not borne witness to complete helplessness and perplexity. Like professional commercial travellers the statesmen travelled from one country to another, from one capital to the next. They paid each other compliments, journalists followed every move of those in power and reported on their every step, and every time it turned out that the visit had been in vain, that they had not succeeded in reaching an understanding, and if they did come to an understanding, it was not about the essential and not about the most important, and that the noose that lies around the neck of the individual countries, and that drags more and more others into its circle[?], is tightening ever more.
The leaders made the impression not of learned doctors but of swindling quacks who want to weaken[?] the misfortune and drive it away with a little wand. One of the magic rulers that is supposed to save the world has become the wild, inflamed, inciting nationalism that goes as far as madness — through Hitler's government in Germany, which wants the rulers of the world to take of its prescriptions..
The contradictions of the prevailing economic and social system have never stood out so sharply and plainly, and one may say so cynically, as in the past year. Overproduction in all fields, an abundance of every good thing, of all kinds of products and manufactures, and alongside it armies[?] of wretched and poor people living in the greatest want and hardship; in America grain is burned, rivers of condensed milk are poured out so that waters turn white for miles; in Brazil hundreds of wagonloads of coffee are thrown into the sea; in Canada locomotives are fired with wheat — and at the same time a host of unemployed, whose number no one imagined could be so great, with a tendency to keep growing steadily. A tragic situation in which, as one publicist wrote: „Millions of healthy hands dangle idle without work, millions of healthy hands cannot earn a piece of bread, millions of working hands cannot make themselves a garment, precious skilled human labour can find no buyer, pure human energy, which can create worlds, can find no taker, and millions go hungry throughout the whole world“.
And with fear and horror the world looks on and waits for what will happen. To what consequences will this wild, tragic paradox lead... Some make strange movements, which are meant to signify that something is being done after all to get the world out of the tight spot. Some wait with closed eyes for the unknown and terrible that must come and take revenge on the world for being badly, very badly governed.
With this fear, with this insecurity, with the torment of unclear expectation, mankind steps into the new year 1924 [sic; read 1934].
En.
A Little Feuilleton. / Cards.

[Będzin — satirical feuilleton; card-playing.]
At the end of the year 1933, 5694 since the Creation of the world, an angel flew over Zagłębie, and to his white, delicate wings was tied a little box of good, excellent poker [?] cards (32-card packs...). By the Będzin castle the box got caught on something and fell down — and Będzin was flooded with cards...
Będzin has become a city of cards. Everywhere, wherever you might turn, people today play for all they are worth.
Everyone plays today: poor and rich, old and young — everybody plays and everywhere people play. Every house today is, "to make a thousand distinctions," like a club — and as for the clubs, that goes without saying...
So I realised that my hatred of cards would bring me no joy, since I would simply be thrown out of "z lepszego towarzystwa" — "the better society", that is. And since one cannot be an eternal "kibitzer", I thought it over and began to play too — I had to do it, for what won't a person do for the sake of society...
And you should know that I can already play with luck. I was a good pupil and I had a good professor — my good acquaintance "Pan X". He is a great expert in this field, and he was my rebbe and mentor.. This merit will stand by him forever, and after a hundred and twenty years he will surely be met not by angels but by aces — four whole aces...
In general my friend "Pan X" is a very successful young man. He does not concern himself with politics, he reads no books or newspapers, but on the other hand he is an "intelligent" in the full sense of the word... In his head he possesses the "intelligence" of "poker", in his feet he possesses the true "tango intellect", and in between he is surely "intelligent"... so that he is intelligent from head to toe..
He is a fine fellow, "Pan X". If you do not want to remain forever a boor at cards, I can recommend him to you; you will certainly not regret it.
Ha-Tsofe.
My Guests!

[Satirical feuilleton — the New Year 1934; taxes and distraint.] By Onkelos.
Happy New Year, a good year!
How did you greet "Nowy Rok" [Polish: New Year]? I, to tell the truth, did not greet it at all this year, because Nowy Rok is not Rosh Hashanah, which one welcomes with the sound of the shofar, accompanied by a groan and a sigh...
Nowy Rok likes to be greeted with a real drop of liquor, so that the feet lift by themselves; and how can I allow myself such a pleasure, when instead of drinking vodka I drown myself in a sea of troubles, and how can I lift my feet to dance when they are swollen from running around looking for a livelihood.
So I thought it over — no, I will not greet it!
I was sure that if I did not greet it, it would not come, and that was exactly what I wanted — we have suffered enough already from this gang of years!
And on Sunday evening I lay down in bed under the featherbed.
— — — — — — — —
Right at 12 midnight there is a knock at the door, and before I know what's what, a "guest" is already standing in my room.
Frightened, I turn on the electric light and see before me some young whippersnapper in a pair of torn trousers — poverty itself.
"Who are you?" I ask, bewildered.
"A thief?"
"No!" he answers me with a mocking smile. "I am an honest fellow, my father's child; you knew my father well. He made himself famous with a great many 'deeds', and even now the world is boiling over his 'deeds' in Germany."
Hearing "Germany", I began to tremble and pressed the featherbed to my naked body...
"So," I say, "he is your father; then we are, after all, a bit related; to us [?] he is a 'grandfather'..."
"You are mistaken!" he interrupts me. "You don't know who I am. My father has no grandchildren yet; I am his only son, his only heir."
"And what was your father called?"
"1933!"
"So that's the story," I finally catch on, "then you are, that is, the..."
"Yes, yes," he doesn't let me finish, "the New Year 1934!"
I was a little ashamed and began to stammer.
"Forgive me for not greeting you — such a dear guest, and there is not even anything to treat you with..."
And I began to pour out my bitter heart to him.
"Your father, your grandfather, your great-grandfather and your great-great..."
"Yes," he says, "I know they did not treat you nicely; they ruined you; you gave everything away in taxes, were left yourself without a livelihood, and now the state will not even give you some little post. But I do not take after my forefathers. Surely you have read in the newspapers the promises to the Jews... That was a deed of mine, even before I came into the world. Now imagine what I will do now that I am already here..."
"So," I say, "from the various unjust taxes that were so cruelly thrown on me I am now exempt?"
"Certainly!" he says generously. "You will see that tomorrow not a single sekwestrator [tax bailiff] will show up at your threshold. What's more: tomorrow you can already take up a state post. Go first thing tomorrow morning to the 'Bank Polski' and take the director's place..."
"You aren't bluffing?" I plucked up courage and asked. "I'm afraid that such a young fellow as you..."
"A young fellow?" he burst out in sarcastic laughter and in a single minute grew old... —
— — — — — — — —
I opened my eyes — beside me stood a second guest, the old caretaker [stróż] of our courtyard, Jacek, dead drunk and tangling his tongue:
"Psiakrew [damn it]... sleeping so late? Winszuję z nowym rokiem... z nowem szczęściem [Happy New Year... new happiness].."
"But Jacek, my dear heart, I have nothing to give you. Wait, I'll get dressed and go to the 'Bank Polski'."
"Zwariował Żyduś [the little Jew has gone mad]," Jacek held his sides, "on such a holiday [święto] as Nowy Rok, when the 'Bank Polski' is closed, he'll go there..."
Only now did it become clear to me why my first guest told me to go and take the director's place and even assured me that on that day no sekwestrators would come to me...
In vexation I turned my shoulder to Jacek, but he "honoured" me: "Wait, wait, now you're a lord, but tomorrow morning I'll send you my son, the sekwestrator. To him you'll give all right..."
And Jacek kept his word: this morning at dawn, while I was still lying under the featherbed, a third guest was already with me, the sekwestrator — demanding that I give him the last featherbed...

Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shemot
The Portion — Torah sayings on Parashat Shemot

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.]
The Portion
a) "And Joseph was in Egypt" (1:5)
"...rather, to let you know his righteousness: he is Joseph who tended his father's flock, he is Joseph who was in Egypt and became a king and remained in his righteousness." Rashi.
The proof from the verse that Joseph remained in his righteousness lies in this: although[?] he became viceroy, and Pharaoh specifically wanted him to be called by a pseudonym, "Zaphenath-paneah", in order to cover up his Jewishness — nevertheless "and Joseph was in Egypt": a Joseph he remained. "And Joseph died" — as Joseph he died, and not as "Zaphenath-paneah". He compelled[?] even Pharaoh to call him Joseph: "Go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do." He did not want to exchange his Jewish name. Kedushat Levi.
• • •
Further on, the verse tells of the Hebrew midwives, who were Miriam and Jochebed (see Rashi, further on, verse 15, and Midrash Rabbah, Emor 32), that Pharaoh called them Shiphrah and Puah — so far did Pharaoh go in exchanging the Jewish names. Apparently he felt that there is a power in the Jewish name, that the name does not let them assimilate. Even Shetiyah.
• • •
Maimonides, in chapter 1 of the Laws of Idolatry, says: "Umiplashben[?] — that one must not resemble the gentiles in names"... The Maharam Schick in his responsa, Yoreh De'ah 169, proves that it is a Torah prohibition to bear a gentile name.
b) "Who knew not Joseph" (ibid., 8)
"Who knew not Joseph" — he pretended not to know that Joseph, who had rescued Egypt from seven years of famine. How quickly they are forgotten, the Josephs who save the countries they live in, and are later rewarded for it with a "Come, let us deal wisely with them"... Divrei Yirmiyahu.
c) "If it be a son, then ye shall kill him; but if it be a daughter, then she shall live" (ibid., 16)
In the book "Sefat Tzaddikim" we find the following witticism:
Pharaoh wanted to weaken the Jewish people. So he ordered the boys drowned and the girls left alive. Well, although fewer boys would remain alive, there would after all be a surplus of women. And since in those days every man was allowed to have several wives — it would now turn out that every man would have to take many wives, since the Jewish daughters would surely not marry Egyptians. Well, Pharaoh knew that if the Jewish men had to deal with many wives, there would be nothing more to fear from them; they would no longer have the head and the strength to stand up against the Egyptians...
d) "And they set over them taskmasters (sarei missim)" (ibid., 11)
Remarkable: "sarei missim" (tax chiefs — "naczelniks") is rendered by Targum Onkelos as "shiltonin mevashin" — hated rulers...
e) "To afflict them with their burdens" (ibid.)
According to the style of the verse it should read: "to afflict him with his burdens". On this Rashi says that "their burdens" means "the burdens of the Egyptians". What, then, is the meaning of the verse?
"To afflict him with their burdens" — the Jews were tormented with the Egyptians' burden. The Jews had to carry the tax burden ("and they set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens") of the Egyptians; they had to pay so much tax in order to cover what the Egyptians were supposed to pay for their own share...
Birkat ha-Shir.
f) "And Moses grew up" (2:11)
"That he grew up not in the way of the world." Midrash.
For in the way of the world, if a Jewish child becomes close to the government, a familiar of an imperial court, he forgets his brothers, whereas of Moses it is said, on the contrary: "and he went out unto his brethren"...
Yalkut ha-Drush.
g) "And he went out unto his brethren" (ibid.)
"That righteous man went out twice, and the Holy One, blessed be He, wrote them one after the other. First: 'and he went out unto his brethren'. Second: 'and he went out the second day' — that makes two." Midrash.
The two goings-out are connected with each other. If at the first going-out it was hard for him to understand why the Egyptian beats the Jew, it was answered for him by what he saw at the second going-out: how one Jew beats another. If Jews beat one another, it is no wonder any more that gentiles beat Jews... Imrei Noam.
h) "Call him, that he may eat bread" (ibid., 20)
"Perhaps he will marry one of you." Rashi.
Jethro's daughters told their father that "an Egyptian man" had helped them. According to the Midrash they said: "his dress is Egyptian and his speech is Hebrew" — he dresses like an Egyptian and speaks like a Jew. So Jethro exclaimed: "And where is he?"[?] "Call him" — call him, "perhaps he will marry one of you": such a son-in-law is just what I need here. A Jew who dresses like an Egyptian in this gentile environment — such a son-in-law is what I am looking for... R' Itzikl of Warka.
i) "And the king of Egypt died; and the children of Israel sighed by reason of the bondage"
When the king of Egypt died, the Jews had to join in the weeping; they were ordered to eulogise their protector Pharaoh... But they did not weep over Pharaoh's death, only over their hard and bitter labour in Egypt.. Sha'ar ha-Shamayim.
• • •
When Empress Elisabeth of Austria was murdered in the year 1898, the government issued an order for all rabbis to eulogise the murdered woman on the Sabbath after the assassination. It is told of a Galician rabbi from the shtetl A., a great simpleton, that when he went up onto the bimah to eulogise the empress, he delivered the following eulogy:
"Gentlemen [printed: rabbotiv], you have surely already heard what has happened. Our great empress, the lawful wife of our great emperor, has been killed. Well, it is a sad thing, but it is, after all, the Sabbath, and 'it is the Sabbath, on which one may not cry out' — on the Sabbath one may not weep...
The rabbi runs out of words and looks for a way to connect the eulogy with the pilpul he had prepared.
— "Well, yes," he catches himself, "we have been speaking here about two things: about killing and about the Sabbath. So I will tell you a pilpul on the Talmudic passage 'he who kills a flea on the Sabbath' (when someone kills a flea on the Sabbath)...
j) "A good land and a large" (3:8)
The Land of Israel is never called "a great land", a big country, but only "a broad (large) one", for in fact it is a small country. But as the Gemara says: "it is written of it 'the land of the deer'" [printed: "hativ" for "ketiv"] — just as the deer's hide is smaller than its body and yet the hide stretches, so too, although the Land of Israel is small, it can still take in all the Jews... By "broad" is meant a spiritual breadth: it is a wonderland which, however small it is, still has the power to take in all its dispersed[?] and scattered children... R' Yaakov Meir Yeshurin.
k) "And ye shall put them upon your sons, and upon your daughters" (3:22)
They[?], the older Jews, did not need any clothes in the desert: "thy raiment waxed not old upon thee". Their garments sufficed them for forty years. They needed them only for their small children — clothes once, for the forty years through... Dvash ve-Chalav.
Radio Chronicle

[Radio — regulations and fees.]
Great facilitations and discounts for new subscribers
The Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs has recently issued a regulation which greatly simplifies the procedure of registering as a radio subscriber.
Article 4 of the regulation states that: "The radiophonic fee shall be collected by the post office in monthly, three-monthly or yearly instalments, according to the request of the radio listener."
Where the radio licence was taken out in the first 10 days of the month, the radio fee is charged for the coming month; where, however, the radio licence was taken out after the 10th day of the month, the radio fee is charged for the coming month, and until the end of the current month the subscriber listens to the radio without any fee.
The regulation further states that when the new radio subscriber at the same time buys the Detefon set at the post office, the registration fee of 3 zł. is not collected from him. For such a radio subscriber the price of a "Detefon set", together with the earphones[?] and all necessary accessories[?], has been fixed at 21 zł. instead of 39 as until now. These 21 zł. are spread for him at the post office into 12 instalments.
With this great discount for new radio subscribers the Post Ministry aimed to make radio listening possible for the broadest masses of the population.
This discount for radio listeners has already given brilliant results. The number of radio listeners is now rising day by day. Statistics have shown that the highest number of radio listeners in Poland was in March 1932 and amounted to 320,000. This number then kept falling and went down to 261.724 in October 1933. On 1 January 1934 the number of radio listeners rose again to 310,000.
From Jabotinsky to Ben-Gurion

[Feuilleton — Zionism; funds and collections.]
For a long time I have not published the conversations I recently had with my neighbour Yankev Yudl, because there were bigger worries. But if this time I nevertheless do so, for my neighbour's sake, and tell the public about our talk, it is because I believe it will interest you greatly.
"I have come to you," my neighbour Yankev Yudl begins, "with a new project" — he immediately corrects himself — "because the newspapers have already written about it, but since I want it not to be merely a newspaper canard but a fact, I want people to write about this matter and to rouse the whole Jewish people, the people of Israel. I mean the project that there should come about a consolidation of all the Zionist groupings, starting from the extreme right, from Jabotinsky, to the extreme left, to Ben-Gurion.
And this is not merely because in Erets Yisroel our rights are being restricted, because England issues harsh decrees against Jewish immigration, forbids tourism and fawns[?] on the Arabs; of course that matters, of course the Jewish people with[?] all its positions and trends must raise a protest against the Mandatory Power and demand that it keep its promise concerning the Balfour Declaration, etc. Naturally, if the Zionists were united, the Erets Yisroel administration would have had to reckon with us. But as I said, the union of all forces is necessary not only because of that, but also because of other things one must once and for all perform a Caesarean section on the quarrels and foolish tug-of-war, and here is why:
As you know, the Zionist Executive has been taken over by the left alone, who, besides the 2 already existing funds, such as the 'Keren Hayesod' and 'Keren Kayemet', have also created an Arlosoroff Fund, for which they agitate and spend money on posters, instructors, emissaries and collectors — and all this costs a fortune. The 'Mizrachi', however, took offence, because [it would] not support the above-mentioned funds, and created a separate fund, 'Keren Erets Yisroel', or as they call it the 'HaShomer HaDati' fund. They too send out emissaries, with instructors, collectors etc., and it costs dear money. Then there are the Revisionists with their Tel-Hai Fund, the 'Judenstaatler', who are not satisfied with the left and lately not with Jabotinsky either, so they are making a bank of their own, and once again money will be collected, and what comes of it one can easily guess.
Just last week I had at my place emissaries of all the fund-collectors; each one ran down the other's fund in order to convince me that only their fund brings the true redemption. I confess that they convinced me. Well, about the 'Keren Hayesod' and 'Keren Kayemet' there is nothing to talk about — I have been paying for so many years, I will not suddenly stop paying. But then came the representatives of the Arlosoroff Fund and demanded that I give a larger sum, so I began to argue: how can this be? What do you want of me, I am no party man, what new funds do you want to introduce? In short, they talked to me angrily, later persuasively, at such length and breadth that I was convinced, took out a few guilders and fulfilled my duty...
That very same day I again had a delegation from the 'Mizrachi'. Fine, respected Jews of the town, who asked for my gift for their 'Keren'. Well, go on, have the nerve and say [no] to these distinguished people of our town.
Then, lately, because of the passing of the Lublin Rabbi of blessed memory, a 'Kofer Nefesh' campaign was also created, and since I am a Jew who cannot refuse, I pledged a few złotys to them too. Meanwhile I learn that the central relief organisation for the Jewish refugees is also holding a collection. Well, what do you think, will one be able to wriggle out and not give them any money?
And all these campaigns are, after all, only secondary, an addition to the regular payments one must pay weeping, as to the Skarb [treasury], to the kehilla, to the Magistrat; besides that there are here perhaps 25 more institutions and societies to which one must pay, otherwise they threaten me that the institutions will go under. How can I take that on my conscience?
When I think about all this, my head starts to spin: until when? How long is the limit, how much strength [is there]? In short[?], they said that today one has to pay everything, and here you have not as many hairs on your head as the amount you have to pay.
There must be an end to it, for if it drags on like this, people will stop paying altogether; therefore it would be high time to unite all the funds — one would save on administration and superfluous expenses, and the money would be used for the main thing. Above all, what is all this quarrelling for? Jabotinsky wants there to be a Kingdom of Israel and wants to build up our one land with funds; Ben-Gurion says that only he will build a socialist Erets Yisroel, and raises a fund. The 'Mizrachi' says that one must have only a religious Erets Yisroel, and again collects a fund. Meanwhile the English stand with the Arabs and show us two figs. One fund, one organisation — otherwise there will be nothing.
I have a project that here too, regarding the local institutions, the same must be done. Instead of institutions with rubber stamps and countless ['dew-and-rain'] societies, there should exist one big institution. But that is a project for later. But at this time, when a danger threatens us all that, God forbid, the gates of Erets Yisroel will be shut entirely, I, Yankev Yudl, say to you: if you want us simple Jews to help and build Erets Yisroel, you must unite, from the extreme right to the extreme left, from Vladimir Jabotinsky to David Ben-Gurion."
Smal.

Years

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-Lefl”; taxes, kehilla.] (A short lesson)
There are, as is known, four [printed “flerlay”] kinds of years: a calendar year, a tax year, a maiden’s year and a kahal year.
The calendar year one gets rid of with one guilder [the price of a calendar]; worse it is with the tax year.
The tax year begins one minute into the New Year, when one must buy out a patent [trade licence], and so one must pay properly until one minute before the end of the old year.
The maiden’s year has the peculiarity that it never ends. The same peculiarity is possessed by the kahal year as well: when somebody grabs a seat, he forgets how long he has already been sitting on it...

The Jewish Queen of Yemen

[Serialized historical tale — Yemen, Pnina the Jewish queen; chapter 1.]
Sh. Berg.

The First Chapter.
This was some fifteen hundred years ago.
Yemen, the land of Arabia, which is now one of the worst lands of exile for Jews — where a Jew is fair game, and Jewish children are snatched from their parents and forcibly converted — once had a Jewish queen. Her name was Pnina. Later her kingdom was destroyed by Christians and she fled to Khaybar [printed "Kha'ibar"]. There she created a new kingdom. She founded a dynasty that reigned for over two hundred years. And about her, the Jewish queen of Yemen, I will tell here.
The Roman emperors inflicted terrible torments on the Jews, and the gentiles taunted the Jews and fired jokes [?] at their hunger [?].
"How much longer will you die for your God?" they asked the Jews. "How much longer will you let yourselves be killed for the sanctification of the Name? Come to us, become equal with us, and we will make you princes."
The Jews bore their sufferings in silence; but when the troubles could no longer be endured, they went off en masse to Persia. And at last Rome's end came. The mighty Roman Empire suffered a great defeat. It fell to pieces and perished. Rome, which had trampled peoples and lands, was trampled by the Huns and Vandals. The whole world rejoiced at Rome's defeat — and what a comfort it was for the Jews!
The Jews who had fled to Persia fared well for a long time. The Persian king was good to them. The Persian priests, who were great fanatics, were angry with the king for this. They incited him against the Jews, but he paid them no heed. He treated the Jews very well, and often invited the elders of the yeshivas of Pumbedita [printed "Pumbrita"], Sura and Nehardea to the royal court and showed them great honour.
But when the good king died and his son became king, bad times came for the Jews. The priests had great influence over the king, and he began to issue evil decrees against the Jews. And when the Jews saw that the blade was already at their throat, they left Persia and emigrated to other lands. Some went to India, where Jews had already lived for hundreds of years, and others went to Yemen, a blessed land of freedom and equality, where Jews had lived since long ago and knew nothing of the torments of Rome and Persia.
And here begins the story of Pnina, the Jewish queen of Yemen.
In Isfahan, the residence city of the Persian kings, there lived a descendant of King David, Huna bar Ukba. He was a weaver and made his living from his work. He had an only child, a little girl, Pnina. He loved her like the apple of his eye, and he devoted his free time to studying with her. He planted in her a great love of God and told her everything that had befallen the Jews from the very first day, since they had become a people, and also everything that had happened to his family — the royal house of David.
"Our people hopes every day that the Messiah will come, that he will redeem us from exile and lead us back to the Land of Israel," Huna would always tell his daughter. "And this Messiah, the Redeemer, will be one of our family, of the royal house of David. And he will sit upon the throne of our forefather King David, and God willing" — he would always add with fervent faith — "you, my Pnina, will be the Messiah's wife, you will be the queen of the Jews."
Little Pnina indeed began to believe that she would be the Messiah's wife, that she would be a queen, and she often thought about it. She studied with great eagerness, preparing herself for the great hour when she would be crowned. Huna, her father, took great pride in her and quietly believed that his daughter was born to be a queen, and he hoped he would yet live to see it.
But he did not live to see it. He died when she was twelve years old, and Pnina became an orphan. Her mother, the widow, carried on the weaving business and fed herself and her only child.
Then the terrible Persian king issued the evil decree to snatch the Jewish children from their parents and convert them by force. The priests burst into the Jewish homes and dragged away all the Jewish children — Pnina among them. The grieving Jewish fathers and mothers stood up against the villains, fell at their feet, tore the hair from their heads, wailed and lamented. But the cruel murderers had no pity; they took the children, and many fathers and mothers lost their lives defending the children.
By kindness and by cruelty the dark priests tried to convert Pnina and the other children, but it did not help them. The children were ready to die for God. And every night, when their guards were asleep, the captive children rose up in the prison and prayed to God in silence.
After Pnina's mother had wept her fill, she resolved to save her child. She learned that the head of the prison was looking for a good laundress [?]; so she went to him and asked for the work. Her washing pleased the head, so she was given access to the prison and often came in to the children.
They saw each other often, mother and Pnina, but never spoke a word, and the guards thought they were complete strangers. Great was the grief of the unhappy mother and her young child when they looked at one another and could not utter a word. But they took strength from the hidden hope that God would help and Pnina would be freed.
A long time passed; the villains tormented the children every day so that they would convert. But the children remained stubborn. They became terribly emaciated, but the fiery will to remain Jews blazed even more strongly in their tormented hearts and shone out of their wonderfully black eyes.

The “Sylvester Holiday” in Zagłębie.

[Będzin — social life.]
Last Sylvester cannot be compared to the Sylvester entertainments of old, of those good “fat years”, when it made no difference to squander a couple of gulden.
In the streets there was a stir of young people, who worked up some “kurage” [kuraż — courage; doubtful reading] and put on the pretence that they were tipsy (after a glass of soda water...); the “drunkards” streamed along Kołłątaja and 3 Maja Street looking for a place of rest where they could celebrate the “Sylvester delight” (oneg Sylvester).
We will not deny that the public did not “have fun” at all; those who still had something in their pocket went to Katowice, where in the local night-spots one even had to resort to pull to get a “little table”. But the owners of the venues made no great profits: most of the guests “caroused” over a glass of orangeade, at best over a glass of coffee with a “kremówka” [cream cake].
But it was lively: the jazz bands worked on all instruments, and the public observed the “Sylvester delight” with awe and love (bi-dkhilu u-rkhimu).
In Katowice the local Revisionist organisation, under the name “Malkhut Israel”, observed the commandment of holy Sylvester; at 12 midnight one of the guests gave a toast speech in honour of the New Year and cried out:
— Le-shana tova tikatevu (may you be inscribed for a good year)...
The Będzin academic youth changed the name: the entertainment it arranged on that night was called “Draczny Bal” [the Jolly Ball].
As reported, the ball did not pass without a quarrel, but in spite of that our youth rejoiced greatly, no worse than the fiery Kock Hasidim of old at the Rebbe's table — they danced not only on the floor of the hall but also on the tables...
In respectable homes too “staiske”[?] celebrations were arranged; people made do with a glass of tea and the music of a gramophone.
But be that as it may, this year's Sylvester did not pass with all the “pitshevkes”[?] [trimmings].
— When one talks of a crisis, it is really out of place...
Tragic Death of a Jewish Boy.

[Będzin — accident.]
On Zaułek[?] Cesl, on Monday morning, a terrible accident occurred which cost the life of an 8-year-old boy.
In a small house on the said street lives a poor family, Rozmaryn — a woman with 2 children.
At the critical moment the mother left the room, leaving the children behind; she had told the elder child, 8[?]-year-old Dudl, to watch the little pot of milk that stood on the burning iron stove. Dudl got down from the bed and stood naked by the stove. Suddenly his shirt caught fire, and the flames engulfed the young victim. The unfortunate child, wanting to save himself, got into the bed, where the fire only grew bigger from the burning straw mattress and bedding.
The neighbours, seeing smoke pouring out of the locked room, broke the room open, and there they saw the great disaster.
The little boy was brought to hospital unconscious, but no rescue could help any more; the child died in terrible agony.
The Coal Relief Campaign.

[Będzin — kehilla and relief.] (Communiqué of the Coal Committee at the Jewish kehilla).

As is known, a committee was created this year at the Jewish gmina (community) in Będzin, whose task is to carry out the coal relief campaign for the impoverished Jewish population of Będzin.
Having acquainted itself with the situation of the local Jewish population, the coal committee has established that, because of the continuing crisis, the number of needy[?] families forced to turn to public support has unfortunately grown considerably this year.
This situation therefore places far greater obligations upon us, so as to be able to come to the aid of the needy population at least to a minimal degree. The committee has therefore resolved to strengthen and broaden the coal campaign, so that the entire Jewish population of Będzin will be drawn into helping with this important cause. The collectors for the campaign are received by the population with a friendly face, and everyone donates to this important purpose according to his means. Thus one sees on the part of the donors an understanding of the important relief task, and we hope that no one will refuse to donate for the benefit of the coal campaign.
But in order for the campaign to be properly carried out in all circles of the Będzin Jewish population, pairs of collectors are needed, who will visit the donors and take the donations from them.
The Coal Relief Committee appeals to everyone who understands the importance and urgency of the relief campaign to come to the premises of the Jewish kehilla in Będzin and enrol as volunteer collectors for the campaign, where they will also be able to arrange partners for collecting and receive the necessary collecting material.
We hope that our appeal will meet with the proper response both among the donors and among the collectors, so that the relief campaign may be carried out among us with due success.
She Lit Candles Before Dying.

[Będzin — people.] On Zamkowa Street an old woman of ninety-some years died this week.
It is interesting that about half an hour before her death the woman got out of bed, lit several candles, said “Shema Yisrael” several times, went back to bed, and a few minutes later she died.

A Dangerous Criminal in the Hands of the Czeladź Police.

[Czeladź — crime.] Last Tuesday a dangerous criminal, who has already been sought for two years by the Częstochowa investigative authorities, fell into the hands of the police in Czeladź.
During the investigation the “bird” declared that he is a former “resident” of the Częstochowa, Piotrków, Będzin and other prisons, where he sat for about 15 years, and that he was a pupil of the burglar famous in Europe, “Spitzburd”.
—o—
Suicide of a Prostitute.
[Będzin — tragedy.] On the railway line in Będzin a young prostitute threw herself under the train. The suicide was torn to pieces.
—o—
Traditional Keren Kayemet Evening at “WIZO”.
[Będzin — Zionism.] On Tuesday evening a board meeting took place at the premises of “WIZO”, at which it was decided that the traditional Keren Kayemet evening shall take place on Saturday the 27th of this month.
—o—
A Fire in a Motor Car.
[Będzin — fire.] On Wednesday afternoon on Kołłątaja Street a fire broke out in the petrol tank of a lorry. Thanks to the quick rescue by the chauffeur, the vehicle was saved.
On the Eve of the Kehilla Elections.

[Sosnowiec — kehilla — elections.] Of the 4 disqualified lists, 2 have been declared valid again.

In the previous number of our paper we reported the decision of the election commission, which disqualified 4 candidate lists that had not been drawn up according to the provisions of the election regulations.
The disqualified lists were: of the Left Poale Zion, the New Artisans’ Union, Rabbi Schwarz and Rabbi Glickman.
The trustees (proxies) of the disqualified lists intervened about this with the starosta, who gave them 8 hours’ time to correct the errors made in the lists.
The trustees of the lists of the New Artisans’ Union and of Rabbi Glickman managed to do so, and thanks to this their lists were confirmed by the election commission.
In the course of the week election meetings were held by the “Mizrachi”, Rabbi Englard, and the Radomsk Hasidim.
In general, the apathy towards the elections is still great.
A Silesian Buys “Golden” Objects.

[Sosnowiec — swindle.] A resident of Wielkie Hajduki, walking along Dekerta Street, was accosted by an unknown “Russian”, who offered the Silesian to buy a ring of “genuine Greek gold”.
While the Silesian was examining the ring, a second person came up, a “connoisseur” of gold, who persuaded him to buy the “bargain”.
When the Silesian went with the “bargain” into a jeweller’s shop, only then did it become clear to him that he had fallen victim to a swindle.
From the New Artisans’ Union.

[Sosnowiec — artisans.] The new Jewish Artisans’ Union, which was founded a few months ago, is developing very well and is becoming a certain[?] factor in the life of the Jewish artisan class in our town.
A number of guilds are already grouping around the union; also next Sunday at 4 in the afternoon a district conference of jewellers and watchmakers will take place at the premises of the Artisans’ Union. On the same day, an hour later, the founding meeting of a tailors’ guild will take place.
The union is also conducting a vigorous election campaign for List 10.
This week meetings of the carpenters’ and butchers’ guilds took place, which adopted resolutions to vote for the United Artisans’ List No. 10.
The election committee of List No. 10 is arranging an election meeting at the “Atlantic”.
Stolen Furniture That Was Intended for the Foreign Consulates in Warsaw.

[Sosnowiec — crime.] A wagon of furniture arrived at the local railway station; it had been sent from Paris for the French, Italian and Japanese consulates in Warsaw.
The railway officials at the local station noticed that the wagon window was open; the matter was suspicious, and when an inspection of the furniture was carried out, it turned out that various objects had been stolen from it.
Where the theft was committed is unknown; the police are conducting an energetic investigation.
A Bloody New Year's Eve in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
On Wschodnia Street in Sosnowiec a group of Christians gathered and began to make merry in honour of New Year's Eve (Sylwester). When they were already drunk, they began to fight. The result was that several of the guests were taken to hospital in a serious condition.

Tax Reliefs for House-Owners
The Minister of Finance has sent out a circular concerning reliefs for house-owners in paying the tax on real estate.
According to the circular, the tax offices, when assessing the tax on real estate, must take into account the cases where the house-owner concerned has vacant premises, or where the house-owner receives lower rent than that which was taken as the basis for calculating the tax, or where the tenants pay no rent and cannot be evicted.
The reliefs, however, are to be granted only in the case where, because of the above-listed reasons, the house-owner's income has fallen by more than 15 per cent.

Sławków — From the Kehilla

[Sławków — kehilla and rabbinate.]
On Saturday night (motzei Shabbat) a meeting of the local kehilla board took place in Sławków, with the participation of the rabbi. In the middle of the meeting the “Ger guard” [Ger Hasidim] arrived with the aim of settling accounts with the rabbi, who had agreed to reduce the pension of the very[?] [—] and respected secretary of the Jewish community (gmina), Mr. A. B. Makowski, who has already been working for 40 years. The secretary's pension had been 1200 zł. a year and it was reduced to 700 zł. a year — while at the same time the rabbi did not allow his own pension, amounting to 3.600, to be reduced. When the rabbi saw the “Ger guard” before him, he left the gmina in haste together with his constant “adjutant”. The rabbi's flight brought still more “bad blood”, and, as people say, the “Ger guard” is getting ready to attack the rabbi once again.
S.[?] Sławkower.
Rights and Duties Concerning Jewish Craftsmen / Picture Exhibition of the Painter Ziegler

[Craftsmen — organisation and legislation; Będzin — art.]
(Communiqué of the Będzin Craftsmen's Association.)
The elections to the chambers of crafts in Poland will take place, in accordance with the new law, in the month of January.
For this reason it is worth reflecting on the broad competences and rights that the new organisation has received, by which it will be able to resolve questions on which it has until now had no right at all. In addition, the amended industrial law, which introduces compulsory guilds, is now [coming into force?].
And this new situation compels the responsible representatives of Jewish craftsmen to reflect on the important problems.
The representatives of the Central Association of Jewish Craftsmen in Poland, which numbers over 600 branches, have — thanks to the trust bestowed on them by the broadest masses of Jewish craftsmen, as well as thanks to their merits in the field of the craftsmen's movement — also gained the trust of the decisive factors, who have appointed them to the most important positions; this will give the 600 associations, together with the guilds attached to these associations, the possibility of making use of the new rights that craftsmen receive through the establishment of compulsory trade organisations.
The compulsion to form cartels will help strengthen discipline among the craftsmen and make impossible the dirty and illicit competition which causes good and productive craftsmen to become beggars, unable to support themselves by their own toil.
The Jewish craftsmen must be ready for every call; they must grow strong, they must rally behind their own banner, which was created with so much blood and so many sacrifices. Let no one ask any more: "What does the association give me?" To this the law will answer: you get rights for the duties you must bear.
With the establishment of compulsory trade organisations there will no longer be in Poland a single craftsman who does not pay his membership dues for the upkeep of his craftsmen's organisation, because his fate will depend on it; just as it is in Upper Silesia, so it will be in all of Poland.
And as soon as a craftsman will not want to bear the duties towards his association, the association will quickly expel him. Equal rights and equal duties for all — this every craftsman must take firmly to heart, and he must get used to it as quickly as possible.
Every craftsman who does not want to find himself outside the camp must rally around the organisation. He must not wait, for it may become too late. Whether the law is good or bad, the future will show. Meanwhile one must be ready.
H. L. Goldsztajn.

Intervention of the Będzin Rabbinate and the Welfare Guardians

With the city commissioner, concerning the sending of poor Jewish patients to Jewish hospitals.
In connection with the fact that the Będzin city commissioner began sending poor Jewish patients to the non-Jewish hospital in Będzin instead of to the Sosnowiec Jewish hospital, a delegation consisting of the rabbis Tellner, Lipszyc and Frydberg, and of the welfare guardians (opiekunki) Mrs. Z. Szajn and A. D. Balimazski[?], went to see the commissioner.
Mrs. Szajn explained the matter and stressed that the rabbinate, which supervises religious affairs, had prevailed upon the Jewish guardians to take part in the delegation to the commissioner, so that he would withdraw his decision concerning the Jewish patients, because the suffering of the Jewish patients is very great, as they are forced to eat non-kosher (treyf) food.
The intervention brought the proper result: the commissioner promised that, just as until now, he will direct the Jewish patients to the Sosnowiec Jewish hospital.
We take this opportunity to point out that the poor Jewish patients cannot be compelled to undergo treatment in the non-Jewish hospital in Będzin.
50-Year-Old Finkelsztajn and 17-Year-Old Cukier

Committed suicide in Sosnowiec.
Sosnowiec can already be counted among the big cities in the field of... suicides.
Last Wednesday two suicides took place in Sosnowiec, which ended tragically.
The 50-year-old Dawid Finkelsztajn from Manduszew[?] had come to Sosnowiec to his brother-in-law.
Finkelsztajn told the members of the household that he did not feel well and asked for a little water. When he was left alone he drank a considerable dose of vitriol[?]. A few hours later Finkelsztajn died.
The second suicide was committed by the 17-year-old Mosze Dawid Cukier, who died after being taken to the Jewish hospital.
The reason for Cukier's dangerous step is said to be that his parents did not want to give him a few złoty to pay for learning Hebrew.
To spite his parents he drank a small bottle of vinegar essence.
— Today's youth...

[Zagłębie — sick fund; labour and welfare.]
Disputes at the Sick Fund
Workers do not have, and do not want, to pay for doctors and prescriptions.
Of the sick-fund institution only the name remains. Its content, however, keeps changing.
From 1 January, as is known, a new law („ustawa“) came into force, under which those insured with the sick fund must make a certain payment when they take a number for a doctor, and later when they go to the pharmacy with a prescription. The payment is small for the time being — 20 gr. and 10 [?] gr. — but even these few tens of groszy are not so easy for every worker to pay.
On this ground regular disputes and even incidents occur at the sick fund. The officials must, after all, carry out the regulations loyally and punctually; the worker, and all the more so the unemployed, will not reckon with this, and when they are told to pay the few groszy they start getting angry, shouting, insulting the officials.
The officials are for the time being showing enormous patience; understanding the anger of the insured, they do not apply any of the means at their disposal, since for behaving tactlessly at the sick fund the same penalty threatens as in any state office.
Some workers leave the sick fund with various outcries.
But the saddest thing is that very many insured people actually go away without a number for the doctor, because they have nothing to pay the few groszy with.

[Poland — crime and police; auctions.]
Fighting the Terror of the „Auction-Goers“
A special circular from the Interior Ministry to the police
A chapter of tears and torment about the so-called „licytacja-goers“ (professional auction bidders).
These are, after all, not chance people who buy something at an auction, but professionals, i.e. people who have made the auctions their livelihood, and accordingly they have imitated the „big people“: they have created a sort of cartel and, God forbid, will not allow anyone to get in their way.
This is not merely a Zagłębie affliction. It is a plague that has already gripped all towns and shtetls. The „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ has written about it more than once. People tried to justify it by saying that this affliction is a state necessity, just like a hangman. Lately, however, the abscess had grown so dangerous that the Interior Ministry ordered an action to be undertaken to combat the professional auction-goers.
The Ministry has sent a circular to the police. The circular draws attention to the unheard-of terror methods used by the auction-goers, among whom there are people from the underworld. In the circular the Ministry points to facts: the bidder-terrorists poured paint over furniture and food products, slashed clothing, stabbed people, if at an auction they did not get the upper hand.
The Ministry calls on the security authorities to take all measures to combat the terror at the auctions.
