Poor Things, They Fell In Badly...

The Warsaw Jewish press, and the afternoon sheets in particular, very often help themselves by "taking" chronicle items and other reading matter from the "Zaglembier Tsaytung". The "work", however, is done incognito, and so that the readers should not, God forbid, find out where the items were taken from, the news is served up under the "stock headings": "From Będzin we are informed"...
This week, almost day after day, the Warsaw press carried items reprinted from the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", but the one who came a nasty cropper was the chronicle supplier of the "Haynt'ike Nayes".
The blunder consists in this: in the previous issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" an advertisement was printed for the "Nowości" cinema about a film showing the trade in "living merchandise". In order to attract the readers' attention, the advertisement was given at the end of the text, but the rules and the number were so conspicuous that every sensible reader understood that this was a paid advertisement. The "item" was received differently in the editorial office of the "Haynt'ike Nayes". They pounced on the sensation like on a roast, and under the screaming headline "Argentine White-Slavers Seduce Young Girls from Zagłębie" there is, poor things, an account of the terrible danger threatening the young girls of Zagłębie.
By the way, the "Haynt'ike Nayes" already knows that "there have even already been cases of young, and precisely pretty, girls being seduced by the white-slavers"...
The Jewish parents in Zagłębie need not despair, however, for, as that very newspaper assures us, "the police of Zagłębie are already on the trail of the cunning white-slavers"...
Appeal of the Yiddish P.E.N. Club / For the Month of the Yiddish Book

To all friends of Yiddish literature!
You are all surely aware of the catastrophic situation of the Yiddish book. Without a school system with Yiddish as the language of instruction, organised and maintained by the state, the normal, natural basis for the organic development of Yiddish book publishing is also lacking. If nothing is sown beforehand, it is futile to expect a time of harvest afterwards [printed "shonim", apparently a misprint for "shnit", harvest]. It is therefore no wonder at all that the Yiddish publishing houses, just like all our other cultural positions, survive on miracles, for apart from the fact that we are dependent on ourselves alone, we have to stand in a struggle against a world of enemies who wish not only to ruin our physical existence but also to suppress our spiritual being, our national life. Meanwhile our Yiddish culture exists as a miracle, especially in the years of the so long-lasting economic crisis[?], when the situation is unbearably catastrophic.
But in a catastrophe one must save at least the dearest, the most important: the spiritual content, the cultural positions, and naturally, first and foremost, the Yiddish book. The P.E.N. Club, as the representative body of Yiddish literature, has for this purpose taken the initiative to organise a month of the cheap Yiddish book and appeals to all friends of the Yiddish word to take an active part in the campaign that has been launched. We hope that none of you will refuse to help, so that the Yiddish book, the foundation of our modern culture, may be found in the bookcase of every educated Jewish home.
Whoever buys the better Yiddish book helps to insure a better future for the Yiddish word.
Friends of Yiddish literature! Do your duty of honour and support the campaign to spread the Yiddish book.
Yiddish P.E.N. Club in Warsaw.

Questions that need to be solved — On a course of price reductions for trams and telephones

On a course of price reductions for trams and telephones.
Not a little has already been said and written about this, and attention has been drawn to it, and yet nothing has come of it to this day; it has remained no more than talk. The matter is the reduction of the price of tram tickets.
The question has been discussed more than once, and we thought that something would come of it after all — that the population would finally benefit and that the tickets would be made cheaper from the New Year on. But the New Year has already passed and everything has stayed as it was. We go on paying the same prices we paid in the good years, back when the gulden [złoty] played no role because one earned it easily. Since those times, however, the economic situation has changed catastrophically, so that today's grosz has become dearer than the gulden of the past.
All the economic parties have recognised this, all the municipal institutions have confirmed it, life itself has convinced us of it; the government itself saw no way out and had partly to reduce taxes and set aside old debts. What more is needed — the government itself has, after all, lowered the prices of its monopoly articles; even the railway, which is almost without competition, also had to adapt to the times and made its tickets cheaper from the New Year. The Railway Ministry had statistics from which it came to the conclusion that citizens do not travel, that travel expenses play a role when prices are not adapted to the times, to everyday use. To that end they began to look for means and devised the reduced-fare trains, which got a large number of passengers, and then they came to the conclusion that the price is too dear, and when an occasional journey comes up, people do travel after all. This gave the Railway Ministry the push to make travel expenses cheaper in general, and the result will certainly be a better one: the volume of traffic will surely grow.
Our tram company, too, can see that the number of passengers has fallen enormously: formerly two cars were packed, and today there is enough room in a single car. So it, too, should have looked for means and tried to find out the reason why people travel little, why traffic is falling. But in the decisive circles no one makes the effort to find the reason, and the end is that both suffer — the company, whose profits have fallen enormously, and the population, for whom the dear tickets matter. Thus, for example, one ride from Sosnowiec to Będzin costs one gulden, whereas by rail it costs no more than 60 groszy. So why should the tram company not suffer, when the journey is as dear as possible because it sticks to this position? Because its income has fallen, it is not in a position to make the tickets cheaper as well — but that is a false calculation, an inconsistent logic, because, first, it has also cut its staff, and besides, salaries are not what they used to be, so that it is indeed able to reduce ticket prices; and second, it can hope that by lowering prices the number of travellers will grow and turnover will rise.
The company, however, makes no attempt to do anything in this field, and that is the reason why citizens avoid the tram whenever they have another option; but one cannot manage with the trains everywhere, so people do ride the tram — where they have no other choice.
The tram company is a private one; nobody has any say over it; it can do as it pleases and as pays it best. But precisely from a purely business point of view it would suit it better to cut prices. At the same time one more thing must be taken into account: the municipal self-governments in Zagłębie are also holders of the tram shares, so that they, too, have a say in the event of certain changes — all the more so when it concerns the good of the citizens, the convenience of their members. The town councils are, after all, obliged to look after the good of their members, the citizens of their towns — so why is nothing done from that quarter to make the trams adapt to the population for whom the transport was created?
No doubt the town councils, the self-governments, can help a great deal in this field, and they are obliged to see to it that prices are reduced, because the tram was not made only for better-situated people but for the whole community — both for the popular masses and for the working elements, who earn the most minimal prices [wages] and who have to reckon with the excessive prices, which far exceed their means and their earning possibilities.
If the tram company does not want to understand this — which, incidentally, is not to its own good — then our municipal institutions must understand it, so that they must put pressure on the tram company to adapt itself to the times and to the conditions in which the population finds itself.
— There is one more thing that begs to be made cheaper. This, too, has already been written about several times. It is the telephone service. It, too, has not budged from its place. It goes on holding to the same price it fixed in its time, and although a large percentage of citizens have given up their telephones solely because the prices are too high, the telephone company has not budged and sticks to its own: if you want a telephone at home or in your business, you must pay the once-fixed price without any excuse; otherwise you needn't — otherwise one shall manage without the other.
And here too one must come to the same conclusion: had prices been reduced, the number of subscribers would not have fallen on such a colossal scale, and the company would certainly have done better business at the cheaper price than with a small number of subscribers at a dear price.
One cannot say that the telephone is as much an article of mass use as the tram, but neither can one say that it is an inferior thing: there are branches and commercial circles that cannot manage without a telephone connection, and yet a large number of firms have had to give up this important thing and have removed their telephones.
In any case a telephone is one of the most indispensable necessities and cannot be counted as a luxury or some other superfluous use, so that this must be reckoned with unconditionally. What more is needed — even the government, to which the inter-city calls belong, has understood that it should lower the price of calls, whereas the telephone company has to this day paid no heed to it.
No doubt the telephone company suffers much from the fact that prices are too high, and not all who formerly had telephones have been able to keep them; and they would certainly have done better had they reduced the subscription fee, since anyone who has a telephone does not want to get rid of it. But a systematic reduction of prices ought to have come, and so both suffer — the telephone company and the population, which does not have the possibility of using the telephone connections the community needs. The tel. co. thus makes its article into a luxury, a superfluous object, regardless of the fact that in the twentieth century it is an urgent necessity.
Nonetheless the question cannot be left standing unsolved like this, because the subscribers who have given up the telephone need it, and a large number of firms that still use it are also on the way to getting rid of it. Many wanted to hold out until the New Year, reckoning that from now on the price would be made cheaper; but since after the New Year everything has stayed as it was, they will not be able to endure it, and many will have to give up the telephone.
We have already pointed out above that the government has understood how to make many things cheaper, and later monopoly products also became cheaper, such as cigarettes [papirosy], spirits, etc. Besides that, cheaper tariffs have been introduced for goods dispatched by rail or post. Calls between towns and telegrams have also become cheaper from the New Year. So the question arises: if the government already sees that everything cannot stay as it was, why should our tram and telephone companies not reckon with this as well?
It would therefore be desirable for the economic and commercial institutions to take up the above matters and to work towards a course of price reductions being carried through on the two questions discussed.
One must not forget that for articles created for the community, for the people, for the masses, one must set such prices as are suited to the strata mentioned.
Selekt.
The History of the Będzin Kehilla in the Second Half of the 19th Century. According to Archival Records. (2)

[History — the Będzin kehilla; serial, instalment 2.] By Moshe Feinkind. According to archival records.
The number of Jewish inhabitants of Będzin, however, kept shrinking from year to year. Thus, of 280 registered householders, 179 paid the etat [the communal budget levy], and in 1858, of 300 householders only 242. The following years are in the same state.
Only in the sixties, when the movement [freedom of movement and settlement] of Jews in Będzin became legal and no longer involved any difficulties, did the number of inhabitants grow from year to year, and with it the number of Jews too. So that in 1897 Będzin counted 23,757 inhabitants, among whom were 10,839 Jews.
In 1848 the following were elected as dozors [members of the community board — dozór bóżniczy]: R' Ajzyk Bialer, R' Aron Neuberg (from 1854 to 1856), R' Herszel Landner, R' Bendet Fiszel and R' Obadia Szancer. The same three dozors were also elected later, but Landner withdrew, and in his place came R' Majer Fiszel (1857—1859).
In the following years R' Bendet Fiszel was also elected dozor. Thus in 1860—62, etc.
With great pomp and with a special prayer in the synagogue — so the records tell — the dozors of those years took up their office.
But they also had a great deal to tell [literally: "to sing and to say"] about their time as dozors in Będzin. R' Lejb Potok brought a lawsuit against them over abuses in the kehilla's finances.
In 1856 R' Lejb Potok turned with a complaint against the three dozors enumerated above to the Radom governor, over various abuses they had committed with kehilla money to the detriment of the "parafia" [the congregation as an official body]. The complaint states [?] that the dozors earn a great deal from the kehilla's revenues that are earmarked for heating and lighting the synagogue; that they take for themselves the money from the "lechayot" [?]; that they do not record the true sums they collect in their official accounts; that they conceal the correct sums they receive from the tax on the mikveh and from the propinacja [the liquor licence], not entering them in the "burushes" [?], etc.
On the basis of the complaint the gubernia ordered a strict investigation of the accused dozors...
The dozors naturally denied everything [literally: "stone and bone"]. A large number of witnesses on whom Potok had relied were also heard, and the books were checked as well; and since none of the witnesses confirmed what Potok had accused the dozors of, and all the accounts tallied too, the judicial-administrative authority did not find the dozors guilty of the alleged abuses, and the gubernia administration resolved at a collegial session to hold Lewek Potok liable for the false accusation and also to make him pay the costs of the investigation, which came to as much as 28 roubles.
The trial stirred up a great to-do [literally: "a great porridge"] in the town. Potok did not sit with folded hands, and went on storming all the higher administrative and judicial instances over the gubernia's verdict. But all his efforts were of no further avail; "one may not question the deeds of a court in any way" — so he was told from every quarter, and in 1858 the files of the official police investigation were handed over to the "protocol" [?; probably a misprint for "prosecutor"] of the Radom criminal court, in order to bring a case against Lejb Potok for slander [?] and for accusing the Będzin dozors.
What became of the trial — the records give no further details.
One can, however, infer that Potok was released from punishment thanks to the manifesto [the amnesty] issued in September [wrzesień] 1856 after the coronation of Alexander II. And we see him as a dozor in the years 1860—1862 and also in the years 63—1865.
At the dozor elections of 1859 the notables of the town ["the face of the town"] submitted a protest to the naczelnik [district chief], in which they write that Lewek Potok and Bendit Fiszel are illiterate, that they bought votes for money, and that people who have no right to do so were put up to vote for them; that a cherem [ban] was proclaimed in the town against those who would not give them their votes, etc. And above all — Bendit Fiszel has no right to be a dozor, because under the governor's rescript of 1854 he was removed from the office of dozor, since he belonged to the banned "Chevra Kadisha" and extorted [literally: "tore"] a lot of burial money from the relatives of the dead, etc. On the basis of the protocol the naczelnik did not confirm the election and ordered a new election, striking R' Bendit Fiszel off the list of candidates.
Again Mark Plessner and that same Potok supported him, claiming that Fiszel is the only one fit to be a dozor, because he is already experienced in the job and conducts himself quite honestly. And since the above-mentioned manifesto applies to him as well, they ask that he be confirmed. In this paper the opponents are naturally also roundly reviled as a gang of "schnorrers" and informers (for tactical reasons I am not listing their names), who at the second election slipped in ballots for other dozors, thereby causing a commotion [sumatokha] in the kehilla, etc., etc.
The result was that the governor confirmed the first election after a strict investigation. Several candidates had meanwhile voluntarily withdrawn from the office, and those left were Lewek Potok and Bendit Fiszel.
The protocol was signed by Rabbi Langfus and the "dukhovny" [duchowny — the official religious functionary] R' Awigdor Sennenholz [?], with the kehilla seal: "Supervisors of the [misprinted „חערת“, probably for „עדת“ — congregation] holy community of Będzin".
But yet another interesting trial took place in Będzin in the fifties — this time against the "Chevra Kadisha". But about that — in the next article.
Kehilla Elections or Rabbi Elections?

[Sosnowiec — Kehilla; Kehilla elections; opinion piece.]
Once again the election campaign has flared up in Sosnowiec.
"Kehilla elections" is what it is called — and passions are running wild. People are angry at one another. The 5000 enfranchised payers of the kehilla tax (the "etat") have split up into no fewer than 17 parties, and every party holds mass meetings at which fiery, heated speakers pour pitch and brimstone on the rival parties...
A question arises: whom do the sermons of the chief speakers bind, if they are not the actual candidates for "parnassim" [kehilla board members]? And above all, why do the leaders of the lists themselves not appear and say what draws them to the kehilla and what they intend to accomplish in the kehilla?
Let us be honest. Chaos ("tohu va-vohu") reigns in the kehilla, and it cannot go on like this. The simple taxpayer also has the right to demand from the outgoing parnassim an account of their "activity" in the past. By the same right the taxpayer may demand from the newly elected parnassim a certain "ani ma'amin" [credo], a declaration of how he intends to carry out what the outgoing parnas did not manage to do. After all, the taxpaying "public" is no golem, and it must protest against the form and content in which the election campaign is being conducted.
Almost all parties put up speakers who will not be parnassim, and what they say does not bind those who will be.
And here the old question arises: why has such a tangled[?] situation come about?
The answer is a simple one. Almost none of the 17 parties that have put up lists of candidates for the kehilla elections is out for the good of the kehilla.
Almost none of the candidates put forward gives himself an account of what is going on in the kehilla; nobody takes the trouble to think how to create order in the kehilla.
With a clear conscience one can state that the largest and strongest part of the parties are out for one thing and one thing only: electing rabbis.
And because the truth is hushed up and kept silent, none of the candidates has the courage to declare openly that it is only this single issue, "electing rabbis," that brings him into the kehilla. Had they been honest and declared this truth openly, they might perhaps have heard the honest answer of the taxpayer: "mochel" [no thanks]. This does not mean, however, that the taxpayer does not want a rabbi. Rather, it would mean: first of all we, the taxpayers, want to see order in the kehilla; first of all the anarchy must be driven out of all the Jewish institutions in town; first of all the lawlessness ("hefkeyres") of the irresponsible people must stop, who regard the taxpayer as a blind tool that does not react against everything that is done in his name and without his consent.
That is the reason why irresponsible people appear at the meetings: because it binds them to nothing, and those who are indeed responsible will later be able to say: we promised nothing, and nothing can be demanded of us.
So such a state of affairs is intolerable. The simple taxpayer says clearly and plainly: parnassim, you should know that the number of well-off taxpayers in Sosnowiec today is relatively small, whereas the number of those without means grows with every day, and you have no right to "bless" the town with 17 rabbis — for almost every party, after all, has a rabbi in its business bag[?]. Be honest and do not reckon without the host, for the host — the taxpayer — is, at best, in no position to take upon himself as great a burden as you will have to lay on him. The same applies[?] to the address of the esteemed rabbis: do not mislead them with promises at the expense of the taxpayer, who cannot meet them.
First of all order must be made in the kehilla, and only then — the election of rabbis.
So, parnassim of every kind, say clearly and plainly: are you holding kehilla elections or rabbi elections?
The taxpayer must know this before he casts his vote for the candidates on the 17 lists.
Will you do it?
Dov Tencer.
Lyon — the "Silk" City

[France — travel piece and interview; the Lyon fair.] A conversation with the former Prime Minister of France — Herriot.
When you travel from Paris anywhere, to Italy, to England, Switzerland or Germany, you have to pass through the city of Lyon. As if placed there on purpose in the middle of the road, one must, willy-nilly, stop in this third-largest city of France, with its six hundred thousand inhabitants and with the greatest silk industry in the whole world.
Where this industry came from, to Lyon of all places, and how it developed so strongly. That it has no equal in the whole world — that cannot be said exactly today. It seems that already the Romans introduced those little flies [i.e. silkworms] that "spit" the silken threads, and here in Lyon they probably found the best place, where they multiplied in such great numbers as could be seen nowhere else in the whole world.
And since Lyon also lies at the centre of all the traffic that links France with the four corners of the world, this silk industry was built up here slowly, slowly, and brought so far that today there is hardly a single city in the world where the silk fabrics of Lyon are not known.
In Lyon there is a textile museum, the largest in the world, and in this museum there are no fewer than five hundred thousand different patterns of silk fabrics made in the Lyon region. One can imagine what work it is, constantly to think up and draw new patterns that will please the world and be suited to the various fashions that now rule all countries.
For hundreds of kilometres far and wide stand the looms of the silk workers who weave for the Lyon factories. In many towns and villages young and old sit almost day and night at work, toiling to finish various silk fabrics, which are then sent from Lyon out into the whole world.
Besides this, however, the people of Lyon are proud of three things: first, of their mayor, the well-known French politician, the friend of the Jews Herriot, who lives in Lyon and has already been French Prime Minister several times; second, of their food, which they reckon the best in the whole world; and third, of their fair, which is held every year from the 8th to the 18th of March.
Already hundreds of years ago this fair was held in Lyon, where all the silk fabrics made there were sold; later they began to bring to the fair all possible articles produced in the Lyon region.
Only in the year 1916 did Mayor Herriot begin to build up the Lyon fair on a grand scale, according to the needs of a modern trade fair (Messe).
Today it is the largest fair not only in France but in all of Central Europe, where manufacturers and buyers from the whole world gather.
Some years ago two palaces were built here in Lyon for the fair; they count among the most beautiful palaces ever built for this purpose.
In one of the palaces all kinds of goods are exhibited, and in the other palace only foodstuffs. There one can see everything the earth brings forth in the whole world and everything produced for eating. Since the French in general are fond of food, and since the people of Lyon say they are the best cooks in the whole world, one can understand that here in Lyon they take the greatest pains to show everything that has even the slightest connection with food.
This year it is expected that many more merchants than ever will come here to the Lyon fair, because Lyon is preparing to prove to the world that French industry has today developed into the largest industry in Europe.
In my conversation with Prime Minister Herriot he was very pleased when I told him about the greatness of the Jewish press in general, and especially when I told him what great influence the Jewish press has on Jews in general. He asked me to convey, through the Jewish press, his most heartfelt greetings to all Jews of the whole world, and to invite them to the Lyon trade fair, which opens on the 8th of March this year.
There are many reductions for merchants from the whole world, about which one can learn at any chamber of commerce or at any French consulate. The visa is free of charge and the railway is greatly reduced; the stay in Lyon and in Paris, too, is at half price.
I am therefore ready to give any information. My address can be obtained from the editorial office of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
—o—
Liability for Income Tax.
[Taxes — legal ruling.] Income tax on wages is not assessed by the tax office (urząd); rather, the employer must pay it in himself, deducting it from the wages paid out.
Income tax is assessed by the office only if it has not been paid in at all or too little has been paid in.
Be that as it may, the employer is liable for such a debt, and by no means the worker — even in the case where the overdue tax debt has to be claimed only after the worker has already left the job.
Heard and Seen.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

"After all, it's our holiday"...
Yet another "Jewish" holiday has been added in the Jewish street — the Sylvester holiday [New Year's Eve], and just as after every holiday, we have "material" for this column from this new "Jewish" holiday.
— From the "Sylvester holiday"...
What we relate here took place in Będzin.
In a hall on Third of May Square [Plac 3 Maja] a group of "proletarian" youth gathered to celebrate the Sylvester holiday. To celebrate the holiday — since in a public hall the youth could not "allow itself" [pozwolić] — they made "a Sabbath of their own": a "homely" crowd [„smaiske" kompania — probably swojska kompania] got together and had a fine time, as is right and proper.
In the house where the festivity took place there also live non-Jewish tenants, who could not fall asleep because of the noise carried from the "Sylvester bibka" [drinking party].
— "Oh, those Żydzi [Jews], those Żydzi, it's still not enough for them. Not only have they grabbed all the trade — they also disturb our night's rest" — whispered the lips of the half-asleep Christian tenants.
And one of the non-Jewish residents, a higher official, was not idle: at midnight he got out of bed and, with clenched fists, set off into the dance hall.
When the official came in to the dancing Jewish youth, the latter assumed that he too had come to have a good time. After all, it is an international holiday.
— Panie! [Sir!] What do you want? Why are you robbing peaceful citizens of their sleep?
— He must already be good and drunk
— a second Jewish young fellow responded. Otherwise he would not talk such foolish words, for what intelligent Christian sleeps on such a "night of vigil"?
— Panie kochany! [My dear sir!] — another young man speaks up, what are you saying? It's the night of Holy Sylvester, isn't it?
— Cóż [So what about] Sylvester? And if so, how do you come to this wedding at all? What has this celebration to do with you?
— "After all, it's our holiday"...

Chatan Bereshit and Sylvester...
We have always known that whoever is honoured with Chatan Bereshit treats the "crowd" of his minyan, or "shtibl", to a kiddush. There are also exceptions: honours of Chatan Bereshit without "kiddushim". But those must already be "the cream of the pot", the purest olive oil. The accepted rule, however, is
— "Chatan Torah or Chatan Bereshit — with a kiddush".
In 5694 a change has come into this system. A Mysłowice Jew, a "mshlgudiber"[?], from the Kielce voivodeship, has made an innovation: that the holder of Chatan Bereshit does not discharge his duty with a "kiddush", but must hold
— a Sylvester ball...
He found a juxtaposition of portions for this, since the rabbi had told him that Bereshit is the first sidra [weekly portion] and — to make the distinction — Sylvester is the first night on which the new year begins...
And our Mysłowice Chatan Bereshit publicized his "idea" in a very nice way. In the special "zaproszenia" [invitations] that he sent to his friends, the synagogue members, he announced that because he had had the honour of receiving, last Simchat Torah, "Khasan Bereyshis" [Chatan Bereshit, in folk-Polish spelling], he is arranging in his "prywatne mieszkanie" [private apartment]
— a "Sylvester evening"...
Incidentally, the "zaproszenie" also notes that the dishes will be strictly "kosher". He, the host — pardon, the Chatan Bereshit — took care of it and invited the rabbi beforehand, who established that a "rytualna kuchnia" [ritual (kosher) kitchen] is "prowadzona"[?] [kept] at his place...
Well, let them say it. That we are living through a spiritual decline, that Jewish culture is not being enriched, that "Moyshe Kapoyer" [Topsy-turvy] occupies the seat of honour. Here a new Jewish "star" has risen in the holy community of Mysłowice, who has innovated that whoever has Chatan Bereshit must, besides the traditional "kiddush", also hold
— the Sylvester holiday...
The one is "closely bound up" with the other, a complete "connection"
— Chatan Bereshit and Sylvester..

"Rummaging in the dung"...
I took a stroll to the "mass meetings" for the Sosnowiec kehilla elections; I went "from strength to strength", from one battle position to the next, listened to the speeches, and from everywhere I came away
— with a feeling of disgust.
I heard no kehilla programme whatsoever, no plans for the future, only:
— thieves, informers, "goose-gobblers"[?], filth, base deeds.
— a veritable lexicon of curse[?]-words.
Coming out of a meeting of this sort, I meet an acquaintance, a full-blown "kol-ulakh"[?] in the current kehilla elections.
— What's new regarding[?] the kehilla elections? — I ask him.
— They — I get from him a short but factual answer
— are rummaging in the dung...

The meaning of words.
At the academy [festive assembly] of the "State on the Way".
Around the presidium table — majors, chief commanders, officers, lieutenants [porucznicy] and other military people, and above all
— Jewish ones...
My eyes saw it and my ears heard how the district commander of Zagłębie gave a speech
— a speech in the Holy Tongue.
A Jewish state! The beginning of redemption! As Rabbi Hager indeed says, when the "simple son" asks you "What is this?" — you shall answer him:
— "With a strong hand"...
But listening to the speeches, my earlier enthusiasm cooled somewhat, for at an academy of such an organization among the nations of the world one hears other words: there they also speak of the past, of bygone times, but the main thing is the real present, the well-founded[?] territorial ambitions. And with us — with us the outward garment is a splendid one, but the reality is a sad one...
— The meaning of words.
Oneg Shabbat (Sabbath Delight)
[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly Torah portion (Va'era); column heading.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's Torah portion. Collected and styled by Yehuda. Parashat Va'era.
Parasha — sayings on the portion of Va'era

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion (Va'era).] Parasha.
a) "And God spoke unto Moses" (6:2).
"He spoke with him in judgment, because he had spoken harshly, saying: Why have You dealt ill with this people." Rashi.
Our tzaddikim and rabbis are in the habit — Rabbi Meirl of Przemyślany used to say — when a calamity befalls the Jews, of saying: There you have it for your sins, God has punished you. That is called flattering the Master of the Universe. And the Jerusalem Talmud in Sanhedrin says: "The righteous know their Master, that He is truthful, and they do not flatter Him." The Holy One, blessed be He, needs no flattery. Moses our teacher, instead of being angry at the Jews for not listening to him, actually had a complaint against the Almighty, as it were: "Why have You dealt ill with this people"; and "He spoke" — He conceded, as it were — that "with him [was] judgment", that Moses was right... Divrei Meir.
• • •
"The Holy One, blessed be He, will in the time to come make a dance [mahol] for the righteous"...
In the time to come the Holy One, blessed be He, will ask forgiveness (la'asot mahul) of the righteous, who suffer so much in this world...
Rabbi Dovid'l of Lelów.
• • •
The Baal Shem Tov once came to Ołyka. He went into the beit midrash and heard a maggid preaching. As usual the maggid enumerated all sorts[?] of sins and transgressions of the Jews: neglect of Torah study, too little fear of Heaven, praying without devotion.
The Baal Shem Tov interrupts him and cries out:
— You dare speak ill of Jews? A Jew toils a whole day in the marketplace, and when evening comes he gives a start: Oh no, I've nearly missed the time for Minha! And he runs into the beit midrash and "snatches" a prayer, not really knowing what he is saying — and it makes a stir in Heaven...
• • •
A maggid once came to Tykocin and in his sermon rebuked the people: Jews steal, murder, etc.
The rabbi, the well-known R' Meirl, heard it; he went up onto the bimah, raised his eyes to heaven and said:
— Master of the Universe, don't listen to him. Not one word he says is true. Jews are holy and their dealings are honest...
b) "The land of their sojournings, wherein they sojourned" (ibid., 4).
Yes, such is the fate of the Jews: even in their own land they were g e r i m ("garu bah"), strangers... The Land of Israel is also called the land of their m e g u r i m [sojournings], because in the Land of Israel Jews are regarded as gerim, as strangers, as "illegals"...
Beit Yaakov.
"And I will bring you out" (ibid., 6).
"For thus I promised him: and afterwards they shall come out with great substance." Rashi.
Had it not been for the great substance, it would have been impossible to get the Jews out of Egypt; they would always have been drawn back to the fleshpots... Only when they were given so much money — the spoil of Egypt and the spoil of the Sea — were they no longer drawn back to Egypt...
Ma'arnei Melekh [sic; probably Ma'adanei Melekh].
• • •
There is a masorah [parallel]: "And I will put a division [pedut] between My people and your people", "He sent redemption [pedut] unto His people", "And with Him is plenteous redemption [pedut]".
To make possible the "I will put pedut" and "He sent pedut unto His people", to make possible the redemption and ensure that the Jews would not want to go back to Egypt — "with Him is plenteous pedut": God had to reward them generously, to send a great ransom along with them...
By way of jest. Ibid.
c) "And I will put a division between My people and your people" (8:19).
A.
Here it speaks of "pedut between My people and your people" — when the Jews are redeemed from the gentiles; and another verse speaks of "He sent pedut unto His people" — a pedut, a redemption from the Jews...
Rabbi Shalom of Bełz.
• • •
Rabbi Eizel Charif was once travelling in winter in a "boyd" [covered wagon], as in olden times. The road was a hard one. The wagon jolted, and on top of that the coachman felt that he had a passenger like R' Eizel, so he began pestering him with foolish questions:
— Rabbi, I've heard that the Jews will have two Messiahs, one the Messiah son of David and the other the Messiah son of Ephraim. What do we need two Messiahs for? Isn't one enough?
R' Eizel grows irritated and says:
— One Messiah will redeem us from g a l u t [exile], and the other from the b a ' a l e i - a g a l o t [the coachmen]...
B.
"And I will put a division between My people and your people" —
If the Jews are perhaps not worthy of being redeemed, yet when I compare them with the Egyptians ("between My people and your people") I see that, with all their badness, they are much better than the gentiles, and are therefore worthy of being redeemed...
Tiferet Uziel.
• • •
"And Your people Israel shall not need one another, nor any other people" —
If only one did not have to plead in the Jews' favour by saying that one is better than the other, and that they are better than the gentiles... That is a lamentable plea in their defence... "And they shall not need".. Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdyczów.
e) "Only let not Pharaoh deal deceitfully [hatel] any more" (ibid., 25).
That is worse than anything — the "hatel", the mockery, the making fun of an oppressed people... Likkutei Shoshanim.
f) "And the thunders ceased!" (9:33).
Twice the Torah mentions "va-yahdelu" [and they ceased]: "And the thunders ceased" and "and they ceased to build the city" (Genesis 11:8). Jews build the Land of Israel when they are beaten, when they are driven out. No sooner do "the thunders cease" than "they cease to build the city"... R' Zalman Kharer.
g) "Korah, and Nepheg, and Zichri" (6:21).
In many Hasidic books we find the following characteristic words:
The Seer of Lublin said that every year in the week of the portion of Va'era the frost must be mild. He based it on the verse "Korah ve-Nepheg" [read as: the ice (kerah) melts away] — the frost must thaw.. "ve-Zichri" — and that is a remembrance for all generations...
Hasidim assure us that since the Seer said these words (more than a hundred and twenty years ago) there has not yet been a week of the portion of Va'era with frost...
Cygler's Picture Exhibition

[Art — exhibition.] At the exhibition Cygler is represented with 60 pictures. That is a sufficient number to form an idea of the artist's many-sided activity, and we shall try to do so, at least in condensed form.
Cygler's works must be classified as graphic and purely painterly.
As a graphic artist Cygler unquestionably occupies an important place among the most significant Polish artists. This is attested by the fact that at the last International Graphic Arts Exhibition in Warsaw a woodcut by Cygler was bought for the state collections. Considering that graphic artists from 23 countries with over 700 exhibits were represented at the exhibition, one must admit that only first-class artists had a chance of having their works bought for a state institution.
Cygler is first and foremost a first-class draughtsman, and that is the most important foundation for a visual artist. His woodcuts are masterfully drawn, very well composed, and bear the specific character of the woodcut technique. In his woodcuts the artist achieves a splendid play of light and shadow. The transition from the white to the black patches is — thanks to his brilliant technique — subtle and pleasing.
Cygler's subject matter is varied. He makes use of social motifs ("The Unemployed", "A Meal", etc.), the landscape, the shtetl, and so on. Everywhere one notices a serious approach to the matter, the striving to achieve purely artistic values, without cheap effects, in which he almost always succeeds.
Besides the woodcut technique, Cygler is also versed in the other branches of graphic art, such as lithography and aquatint.
Now about Cygler's purely painterly works.
The 40 oil paintings and watercolours consist mainly of landscapes in the south of France and Kazimierz, as well as some still lifes. In the works from the south of France the green and red colour tones dominate, which are characteristic of the local landscape. The artist has succeeded in achieving very juicy yellow-green colour chords, as well as fine and subtle red nuances.
At a considerably higher artistic level are the works from Kazimierz.
Although Cygler's colour scale is not a broad one, he nevertheless succeeds in bringing out the most varied pleasingly effective nuances of colouring. In his landscapes the artist mainly uses the tonal scale from blue to grey, but they are so happily harmonised that they capture the eye and rivet the viewer to them.
"The Horses at the Fair" prove once again how enormously important it is for a visual artist to master the technique of drawing. Not many artists will manage to draw so precisely and with such verve so considerable a number of horses in motion.
"The Synagogue in Kazimierz" is painted with temperament. The fine drawing and the splendid light effects create a harmonious line in the colour composition, which make the picture a small masterpiece.
The pictures "The Shtetl" and "The Alley" are kept in a lively, pleasing colouring, and in them the characteristic features of the Jewish shtetl are captured with talent.
One must also mention the large oil painting "The Hasidic Dance" (from the Dybbuk cycle), which is kept in quiet, dark tones and breathes a mystical ecstasy.
Cygler is certainly a powerful talent who is at a stage of his artistic development, and it is to be hoped that on his artistic path he will reach a very high creative level.
Sh. R.
Greetings from Home

[Feuilleton — satire; Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec, rabbinical and kehilla elections.] (A bundle of letters between Yosl Varshaver and Berl Zaglembier.)
Handed over for printing by Y. B. Zayants.
Dear friend Yoselé, may he live long! Since I haven't written to you for such a long time, you are surely cross with me; but believe me, dearest Yoselé, that if you were here with us in Zagłębie, in this tormented Zagłębie of ours, and saw what goes on here, then — upon my life — you would not hold it against me at all; always busy[?], always overworked[?], so that truly one never has oneself in mind, except sometimes when one does something for the public good... Now, my friend, let us get to the point: when I and my missus — may she be healthy and strong — sometimes talk about you, [we say] it is truly a [shame][?], upon my life, that you have settled yourself there in the big city by the Vistula and won't budge from the spot... Between us, Yoselé: if that's how it is, "it shall not prosper" — such a shlimazl as you are has to this very day not been elected there as a Sejm deputy; if such an uncle as you does not now sleep in the city council, and above all, if a Jew with such long hands as you have has never yet been a dozór [board member] of the Warsaw Jewish community — what are you wasting your life for, you robber, in that great metropolis with the skyscrapers, and don't see that you'd do better to dash over here to Zagłębie, where money is scraped up in the streets and anyone at all here makes the "masnia"[?], so that he goes to sleep a pauper[?] and gets up a multiple millionaire...
Now, here we have rabbinical elections in the holy community of Dąbrowa, and you surely understand that half a world of "crowned rulers" in shtreimels want, poor things, to "push their way in" right here into this coal basin, to grab the rabbinical throne here by force... But "no" — with a [?]: the Dąbrowa kehilla wants a "bridegroom" with all the virtues, and such a "jewel" is hard to find nowadays because of the various parties and little parties. Therefore, dear Yoselé, if you can pack up there in your "Beersheba" such a little rebbe who on Shabbat will be a "table-sitter" in Belz[?], on Sunday an assimilationist in a frock coat and top hat, on Monday will buy a "shekel" and be a Zionist, on Tuesday will comb his little beard and become a Mizrachi man, on Wednesday will sit down on a cobbler's bench and become an artisan... if you manage that, if you, Yoselé, can pack up such a "bird" there, bring him down here at once by the express, and in Dąbrowa we'll literally sugar him up...
You think, my Yoselé, that you're already off the hook? Don't hurry, don't grab the tsimmes before the noodles...
Together with these rabbinical elections in Dąbrowa, we also have elections here in the Jewish community of Sosnowiec, and here, brother Yoselé, there'll be a bone worth licking, because for the "pot" there are so many contenders there that one person[?] from there even submitted a list of a dead candidate, on the grounds — so they claim — that since the Sosnowiec Jewish community will in any case forever remain nothing more than a "shtibl of the dead", the dead too want to have a "share"[?] in the bowl there...
To tell the truth, the Sosnowiec elections are nowadays a hard bit of Maharsha, because our Sosnowiec possesses, thank God, quite a few "upstart" rich men. These are creatures who, if not for the World War, would have lived out their years in peace and tranquillity in their basement rooms and later been buried with great joy in the cemetery behind the park... But now that they have indeed "come out on top", so why on earth shouldn't they, like the others, also once jump up onto the "old nag" of the Community of Israel and give her a lash...
In short, dear Yoselé, if you have it in mind to become a man of standing, if you want to do the real business, follow my advice and come straight to Sosnowiec; here they'll put you up as a candidate, and we'll first[?] come to terms with a certain "kehilla-digger", a well-known personality with a big mouth, who will get so-and-so much from us — and you'll see, brother Yosl, what he will proclaim about you aloud before the whole congregation... He'll shout that you are as pious as our father Abraham, as wise as King Solomon, an orator like Balaam's donkey, a Zionist who drinks a whole barrel of Carmel wine in one breath, and on top of all that, since when you talk you gesticulate with your hands, you are anyhow an "artisan" as well; they'll snap you up here like a roast and seat you in the Sosnowiec Jewish community as president, and I'll be your secretary here, and we'll rob "dead and alive" without a speck of fear, because for the living it's enough to have a polished brick [i.e. a smooth tongue] with sweet little words, and the dead, on the other hand, have the advantage that one may steal from them however one likes — it always remains a secret...
Don't be a shlemiel, Yoselé, and come here at once, because "the time is short and the work is great".
Your friend
Beril Hitskop.
Where Is Justice, Mercy? (A Humoresque)

[Humoresque — housing; landlord and tenant.] By B. Kowner.

They put my uncle Eliyahu out on the street with all his wretched belongings.

So I run off to the landlord — a "macher" [big shot] in some society — and I ask him:

"Panie [Mr.] Grablien! How are you not ashamed to throw out onto the street a pauper like my uncle Eliyahu? A Jew, a destitute man, who hasn't even got the money for rent. — Pfui, you may well be ashamed; that one Jew should throw another out onto the street over such a trifle as rent. How much does he owe you altogether? Surely [?] three or four months. And even if it were six, so what? The very fact that he has not paid you is the best sign that he hasn't got it. Whoever has it, pays; nobody wants to be thrown out onto the street. Why should the whole world have to see that he is a poor man? That he has broken beds, rusty ones, with old mattresses, with a Singer machine that won't sew, with an old gramophone that won't play? When someone is rich and has the beautiful, the rich furniture, with the big mirrors, with the Japanese vases, with the expensive oil paintings and statues by great artists, and he is put out on the street, he is not so ashamed; on the contrary: let people see what a rich man he is, what furniture he has. But to throw out a Jew like my uncle Eliyahu — that is not nice [?], and for what? For rent! What part does five or six months' rent play for a Jew like you, with such a name? But for my uncle it is a fortune, a treasure of money.

"Pfui, what is this supposed to mean! Now he sits there in the street with his four little children, and they guard their bit of poverty.

The landlord began to stroke his beard, looked at me, smiled and wanted to say something, to put forward arguments, the excuses of yesterday, but I did not let him get a word in; I knew [?] beforehand what he would answer me; I know them by heart, the owners of the houses; I wish I did not know them so well!

So I did not let him get a word in, but went on talking:

"If I were a landlord, I would act differently. I would take into my houses precisely the poorest people, the greatest paupers, and I would say to them: 'Children! Live with me as long as you like; don't worry about rent; if you have it — you'll give it; if, God forbid, you don't — it won't bother me either; only it would be better if you did have it.

"'And children — you may have as many as you yourselves like; the more children, the better, the merrier. And the children would enjoy every freedom with me: you want to smash windowpanes — smash away, in good health! The glazier has to make a living too. You want to write on the walls — write! The house painters are going about idle; they'll have something to do. You want to take the handles off the doors — in good health! If it gives you pleasure, why not? You want to stop up the bathtubs — stop them up: who's stopping you? You want to dance about in the courtyard with other children — dance in good health! You may even shout and make a racket and beat one another, as long as it gives you pleasure.'

"And to the mothers of the children I would say: 'You want to throw rubbish out of the windows — throw it! Carrying it down to the courtyard is too much work; you have to go down the stairs and that is hard: you are left out of breath. And if you want to hang your bedding out of the windows so that it dries and airs, that doesn't bother me either; you may cover all the windows with your featherbeds and quilts and rags and nappies and underclothes [?] and socks and handkerchiefs; if it doesn't bother me, it needn't bother you. And should you want to quarrel and invent gossip, "plotki" about one another — you may do that; don't be ashamed before anyone; don't give a fig for the world!

"'You may even pull one another's hair, scratch out one another's eyes, insult one another, drag one another through the mud.

"'Everything is permitted to you!

"'And if you want to sit outside on the balcony — you may do that too. When you have every freedom — that's nice, isn't it! You can even slander [?] your neighbour, and me myself, ten times a day, demand that the flat be painted twice a year, that electric iceboxes [?] be installed. You can demand anything, anything, and I will give in to you in everything.'

"That is how I would act if I were a landlord.

"It goes without saying that I would have a good name and all the poor people would want to live in my houses.

"And you, such a fine Jew, such a rich Jew, a macher in a society, a Jew who stands at the eastern wall next to the rabbi, you who play the great part — you are not ashamed to throw my uncle Eliyahu out onto the street over a few months' rent!

"Where is justice? Mercy? Humanity? One must have a heart, after all — [even] that of a robber, of a bandit! What, will you take your houses with you to the next world?! Either way you will get no more than four ells of earth, the same as my uncle Eliyahu... So why are you tearing the world apart? You are no longer a young man: any moment now you'll go your way [die], and I swear no one among our people will leave a tear after you, or even heave a sigh. Who knows! It will even give us a great deal of pleasure [?]."

That is how, as you hear, I talked to the landlord for perhaps half an hour without a break [?]. Him I did not let open his mouth.

And do you know what the end was? Uncle Eliyahu sat in the street so long, guarding his belongings, until it started pouring with rain, and I had to take him and the children in to my place...
My Prophecies for the New Year

[Satirical verse — prophecies for the new year; Zagłębie, Hitler, Jabotinsky.] By Graf Kali.

I prophesy.
What will be in the new year?
Whoever has been a pauper
Stays a pauper — that is clear!

There will be no more protested bills,
That I also have perceived,
Because there will not be the złoty
To pay the notary [rejent]...

The Sosnowiec Jewish kehilla
Will stay true to itself as before:
Coal will be distributed there
On the twentieth of the month of May...

Zagłębie will become fine and bright,
Finer, more elegant too:
From hundreds of factories
Smoke will cease to rise...

The Yiddish theatre
Will begin to stir [?] from its sleep,
Genuine, true artists of the "Muse"
Will start touring again.
No one will any longer count as a star [?]
Those who can [only] wail [?] "folk" [songs],
For to listen to whose nasal twang
You have to be stronger than iron.

* *

This, gentlemen, is my local prophecy. Now you surely want to know what will happen in general in our poor little world? Whether Hitler will die an unnatural death, and who will be the president of the Zionist Executive?

Then listen a little, gentlemen, I will think it over... Like this:

Hear, then, further my prophecy [printed "gviot"],
Children of men, hear it fast,
What in nineteen thirty-four
Is fated to come to pass...

Adolf Hitler, there in Germany,
Will soon be rid of power.
Only, before long, he will be
Laughed to utter scorn...

Besides his high, fine post
He will also lose his glory;
Like his old, proud Kaiser
He will have to abdicate in shame...

* * *

Vladimir Jabotinsky
Will this year come "to power".
And he will, with Great Britain,
Measure himself in battle —
Not with tanks, aeroplanes,
Not with mighty legions;
He will fight only with justice
And will demand... demand... demand...

*) For technical reasons the "prophecies" are printed slightly late.
The Jewish Queen of Yemen (2)

[Serialized historical tale — Yemen; installment 2.]
Sh. Berg.

The guards had by now grown so used to Pnina's mother that they no longer watched her. So she decided that the time had come to save her child. She worked out a plan and secretly passed Pnina a note, instructed [?] her what to do in order to be able to escape, and told her to be ready the next day.

The whole night the poor mother stayed awake and prayed to God that He might stand by her, that she might be able to save her only child.

The next morning Pnina's mother came to the prison as on every day, with a big basket of laundry; she handed out the laundry, and the empty basket she set down in the front house. Pnina quietly climbed into the basket and covered herself with a sheet, and the mother took up the heavy burden — which was so light and dear to her on her shoulders — and walked past the guards. They did not stop her; after all, they knew her well.

Outside a wagon was already waiting, and she lifted the basket onto it. They no longer went home but drove straight out of the town. A whole day they travelled in great haste, until they reached an inn where many Jews were waiting to travel to Yemen.

Only at the inn did Pnina come out of her hiding place in the basket. Mother and child fell on each other's necks and wept hard for joy, and they thanked and [printed "in" for "and"] praised God for having saved them from the hands of the gentiles. With a bitter heart they left the land where Jews had lived quietly and securely for six hundred years and where they had left behind so many precious graves. They boarded a ship and sailed for Yemen.

For some time they sailed on the sea. They lived through many terrors. Storm winds often hurled the ship up above the clouds and flung it down deep toward the abyss. They thought they were going under. And the fear of the sailors, lest they do Pnina some harm, was no small matter either. At last they came to the shore from which they were to go on to Yemen.

They had to cross a great desert, from the sea to Yemen. So they hired camels, loaded onto them their bit of belongings, prepared food and water, and set off on the road, across the great desert.

A fear, a strange fear, came over them when they entered the desert. No village, no tent is to be seen here. Not even a bird, not a living soul, not a tree, not a blade of grass — only sand that burns like fire and is fine as dust.

Two nights they spent in the desert; the camels' backs were their bed, and above them the clear sky with the wondrously shining stars. By day the heat tormented them and by night — the cold. On the third day they came to a mountain that looked like an island in the middle of the sea. On that mountain there was a patch of fertile field with six great, broad-branched fig trees and precious shade, where hundreds of weary wanderers with their camels rest and refresh their hearts. Beside the trees they found a fresh spring gushing [?] from a rock. They [printed "hab"] stopped, drank their fill of fresh water, watered the camels and sat down to rest in the shade.

Soon they opened the packs, took out copper pots, gathered dry branches, made a fire, cooked a pot of millet [?] and ate their fill; then they set off on the road again.

For a few hours they walked through the desert. Suddenly the sky turned green, and the sun red as blood. A terrible stifling heat fell upon them and they could hardly breathe. The camels at once stretched out on the ground, lowered their heads and buried mouth and nose in the sand.

They understood that the samum was coming — the terrible storm wind that is full of poisonous dust, and whoever breathes it in dies on the spot. Only he can save himself who lies down on the ground and hides his mouth in the sand. Quick as lightning they got down from the camels, stretched out on the ground, buried mouth and [printed "in" for "and"] nose in the sand, and the angry storm raged wildly over them with a fearful [?] whistling and burned their skin as if with burning sulphur.

At last it grew quiet. The angry storm stopped, the camels got up, the people raised themselves. The heat fell, a pleasant breeze began to blow, and they walked on until sunset. Soon after sunset it became terribly cold. They shivered with cold, and again a strong wind arose; it carried clouds of sand, as if it wanted to cover and bury everyone.

A wild terror fell upon the wanderers. They saw that a disaster was coming upon them, and they broke into loud weeping and begged God to have mercy on them and save them from death. Pnina's mother quickly covered her only child with a sheet over her face and pressed her tightly to her heart.

The camels went wild and threw everyone off. And before they could look around they were already lying under a mountain of sand. And the mountain grew ever bigger and heavier. How long it lasted Pnina did not know; but when she dug herself out of the sand, the storm had already died down, and her mother lay beside her, buried under the sand; only her hand stuck out.

Pnina seized her by the hand, wanting to help her dig herself out. But the hand was ice-cold. Pnina called her — Mama, Mama, Mama — but she did not stir, did not answer. Pnina screamed, wept, lamented. She wanted to call her mother back to life, but it was in vain. The mountain of sand had smothered her. She was dead in her grave of sand.

She cried out for help and no one answered. All the wanderers lay dead, buried under the sand; only here and there [?] could one see the packs the camels had carried. And what could Pnina do, a twelve-year-old child, she, the only one saved from the disaster? She scraped the sand off her dead mother, threw herself upon her with a wail, washed her face with tears, until she no longer had the strength to weep.

For a while she lay like that; she wanted to die next to her mother. But the power of life was stronger, and she decided to go on through the desert until she came to a settlement. She wrapped her mother in the sheet in which her mother had wrapped her and thereby saved her from death, heaped over her a high mound of sand, and moistened her mother's grave with her tears.

Mute, she stretched out over the grave; she could no longer weep, and she fell asleep. When she woke up she did not know how she had come here. She thought that it had all been only a bad dream. But then she saw the grave and burst into hard weeping again; afterwards she prayed from the heart, took leave of the dear grave and set off at God's mercy [?], not knowing where to or how.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: A Long-Term Loan by the Magistrate

[Będzin — Municipality.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 25 Tevet 5694 — piątek 12 stycznia 1934 [Friday, 12 January 1934].)
Będzin
A Long-Term Loan by the Magistrate.
At the last meeting of the Council of Commissioners it was resolved that the Magistrate [municipality] will take a long-term loan from the "Bank Polski" in the sum of 45 thousand zł.
At the same meeting it was decided to pay the surveyor (geometer) Mr. Berecki [?] a sum of 19,780 zł. for surveying the town...
A Concession for the Owners of Houses Not Yet Connected to the Water Mains

[Będzin — Municipality and housing.]
As is known, the owners of houses that are not yet connected to the water-mains installation are being called upon by the Magistrate to pay 60 percent of the water lump-sum charge (ryczałt).
In this matter the Association of House- and Plot-Owners turned with a memorandum to the Kielce Voivodeship office. The memorandum stressed that, because of the hard times, the house-owners are not in a position to connect their houses to the water mains, and therefore the levy which the Magistrate demands from the house-owners is not justified.
"This week the association received a reply that the Voivode has instructed the local Magistrate not to demand the tax imposed for water, and that the deadline for laying on the water mains is to be extended until the 1st of April (kwiecień) of this year.
The Great Success of Cygler's Picture Exhibition

[Będzin — Culture and art.]
As we have already written, the picture exhibition of the well-known artist-painter Mr. S. Cygler was opened last Saturday in the premises of the Jewish Society for Knowledge of the Land (Żydowskie Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze).
The success of the exhibition exceeds all expectations. In the course of the week the exhibition was successfully visited, and a considerable number of pictures were bought by the visitors.
The exhibition, which will remain open for a few more days, must absolutely be visited by every educated person.
A Local Relief Fund Has Been Created

[Będzin — Relief and the unemployed.]
In connection with the fact that the local Committee for the Support of the Unemployed is in the process of liquidation, a meeting of a number of Jewish and non-Jewish public figures took place this week at the Magistrate. At the meeting it was resolved to create a local relief fund, from which, besides the unemployed, poor families who are not registered will also be supported.
The committee appeals to the population to support the campaign of the local relief fund, so as to make it possible to alleviate the situation of the camp of the poor.
—o—
From the Anti-Hitlerite Youth Action in Będzin.
[Będzin — Boycott of German goods.] A few weeks ago, as is known, a youth committee was founded in Będzin whose task is to propagate the boycott of German goods.
The committee distributes among doctors, pharmacies and merchants lists on which are enumerated which articles can be imported from other countries instead of from Germany.
The committee asks everyone who knows who is trading with Hitler-Germany to inform the committee about it; the committee is on duty in the premises of the youth organization "Akiba", Będzin, Podgórska 4.
—o—
Consultation of the Most Respected Citizens on the Budget for 1934
[Będzin — Kehilla.] In connection with the draft budget for the year 1934, the presidium of the kehilla board has called a number of the most respected budget-payers to a consultation.
—o—
An Amateur of Electric Light Bulbs...
[Będzin — Crime.] On Monday towards evening a young Christian was caught red-handed ("in the hot minute"), who had unscrewed the electric light bulbs in the "German" synagogue on Kołłątaja Street.
—o—
New Head of the Tax Office
[Będzin — Taxes.] The hitherto head (naczelnik) of the local tax office, Mr. Krakowiak [?], has left the office. In his place the hitherto head of the tax office in Olkusz has been appointed.
Sosnowiec — Convention of Brit HaHayal of Zagłębie and Silesia

[Sosnowiec — Revisionists; Brit HaHayal and Betar.]
On Sunday the members of Betar and of "Brit HaHayal" from all of Zagłębie and Silesia gathered in Sosnowiec. The latter drew attention to themselves because of their military dress; among them were genuine Jewish officers and captains.
The celebration opened at 9 in the morning with the parade report, which was taken by the chief commander of "Brit HaHayal" in Poland, Consul Eng. M. Szeskin, and the commander for [?] the Kielce voivodeship, Mr. Henech [?] Ehrlich.
After the report a festive prayer service was held in the town synagogue. After the cantor Mr. Leichter sang the appropriate chapters of Psalms with the choir, the chairman of the patronage committee of "Brit HaHayal" gave a spirited speech on the difficult situation of the Jewish people, on the role of the Jewish leader, and on the great merit of Ze'ev Jabotinsky and of "Brit HaHayal".
After this speech the orchestra of the Będzin "Hakoach" played the Polish and the Jewish anthems. Then a procession of "Brit HaHayal" and Betar was formed, of nearly 1000 men, who marched through the streets to the cinema hall "Palace", where a festive academy [assembly] took place.
A crowd of a couple of thousand people came, but not all could get into the hall, and many hundreds of people remained outside. After the Polish and the Jewish anthems were played by the orchestra of the Będzin "Hakoach", the district commander Mr. Ehrlich opened the academy.
In his opening speech, which was delivered in Hebrew and in Polish, he said that "Brit HaHayal" stands at the service of the entire Jewish people, following the orders of its leader Ze'ev Jabotinsky.
Jabotinsky's telegram of greeting was received with loud applause.
On behalf of the patronage committee a greeting rich in content was given by the chairman of "Brit HaHayal", Rabbi Hager, who said that he is proud to stand at the head of such a movement, which has inscribed on its banner: self-sacrifice (mesirut nefesh).
Then the member of the district command Mr. Yosef Klarman gave a longer speech in which he dwelt on the agitation (Hetze) that has lately been conducted against this movement.
Speaking of the latest Palestine decrees, the speaker appealed [to the audience] to take part in the petition proclaimed by Ja[bo]tinsky.
The last to speak was the chief commander Szeskin, who dwelt on the latest events in Zionism and in Palestine.
The speaker gave a survey of the development of events, which, in his opinion, are a consequence of the bad Zionist policy. The speaker appealed to those assembled to draw conclusions from the latest events in Germany and to [rally] [?] under the blue-white flag, which symbolizes the liberation of the Jewish people in its own land.
All these speeches were heard by the huge crowd with attention, and the speakers were rewarded with loud applause.
The second part of the academy began with a sound film of a Polish "Brit HaHayal" convention in Warsaw. In an elevated mood the academy was closed.
On its march back the procession was greeted by the thousands of people in the streets.
The procession, with the "Hakoach" orchestra at its head, marched through the streets Warszawska, Modrzejowska, then on to Małachowskiego, where at the premises of "Brit HaHayal" the march-past took place, taken by Consul Szeskin.
In the afternoon the conference of the commanders took place at the premises of the Revisionists, chaired by Mr. Szeskin.
The commanders took part in the debate on future work: Bester (Kraków), Brandwein (Bielsko), Captain Sachs (Katowice), Dr. Herber (Bielsko), Capt. Glidman (Będzin), Majerczyk, Ehrlich (Sosnowiec). Praszker (Żarki).
A series of important resolutions was adopted at the conference.
In the evening the festive opening of the premises took place. After the Betar choir sang "Mizmor shir hanukkat ha-bayit" (A Psalm, a song at the dedication of the house), the ribbon was cut by Rabbi Hager. Mr. Klarman opened the evening with a speech in which he dwelt on the development of the Revisionist movement in Sosnowiec. After he welcomed, among others, the vice-chairman of the patronage committee Dr. Glanc, a series of greetings were given by Rabbi Hager, Szeskin, Brandwein, Triger, Miss [?] Fiszel, Glidman and others.
The Endek "Kurier Zachodni" is in a rage over the celebration that took place.
After a lengthy discourse on the celebration in the style of Nowaczyński, the writer says that "it would be quite right for the Brit HaHayal men to renounce Polish citizenship and emigrate to Palestine, where they could train as Jewish military men".
The 'Beit Lehem' society legalized.

[Sosnowiec — relief; the "Beit Lehem" society.]
For more than a year already the idea has been ripening among several local [?] activists of creating in our town such an institution as would support the poor strata of the Jewish population in a time of trouble.
"Beit Lehem" had the same fate that all Jewish institutions in our town have had. But for everything — says King Solomon — there comes a time; after much effort by the organizers and long waiting by the poor, "Beit Lehem" was finally legalized. But after the legalization the situation has not changed at all: the few individuals who work to bring the institution to life remain helpless in every attempt at any action whatsoever. Thus, for example, the provisional board undertook a coal campaign, and for this purpose dozens of letters were sent to the notables ("pnei") of the town asking them to support the coal campaign.
And what does the result look like? — a very sad one: of some fifty, no more than 4 (read: four...) responded. Optimists explain that this is a consequence of the election campaign; the public has no time to reflect on the sad situation of the hundreds of Jewish families in Sosnowiec who live in want and in need.
Next Sunday a meeting will again be called about the activity of the new institution "Beit Lehem", and at this very meeting the final verdict will be given: whether to send back the legalization, or whether "Beit Lehem" is to become the relief institution for the great number of needy.

On Wegrada [?] Street in Sosnowiec a group of boys were skating [on "liushves" — probably łyżwy, skates]. One of them, 18-year-old Majka, while skating, performed various "stunts"; during one such "stunt" Majka went under a passing automobile, by which he was mortally injured.

67-Year-Old Woman Falls Out of a Tram and Meets Her Death.

On Third of May Street [ul. 3 Maja] a tragic tram accident befell 68-year-old Mrs. Mazan. The woman was riding in the attached trailer car. “L.O.P.P.” (Air and Anti-Gas Defence League)

[Będzin — air defence; L.O.P.P.] (Sent in by the Będzin L.O.P.P. committee [LOPP — Liga Obrony Powietrznej i Przeciwgazowej, the Air and Anti-Gas Defence League]).
(Sh.) The World War, the peace treaties, the position of Germany and the general political situation in Europe after the war convince us that the only argument suited to the present political conditions is readiness to repel at once any tendency of occupation with regard to the integrity of the state.
Germany's appetite for our Pomorze, the demand to revise the borders — these are warnings which must strengthen our courage and give an impulse to intensify the preparations in case of war. What the future war will look like, given today's technical progress, is hard to say; in any case, different from what it has been until now.
The development of aviation and of gas weapons has invalidated the former notions of borders and fronts. Wars until now used to cover certain areas, and only soldiers used to take part in them. Today the situation has changed completely. Today the front is the whole state, which is attacked by the enemy air force. In such a state of affairs the whole population must take part in the struggle and must be able to defend itself — one must be prepared for defence. The institution that deals with this preparation is the "L.O.P.P." (League for Air Defence), already well enough known among us. The League teaches how to organise the defence. To this end it holds special courses throughout the country, publishes and supports a whole series of publications, organises appropriate organisations [garbled repetition as printed], provides them with the necessary equipment, builds anti-gas shelters, etc.
The activity of the "L.O.P.P." in this field is, however, limited, because although the "L.O.P.P." is the strongest organisation in Poland, which in the course of 10 years has drawn a million citizens to itself, it does not have the proper means to organise the whole of society; for the League to be able to fulfil its task, the cooperation and support of the entire population are necessary.
Let us not wait for the last moment, for then it will already be too late to expect help, because the organisational-technical preparations will be limited to the material means. One must therefore not neglect the matter, all the more so because we do not know what the future may bring us. Already today some states possess such bombing means and gases as we cannot even imagine. Let us not forget that, in parallel with the peace negotiations and the well-functioning apparatus in Geneva, there actually [?] reigns a fever [?] in the field of armament and of the invention of ever newer means of combat.
Because of the preparations and the war fever that has gripped all of Europe, we must take account of the necessity of preparing for the events that may occur. The strength to protect the state must be gathered in the "L.O.P.P.", whose task is to prepare society, without distinction of race, religion or political outlook, to defend itself against gases and other calamities of war.

How 4 Unemployed Men Swindled the Coal-Dealer Berman of Czeladź / Last Days of Ziegler's Exhibition / A Young Zionist Activist Died Suddenly / Big Revisionist Election Meeting / From the Anti-Hitlerite Youth Front in Będzin / Sosnowiecers on the Other Side of the Ocean... / A Terrible Act of Revenge[?] by a Butcher's Worker / Tram Employees against the New Insurance Law

[Czeladź — trial; fraud.]
Before the Katowice district court the trial took place on Wednesday against 4 unemployed men who had, in a fraudulent manner, tricked 1.500 zł. out of Binyamin Berman of Czeladź.
Berman, who had been buying coal from the unemployed from the „bieda-szyby“ [biedaszyby — primitive illegal „poverty pits“], turned to the suppliers asking them to deliver a larger quantity of coal.
A few days later the workers came to Berman and told him that at a certain coal mine in Upper Silesia large stocks of coal were lying which could be bought at cheap prices.
Berman believed what the workers said and gave them an advance („konto“) of 1.500 zł. for it.
Later, when Berman demanded the coal, he only then saw[?] that he had been swindled.
The chief „merchant“ was sentenced to 6 months and the rest to 3 months in prison.
—o—
[Będzin — art; exhibition.]
Last days of Ziegler's exhibition.
As we have already reported, the picture exhibition of the artist-painter Mr. S. Ziegler in Będzin has had a colossal success. The greater part of the pictures were bought right in the first days.
The picture exhibition will thus, as we are informed, remain open until next Sunday, the 21st of this month.

[Upper Silesia — obituary; Zionism.]
A young Zionist activist died suddenly
In the bloom of life, at the age of 38, the well-known Zionist activist Ziskind (Siegfried) Miarczyk[?] died suddenly in Königshütte [Królewska Huta / Chorzów]. The death of Mr. Miarczyk made a shattering impression on the Jewish as well as on the non-Jewish population.
In the course of recent years there was not a single public cause into which he did not throw himself with all his energy; suffice it to mention his activity for „Maccabi“, the Hitachdut, the artisans, the small traders, the relief fund, the children's colonies, the relief committee for refugees from Germany, the Keren Kayemet, and above all his fatherly attitude toward the veteran halutzim. Last Friday, when the funeral of the deceased took place, the town was turned into one general mourning, in which the non-Jewish population also took part; a crowd of a few thousand heads in closed ranks came to pay the last respects to the one who had sacrificed his young life for the common good.
A moving eulogy was delivered by Rabbi Dr. Kohlberg; the crush at the cemetery was so great that the police had to keep order. At the open grave spoke representatives of the Hitachdut, „Maccabi“, the Jewish community, the Zionist organisation, „Kvutza Vatikin“, the small traders, the artisans, Poalei Zion and the Revisionists; out of a whole series of private eulogies the farewell speech of a Christian, in the name of the hundreds of Christian co-workers, drew attention. With the sad awareness that Königshütte had lost its son, the huge crowd dispersed.

A terrible act of revenge[?] by a butcher's worker
On Wednesday a Christian butcher's worker in Załęże (Upper Silesia) committed a terrible murder of his fiancée.
The murderer went into the shop where his fiancée worked, and after a short exchange of words he snatched a [?] knife from the table, with which he inflicted several severe wounds on her; seeing that his fiancée was still breathing[?], he finished her off and then dragged the dead body across the floor.
The murderer has been put in prison.
