The Rabbinate Question in Dąbrowa

The rabbinate question in Dąbrowa has already, as they say, come out of the "eggshell" and is taking on real form.
The candidates for the Dąbrowa rabbinical seat are already being invited by the kehilla to deliver the appropriate sermons, the so-called "examinations".
The first to present himself for the "examination" was the son of the Krzeszowice [?] rabbi, Rabbi Menashe Klingberg, who was in Dąbrowa last Sabbath and appeared with sermons on Friday night and on the Sabbath after the Torah reading. The sermons made the proper impression on the packed audience in the town synagogue.
On Sunday morning the rabbinical candidate was invited to the kehilla premises, where he spent time in an unofficial conversation with several representatives of the board and of the kehilla council.
The main "examination" took place the same day at 8 o'clock in the evening, with the participation of some 60 of the most respected householders and larger "etat" (kehilla-budget) taxpayers of the Dąbrowa kehilla.
Without an invitation entry was forbidden. A special guard of the local "Brit HaChayal" saw to that. But since "after all, we are Jews", many of the uninvited also got into the hall.
On behalf of the board, the chairman Mr A. Neufeld greeted the distinguished guest, explained the purpose of the meeting and gave the floor to Rabbi Menashe Klingberg.
The rabbi takes his place at the special "tribune", face to face with the audience, before whom in his hour-long lecture he gave a historical survey of the opinions of the Sages (Chazal) on the language question among Jews.
After the analysis the rabbi switches to Polish, which arouses enthusiasm among the assembled audience. Here stands a young rabbi, the candidate for the Dąbrowa rabbinate, and besides his ordinations from well-known geniuses (gaonim), he also speaks a fine Polish.
In the Polish language the rabbi speaks about the press of former times and of today, and concludes that one must not despair
— Am Yisrael chai le-olam (the people of Israel lives forever)!
The rabbi's speech was received with sympathy.
From Wednesday On One Must Pay at the Sick Fund (Now — the Social Insurance Institution)

From Wednesday on, the new law comes into force under which the insured must pay for a doctor's visit and for medicines.
Under the new regulations one is charged 20 groszy for every medical consultation, 10 gr. for every treatment, 10 gr. for every medicine, remedy and aid, and 30 groszy for a specific (proprietary drug) and a preparation.
If the treatment takes place during the medical consultation, it costs 20 gr. altogether. If the doctor prescribes several medicines, one pays 10 groszy for each of them.
The sick fund takes no co-payment for surgical procedures, observation procedures, quartz-lamp irradiation for children up to 8 years, for infectious and acute illnesses, and for illnesses that cause an interruption of work of more than 4 weeks.
Nor is any co-payment taken for medicines and dressing materials applied to the patient by the doctor or the medical staff, for various vaccinations, or for medicines in illnesses for which no visit fee is paid. Nor is a co-payment taken from persons who fell ill because of an accident at work, from those ill with an occupational disease, from those who earn up to 2 zł. a day, or from insured women in childbirth.
Extended until 1 February

As is known, Tuesday was the last deadline for employers to re-register their workers and employees. It turned out, however, that with the best will in the world the officials could not possibly deal with all the registrations by yesterday.
In the sick funds long queues ("ogonki") of hundreds of people formed, who had to stand for several hours.
In the end the ministry decided to extend the registration deadline until the 1st of February.

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
Anti-Jewish demonstration in a cinema.
In the Katowice cinema „Capitol“ the Palestine film „Sabra“ was shown, which depicts the life of the new Jewish Yishuv in Palestine. The introductory speech in the film is given by Nahum Sokolow. But in the middle of the speech a tumult broke out and there were shouts: „Down with the Jews!“, „Long live Fascist Poland!“.
Among the large number of Jewish patrons panic broke out and everyone hurried to leave the hall. Police came to the scene and arrested the demonstrators. They belong to the Polish Hitlerite party.
The Warsaw „Unzer Ekspres“ carries the report in large letters under the heading: „Great scandal and rows at a lecture by Nahum Sokolow in Katowice“.
In the report, which the editors probably received from their Zagłębie correspondent, the following is related: „The president of the Zionist Executive, Nahum Sokolow, gave a lecture in Katowice on the situation in ‘Eretz Israel’.
While the president was speaking, several young men burst into the hall and made a row, so that the meeting was broken up“...
In our opinion this report should go into the programme of the „Jewish gang“ under the title „Nisht geshtoygn, nisht gefloygn“ [neither risen nor flown — i.e. a pure fabrication]...

Homely Mustiness and Accumulated Mould

[Article — Sosnowiec, public life.] A hard, a very hard task it is nowadays to write about public affairs. Writing is not hard because times are bad and one cannot ask the other fellow to give[?]; no, it is hard to write only because there is nothing to talk about and no one to talk to — that is what is worse, that is what is more bitter, more vexing and more painful than anything.
Public life has somehow sunk so deep, become so petty and ridiculous, that we could never have imagined it. So much mould has accumulated in the mustiness that one is simply unable to clean it out. Even if one were to set about it intensively — not to mention that one does not want to touch[?] it at all. And not only does one not touch it; on the contrary, it is more comfortable to bathe in this filth; and more painful still is that this very filth and mould are even sanctified, and one does not want to touch them, because they have become a kind of holiness, a holy being[?], and like something sacred one wants to guard them, to spare them. It is simply incomprehensible where people get such notions, such ideas.
That Sosnowiec is backward in the public sphere there is no doubt; everyone knows it everywhere, and the townspeople admit it with a quite light conscience and do not regard it at all as a shortcoming. Public activity, philanthropic work, supporting the poor and the helpless — they consider all this a superfluous thing, a luxury matter, so that whoever feels like it may busy himself with such a toy. That is roughly how the public problem is treated in Sosnowiec. Hence it is no wonder that so much lawlessness and apathy reign in these fields.
But worst of all is that, despite finding oneself at such a low public level, one still wants to play a role and keep up with others.
Thus, for instance, one sees how other towns — of course smaller ones, and in worse conditions than Sosnowiec — organise relief campaigns; so that Sosnowiec should not be backward, it imitates them, but nothing comes of it; it is all done for show only, for publicity, so that meanwhile the bells may ring; and that the whole thing will end in nothing [literally: "come out in the attic"] — that, it is reckoned, nobody will know later; as long as one keeps up with others and imitates all the other towns.
Thus, for instance, people suddenly remembered, out of the blue, that it is winter, and undertook to proclaim a coal campaign; but we know that as long as the winter lasts they will wrangle over the matter, and when the winter is over the coal will not be needed anyway — coal for which, of course, there will be no money anyway.
If only a philanthropic institution took it upon itself, it would still be understandable, since a "Beit Lechem" is called to do so and must be supported in town. But how can one look on while a party comes along and sticks out a foot, so that it too collects money for a coal campaign? How does a party, a narrowly partisan party, come to philanthropic work? It would still not be so embarrassing if it did not amount to disrupting the activity of the institution whose calling is to deal with a coal campaign; and we know what the end will be: the young people will achieve nothing, and the institution will be harmed[?] in its work, which limps badly enough as it is.
Perhaps people will come and say that it does not matter: let one institution give coal and let a party do the same; who cares if those people become philanthropists. That is how one might think superficially. In reality, however, one must not think so, because, first, the citizen must know to whom he gives his donation; he must have responsible people, with definite obligations, who will guarantee the carrying-out of the campaign undertaken; and secondly, such lawlessness must not exist. Once one institution has undertaken a campaign for such-and-such a product, a second institution must not come and do the same, because that only brings disharmony into the activity. Besides, we do not have so many donors that they could favour everyone at every step[?] with the proper donation — let alone when it concerns a party that is not called to this campaign.
It is a crime to come and interfere, and such lawlessness must be reacted to unconditionally, because after all there must be responsibility for public activity, however much it may be made light of.
Possibly this has a political background, for we are, after all, somewhere near kehilla — or, more correctly, rabbinical — elections, and where it comes to fights, to quarrels, to high temperatures, people stop at nothing, so long as they achieve what they wish, what they have calculated and what they have planned.
That is how it is in our town: nothing can be done without uproar and without misunderstandings; whatever is understandable, logically grounded, worked out with common sense, will never be realised here.
How many times have we been reproached that in the anti-Hitlerite field nothing has been done here; one does not know whether there is or is not a committee in town to combat the Hitlerite murders; on the other hand, one knows perfectly well that nothing has been done in this field, and however often one wanted to talk about the matter, no meeting ever came about. People have more important business than talking about such "nonsense". So Mr. Tencer hit on quite an original idea: since the Jews of Sosnowiec are temperamental and — Mr. Tencer knows — where it is a matter of inflaming passions, no Jew will stay at home, he applied to the election committees asking that at the opening of each party's rally he be allowed to speak for just a few minutes, in all, about the duty to combat the Hitlerite deeds. And one must admit that the idea is truly brilliant, for when else, if not this time, could there be an opportunity to speak about the question before this motley crowd?
That is just how it is with us: we can only get the public when passions are inflamed, when it will be "jolly and lively" and things will happen on tables and on benches; otherwise people stay chained at home, or do whatever it may be, as long as they do not fulfil public obligations.
And indeed, whom can public problems, philanthropic help, practical benefit for the community interest? One would have to be stronger than iron to keep sitting through such sessions. On the other hand, when one comes to an election rally, one at least hears something, and it is worth it, because besides learning the very most interesting secrets, one can also behave frankly and freely and do whatever one likes. When one comes to these rallies it is worth something after all: one finds out about everything there, and besides, one is promised a little of both the world to come and this world — so how can one restrain oneself and sit at home?
That is what explains the great success of the rallies and the apathy towards all other public problems.
Can one call this anything other than comedy games? Can one allow serious questions to be made so light of by the whole community? But one can say quite boldly and openly that the community, the masses, the public are little to blame here. First and foremost the leaders are to blame, those who direct public problems; had they had more understanding, more regard, more reverence, more responsibility towards the community, the questions would not have been treated so lightly. The whole trouble is that everyone becomes a ringleader and does what and how he pleases, what and as he sees fit, and nobody reacts to it. Otherwise public problems would not stand at so low a level, and not everyone would allow himself to do whatever he pleases.
Had people understood that public prestige is the pride of a people, they would not have allowed their own dignity to be so debased, because after all society must have its representation, which should take pride in its citizens, and this representation must strive to educate the elements it represents; and, of course, the task of the representation must be to raise the masses to a proper level of awareness and self-respect.
Had there been understanding for this, not only would so much mould not have accumulated in the homely mustiness, but on the contrary, the air would have been cleansed, so that it should be easier to breathe, and the accumulated mould would have been swept out with brooms.
Is anyone among our intelligentsia and responsible citizens interested in our reaching a better level? We do not see it. Unfortunately, at every step we meet more disappointment, more lawlessness, more irresponsibility and degradation.
Dr. Papuri.
The History of the Będzin Kehilla in the Second Half of the 19th Century. According to Archival Records. (3)

[History — the Będzin kehilla; serial, instalment 3.] By Moshe Feinkind. According to archival records.
A very characteristic trial took place in Będzin in 1854—55 against the Będzin "Chevra Kadisha" [burial society]. The trial dragged on for three whole years, and the government authorities, as well as the kehillas in Poland, took an interest in it.
The "Chevra Kadishas" were not permitted to exist in Congress Poland. The first namiestnik [viceroy] had already forbidden them to engage in burying the dead, because they "tear" [extort] from the dead and the living, and no accounts were ever seen [?].
This was the result of the frequent denunciations that kehillas or private persons made to the authorities; above all, the Warsaw kehilla brought it about.
This function was recognised as one of the attributes of the kehilla, and it had to show [?] in the kehilla budget the income it had from burying the dead and from weddings.
But the sums were fictitious. Thus Będzin showed in 1859 23 weddings and 29 dead, in the year 1860 — 21 weddings and 39 dead, in the year 1868 [?] — 26 weddings and 24 dead, with paltry sums of some twenty or thirty roubles of income.
This, however, was only de jure; in fact the anonymous "Chevra Kadisha" never ceased to exist in every town, and against it no struggle and no denunciations to the authorities were of any help.
Among the great number of towns in which a struggle was waged against the "Chevra Kadisha" was also Będzin, which left traces [?] of its wrangling with this society in the archival records that I quoted in my first article.
There a trial with the Chevra Kadisha is described. The story was as follows:
A Jew from Breslau [Wrocław] named Jakob Reichman bathed in August 1853 in the river at Gzichów [?] and unfortunately drowned. The dead man was brought to Będzin to be buried, because Gzichów belonged to the Będzin district.
The "Chevra Kadisha" left the dead man lying until it received, sent by the drowned man's son-in-law, Hensel of Breslau, one hundred and thirty Reichstaler of burial money.
The gabbaim of the "Chevra Kadisha" at that time were R' Hendel Ehrlich, Mark Eide, Markus Fraenkel and Bendit Fischel.
The money from the drowned man's son-in-law Hensel was received by R' Hendel Ehrlich, and the dead man was given his due.
This, however, angered the town, and the whole Chevra Kadisha was denounced to the authorities, and an investigation was conducted against the gabbaim (1854).
Chiefly the authorities turned to R' Hendel Ehrlich, demanding that he deposit the money, which amounted to 117 roubles, in the state treasury.
The Radom governor ordered the Olkusz powiat naczelnik [district chief] to quarter a military "execution" [soldiers billeted as a coercive measure] on R' Hendel Ehrlich at his expense, and that it should remain there until he returned the burial money for the Jew Reichman.
The Będzin burmistrz [mayor], to whom the naczelnik turned about carrying out this order, did not hurry with the execution, wishing thereby to wait for the result of the investigation.
This investigation was conducted by two instances, by the administrative authority and by the judicial authority.
On 28 September 1885 [so printed; read 1855] the trial took place against the above-mentioned gabbaim of the "Chevra Kadisha" in the so-called "simple police court" in Olkusz, and the accused gabbaim were acquitted for lack of evidence.
Things went differently, however, with the investigation by the administrative authority.
The governor would hear of nothing and ordered that R' Hendel Ehrlich be compelled at all costs, by a military execution, to deposit the burial money, giving the Będzin burgomaster a severe reprimand for having neglected until now to carry out the execution, and also making him responsible for the consequences of his hesitating to carry out this order.
In the meantime R' Hendel Ehrlich died, and the burmistrz quartered the military execution on his son, R' Dawid Ehrlich.
R' Dawid Ehrlich then turned with a petition (24 April 1856) to the Olkusz naczelnik to free him from this execution, presenting the following Jewish [?] document, signed by Reichman's son-in-law, Hensel, which reads:
"I, the undersigned, hereby certify that I have willingly come to an agreement with the gvir [notable] Chanoch Hendel Ehrlich of Będzin for all the funeral costs of my late father-in-law Mr. Reichman of Breslau, may God grant him eternal rest, for 130 Rt. [Reichstaler], and I have with good will and glad heart come to an agreement with the gvir Chanoch Hendel Ehrlich of Będzin, as I have no objections whatsoever to it. Będzin, the 2nd of August 1853. Signed in my own hand (in German) Hensel."
The sworn translator (translator) of the Hebrew language at the tribunal of the Radom civil governorate in Kielce, Ziskind Rosenblum, translated the document.
Besides this receipt R' Dawid Ehrlich also submitted a bill which, as he claims, he found in the table drawer after his father's death, in which were written down the expenses [printed "מוצאות"] for the preparation [of the body], the funeral and the burial of the late Reichman.
And having proved with these documents that his father had spent all the money he received from the drowned man's son-in-law, down to the last penny, for the needs of the dead, the naczelnik deferred (printed "prolongirt") the execution for 8 days, until an explanation of the whole matter arrived from the Będzin burmistrz.

In Sosnowiec There Is Nothing New...

[Sosnowiec — kehilla; elections.] Had the kehilla in Sosnowiec, in connection with the present elections to the kehilla council, issued a bulletin reporting on the course of the whole election campaign, then surely the essence, the entire content of that bulletin would have been interwoven with one single thought: "In Sosnowiec there is nothing new"...
At first glance it seems a paradox!
Is there really nothing new in Sosnowiec? Is there really such an idyll in Sosnowiec that before the elections to the kehilla, when in just a few days the fate of this institution must finally be decided, peace, unity and calm should reign, and the quiet "Jewish air" should not be disturbed by a storm, not even by a little breeze?
And yet — there is nothing new!...
Even the 16 lists, which glitter [?] with dozens of candidates' names that are supposed to be the "cream" [lit. "fat"] Sosnowiec possesses; even the hundreds of posters and election appeals that wink down from the walls and peer out of the shop windows; and even the dozens of election meetings, the fairs at which every single party, every little shop, laid out goods for sale, shouting and clamouring: People, buy from me!... Only from me and not from anyone else will you get such precious goods, such good goods for cheap money! — have not managed to bring anything new into Jewish public life.
A folk tale relates:
Once there was a poor Jew, burdened with children, who occupied a small, cramped little room. For years this Jew suffered in that room, until one day his wife says to him: Chaim, how much longer must we torment ourselves in this crowding? Go to your rebbe and ask him for advice.
Chaim obeyed his wife and went to the rebbe.
— Rebbe — he says — give me advice: what does one do about the crowding in my room?
The rebbe pondered a while and said:
— Chaim, you have a goat; take it into your room...
Chaim barely understood the rebbe's answer, but since he was a believer, he followed the rebbe's advice and took his goat into the room.
So the room became more cramped, stuffier. Chaim runs crying "gevald" to the rebbe and shouts: Help, rebbe, it has become even more cramped; rebbe, give me advice so that it will not be so cramped and stuffy.
The rebbe says to him: Chaim, do you have chickens? Take them into your room...
A believer Chaim was, so he followed the rebbe's advice and took the chickens in with him.
So the room became still more cramped, the air stuffier.
He runs with a great outcry to the rebbe: Rebbe, save me, I am perishing of the crowding!
The rebbe pondered, raised his eyebrows, looked at Chaim with compassion and said: Chaim, go home and throw the goat out of the room...
A believer he was, and so he carried out the rebbe's order.
— Rebbe — Chaim again comes running — you have saved my life; the room has become a little roomier, but give me advice so that it becomes a little roomier still, so that the air will not be so stuffy?
— Go, throw out the chickens, and it will surely become roomier for you...
Chaim followed the rebbe's advice, threw out the chickens and ran off joyfully to the rebbe, exclaiming: Dear, holy tzaddik, you have saved my life, now it is a pleasure to be in the room, so big, so roomy...
In this very folk tale lies hidden the whole truth about the hypocritical struggle that will be played out on Sunday in Jewish Sosnowiec; and if we want to be sincere, we must say that these elections will renew nothing, will not change at all the situation of the Jewish kehilla and its management. It will be the same Yente, only veiled differently...
It is very hard for me to speak out this truth. But it would be a great crime to keep silent about it, when already on Sunday the Jews of Sosnowiec will stand before the ballot boxes in order to decide with their votes the victory of this or that list, when already on Sunday every single voter will have the opportunity to decide the fate of the community.
That my words are not, God forbid, empty phrases can be proved by the very fact that almost the entire Jewish population goes to the elections "cemented" — so strong is the "unity" — for after all, only 16 lists in all have been put forward... Alas and alack for the future kehilla, which will be led by such a hodgepodge, in which every single clique will have only its own interests in mind.
It looks like an utter impossibility that, with such a composition of forces, with such fragmentation of Jewish society, anything positive could be created.
One need not be a pessimist [lit. "black-seer"] to venture already today the guess that the future kehilla council will produce from among itself an administration that will be utterly incapable of work and will achieve for Jewish society exactly as much as the one until now.
The second point, the one that strikes the eye most, is the individual, materialistic interest of a large part of the lists, which arose not because they have the good of the community in mind, but because they must defend the private pocket interests of individuals...
It is truly remarkable that not a single list, not even the boldest, has clearly underlined this very point in its programme.
Those who should have done it first and foremost are the ones who have many times had the courage to stand up openly against the demoralisation of Jewish society — and yet they have not done so...
— In Sosnowiec there is nothing new...
Hypocrisy will go on reigning, the lie will go on raging, and like a terrible storm it will completely overturn the ruins left behind by the outgoing kehilla administration. The future kehilla leadership, which will be born of such "love", will certainly not erect any new buildings.
It truly becomes gloomy at heart; a sad melancholy envelops one, a kind of invisible resignation, when we reflect on the terrible state of Jewish public life, on its lawlessness and demoralisation, to which, it seems, there will never be an end. And yet we, resigned as we are, must not fold our hands, must not poison our hearts with feelings of despair, but must look at life with open eyes — at hard life — driving away all those who want to block out the light with their shadows, the very light that makes our life finer, more glorious...
And that is precisely why we must go to the elections. Each one of us must strive with our "vote" to drive away the shadows that lie in wait for our freedom.
For whom to vote?
— I do not want to point it out, but let everyone, when he casts his vote, reflect for a while whether his vote helps the building up of the Jewish kehilla. [Not only the] elected bear afterwards the responsibility for the bungled management, but every single voter who, with his vote in the ballot box in Sosnowiec, contributes to strengthening its management — or, on the contrary, helps towards its destruction, its ruin?
For not the representatives, the elect, but he alone is the actual subject [printed "object"] who bears the responsibility for the activity of his representatives.
For the time being there is nothing new in Sosnowiec...
But something new can happen, if you, voters, understand the importance of the moment and do what your clear conscience dictates to you and what the good of the community commands you.
On Sunday the voter has the floor — he must strive to make sure that in Sosnowiec something new does happen after all...
Tanai.
A Ridiculous Kehilla Philosophy

Farewell to me, my dearest, beloved Sosnowiec kehilla!
Like a white, white legend of happiness, like a wondrously beautiful magic dream, like a sweet, sweet memory of love, like the mysterious stillness of night on the mountain peaks, like the whiteness of snow facing the moon, like the mournful sadness of a heroic song, like the echo of white, white echoes —
so abyss-deep, oppressively melancholy, an incomprehensible riddle are you in your tragi-comedy and comi-tragedy...
* *
When I happen into your hall, something like a strange stench of vanity pierces the deepest depths of my soul... My imagination runs wild; before my eyes there surface from the benches, tables and walls congealed, trinket-like, "tal-u-matar-ish" little thoughts of "flabby little brains" — they wriggle [?], clown-like, suddenly turning into a great Mephistophelean licker [?]...
In my soul a kind of feeling of pain stirs [?]. Outside, Time giggles and tells me:
In the days of Creation, at twilight, when the tail of Abraham our father's ram, the mouth of Balaam's ass and the demons were created, the angel in charge of ridiculousness gave a yawn, and —
the Sosnowiec kehilla was created...
* *
Two thousand years tormented, consumed, seventy-seven dark generations stuffed with troubles, fattened with evil decrees, and —
no joy at all!
Narrow-heartedness, trivial begging for honours, clumsy-idiotic bench politics, needless envy and hatred, disgusting, loathsome, rusty polemics, sickening, nauseating squabbling — rule our world.
In our kehilla, may its glory be exalted, the specifically Jewish Don-Quixotism is mirrored in all its tragi-comedy. Bearded, side-locked, skull-capped and girdled comedians of piety clown about, supposedly hauling the kehilla windmills up into the heavenly heights; while on the other hand [?] the hyper-Europeanised, ultra-secular, up-to-date modernised kehilla Don Quixotes crank the windmills enthusiastically, self-sacrificingly, arrogantly, in order to hurl them down into the earthly, everyday turmoil and hullabaloo —
it flashes, it thunders, ownerless winds play pranks...
* *
Fare thee well, my dearest Sosnowiec kehilla!
Mournfully comic, painfully beautiful, splendidly melancholy, your yawning symphony echoes into the well of the future...
A. Ch. Szifer.
Letters from Home

B"H, Friday, eve of the holy Sabbath, of the portion "and there was darkness" [Bo]...
My friend R' Shlomo, may his light shine.
Your letter, in which you pour out your bitter heart over the difficult economic situation in your country, really cheered me up, and every moment I give praise to the Almighty that I did not let myself be influenced by your optimistic promises, just so I should find myself in your place. Yes, a fine face I would have now: I would have had to groan [?] together with you and philosophise about world morality, about the Hitlerite regime that is poisoning the air in Europe, about the decline of civilisation and similar "nonsense", which are a matter for idlers, good-for-nothings and pessimists. Here with us in Zagłębie one neither knows nor talks of such matters. An exception in this field is — Sosnowiec. This very town, which possesses the head offices of the sick fund, the telephone company, the chamber of commerce and so on and on — has taken into its domain the whole arsenal of ammunition and explosives, which go off from time to time and leave bad smells behind for several years..
As you know, R' Shlomo, Jewish Sosnowiec is dancing for the second time the
— election dance to the kehilla.
At a time when in the neighbouring kehillot normal activity goes on — for instance, Będzin is thinking of finishing Noah's ark, pardon, the historic mikveh building, and Dąbrowa is examining the rabbinical candidates as to whether they master the Polish language — Jewish Sosnowiec is still at Genesis, at the portion of the "first" kehilla elections.
And there is something else you should know, R' Shlomo: the Sosnowiec kehilla elections differ from all elections to the kehillot in Poland. Everywhere, in all the Jewish dispersions, where kehilla elections take place, it means that one goes to elect the kehilla representation, the emissaries of the public, those who must build up the kehilla system, etc., etc.
Different is the situation in Sosnowiec, in the town where form and content go separate ways, as the saying goes: "It's not the Haggadah they mean, but the knaidlach"...
Here speakers take the platform, loudly make "kiddush", even ask in the chant the four questions of the four sons, but the main thing, the aim is
— the Shulchan Aruch... the rabbinical chair...
As I already wrote to you, no fewer than sixteen "troupes", home-grown "amateur forces", are taking part in the election performance that takes place this coming Sunday...
Among the 16 lists there are 5 in which the leading role is played by rabbis, the candidates for the rabbinical seat in Sosnowiec. There is one more important factor, namely living numbers, with which acrobatic stunts are performed.
The "living numbers", which by the way are a novelty in the electoral field, have a very important significance for the development and fertility of the Jewish people...
I believe this means to victory will also become popular throughout Europe and especially in the United States, for in America, which surpasses Europe with its election advertising, they have not yet hit upon the bright idea that during the presidential elections one should, among other merits, not forget to mention
— how many children the candidate has...
And one more merit must be credited to Jewish Sosnowiec. We know that in elections the merits of the candidates standing are presented at election meetings; each group strives to show off its candidates with honour and glory. With us in Sosnowiec, however, it is different: here one does not talk about future work, only about what has already been... and what has been — I do not want to write to you, for I am afraid you would lose your respect for the town in which you lived half your years...
The Sosnowiec election campaign ought — in my opinion — to be immortalised in a sound film entitled "Woe to the ears that hear this"...
There are, however, lists that are not harnessed to the rabbinical wagon and are after only one thing — "to save Judaism"...
To tell the truth, we believe with perfect faith that none of the lists has any ulterior motives; rather their entire aim is
— to erase [so printed; probably for "to strengthen"] the religion... I underline the words "to erase [strengthen]", to strengthen, because in the religious field the "Torah-loyal" have created a great deal: for instance, a mikveh building was built according to the latest technique and in perfect ritual purity; and now, what about the Talmud Torah, which is one of the model institutions, and the like...
Yes, R' Shlomo, about the holy lists I have a lot to write, but here I receive an invitation to speak at a meeting, so I must cut the letter short, because I have to learn by heart a lexicon of words and curses of the people of the underworld..
And so have a good Sabbath, wishes you
Ben Amotz.
The main thing I forgot! I can write you good news — the Jews of Dąbrowa are learning to speak Polish out of envy... It comes from the fact that one of the rabbinical candidates also gave a fine exposé in Polish.. But about that — another time at length.
The above.
Can Anything Still Be Done?

[Article — the economic situation of Polish Jewry; the Labour Fund.]
Can anything still be done for the Jews in Poland?
At first glance one might think that there is nothing left to do.
For if there are hundreds of thousands of unemployed Poles in the country, how can we hope that anyone will look for work specially for Jews? Even without antisemitism the rule holds that one's own shirt is closer to the body!
And if Polish compulsory education every year takes into its arms hundreds of thousands of new peasant and middle-class children, and every year thousands of freshly „greased" intellectuals come out, how is it possible that any new public post at all should remain open for Jews?
And what does it help that we will repeat early and late that „national" does not necessarily mean Polish-Catholic, but simply Polish-civic, so long as life takes no account of any theories, but only of natural egoism, and everyone wants first of all to provide for his nearest!...
And if so, then perhaps those are indeed right who let their hands drop in despair at local politics and do not want to let themselves be drawn into such hopes, which will surely mislead!
It turns out that something can still be done — not much, but something nonetheless.
There exists in Poland a Jewish economic committee which has turned to the directorate of the State Labour Fund [Fundusz Pracy] with a characteristic memorandum on help for the impoverished Jewish population, and there, in the memorandum, 5 main points are given on how one could help the Jews.
Anyone in his own town can see with the naked eye what large works are being carried out by the Labour Fund (so a painted signboard announces) — and you look there in vain for a Jewish worker.
While here in Będzin the elected magistrate (municipal board) was functioning, the Jewish board members („ławnicy") saw to it that Jews should get their proper share of public works; now, under the rule of the commissioner, the Jewish eye has been taken away and Jewish workers are being passed over.
The memorandum demands in its first point that the Labour Fund issue a circular to all towns that a share of the work be allotted to Jews as well.
And we ask: how has the criminal exclusion of the Jewish unemployed been permitted until now? It is simply unheard of!
With this the matter is not yet exhausted. The memorandum has a whole series of further means by which Jews could be helped.
Here, for example, subsidising investment works of Jewish kehillas. A few words about that. Since ancient times Jews have built institutions. First of all houses of prayer, mikvehs, hospitals and the like, and in every larger town there are dozens of buildings belonging to the Jewish kehilla. Lately, however, the impetus for building has stopped, and above all Jewish temperament cools when it comes to building modern institutions, and precisely those whose necessity nobody can deny, such as, for example, a Yiddish or Hebrew school, a Yiddish theatre, a people's house — all those premises whose rent squeezes the marrow out of our bones.
The Jewish kehillas would certainly take such burdens upon themselves if the sums were lent and if part of them were borne by a government institution such as the „Labour Fund"; but one has to demand it energetically.
And further there follows a whole series of means, precisely detailed, by which many thousands of Jewish families could make a living.
And finally the productivisation of Jews, the placing of Jewish masses in various kinds of work, especially in gardening, orcharding, all sorts of plantations and the like. For this an allocation of 6 million is required, and the memorandum asks that it be entrusted to the „CEKABE" with its 750 branches throughout Poland.
The „CEKABE" — that is the organisation of the interest-free loan funds, at whose head stand the banker Rafał Szereszowski, Prof. Schorr, Dir. Giterman and others.
Whether this organisation is fit to direct such a grandiose work and to dispose of such a huge sum for the people's needs — we cannot know. Possibly, on coming closer to realising the programme, a reorganisation with broad democratic elections would be necessary.
Above all, the „ORT" activists ought to have been drawn in here, since the productivisation of Jews lies closest to their hearts.
What is important, however, is that by no means all possibilities of doing something for the Jews in Poland have dried up yet; that we can be helped a great deal by the government machine itself, if only it functions justly, with an honest, equal measure towards all citizens; and that a great deal more we Jews can still accomplish ourselves with our energy and professional knowledge.
One must not lose one's head, must not let one's hands drop, must not say that here the sky has completely come down to earth.
P. K.
Before the Decisive Moment

[Sosnowiec — kehilla and elections; opinion piece.]
In my previous article about the kehilla elections I put forward the supposition that what is at stake is mainly "rabbinate elections". And I believed that the gentlemen candidates for parnassim [kehilla councillors] would think better of it at the last moment and come out publicly with programmes and take upon themselves obligations to bring order into the kehilla.
Unfortunately this has not happened; on the contrary, the agitation at the mass meetings shows clearly that the only problem with which the candidates for parnassim are charged by their parties is — to entrench and seize the kehilla for the sake and on behalf of the rabbis who wish to be candidates in the future for the rabbinical seat in Sosnowiec.
On most of the posters that call the mass meetings, the speakers announced are — precisely those rabbis who are personally interested in the outcome of the elections in their own favour.
With the greatest respect that I have for the shtreimel in general, I wish to express the opinion of a large part of the kehilla taxpayers ("etat"-payers): this is not the way; this is not the right path on which rabbis should walk. I belong to the old generation, to whom the ways by which rabbis used to win the sympathy of the community are not unfamiliar.
The rabbi's place is in the beit midrash, and the weapon with which the rabbi influences his listeners is the power of the holy Torah.
The rabbi must stand above all parties, above programmes; and if the rabbi lets himself be drawn into the net of party disputes and lets himself be influenced by party ringleaders who do not choose their means to fight their opponents — then, let us say it openly, they profane the sacred, and then we must say — "Sages, be careful with your words."
Do not overdo it, for you should know that the situation of the kehilla is far from rosy [?]: apart from debts up to the neck which the kehilla cannot pay, there are further worries about where to find the means to cover next year's budget as well.
Perhaps you do not know that the kehilla owes the Jewish hospital over 20,000 zł. Because the hospital is neglected and run down, the women gabbaim "buy themselves mitzvot" [i.e. earn merit] and go begging from house to house for bedding and linen, and so far there is nowhere to get it from. Perhaps you do not know that the kehilla owes the old-age home about 7000 zł., and if this is not covered the old-age home will have to be closed and the old people will be left homeless wanderers.
Perhaps you do not know that the religious functionaries are owed over 15,000 zł., and there is nowhere to get it from, because the till is empty.
Perhaps you do not know that the subsidies for the education of poor children are not being paid out, and it seems to me that the kehilla also owes the orphanage a certain sum, and that too is not being paid.
If you perhaps say that the kehilla has money owing from the taxpayers — you are mistaken, for most of the money cannot be collected, because, as I already mentioned in my previous article, a large part of the taxpayers have become impoverished, and those who are still able to pay the tax must also be spared.
In such a catastrophic situation nobody has any right to place on the relatively small number of members still greater burdens than until now, and whoever dares to do so will bear the responsibility on his conscience.
Therefore we say: enough strife! Order must be created, and those who brought about today's situation and those who wish to continue the work of chaos should take their hands off the kehilla.
Dov Tenzer.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bo)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bo
The Portion
—o—
a) "Go now, ye that are men, and serve the Lord" (Ex. 10:11)
Moses told Pharaoh that the Jews wanted to go outside Egypt to hold a congregational prayer to God. Pharaoh asked him: "Who are they that shall go?" After all, only men need go to pray... But Moses answered him: "With our sons and with our daughters" — even our daughters want to come along. Then Pharaoh put on a pious face: "Go now, ye that are men" — if it is to pray, let only the men go. "For that is what ye desire" — you mean only the praying, as you say; and do you really believe that when you have the wives and children with you, you will be able to pray?...
Sefer ha-Berit [?] (Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Kalischer).
•
The Gemara (Hagigah 3) says: "Why do the little ones come? To give a good reward to those who bring them." Tosafot remarks on this: from here it follows that one must bring the children along to the synagogue for prayer...
•
The "Holy Jew" once came as a guest to the Maggid in Kozienice. The "Jew" was the first to introduce late and quick praying, as the Kotsk Hasidim later did... The Kozienice Hasidim grumbled: how does the "Jew" stand and pray before God like that? Until it was told to the Maggid. The Maggid said to the "Jew" and to the Hasidim around him:
— "This thy stature is like to a palm tree [tamar]" — your standing before God is like Tamar... The deed of Tamar, had another woman done it, would have been counted as impudence. But Tamar meant it for the sake of Heaven. So too the "Jew" truly means it for the sake of Heaven with his late and quick praying; but when the Hasidim imitate him — they become like another woman who imitates Tamar...
"Hitorerut ha-Tefillah".
—o—
b) "We will go with our young and with our old" (ibid., 9)
Moses told Pharaoh that even "with our old we will go" — even the elders want to leave Egypt, not only the young are rebelling. It is already so bitter in Egypt that even the old want to get out...
Imrei Noam.
—o—
c) "For in the day thou seest my face thou shalt die" (ibid., 28)
The Targum Jonathan says on this:
"For on the day that you see my face my anger will grow strong against you, and I will hand you over into the hands of those men who were seeking your life to take it."
The meaning of the words is: Pharaoh did not threaten Moses that he, Pharaoh, would kill him — he had already seen enough how brave and bold Moses is and pays him no heed. And if he now wanted to frighten Moses, he could frighten him only by saying he would hand him over into the hands of Dathan and Abiram, into the hands of the little Jews — and they can surely finish off a Moses better than he, Pharaoh, himself...
Sefer Yenahenu.
—o—
d) "Speak now in the ears of the people, and let them ask... jewels of silver and jewels of gold" (11:2)
"So that that righteous man should not say: 'And they shall serve them and they shall afflict them' He fulfilled for them, but 'afterwards they shall come out with great substance' He did not fulfil for them." Rashi.
The Midrash (Bereshit Rabbah 44) says that God let Abraham choose for his children: either Gehenna or exile. Abraham chose exile. Therefore God promised him that the Jews would come out of exile with great substance.
That is what Rashi says: so that that righteous man should not say — that Abraham should not claim — "and they shall serve them and afflict them" He fulfilled: what I, Abraham, chose — exile — God hurried to fulfil... but what He, the Holy One blessed be He, promised — great substance — that He did not hurry at all to fulfil...
Eser Tzahtzahot (by the Rebbe of Sanz [?]).
•
"Speak now in the ears of the people" — by "the people" is meant the common folk, the poor masses. To the rich the Egyptians quickly lent jewels of silver and gold — no difficulty there, they were given credit. The poor were only afraid to come [?] and borrow, for who would give them credit?
Therefore God said: "Speak now in the ears of the people" — let them, the poor, borrow, so that that righteous man should not say "and they shall serve them and afflict them" was fulfilled — for in Egypt it was mainly they, the poor, who were made to work, since the rich had probably bought themselves out with money... and now, when it comes to the reward, to the great substance, again the rich would get the substance, because it is to them that things would be lent, and the poor, who suffered most of all, would not be rewarded at all... Therefore "speak now in the ears of the people"...
Yalkut ha-Derush.
—o—
e) "What mean ye by this service?" (12:26)
The author of the Haggadah counts this question as the question of the wicked son, whereas the wise son asks: "What mean the testimonies, and the statutes, and the ordinances, which the Lord our God hath commanded you?"
The question arises: what is the great difference between the question of the wicked and the question of the wise?
But the wise son will take part in the Passover offering, and while eating he asks: "What mean the testimonies, etc.?" — fair enough, he wants to know the reason for the commandment. Whereas the wicked son asks: "What mean ye by this service?" — he does not let the Passover be made in the first place. Even before the Passover has been done, he is already asking: "What mean ye by this service?" ("The service" shows that he speaks during the work, while the Passover is being made.)
Birkat ha-Shor.
—o—
f) "Ye shall say: It is the sacrifice of the Lord's passover" (ibid., 26 [sic; should be 27])
Not "ye shall say unto him" — to him, the wicked one, you should not answer at all. Just speak out into the world, so that he will hear, for with a Jewish apikoros one must not argue...
Be'er Yitzhak.
•
R. Gershon Henoch of Radzyń used to say:
"Know what to answer the apikoros" — why does the Tanna not state outright what to answer, but merely hints with "know"? — The Tanna means the second verse of the Song of Songs... for with logical answers you will not get the better of him, the spiteful apostate...
—o—
g) "And they let them have what they asked" (ibid., 36)
"Against the will of Israel, because of the burden" (Berakhot 9).
Money is a burden, and just as one who carries a burden cannot walk up a mountain, so too one who has money... "Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord — he that hath clean hands"... He who does not have clean hands can have no ascent...
Sefer Bat Rabbim.

The Social Restructuring of the German Jews in Eretz Israel

[Eretz Israel — immigration from Germany; Keren Hayesod.] (From our special Eretz Israel correspondent.)

In the past the following anecdote used to go around in Germany: what does every Jew's fortune consist of? And people would answer: every Jew's fortune is — a doctorate. The German Jews used to tell this joke with a certain pride, because it showed how far the majority of German Jewry had climbed up the social ladder. For a family that had any means whatsoever — and even if it had to save for it from its own mouth — it was a matter of course. — that the sons, and often the daughters, had to study at university. A young man who did not have the title of doctor had no great chances in the better circles.

This surplus of people with an academic education in German Jewry has now taken bitter revenge, because it is precisely the free professions that have now been completely closed to the German Jews. They may no longer work as doctors or lawyers; they may not be officials or editors. Many thousands have simply been thrown out of these professions, and the Jewish student youth no longer has any prospect of passing an examination in Germany and of learning the profession to which it is inclined. And therefore one need not wonder that the German emigration to Eretz Israel yields such a high percentage of people in the free professions, such as doctors, lawyers, lecturers (Dozenten), writers, whose means of livelihood in Germany have been completely cut off and who in Eretz Israel must begin anew in order to build themselves a new life.

But this whole [?] stream of people in the free professions Jewish Eretz Israel cannot by far absorb. A few doctors can still find a modest practice — those who have a rare specialty, or when they are very famous — and if immigration continues on a large scale, one or another may still have a certain hope. But with a single ship that brings hundreds of new immigrants, no fewer than 20 doctors arrive in the country. How will they be able to hope to earn their bread with their profession so far? And it is even worse with the lawyers. They have to pass a very difficult examination here before they are allowed to practise in a legal system that is completely foreign to them, and on top of that [?] three new languages, which are no less foreign to them. Most of them simply cannot hold out financially, not to mention the difficulties of studying. This same problem surfaces among the women too. What, for example, can a woman art historian begin to do in Eretz Israel with all her scholarly knowledge? Or, for instance [?], that young lady who went to the Eretz Israel government and asked to be employed in her profession so far — as a welfare worker [?] in a prison: how astonished she was when she learned that no such institution exists in the country at all.

Therefore the slogan among almost 90 percent of the German Jews now coming to Eretz Israel is: r e s t r u c t u r i n g. To throw away the former professions, which are completely useless here, and to go over to others, which the country demands. There is no help for it; one must set the title of doctor aside and instead become a "chaver" — a Jewish worker. Back to the soil, back to manual labour! That is the only possibility of integrating the German Jew into the upbuilding of Eretz Israel.

The Keren Hayesod, the economic centre of this upbuilding, devotes special attention to the restructuring problem — the re-stratification of the Jews — because this is no easy matter, neither from the practical point of view nor from the psychological one. For the German Jews, social restructuring is for the time being still bound up with the feeling of "proletarianization", a concept that cannot exist in a country like Eretz Israel, where no one is held in such high esteem as the person who does productive work.

Parting from the old profession is much harder for the German intellectual than for the Jew from Eastern Europe, because on the one hand the consciousness of social rank was developed in him in Germany. On the other hand, however, his profession will no longer be a means of earning his bread; besides, these academics are for the most part no longer at the age of first blossoming youth. Most of them are people in their forties, for whom physical labour, at least at first, involves certain difficulties.

Despite all this, the restructuring succeeds extraordinarily well with those who hasten to adapt themselves to the new conditions without superfluous preparations. The new immigration has created a strong boom in the building trade in Eretz Israel, which comes to the aid of the social restructuring, because when there is a shortage of workers even the inexperienced find employment more quickly in unskilled labour. Thus [?] even a former lawyer quickly learns how to fill sacks with cement or stack bricks in rows. And a doctor who very often deftly wielded the surgical knife learns how to use a plane or the saw properly. Among the new candidates in the building trades there are, of course, also some for whom, so to speak, all the work is wasted; but opposite them stands the large number of those who overcome the first difficulties thanks to their strong will and natural aptitude, and after a certain time they find their place in the upbuilding of the country as full-fledged workers.

The same experience that was gained in the building trade has also proved good in paving streets. In every Jewish colony, on all the thoroughfares of Eretz Israel, one sees strong building gangs, among whom it is very easy to recognize the "greenhorns" from Germany. They quickly learn the methods that make the work easier. Their skin gets as sunburnt by the sun's rays as that of their "native-born" comrades, and very soon they understand that tennis shoes and flannel trousers are not the proper work clothes. If one talks with them, it turns out that one not only hears various German dialects, but one also soon learns that almost every one of these freshly baked street pavers [?] was formerly an intellectual: a doctor, a lawyer, a bank director, etc. But the main thing: they feel good in their new occupation, which gives them a living and is also, as they feel it, important for the upbuilding of the country.

What is now taking place in Eretz Israel — the social restructuring of an entire population stratum, from intellectual to physical work — has no precedent in the world. If this restructuring really succeeds on a large scale, it would be a new proof of the tenacity of life and the courage to live of the Jews, who do not accept great misfortunes fatalistically but draw from them the necessary consequences and quickly adapt themselves to the new forms of life.

And yet this "leap into life" would have had no success whatsoever were it not for the Keren Hayesod, the Jewish reconstruction fund, which laid in Eretz Israel the foundation for everything now being created here. For in the end private initiative, too, is based [?] on the activity of the Keren Hayesod. And although [?] the new immigrant must himself bring with him what is most important for the restructuring — the conviction of how necessary such a restructuring is, and the moral courage to carry it through — it is to the Keren Hayesod that one owes the fact that the conviction brings results and the courage is not put to shame.

Y. K.
Summaries (valid even after New Year) — a little feuilleton

[Feuilleton — the year 1933 in review.] (Valid even after New Year)
(A little feuilleton).

Economics.
I found a notebook in which a Jew had recorded his budget for the past year, and I pass it on here word for word.
"In January 1933 I had fifty-eight protested bills of exchange and 94 protested cheques.
In February I was thrown out of my flat, and I knocked about in the street with my household and my household goods [?] for several days on end, until a neighbour took pity on me.
In March I lost two thousand złoty of other people's money and had to uproot myself from my permanent residence to a strange place.
In April one of my good friends lent me an interest-free loan (gemilut chesed)!
In May my wife's family came to stay with me for a couple of weeks and ate away a... couple of months [?].
In June... in July... in August...
In September I got my head so muddled that the whole time I went about with the peak of my cap at the back.
After that the 'urushaner' [?; apparently the bailiff] sold off my belongings.
In short, I had a fine and good year."

Politics.
In world politics, to tell the truth, I took very little interest. On the other hand, I had my own politics.
Every morning I had to 'make politics' with my wife, who demanded that I give her money. In the morning money, in the daytime — money, towards evening — money, and even at night — money..
There was even a moment when I thought of resigning.
I wanted to resign from my post of finance minister in my house, but since even real ministers have no intention of handing in their resignation, although they haven't a grosz to their soul, I didn't resign either.
On the whole I had, one may say, just as political a year as all other politicians.
Rebus.
The Jewish Queen of Yemen (3)

[Serialized historical tale — Yemen; Pnina with the Arab sheikh; installment 3.]
Sh. Berg.

All alone in God's world, between sky and sand, Pnina was left. Wherever her eyes carried her, she walked, hour after hour. And yet her luck was not entirely dark. She came to an oasis. She lifted her eyes to heaven in thanks — here she would see people again. She would come to a settlement; and she sat down under a tree to rest. She had not sat long under the tree when she heard little bells ringing far off [?]. She followed the sound and came to a well.
By the well sat a band of Arabs with camels. From afar she saw a large village full of tents. And sad as she was after all her misfortunes, she rejoiced. She was saved.
"Who are you, where do you come from?" the Arabs asked her in wonder, seeing a strange girl all alone, covered in dust.
She was weak and tired, she could hardly speak; the Arabs saw how weak she was and told her not to speak at all, but first to eat and refresh her heart.
"Whoever you are and whatever you may be, you are hungry [?] — here is bread for you," an elderly Arab said to her, handing her a piece of barley bread with butter. "You will tell your story later."
It was poor bread. Once, at her father and mother's, she would not have put such bread in her mouth; now it was very tasty and sweet as sugar. After eating and a good drink of fresh water, when she felt stronger, she told her sad story. They had great pity on her and advised her to go to the sheikh of the tribe, their prince, and tell him everything.
"The sheikh is good-hearted and hospitable," they told her. "He will protect you from all evil; a girl, an orphan, needs a protector."
She thanked them warmly, and the good Arab who had given her bread led her to the sheikh's tent. First there came out a dark, graceful girl of Pnina's age, who looked her over with curiosity. Then two handsome youths came out with the sheikh — a man of about fifty, with a long black beard down to his belt and an honest, wise and kindly face.
"Come into my tent, young wanderer," the sheikh invited her warmly. "You will quench your thirst and gather strength in the shade of my house."
She went into the tent. The girl handed her a glass of sour cream (smetana), and the sheikh told her to drink first and then tell what had happened to her. She told him everything, and the tears choked her; but when she saw tears in the sheikh's daughter's eyes, she took it as a sign that she would find shelter here. They were good people. The sheikh was deeply moved by her troubles; he comforted and calmed her, saying that their mother Hagar had also wandered in the desert, but God had taken pity on her and sent her an angel to help. He ordered her to be taken into the women's tent to rest. She lay down and slept peacefully until one o'clock [?].
When she awoke, a good meal was already ready. They all ate, and after the meal the sheikh told Pnina that in Yemen there is a Jewish king, Yusuf Dhu Nuwas [printed "De Niuas"] is his name; they call him "Dhu Nuwas" [printed "De Nias" (?); "he of the locks"] because he has great, beautiful locks. He is a rare war hero, and he forces everyone to accept his faith.
"Yusuf sent me an order too, that I and my tribe should convert to Judaism," the sheikh went on telling her, "but we will not obey him. Free men are we; we will submit to no one. We answered him that we did not want to. Well, he sent us a chest of pictures of various weapons and wrote that with these weapons he would make us his subjects; so we sent him a chest of sand and wrote that the sand of the desert would be our protection. And he did indeed march against us with a great army," the sheikh went on, "but when he entered the desert a great storm came, such as sweeps you off the road [?], and the greater part of his army was buried alive under the sand. In remorse King Yusuf returned to his land. Now we are sure he will leave us in peace.
"And now, Jewish child, if you wish you can stay in my house, and if not you can go to Yemen, where one of your brethren is king," the sheikh said to her.
And before Pnina had time to answer, the sheikh's little daughter ran up to her, hugged and kissed her, and begged her to stay with them. She also begged her father to ask Pnina to stay. So she agreed and stayed. She helped the women with the housework, and since she was educated and could play and sing, she taught the sheikh's daughter to write and read, to sing and play. She told her the history of the Jews, and the girl liked it so much that she said she wanted to become a Jewess. Tsarida — that was the name of the sheikh's daughter — grew very fond of Pnina and became attached to her as to a sister of her own flesh and blood.
So some three months passed, quiet and peaceful. One night, when everyone was asleep, they were woken by terrible cries:
"Allah! Allah! Allah!" (God!)
Terrified, they leapt up from their beds and saw a gruesome sight. The whole village stood in flames. Soldiers were running with bare swords and torches in their hands. A terrible cry rose from the fleeing men and wailing women, mixed with the weeping of frightened children and the bellowing of camels. Above it all rose the war cries of the enemy, the invader, and the earth shook.
(To be continued.)
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: On the Eve of a Strike by the Kehilla Employees

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Kehilla.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 3 / 3 Shevat 5694 — piątek 19 stycznia 1934 [Friday, 19 January 1934].)
Będzin
On the eve of a strike by the kehilla employees.
The presidium of the kehilla board has resolved to change the system of paying the salaries („pensje“) of the kehilla employees.
The change consists in the following: the salaries will be paid every month in full, the whole 100 per cent, but the debts which the community („gmina“) owes the employees will be covered in instalments; for example, in the new budget a sum amounting to 20 per cent of the debts is provisionally set aside.
The new „order“, which was already introduced on the 15th of this month, has raised a storm among the employees. The lower employees accepted the few złoty — after all, they have nothing to lose either way; the rabbinate, the shochtim (ritual slaughterers) and the office („biuro“) employees, on the other hand, refused to accept the salaries until they have a full guarantee for the debts owed them by the kehilla.
The first to go out into the fight were the shochtim, who turned to the presidium with an ultimatum: if the resolution is not withdrawn by Wednesday at 11 o'clock in the morning, they will go on strike.
And at the appointed hour a delegation of the shochtim came to the community office and was received by the president, Mr. Rubinlicht.
Mr. Rubinlicht explained to the shochtim that the resolution on the system had been adopted in order to bring order into the kehilla's finances; as regards the security of the debts, every employee will receive an official confirmation of the sum due to him from the community. „If you do not agree to this,“ Mr. Rubinlicht declared, „you have the choice to do as you please.“
The answer, as it turns out, did not satisfy the shochtim, and up to the 15th of this month they have refused to accept the salaries.
The office employees, too, have sent the board a letter in which they ask that the resolution be withdrawn, so that they should not be forced to take stern steps.
The deadline for withdrawing it is Sunday at 11 o'clock in the morning.

„When Hitler Comes, He'll Sort Things Out“ — Says a Secret Agent to a Jewish Passenger

[Będzin — Antisemitism.]
Travelling from Łódź to Będzin, Mr. Ber Rozenblum of Będzin was accosted in the railway carriage by a Christian who was slightly tipsy. In the course of the exchange of words the Christian let drop: „When Hitler comes here, he'll sort things out („porządek“) with the Zhids („żydy“, a Polish slur)“.
Mr. Rozenblum did not let the Christian out of his sight any more, and already at the next station called the police, who drew up a report against this follower of Hitler.

On Tuesday the furniture of the Szwinkelsztajn family was sold at auction for a tax debt. As an illustration it is enough to note that a wardrobe was sold for... 4 zł.
Even the policeman who was present could not tolerate this 'slaughter', and although the sold items were already on the cart, the policeman went to a nearby telephone and asked the commissioner by telephone what he should do in such a case.
The commissioner, on receiving the telephone report, ordered that the sold items be taken back out of the auction-goers' hands.

On Kołłątaja Street the wife of a poor Jewish shoemaker poisoned herself. Thanks to quick rescue her life was saved.
On the eve of the kehilla elections

As is known, next Sunday kehilla elections will take place in our town. In connection with this, countless election meetings took place in the course of the past week, and the agitation is going at full steam.
The election fever, which began on Sunday, gave material to the Polish press, which had a story to tell that the Jews in Sosnowiec hold stormy election meetings.
The 'storm' came from the election meeting in the 'Zagłębie' cinema, which was organised by Rabbi Englard's list. Not relying on their own forces, the organisers asked the police for protection, which, by the way, carried out its duties properly.
In front of the hall where the meeting took place one had to be a 'walker' — standing still was not allowed. Thanks to that everything passed off in peace, and to the 'blessings' of Rabbi [printed: H"B] Englard, who in person delivered a speech at the meeting, his 'holy flock' answered:
— Amen, amen...
On his way home Rabbi Englard also had the proper guard: in front — police, then several faithful adjutants, and behind — mounted police.
The guard aroused enormous interest, as a result of which the surrounding streets were black with people.
There were also election meetings at which the rival lists were 'honoured' with 'reverent' expressions.
In the election posters, which are found in almost every shop window, there are promised: the honour of the Torah, good management, this world and the world to come...

In the end he agreed to Wolf...

A young man comes into the gmina [municipal registry], evidently no great intellectual. He wants to enter a little boy in the books.
— What name are you giving him? — the official asks.
— Witold.
— What? Witold is not Jewish, and we cannot register it like that in the books.
— I'll go and complain to the authorities.
— We can register Wolf.
— No, I don't want that.
— It doesn't suit you? The grandmother is called Malkale, the great-grandmother was well known under the name Sheyne-Yakhne, — a bystander chimes in.
The father of the newborn child turns red and in the end agrees to Wolf — a name after the grandfather Wolfke.

At the Sosnowiec Jewish hospital a ward has been opened for sick children aged from infants up to 14 years old.
The ward will be run under the direction of Dr. Liberman.

Jews Talk — Gentiles Act

[Zagłębie — the boycott of German goods.] A characteristic curiosity occurred these days in the local merchant world, which illustrates most strikingly how Jews clamour and make noise and get by with... talk. Whereas gentiles, who know nothing of clever tricks, subtleties and sub-arguments, hold only by deeds.
A respected local Jewish merchant had for a long time been owed a debt by another Jewish merchant — a few złoty. One fine day the second merchant says to the first: since I cannot give you back those few złoty, be so kind and take, for the debt, German goods that I still have lying around from before the German boycott. (They all say that...) And done with the matter. Having no choice, the creditor took the bit of German goods, and no one would have known a thing (literally: "not even a rooster would have crowed")...
Then it so happens that the first merchant receives an order from a Christian firm in Poznań. So he goes and sends it the order straight away and packs into it the German "bargain"...
It does not take long and a letter arrives from the Christian Poznań firm, written in a tone of indignation: — How can this be?! And once again, how can this be?! Have you Jews not been beaten enough in Germany, that you consider it a happiness to smuggle in to me at least a little [German] goods?! You should be ashamed of yourselves!
Thus "replied" a Polish firm from Poznań, and we admit that we ought to be deeply, deeply ashamed!

The Bistritzky Days in Zagłębie

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — Zionism; JNF, the „Kfar Ussishkin“ campaign.] For 3 days now Jewish Zagłębie has been under the sign of the Bistritzky festival. It will be no exaggeration to say that all who had the chance to be even for a little while in the company of the brilliant poet Natan Bistritzky will long not forget the delight he gave everyone.
Bistritzky, who is staying with us in connection with the Kfar Ussishkin campaign, arrived in Będzin on Thursday evening. In honour of the distinguished guest an academy (festive gathering) was held in the „Świtowid“, organised by the local K.K.L. (JNF) committee.
After the chairman Mr. A. Liwer opened the academy with a short introductory speech, the „Hakoach“ orchestra played the Polish and the Jewish anthems, and the floor was given to the poet Bistritzky, who delivered a brilliant lecture entitled „The Cultural Crisis in Europe“. In a splendidly beautiful Yiddish the speaker unfolded the picture of today’s cultural barrenness. The golem with an axe in his hand has once again come to power, and the first victims — he says — are we, the Jews.
The lecturer is showered with stormy ovations. The orchestra is carried away and plays the „Hora“.
Then a youth choir sings several Eretz-Israel songs, and Bistritzky goes into a dance with the young people.
———
On Saturday a youth meeting took place in the same hall with the participation of Mr. Bistritzky.
In the evening Bistritzky gave a lecture at „WIZO“ entitled „The Tragedy of the Jewish Woman and Her Liberation“.
The same evening a banquet took place at the „Merchants’ Association“, with the participation of Zionist activists from Zagłębie and Upper Silesia.
On Sunday morning the festive opening of the district conference of the K.K.L. took place in the „Apollo“.
Delegates and guests from the surrounding towns came to the conference. A series of resolutions was adopted, among them to work on the kehilla leaders so that items for the K.K.L. be included in the kehilla budgets.
In the evening Bistritzky paid a visit to the premises of „Hashomer Hatzair“, where he had a cosy chat with those assembled, interwoven with Eretz-Israel songs.
On Monday morning Mr. Bistritzky visited Fürstenberg’s gymnasium, where he gave the children a lesson in geography, interwoven with Eretz-Israel songs. The enthusiasm of the pupils was beyond measure.
On Monday evening Mr. Bistritzky captured the „fortress“ of the „Social Club“. Taking that position was no easy matter; the „great ones“ of the „Club“ trembled with fear that the lecturer might speak precisely about what is not „pleasant“ (przyjemnie) for the club; but on hearing Bistritzky’s scholarly lecture, something like an electric current went through those assembled, which gave them a „pinch“ at the „pintele yid“ (the Jewish spark within), and almost all declared themselves ready to work for the upbuilding of Eretz Israel.
After the lecture a banquet took place in the same premises.
A colossal success was had by the lecture of the poet Bistritzky on Tuesday evening at the „Nowości“, entitled „Jerusalem or Moscow“.
After the greeting by Mr. Wygadzki[?], the floor was given to the distinguished lecturer, who described the tragic situation of Russian Jewry, which finds itself in the land of a people whose source runs from Tsar[?] Peter the Great to the present-day dreamers of a world revolution.
On Wednesday the „Kfar Ussishkin“ campaign began in Sosnowiec with a festive academy in the municipal theatre.
The academy, which for formal reasons began an hour late, was opened by Rabbi Hager. After a very successful Hebrew greeting by Mrs. Rasner[?], the poet Mr. Bistritzky was given the floor for his lecture „Heavenly Jerusalem and Earthly Jerusalem“ („Yerushalayim shel maala vi-Yerushalayim shel mata“).
The lecture called forth a storm of applause.

Broderzon Celebration in Będzin
The Jewish literary world is now celebrating the 20th jubilee of the well-known poet Moshe Broderzon.
And together with all the other larger cities in Poland, a Broderzon celebration will also take place in Będzin, in the „Nowości“[?] hall, on Monday the 29th of this month.
At this evening the jubilarian himself will appear and will recite the newest of his literary creations.
It is to be hoped that the friends of the Yiddish word and of Jewish culture will help the jubilee celebration to have the proper success.
