A Libel against the Jews of Wolbrom, that They Killed a Christian

[Wolbrom — blood libel; community.] A slain man found near the Jewish cemetery. — 200 Jews arrested. — Intervention with the starosta. — The rabbi decreed a fast.
The Jewish population of Wolbrom went through great fear and pain this week because of a Christian who was found killed by the wall of the Jewish cemetery.
The misfortune happened on Sunday. On that day 3 funerals took place in the town, among them the funeral of a young woman who on Friday towards evening had fallen down the stairs of her new apartment and been killed.
After the public, which had gone through so much grief, came home from the third funeral, a Christian came running into the police station and told that the Jews had killed a Christian, who is lying by the Jewish cemetery (the "cmentarz"[?]).
On the basis of this accusation about 200 Jews were arrested, among them the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha and the gravedigger Wingerman, who were made responsible and told that they would not be released until the Jewish murderer of the Christian was handed over. No intervention by some of the town's notables helped, and the arrested were not released.
Then a delegation intervened with the starosta in Olkusz, who delegated the Olkusz examining magistrate to Wolbrom, and all the arrested, except the gravedigger, were released. The Christian who had come first with the news of the slain Christian was also arrested.
The next morning, Monday, a public fast was held because of the blood libel and because already for the second time 3 funerals have fallen on one day.
In the town people say that the punishment is because the dozór (community board)[?] ordered a row of trees in the cemetery to be cut down.
Yitzhak Lichtenstein

[Sosnowiec — art; exhibition.] (On his painting exhibition in Sosnowiec).
In the "Bridosz"[?] hall on Dęblińska Street the painting exhibition of the artist-painter Yitzhak Lichtenstein is on.
Yitzhak Lichtenstein is a new face here, known only in the circles whose whole being is permeated with what happens in the Jewish art world. But when we leaf through the Jewish and non-Jewish world press, which devotes whole pages to Lichtenstein and speaks with appreciation of Lichtenstein's works, one comes to the conviction that Lichtenstein belongs among the artists — among the quiet, fine troubadours of painting.
Here is what Mr. Leo Koenig writes about Lichtenstein in the London "Tsayt":
A Lichtenstein exhibition is, so to speak, a painterly ingathering of the exiles: Polish Jewish shtetls, London restaurants, Paris cafés and boulevards, Palestinian Sephardi sages, Yemenite women, labyrinth-like Jerusalem alleys and Scandinavian snows...
The painting exhibition, which opened in these days, will, we hope, be visited by Jewish society and will have the success it deserves.
Murder and Suicide in Front of the "Renard Hospital"

[Sosnowiec — crime.] In front of the "Renard" hospital in Sosnowiec a bloody tragedy took place on Saturday at 6 in the morning.
The 41-year-old Dąbrowski, with several revolver shots, seriously wounded his beloved, a nurse at the hospital, and afterwards took his own life.
Two years ago Dąbrowski left his wife and children and lived with his beloved. But when he was laid off from his work in the coal mine, frequent quarrels arose between the enamoured couple, which led to Dąbrowski falling out with his mistress and making peace with his former wife. He could not, however, forget his beloved, and since she refused to come to him he decided to take revenge.
On Saturday morning Dąbrowski lay in wait for her as she was going into the hospital, and after an exchange of words he fired at her several times. Then he went off home and told his wife to bring him fresh water. When the wife went out into the yard, Dąbrowski shot himself.
A Patent Is No Proof that the Business Belongs to the One Who Took Out the Patent

[Law — commerce; Supreme Court ruling.] The fiscal authorities sequestered the goods and property of a well-known firm, because the patent (trading licence) for the business had been taken out not in the name of the person in question but in the name of a female cousin of his.
The matter went through several court instances until it reached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court issued a decision that taking out a patent is proof that the State Treasury has received the corresponding sum. With this patent, however, one cannot open an enterprise that requires a concession. Nor can a patent serve as proof that the person in whose name the patent is issued is the actual owner of the enterprise that is run on the basis of the patent.

A Whole Peasant Family Poisoned with Denatured Spirit

[Village — poisoning with denatured spirit.] In the village of Radłowice[?] beyond „Kauszial“[?] a peasant, a certain Kauszal[?] („as his name, so is he...“), made merry with his sons, drinking denatured spirit.

The result was that old Kauszal died at once, and the sons are fighting for their lives.
Tax Relief for New Houses.

[Taxes — relief for new construction.] The Treasury Chamber (Izba Skarbowa) has received a circular on granting tax relief for newly built buildings. According to the circular, tax relief will be granted for residential houses in the towns on the basis of individual, properly substantiated applications, which must be submitted to the appropriate treasury offices.
New houses, as well as partly extended and rebuilt houses, which are completed by the end of 1940, will be exempted from taxes for a period of 15 years, counting from the moment the house is handed over for use, even partially.
In addition, relief will be granted to persons who build residential houses by the end of 1940. Here the right will apply to deduct from the total income subject to income tax the sums spent on building costs, excluding the domestic loans. The latter will depend on the wish of the taxpayer — he will either deduct it at once or over at most 5 years, beginning with the year after the completion of the building.
In particular, the tax relief will be applied to new houses completed after 20 October 1930.
To an application for tax relief for new houses one must attach the appropriate documents establishing the right to this relief.

Dear Mr. Editor! We ask you to print our statement in your esteemed newspaper.
In connection with the notice in your esteemed newspaper about the payment of pensions, we declare the following:
The former kehilla administration, on leaving office, left behind nearly 90 thousand zł. of debts; there are officials who are owed arrears of pensions, from 1 month up to 15 months. Since the present administration pays full 100 percent pensions, it has been decided — in order to be able to run a normal economy and also to be able to cover the various social payments properly — to pay from 1 January 1934 the pensions for the current period, whereas the old debts are to be paid off over several years in instalments.
The Presidium of the Będzin Jewish Kehilla Administration,

Responsible Tasks. (An Apathetic Attitude Harms Society.)

More than once we have said that one must react to institutions that exist on paper, exist for the sake of power, exist as advertising, exist for their own benefit, and even exist to do harm at every step — and they already do harm by the very fact that they bring no benefit to society, to their members. What, then, do we need these comedies for? As soon as it comes to electing a new board, a chairman, in whatever institution it may be, the wire-pullers appear, and each one also[?] puts forward his candidacy and comes to the conclusion that he is the one called upon to raise this or that institution to its proper level.
In fact, however, we see that it is all bluff, all frivolity; members are ignored in everything, and hardly any of the leading figures lifts a finger [literally: "puts his hand into cold water"], and meanwhile, meanwhile one relies and believes that the association is already taking care of its member so that no harm comes to him, so that he will not have to pay a needless fine. That is how harm is done to the community, that is what is damaging to society. Whereas if people did not know that someone cares for the member, if there were no one to rely on, everyone would know to take care of himself in time, to take care of his own "I".
Most glaringly one sees the damage the economic institutions cause us precisely when something has to be settled, when one has to — when a civic duty has to be fulfilled.
A new ordinance has been issued by the authorities, according to which all employers must re-register their employees with the sick funds. The press hardly reported on the regulation, and it was not known to the population, so that suddenly, last Monday, the 15th, it became known that this was the final deadline — well, well, there arose a great outcry ["vayitsaku"]. All the premises of the sick funds were besieged, and it was not easy to obtain the new forms; but the public could not find its way exactly in how to fill in all the sections, and the officials would not give any explanations. The queues ["ogonkes", from Polish ogonki] began to grow, and most of the filled-in forms were refused because they had not been filled in properly.
A "miracle" happened: "writers" were found at once who filled in the forms for a certain fee; but they too were swamped with work, because rather than dread paying a fine of several hundred gulden [złoty], everyone paid the few groszy to put his papers in order.
Luckily it later turned out that it was impossible to deal with everyone within those few hours, and the blank forms were also running out, so acceptance was extended by a day or two. Meanwhile, after the deadline, an ordinance came out that the re-registration is finally extended to 1 February ["luty"], so that the harried [literally "choked"] public began to breathe more freely and was for the time being freed from the yoke that had befallen it.
Before that, however, when nobody knew anything about all this, the public ran about as if dazed. First of all everyone ran to his association for information; but one association was closed, a second advised first of all to hand [the forms] in — and if he does not know where the way in is and where the way out, surely the association is not to blame for that; a third association did not know at all what this thing was and what it was needed for in the first place, so that they actually learned the news from the member.
Such was the "information" the institutions gave their members at the moment when time played a role and he [the member] was left helpless.
One would think that a matter as popular as the sick-fund regulations is something economic institutions should certainly take up — and not just one institution but indeed all existing ones, since there is hardly a household without a registered member.
This question should have occupied both the merchants' and small traders' associations and the associations of artisans, tenants ["lokatorn"] and house-owners, since the members of all these professional institutions had registered their employees with the sick funds.
It is truly ridiculous that they did not want to take up so topical a matter; but more painful still is the fact that, seeing the nervousness of the citizens, none of them wanted to intervene with the proper bodies to have the deadline extended. What would have happened, then, had the extension not come out in Warsaw [Warszawa]?
How then is one actually disposed toward matters that concern the community and with which precisely the professional economic institutions ought to deal? And it would seem that they all also have secretaries, whole teams of "lawyers" and fixers ["makhers"], and yet they remain helpless when it comes to the good of society, to helping members with advice and information.
That is how it is when institutions take an interest in everything except what belongs to them, while the member deceives himself thinking that his association is already looking after him. And as much as we once needed professional associations, one needs them in this critical time even more; but just as we need their intensive activity[?], their useful work, so they are superfluous to us when they do nothing. Thus they harm the community when they exist only to serve their own interest. Such apathy, such indifference leads the merchant and the artisan to the abyss, to complete ruin.
And here again is news, and not good news — not the kind that would bring relief and comfort, but just the opposite: added hardship, despair.
Regulations are to be published under which, for trading after 7 in the evening, the merchant's shop is to be sealed up ["farkhasmenen"].
One can understand orders concerning the limitation of trading hours, but one cannot agree to such heavy penalties, which threaten the complete destruction of the element that works hard and bitterly until it earns its daily living. Why does one think only about how to restrict small trade at a time when taxes are not being reduced but, on the contrary, people keep going around with new taxes that will press still harder on the toiling, overworked element?
And one might once have thought that things had already reached the culminating point, that in the decisive circles they would finally feel that it cannot go on like this and would begin to seek means to ease the conditions of life, the conditions of dragging the yoke of labour. People[?] kept expecting tax relief and better conditions of existence.
But of these hopes we have, for the time being, nothing [printed "oyspips"; reading doubtful], and we are crushed under the heavy burdens of civic obligations.
We expected relief, but instead of all this new surprises are on the way, which will make the already hard enough life of the middle class harder still. Instead of help we receive decrees.
Thus whole branches of Jewish livelihoods are taken away, and further hardships are foreseen that can ruin the merchant over the slightest trifle.
Can one pass over these grave problems of life with indifference? May one tolerate all this as if nothing at all had happened? Why does one pick only on the helpless and the oppressed, on the one who leads a hard, bitter and stubborn life?
Why does one think only about how to make the oppressed man's livelihood harder, while the industrialist is allowed everything: he may run as many shifts ["zmianes", Polish zmiany] as he likes, he may run the factory on Sundays — whereas the harshest decrees fall on the one who is helpless.
And at such a time our professional and economic institutions find themselves in a dreadful state. Who, then, will stand up against this new decree? Is anyone trying to think it over? Have they already met to confer about it? Do they give themselves an account of what ruin this may bring into the situation, dark enough as it already is, or are they shutting their eyes here too to the sad reality?
Yes, there is work for the institutions mentioned, and a great deal of it, very responsible work, so that they must manage to stand at the proper height; if not, it would be better that they be liquidated altogether, and then at least we will know that we do not have the body that is supposed to care for its members.
R. Lct[?].
The History of the Będzin Kehilla in the Second Half of the 19th Century. According to Archival Records. (4)

[History — the Będzin kehilla; series, part 4.] By Moshe Feinkind. According to archival records.
To this the burmistrz [mayor] replied to the naczelnik [district head] only in August [sierpień] 1856, explaining in his report that Reb Hendl Erlich had had the full right to use the burial money at his own discretion and had not needed to give anyone an account of it, because Wenzel [?] had sent it to him voluntarily and has no claim against him on the basis of his receipt.
The burmistrz further explains that neither the inquiry conducted by the naczelnik's assistant nor the judicial authority had established that a "Chevra Kadisha" exists in Będzin (the burmistrz of course did not know of the "pinkas" of the Chevra Kadisha, from which a few leaves are missing, as my friend the teacher Mr. Warmund writes to me); and since the dozors [members of the kehilla board] did not occupy themselves with burying the dead man, one surely cannot demand from individuals, on whom the blame is being laid, nor from the dozors, nor from the Chevra Kadisha, which does not exist, that they pay this money into the kehilla treasury.
For this reason he also did not consider it justified to demand money by coercive measures from people from whom nothing can be got and who owe nothing but their soul to God.
There then follows in the report a large number of arguments with which the burmistrz himself defends himself regarding the whole affair, but which have no connection with the case; at the same time he informs the naczelnik in his report that Reb Hendl Erlich left no property — he died poor — and therefore the magistrate asks that everyone be released from repaying the contested [?] burial money, and in particular that the son, David Erlich, also be released from the military execution, and that the whole affair be annulled.
What became of the matter with the administrative authority — further details are missing from the records; but, as I already noted in my previous article, Reb Bendit Fiszel, then a dozor, was dismissed because he had been a gabbai of the Chevra Kadisha, but the coronation amnesty of Alexander II amnestied him. The same may also have applied to the other gabbaim listed above.
The military execution for collecting the burial money from the gabbaim must also have been annulled because of the amnesty.
On this occasion I want to explain to the young generation what a "military execution" was, since one has to speak of it so much here.
A military execution consisted of several armed soldiers who were quartered in the householder's home as a means of compulsion to collect a debt or taxes, and also for various administrative fines...
According to the size of the sum demanded, so large was the number of soldiers quartered there.
The householder himself had to feed the soldiers and give them drink of the very best. If he simply did not have the means for it, the soldiers — who mostly were "khokhly" [Ukrainians] or "katsapy" [?] [Russians] — made the householder's life a misery. They took over the beds and sold from the house whatever they could grab, and so on, and so forth.
But Będzin never had any peace with its "kehilla". Modrzejów [printed "Mandzhev"], which belonged to the Będzin district, rebelled and strove to break away in order to become an independent kehilla.
As already noted in the previous article, in the year 1854 [?] the Rabbi of Sieradz, Reb Yochanan David Langfus, was elected rabbi of Będzin.
But this rabbi did not enjoy length of days on the rabbinical seat of Będzin. After ten years as rabbi in Będzin he passed away, on 30 November [listopad] 1864, being barely 60 [?] years old.
In his time the new beit midrash was built (1859 [?]), which cost about two and a half thousand rubles. Reb Yosef Kacenel(l)er [?] left 600 rubles for this purpose, deposited with Reb Itzik Gelerman [?]; for the remaining money a "rozkład" [levy apportioned among the householders] was made.
But after the death of Rabbi Langfus the Będzin kehilla had no possibility [?] of engaging a new rabbi, because, as it writes, it had no means for it. The kehilla petitioned the authorities to allow the present dukhovny [official religious functionary], Reb David Szlezinger, to fill the rabbi's place temporarily, with the same salary of 180 rubles a year which the late Rabbi Langfus had received.
The dayan Reb David Szlezinger had already been moreh hora'ah in Będzin since 1849 [?], and in 1852 he received a licence for it. In 1851 Rabbi Szlezinger received the right to wear traditional Jewish dress, and the town was always [?] satisfied with him, because he was a very modest man and a hater of gain. He hated money, and besides he was a great pursuer of peace.
This petition was signed by the dozors Reb Bendit Fiszel, Reb Hershl Langner [?] and Reb Leib Pa…sk [?], the one who had brought the protest against the dozors over abuses, about which we already wrote in the earlier article.
The Radom governor understood that this must be a ploy of the dozors, who wanted in this way to block the post of a rabbi; so, regardless of the great efforts the kehilla made on behalf of the moreh hora'ah, he would not agree that Rabbi Szlezinger merely fill the rabbi's post voluntarily, and urgently called on the Będzin kehilla to present, within a short time, a candidate for rabbi in Będzin.
In October [październik; printed form doubtful] 1865 the kehilla presented as candidate for the Będzin rabbinical seat, in place of Reb David Szlezinger, the Rabbi of Szczekociny, Reb Meir Englard, who held an appointment as rabbi from the former Gubernia Office in Kraków from the year 1840.
But the Radom governor would not recognise this "nomination", demanding that Rabbi Englard produce a heter hora'ah [rabbinical ordination] from rabbis showing that he is a qualified rabbi.
The kehilla had agreed with Rabbi Englard on 500 rubles a year salary and a free apartment, etc.
Because of the difficulties the governor made, Rabbi Englard renounced the Będzin rabbinate entirely, taking the rabbinical seat in Szydłowiec, where he died a year later (May 1866).

"Ubezpieczalnia"...

[Article — social insurance; Zagłębie and Poland.]
"Ubezpieczalnia" — that is the new name of the sick fund [Kasa Chorych], of "ZUPU" [the Salaried Employees' Insurance Institution] and of all the other insurance institutions, for manual and for mental workers.
We are not yet taking the trouble to translate the word "Ubezpieczalnia" into Yiddish. The literal translation is not so burningly topical. Jews will themselves find a term of their own, the fitting word and the right name.
And then it will [?] be a name not out of any dictionary, but — out of life.
In a Polish newspaper we have already read such punning names as "Wynadziwalnia" [?], "Wymordowalnia" ["murder-house"], "Wykańczalnia" ["finishing-off house"] and the like.
These Polish epithets already bear witness that among the insured the insurance institutions are regarded as practically finished. That does not mean that they cease to exist; nor does it mean that the employers' demand to be freed from the social taxes is being satisfied. Neither the workers' demands nor the employers' have been directly satisfied here. The burden of the contributions will remain the same for both sides, if not heavier still. But the institutions, as insurance institutions, cease to have any meaning.
The apparatus becomes more bureaucratic, stiffer, and stops seeing what is happening in the street. It stops reckoning with life.
Figures: an employee who earns 295 [?] zł. a month pays 11 zł. 90 gr. for "ZUPU", 10 zł. 35 gr. for the sick fund, and then come further smaller contributions to other insurance funds, not counting 8 zł. 54 gr. tax to the Urząd Skarbowy [?] [tax office]. These figures have nothing to do with the employers' contributions to the same institutions.
When times were good, the insurance institutions used their enormous revenues to buy hotels, build villas, set up a huge administration with countless posts and offices. The insured were hardly taken into account.
And when the crisis began, they began more and more to tear down the existence of social insurance. Not a year passed without something else being taken away: the benefit period for the unemployed was shortened, the contribution to "ZUPU" was raised for mental workers, and now comes the fee for doctor's visits and prescriptions in the sick funds. Ever more taken and — ever less given.
The employer, who thought he would be freed from the social taxes, was disappointed; still more disappointed was the employee, seeing how precisely in a time of unemployment, when hunger and want increase the number of illnesses, the sick fund becomes for him an even crueller stepmother.
Once the present-day users of the sick funds [i.e. those now in control of them] argued that these institutions were fortresses of the workers' parties, so they set about "cleansing" them. But what do they look like after the cleansing? Are they not still fortresses of partisanship? The apparatus was not reduced precisely because every official in the insurance institutions grabbed in [people] from the circle of his own family.
And when an ordinary worker today enters the splendid building on Third of May Street, he feels an immense hatred for it; the hatred is, God forbid, not for the officials — it is hatred for the whole institution. And that is far worse and sadder.
That the whole reorganisation of social insurance cannot stand the test of life is shown to us by the fact that the "Ubezpieczalnia" has already led to a mass dismissal of domestic servants.
And therefore it is also no wonder that around the "Ubezpieczalnia" a united front of all the workers' parties has formed in the country, which found expression in the protest strikes in Łódź, Białystok, Warsaw, Zagłębie and in the protest meetings throughout the country with which the workers received, at the beginning of the New Year, the new laws on social insurance.
One must admit that even in some of the government newspapers strong voices are heard against the way in which social insurance has been "reformed".
"Ubezpieczalnia".
We are in no hurry to find a Yiddish term for this institution, because we are convinced that very soon life itself will show how false are the foundations on which they now want to base social legislation.
"Ubezpieczalnia" — a temporary name.
Y. Nisenbaum.
The Bottom Line.

[Sosnowiec — Kehilla; elections.] The result of the elections, which is to decide the fate of the kehilla in Sosnowiec, was awaited with impatience.
And I shall try to make a reckoning of the soul, to sum up everything that has been done and to know where we stand in the world.
The fair that took place in town was a big one: couriers, droshkies, cars plastered with various [list] numbers flew like an arrow from a bow, leaflets with numbers beyond measure strewed the streets, and above all Magrushever [?] Street, which looked like a battlefield.
But the main thing: the content of all the speeches and all the leaflets is a sad one, and perhaps also a disgrace for the kehilla.
On the one hand we heard a great outcry from the religious functionaries, expressed in the words "we are starving", and respectable people tell that in some homes there is not "al minyan [sic] one meal" [probably meaning: not even a single meal], because the kehilla does not pay; and from the institutions that depend on the kehilla, too, the same outcry is heard — we are starving! The sick receive no help, the schoolchildren of the cheder go naked and barefoot, melamdim and teachers do not get their wages, and all the needy, ruined merchants get no loans from the Gemilut Chesed fund, because there is no money.
And when one listens to the insults hurled by one rabbi at the other, one's face turns red with shame: are these your teachers, O Israel! And if the flame has fallen upon the cedars? If the heads of the people, if those for whom we are accustomed to have respect, are unable to keep within proper bounds of ethics and of dignity — what can one then demand of the common people?
The upshot of all this is a third question, namely: if the force of the elections could rouse the Jewish population of the town to such great enthusiasm that it spared no money to achieve the victory of the parties — why do they not hear at the same time the outcry of the needy and hungry families and institutions in town?
Some sort of "demons' dance" [?] is going on in our town: the ear does not hear what the mouth says, and people dance and show off.
Therefore it is the sacred duty of the newly elected parnasim, regardless of which faction they belong to, to put an end to the present situation, so that the plague which poisons the Jewish institutions and demoralizes the Jewish population may vanish from among us for ever and ever.
Yes, it is easy to say "make order", but in truth it is not so easy, and the gentlemen parnasim should have prepared for it beforehand; and if they did not know it, they will now learn that the kehilla has a deficit of nearly 150 thousand złoty, besides which the budget for the current year has not yet been drawn up.
I want to return to the flaming speeches delivered at the mass meetings, of which it is worth dwelling only on the speech given by the member and vice-president Liwer of Będzin.
The latter appealed to the exemplary order reigning in the kehilla there, which ought to serve as a model for Sosnowiec too.
Yasher koach, Mr. Liwer. Only one thing you forgot to tell, namely that you increased the budget by 77 thousand złoty — so we read in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" — and that the religious functionaries have announced a strike over arrears of wages.
Not bad prospects for the Sosnowiec kehilla taxpayers, but still a hard "Rambam" [a hard nut to crack] for the new parnasim...
Pity the people — they sweated for nothing.
Dov Tenzer.
"To Raise Him to Torah and to Skating"... (A Short Feuilleton)

[Feuilleton — upbringing and ice-skating.] Among Jews the greatest blessing was that one should raise the children to Torah, to the wedding canopy and to good deeds.
How much Jewish parents sacrificed so that they could pay tuition fees for their children; not to speak of when it came to marrying off a child — that was a matter of mortal danger, and they raised heaven and earth.
But now new songs have arisen — new times.
Parents want first of all that their children should be good sportsmen, because sportsmen are today the top of the heap [?], the ones people boast of being connected with, and study is only in second place, and perhaps even in the last.
I remember, when I was a 6-year-old boy and already learning Chumash and Rashi, I once wanted to go skating; my father, of blessed memory, noticed it and gave me a stern "moral lecture": that this is a gentile practice, and that a boy who is already learning Chumash and will soon begin to learn Gemara must not skate like those good-for-nothings; and wishing truly to be a Jew, created for other, higher matters, I never skated again.
Today, however, if you go out into the street you will see that not only 6-year-olds but even 10- and 20-year-olds and still older children — not only do they skate, but special skating costumes are made for them; the parents themselves take their children to the rink and take delight when their little ones skate and have mastered the craft, and when parents get together they brag.
Instead of what people used to tell — that my boy is already learning Gemara and will amount to something — they now say: my Stefek or Józek is a brilliant skater, he performs real wonders, he will grow up to be a "tanna bara" [a giant] in this field, and the world will yet ring with his name. And meanwhile the mother's heart swells with pride and happiness.
If so, I hold that the notion of the blessing customary among Jews for ages and generations must also be changed: instead of wishing, as was customary among Jews, "to raise him to Torah, to the canopy and good deeds", from today on people should wish one another "to raise him to skating, to skis [?] and to good dances, amen"...

After the Election Fair (Snapshots)

[Sosnowiec — satirical feuilleton; rabbinate and kehilla elections.] Snapshots — by Ben Amotz.
I have already put it in.
An elderly Jew, small and overgrown, his white-grey beard bears witness. This Jew is careful about the tip of a yod; he does not let even a single hair fall
— from his beard...
A gang of youngsters with their sidelocks hidden behind their ears fall upon him, the old man, and each of them, of these young [?], tugs and tears pieces off him.
— Come with me, grandpa, our list is a dispute for the sake of Heaven, you will surely buy yourself the World to Come; it is an explicit saying: "One may acquire his world in a single hour", and now is truly the right opportune moment. — What do you want of me, you young whippersnappers?
— We want you to vote for the true Jews and not for the heretics.

— So what will you do?

The Shofar...
The election meetings proceeded at the same tempo as the prayers of the Days of Awe.
The first meetings were held in the tone of the first Selichot, later already a bit warmer
— as at "Zekhor Brit"...
But in the last week they were already speaking with fervour
— Rosh Hashanah-like...
And on the last Sabbath
— Ne'ilah-like...

A debt repaid...
Comfortably seated on a droshky sits an old Jew; he has great "merit of the fathers"; he still remembers the Polish uprising [?], when "Swedish [?] horses drank from the Przemsza". He is shut in "on all sides" so that he should not "catch" an "evil eye"; he is led under strict guard, as the police lead a criminal sentenced to a heavy penalty.
The droshky stops at the polling district and the voter is led in like a bridegroom under the wedding canopy. Suddenly he is stopped by a young fellow [?] he knows, an agitator for another list, who tries to persuade him to vote for his list.

By the merit of righteous women...
The pessimism toward the whole [?], the thought that all the work, all the hullabaloo would in any case go to waste — vanished from me on election day, and I believe with perfect faith that the present elections will endure and that the city of Sosnowiec will at long last be redeemed from slavery to freedom...
For what reason? — not because the public is already tired, but because in the election campaign there took part en masse
— righteous women. Wives in head-kerchiefs [?], women in wigs, young ladies [?] with painted little lips, and ladies who have a "manicure"...
— By the merit of righteous women...
Therefore happy are you, Sosnowiec, that you have been privileged that in the kehilla elections, more precisely, in the rabbinical elections in your town, there should also enlist [—] [?] kosher, modest and splendid little women
— By the merit of righteous women...
Meanwhile Mephisto Laughs... (After the Kehilla Elections in Sosnowiec)

Finally, with Sunday's election day, the struggle over the elections to the kehilla has come to an end — elections that for weeks kept the entire Jewish population of Sosnowiec in tension, in feverish expectation; a population that wanted, in these elections, finally to find the key to tranquillity, to the dreamed-of peace for which it has been longing through the long years of continuous struggle and strife.
Unfortunately, however, Sunday's election result has brought no clarity whatsoever into the unbearable situation, no decision at all that could have put an end to the abnormality of Jewish public life.
Outwardly it seems that the struggle is already over, that apart from the election literature, which lies about in the streets like dried-up leaves in autumn, and apart from the marks on the walls of the houses, no trace of it all has remained... So it looks on the surface. But if one looks closely into the faces of the worried Jews who wander about the streets seeking a piece of bread for their "household", if one listens to their conversations, one senses in their words a fear, a strong fear for the future of the Jewish kehilla and its institutions.
Even those who rejoice at the outcome of the elections and openly show their satisfaction are, deep in their hearts, surely not at ease[?], because they understand from the outset the consequences that such an outcome will bring with it.
Meanwhile Mephisto laughs...
— Mephisto laughs... His voice giggles and penetrates the ears, reaches the dull brains of all those who, in the hour of destiny, at the decisive moment, did not have the good of the community in mind, but placed the suffering and need of one man above the suffering and pain of hundreds of poor Jewish families who are perishing of hunger and cold, and who had the right to demand of Jewish society that it take an interest in their fate and help them out of their terrible need.
It may be that if today's elections had not been rabbinate elections, the result might perhaps have been quite different; then perhaps a large part of the electorate would not have been guided by sentiments of compassion towards one family burdened with children, but would have voted as public responsibility demands of them — which must be the highest credo of every single individual.
All this, however, cannot justify the conduct of a large part of the Jewish population, which showed its immaturity at important moments that could have been a turning point in the history of Jewish Sosnowiec and could have entirely changed its public face.
— Meanwhile Mephisto laughs...
He laughs at the immaturity of the Sosnowiec population, which ought, when casting its ballots, to have considered whether[?] its votes would help to put an end to the quarrels and squabbles, to the desecration of God's name and the disgraces, to open a new era for the economic flourishing of all kehilla institutions — or not?
For it is more than certain that the future administration will hardly be able to attend to all the ruined institutions that it has inherited from the former rulers and that were entirely neglected during their term of office, as it will remain absorbed in the painful rabbinate problem.
A sad result is what today's elections have produced, sad and at the same time tragic, because it has taken from hundreds of people the feeling of hope, robbed them of the feeling of confidence in a finer, more splendid beginning for Sosnowiec public life.
Neither the National Bloc, which won six mandates, nor the second side with its five mandates holds the key to this enigmatic[?] situation, but precisely the third side, which consists of three separate cliques with different aims and interests.
This very "third side" has the possibility, given a certain understanding of the situation that has arisen, to correct somewhat the sad sum total of the elections, to repair the mistake the voters committed through their premeditated[?], irresponsible action.
They must do it, they are obliged to do it, in order to put an end to the lawless situation in which Sosnowiec Jewish public life is drowning[?], so that the rusted kehilla wagon may budge from the deep swamp in which the outgoing administration left it stuck.
They must do it for the good of all the declining institutions that are waiting for their redeemer, for the sake of the hundreds of needy, poor Jews who come to seek help at the Jewish kehilla, and for the whole Jewish population, which wants to see in the Jewish kehilla its only autonomous institution in the Diaspora.
I am sure that in the end healthy public sense will prevail, that in the end individuals will have to capitulate before the interests of the community, because perhaps no other town is in such need as Sosnowiec of a complete "restoration" of public life.
Only quick, consistent action on the part of the responsible representatives is able to open a new, splendid page in the history of Jewish Sosnowiec, has the power to repair the distressing[?] result of the elections and to change its sad sum total.
The newly elected parnassim face a difficult examination in public responsibility, which they will have to pass at the very beginning of their rule, and which will be the first certificate of their maturity and understanding in important public matters.
With trembling impatience, Jewish Sosnowiec awaits the outcome of this examination.
Meanwhile, however, Mephisto laughs...
Tanai.
Theatre Notes

[Theatre — review.] “Der Urteyl” (“The Verdict”), a reportage play in 3 acts, 5 scenes, by S. Levitska [Lewicka?], performed at the cinema “Światowid”.
When you see in the street a poster from which the name of one actor screams down in letters as big as for the Blessing of the Moon, you can be sure that the aim is to draw the public with the ineffable name of a “star”, and that in this case neither the play nor the ensemble plays any role at all.
This time the actor Sandler was supposed to be the “shining star”, and his wife and daughter the 2 comets (on the poster in smaller type), who are meant to draw the naive theatre public.
But first of all about the play itself.
During the war between the Bolsheviks and the various White generals, the Reds [printed “roise”] occupy a town. A Bolshevik commissar is quartered in the flat of a counter-revolutionary family, and he falls in love with the young, beautiful daughter of the householders.
The parents of the young woman are under suspicion of espionage. During a search, weapons and compromising material are found in their home. The daughter takes the blame on herself; all are arrested, the parents are shot, and the daughter is released for lack of evidence.
After her release, the commissar's wife runs over to the White general staff, where her brother is. There she is persuaded to run back to her husband and carry out an espionage mission.
She is discovered and sentenced to death. The sentence is carried out personally by her husband, the Red commissar.
That, in brief, is the content of the play.
It is clear that we are dealing with a play of bad quality; it is a kind of shoddy, cheap concoction in which the heroes[!] chew the cud of threshed-out phrases that have no effect and convince nobody.
Inspired by the success of “Roar, China!”, which is truly a masterly reportage breathing genuine revolutionary pathos, certain writers have begun to produce pseudo-revolutionary “bigos” hodgepodges that have no artistic or educational value whatsoever. To this kind belongs the above-mentioned play as well.
The acting of the artists: Sandler doubled in the role of the Red commissar and of the Tsarist general. In the first role he is pale; his acting leaves one cold and makes no impression. He is considerably better in the second role, where he gives a finely drawn type of an old, degenerate and nervous general.
Mrs. Sandler, in the role of a Bolshevik agent, was not in her right place. This is a role for a young, temperamental actress and not for an actress suited to mother roles.
Miss Sandler, in the role of the commissar's wife, has all the outward qualities to be a subtle actress. Her acting holds up somewhat less well: she had several good moments, but in the final scene, when she begs her husband to spare her life, the actress does not act directly by purely artistic means but with the help of an overdone, hysterical weeping that provokes revulsion.
The remaining 20 “first-class actors” could indeed have been first-class extras, for there happen to be some well-built young fellows among them. I refrain from writing about their acting, because it is a waste of time.
The “sets” — more than scandalous.
2 examples by way of illustration:
In the office of the Tsarist general they leave the same props from the flat of the Red commissar.
4 boards set up, by which 4 soldiers sit and sing sentimental songs, are supposed to represent a trench of Russian front-line fighters.
Further comments are absolutely superfluous here.
On the whole it was a performance such that whoever did not see it need certainly have no regrets.
Sh. R.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Beshalach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Beshalach
The Portion
—o—
a) "And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him" (Ex. 13:19)
"'The wise in heart will take commandments' — this is Moses: for all Israel busied themselves with the spoil, and he busied himself with a commandment, with the bones of Joseph." Tractate Sotah.
All the Jews were busy with the spoil of the sea, fussing over the gold and silver of the dead Egyptians — and then Moses our Teacher carried the bones of Joseph past them, to remind them that of all the gold and silver, what remains of a person is just these bones... Chavot Yair.
—o—
b) "And behold, Egypt marched after them" (14:10)
"'Marched' (singular) — with one heart, as one man." Rashi.
See: the Egyptians were of one heart and as one man, therefore of them the singular "marched" is used; whereas the Jews, the "asa-kirte"[?], already have "after them", the plural — the Jews were not of one heart and as one man. Even when the danger was so terrible they could not unite at least like the Egyptians... Ktav Sofer.
—o—
c) "And the waters were divided" (ibid., 21)
The Gemara says: "A man's livelihood is as hard as the splitting of the Red Sea." In what way, one asks, is livelihood like the splitting of the Red Sea of all things? But the Gemara in Arakhin (15a) says that the Jews passed through the sea "like half a round threshing floor", that is, they walked in a circle. Each tribe formed another[?] circle — twelve circles one around the other. It follows that one had less distance to the goal, and another had to crawl around a longer way. So it is with livelihood too: one reaches his piece of bread by a nearer circle, and another by a more distant road...
R' Eizikl of Zhidachov [Żydaczów].
—o—
d) "And the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand and on their left" (ibid., 29)
In Sanhedrin (103a) the Gemara says that this is why "chomah" is written without a vav (as "chemah", wrath): because the sea was filled with "chemah" (wrath) against them on account of the idol of Micah, which they had taken along with them into the sea.
One asks: why in verse 29 is "chomah" written in full, with a vav — why then was the sea not filled with wrath against the Jews?
Because then, while the Egyptians were still alive, the sea could not be angry with the Jews — the Egyptians were no better... Only now, when "there remained not so much as one of them", when the Egyptians had perished, did the sea grow angry, because it no longer had anyone to point to as worse than the Jews... Apiryon.
—o—
e) "Thou shalt bring them in and plant them in the mountain of thine inheritance... For the horse of Pharaoh went in with his chariots and with his horsemen into the sea" (ibid., 15:17–19)
Just as at the splitting of the Red Sea, at "the horse of Pharaoh went in", the angel of the sea argued: "These are idol-worshippers and those are idol-worshippers" — the Jews are no better than the Egyptians — and yet God redeemed them; so too one day, when it comes to "Thou shalt bring them in and plant them in the mountain of thine inheritance", when the future redemption comes and people will again rise up with claims: the Jews are no better than the gentiles... God will again pay no heed to it and will redeem the Jews... Arono shel Yosef.
—o—
f) "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you... that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no" (16:4)
R' Mordechai of Neskhiz used to say:
The world says that whoever is pious fares badly. Therefore people are afraid to be pious. But we see[?] that sinners also fare badly, and we see[?] that pious Jews also sometimes fare well.. Therefore: "Fear the Lord, ye his saints" — fear God, for "there is no want to them that fear him", for want, poverty, has nothing to do with the fear of God, since "the young lions [kefirim] do lack and suffer hunger" — we see such unbelievers [koferim] who go hungry and are poor; and further we see that "they that seek the Lord shall not want any good thing" — that there are such pious people who have all good things; one can be pious and also be rich...
Toldot Yitzchak.
• • •
To the Aleksander Rebbe, R' Yerachmiel Yisrael Yitzchak, a Hasid complained that he had no livelihood. The Rebbe raised his eyes to heaven and argued it out with the Master of the World:
— What would it harm You to give the Jew a livelihood, dear God in heaven, what's the problem? "The Holy One, blessed be He, takes from this one and gives to that one" — God takes away from one and gives to the other. Well, the Blessed Name does not want to take from another Jew, since that one too will have grievances against God. But, Master of the World! You can take from an unbeliever — that one won't have any complaints against You, since he says he doesn't believe in You...
—o—
g) "And the children of Israel did eat manna... until they came to a land inhabited" (ibid., 35)
In the desert, in exile, the Jews had to eat manna by the merit of Moses, drink water by the merit of Miriam (Miriam's well); but when they arrived in the Land of Israel all these merits ceased — one no longer needed to live by anybody's merit... Before[?] the Ostrowiec Rebbe, of blessed memory.
—o—
h) "And it came to pass, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed" (17:11)
"But did the hands of Moses make war? Rather, it is to tell you: as long as Israel looked upward and subjected their heart to their Father in heaven, the hands of Moses prevailed." Tractate Rosh Hashanah (chapter "Ra'uhu Beit Din").
Moses, the emissary of the congregation, can only act when the congregation acts. "If the emissary of the congregation errs, it is a bad sign for those who sent him": if a prayer leader makes a mistake, it is a sign that those who sent him are no good... The emissary of the congregation by himself can do nothing if the congregation stands at a distance and just looks on.. Ktonet Or.
A Problem of the Moment

[Essay — the Jewish question; Hitlerism and nationalism.] By Rabbi Y. L. Graubart.
The Jewish situation is very critical and tragic. Not a single year goes by quietly and peacefully, without misfortunes, without persecution. Remember the events of recent times: slaughters, murders in Ukraine; pogroms in Romania, Hungary. And now the cruel Hitlerism. One cannot say that this is a temporary accident, a thing of the moment. No! It is a permanent illness. It is like a weak organism: sometimes the illness seizes one limb, sometimes another. Now the head aches; later the pain is in the belly and in the hands. The Jewish organism is an eternal sufferer. Sometimes the calamity strikes in this country, sometimes in another. It is an epidemic, a "makat mehalekhet" (a spreading plague).
Our sad condition is natural, a law of nature, like the fixed seasons of summer and winter. It must be so; it cannot be otherwise. It is not a catastrophe but a tragedy, which happens according to[?] calculated circumstances.
Every nation sits on its own soil, "am ha-aretz" (the people of the land). We, however, are in a foreign place, have no home, no territory of our own; that is not normal. It is a crippled situation. The Jewish question, "she'elat ha-yehudim", is in reality no Jewish question but a gentile question — a world question and a universal problem, without a solution and without a decision.
So when we come in the name of philanthropy, when we demand our rights with the claim of justice, of hospitality — the "love of the stranger" that the Torah commands, bidding us to respect[?] and treat strangers well — still one cannot root out, eradicate natural egoism. Man is envious; he cannot indifferently tolerate the stranger who is more successful, more capable than he. And when the gentile, the old-established citizen, sees how the stranger, the Jew, competes with him on the economic field and takes away his livelihood, it must vex him, and he cannot remain content.
The very fact that the Torah repeated many times the command to protect strangers and to live harmoniously with them is the best proof that nature resists it and that it is hard to carry out.
And not only Jews: other national groups (landsmanshaftn) that emigrate to foreign countries are also not welcome guests. People treat them with antipathy, and yet they do assimilate with them. What wonder, then, that people look askance at Jews, who are a different race, different in appearance, and keep apart by themselves — "a people that dwells alone"!
If we are to be impartial, if we will not be one-sided, we must acknowledge that the gentiles have arguments to raise against us. And we cannot raise a firm voice, demand our right according to the dry letter of the law, by strict justice: "If you probe the depth of the law, who will be acquitted?" We can only plead, in a soft tone, in the name of high morality, of c-o-m-p-a-s-s-i-o-n (rakhmones), of mercy. But compassion can be used only with the better class of people, and only sometimes; before the whole world, however, and constantly, forever, compassion is no marketable commodity. A nation of 17 million cannot depend on compassion and maintain a place for itself on hospitality.
But our correct argument, our true claim, is necessity, the "must". The Jewish people has no way out, no counsel; we are living creatures, we exist. We have no land; we m-u-s-t be among other peoples and in gentile countries. Everyone reckons with necessity. Everyone m-u-s-t tolerate what he must, and becomes indifferent to it — just as one grows used to the sight of death that one sees day after day, because one must survive and remain content.
The normal way would have been for us to possess a land of our own, like all peoples, and to be freed from the old, two-thousand-year-old, entangled and crippled question of eternal sorrow. But no place has remained for us on the globe. Even Eretz Israel cannot take in a quarter of us. Moreover, the Arabs occupy the land, act as masters there, regard themselves as its owners and crowd us.
In ancient times the peoples were primitive, naive. Nationalism was alien to them. They were internationally minded, and strangers settled in well everywhere, in all countries (if religion did not interfere).
In the latest epoch, with the spread of civilisation, nationalism developed.
Patriotism was created; every nation breeds nationalism, closes itself off, drives out foreign national groups — just as the human body spits out foreign elements, foreign materials. The motto is: "Mine — mine", my property for myself alone, for my race, my nation. It may be that the idea is right. But for us it is harmful; this principle is our Satan, because we have no "mine-mine", we possess no soil of our own. So we are driven from all positions and hang in the air.
Fundamentally, brutal Hitlerism is not antisemitism and is not aimed specifically against Jews. It is nationalism, which now dominates the world in an exaggerated form — a wild nationalism, which leads to chauvinism and is perfected in Hitlerism. Every nationalism harms us to a certain degree; Hitlerism ruins us.
Hitlerism threatens, like a plague epidemic, to spread through the world, and it conducts propaganda to create comrades for itself in America and Canada too.
Besides this there are egoists, who care only for themselves and ignore the people: the individual, the single one is everything — "What is klal Yisrael to me, as long as I make a living." These persons are beneath criticism. And unfortunately there are a great many of them.
Many are optimistic: things will get better; these are not the Middle Ages, we live in a modern, civilised time. But experience, the facts, show precisely the reverse. Germany is a convincing proof and serves everyone as evidence that civilisation is no armour against atrocities. The Germans are the bearers of culture, there is the fortress of learning — and yet its civilisation agrees with barbarism, and humanity with terror; they are united and go hand in hand.
How can we help and alleviate the misfortune? What is the duty upon us? Nothing new at all: one must merely call attention to what is known to everyone. Everyone knows it, and yet it is not superfluous to say it and recall it once more.
We must be careful. Whoever cheats over a single dollar — klal Yisrael pays for it in hundreds, and with lives.
One may answer that swindling is a crime, but gentiles swindle too — they are allowed! Their fire[?] is not seen. When a son sins, the father, the elder, keeps silent. He is one of their own; he is forgiven. But with a stranger's transgression, a speck of dust, of sand[?], becomes a mountain. Our smallest fault is examined through a telescope. We must be clean, noble and kosher, like a newborn child.
Antisemitism can be felt in the air. The bacilli stir and move; one must use disinfection, means of cleansing.
We must know for ourselves how things stand with antisemitism, but not spit it out; that is a dangerous step, because it manufactures hatred. When one says to somebody, "I know you are my opponent, my enemy", one provokes the fight and turns that person into a foe, when it had never occurred to him.
Do not fan any sparks. Keep wisdom to yourselves: "a fence for wisdom is silence".
Important Decisions of the Supreme Court

[Law — decisions of the Supreme Court; regular column.]
Proper business books
If it concerns a transaction on credit, it must without fail be indicated: in a purchase — who the supplier was, and in a sale — who the buyer was.
As regards transactions concluded for cash, the buyer or supplier must likewise also be recorded; only in exceptional cases can a booked purchase or sale transaction in which the supplier or buyer is not stated be recognised as valid. This applies to small purchases from a peasant at the fair (targ) or market, where it is truly difficult to establish the seller's identity and to demand a receipt for the sum paid; likewise the names of chance customers for small purchases[?] (sprawunki) for their own use cannot always be ascertained.
Objections against judgments by default (wyroki zaoczne)
In an objection against a default judgment in a civil case, the reasons why the defendant did not appear at the trial need not be stated; but the pleas against the claim must indeed be stated, and the pleas must be substantiated with facts and documents, or possibly be grounded in other evidence.
The Jewish Queen of Yemen (4)

[Serialized historical tale — Yemen, King Yusuf Dhu Nuwas; installment 4.]
Sh. Berg.

"Woe unto us!" the sheikh cried out in confusion. "It is Yusuf Dhu Nuwas [printed "De-Nuwas"] with his army, he has come and fallen upon us suddenly!" Quickly he put on his sword, stuck a sharp knife in his belt and went outside, and his household with Pnina after him [printed "after her"]. And no sooner were they out than their tent too began to burn.

The villagers saw their sheikh, roused themselves and all took up arms; they surrounded him and stood against the enemy. But the enemy was stronger, and after a heroic battle all the men fell dead.

The women saw the sheikh fall dead; they snatched up the children and wanted to flee. But Yusuf Dhu Nuwas had surrounded the village with soldiers and let no one out. The soldiers captured the women and children, Pnina and Tzarida too, and tied them two by two onto donkeys [?] and camels. They gathered up whole fortunes, and when the last tent had burned down, Yusuf Dhu Nuwas, at daybreak, took everyone away with him.

Yusuf Dhu Nuwas, the Jewish king of Yemen, was a man of about twenty-five, tall, broad-shouldered, with a little black beard and big, thick locks down to his belt. His face was brown, burnt by the sun. On his head he wore a red turban, on his shoulders a dark-green silk cloak, and on his loins a silver belt set with precious stones. From the belt hung his Damascene sword.

When they had left the village, Yusuf Dhu Nuwas rode up to the captives and looked them over. He stopped beside Pnina and looked at her.

Pnina was frightened. She trembled before the man who had just so cruelly destroyed a whole village. But she steeled herself and looked him straight in the face, and she calmed down a little. Besides his tremendous courage, which his face expressed, it had a great deal of charm, and his look was gentle and pleasant. He began to speak to her and said:

"Girl, you are, it seems, not from that village. Where are you from?"

"From Persia."

"How do you come to be here?"

"The king of Persia torments the Jews terribly," she told him, "so many Jews have left the country. My mother took me and we all set out for Yemen to find protection with you, great ruler, for you too are a Jew. Near that village a bitter storm-wind rose and buried everyone under the sand. My good mother perished too. Only I alone remained alive. When I came into the village, the sheikh took pity on me and kept me like his own child."

"Are you a Jewish child?"

"Yes, I am descended from King David."

"Have you proof that you are telling the truth?"

"I have the genealogy scroll with me; it hangs around my neck."

"If what you say is true, then you are of my family. I too am descended from King David, I come from King David. You know, King Solomon fell in love with the Queen of Sheba. She converted to Judaism and married him, and she bore him a son. The son reigned after his mother, and he is the father of our royal family," Yusuf Dhu Nuwas told her, and said:

"Show me the genealogy scroll."

She handed him the genealogy scroll, and after he had read it through he pressed it to his forehead and to his heart and kissed it with holy awe. He at once ordered Pnina and Tzarida to be untied from their camel with the other captives. He seated them on a camel beside himself and showed them great honour. He also at once issued an order to his soldiers that they must not dare to disturb the captives.

After sunset the camp halted. They pitched the tents: Yusuf with his army separately, the captives separately, and Pnina with Tzarida separately. Soon Pnina and Tzarida were brought into the king's tent. Yusuf Dhu Nuwas sat on a costly divan; he bade them sit and asked Pnina to tell him how the Jews were faring in Persia. She told him what troubles the Jews were enduring, and wept bitterly. Yusuf Dhu Nuwas was deeply moved, and tears came to his eyes.

"Enough for today," he checked himself. "You are tired, you must rest. You will eat supper with your friend and go to sleep. Tomorrow you will tell me more. I have a great deal to talk about with you. And we have time: it will take 5 days until we reach my capital."

They had a fine meal of roast meat with dates and lay down to sleep. At daybreak they moved on. Pnina and Tzarida rode beside him, and they were already talking like old acquaintances. After Pnina had finished telling about the situation of the Jews in Persia, Yusuf Dhu Nuwas asked her to tell him the history of the Jews since the destruction of the Second Temple. What had happened up to the destruction, he said, he knew well; and she told him everything.

On the sixth day at noon they arrived in Sana'a, the capital of Yemen. Pnina was disappointed. She had come from [printed "in"] Isfahan, the Persian capital, with its wealth and grandeur, and Sana'a looked to her like a small village; a small town in Persia was bigger and more beautiful than the capital Sana'a. But in Arabia, the land of the desert, where most of the inhabitants are Bedouins with wandering tents, it was enough for Sana'a, with its few streets and little wooden houses, to be a capital. And the two-storey stone house, painted green, was there already worthy of bearing the name "royal palace."

Towards evening Yusuf Dhu Nuwas divided the spoils of war among his soldiers. Pnina and Tzarida he took into the palace and gave them an apartment on the ground floor. They were not kept as captives but as members of the royal household. Tzarida he treated so well for Pnina's sake.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: City Council Elections to Take Place in March

[Head of the local section; Będzin — city council elections.]
What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 10 Shevat 5694 — piątek 26 stycznia 1934 [Friday, 26 January 1934].)
Będzin
City council elections to take place in March.
As we are informed by an authoritative source, the date of the city council elections is approaching. It is already almost certain that the elections will take place in the second half of March.
The Stubborn Stance of the Local Shochtim

[Będzin — Kehilla; ritual slaughterers.]
As we have already reported, the kehilla presidium decided to withhold the payments of the debts to date that the gmina owes its employees.
The shochtim (ritual slaughterers) do not want to agree to this decision, which came into force on the 15th of this month, and do not want to accept the salary (pensja) for the current month.
As is reported, the shochtim wanted to strike this week, but the strike is being held back because the older shochtim fear that a strike could harm the young shochtim, who are not yet included in the budget.
Delegation of Synagogue Worshippers on Engaging Cantor Mr. Kamieniecki

[Będzin — Kehilla; cantorate.]
Last Sabbath the well-known cantor Mr. Kamieniecki led the prayers for the second time in the city synagogue, further strengthening his chances for the post of cantor in our town. On Sunday a delegation of 25 synagogue worshippers approached the vice-president, Mr. Liwer, with a proposal to engage Mr. Kamieniecki as the cantor of Będzin.
Mr. Liwer declared that the proposal is being taken into consideration, but the question can be finally settled only when the new budget is approved.
A Gang of Swindlers Falls into the Hands of the Police

[Będzin — crime; followed by five short news items: Czeladź, Będzin, post office.]
A few weeks ago — as our readers know — pieces of merchandise were stolen in the cloth shops of Messrs. Blumenfeld and Szwajcer. The thefts were carried out by skilled swindlers, who entered the shop supposedly to "buy", and when the "customers" had left, the owners of the above-mentioned shops discovered that pieces of merchandise had been stolen.
Last Wednesday our [?] Jewish "customer", a middle-aged Jew, came into Szwajcer's shop and asked to be shown various goods.
In the shop was Mr. Szwajcer's son, who, despite having recognised that he was a thief, obliged him and showed him the requested samples. But when the "customer" was about to leave, declaring that he would come right back with the tailor, Szwajcer's son revealed a "secret" to him: that he should not go yet, because — the police are coming here at any moment.
The "customer" began to protest, swearing the holiest oaths that "he owes God his soul" [i.e. he is guiltless], that he is an innocent soul. Soon, however, the police arrived and took the "customer" off to the police station.
A little later 3 more partners were arrested while they were sitting in a local restaurant over a tasty lunch.
Various documents and objects were found on the arrested men which confirm the accusation levelled against them.

Trade Licences Must Hang in a Visible Place, and One Should Write Fewer Petitions

[Będzin — taxes and trade.]
A delegation of the Merchants' Association, in the persons of Messrs. Rubinlicht and Goldfeld, was received by the new head (naczelnik) of the local tax office.
During the conversation about a series of current matters, the head asked, through the mediation of our newspaper, to draw the merchants' attention to the following: 1) that the trade licences (patents) must be located in a visible place, and 2) to act so that not so many petitions are written about free licences and about tax reliefs which are not provided for in the tax law.
The head added that because of the great number of petitions, those of the people who are actually entitled to enjoy the above-mentioned reliefs cannot be dealt with.
The New Kehilla Budget at the Plenum of the Kehilla Board

[Będzin — kehilla.]
The new kehilla budget was before the plenum of the kehilla board at Sunday's session.
At the session the presidium, Messrs. Rubinlicht and Liwer[?], reported on the budget, which has been increased because of the sums earmarked in advance for investment purposes; and in order — says Mr. Rubinlicht — to put the budget on a realistic footing, a reduction of 10 percent in the officials' pensions has been provided for that purpose.
The board members (dozór) Banhart and Skocylas[?] came out against the reduction.
Board member Hampel criticised the fact that the budget contains no item for broad social welfare, and that care is taken only of the religious functionaries (klei kodesh).

The Result of the Kehilla Elections in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — kehilla elections.]
The election campaign. — 82 percent take part in the elections. — Lists that failed. — No victors and no vanquished.
The kehilla elections in Sosnowiec, which took place last Sunday, have brought no decisive change in the situation as it has been until now. After the months-long struggles, the effort expended[?] and the large sums of money, after so many speeches and so much abuse, it is again — status quo... So that both main contending sides, both the Mizrachists and the Englardists [supporters of Rabbi Englard], did not obtain the number of mandates that would form a majority and not need to depend on other people's favours.
—
As we reported in our special edition, the turnout was high. Of the 4,600 eligible voters, 3,737 voters took part in the elections, that is, about 82 percent. A feverish commotion reigned in the streets; almost all the taxis, buses and droshkies were “occupied” by the election canvassers, who brought the “uncertain”[?] voters from the most distant streets, sparing not even the seriously ill and even cripples.
On election day the kind of “election literature” with which Jewish Sosnowiec had been fed during the whole time of the election campaign did not appear; only number 11 (Rabbi Glikman's side) received for “Ne'ila” [the final hour] an “urgent telegram” from the Belzer Rebbe, who calls for voting for list 11, and in return he promises abundance, blessing and success in everything good...

At the Headquarters of the Polish Hitlerites in Katowice.

[Katowice — Polish Hitlerites.] A contributor to „Kurier Poranny“ paid a visit to the headquarters of the Polish Hitlerites in Katowice, whose organ is „Błyskawica“ („Lightning“), a little sheet that preaches and makes noise about fascism, Hitlerism and antisemitism.
The Goebbels of the Polish Hitlerites is a certain Chamiec. He styles himself professor. He himself has already served every idolatry and bustled about in every party. On his lapel he wears a miniature cross of Bułak-Bałachowicz's army.
The „party“ is already 8 months old and has 80 organized groups in various towns, mainly in Upper Silesia, Pomerania, Danzig and Zagłębie.
The party (N.S.P.R.) already also has its own economic organizations, which intervene in matters of taxes and tax reliefs, and perhaps that is why the „chief of staff“ is a certain Sim Niak [?], an official of the tax office. Tax reliefs and a little patriotic propaganda mixed with socialism bring followers. The N.S.P.R. leaders boast that they already have 30 thousand followers. „Błyskawica“, however, sells only 4 thousand copies. The N.S.P.R. is also waging a struggle with other Polish-Hitlerite parties, which are now springing up like mushrooms after rain and compete among themselves.
„Kurier Poranny“ asks who pays for all the expenses that the Polish Hitlerites incur, the drinks and the feasts held in the restaurants while recruiting members.
The paper assures that the whole affair need not be taken seriously, because with one ordinary police order the whole business of Polish Hitlerism could be liquidated in a single day, before it tries to penetrate other regions of Poland.
— But when will that happen?

[Będzin — Accident.] 26-year-old Jewish young man from Będzin killed in tragic circumstances in Warsaw.
Yesterday the Rembiszewski family in Będzin received a telegraphic message from Warsaw that their son Avraham, 26 years old, had been killed there in tragic circumstances.
The tragic accident took place in the following circumstances:
On Tuesday before dawn Avraham Rembiszewski, a gardener by trade, was going to his work in Mokotów. While crossing the railway tracks near Taranska [?] Street he did not notice, because of the darkness, that a freight train was approaching. When he noticed it, it was already too late. The train ran over him and killed him on the spot. Only in the morning was the victim identified and the family in Będzin informed.
This is already the second tragic case in the same family: some years ago their son died tragically in Eretz Israel.
The news of the tragic loss of Avraham Rembiszewski made a shattering impression.

„S.O.S.“ at the „Apollo“ cinema.
„S.O.S.“ — that is the signal of desperate people who alarm the world that someone should come to rescue them from disaster.
This time it concerns a group of scientists who set out for the polar regions to do research.
The film has no love content, no star actors play in it, and yet one watches it with the greatest suspense. For what value have all the love stories and heart-tragedies against the terrible truth that nature is able to show us? With a shudder one sits in the cinema and watches the ice wastes and the bold scientists crawling forward over the pieces of ice.

Polish „People's Socialists“ (National-Socialists) as Hitler's Servants

[Katowice — trial; the Polish Hitlerites.]
President of „Błyskawica“ [„Lightning“] sentenced to 3 months in prison — a sensational trial in Katowice.
Before the Katowice district court a trial was played out on Wednesday which uncovered the behind-the-scenes politics concerning the activity of the Polish Hitlerites in the territory of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia.
The hero of the sensational trial is the already well-known „Führer“ of the People's Socialists [National-Socialists] in Zagłębie, the advocate Kozielski of Sosnowiec, who brought charges against his party comrades in Upper Silesia, who had accused him that he — Kozielski, that is — had struck up relations with the German Hitlerites in order to work for the benefit of their idea, and that for this he was to be satisfied with a sum of 20 thousand German marks.
In the dock sat 3 accused, who are in the presidium of the Polish Hitlerite party in Upper Silesia and are the publishers of „Błyskawica“.
A series of witnesses was heard, among them the chief witness, the president of „Błyskawica“, engineer Żmudziński[?], who supports the accusation and adds that the sum of the 20 thousand marks was to be received by Kozielski at the Dresdner Bank branch in Katowice.
Late at night the court pronounced the verdict, according to which the president of „Błyskawica“ is punished with 3 months in prison.

In today's issue we report on the peace agreement concluded in Sosnowiec concerning the rabbinate question; but, as it turns out, the fighting camp has not yet let the „stratagems of war“ out of its hands and is striving to have the kehilla elections invalidated.
In the complaint, which — as we are informed — is already prepared, it is pointed out that: 1) the elections did not take place according to the regulations, 2) votes were cast by people who are away on military exercises, 3) votes were cast in the names of persons long dead, and 4) many voters were not admitted to the ballot boxes at all.

Yesterday, on the name day of the President of the Republic, Prof. Ignacy Mościcki, a solemn prayer service took place in the Będzin synagogue, in which the rabbinate, kehilla representatives, school youth and others took part.
Mr. Baum with the choir sings the appropriate prayers, recites „Mi Sheberach“ blessings for the President of the State and Marshal Piłsudski; then each member of the rabbinate says a chapter of Psalms, and the school orchestra plays the Polish and the Jewish anthem.

The Sosnowiec commissioner, Mr. Kuźniak[?], received a delegation of the residents of Prez. Mościckiego Street and of Jagiellońska. Meeting of the Jewish Metal Guild in Sosnowiec
In the premises of the New Artisans' Association, Modrzejowska 19, the annual general meeting of the members of the guild takes place next Sunday at 5 in the afternoon. Christian Hooligans Attack the Jewish Girl Pupils at the Evening Courses
The Jewish pupils, and above all the girl pupils, who attend the evening courses at the Będzin Magistrate have to endure bitter troubles from non-Jewish pupils, who lie in wait for the moment the Jewish girls leave the school, and then they are pelted with stones and attacked in a base manner.
Last Tuesday evening, during such an assault, Mr. H. Broner[?] intervened at the police station. A przodownik [police sergeant] soon went there and drove the hooligans away.
One can only wonder that the director of the courses does not react to such hooligan deeds — or does he not know of them?

An Original Demonstration in Katowice
Yesterday an original demonstration took place in Katowice which aroused wide interest. Before the Voivodeship office 20 carriages drove up with citizens of Chorzów — merchants, artisans with their wives and children — who had come to protest against the proposal that Chorzów should belong to Königshütte [Królewska Huta].
