A protest meeting on the rabbinate question in Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — rabbinate; kehilla.] In the "Wenus" hall in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] a meeting on the rabbinate question took place on Sunday morning, chaired by the former president of the kehilla, Mr. Mitelman.
Notwithstanding that the competence to elect a rabbi lies exclusively in the hands of the kehilla council, a committee has nevertheless been formed (as we are informed, this is said to be a political manoeuvre of the "Agudah", so that the kehilla should open a second competition for rabbis), which occupies itself with the rabbinate question.
At the meeting a series of "speakers" came forward, who protested against the ruling of the rabbis that the rabbinical seat belongs to R' Baruch Epstein, the son-in-law of the deceased rabbi, who does not have the proper qualifications.
In this spirit appropriate resolutions were adopted.
1) In the name of today's mass meeting we express our mighty protest against the unheard-of injustice, in that they want to impose by violent means a candidate as rabbi and local rabbinic authority (mara de-atra) in the person of Mr. Baruch Epstein, who is not equal to the office [lit. "not grown up" to it]. We establish and declare categorically that we will react to this with all possible means.
2) We turn to all the rabbis and great men of Israel in Poland and in all the dispersions of the Exile with the request not to issue any opinion whatsoever regarding the rabbinical seat in Dąbrowa before they have acquainted themselves with public opinion on the spot; and those who have already permitted themselves to express their opinion without an understanding with the town should revise the decision, because they were badly informed by interested persons.
3) We turn to the gentlemen representatives of the kehilla to take into account the public opinion of the Jews of Dąbrowa and not to take the candidacy of Mr. Baruch Epstein into consideration at all.
Zagłębie on the Birthday of the New Constitution

[Zagłębie — state and constitution.]
The decorating of the houses with state flags on Saturday at first aroused astonishment. People did know that the constitution was being discussed in the Sejm, but nobody expected that a miracle would happen in the Sejm and that the constitution would be born so quickly.
In honour of the adoption of the new constitution, manifestations took place throughout Zagłębie and a resolution was adopted, in which the citizens of all strata of Zagłębie society welcome this great act of the people's representatives and with joy and pride wish the government, with its President at its head, that in the new organisational framework of the Polish state they may find enthusiasm for further untiring work for the fatherland and for the Polish people.
In all elementary and secondary schools ceremonial assemblies („akademies“) were held.
In the Sosnowiec synagogue Rabbi Hager delivered a sermon on Saturday morning about the new constitution.
Shlomo Gutman, of blessed memory (A Few Words in His Memory)

[Będzin — Memorial tribute; black-bordered.] On Monday [29 January 1934] the orphaned Jewish community of Będzin accompanied to his eternal rest one of its noblest citizens, the highly deserving communal worker Shlomo Gutman [Salomon Gutman], of blessed memory, who was suddenly torn away at the age of 63.
We would not be at peace with our civic conscience if we did not devote a few words to the exalted figure of the noble deceased, the fine man and warm Jew — two qualities that one very seldom meets among the communal workers of the present generation. The late Shlomo Gutman, of blessed memory, belonged to that type of communal worker whom one now encounters very rarely on the Jewish street, for he united in himself modesty, earnestness, wisdom and, what is most important, a large measure[?] of tolerance towards his political opponents.
For us, for the representatives of national Jewry, for those who take an interest in all Jewish problems — cultural, socio-economic and national alike — the death of Shlomo Gutman, of blessed memory, is an enormous loss. Those who have been engaged in public work in our town for a number of years know very well that whenever a public institution was founded, one could always count on the vigorous help of Shlomo Gutman, of blessed memory. One knew that with his deep understanding, noble heart and open hand he would help to found the institution and to lead it. It would be a great injustice to pass over in silence what Shlomo Gutman, of blessed memory, actually was for a number of years to the Jewish gymnasium in our town.
He was one of the few founders of the school; over the course of years he supported it with an open hand, and for a number of years he was its tireless president.
But when the great philanthropist of our town, Mr. Szymon Fürstenberg, erected a splendid building for the gymnasium, Shlomo Gutman, of blessed memory, understood that he must yield his place to Mr. Fürstenberg, and he left his honorary office quietly and calmly, with the feeling of a responsible public worker that the institution which he had co-founded and represented had grown enormously and that he was handing over its further fate into solid and secure hands.
Honour to his memory!
Szymon Żmucki[?],
member of the Supervisory Board of the Jewish Gymnasium named after “S. Fürstenberg and wife”, Będzin.

At the helm of the kehilla's affairs — The civic committee set up in Będzin and the Jewish kehilla

The civic committee that has been set up in Będzin and the Jewish kehilla.
A week ago, it seems, a brief notice slipped through the newspaper saying that a committee is being created in Będzin whose task will be to support the unemployed — and, most important of all, to combat begging. But, as it appears, what for us is the main thing, the essence, is for the newly created committee a side matter, a concern of the second category.
It goes without saying that we have nothing against the founders of the committee that has been created; and not only do we have nothing against them — their initiative is surely to be welcomed, for it is most certainly a good one, most certainly a devoted one. And yet it is not what we had in mind, not the thing about which we have so many times written and spoken, agitated and shed light. Besides, the creation is, as it turns out, more of an official matter, a general municipal one, because it is being formed around the magistrate [the city administration]. This committee is truly desirable and can without any doubt bring the town much benefit, given intensive activity and a proper understanding for those who are unemployed and have been drawn into the net of begging; and yet this is not what we had in mind. We would have needed a specifically Jewish committee, which would occupy itself with the special, specifically Jewish interests, with their sufferings and their poverty. We need a committee of Jews for Jews. Non-Jews cannot understand our impoverished sufferings; and besides, with us it is not only a matter of the professional beggars and the unemployed. We have, after all, a whole camp of, so to speak, "respectable ones" ("bekovede"), who indeed make their living from it — and that is something a non-Jew cannot understand, and besides one cannot make him understand it with the best will in the world.
In its time we made a suggestion to the Jewish kehilla representation, and we said then that however petty they may be, and however helpless and poor they may feel, they must nevertheless bring about the creation of such a committee. Be that as it may, they do after all claim to be raising Jewish honour — and how much merit our kehillas would have earned had they undertaken to solve the question that so darkens our already sufficiently darkened horizon.
Our kehilla representations — in recent years we have demanded nothing of them, because we knew well how far they are incapable of working, how far they have fallen behind, and to what extent everything was on every occasion calculated so that the activity should bring harm and loss. And it is indeed no wonder: every person with a logically thinking mind knew that nothing can be demanded of this "non-party" body, because it is a general rule that where one sows wind, no fruit can grow.
Did they, then, do anything more than quarrel and play, all the while, a behind-the-scenes politics in which the only aim was for one to trip up the other? And the moment anything came up, no meeting was called; it was considered superfluous to take counsel in order to find a way out — instead they at once carried the matter over to the authorities, at once went off to inform, and let them there, at the "high windows", find the solution. It goes without saying that thanks to these tactics nothing was done for the good of the Jewish citizens, for the good of the members of the Jewish kehilla; and not only was nothing done for their good, but on the contrary, everything began to sink and go under, and poverty on the one side and idleness on the other began to take the place of honour.
Well, when one finds oneself in such a stage of decline, in a kind of stage of losing one's balance, it is surely understandable that they have to keep out of the way of the public, of society, of the press.
The Jewish kehilla representation gives its member nothing; it does not come to his aid with anything at all, and if a citizen asks for something, he must pay separately for every trifle. The representatives take no account of the fact that he is burdened by them with the due taxes, and that he must hand over a share to the kehilla from his bit of meat even before he puts it in his mouth. None of this do they even begin to take into account; and had they taken it into account, had they at least wanted to take it into account, they would then have tried to see to easing and brightening Jewish life — naturally according to the most minimal possibilities at their disposal. The worst of it, however, is that nothing interests them. They seek only to obtain the "chairs", and afterwards let God take care, if things are not done as they should be. When they take over the chairs they consider it a duty to read out declarations and to paint the future work in bright colours, and soon after the declarations have been read out they immediately forget what they said, what they undertook to accomplish for the common good.
A chaos they knew how to bring into the Jewish kehillas, a fire they were able to fan, so that we should have to hide for shame; on the other hand they do not even think about improving the situation of the kehilla representatives [sic; evidently the kehilla representations] — if only they had given a thought to raising up these institutions, if only they had taken an interest in raising Jewish honour as far as it can possibly be done!
When the present leaders took over the leadership of the Jewish kehilla in Będzin, we told them that we certainly do not envy them the household they are taking over, because we knew quite well how everything there is rotten and mouldy and how poverty whistles everywhere; but still — we said — one must not stand by and look on indifferently at the sad state of affairs, because then everything becomes still more neglected and the situation grows still more dangerous, still uglier and more repulsive.
We told them then: if you cannot do anything at all, if you are not capable of raising up the Jewish representation to any extent whatsoever, you must nevertheless organise Jewish poverty, concentrate it in one place, because as things are we have both disgrace and humiliation and also pain and suffering; on top of that the public is being fleeced, and the sufferers do not have what they could and ought to have.
We said: begging is spreading more and more all the time and is taking on repulsive forms, because under the same mask individuals are operating, so that the citizens are fleeced and the truly oppressed, suffering and hungry person gets scarcely anything out of it.
Take this — we said — into your hands; see to bringing into order the matter which the time of crisis has called to life and which has become an everyday phenomenon, such as one sees among no other people in so broad a form as among us Jews; do not allow the harmful thing to take root in our body. Concentrate Jewish hunger and suffering around yourselves, create a fund for them. Every citizen will gladly give you what the regular alms cost him, and perhaps even more, and you will be the distributors, the representatives, the highest Jewish representation.
We said then: if you have done nothing until now towards improving the kehilla's household, then by creating this necessary institution you will have accomplished much to raise Jewish honour, and at the same time have set up an important undertaking.
But, as it appears, this is for you a burdensome thing or a superfluous matter, so that for the time being one must be content with the committee that has been created on the part of the magistrate's leadership — although this is not what we had in mind and what we had imagined.
This is what the activity of the present kehilla representatives in Będzin looks like, those who stand at the ruling helm.
R. Les.
The History of the Będzin Kehilla in the Second Half of the 19th Century. According to Archival Records. (5)

[History — the Będzin kehilla; serial, instalment 5.] By Moshe Feinkind. According to archival records.
In the meantime Modrzejów [printed „מאנדזשעוו“] rebelled, and in 1865 the local dozór members [community board], M. Szarf, J. Szajnweksler [?] and M. Goldfeld, turned to the governor with a petition in the name of 7[?] local Jewish families: since Modrzejów is a town inhabited mostly by Jews, who have their own synagogue there, a bet midrash, a mikveh and also a cemetery, and since from them to Będzin is a distance of seven versts and one cannot afford to travel to Będzin over every trifle to attend to one's religious needs, they therefore ask that the governor confirm a separate rabbi for Modrzejów; and as candidate they put forward R' Dawid Bunem Brechner, a local resident, to whom the town undertakes to pay one hundred roubles a year salary and a dwelling.
In fact Modrzejów had already, in the year 185[—], taken on R' Ruben Biksman [?] as rabbi, but because the town had not declared the undertaking, the governor held back from issuing the konsens [official licence], and by the time they were about to give him the konsens he had already left the country.
Now the mayor [burmistrz] came out in favour of R' Dawid Bunem Brechner and wrote to the gubernia that Rabbi Brechner knows Polish, German and Yiddish; Brechner also presented other good documents showing that he is politically unobjectionable and respectable, together with the rabbinical ordinations [heter hora'ah] from the rabbi of Olkusz R' Moshe Zajonc [?], from the rabbi of Żarki R' Moshe Baum, from the rabbi of Pławno R' Yisrael Itzik Kreinger [?] and from the rabbi of Radom R' Gabriel Danziger [?].
The rabbi of Pławno, Rabbi Kreinger [?], who had been a moreh hora'ah [rabbinical judge] in Piotrków, writes that R' Dawid Bunem Brechner studied with him continuously for 6 years, from 1858 to 1864 [?], and greatly distinguished himself in halakhic ruling so as to be a rabbi. The other rabbis write the same about him.
Because Rabbi Brechner is a native of Będzin, I wish to add that he was born there in 1844 to his parents R' Yochanan Joachim and Gitl. His father was a merchant. Until the age of 14 he kept [?] at his studies at home. Then Rabbi Brechner went to Pławno to study with Rabbi Klinger [sic]; having received ordination from the rabbi of Pławno, Rabbi Brechner married in [?] Modrzejów and became a dayan there, deputising there for the rabbi of Będzin, Rabbi Langfus, and receiving from the townlet a few gulden [złoty] a week.
The governor of Radom did not confirm Rabbi Brechner as rabbi in Modrzejów, as the dozór members had demanded, but only as assistant to the rabbi of Będzin (1866).
The Modrzejów dozór members, however, were not satisfied with this, and through the naczelnik [district chief] of Olkusz they addressed a second petition to the governor about separating Modrzejów from the Będzin kehilla and creating a separate district out of Modrzejów, Niwka, Sosnowiec and Sielce [printed „שעלצע“], and also about freeing them from paying the etat [community tax] in Będzin.
The naczelnik did indeed agree to this, but the governor found the separation of Modrzejów from Będzin very complicated because of the financial question and the like, demanding of the naczelnik that he submit an exact plan of the expenses connected with the separation, so that it should bring no harm to the Będzin kehilla, as well as statistics of the householders living in the proposed district, etc., etc.
Meanwhile the governor of Radom sternly called upon the Będzin kehilla to present at once a candidate for rabbi; otherwise he would be compelled to appoint a government rabbi himself.
Modrzejów, however, would on no account agree that the new rabbi of Będzin should have a say in their townlet, and a dispute „for the sake of Heaven“ flared up between the two towns. Będzin itself could not carry a rabbi on its shoulders. It had also undertaken, after Rabbi Langfus's death, to pay 30 roubles a year to the rabbi's widow; this sum it had previously paid to the old rebbetzin Gitele Majman, who just now had also died.
And wishing likewise to save the situation, Będzin now hastened to choose a rabbi. The kehilla put forward as candidate for the Będzin rabbinical seat the Piotrków moreh hora'ah R' Itzikl (Itshele) Kimelman (1866), with a salary of 360 roubles a year and free lodging, etc.
R' Itshele Kimelman had already held a konsens as dayan of Piotrków since the year 1853, which he had received from the governor of Warsaw, to whom Piotrków then belonged.
But because Rabbi Kimelman did not submit the original of his konsens, Radom confirmed him provisionally as deputy for a rabbi in the Będzin district. Only some time later, when Rabbi Kimelman had submitted the original, was he appointed permanent rabbi in Będzin. And Modrzejów remained, as before, a branch [filia] of the Będzin kehilla.
The early sixties were very hard for the Będzin kehilla.
Because of the „powstanie“ [the Polish uprising of 1863] Jewish trade was completely paralysed.
The Jews of Będzin sympathised strongly with the uprising, just as they had sympathised with Kościuszko's uprising (1794), collecting money for the benefit of the uprising; and many of the Będzin householders even took part personally in the fight for freedom. As is recorded in the gendarmerie's gubernial control books, Joachim Manszajn [?] of Modrzejów was punished with three years under strict police supervision for spreading lampoons against the government, as were many other Jews (Police Supervision of the Piotrków gubernia, page 294 and others).
The Jewish population, it seems, became greatly impoverished at that time, being unable to pay any large etat.
The etat for those years amounted in all to 226 roubles. The highest sum came to three roubles. Of 235 registered householders only 175 paid the etat. With the engagement of the rabbi the budget rose to a sum of 840 roubles, and the assessment [rozkład] was for 331 roubles, which were imposed on 341 householders, and the highest sum was now 5 roubles.
It will not be superfluous to give here a few biographical details about the rabbi of Będzin, R' Itshele Kimelman.
R' Itshele Kimelman had earlier been a dayan in Pilica [Pilts]; in 5608 (1848) he became head of the rabbinical court in Piotrków, where he distinguished himself both in learning and in piety. In Piotrków he received a salary of 150 roubles a year.
And since he was a great hater of gain and yet could not manage on that small salary, the town wanted to give him an increase, but the authorities refused this because of the critical time of the year 1863.
But after great effort the governor of Warsaw finally agreed to double his salary.
Meanwhile Rabbi Kimelman accepted the rabbinical seat in Będzin and was rabbi and head of the yeshiva here for 27 years, spreading Torah in Israel.
Rabbi Kimelman corresponded in halakhic responsa with the greatest geonim of his time; the „Chiddushei HaRim“, in a responsum to him, titles him „the sharp and erudite rabbi“ (the monthly „Or Torah“, issue 1, 5691 [1930/31]).

Trade in Liquidation

The situation of trade and of merchants in Zagłębie is well known to me. Almost every day I meet with these matters, and I have the opportunity to become more closely acquainted with the painful and sad phenomenon in the present state of trade.
My article is devoted to the cruel economics that reign in Zagłębie. I am convinced, however, that in other towns the situation is no better, and that wherever commercial life still pulsates the same rhythm is being played out, so that my observations and remarks will everywhere be a reflection of the sad reality.
A small, or perhaps a large, part of the readers, on reading through the title of my article, will surely regard me as a hundred-per-cent pessimist, or a fantasist, because I write about a trade that is in the stage of liquidation at a time when, in the streets of our town, the number of commercial enterprises is not growing smaller at all but, on the contrary — one sees, after all, that in this street or that, dwellings are being rebuilt into shops, and in the newly built houses commercial premises are being fitted out; where, then, is the ground for speaking of the decline of trade? Such superficiality may indeed call forth the opinion that I have exaggerated and overrated the situation of trade. After reading my article through, however, you, esteemed readers, will come to a different conclusion and will certainly agree that there is not the slightest shadow of pessimism or fantasy here.
A correct and indisputable criterion, and a thermometer that cannot mislead, is in every field the quality and not the quantity [said twice in the original, once in Germanic and once in Hebrew terms: „der eykhes un nisht der kames“]. Just as in a river it is not the multitude that decides but the kind of fish found in it. A picture, too, we value according to its quality, and we take little account of its artificially gilded frame.
The shops existing in our town are — through the fiscal tax burdens and the scanty credit, or the complete absence of credit — so poor in goods that pity seizes a person looking at the merchants who seek the protection of Mercury. They stand from early morning until late in the evening in their shops, into which tuberculosis bacilli are constantly stealing, making a consumptive skeleton of the commercial enterprises that only a short time ago were blooming and growing.
Merchants have always been regarded as people of initiative, orientation and a spirit of enterprise, with the qualifications of knowing people and markets. Formerly, at the beginning, they opened small shops, which later — for the most part — grew into stores [magazinen], warehouses and trading houses. Today, by contrast, we see how for 3 years now the same merchants, at the season for purchasing the trade patents [annual trade licences], change their patents in the minus and not in the plus, i.e. they reduce their patents, and this goes together with the shrinking of consumption and of the stock of goods [„skhoyre-laze“ — doubtful reading]. Some merchants, who are no longer able to carry on the sick and consumptive trade, liquidate their commercial enterprises entirely, and in their place hairdressing establishments, chemical laundries and bakeries are opening.
Our eyes, which once saw shop-windows with all kinds of goods — we now see laundered collars, ladies' coiffures, bagels and pastries [„tshastes“ — Polish ciastka].
Trade has always been regarded as a spreader of prosperity. It was also maintained that it helps people and nations to become acquainted with one another, to spread culture and to increase the power and influence of industry. Do you know what role it plays today? It has become a „superfluous middleman“.
Once trade had the possibility of enjoying all the good things the world possesses, which were brought by various merchants from various points of the whole globe. One could wear an Italian hat, smoke a cigarette of Turkish tobacco in French cigarette-paper [bibulke], write with a Waterman pen on German [?] paper, sitting on a Viennese chair in an English suit of Australian wool, drinking Ceylon tea with an Italian lemon from a Czech cup (please do not suspect me of praising what is foreign and disparaging what is our own). Today, by contrast, we have import quotas [contingents], compensations and, in general, restrictions that make import impossible, even on the smallest scale.
Almost all states suffer from a mania of autarky (self-sufficiency). They lock their doors against the import of foreign manufactures and products. At the same time they support export at home and take no account of the dumping they create in other countries. The consequences are that when a state comes up against high customs duties, it shuts itself up behind its [?] locks and does not allow products to be imported, even such as are lacking in its own country and whose lack makes itself painfully felt.
Here we come up against roads closed to trade. Mobile trade, which tolerates no restrictions, has contracted a hardening of the blood and can no longer circulate freely. A blood-bearing artery has become calcified — the so-called sclerosis — and has ceased to circulate.
Does one not see here plainly the beginning of the liquidation of trade?
(Conclusion to follow.)
A. Perin.
“Reb Lekachs”... (A Type from Type-Land)

[Sosnowiec — satirical feuilleton, kehilla.] (A type from Type-Land)
Many decades ago, in the town that lies on the little river “Przemsza”, there were dozors [members of the kehilla board, dozór bóżniczy] who were called “Reb Lekachs” [from Hebrew lakach, “took”: “the Takers”].
And in the town lived Jews of all kinds: pious ones, free-thinkers, clever ones and fools, wicked and righteous. The town possessed everything: rebbes, rabbis, ritual slaughterers, religious judges, melamdim, idlers, a burial society, gravediggers, gabbai-women, a bathhouse, mikveh attendants and — to distinguish “by a thousand distinctions” — also a “holy congregation” (hold your noses!...)
Naturally, if there is a kehilla in a town and Jews by the name of “Reb Lekachs” live there, those same “Reb Lekachs” must be members of the kehilla board, for who on earth is fit for the kehilla if not “Reb Lekachs”?...
So our dear “Reb Lekachs” did indeed sit in the kehilla and turned the wheel there as they know how and as it paid them..
The “Reb Lekachs” flattered everyone: the artisans, the common crowd, the intelligentsia, the Hasidim, the rabbis, even the adherents of “Beit Yaakov”. But in mind they had only themselves... as is the way of a Jew whose name is “Reb Lekach”....
In this way the “Reb Lekachs” became the masters of the town. If a shochet wanted to settle there, he first had to “see” one of the “Lekachs”... If someone wants to lease the bathhouse, he must first come to terms with “Mr. Lekach”; if someone needs — may “He will swallow up death forever” come true — a burial slip for a deceased, he must first “pay a visit” to “Mr. Lekach”.. When one speaks of the “master” of the town, it goes without saying...
In this way the kehilla's economy went to ruin, institutions went under, societies closed down, poor people perished in the winter frosts of hunger and cold — all because of the deeds of the “Reb Lekachs”, who used to make mock of everyone, indeed of everyone, even of the “wise men” who had propped them up and put the “government” into their hands... They, the “wise men”, used to quarrel with each and every one, to buy themselves dozens of enemies, and all so that the “Reb Lekachs” might be able to do everything that their “upright conscience” permits them — the well-known conscience of “Reb Lekach”...
—
An old Jew told me this story, which happened long years ago; today, in the twentieth century, such a thing could not happen even in Sosnowiec...
Eh, what do you think?
X [Iks].
Art and Criticism

[Zagłębie — culture; essay.] From my book of essays.
To cut open the warm, feathered little throat of a nightingale and want to touch her song with one's hands, or to pluck apart a rose, a flower, a chrysanthemum, and want to sense its fragrance with a polyp-ridden [?] nose — to what may this be likened? — it is like a surgeon in a white coat, a vivisection knife in his hand, who steps up to perform an autopsy on the soul of a little book of poems...
The poet's heart is a holy of holies, a mysteriously hidden tent into which he himself, too, enters only in rare minutes and long-yearned-for moments — there hangs a golden string, a lyre...
The poet's heart is a blue sea-mirror in which an outsider's eye does not discern when stormy waves are about to roar up and the mirror will be shattered [?].
A reservoir of concentration, a cable of thousands of knotted threads.
Such is the poet's power of imagination: it weaves, it spins, it plaits; something has caught fire, something is burning — a fire, a flame, a flickering —
It is the mighty feeling of a creative season.
Thus the poet is fertilized, swept along and choked like a drowning man in a sea of bell-like [?] convulsion. He wraps himself in waves of the creative element. He drinks the chaos of a mighty feeling, until a tremor runs through — the golden string in the poet's heart; sounds flow apart in stormy emotions; a secret hand takes down with fiery tongs the glowing coal from the creative altar and touches with it the artist's lips, and drives him, chases him like a dreadful fate [fatum]; he chokes in long-yearned-for torments. Of birth-pangs, until he trembles awake, grows ripe. A flash of spiritual radiance. The secret of communion...
And the poet's womb bursts open. Flung wide are the doors of his hidden sanctuary —
The poet spits out a poem...
Yechiel Feiner.
Heard and Seen.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

On the other side of the bridge...
In the Chumash, in last week's Torah portion, it is told:
"The Jews walked in the wilderness and found no water. So the 'people' came to Moses with the complaint:
— Give us water to drink!
And the Almighty, as it were, said to Moses: strike the rock at Horeb with a staff and water will come out of it; and Moses did so, and the people had water to drink."
I was reminded of that miracle when I found myself in the home of an acquaintance of mine, who lives
— on the other side of the bridge...
The clock already showed that it was time for the afternoon prayer (Mincha), but the people of the house had not yet eaten their midday meal.
Not, heaven forbid, because the grosz was lacking to buy the necessary "potrawy" [dishes] for the meal, but because of a trouble that happened precisely in the wilderness
— there is no water...
Ever since the magistrate [city hall] bestowed a water main upon the town, the inhabitants there have been suffering from
— the water trouble.
In the early days water was still drawn from the wells; true, to get a bucket of water one had to toil hard and bitterly, but it was, as they say — half a trouble. But for several months now the inhabitants of the streets Browarna, Gzichowska and half of Czeladzka have been as thirsty as the Jews of old who wandered in the wilderness, and they cry out to the magistrate:
— Help! Give us water..
And the magistrate fobs off the water-criers with promises, has even already assigned a certain sum for the work, but meanwhile a little water on Browarna Street is held in greater esteem than genuine Carmel wine...
People do not allow themselves — so I am told — to wash properly; they do not let go to waste
— a drop of water; and the little story from the Chumash repeats itself, not, heaven forbid, in the deserts, but
— on the other side of the bridge...

It came a little late...
A new chapter in the Arlosoroff tragedy: "The chief prosecutor in Jerusalem has arrested two Arabs who are said to have confessed to committing the murder of Dr. Arlosoroff" — so it is reported from Jerusalem.
The sensational news was carried by the entire Jewish press; the only difference is this: in the newspaper that stands close to Revisionism we read that "the Arab murderers have confessed", while the newspaper where they wink with one eye at the radical Zionists brings the news with caution, for example: "the Arabs are said to have confessed".
And the third side, what does it say? The "side" that looks at the course of the trial a little more soberly — repeats the same thing it said right at the beginning of the accusation against the Revisionists, namely that
— "an Arab hand is in the matter".. that the unforgettable Dr. Arlosoroff fell at the hands of Arab murderers, of the same killers who have already slain enough innocent martyrs.
Well, and why has the truth been discovered only now? — For that, too, my neighbour has an answer.
It is exactly — he says — like a married couple that keeps on fighting, and the only way out that would put an end to their tragic life is to go to the rabbi and
— take a divorce...
But when the rabbi hears out the foolish reasons that cause the quarrels, he intervenes and makes peace between the couple...
Whether the peace is a lasting one or not is a matter in itself; the main thing is only that in the first period after the peace is concluded the couple lives like little doves...
The moral? Both sides, the "Histadrut" and the Revisionists, have always lived with one another like cat and mouse; well, once the murder came along, it was surely an opportune moment to raise an outcry
— The Revisionists are upon thee, Israel!
Such "bombs" as "murderers, pimps, knife-stabbers" are very good instruments of war, especially for Congress elections... But when the hot blood is already growing cooler, and the mutual attacks are already overstepping the bounds of ethics and morality — suddenly the great "secret" was discovered, the covering veil was removed, and then one beheld
— the Arab murderers...
Good tidings, upon my life: the news has removed the mark of Cain not only from the Revisionists but from the whole of Jewry; it is, however, to be regretted that the tidings
— came a little late...

An easy income...
For the institutions, both communal and philanthropic, we have a proposal that can improve their budgets, secure their existence and rid them at one stroke of the constant worry
— where does one get money?
Our proposal is that in every institution, every society, there should be opened
— a card club...
A small expense, and the income — a great deal.
As an example that our proposal is a practical one and can bring enormous material benefit, we may cite the budget of the new "Klub Towarzyski" [Social Club] in Będzin.
Here we read in black and white that the income side of the budget foresees a revenue of 3,600 gulden [złoty], that is to say, a firm 300 gulden a month from
— card-playing...
Such a "dochód" [income] no event whatsoever can bring, no "wieczór taneczny" [dance evening], and not even a premiere of the "Muza"...
Therefore our proposal is that every society, association, and likewise every organization that wants to have a "zapewniona egzystencja" [assured existence] should open
— a card club.
A small expense and a large income; the main thing is
— an easy income...

If only not...
Having heard the good tidings that in Sosnowiec, in the quarrelsome town, the "Burgfrieden" [civil truce] has been concluded, I dropped everything, bag and baggage, and off I went to Sosnowiec.
I hoped to find a jubilee mood; in my imagination pictures were weaving themselves of "And it shall come to pass in the end of days": hatred over, quarrels over, the sins committed in the "Seven Years' War" forgotten.
— Peace upon Sosnowiec!
But on entering "Modrzejowska" Street I see "two Hebrew men striving": two Jews quarrelling, cursing each other with the vilest curses.
— What is the matter with you? What is it again? Surely there is already peace in your town?
— Eh? What are you saying — peace? You surely remember the saying in the Midrash that at the creation of the world, in the order of the work of Creation, on Friday at twilight there were created
— demons...
The peace too — says one of the quarrel-mongers — was likewise made on a Friday, 2 minutes before candle-lighting, and it too can create new
— demons...
Ashamed, I went away from the quarrelling camp and quietly murmured:
— If only not...
The Story of an Old, Sturdy Tree...

[Feuilleton — a parable for Tu BiShvat.] By Dovid Zisman [Dawid Zysman].
(A little tale for the Fifteenth [of Shevat])

It was long, long years ago, in an old, an age-old time; it was in the time when human wickedness had not yet penetrated everywhere, and over the kingdom of the trees no one yet had any dominion. It was still before Tubal-Cain, the first master of iron, came into the world. No axe and no saw had yet been invented, and freely the trees then lived in the forest; they feared no one. Freely they developed, freely they grew; their tips they sent far, far out beneath the heavens [printed: „ארונטערגעלאזט“, literally "let down" (?)]; their body was strong and thick, but their stem too was strong. Deep they drew their roots into the earth, and, drawing nourishment from the most hidden, deepest springs, they fortified and strengthened their stem, so that even the greatest winds had not the power to tear them out of their stem...

And it was good for the trees in the forest, and ever higher, broader and deeper they grew, and ever finer and tastier were the fruits they bore, and ever more fragrant became the air around them, which filled with heavenly scents; and good and contented, harmonious and merry was the life of the trees in the forest, and they kept on praising the Creator of the world without cease, and in their rhythmic swaying they would compose and fervently sing songs and praises to the Master of the Worlds.

But other times came.
By the side of the forest a second forest grew up, which was stronger, mightier and taller than it, and its heavy, thick branches it stretched over the forest's sky and covered the sun from it.

And it grew dark in the forest. The song of the trees fell silent, and their free life, their free development, came to a halt. They could no longer grow upward, because the neighbouring trees did not let them. And so years upon years went by. The one forest grew ever darker and the trees ever weaker and more dispirited. Rarely, rarely it would happen that a single tree, which could not bear this situation, would break through by force through the dense, cruel branches; but, coming out into the high air of freedom, it would at once be scorched by the sun's rays and wither away from its stem altogether... But worst of all was this: that the trees had already ceased altogether [?] to strive to tear themselves out of their situation. They remembered that once it had been very good and merry among them in the forest. But all of that seemed to them like a legend... And ever quieter became their swaying, and ever lower their branches would bend, and their skin grew pale...

Times went and times came, and in the forest a new generation of young, tender little trees grew up. Great was the love of the old trees for them, because with their beauty and charm they reminded them of their own youthful days; it became a little noisier and more comfortable in the forest; the young little trees would somehow sway and wink among themselves more noisily. And all at once they all began to argue with one voice: „It is cramped for us in the forest, we want to grow upward, we want to break through the branches that cover us, we want to reach the sun, the light.

Then the old trees shook themselves angrily and began to rage: „Why are you straining toward the sun?“ Better grow in breadth, better take root in your stem; it is dangerous to look straight into the sun, one may yet be blinded by it.

But the young ones did not want to listen; to the sun, to the light — they cried — we are not afraid!

And a terrible quarrel broke out among the trees in the forest, and when the moment came when the fate of the trees is decided, when the New Year of the Trees came, the old trees prayed to the Master of the Universe that He should mend the thoughts of the young little trees, or else destroy them altogether.

The young little trees, too, wanted to set about asking something of the Master of the Universe, but they did not know any „ivre“ [how to read the Hebrew of the prayers]..

And God then grew angry at the trees, and as a punishment He then created „Tubal-Cain“, the first master of iron; he devised an axe and a saw, with which the trees are continually destroyed — but not only the young ones“...

* * *

Dear readers! You surely understand the meaning of this little tale. You know the story of the old, sturdy tree, for whom it was at first so bright and afterwards became so dark, and you surely remember the quarrel between old and young; their separate currents and prayers always bring harm. Always, after that, a Tubal-Cain rises up with an axe in his hand and ruins both the young ones and the old...

Harmony must be brought in between these currents. Let the old not wish to cover with dense branches the free air from the eyes of the young. But let the young take better root in their stem, let them learn „ivre“ more thoroughly...
Radio Bulletin

[Radio.]
Yossele Rosenblatt on the radio!
In order to honour the memory of the late king of Jewish cantors, Yossele Rosenblatt, Polish Radio will give the Jewish radio listeners several of his best cantorial creations on gramophone records.
This broadcast will take place on Tuesday, 6 February, at exactly 10 in the evening.
The Jewish radio listeners will certainly listen with pleasure to this concert of the finest cantorial music.
—o—
Stavisky's swindles on the radio.
It now turns out that the notorious Russian swindler Stavisky made use of the Paris radio for his swindles.
He came to an understanding with the radio station of the Eiffel Tower, which received 200 thousand francs for two radio advertisements about the credit bonds of the Bayonne pawnshop.
In connection with this, arrests are being made also among the management of the French radio station.
—o—
Japan's flirt with Germany.
For a short time now one can notice in the "air" how Germany and Japan are flirting with each other. Over the radio waves the two states send each other the most cordial greetings. Besides this, a mutual exchange of programmes often takes place. On the radio the Hitler people put on Japanese gramophone records, and the Japanese envoy in Berlin gives a speech on that occasion for the German radio listeners. The same also happens in Japan, where the transmissions of German records are given with an introductory word by the German ambassador in Tokyo.
The reasons for this pronounced radio flirt must be sought in the analogous political circumstances of the two countries. Both Germany and Japan have left the League of Nations, and their common enemy is Soviet Russia.
—o—
Radio sets in all schools.
The Italian government has recognised radio as an important factor in the field of Fascist propaganda.
To this end Mussolini has ordered that in all Italian schools there must be a radio set.
The Ministry of Posts has already set about producing a model of such a school set, which is to pick up solely the one station of Rome.
The whole plan of "radiofying" the Italian schools will be carried out this year.

Parashat Yitro
The Portion
—o—
a) "And Jethro heard" (Ex. 18:1)
"What report did he hear, that he came? — The splitting of the Red Sea and the war of Amalek." Rashi.
He came to see such a remarkable people: a people before whom the sea splits, a people of miracles and wonders, a people of the splitting of the Red Sea — and nevertheless "and the war of Amalek". And nevertheless the Amalekites are not frightened by that and pick a fight with it... Imrei Noam.
—o—
b) "And it came to pass on the morrow, that Moses sat to judge the people" (ibid., 13)
"And it came to pass on the morrow — it was the day after Yom Kippur." Rashi.
It was the night after Yom Kippur, only a few hours after everyone had forgiven one another everything — and already Moses was besieged by litigants quarrelling with each other, by a whole camp of wrangling parties... That is how Jews were already in their first desert period.. Parpera'ot la-Chokhmah.
—o—
c) "From the morning unto the evening" (ibid., 14)
"...rather, every judge who judges a case with absolute truth... it is as though he became a partner of the Holy One, blessed be He, in the work of Creation." Rashi.
The rabbi of Lemberg, R' Z. W., once conducted a din-Torah and, as was his custom, issued a "lukewarm" ruling, a compromise one, neither this way nor that.
As he was leaving[?], one of the arbitrators accompanied him. The day was a mild one, and R' Z. W. talks about the weather... "Good weather, not hot and not cold"...
— That is — the arbitrator answers — because you have become a partner of God in the work of Creation. So the weather belongs to the two of you, and "a pot of partners is neither cold nor hot" (Eruvin 3); therefore the weather is neither hot nor cold.. The thing is, however, that in your ruling God is also a partner, and the ruling too is "a pot of partners", which is neither warm nor cold...
—o—
d) "And God shall be with thee" (ibid., 19)
If you will not heed me — Jethro argued to Moses — and free yourself a little from communal affairs, the Divine Presence too will not be with you, because communal affairs bring sadness with them, and "the Divine Presence does not rest amid sadness". If you give yourself over so much to communal affairs, you will forfeit the world to come as well.. Therefore: "I will give thee counsel, and God shall be with thee"... Ma'amar Avraham[?].
—o—
d) [sic — the letter is printed twice] "Hating unjust gain" (ibid., 21)
Today's rabbis — said R' Yoshe Ber — are true haters of gain: they hate money and give it away for the rabbinical chairs..
• • •
Once, he who was a prodigy with a "good head" and possessed no money became a rabbi, and he who had money became a merchant. Today it is a topsy-turvy world. He who has money becomes a... rabbi, and he who has a prodigy's head for "wheeling and dealing" and has no money becomes... a merchant. Nachalei Devash.
—o—
e) "In the sight of all the people" (19:11)
"This teaches that there was not a blind man among them, for all had been healed." Mekhilta.
R' Aharle of Chernobyl[?] once argued it out with the Master of the Universe thus:
You want us Jews to fulfil the Torah. But recall, Father in heaven, under what circumstances You gave the Torah to the Jews: at that time Jews were rich. They had the spoil of Egypt and the spoil of the sea; Jews were healthy, the blind had become seeing and all the sick had been healed; the Jews were free. If You want us to fulfil the old Torah today — see to it, Master of the Universe, that today too we are all healthy and strong as at the Giving of the Torah, that today too we have a spoil of Egypt and a spoil of the sea... and that we too, as then, be free of exile... When all that comes to be, we too shall today renew the receiving of the Torah.. Eretz ha-Chayim.
—o—
f) "Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain" (20:7)
"The whole world trembled at the moment the Holy One, blessed be He, said 'Thou shalt not take'." Tractate Shevuot.
Why precisely at this commandment did the world shudder?
It is just that at "Thou shalt not steal" and "Thou shalt not murder" the world did not tremble: never mind, a dispensation will surely be found to steal after all, supposedly for the sake of Heaven... for God's sake; likewise with all the other transgressions — under the mask of holiness one will be allowed to commit them... But when God said "Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain" — do not take God's name for your falsehoods — the world shuddered: now one will no longer be allowed to commit all the thefts and murders in God's name... Chezyonot Avraham.
—o—
g) "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house" (ibid., 14)
The Gemara (Sanhedrin 86) infers that all the Ten Commandments refer only to "souls" [capital matters]: by "Thou shalt not steal" is meant "one who steals souls" [kidnapping]; by "Thou shalt not murder" the soul is certainly meant; the question then arises: "Thou shalt not covet" refers only to "thy neighbour's house" — here, surely, it is not a person's life that is spoken of but his property?
To this R' Yechezkele of Kuzmir answered: whoever covets a person's property thereby covets his life — "for it takes away the soul of its owner"; a robber often takes away not only the other man's money but also the other man's life... Nechmad mi-Zahav.
• • •
R' Nachman of Bratslav expresses this in his own language:
A person's soul is scattered through his property and his belongings, and whoever robs a person's property robs his soul too... Likutei Moharan.
—o—
h) "Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long" (ibid., 12)
Why was long life promised precisely at the commandment of honouring?
Because for the most part parents become a burden to their children when the parents are already in old age, and then the parents' length of days is too great in the children's eyes. More than one daughter-in-law says: the old woman is already old enough... Therefore the verse says: Honour thy father and thy mother — let their length of days not be a burden to you; by that merit you too will live long. Kad ha-Kemach.
—o—
i) "Ye shall not make with Me gods of silver" (ibid., 20)
Do not serve Me — says God — for the sake of money; do not be God-fearing because that can bring you money... R' Yaakov Aharon Voloshiner[?].
The Coming City-Council Elections

[Municipal politics — the city-council elections.] By Advocate E. Kamerman.

The city-council elections are approaching. Attention must therefore be drawn to the fact that the authoritative circles want to publish the date at the last minute, or at such a date that there will not even be time left to think about election preparations, and still less about the candidates.

After the date of the elections is published, the lists of candidates will have to be submitted at once, and within a very short time the elections will take place. So it was during the elections to the commune (gmina) councils in the villages and, lately, in the towns of Pomerania [Pomorze].

From this we Jews must draw the proper conclusions. Practice up to now shows that, notwithstanding the losses suffered, the same mistakes are often repeated at elections instead of being avoided. It is characteristic that the Jewish groupings always submit a large number of candidate lists. More than once there have already been cases where there were more[?] lists than groupings. This is explained by the fact that within the political groupings themselves quarrels broke out over the persons put forward, and at the last minute they split into factions which, out of personal ambition, put forward representatives of their own. There were also cases where people not politically engaged came to an understanding among themselves and submitted candidate lists. The effect of such a policy is always the same: the scattering of votes has never brought anyone any benefit.

Least of all have we Jews, as citizens, reckoned with this; and when it turned out after the elections that we had lost a great deal because of it, we were compelled to acquiesce, without drawing from it the necessary conclusions as regards the mistaken policy of our representatives. So it was, for example, at the last Sejm elections, which led to the result that, because of the large number of Jewish lists, the votes were splintered, and that is why we have today the smallest number of Sejm deputies since the Polish parliament has existed.

With the city-council elections, as far as one can infer from the policy pursued until now, it will not be much better. And if one also takes into account that the elections will be held according to the new electoral ordinance, on completely new foundations, which complicate the electoral system to a great degree, the prospects[?] are quite sad.

It is difficult, within the frame of an article, to discuss these regulations precisely; nevertheless we want, simply for the sake of orientation, to stress that the present electoral system is an entirely new one. First of all, the age qualification for voters and for those elected has been raised. The active franchise [so printed] belongs to one who is over 30 years of age and commands the Polish language in writing and in speech. As far as Jewish councillors are concerned, no attention has been paid until now to their writing in Polish. The passive franchise [so printed] belongs to one who is over 24 years of age and has lived for more than a year in the given locality (until now: the age of 21 and 6 months' residence in the given locality). Towns with more than 5 thousand inhabitants are divided into electoral districts, and for each district separately, depending on the number of inhabitants, the number of seats is fixed.

For Jews, the manner of the division into districts, and the population that will belong to a district, will be very important. To each electoral district a minimum of 3 seats will fall. A novelty in the elections will be that in each district the councillors are elected by a vote by name, instead of, as until now, for a list. The place on the list has no decisive significance, because the voter does not vote for a list but, as we have mentioned, for persons. Since the election of this or that councillor depends to a great degree on the will of the voters, discarding the principle of lists, the law brings the voter into an "umdirektn"[?] [so printed; by the context: immediate, direct] contact with the candidate, bypassing the political groupings that are represented by the lists. The law proceeds here from the premise that local economic, cultural and administrative questions need not be settled on political ground. The number of candidates on the individual lists may not exceed 3 times the number of seats of the given district.

A novelty is also the form of voting: every voter disposes of as many votes as the number of councillors the given electoral district elects; if, for example, 3 councillors are elected, every voter has 3 votes; if 4 councillors — 4 votes, and so on. The voter may give each of his votes to separate candidates, and for that purpose may write on the ballot paper the full number of candidates that falls to the district. The voter may also give all, or part, of his votes to one and the same candidate. The voter may, however, vote only for persons who figure on the same candidate list. The manner of distributing the seats is already very complicated.

As can be seen from the above, the manner of exercising their franchise is so far unknown to many Jews — to say nothing of the manner of drawing up the candidate lists!... This proves that it is necessary first of all to acquaint the broad public with, and teach it, the fundamental laws of the new electoral ordinance. It is therefore necessary to work so that the danger of putting forward a large number of candidate lists, which helps to splinter the votes, is avoided.

In the name of the general Jewish interest, properly understood, it is necessary to create one Jewish electoral bloc.

The chairmen of the individual factions or groupings must place the general interest above their private one and adopt all possible means to unite Jewry in the individual electoral localities. They must remember that for the outcome of the coming elections, and for the struggle for the rights, existence and honour of the Jewish people, it is they who bear the responsibility.

It must be stressed here that this has already been understood by the Jews in other countries, where all, without distinction of party and tendency, have, in view of the threatening danger, begun to unite. Thus there lately came about a general Jewish electoral bloc for the parliamentary elections in Romania, which gave good results.

According to reports reaching us, the Jews in Warsaw are beginning to understand this, and they too are endeavouring to create one Jewish electoral bloc for the coming city-council elections.

We cannot pass over[?] the fact that the Polish municipal groupings have long been conducting pre-election negotiations among themselves, and echoes reach us of various talks on the composition of persons and on the number of candidates.

We therefore hold that we Jews, too, must not remain indifferent to the pre-election campaign. The most proper thing would be for the Jewish councillors to convene a conference at which all matters connected with the coming city-council elections would be discussed, and also to elect a committee that would occupy itself with the further work in this field. The committee must also convene information meetings, where the form and technique of the elections would simply be taught.

One must remember, however, that time is short and that one must set to work as quickly as possible.

Regulations concerning auctions

[Law — notice.] The rule that the buyer of an article at an auction need pay at once only 20 per cent of the purchase price has been accepted by the new Code of Civil Procedure — but only in cases where the articles bought amount to over 5 thousand złoty; if, however, a smaller sum is involved, the buyer is obliged to pay in immediately.

In the contrary case the purchase is annulled, the auction begins anew, and the buyer no longer has any right to take part in it. Moreover, the court may even impose on such a bidder a fine amounting to one fifth of the price offered.

—o—

Turnover tax of artisans

[Taxes — notice.] One and a half per cent for the year 1932, and one per cent of turnover for the year 1933 and for the following years, will be paid only by those artisans who possess artisan's cards.

As for those craftsmen and industrial entrepreneurs who do not possess artisan's cards, they must pay 2 per cent turnover tax.
The Jewish Queen of Yemen (4)

[Serialized historical tale — Yemen, King Yusuf Dhu Nuwas; installment 4.]
Sh. Berg.

Yusuf Dhu Nuwas [printed "De Nuwas"] was a decent [?] man. He had all the virtues and all the faults of his people, the Arabs: a broad heart, heroism, and great hospitality. He protected travellers passing through and often helped them. But he also loved to plunder. In this he was a true [?] child of the desert. Especially great was his will to force his faith upon others by violence and, with the power of his sword, to compel them to convert to Judaism. He was seldom at home. He was always busy making order in the lands that were under him, or away at war with peoples near and far. But when he was at home he loved to spend his time with Pnina and Tzarida. They played and sang, and he told them of his experiences in his wars.

He had not married and did not think about love. His fanaticism for his faith and his thirst for victory had so hardened him that he did not look at women at all. Pnina and Tzarida were the mistresses of the house and they ran the household. They had many slaves and maidservants at their command.

So three and a half years went by. Pnina turned seventeen [?]. Her beauty blossomed like a wondrously lovely flower, and her charm had no equal. Yusuf Dhu Nuwas came home from a victorious war and brought with him a great deal of booty. And when he caught sight of Pnina in her full beauty, a wondrous change took place in him. He suddenly saw the woman, and his hardened heart was kindled with the blazing [?] fire of Eastern love. And he never acted slowly, with calculation, but did everything quickly, with storm, suddenly.

As soon as Yusuf Dhu Nuwas felt that he loved Pnina, he sent for her. She was accustomed to play and sing for him. So she took her harp along and went in to him. She never used to sing any love songs — he did not like them. So she always sang religious songs, mostly chapters of Psalms. How surprised she was when he told her to sing a love song. But she mastered herself and at once began to sing one of the most beautiful love songs of the East.

Yusuf caught fire. His face [?] became a blaze of flame. Sparks flew from his eyes and he stormed [?] like the storm of Yemen. He could hardly wait for her to finish, and he threw himself at her feet and spoke in a trembling voice:

"Pnina, Pnina, my captive! You are no longer my captive — I am your captive! I am your slave and you are my mistress!"

Pnina stood trembling, at a loss, and could not utter a word, and he went on speaking and pleading:

"Pnina! I could have treated you as a captive. But I did not do so. I paid you great honour, I honoured you so because I serve the God whom you serve. You were a sister to me, because you are descended from King David, my great-grandfather; now look. See, King Yusuf Dhu Nuwas, before whom nations tremble, lies at your feet and bows down to the dust of your footsteps, Pnina! This comes from my great love for you; I have never loved. Pnina! You are the first love of my life; you are the first woman who rules over me. It is the power that drew Samson the Mighty to itself."

Trembling, Pnina stammered out:

"Who am I, then, good, strong king? By what have I — a poor girl, an orphan, a captive — deserved that the mighty ruler of Yemen should lower himself and marry me?"

"Do not be lowly and fallen in your own eyes because of your poverty," he pleaded. "Soon Yemen with its rich treasures will lie at your feet. You will be the queen of Yemen and the most beautiful queen in the world. You will be the ruler of my kingdom and of my life. It is nothing that you are poor: our ancestor, King David, was also a poor boy, a shepherd boy, and God chose him and made him the ruler of his people. You know, after all: God loves the poor and the oppressed. Because you are poor and have suffered so much, you are seven times dearer to me. I, too, was not brought up in a royal court. Oh, how much I suffered until God took pity and returned to me the crown of my forefathers. If you marry me, I will tell you at our wedding the story of my family and of my life. I am a Jew, after all, and as a Jew I have suffered a great deal. Love me, Pnina!"

His ardent words and the sadness [?] in his eyes moved Pnina deeply. She had always liked him. She knew that not only poor girls but princesses would have felt happy if he loved them. But she had always been afraid of him. However good he was to her and to her companion, and however grateful she was to him, she could not forget that evil night when he had so savagely fallen upon the village of the good sheikh and so cruelly killed everyone. When she remembered it she shuddered, and she was afraid of him and trembled. And even when he lay at her feet she stood full of fear.

But she thought it over and concluded that it would be better if she married him. She would influence him to stop waging wars and to live in peace with his neighbours; she would help him build a kingdom by which the world would bless itself. She put her trembling arms around him and said:

"Very well, I will become your maidservant, King Yusuf, and will wash the dust from your feet."

He caught her up and pressed her to his heart, covered her face with hot kisses, and cried out in joy:

"Pnina, my dear, my beautiful bride! You will not be my maidservant but my queen; you will see how good it will be. We, two grandchildren of King David, conclude a covenant of love and faithfulness. We will sit together on the throne, we will build up a fine Jewish royal house that will be famed and praised. We will secure and strengthen the royal house of David."

Many words of joy and happiness did Yusuf speak to Pnina, and she grew calmer and calmer, and her fear of him vanished entirely. She asked him to be good to her companion Tzarida and to find a husband for her. And he promised her that one day after their own wedding ceremony Tzarida's wedding would take place as well. He already had his eye on a bridegroom for her. And he set the wedding for a month's time.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The New Kehilla Budget before the Plenum of the Board

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Kehilla.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 17[?] / 17 Shevat 5694 — piątek 2 lutego 1934 [Friday, 2 February 1934].)
Będzin
The new kehilla budget before the plenum of the board
The salaries of the rabbinate reduced by 10 per cent, office employees by 5 per cent. — „Agudah“ against the reduction.
On Saturday night the kehilla board held a meeting. On the agenda — the kehilla budget for the year 1934. Before the agenda is taken up, the board member (dozor) Mr. D. Skoczylas and his group submit a protest against the conduct of the presidium, which did not invite to the meeting the moreh-tzedek, Rabbi R' Yehoshele, who carries out all the rabbinical functions during the Rabbi's leave, and they declare the meeting unlawful.
In reply, the majority of the board submits the following declaration:
„We regard the protest of Mr. Skoczylas and others as a means of disturbing and undermining the normal work of the kehilla. The gentlemen behind the protest, instead of helping and co-operating in running a normal and productive economy, are out to bring chaos into the kehilla's work. We protest against such a tendency, because every member of the kehilla has a duty to help and not to disturb“.
Then the board members Manela and Najmark put an interpellation: why is the kehilla board not given the possibility of acquainting itself with the whole of the kehilla's correspondence, but only with a part of it.
The president, Mr. Rubinlicht, demands that the interpellation be submitted in writing.
In the income part of the budget Mr. Hampel proposes to enter a sum of 10 thousand złoty, to be taken from the rabbinate's revenues. Mr. Hampel takes the standpoint that all revenues which the rabbinate has must belong to the community (gmina).
The secretary, Mr. Frajlich, declares that the proposal is contrary to the regulations, for according to the regulations the revenues belong not to the rabbinate but to the Rabbi.
After the discussion of Mr. Hampel's proposal, the proposal of the vice-president Mr. Liwer is adopted: that the board proposes to the rabbinate that it voluntarily renounce the side revenues in favour of the community, and as compensation they will receive a special material remuneration.
A lengthy discussion, lasting several hours, took place around the presidium's proposal to reduce the salaries of all kehilla employees by 10 per cent.
The „Agudah“, for understandable reasons, spoke out against a reduction — neither for the rabbinate nor for the office staff.
Mr. Hampel is in favour of only the salaries for the rabbinate being reduced, by 20 per cent.
Mr. Manela is for a compromise proposal — to reduce by 5 per cent.
In the votes all the proposals were rejected and the presidium's resolution passed; only for the salaries of the office employees was Mr. Manela's proposal to reduce by 5 per cent adopted.
Under the shechita item, the „Agudah“ board members demanded that a full salary be fixed for a fourth shochet. The proposal was rejected, and a vacancy sum of 2,500 złoty was budgeted.
A sum of 900 złoty was also budgeted for a cantor in the beit-midrash.
Mr. Hampel's proposal to strike out entirely the salary for a synagogue cantor was rejected.
At 3 at night the meeting was closed at the „dead item“ — the expenditure and income of the cemetery...
In Houses Where There Are Water Meters, the Tenants Have the Right to Demand the Water Bill

[Będzin — Housing.]
We draw the attention of the tenants who live in houses where there is a meter (licznik) for water consumption, that they need not pay as much as the house-owner demands; rather, they have the right to demand the bill showing how much the house-owner has to pay, and to have the sum charged proportionally to all the tenants of the house.
Deputy Mincberg Intervenes with the Kehilla President Mr. Rubinlicht That He Withdraw the Resolution Concerning Payment of the Rabbi's Salary

[Będzin — Kehilla.]
As is known, the presidium of the kehilla board resolved to hold back the debts which the kehilla owes its employees up to 1 January of this year.
The rabbinate and also the shochtim absolutely refuse to submit to the resolution and are not accepting the salaries for the past month.
As it turns out, the dissatisfied are applying other means, intended to bring it about that the presidium withdraw its resolution concerning the salaries.
This week Mr. Rubinlicht received a letter from Deputy R' Leibele Mincberg, who draws Mr. Rubinlicht's attention that he should not apply the above-mentioned resolution against the klei-kodesh (religious functionaries), so that he should not be compelled to intervene in this matter with the proper authority.
Yitzhak Lichtenstein's Exhibition of Paintings / A Festive Completion of a Torah Scroll

[Będzin — Art; Będzin — Religious life.]
Yitzhak Lichtenstein's exhibition of paintings.
Today, Friday, there opens in the „Club“ of the Society for Knowing the Land (Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze) an exhibition of paintings by the well-known painter Yitzhak Lichtenstein (Paris).
In recent times the artist has exhibited his paintings with great success in almost all the European capitals. The critics responded very warmly regarding the high artistic level of Lichtenstein's creations. In the Jewish world Lichtenstein is known as one of the pioneers of modern art. It is to be hoped that the exhibition will have a great success.
In the same premises, in connection with the exhibition, there will take place next Sunday at 4.30 in the afternoon a lecture by Yitzhak Lichtenstein on the theme: „The New Face in Art“.
—o—
A festive completion of a Torah scroll (siyum ha-sefer).
The Żarki Hasidim in Będzin celebrated a siyum ha-sefer on Tuesday evening. In honour of the celebration the Żarki Rebbe, who now lives in Częstochowa, was specially invited.
The scroll was carried under a canopy, with singing, at 11 in the evening[?], through the streets right into the synagogue.
Sosnowiec — Peace Agreement Between the Rabbis

[Sosnowiec — rabbinate, kehilla.]
Hager, Frommer and Glikman.
Satisfied and dissatisfied sides. — A committee to continue the rabbinate struggle. — New kehilla elections?

As our readers already know, the kehilla elections in our town [Sosnowiec] brought such a result that neither of the main candidates for the local rabbinate — neither Rabbi Hager nor Rabbi Englard — obtained the requisite number of mandates that could have led to a victory without the help of the smaller “firms”...
And because of this outcome each of the above-mentioned rabbis began negotiating on how to obtain a majority and also to restore the long-awaited peace in the town.
The “scale pan” of the majority was the Koziegłowy side [the camp of the Rabbi of Koziegłowy], which was showered with various concessions. But the Koziegłowy side, which in the present situation also had practical benefits in mind, decided to unite with Rabbi Hager.
The “heads of chapters” [outline of terms] were written on Friday before candle-lighting, and on Saturday night the “tnoim” [the formal contract] took place. As we are informed, the peace agreement provides that Rabbi Hager receives the office of rabbi, and the Rabbi of Koziegłowy, Rabbi Frommer, receives the title of head of the rabbinical court (rosh beit-din).
The union was also joined by the hitherto moreh-tzedek [rabbinical judge], Rabbi Glikman.
The news of the peace agreement made a great impression in Orthodox circles, because in those circles people had been almost certain that the Koziegłowy side would go together with Rabbi Englard.
—
The side that feels most hard hit is Rabbi Englard's, which is moving heaven and earth and devising ways to be able to invalidate the elections.
On Saturday night a large meeting took place in Rabbi Englard's apartment, at which it was resolved to fight the peace agreement. Those assembled pledged to give Rabbi Englard various sums of money, so that he should have the means to continue the rabbinate struggle waged until now.
It is also said that material is being collected which is to serve as an argument for invalidating the elections.
The majority of the town, however, is satisfied with the agreement, which is the beginning of an end, at long last, to the ugly quarrel and the terrible baseless hatred among the local Jewish population. All the more so as the united rabbis are in favour of also taking Rabbi Englard into the future rabbinate collegium.
The committee that was created at the meeting in Rabbi Englard's apartment has issued an appeal.
In the appeal the committee calls on the Jewish population to work towards having a beit-din (rabbinical court) pronounce its opinion on the local rabbinate question.
Health Certificates Will Be Issued at the Small Traders' Association

[Sosnowiec — municipality, small trade.]
At the local magistrate [municipality] one had, as is known, to pay 5 zł. for a “świadectwo zdrowia” [health certificate]. No requests whatsoever helped; the magistrate had its fee of 5 zł.
Several weeks ago Councillor Oliner raised the question at the plenum of a session of the commissioner's council, and after a lengthy discussion Mr. Oliner's proposal was adopted, that such a certificate should cost only 2 zł.
The resolution, however, remained on paper, and the old fee continued to be in force. Because of this Mr. Oliner this week held a conference with the district physician, who agreed that the “świadectwa” [certificates] should be issued on the premises of the Small Traders' Association and cost only 2.50.
A House Watchman Who Has a “Weakness” for Stealing...

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
For several weeks in a row, almost every night, a few złoty were stolen from the drawer in Hamburger's shop on Dekerta Street. The theft occurred so systematically that it was hard to find out who the thief was.
Last Tuesday Mr. Hamburger and his son-in-law stayed overnight in the shop in order to find out who the thief was. In the middle of the night they heard the door being unlocked, and in came the stróż [caretaker-watchman] of that same house. He even tried to escape, but he did not succeed; before his eyes a policeman at once appeared, who led the “bird” off to the police station (komisariat).
The thief is the chief “in-law” [a leading figure] among the local Hitlerites.
Wajntrojb Sentenced to 8 Years and Ważnica — to 5 Years in Prison

[Sosnowiec — court.]
In the local district court the sensational trial against the communists Lejbl Wajntrojb and Sala Ważnica, who were accused of carrying out an attack on Beryl Włodzimierski, came to an end on Tuesday.
After the speeches of the prosecutor and the defence counsel, the court withdrew for a two-hour deliberation and then handed down a verdict, that Wajntrojb is sentenced to 8 years in prison and Ważnica to 5 years, and to loss of rights.
The candidate of List No. 1 has given up his mandate.

[Kehilla — elections.] The newly elected parnas (community councillor) Reb Hershl Pachter of List No. 1 has, through the mediation of the gmina (the kehilla board), applied to the starosta asking to be released from the mandate, because Mr Pachter does not feel fit for the post on account of his weak health.
The Sick Fund is increasing unemployment.

[Zagłębie — labour and social insurance.] Mass dismissal of domestic servants.

The Sick Fund, or by its new name the “Ubezpieczalnia” (Social Insurance Office), with its new demands and above all with the high contribution, is now bringing it about that unemployment in Zagłębie will grow considerably. First of all this concerns domestic servants. The contribution for a cook or for a maid has been raised so much that people have begun outright to give notice to their employees. Already now it happens that several neighbours together make do with one maid, while others try to manage with the help of the house-watchman's wife. In any case the maids and cooks are losing their positions and are left without bread and without a roof over their heads.

The writer of these lines had a talk about this with a senior official of the Sosnowiec Sick Fund, who stated the following:
— We know about the panic over the dismissal of domestic employees, but we hold that people are exaggerating when they persuade themselves that the contribution will really be a high one. [Radio — Katowice; letter to the editor.]
Two weeks ago the religious concert performed by Cantor Sirota of Warsaw was transmitted by all the Polish radio stations. An exception was the radio station in Katowice, which begrudged the Jewish radio subscribers in Zagłębie and in Upper Silesia the hearing of the concert.
We received many letters of protest from our readers about this tactless conduct, but we passed over them in silence, reckoning that it had happened because of a mistake on the station's part.
But the Katowice radio station made the same „mistake“ this week and did not broadcast the concert of Yossele Rosenblatt (on records).
In connection with this we have received from Mr. Szlomo Frenkel (Bystra) the following letter.
Dear Mr. Editor!
As a Jewish citizen of Będzin I take the liberty, through your esteemed newspaper, of turning to our Jewish citizens of Zagłębie and drawing their attention to the terrible wrong which the Katowice radio station is committing against them. It is not enough that we are the majority in number and in substance of the radio listeners, that we have the right to demand that the radio programme include every day at least half an hour of some Jewish or Hebrew broadcast, or at any rate once a week — a right which is in fact due to us not only morally but also legally — yet, although the concert of Sirota on the radio was announced in all the newspapers for several weeks running, all the Polish radio stations in Poland broadcast the concert except Katowice. The same thing repeated itself on the 6th[?] of this month, when Warsaw broadcast several numbers by Yossele Rosenblatt on records — Katowice did not even find it necessary to mention a word about it. The wrong is mostly[?] against the Jews of Zagłębie.
It is therefore a duty that Jewish society should draw the attention of the Katowice radio station to this; let them at least know that we do not let ourselves be spat in the face.
I thank you very much, dear Mr. Editor, for publishing this letter, and sign
with respect,
Szlomo Frenkel.
