The Rabbinate Question in Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — rabbinate; kehilla.] "Mizrachi" puts forward a candidate. — Lecture in the "Wenus". — Police drive the crowd on with rubber truncheons.
Ever since the rabbinate struggle began in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza], the Jewish population there has had free "entertainments". Almost every Sunday a crowd gathers in a hall and listens to the sermon of this or that candidate.
Last Sunday the Central Committee [Ts. K.] of "Mizrachi" delegated the Rabbi of Olyka [printed "Oliki"; Ołyka?], Rabbi Reuven Horowitz. Some 6 months ago the rabbi left the "Agudah" and joined "Mizrachi".
Together with Rabbi Horowitz came the parnas [kehilla board member] Mr. Szczerański of Warsaw, for the purpose of conducting a campaign for the benefit of the "Keren HaMizrachi".
The "Wenus" hall, where the rabbi gave his lecture, was packed with men, women and children. A "miracle" happened, in that about 50—60 persons were invited to the presidium... thanks to this nobody was crushed in the hall, for in Dąbrowa people hold strongly by "from all my teachers I have gained understanding". If the "Agudah", during the lecture of the Rabbi of Preshov ["Preshover Rov"; Preszów?], invited a minyan of people to the presidium, along came "Mizrachi" and showed its hospitality and invited, besides political ones, also philanthropic institutions...
The meeting is conducted under the chairmanship of the kehilla president Mr. A. Najfeld, who greets the rabbi, Mr. Szczerański and all the visitors, and gives the floor for the lecture to Rabbi Horowitz.
In the first part of the lecture Rabbi Horowitz, who is a brilliant speaker in the modern sense, depicted in vivid pictures the bankruptcy of democracy in the present epoch, but later he illuminated the tragedy of the Jew of the Exile, who creates and builds for foreign peoples on foreign soil, and for all his faithful work he must yet beg for a permission — as Joseph once did of his brothers — that they should remember to take his bones along to the Land of Israel...
The lecture enchanted the listeners, and the rabbi was rewarded with stormy applause.
After the lecture Mr. Szczerański spoke about supporting the Keren Kayemet. The young men who were in the hall shouted "Keren HaYishuv". Then a great tumult arose; the national youth sang "Hatikvah", the "Tze'irei Emunei" [Agudah youth] — "Nisht fartsveyflen" ["Do not despair"], until people began to come to blows. The policeman present then began to drive the crowd on and, while at it[?], did not spare blows with his rubber truncheon.
Later, in the apartment of Mr. Izrael Welner, where the rabbi was staying, a larger number of householders gathered, among them also some from the "Agudah", with whom the rabbi had a talk about today's youth.
The rabbi's visit left a strong impression and, as we are informed, the candidacy of the Preshover or the Olyker rabbi is being taken into consideration.

Noisy and merry was the representatives' ball in Dąbrowa, arranged by the Committee for the Care of Orphans with the co-operation of the local "Maccabi".
The representatives' ball was true to its name: it represented the whole elite of Dąbrowa and select individuals from the neighbouring towns, and everything revelled[?] in the highest degree. The "zabawa" [Polish: party, entertainment] had one particular virtue: elsewhere the organisers lie in wait for the guests, that they should pour and stuff into themselves as much as possible; here it was different — the guests, especially those who stand at the helm of Jewish communal work, spared no effort and, above all, no ready cash, so long as the ball should have its proper success and the mood should be an elevated one... Apparently that is why none of the guests really wanted to look at the clock...
"And when the king's heart was merry with wine" — when the crowd was already a little "in courage" [tipsy] (but that too decently, solidly; no drunken voices were heard...) — several connoisseurs were chosen to give their opinion as to which of the fair sex deserved to receive the title of "queen of the ball".
The candidates for the "crown" were very many, and in each one's heart it throbbed:
— "Może mnie" [Polish: perhaps me]...
But the connoisseurs came to the decision that the "queen of the ball" must be Miss Tania Żeryker, a daughter of Dąbrowa Górnicza, where the "black diamonds" [coal] grow..
Only one small "error" did the organisers commit — not, God forbid, that the title was not properly awarded, but that the "queen" was elected only at the break of dawn, and a large part of the dancers no longer "had the privilege" of dancing the mitzvah-dance with the "queen"...
But let such trifles be forgiven; the main thing is that money was taken in and a handsome profit remained, a bigger one than from the balls in Będzin.
A special "yasher koach" [well done] was earned by the local "Maccabi" for its active co-operation — it kept order for the benefit of the useful event. Although their exertion was for the sake of receiving a reward — 50 per cent of the net income went to the sports club — "Maccabi" nevertheless took pains that the ball should succeed.
A bit of a share in the mitzvah also belongs to Simcha Lustig and his band, who played beyond their strength and not according to the fee... Thanks to that, you may perhaps have happened to overhear a conversation of the "młodzież" [Polish: the young people], that at the ball in Dąbrowa a good time was had.
— Oh, what a good time was had!..
—
The committee, which consisted of the ladies [Mrs.] Engineer Kawa, Sztajnberg, Birnbaum, Żmigród, [Mrs.] Dr. Mitelman, Futerko, Hajnryb[?] and others, worked very ably at the sale of tickets and also at the ball itself, at the necessary tasks.
The net income was about 600[?] zł. Half of the sum goes to the Będzin orphans' home, where orphans from Dąbrowa are also brought up.
Trade in Liquidation (conclusion)

2.
A well-known economist and sociologist once said: trade is, for our state treasury, a good milch cow (I shall not give figures, because there are very many of them). Everyone knows well that trade gives the state, proportionally, far more than all the other branches of the economy. He added that every good farmer — when he comes upon a good milch cow, he provides her with good pasture and takes thought for her, so that she may keep up her profitability.
What kind of pasture does trade receive, which in relation to the state is a good milch cow? Maximum levies and tax burdens and, as extras, cartels, syndicates, étatism; and the consequences are: pauperisation.
Are not the above-mentioned ways such as lead, in the end, to the destruction of the cow and to making a skeleton of her?
A good gardener who has established that his garden gives him less fruit than before, although he has planted new trees, sets about at once to establish what cause has brought about this state of affairs, and once he knows it he spares neither work nor toil in order to make the dying trees healthy and fruitful again. He does not wait and does not rest, but applies every counter-measure so as not to allow even a small number of trees to wither; he knows and understands that a small diseased part can infect his whole garden.
What is being done against the catastrophic and consumptive condition of trade? People look on at its hard situation with the greatest indifference, despite the fact that they know and see that it is still possible now to save and preserve it, and that later it may be too late.
Every change in economic life strikes trade heavily and hard: the moratorium that was granted to agriculture hit trade hard; the reduction of the pensions and salaries of the whole body of civil servants also dealt trade — because of the shrinking of the consumers — a death-blow; the internal loan — whose success is of the greatest importance for economic life and to which the merchant class contributed in great measure — also obliged the trading class to certain exertions. The last is indeed a civic duty, but it ought nevertheless to be taken into consideration in favour of the merchant estate and so as to ease its situation.
The new decree of December last year, which grants tax reliefs for all tax arrears that arose before 1 October 1931, is unfortunately not the remedy that can give the gravely ill trade any relief whatsoever, because those who owe taxes consist for the most part of ruined merchants and liquidated enterprises, and if there is a minimal part that will now be able to put itself on a sound footing and pay off the taxes, this will bring no essential improvement into trade.
Industry, trade and the crafts are three economic arteries that are closely bound together. Trade stands in the middle, because it is the most important artery, for it nourishes the others and brings them abundance. It takes from the manufacturer and gives to the craftsman or the consumer. We saw then that when trade went bankrupt or became insolvent, it dragged industry and the crafts along with it, because when it could no longer give the necessary blood injection, they had to follow and likewise came to the sad condition in which they find themselves today.
The paths of the three economic rings never cross. The revival of one of them is a source of life for the other. Therefore all three need to unite and seek help and rescue from the hard situation in which they find themselves today.
I am no economist and no sociologist. Sometimes, however, great initiatives come from average people.
I propose that the three economic sister-arteries should — through the mediation of their chambers of commerce and chambers of crafts — call an economic congress, in order to organise themselves together in the struggle against the danger of ruin.
We must tell ourselves openly that the authoritative circles cannot do it and do not have the possibility, even if we grant that the will is there.
In order to improve tomorrow we are obliged to do something substantial ourselves. The best help is when one helps oneself.
I believe that if the three economic forces set about, with joint energy and diligence, improving their own lot, they will certainly have success and will certainly change the situation for the better, for "nothing stands in the way of the will."

On Guard: Compulsory Guilds

[Editorial — artisans; legislation.] On Guard. Compulsory guilds.

It must be assumed that the matter of compulsory guilds will be carried through. The amendment to the Industrial Law has already been adopted at the first reading in the Sejm and will surely also be adopted in full.

From the conferences, consultations and negotiations that have taken place on this matter between the Chambers of Artisans and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, one must assume that the Central Union of Jewish Artisans, too, has also agreed to compulsory guilds — and not separate Jewish ones and separate Christian ones. But unified, general compulsory guilds.

We must stress that the question of compulsory guilds has been discussed little, or almost not at all, in the ranks of the Jewish artisans; one still has to consider carefully whether the introduction of general compulsory guilds will be to the benefit of the Jews.

The guilds, which will now receive broader powers, will have to deal with practical life. They will be in contact with the artisans themselves. They will have to settle the artisans' day-to-day interests; it is they who will be the final arbiters in all artisans' questions, and the Jewish artisans, too, will be dependent on them. What will the situation of the Jewish artisans look like then? We must picture the matter as follows: there will be no Jewish "starszy" [guild elder] in any guild whatsoever. Even if we take the largest Jewish guild in Zagłębie, which consists 80 per cent of Jews, it too will not want to put forward the candidacy of Jewish elders — just as it is in the towns where Jews are a majority and yet no Jewish elders are elected; what is there to say, then, of the guilds where there is a non-Jewish majority — there is the danger that the Jews will not be represented on the boards at all.

But that is not all. The structure of Jewish artisanry is different from that of the non-Jewish. The running of the workshop, the selling, and other matters connected with the trade are, among Jewish artisans — who are bound almost exclusively to the Jewish consumer — quite different from what they are among non-Jews; one can therefore imagine that in the general guilds, where membership will be compulsory, the Jews may suffer an injustice, even one that is not at all malicious and not intended; but how many acts of ill will there may also be in this on the part of particular people and particular guilds — that cannot even be reckoned.

Perhaps the principle of compulsory guilds would be a correct one (that, too, would still have needed to be discussed), but the general compulsory guilds are entirely wrong. We may therefore have a grievance as to why so important a question for the whole body of Jewish artisans was not brought out publicly before the artisans themselves, but was settled in the board rooms and not at general assemblies and meetings of the artisans. Even now the Jewish artisans need to think it over, to reckon up all the pros and cons, and to prepare themselves for the new amendment, if that clause can by no means be changed any more. One cannot rely on people's kindness and understanding. The Jewish artisans must have it written and signed that their rights will be protected; only then can the struggle for the protection of those rights be waged. Otherwise the struggle does not even have anything to lean on.
The History of the Będzin Kehilla in the Second Half of the 19th Century. According to Archival Records. (6)

[History — the Będzin kehilla; serial, instalment 6.] By Moshe Feinkind [Mojżesz Feinkind]. According to archival records.
In the time of Rabbi Itshele Kimelman, Będzin began to develop strongly with coal production and the iron industry, which brought a great abundance of livelihood for the Jews of the whole region.
The number of inhabitants also grew greatly here because of this. In the year 1897 Będzin already counted about 24 thousand inhabitants, among whom there were about 11 thousand Jews, i.e. forty-odd per cent.
But in Rabbi Kimelman's times, too, no great peace reigned in the Będzin "gemoyekhts" [?] [doubtful word in the print; apparently a mocking term for the kehilla's affairs].
There were great frictions over the leasing and the repair of the mikveh. The governorate [gubernia] was showered with "papers", the sides accusing and reproaching each other of mismanagement and of putting up fictitious bidders at the kehilla's expense, and so on.
Several times, therefore, the mikveh auctions were indeed held. The auctions for the "tsol-benk" [apparently paid seats/benches; ?]; the expenditures and the revenues were contested — in a word: it was "cosy" in the Będzin kehilla, things were boiling.
And in this muddy water Modrzejów [printed "מאנדזשעוו"] meanwhile caught fish. It succeeded in tearing itself away from Będzin and becoming an independent kehilla with all the trimmings, over which Będzin no longer had any influence at all.
After Rabbi Brechner, R' Yeshaya Englard took his place (Piotrków gubernia, under number 1913-290).
And since Rabbi Itshele of blessed memory [was] a simple, guileless Jew and meddled little in all the quarrels, everything was run just as people pleased.
In the end the supposedly aristocratic crowd grew sick of him too. He was already advanced in years, weak and ill. So they pestered the district chief [powiatowy naczelnik] to obtain from the governor that he be removed from the rabbinical seat and that the kehilla be told to elect another in his place, as I have already described all this in my "Memoirs".
But before the governor managed to reply to this, R' Itshele passed away (28 Tammuz 5653 [1893]) and elections for a rabbi were fixed.
Meanwhile R' Yehoshiele Telner [?] occupied the rabbinical office.
The town then unanimously, to the number of 300 householders, elected Rabbi Graubart as rabbi (1893), about whom I have already written at length in my "Memoirs" in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" in connection with his 20th yahrzeit.
But after the passing of Rabbi Graubart a great dispute over the rabbinical seat flared up in Będzin once more.
Soon after Rabbi Graubart's passing the Będzin naczelnik reported to the governor that he had died on 12 November 1913 in Breslau [Wrocław], and that he had ordered the kehilla to make preparations to elect a rabbi in the place of the deceased, fixing the elections for 17 December, i.e. 30 November [so printed; probably meant 30 December] (according to the new style).
This order, with so short a time limit, threw the town into great turmoil. Parties were soon formed, around which various elements grouped themselves.
Several householders (for quite understandable reasons I cannot cite anyone's name here) hurried to ask the naczelnik to permit them to arrange three pre-election meetings about the rabbinical candidacy; he refused their request. So they turned about this directly to the Piotrków governor. In their petition they explain to the governor that the Będzin kehilla is a widely ramified and large one. One therefore needs here a rabbi who would be an authority not merely in the religious field, but who would also be capable of directing all the affairs of the kehilla.
The householders said things that were untrue: that the deceased rabbi had paid little attention to this and had taken no interest whatsoever in communal matters, on account of which the synagogue, the bet midrash and the mikveh are in a very lamentable state.
Therefore — they declared — the town of Będzin now wants to seek out a candidate who, by his character and his calling, would answer the wishes of the whole community, so that he would enjoy full confidence and have influence with the entire Jewish population.
And so — those householders go on to write — since the naczelnik did not permit us to arrange pre-election meetings in order to come to an understanding about the candidacy, they ask the governor to permit them to arrange three such pre-election meetings, in order to avoid various misunderstandings and unpleasantnesses...
This petition lay in the governor's chancellery untouched for a longer time, and when it was taken up for consideration the rabbinical elections had already taken place in Będzin; the petition was thus no longer topical and indeed was not considered any further. Of which the naczelnik in Będzin was ordered to inform the petitioners...
The rabbinical elections took place on 30 December in a very tense atmosphere. Two sides formed, which fought each other with the whole fire of their strength — if I am to speak in lofty style, I must say: for life and death — as can be seen from the "scribblings" with which the governorate was showered from a certain side, not sparing even the honour of the great deceased, who was in every respect a great Orthodox Jew and scholar and an authority in the Talmudic field.
One side, around which the greater part of the town grouped itself, stood like steel and iron for the candidacy of Rabbi Graubart's accomplished son, the twenty-one-year-old R' Yekutiel Zalman. The opposing side, which was recruited from the Sochaczew Hasidim, put forward Rabbi David Bornsztajn of Wyszogród, today's Sochaczewer Rebbe, as their candidate.
Registered on the voters' list were 1091 payers of the etat [kehilla tax], of whom eleven had died in the meantime and eighteen had emigrated to America. Thus there remained 1062 voters, of whom 707 voted. Rabbi Graubart received 477 and Rabbi Bornsztajn 229. So the former got through by a majority of votes as rabbi of Będzin.
But the adherents of Rabbi Bornsztajn could not make their peace with the victory of the opposing side, and they began to bombard the governorate with paper protests.

On the Eve of the Elections to the City Councils

[Zagłębie — on the eve of the city-council elections; opinion article.]
In the very near future elections to the city councils in Zagłębie will be ordered.
This fact obliges us to reflect calmly and objectively on the position that Jewish society in Zagłębie ought to take — and to do so not under the influence or at the command of outside factors, but simply because for the Jews of Zagłębie this question is closely bound up with the great chain of burning problems that make up Jewish life in Zagłębie.
First[?] of all a few general remarks — not necessarily purely local ones, because in their light it will be easier for us to deal with the specific relation of Zagłębie Jewry to the city-council elections.
The new self-government statute (ustawa) very seriously alters the form, the scope of activity and the significance of the representative body and of the administrations of the municipal economy. The autonomy of municipal self-government has been greatly narrowed and subjected to the control and far-reaching interference of the state authority. The centre of gravity of self-governmental power has been transferred to the magistrates (the city executive boards). The presidents and burmistrzes (mayors) of the towns, their deputies and the ławniks (aldermen) will have considerably broader prerogatives than was the case until now. To the municipal representative body there has been left merely the right to control and to criticise the activity of the city administration.
The elections that are shortly to take place will thus elect the councils and administrations for the new system. The Jewish population, being a distinctly urban one, is very strongly interested that its representation in the representative body and its share in the administration of the city should not be diminished, and that what it has held until now should be preserved. Too many questions — economic ones, taxes, levies (daniny) and fees — are bound up with the city administration, even in its new form, for the Jewish population not to appreciate the significance of the coming elections.
But before we do that, one „reservation of principle must be made, which is necessary because of the events of the last few days on the Jewish street.
We regard ourselves as citizens of Poland with full and equal rights, whose welfare and power lie close to our hearts too. We know and understand that a strong and mighty Polish state is the source and foundation of happiness and contentment for us also, as its citizens.
But with all our understanding for this cardinal thesis — we nevertheless do not wish to be a component part of anyone [letter-spaced for emphasis in the original] in striving, together with other citizens of the state, toward the goal clearly indicated above. We also understand this: that within the state we have a whole series of separate, distinctive postulates, and that to fight for them on the narrow sector of the front that is self-government we regard as a weighty task and one of our own; and that these separate interests do not permit us to dissolve in outside waters in order to become a component part of somebody else, but exactly the opposite — although we strive together with Polish society toward one goal, we must nevertheless quite often go toward that same goal by separate roads.
We stand on the position of principle that everything must be done so that — with due regard for the reservation of principle already mentioned — it should be possible to create a strong and united Jewish front, which would be able, facing outward, to carry through successfully the postulate of a proper Jewish representation both in quality and in quantity — a proper share in the city administration.
In order to attain this goal one must come to an understanding with all the Jewish groupings that represent a force or a social value. As the platform for the understanding there should be put forward solely Jewish solidarity and the postulates of principle of defending the interests of the Jewish population, in accord with the idea of national-Jewish policy.
In the negotiations, which ought to take place and certainly will, all private or personal interests must be laid aside. Decisive here must be the interest of the community as a whole and the deep awareness that the mandate of a Jewish councillor or of a member of the city administration is not merely an honour but — what is no less important — demands readiness for sacrifice, patience and tenacity; and that in order to be able to fulfil the duties one must have social preparation for them and a pure will truly to serve the community, and then also to represent certain ethical values.
We understand perfectly well that a lack of solidarity must lead to a weakening of the Jewish representation; we understand that in this respect a great danger threatens us, and that if it should come to a fight within Jewish society, then in the atmosphere of that fight personal ambitions, private reckonings and local intrigues will resound still louder, and that on the arena of public life there may then step forth not the interests of the community but the interests of profiteers and swindlers (aferzyści), who have lately been spreading more and more in Jewish public life.
Into municipal self-government there must enter, in the name of the Jewish population, people who by their life up to now, by all their communal work, have proved that they work out of idealism and have pure intentions; people who do not seek any personal interests but take upon themselves heavy communal duties which they are willing and able to fulfil — and not persons who, having been presented with mandates of honour, quickly become disappointed and desert their posts (placówki).
One must therefore come forward with an initiative to create a united, self-reliant, independent Jewish front. And in order to achieve this one must apply great effort and not draw back, even if this should involve certain sacrifices of a party character.
And if, after all that, it should nevertheless not succeed and it should come to an election fight between Jewish lists — such a fight must be conducted on an ideological platform of defending the specifically Jewish interests, i.e. on a platform of a self-reliant and independent path of its own for Jewish policy, in complete harmony with the interests of self-government and of the state.
The Jewish population must render itself an account that the whole election campaign has to be adapted to the present conditions: on the one hand, the new system introduced by the new self-government statute, and on the other hand — the ruthless struggle, with all possible means, against that — fortunately insignificant — part of Polish society which openly strives to oppress us and to rob us of the most elementary human rights.
Dr. M. Altman.
Important rulings of the Supreme Court.

[Poland — law and courts.] Defence in administrative penal matters.
In administrative penal matters, which are tried in the starosta's offices [starostwa], no participation of advocates is permitted.
Insurance of white-collar ("intellectual") workers.
Subject to the insurance of white-collar workers are, in principle, also the parents (father-in-law, mother-in-law). grandfathers, and even the wife of the entrepreneur as well, if they are employed as white-collar workers in his enterprise.
Likewise the law on insuring white-collar workers extends also to children, stepchildren, the children and wives of stepchildren, insofar as they do not live together with the entrepreneur.
In all the cases enumerated, however, one may, on the basis of one's own application, be released from the obligation to be insured as a white-collar worker.
Industrial law.
The licence to run an industrial enterprise at the same time also entitles one to sell the same articles, even if they are of someone else's production. A special card ["zaloishenie"?] for selling is no longer necessary.
Dance, Dance — It Is a Mitzvah-Dance...

[Feuilleton — humoresque.] (A humoresque).

Years run, life moves on, the world turns — and we dance, and time, time leaps. It turns somersaults and throws out of its bowels whole heaps of epochs and little epochs. The exalted are brought low, the lowly are exalted, and so on without end and without finish.

And [from?] the epochs of the heart and of the mind we have now arrived at the epoch of the foot (footballism, dancingism). The lowest, the humblest of all the limbs — the foot has been given the floor. It is on the go. Not the going of old, on its everyday errand, for the sake of the stomach, for the sake of eating: this is quite another going — a game, a dance of the spirit of the age. Heart, mind, feelings lie strewn on the ground, under the feet, like cut-down sheaves, and they, the feet, tread and stride over them with giant steps to the order of the day.

We, the unprepared, not grown up to this new epoch, must, poor things, like little babies, shuffle along by the little stools and only now learn to set down a foot.

*

Fat Keyle turns about the hall, panting, working like a donkey with every limb. Now she leans for a moment on a table, lifts her feet, bends them there and back and counts: one, two, three. Tshipe, her old mother, sits with a quiet longing on her wrinkled face. She shakes her head and sighs: “Like a dream. A dream”... “How long is it, after all, since her Beyle [so printed], just as now, shuffled along by the chairs, learning to walk”?!

Yes, all of us must now set about learning anew how to place our feet, just like the little children by the little stools...

And everything dances: young, old, poor, rich, regardless of nationality, estate, class; all lift their feet, everything dances, hops — all of them devoted, earnest children of the foot-epoch.

*

I come into a hall; everything is turning in a circle. Tables and benches along the walls. One of the stewards catches sight of me; before I can look round, he already has me by the arm and is driving with me across the room. I resist with all my strength. I want to free myself from him, but as if through a nasty storm I am at once carried over into the arms of Madame herself, the chief hostess [“hoypt-mekhuteneste”] of the evening. My resistance grows, naturally, weaker. For how can one tear oneself so quickly out of soft womanly arms? A minute — and I am swaying with everyone in the circle. One of them, a young man, gives the commands: right, left, gentlemen out with the right, ladies in with the left!

Five minutes already that I have been swaying like this; my breath grows heavier, the heart is pounding in my Madame too... I would like to stop, to catch my breath for a minute, but how does one break off in the middle?

She will surely say of me that I am already danced-out [a has-been]... I feel that my Madame, too, would already like to rest. But she is afraid, evidently, of the same thing as I...

— Eh, this is no dance — I look for a way to wriggle out. — A foxtrot would have been better[?] — but my partner does not stop and dances on and on. At last the happy minute comes. The music stops, we let ourselves drop like two heavy loads onto the armchairs and pant like bellows — a real asthma.

— Ah, how nimbly you dance! — she says to me, — may I have so good a year, ten thousand times better than today's young folk.

— And you? — I pay her back a compliment — today's girls may go and hide before you; why, you positively do not touch the floor — and my heart is all but jumping out of me...

— The new foxtrot! — the young man gives a command.

And again I turn in the circle, locked in my Madame's arms. I plead with her: I have no strength; but it does not help, I am harnessed as if between the shafts of a cart, and she keeps on teaching: “That's it, ah, straight. Oh, splendid! A little more and you will be able to show yourself in the best dancing-hall”...

— Ah — I answer her — you do it simply splendidly!

When I got out of the hall I looked round behind me a few times, to see whether I was not being taken to dance once more. Now I understood the point of the punishment in the world to come, which a sinner must serve by dancing with a female day and night, without end and without finish.

The next day I call on an acquaintance of mine.

— Where is Hersh-Leyb — I ask the children.

— Daddy has gone dancing, — pipes up a little boy of about three.

— Just ask him how his daddy dances? — a girl with a tousled[?] head winks at me

— Velvele! Show the “pan” [the gentleman] how daddy dances — chimes in a grown lad with a small cloth cap on his head — and the three-year-old Velvele, with his runny little nose and unbuttoned little trousers, begins to spin about the room with his little hands spread out, and the whole household claps along: that's the way, that's the way, hop-la! hop-la.

And not only in the homes are feet being lifted, but also in the streets, in the shops. Here stands a shopkeeper, a Jew with a thick little beard, leaning with his hands on the table and turning his feet underneath, somehow down and up.

— Rheumatism, no doubt? — I ask.

— No, heaven forbid — smiles his dark, charming little wife.

— Ha! — say I, seeing so earnest a face on the man — from heartache, a little bill of exchange, a little protest...

— He is doing his “lekcja taniec” [“dancing lesson”], he is getting ready for the Dobroczynność [charity society] ball — the wife leads me out of my embarrassment.

Here a young man suddenly turns off the street into a side lane and looks round a few times, to see whether anyone is watching him, and at once begins to turn his feet. He too is doing his “dancing lesson”.

And it is not only with the feet that people are “occupied”; they also talk, they philosophise about dancing, whole discussions are held.

One of them, a young man who evidently has no understanding of the present spirit of the epoch, falls upon[?] the dances, crying out with pathos: This is decline, the death-agony of culture!

Not true! It is art, plasticity, music! — a second one cries out — the soul, the heart have found their redemption [tikkun] in the feet. It is rhythm, measure.

— The matter of dancing — he says — is a deep problem. Look closely at the dancing couples, what earnest faces they have. It is a mitzvah-dance. Do you remember the mitzvah-dance at a Jewish wedding? And he begins to paint: before daybreak, long after the wedding canopy, after the “golden broth”, after the announcing of the wedding gifts [“droshe-geshank”], many of the guests have already gone their ways. Towards dawn. The bride in the middle of the room; Jews with pale faces, bathed in the wan light of dawn, turn like shadows around the bride, and the klezmer musicians, sleepy, with dishevelled beards bent over their fiddles, draw their bows across the strings with closed eyes, strumming a half-melancholy, half-merry tune.

Each time another Jew goes up to the bride, takes hold of the kerchief she holds in her hand and turns around her so a few times in a circle. Suddenly — the bride has vanished... Where has the bride gone? She has finished dancing; it was her last dance, the dance at the parting of the ways, on the threshold of two worlds, the old and the new, a dance on the way to new generations, to a new life...

*

And I think to myself: perhaps the last one is indeed right? Perhaps this too is the dance at the parting of the ways, the last dance?

And I resolve: whomever I may meet, I shall say:

— Dance, dance, it is a mitzvah-dance!

Y. P.[?]
Heaven and Earth and Jews

[Article — economic self-defence of the Jews.]

The offensive of the antisemites against the Jews, almost all over the world, keeps growing stronger. Day after day reports arrive of incessant harassment of Jews, and one can no longer tell them apart: whether from Harbin — the cruel, bestial murders that make the blood freeze in one's veins: abducting Jews and cutting off pieces of living limbs in order to extort ransom money from the family — or in Cuba, the attack on Jews. Of Hitler's land there is no need to speak any more; Romania, too, has its say, and so on. In a word: the nations, it seems, have sworn to torment the Jews day in, day out, in all kinds of ways, which it is superfluous to enumerate.

In short: what should the beaten Jews learn from this? — Self-defence!!

Self-defence not only as in Romania, [where] they meet the hooligans like heroes when they are attacked; not only as in Palestine — the Haganah; but also self-defence on the economic front!

Self-defence on the economic front is, at the present day, the most important task for the Jews, without distinction of party or trade union. If the acts of violence against Jews bear a permanent character, the systematic economic pogrom against the Jewish economic positions is stormier, more dangerous. One position after another is taken, and one is not even allowed to weep.

Can Jews defend themselves with the economic weapon or fortresses[?]?

Certainly yes!

The common danger compels it.

Since the governments of some states directly lead the boycott of Jewish economic positions — whether with gloves or without gloves, whether by compulsory liquidation or by handing the businesses over to the natives — the Jews must pass without delay to economic self-defence through self-sufficiency. That is: Jews must be employed by Jews, Jews must buy from Jews. Clearly. We would not have to feel the economic pressure so strongly today if a firm such as Poznański, Oskar Kon [printed: Kahn] and thousands of others had from the very beginning employed, if not exclusively, then 50 percent Jewish workers, who are suitable both in their trade skills and, above all, in their prices. The Jewish workers, especially the factory workers, who work for individual Jewish manufacturers, quickly became at home in the factories.

We know of such factories in the Zagłębie area where Jews have been employed for a long time, even since before the war, and the manufacturers have had no complaints whatsoever against the Jewish workers. Well known are Fürstenberg's zinc factory and the Klein Brothers in Dąbrowa.

Nor does the Sabbath question interfere with the work. Besides, in case of necessity the Sabbath is overridden by... the war for a livelihood!

We give the names of the factories in order to substantiate our claim that there are no physical or financial difficulties whatsoever on the part of the Jewish workers. The Jewish workers' organizations, which raise the alarm about the right to work for Jews and achieve as much as the drunkard who bangs his head against the wall to make himself a way through (the results of the interventions are pitiful), would do better to turn their attention and action to the Jewish manufacturers and, together with the Jewish communal activists, bring about the steady taking-on, at every opportunity, of Jewish workers. After all, the Jewish manufacturer can easily take on Jewish workers at the start of the work, in order to avoid conflicts with the other workers. If Jews are taken on right at the beginning, every dispute can be avoided. This can happen only with good will on both sides.

In any case a Jew earns as a day labourer no more than 3—4 zł. a day, the same as the Christian. (Even married men do not get more.) Strikes occur less often today because of the general crisis; thus the Jewish manufacturers' penny-argument about the expensive Jewish worker has been taken away.

We must learn from the German Jews, who have been forced by Hitler to protect themselves economically. We read reports from there of how one Jew supports another with work.

Strong propaganda must be conducted in this respect, and we are sure that the instinct of self-preservation, out of the natural urge to live, must compel the Jews to create economic defence positions for themselves. The initiative must be taken by the Jewish economic and trade organizations. The result will certainly be a satisfactory one!

Sh-ski.
Menachem Kipnis (On His Musical-Literary Jubilee)

[People — jubilee.] (On his musical-literary jubilee.)
Menachem Kipnis is one of the few who have been granted "two tables" [shnei shulchanot]: he is both a celebrated folk singer and a popular feuilletonist and reviewer.
He never fantasised about being a "great man in Israel", nor did he strive for it. His career began very modestly. A lad with a little voice, he was a choirboy (meshorer) with cantors, and wandered with Zeidel Rovner as far as Warsaw. Here he stayed, became a chorister in the synagogue and in the theatre, and tried his hand at writing music reviews in the newspapers.
And suddenly he began to go uphill. In music he became one of the "divers" ["vaser-krikhers"], who lowered himself into the depths of the people and fished out from there new folk songs, of which he himself became the populariser. This light genre, in Kipnis's heartfelt rendering, greatly pleased the masses, and his concerts became the greatest public attractions.
And strange was the double role that Kipnis began to play in the musical field. Being himself a singer, an object of criticism and appraisal for other connoisseurs, he became at the same time the most accepted reviewer and critic in Warsaw for concerts, operas and especially for cantors, who used to make guest appearances in the capital. For Jewish singers Kipnis's apartment was a veritable Mecca, to which all streamed for a blessing, a good word...
And in the provinces Kipnis's opinion of a cantor or a singer is like the word of a prophet. Whomever he recognises — that man's success in Poland is already assured; and whomever he tears down — that man may as well pack up and take himself off...
Lately Kipnis the singer has already fallen silent; only his printed selected folk songs will remain an important contribution to Jewish musical literature. Kipnis the reviewer, on the other hand, is still rising in his influence and is becoming ever surer and richer in colour in his appraisals.
And simultaneously with his musical ascent he was also, as if suddenly, revealed in the writer's craft. He is no "splitter of heavens", never pushed himself to become a great man, and yet he has become one of the most popular feuilletonists, for whose feuilleton thousands of readers of "Haynt" wait impatiently every Friday.
And thus, ever so quietly, he has even worked out for himself a genre, a style of his own, by which you will recognise him even without seeing the signature. His broadly sprawling description of a "Pan Mecenas" [Polish form of address for a lawyer], or of a wise man of Chelm and the like, underlined with a little invention that is more mischievous than witty, has for the broad public the taste of a tasty, well-larded krupnik [barley soup], and people lick their fingers over it.
Kipnis has become a brand name in the newspaper; he surely has more readers than other heavyweight "log-choppers" or over-sharpened hair-splitters.
He knows nothing of politics, of any orientation, does not meddle in the party squabbles; all that is no worry of his [literally: "not his grandmother's worry"], so long as he has grabbed some light little subject with which to play a prank.
And just so, slowly and gently, going forward with small steps, there has grown up before us the meritorious Kipnis, a Jew who already has a serious past, for whom a jubilee is already being celebrated.
He has honestly earned it. It is a jubilee of work, of creation, of honest and faithful service to the Jewish people, and we wish the celebrant from the bottom of our hearts that he may live and create for a long, long time yet!
Chanan.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Mishpatim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Mishpatim
The Portion
—o—
a) "If thou buy a Hebrew servant" (Ex. 21:2)
A Ger Hasid, a famous Warsaw magnate, the landlord of a large house, once wanted to throw out a poor tenant who owed many months' rent. The Chiddushei HaRim [R' Yitzchak Meir Alter, the first Rebbe of Ger] sent for him and asked him: How can this be?
The magnate answers:
Why am I obliged to make him a gift of so much money? If he is a poor man, let money be collected for him for a dwelling; I myself will give the largest donation. But why must I keep him entirely for nothing? Does the commandment not apply to other Jews, who are not landlords?
To this the Chiddushei HaRim answers him:
The Gemara says in Chagigah: "One who is half slave and half free — his master is compelled to make him a free man" (a slave of two partners, whom one of them has freed — the rabbinical court compels the second to free him as well). Your question arises there too, after all: why must he, of all people, free him? Let the court collect money and redeem him. But it must be so: because that man happens to be his slave, the commandment to free him lies upon him. So too here: because the tenant happens to be your tenant, because Providence has so arranged it, the whole obligation and the commandment to make him a gift of the rent lie upon you...
Imrei Tzaddikim.
—o—
b) "Neither shall ye lay upon him interest" (Ex. 22:21 [as printed; in the Bible 22:24])
R' Yitzchak Nissenbaum relates in his book "Alei Cheldi" about a Vilna usurer who was such a devourer of interest that if someone borrowed money from him in the middle of the day, he reckoned that day as a whole interest-day. And when the money was returned to him in the middle of the day, he reckoned that day too as a whole day, although, counted from hour to hour, this came out as an extra day... He does not recognise half-days, he said. So people applied to him the verse "Men of blood [damim — also 'money'] and deceit shall not halve their days" [Ps. 55:24]: the men of blood-money and deceit do not want to divide the days in half...
—o—
c) "And ye shall be holy men unto Me" (ibid., 30)
In your holiness you shall be human; not wildly holy, but humanly holy shall you be... "and holy men".
Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk.
* * *
A young man once came to R' Zalman Miropoler [of Miropol] to receive rabbinical ordination: he wants to become a rabbi, he is versed in all four parts of the Shulchan Aruch.
— But are you versed in the fifth Shulchan Aruch too? — asks R' Zalman.
The young man is astonished: there are, after all, only four Shulchan Aruchs, not five.
R' Zalman says to him:
— There is indeed a fifth Shulchan Aruch, which a rabbi must observe; it begins with the paragraph: "A person should always be a man [adam]"... (Be a mensch!...)
—o—
d) "Ye shall not eat any flesh that is torn" (ibid.)
In Slutsk a commotion was once raised about "outside meat": meat is being brought in from elsewhere. People ran to the rabbi, to R' Yoshe Ber [R' Yosef Dov Soloveitchik]: Help, outside meat is being brought into town!
R' Yoshe Ber asks innocently: And what is "outside meat"?
— How so, Rabbi, — shouts one householder, — do we then know the slaughterers who slaughtered the foreign meat?
R' Yoshe Ber answers:
— If with the Slutsk slaughter, whose slaughterers you do know, you nevertheless eat of their slaughtering... then you may certainly eat of the slaughtering of slaughterers whom you do not know, and of whom at least you do not know for certain that they are "klakes"[?] [apparently: bunglers, good-for-nothings]...
Midor Dor.
—o—
e) "Ye shall cast it to the dog" (ibid.)
"And ye shall be holy men unto Me"... Do not be like the dogs: when one dog barks, all the dogs raise a barking, not knowing themselves what is going on... first of all one barks along... You shall not do so... "And ye shall be holy men unto Me"...
Midrash.
—o—
f) "Nor curse a ruler of thy people. Thy fullness and thy tear [the first of thy ripe fruits and of thy liquors]" (Ex. 24[?] [should be 22]:27–28)
The Midrash says on this: "If you curse the judge, you are cursing nothing but your own produce." For when Jews have an ample livelihood, they take to quarrels, to wrangling with rabbis; therefore — say the Sages in one place — "the Lord sends leanness, and they are occupied with livelihood and with worry, and will no longer judge their judges"... (When God sends a famine, they are busy with making a living and no longer quarrel with the rabbis...) Therefore "thy fullness and thy tear": if you want to have a livelihood — "nor curse a ruler of thy people": do not brawl with your leaders, and do not bring it about that God must bring a famine so that you leave off the quarrels...
Ktav Sofer.
—o—
g) "And the feast of ingathering, at the going out of the year" (Ex. 23:16)
From this verse it appears that Sukkot is in the last month of the year, that is, Elul. And in the portion "Kisa" [printed "קשא", a misprint for Tisa] (34:22) it is said "and the feast of ingathering at the turn of the year" — that Sukkot is in Tishrei. So the verse here is strange: Sukkot in Elul, of all things?
But in the Yalkut, portion Pinchas, it is said:
"Resh Lakish said: Every month God wanted to give the Jews a festival. In Nisan He gave them Passover, in Iyar — the Second Passover, in Sivan — Shavuot; in Tammuz He wanted to give them a great festival (Rosh Hashanah), in Av He wanted to give them Yom Kippur, and in Elul — Sukkot. The Jews made the Calf, and so Tammuz, Av, Elul (the days of the Calf) remained without a festival, and Tishrei took everything: Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret."
Thus, before the sin of the Calf, Sukkot was meant to fall in Elul. That is why it says here "at the going out of the year", for this verse was said before the sin of the Calf. But in the portion Tisa, after the sin of the Calf, it already says "and the feast of ingathering at the turn of the year" — that Sukkot falls in Tishrei...
Kneh Chokhmah.
—o—
h) "And ye shall serve the Lord your God, and He shall bless thy bread" (ibid., 25[?])
Of prayer the plural is used: "and ye shall serve" — in spiritual matters there is a joining together. But of eating the singular is used: "and He shall bless thy bread" — one eats only for oneself; one can pray for another, but not eat...
Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk.
* * *
"And ye shall serve" — to serve God all are equally obliged. The rich man has no other commandments than the poor man. But "and He shall bless thy bread" — of the reward for the commandments the singular is already used: each is rewarded differently for the commandments. One with riches and one with nothing[?]..
R' Moshe Sofer [the Chatam Sofer].
“Der Kokh-lefl” [The Ladle / The Meddler] — Humour and Satire. Compiled by Amutslo[?]. — After the Election Battle

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; verse.]
After the battle —
the public is left standing,
with heads dazed by fumes,
with hearts poisoned[?],
with brains deafened,
with votes robbed,
with hopes crumbled away,
and it stands and waits,
withered and shrunken[?],
and it perceives
(when it is already too late)
that with all this[?] it has been
fooled!

That is just the trouble —
well, never mind, what’s lost is lost —
that the public grows clever
only after the elections.
The public turns into a sage,
but during the fight
it is, poor thing, a golem.

And now, brothers,
when it is already over,
the blizzard of talk,
and one no longer hears
the splashing from the pots of filth —
what, then, has remained
of all the shouting,
of the chewing and the jabbering,
except a taste
of spittle on an empty stomach?

So it will remain,
no shouting will help,
as long as the old parties
rule,
no matter who has
won, —
for the best of them
are fit only for the fire.
“This one is better, that one is worse”
— it is simply laughable!
What good to you, brothers,
are all these things?
Out of a tail
you cannot make a shtreimel.
I Am Off to Częstochowa.

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; feuilleton.]
Jews, things are bitter! The million that came out in the last lottery has rolled itself away all the way to Częstochowa.
God willing, by the coming 4th class I shall already be a Częstochowa man. What will I gain by sitting it out in this luckless Zagłębie? Here one cannot even hope to live to see a little win of 20 thousand.
But a little win of some sort did drop in after all.
At the sub-collector’s, where I take a third share in a “quarter” ticket, the wife has won... a baby boy. A birth at the time when the last class is being drawn is, among lottery collectors, a sign of luck. So the poor sub-collector ran round to his clients and announced the tidings to each one — We’ve won! We’ve won!
— Won what, won how much?
— My wife has won a boy, and this time the million will be at my place.
He hit it right on the dot..
On the other hand, how is he to blame? Będzin or Sosnowiec are luckless towns; at most a woman here can win twins.
When one has to do with a shlimazl, it is bad. No cleverness helps.
Go and do business and win in the lottery when you have to do with a shlimazl.
I am off to Częstochowa, and fare you all well.
Yosef.

A Carnival Lesson for a Modern Lady.
The mother teaches the daughter:
— Salcze, when you dance the tango and your partner permits himself to press you tightly to him and kiss you, then remember and do not push him away from you; your father, the idiot, I too caught in the trap in just this way.
What Does the New Constitution Give Us?

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”.]
Jews! We have, with good luck, a new constitution, and do you at least know what privileges the new constitution gives us?
For example, until now we used to elect strangers to the Sejm; from now on everyone will elect himself — we shall all be deputies, and our wives will be “nietykalne” — untouchable [immune].
The new constitution introduces the following freedoms:
Freedom of speech: one will be able to speak freely — to the wall, to the daszek [the cap-peak] and to the lamp.
Freedom of assembly: every citizen will have the full right to arrange gatherings of... creditors, melave-malke[?] meals and other similar “zebrania” [meetings].
According to the new constitution the whole of life will be changed: from now on bachelors will give the dowry,
mohels [circumcisers] will have to have a “karta rzemieślnicza” [craftsman’s card] from the Chamber of Crafts and a master’s certificate for “men’s made-to-order work”[?]..
Midwives will have to have “zaświadczenia” [certificates] that they are “roeh et ha-nolad” [“one who foresees what will be born”].

The Noble Landlord. Where Is His Address?

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”.]
I tell you that not all landlords are scoundrels. Why, this very week I spoke with a landlord — a real human being.
— You know — said the landlord — I do not hold with any evictions... Even if I were to be gilded I would not carry out an eviction; how can one take a man with a wife and children and throw him out on the street — feh!
— And what do you do, Mr. Landlord, when a tenant really does not pay you any rent?
— What should I do to him, what? If he does not pay, it is a sign that he has nothing to pay with; one must after all have a little humanity, is it not so?
— Absolutely! And what do you say about the campaign to make rents cheaper?
— Rent absolutely must be reduced by 30 per cent. It is a scandal: at a time when everything has become cheaper and rent has not — I ask you, where is the sense? Where is justice?
— What do you say, dear readers, to this remarkable landlord? A fine person, isn’t he? Whoever among the readers wishes to see the noble landlord, we give his address:
You can see him in the madhouse in Bushevovits[?].

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”.]

The Jewish Queen of Yemen (6)

[Serialized historical tale — Yemen, King Yusuf Dhu Nuwas; installment 6.]
Sh. Berg.

Yusuf sent couriers throughout all Yemen and to the peoples under his rule, and everywhere they announced that the king was getting married and that all were invited to the wedding. He called together the elders of his army and told them that for the whole month there would be no war — during the time of the wedding certainly not — and that he hoped to have peace from this day on. He gave the soldiers leave, and the joy in all Yemen was great.

Tzarida [printed here "Tzaraida"] was happy too: her friend, whom she had come to love from the first day she saw her, was being so blessed. She was becoming a queen, and she herself was not forsaken [?] either — the king had promised her a husband, and no ordinary one. So she was even merrier and more cheerful than Pnina. Her heart still ached over the great misfortune that had befallen her father. She had always been afraid, like Pnina and perhaps even more, of Yusuf, who had killed her father and laid waste his village. But she was grateful to him for his good treatment, and her sorrow had grown weaker. Now her joy was so great that he had already become dear and precious to her as well.

The wedding was celebrated with great pomp. Representatives from every corner of the land and from the subject tribes came and brought costly gifts. The generals and all the elders of the army were there as well. A lavish feast for all the poor was given before the wedding ceremony, and the wedding for the guests [so printed, with a full stop in mid-sentence; i.e. the wedding feast] was as rich as a feast at King Solomon's. Those who led the couple to the canopy were Tzarida and her bridegroom Mede'a [?], a Jewish sheikh, and the rejoicing was very great in all Yemen.

At the wedding meal Yusuf Dhu Nuwas [printed "De Nuwas"] gave a sign, and it grew quiet, and he began to tell his story:

It was when King Solomon reigned. The Queen of Sheba heard how great, rich and wise King Solomon was, and she wanted to see him, to hear his wisdom. She came to him and fell in love with him, and became so attached to him that she converted to Judaism and learned all the branches of wisdom from him. He married her, and she bore him a son. She gave the son the name Menelik.

When she later returned to Sheba, she called her ministers together and told them everything. They recognized her son as the heir to her throne. In those times Sheba was a great kingdom, stretching from Arabia to Abyssinia. After the Queen of Sheba died, Menelik became king, and his children and grandchildren after him occupied the throne. All the kings who were descended from Menelik believed in the Jewish God and in His Torah. But they did not force their faith upon the peoples. The land was free, and everyone served the god of his fathers.

Some time later the kingdom was divided between two brothers: one took Arabia and the other — Abyssinia. Kahan [?], the king of Arabia, chose Sana'a as his capital city. From him all the kings of Arabia are descended to this very day. The children of the two brothers, the kings of Arabia and Abyssinia, lived well with one another as long as they served the Jewish God.

Until the king of Abyssinia abandoned his faith and became a Christian. Then quarrels began between the two kings over the faiths, and the kinsmen became strangers and enemies.

Yusuf's forefathers had not wanted to force their faith upon the idol-worshipping Arabs — until the Christians spread their dominion over the surrounding lands. When Yusuf's father, Abu Karib, became king, the fanaticism of the Christians brought him to begin forcing his faith upon the neighbours. Abu Karib was famed for his wisdom and heroism. He was the mighty ruler of Yemen. When he felt his might, he assembled a great army and went to wage war on the emperor of Byzantium, to tear all Arabia away from him.

He passed with his army through Yathrib and left his son there to keep watch over the provisions. In Yathrib there lived Jews and gentiles, and the gentiles killed the son, Yusuf's brother. When Abu Karib heard of this, he resolved to take revenge on the city. He meant only the gentiles. But the Jews defended the city together with the gentiles. For a long time he besieged the city and could not take it.

He cut down all the date palms, so that the besieged should perish of hunger. Suddenly he came down with fever, and there was no fresh water for him to drink. Two Jews, from among the most respected in the city, brought him fresh water and he recovered. He was grateful to them, and they begged him to have mercy on the city and not to destroy all the Jews and the innocent Arabs on account of a few murderers. Abu Karib heeded them and departed from the city. But he took the two respected Jews along with him, and they helped him convert the whole army to Judaism.

When the Arabs of Yemen heard that Abu Karib had converted the soldiery and that he wanted to convert the whole people, they rose in revolt. When Abu Karib returned home, the rebels locked the gates and did not let him in with the army. A great battle would have broken out, but the leaders of the revolt took fright and agreed to make a trial of who was in the right, Abu Karib or they.

Near the city there is a wonder-cave; whenever a quarrel broke out, both sides went to the cave, and from the cave a fire came forth and burned the guilty. Those who came out whole were in the right.

To the cave went the respected Jews with Torah scrolls and the Arab priests with their idols, and a fire came forth from the cave and burned the priests together with the idols, and the Jews with the Torah scrolls remained whole. The people took this as proof that Abu Karib and the Jews were in the right, and all of them converted to Judaism.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Continuation of the Budget Debate at the Plenum of the Kehilla Board

[Head of the local page; Będzin — kehilla, budget.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 24 Shevat 5694 — piątek 9 lutego 1934.)
Będzin
Continuation of the Budget Debate
at the plenum of the kehilla board.
In the previous issue we gave the report of the first session of the kehilla board called to consider the budget for the year 1934.
Last Saturday night, under the chairmanship of Mr. Rubinlicht, the continuation of the budget session took place. The session began with the items of expenditure and income of the cemetery. Before the agenda is taken up — a protest is submitted for the second time by the Agudah faction, which protests against the presidium because R' Yehoshuale was not invited to today's session in place of the absent rabbi.
Vice-president Mr. Liwer submits a counter-motion: "Since Mr. Skoczylas endeavours at every board session, by various means, to disturb the normal work by submitting protests against resolutions that have already been adopted by a majority — he proposes that Mr. Skoczylas be excluded from the sessions at which the new budget will be dealt with. This will be a guarantee of moral and productive work for the benefit of the community (gmina), and this is also the wish of the entire (?) Jewish public.
Mr. Rubinlicht declines to put the motion to a vote, on the grounds that the community does not have the proper rules of procedure.
The section "Cemetery" (cmentarz) is, on Mr. Rubinlicht's motion, adopted en bloc according to the presidium's draft.
A passionate discussion developed over the section: culture and social welfare. Mr. Neumark proposes that the Mizrachi school be placed in third place together with other schools.
Mr. Piekarski — that the Talmud Torah be placed in first place. The Painter Icchak Lichtenstein

[Art — Będzin.] Icchak Lichtenstein entered the family of Jewish painters some 25 years ago. That was a time when among Jews only the names of a few painters were known, such as: Hirszenberg, Pilichowski, Trębacz, Minkowski and a few others, less well known.
All these artists had mostly come from the Munich Academy of Art, from which they brought with them German exactness[?] and precision, but at the same time also their conservatism and rigidity.
All the Jewish artists of that time mostly took their subject-matter from Jewish, religious life. What dominates in their pictures is: the house of study, the yeshiva, prayer-shawls, shofars, lulavs and in general the whole stock of sacred-object props. This subject-matter spoke to the heart of the Jewish public, which understood very little about art and therefore demanded no other, purely painterly values, but mainly the Jewish, religious motifs.
Lichtenstein brought a new, fresh breath into Jewish painting.
Being by nature a true artist-bohemian, he has wandered in the course of the years over almost the entire globe. He is the true cosmopolitan, whose fatherland is the whole world.
If he comes to a port with the intention of sailing to America and just then meets a ship that is going to Scandinavia, Lichtenstein does not think long and sails to Scandinavia. It does not bother him that he has nobody there, that he has no command of the local language, because far mightier than the spoken tongue is the language of colour; it is more convincing because it is truer.
The restlessness in Lichtenstein also finds striking expression in his creations.
In his pictures it is hard to find the marks of a definite school. There are in them no stable forms of the various „isms“ in art. Lichtenstein is the eternally restless spirit, who cannot fit himself into the narrow frames of any forms whatsoever; he is in a state of permanent searching for new paths and possibilities, and hence the great diversity of his canvases.
Not stability, not being satisfied, are characteristic of a talent; rather it is precisely the restlessness and the eternal searching that bear witness to the true artist.
Leonardo da Vinci stands higher than Michelangelo in this, that the former was the always unsatisfied one, the one hungry for new forms and possibilities. It took 20 years until Leonardo found a model for Judas Iscariot for his picture „The Last Supper“, which was [otherwise] entirely finished. In the course of the long years no model whatever satisfied him, until he found that one, whom he had seen in his visions. Da Vinci never completely finished his works, and in this lies his greatness.
Michelangelo's „Moses“, „David“ and „Pietà“ are finished masterpieces, but in absolute finish there lies hidden the danger of decline.
Lichtenstein shows[?] us the gloomy skies of the North and the bright, sunny landscape of the South; everywhere he is original in the manner of bringing out purely painterly values. He often makes use of only a certain colour-tone, such as, for example, grey or blue. But he succeeds in bringing out rarely fine vibrations of colouring[?], which create subtle and harmonious chords of colour.
The artist is very varied in his subject-matter. He paints urban views, landscapes, still lifes and constructivist pictures.
The graphic technique is not foreign to him either; his copper engravings, done with the cold needle [drypoint] (a kind of technique), are executed in a very first-class way; they are well composed, finely drawn and make their effect through their subtlety.
Icchak Lichtenstein is unquestionably one of the most intelligent and most original artists in the family of Jewish painters.
Sh. R.

Sharp Exchange of Opinions over the Będzin Kehilla Budget

[Będzin — kehilla; budget.]
The vice-president of the kehilla council, Mr. G. Landner, summoned the parnasim (board members) of the national camp to a consultation, for the purpose of talking over the new kehilla budget.
The meeting, which took place on Wednesday evening, bore at moments a stormy character.
The chairman, Mr. Landner, opens the consultation and declares that it was called in order to establish the position of the national parnasim at the plenary session that will take place this coming Sunday.
A sharp discussion developed over the first budget item — the salaries („pensyes“) for the rabbinate. Some of the parnasim present expressed the view that, because of the large side incomes the rabbinate has, their salaries should be reduced by 50 per cent.
The kehilla presidium defended the budget, arguing that in the neighbouring towns too the new kehilla budgets have been raised.
After the discussions, which lasted several hours, it was resolved to reduce the rabbinate's salaries by 15 per cent.

What's New in Częstochowa?

[Częstochowa — local report.] A strike of 200 Jewish home-workers.
For the third week now a general strike of 200 Jewish home-workers ["chalupnikes", chałupnicy — outworkers] has been going on in Częstochowa, among them the ladies' tailors working for the "magazines" [ready-made clothing stores]. The strikers demand a wage increase of 50 percent.
—o—
A harsh decree for the small traders.
It is already quite some time since the municipality rebuilt the area at "Zavade" [probably Zawodzie] behind the town, in order to move the market traders from the New and the Old Market to that site, which is very inconvenient for the Jewish traders, because in the first place it is by no means a safe place and it is simply a danger to go there, and in particular trade will be greatly weakened.
Lately, however, the authorities have set about carrying out the plan, and the decree is to be implemented in the very near future.
In connection with this, meetings of the small traders have been taking place lately; they are seeking various means to soften this decree, which is catastrophic for the small-trading class, which consists exclusively of Jews.
Perhaps these interventions would have yielded some results, but the calamity is that Częstochowa has 2 small traders' unions. Taking advantage of the occasion that the handful of Jews are to be driven from the municipal markets, the two small traders' unions have set about fighting each other, in the form that each wants to outdo the other with positive deeds, and all this meanwhile goes on at the expense of the poor small traders...

Antisemitic attacks on Jews again.
About 2 weeks ago a member of the Endecja [National Democrats] was punished with a year and a half in prison for assaults and for wanting to kill a Jewish editor.
It appears that the Endek youth of Częstochowa were little frightened by the verdict and are renewing their antisemitic deeds.
Last week the pupils of the Christian artisans' evening courses spread out through the town and beat the Jewish passers-by. Larger groups formed along the avenues, smashing several shop windows of Jewish stores, and they went about their work undisturbed as far as the New Market, where they beat Mr. Yaakov Frein[?] murderously.

What's New in Upper Silesia? — Changes in Katowice Kehilla Life

[Upper Silesia — Katowice, kehilla.] The rabbinate's income reduced. — For the first time a fee is fixed for the slaughter of poultry.
Under the chairmanship of the president, Mr. Meyer [מייער], a meeting of the Katowice kehilla council took place, which dealt with the new kehilla budget.
After a lengthy discussion the budget was adopted according to the board's draft, but with the exception of several items, which were altered by the kehilla council.
The changes introduce new chapters into the life of the Katowice kehilla. As is known, the slaughter of poultry was free of charge for the Jewish population of Katowice. But because of the financial crisis, which also affects the income of the community (gmina), it was decided to take a fee for the slaughter of poultry.
The fee is: 50 groszy for a turkey, 30 groszy for a goose or a duck, 20 groszy for a hen and 10 groszy for a chicken (kurczak) or a pigeon.
The hitherto existing system of schooling has also been abolished. Tuition will be charged for every child who studies in the community schools. The scale of the fee is as follows: those who pay a kehilla tax („etat“) of 30 to 60 zł. will pay tuition of 2 zł. per child; from 60 to 150 — 3 zł.; from 150 to 250 — 4 zł.; from 250 to 500 — 6 zł. Whoever has 3 children in the school will pay for only 2.
The Orthodox faction put forward a proposal that with the income from the shechita and from the schools a town[?] building should be built, in which there would be a Talmud Torah, a mikveh and the like.
The proposal was rejected.
The kehilla council struck out the sum of 4 thousand zł. which the rabbinate received for teaching religion in the community schools, and also abolished the income which the rabbinate had from weddings and funerals.

Moshe Feinkind

[Literature — jubilee.] (On his 50-year literary jubilee.)
Quietly and modestly, without noise and tumult, the 50-year literary jubilee of the well-known writer and national communal worker, R. Moshe Feinkind, was celebrated last Sunday in Piotrków.
At the age of 17 Moshe Feinkind specialised in Jewish studies (Chochmat Yisrael) under Dr. Cassel, Lazarus, Dr. Hildesheimer and others, and translated into Hebrew poems by the German classics.
Moshe Feinkind begins his activity as a writer in the year 1884, in "HaNitzanim", in "HaTzefirah", and later, in the Jewish and Jewish-Polish press of Warsaw, Łódź and Lemberg, Moshe Feinkind occupies an honourable place and becomes popular through his dozens of publicistic and historical articles.
Among the readers of the Warsaw Jewish press in general, and of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" in particular, the esteemed jubilarian is likewise well liked for his frequent articles on historical dates, especially for his articles on the history of the Będzin kehilla.
At the age of 68 our esteemed contributor R. Moshe Feinkind celebrates his 50-year literary jubilee. He has honestly earned it; it is a jubilee of serious work, of tireless creation not only in the literary field — he also has great merits as an ardent, devoted national Jew, and we wish the old-young jubilarian long life, to go on freely spinning the thread of his literary activity.
