A National or a Civic Standpoint

By Leo Koenig[?].
It may be that in our struggle against Hitlerism we have taken our stand too much on the national standpoint and too little on the standpoint of our civil rights.
That is to say, in almost all our reactions to Hitlerite antisemitism we have acted mostly, and in the first place, as Jews, as members of one whole and separate people, and not as citizens of the countries to which we belong.
It was the Jewish people that protested against the savage Nazi attacks, and not the English-Jewish, American-Jewish or Polish-Jewish citizens, and so on.
And it was not consciously that Jews all over the world adopted this national standpoint. The greater part of the present-day Jewish people is neither national-Zionist nor national-Folkist.
And yet the great majority of our actions and reactions against Hitlerism were separatist-national.
Our separate civil statuses only coloured, so to speak, nuanced to a certain degree, or sometimes even disturbed the national character of our actions.
But in the main, all our actions against Hitlerism bore a national character, and they bear it to this day.
Why did it happen so?
Chiefly for historical and atavistic reasons:
We Jews ourselves have not yet grown accustomed to living with our emancipation, even in the "most advanced" countries; we have not become sufficiently naturalised, so to speak, in our civil rights. Psychologically we do not feel ourselves entirely to be equal citizens in the countries of our citizenship. Jewish emancipation is still comparatively young, it is not yet in our blood; in our blood there still lives the feeling, or the subconscious sense, that we are a separate, persecuted people. And even in the most conscious and most natural of our assimilationists the instinct, or the half-consciousness, still smoulders.
In our non-Jewish fellow citizens we do not have full confidence.
It seems to us that they will not really stand up for us, their Jewish fellow citizens. We do not believe it — or is it that the Exile psychology still lives in the freest among us, in the most assimilated among us.
That is why we all become, as if suddenly, as if out of the blue, national. And our assimilationists, even our apostates, raise the same "vayitzaku" [Hebrew: "and they cried out"] as our ghetto Jews, as though all of them together had only just come out from under Mount Sinai.
And all in all we fall into a kind of "nationalism of affliction". Only our troubles drive us to national actions.
And [printed "un"; read "in"] in more or less normal times the majority of Jews do not want to know either of a land of their own, or of a language of their own and a culture of their own. They speak with such slavish pride of their English, German or French culture.
But as soon as a Jewish trouble comes, we forget our proud citizenship and become such submissive, pitiful and grateful citizens.
And we protest and cry out not as Englishmen, Americans or Frenchmen, but as Jews, and persecuted Jews at that.
———
The Jews all over the world responded to the attacks of Hitlerism only as Jews.
It is true that Hitlerism attacks not merely the German Jews but the whole Jewish people, the whole Jewish race. And from a civic standpoint this could have become our sharpest weapon against Hitlerism.
But with our "purely Jewish" actions we have in fact fallen, to a certain degree, into the Hitlerite "trap" [pastke], because by them we confirmed that there does exist one Jewish people with separate fighting organisations and aims, which stand outside the bounds of our civil rights.
And what is perhaps far more important still: because by the national character of our struggle against Hitlerism we have actually weakened the struggle and made it less effective.
A national struggle is natural and necessary when a people is assaulted, attacked savagely and brutally; but when does that hold? When the national struggle has behind it a real national force: a land, an army, or an economic power of its own.
We have no national power, and it may be that with the atavistic, spontaneous national front which we set against Hitlerism we have only weakened our other means of struggle, namely the civic ones. With our "national front" we have to a certain degree atrophied and weakened the actions which the non-Jewish governments would have taken against Hitlerite antisemitism. Many of the nations of the world perhaps think now that we Jews will somehow hold our own by ourselves against Hitler, and why should they meddle too much.
———
And it may be that it is already time for us to ask ourselves: would it not have been better and more to the purpose if, instead of an all-Jewish [klal-Yisroel] fighting front against Hitlerism, we adopted a civic one? And is it perhaps not an idea that we should now change our line of battle?
Our "national" struggle against Hitlerism has helped almost not at all. We must admit it to ourselves: we were not able to organise the so much discussed boycott? [question mark thus in print]. Palestine cannot help the German Jews either practically or with its prestige. And [printed "in"] all our klal-Yisroel protest meetings have not stopped Hitler's insolent attacks on the Jews of the whole world.
Hitler attacks our civic dignity in all countries. Is it not our duty to defend ourselves, as citizens of our countries, against the attacks; it is our duty to demand [this] of the governments of which we are equal citizens with full rights.
Productive Kehilla Work

(A visit to the Katowice kehilla kitchen — by S. Lewkowicz.)
Having moved away for a short while from the home-grown morass that blossoms and spreads ever more over the body of the Jewish public in general and over the ruins of the Zagłębie kehillas in particular; having distanced myself a little from the reports that reach us about the behind-the-scenes politics of the Sosnowiec kehilla, where after barely two years of fighting they are only just at the "aleph"; from the rabbis' examinations[?] in Dąbrowa; and even from the good tidings of the new Będzin kehilla administration — I snatched a moment for a visit to a neighbouring town, to take a look.
— At the Katowice kehilla, to get acquainted with the activity of the Katowice kehilla. As we entered the courtyard of the synagogue building, my companion drew my attention to the fact that my first visit ought to be
— to the community kitchen.
It is — he says — dinner time; it will be interesting for you to have a look at the community kitchen [Gemeinde-Küche]".
And my companion was right; as the saying goes: "A guest for a while sees for a mile." The activity around the kitchen already gives a clear picture of what people call
— kehilla activity, or more correctly, communal work; and upon my life, it would do no harm at all if our women (they may again find themselves offended...) were to take a lesson in how to conduct oneself in a communal kitchen...
It was dinner time. Around the clean tables covered with tablecloths sat some 50—60 diners. Portions are also given out to take home. But the giving out, and the taking, are very far from "shedding blood" [i.e. putting a person to shame]; everything in the most decent manner, without shame, without shouting.
— "Bitte sehr, zum Wiedersehen" [German: "If you please, goodbye"] — are the words that accompany everyone who makes use of the kitchen.
During the meal quiet reigns. The diners behave as if in their own home; people read a newspaper, and more than a newspaper. Here a young man sits at the table and studies the scores of Mozart...
The kitchen has existed for 6 years already — the directress explains to me, the wife of Dr. Kaufmann, who never fails to come to the kitchen every day and is present when the dinners are given out. According to the regulations one is to pay 20 groszy for a dinner (meat every day), but from the 120 dinners that are given out the income is barely four złoty... Perhaps — she says — the Zagłębie religious communities would subsidise the kitchen. "Wir haben doch so viel von Bendzin" [German: "After all, we have so many from Będzin"]...
Leaving this important institution, the suggestion comes to my mind: that for the leaders of the Zagłębie kehillas it would be very necessary to get acquainted with what is called, among other people,
— productive kehilla work.
Important rulings of the Supreme Court.

[Law — Supreme Court rulings.]
Begging is permitted.
Article 32 of the Decree on Petty Offences [Prawo o wykroczeniach] provides a penalty of up to one month's arrest for begging, but only in the case where it is done in an insolent or fraudulent manner.
For begging in a decent manner, on the other hand, the Decree on Petty Offences provides no penalty whatsoever.

Insurance of intellectual [white-collar] workers.
Persons employed by travelling troupes are not subject to the insurance of intellectual workers.

Industrial law
The provision that every enterprise must be furnished with a signboard is laid down not only by the law on the industrial tax but also by the industrial (guild) law.
Our Panorama

[Będzin and the region — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.
(The foundations of the world are shaken. — Blood in the Czeladź beit midrash[?]. — A shammes crisis. — In Wolbrom it is merry, — Sabbath-keepers[?] set boundaries. — The young wives are already “going”. — A holy war in the Żarki shtibl.)

We are not destined to have one restful day. The Sarajevo shot in the year 1914 shook the foundations of the world, and the world-fire that was kindled then has not been extinguished to this very day. Hardly have we breathed a little more freely after the bloody events in Austria, and already blood is flowing again in Czeladź — and not only blood: stoves fall, benches fly, and, the main thing, the shammes of the beit midrash threatens to tender his resignation.

We do not wish to state our opinion as to on whom the blame falls; we wish to be “neutral” and pass on the official report that we received from the holy community of Czeladź word for word, written according to the “nusach” (“nisekh”) of the Little “Folkstsaytung” [Kleine Folkstsaytung].

“Mister Editor I make known to you about the Czeladź synagogue what happened this Sabbath at the prayers a little boy of 5 years went up onto the bimah the shammes went and gave the boy a slap he drew blood from his face he asked the shammes why he had hit the child and out of this there arose a fight with knives in the synagogue and the gabbaim did not respond because they are afraid of him it would already be time[?] that one be rid of him from the beit midrash many people weep because of him such a coarse person as he there is not in the whole world as he is”.

———

The “when Adar enters, joy is increased” is being strictly observed this year in Wolbrom. Joy reigns in every home; all faces, and especially among the older generation, beam with gladness, and it is “la-Yehudim”-like [as in “the Jews had light and gladness”].
And indeed the joy ought to be complete — a trifle, one might say, to vanquish the Angel of Death...
And this is how the story went:
Once, on an ordinary Sunday in the morning, the shtetl is shaken by the news that there are 3 dead in the shtetl. True, these were no young people: one who himself no longer remembered when he had been healthy; the second lacked 2 more years to make his illness a 20-year one; and the third? Also of the same sort. But what has that to do with the matter? The main thing is the living, sad fact
— 3 dead. 3 funerals in one day...
Well, in another town, where the evil inclination has already firmly established itself, where the forty-nine gates of impurity have encompassed all branches of Jewish life, such a matter of three dead is waved away with the hand. Died, buried, and on with the sinning.
Quite differently was the thing received in Wolbrom. Why, this is a real “epidemic”, Heaven preserve us; is it possible? 3 dead! So the seven notables of the town assembled and set about devising counsels and means how to check the epidemic...
And “I toiled and I found”. It became clear that in many dwellings[?] the beds stand tightly pressed together like one piece... and the young wives are not careful about the first of the three commandments [the women's commandments: niddah, challah, candle-lighting]...
And since “the Rebbe Elimelech wanted to be merry” — this is what he did: he sent out several dozen inspectors, who measured the length of the beds in every home and set boundaries.. Then the guardian of family purity was summoned and called upon to keep an exact register of those who “go” [to the mikveh], according to which the number will become clear of
— those who do not go...
Well, perhaps you still think that the measures did not help? — you are greatly mistaken. As our correspondent assures us, the situation looks like this: hardly had they begun to move the beds apart and the young wives begun to “go”, when at once
— the plague ceased, and in the shtetl there is gladness and joy; it is hoped that it will now be “death swallowed up for ever”, no one will die in Wolbrom...

———

In the Żarki shtibl of Będzin the first Sabbath of the month of Adar was, alas, disturbed. On whose account, do you think?
— On account of the Będzin “Mizrachi”, which took a fancy, no more and no less, to arrange a lecture by the Rabbi of Tomaszów, Rabbi Brodt. What is more, a craving of the Mizrachists: to hang up a poster in the Żarki shtibl — was such a thing ever heard?...
But Israel is not widowed; Jewishness is, thank God, still strong enough. Let the “Mizrachi” not triumph that religious Jewry is permeated with the Land-of-Israel idea; no, it is a lie. And the proof? The gabbai of the Żarki shtibl, who is ready to perish for the sanctification of the Name, so long as no spark of his Hasidism be lost.
And the gabbai “can” prove this not merely theoretically but also practically: when he actually caught sight of the heretical poster, the Hasidic ardour flared up, and roaring like a lion he fought for the sanctification of the Name and[?] removed the Sitra Achra out of the shtibl...
Many of our readers will perhaps wonder and doubt whether this happened, for the physiognomy of the gabbai is a contradiction to his deeds; but for us this is already a familiar thing: we know that the gabbai of the Żarki shtibl belongs to those who are punctilious over the very tip of a yod; he will not, for example, eat a crumb of sugar-cake on the eve of Passover before he asks a rabbinical question about it... But be that as it may, the Żarki Hasidim in Będzin had a disturbed Sabbath.
Ben Amotz.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Tetzaveh)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Tetzaveh
The Portion
—o—
a) “And you shall command” (Ex. 27:20)
The Baal HaTurim says on this verse that this is why Moses' name is absent from the portion — whereas there is not a single portion in the Torah, from the time his birth is told, in which Moses' name is not found — because at the affair of the Calf Moses pleaded: “Blot me, I pray, out of Your book which You have written”, and the curse of a sage “comes about even when made conditionally”; therefore his name was erased from one portion.
• • •
The question arises: for that reason his name ought rather to have gone unmentioned in one of the portions after Parashat [Ki] Tisa, after the affair of the Calf —
But Moses said: Blot me out of Your book which You have w r i t t e n — out of the portion that You wrote earlier, out of the portion before Parashat Tisa, where the affair of the Calf is mentioned — out of Parashat Tetzaveh... Kehillat Yitzchak.
—o—
b) “To cause a lamp to burn [lit. to raise up a lamp] continually” (ibid.)
In Parashat Behaalotecha Rashi says: “‘When you raise up...’ — there was a step in front of the Menorah, on which the priest stood and trimmed [the lamps]”, meaning that this is why the expression “raising up” is used of the Menorah: because in front of the Menorah there was a step to go up on. The question arises: why does Rashi not remark on this here too, at “to r a i s e  u p a continual lamp”?
But the Menorah was three cubits high (eighteen handbreadths), and the height of a man is also three cubits. Therefore there had to be a step, so that Aaron could stand higher than the Menorah and clean it. But here, in this portion, the text is after all also speaking of Moses (who performed the service during the eight days of consecration), and Moses was ten cubits tall, as the Sages say — so he needed no step to the Menorah... Mayim Yechezkel.
—o—
c) “And you, bring near Aaron your brother... from among the children of Israel” (28:1)
Not you, Moses, can become the priest — you are too tall; but Aaron, the one who comes “from among the children of Israel”, from the people, the one who “mixes with people”, the “pursuer of peace” — he can be the emissary of the people. Ohel Yaakov.
• • •
In Radin [Raduń], in the yeshiva of the “Chofetz Chaim”, a celebration was once held. In the midst of the rejoicing one of the students went up to the “Chofetz Chaim” and wanted to lift him up on his hands, as is the custom among people, who lift a beloved leader on their hands. The Chofetz Chaim grew angry at the student and said:
— One does not lift a man up higher than he is...
—o—
d) “Four rows of stones” (ibid., 17)
The author of the Akedah says that among the stones of the breastplate there were the most precious stones as well as the cheapest stones, because the breastplate atoned, as the Sages say, for the perversion of justice. This showed that when justice is perverted, “a case of a penny is like a case of a hundred”, and there is no difference whether one perverts justice over a grosz or over a million.
• • •
And that is why it is said of the breastplate “and it shall be upon Aaron's heart” — Aaron wore it on his heart, because these are matters entrusted to the heart, and the outside person does not know to what extent the judge has perverted justice... Taamei HaMitzvot.
—o—
e) “And engrave upon it, like the engravings of a signet: Holy to the Lord” (ibid., 36)
The head-plate (tzitz) atoned for brazenness. Brazenness in holiness, however, is permitted. That is why the head-plate bore the inscription “Holy to the Lord”. For only when it is holy to the Lord, when by brazenness in holiness one means solely and only the sake of Heaven, is it permitted... The head-plate revealed which brazenness is “Holy to the Lord”. R' Moshe Sofer.
• • •
And that is why the Tanna says in Avot: “The brazen-faced go to Gehenna... May it be Your will that the Temple be rebuilt” — because today, too, everyone says that his brazenness is holy to the Lord, that with his brazenness he is only aiming at the sake of Heaven... Therefore the Tanna prays: “May it be Your will that the Temple be rebuilt” — and then the head-plate will reveal whose brazenness is truly for the sake of Heaven... Ktav Sofer.
A Quiet Struggle

[Commerce — Sunday rest and trading hours; article.] One of the chief demands (postulates) of the Jewish population in Poland to the government is the amendment of the law on Sunday rest. Bound up with it is also the question of regulating trading hours.
It is by now superfluous to demonstrate that in today's hard times, with the heavy tax burdens, with the heavy payments for social insurance, the merchant must make all manner of exertions [?] to extract from his small shop his bit of livelihood. The shopkeeper must seek out and hold on to the buyer and consumer, must adapt himself to him and arrange his trade so that the buyer can, and will want to, buy without difficulties. But for the Jewish shopkeeper this is made harder: the Jewish shopkeeper must suspend his trade on Sunday, then on Saturday, and in wintertime another half of Friday. Can a shop exist if it is to be active only 4 and a half days a week?
That is almost impossible. For a certain time people still hoped for the regulation of trading hours. Certain categories of shops were able to stay open after seven o'clock in the evening, just when it is most convenient for the buyer to shop; now the restrictions in this respect have come, and the heavy fines for trading after seven o'clock.
On this point a quiet struggle is being played out between the Christian and the Jewish small traders. The Christian small trader has no interest in trading longer than until 7 o'clock, because in return he has the half Friday and the Saturday; he trades a normal six days a week. In trading after 7 he sees competition to himself on the part of the Jewish shopkeepers, and therefore the Christian merchants' organisations have recently begun a sharp fight to restrict trading hours.
The Jewish merchants' associations, by contrast, are waging the fight to permit trade after 7 in the evening, and show with every argument that nobody loses by it — not the state, not the consumer, not the merchant and also not the employee, whom the shopkeeper is willing to release at 7 o'clock in the evening.
This struggle is conducted by means of memoranda. The Jewish small traders' associations send a memorandum to the ministry about abolishing the restrictions — at once a second memorandum comes from the Christian side about applying repressive measures against those who trade beyond the permitted hours. The Jewish representatives of the small traders in the Chamber of Commerce demand an intervention for abolishing the restrictions — the Christian representatives bring that intervention to nothing.
The whole struggle takes place in silence and is not carried out into the public. In our opinion, the most proper thing would be for an attempt to be made to bring the Jewish and the Christian representatives together at one table, so that a single position might be reached on this question. Given a unity of opinions, the Ministry of Commerce would surely have no interest in opposing anyone, and the matter would be settled, because, as we have already pointed out, nobody suffers any harm by it. The attempt must be made. The initiative should be taken in the first place by the Chamber of Commerce. If that is not possible, the initiative must come from the Jewish small traders' associations, which, after all, must themselves at long last have a uniform position on the question. Until now that has not been so.
D.
Salomon Gutman, of blessed memory (For the Shloshim)

[Będzin — memorial tribute for the shloshim (thirtieth day of mourning); headline in a black frame.] As a representative of the Jewish community of Będzin, I not long ago took leave of one of the oldest and most respected householders in our town, my best friend Salomon Gutman, may he rest in Eden.
I cannot bring myself to believe that he is no longer among us. Merciless death tore him from us suddenly. Like a thunderclap the news struck everyone that Shlomo Gutman, may he rest in Eden, was no longer alive, and still more did it strike his friends, who had lived side by side with him for many years.
The deceased was, as far back as some twenty-odd years ago, a founder of almost all the larger and most important societies in our town. Already before the war he was a founder of our Merchants' Association and afterwards its president for many years. He was also the founder and long-time president of the Będzin Jewish gymnasium, then "Yavne" and now bearing the name "Szymonostwo Fürstenberg" [i.e. "Mr. and Mrs. Szymon Fürstenberg"]. It was a fantasy at the time, when a small group of people with the deceased at its head — we sat together in the year 1915, in the time of the German occupation, and resolved to create in Będzin a Jewish gymnasium, which is today a source of pride for the whole of Jewry in Zagłębie, thanks to the understanding of our benefactor Mr. Fürstenberg, who erected a splendid building for the gymnasium, in which 450 Jewish children now study; and with that the idea of the small group of people headed by the deceased was made everlasting.
The deceased was also for a number of years a councillor in the Będzin Town Council in the time of the German occupation, and took part, with counsel and deed, in almost all the larger communal institutions.
In his family life, too, he was exemplary: his relation to the children and wife was that of a friend, and not of the one who gives the orders in the family.
His conduct towards people was always calm and modest, and for that reason he won so much sympathy among the people of our town.
A crowd a thousand strong took part in his funeral; at the open grave representatives of various organisations eulogised him and comforted the family left in deep mourning.
To the mournful singing of Hatikvah the grave was filled in of my best friend and modest communal worker, may he rest in Eden, Shlomo Gutman.
He has been torn away from us and is no longer in our ranks. But his memory remains with us for ever.
Chaval al de'avdin [Alas for those who are lost].
Eleazar Rubinlicht,
President of the Jewish Community in Będzin.
Panna Sabina [Miss Sabina]

[Feuilleton — a satire on assimilation.] I was invited to a "herbatka" [Polish: a tea party] at the home of acquaintances of mine, in honour of their little daughter's birthday.
In the brightly lit room there is a hum of noise.
At many little tables sit small groups of guests, deeply absorbed — some in a game of poker or "król" [a card game], some in a discussion.
Most of the women had gathered round a separate little table and were enthusiastically talking over the newest fashions and other similarly important events.
Particular attention was drawn to herself by her — Panna Sabina.
Leaning back on her chair, a cigarette in her mouth, and with the air of a woman who is called "Sabina" and understands the magical ring of that name...
And indeed, every time one of her girlfriends ["koleżanki"] addressed her by that melodious, supremely modern name — "Sabina" — a kind of inner joy showed on her face, and one could positively sense that it gave Panna Sabina great pleasure.
It goes without saying, and it is superfluous to add, that her girlfriends looked at her with envy and no doubt deeply regretted that fate had shamed them and endowed them with such unmodern, small-town names, inherited from the ancient grandmothers Sarah, Rebecca...
And our Sabina did indeed reign the whole time over all her company.
She threw out topics for conversation, she set the tone of the discussion, which was conducted, as is the custom, in... but never mind, Russian or Polish — the fact is that the nice company did not, Heaven forbid, disgrace itself with "jargon" [the disparaging name for Yiddish].
New guests keep arriving; at the card tables it grew ever more crowded and hotter; the gramophone kept serving the company a fresh portion of hit songs — "Może kiedyś" ["Maybe some day"], "Pierwszy znak" ["The first sign"].
And at that little table she still reigns — Sabina.
She is now conducting a very serious conversation: who spent the carnival well. Well, you understand of course that most of the questions were addressed to her — to Sabina.
"I," Sabina solemnly declared, "was at the ball of the Polish intelligentsia and 'enjoyed' ['cieszyłam się'] a 'wild success' ['szalone powodzenie']." There she had made the acquaintance of someone — it seems to her with the rank of a porucznik [lieutenant], and perhaps even higher. But... what does the rank matter to us here — the fact is: "mężczyzna i w mundurze" ["a man, and in uniform at that"]. This man, let him be a lieutenant — Sabina relates — admired her slender figure, her grace, showered countless compliments upon her, and altogether she — Sabina — stood at the centre of interest of the whole Polish intelligentsia... The girlfriends, with envy-filled eyes, swallowed Sabina's every word.
And every time the word "porucznik" was mentioned, one could see how it positively pained them.
Some of them actually decided (what envy will lead to!) to steer the talk onto other paths, and by chance they came out upon the subject of reading as a sport.
Here Panna Sabina displayed great erudition in the works of Pitigrilli and in others of the same kind.
One of the girlfriends unwittingly let slip something about Sholem Asch.
At this Sabina pricked up her delicate ears and, with wide-open eyes, asked:
"Co-o?! [Wha-at?!] 'Niestety' [unfortunately], she is not acquainted with the jargon literature... In the 'towarzystwo' [the society] in which she 'obraca się' [moves], that Szalom Asz is a 'nieznany pisarz' [an unknown writer]..."
The girlfriend blushed, and the others put on an expression as if to say: now that is what you call intelligentsia...
In the end the conversation had got to the point where she — Sabina — was relating her "wrażenia" [impressions] of when she "bawiła" [stayed] with her "wujaszek" [uncle] on that Jewish holiday — well, what do they call it there, "Kuczki" [Sukkot] — well, the time when they blow the "trąbka" [the little trumpet]...
But at this point the door suddenly burst open and an elderly woman rushed hastily in and, wringing her hands and turning towards Sabina, broke into weeping:
"Sore Trayne, gevalt, come quickly, father has collapsed."
The girlfriends exchanged a glance, and on their lips a smile of satisfaction seemed to turn to stone.
Dear reader, the fate of "Sabina" is sealed...
B[?]. Rozenfeld.
Three Weeks Later.

[Literature — a sketch.] By S. Michael.
(A sketch)

Dovid, a young man of thirty, fell ill. He fell so gravely ill that the family doctor, Wolfson, ordered a consilium to be convened, then another consilium, and yet another consilium. And the old professor and the young Doctor Wolfson agreed that the patient must undergo an operation.

Dovid's young wife, her eyes red with weeping, was the first to take it upon herself to tell the sick man. She sat down beside him on the bed, stroked his forehead, which was covered with clammy sweat, and quietly, with her head lowered, began:

— My dear friend! They have decided that the very quickest way to be rid of your illness is an operation. The operation is not a serious one. In two weeks' time you will be well again and will be back at home again...

Here she raised her eyes, and, meeting his eyes, bloodshot from sleepless nights, she suddenly fell silent, as though she had choked on the word.

Dovid looked at her with that heavy, fixed stare with which he had begun to look at her as far back as half a year ago. She knew what that look meant: jealousy and suspicion. And even now, lying ill, in so grave a condition, he had still not stopped being jealous and harbouring a suspicion against her.

He is especially restless when Wolfson, their family doctor, comes to him. The sick man then does not take his heavy gaze off him, off her, off the two of them. At such moments, seeking somehow to smooth over the awkward[?] situation, the wife begins to talk with exaggerated attentiveness. She keeps her tongue grinding without a stop, talks and talks, as though she wanted to talk someone out of his senses. Wolfson, the young, handsome doctor, evidently feels flustered too, and he questions the patient in an exaggeratedly loud voice.

Dovid is silent. He takes pleasure in their confusion, as in a sweet revenge. He looks them through and through. He probes them with his dull, heavy gaze and does not answer the questions. As a sick man he has the right to be "capricious".

— His caprices are more than one can bear! — Dovid hears his wife complaining to the doctor in the next room, and it seems to him that she is saying it like that on purpose, so that he should hear and should think that she is talking with the doctor about the most ordinary things, and that that terrible accusation which he flung at her not long before he fell ill really is nothing but the "fruit of his crazy jealousy", as she cried out at the time.

"Crazy jealousy"... Then why does she blossom so when that man comes in? Why does she send for him straight away over every bit of foolishness. Over every slightest thing? What is this — "Doctor Wolfson" and "Doctor Wolfson"! The name simply never leaves her lips! And when she utters that name it seems to him, to Dovid, that together with the word "Wolfson" a vapour flies out of her mouth, a sweet and mysterious one; it is so unpleasant when she utters that very word!

His jealousy has grown still greater during his illness. Under the pretext of supposedly medical visits to the sick man he comes to see him, this Doctor Wolfson, twice a day. And it seems to Dovid that after these visits his pains become even stronger. He is altogether much worse after the doctor's visits!

— That doctor of yours doesn't know what to do with himself, he is so full of life! Why has he taken[?] to turning up here, like all the devils? — Dovid complains to his wife.

— You are such a capricious man! — she answers patiently, straightening his pillow or handing him a spoonful of the medicine that Doctor Wolfson has prescribed. All the while there flits across her face an expression of martyrdom, the look of an innocent victim. And that irritates him and pains him. But from the mere fact that she is beside him, that he sees her right here next to him, he feels a little easier.

At the first words about an operation the thought that flashed through him was not about his own life, but only about them, about her and Doctor Wolfson. He, Dovid, will be taken away to the hospital, and she will stay alone in the house, and Doctor Wolfson will come to her...

And fixing on her a heavy, hard stare, he brought out in weighty, clipped words:

— I do not want any operation!...

But at that very moment Doctor Wolfson came into the room. He came in from outside, from the winter frost, fresh, cheerful and, above all, healthy. He came in rubbing his hands from the cold, and as he came in he uttered that phrase which is ordinarily used by all doctors of all countries and all peoples:

— Well, and how are we feeling today?

———

The first night in the hospital, before the operation, was for Dovid a terrible night, a nightmare. His wife had not been allowed to stay overnight, and he was left all alone with his torments and with his fear. It was not the operation he was afraid of, but something else: jealousy gnawed at him and ate away at him with the dismal pictures. Now he will die... he will surely die... and she will marry Wolfson... His wife and — Doctor Wolfson!... His hair stands on end with dread and heartache. And the more he thinks about it, Dovid, the less he wants to die. He does not want to die! He does not want to die! No, he does not! He wants to live, to live, to live!...

He began to feel unwell. So he rang, calling the attendants.

— How you do upset yourself! — said the nurse, counting his pulse. — Be strong, take yourself in hand! Be a man!...

"I must not, I must not die!" — came the answer inside his head. — "Die?"

———

Three weeks later he was sitting in his own home in a soft armchair, emaciated, pale, and his wife — on a little stool at his feet. For the hundredth time they recalled and went over how it had all happened; how he had been ill, how he had been operated on, how he had very nearly died, how somehow, by some miracle, he had recovered, how all the doctors had already given him up, and only Doctor Wolfson alone had given her hope. He was a friend to the end. Now he hardly shows himself — he is no longer needed...

Dovid feels a slight stab in his heart when she utters Doctor Wolfson's name, but the old, bad feeling is indeed at once replaced by another feeling, which masters and swallows up all the others, the strongest, the mightiest feeling — the joy of living.

He is alive, he has not died. He can move, look at his wife, stroke her hair, look into her eyes.

He no longer broods over what tormented him during his illness. All that has been wiped away, has evaporated, just as if it had entirely steamed away together with the smell of the ether he was given during the operation. "What, after all, is there better than life" — he thinks to himself, and, slightly lifting his wife's face by her little chin, he says aloud:

— He did a great deal for me, Doctor Wolfson! We shall have to thank him with something...
Little Feuilleton. The Jew in the "Gentile Paradise"...

[Little feuilleton — political satire.] Signed: P.

A simple characterization.

A peasant from a village once told me — speaking in all innocence — his dream.

— I dreamed — says the peasant — that I had died and at once flew straight into Paradise.

The peasant describes the splendours in heaven, in Paradise, and concludes:

— Ha, ha, ha! As fine as at the king's! [in Polish: Ładnie jak u króla!]

— In Paradise — the peasant goes on with his story — there stood great chests full of okovita [strong spirit], tin quart-mugs were fastened on iron chains, and everyone may drink as much as he pleases.

But hardly had I scooped up a quart of spirit and was already holding it to my mouth to drink, when a "Żyd" [Jew-boy] Moshke caught me by the hand:

— Psiajucha [damn you]! Have you paid yet? [in Polish: Psiajucha! Czyś ty już zapłacił?]

And the peasant concluded:

— The devil take it! There is a Jew even there! [in Polish: Niech to szlag trafi! I tam jest Żyd!]

———

I am reading about a heated debate in the Sejm. Deputy Rybarski of the Narodowcy [the National Democrats] criticizes very sharply.

Among other things he says:

Foreign capital in Poland has made great progress, and he only regrets that no statistics have been published on the growth of Jewish capital.

How they do manage to drag the Jew in!

Never mind! When Deputy Żuławski says in the debate:

— The strength of the "BB" [the Non-Party Bloc for Cooperation with the Government] rests on the Radziwiłłs and the Wiślickis, — he too is not far from that peasant who says:

— A Jew there too! [in Polish: I tam też Żyd!]

The Jewish Queen of Yemen (8)

[Serialized historical tale — Yemen, King Yusuf Dhu Nuwas; installment 8, the last.]
Sh. Berg.

The Christian priests heard of this, and they called upon the emperor of Byzantium to march on Yemen. On his own, however, he was afraid that his army might be buried under the sand of the desert before it reached the border of Yemen. [So] he concluded an alliance with the king of Abyssinia, and together they are marching on Yemen with a mighty army; they are already not far from the border — and this is what the general had announced to him.

He saw her fright and he calmed her. The army is mobilized. Overnight it will be ready, and at the very break of day he will lead it against the enemy. She understood that he was only comforting her, but that a terrible war lay before him. And although she knew that he himself was to blame — he should not have attacked the Christian merchants, and he had also been cruel to prisoners [?] — still [— (smeared line; perhaps: "there was no help for it now")], and he is her husband, she loves him, [she would have] given [?] her life for him; yet she said nothing at all about it. She only begged him to lie down and rest before the hard journey.

They lay down, but could not close an eye. He tossed from side to side, and from her eyes tears flowed silently and wetted the bed.

Before sunrise the sound of a trumpet was heard. Yusuf sprang up from [?] the bed, and Pnina after him. She handed him a fresh drink, he put on his weapons, threw himself upon her neck, kissed her ardently and said:

— Farewell, Pnina dear, we shall see each other again. Do not worry. Here, or there in… heaven!

He tried hard to smile, but he could not. Tears ran down his cheeks and over his handsome [?] beard. Pnina wept bitterly and wished him [?] that he might go in good health and come back in good health and win a great victory. She begged him to swear to her by God that he would never again force anyone to become a Jew. Jews dissuade a gentile who wants to convert, telling him not to do it — she said to him. And that he would never again attack anyone. He swore it to her. With great love he pressed her to himself, they embraced and kissed and could not tear themselves away from one another.

A knock was heard at the door. He tore himself from her arms, kissed her for the last time, and, wiping away her tears, went out quickly.

Pnina wept for a long time; her heart pounded stormily, as though it felt [?] that she would never see him again.

About an hour later the army set out [?] on its way. Yusuf rode ahead on a wondrous horse — a handsome, proud, courageous hero led the army; this was how Pnina had first seen him in the Arab village. But she knew that now it was different: he had to wage war against a united army of mighty kings. Quietly saying a prayer, with tears in her eyes, she followed him with her gaze until he was swallowed up in the distance.

By the Red Sea Yusuf met the enemy. The battle began. Yusuf's army worked wonders; it dealt the enemy mighty blows. But it also suffered heavy losses. And as the enemy's army was greater in number, in the end Yusuf's army lost and began to retreat.

Yusuf saw this and he resolved to die like a hero rather than live in shame. He rode his horse up onto a rock and leapt down into the sea. The sea became his grave.

The victorious army took Yemen and slaughtered many Jews. But before the enemy reached the capital, Sana'a, there arrived Tzede'a [?; in installment 6 "Mede'a" (?)], Tzarida's husband [printed here „צאריידאס מאן“], who had been in Yusuf's army. As soon as he saw Yusuf leap into the sea, he ran like an arrow from a bow to Sana'a, to rescue his wife and the queen. In haste they fled, and with them a great, great many Jews, and they settled in Qamus, in the land of Khaybar. There they built a strong fortress to protect themselves from their enemies, the Christians.

Two months after the death of Yusuf Dhu Nuwas, Pnina gave birth to a son and named him after his father — Yusuf. The son was the consolation in her misfortune. Pnina, the Jewish queen of Yemen, who had so quickly lost her husband and her kingdom, did not forget her husband all her life long, and she never married again.

The people of Qamus crowned Pnina as their queen, and after her death her son Yusuf inherited the crown, and the dynasty ruled the land for over two hundred years.

(The end.)
No Agreement Reached Between the Zionist and Mizrachi Parnasim on the Salaries for the Rabbinate

[Będzin — community.]
[Head of the local page:] What's New in Zagłębie? (Friday, 8 Adar 5694 — piątek 23 lutego 1934.)
Będzin
In the course of the past week consultations took place between the Zionist and Mizrachi parnasim [kehilla councillors] regarding their stance towards the budget.
Sharp differences of opinion came to the surface while the salaries for the rabbinate were being dealt with. The Zionist parnasim take the standpoint that, apart from the 10-percent reduction, according to the board's draft, the item of rent money for the rabbi's dwelling should also be taken away, the salary for the beit-din beadle should be struck out, and the like.
The Mizrachi parnasim are against striking out the special supplementary items and, in general, [hold] that the salary reduction should be by only 5 percent...

“The Jews Rob the Polish State.” Such a Lesson Is Given by the Director of the Evening Courses.

[Będzin — antisemitism, education.]
Several weeks ago we carried in our newspaper a notice about the harassment of the Jewish children who attend the evening courses, on the part of their Christian classmates. On that occasion we drew the attention of the Pan Director to it, that he should take steps so that the attacks and harassment should not recur.
As it turns out, the Director took offence: how can it be? A “jargon” [“żargonowa”, i.e. Yiddish] newspaper should preach morals to him? And indeed, instead of reprimanding his Christian pupils, last Thursday he delivered a lesson like this:
“A żydowska [“Yid”] newspaper wrote that the Jewish children who attend the evening courses are being beaten. When the Jews are beaten — says he — they come here to Poland, where they receive protection, and afterwards they rob the Polish state.”
The Director was still not content with this and “prophesied” that “in Poland the same will happen to the Jews as in Vienna.”
After the “moral” lesson the Jewish pupils left the courses in protest.
Our informant describes to us the severe torments of the Jewish children who attend the courses. For example, the non-Jewish pupils threaten them with knives, shout “Hitler is coming,” and so on.

To the Jewish Population in Poland!

[Warsaw — appeal; the refugees from Germany and the struggle against Hitlerism.]
(Sent in by the United Jewish Aid Committee for the Refugees from Germany, Warsaw.)
Brother Jews!
Hitlerism, which has now ruled in Germany for a year, has convinced us that the madness of hatred and the policy of extermination towards Jews, which is being spread by the race fanatics, is no passing phenomenon. The tendentious reports that a certain weakening has occurred in the Hitlerite anti-Jewish action have no foundation, for the adherents of Hitlerism are again preparing and carrying into life a planned and systematic struggle against the whole of Jewry, not only in Germany but also in many other countries.
Since the times of medieval barbarism, since the times of the Spanish Inquisition, Jewry has not been exposed to such heavy trials: the entire German state apparatus and the unlimited propaganda funds stand at the disposal of the adherents of the wild hatred, working upon the lowest human instincts.
Against this organized hostile action the whole of Jewry must organize itself and prepare for a long-lasting, embittered struggle; only in unity does our strength lie, only our unity can lead to a victory. In this matter there are no party differences whatsoever, the whole Jewish community has only one opinion, and everyone is unconditionally obliged to submit to the orders of those who have taken upon themselves the heavy burden and duty of leading the struggle.
In order to carry out this action properly, a proper fund is necessary. It should on the one hand be able to be used to relieve the distress of the refugees who are in Poland, to settle them in Eretz Israel, and on the other hand for the energetic combating of the Hitlerite propaganda.
In order to give the action a uniform character, the representatives of all parts of Jewish society have unanimously empowered the United Jewish Aid Committee for the Refugees from Germany to carry out in the year 1934 a mass collection in the form of a one-time obligatory self-taxation, which will be carried out on the basis of precisely fixed norms. The proper carrying-out of the action will take place under the supervision of specially appointed citizens' committees. Everyone is obliged to contribute the sum according to these fixed principles.
By paying in the one-time self-taxation we shall only be fulfilling our duty towards the community and towards ourselves.
Not fulfilling this important national duty will be tantamount to supporting the hostile Hitlerite action.

A Jewish merchant from Tel Aviv

Conducts commercial negotiations with a German firm.
A certain M.[?] H. Jungster of Tel Aviv approached a German firm on business matters.
The German firm, not knowing the creditworthiness of the party making the offer („der Oferte“), turned to its former customer, the haberdashery firm of Mr. N.[?] Abramczyk, for information concerning Mr. Jungster.
Mr. Abramczyk gave the German firm the following reply: I cannot supply the requested information because 1) it is almost unbelievable to me that a Jewish merchant from Tel Aviv should have any commercial relations whatsoever with a German firm, and 2) even if this should indeed be true, I likewise refuse to give any kind of information to a firm from present-day Germany.

The building committee of the beit midrash in Pogoń turns to Marshal Piłsudski about its claim against the Sosnowiec kehilla.
As is known, the building committee of the Pogoń beit midrash [Pogoń, a quarter of Sosnowiec] has remained owing a sum of 4000 zł.; the sum was lent by several Christians, and to this day they cannot collect the debt. The committee, and especially its chairman, the shochet (shub) R' Dawid Zweigenhaft, has turned many times to the kehilla representatives. The “Meter” Betrayed Them...

[Zagłębie — everyday life, a true story.] Two young, pretty, modest friends[?], innocent doves, rented lodgings — a separate room, a separate entrance; all day they worked in a “biuro” (office), came home in the evening, slept the whole night and duly paid the rent as subtenants.
The old couple was pleased with the two lodgers. They themselves went to bed with the chickens and slept so soundly that even Dollfuss with his cannons would not have woken them.
At the end of the month the couple noticed that the bill from the power station had somehow grown threefold. How come? The lodgers, after all, sleep the whole night? They are, after all, quiet, decent children?
So the little old woman began to check, and very quickly convinced herself that the “office girls” (biuralistki) do not at all like to sleep at night: by day they lie in their beds, and by night they hold “conferences” with young men, and such “conferences” take place some ten[?] every night — and that is why the meter (licznik) turns and the bill grows.
The matter has gone to court; the couple demands eviction (eksmisja) of the “office girls”. The evidence against the lodgers is the statements of the main householders and the bill from the power station.
Will the court grant an eviction on that basis?
A well-known publicist, who writes articles about politics, has a ready answer to such a question: the future will show.

A Letter to the Editor
[Sosnowiec — history of the kehilla, letter to the editor.]
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
We, the undersigned, take the liberty of drawing attention to some incorrect passages in the article by Mr. Moshe Feinkind of last Friday, entitled "The First Period of the Sosnowiec Kehilla".
1) It is not correct that the first Jews who came to Sosnowiec were mostly tailors and that therefore the first minyan that arose in our town was a tailors' minyan; on the contrary, in so small a number of Jews as there then was in Sosnowiec, 90 per cent among them were of the wealthy strata.
2) Nor is it correct that the Sosnowiec Jews tore themselves away from the Będzin kehilla by great efforts with the Piotrków governor; in fact the great Jewish industrialists of Sosnowiec worked in Petersburg and brought it about that Sosnowiec is an independent town with a Jewish kehilla of its own.
3) Nor is it correct that Rabbi R' Abraham Meir Gitler of blessed memory was the first rabbi in Sosnowiec, for the first rabbi was Rabbi R' Arie Leibish Gitler of blessed memory, the father of Rabbi R. A. M. [R' Abraham Meir] of blessed memory.
4) Again, concerning the rabbinate in Sosnowiec the writer's account is not correct. Rabbi R' Abraham Meir Gitler of blessed memory was a licensed ["concessioned"] rabbi from among the old rabbis; after the passing of his father of blessed memory the Sosnowiec Jews accepted him as rabbi. Later, when Sosnowiec became independent and the government demanded an examined rabbi, the Jewish kehilla again unanimously elected Rabbi Gitler of blessed memory, and the papers were sent to the gubernia for confirmation together with his licence, which served[?] him. Unfortunately, however, there were already at that time "modern" rabbis, and one of the "modern" rabbis, Rabbi M., had a great appetite for the Sosnowiec rabbinate; unable to attain it, he found a way out with a little denunciation to the gubernia, which he sent in, arguing therein that Rabbi Gitler's licence lapses, because more than 5 years had already passed since Rabbi Gitler exchanged the rabbinate of Pińczów for Sosnowiec. (At that time such was the Russian law.)
How beloved Rabbi Gitler of blessed memory already was among us then may be shown by the fact that, after Rabbi Gitler of blessed memory lost the licence as crown ["kazyonny"] rabbi, the Jewish kehilla took, as a label [a mere figurehead], the late Mr. Dawid Sztajnzalc and made him crown rabbi, so as not thereby to let in any "modern" rabbi — for already then we understood what a "modern" rabbi is. Yet after a few years Rabbi Gitler of blessed memory received his licence back from the government with full authority.
5) As for the "third" dozór [kehilla-board member], R' Lejb Englard — you did not find his merits in the files, because his activity was exclusively in the religious field alone; and secondly, we see[?] nothing of importance in the files at all.
With respect,
A group of Sosnowiec Jews who still remember how present-day Sosnowiec was a forest.

A New Decree

[Poland — economy and trade; article.]
The Polish merchants' associations have already declared themselves in favour of the proposal to introduce an educational qualification (census) for merchants.
And what does the proposed educational qualification for merchants consist of:
1) In order to run a commercial enterprise of the 4th category one would have to have completed 6 classes of an elementary school. Besides that, one must complete a one-year commercial school and go through a proper commercial apprenticeship. 2) The right to run an enterprise of the second and third commercial category is to belong only to persons who complete a commercial gymnasium, a one-year commercial school, and go through a proper commercial apprenticeship. 3) Only persons who complete a commercial lyceum and go through a proper commercial apprenticeship are to be permitted to run an enterprise of the 1st commercial category.
The cup of decrees is apparently not yet full... But whereas people try to justify decrees — for example in the field of tax policy — by saying that the State Treasury is in need of revenue, for the proposed decree quoted above, which incidentally was also put forward during the debate on the budget of the Ministry of Commerce by the BB [BBWR, the Non-Party Bloc for Cooperation with the Government] deputy Czernichowski[?], there is no excuse whatsoever that could satisfy an honest person.
It is superfluous to point out that progressive Jewish society has lately been striving, with deeds, for Jewish youth to receive the necessary vocational training before it enters the day-to-day struggle for existence in every occupation. Witness to this are the large hosts of Jewish young men and girls in the commercial schools, in the artisans' schools, and so on. Jews have founded many commercial schools, communal and private, so that the future Jewish merchant and the person employed in the commercial branch should have, apart from his practical knowledge, which he will acquire later, a theoretical preparatory education as well. This is being done in their own interest, so that the Jew should be able to compete at a time when all fields of life are progressing; and nobody can now accuse the Jews of a lack of understanding for schools and educational institutions. The eternal[?] “People of the Book” surely[?] sometimes[?] gets a moral lesson on account of its excessive diligence in learning.
But if one comes at the present time with the demand to introduce legal regulations in this field, it means, on the other hand, an assault on the Jews, who have not yet managed to go through this process of development; long years will yet pass before that happens. A great obstacle to it is the difficult economic situation of the Jews, which does not in every case allow them to study.
The antisemitic face of this proposal is a glaring one. From the insufficient education of the Jewish shopkeeper nobody suffers but he himself; his “educated” competitors, however, cannot withstand, in the natural way, the competition of the “uneducated” Jewish merchant, so they endeavour to get rid of him by way of the law.
Let us hope, however, that this decree will not come to pass!
N. H.
Mechanisation of the Bakeries Postponed for 3 Years

[Poland — regulations; bakeries.]
The Ministry of Public Supervision [“Ministerium fun efntlekher oyfzikht” — apparently the Ministry of Social Welfare, Ministerstwo Opieki Społecznej] has published in the “Dz. Ustaw” [Dziennik Ustaw, the Journal of Laws] an ordinance which introduces the following very important changes in the field of the production of baked goods and confectionery.
A bakery that is located in an area where there is a water supply and sewerage must be set up only in premises that are connected to these two important factors. A bakery may not be located in any basement. The rooms of the bakery must be large enough for there to be at least 4 square metres of space per worker. Bakeries located in places where there is electric power must have mechanical installations for sifting flour, and for mixing and kneading the dough.
The bakery may not be directly joined to the dwelling; it cannot serve as a place of residence, as a resting place or sleeping quarters, nor as a passageway [“ferkers-shtel”]. The sale of baked goods or confectionery in the street, at stalls and in the markets is permissible only in the case where means are applied which safeguard the products from uncleanliness (keeping the baked goods in small cabinets or in glazed carts). Door-to-door peddling of flour products is forbidden.
Bakeries and confectionery factories which, at the time the said ordinance is issued, are located in basements may remain there for the time being in the case where the depth of the bakery does not go further than half a metre below ground level and the windows are at least one metre above the ground. On the other hand, bakeries located in deeper basements may also remain, if they meet all the regulations. However, each individual case is decided by the powiat [county] administrative authority. This authority will determine time limits — which bakeries, and for how long, may remain in these conditions. In any case the time limit will be no longer than until 24 November 1936.
When a bakery or confectionery factory is located in a basement, exemplary ventilation must be installed there.
The provisions concerning time limits for remaining in the basements are not applied with regard to confectionery manufacture.
The time limit for “mechanising” the bakeries and confectionery factories is decided by the powiat general administrative authority, depending on the local economic and technical conditions. In any case the time limit cannot be put off later than until 31 December 1936.
All mills and sales points for flour which do not meet the provisions of the ordinance are closed as of 22 February of this year.
Adar-ish (A Little Feuilleton)

[Purim — little feuilleton; a play on words: “Adar” (the month) / “oder” (either–or) / “odern” (veins).]
If every month has its own psychological significance — I mean, its name has its own significance — then the month of Adar certainly has its special significance.
It has altogether now become a rule: either — or [“oder, oder”].
The politics of the last few days proves that the world has become an ardent adherent of “Adar”, i.e. either — or.
Here we have Purim. Years ago one used to feel, already beforehand, a certain elevated mood among Jews. People prepared for the simplest and perhaps the merriest holiday we have.
True, often the joy was more an artificial than a natural one; people made themselves merry, as if it really were merry in the heart; but it was already enough that one could at least make oneself merry.
Today, however...
The Hamans have raised their heads; they have come down from their historic, so to speak, gallows and are setting about hanging their enemies.
And the greatest Haman is the time itself; it takes revenge without limit and without measure; true, it makes no distinction between nation and people, but in the end we Jews feel better than anyone else the taste of the present time.
Among us, more than among anyone else, the Adar-ish spirit prevails, i.e. either, or...
The golden mean has vanished, and in its place has come the extreme: either one lives quite well — or one “expires” of hunger... There is almost no middle now.
It is, gentlemen, Adar-ish in the world!
———
“When Adar enters, we increase in joy.”
So it used to be once. But now...
Where does one now get a little bit of joy, even just a little bit, of the joys of old?
Ah, if only one could have saved up a little gladness and contentment from the good old years for now!
If only joy were like money! After all, some people did save up money from the earlier years for now — why then should one not have been able to save up a little gladness too?
Adar-ish...
It positively cuts[?] through all our veins [“odern”].
Rebus.

And so the needs of the kehilla did indeed grow greatly as well; thanks to this the kehilla's budget also increased many times over, and the Sosnowiec kehilla was reputed to be one of the largest and most important in Poland.
3.
In writing the history of the Sosnowiec kehilla in the first period of its existence, one must also mention the characteristic lawsuit that was conducted in 1907 against the local gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha, Messrs. Yevsey[?] (!) Slutshevski [Słuczewski], Yaakov Stahl and Leib Federman[?], for extorting burial money from Messrs. Pachter and Fischhof for the burial of one of their relatives.
Mr. Pachter lodged his complaint against them with the chief prosecutor of the Warsaw Court of Appeal, and Mr. Fischhof with the Governor of Piotrków.
I wish only to give here, briefly, the content of the two complaints, leaving out, of course, all the insulting expressions which they contain addressed to the Sosnowiec Chevra Kadisha.
This is what is written there: the Chevra Kadisha in Sosnowiec has a monopoly on burying the Jewish dead. It extorts from the relatives of the deceased large sums of money, at its own discretion and according to the financial circumstances of the deceased or of their relatives, without rendering any account whatsoever of where the money goes.
On 9 February 1907 the widow B. died (I omit the name so as not to shame the dead). In her old age her children had had to support her. Yet the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha demanded from her relatives burial money of no more and no less than 1,200 rubles.
Not wishing to give such a large sum of money, the children invited[?] several women who occupy themselves with sewing shrouds[?] to perform for her the last rites due to her; but the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha strictly forbade them to attend to the dead without their permission, so the women dispersed and the deceased was not brought to burial.
On the third day after the death the gabbaim were already demanding a full 2000 rubles; otherwise they would have her buried with a "donkey's burial".
So the children took the dead woman by night to Modrzejów, in order to bury her in the cemetery there, and as they were proceeding to the burial Slutshevski wanted[?] to telephone to those attending to the burial that they should not dare to do it for all the money in the world.
So the deceased had to be carried back again to Sosnowiec, and only after great effort and haggling did the gabbaim agree to take 1200 rubles — 600 rubles in cash and bills of exchange for the remainder, which were paid when due.
Only on the fourth day, at night, after the death was the deceased given her due, for which the burial attendants again had to be paid separately...
The complaint goes on to describe the "disgrace of the dead" when, among Jews, burial does not take place soon after death, and the humiliations inflicted on the complainants by the keeping of the body for 4 days in the house, which, it goes without saying, had a very harmful effect on the living. Therefore the complainants turn to the prosecutor, that he should bring the above-mentioned gabbaim to judicial responsibility for extorting money by violent means, at the same time naming a large number of witnesses who will confirm all the facts.
The prosecutor handed this matter over to the Governor-General of Warsaw, who in turn forwarded the complaint to Piotrków, to the Governor, to carry out an investigation of the matter.
The investigation was conducted by the Sosnowiec "zemsky nachalnik" [chief of the district land guard], and many witnesses confirmed the incriminated facts, while many others claimed that nothing of the kind had ever happened — they knew nothing to tell.
The gabbaim, for their part, defended themselves by saying that they are not obliged to comply with the wishes of a dead person's relatives regarding a burial plot and so on[?], and since Yevsey[?] Slutshevski was at that time also the head of the kehilla's dozór [supervisory board], he had used the money for the needs of the kehilla.
It would lead too far to give here all the characteristic claims that the interested persons put forward at the investigation — that the Chevra Kadisha had also taken 1,500 rubles from Fischhof as burial money for a distant relative of his, and so on[?]. Here I wish to be brief and pass on to the matter itself.
The zemsky nachalnik sent the investigation files to Piotrków, to the Governor, and on 2 September 1908 the case came up at a sitting in the provincial (gubernia) administration, and it was resolved to hand over to the prosecutor of the Piotrków District Court the matter of the above-mentioned gabbaim, for taking 1,200 rubles of burial money without handing it over to the kehilla treasury.
The files, together with the resolution, were sent to Warsaw to the Governor-General, by whom the investigation had been ordered; there they did not agree with the resolution of the Governor of Piotrków and annulled it (end of October 1908). And hardly had this sensational news reached Sosnowiec (8 November 1908) when the interested complainants lodged a cassation appeal with the Senate in Petersburg against the decision of the Governor-General of Warsaw.
The pleading of the cassation appeal was entrusted to the Petersburg expert in Jewish affairs, the advocate Mil[?].
The case in Petersburg dragged on for a long time. Meanwhile the World War came and made "peace" between the warring sides in Sosnowiec; and since most of them are already in the World of Truth, let history too judge them no longer, and remember them for good on the day of the 35th jubilee of the existence of the Sosnowiec kehilla.

"Jus Primae Noctis"

[Article — Nazi Germany; the status of women.] By Sh. Rotenberg.

It has not been established whether there really existed in the Middle Ages a law on the "right to the first night", under which every peasant maiden had, on her wedding night, first to give herself to the lord of the manor; but it is a fact that such a custom prevailed in various countries during feudal rule. And even if there were no historical proofs of the existence of such a custom, plain reason would simply oblige us to invent it, for it is surely clear: if the lord was master over the life and death of his serfs, whom he regarded as an inventory with which one may do whatever one likes at any time — then who and what could have held him back from committing a sexual excess upon a pretty maiden who took his fancy?

Of that dark epoch every cultured person speaks with disgust and anger. That time was regarded as one that had vanished for all generations, one that would never again be repeated and would remain only as an ugly stain of shame on the pages of human history.

But who would have believed a few years ago (nowadays one can believe anything) that in the year 1934 a "scholar" would come from a country in the very heart of Europe and propose to reintroduce the "jus primae noctis"?

It is not hard to guess that this highly "cultured" and "civilised" country, from which the author of the "humanitarian" project hails, is bloody Nazi Germany.
