On Guard Against a Catastrophe. (XX. Antisemitic Modernism. — How Do We React to This Phenomenon Among Us?)

[Editorial — antisemitism and Hitlerism; instalment XX of the series.] By L. Szpigelman.

Everything has its time and its season, its expectations and its span of endurance[?]. Thus, for example, the season of antisemitism has arrived nowadays, the season of oppressing and choking every free phenomenon, every ideal aspiration. Hitlerism has clamped the fist firmly in its paws and has begun pitilessly to beat down on human heads, until everything was dulled; and although the spectacle has lasted only a year, people have almost forgotten that not long ago the world looked different: people felt with people, suffered with them, your sorrow was also the other man's sorrow and, conversely, my joy was also the other man's joy.

At the present moment a season of brutality has come, and the stronger the brutal rule is, the more secure people feel, and regrettably the more adherents it gains.

After German Hitlerism, after so much innocent blood was shed there, came Vienna and showed us that within a few days it was possible to destroy and wipe out everything that had been built and cultivated for years and that people had prided themselves on. The great, beautiful social ideal was annihilated in the blink of an eye, as if it had never existed, never worked in life, never been a beautiful ideal that showed light and wonders. And although in beautiful, cosy and free Vienna so much blood was shed, the blood of innocent young women and children, the fist nevertheless makes progress there, and all kinds of dark individuals are beginning to take the helm into their hands, and their might will consist in destroying every free thought, every ideal aspiration and phenomenon.

And in the world people envy these "heroes", who know how, and have the courage, to destroy everything, to kill everything, so that those who do not stand at the helm learn from the dark elements how to fight their way through to power; and if such a course prevails throughout the world, why then should Poland lag behind them, especially when Poland possesses a fair percentage of "hostile" elements, consisting mostly of Jews, around whom there is something to be accomplished.

For months now our antisemites have been competing among themselves, each party wanting to show more greatness and more achievement in its field with regard to antisemitism against the Jews, and meanwhile they fight and quarrel for all they are worth. One intrigues against the other and they tussle, and meanwhile nobody has yet shown any wonders. Each forges antisemitism on his own account, according to his own conception and understanding. What Katowice, for instance, determines does not please Sosnowiec, and vice versa. And meanwhile, meanwhile, things are going for them, poor fellows, butter-side down, do what you will.

But although here among us there is the nest of antisemitism and Hitlerism, and the prospects are not brilliant, not optimistic, black crows are nevertheless beginning to spread their wings too in various corners of the country, threatening that Hitlerism already rules over Poland; and however much of a utopia that may be, one must not forget that we are now living in a period of antisemitism. When such a course prevails, that is the end of everything.

Do we not see what our various antisemites are aiming at? Do we not see what they are aiming at in Warsaw? Do we not hear the speeches of their deputies in the Sejm and in the Senate? Do we not feel how they strive to poison the air and how they want the horizon to be filled with lead? Are they not preparing for this loathsome work of destruction?

Yes, truly one needs no deeply penetrating eye to see this, to grasp this. And what are we doing to ward off the bullets that are aimed at us? It is, after all, no feat of wisdom to stand with folded arms and watch all this indifferently from afar, as if it were not we who are meant here, as if it were not the Jew whom they want at every opportunity to make into the scapegoat [literally: the atonement chicken]. They concoct stories, they search, they rummage, they try to clutch at the rotten wall, only to prove that, whatever it may be, the Jew is to blame.

We supposedly have committees whose aim is to fight against Hitlerism and antisemitism, but are they at the proper level? Do they fulfil their tasks? One can say quite boldly that they are far from the proper level and far from doing what is incumbent upon them. At best the activity of the committees consists in holding meetings which achieve nothing by their sitting and merely postpone one meeting to the next. But all that was once, in the heat of the blaze. Now people have weaned themselves even from that, and even the meetings, which yielded a minimum, no longer take place, so that everything has congealed, and it comes to the same thing whether a town has a committee or not.

The question arises, however: may we remain indifferent to all that is happening around us? Are we not committing a crime when we stand by with folded arms at the present moment, when various individuals want to tear the Jew out by the root?

True, we live in very hard conditions; to earn a penny, so as to have a livelihood, one must work hard, and one is sold day and night, so that there is no time to come together to consider the gravity of the hour and to seek remedies for it; those, for their part[?], who have too much time have dropped out altogether; they are, so to speak, without heads and do not know how to consider such serious problems; they have no courage for it and have withdrawn entirely from communal activity.

Yet one can tell that for "lighter matters" there is indeed time, and patience, and courage, and strength. No sooner is it a question of Jewish affairs — of the Chevra Kadisha, the synagogue, the shtibl, the cantor, the rabbi or other intrigues — ah, then people stop at nothing, then they will fight to the death, each will strive with the heaviest weapons to defeat the other. Each will exert the most energetic means so that things remain as he wants and not the reverse. At such a moment neither money nor time nor courage is lacking, so long as one gets one's own way.

Yes, for petty intrigues, for home-grown squabbling[?], when it is a matter of destructive work, people with strength and energy will always be found; by contrast, all this vanishes when it is a matter of grand work, of serious deeds on which Jewish existence, the Jewish future, Jewish being depend.

Nevertheless one must render an account of the prevailing situation; one must penetrate with full awareness into the position in which we find ourselves and see how they lie in wait to exterminate us, and then one must come to the conclusion that the situation is too serious for us, too dangerous, too grave, for us to remain standing indifferently and watch all this as if frozen, as though it did not concern us, our present and our future.

On no account may the leading Jewish elements remain indifferent to all that is happening around us; the representative Jewish elements must employ every possible means so as not to allow us to be made into what all kinds of antisemites want to make of us.

Many are of the opinion that "Israel is not widowed": we have already been burnt and roasted, we have already survived various Hamans, and the Jewish people lives and will live, and will also outlive all kinds of Hitlers in the most varied guises.

Today, however, the serious question cannot be solved with such arguments. We must stand on guard and protect that which can be destroyed, that which we must not allow to be destroyed. True, we have already lived through and suffered through all sorts of things and endured everything; we are as elastic as rubber in enduring all kinds of troubles that other peoples would perhaps not have endured; and yet we must not submit to the troubles merely because we are able to endure them and because our forefathers grew accustomed to them.

If one were to draw up a little statistical survey of the Jewish situation in recent years, one would come to the conviction that we have been terribly degraded, that our condition has sunk deep. Poverty and powerlessness occupy the place of honour everywhere among us.

True, this has much to do with the crisis, which has spread so widely over the whole world, and without doubt it was bound to strike us too. But had it touched us only to the extent that pertains to the general world crisis, we would in that case be the fortunate ones, for it is self-evident that it could not and need not have avoided us and passed us over in silence.

We would — as has been said — be content if we suffered from the crisis indirectly, on a par with all other peoples. Worse and more painful, however, is that we also suffer directly: once as citizens and a second time as Jews. The moment anything happens, no sooner does the general situation become less than splendid, than our antisemites at once begin to look for the guilty, and as the scapegoat they instantly find, in the first place, the Jew; and this at once becomes clear and evident to them, and on these self-evident truths of theirs "theories" are built and arguments are made.

We live in the twentieth century, when antisemitism has in recent years, for the moment [letter-spaced for emphasis], become a modern phenomenon; we must see to it with all our forces, however poor and modest they may be, to root out the dangerous "modernism" before the eyes of honest people, of those who want to see the truth just as it is in reality, without any imitation whatsoever.

After all, we have representatives who represent the Jewish people; let them take upon themselves the great and responsible mission and not allow the Jewish people, which has shown wonders so many times already, to be made a mockery and a laughing-stock.

Let people give this matter some thought in a serious hour.
The first period of the Sosnowiec kehilla — for its 35th jubilee (1899–1934). Part 3 (end)

By Moshe Feinkind. The first period of the Sosnowiec kehilla. For its 35th jubilee (1899–1934). (Instalment 3.)
For today's generation it will also be interesting to tell of the birth pangs of the Sosnowiec kehilla, on its 35 years of existence.
The notables in Sosnowiec had to fight on two fronts. In the first place with Będzin, to whose district Sosnowiec belonged.
The Jews of Sosnowiec covered the greatest part of the “etat” [kehilla tax] of the Będzin kehilla and had nothing from it, apart from the salary that it paid to the Sosnowiec moreh hora'ah [rabbinical judge].
Naturally, Będzin did not want to let such a fat morsel out of its mouth, and defended itself with all its strength.
On the other side the notables had to fight with the local population, which was quite apathetic and indifferent to the whole matter.
But the healthy instinct of the intellectual forces of Sosnowiec prevailed — among whom the Lithuanian [Litvak] element played no small part, introducing trade and culture into the newly thrown-together little town, as can be seen from the natchalnik's [district chief's] report — and the town had already agreed to tear itself away from Będzin and create a kehilla of its own.
The motives which moved the Jews of Sosnowiec to turn with a petition about this to the Governor of Piotrków are quite matter-of-fact and convincing, without touching the other side's honour.
In this petition it is said that the number of the Sosnowiec Jews exceeds the number of Jews of Będzin*, giving along with this a picture of Jewish intellectual life in Sosnowiec, [and] declaring themselves at the same time ready to bear all the expenses that are connected with maintaining an independent kehilla, etc., etc.
This petition was signed by Doctor Neufeld (a contributor to the “Kurjer Sosnowiecki”) published by the Będzin advocate Wieruszbowski[?], the firms “Oppenheim”, “Landau”, Reicher and hundreds of others.
The Będzin kehilla together with the rabbinate protested strongly against tearing Sosnowiec away from their kehilla. For the budget is calculated, among others, on Sosnowiec too, and the tearing away of this town is liable to undermine the existence of the Będzin kehilla, etc. For Będzin has a poor population and will not have the possibility of covering the deficit without Sosnowiec.
The Będzin powiat natchalnik [district chief], to whom the guberniya administration had turned for information and an opinion, stood on the side of the Sosnowiec petitioners. It may be on account of particular sympathies which he had for them, or for reasons of money, [he] replied to that inquiry that he had nothing to object to Sosnowiec having an independent kehilla. And as concerns the “budget” of the Będzin kehilla, the fear is not as great as the Będzin dozors [kehilla wardens] present it; there are in Będzin enough rich men, magnates, who can themselves cover it in case of a deficit, and who also need not be beholden to anyone.
Altogether — the natchalnik declares further — Będzin has a large district with a large Jewish population, which is little burdened with “etat”.
And as I have already reported in my first article, Governor Miller confirmed the request of the Sosnowiec Jews (July 1898).
Będzin became indignant at this and people prepared to appeal; lawsuits before rabbinical courts without end began between the two towns, and without having the slightest chances of winning. And the Będziners also did not want to fall out with the Sosnowiec bankers and forwarding agents, with whom they stood in business relations; and it was also wanted to give the Będzin rabbinate a certain satisfaction for the damage which they had on account of the tearing away.
So no appeal was made; the individuals who had been steel and iron on the side of Będzin also remained with folded arms.
No satisfaction, as it seems, did Sosnowiec give anyone. Or it may have promised nothing at all, in the “and wrath came”[?] [in the heat of the quarrel].
Meanwhile the Sosnowiec kehilla organised itself and elected as its dozors the persons already mentioned by me in the first article (Doctor Neufeld, Reicher and Englard).
And wishing now to avoid Będzin altogether, the Będzin powiat natchalnik officially invited to Sosnowiec the Rabbi of Częstochowa, the Rav HaGaon R' Nachum Asz, to take the oath from the dozors as the law then prescribed, which took place in the Sosnowiec synagogue in the presence of the higher officials with the natchalnik at their head, with great solemnity.
The whole Jewish population took part in the “holiday” of strengthening the new kehilla.
Of this the natchalnik informed the Governor.
(End.)
A dark cloud is moving in upon the Jews in Poland

[Editorial article — Poland; economic legislation and antisemitism.] A terrible cloud is moving upon the Jews in Poland. The Trade Commission of the Sejm has adopted a bill concerning a series of new decrees in the field of trade and industry, which can ruin thousands of Jewish livelihoods [literally: existences].
All these planned amendments [novelas] look at first glance like means of bringing civilization and culture into the ranks of the urban merchants, artisans and manufacturers. And so they[?] indeed are, in truth. There is, after all, no doubt that an educated artisan, an intelligent shopkeeper and manufacturer can make better use of their trade, more productively and profitably, than an illiterate.
And yet it has been pointed out more than once that in the regrouping which must take place in the process, it turns out of itself that it is the Jew who suffers.
But it appears that the authors of the bill are not content with that "of itself"; they actually want to create a real force that will push the wagon along in the direction of Jewish extermination [i.e. economic elimination]. Therefore such cleverly masked tricks are provided for as will push the Jew out of his positions outright, with their own hands.
For example, a few merchants and industrialists can demand of the minister that he introduce "professional qualifications" both for merchants and for industrialists, and the minister has to comply with them.
What does that mean: "a few"? How does a minority come to be able to squeeze a majority? Let us understand it simply: in every town there are, after all, a handful of Polish merchants, artisans and manufacturers; they will be able to point out to the minister that shopkeepers and artisans must know the Polish language better, or know how to treat a customer, or keep books and the like. And the minister will agree with them, and a purge will begin of the unqualified... Jews.
A second dreadful means of actively de-Judaizing trade and the crafts is the compulsory organization. According to the bill it comes out like this: in a town there must be an organization, which is not obliged to admit everyone, but whoever does not belong to the organization is exposed to the most terrible antagonisms. Thus, for example, a shoemakers' guild is created, which from the outset admits only a certain portion, the favoured ones, of the trade; the rest remain outside, and afterwards they suffer bitter years [literally: "cut years"], having no one to stand up for them. Does one still need teeth for borscht? [Proverb: it is obvious.] Do we not understand that the favoured members of the guild will for the most part be non-Jews, and that masses of Jews will be left overboard?
Immensely great is the danger of concessions [licences]. This too is, at first glance, a reform. The state wants to control all enterprises and works, in order to be able to introduce order into them. And in order to have supervision over everything, there is no better means than through concessions. But if porterage or courtyard trade [peddling in courtyards] is going to be regulated by the government, we can already know in advance that many Jews will drop out of these occupations. Here, for example, the occupations of porterage at the railways and of courtyard-watching [house caretaking] are regulated — how many Jews find their livelihood in them?
— Wherever there is a "vayehi" ["and it came to pass"], they say, it is a trouble for Jews [after the Talmudic dictum that every "vayehi" signals distress]; as long as things still drag on as before, never mind, but if something new happens, Jews must at once suffer from it...
And here, it seems, the "vayehi", the novelties, are being brought in on purpose, precisely in order to be able to smoke Jews out — in the spirit of the Endek [National Democratic], Jew-devouring programme, only not in its forms: "in its image" but not "after its likeness"...
*
Of[?] these dangers the Jewish deputies of the Koło [Koło Żydowskie, the Jewish parliamentary club] informed the Jewish public through a press conference which they arranged in the Jewish Sejm club. They appealed to the Jewish press, to Jewish society, to help them in the impending bitter struggle for the elementary Jewish rights to live.
They called the press conference, it appears, in order to cast off from themselves the responsibility before history. Let it not be said that events take them unawares; look, they know beforehand, they know and warn, warn and fight — but what could they do against the powerful?
It is still a great question whether history will accept their justification. The Jewish political leaders in Poland certainly have some share — if not indeed a large one — in the troubles that are clouding over us. It is known, after all, that the Jewish artisans' organizations all but approved the bill; the merchants, too, did not protest very sharply. Well, these organizations, we understand, have no broad historical perspectives; they care[?] only about the "ba'asher hu sham" [the here and now]. But the politicians in the Sejm, who surely think about the people, about the future — what have they done? Why did they look about them only at the last moment, to call the press to their aid? Why did they not raise an outcry to the whole world, not "tear open graves" [i.e. leave no stone unturned], while there was still time?
And worse still is that they pose the Jewish question altogether in such a way that all these open and disguised antisemitic tricks do not look so strangely wild at all. For since the whole of life here is no more than a vestibule, a passage — then what is the disgrace[?] if in the corridor there are not so many comforts, so many freedoms? One will somehow push the time through, until one comes into the parlour!...
*
They are now preparing to introduce this novelty: the activization of the masses with regard to the Jewish question; one might say: the democratization of antisemitism, if one were permitted to mention that unkosher [treyf] word.
Until now the extermination of Jews proceeded, as it were, automatically, and used to be carried out by the bureaucracy in a very polite form, with a smile on the lips, for on politeness we are very particular here... And the bureaucracy by itself was not able, within the framework of the laws existing until now, to accomplish very much.
Now, however, the people will have the say; it will be able to stimulate the minister, to inspire the various authorities to take steps to "raise" the level of trade and crafts in Poland, and at the same time to keep strict watch that this raising should not, God forbid, be at its own expense...
That is the "vayehi" of the new Polish economic policy, which is moving upon Jews like a dark cloud.
P. K.
It is already time for the matzah campaign

[Editorial — relief; the Passover matzah campaign.] The date of the Passover holiday is drawing near. It is not necessary to recall how great the need now is among the Jewish population; but it certainly is necessary to recall that this year one must not wait with the traditional Passover campaign until the last days.
The people who occupy themselves year after year with this campaign should already now set to work and also find new ways and means of increasing the income of the Matzah Commission, so as to be able to satisfy in proper measure all those who this year will have to turn to the Matzah Commission for help.
The charge [levy] on matzah and the voluntary collection of ma'ot chitim [Passover "wheat money"] alone may this year prove too little; means must also be found of ensuring that at the very least all buyers of matzah pay the required charge to the Matzah Commission. Possibly one ought to come to an understanding about this with the matzah bakers and matzah sellers; there are various means available.
All this will be possible to do if one does not wait with the matzah campaign until the last days.
We hereby give a reminder of this!
Important Rulings of the Supreme Court.

[Law — rulings of the Supreme Court.]
Turnover tax on banks
In calculating the turnover tax, the commission which the banks receive for the collection (incasso) of bills of exchange must be included; by contrast, the protest costs which the banks take back from their clients are exempt from turnover tax.
Limitation (prescription) of bill-of-exchange debts.
A bill-of-exchange debt with respect to the issuer becomes time-barred after three years. As soon as the holder of the bill can prove that the issuer was enriched by it, the issuer bears the liability for the bill debt for a further 3 years. In that case it is all the same whether the bill was protested in its time or not.
As regards the manner of proving the issuer's enrichment, it is sufficient that the bill bears the remark that the value (waluta) was received, although under the bill-of-exchange laws in force such an annotation is not necessary at all.
Letters from Home.

[Satirical feuilleton by "Ben Amotz" (pen-name) — Zagłębie, communal life.]
With God's help, in the week of the portion "The people bring much more [than enough]"... [Exodus 36:5 — parashat Vayakhel]
My friend Reb Shlomo, may his light shine.
I have only just come home from the night sitting of our "parliament" (gmina in the vernacular) [here: the kehilla council], said the morning prayer and at once sat down to write an answer to your last letter, which caused me great sorrow.
How much longer, Reb Shlomo, will you be so naive and take things so very much to heart? True, as a warm Jew it pains you and your heart is full of suffering because of the daily decrees that pour down on our heads; certainly one can fall into the greatest despair, seeing how all the evil spirits have united in order to realise Haman's slogan of:
— "to destroy and to annihilate all the Jews".
The only difference is that in the process of extermination the "to kill" is missing; that system is no longer modern. Why beat, why murder, when one can annihilate the whole of Israel in white gloves... And yet, do not take it so to heart. If you, Reb Shlomo, were to come here to us and get acquainted with our forms of life, were to watch our wars over "an egg not yet laid", over yesterday's days [= things that never were], over worthless matters, your pessimism would diminish a great deal...
So here I do want to fulfil your request and write to you about the actions which Jewish society in Zagłębie has undertaken against the new decrees.
One of the most important counter-actions, which the powers that be will presumably reckon with, taking our demands into consideration — is the dancing... In this field a great deal was done before this year's turnover-tax assessments; the local authority was showered with dozens of "memorials" concerning the
Purim balls...
Even in the smallest Jewish settlement, where since the creation of the world no ball has ever yet taken place, this year, "to spite" our enemies, several balls were arranged... in order to show the nations of the world that Israel is not widowed [Jeremiah 51:5], that the more decrees they think up, the more we shall
— dance...
Our second defensive force we display at our "parliament" sittings. I tell you, Reb Shlomo, that the greatest socialist leaders, even MacDonald himself, ought to drop in on such a "parliament" sitting and get acquainted with what is called
— socialism...
As an illustration it will, I think, be enough for you to hear a few proposals brought in by the parnasim [councillors] who came into the kehilla "to combat the Jewish clergy"... First of all they demand that the reactionary-fascist-clerical system of burying the dead be changed in this sense: a reactionary corpse should be buried face down, and a proletarian one, from the masses of the people, face up. Then, on the site of the new, future mikveh building a crematorium should be built, and on the plot of the Talmud Torah monuments should be set up to the fallen revolutionaries in Austria...
And last but not least. The greatest energy, money and blood, our last strength we give away to
— spiritual matters, for however bitter things may be for us, we must after all remember that "man does not live by bread alone", that bread alone does not satisfy the plain creature of flesh and blood; our whole existence is, after all, only thanks to our helping to see that the creative spirit should not cease to bubble...
For that very reason the fighters for higher matters in Zagłębie have joined hands and are waging a holy war, a dispute for the sake of Heaven. The difference is that Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa fight over a rabbi, and Będzin — over a cantor.
Well, the Sosnowiec "7-year war" is already well known to you, Reb Shlomo. That is by now a popular matter not only among Jews but also towards the outside world. A simple gentile newspaper carrier is more versed in the Sosnowiec rabbinate question than a Zionist is in the map of the Land of Israel...
The Będzin cantorship, too, already has a "rich" past, and it is still a matter of which there will be much "to sing and to tell"... This time, Reb Shlomo, I want to explain to you the state of the very young dispute that is quietly burning around the Jewish kehilla of Dąbrowa.
You surely remember that a beit din issued a ruling that the rabbinate in Dąbrowa belongs to the son-in-law of the Dąbrowa rabbi. So according to reason and according to the holy Torah it followed that the first to recognise the ruling would be those who "carry high the banner of the Torah", those "whose forms of life are solely in the spirit of the Torah"...
But along come the Ger Hasidim of Dąbrowa and say: "Lo fidalti"[?]! [a mock-Hebrew quip: "I couldn't care less".] The ruling of the beit din, which was also confirmed by the Union of Rabbis [Agudas HaRabonim], has for us the same importance as the yearly prohibitions on outside matzot and on outside slaughter... Not the study is the main thing but the deed; the main thing is — only the merchandise, a fat goose... let it even be from elsewhere...
You will surely ask: how can that be? Does it then turn out that the Hasidim, Heaven forbid, do not obey what their own Rebbe says? So I shall tell you this:
Before the blowing of the shofar several young men were standing in the courtyard of the Ger beit midrash, debating the Gemara's difficulty on the verse "Happy is the people that know the teruah [the shofar blast]". The Gemara asks: "Do the nations of the world not know how to sound a blast?" At that moment the Sfas Emes of blessed memory [the Rebbe of Ger, R. Yehuda Aryeh Leib Alter] passed by and dropped a remark:
— They really cannot.
Some time later, in the shtetl where those same young men lived, there appeared in the market a Cossack with a shofar in his hand.
The Cossack with the shofar caused a great commotion among the young men, and the majority of them said that the shofar must be torn out of the Cossack's hands. The sober ones among them were against fighting with the Cossack: and if it turns out otherwise than the Rebbe said — that too cannot be helped; who would dare to fight with a Cossack?...
The same excuse is used by the Ger Hasidim in Dąbrowa as well. We want — they say — a suitable rabbi. And if it turns out otherwise than the Rebbe says — that too cannot be helped... The matter of the rabbinate — they argue — does not, after all, consist merely in being able to hold a shofar...
That is how the situation looks on our internal front. "Without, the sword shall bereave" [Deuteronomy 32:25] — from outside the sword of Damocles waves over us, but inside, within our own "camp", a behind-the-scenes politics is being conducted, a hypocritical trade, and a dreadful dance of demons is taking place.
To your inquiry concerning the conflict of the dollar-shochtim [the ritual slaughterers] with the kehilla board you will receive an answer in the next letter. Meanwhile have a good Sabbath, as is wished you by your friend
Ben Amotz.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayakhel-Pekudei)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayakhel-Pekudei
The Portion
—o—
a) "And Moses assembled all the congregation of the children of Israel... and on the seventh day there shall be to you a holy day" (Ex. 35:1)
The only portion in the Torah — as the Yalkut remarks — that begins with "Vayakhel" ("and he assembled") is the portion of the Sabbath. For Moses said this to the Jews: if all week long business, the sinful livelihood, calls forth among you envy and hatred, quarrels and scuffles — on the Sabbath, when you conduct no trade, be at least then "in assembly", be at least then in unity... Imrei Noam.
* * *
The Torah was given on the Sabbath, when no trade is done and Jews can at least come to an understanding with one another. "The Lord will give strength to His people, the Lord will bless His people with peace." The Torah is meant to bring peace among Jews, and that is possible only on the Sabbath, when for one day one forgets about "business"... Iyun Yaakov.
* * *
At the Sabbath afternoon prayer we say: "You are One and Your name is One, and who is like Your people Israel, one nation on earth" — at any rate on the Sabbath, when economic affairs, when the bitter war for a livelihood (in which "men swallow one another alive") is weakened for a day — at least then let us be "one nation", and not splintered and divided... Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
—o—
b) "You shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations on the Sabbath day" (ibid., 3)
The prohibition of doing work on the Sabbath is expressed through two light labours: kindling fire and going for a walk beyond the Sabbath boundary ("let no man go out of his place" [misprinted in the paper]), so that one should not think that a trifle — lighting a cigarette — does not count as work... R' Zvi Hirsch Kalischer.
—o—
c) "A Sabbath of solemn rest to the Lord" (ibid.)
"If Israel had only kept two Sabbaths they would have been redeemed at once." Midrash and Talmud.
With this the wording in the Sabbath table-hymn "Kol Mekadesh" becomes understandable:
"Lovers of the Lord who await the building of Ariel, rejoice and be glad like those receiving the gift of Nachaliel."
For through the Sabbath one does after all arrive at redemption, at the building of the Temple (the building of Ariel), and the Sabbath is after all equal in weight to the whole Torah; therefore: "like those receiving the gift of Nachaliel"... Dvash ve-Chalav.
—o—
d) "These are the words which the Lord has commanded, to do them" (ibid.)
The words God commanded to do — not merely to speak, but to do... Beit Yaakov.
—o—
e) "Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah" (ibid., 30)
The Mishnah in Avot says: "And all who occupy themselves with the needs of the community should do so for the sake of Heaven, for the merit of their fathers assists them." So then, one needs the merit of the fathers in order to be a faithful worker for the community's needs; a person needs such help from Heaven in order to be faithful [the print has "ba-umah", apparently for "be-emunah"] in communal needs that he actually needs to have the merit of the fathers... That is why, in the case of Bezalel, who worked with the gold and silver of the Tabernacle, his ancestral merit is recounted: son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah... (see also in the Midrash). Kli Chemdah.
* * *
Those who occupy themselves with communal needs for the sake of Heaven therefore need the merit of the fathers so that they should have something to eat; for if one devotes oneself to communal needs and derives nothing at all from it, purely for the sake of Heaven, one truly needs the merit of the fathers in order to have a piece of bread to eat... (see Berakhot, chapter 1): "A righteous man for whom it goes well [the print has 'for us'] — a righteous man, son of a righteous man." So then, the merit of the fathers is what brings a livelihood (also Psalms 37:25, "yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread"). Solet la-Mincha.
* * *
In his book "Divrei Chaim", in the addenda on the portion of Vayakhel, the Rabbi of Sanz [Nowy Sącz; R' Chaim Halberstam] writes:
"The rabbis and the Hasidim and the householders of this generation are, for our many sins, mostly of the mixed multitude [erev rav], and they want to rule over the community, and all their deeds are only for themselves, to acquire honour and money; therefore one must not join with anyone except those who work in truth and sacrifice themselves for God, not hoping for any benefit to themselves"...
—o—
f) "The children of Israel brought a freewill offering to the Lord" (ibid., 29)
The verse says: "Every man and woman whose heart made them willing to bring for all the work which the Lord had commanded to be done by the hand of Moses" — that is to say: whatever their heart desired to bring as an offering, only they did not have it — "the children of Israel brought a freewill offering to the Lord": they brought merely their will, their readiness... and that, too, was acceptable before God... Likutei Peninim.
* * *
Rabbi Chaim of Sanz used to say: the virtue of charity I learned from the Rebbe R' Hirsh of Rymanów, but I did not reach his level. With the Rebbe R' Hirsh, when a poor man came to ask for alms and he no longer had anything to give — his pockets had already been emptied — it was for him at once as though he had given the charity. "If a man intended to perform a commandment and was prevented and did not perform it, Scripture credits him as though he had performed it." But I — if a poor man comes to me and I have nothing to give him, my sorrow is greater than his... Dor De'ah.
—o—
g) "And the people were restrained from bringing" (36:6)
This proved that it was not merely out of prodigality that they were bringing to the Tabernacle; for it could have seemed that they did not mean the Tabernacle at all, but rather "asked for the Calf — they give; asked for the Tabernacle — they give". The people already has such a psyche: to throw gold about when it is called upon, without considering for what. That is why Moses took fright at "the people bring much more than enough"; and when at his call the people stopped bringing, it was proven that the present bringing was not merely a psychosis of prodigality... Divrei Shaul.
* * *
"He has scattered abroad, he has given to the needy; his righteousness endures for ever" —
For one who is a spendthrift in general, his charity has no great significance. But he who "has scattered, has given to the needy" — who gives his prodigality away to the poor — "his righteousness endures for ever", his charity has worth... Ibid.
* * *
"And Moses gave commandment, and they caused it to be proclaimed throughout the camp, saying: let neither man nor woman make any more work for the offering of the sanctuary" —
What other leader would have called out to the people: bring no more, there is already enough gold and silver?... Ramban [Nachmanides].
From the Book Table.

[Book review — Yiddish poetry.]
Hirsh Gutgeshtalt — "Man and Landscape" ["Mentsh un landshaft"], (poems), "Shtaplen" ["Rungs"] publishing house, Warsaw, 1934.

In the present hard times, under the worst conditions, such as perhaps have never been before, when the situation of the Jews in general and the Yiddish book market in particular is so depressed, so threatened — when a Yiddish book by a Jewish poet still sees the bright light of day, one simply feels like crying out for joy:
— And yet the Yiddish book lives! And yet our poets sing!
And this is because the Jewish troubadour lives by the same fate as the Jewish man of the people, the everyday Jew: stubbornness and obstinacy! This Jewish trait is the eternally proven weapon with which the eternal Jew defends himself.
Hirsh Gutgeshtalt is one of the pleiad of young poets who group themselves around the central literary periodicals, such as "Literarishe Bleter", "Vokhnshrift" and others. His poems published so far in the said periodicals have clearly shown that he is a distinctive poet with a path of his own.
His book "Man and Landscape" comprises the following cycles of poems: "With Roads in the Chase", "What Was", "On the Side of My Threshold", "From Man to Man", "When Fates Sway". From the so-called landscape poems one sees that the European continent is no stranger to the poet: on his wanderer's way he reaches the Danube, the Lido, Venice — and all of this he sings with such a light spirit, with so little care; he does not want to remember the past, he lives with today, with his individual today; his yesterday has died, and there is nothing to regret.
In his so-called poems of man, too, he is full of buoyant confidence and faith; though he may see the dishevelled head and bared chest of a tramp who stretches out a fist, angry and dark like a warning, into the flung-open door of a café full of jazz, wine and woman, or other such things — this nonetheless does not disturb his deep faith in a better tomorrow.
He can dream:
"I shall rise at dawn,
outdoors it will be frosty and blue,
light will swell up, and hour after hour will grow
the joy and carefreeness, and run like a little brook.
I shall think about nothing
and know the answer to everything."
The most successful, however, and poetically the most emotional, are the poems in the cycle "When Fates Sway". In these poems, however, the poet is no longer of such a light spirit; on the contrary, here he is embittered to the utmost, for in these poems the purely Jewish tragedy finds expression, the bitter fate of the Jewish people and its just grievances against the world. Thus we have here, among others, the following poem titles, which give more or less an idea of their content, such as: "We, the Strangers", "We — the Moneybags", "We the Shopkeepers and Brokers", "We and the World War", "We and the U.S.S.R.", "When Europe Is Victorious". In the introduction to the said poems the poet says:
"We with old blood and plain limb,
we thousand-headed, thousand-year-old, dust of millions,
lepers in the world and chosen ones,
I take your burden upon myself,
harnessed to your fate,
and want to play the picture of your clotted blood,
burn-wounded, festering sorrow
and the young unrest of your old spirit —
Jews!"
Finally, a question: why are rhythm and verse metre so little observed?
Hirsh Gutgeshtalt is a gifted young poet, and it is to be hoped that in future he will pay more attention to this trifle. The book is aesthetically and tastefully produced.

Leyzer Shikman
I Cannot Be Cheerful.

[Satirical feuilleton — taxes, collections and charity wardens.]
Shiele [Szyjele].

My editor, my readers are cross with me. How can it be, they say: a feuilletonist must be cheerful, he ought to provoke laughter — and that is what the cross editor together with the readers is waiting for. They demand this of me; although I know that they are one hundred percent right, I nevertheless cannot write so that people should laugh, because, first of all, one may not laugh when one wants to, nor may one laugh when one ought to, but only when chance brings it about.
Just as among Jews there are special times for laughing — Simchat Torah, Purim, a festival — so it is with our scribbling too. The season itself supplies "Purim heroes" and hakafot-bearers, and then one laughs, instinctively, without meaning to; then one laughs at one's own brother, friend, father, at one's own child, at the rulers, at the protectors, at the gods, at everything and everyone; the laughter is a natural, a hearty, a human one.
But I myself no longer feel like laughing, for, as you know me, I am a Jew, a shopkeeper; I have a patent [trade licence] and must pay obrotowe [turnover tax], dochodowe [income tax], majątkowe [property tax], lokalowe [premises tax], drogowe [road tax], szyldowe [signboard fee], szpitalne [hospital levy], kryzysowe [crisis tax], pożyczkowe [the (National) Loan], 10 percent, the "payove" [?] surcharge [dodatek], the electricity charge, etatowe [?], the radio fee, the postal fee, chorobowe [sick fund], meldunkowe [residents' registration fee], the advertising fee, członkowskie [membership dues], ubezpieczeniowe [insurance], stróżowe [watchman's fee]; besides this I am "related by marriage" to Linat HaCholim, Gemilut Chesed, Beit Lechem, the old-age home, the Friends of the Hospital. The Friends of the School ["shul-fraynt"; possibly: of the synagogue], the Friends of the Gymnasium, the Small Traders' Association, the LOPP [League for Air and Anti-Gas Defence], the Liga Morska [Maritime League], the yeshiva, the Talmud Torah, Beit Yaakov, Tarbut, the Anti-Hitler Committee, the Tenants' Association, the Women's Association, my party and all the other funds, parties and clubs. All the associations, parties and institutions enumerated carry out on average dozens of campaigns in the course of the year, and they want no great things from me, only money; some of them take monthly dues, yearly dues, quarterly dues. Others take constantly, without cease, at every opportunity. They take into kerchiefs, into briefcases, into collection boxes and little bags; they sell tickets, they collect raffle prizes [fanty]; they take festival money, Passover money, Sukkot money, Tisha B'Av money, Fifteenth [of Shvat] money, Lag BaOmer money, Chol HaMoed money, Yom Kippur money, Rosh Hashanah money, Purim money; and all those enumerated have collectors, sequestrators [tax-seizure officers], bailiffs, ordinary and educated lady wardens, gallants, dressed-up young misses, young Jews, youths, matriculants, girl students, masters of arts, professors, directors, office clerks, presidents, secretaries, doctors, chiefs and plain idlers — and this whole camp of "do-gooders" drives every sign of cheerfulness out of me; although today it is already the eve of spring, I cannot be cheerful.
Just listen how I spent last Purim.
No sooner had I opened my little shop in the morning than the sequestrator came in to me with a bailiff and demanded obrotowe, szyldowe, etatowe; no sooner had they left than the collector came in for the stróżowe; after him came the briefcase [?] for the electricity ["elektritshnoshtshove" ?] — and to them I had to give, for do I have a choice? After them the landlord came in for the rent. He already has an established right, he says, to take the rent from his tenants on Purim; for him that is the best mishloach manot. After the landlord came the campaigners: the Purim campaign of Beit Lechem, the Purim campaign for the yeshiva, the Purim campaign for Keren Kayemet, the Purim campaign for Beit Yaakov, the Purim campaign for Matan BaSeter, the Purim campaign for the Talmud Torah, the Purim campaign for the German refugees, and on top of that a few private campaigns without a name. Apart from the campaigns, the associations come for membership dues; now there also come the "LOPP" and the "Liga Morska i Kolonialna" [Maritime and Colonial League], which want to save us from all dangers; refuse them you may not, for otherwise you are not a loyal citizen. Now come the concerts, balls, performances, masked balls, routs [evening parties], children's performances. Here come the ladies, the young misses, the intellectuals; they ask no more than that you buy two tickets from each of them — and of such there are dozens. Refuse them you may not, for they take offence; especially if you are a shopkeeper, you may yet lose customers; so you must even smile at them and thank them for their noble honorary work, for the good cause of our "współczesne towarzystwa" ["contemporary societies"].
After them comes a flood of plain beggars and merciful lady wardens, women, ladies of pedigree, beadles, cantors, preachers, the deaf, the blind, the lame, the mute, the old, the unemployed, those without a livelihood, degenerates, alcoholics, madmen, paupers and plain vagabonds, who are fruitful and multiply; their bearing is still more insolent.
They curse, shout, demand, dun, abuse, get worked up; by force they take their groszy; they drive out of you your patience, your joy of life, your cheerfulness, your laughter; the hand grows tired of giving, the mouth — of talking, the eyes — of looking; like a cloud it darkens the day and drives away laughter, and one cannot be cheerful.
Well, I ask you, how can I satisfy my editor and my readers with a cheerful feuilleton, when my heart weeps within me for my poor, hard-toiled-for few groszy and for my worn-out hands, which keep on doing gymnastics, taking out of the drawer and giving, giving without end...
We Shall Repair the Mistake

[Article — Eretz Israel, Keren Hayesod and the refugees from Germany.]
In Eretz Israel a new Jewish life is being created. In the year 1933, notwithstanding all the certificates and other restrictions on aliyah, over 40,000 Jewish immigrants entered Eretz Israel; almost all of them have settled in there, and the hunger for working hands is still great and there are still workplaces for many people. No government, no state power whatsoever shows the Jews any financial help in the colonisation of Eretz Israel. On the contrary, the Mandatory power has made of the Jewish immigration a source of revenue for itself, and the income that derives from Jews is partly used to strengthen Arab immigration; and in spite of this, in the course of one year, without any state help at all, 40,000 new Jews entered Eretz Israel.
In the course of the last 7 years the mighty Soviet Russia of 150 millions, with the help of an entire state apparatus and of state funds that are linked with the Jewish American Joint (Agro-Joint), has not managed to settle in Biro-Bidzhan even a quarter of that number. The colonists and immigrants in Eretz Israel enjoy prosperity and the latest achievements of culture and civilisation. The Jewish colonists in Biro-Bidzhan suffer torment in the most primitive and anti-sanitary conditions of life and work, and run away from there at the first opportunity.
Despite the noisy promises it has turned out that settling one family on the land in Biro-Bidzhan is considerably more expensive than in Eretz Israel, although the Soviet government gives the soil for nothing — which we do not have in Eretz Israel.
Since the Hitler upheaval, several thousand Jews apiece have settled in a few large states that lie in the neighbourhood of Germany. They have settled chiefly as temporary guests, having no possibility of establishing themselves there, and provoking against themselves an organised defensive action on the part of the local trade organisations. This proves that the greater part of the refugees from Germany will soon have to take the wanderer's staff in hand and wander on, seeking for themselves some wild Angola or an uncertain Uruguay. The action for the temporary sojourn of this wandering mass has already cost Jewish society tens of millions of złoty. In the same time over 9,000[?] Jewish refugees from Germany have settled and established themselves permanently in little Eretz Israel. Jewish society throughout the world has until now given pennies for that purpose.
The contrasts we have underlined are explained by the fact that, while everywhere else we have to do with Jewish philanthropic actions, possibly even with non-[?]state-political actions (as is the case, for example, with Biro-Bidzhan), the Zionist colonisation in Eretz Israel is the product of a consciously organised, national-statelike Jewish self-help action. Zionist Eretz Israel — that is durability, purposefulness, finality. It is the idea that joins sentiment with reason and with the political justification of existence. Everything apart from it is vacillation, planlessness, temporariness; it is only sentiment and Jewish good-heartedness, or else bare reason without sentiment and heart.
We talk a great deal about the economic crisis of the Jews (which Eretz Israel does not feel at all), about the Hitler catastrophe. If Eretz Israel had numbered at the beginning of 1933 not 200,000 Jews but 3 times as many, that is, if Eretz Israel had already had a Jewish majority and thereby also a correspondingly enlarged economic property, the victims of the crisis, of poverty and of Hitlerism would have felt the burden of the misfortunes less, because they would have had a way out and a possibility of establishing themselves in Eretz Israel. To attain that number lay within our power; it was only necessary to provide greater means for the upbuilding of the country, so that in the course of the past 12 years it could take in more Jewish immigrants and provide them with more work and earnings. The collecting of these means is the business of Keren Hayesod — a voluntary collection of a permanent character. We did not do it, we gave too little, and now we are being punished for it. It was a mistake; the mistake which we allowed ourselves at a time of better economic conditions we must now make good under far harder economic conditions.
As energetically as possible let us set about providing the temporary, speedy help for the Jewish refugees from Germany. Jewish public opinion will brand those who, having the possibility to do so, refuse this help. But let Jewish society remember that still more important is the stable and lasting help, both for the exile from Germany and for the victims of economic misfortune in general. Whoever gives for the first aim — and refuses the second — fulfils his Jewish duty only for appearance's sake, and in reality he refuses to give help to Jews. One must do the first and the second. Those who refuse to give help in the first case will be branded by the public opinion of the present moment; those who refuse to fulfil their duty in the second case will be branded by the national-Jewish public opinion of the present moment and by the judgment of the history of the Jewish people.
Let us not repeat the same mistake! Let us see clearly its consequences up to now!
Let us repair it, and let us give as far as possible!
A. M. Hartglas (Warsaw).
People Are Pondering (A Little Feuilleton)

[Little feuilleton — the crisis and the approach of Passover.]
Passover is coming on now, so Jews sit and ponder; one ponders how to earn a złoty and how to take a fresh little interest-free loan; one man „clears“ [klert — both „ponders“ and „clarifies“] mead, and another ponders about matzah for Passover.
Jews are a wise and understanding people. One ponders about oneself, about the other fellow, about the whole community of Israel, but one ponders nothing out. Here, once upon a time people among us pondered about making the electricity cheaper, so they pondered and pondered. A committee was picked. They sat whole nights, until the electricity went out and the little committee fell asleep...
The whole world is pondering how to get rid of the crisis and cannot find any counsel for itself. Nobody has so far pondered anything out. Kreuger went off from his matches with the fire, and Rothschild's fortune is now going off with the smoke...
How long ago was it that every one of us wished to have at least a part of Rothschild's fortune? All the New Year wishes were, after all, full of his name, and mothers used to lull their children to sleep with his „golden ducats“, and now — the crisis has lulled him himself to sleep...
And then Coty? — which Jewish girl or young wife has not smeared and dipped herself with his perfumes, powder and paints? Thanks to him, after all, hundreds of druggists' shops have sprung up in every street and lane, and there has come forth a generation of nothing but „beauties“! And to whom do all the „Misses“ and uglinesses[?], queens and vice-queens, owe their paper crowns, if not to him, the almighty enemy of Israel, Coty? Now he has lost half of his fortune and has himself got the real pretty face...
Or did any of us ever think that little America, that rich „golden land“ which used to send over to us, the greenhorns, so many dollar bills, would itself, poor thing, turn green, and would not be able to help out our ailing institutions for Passover, so that we might be spared[?] knocking on the doors and tables of the magistrate [the municipality] and having to resort to Esau...
So Jews sit now and ponder what will be further, how one is ever to get rid of the crisis; the borders are closed[?]; one is oneself limited, and to the troubles too there is no limit. Livelihood — none[?], the businesses lie in the ground; perhaps one should really take to working the ground?...
So one ponders about cheaper rent, about marrying off daughters, about taxes that have to be paid, about the bits of household goods that will be taken away, and while pondering one goes back to the old trades of beadle and warden, of wedding-jester and cantor, to the truly Jewish, kosher livelihoods of baking matzot and making charoset...
Ch.[?] Matinka.
A Blood-Stained Envelope Uncovers a Tragic Story from the World War

[Serialized story — World War, espionage.]
By Y. Shteger.
An Austrian officer is forced to shoot his own wife. — She was the daughter of an Austrian nobleman, but she gave away military secrets to Russia.
A good few years have already gone by since the World War, but every day new terrible tragedies from that terrible time are still being uncovered.
Not long ago, here in Budapest, the secret documents of the war that were left over from the Austro-Hungarian government were opened; among the various documents a short letter was found.
The letter lay in a torn-open envelope that bore several brown stains, traces of human blood. On the other side of the envelope is written: “Committed suicide with his own revolver.” The scholars who found the letter became greatly interested in it, set about investigating, and dug up — a remarkable tragedy.
The tragedy begins in the spring of the year 1916.
In the course of the whole winter of that year the Austrian commanders made all the preparations to attack and smash the armies of the Russian General Brusilov; it seemed that this would not be so hard, and it was hoped that once they were smashed the road would be entirely free to march into Russia and even to take Petrograd.
The attack on Brusilov was supposed to begin from a corner in which the Russians were quite weakly protected, because they had no need to expect an assault from that side. In secret the Austrian generals brought over several fresh battalions to begin the attack.
But suddenly a disaster occurred. Instead of the Austrians falling upon the Russians, it was the Russians who, at that very point, began an attack on the Austrians! An attempt was made at once to get in touch with the generals of those divisions, but it did not succeed, because the telephone line had been cut.
The Russians penetrated deep and smashed the entire Austrian protective wall. In that battle Austria and Germany lost about 50 thousand soldiers captured, wounded and killed.
It was a catastrophe that nobody had expected. After all, the preparations had all been made in secret, and only a handful of people knew of these offensive plans. Who, then, gave away the great secret?
Wilhelm, the German Kaiser, raged[?] and shouted; old Franz Joseph fell into hysterics, and when he had calmed down he ordered the commander-in-chief, Baron Hatzendorfi [as printed; i.e. Conrad von Hötzendorf], not to rest until the traitor and spy who had handed the secret Austrian plans to the Russian General Brusilov was found out.
Spies came down from Vienna and searched and rummaged in order to find any evidence whatever or a trace leading to the guilty party. Experienced secret agents from Berlin helped them in this. But nothing came of it, and it looked as though the mystery of how the Austrian war plans had been handed over to Russia would remain a secret for ever.
But unexpectedly, through a strange chance, everything was cleared up.
In the middle of the night several soldiers were patrolling the streets of the town of Brünn [Brno]. As they rode they noticed a man suddenly fall down and not get up. They ran to him at once and saw that the man suffered from the falling sickness. When the soldiers began to lift him they felt papers crackling in his large breast pockets. On him were found several large envelopes stuffed with a number of letters, written in French, in which exact information is passed on about all the war plans of the Austrian General Staff, which was located in Baden.
The epileptic was Captain Mikhailovich, a Russian spy, one of the assistants of Major Ivanov, head of the Russian espionage agency in Austria.
When Mikhailovich was brought round he saw where he had landed. The Austrians did not stand on ceremony with him for long, and before dawn he was shot.
A few hours before Mikhailovich was caught by the Austrian patrol, the young Lieutenant Schalzi[?], one of the bravest assistants of General Hatzendorfi, had been sent off to the front, carrying with him secret instructions about the further steps of the Austrian army.
When Baron Hatzendorfi was handed the documents that had been found on Mikhailovich, he shuddered with anger, pain and vexation; his astonishment knew no bounds. The documents were a complete translation of the instructions he had handed to Lieutenant Schalzi[?]. And more than that: they had been written on the same typewriter.
Suspicion soon fell on the private secretary of the commander, Baron Hatzendorfi; the secretary's name was — Margit von Pimala[?].
Hatzendorfi at once sent several secret agents to Margit's apartment, and they searched among her wardrobes and found German and Swiss banknotes sewn into many of her coats and blouses. When the money was counted, the sum came to 180[?] thousand dollars.
Now there was no longer any doubt at all that the Baron's faithful secretary Margit was an agent of the Russian espionage bureau. And she also confessed to it as soon as they began to interrogate her.
Margit von Pimala[?] was the only daughter of an Austrian nobleman, a great gambler, who a year before the war had lost his palace and his estates. His daughter therefore could not live in the same luxury as the daughters of the other Austrian nobles, and so he sent Margit to study at a commercial school, to specialize in secretarial work and business management.
Margit finished the commercial school at just the time when the war began. Good secretaries were then in demand, because the men had all been called up to go to the battlefield.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Continuation of the Budget Sittings of the Kehilla Council

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Kehilla.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 22 / 22 Adar 5694 — piątek 9 marca 1934 [Friday, 9 March 1934].)
Będzin
The continuation of the budget sittings of the kehilla council.
Interpellation about the bloody events in the synagogue. — A promise that order will be restored. — Declaration of a left-wing parnas. — The budget item for a secular school struck out.
At the Saturday-night sitting of the kehilla council one would, according to the law, have been permitted to celebrate „Sheva Brachot“ — the kehilla council received a „new face“ [panim chadashot]. The place of parnas [council member] Fajner — is taken by his substitute, parnas Jechiel Kornfeld, who strives for Karl Marx's theory to be realised in the kehilla shtibl...
The beginning of the agenda at the sitting was the department — „cmentarz“ [cemetery]. Around this „dead point“ a „lively“ discussion develops. Very little was lacking for the 2 buckets [„wiadra“] of water that had been made ready to be used for „tahara“ [ritual purification of the dead] purposes...
At the sitting cultural problems were dealt with. The parnasim and board members, those who took part in the discussion around the culture department of the budget, endeavoured to show off their expertise about darkness, science, fascism and... socialism. Jewish personalities were invoked, among them Sokolow, Bialik and others.
— It was a „scientific“ sitting.
The president, Mr. Kurland, opens the sitting and announces that parnas Fajner has, for material reasons, withdrawn from the kehilla council and that Mr. J. Kornfeld has been invited in his place.
Before the agenda, parnas Mr. Klajman brings in an
urgent interpellation
addressed to the kehilla council, in connection with the bloody events that took place in the synagogue courtyard; Mr. K. asks what measures the kehilla council will adopt so that such things shall not be repeated.
The vice-president, Mr. Londner, expresses himself in words of regret about the events and declares that the board has a project to reorganise the order in the synagogue, only because the board was exhausted [„ershept“] last week the reorganisation plan could not be realised.
Parnas Kornfeld reads a declaration in which he announces
a struggle against reaction
and against the way the kehilla has been run until now.
The first budget item at the sitting — is the cemetery department. Parnas Rozenblum makes a proposal that in conveying the dead to the cemetery no exception should be made. The same wagon that is used for the rich should also serve for the poor dead. The proposal of Mr. Rozenblum is taken note of.
A lively discussion takes place on the item
Culture and schooling.
On this item countless proposals were brought in, both from the right and from the left; the forces of the silk żupica [Hasidic coat] measure themselves against... the red flag. After the 2-hour discussion almost all the subventions are adopted as the board had projected.
Parnas Rozynker proposes that, together with other libraries, the Arlosoroff library, the organisation „Vitkinia“ [„ויתקינה“] and the sports club „Przemsza“ should also be subsidised.
Parnas Klajgman[?] proposes to budget 5000 zł. for the benefit of artisans' courses for those who want to emigrate to Palestine.
All these proposals are, after the explanation of the dozor [board member] Mr. Manela, put off to be considered after all the items of the department have been dealt with.
On the subvention for the benefit of the Talmud Torah, Mr. Welner brings in a proposal to increase the sum from 3,500 zł. to 4000 zł. Against this speaks Mr. Liwer, who points out that the previous board budgeted 5000 zł. but the subvention was not paid out at all, whereas the present board promises that the budgeted sum will be paid out in full.
The dozors Piekarski, Welner, Szenberg and others also speak, and the proposal of Mr. Welner is adopted.
On the subsidies of the „Yesodei HaTorah“ and „Mizrachi“ schools Mr. Kornfeld delivers a proletarian speech, but when he gallops too far, the floor is taken away from him.
A broad discussion about
„light“ and „darkness“
develops during the item of 5000 zł. for a secular school.
Messrs. Hampel and Kornfeld fight with all the socialist fire they possess for the item to be kept, but the majority is against it and the item is struck out.
Owing to the late hour the sitting is broken off at 2 o'clock at night.
Sharpened Conflict between the Shochtim and the Kehilla Board.

[Będzin — Kehilla, ritual slaughter.]
The 2 „shochtimlekh“ [junior shochtim] given notice. — At slaughtering 4 shochtim must be present. — Ultimatum from the shochtim. — Intervention of the city commissioner.
As readers already know, the shochtim do not want to take the monthly salaries [„pensje“] until the gmina [the kehilla board] guarantees them that the arrears [„zaległe“ debts] will be paid. The shochtim have already intervened in this matter with the labour inspector, who, after acquainting himself with the matter, agreed with the decision of the kehilla presidium.
This week the conflict took on a serious character. The relations between the interested parties became so sharpened that it was thought that any moment now a fiery quarrel would flare up in the local kehilla. Ultimatums were sent from one side to the other, there was a sharp exchange of words between the rabbi and the kehilla president, but at the critical moment the municipal commissioner intervened in the matter and tempers calmed down.
The course of events is as follows: on the 1st of this month the kehilla presidium gave notice to the 2 „shochtimlekh“ because no salaries had been budgeted for them in the budget. As a protest the „shochtimlekh“ no longer came into the slaughterhouse on Saturday night. It also happened that R' Berish Makower had to go away because of family matters and R' Shlomo the shochet was unwell, so that in the slaughterhouse there was only the shochet R' Avraham Gerlitz, who declared that even if a second shochet were to come he would not slaughter, because the rabbi demands that during the slaughtering on the days Thursday, Friday and Saturday night 3 shochtim must be present, and on the remaining [„vayterdige“] days there must be no fewer than 4 shochtim.
On Monday the shochtim gave an ultimatum: if the presidium of the kehilla board does not withdraw the decision regarding the salary payments, they will go on strike. The time for withdrawing was given until Tuesday, 1 o'clock in the daytime.
When the city commissioner learned that things were heading for a shochtim strike, he took an interest in the matter and succeeded in getting the shochtim to extend the time of the ultimatum until Wednesday, 1 o'clock.
On Tuesday the shochtim summoned the president, Mr. Rubinlicht, to a din Torah at the local rabbinate. Mr. Rubinlicht rejected the proposal, giving as his reason that the shochtim, the believers in kashrut, ought first, before they turned to the labour inspector and to the commissioner, to have summoned him to a din [religious court]...
———
On Wednesday, at the appointed time, a delegation of the shochtim came into the gmina to announce that the shochtim had decided to strike.
The kehilla presidium was not impressed by the „revolutionary“ step and decided not to change its decision.
Bloody Brawl in the Courtyard of the Będzin Synagogue.

[Będzin — the synagogue.]
The lawlessness that has reigned for several weeks in the local synagogue — led last Sabbath to a bloody brawl among the elements who have lost their respect for the synagogue and who voice opinions in matters that ought to be decided by the heads of the kehilla and by the rabbinate in particular.
It is already high time that order be restored in the synagogue; we expected this first of all from the new kehilla board, but when will it finally happen?...
Until the 15th of This Month the Water-Main Tax May Be Paid with a Half-Percent Penalty

[Będzin — municipality, taxes.]
In the year 1931 the magistrate (municipality) imposed on the house-owners a special tax for carrying out the water-main works. The house-owners appealed against the tax at the time, but after 2 years the appellants received an answer that the appeals are rejected.
In the magistrate's reply to the House-Owners' Association attention is drawn to the fact that those who pay the tax (podatek) by the 15th of the current month will be charged only a half-percent penalty.
A General Meeting at the “Muza”

[Będzin — societies, culture.]
On Saturday, the 2nd of March, a general meeting took place at the “Muza”, at which, after a lengthy discussion of the activity up to now, the following board was elected: chairman Jakub Winer, vice-chairman Szlomo Kronental, secretary Izrael Wierzba[?], treasurer Icchak Feldbaum, board members: Lejb Staszewski, Mendel Kaner and Dawid Klajner.
As we learn, the board has already set about a widely ramified activity, and it is to be hoped that in the nearest future the new leadership will show decent fruits of this work.

Sosnowiec / The new kehilla budget at the same level as last year

[Sosnowiec — kehilla; budget.]
The new kehilla budget at the same level as last year.
The community-tax assessment ("etat-rozkład") smaller by 19 thousand zł.
On Sunday a sitting of the kehilla board took place, to consider the budget for the year 1934. As is known, 2 weeks ago a special budget commission was elected, which was to work out a draft budget. But at the sitting the commission did not come with any new proposals at all.
The chairman, Mr. Zendel, brings in a proposal that the officials' salaries be reduced by 10 percent and the retirement (emeritura) pensions by 25 percent.
The dozór [kehilla board member] Mr. Sztyglic is in favour of all salaries being reduced by 30 perc.
Both proposals fall, and by a majority of votes it is resolved that the new budget shall be at the same level as in the past year, whereas the community-tax assessment (etat-rozkład) shall be smaller by 19 thousand zł.
Mr. Zendel submitted a votum separatum [dissenting opinion].
A festive examination ceremony of the "Keter Torah" yeshiva

[Sosnowiec — yeshivas; religious life.]
Last Sunday the circle of Torah scholars in Sosnowiec had the opportunity to become acquainted with the brilliant development of the "Keter Torah" yeshiva in Sosnowiec in the field of study. On that day the annual examination ceremony of the "Kibbutz Gavoha" [advanced study group] took place in the "German" synagogue ("Daytshe shul"), with the participation of about 70 students of the yeshiva.
The examinations were conducted by the Rabbi of Będzin, Rabbi Vogelmann (Katowice), Rabbi Yosef Blumenfeld (Königshütte [Królewska Huta]), Rabbi David Halberstam (brother-in-law of the Radomsker Rebbe), the Będzin rabbinate, the member of the Kraków rabbinate Rabbi Reinhold, the heads of the yeshivas in the surrounding towns and townlets, and a large audience of Torah scholars from Zagłębie, who admired the great erudition and acuity of the students, among whom there are several prodigies (iluyim).
After the examination Rabbis Vogelmann and Blumenfeld, in their speeches, pointed to the importance of the "Keter Torah" yeshivas, which are being created and maintained by the Radomsker Rebbe, and in particular to the great achievement of the president of the yeshivas, the eminent Rabbi R' Moshele, thanks to whom the yeshivas are developing so well.
Afterwards a banquet took place in the beit midrash of the Radomsker Rebbe, at which the chief president of the "Keter Torah" yeshivas in Poland, R' Moshele, delivered a sermon rich in content on matters of the day. The cantor Mr. Weiss of Lemberg [Lwów] delighted those present with song.

[Sosnowiec — crime; theft.]

From the "Keren Hayesod" Campaign in Będzin

[Będzin — Zionism; Keren Hayesod.] On Sunday morning the ceremonial proclamation of this year's "Keren Hayesod" campaign took place in the "Apollo" cinema, in a hall packed full. After the Polish and the Jewish anthems have been played, the academy [festive assembly] is opened by Mr. Marek Szajn; with very matter-of-fact and logical arguments he points to the harmful tactics of the opposition, which makes use of boycott methods against the national funds that form the basis of our work of upbuilding in Eretz Israel, and he describes the deed as a national crime. In the name of the Keren Hayesod patronage[?], Mr. Sz. Fürstenberg gives a greeting in warm words, appealing to those assembled to tax themselves for the benefit of the "Keren Hayesod". In the name of the Jewish kehilla the vice-chairman, Mr. A. Liwer, gives a greeting, pointing to the positive attitude of the present kehilla towards the Keren Hayesod.
Then the distinguished guest, Mr. Hartglas, delivers his lecture, rich in content, on the great significance that Eretz Israel has at the present moment for the Jewish people, as the only place of absorption for the great Jewish masses. The speaker is interrupted several times with various heckling calls by opposition parties, which however receive their due answer from the speaker, who ends his speech amid enthusiastic applause from the audience. In conclusion the delegate of the Directorate, Mr. Garuszałka[?], speaks; he delivers a very warm speech interwoven with sayings of the Sages, and dwells on the symbol of the menorah, which unites in itself the branches of the right and of the left. The speaker is greatly disturbed by the opposition, yet his speech is concluded in an elevated mood; with the singing of "Techezakna" and "Hatikvah" the academy is closed.
In the afternoon a second lecture by Mr. Hartglas took place in the "Social Club", which made a colossal impression on the assembled audience. After the lecture a glass of tea was held, at which those assembled declared themselves ready to work for the benefit of the Keren Hayesod. It is to be hoped that this year's campaign will pass off with success.

A father punished with 8 months' prison for tormenting his children from his first wife.

A Terrible Catastrophe with Human Victims in Będzin

[Będzin — disaster.] A balcony with people on it falls onto the pavement — a Jewish girl killed — 11 injured.
On Wednesday at 4 o'clock in the afternoon the town of Będzin was shaken by the terrible news that in the courtyard of Winer's house on Potocki Street [ul. Potockiego] a balcony had collapsed and that there are many human victims.
The catastrophe happened for the following reasons: a group of acrobats was performing in the courtyard and drew many curious onlookers, above all children, who gathered on the balconies. Suddenly a loud crack was heard. A balcony on the 2nd floor collapsed, and those who were on the first floor were buried under bricks and stones; those who fell onto the pavement suffered most.
From under the ruins there were pulled out, already in a dying condition: Chana Shivtsharsh [Szwiczarz?], Anna Wincarz[?], Maria Szlusznik and Stanisław(a) Grańska[?], who were taken to the local hospital.
A large number of Jewish children who were on the first-floor balcony were also injured by the falling stones and bricks. Some of the children had all their teeth knocked out.
Dr. Wasercwajg gave the children first aid and sent the more seriously injured to the hospital. Their state of health is not dangerous.
A wondrous miracle also occurred. Two Rozenbaum children, a little girl of 3 and a little boy of 5[?], were left hanging in the air on the iron bars of the balcony.
Before the children were rescued, several women fainted from fright.
The tragically killed Chana Shvitsharsh, 22 years old, from Pińczów, was a maidservant at Mr. Matus(z) Winer's. She had been taken on in the position only a week ago. While washing the dishes after the midday meal she heard the music in the courtyard and went out onto the balcony, where she fell a victim of the catastrophe.
At the scene of the catastrophe and in the surrounding streets thousands of people also gathered. The impression in the town is a terrible one.
—————
From the hospital we are informed that the condition of the injured, and especially of Mrs. Wincarz[?], is very grave.

A Public Fund-Raising Campaign for the Yiddish Secular School System in the Country.

[Będzin — education, CYSZO.] The extraordinarily sharp crisis on the Jewish street has made itself felt especially in all Jewish cultural institutions, and almost unbearable is the bitter struggle of the Yiddish secular schools, which were supported and maintained chiefly by the broad working Jewish masses.
In order to help, at least in a minimal measure, to ease this acute distress a little, the Central Yiddish School Organization [CYSZO] is now conducting a broad campaign of public enlightenment, combined with fund-raising drives throughout the country.
In recent days a relief campaign has begun here in Będzin too, led by the long-standing school and cultural activist Mr. M. Mandelman, instructor of the "Y.Sh.A." [so printed; i.e. CYSZO]. Several conferences and consultations with the local friends of the schools and of culture have already taken place, and it is to be expected that the democratic part of the local Jewish population, as well as all friends of modern Yiddish secular culture, will do the utmost to help preserve the splendid school edifice, to encourage the teachers and school activists to carry on with the very important school and educational work on the Jewish street.
