A Letter to the Editor

Esteemed Mr. Editor!
In a letter from a group of Sosnowiec Jews who still remember that Sosnowiec was a forest, which was printed in the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” no. 9, attention was drawn to several incorrect passages in my article about the Sosnowiec kehilla in the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” no. 8.
In truth I had no intention whatever of reacting to it, since everything I wrote there about Sosnowiec is founded on archival files, official reports etc.; but so that it should not be said that “silence is tantamount to admission” (shtika ke-hoda'a damya), and for the sake of historical truth, I establish the following:
1) It is correct that the first Jewish settlers were tailors, and that the wealthy strata of Jews, of whom the “group” boasts so much, came some time later, when Katowice had become a great commercial city, setting up in Sosnowiec businesses, forwarding offices and trading offices etc.
Until the year 1862 no Jews at all were permitted to live in Sosnowiec, because of the so-called “border strip” (grenits-pas). Only artisans used to stay there illegally.
2) It is correct that Sosnowiec waged a struggle with Będzin over breaking away from it, as I wrote in detail in no. 10 of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung”, and because of Będzin's resentment the rabbi of Częstochowa was officially invited to administer the oath of the dozors (kehilla wardens). From Częstochowa this fact has been confirmed to me.
The “group”, begging their pardon, contradicts itself in its own words when it maintains that great Jewish industrialists obtained in Petersburg an independent kehilla in the town
If the matter had been obtained in Petersburg, which was the last instance, it would after all first have had to pass through the instances in Piotrków and in Warsaw, and there the matter would have had to be decided to the disadvantage of Sosnowiec. But this was not the case here. Piotrków decided on an independent kehilla for Sosnowiec, and this happened on 23 July, Old Style, 1898, as I wrote. Petersburg, on the other hand, decided on recognizing Sosnowiec as a town, because only Petersburg had the right to do that, after it had passed through the two first instances, Piotrków and Warsaw; and this happened only some 3 years after the kehilla came into being, i.e. in the year 1902, and the magistrate began to function only in the year 1903.
3) It is correct that in the official files and in the kehilla budget Rabbi Gitler figures only as “duchowny” (clergyman) and not as rabbi. One can also convince oneself of this from the “Pamyatnaya kniga” (official yearbook) of the Piotrków gubernia for the year 1913, where Mr. Steinsalz figures as rabbi.
I did, however, say expressly that the actual head of the rabbinical court (av beit din) was indeed Gitler, and that is also how he signed himself, “Rabad”, on the letters that are to be found at the Piotrków rabbinate.
Nor do I dispute that before him his father may have been rabbi there, but officially he does not figure at all.
4) It is correct that Rabbi Gitler had no concession for the rabbinical seat in Sosnowiec, which they themselves confirm, as does the fact that for appearance's sake one had to have a crown (“kazyonny”) rabbi in the person of Mr. Steinsalz.
5) It was not my aim in my articles to offend anyone's honour, seeing that I did not mention the Gitlers as rabbis. For “cleanse me from hidden faults”. Nor the honour of the dozor Englard, for in recounting the “virtues”, so to speak, of the first two dozors, I merely wished, in Englard's case, to excuse myself by saying that about his “virtues” I found nothing in the files.
6) Finally I want to underline one more thing: between the lines I read that that “group” was concerned only about the “rabbis” and not about the substance of the matter. Probably they are interested parties in this affair; and whether the “group” considers the content of the files about the Sosnowiec kehilla important or unimportant is a matter of complete indifference to me. For Jewish regional historical research they have a historical value, and precisely this and only this moved me to write the articles in question.
Respectfully,
Moshe Feinkind.

Festive Opening of the “Golden Book” at the Free-Loan Fund in Katowice.
(H. P.) On Sunday the festive ceremony of opening the “Golden Book” (Sefer ha-Zahav) took place in the “Concordia” lodge in Katowice; the book was created at the “Gemilut Chasadim [free-loan] fund” in Katowice on the initiative of Messrs. Benendelman[?] and Goldwasser.
In the presence of a large number of assembled delegates and representatives of all the Katowice Jewish associations and parties, as well as the delegation of the Będzin free-loan fund, Messrs. Wygodzki, Bożykowski, Goldstein.
The meeting is opened by the chairman, Dr. Kaufmann, who greets all those present and invites Mrs. Wilner, president of the Women's Association, to cut the white-and-blue and white-and-red ribbons of the golden book.
The first to be given the floor is Rabbi Dr. Vogelmann — first in Polish and then in Yiddish. He criticizes Katowice Jewish society, which is not yet mature enough to understand the necessity of a free-loan fund, and very sharply and with bitterness reproaches all those who did not come to take part in so necessary an action.
A matter-of-fact speech is delivered by Mr. Wygodzki, who appeals chiefly to the women, who have not yet been so swept along by the crisis and can surely accomplish more than the perpetually preoccupied man. The speaker says that evil spirits, and with terrible, incomprehensible decrees, seek to exterminate the Jewish people, and only the free-loan funds can to a certain degree alleviate our situation.
Further speakers are Messrs. Goldwasser (small traders), Dawid Ehrlich (Mizrachi), Szymon Kaufmann (artisans), Neumann (president of the Concordia lodge) and others.
The following signed (subscribed) in the “Golden Book”: the Women's Association (100[?] zł.), the Merchants' Association (50 zł.), “Mizrachi” (50 zł.), the Jewish artisans (25 zł.), the small traders (25 zł.), Right Poalei Zion (25 zł.), Ż.K.S. [Jewish Sports Club] (25 zł.), the Revisionists and Brit HaChayal (25 zł.), the free-loan fund in Będzin (25 zł.), as well as Messrs. Kowbski[?], B. Rechnitz, J. P. Blumenfrucht, Muszyński, Benendelman[?], Dam[?] and others.
Dr. Kaufmann thanks everyone for their assistance and, calling for further intensive work, closes the official part. Over a modest glass of drink and fruit the company converses until late in the evening.

Small Remarks on Great Matters

[Będzin and the Zagłębie — opinion column in two parts: the Passover relief campaign; antisemitic assaults in Gzichów.]
More on the Passover campaign.
Two weeks ago we pointed to the necessity of creating a Passover campaign for the Jewry of the Zagłębie, which over the last, let us say, 2—3 years has become greatly impoverished, and the poverty, moreover, grows stronger and stronger as time goes on, so that each time it seems that it has now reached its culmination point. Unfortunately, however, things get worse and worse, and as time goes on it becomes harder to breathe and to get through the process of existence.
And it is for that very same reason that we find ourselves once again touching on the same question. One must not forget that the pre-Passover season has already drawn near [printed: „אפגערוקט“], when every Jew is preoccupied with the one thought: where does one get the means for Passover? How does one meet this heavy burden? And not a few families will be unable to free themselves of the load right up to the day of Passover itself.
One must therefore enter into the situation of these families, who will be at a loss what to do and will not have the possibility of making Passover.
If we had kehilla representations as they ought to be, which truly stood for and represented the Jewish citizenry; if we had Jewish self-governing bodies in the true sense of the word; if the very first place there were not taken up by intrigues and behind-the-scenes politics and mouldy petty scrabbling[?] — one would have had to hand the mission over, in all the towns, to these representations, which in fact embrace the whole of Jewish life. Unfortunately, in the present state of the Jewish communities („gminas“), nothing more has remained than the bare names; nothing more exists than a firm, a signboard, so that nothing real whatsoever can be created with them, and once again we find ourselves turning to the philanthropic institutions, that they should take over this responsible mission.
The Jewish Zagłębie possesses „Beit Lechem“ [„House of Bread“] societies and other philanthropic institutions, which are called upon to take the mission of a Passover campaign into their own domain. Let them therefore occupy themselves with the necessary campaign, for which, incidentally, not much time remains. Passover is drawing near, and there is much work, and what is more, very, very responsible work, very, very cautious, very, very precise. One must not forget that this year many families will have to take for Passover who only a year ago were themselves givers, and therefore one must know in what manner to benefit these fallen families. In addition one must be very careful in gathering the material about them, because they are even capable of preferring to go hungry rather than that the street should, God forbid, learn of their sad situation.
To our appeal on this question there responded in Będzin the president of „Beit Lechem“, Mr. Bolimowski [באלימאווסקי], who is willing to take upon himself the carrying out of the necessary Passover campaign on a broad scale. He demands, however, and indeed must demand, the assistance of the citizens. The assistance of the public at large. There are broad possibilities for giving, and so there must accordingly also be the same possibilities for taking. In order that it should be able to hold out, everything must be done in parallel. It is therefore necessary to carry out the campaign in the broadest possible forms, and both the public at large and rich individuals must come to the aid of „Beit Lechem“; it [the campaign] also ought to be subsidised by the proper competent authorities, whose task it is not to let citizens fall who themselves gave when they had the possibility.
For a number of years now „Beit Lechem“ has been carrying out Passover campaigns which are sufficiently satisfactory, and this gives us the possibility of having confidence in the leaders of the institution and of patronising their activity. May they have the courage to carry out the necessary campaign on as large a scale as possible, so that it may bring benefit to as many of the fallen, as many of the oppressed, as many of the suffering as possible.
That is as regards Będzin. But what is being done in the other towns of the Zagłębie? Who, and in what manner, will carry out the Passover campaigns in such towns as Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa, Zawiercie and the surrounding settlements? Of them we hear nothing. And when one hears nothing, it is not to the benefit of the public.
The representatives of the said towns must not forget, however, that time does not stand still and Passover is drawing near; it is no longer merely on its way, but is already almost knocking at the door, so that there is no time here to be spent on pondering and on calling meetings — at which it is resolved, as usual, to call a second meeting and a third and so on continually, and meanwhile Passover will come and the hungry and the fallen and the oppressed and the suffering will go hungry.
One must therefore set about the work at once, and the work must be consistent, systematic, so that it should bear fruit. First of all the campaign ought to be concentrated under one society, and not that every institution should „make Sabbath for itself“, because in our poverty disunity is a misfortune, and in that case „the challah goes into the hamotzi“ [i.e. everything is used up on the preliminaries and nothing is left for the purpose itself].
It is therefore high time to set about energetically carrying out the Passover campaigns in the Zagłębie, so that everywhere the fallen and the impoverished should benefit from them; and as soon as the initiative arises from responsible communal workers, who know how to carry out the said campaigns, they will certainly be supported in broad measure both by the population and by the communal [municipal] institutions.
And therefore the most important thing is not to waste a single day, but to set about the work at once at full speed.
Antisemitic assaults in Gzichów [a district of Będzin].
Several times already we have had occasion, in the columns of our newspaper, to deal with incidents of beatings which take place in Gzichów, committed by antisemites against peaceful Jewish citizens passing by. We recorded them with the intention that measures should be taken, so that it should not come to serious events. Unfortunately the incidents are assuming an ever more serious character, so that at the present day there are already sick and wounded both in hospitals and in private dwellings. It would seem that the Hitlerite hooligans are making progress and are boasting that their work is fruitful.
Wounded people come with their bitter hearts to the office of the kehilla and to our editorial office, begging that one should come to their aid in their torment; they are afraid to go out of the house and do not have the possibility of being occupied at their normal work, because in the evening they cannot come home, fearing serious events.
One surely cannot, nevertheless, permit that in that corner of the town hooligans should do with people whatever their hearts desire, and that only because the passers-by are Jews.
After all, the attacks in Gzichów are an everyday phenomenon, so that beatings and assaults are no longer any news at all; the inhabitants there expect them. Yet one cannot remain indifferent to this antisemitic campaign of incitement; one must react to it properly, otherwise it may assume terrible forms, and then one may already have to react in another manner, which will no longer be as easy as now.
At the time we write these lines nothing has yet been done by our representatives; possibly, by the time the newspaper appears, something or other will already have been done. Yet we consider it necessary to remind our municipal [communal] representatives and communal workers that they should not make light of the question, because antisemitism is assuming ever stronger forms and we must see to warding off the bullets that are aimed at our camp, whether they are hurled by conscious, organised[?] antisemites, or whether these are blind tools in someone else's hands.
We know, after all, that there are various shady characters here who do not know what they want and merely carry out their mission: they are told to beat and they are let[?] — so they beat, because otherwise they will not be admitted into the company.
Our representatives, if they have begun to do something or other in the question, and possibly it will become quieter, must nevertheless stand on guard and see that the deeds are not repeated with still stronger forces.
We believe that the municipal authority as well as the police will come to the aid of those who will take an interest in the undesired events, and that they too will endeavour not to permit that corner to be brought to an abnormal state, only because hooligans want to run riot and provoke serious events.
One must therefore see to it, calmly and consciously, without noise and tumult, that the orgies at which the hooligan gangs aim — gangs which have been stationed in Gzichów in order to torment peaceful Jewish inhabitants — are put a stop to.
Let the question be taken up by such people as understand how to react to the antisemitic assaults.
Selekt.
The history of the Dąbrowa kehilla — according to archival records

By Moshe Feinkind. The history of the Dąbrowa kehilla. According to archival records.
To tell the truth, the Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] kehilla does not yet have a history in the full sense and meaning of the word. It is, after all, not even 25 years old, and what I am going to relate here will be only the birth pangs of the emergence of this kehilla.
Dąbrowa itself is also still young, barely 60 years old. The first to settle in the Dąbrowa area were the "Prussians", who, occupying Poland, founded here in the year 1796[?] the first mine, by the name of "Reden", around which there arose merely a colony of workers and other inhabitants.
In the second quarter of the nineteenth century there further arose there the "Huta Bankowa", "Ksawer" [Ksawera] and so on. Then all the colonies were united under the general name "Dąbrowa", which lies in the centre of all the colonies, being counted as part of the complex of Crown estates.
Jews settled there only in the second half of the nineteenth century, and the Jewish population of Dąbrowa in the year 1897[?] amounted to not quite 500[?] souls.
So the Jews of that area belonged to the Będzin kehilla, where they paid the etat (the community tax) and buried their dead, and so on.
And when Rabbi Reb Berish Graubart of blessed memory took over the rabbinical seat of Będzin (1893), the revenues from the small towns of the whole district, Dąbrowa among them, were also reckoned in for him.
But since, owing to the development of the iron industry in that region, the number of Jewish inhabitants also grew from day to day, they no longer wished to be dependent on Będzin and set about creating an independent kehilla in Dąbrowa.
I do indeed wish to set down here, on the basis of the documents that are in my possession, the details concerning the creation and emergence of the Dąbrowa kehilla.
The story is as follows:
Several householders from Zagórze, Józefów, the "gmina Górna" [probably gmina Górnicza] of Gołonóg, and Ząbkowice applied in the year 1908 with a petition to the Governor of Piotrków, to detach them from the Będzin kehilla and to permit them to create, together with Dąbrowa, an independent kehilla under the name "Dąbrowa kehilla".
The petition was motivated by the argument that, because of the distance from Będzin and not having on the spot their religious necessities, in which the Będzin kehilla takes no interest whatsoever, they absolutely must have an independent kehilla, and that they were already preparing to build a house of prayer in Dąbrowa, and so on.
The gubernia administration forwarded this petition to the county chief (naczelnik of the powiat) in Będzin, for him to give his opinion on the matter.
To this the naczelnik replied that the Jews in Dąbrowa and in the other places enumerated in the petition are the very poorest of the Będzin kehilla, and that it is with great effort and difficulty that the authorities manage to collect the small etat sum which they have to pay. And once they have an independent kehilla, it will of course be necessary to burden the Jews there with a great deal of money, as for instance for building a synagogue, a mikveh, for buying a plot for a cemetery, not to mention the budget of several thousand roubles a year for paying a salary to a rabbi, a cantor, beadles and so on — which will be so great a burden for the poor, small population there, and it is liable to impoverish them still further.
In particular, the greater part of the householders of that area had also applied to the Governor with a petition of their own, asking, for the above-mentioned reasons, not to tear those places away from the Będzin kehilla, and so on and so forth.
And taking into consideration the motives enumerated by the naczelnik, the gubernia administration, at its sitting of 23 June 1909, refused the petition for the creation of an independent kehilla in Dąbrowa (ukase no. 4592 of 1 July 1909).
But that little band of Jews did not yet regard the matter as lost, and lodged a cassation appeal against the Governor's decision with the Senate in Petersburg.
But hardly had the Senate received the appeal for consideration when householders from Dąbrowa proper, Huta Bankowa, Reden and Gołonóg submitted to the Governor a second petition to detach them from the Będzin kehilla; and the other side in turn worked for the "revolutionary" petition of the present petitioners to be refused once again, declaring that they are satisfied with the activity of the Będzin kehilla, which also looks after the religious interests of their localities, and above all that they will not be able to maintain an independent kehilla with their own strength and means.
The gubernia administration then further ordered the naczelnik to make inquiry in each place and establish the number of those who wish to break away and of the "nay-sayers", and also whether they are willing to take upon themselves all the expenses connected with an independent kehilla.
The naczelnik called together, in the places that wished to break away, all the Jewish inhabitants, asked each one separately what his opinion was, and on compiling the minutes of the inquiry — more correctly, of the "enquête" (poll) — it turned out that the majority of householders were for an independent kehilla in Dąbrowa.
Of 136 Jewish inhabitants in Dąbrowa, the colony "Huta Bankowa", Reden, Józefów and Gołonóg who had the right to vote as payers of the etat in the Będzin kehilla, 125 agreed and 11 were obstinate and said "no".
The well-to-do etat-payers of Dąbrowa, Huta Bankowa and Reden also declared themselves ready to bear at their own expense all the outlays and needs of the new kehilla, should the authorities not agree that Zagórze, Józefów, Gołonóg and Ząbkowice should belong to the Dąbrowa kehilla.
The opposing side went on to lodge a protest, that is, an accusation, with the Governor, that the public had been bought off, and that this was why the very people who had earlier also been "nay-sayers" had now joined the "yea-sayers"; and since an artificial majority had been created, the "enquête" should not be taken into consideration, and so on — for nobody, after all, is going to pay any etat.

The Renewal of a Shameful Deed

[Opinion — the Transfer (Haavara) agreement and the boycott of Hitler's Germany.]
By Sh. Rotenberg.
When, months ago, institutions that stand under Zionist supervision concluded the sadly notorious transfer agreement with Hitler's Germany, it called forth tremendous protests from the broadest strata of Jewish society. Almost the whole Jewish press throughout the entire world was conducting a strong anti-Hitler campaign and calling for a boycott of German products. From the front pages of the Jewish press all manner of slogans about boycotting Hitler's Germany cried out in letters as big as those of the Blessing of the New Moon. Thousands of articles on the matter were written by journalists and communal workers of the most varied shades; protest meetings took place which condemned the shameful act. All this put the initiators in a very uncomfortable position, and they tried by every means to defend their dirty piece of work.
Among the many excuses they also offered one for which one could perhaps find some justification. They argued that the agreement had been concluded while the pre-Hitler government was still in office, and that there had been no possibility of withdrawing.
Everyone, however, was sure that the "brilliant" deal-makers were inwardly convinced that they had made a mistake, and that they wished the public would talk about it as little as possible and in time forget it altogether. It is quite possible that this is indeed what would have happened, for when new troubles and worries arrive one forgets the old ones for the time being.
But the high politicians and business strategists of certain Zionist currents held an entirely different opinion about it.
Public opinion, the broad masses, democracy and so on — these are quite pretty words, yet nothing more than empty sounds, with which one can by no means do any "business". A practical commercial agreement is something else — let it be with Hitler — so long as one can snatch a nice[?] little profit.
Like a spit in the face, therefore, came the news that the transfer agreement has not merely been renewed but also enlarged, from 3 million to 8½[?] million marks. There sit[?] a couple of ringleaders who think with bookkeepers' brains, for whom the needs of world Jewry are nothing at all, and they keep concluding transactions with the bloodiest enemy of the Jews — Hitler.
The question arises: by what right does one demand of tens of thousands of Jewish merchants and millions of consumers that they boycott Hitler's Germany, at a time when official Jewish institutions openly and freely do business running into millions?
Here no twirling of the thumb [Talmudic hair-splitting] will help, no sophistry about higher national tasks; this remains a shameful breach of the boycott all along the line. Such a "shining" example has a thousand times more demoralising effect than, for instance, an Ellenberg affair, because the transfer agreement was sanctioned by public Jewish bodies. No jester would have been capable of devising a more ingenious mockery than the one the authors of the transfer agreement have made.
After all, the boycott has had a fatal effect on German exports, which fell in the year 1933 by 870 million marks compared with the year 1932. But while German imports fell throughout the whole world, in Eretz Israel — which ought to have served as a model with a one-hundred-percent boycott — they rose from 6,364,000 marks in the year 1932 to 10,027,000 in the year 1933, i.e. a surplus of 3,663,000, that is, 75 percent more. These figures, taken from official German statistical sources, are given by Dr. A. Marcus in the Eretz-Israel newspaper "Haaretz". One should know that Dr. Marcus is a well-known specialist in the field of economic questions; for long years he was active as an expert on various German newspapers, and he therefore deserves the fullest confidence.
It may sound like a paradox, but in the light of a transfer agreement one has to defend the various Ellenbergs; for if Jewish institutions which day in, day out preach boycott break it, then why should a private firm not do so? Why, for instance, should one declare kosher such a purely German firm as Oetker and disqualify such a "leader in Israel" as Ellenberg?
To preach boycott and to break it oneself — that is surely "immersing while holding the unclean creature in one's hand"; that is surely a deed of shame which no national fig-leaf has the power to cover.
Let the renewal of the transfer agreement be a warning to the broadest masses not to let themselves be led astray by the "leaders". The "Führer" Hitler is dragging Germany and the whole world into the abyss of the blackest reaction, and in this the Jewish "Führers" are lending a hand.
It depends only on the millions of consumers whether the boycott against Hitler's Germany will continue to be conducted with success. Here it is no longer a matter of class interests, but of supporting a regime which wants, with fire and sword, to drag humanity back into the dark Middle Ages — a dictatorship which strangles with an iron paw everything that the free human spirit has created in the course of long generations. Hitler, Dollfuss[?] and other mass-murderers must serve as a terrible warning that an endless night of the bloodiest reaction is approaching. A struggle must therefore be taken up against the new invasion of the Huns, which threatens to exterminate human culture and civilisation. And in this humanitarian struggle honest people, too — as the one and only exception in world history — may make use of the Jesuit maxim: the end justifies the means.
Trifles.

[Economy — satirical feuilleton.] A little watch thrown in...

A well-known barbed saying with which merchants answer those kind-hearted customers who want to buy "cheap":
— I'll give you a little watch thrown in as well!
And had anyone once said that a time would come when a watch really would be thrown in, people would have thought that whoever said so was mad.
And now we have lived to see such a time, when customers are given a little watch as an extra.
In the I.K.C. [Ilustrowany Kuryer Codzienny, the Kraków daily] we find the following item:
— The absurdity of dumping. They give flour away for nothing and pay on top of it.
The newspaper relates the following:
In connection with the constant growth of dumping, cases are beginning to multiply that show what absurdity one arrives at through the system of granting export premiums.
One of the firms in Trieste approached the Austrian bakers with an offer that they should take Italian flour from it not only absolutely free of charge, but that it, the Trieste firm, would pay the Austrian bakers an additional 15 to 20 lire for every centner of flour, on condition that the recipients of the flour pay the border duty and deliver the receipts to the Trieste firm.
The reason why the Trieste firm came forward with such an original offer is that the Italian government, wishing to support the export of wheat flour, in which Italy is now rich owing to the good wheat crop of the last harvest, decided to grant export premiums. These amount to so much that it pays the Trieste firm to give the flour away for nothing and to pay something on top, as long as it obtains documents showing that it has exported as much flour abroad as possible — and then it receives the premiums.
There you have "free of charge, with a little watch thrown in".
And if we are speaking of watches, it is also true that for 20 lire one can today get a whole kilo of Japanese watches, because Japan is dumping watches.
Presumably other states too will follow the example of Mussolini's state. Poland, for instance. Presumably one fine day we shall begin sending sugar to England no longer at 13 groszy a kilo but entirely free, and as an extra — a piglet[?] for every Englishman who consents to enjoy free Polish sugar; and presumably we shall begin sending ready-made clothes to Africa, and not merely without money: in the pocket of every garment we shall put a złoty, so that the Negroes [the period term of the original] may have something for small expenses. To Germany we shall send geese with a supplement of eggs, flour and skins[?], with which to fill the goose stomachs later on.
These are true pictures of today's international trade relations. The states bestow all kinds of dumping gifts on one another, and their own citizens are left more and more without watches, without clothes, without flour and without shoes on their feet.

Heard and Seen.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

A branching front...
The Jewish "danger" casts fear over all of Europe; those in power rack their brains to find the means and the systems that will annihilate[?] once and for all, so as not to be subjected to Jewish rule over every domain in the whole wide world.
And the holy work of extermination is done systematically; every step, every chess move is calculated according to a plan. The rope that is thrown around the necks of the Jewish merchants is not enough; it is still too little that the growth of the Jewish artisan class is cut short by decrees. No — they take the means of incitement against Jews out of the old archive and show them to today's "cultured" generation, so that it may have an idea of what such a thing really is
— the Jew...
In Warsaw, Shakespeare's "Shylock" has been staged these last weeks in such a form that "the Jew's lust is only to cut a pound of flesh out of his Christian debtor...
And in Będzin the holy work goes further and stronger. Here it is not the individual deeds of Shylock that are shown; here they show how "Jews crucified Jesus at the time of Jewish rule in Palestine"...
The holy mission of staging this has been taken upon itself by the Association of the Hallerczyks [veterans of General Haller's army] in Sosnowiec, for playing theatre for theatre's sake is not topical in the present epoch; every performance must have a definite aim, so that it may bear fruit...
— "Shylock" in Warsaw and "Judasz" ["Judas"] in Będzin...

— but that we have mentioned only by the way, in passing; what we are really after is something else: to touch once again upon the old plague that is deeply rooted among our Jewish daughters,
— their hatred of Yiddish...
The greatest distress is caused to the modern Jewish ladies [panie] when they are forced to let out of their delicate little mouths
— a Yiddish word.
And we had the following spectacle: the Englishwomen deeply regretted that they did not have the possibility of delivering their talks in plain Yiddish, but only in a high-flown[?] German; whereas when any one of the women delegates took the floor, they trembled with fear lest, God forbid, a "jargon" word slip out...
However many times the London ladies begged the delegates to speak mame-loshn [the mother tongue] — they did not succeed.
And a deep sorrow was poured over one of the Sosnowiec delegates, who declared:
"I cannot express myself [wysławiać się] po żydowsku [in Yiddish]"...
And one may believe that the declaration given accords with "reality"; and why not — the ladies from London cannot speak Yiddish either; it is, after all, a matter of course; how could it be? Where would an intelligent lady get the ability to speak Yiddish?.. And altogether, how would that be fitting?
And because of this one really cannot have any complaints against her.
— She really cannot "express herself".

Time is money...
An old, well-known saying; even in the present time of crisis the adage is still used. True, not everywhere, but in the firms that still enjoy "prosperity" one is to this day pointed to the little plaque that hangs on the wall, in a conspicuous place
— time is money.
The slogan is observed best of all by the present Będzin kehilla council, which applies[?] every means so that at its sittings time should not go to waste, because
— time is money...
There is no talking there just into the air, for the sake of demonstration, to needle[?] the other fellow; rather, every word is as if measured, polished, well founded, because once again the same thing
— time is money...
As an illustration, in my view, the following little picture will suffice:
The Będzin kehilla council "thrashed out" (Comrade Kleinman says: "mangled"...) the budget over 6 sittings. Each sitting lasted about 6 hours; so 30 dozors [board members] (the board and the council) sat for 6 hours each time, and we have an established total of 1,080 hours.
— The positive deeds? — The council raised[?] the budget by 10,000 zł. By this reckoning, an hour of work and sweat comes to about 10 zł.
In former times, when earning a few gulden [złoty] was one of the easy things, an hour of work ought to have cost more; but, for our many sins, at the present time a price of 10 gulden [złoty] an hour is not a bad one either. Besides, what matters here is not the amount of the payment for the trouble taken; the point here is that the kehilla council has once again confirmed that
— time is money...

The beginning has been made...
We were invited to a children's performance at School No. 8 (headmistress: Mrs. Brojda[?]) in honour of "Mother's Day".
The desire to go "caught hold" of me on hearing[?] the "detail" that, besides other songs, recitations and choral[?] singing, Hebrew songs would also be sung —
truly a sensation! A powszechna [state elementary] school and Hebrew songs...
The content of the songs, too, is topical, very topical; "Awake, Israel!" the very young, likeable little children cried out
— "Wake up, Yidl, take your fiddle".
We shall not deny the truth that the Hebrew word still comes out a little foreign in the mouths of the Jewish children; songs in another language sound better, come out more distinctly. But we believe, all the same[?], that appetite comes with eating.
— The beginning has been made...

The gallery.
The gallery plays a great role in the budget debate.
The Right reproaches the Left that it brings in demonstrative motions in order to show off[?] before the gallery; the Left in turn reproaches the Right that by defending reaction, fascism, clericalism, it wants to find favour with the gallery; in short, everyone flirts with the gallery.
And who is this gallery at the plenary sittings of the kehilla council?
The barrier and the doors have been taken out, and in the narrow strip of space stand Poale Zionists, Right and Left, Gordonists, a few Aguda lads, kibbutzniks of no particular kind — and that is the gallery.
It brings to mind the joke about that yeshiva student who sat in an attic room and shouted: "The world asks[?] a question[?]"?
This Year's Purim Celebrations in Tel Aviv

[Eretz Israel — letter from our correspondent.] A letter from our Eretz Israel correspondent Sh. Y. Tzviali (Rishon LeZion).
This year the “Adloyada” celebration took place before a much larger audience than last year, but on the other hand the content was poorer than last year.
On Friday, 23 February, one already began to feel Purim. On Saturday night work began around the “Esther's Palace” (Armon Esther), which is set up every year on the square of the Mograbi Opera and at Purim is called “Adloyada”.
On “Vayitapak Haman” Street (the Allenby—Nahalat Binyamin square) 2 beautifully painted gates with pictures from the Megillah were set up, and a carousel with hanging dolls representing the heroes of the Megillah.
The municipality issued appeals to the population to welcome the arriving guests, and the population complied with this very well. All the shop windows were decorated.
A great campaign during the Purim days was conducted by the “Union for the Products of the Land” (Igud lema'an Totzeret HaAretz).
Loudspeakers (megaphones) were set up along all the streets of Tel Aviv.
On Wednesday evening the public reading of the Megillah took place, and through the loudspeakers it was heard in all the streets. After the Megillah the crowd streamed to the “Adloyada” square, where the “Esther's Palace” stands. The surrounding streets, balconies and roofs were packed with people.
After 7 in the evening 4 men appeared on the stage and announced with trumpet signals that the Purim performance by “HaOhel” was beginning.
After the opening people began dancing through all the streets to the accompaniment of music from the loudspeakers.
The same evening many balls also took place, public and private. The dancing in the streets and in the cafés, the balls, etc., lasted a whole night.
On Thursday before noon the Tel Aviv radio station, with the help of the loudspeakers, broadcast various Eretz Israel songs, and in many places young people stopped and started dancing, thus even holding up the traffic — for who asks anyone here... after all, today is Purim and we are at home.
The procession — the Adloyada — was set for 2.30, but already well beforehand the streets through which the “Adloyada” was to pass were packed, and the roofs were “mobilised”. The “Adloyada” set out from the street (in honour of Purim the names of the streets are changed to names from the Megillah) “Umedaber kilshon amo” [“and speaking the language of his people”] (Eliezer Ben-Yehuda Street) and passed through the streets “Shushan HaBira” (Allenby), “Medina umedina, ir va'ir” [“every province and every city”] (the Tel Aviv–Jaffa road), Vegadol baYehudim [“and great among the Jews”] (Herzl Street), “Ish Yehudi” [“a Jewish man”] (Ahad Ha'am), “Esther HaMalka” (Nahalat Binyamin), “Shushan HaBira” (Allenby), and back to “Umedaber kilshon am va'am” Street.
Ahead of the Adloyada, members of “Hapoel” and “Maccabi” rode on motorcycles.
In front marched the band of “Maccabi HaEsh” (the firemen). Then came the car with the Adloyada committee, and after them 2 flags were carried (the national one and that of the Adloyada). Beside the flags rode on horseback the mayor of Tel Aviv, Mr. M. Dizengoff, and the well-known Avraham Shapira of Petah Tikva, accompanied by a troop of horsemen.
The first part of the procession was “The Tribes of Israel in Days of Old”, in which the 12 tribes were shown, each tribe with its flag and emblem, and at the end the tribe of Levi, who carried the “altar” and upon it “Aaron the Priest”; this lasted over an hour.
In the second part “Russian Jewry” was shown, where “Katsaps” [a nickname for Russians] were presented with Russian nagaikas [whips], waging war on religion, leading Zionists off to prison, etc.
“Polish Jewry” presented Hasidic Jews in torn kapotes, walking with various instruments and playing Hasidic melodies, holding signs “We are without a livelihood”, and yet[?] there stands the sequestrator [the tax bailiff] and shouts “Hav kesef” (give money) for taxes.
“American Jewry” showed that when one comes to them for money, a donation for various causes, they answer: “The dollar has fallen”, “We are poor people” — and yet they dance and have a good time in America.
“German Jewry” presented a car in the form of a snake with the Hitler emblem; on the car sits “Einstein”, in mourning, with a suitcase; behind the car “walked” the books of Einstein, Freud, Wassermann, Remarque, Bialik[?] and others, which were burned in Germany.
“The Jewry of Eretz Israel” — here the “Maccabi” band marched in front. A group of young, hot-blooded fellows with song; a car in the form of a worker with his tools in his hands; and “And it shall come to pass in the end of days”, in which were shown a “Hapoel” man [worker], a “Betar” man, a householder, an Ashkenazi, a Sephardi, a Yemenite, a Mizrachi man, a General Zionist, dancing and kissing one another; they were loudly applauded by the whole crowd. Then came various institutions.
The Yemenites this year displayed great activity in taking part in the celebrations with their very successful presentations. Here comes a wagon with small children (even ones in swaddling clothes[?]), all dressed up in white, and above them a sign “Long live the internal aliyah, by licence of the Government”... Then arrived “King David”, “Saul”, the heroes of the Megillah and the “Queen of Sheba” with the Yemenite “Queen Esther”; and here is the well-known Yemenite Moshe with his “fortune” — 10 children from one wife, apart from the second one (Yemenites even today have several wives each) — with a sign “An answer to the enemies of Israel — natural increase”. The catching of the tourists was also presented, and so on.
At night the closing of the celebration took place, with a trial over the burned books in Hitler-land. Then hora dances took place through all the streets; on “Vayitapak Haman” square the Betar members danced on one side and sang “Jabotinsky lives and endures”, and on the other side — the workers with the “Internationale”.
Late into the night the crowd spent its time at the balls, until the grey of dawn.
It is interesting that very many Arabs from the whole country also came to attend the celebration.
On Friday an incident occurred that disturbed the rejoicing: a clash between the Betar members and a band of Histadrut men; police arrived, and after a lengthy struggle the police succeeded in dispersing the crowd. 20 Betar members were left on the spot severely wounded.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayikra)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayikra
The Portion
—o—
a) "When any man of you brings an offering" (Lev. 1:2)
Today prayer stands in place of sacrifice ("so will we render the bullocks of our lips"), and just as a sacrifice does not atone without intention, without repentance, so too prayer has no value when there is no intention in it. Arono shel Yosef.
* * *
After the Shemoneh Esreh prayer we say "May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable"; but we often say the prayer only with the mouth and not with the heart — it is then merely "the words of my mouth" and not "the meditation of the heart" — so how do we still dare to say "May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable"?
Only, we say that verse itself without intention too, without the meditation of the heart...
* * *
"And when you pray, know before Whom you are praying."
For many pray not before God, but before — people... Yavin Shemua.
* * *
In Sanz [printed "Sondz", Nowy Sącz], at the Rebbe's, there was a prayer leader, R. Abish Meir. Once the Rebbe told him to go up to the lectern. R. Abish Meir answered that he had no strength; then the Rebbe said to him:
— A cantor is given help. If he prays honestly, God helps him; if he does not pray honestly, the Adversary [Satan] helps him... (Mekor Chaim.
* * *
Rabbi Henech of Aleksander [Aleksandrów] was once together with Misnagdic rabbis. The Misnagdim prayed, as is their way, the prayer in its proper time, at daybreak, and Rabbi Henech waited with his praying, as Hasidim do, until twelve o'clock. Then R. Henech stood up and said:
— From heaven I am being informed that I should now go and pray...
One of the Misnagdim asked him:
— Why am I not informed from heaven when I should go and pray?...
— I will tell you — smiled R. Henech, who was fond of a witticism — you pray at daybreak, the prayer in its proper time. I, however, dawdle about until after twelve, and then, when hunger already begins to gnaw at me, I know that I am being informed from heaven that I should go and pray...
—o—
b) "And if his offering be a burnt-offering of fowl" (Lev. 1:14)
In Zevachim (Mishnah, chapter 1, 2, 6 [?]) it is said that the blood of the burnt-offering of a bird was sprinkled below the "red line" [chut ha-sikra], and that of the sin-offering of a bird — above the "red line". With an animal it was the reverse: the burnt-offering — above the "red line", the sin-offering — lower.
So, with a bird, which a poor man brings, the burnt-offering was more important than the sin-offering; with an animal, which a rich man brings, the sin-offering was more important than the burnt-offering.
For with a rich man a burnt-offering, which is merely a gift to God, is not so significant; whereas a sin-offering — that a rich man should own up to a sin — that is already rare, and therefore it deserves to be distinguished... The reverse with a poor man: with him it is no wonder when he owns up to a sin and brings a sin-offering... but it is welcome and precious when he brings a burnt-offering, a gift to God.
Siftei Tzadikim (Rabbi Shmelke of Nikolsburg [Mikulov]).
—o—
c) "And when a soul brings a meal-offering to the Lord" (Lev. 2:1 [?])
"'Soul' is not said of any of the free-will offerings except the meal-offering. Whose way is it to offer a meal-offering? — The poor man's. Said the Holy One, blessed be He: I account it to him as though he had offered his soul." Rashi.
The order of the sacrifices is: first cattle, which only a rich man brings; later sheep, which a man of middling means brings; further on a bird, which a poor man brings; and last of all a meal-offering, which a really poor man brings — because with sin, too, it goes in this order: the poorer one is, the less one sins...
And one more thing: of the cattle-offering [?], the offering of the rich man, it is said: "its inwards and its legs he shall wash in water" — only the inwards of the offering, the innermost part of the offering, can be cleansed; whereas his own inwards, his own soul, the rich man's, remains sinful as before... But of the poor man — "as though he had offered his soul": the poor man cleanses his soul, brings his soul as the offering. Kli Yakar.
—o—
d) "If the anointed priest shall sin, to the guilt of the people" (Lev. 4:3)
If the anointed priest sins — "to the guilt of the people": it must inevitably end in the sin of the people. Under such a priest there can no longer be a people of righteous men... Divrei Shaul.
* * *
"For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek Torah from his mouth" (Malachi 2).
If the priest's lips keep that which they teach, if they themselves fulfil what they preach to others — "they should seek Torah from his mouth": only from such a priest does one want to learn... Shaar Bat Rabim.
* * *
"The Torah is destined to be forgotten in Israel" (Shabbat 131 [?]).
That is in order to bring the Redemption nearer; for it is chiefly our leaders and teachers who do not let the Redemption come, because they know that then "the earth shall be full of knowledge" and nobody will need to turn to them... Only once Torah is forgotten in Israel, and even in exile the teachers with their Torah are no longer needed, will the Redemption at last be able to come...
By way of a jest. Lachmei Torah.
—o—
e) "To him to whom it belongs shall he give it, on the day of his guilt" (Lev. 5:24)
The "on the day of his guilt" is incomprehensible. Is it speaking here of the day on which [?] he sinned? Here, after all, it is already speaking of his repentance.
All the commentators try to explain the difficult verse. The most correct seems to be the plain reading of R. Tzvi Hirsch Kalischer, namely: it should be vocalised "ashmato" (a sheva under the "shin" and not a kamatz), and that means: on the day of his excusing himself... of his owning up to the sin... like the "yechata" [shall sin] of verse 23.
London — Będzin

[Będzin — Zionist movement, WIZO.] It sounds like a witty conceit, like a paradoxical play on words that raises a smile, as though a giant and a dwarf were standing side by side. But in Zionist matters this is no comic piece of nonsense. In Zionist matters a small Jewish town in Poland comes together with the largest city in Europe.
Last week Będzin had distinguished guests from London.
The ladies Sieff and Goodman came — members of the executive of the world women's organisation "WIZO", which embraces fifty-odd countries. The two women, Sieff and Goodman, play the most eminent roles not only in the Zionist women's movement; they also hold an important position in English society. England is a land of tradition, and there a fine Zionist tradition has also been created.
The most prominent personalities of English Jewry regard it as their duty of honour to sacrifice their time and effort to the idea of the national renaissance of the Jewish people.
In the first ranks, together with the ladies Lady Erleigh, Vera Weizmann, Lady Samuel and others, stand the ladies Sieff and Goodman.
Now they have come to Poland in connection with the problem of hachshara (training) for girls — a problem which at the present hour is recognised as the most important question in the Zionist women's movement.
Miss Sieff and Goodman have been commissioned by the world executive of "WIZO" to study precisely the hachshara problem in the countries of the Diaspora, so as to be able in this way to find a practical and financial solution for this important problem.
With great effort it was achieved that the distinguished guests should visit the "WIZO" of Będzin, which on that account also invited women delegates from the surrounding towns to a consultation.
People knew that they had before them important individualities, that they had before them women who devote their whole lives to the Zionist cause. Women who belong to the highest aristocracy of England, who are welcome guests in ministers' palaces, around whom the intellectual world gathers. These women left their palaces, came down to the Jewish masses throughout the world, drew near to them, understood their misery and their sufferings, and took their place in the first ranks of the fighters for the upbuilding of the Land of Israel.
The speaker, Miss Sieff, gave expression in her address to her astonishment at the strange fact that at a time when the Jewish woman in England — who enjoys all civic privileges together with her Christian fellow-citizen, who knows nothing of oppression or misery — regards it as her duty of honour to be a Zionist and to work actively for the realisation of the lofty Zionist ideal, at that same time there are women in Poland who have no understanding whatever for the renaissance of Jewry in the Land of Israel, who hold that it is not good form to take an active part in a Zionist organisation.
And we can also add that the fact is truly astonishing, and characteristic, that even the great tragedy of German Jewry, which has given such a dreadful example of the fate awaiting Jewry in all countries — that even this has brought about no upheaval in the soul of the Jewish woman; this is a sad phenomenon.
It is simply a crime on the part of those Jewish women in Poland who, in the present critical hour of history, still stand far from Zionism. It is high time that all should mobilise around the Zionist banner. It is high time that all Jewish women should walk with dignity and pride in the ways of the English Jewish woman and help build the great monumental work — the Land of Israel.
For if not now, when?
The London guests brought enthusiasm with them; they roused us with their deep spirit and their warm, Jewish, feeling heart.
Necha Ratner.
What Should One Pray For? (A little feuilleton)

[Feuilleton.] An Orthodox Jew was arguing with me.
"Do you still not see that your liberalism is finished, that the chauvinist-fascist waves are flooding over us ever more strongly? How much longer will you hold on to the belief in the progress of mankind?"
And further:
"It is simply a piece of luck from Heaven that all these troubles have now come pouring down on us — otherwise, who knows how far we would already have strayed with our liberalism and progress..."
And further still:
"As it says in the verse: 'Al tivtechu' — do not rely — 'bi-nedivim' — on liberals — 'she-ein lahem teshua' — who are themselves helpless — 'tetze rucham' — their spirituality departs — 'yashuvu le-admatam' — they turn back to their earthliness... No sooner does a Hitler show himself with his Aryan theory than they at once forget all their ideals and become dogged egoists, coarse creatures of this world, and like beasts they drive the weaker Jew away from every bite of bread, throwing themselves upon it with bestial greed."
And finally:
"Do you not see for yourself that you no longer have anyone to hope in, except your Father who is in Heaven?" — —
•
Having heard out my Orthodox friend's tirade, I answered him:
"You are right, my dear fellow. Only last night, 'upon my bed at night', I did indeed come to see that one must become more pious, that all gates are locked before us and only the gates of tears are still open. Weep and pray we may, as much as our heart desires. I did indeed resolve to pray to the Creator of the world; but when it came to it, I did not know what to pray for. Should I pray for a downfall for Hitler and for Hitlerism — well, what will be the outcome? Liberalism will spread through the world again, Jews will become lawyers and professors and ministers and will once more forget God, as in the good old days. Should I, on the other hand, pray that Hitlerism be strengthened, so that Jews may indeed remember the 'put not your trust in princes' — why, it, Hitlerism, is here now anyway, even without my prayer."
What, then, should I pray for?
Abi-ver ["Whoever" — a pen-name].
Important Decisions of the Supreme Court

[Law — rulings of the Polish Supreme Court.] Liability for a false oath.
A person can be called to account for giving a false oath only when this was done out of express ill will; accordingly the new Penal Code sanctions the non-punishability of a false oath given through negligence or for some other reason that is not malicious.
Accidents at work.
A worker has the right to claim compensation from the employer for the injury suffered at work not only when he was not insured at all in the accident-insurance institution, but also in the case where, because of the employer's belated notification to the insurance institution of the accident in question, the injured worker has lost the right to receive an appropriate pension from the said institution.
What exactly is a "parcel".
In applying a reduced railway tariff to railway parcels, the rule to be adopted is that a consignment declared on one freight bill [the original has only "oyf eyn frakht"] is recognised as a separate parcel, irrespective of the number of goods or articles it contains.
Deferment of payments.
The concession of deferring payments which has been granted to a partnership firm extends at the same time to each partner individually and covers not merely the obligations connected with the enterprise but even the personal debts of each partner individually; the concession does not, however, apply to maintenance (alimony) obligations.
A Blood-Stained Envelope Uncovers a Tragic Story from the World War

[Serialized story — World War, espionage.]
By Y. Shteger.
An Austrian officer is forced to shoot his own wife. — She was the daughter of an Austrian nobleman, but she gave away military secrets to Russia.
(2)
Since Margit was the daughter of an Austrian nobleman about whose patriotism towards "Kaiser and Fatherland" there could be no doubt whatsoever, she was engaged as the private secretary of Baron Hatzendorfi [as printed; i.e. Conrad von Hötzendorf], the Austro-Hungarian commander-in-chief for the Russian front.
The Baron was exceptionally pleased with her work. Margit could work 24 hours on end and not even complain about it. She was a "true Austrian daughter", as Hatzendorfi expressed himself about her with praise and gratitude. When he once asked where she got so much energy from, Margit explained to him that she had no friends and did not go to any amusements. "When I get up in the morning, I eat and go to work. When I come home from work, I eat and go to sleep; that is why I am always rested, Your Excellency."
Many of the officers at the staff headquarters in Baden tried to become more closely acquainted with the Baron's secretary, but she ignored them all; only one of them had success: this was Lieutenant Stefan Szalay [printed: Shalei], who did not flirt with her like the others, but really showed true love and adoration.
Margit was touched by Szalay's attitude towards her, and she responded to his love. They began to meet in secret; their meetings used to take place in a separate room of an inn near Helenental [printed: "Henental"], a few miles from Baden.
At one of these meetings they decided to marry, but Margit stipulated that their marriage should be kept secret until after the war. Margit gave Szalay to understand that if Baron Hatzendorfi found out that she had married, and that she might therefore yet share her state secrets with him, he would send him, Szalay, away somewhere else, or he would dismiss her, Margit, from her post.
In the middle of April 1916 Stefan Szalay and Margit travelled to Vienna, where they took out marriage papers, and on the following day they were already back in Baden. No one apart from the two of them knew of this wedding, and Szalay himself did everything so that the secret should, God forbid, not be discovered.
Just then, when Szalay was at the war front, it was found out that Margit von Pimala[?], the secretary of Baron Hatzendorfi, was a paid agent of the Russian espionage bureau in Austria.
Margit was brought before a court-martial, under the chairmanship of Prince Friedrich, a cousin of the Austrian Emperor Franz Joseph.
The trial was conducted in secret and the outside world knew nothing of it. Here, after all, they were trying the traitress who had worked in the Austrian military headquarters and had given away those secrets which had led to the defeat of the Austro-German armies in the spring of 1916 and to the victory of the Russian battalions under the leadership of General Brusilov.
At the trial Margit related that she had been drawn into the espionage work by Mikhailovich, who had promised to pay her enough money for her services that she would be able to buy back the palace and the estate which her father had lost. When Margit already had enough money and wanted to stop supplying information to the Russian espionage bureau, she found out that she could no longer wriggle out of the hands of Ivanov and his assistants, and she had to continue the work.
At the secret trial Margit also reported that in the war zone there was another Austrian who was in the service of the Russian government. He is an elderly man who makes friends with the soldiers and brings them various sweets and drinks, so that everyone trusts him. In the darkness of the night he crawls quietly over to the Russian side, where they already know him and no one shoots when they see him moving, and he handed over to them the secret documents that Mikhailovich had received from her.
As soon as Margit had told this, a telephone call was made at once to the war front; the man in question was immediately arrested, and he was shot without a trial.
The court-martial that tried Margit did not need to think much about the verdict. It was unanimously decided that she should be shot; the sentence, however, was not carried out at once — it was postponed for several days in the hope that more information about the Russian espionage work in Austria could be got out of Margit.
When Lieutenant Stefan Szalay returned from the front, he at once burst into the main office, ostensibly to hand in his report, but in truth he wanted to catch a glimpse of his ardently beloved Margit.
Szalay was surprised to find another person in her place. He did not ask where she was, however, so that he should not be suspected of having a special interest in her. He had, after all, agreed with Margit that no one must find out that they were man and wife, or even close friends.
Szalay waited impatiently for the moment when he would be released from his duties, so as to run to Margit and find out what was the matter with her. Hatzendorfi and several of his assistants were at that moment holding a secret consultation to determine who should command the 12 soldiers who were to shoot Margit.
And that really was a difficult problem. All the lieutenants and officers of the staff had known Margit for a fairly long time, and not one of them had the courage or the desire to be the commander of the soldiers who were to shoot her, notwithstanding that she had been a spy and a traitress and did not, in their opinion, deserve any pity or sympathy.
One of the officers who took part in the consultation then stood up and said the following.
"Gentlemen! The trial of the traitress was conducted in secret. When each one of the assistants came into the staff headquarters and saw that Margit was missing, he asked what had happened to her and whether she was, God forbid, ill. Well, they have certain sentiments for her. The one exception is only Lieutenant Stefan Szalay. When he came back from his mission to the front and, on coming into the office, did not find Margit, it did not even occur to him to ask where she was. That is the best proof that he has no connection with her whatsoever, and therefore he is the suitable man to direct the execution…"
(Conclusion[?] to follow.)
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Ne'ila Sittings of the Home-Grown "Parliament"...

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Kehilla.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 29 / 29 Adar 5694 — piątek 16 marca 1934 [Friday, 16 March 1934].)
Będzin
The Ne'ila [closing] sittings of the home-grown "parliament"...
Hebrew courses at the kehilla. — A plan for a trade school. — Fire and water. — Not "dobroczynność" [charity] but social welfare. — The shochtim's struggle with the kehilla. — A loan of 15 thousand zł.
After heavy toil and trouble, after 6 sittings, the kehilla budget has at last been adopted by the council. The last sitting took place on Sunday evening. The sitting was rich in... attractions: not only the "revolutionary" numbers of the left-wing parnasim [council members], during which they even invoked Lenin's soul... but also attractions provided by the electricity and the water mains. During the sharp discussion about "whether dozor [kehilla board member] Manela[?] meant it this way or otherwise with his proposal", the electric light "went on strike" and the hall went dark; the darkness made the gallery "lively", and the sitting "conducted itself" without a chairman. The dark picture suited the general mood; it looked like a beit midrash before the reciting of Eicha [Lamentations] — all that was missing was for the tables and benches to be overturned, and then the true face of our "parliament" would have come out...
At Thursday's sitting,
which took place under the chairmanship of vice-president Mr. Landner, the continuation of the culture section was dealt with. After the reading of the minutes of the last sitting, the chairman makes a proposal that, because of the present strong urge towards Eretz Israel, the kehilla should organise Hebrew courses. The courses should also be for the children who study in the public elementary [powszechne] schools.
Dozor Hampel says that for the sum of 5,000 zł for courses, a children's home should be created.
During the consideration of Kleinman's proposal to allot 5,000 zł for a trade school, parnas Landau says that the trade school should be set up in the "Talmud Torah". The number of proposals of this kind keeps multiplying, a tumult arises, president Rubinlicht rings the bell. At last the "storm" is liquidated and the proposal of parnas Kisner is adopted, that 500 zł be budgeted for a plan for a trade school; with that the matter is settled.
On the further items dozor Mr. Piekarski takes the floor; he proposes to budget 1000 zł for the "Keren HaYishuv".
By a majority of votes the proposal of parnas Rozenker[?] is adopted, to pass over the proposal to the order of the day.
Because of the late hour the sitting is broken off at 1 o'clock at night.
———
With a delay of 1½ hours there begins
Sunday's sitting.
Before the order of the day, an urgent motion is brought in on behalf of the board, that the council authorise the board to take out
a loan of 15000 zł,
which is to serve for carrying out the planned Passover campaign. The motion is adopted unanimously.
After the "granting" of the loan, the light breaks down and it becomes dark. The tightly packed gallery public takes advantage of the opportunity and feels at home, more than the parnasim...
At last the light is put back in order and they proceed to the further deliberations.
Parnas Kisner[?] comes with a proposal to assign
1000 zł for the "Prisoners of Zion".
The left raise a tumult, but in the end the proposal is not put on the order of the day, for political reasons.
Then a second "miracle" happens. Water suddenly began to pour stormily from the water mains. The wags of the generation say that the water pipes could not withstand the amount of water that had accumulated from the speeches...
After the events of "fire and water" they proceed to the item: subventions for philanthropic institutions.
Parnas Kornfeld is not satisfied with the title "dobroczynność"; he demands that the "dział" [budget section] be called
Social welfare
After the explanation of the presidium the proposal is withdrawn.
Parnas Kisner protests against the fact that the letter from Betar concerning a subsidy was not dealt with, and as a protest he leaves the sitting.
Vice-president Mr. Liwer speaks about the subventions and subsidies and appeals that the council should not alter the board's draft.
Parnas Kornfeld is against the expenditure on kosher food for Jewish soldiers and prisoners at Passover; the money should be given for social aid. Parnas Rozenblum also speaks in this sense; at the same time he proposes to increase the sum for supporting poor emigrants to Eretz Israel.
Parnas Rechnic is for increasing the subventions for the institution of the "Linat HaCholim" society.
Mr. Liwer proposes to strike out the subventions — 2000 zł for "Keren Hayesod", 1000 zł "Keren Kayemet" — and instead to increase the support fund for emigration to Eretz Israel and other countries from 4 to 7 thousand zł. The proposal is adopted. All the amendments brought in fall, and the whole "dział" (37,000 zł) is adopted en bloc. It is also resolved to give a subsidy of 300 zł for "Beit Lechem".
Parnas Kornfeld proposes that the council express its wish that the board take steps so that the institutions subsidised by the kehilla should not carry on any separate
schnorring at celebrations.
On this question Mr. Rubinlicht answers that the board is going about with a plan to have a control over the activity of the philanthropic institutions and to concentrate them at the kehilla. Mr. Rubinlicht relates, by the way, that a certain institution in Będzin had, in the course of one year, an income of 2,600 zł, and of that sum 2,200 zł was spent on administration.
Then a letter is dealt with from one of the morei hora'ah [rabbinical judges], who asks that the council allot him
a gratuity of 1000 zł.
Mr. Liwer delivers a longer speech on the question, in which he speaks out against giving gratuities to members of the rabbinate, if only because that same rabbinate is leading the shochtim's struggle against the kehilla. For what good deeds are gratuities due to them — Mr. Liwer cries out — where were they when Jewish Będzin demonstrated against the Hitler regime? What has the rabbinate shown in the field of education? Do they take an interest in orphans or in other institutions?
Mr. Rubinlicht speaks in the same sense; he quotes a part of the letter that the shochtim wrote to the commissioner of the municipality, to whom they pass on slander directed at the kehilla presidium.
Messrs. Skoczylas, Piekarski and Goldsztajn support the request; it is not logical — they say — to tie the struggle of the shochtim together with the moreh hora'ah in question, who is, by the way, the most capable one and is esteemed by all strata of the Jewish population of Będzin.
Messrs. Landner and Herszlewicz also speak, and the proposal of Mr. Goldsztajn is adopted, and the matter is handed over to the disposition of the presidium.
The last attraction of that merry evening was the discussion about the expenses and income of the mikveh.
Parnas Kornfeld came out, as always, with a social proposal: that the 37 thousand zł which the mikveh is to cost be given for the unemployed. With this proposal Kornfeld mentioned Lenin and the idlers ("editors" of the mikveh-sheet) who had taken a levy on kosher milk...
The whole part is adopted en bloc.
That was the last part of the kehilla budget, on which as many as 6 sittings were held.
At midnight the "historic" sittings came to an end.
A Kimcha [de-Pischa] Commission Created at the Kehilla.

[Będzin — Kehilla; Passover relief.]
On Tuesday evening a sitting took place in the premises of the kehilla [of Będzin], at which a Kimcha [de-Pischa, Passover flour relief] commission was created, consisting of Messrs. L. Rubinlicht, A. Liwer, J. Gutman, J. Goldfeld, Mrs. C. Szajn, Mrs. Dr. Parashtiska[?], M. Rozensaft[?], Sz. Piekarski, M. Lewin, N. Landner, B. Rembiszewski and A. D. Galisowski[?].
All those who wish to benefit from support for Passover must register at the office of the kehilla from 5 to 7 o'clock. Respectable families can apply themselves or through others to the members of the Kimcha commission.
A Christian Woman Wounds a Passing Jew in Gzichów

[Będzin — incident; antisemitism.]
On Tuesday evening a Jew from out of town, while walking along Gzichowska Street [Będzin], was attacked by a Christian woman, a local resident, who wounded the Jew in the head with a blunt piece of iron.
Sosnowiec — The Kehilla Books from 1927 Taken Away

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] A search at the kehilla secretary's. — Dozors (board members) at the investigation office. — Echoes of the kehilla's lawsuit against Rabbi Englard.
Last Sunday Jewish Sosnowiec was in an uproar because of the "sensational events" in the kehilla.
On Sunday morning 2 secret agents came to the premises of the kehilla office and declared that, on the strength of an order from the prosecutor's office and from the municipal court, they had come to take away the books of the kehilla's activity from the year 1927 until today.
After taking out the books demanded, the same men carried out a search in the dwelling of the kehilla secretary, Mr. Lewenhof; although nothing whatsoever suspicious was found in the search, Mr. Lewenhof was nevertheless detained and taken to the investigation office.
The dozors were also summoned: Zendel, Bachmajer, Sztiglic, Gabetia[?], Zaks, Brahn and Broner, from whom explanations were demanded as to on what grounds the kehilla board had permitted itself to dispose of about 18[?] thousand zł. of kehilla money, which was used to conduct lawsuits against Rabbi Englard.
To this the dozors declared that the sum was spent in accordance with a resolution of the board and the council. The sum that the trial procedure cost — the dozors declared — brought the kehilla a gain of many tens of thousands of złoty, for had Rabbi Englard won the lawsuit, the kehilla would have had to give him the yearly pension, starting from 1927 until today.
After the explanations the dozors were released at once, whereas Mr. Lewenhof was released only at 5 in the evening.
Commissary Council Against the Proposal to Subsidize the Jewish "Moshav Zkenim" (Old-Age Home)

[Sosnowiec — municipality.] At the last sitting of the local commissary council [the appointed city council of Sosnowiec] it was resolved to burden the citizens (read: the Jewish merchants) with an investment tax in the amount of 100 thousand zł.
After the proposal had passed, councillor Mr. Aliner turned to the council with an appeal that the Jewish "Moshav Zkenim" (old-age home) be given a subsidy of 1,500 zł.
Aliner's proposal was put to a vote and was rejected.
Then Mr. Aliner left the session hall in protest. It is worth noting that since the "Moshav Zkenim" has existed in the new building, the magistrate has not given any subsidy whatsoever.
When the State's Revenues Grow, the Crisis Will Shrink

[Sosnowiec — economy, lecture.] So says Senator Targowski.
In the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec a lecture by Senator Targowski took place on Saturday, under the title[?] "Polish policy in relation to the important economic problems". Present at the lecture were: Starosta Boksa, the president of the Chamber of Commerce Gadomski, the president of the district court Zbrowski[?], deputy Ganszewski[?] and a number of representatives of the local industry and trade.
In the introduction to the paper Senator Targowski gave a survey of the general economic situation in Europe as a whole and of the economic problems in Poland in particular. The lecturer states that we stand before a better tomorrow. The lasting crisis in Poland — he says — depends on society. State policy must be conducted in the direction that the incomes of society should grow.
The lecturer also analysed on a broad scale the question of devaluation and underlined that Poland has shown a great success in the field of maintaining the currency.
At the end of the paper Sen. Targowski reported on the new trade agreement with Germany, the growth of the port in Gdynia, and came to the conclusion that economic policy in Poland is going along a good road.

A successful children's performance.
In the premises of Elementary School No. 8 in Będzin (headed by Mrs. Brojda) a children's performance entitled "Mother's Day" took place on Saturday evening; it left a very good impression on the parents present and the invited guests.
The programme, which was rich in singing, recitations and musical numbers, was brilliantly performed; the tiny troupe played their parts freely, almost like "professional actresses".
A very successful number was the one-act play, which presents children's self-sacrifice for their parents; the one-act play, written by Mrs. Eng. Sznajderman, is good material for school youth.

On Wednesday afternoon the 70-year-old Aron Kugel threw himself from the third floor of Liberman's house on Targowa Street in Sosnowiec. On the way to the hospital the suicide died.

[Sosnowiec — accidents.] At 37 Modrzejowska Street in Sosnowiec there is a "Hachnasat Orchim" (hostel for wayfarers); Mrs. Zweigenhaft[?] was staying there with her children.

The first tram strike in Zagłębie.

On Wednesday at 12 midnight a meeting took place, attended by all the tram employees, at which the new wage-reduction proposal of the tram management was discussed.
After the report of the delegates that the management was holding firm to a 12 per cent reduction, a resolution to strike was adopted.
Until 12 noon tram traffic was completely halted; only later did the trams run, operated by the inspectors (controllers), on the line from Huta Bankowa to Sosnowiec; to Czeladź the trams did not run.
In the course of yesterday negotiations were held between the two sides; the employees proposed a reduction of 7 per cent.
In the afternoon the strike was called off.
On Sunday the shops will be open.

According to the regulations all shops may be open this coming Sunday from 1 p.m. until 6 in the evening.
On the remaining days of the week the shops may be open until 9 in the evening.

Why should there be no intervention with the tax authorities to suspend the distraints until after the holiday?
We point out that every year at this time the municipality (Magistrat) used to suspend the distraints for local tax until after the holiday; now, however, the local tax has passed to the tax offices, and it would therefore be only fair that the Jewish economic institutions intervene with the tax authorities so that they, too, take the eve of the holiday into account.
Without doubt such an intervention would be necessary, and not only regarding the local tax, but — to suspend until after the holiday the distraints for all kinds of taxes.

The health office of the Będzin Magistrat has informed the bakers' guild that all those employed in matzah baking must hold health certificates.
