Jews of Sosnowiec, fulfil your brotherly duty!
The Sosnowiec Kimcha [de-Pischa] committee points out that, in connection with the terrible want prevailing among the broad strata of the Jewish population of Sosnowiec, the number of needy has doubled compared with previous years. A number of householders, however, have not given any Kimcha de-Pischa, and this disrupts the payments to those who are waiting to be helped for the holiday. An appeal is therefore made to those who have not yet fulfilled their brotherly duty to pay the Kimcha as soon as possible at the gmina (community office).
For not paying in the restaurant.

Two women came into a Katowice restaurant, ate their fill and refused to pay.
This week they stood before the Katowice court, which sentenced them to 4 months' prison.
500 thousand tons of coal to Denmark.

A Danish shipping company has approached the Polish government with a proposal for the following exchange: the company is to give 2 passenger ships in return for 500 thousand tons of coal.
In the coming days a plenipotentiary of the shipping company is arriving in Poland, who will negotiate on this matter with the coal industrialists.
Distraints over Small Tax Debts

[Poland — taxes.]
The Ministry of Finance has sent an explanatory circular to all tax offices concerning the manner in which smaller tax sums are to be collected. It happens very often that when a few złoty, or even 15—18 złoty, are owed, the tax bailiff comes and carries out a distraint (zajęcie), which involves large expenses, entirely out of proportion to the debt.
For this reason the tax authority in Warsaw has ordered all the offices [?] in the provinces that, in the case of small sums, before the cart is sent, a further reminder (upomnienie) should be sent, stating that if payment is not made within five days, the goods will be taken away on the cart.

Imposing Celebrations in Zagłębie in Honour of Piłsudski's Name Day

[Zagłębie — Piłsudski's name day.] This year's celebrations in honour of Piłsudski's name day in Zagłębie bore a festive character.
The beginning took place
in Dąbrowa.
The present kehilla administration [of Dąbrowa Górnicza] got in first [“had had” — doubled in print] and arranged a festive divine service in the synagogue on Sunday afternoon. In honour of the celebration the well-known Preshever[?] rabbi, Rabbi Levi[?], who now lives in Kraków, was invited to speak on topics of the day. Representatives of the police, municipal and administrative authorities were also invited. Because of the latter the celebration did indeed take place punctually. It is, after all, a well-known thing that we have respect for all the nations, only not for ourselves. While a non-Jew is in the synagogue, it is calm and quiet; as soon as he leaves the synagogue, there is already a noise as at a fair... This was confirmed again during the celebration. Hardly had the representatives of the authorities left the synagogue when everyone found his tongue, and it echoed with — Sha! Sha!..
The celebration begins with “Mah Tovu”, sung by Mr. Baum with the choir (from Będzin). Then the above-mentioned rabbi, wrapped in a tallit, takes his place before the Holy Ark, and after an introduction about Joseph's deeds for the land of Egypt the rabbi passes over to Polish, in which he describes, rich in content, the great work of Marshal Józef Piłsudski for the liberated, independent Poland.
With the cry “Niech żyje” [Long live] for the President and for the person of the jubilee the rabbi ends his speech in the Polish language.
Then the rabbi opens the Holy Ark and says the chapter “Ha-Noten Teshua”. After that he speaks in Yiddish about the greatness of Marshal Piłsudski, who grants equal rights to all citizens; especially great are his merits — says the rabbi — in that he helps to educate the Jewish children in the Jewish spirit and to strengthen the Jewish faith.
The packed audience is so enchanted and delighted by the rabbi's speech that people forget they are in a synagogue and answer [misprinted “etfert”] with stormy applause.
Mr. Baum sings mi-sheberakhs and other chapters of Psalms, and with that the official part is ended.
But the audience does not want to leave the synagogue and demands that the rabbi speak more. The demand is fulfilled, and the rabbi speaks about the festival of Passover and appeals that in the present hard time the well-fed[?] should also remember the hungry.
In front of the synagogue hundreds of people had gathered, waiting for the rabbi. Because of this a great crush arose, especially when the photographer performed wonders with his camera..
Będzin
On Sunday and Monday Będzin stood under the sign of Marshal Piłsudski's name day.
All houses were decorated with flags. On Third of May Square the monument was decorated with pictures of Marshal Piłsudski and adorned with greenery.
In the synagogue, with the participation of the rabbinate headed by the rabbi, kehilla representatives, representatives of the authorities and the school youth, a prayer took place, conducted by the beit-midrash cantor Mr. Piotrkowski.
For the first time the new orchestra of Fürstenberg's gymnasium took part, playing the Polish and the Jewish anthem. Speeches on topics of the day were given by the rabbi and Director Einhorn. The latter spoke about the important stages Piłsudski went through until he created a great, mighty Poland in all fields.
The orchestra plays “Sto lat” and a “tusz” [fanfare]; the rabbi and all the rabbinical judges say the appropriate chapters of Psalms, and Piotrkowski makes mi-sheberakhs in honour of President Mościcki and Marshal Piłsudski.
At the end “Hatikvah” is played, at which the head of “Yesodei Torah” showed his “love” for the Land of Israel: while “Hatikvah” was being played, the “gots-drapcze”[?] did not let the pupils of “Yesodei Torah” stand up.
After the march-past through the town the school youth took an oath to be loyal to the government.
Delegations of Jewish merchants' institutions and of artisans submitted congratulations at the starostwo [district office].
In Sosnowiec
a divine service took place in the synagogue, conducted by the cantor Mr. Leichter with his choir. Then the Jewish school youth joined the general procession, which marched through the town to the sounds of several orchestras.
A series of academies [festive assemblies] took place.
In Wojkowice a Jew Sells Pork Cheaply...

[Będzin district — trade.] The Christian butchers in Wojkowice (Będzin district) have got a “dangerous” competitor. A Jew has opened a butcher's stall with pork there and sells more cheaply than the Christian butchers.
What's New in Upper Silesia? — Annual Meeting of the Zionist Organisation in Katowice

[Head of the column: What's New in Upper Silesia?; Katowice — Zionism.]
What's New in Upper Silesia?
Annual meeting of the Zionist Organisation in Katowice.
(L. S.) In its own premises, before a packed hall, the annual general meeting of the Katowice Zionist Organisation took place.
The meeting was opened by the outgoing president, Mr Dr Rapaport, and after greeting the president of the Kraków Zionist Executive, Mgr. Salpeter, who was present, President Rapaport gave a general report on the activity to date. Crisis and Antisemitism

[Poland — Jews, economic crisis and antisemitism; article.] By L. Szpigelman [editor of the paper].
Antisemitism as a direct means of annihilation in a crisis which ruins us indirectly.
Crisis and Antisemitism.
Both of them are unpleasant and unwanted; it is not that we long for them, nor can we stop them. The first — the crisis — is a plague upon mankind, and like every misfortune, it is first and foremost the one without means who suffers: the working masses, the middle class, he who lives from his daily earnings; and as such the Jewish people suffers to a very great degree. Indirectly we all suffer from the crisis more than all other peoples, if only because we are restricted at every step. That is the reason why the crisis spreads its fearsome wings more over Jewish heads than over all other peoples; indirectly we, as the weak ones, therefore suffer more than all the other independent peoples, who feel secure on their soil and in their land, in their home.
So much for the crisis. The second item, on the other hand — antisemitism — was created especially for our sake and aims to do us direct harm, a full hundred percent. Moreover, it now comes with entirely new conceptions, much stronger and more dangerous than in the darkest times of the Middle Ages; every possible means is employed so that the forms be as strong as possible and that the teeth of the bestial instincts sink with full force into the Jewish body.
True, we have already been tormented enough; we have already been burned and roasted and have gone through the most terrible sufferings and pains; we have behind us a generations-long past, rich in blood and tears, in sufferings and in heroism, so that nothing frightens us any more. In the face of everything we remain steadfast, and to the saddest phenomena, which perhaps oppress us, we pay no attention; and we are still the ones who seek to console ourselves, to talk ourselves into things.
Yes, this is perhaps a hard role[?]; this is, possibly, our tragedy — when we must console ourselves, when in our greatest despair we must seek comfort and arrive at the conclusion that it will not always be so, that we will not always be bitten by wild creatures. Our common man is accustomed, in the greatest despair, to raise his eyes to heaven, to stare at it and wait for salvation, for a miracle that must come, not knowing how.
Today we live in other times, in another period. We find ourselves in the 20th century, after the Great World War. Thanks to the fact that mankind has progressed so much in all fields of life and knowledge — with that same power, with those same inventions, they want to uproot the Jewish race, without regard to the fact that it has given the world so much that is sublime and ideal; and who knows, perhaps precisely for that, and only for that, they want to exterminate and destroy us?
More than once it happened in our ancient history that just then, when it was already quite dark, when it was already truly "darkness which may be felt", the sun shone forth for us and it became light in our corners too. The sun's rays were so strong that they pierced the deepest darkness and shone into the place where it had seemed an impossible thing that a ray of light could penetrate there.
Today, however, we cannot hope for such miracles, and one certainly cannot build on them, because in the meantime the Jewish middle class is being completely ruined, so that one cannot sit down and wait for miracles with folded hands.
Before the war, when things were bad in one country, when we were not admitted to this or that profession, to this or that institution, a world was open; people emigrated; wherever the world had an end one could reach, and Jews developed their [—][uncertain word: "falansn"] wherever they turned. It is quite different now, however, when no country admits anyone, and everywhere emigration has been stopped. So where are people to go? The only hope is to emigrate to Palestine, but woe to such a hope, when England admits there only chosen individuals. But the community at large, the great Jewish mass of people — where is it to go?
Meanwhile both poverty and antisemitism are growing; both are progressing. True, it is not very pleasant to lay heavy stones on hearts already tormented enough, but why deceive ourselves, why cover the truth from reality, since it can certainly bring nothing but harm. It is better to look the truth in the face, however terrible and sad it may be, however unpleasant and bitter it may appear to us.
If we see the tragedy of naked reality, however terrible it may be, we can have the courage to seek a remedy for it, no matter whether it will cure the patient or, God forbid, not. For a people it is important not to lose hope and the courage to seek and explore and study a better tomorrow and a brighter future, even for the nearest time.
The Jews in Poland live in compact masses; they suffered together with the Polish people in the building up of the country; together with the Polish citizens we carried brick upon brick, stone upon stone, to the great work of construction called "Free, Independent Poland", and therefore we also have the right to demand that we be treated as citizens who sacrifice themselves for the country, for its soil and for all its treasures.
We must not let ourselves be underrated just because there are blinded individuals who want to float up to the surface on the ruins of the Jewish people and play careerist, adventurist roles, which will certainly bring the country no benefit.
It is important for us, besides repelling at a vigorous pace the bullets aimed at the Jewish camp, also to illuminate from all sides the problem of Jew-baiting — not for our own sake but for the Polish people, which, willingly or unwillingly, is swept along by the enormous current and by empty promises that Poland will be a paradise as soon as the Jews are driven out, who bring into the country everything that is undesirable, everything that is dangerous for the Polish patriot. It goes without saying that this is not proven by any logical arguments; a few watery sermons suffice, and the mob is sure that things are as it has been talked into believing. The unconscious elements, the average citizen, are not capable of taking account of the fact that it may be far from what he is being told. And therefore we say that it would be very, very important that our communal workers not take the question lightly, but that an enlightenment campaign be carried out, aimed at refuting and responding to the lies with which one wants to blind the eyes of the Polish people. This would be a very, very important mission and, of course, also a responsible one; therefore it would have to be approached with the greatest caution and decency, so that it could bring the proper benefit and again, as once before, clasp together the Polish and the Jewish people in peaceful conditions.
At the same time it must also not be forgotten that the crisis, which is truly not aimed specifically at harming the Jew, is ruining us extraordinarily, so that from day to day it gets worse and more bitter. Usually one is accustomed to the idea that a crisis lasts a certain time and one need only hold out, as the saying goes, "until the inn", and after that things become easier and the situation begins to become normal again. So "until the inn" each one manages as best he can: a little interest-free loan, a little loan, and so on. All this, however, applies when it is a matter of a crisis that lasts a shorter or longer time. With us, though, the crisis has already lasted a good many years, so that it has become a chronic disease which swallows up the largest fortunes; therefore there is no longer any way of helping oneself "until the inn". Everything has already come apart, and the crisis is no longer a crisis in the sense of a passing phenomenon, but rather a law to which one must adapt; the situation prevailing today is therefore an everyday phenomenon.
One must therefore assume that we are already living in this very stage and must adapt to the prevailing conditions; that is, one must limit one's expenses. Economy plays one of the main roles here: one must not spend beyond one's means; at such a time one must not make the false calculation that if I spend more today, I will earn the difference tomorrow, because one sees plainly that tomorrow is not better and there is nothing to count on regarding earning more.
If times are hard, calculation plays a very great role, both in business and in private life: expenses must under no circumstances exceed income; otherwise one begins to lose one's balance and departs from the straight line on which one must keep oneself, as the saying goes, with iron tongs.
Certainly such a calculation is not easy to carry out in our day, when all around the expenses are enormous and almost nothing remains for oneself; but when there is no other way, there is nothing to say.
In any case, these two hard problems embitter our lives: crisis and antisemitism.
The History of the Dąbrowa Kehilla. According to Archival Records. (2)

[History — the Dąbrowa kehilla; serial, instalment 2 and last.] By Moshe Feinkind. According to archival records.
When it turned out, however, that almost all the Jews who were the "yes-sayers" [supporters of secession] had undertaken to pay punctually the budget [etat] for maintaining a rabbi and for other needs, securing this with their property and goods, the provincial (gubernia) administration resolved at its session of 16 September 1910 to grant the petition of the majority of Jews in the localities listed earlier, and permitted the founding of an independent kehilla in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza], to which the colony Huta Bankowa, Reden and the village of Gołonóg were also to belong, which took upon themselves the obligation to maintain the new kehilla at their own expense and from their own means.
Consequently the cassation appeal that the petitioners had lodged against the gubernia's first decision of 23 June 1909 now became void.
On the basis of this concession the Dąbrowa kehilla came into being on 1 January 1911, i.e. 23 years ago.
I must remark here that in Dąbrowa's struggle etc. to break away from the Będzin kehilla, the latter did not get involved and did not even oppose it, as if it did not interest them at all, which gave the impression that Będzin was actually pleased with Dąbrowa's breaking away — whether because the Jews there did not want to pay the budget willingly anyway, or for other reasons, cannot be established from the records.
That the Będzin rabbi, Rabbi Graubart [?], suffered great distress over it becomes clear only when elections for a rabbi took place in Dąbrowa, since he thereby lost income and his livelihood was curtailed.
• • •
Soon after the kehilla was organised, the public set about electing a rabbi, and the candidate for the rabbinical seat was Rabbi R' Alter Lechi [?] of Patshine [?], who died not long ago.
Only now does the real war between the "no-sayers" and the "yes-sayers" flare up...
Only now is the intrigue exposed that was conducted by a certain side against the Będzin rabbi's rabbinical seat in Dąbrowa.
As can be seen from the protests of the "no-sayers", the Patshinov [?] rabbi had bought himself a house in Będzin three years before Dąbrowa broke away from Będzin, and lived there after leaving his little town.
From time to time he travelled over to Dąbrowa and managed the religious needs of the Jews.
The Będzin rabbi regarded this as an encroachment [hasagat gvul] and turned about it to the rabbi and gaon R' Chaim Meisel [?] in Łódź and to the Krimilov rabbi R' Natan Nachum Rabinowicz.
The Łódź gaon and the Krimilov rabbi were indeed against the encroachment, but beyond writing letters they had no power to apply other means. The Patshinov rabbi justified himself in a letter of 5/18 November 1910 [?], saying the affair had already cost him some three thousand roubles ("the sum of gimel [three] thousand I have spent so far" — printed "גומל"), which letter the "no-sayers" obtained from the Krimilov rabbi and submitted in their protest to the governor.
Lampoons flew from one side to the other. And the end was that the Patshinov rabbi was elected to the Dąbrowa rabbinical seat by a large majority, and on 20 June 1911 the governor confirmed the election.
Having then sworn allegiance to the state, as is customary, he officially took over the Dąbrowa rabbinical seat in the month of July, to the satisfaction of the whole population, except for the embittered "no-sayers".
The "no-sayers", however, did not keep quiet and appealed against the governor's decision to the governor.
In their appeal they repeat all their arguments that they had written in the protests to the governor: that it had been promised to exempt the Dąbrowa Jews for a certain time from paying the budget as soon as the rabbi was elected; that many "no-sayers" had been bought over to vote for Rabbi Lechi [?]; and other arguments from the legal side. They referred to the two submitted letters from the above-mentioned rabbis and also to a large number of witnesses who would supposedly confirm all this.
The authorities, however, did not examine the witnesses, and could not make sense of the "encroachment" the rabbis had written about; and also disregarding the fact that under Russian law a rabbi applying for a rabbinate in a town of another gubernia had to have a confirmation from the rabbi residing in the gubernia town that he had the necessary qualification to be a rabbi — on which the "no-sayers" had relied — Governor-General Skalon confirmed the rabbinical election.
The "no-sayers" girded their loins and filed a cassation against the Governor-General's decision to the Senate in Petersburg.
In the cassation all the objections are repeated again, and meanwhile [?] the World War broke out and also put an end to the Dąbrowa war.
The end was that Rabbi R' Alter Lechi [?] remained riveted to the rabbinical seat in Dąbrowa, which had only a few years earlier turned from a village into a town, "and none opened his mouth or chirped"...
Because of the war, the Dąbrowa heads of the community also did not manage to submit a report to the gubernia on their activity in the first years of their term, nor on the "budget" of the new kehilla for the years 1912—14.
But the wheel of history keeps turning in the holy community of Dąbrowa too.
After the death of their first mara de-atra [rabbi of the town], a dispute over the Dąbrowa rabbinical seat flared up again. But that I leave to the younger regional historians.
(The End).
A Commandment of the Hour

[Opinion — Poland, economy; the trade and crafts decrees.]
S. Rotenberg.
The Jewish street has sunk into a dreadful chaos of lawlessness and demoralization. A twilight of material and spiritual depression reigns there.
This state of affairs is a consequence of the terrible impoverishment and need of the broadest masses, who have become dulled because of hopelessness about a better tomorrow, and have therefore become incapable of reacting even to the most terrible deeds of their „leaders“. This state of lethargy of the masses is exploited by the various ringleaders, who perform acts of deception that may have the saddest consequences for the whole Jewish community in the country.
In the previous issue of our paper we already wrote about the sad fact of the „transfer“ heroes who, despite the most powerful protests of almost all strata of the Jewish population, have again carried out the agreement with Hitler. Now we again face a criminal piece of work on the part of a couple of stranglers of Klal Yisrael, who have consented to decrees that may bring about the complete downfall of the whole of Polish Jewry.
It concerns the amendment („novella“) to the Industrial Law, which was adopted by the Sejm and Senate and which threatens the whole of Jewish trade and crafts in Poland with the most fatal consequences.
The broad public learned of these decrees only from the press, when they had already become the subject of the Sejm debates. But those who stand at the head of the Jewish economic institutions in Poland were informed of the planned decrees many months earlier, and not only did they not react to it, they even gave their fullest consent.
These gentlemen did not find it necessary to call a conference of Jewish merchants and artisans in Poland in order to hear their opinion and to consult about the position to take on the matter; instead, on their own responsibility, they consented to laws that extinguish the last rays of hope for the [already?] precarious existence of the Polish Jews.
Here a secretary of a local economic institution tells me that he had in fact received directives from the central office to conduct a survey among the members on this matter; only one small thing happened: instead of receiving the instructions at the right time, i.e. a few months ago, he received them when the matter was already before the Sejm plenum. What should one call such criminal conduct on the part of the „leaders“?
The new decrees might perhaps have had some sense if they were to come into force only some 10 years from now, and if in the course of that time the government were to spread over the whole country a large network of free vocational schools and evening courses for the most various branches of trade and crafts. But that is not what is being considered in the decisive circles; there they think only of destroying and not of building.
In vain do the Endeks [National Democrats] fear that the Jewish question in Poland will not be solved according to their will and inclination[?]. The new decrees show clearly that the Sanacja does it absolutely no worse than they do, with the difference that instead of the Endek methods of cutting off beards, smashing windowpanes and making pogroms, it is done in silk gloves, by way of law, according to the European formula of the B. B. [BBWR] leader Miedziński.
Instead of giving trade and industry free opportunities for development, we are going back to the medieval system of compulsory guilds. But anyone who is even a little versed in world history knows that it was precisely the guilds that were the greatest hindrances to trade and crafts, and that the flourishing of commerce and manufacture became a fact only after the guilds were abolished.
The founder of modern political-economic science, the Englishman Adam Smith, writes in his book „The Wealth of Nations“ that the less the government interferes in the economic life of a country, and the more it lets the national economy develop freely, the better it is for the country. Here, however, free initiative is hampered at every step, and especially that of the Jews, who are being pushed into a blind alley from which there is no way out at all.
Of course Adam Smith's remarks are relative, for in Soviet Russia the government absolutely dominates the whole economic and commercial life, and as the journalist Otmar writes in the Sanacja paper „Gazeta Polska“, the situation in Soviet Russia is steadily getting better and better. The population is getting ever better food and clothing. But methods[?] that suit a workers' government by no means fit into the framework of a capitalist economy, because here it is first and foremost the broadest popular masses who suffer, while the upper ten thousand enjoy the benefits.
It is high time that a conference of all Jewish economic institutions in Poland be called as quickly as possible; they must elect such leaders as will not barter away our most vital (literally „bloodiest“) interests for a pot of lentils.
This is the present commandment of the hour.
At the Seder Let There Be Light for Everyone!

[Zagłębie — Passover, maot-chittin relief.] At this moment, before the holiday, special attention is deserved by the institutions in Zagłębie: the kimcha [Passover-flour relief] committees, and in particular the kehilla administration in Będzin, which this year abolished the kimcha system hitherto in use — a system of beggary.
At the committees the strain is now at its peak: before Passover they must satisfy hundreds and thousands of petitioners [printed "petentn"], and they are waiting for the generosity of the better-off elements.
On Passover, when one sits down to the Seder, everything must already be done. According to the old, beautiful Jewish tradition, every Jew, poor or rich, [must] sit at the Seder with joyful brightness in the home and in the soul, at a fully provided table, with holiday serenity on his face.
For this the poor man does not need much: he must receive the few złoty at the committee, provide himself with a little matzah, something of meat — and he already has a joyful holiday.
But where are the institutions to take the necessary money from?
Once there was America, and today it is gone [?].
We ourselves, here on the spot, give donations more easily than loans [?]. The matzah campaign used always to be filled for the greatest part by ourselves, but America would [?] help. Today, when America has sent nothing, the committee is in a fix. Zagłębie gives, and with a generous hand, but it is not enough for "matan beseter" [secret charity] for the respectable needy; it is not even enough for matzah for the beggars. Will people be hungry this Passover?
One wants to believe that the committees will surely multiply their efforts tenfold and that the public will meet you [?] halfway. However hard it may be, in the end, at the Seder, the table will be ready at everyone's home — even at the poorest of the poor — for in Zagłębie there are Jews who, at the first call to them that the kehilla treasury needs several hundred gulden, bring it in at once and gladly.
Now, on the eve of Passover, is the right time when one can make good [?] one's kind-heartedness in the awareness that one is saving Jews.
Here and there sit Jews, communal workers, worried; they want to satisfy all those in need, and their means are small.
We must meet them halfway, we must help them. If any of you has not yet brought in the requested [?] budget account [?] contribution, do not put it off until tomorrow, for the poorest, the weak, must be helped.
Help, so that at the Seder there will be light for everyone — in the home and in the soul.
New Circulars.

[Poland — laws and regulations.]
Distraint on a horse.
The Minister of Justice has issued a circular to the bailiffs [komornicy] that if they have occasion to carry out a seizure [zajęcie] for a debt on a horse, they may not take from the owner the so-called "pass" [horse passport] of the horse; the pass must remain in the owner's possession as long as the horse has not been sold at the auction [licytacja]; only then does the bailiff take the pass from the debtor [printed "ba'al-hov"] and hand it over together with the horse to the buyer.
Money collections.
According to a circular of the Minister of the Interior, money collections will take place every year on the days from 1st to 10th September throughout the territory of the whole state for the benefit of the Red Cross, and therefore no other institution will be issued a permit for a money collection during the said period.
Where must a person liable to conscription report to the commission?
The Ministry of Military Affairs announces that if a conscript [poborowy] is in the territory of another P.K.U. [district recruiting command] and must for important reasons report to the draft commission there, he must have for this a permit from the starostwo [district office] where he figures in the draft lists.
The application for such a permit must be submitted by 1st April at the latest.
The League of Nations and Hitlerism

(Conversations)
By Avraham Tiktin.
The League of Nations has refused to intervene in Germany concerning the Hitlerite antisemitic campaign, explaining its refusal on the grounds that this would have meant interfering in Germany's internal affairs.
This standpoint cannot be accepted as correct. Firstly, since [?] the League bears the name League of Nations and not League of States, there therefore rests upon it the duty to protect and defend the interests of all peoples and all states when they — and their elementary human rights — are unlawfully [?] harmed and oppressed.
This is one of the postulates that the League of Nations foresaw at the time of its founding, and therefore such an act cannot be regarded as an unjustified intervention.
Secondly, the minority-rights clause was not included in the Versailles peace treaty with Germany solely because of the request of German Jews, who gave assurances that they had no need of such a clause. Orally, however, the German delegates on 19 May 1919 undertook to strictly observe minority rights in Germany, and on 16 June the representatives of the United (Allied) States informed the German delegation that their declaration had been taken note of. Ethically, an oral commitment stands higher than a written one: for not paying a card debt it is accepted to pay with one's life, because the debtor was trusted on his word — this is called a debt of honour.
Another question is whether the League of Nations' intervention would have had a positive effect. To this question one can answer, without much reflection: certainly not. Not only now, but even if at the time [?] the minority clause had been included in the Versailles peace treaty. Well, what would Hitler have answered to that? He would have given the same answer that he gives to the question why Germany is arming, organising great armies, manufacturing poison gases, building aircraft and other such fine things, which Germany had undertaken not to do.
Hitler said in his book "Mein Kampf", and before he became chancellor at every opportunity in speeches and on the radio, that Germany would not rest until it got back every foot of soil [?] that had been taken from it. Now, as a responsible chancellor, he refrains from saying so, but he is only waiting until he has Hitlerised and united a hundred million Germans and is strong enough to carry out what he wants by force.
Let the League of Nations try, for the sake of peace, to give back to Germany the Corridor, Danzig, Memel, Upper Silesia — just as Briand conceded many things to Stresemann at Locarno — Hitlerism will not be appeased by it, and will later demand that it be given back the colonies, Alsace-Lorraine, Eupen-Malmedy, and afterwards, as a hinterland, Lithuania, Poland, the Baltic states, and White Russia as well.
Hitlerite antisemitism is still only a small part of the broad and ramified Hitlerite programme, built on the lowest, egoistic, bestial instincts which civilisation and culture have taken such pains, for the sake of the existence of the whole, to pluck out and uproot from humanity. If Hitler has put the antisemitic part of his programme into practice before all the other parts, it is only because for carrying out that part he already possesses [?] the necessary power, whereas for carrying out all the other parts he still has [?] to gather the necessary power.
The League of Nations is simply blind if it does not see in the open, brutal Hitlerite antisemitism the dark omen, the memento mori, which the world has to expect in the future from the lurking, aggressive, offensive Hitlerism. No civilised nation in the world would have been capable, in the twentieth century, of tearing [?] off its human mask and displaying before all mankind its horrid, medieval, bestial face.
To the sober [?] practical person the pose appears ridiculous in which statesmen conduct negotiations with Hitlerism and search for means of getting out of Hitler a little signature under a disarmament act — as if that little signature were all that world peace lacked. God willing, once they obtain the "good signature" (chatimah tovah), they will put the disarmament act in their pocket, appoint a control commission and go to sleep peacefully.
This is a great and dangerous mistake. There is no signature that can bind present-day Germany while she regards the obligation as inconvenient for herself. When Germany at the beginning of the World War brutally broke her signature under the Belgian neutrality guarantee and militarily invaded Belgium, Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg justified [?] this fine deed by saying that every written act represents nothing more than a scrap of paper...
The importance that Hitlerism attaches to the German state's signature on the Versailles peace treaty we see with our own eyes. In the Locarno agreement Germany undertook never to try to change her eastern borders by means of war.
And if all this is not enough, we, the present generation, have had the privilege of witnessing how representatives of the entire German population, of all its strata and classes, fifteen years ago created [?] the Weimar constitution, which assured all German citizens, without distinction of race, nationality and faith, the possibility of enjoying all civil rights. The President of the Republic, the ministers and even the deputies in parliament swore, before they took up their functions, to guard sacredly and put into practice the provisions of the constitution. How the Hitlerite government observes the provisions of the Weimar constitution with regard to Jewish and even non-Jewish German citizens is shown by deeds which have brought the whole of cultured humanity into tremendous agitation.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Tzav, Shabbat HaGadol)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Tzav
The Portion
—o—
a) "Command Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the law of the burnt-offering" (Lev. 6:2)
"'Command' always denotes urging." Torat Kohanim[?].
"The burnt-offering comes to atone only for arrogance." Midrash Rabbah.
To urge concerning the burnt-offering, concerning the sacrifice that atones for arrogance, one needs precisely "Aaron and his sons" — the sons of Aaron, those who take over the priesthood by inheritance and often without any qualifications. And precisely among these, arrogance is frequently found. Precisely they, who possess nothing but a "[—]", must be urged about pride... Ktav Sofer.
—o—
b) "And this is the law of the meal-offering" (ibid., 7)
The Gemara in Zevachim 7b derives from the verse "The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination" that a sacrifice without repentance does not atone. The Gemara also says (Menachot 50) that a meal-offering is not included in "sacrifice". So it follows that a meal-offering, the poor man's offering, atones even without repentance, because "poverty atones for transgressing the will of one's Maker": it is enough that the poor man scrapes together a few groszy for an offering; but to collect one's thoughts in order to contemplate repentance — such composure[?] and peace of mind only a rich man can afford... Tefillat Mordechai (the Maharsham of Berezhany).
—o—
"Let Thy mercies speedily come to meet us, for we are brought very low."
Once one brought a sacrifice for a sin; today charity atones. "Whoever has mercy on creatures is shown mercy from Heaven," measure for measure. But today we cannot even manage to buy off our sins with charity, because "we are brought very low", because we are poor... Therefore "let Thy mercies speedily come to meet us": have mercy on us, God, and do not wait until we buy off our sins through charity and compassion, for we are brought very low — we have no money for it... Maharsha.
—o—
c) "And Moses did as the Lord commanded him, and the congregation was assembled" (8:4)
For there to be "and the congregation was assembled", for a congregation of Jews to gather around a rebbe, there must be "and Moses did as the Lord commanded" — the tzaddik must do everything God commands... Today, for our many sins, people travel to such rebbes about whom one doesn't know[?] whether they do everything as the Lord commanded... Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk.
* * *
And Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk used to say further:
— What is the difference between a Hasid and a Mitnaged?
— A Mitnaged fears the Shulchan Aruch, and a true Hasid fears God...
* * *
In a certain town there was a rabbi about whom people grumbled that he was so headstrong that he did not fear even God... Once a maggid (itinerant preacher) came to him, having been told in town about the rabbi. The maggid tells the rabbi that he wants to hold a din Torah (rabbinic lawsuit) before him against the Master of the Universe, because He does not give him a livelihood and so on. The rabbi asks him: Why do you summon the Holy One, blessed be He, to a din Torah precisely before me? Are there no other rabbis to whom you could summon God to judgment?
The maggid answers him:
— All rabbis are suspect in my eyes of bending the judgment in God's favour, because they fear Him. You, as I have heard, are so headstrong that you have no fear even of God — so I believe you will not bend the judgment in favour of either side and will judge justly between me and God...
—o—
d) "And Aaron and his sons did all the things" (ibid., 36)
"To tell their praise, that they turned neither right nor left." Rashi.
There is a kind of pride that consists in supposedly not wanting to accept honour. When one comes to such a Jew and offers him a full post as an honour, he supposedly shrugs his shoulders with a groan: I know[?], I am not worthy of such an honour... But in truth he prays in his heart that, God forbid, they should not change their minds and stop asking him. That is the praise of Aaron, "that he turned neither right nor left": he did not turn his head right and left, but straightforwardly, with natural simplicity, took on the priesthood.
Dvash ve-Chalav.
* * *
"Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in His holy place?"...
Who should ascend the mountain of the Lord, ascend to greatness? — He who constantly[?], already in his high office, "shall stand in His holy place": will remain in his place, will not step out of the bounds of his essence, will not puff himself up, and will go on being worthy. R' Moshe Alshich.
—o—
"That he turned neither right nor left."
The novelty is "that he did not turn to the right" — that he did not make himself too pious. "And Aaron and his sons did all the things which the Lord commanded", and no more than what God commanded — he did not become too pious. That is the novelty. Kiflayim le-Tushiya.
Shabbat HaGadol.
e) The Rabbi and the Hasid.
In Orach Chayim, Laws of Passover, section 429, it is said: "One asks and expounds [the laws of Passover] thirty days before Passover." On this the Rema says: "Gloss. And it is the custom to buy wheat to distribute to the poor for the needs of Passover." The question arises: how does this gloss belong to the law of "asking and expounding"?
To this Rabbi Meir of Przemyślany said:
The author (of the Shulchan Aruch) speaks as a rabbi — and what does a rabbi think about before Passover? About sermons... The Rema speaks as a Hasid: never mind the sermons; the main thing is, one must provide the poor with matzot... Divrei Meir.
* * *
Today one should not call it "maot chittin" (wheat money) — said R' Yaakov Aharon of Załoźce — but "maror money", because what one gives the poor today for matzot is barely enough for maror (bitter herbs). Beit Yaakov.
Erev-Pesach Thoughts.

[Feuilleton — the eve of Passover.] That the eve of Passover is the best season of the year — on that, surely, there is no dispute. No small thing, the spring, the dear spring! It would seem that spring is no longer a novelty to any of us, every year one and the same. And yet there lies in nature's freeing itself from the hard winter a wondrous power, and every year we live through the joy anew, exactly as though we were seeing it for the first time. Upon my life, all the other good things in the world nevertheless become tiresome; we are bored not only by all sorts of elections, meetings, party splits, constitutions and votes, but even the best that the present era possesses, fascism and dictatorship, have already become unpleasant too...
Therefore the Almighty has sent us this year, as compensation for our bundle of troubles, an early spring. But unexpectedly we realised that we no longer have any snow or ice; the dear sun shines and caresses tenderly. And the poor are already spared standing in the "ogonek" (queue) at the kehilla for coal.
May this indeed be a good sign that not only the winter, but also the crisis in person will soon take itself off?
Meanwhile, on that basis, the "ubezpieczalnia" (social-insurance office) has already sent the workers and the householders swollen bills, so that everything went dark before their eyes; the "urząd" (tax office) has already raised the "obrotowe"[?] (turnover tax) — and all on the strength of the confidence that spring is coming to the world.
In general, the gentiles have lately caught from us Jews the disease called bitachon (trust in Providence). Lately they build far too much on the "konto" (account) of mere trust, and that, I fear, is a very bad sign, simply a sign of poverty.
And one more thing they have learned from us: rattling the charity box. They too now hold "actions" with "funds" (from the Jewish foreign tongue), and already go round from house to house with the red[?] "pachyle"[?] and make "zbiórki" (collections) in the streets — all just as among kosher Jews, to make the distinction. And meanwhile spring does its thing. Merrily, hopefully the waters bubble in the brooks and puddles, little birds chirp, hens cackle — and Jews wrinkle their foreheads and worry about what to do with the plagues of Passover.
Thus, for our many sins, the dear, enchanting spring is turned into a wicked uncle[?] whom one cannot satisfy. Thus the poor little Jews torment themselves with their merry Passover; thus they have bitter troubles from their holy Festival of Freedom, from the Season of our Rejoicing. In short, gentlemen, I do not like at all the way our little world is run; not all is in order "in the kingdom of Denmark"...
Rabbi Yaakov.
Reb Ozer Goes to the Examination

[Zagłębie — satirical feuilleton, small trade.]
(If you like, this is no made-up fantasy of a feuilletonist.)
My neighbour Reb Ozer let himself be reassured by Senator Iwanowski and by the assurances of the Central Artisans' Association that the laws[?] on qualifications and concessions are simply a salvation for Jews, and like a loyal herring-shopkeeper he went off to the examination, so as to be able to go on standing in the market and drawing his livelihood[?] from his little barrel of herring.
And here is what the examination looked like:
— What do you want?
— Take a sniff — can't you smell what I deal in?!
— Herring?
— It smells of herring, of beggary, of pauperdom, of worries, and of whatever else His Most Illustrious Lordship [“jaśnie wielmożny pan”] wishes.
— Why did you pick precisely the herring trade?
— What then, should I have become a colonel [“pułkownik”]?
— So what is it you want?
— Examine me, or just be done with me.
— A herring merchant must know first of all where herring come from.
— My dear sir [“panie” + Yid. “lebn”], everything comes from Heaven — only the herring swim about in the Dead Sea.
— What sorts of herring are there?
— Big herring, little herrings, with roe, with milt, with a smell, [?]-ed [“gevenzlte”] herring, frozen herring, rotten herring, stinking herring, herring on credit, unpaid herring and marinated herring.
— But their quality, their anatomy?
— I don't even know the meaning of these foreign words, but I guess what you mean. With us, for instance, people say: that's no cantor, just a herring; the little bridegroom looks like a soaked herring; and when a Jew is a fool they say: take the herring away [i.e. he is a herring]. Nowadays, for instance, out of some herring have come doctors, councillors, and the sour herring have become fixers [“makhers”] and fill the corridors of all the offices.
— What are herring used for?
— When one has no fish for the Sabbath, one makes do with herring; when the rich man is stingy, he treats his guests to herring; and in Lent [“post”] one sometimes earns a grosz on a herring from a peasant.
— How do herring swim?
— With the head, with the brain; such[?] a little herring, a nothing with a nothing, suddenly flips over and already “sits” [Pol. “siedzi”] on top, like a president — although altogether it consists of a tiny little head and a big tail, “Schwanz” in the foreign tongue.
— What is the difference between herring and fish?
— From a fish one scrapes the scales, while our present-day herring scrape the scales off the whole world themselves.
— What does one wrap herring in?
— Once they were wrapped in a newspaper sheet; nowadays one gets cheaper[?] [“bi-liner”] paper, for instance the matura certificates of the daughters, the diplomas of the sons, the engineers, and other such important [“ważne”] papers on which Jews squandered fortunes until they obtained them for their children.
— And arithmetic, do you know it?
— A little; I learnt it when I was a director in a cooperative bank.
— What does a merchant do to become a councillor in the Chamber of Commerce?
— He pays 4 thousand zł.
— What is meant by import?
— Ask, if you'll pardon me, at Wiszlicki's.
— What does the export look like?
— Mostly, pigs are exported from Zagłębie. And yet their number grows every day; nowadays, as soon as you move, you run into a pig.
— What is meant by a merchants' association?
— I'm ashamed to say; better ask Rubinlicht.
— How does a merchant obtain credit?
— One pays 20 groszy for a “window”[?] [“fenster”] — you may have 5 and pay for only one; one begs one's way to a declaration, one pleads and weeps and faints before the board, one seeks protection with President Rubinlicht, and if one brings a lot of good guarantors, one need only wait until Giterman sends a new portion of money from the “Joint” to the relief committee.
— Where is the main source of herring?
— Once this article was to be had only at Hampel's, and nowadays at anyone's you like.
— How does one pack herring?
— One makes promises, hands out mandates and gives people to understand that it could be even worse.
The examining official put to Reb Ozer a further series of questions on ichthyology, technology, philology, climatology, bankruptology, “boorology” [from Heb. “bur”, ignoramus], oceanography, seismography, demography and photography; since Reb Ozer gave no satisfactory answers to these, the examiner postponed the examination to a later date and meanwhile sent him off to enrol in the evening courses of the herring section at B. B.
A. Szwarcer.
Economic Men and Politicians

[Article — Jewish politics in Poland; economic activists and politics.] By P. K.

It is, it seems, already high time that our economic activists should take stock: what they may and what they may not do, what they are called to do and what lies beyond their competence.
In recent years the economic organizations have pushed the political parties into the background.
Whether this was because wild wars flared up around the mandates of the artisans and merchants among the various politicians — Zionists, Folkists and Agudists — and the poor man of the masses suspected that what was meant here was not his good, but that people were scrambling for seats;
one way or another, the decisive stance of the economic masses turned their organizations into fortresses for the strata engaged in crafts and trade — fortresses not only economic, but also political.
Because government policy in Poland has lately followed the line of relying on real forces and not on ideologies, the chambers of commerce and the chambers of crafts have therefore become the government's closest advisers in its most important political steps.
Our economic circles found themselves very comfortable in this situation. It seemed to them that if one satisfies the activist's self-love and takes his opinion into account, one has already satisfied the interests of the masses. Sometimes, indeed, some small thing was achieved, fought for, shouted out, and above all there was the certainty that fate lay in one's own hands, that no outside factor could conduct any politics over their heads, at their expense.
But precisely in Poland and under the present circumstances we must be especially careful in this respect.
Jews, on the one hand, have suffered under various regimes in all sorts of countries from terrible decrees and persecutions, against which they had to fight bitterly[?]; and on the other hand they had the feeling that what they do for themselves will as a matter of course also be valid for their children and children's children.
But there, where antisemitism goes about in gloves and wants to carry out a bloodless de-Judaization of all kinds of economic fields, one must stand on guard, keeping before one's eyes a perspective of political far-sightedness[?], because it is possible that in the near term one will not see any decree at all...
Precisely in such a situation we find ourselves now in Poland. The new cloud of decrees that is moving in on us carries within it, without any doubt, a curse for Jewish trade and for Jewish crafts — but only in the time to come; for the moment there is peace and quiet, and even when the laws come into force, their validity will extend only to new merchants and artisans and not to the old ones.
And here our economic men are already short-sighted. What is more: just as they had no trust in the intelligentsia to look after their professional interests, we cannot have any trust in them themselves, the economic men, to look after the interests of the coming generations.
We have already seen how the craftsmen relate to the question of apprentices, to the question of vocational schools, how they care for Klal Yisrael [the Jewish collective] — that it should be strengthened[?] in crafts and found its future on real and productive foundations.
We have also seen, in the matter of the latest decrees themselves, an indifference among the artisans towards the approaching clouds, and things were not much better among the other economic strata either.
Therefore, in our opinion, the matter of Jewish political representation is now becoming topical again. The professional associations of the Jewish economic strata ought to look after their purely internal affairs, as well as mediation and interventions with the organs of power concerning taxes, fines and the like; political representation, however, they must hand over to people whose view reaches into broader sectors and further perspectives, who care not only for the particular but even more for the general, and not only for the present moment but even more for the future of the nation.
Jewish politics in Poland is now altogether an abandoned field, which must first be ploughed and sown in order to bear fruit later. But the ploughshares and the cutting knives must lie in the practised hands of good politicians and not of professional activists.
At the present hour this must be given special thought.
P. K.
Cheap, Cheap — Everything Cheap. (Reflections)

By Y. D. Petshenik.
(Reflections).
We live in a time when everything is cheap!
Cheap eggs, cheap meat — all foodstuffs cheap; cheap love, cheap hatred, cheap feelings — everything for a penny [grosz]. Cheap ideas, cheap programmes, everything is cheap, even —
being a ruler over millions of people.
Cheap is a human being's life, cheap all traditions, cheap morality, honesty, ethics — cheap, rag-cheap.
Cheap too have become treaties between nations and all obligations.
It costs little to become a party man and a party leader.
Once everything was expensive.
Today everything costs little, dirt cheap.
Take, for instance, how much effort a young man once had to make in order to exchange a single word with a young lady, and what superhuman exertions a woman had to make to allow herself to give a man a smile? Today it is all cheap, without effort and without trouble.
And how many sacrifices, for example, did a Jew have to make in order to be counted as God-fearing? Real self-sacrifice, kiddush ha-shem. Today it is done cheaply:
A member of the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel] and a "pious Jew".. — done.
And how much work and strength one had to give in order to become a party man! Not to speak of becoming a party leader!
First of all one had to know things, know a great deal. One had to be versed in the Rishonim and Acharonim, and besides that one had to have a fine record of work.
Today it is cheap.
A few hackneyed phrases, a lot of demagogy, a pair of strong fists and —
— a party man is ready.
Add to that a little chutzpah and a bit of a voice and —
a leader is ready.
To become a writer it is enough to know some alphabet or other; to become a critic — not even that. As long as there is a nose that one can turn up — a sign that it is no good.
Today, how much does it cost, so to speak, to become a public worker?
In former years someone engaged in communal affairs first of all had to be a great philanthropist himself, a person of standing, with a Jewish heart; with many more humane and specifically Jewish good qualities; he indeed also had to be somewhat versed in the small print.
Today? Today it is done cheaply; the qualifications for a present-day Jewish public worker can be obtained in a twinkling [?]. A bribe/flattery for the squire [„shishke“], a fig [rude gesture] to one's own comrade and... a blow to the community and —
a public worker is ready.
And how much does one need today to be an intellectual? One trifle: not to speak Yiddish, not to "frequent" [?] any Jewish society, and in general to criticise everything that is Jewish — and a Jewish intellectual is ready.
What a precious time this is!
How fortunate is our generation, which has become so cheapened...
A Blood-Stained Envelope Uncovers a Tragic Story of the World War

J. Steger.
A Blood-Stained Envelope
Uncovers a Tragic Story of the World War
An Austrian officer is forced to shoot his own wife. — She was the daughter of an Austrian nobleman, but she betrayed military secrets to Russia. (3

The others agreed to this, and an officer went at once to Lieutenant Szalay to tell him that tomorrow, at 5 in the morning, he was to come to the city prison and command the firing squad at an execution.
When Szalay asked whom they had to send into the next world, the officer told him about Margit von Fimala and her crime.
Human language is too poor to convey Szalay's feelings when he heard who the victim was and of what crime his wife had been found guilty.
All night long Szalay, half out of his mind, paced up and down his room, rummaging in his brain for a way out of the terrible situation in which he found himself.
At first it seemed to him that the best thing for himself and for his ardently beloved Margit would be for him to commit suicide. But soon a thought crept up on him: perhaps she actually needed him to stay alive, so as to help her, even at the last moment, to prove that she was innocent, for Szalay could by no means bring himself to believe that his wife had really done the things of which she was accused.
At half past four Szalay left his room. His whole body was feverish, and with heavy steps he set off for the prison where Margit sat waiting for death.
When he arrived there, the 12 soldiers of the firing squad were already standing ready to carry out his orders. Each of them handed Szalay his rifle, as the law requires, and he mechanically checked whether they were loaded. Examining the rifles, he tried to console himself with the thought that perhaps Margit had married him in order to worm certain military secrets out of him, but he soon drove the thought away: no, she is innocent, and he still has to carry out the sentence on her — on his dear Margit...
He took his place at the side and waited.
The iron door of the prison opened and Margit was led out, escorted by four soldiers and a priest, who had finished the last prayer for her soul.
Margit glanced at the soldiers standing in line with loaded rifles, and her gaze fell on their commander, on her husband; she immediately drew her gaze back, and Szalay read in her eyes that her love for him had been just as sincere and honest as his.
Margit was led to the grey stone wall; a soldier blindfolded her, and she was left standing alone. Was Margit[?] thinking at that moment only of her life, which would soon end, or of her Stefan, who would give the order to shoot her?
Szalay did not want his Margit to suffer too long; in a hoarse, squeaky voice, his head turned aside and the gleaming sabre in his trembling hand, he gave his orders:
— Present arms!
— Down!
— Fire!
The crack of 12 rifles rang out, and Margit von Fimala, the wife of Lieutenant Stefan Szalay, fell in her own blood.
As the law requires, the commander of the firing squad must go up at once and check whether the executed person is completely dead. If not, it is his duty to finish her off with his own revolver.
There was no more life in Margit's body, and Szalay considered this a great "piece of luck," because had she still been breathing[?], then — not enough that he had had to give the orders at the execution of the sentence — he would also have had to drive a bullet or two into her himself...
All this took place on 17 June 1917.
The commander-in-chief, Baron Conrad von Hötzendorf [printed "Harcendapi"], appreciated Szalay's obedient execution of the sentence on Margit von Fimala and released him from duty for a few days.
Lieutenant Szalay went to Vienna, the merry Austrian capital, which was the paradise of all officers. Instead of drowning his pain in drink and forgetting it in one of the cheerful coffee houses, Szalay locked himself in a small room and shot a bullet into his heart.
When they broke open the door of the room, they found him lying dead on the floor. In his breast pocket they found a letter addressed to Baron Hötzendorf. The envelope was stained with a few fresh drops of the blood that had streamed from his heart...
A courier went at once to Baden and delivered the suicide's letter. Hötzendorf tore open the envelope, in which there was a message to him and the document confirming the marriage between Stefan Szalay and Margit von Fimala.
A shudder passed through Hötzendorf's body as he read the letter. Szalay had written the following:
"Excellency!
"You will understand my action, honoured sir, when you learn that the condemned woman was my wife. I loved her. She was the only thing I had in my life. I still love her even now; I cannot forget her beautiful eyes, which will never open again, nor her lips, which lied to me[?] from the day I met her.
"I have done my duty, sir, but how I was able to carry it out, I myself cannot account for.
Stefan Szalay, Lieutenant."
Hötzendorf controlled himself and bit his lips. He put the letter with the marriage certificate back into the envelope, wrote on the other side: "Committed suicide with his own revolver," and in a dry voice ordered his aide to place the document in the shiny black steel box where the most secret papers of the military headquarters lie.
Thus the said letter lay hidden for a long time, and only years later, after the crowned heads who had declared the war had fallen and the Austrian empire had been shattered, did people set about studying the secret war documents. Among them lay also the last letter of Lieutenant Stefan Szalay, which tells of this remarkable tragedy, one of the thousands of heart-rending occurrences in the time of the last World War.
(The End).
What's Doing in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Great Uproar over the “Bread of Affliction”.

[Będzin — Passover, matzah baking.]
Year in, year out, as the time for baking matzah draws near, the great uproar begins and all sorts of plans are worked out so that everyone who has the slightest chance can make a living from the “bread of affliction” (lechem oni)... When the bakers have already come to terms among themselves about the price, then comes the side that looks after kashrut and declares: “we have the main say”...
This year too a sharp conflict arose because the rabbinate demanded of the bakers that, besides the ne'emanim (kashrut supervisors), chief supervisors should also be appointed, whose wages were to be paid in advance.
The conflict between the bakers and the rabbinate over this matter ended only on Tuesday, and on that day they began baking matzah — at a time when in the smaller neighbouring towns matzah baking had begun a week earlier.
—o—
[Będzin — the Rabbinate; notice.] The Będzin Rabbinate on Passover salt
[Będzin — the Rabbinate; notice.]
R' Shalom Batysta [?] of Będzin has brought from Hipolitshka [?] a wagonload of salt, which was ground and packed under strict supervision by a proper supervisor (ne'eman). We therefore warn the inhabitants of our town not to use any other salt. Every sack bears the mark „Pesach“.

A Jew from Dollar-Land Repays a 30-Year-Old Debt.

[Będzin — human interest.]
Our well-known Reb Shalom Kleiner borrowed, 30 years ago, an interest-free loan (gmilus-khesed) of 20 roubles from Mr. Yitzchak Meir Wigraich.
At that time Reb Shalom emigrated to New York and completely forgot that he owed a debt in Będzin.
This past Purim, Reb Shalom is sitting with his family at the Purim feast, and they are telling stories of the old home, of neighbours, of bygone times, and —
“Oh, I still owe Itche Meir Wigraich in Będzin a debt of 20 roubles!” — cries out Reb Shalom.
The next morning Reb Shalom went into an office and sent 10 dollars to Wigraich in Będzin, according to the dollar rate of that time. (One dollar was then worth about 2 roubles.)

Pledge Campaign (Nedarim) for the Gemilus Chesed Loan Fund.

[Będzin — charity, interest-free loan fund.]
As every year, the board of the local Gemilus Chasodim fund has proclaimed a pledge (nedarim) campaign during Passover week.
The fund, whose task is to sustain the weak and struggling merchants who still want to stay on their feet, needs a large sum of money. Once there was America, and today we ourselves, here on the spot, must support the Gemilus Chesed fund, because nobody wants to lend money to the shopkeeper; only in the interest-free loan fund, in the modern Jewish “Gemilus Chesed”, does he get the loan — yes.
This year the loan fund has particular difficulties because the “clientele” is growing; the institution must have fresh injections.
For this purpose a pledge campaign has been proclaimed this year too. Let everyone, when called up to the Torah, fulfil his great duty. One should not just discharge oneself for form's sake, but everyone should take stock of the great importance of this financial institution in the present hard times.

The Gentile Did Them In “the Turkish Way”...

[Sosnowiec — Jewish community.]
The local Jewish world is abuzz with the story of certain kehilla activists — clever merchants, by the way — and yet a non-Jew from Milowice did them in “the Turkish way” [tricked them].
The story went like this. The activists, who play the main roles in this tale, were authorised to negotiate with a Christian from Milowice about buying a plot for a cemetery.
The Christian asked 45 zł. per “pręt” [a land measure], but instead of bargaining with him the activists told the seller that they would accept the price on condition that they would get 5 zł. from every “pręt” as broker's fee, to which the seller agreed.
Before signing the agreement at the notary (rejent), the activists demanded the sum as agreed (about 1,500 zł.); the Christian then declared that he had no cash, but gave them a letter [?] in which he confirmed that he was to give the persons such a sum within a few days.
A few days later the gentlemen indeed went off to the seller and demanded their reward, but instead of money he told them “lo madalti” [?], I don't want to give you anything, and you can call me a “nutcracker” [i.e. call me what you like]...
And when the gentlemen began to threaten the seller of the plot, he went into the gmina [municipal office], where he revealed the whole affair...

Erman's Picture Exhibition

[Będzin — art; exhibition.] The painter Mr. Erman is a graduate of the Kraków Academy of Arts, where he was a pupil of the well-known artist Prof. Weiss.
At the exhibition Erman is represented by 18 oil paintings and 20 [?] graphic works.
In his oil paintings it is still hard to find an individual approach to the treatment of painterly problems. What dominates there is the purely academic conception, which expresses itself in the good sense of composition, in the fine draughtsmanship and in the correct handling of texture (facture).
These are, without doubt, very important basic qualities for a young artist, without which it is hard to imagine further artistic development.
Erman's colour scale is not a broad one; he operates with only a limited number of colour tones, yet he nevertheless succeeds in creating pleasant, effective colour contrasts.
It is worth singling out the picture "The Blind Man with the Flowers", which is set down with temperament and painted in a warm, lively tone.
Erman's graphic works stand at a considerably higher artistic level.
If in his oil paintings it is still hard to find individuality, in his graphics it is already strongly evident.
Erman masters the various graphic techniques, such as lithography, aquafortis (etching), aquatint and the woodcut. Most interesting, however, are the woodcuts, which the artist treats not according to the accepted pattern and not with white and black patches, but with the help of a very subtle shading, and they therefore bear a more painterly character.
Usually [?] graphic artists who treat a woodcut with black-and-white patches must stylise the drawing, otherwise it would come out too brutal and unpleasant. Erman has absolutely no need of this; he does not stylise, he is realistic, and he achieves the subtlety with the help of his singular shading technique.
In his woodcut "The Synagogue in Żółkiew" [?] the artist has brought out a great many fine details and the specific mystical mood characteristic of such a motif.
In the composition "Samson" the musculature of the nude is treated subtly; the transition from the dark to the light patches is not sudden but gradual, and the play of light and shadow is therefore more pleasing.
In general Erman shows much love and perseverance in his graphic works. His mastery of drawing and graphic technique and his sense of composition bear witness that the artist stands firmly on the rails of his artistic career.
Sh. R.

From the World of Sport

[Będzin — sport (football).] "Hakoach" — "Brynica" 0:1
The opening of the football season began with the championship match between the two above-mentioned clubs.
This match, which was a "continuation", lasted no longer than 25 minutes, and during that time neither team managed to score a goal, so that the result of 1:0, which "Hakoach" had achieved in the first round, remained unchanged.
With almost all the "Hakoach" players one could notice that they were on the sports field for the first time this year, and that throughout the whole winter they had not yet had any training.
It is to be hoped that the "Hakoach" players will take full account [lit. give themselves a reckoning] of the fact that they are the only representatives of Jewish football in class "P"[?] in Zagłębie, and that by the big championship matches they will already be somewhat better prepared and will also fight with more ambition.
Puterka, who in this match appeared for the first time in the first team, passed the test very well. It would be worthwhile for the management of the football section to pay a little more attention to the reserve team, in which there are players who could quite boldly replace the old "stars". Puterka's performance confirmed this.
A gratifying phenomenon was also the fact that the entire board of "Hakoach" and of "Korpore"[?], headed by the chairman Mr. Michał Gutman, were present on the sports ground before the start of the match and kept order.
The order on the ground was, for that reason, truly exemplary.
A. Wrocławski.

The Lawsuit of the Jew Bernheim
against the Hitlerite state for violating minority rights in German Upper Silesia.
This week, in Katowice, before the Mixed Commission for Upper Silesia, the case of the German citizen, the Jew Bernheim [Franz Bernheim], against the German state took place.
The case took place because of the petition that Bernheim had submitted at the time to the Council of the League of Nations.
The League of Nations referred the question for decision to the Mixed Commission for Upper Silesia.
Bernheim had for many years been an employee in the department store of Delmak[?] in Gleiwitz [today Gliwice]. This firm was on the well-known list of the National Socialists, which was also supported by the German government; the reason for boycotting the business was that the enterprise was financed by Jewish capital and employed Jewish staff. Because of this Delmak decided to push out the Jewish capital and removed all Jewish employees, among whom was Bernheim. Only then did the firm receive a certificate ("Bescheinigung") that it was "judenrein" and not subject to the boycott.
The dismissed Bernheim, through the Jewish communal leader in Czechoslovakia Dr. Margulies, lodged a complaint with the League of Nations, stating that he had lost his livelihood because of the boycott and that this violated the rights of the national minorities in Upper Silesia, which are guaranteed by the Geneva Convention.
Bernheim demanded compensation from the German government.
The deliberations of the Mixed Commission were secret; the German government was represented by Kampmann, and Bernheim was represented by the Katowice lawyer Reichman. The verdict will be handed down in a few days.

Hitlerism in the Passover Days — The Great Protest Movement and the Solidary Struggle

The Warsaw Relief Committee for the refugees from Germany has proclaimed a great protest campaign of Polish Jewry against the persecutions of the Jews in Germany.
It has been decided that the Passover days shall be used throughout the country as a great protest demonstration, which shall find expression in a solidary struggle against Hitlerism.
Two things are at stake, which must be dealt with seriously and thoroughly [?] and [?] — carried out: on the one hand, material and moral support must be given to the expelled, unfortunate, helpless and broken people, who were forced to live like other people [?]; and on the other hand, the boycott of all German goods must be intensified. One must in every way [?] take all possible and impossible measures not to use oneself, and not to let others use, any article whatsoever that comes from Hitler-land.
At the beginning, when one could not imagine how terrible the Jewish sufferings in Germany would turn out, the boycott was taken lightly; people reckoned that perhaps the devil is not as terrible as he is painted, and at other times again people thought: eh, nonsense, the great German industry will not be diminished if Polish Jewry does not use German goods.
But what have we seen? Time has shown us that the devil is even more terrible than we had pictured him; that Jews are tortured there and restricted in such a way that no modern person would have believed that in our day such barbaric deeds as the Hitler-vandals have devised could be applied against [?] human beings. As for the boycott, we have further seen that we underestimate our strength. It is far from good to deceive ourselves and overestimate our strength, to say that we are a force at a time when we remain helpless; on the other hand it is also a mistake when we underestimate our modest strength.
With the boycotting of German goods by Jewish firms throughout the world, we have seen that German commerce and industry feel broken and beaten down, and this is thanks to the small handful of Jews who no longer want any dealings with Hitlerite Germany for as long as no other order sets in there that would assure the Jews there a normal existence, as it was until the coming of Hitlerism.
We have seen that thanks to the Jews the Leipzig Fair — the great traditional world fair — was a hundred-percent failure, so that there was simply no one for whom to open the great gates, at a time when year after year the greatest transactions between merchants and manufacturers from various parts of the world took place there. For Germany is now trying to send incognito, both to us and to other countries, her agents, who include even "ma yafit" Jews [toadying Jews], and they try to prove that in Germany, God forbid, nothing at all happens to the few Jews and everything is in the best order — and so, pardon us, to worm their way in [?], in order to establish trade relations. This is the best proof that they need us, that they cannot manage without a great world export, and for that one needs Jewish mediation, Jewish capital and the Jewish head that knows how to work out how the calculation will come out better.
We here, in the Upper Silesian and Zagłębie region, have for many [?] years been tied to the German industrialists, and it is not so easy to cut at one stroke the cord that is so firmly knotted together and grown together; this perhaps explains why a traffic with Germany is still felt in our area.
Unfortunately, to our regret, to our greatest pain and sorrow, all kinds of goods and articles from Germany are still being brought in to us, and for the most part they are imported by our brethren, the Children of Israel. Now we must put an end to all this. The committees must take up this question and in every way [?] put in the pillory all those who do not feel pain over our sufferings and anguish, all those for whom filling their pockets with money stands higher than the interests of the people and the spilled blood of the tortured martyrs.
Despite the fact that so much Jewish blood has already been spilled there in the concentration camps, despite the fact that so many Jews have already been tortured there and consequently have been ruined and lost every livelihood, the persecutions are now beginning to appear once again against the few Jews who are still in Germany.
And we — what shall we answer to this? What shall we do about it? How shall we react to the fresh renewal, to the new extermination? Shall we go on standing helpless like this and watch our brethren go on doing business with Hitler Germany and, on top of that, buy the goods? Or perhaps the work will consist at most in helping by letting out a groan? Such toleration, such levity, such coldness and apathy are surely unheard of.
In Będzin there is a committee, in Sosnowiec too. [?], but we do not know whether it does not come to the same thing [?], since neither here nor there is anything real, positive being done. To our great regret no position has been taken on how to react to the criminal deeds of our brethren, who blacken our face because they are out for nothing more than filling their pockets with money, even if it comes from Hitler-land, which is so drenched with the blood of our martyrs and saints.
The Passover days must therefore be used in all the towns of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia to carry out a great protest movement against the persecutions of our brethren in Germany. Protest meetings must be organized everywhere, to demonstrate our solidarity in the struggle against Hitlerism. Efforts must be made to organize demonstrations against the outright ["formal"] pogroms upon the Jewish population in Germany. Mass meetings must be organized in the open air, in which every Jew in whom a Jewish pulse beats should take part.
That concerns solidarity in the political field; but one must not forget that this is not everything. There are refugees, broken unfortunate souls, who have nowhere to turn and face the greatest catastrophe. We must help the unfortunate, desperate victims, and for that money is needed — money not as for beggars, who are content with a grosz. We must not forget that we are dealing here with people who lived in the best conditions, material as well as political and hygienic — so that we have before us here an entirely different element! An element that lived as citizens, bore obligations [?] as citizens and as social beings, kept a household, raised children and was therefore devoted family parents — and here they have been broken and driven out of their old places where they had been long settled.
