Can we imagine this tragedy? Can we imagine how hard it is for the Polish Jew in the present hard times to help this category of people? We know that it is an almost impossible thing; we know that we are all financially broken and have no strength to pull the yoke of our existence, of our being here — and yet, and yet we cannot and must not remain standing helpless at a distance. And if the Jewish people as such could bring itself to stand at a distance before this dreadful fact, because it has no strength to help positively, it would then undoubtedly suffer more morally, ache more morally, for after all their flesh is also our flesh, their blood also our blood.
And if we cannot help them materially as they have deserved — for after all their hearts did not remain petrified when we needed their help — if, then, we have no strength to repay them as they have deserved and as they need it, then let us come to their aid according to our ability. And since one must tell the truth, there is no ability at all in the present bitter time, so we must do beyond our ability; we must come to their aid beyond our possibilities. We must share our morsel exactly as is done between parents and their children, who give away to them more than falls to their share.
At the same time, however, it is important that order should prevail in the material field, and that the money, which is now so hard to give, should be used for the set purpose, for the necessary goal.
Let, then, the present protest campaign and the great fund-raising be a new expression of our unity and our determination to fight against the new Hamans and Pharaohs who want to oppress and annihilate Jewry.
Dr. Maori [?].
Passover — the Festival of Freedom

[Passover — reflective essay; exile, redemption and the Land of Israel.]
"Wherefore criest thou unto me? Speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward."
(Exodus 15:14) [so printed; the verse is Exodus 14:15].
For three thousand years now the Jewish people has been celebrating the festival of Passover as a festival of liberation, "the Festival of Freedom" (Chag ha-Cheirut).
But the most remarkable thing about it is that the festival was celebrated as "the Festival of Freedom" even in such times when doing so was bound up with real mortal danger; and although conducting the Seder does not belong to the commandments of "be killed rather than transgress", the Jew never gave it up and never renounced it.
Thus the Jews celebrated Passover with the greatest splendour and magnificence, as true free men, when they lived in their own land, the Land of Israel; and thus they also celebrated Passover throughout two thousand years of dreadful, dark life in exile, in the times of inquisitions and pogroms.
Take, for example, the time after the Second Destruction by Titus, when the people, which had still seen with its own eyes the period of glory of its land, now sees the great dark destruction of its dear and holy fatherland: how its sanctuaries are desecrated and laid waste, its best children defiled and slain, its property robbed and plundered, and the remnants of its best children are driven off to Rome, where they are forced to fight the starved wild beasts in the "circus" amid the jubilation of tens of thousands of assembled bloodthirsty Romans; and precisely at that terrible, tragic moment — which, according to the account of some historians, fell exactly on the night of Passover — the holy martyr-heroes, their fists clenched in grief and wrath, whispered the "We were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt", but "today we are free men"!...
Or a second fact: the Jews are in the Spanish exile, in the bloody land where the "Holy Inquisition" reigns, and woe to him who is caught, or even merely suspected, of observing any ritual tradition whatsoever — after being tortured with inhuman sufferings, he is burned at the stake. Nevertheless, when the festival of freedom, Passover, comes, Jews gather together with the Marranos in underground caves, where, in mortal terror but at the same time also with trust in God, and with scorn and contempt for the cruel enemy, they conduct the Seder, and courageously and proudly recite the "We were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt" but "today we are free men"!...
But let us take a third, generally known fact — the sadly familiar blood-libel stories. A libel is made up that the Jews slaughtered Christian children in order to use the blood for matzot. Can there be a greater irony and a more tragic curiosity of fate? Thousands of Jews are arrested, tortured with the most gruesome pains, their skin is flayed from them alive, their flesh torn, burned and roasted; the whole community of Israel is persecuted and subjected to pogroms, seas of blood and tears are shed — and yet! When Passover comes, the Jew conducts the Seder in mortal terror of the enemy on one side, and with scorn and contempt for that same enemy on the other, and proudly says the "We were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt", but "today we are free men"...
We could bring a whole series of examples and facts showing that even in the most dangerous conditions and the most terrible moments, when the sword of Damocles hangs over the Jew's head and he finds himself in mortal danger — nevertheless, when the Passover night comes, he feels himself a proud and free Jew, a "free man" (ben chorin), and the greatest pain and suffering can break him only physically, but in no case spiritually and morally.
And the question arises: wherein lies the great secret that gives the Jew so much courage and strength to go to self-sacrifice in the most dangerous moments, just so as not to give up or resign from demonstrating that only once were we slaves, but today we are "free men"?
The answer to this question we can find in the above-mentioned quotation from the Torah: "Wherefore criest thou unto me? Speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward"! The Jewish people finds itself in the greatest danger, between two fires: in front the deep, endless sea, and from behind [printed: "from below"] the Egyptians pursue them; there is no way out, the people despairs, weeps and cries hopelessly, and only at the last moment comes the divine counsel "Wherefore criest thou unto me?" — that it is not with weeping and crying that freedom can be won, nor can one become a free people through miracles alone, but only "Speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward"! There must be self-sacrifice, sacrifices must be brought upon the altar of freedom; and only then, when Nachshon son of Amminadab leapt into the sea up to his neck, and after him the whole people, and only after the great self-sacrifice, did they become a free people. And that is the secret why the Jewish people holds the Passover night so holy and dear: because the Passover night is the symbol of the freedom which the Jews won with the greatest self-sacrifice, and thereby were freed not only from bodily slavery but — and this is the main thing — received the great spiritual freedom and the maturity to accept the universal teaching called "the Torah of Moses", and to take possession of the Land of Israel and to develop spiritually and economically, as befits a free and cultured people.
When we consider today our present sad situation in exile, we notice a remarkable similarity to that ancient Egyptian epoch. How, actually, did the hatred of Jews begin to develop? We know, on the contrary, that at first the Jews were a blessing for the land, and therefore Pharaoh and the Egyptians received them with open arms; was it not none other than the Jew Joseph who saved them from death by starvation, introduced various useful social reforms and raised the country to a high cultural level?
But the good fortune lasted only as long as the Jews were a small, negligible minority; from the moment the Jewish people naturally increased, the Egyptians saw in the Jews a competitor and took fright that their economic positions were threatened — and then the first antisemitic slogan was raised: "Come, let us deal wisely"! They did not wait long and found a remedy: "Therefore they set over them taskmasters" [printed "vayishumu" for "vayasimu"] — they laid enormous taxes on trade, so that trading should not pay and the Jews would consequently have to emigrate from the land; from the Jewish workers (the uncultured Egyptians still employed Jewish workers) they in turn demanded strenuous, abnormal physical labour — "and they made their lives bitter" — embittered their life, so that they would be forced to abandon work and emigrate from the land. But when the latter succeeded, and they are freed from the Egyptian yoke, take the wanderer's staff in hand and emigrate, they again meet an obstacle of nature, the sea; again they remain in despair, until the call of the Almighty comes: not to cry, not to weep, but to fight the obstacles with self-sacrifice! Do we not see the same phenomenon also in the present time of the "birth-pangs of redemption"? In contrast to the persecutions of the various exiles, which almost always bore the character of national or religious fanaticism, today's persecutions are mostly on economic and social grounds. What else are the hellish persecutions of our brethren in Germany, and what is the meaning of the dark decrees that pour down on our heads incessantly, robbing us of our political rights, pushing and thrusting us out of the economic and cultural positions we have occupied? And when we already tear ourselves out of exile, we meet on the way an endless sea of decrees and restrictions against entry into the Land of Israel — by the English government? Let these sad facts serve us as a moral lesson that one must not rely on any miracles — "one does not rely on a miracle". But if we truly want to become "free men", we must build the Land of Israel, and if build — one must prove it with deeds, and not with words, declarations and petitions, but only with sacrifices and self-sacrifice. We must have Nachshons son of Amminadab, and listen to the almighty call of this so tragic and yet at the same time historic hour:
"Wherefore criest thou unto me?
Speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward!"
Y. Wygodzki [?].
The Bloody Spectacle.

[Essay — society and politics; crisis, despair, Hitlerism and antisemitism.] By L. Szpigelman.
The mass murders [i.e. mass suicides], the difficult situation and starving humanity. The reasons why man was turned into the shape of a beast.

People who have been through a great deal in life, people who have many acquaintances in various circles and spheres, people who have all kinds of friends [?] and enemies in the world, can tell various things about humanity; all sorts of surprises often occur, by which one is shaken more than once.

Thus, for example, one quite often hears of suicides that remain a riddle to acquaintances. They know how to tell the very best about the person to whom the catastrophe happened; they can describe to you the calm and decency of the person. They can describe to you for hours his good qualities and the common sense he possessed all his life, and they cannot answer the great question mark: why and how did he bring himself to commit suicide?

One can sometimes debate such a matter for whole days and no decision can be reached, because opinions on the hard question differ, and a solution cannot easily emerge.

One is often shaken [?] by this or that catastrophe: what does it mean — after all, we knew him so well: his character, his conduct, his decency, his steadiness both in private and in public life — and we can by no means understand how he could bring himself to cut off the thread of his life without considering that only [?] he himself is freed in this way from the suffering and pain, whereas they are passed on to the members of his family whom he left behind. And we do not understand how he could bring himself to cause still more suffering to those closest to him by taking his own life, when in his lifetime he could not bear to see their sorrow.

And another example: we see a man suddenly begin to drink. A man who was known to us as a solid gentleman, and then we see him become, step by step, lower and more worthless, until he reaches the level of an utter idler.

We meet the same thing in people who become card players and reach the level of professionals. They then begin to forget themselves, their family and everything that interested them as human beings and that they wanted [?] in life.

And every time we ask ourselves: what has happened here? What has become of these people? What causes brought them down and led them to the level of the abyss? And however one looks at the serious question, however one may wish to solve the hard problem, one must come to the conviction that what led to these terrible deeds is only despair — the loss of hope that things can still be good for him, that he will be able to endure the bad time. Despair is the worst and most dangerous thing. Despair puts an end to everything. Despair puts an end to one's own "I", however much he may love it and however egotistic he may be. Despair leads to cutting for ever the thread of a person's life. Despair does not reckon with a strong will, with the enormous force of life, with intuition. Despair is stronger than everything, and it leads down to the abyss of destruction.

Several years ago, as soon as the crisis began to prevail, mass suicides began all over the world. Citizens could not endure the terrible suffering, so they put an end to their lives, not reckoning with what would come later. And despite the great number of suicides, despite the mass epidemic which swept away whole cities and countries, they nevertheless bore a private character, and it turned out that they harmed only the closest relatives and those around them, with whom the suicides had been connected. In any case, the suicides everywhere bore a private character, in which neither society nor the governments as such took an interest.

And why should one take an interest in private persons, in individuals, however great their number might be, so long as they did no harm to the community, to broad society as such? So, at least, people thought about this terrible phenomenon.

But the grave process continued according to natural forms; nature did its part; it took little account of the fact that the world regards the mass murders as private, as egotistic — and they inevitably became socialised.

If we look a little further, strain our eye harder, cast our gaze deeper, we must come to the conclusion that the upheavals in Germany and the revolution in Austria are a consequence of despair.

In Germany and Austria things became bad and bitter; people fell into despair and took their own lives, and then came the dark elements, those who want to fish in troubled waters, and said to the masses: Don't you see how bad and dark things are for you? Don't you see that you are eternal slaves of the Jews, and of philosophers who descend from Jews, and of the socialists? So why should you go on languishing under their whips? Have you anything left to lose? Come to us, we will turn everything upside down, murder the stumbling blocks [?], and then we will take the helm into our hands, and you yourselves will be the rulers and the masters, and we [?] will oppress those who oppress us.

And those who truly suffer and hunger, the great number of unemployed, had nothing to lose; they had long lost hope in a better tomorrow. The individuals captured their hearts by assuring them of work, so that with this the revolution began and the intended upheaval was achieved.

Here one was dealing with people who had remained desperate and had long since given up all hope, so that they had nothing to lose, since in any case they are hungry, in any case they wander about like superfluous shadows; and this explains why they were turned into beasts. About their bestial deeds historians will have many books to write, and without doubt future generations will not be able to grasp how the plague could spread in the 20th century in the heart of Europe and exterminate people, cities and countries.

Our Polish antisemites too envy the Hitlerites and also perform deeds in order to bring about upheavals; meanwhile they are out [?] to fish in troubled waters, and first of all they want to seize upon the helpless one — the Jew, on whom the reproach used [?] to be poured out at all times. Here too the unemployed man is persuaded that because of the Jews he has no employment, although a Jewish factory worker is never to be seen in the light of day; but one can talk people into anything in the world — especially against Jews.

Our Hitlerites preach how good it would be for the Polish people if the Jews were expelled — a real paradise there would be in Poland. Here too they want to persuade the helpless and miserable citizen, himself hungry, that the Jew is to blame for everything — regardless of the fact that we no longer have the strength to drag upon ourselves the heavy tax yoke, the greatest proportion of which falls on our shoulders.

We are simply crushed under the heavy yoke of taxes and under the great burden called livelihood. We kept thinking that the yoke would be eased, that taxes would be reduced; we hoped that the government would realise that we no longer have the strength to languish under the hard conditions, and that relief and reductions would come. Meanwhile, instead of relief, we hear of new decrees, fresh projects, which would make our already difficult situation even more unbearable; and on top of that they cast a covetous eye on us and keep inciting, keep agitating, keep stirring up that the Jew is to blame for everything.

Our Jewish representatives in Poland ought [?] to treat and consider this tense situation somewhat more seriously. One must not forget that the danger is great, and one must not take our situation lightly.

The result of all this, however, is that hunger and want occupy the top place in the whole world, and this element — the hungry and suffering population — is used as a blind tool, and they are incited by being shown all good things from afar, like a beast which [?] could swallow and wants to throw itself upon it; exactly so, to the same level, the hungry man is led. And the hungry man loses nothing; he is desperate, he has given up everything and easily believes anything; he is made drunk, and then he is used to carry out any experiment.

But one cannot always remain in a state of intoxication; one must sober up at some point, and then one rises as from a long lethargic sleep, rubs one's eyes, stretches [?] and begins to look around: what has happened here around me, around us? And still one sees no paradise, despite having "purged" so many "dangerous elements".

The Hitlerite bluffs, which promised the German people bread and work, and which seemed to them a reality, have turned into a fantasy.

— The people begin to sober up and see the naked truth: that the bloody struggles were nothing more than a spectacle, performed by suffering, hungry people through harmful individuals.
The Haggadah

When our grandfathers uttered these words [“Ha lachma anya” — “This is the bread of affliction”], they saw before them the dark, muddy shtetl, with its crooked[?] little houses, the cramped space, the poverty, the dog's, crawling[?] life, the constant hopelessness, the whole doleful this-world, which was compensated with a fantastic world-to-come... That was the “lachma anya” of olden times.
Before the War one saw before oneself a barrel stuffed with herring — the Pale of Settlement — a wild striving for freedom, for equality, for the possibility of breathing in the broad Tsarist empire; bread dipped in blood and tears, in apostasy and desertion; a pot of lentils, bought at the price of the sons' souls, the daughters' honour, the denial of one's own self — that was the pre-war “lachma anya”.
During the War it again acquired another meaning: peel-cooking, tea with saccharin, rye matzah, sandy bread...
And today — today's “lachma anya” is doled out to us by the sequestrator [the tax-distraint officer], who snatches[?] it from our mouths. Today's “lachma anya” passes through sevenfold taxes that chase us from morning till night and even into our restless dreams. It is a “lachma anya” of constant fear of war, crisis torments, antisemitic afflictions, with pogroms and excesses[?]. A “lachma anya” of étatisms and monopolies, revoked licences, numerus clausus, paper constitutions, iron chains, discrimination and pauperisation. It is, after all, a “lachma anya”...
That is how Jews interpret the Haggadah and lick their lips with pleasure.
But the trouble is that all our other, weekday sayings too have now become: haggadah, a stock formula. We have, after all, speechmakers and penmen, Lamentations-wailers, bearers of tidings, who deafen our ears from the platforms and from the newspaper columns. And everything they say is haggadahs — yesterday's question with yesterday's answer.
After all, we do breathe with the dynamics of liberation, of rise and ascent and striving towards a new, free life. But we hear no word, no new slogan resounds. Today as yesterday, as the day before yesterday. Songs sung out, a Haggadah recited, questions asked out and answers answered out.
Our whole life is filled with sayings that say nothing.
Sayings we have, thank God, enough; we simply don't turn to a siddur, a machzor, a chumash or a Psalter. We run the town, we hold posts, and a child must, after all, be taught Jewishness. We guard the synagogue tradition with all its tinsel, and over a cantor it is right to kill one another, as the great-grandfather did...
But today's saying, the Haggadah, has a special merit with us. It is the only time in the year when the saying is bound up with eating. All our prayer books can live out a whole life, from the bookbinder to the cellar of the shemos [the genizah], without ever seeing the home. They can lie locked in the lectern and wait from prayer to prayer. The Haggadah is just the opposite: it can live out a whole life without seeing the synagogue; it lies a whole year dusty on the shelf, until people begin to prepare[?] for the Seder. Then one lays on the table, together with the three matzahs, four cups, charoset, zeroa and maror, the Haggadah as well, exactly as if it too were a dish for the table...
On Yom Kippur, it seems, there is more to say, beyond measure to say — it suffices for a full twenty-four hours with another hour added; nevertheless, when one has to fast it out, one is exempt from the saying. On Passover, however, the Haggadah lies on the table: a saying and a bite, a bite and a saying. Not for nothing does the Haggadah say: “Whoever expands on it is praiseworthy”...
All this is nice and fine; that is what we are Jews for: if we were to drink down four cups of wine at once, we would get drunk. So it really is better to drink with pauses and fill the time with saying.
But it is a little uncomfortable that one says the same thing every year. When my little boy begins to ask the Questions, it seems to me that I see a hidden little smile at the corners of his lips; he still remembers the answer from last year, and he also knows that in that same book no new answer has been printed in the course of the past year; nevertheless he asks, just for the sake of fulfilling the duty[?] — so what sense can my answer still have? Such a question troubles me:
Passover, after all, is the only Jewish holiday that possesses movement, dynamics, revolution. All the holidays are expressions of statics, of stability, of a life that flows smoothly from yesterday into tomorrow through today. Only Passover is a holiday of liberation, redemption, breaking out, escape from bondage, burning the bridges behind one, striving towards unknown distances, towards a new Torah, a new land, a new life for the people. Here, surely, the new word should have come, the bubbling, rousing, stimulating call. In the end — here you have the Haggadah from last year, from two years ago, from a hundred years ago, the old question, with the old answer, down to the old Chad Gadya...
There is still one defence of the Haggadah: one can put into it, as into all our old books, new interpretations every time, according to the spirit of time and place.
For example, we say: “Ha lachma anya”; how many flavours we feel in it!
Argus.
Two Seders

[Passover — literary sketch.] By Yehuda Yafet.
...In a remote German small town, at a Jewish family's home. Until not long ago the town counted a few dozen Jewish families. But for a year now the majority of the Jewish families have had to emigrate, leaving behind all their belongings; some are still in the concentration camps and under arrest for various "Jewish sins" — so that only a handful of Jewish families remained, and today, on Passover evening, there was barely a minyan in the little synagogue, even counting [?] the small children. The minyan was completed by the seder instructor, who had been sent down specially by the Frankfurt communities' central office for the purpose of conducting the seder with the ignorant [?] Jews who are holding the seder for the first time in the year 5694.
Doors and windows are bolted. God forbid the gentiles should find out what is going on here — one would not be sure of one's life. Just so their grandfathers once trembled on Passover night lest enemies plant a murdered Christian child. Today's enemies do not even need a blood libel in order to destroy Jews.
All the Jewish families are gathered in this house [?]. Most of them were of those who had remained — such as had been at the front and lost there, for the German fatherland, a hand or a foot. Others again could prove [?] that their forefathers have been living on German soil for hundreds of years.
The instructor, a former student of a rabbinical seminary that has been dispersed [?], explains to those present the meaning of Passover, recites the Haggadah and translates every sentence into German. "And it is this that has stood by — he translates — our fathers and us, for not just one has risen against us to destroy us, but in every generation they rise against us to destroy us, and the Holy One, blessed be He, saves us from their hand."
Not only in this town [printed "shtele"] but in many similar ones the listeners' eyes lit up with a glow; they wondered and did not understand: had the very same words already been said years ago, even when Kaiser Wilhelm, His Highness, was reigning?...
The seder customs, the strange words of the Haggadah — all this so amazed them, wafted over them with generations of Jewish history, with millennia of Jewish suffering.
They came to "Pour out Thy wrath". The seder instructor points to little Fritz:
— Well, now open the door.
Everyone is frightened: "Open the door? Across the way the neighbour, a Nazi, will overhear how we say here 'Pour out Thy wrath upon the nations'." He will find out what is going on here? No [?] — they might still be attacked this very night.
But the instructor explains: now no Nazi will come in, now the prophet Elijah will come — here, I pour out a cup for him.
And the seder instructor tells who the prophet Elijah is, his story as the Bible tells it, his deeds over thousands of years in all Jewish settlements, seeing the Jewish troubles and bringing help and consolation everywhere.
For a long time the instructor spoke, describing the legendary figure of Elijah who lives forever and hovers over all the lands of the Diaspora, there as a child becomes [?] a Jew — on Passover at the seder, and in poor hovels of want.
And little Fritz saw before him such a picture:
...On Carmel stands a prophet girded with a leather belt. Long hair that strikes terror; around him eight hundred and fifty Phoenician priests. The whole land of Israel has become full of temples in honour of Baal, in honour of the Asherah, in honour of Ashtoreth; Jezebel, the daughter of the Tyrian king Ethbaal, the wife of Ahab king of Israel, has flooded the land with Tyrian idols. Jews served both them and the God of Israel... Prophets and preachers had already devised [?] a sect between Judaism and "Tyrism", made peace between them.
Elijah stands on Mount Carmel and thunders with his divine voice:
— "How long will you limp between the two sides? If the Lord is God — follow Him; if Baal is God — follow him."
And the people answered not a word.
The people liked it and found it comfortable precisely to limp between Baal and the Lord. A peace had been found between them, in both faiths — which means, in any case, denying neither.
All this little Fritz pictured to himself according to the instructor's description, and he did not know that he was seeing the vision of his own home, his own tragedy. Year after year Elijah knocked on the doors of the German Jews, calling to them: "How long will you limp between the two sides?"
But the German Jew bolted his doors against the prophet's call, limped and limped on both sides, until he slipped so terribly.
Exactly ninety years ago, in a German city, in Braunschweig, at a "rabbinical conference", much was said about this very Elijah. It was then resolved that the "messianic idea" deserves high consideration, but with distancing [?] from everything politically national. Elijah will indeed appear on the great festive [?] day, but that has nothing to do specifically with Jews. It is a lofty idea of world redemption. Elijah will come to the world. The German Jews do not need him, they are well and fine, Elijah need not bring them to Jerusalem, because — as the German Jews, according to the book "Ma'aseh Nissim", answered in the days of Ezra to the call to go up to the Land of Israel — "We have already given up on old Jerusalem; therefore we have on the Rhine a new Jerusalem, which in our eyes is no less important than the first."
At the table the conversation has now turned to how to obtain certificates for the Land of Israel. Above all the master of the house wants his Fritz to be raised already in Jerusalem — in Jerusalem, not on the Rhine...
* * *
...In Tel Aviv, on the first Passover night of 5694.
Joyful and merry is the night of redemption in the land of redemption. Jews from the four corners of the earth are gathered, the heart wells up [?] with joy; in a spirit of freedom they celebrate [?] the public seder in one of the restaurants. Jews from all the lands of the Diaspora sit at one table; the ingathering of the exiles is here already a fact; from all hearts a song of freedom rings out.
The eldest of the company leads the seder, recites the Haggadah, begins "Ha Lachma". "This year we are here, next year — in the redeemed Land of Israel. This year we are slaves, next year we shall be free."
For a moment the faces are shadowed. We are not yet in the redeemed Land of Israel, we are still slaves, even here, in the Land of Israel... Most sharply of all the face clouded over of one Jew, an "illegal", who faces at any moment being expelled from the country, arrested, sent to Acre — he, his wife and even his child...
But soon the faces brighten again. The Haggadah goes on merrily, people eat and drink and sing songs of the Land of Israel. The four cups have long been emptied; the fifth cup is poured for Elijah.
The four cups — explains the elderly Jew who leads the seder, the "king" — correspond to the four expressions of redemption: "I will bring out, I will deliver, I will redeem, I will take." This present fifth cup corresponds to the fifth expression of redemption, to "And I will bring you into the land". With those four cups we already manage somehow. "I will bring out, I will redeem, I will take" — not so bad. With the Pharaohs of our Egypts we have long been finished with "letting us out"; but what does one do with the Pharaoh of this land, the Pharaoh who does not allow "And I will bring you into the land"?... Ah, the cup corresponding to "And I will bring" is the bitterest cup...
And when the door was opened and they said aloud: "Pour out Thy wrath upon the nations that know Thee not, and upon the kingdoms that call not upon Thy name, for they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling", the "illegal" Jew said the words in a terrible voice and with tears in his eyes...
And again the conversation turned to Elijah, to the wondrous figure in Jewish history, to the great zealot [?], to the prophet of zeal, who was merciless towards the worshippers of Baal, and yet it was said of him "Behold, I give unto him My covenant of peace", and yet he is the angel of peace who will "turn the heart of the fathers to the children and the heart of the children to their fathers". The zealot towards strangers and the angel of peace towards his own.
And one of the listeners searched with his eyes for the angel of peace, who is now so needed in the Land of Israel — the angel of zeal towards strangers and the angel of peace towards one's own...
King Solomon — A Passover Humoresque

[Passover humoresque — story.]
A Passover humoresque.

Contentedly Shloyme Aynbinder [i.e. "Bookbinder"], or Shloyme Shlimazl, as they called him in the shtetl, sat down to the Seder.
He had crawled into the white[?], freshly washed kittel, poured the four cups — not raisin wine as every year, but really good, genuine wine; in honour of the holiday — he thinks to himself — let there be a glass of drink, just as at a king's.
Zlate, his little wife, looks like a queen, in a white apron with pleats, a white silk kerchief around her neck; the face itself — simply regal, a delight, contentment; and poured out over her thin, always bone-[?]sharpened little lips, from which curses used to pour on him without end like hail — today everything has vanished; even her little hands, which all year are dirty and smeared, are washed clean as never before.
The room itself — a refreshment; the floor scrubbed, gleaming clean, strewn with yellow sand — wealthy, kingly.
He said the Kiddush, drank the wine, sip after sip, in small swallows, not[?] all at once — is it raisin wine, then?!
The "Mah Nishtanah" was asked by his Zlatkele (for they had no children). Expansively he recited the Haggadah as never before, and indeed conducted himself like a king.
"Rachtzah!" he commands; she understands the orders in the Holy Tongue; a scoop[?] of water, a basin, a white towel — she brings them. He is served just like a king.
His heart melts with joy — no small thing! All year he is used, besides his trade, to doing several small kitchen chores, just so as not to catch his Zlatkele's well-rounded curses; but today —
With courage he sang through the Haggadah; "Chad Gadya" he already went through as if on a hilly highway. His eyes tired [printed "mir", read "mid"], his mouth barely opens; the "Next year in Jerusalem" came out of him by now more through his nose...
Tipsy from the wine, barely keeping himself on his heels ["pyentes", Polish pięty], Shloyme, drowsy, in his kittel, fell onto the bed in his clothes and with a solid snore fell asleep.
On his contented face and laughing expression it could be seen that the angel of dreams was spinning for him lovely, charming little threads, interwoven with splendid pictures, decorating with them fantastic, wondrous scenes.
He finds himself among a camp of Jews, all dressed in soldiers' clothes; he himself at their head, wearing an officer's coat, a sword at his side; together they all climb up a high mountain, dragging along cannons and other implements of war.
From the mountaintop he sees the Land of Israel; an army of Turks stands against him, ready[?] for war; his Jewish army speaks only the Holy Tongue.
He commands:
— Kadesh! His army gets ready for battle.
— U-rechatz! The gunners quickly wash the cannons all round.
— Karpas, he calls in a stern voice; the artillery advances to the front line. The cannons are loaded with balls.
— Yachatz! he cries out. The cannons fire. There is smoke; from the other side, at the enemy's, a wave of cloud rises; his soldiers shoot, fight bravely. The enemy stops shooting; he adds courage with a general's order:
— Maggid! His army bursts out with a feverish[?] cry "Hurrah! Hedad!" over to the surrendered enemy; they took [printed "gegumen"] the Turkish army with its ammunition into captivity.
His soldiers are full of joy, officers carry him on their hands, all call out "Long live the king! Long live our King Shloyme!"
As he was led into Jerusalem, the inhabitants of the city came out to meet him with Torah scrolls, led him in with a great parade into a magnificent royal palace, and set on his head a royal crown of gold studded with precious stones.
From outside, in the street, he hears the joyful singing of the public; the Jewish military orchestra plays "Od lo avda tikvatenu", blue-and-white flags with Stars of David flutter.
—
In the midst of it all [printed "drigen", read "drinen"] he remembers his Zlatke: to her he must bring the tidings that he is the Jewish king and she, Zlatkele — queen; let her share the kingdom with him.
The angel of dreams carried him in a minute [printed "migut"] home to his house...
— Shh, quiet — he says to himself — she is asleep, don't wake her, she is a queen after all.
Tired himself from the war, he thinks, he needs [printed "goytigt", read "noytigt"] to rest a little until his queen wakes up; to tell her the tidings of who he is now and take her with him into his palace, put the crown on her: he — King Solomon, she — Zlatka the Queen — — —
Suddenly he feels a tug at the blanket.
— Enough sleeping for you! — he hears the familiar squealing cry, angrily, of his Zlatkele — it's time to get up already!
The windows were still shut; the darkness of the room kept him still under the gentle influence of his sweet dream.
— Zlatke! Zlatke! — he calls merrily, wishing to continue his eminent mission — Zlatke! Quickly, first just give me a glass of good tea, then hurry, dress in your finest garments and come with me!
Zlatke, unused to hearing such commanding words from her husband, fixed on him a pair of stern[?], glassy eyes as on a madman.
— You shlimazl! What sort of talk is this today?
— Tea, let it be, quickly, don't forget who is speaking to you.
Such talk [printed "gererekhts", read "geredekhts"] from her husband did not please Zlatke at all; she comes up to him, measures him with her familiar angry look, biting her thin little lips and pursing them, and wanted to fling herself at him, as is her way in such cases, to honour him with a "gift of the hand" [a slap].
Shloyme, still under the dream's influence, could no longer stay patient. With a raised, heroic, proud head he went up to her, seized her by the hands, looked at her with pride and dignity and said excitedly: "Respect, Zlatke, know who I am!"
Feeling her hands pressed tight in Shloyme's hands, Zlatke in anger spat into his face. That drove him entirely out of patience — a smack was heard in the air. Zlatke's cheek turned red, marked[?] with welts[?] of fingers...
At Zlatke's screaming, squealing and cursing the neighbours came running together. Opening the door, they still found Shloyme standing in his kittel, shouting at his slapped wife: Now will you know who your husband is? I am King Solomon! Understand? And — —
The neighbours burst out in wheezing laughter.
Shloyme, only now noticing in the light the holiday clothes of the children who had come running, with bits of matzah in their little hands, only then came to his senses, that it had all been a foolish dream... only the slap with which he had honoured his Zlate [printed "Zlaten"] had not been a dreamlike one... but — lost, it has happened.
The dream brought him a double benefit: Zlatke was now afraid to hit Shloyme, and instead of his former name Shloyme Shlimazl, he was now called — King Solomon...
H. Salnik.
The Festival of Liberation and Everyday Reality

[Passover — essay.] We truly are a people of romantics and dreamers.
Just take Passover, our festival of freedom.
With enthusiasm we celebrate this festival of a liberation of long ago. That bygone liberation which the centuries have long since buried, erased from reality.
But what — one pretends not to know. Passover is the festival of liberation, and no other festival will take the crown from its proud head... And already weeks beforehand one makes stormy preparations to welcome freedom — the 8-day freedom! — in a worthy manner. Want and worries and troubles suddenly become chametz, and one searches them out... one burns them... even today, when chametz is so dear, when so many needy people "long" all year for a little piece of chametz... And whether in Hitlerite Germany or in hooligan Romania — on Passover every Jew is a rich man, every Jew is free, there is no unemployment and no crisis.
It is, after all, a festival of liberation.
And that is the miracle of faith, the miracle of Israel's strength, of its survival.
Here you have a Jew who all year pushes a little cart with a "shop" worth a few złoty... earns just enough not to starve... but go in to him on Passover night, to the Seder!.. Here you have a Jew who barely, barely saved his poor bit of life from the German hooligans... and just look how expansively he has settled himself at the table and says only "we W-E-R-E slaves"... proudly opens the door, so that Elijah the Prophet may come in... knowing full well that Elijah, for whom he has been waiting his whole life, will not come — short of a miracle — and that sooner some hooligan, l'havdil, will come in through the open door.
He knows that he is not free, he knows that he is celebrating a liberation of long ago. He knows that in the end he is tearing these few days of the festival of freedom out of his enslavement. He knows that this festival he is now celebrating is a kind of staged performance, that it contradicts reality... But his faith and his longing for freedom have mobilised all his dreams, hopes and illusions, so that reality really does vanish to one side, just like the chametz.
And on Passover the Jew truly feels free. He celebrates the festival of liberation with all his religious and national ecstasy, with all his longing for the religion of freedom.
* * *
And one does not want to disturb the festival, and one does not want to sober up — and yet.
Should we not, on this very festival, remember that we have lost our freedom, and should not this moving and inspired "remembrance" of the bygone liberation forge our energy and our faith for the struggle for a renewed liberation?
For slaves we are. The Jew in exile is a slave everywhere, whether in the countries where antisemitism has already passed to deeds or in the countries where it is still dozing. The Jew in exile is not free spiritually, not morally, not economically. Look at how the Jew walks in the street. It is quite a different step, quite a different bearing from that of the native masters of the house. In the rhythm of his steps one senses that he is carrying some burden. That is the burden of servitude. Whether he knows it or not. Unconsciously he feels that he is not equal to everyone. He wants to forget it, wants to free himself of what is called, by a false observation, "exile psychology". But it does not help. From some remote little corner a miniature incident will jump out to remind him that he is not free, that he is a stranger.
Everywhere in exile. And here too, among us, here too people are already whispering in the corners about Jews... against Jews... And the more you carry your Jewish consciousness with you, your pride as a Jew and as a human being, the more it hurts. You already have here groups of Hitlerites, dark elements, who tell you openly that they hate Jews; they have not yet taken a position on the Jews, that is, against the Jews. But we have already been informed that in their ranks there is a strong current against Jews... They have an organ, and it will be enough for us to point out that the source from which they draw their wisdom and their theories is Hitler's "Völkischer Beobachter"...
This is, of course, only a beginning, but the beginning will lead to a development, to growth... For now there is still grace: we are not yet a political factor, we are after all still politically neutral, although the Endeks reproach us that we are their opponents, that we are not loyal...
Neutralists? Maybe — we were assured — but not loyal ones. And arguments were put before us that were truly heavy stones.
One more thing we wish to note: the time is already very near when the Jewish voter will have to vote, will have to declare himself for this or that party, will become an active factor in the political life of the country.
Can you say how he should orient himself? Do we even have the right to tell him? Certainly not, for he will join this or that political party not as a Jew but as a citizen, and the Jewish collective cannot be a political guardian over his political views...
But here a whole complex of questions already surfaces, which we must postpone to another time.
H. Cwir [?].
Help, “Reductions”!...

[Feuilleton — humour.] (A little feuilleton.)
— What do you say to the new trouble, eh? The plague of "ulgi" [reductions], I mean — heaven and earth and "reductions"! They just keep making life easier for me. The tax office does me a favour and gives me "reductions" — it takes my few groszy from me in instalments. The magistrate also grants me a "convenience" and orders the sequestrator to pull out my guts in a "reduced" manner. Every quarter the landlord promises me "reductions" on the rent. My Maniek uses a reduced-price booklet to go to the cinema and the theatre. What an effort it cost him! Only through the protection of a highly placed personage did he finally get it, and he came home in triumph:
— Dad, I've grabbed one!
— What have you grabbed, I ask.
— What do you mean, what? A reduced-price booklet for the cinema.
My daughter, for her part, uses "reductions" at the dancings in Katowice, my wife has a reduction at the hairdresser's, my father-in-law a reduction at the mikveh — in short, heaven and earth and reductions. It's such a racket [?] — dragging the few groszy out of your pockets.
And as if all that were too little, along came a fresh misfortune: reduced-fare trips. They seek out all sorts of days off and give the public a chance to travel to Warsaw for a small price. Well, what can you do — my wife, my son, my daughters and even my mother-in-law are all now keen to go on the "wycieczka" [excursion]. With signs and wonders they prove to me how much money one earns on such a trip. 80 per cent — they argue — stays in your pocket as clean money.
— And where does one get the 20 per cent? — I ask them.
But they listen to me as to the cat, and off they go to Warsaw, and hardly have they been brought to Warsaw when they are already charged enormous prices in the restaurants and hotels — but all in a "reduced" manner.
I tell you, gentlemen, I'll become a pauper because of the "reductions". Who invented this plague? Bring me the thief and I'll make kreplach-meat of him.
Esne.
This Year Here, Next Year in the Land of Israel.

[Sosnowiec — Passover political-satirical feuilleton; Nazi Germany, Zionism.] By Yosef Perlmutter.
(Almost a political letter from a merchant on Modrzejowska [?] Street [Sosnowiec] to a Łódź merchant).
My friend! I know in advance that when you receive this little letter from me today, you will surely open a pair of big eyes and ask in astonishment the great "Mah nishtanah": how come, all of a sudden, after such a long silence, so-and-so remembers to write a letter, just on the very eve of Passover.
To all your questions, my friend, I will answer you in two simple words: I had adopted a "wait-and-see stance".. Lately I have been watching all the great world politicians. I noticed that lately almost all of them stand hidden behind the curtain and you hear not a peep from them at all. For there is sometimes a time when one must keep to the saying "a word is worth a sela, silence is worth two", and that is exactly why, you know, I did not take [?] the floor on any of the latest great world events, such as the Stavisky scandal, which made a proper uproar in France, so that a whole literature with "prophets" has almost been created about it and "the whole world" has split into two camps: "yes guilty, not guilty"...
Likewise I took care not to say a word about the great shochtim strike that took place here recently in Zagłębie...
And I am also holding myself back with all my strength from getting involved in the great Revisionist battle that has broken out so sharply between the two best former friends — the Zionist Executive [printed "ekuekutive"] and Grossman-Jabotinsky.
But you know, my friend, if on all the questions listed I could still somehow restrain myself and not say my great, daring word, I really can no longer bear to watch the new wild, crazy deeds in Germany since [?] the house-painter [?] Hitler the wicked rose to the highest political rung in such a cultured state as Germany, and there they are bent only on exterminating their own devoted, self-sacrificing citizens, merely because they bear other names...
This, you know, can no longer be passed over in silence, and I must point out to you that this is how the beginning of a people that is starting to decline and vanish begins... It is the same path, the same stage, which far mightier peoples went through before they began to disappear... Plainly: one becomes big and strong, one grows in length and in breadth, and once one is so big, one becomes "firm in one's mind" [printed "bre'ato"] and wants to impose one's opinion on the whole world, and when the other will not submit, one goes to prove one's greatness with the might one possesses, and gets the first blow on the head... (if one wins — fine, if not...) Unable to vent the hatred and fury on strangers, one vents it on one's own citizens, though they are as innocent as can be [literally "owe God their soul"], and instead of [?] and imposing rule on strangers, there spring up as if from under the ground dark persons who preach and sow the same hatred and fury against their own, and they torture and murder for so long until a terrible civil war breaks out without end and without finish... And it is already an old rule that "if thou hast begun to fall... thou shalt surely fall"... And the end will be that "thou art undone, O people of Chemosh" [printed "avrat am kemosh"] — Germany, you are going under, you are lost beyond rescue... "Relief and deliverance shall arise to the Jews from another place", for we are already an old, tried people, "a people accustomed to miracles" [printed "kenisim" [?]]. "And thou and thy father's house shall perish"...
And perhaps you think, my friend, that the combination of the Four Sons will help him somehow — not at all.. You will indeed see tonight, when you sit like a prince at the Seder, that we have long since forgotten that "the Torah speaks of four sons", and you will see how he will come back with knocked-out teeth and — "and you, set his teeth on edge" [printed "hakeh"].
The first crack in the teeth he has already received from us, so that he has indeed already lost his tongue a little...
The beginning has been made and the rest will come of itself...
And perhaps you want a hint about it — I will give you that too, since without it, as is known, it doesn't work.
Here, on Modrzejowska [?] Street, people actually say that "Pharaoh" too was neither more nor less than a "Hitler", and if you work it out [by gematria], you will see that it adds up...
And with whom did he begin, the paintbrush-politician? With a people that works wonders: for at a time when tens of millions of people with old, well-founded foundations wander about superfluous, like those sentenced [?] to death, our brothers stand and build and plough and sow and [?] literally stretch out their hands to the work... A people that has been hammered into one single body, in one piece, so that if you strike a blow in one place, it echoes at once, as in a great body, and it reacts with dignity and with pride...
And perhaps that is exactly what the sages meant by the saying "The Holy One, blessed be He, did Israel a kindness by scattering them among the nations" etc. — that if one ever has to react against a monstrous murder, such as is now being done in Germany, the whole of Jewry across the entire globe should indeed respond...
And seeing the united protest of the whole Jewish people, one begins to believe with perfect faith in the words I once heard from Jabotinsky, that in twenty years' time the question of who is [?] to have the say over Eretz Israel will no longer exist, because all of us — I and you — will be the ministers and the administrators of our state, which is called Eretz-Israel (including also Transjordan), and all the problems, all the disputed questions over which we fight each other now, and all our enemies, with the Hitlers, who poison our lives at every step, will in twenty years' time, when our children will have to take over the helm, no longer exist, and there will instead be people who go their own way and build their own land, calmly and securely...
And to you, my friend, as also to all your colleagues, the Łódź manufacturers, I wish that if they must lose a strike, they should rather be privileged to lose it to their own Jewish workers, in their own land, in Eretz-Israel, because I know that this is what they hope for, and this is what they will surely have in mind when they say tonight at the Seder: "This year here, next year in the Land of Israel"...
Sosnowiec, Erev Pesach 5694.
In Honour of Passover. Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around the Passover Haggadah.

In Honour of Passover.
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around the Passover Haggadah.
Collected and styled by Yehuda Yafet.

a) "We were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt"
To the questions we ask — why one must eat matzah, sit reclining, etc. — the answer is: "We were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt", and in Egypt we had to do harder things: to work in mortar and bricks, and we asked no questions... So we may also fulfil the commandments and ask no questions...
The Rabbi of Lissa [Leszno].

b) "In the beginning our forefathers were idol-worshippers."
A Hasid came to the Kosów rebbe, R' Yaakov Shimshon, and told the rebbe that he had, in a lucky hour, signed the betrothal terms for his daughter. The rebbe asks him what sort of groom he has taken; the Hasid answers:
— A modern, of-today's-world one.
The rebbe asks him: what does such a thing mean, "of today's world"? The Hasid explains: he is a bit irreligious, not careful about this and that — in one word: a goy...
The rebbe laughs innocently: that is what you call "of today's world"? "In the beginning our forefathers were idol-worshippers", says the author of the Haggadah — our ancestors were goyim long, long ago; so your son-in-law is not "of today's world" at all, but a very, very old-fashioned one, from the days of Terah...
Daat Zekenim.

c) "Your seed shall be strangers... And it is this that has stood by our fathers and us."
"And it is this" — that we feel ourselves strangers in the lands of exile, that we do not want to join with the nations and crawl at their feet — this is what has stood by us and our fathers... The Gemara in Pesachim (116, as printed) says: "What caused Israel to be scattered among the nations? — They delight in approaching [them]", because they want to come close to the nations, to become like them — and thereby they sink even deeper into exile. We must always remember "your seed shall be strangers in a land not theirs": when we find ourselves in a land not ours, we must always feel like strangers.
R' Naftali Zvi Yehuda Berlin (the Netziv).

d) "Go and learn what Laban the Aramean sought to do."
Laban actually had only money quarrels with Jacob and nothing more; on the contrary, he even protected him from Esau — and yet the author of the Haggadah says that "Laban sought to uproot everything": by associating with Jacob, with his flattering speeches, by supposedly protecting him from Esau, he wanted to uproot from the root his whole Jewishness.
Imrei Shefer.

e) "You grew and became great and came to excellent beauty."
Once at the Seder the Sanz [Nowy Sącz] rabbi interpreted wittily the verse "You grew and became great and came to excellent ornaments; your breasts were fashioned and your hair was grown, yet you were naked and bare". "You grew" (va-tirbi) — sometimes a Jew "rebbes" himself, talks himself into being a rebbe; "and became great" — considers himself great; "and came to excellent ornaments" — adorns himself with finery; "your breasts were fashioned" — disciples and Hasidim receive from him his Hasidism too; "and your hair was grown" — a broad beard and sidelocks; but in truth — "yet you were naked and bare": you are naked and empty of commandments and Torah...
Mekor Chaim.

f) DeTZaKh, ADaSh, BeAHaV.
Once R' Yitzhak of Volozhin [Wołożyn] and R' Mendele of Lubavitch were summoned to Petersburg to the Minister of Education about a series of religious matters. As often, a dispute developed about the Jewish religion. A prominent [?] priest took it upon himself precisely to prove that Jews need blood for matzah. The rabbis refuted all his "proofs". Then the priest appeals with a new proof: in the Haggadah one says the acronyms DeTZaKh, ADaSh, BeAHaV. What are these secret acronyms for? It is surely a secret sign: DeTZaKh — "dam tzrikhim kulam", "all need blood". This is a secret sign that everyone should use blood for the matzot at the Seder.
The rabbis try to answer: these are the initials of the plagues — blood, frogs, lice, etc. But the priest sticks to his own: why initials of the plagues? There must be a secret sign here, and it has to do only with blood. R' Yitzhak sees that with the truth nothing will be achieved here, so he says to the priest:
— True, these are acronyms about the blood libel, and here they are: DeTZaKh — "dovrim tzorreinu kazav" (our enemies speak lies), ADaSh — "alila dam sheker" (the blood libel is a lie), BeAHaV — "bnei Avraham chalila be-zot" (the children of Abraham — far be it from them).
With this R' Yitzhak showed how "strong" our enemies' arguments against us are: acronyms, which one can interpret as one likes.

g) "With matzot and bitter herbs they shall eat it."
Today we fulfil it — said R' Hershele of Halberstadt — today we eat matzot together with bitter herb, because the matzot come to us with bitterness... (with hardship, until one earns enough for the matzot).
Tzvi la-Tzaddik.

h) "Mighty is He, may He build His house soon, speedily, speedily in our days, soon."
The Gemara says in Gittin (68) that with God "speedily" means eight hundred and fifty-two years — that is "speedily", fast, with God... So we say: build the Temple "speedily in our days" — in our "speedily", and not, God forbid, according to Your "speedily"...
Machatzit ha-Shekel.

i) Seder matters.
The Midrash on Beshalach says: "God led them about by the way of the land of the Philistines — hence they said: even the poorest in Israel shall not eat until he reclines". Actually a poor man ought to be exempt from reclining, since for him the symbol of lordship is only an irony — and yet he is obliged to recline. The Midrash derives it from "God led them about by the way of the land of the Philistines": there the redemption happened in a supernatural way, and the poor man too cannot know whether help beyond the natural order is not destined for him, whether the symbol of lordship will not become true for him...
Ktav Sofer.
• • •
The commandment to drink wine on Passover the Jewish scholar R' Yitzhak Ber Levinsohn tries to interpret in a scientific way:
As is known, the ancient Egyptians did not drink wine; they believed that wine is the blood of their [—?] whom the evil god Typhon (Baal Zephon) had turned into wine. Only the Pharaohs themselves were allowed to drink wine. Therefore on Passover one drinks wine in memory of the liberation from that idolatrous cult.
Efes Damim.

j) The Seventh Day of Passover.
The Sages say that at the splitting of the Red Sea God did not know whom to drown: "these are idol-worshippers and those are idol-worshippers" — the Egyptians and the Jews were alike. And therefore — the world says as a jest — a man's matchmaking is likened to the splitting of the Red Sea: because mostly, in a match, each seeks to fool the other, but in truth both fool each other — "these are idol-worshippers and those are idol-worshippers" — it is hard to determine whom to drown...
———
In Galicia, as is known, the Hasidim strongly hated the Zionists, and what galled them was that the Zionists were mostly freethinkers who had no fear of the rabbinical bans and curses. So Rabbi Yehoshua'le of Dzików interpreted "and he became there a great nation (goy gadol) — this teaches that they were distinctive there": if you come to a town where you see Jewish goyim (a "great goy"), this teaches that Israel were "distinctive" there — that the Jews there are Zionists...
Yitzhak Katzenelson — From Egypt to the Land of Israel (Eastern Motifs)

Yitzhak Katzenelson
From Egypt to the Land of Israel.
(Eastern motifs)

I.
O low Egyptian sky, you are heavy as lead,
and black you are, and sticky, like pitch;
height does not serve you, nor does freedom[?] serve you —
O you [gagbi]-sky[?], you are coarse and fat and brazen...
Something pulls you down... down into the valley, as
a drunkard is pulled to a barrel of wine, both full and big;
it pulls you to the valley, to the Nile valley, as a Jew is pulled
to a kosher home... and as the lecher to a harlot's lap...

Every sky dips itself piously in a salty sea,
as a modest woman immerses in the clear spring of a mikveh;
but the sky rises again, quiet and mute,
and repays the earth with sweet drops for the salty ones —
O sky-blue! —

But you, sky of lust, you hang over the Nile valley...
you hang
and breathe heavily and whisper openly and freely, and everyone
hears,
and everyone knows of your desire and what you long for —
O sky, Egyptian sky — you smell
of sin, of earth...

II.
From Shem to Ham — brothers, it is not far after all,
from the Land of Israel to Egypt is nearer still;
whether I come from Zion or from Zoan, dear people —
I come from both these places, and more sunburnt..

I am from Nob, a city of priests near Jerusalem;
Nob, my city, rhymes with Moph, which is Egypt;
Nob and Moph — to this day I cannot free myself
from either —
Nob and Moph — ah, two wives of one lover...

If one wishes, the Land of Israel is far from Egypt;
if one wishes, a desert lies wide and great between the two;
and if one really wishes, one makes this journey in a short time —
one can make it in suffering and also in joy...
Moshe Feinkind — The Prager Rabbi and Yakl His Servant (A Passover Tale)

Moshe Feinkind.
The Prager Rabbi and Yakl His Servant.
(A Passover tale).

The old Prager rabbi, R' Yosef Prag, had a servant; Yakl was his name.
The rabbi was an excitable man, and Yakl, for his part, a great jester.
He would make fun of and mock even his own rabbi.
But being a faithful servant, the rabbi forgave him his jokes and nonsense and kept him by his side all along.
In the rabbi's house Yakl, the servant, listened in a great deal and also became a little acquainted with the "small letters" [the fine print of commentaries], and as the saying goes: "Even the rabbi's servant can rule on a halakhic question."
But in the synagogue he was not called up to the "Torah reading" as "Haver", as was done for others of his kind.
The synagogue beadle called Yakl up merely as "Ya'amod Yaakov ben..."
His rabbi would on no account give him the title "Haver".
And in those days, when the town rabbi had not granted someone the title "Haver" or "Morenu" in writing and over his signature, that person could not be called up to the Torah with such an honorific.
This hurt Yakl badly, and when he asked his rabbi about it, the rabbi would always[?] put him off with the answer: "Yakl, you are not worthy of it."
Because of this our Yakl also suffered great humiliation in the synagogue: every time the beadle called him up to the Torah, the congregation, as if out of spite, shouted a great cynical laugh after him: "Ya'amod Haver Yakl ben..."
So Yakl grew angry[?] and resolved to take revenge on his rabbi for the shame he caused him and for not wanting to give him the "Haver title"...
* * *
It was the eve of Passover. R' Yosef Prag sent his servant out to the market to buy apples and nuts for the "haroset".
Yakl dawdled in the street a good[?] while, loafed about[?] and joked about everything under the sun.
The rabbi waits for the fruit with great impatience; he wants to prepare in good time for the "Seder", and Yakl is nowhere to be seen.
He waits nervously and sends someone to look for him. Yakl does come home, but instead of going into the rabbi's room he gets to chatting in the kitchen with the cook, etc.
This impudence of his servant made the rabbi lose his patience, and in great anger he wrote in chalk on the door through which Yakl had to come in to the rabbi the word "behemah" [beast]...
Coming to the door, Yakl noticed "behemah" written in the rabbi's hand; Yakl felt insulted, understanding perfectly well that the rabbi meant him by it, and added to it the word "atah" [you are].
And when the rabbi, coming out of his room, noticed his servant's addition, he grew very angry at him for his great impudence in taking him, the rabbi himself, for a beast, when he, the rabbi, is the mara de-atra [chief rabbinic authority] of a "mother-city in Israel".
Yakl asks the rabbi [printed: "der rov"] why he calls him "behemah"; R' Yosef Prag excuses himself, saying that he [Yakl] is in the first place[?] a great ignoramus: the word means "Ba-shuk hayita, mah heveta" — you were at the market, what did you bring; put the initials of these words together and you get "behemah".
If so, Yakl plays the innocent, the word "atah" means "Egozim ve-tapuhim heveti" — I brought nuts and apples.
But R' Yosef Prag sent his servant into town a second time to take care of something more before the holiday, and then wrote on the same door the word "ain-peh" [ע"פ].
Yakl, coming home, noticed this too and added the word "lamed-shin" [ל"ש].
The rabbi interpreted it as the servant calling him "loke'ah shohad" [a bribe-taker].
That really made R' Yosef Prag lose his temper, and he gave him the "proper ruling", as was due for the insult.
Now Yakl asked: why does the rabbi call him "azut panim" [brazen-faced]?!
Our rabbi again excuses himself: he did not at all mean to offend him with the two letters; he only wanted to remind him that today is "Erev Pesah" and he should not dawdle long in town.
If so, Yakl explains in turn, he too only wanted to remind the rabbi that tonight is "Leil Shimurim" [the night of vigil]...
* * *
On Passover morning the congregation noticed the old rabbi calling the synagogue beadle over before the Torah reading and whispering something in his ear.
The congregation thought: who knows what blood libel or other misfortune hangs over the town once again, such as always used to befall the Jews there at Passover time.
But how surprised and astonished the congregation was to hear the beadle call up the rabbi's servant to the Torah on the first day of Passover: "Ya'amod he-Haver Yakl ben"...
Naturally the congregation grew curious to know what could suddenly have happened that Yakl should now be called "Haver"...
So they asked the rabbi about it, and the rabbi had one answer: my Yakl earned it honestly ["kosher"] this Passover — and basta.
Only after the rabbi's death did the town learn the real reason why Yakl the servant became a "Haver": because he was an expert in initials.
But by then Yakl was already being called up to the Torah as Haver; they did not want to annul the old rabbi's ordinance.
"Zangen" (Ears of Grain) — section for theatre, literature and culture; Leyzer Shikman: Coal Miners

Zangen ["Ears of Grain"]
Section for theatre, literature and cultural matters

Leyzer Shikman.
Coal Miners.

Zagłębie has many of them, the coal miners,
the darkened tuberculosis-diggers [?]...

I do see them in the streets,
when they trail out of the pits, wet with sweat,
with little carbide lamps in their hands,
and with faces smudged [?] with coal, pale...

Like their faces, so are their lungs;
two kinds of death are prepared for them:
one is devoured by tuberculosis,
another is buried alive in the pit..

In the caves of death down there,
in the gloom-filled abysses of the pits,
far from light, air and sunshine;
in the kingdom of "black diamonds"
the lives of coal miners quickly wither, pass away..
Spiritual and Moral Bankruptcy

S. Rotenberg.
It is a sad fact that the material decline, the want and misery now reigning in the Jewish street, are accompanied by a frightful spiritual depression. Almost the entire Jewish press has been terribly debased by "shund" [trash literature]; the Urke Nachalniks and Maciejewskis [?], criminals and hangmen, have become the literary tone-setters for tens of thousands of readers. No better — apart from small exceptions — looks the theatre, which keeps sinking into the spiritual filth of banal erotic conflicts, of husband-and-wife acrobatics chewed over for the thousandth time. The public, taken in by the hallowed name of a star or by tendentiously written reviews, sees, instead of true artistic performances, contrivances of the worst sort; instead of experiencing purely artistic emotions, one breathes the brothel atmosphere of the various "Din Toyres", of "A Night in Bravilin" [?]. Stupefied by such spiritual narcotics, the mass is diverted from the most pressing social problems; it becomes incapable of reflecting on its extraordinarily sad situation.
"Bread and theatre-games" — this demand of the Roman plebs should not be regarded merely as a coarse lust of the mob. Bread and theatre (as well as art in general) belong to the essential foods without which a normal physical and spiritual life is hard to imagine. And just as physical existence needs vitamin-rich nourishment, so it is with intellectual life, which for its sustenance must have spiritual vitamins in the form of artistic emotions. The urge to consume art in its most varied expressions is a necessity deeply rooted in the catacombs of the human soul. And a crime is committed by those who produce trickery and clown-spectacles instead of true, pure art.
A further proof of the moral and spiritual decline is card-playing. Today it belongs to the bon ton of "better" society to be versed in this "art". Otherwise one is exposed to the danger of being regarded as an idler. Cards are played alone and in company, privately and in society. For card-players the problem of time and space does not exist; at every moment and wherever they meet, their brains are at once dominated by the strategy of the "Obers" and "Unters".
About card-playing Schopenhauer writes in his "Wisdom of Life" that: "Card-playing is the yardstick for measuring the worth of society and the acknowledged bankruptcy of thought. In truth, since people have no thoughts they could exchange with one another, they exchange cards and seek to take each other's money."
If one takes into account that the great camp of card-players also includes people with half and whole diplomas, people who ought to have served as a model for the growing generation by their serious attitude to life and to all the problems on the agenda, the picture becomes even starker and sadder.
Another unmistakable sign of the moral and spiritual decay is "shmendrikism" — the being ashamed of Yiddish by all sorts of pseudo-intellectuals and above all by the "Nasz Przegląd" intellectual ladies.
It happens that one meets such an "intellectual lady", whose entire cultural baggage consists of a few modern novels read through (but badly digested) and connoisseur's opinions on films and movie stars; such a "spiritual giant" [?] blushes with shame when spoken to in Yiddish, especially in "better" company.
Among what other people will one find such moral decay and self-denial, such shame of one's own language and culture? These poor people do not know that this is a morbid phenomenon, which psychoanalytic science designates by the term: inferiority complex.
This chaos and disorientation of the masses is exploited by the various "leaders", who ride on the people's neck and perpetrate all sorts of swindles; like Judas they sell the most vital [lit. bloodiest] interests of the people for pennies, without asking anyone. They confront the masses with accomplished facts.
But the greatest tragedy in all this is that the youth too is being dragged into this moral and spiritual swamp. People do not know that, just like a tender plant, youth too must have a pure atmosphere and enough light in order to blossom and develop. A true youth cannot breathe in moral corruption. Otherwise it must degenerate and perish.
Does this mean that under the prevailing conditions one must give up the struggle against the spiritual and moral filth and against the existing injustices in general?
No, and a thousand times no!
Resignation is worse than death, for with death comes also the dying away of consciousness, whereas resignation means having the consciousness of eternal powerlessness and decay. It is a slow agony without that heroic [?] happiness and enthusiasm which struggle brings with it.
And let the spring that has arrived — that wonderful, eternally self-renewing mystery, which awakens from the long winter sleep a fresh, young life, striving towards the light and creating — serve as a symbol that the long, dark night will not last forever, that in the East a strong light is already appearing of a new, rising, better tomorrow for the million-strong camps of the working and creating.
—o—
Literary Chronicle.
The situation of the Jews in Germany in the year 1933.
In Paris an important book has just appeared on the situation of the Jews in Germany during the last year, that is, since the barbaric Hitler regime came to power.
The book is published by the "Committee of Jewish Delegations" and is called "The Black Book — facts and documents on the situation of the Jews in Germany in the year 1933". The book, over 500 pages, relates in a scholarly manner how the Jews were humiliated and persecuted during this time in a horrifying and shameful way.
Old Jewish folk tales in English.
These days an important and interesting book, "The Story Book" [Ma'aseh Book], has come out in Philadelphia, especially for Jewish children in English-speaking countries.
The Ma'aseh Book consists of two volumes and contains a treasury of splendid Jewish tales and legends from the Middle Ages and earlier periods of Jewish history. They were collected and translated into English by the London Jewish scholar Dr. Moses Gaster, who is a specialist in old Jewish folklore.
Almost half of these tales and legends are taken from the Talmud and Midrash. The rest are from the medieval period, mostly about Jewish rabbis and tzaddikim.
A new work on Oscar Wilde.
The well-known Jewish poet and essayist Imber has just published (through the Warsaw publishing house "Gebethner and Wolff") a book about the famous English poet Oscar Wilde.
The book is called "The Song and the Soul of Oscar Wilde" and expresses a new view of the talent and interesting personality of the great poet.
The history of child-snatching among the Jews in Russia.
In Warsaw there appeared not long ago a large historical work entitled "Cantonists", by A. Levin. It is the history of the saddest of times, under Tsar Nicholas I, when young Jewish children were seized in a cruel manner and given away to serve as soldiers for twenty-five years.
The book contains a mass of important material on military service for Jews in Russia and Poland in those dark times.
An increase in books in England.
The official organ of the book publishers in England reports that in 1933 more books were printed in England than in the year 1932.
The number of new books in 1933 is 15,022 [?]. In 1932 the number was 14,834.
The increase was in the sections of books on sociology, biography, religion and philology.
The number of new novels was also greater than in 1932. The greatest number was in October — 256 new novels.
Sholem Aleichem institutions asked to send material.
The Yiddish Scientific Institute of Vilna [YIVO], which is now preparing for the celebration of the 75th birthday of the great Jewish humorist Sholem Aleichem, is seeking material for the celebration; the executive of the Institute appeals to all establishments and institutions that bear the name of Sholem Aleichem to send the Institute whatever material they have in connection with Sholem Aleichem, such as pictures, printed matter, reports of their activity and the like.
The address of the Institute is: Vilna, Wiwulska [Wiwulskiego] 18.
From the Book Table

Yakov Reyzfeder: "Azoy iz es geshen" ("That Is How It Happened"), a novel, Kultur-Lige, Warsaw 1933.
A book of big-city misery. Of tragic love and of glorious struggle.
As if on the edge of an abyss, two young lives struggle in despair, reach for simple life like a plant toward the sun, cling to it with their last strength as to pieces of a sinking ship — and are lost in that abyss called the big-city hell. For the big-city stream of life races and roars with impetus and haste; it sweeps away and — wipes out, tramples and destroys, mercilessly[?], hundreds of lives. People cast out by want, by utter abandonment. Who looks at them, whose concern are they? And when that one poet comes and shows us, describes for us with his heart's blood their enormous suffering, fight and struggle, their miserable path of life — we are shaken and cannot free ourselves of it for a long time afterward, even when we wholly disagree with some of the author's conclusions.
What does Y. Reyzfeder tell us?
Of a tragic love between a 28-year-old unemployed, hungry office clerk named Victor and a young street girl, Irena, an orphan, who sold herself for the first time out of want, wishing to save with the money earned her beloved from his deathbed — he who was the last content of her life. But Irena had already remained on the street. And then the two outcasts of life met by chance: the unemployed clerk and the street girl. They became acquainted, became friends, and she shared with him in that [—] her poor bread. Their life together began, in want and in looking for work. But they found no work, and hunger became a true resident with them. Irena, forced by hunger, began again to — sell herself in secret. Victor suspects her and follows her until he discovers the truth. Irena cannot bear the shame and commits suicide. That is more or less the content of the novel.
It is, however, desirable that the reader get to know the book himself, for even the best retelling cannot convey what is essential, the intimate warmth and the pain that vibrate between the lines. And Reyzfeder's novel is more than literature: it is unmediated naked life itself in all its terrifying[?] struggle of rise and fall, of upsurge and resignation, which grips us right at the beginning and keeps us in suspense to the end. The heroes are drawn so vividly, above all Irena, that we are overwhelmed by their fate, rejoice at their victory and ache at their failure, and it illuminates for us all the hidden chambers of the human soul and all its vibrations. In Reyzfeder above all the lyrical and purely human feeling dominates, which forces its way through all human stumbling; through social injustice a person — in this case Irena — is pushed by force into the arms of the swamp, from which there is no longer any way back.
