But Reyzfeder has not shown us the source of this evil, this accursed order which has brought it about that such Irenas — children of poor homes — must sell themselves for bread and go under; he contents himself with saying, in one place: "I think of the time when fire-winds will overturn the order of our present life, how much gold we will find in the swamps of want and degradation." — But to us these are fine words that are not based on any force. Also not right is the situation in which Victor, having convinced himself that Irena is selling herself anew — becomes her stern judge.
Knowing full well that she did it out of her great love for him and so that they would not both die of hunger — should one judge Irena, who suffers so much and is so tormented by life? Also not right is the novel's finale, that Victor, after he had already lost everything, no longer wanted to live — that is what all weak natures do, who learn nothing from life, who instead of going out into life with clenched[?] fists, rousing, fighting and demanding — give up at once. As for the descriptions, they are vivid and compact[?]. The language is fluent, and in places, in the nature descriptions, Reyzfeder succeeds in rising to purely poetic tension. The dialogue — concise and polished. This problem is something new in our literature. The book pains, purifies and uplifts.
N. Shternberg, Warsaw.
In the Children's World.

[Children's section — poetry; for Passover.]
A section for our children in honour of Passover. — Compiled by S. Libassohn [?].

Spring Is Coming!

The days start growing longer,
One begins to feel better:
  Spring-life is coming —
  Spring is a joy!

And the nights, they grow shorter,
They grow ever more beautiful:
  A fresh breeze is blowing —
  Spring is a joy!

Birds go strolling in the air:
On the fields begins to stir
  All that has been sown —
  Spring is a joy!

On the eve of spring, sun rays —
Doors, windows, they fall upon them!
  They open them wide —
  Spring is a joy!

For spring, the long-awaited...
They look out eagerly and wait,
  All, young and old —
  Spring is a joy!

One begins to feel the spring,
The children start to play,
  Singing, gladdened —
  Spring is a joy!

For the sake of the little children,
Spring brings a fortune;
  Light and warmth —
  Spring is a joy!

Spring shines and spring warms!
It comes shaped [?] with sunshine...
  Spring-life is coming —
  Spring is a joy!

Ch. Y. Farber.

Let's Make a Holiday.

By Ch. Y. Farber

Spring is once again
Here with us as a guest;
Let's make a holiday,
As befits the spring!

  Let's make a holiday
  Out in the open field:
  Every child should come,
  There will be a whole world there!

Every child should come
To go out to the field;
No one should be missing,
Then it will be [—] [?]!

  No one should be missing
  With his merriment;
  Come, lovely games
  Are all prepared!

Come, lovely games
To play them nicely;
One of the games
Will be the loveliest!

  One of the games
  Will consist of this:
  Every child a little tree
  Shall plant on his own!

Every child a little tree
Shall diligently plant;
A whole forest
Will grow from them one day!

  A whole forest will come
  Out of the game;
  Fresh, young little trees
  Spring makes them big!

To the fresh young little trees
Spring gives strength!
And to us — all the children,
It brings nothing but happiness!

  Spring is once again
  Here with us as a guest;
  Let's make a holiday,
  As befits the spring!
The Disappointed Little Sheep

[Children's section — fable.]
(From Yehuda Steinberg's fables.)

A persecuted and long-suffering little sheep, which day in, day out was treated very cruelly by the unfaithful shepherd, — once sank deep in thought:

— Why are we, foolish sheep, forced to suffer such lifelong torment under the evil rule of base shepherds, as though our feet had been forged into chains? After all, the wide world is always open to me. Look, not far away green hills reveal themselves, covered with fresh grass, fertile valleys, full rivers with clear waters! And even when the gloomy autumn days and cold winter evenings arrive — the unwelcome time for the poor sheep — well, if my wool warms the shepherd and many people sate themselves from my blessed breasts — why then should my wool not serve me myself as a protection and defence against the cold, and my milk — to sate me during the short course of the few cold winter months?

The pensive little sheep, as she thought, created for herself beautiful notions, lofty ideal plans of "liberation" and "redemption", which await her in the very near future. She resolved within herself to wait a little while longer, until her recently shorn wool grows back; then [printed "he"] she would tear herself away from the herd [?] and run off wherever her eyes might lead. She even pictured to herself, foretasting the [savour] [?] of revenge, how her hostile shepherd would acknowledge his guilt and beat his breast with "chatati" ("I have sinned") for the sin he committed against his poor little sheep, who had given him his bread and drink and had also clothed his nakedness.

A very fine thought and a happy idea this would have been for our poor little sheep, had the shepherd not caught her in time and sheared off her newly regrown thick wool, and had he not milked the fresh milk from her fat, laden breasts.

And so, naked, frozen with cold, with emptied, shrivelled breasts, our little sheep now stands, saddened and disappointed, in a lonely corner of a cold stable; she is ashamed of her own thoughts, and of the happy plans which — to her grief and shame — did not succeed.

Oh, poor little sheep!
If You Want to Please Everyone (A Little Tale)

Once a father and his son were travelling a long way. There were no railways yet, so they took a donkey with them. The father rode on the donkey and the son went on foot. Meanwhile a passer-by came upon them and addressed the father: How have you no pity on your weak child?
The father was ashamed, climbed down from the donkey and set the child on it, and so they continued their way.
A second passer-by met them, who addressed the son:
— You shameless one, how have you no pity on the feet of your old father?
Hearing these words, the father too climbed up onto the donkey, and the two of them rode together on the donkey.
A third passer-by met them and, seeing how the poor donkey was worn out, dragging the father and son on its back, he called out to the riders:
— Ah, you wicked people, how have you no pity on a weak animal, that you ride the two of you together on the donkey.
Wishing to comply with the third passer-by, they both climbed down from the donkey and went on foot, the three of them — the father, the donkey and the son.
A fourth passer-by met them and laughed at them, saying:
— Look, there go three donkeys and not one rides on the other...
They thought to themselves: how does one manage to please everyone?
And they decided: the father and son will go on foot and the donkey shall ride on them...
Translated from the Hebrew
Akiva Rabinowicz.
Passover Tales.

Before Passover a teacher told his pupils about the ninth plague, with which God punished the Egyptians — the plague of darkness.
The darkness, the teacher said, was so great then that no one could see his neighbour and no one could move from his place.
When Pharaoh saw that things were bad, he sent for Moses, asking him to pray to God that it should become light again.
— How could the messenger see in the darkness to go and call Moses? — a pupil asked.
— You fool, — a second pupil retorts, — he must have spoken to Moses on the telephone.
Spring. (A Picture)

Beautiful is the spring! Beautiful with clouds and fog drawn out into pieces, threads and cobwebs, torn and broken. Beautiful with the quiet, charming, radiant, blue-smiling patches of sky. And with the sun, which swims [?] — a tearful bride — out of the white veil of fog and dives back under, ashamed.
And beautiful is the first trembling of the forest — awakened from a good dream by good tidings. It trembles, it wants to throw off its snowy shrouds and spread newly blossomed branches for the winged singers who come from abroad.
Beautiful is hoping; beautiful are the tidings that are carried on the light wings of the wind, over valley and mountain, over river and forest — — —
Downhill, downhill rush, murmuring, ringing, winding, deep-blue little streams between white snowy fields; pointed-green, life-thirsty little heads already peep out here and there from the snow and ask: When?
After I. L. Peretz.
Perished for the Sanctification of God's Name

[Fiction — pogroms; serial.] H. Asterman.
(A tragic story of a Jewish daughter at the time of the Ukrainian pogroms in 1919).

In bygone years, when Jews had the custom of recording every important event that took place in the shtetl in a pinkas (communal register), in those years an event such as the one I am about to tell you here would surely have been recorded not only in a pinkas but on parchment, and the parchment would have been handed down from one generation to the next, and on every yahrzeit the rabbi of the shtetl would have read the story aloud like a megillah before the congregation of Jews, and all the Jews would have wept tears of blood over what the rabbi read, and the rabbi together with the Jews would have said Kaddish for the Jewish martyr Chana Hornstein, who on the nine[?] days of the month of Av, on Tisha b'Av, in the year 1919, perished for the sanctification of God's Name (al kiddush ha-Shem).

In that shtetl where Chana Hornstein died, however, the events of the shtetl were not recorded in any pinkas, and the world would never have known of the remarkable story of the holy girl Chana.

Yet it was fated after all that the brutal[?] and wondrous deeds of 18-year-old Chana should not be forgotten in the world: I met the parents of that holy girl, and through them I learned the whole story.

The tragic story happened in Ukraine, in the shtetl of Bilovka [Biłówka?], which lies not far from Proskurov. There lived a Jewish rich man named Chaim Hornstein.

And there was a great difference between the rich man Chaim Hornstein and other rich men. Although he was wealthy and possessed almost so much money that he could by himself have bought up the whole shtetl of Bilovka, he was nevertheless, in himself, very plain and modest. His modesty went so far that he really behaved, as the saying goes, lower than grass and quieter than water.

A few hundred Jewish families lived in Bilovka, and they had their own synagogue and, to make the distinction, a bathhouse, and Reb Chaim Hornstein did not seek, here or there, that people should pay him honour. In the synagogue Reb Chaim did not have his "seat" at the eastern wall, and, to make the distinction, in the bathhouse he did not "puff himself up" as is the way with rich men. Reb Chaim Hornstein never spoke a haughty word to anyone, and for that everyone loved and esteemed him. He was a timber merchant.

And modest as Reb Chaim was, his wife Gitl was in herself even plainer. The Hornsteins lived in a house of their own with many rooms, large and [spacious?] as the forests, and one can imagine that Gitl Hornstein could have afforded to keep not just one maid, but even three maids.

Nevertheless Gitl kept no maids and did the housework herself. At the same time there was not a single communal matter in Bilovka for which Reb Chaim Hornstein did not give the largest donation — from money for matzah for poor Jews to dowering brides (hachnasat kallah).

These were all things that everyone in Bilovka knew; less[?] [known was] what Reb Chaim Hornstein used to give so that no one should know;

But Gitl Hornstein never took a maid into her house, because she feared that in Bilovka it would be interpreted as arrogance, as putting on airs.

Reb Chaim Hornstein, as said, was a timber merchant. The great forest that lay between Bilovka and Nemirov Reb Chaim had held for many years on lease (arenda) from the Bilovka squire (poritz), to whom Bilovka also belonged, along with several other surrounding shtetls and villages.

The squire Shcherbatov came of very high lineage, from counts and princes, and it was even said of him that he had access to the imperial court in Petersburg. And once Chaim Hornstein was the leaseholder of the forest, the Bilovka paupers no longer had to worry about a cold winter. Reb Chaim Hornstein provided all of them with firewood. And they did not even have to go and ask Reb Chaim: he already kept a list of all the needy, and as soon as the last day of the Jewish holidays came, Reb Chaim would already begin sending out whole stacks of wood to all the Bilovka poor.

The Hornsteins were both still young people when Reb Chaim began to grow rich; it was only five years after their wedding when Reb Chaim leased the forest from Shcherbatov. From year to year the Hornsteins' fortune kept growing. And when Hornstein had held the forest on lease for the tenth year, he was counted as the greatest timber merchant in Ukraine.

The Hornsteins had one and only daughter, named Chana. In her virtues Chana took after her parents: kind, quiet, decent, and on top of that very beautiful. When Chana turned ten, she was already esteemed in Bilovka and in many shtetls as a very accomplished girl. There was no gymnasium in Bilovka, and when Chana finished the Bilovka elementary (folks-) school, she had nothing further to learn there, and the Hornsteins could not bring themselves to send her away to a bigger town.

The Haggadah

Koshered and cleansed — by — Bz Amotz

Biur Chametz (Burning the Leaven).
This year we had a fine bit of work burning the chametz of the communal institutions.
Hear what we had to burn.
In the city councils the commissioners ordered the archives of the former city councils and magistrates burnt, along with the photographs of the "city fathers"[?].
And in the Merchants' Association Rubinlicht ordered the copies of the memoranda about remitting tax arrears ("zaległe" taxes) burnt.
In the Jewish banks the directors ordered the protested bills of exchange of the board and council members burnt.
In the kehilla the presidium ordered the letters about the "clean" hands of the parnassim burnt.
Thus we have koshered the Zagłębie communal institutions, and therefore our "Haggadah" is kosher for Passover...

The Modern Seder
Kadesh. One reads[?] Miedziński's speech, and the new aliyah restrictions, and one makes kiddush...
U-rechatz. If you are a member of the tax-assessment commission, wash your hands and say that you had nothing to do with it...
Karpas. Take the coal campaign of the Sosnowiec "Beit Lechem", dip it into the plans of the Będzin mikveh and say "borei pri ha-adamah".
Yachatz. After the "good" winter season, share with your creditors — but see to it that the bigger half stays with you.
Maggid. Promise everyone that
Rachtzah. That the Treasury (Skarb) has already washed you out.
Motzi. That one can already give you a fresh "motzi".
Matzah. All the institutions and the banks are becoming dry as matzah.
Maror. Those who keep commercial books already tasted the taste a few weeks ago.
Korech. Take the peace proposal of the Sosnowiec rabbis, put a few "chal"[?] appeals in the middle, and say: "In memory of Orman-and-Bimka"[?].
Shulchan Orech. Buy a "position"[?] from the Magistrat, so that the "bezrobotni" (unemployed) may have a glass of liquor.
Tzafun. A fresh hidden affair of Sosnowiec public figures has been discovered..
Barech and Hallel go hand in hand: one just keeps praising how good and fine we have it here. A real Garden of Eden.
Nirtzah. Therefore one is indeed[?] an approved "apivatel"[?].
———
(One takes a plate; at the back one puts the distraint receipt for the arrears budget ("zaległy etat"). In the middle — the receipts of the "paushetshke"[?], and right on top — the wife's[?] bill for the pre-holiday goods; and one says with great devotion:)
Ha lachma anya. This is what a merchant of today looks like; di akhalu — one eats up the few gulden; be-ar'a — everything lies in the ground; kol dikhfin — everyone is hungry for a złoty; ve-yekhul — because everyone wants to eat; hashata avdei — today we still have a bit of a say over our "majątki" (property); le-shanah ha-ba'ah, in a year's time, b'nei chorin — we shall be free of everything...
If you believe there is still a person who will listen to your questions, then ask:
Mah nishtanah. Why is the Sosnowiec Magistrat so "democratic"? She-be-khol ha-leilot — in all towns the magistrates maintain the old-age home, but in Sosnowiec the commissioners' council has refused the subsidy?
She-be-khol ha-leilot. All along we thought that once the kehilla passed to the national camp, something substantial would be done for the kehilla; ha-laylah ha-zeh — but when one looks at its activity twice (shtei pe'amim), we see that we have been fooled twice: apart from paying pensions, nothing is done.
She-be-khol ha-leilot. In all times it was known that pious Jews bring their claims before a beit din, and the wild youths run to the gentiles; ha-laylah ha-zeh — but in the present dark epoch, kulo maror, all the fine Jews, the "olive oil", run "nut"[?] to the "sgefl"[?]...
She-be-khol ha-leilot. Once there was a husband and a wife; ha-laylah ha-zeh — but the wife is a "bridge-player"[?] and the husband sleeps at home[?].
And[?] the answer: Avadim hayinu. We are "farkapet"[?] (buried, stuck) and will go on being servants to every good-for-nothing. Therefore mitzvah aleinu — a duty lies upon us — le-saper, to tell everything that is done by our kehilla providers.
Ma'aseh. There was a story in the town of Sosnowiec: a few public figures wanted to make a little deal ba-laylah, so that nobody should know of it, but the arel (gentile) came, va-yomru lahem, and said to them: "Rabboteinu, Panowie (gentlemen), I shall go to the gmina (municipality) and tell everything."

Ma'aseh be-Rabbi...
Ma'aseh — there was a story of a rabbi... (why mention the names of such holy "tannaim") she-hayu merubin ("who were many", for "mesubin", reclining); they sat reclining at the table in the Skarb (Treasury office), ve-hayu mesaprim — they told what one need not and what one may not — bi-tziyat Mitzrayim: that the Jews of Zagłębie carry all the money (vislern[?] gezogt) out to Palestine; ad she-ba'u — until the naczelnik (district head) declared that it is a lie; va-yomru lahem — he said to them: "Rabboteinu, moi Panowie (my gentlemen), higi'a zman — the time has already come when there is hardly anyone left to take from..."

The Modern Ten Plagues
Blood — when you see the bailiffs before you, your blood freezes.
Frogs — they run about the streets in the new uniforms like "żaby" (frogs).
Lice — an article every merchant carries in his pocket...
Wild beasts (arov) — when the Jewish merchants of Zagłębie heard the words of the inspector from the Izba (Treasury Chamber), they became all mixed up...
Pestilence — the "podatki" (taxes) have killed off the Jewish merchants.
Boils — a topical plague: it is getting close[?] to the city-council elections...
Hail — there will be a hailstorm of candidate lists.
Locusts — before the holiday the Jewish merchants were starved for a "złoty" of takings.
Darkness — never yet has it been so dark in the Jewish street.
Slaying of the firstborn — the "prima" firms. When they draw up a balance sheet, only then do they see that they have taken a beating..

Va-yehi ba-chatzi ha-laylah ("And it came to pass at midnight").
In the "intelligentsia clubs" they play "bridge" — at midnight.
In the gmina they draw up the budget — at midnight.
Meetings of Jewish institutions end — at midnight.
Enough already of telling what goes on — at midnight.

Az rov nissim ("Then many miracles")...
When peace reigns in the Jewish kehilla — there will be many miracles.
When the Jewish institutions receive subsidies from the Magistrat — there will be many miracles.
When the Będzin mikveh is finally finished — there will be many miracles.
When today's Jewish gymnasium pupils are able to say "Modeh Ani" — that will be many miracles...

Echad Mi Yode'a? ("Who Knows One?")
One I know: if you lend someone a few gulden today, you never see them again.
Two, who knows? Two I know: the chairman and the vice-chairman run the whole kehilla apparatus.
Three, who knows? Three I know: three Jewish banks — the Kupiecki, the Spółdzielczy and the Kredytowy — rest in the Garden of Eden.
Four, who knows? Four I know: 4 Będzin magnates raised the budget themselves.
Five, who knows? Five I know: the declarations of the parnassim at the budget[?] sessions lasted 5 hours.

Chad Gadya, Chad Gadya...
Father bought a little goat for 2 gulden and put it in a stable.
Ve-ata — then came the tax office and ordered turnover tax ("obrotowe") paid.
Ve-ata — then came the assessment commission and ordered income tax ("dochodowe") paid.
Ve-ata — then came the Magistrat and ordered premises tax ("lokalowe") paid.
Ve-ata — then came the sick fund and ordered contributions ("składkowe") paid.
Ve-ata — then came the Chamber of Commerce (Handelskamer) and ordered an examination fee ("examinacja"[?]) paid.
Ve-ata — then came the landlord and ordered rent ("komorne") paid.
Ve-ata — then came the kehilla and ordered the communal levy ("etatowe") paid.
Ve-ata — then came the Starostwo (district office) and ordered the unemployment levy ("bezrobotnowe") paid.
Ve-ata — then came the bailiff and took away the little goat that Father had bought for two gulden, for not paying any obrotowe, dochodowe, lokalowe, składkowe, examination fee, komorne, etatowe and bezrobotnowe.
—o—
A Hint in the Haggadah.
To a debtor came someone [to claim] a debt that had been owed for a long time.
When the debtor saw the dunner, he recited the 3 words: Pesach, Matzah and Maror, and says: "Now I owe nothing any more."
"How so, Reb Borukh," asks the dunner, "where is my money?"
The debtor answers:
"Why, the author of the Haggadah says: Whoever has not said these three things on Passover has not fulfilled his obligation (lo yatza yedei chovato) — Pesach, Matzah and Maror:
so I am already quit of the debt."
The dunner answers: "But there it says: on Passover."
The debtor: "With me it is Passover today too — clean, without a penny; I've got plagues, and the sequestrators have cleared out my home."
Leyb Shtabinski.
—o—
Zman Cheruteinu ("The Season of Our Freedom").
Once, when the Jews were redeemed from the Egyptian exile and became independent, Passover was called "the season of our freedom" — today, for Jews, the whole year is a season of freedom. That is:
1) The flats are free of furniture.
2) The pockets are free of a penny.
3) The shelves are free of goods.
4) The worker is free of a stitch of work.
5) Everything is free. Hefker petrushka (a free-for-all)!
Leyb Shtabinski.
When the King

[Passover humour — poem and satirical squibs.]
(A Seder idyll).
À la Konopnicka [after the Polish poet Maria Konopnicka].

When the king recites the Kiddush,
night is steeped in glow and splendour,
the festive joy sings on the table,
and sorrow creeps into its sheath.
———
When the king sips his cups,
worries are pushed down deep,
a spring of melody opens up
and the Seder ball sparkles.
———
When the king cracks the matzah,
everyone crunches along in time,
from the kitchen wafts the sweet aroma, —
fish and meat, compote and broth.
———
And the queen sits by[?],
watches joyfully how the Seder is conducted;
the king finishes "Chad Gadya"
and confers with the radio.
Pantsh.

Because the Wise Son doesn't want to marry at all, the Wicked Son wants the dowry and doesn't want a wife, the Simple Son demands 5 thousand dollars, and the One Who Does Not Know How to Ask doesn't know what he wants..

What do they like best?

What's New in Zagłębie? — Mommy, Don't Drown Me!...

[Head of the local section; Sosnowiec — crime, court.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 14 Nisan 5694 — piątek 30 marca 1934 [Friday, 30 March 1934].)
Mommy, Don't Drown Me!...
The harrowing confession of a child-murderess.
A few weeks ago the dead body of a little girl, a few years old, was found in the river by the Pradła [?] fields.
The investigation established that the murderer of the child was none other than her own mother, the 27-year-old Będkowska [?].
This week the child-murderess stood before the district court in Sosnowiec. Before the judges' bench the child-murderess confessed to the terrible murder. "I was," she says, "without work and had nothing with which to feed my child." At the critical moment she led the child out to the river; there she tied a heavy stone to the child's neck and then threw her into the river...
Weeping, she goes on to relate that when the child sensed the bitter end awaiting her at the hands of her own mother, she begged her, crying:
— "Mommy, don't drown me."
The last words of the child-murderess moved everyone present in the courtroom to tears; several women simply went into spasms.
Będkowska was sentenced to 7 years in prison and to the loss of civil rights for 10 years.
It Is Not Provided for in the Budget...

[Będzin — kehilla, municipality and Passover relief.]
Every Passover campaign of the Będzin kehilla has been supported by the magistrate [municipality] with several hundred złoty. This year too the kehilla board turned to the commissioner [the appointed municipal commissioner] asking him to support the kimcha [de-Pischa] campaign.
In his reply the commissioner explains that he cannot give any holiday support whatsoever, because it is not provided for in the budget.
On the Conclusion of the "Keren Hayesod" Campaign in Będzin

[Będzin — Zionism, Keren Hayesod.]
Last week the "Keren Hayesod" campaign, which was conducted with the participation of the delegate Mr. Yakov Goruszałka [?], was concluded.
The result, despite the most varied disturbances, technical and political, is a very satisfactory one; although the number of declarants [pledgers] did not increase, the sum collected rose considerably.
It is also worth noting that this year the campaign lasted much less time than in previous years.
All this happened thanks to the patronage committee that was created, headed by its president, Mr. Fürstenberg, member of the Jewish Agency, who showed fitting activity in carrying out the campaign.
One must also point out the gratifying phenomenon that this year many new contributors were gained, who contributed for the first time to the building of Eretz Israel, from circles that until now stood very far off.
In general, all contributors showed a hearty and very warm attitude to the campaign, and some contributors considerably increased their pledges this year, by fifty, a hundred and more per cent — which must be attributed to the higher and much deeper understanding of the Eretz Israel cause among the Jewish population in the last year, and to the correct appreciation of "Keren Hayesod" as the central financial apparatus of the Jewish Agency.
In the name of the local "Keren Hayesod" committee and in the name of the central office in Warsaw, the deepest thanks and recognition are hereby expressed to all the esteemed public workers, members of the patronage committee, especially Messrs. President Sz. Fürstenberg, Jakub Gutman and Chaim Szajn, for their devoted and untiring work for the building of a Jewish Eretz Israel for the Jewish people.
Report Meeting of the Sosnowiec "Linat ha-Cholim"

The First Days of Passover in Zagłębie.

[Zagłębie — Passover: Będzin and Sosnowiec.]
On both days of the festival the weather was sunny and coolish. Those who had no new summer coats "refreshed themselves" in their winter clothes; the streets were full of strollers.
This year the Seders at the Będzin orphanage were held in splendid fashion.
The guests present (by the way it must be noted that a large part of those invited did not come...) were shown how Jewish traditions come out richer in content when they are given the proper garb, the proper décor.
And so the teacher Mr. Elchanan Zyder did indeed succeed to a certain degree; he, so to speak, modernised the content of the Haggadah, staged the important passages, wove in suitable Hebrew songs, and the result was a "living Haggadah"...
The children, dressed up in new holiday clothes, sit around the long tables decorated with flowers. The master of the Seder, Jakub Malinowicer, greets the guests in Hebrew and [?] Ferstenfeld — in Polish.
After singing "Hatikvah" and "Chag ha-Pesach" the Seder is conducted, in which Malinowicer, Piniek Golder, Zegelman, Treisman, Danaiger and others take part.
In fluent Hebrew they ask the Four Questions, give the answers, and the whole company bursts merrily into "Vehi she-amda", "Shir chaverim", and then they turn to the Shulchan Orech, to the tasty dishes, which were prepared no worse than in wealthy homes.
The festive Seders end with merry dancing and singing late in the evening.

Year in, year out the Jewish soldiers are provided with Passover food by the kehilla. Present at the Seders were the presidium of the kehilla board, of the council, and public figures, who spent some pleasant time with those torn away from their homes.

Small Remarks on Big Matters

[Zagłębie — community and society; commentary.]
The magistrate's subsidy for Passover.
How far poverty reaches, how terrible the sufferings are of those who are hungry in the literal sense of the word — this can be shown to us by the statistics of those who took kimcha [Passover relief] this year. Jewish Zagłębie has been impoverished to the highest degree.
It is enough to relate that kimcha was received by people who have open shopfront stores on the main streets of Zagłębie. In need of human charity [?] were people who to this day are taxed with quite respectable sums, and people to whom one used to come for donations.
And when we take stock of all this, we arrive at the conviction that the hunger, want and degradation [?] have already reached the point of culmination. Unfortunately, not a crumb of bright light is to be seen on the horizon, regardless of the fact that spring is soon arriving, whose sunbeams will call to a new life and to encouragement.
The pre-Passover mood in the Jewish camp was somehow so depressed, so grey, that no consolation whatever appeared. And when we took a look at whom all had to be provided with kimcha, we had to lower our eyes out of shame and pain.
Moreover, the chronicle tells us that when the representation of the Będzin Jewish kehilla turned to the magistrate [the town council] for support for the kimcha campaign, it received a refusal. It is characteristic: every year the kimcha committee is supported by the magistrate, and precisely this year, when hunger rages with such force, when one could have counted on an increased subsidy, nothing at all was taken into account and the request was rejected entirely. An excuse was found, that no such item is provided for in the budget; but we surely know that if only there had been a will [printed "bewolt"] to help the hungry, a way could have been found and a subsidy would have come about. And who more than a magistrate must care for the town's fallen citizens, for those who paid and still pay taxes to this day and have obligations towards the town and its economy? The magistrate is, after all, the father of the town, who must care for its inhabitants as a father for his children — so how can such a municipal institution remain indifferent while it sees its members suffering?
The magistrate's refusal, its disregard of a topical, urgent request from the representation of the Jewish kehilla, is far from appropriate and gives cause to vex Jewish Będzin, which at all times fulfils its obligations beyond its means.
—
The premises and prestige of the Sosnowiec Small Traders' Association.
At last the Small Traders' Association in Sosnowiec has moved into new premises, so that it only remains to wish it fruitful public activity for the benefit of its members.
Why do we dwell on this fact, which is nevertheless not such an important event? Quite a few institutions move and we do not mention it — but here it is indeed worth devoting a few lines, and this because the writer of these lines once had the occasion to view the former [?] "premises"; but before we climbed up there, to the little attic rooms, a dread seized us; it somehow seemed to us that someone wanted to lure us up there and take revenge on us there — a question about a story: once, perhaps, an untactful note had been written about them — so that it was not easy to reach the doors [?] until they managed to get us up. And arriving at the "departments" there, we felt sad at heart, seeing how low our public life has fallen, that such an institution does not even have premises where the members could be received and where one could meet with people properly [?].
And therefore, now that we see the renewal of the premises, we must tell them that they should not let themselves decline and should keep themselves at the proper level, because the association is not some private little shop, and first and foremost one must surely have decent premises, where people can come in and not have to think that they are hiding [?] something in a concealed place.
It goes without saying that the premises are not yet everything; along with the premises one must have people with initiative, who will run the institution.
That the small traders are living through terrible days is no secret; at the same time the institution has many tasks to fulfil in the prevailing difficult period of our existence. Let the institution take up activity that will help lead — according to its means, of course — the members to a better future. And there is a great deal of work for it today, and of course very, very responsible, ever more serious; it must therefore stand on guard and protect its interests as it should.
—
How is the Sosnowiec kehilla reacting to the new "transaction"?
Well then, we have read the note about the Sosnowiec plenipotentiary [?] public figures, who, in buying a plot for a cemetery, demanded for themselves separately that so-and-so much be let down into their pockets. Nevertheless it is interesting to hear: what do the owners of the transaction say? What do they, the brokers, say about the matter? Surely they too have something to say — so why is not a word heard from them? Have they nothing to tell Jewish Sosnowiec about the reasons for which they set out on this path? Have they nobody here to blame? In our day everything is kosher and for everything one can find a dispensation — so why have they placed themselves behind a fence, as it were, so that they cannot be seen at all?
And one more thing: the gmina, the kehilla representation, the one that issued the powers of attorney — why does it not come forward to say a word on the question? After all, Jewish Sosnowiec knows clearly and plainly everything that goes on on its shoulders — so why is it silent? Why should it not officially communicate what has happened here, how it came about and who the guilty are?
Of course this is no tasty morsel; of course one must be ashamed to raise one's eyes when one lets things sink to such a degradation; of course, had the kehilla stood at the proper level, such humiliation could not have come about — yet this fine piece of work must not be wiped away. We must not wipe it away, neither for ourselves nor for those who made themselves so broadly at home with public money, which today is not at all easy to extract from the impoverished population.
By the deeds of the transaction-makers the Sosnowiec kehilla representation has undoubtedly been humiliated, but that is not enough [?] reason for it therefore to sink further into the mire [?]. It must unconditionally react to the disgraceful deeds, and the verdict must be made public.
If public money is squandered, or even if it is not spared, this must not be taken lightly; otherwise the community may come and ask: what did you, the representatives whom we elected, do about the untactful deeds — and then you will have to give an answer for your deeds before the Jewish population?
If you do not react to this properly, it means that on the one hand you accept that what was done was done with your consent, and on the other hand one may permit oneself to go the same ways again, for it is no crime at all, since no punishment whatever fell upon the guilty; so that this amounts to saying that everything is in perfect order and one may go on along the same paths, and nobody will say that it is not good so. And therefore we ask: what do the kehilla representatives say about the deeds that were done, and how have they reacted to them?
On the contrary, it is worthwhile for them to say a word on the question.
Selekt.
How I Celebrated My Dictatorial Seder...

[Humorous feuilleton — Passover.] Different people give different answers to the question: what is the best thing in the world? Some say: wealth; others — brains; and still others — a good wife. Each one answers according to his notions, according to his understanding and according to what he lacks.

And they are indeed all as right as day, but the rightest of them all am I, with my small pretensions and even smaller aspirations, but with practical experience of life instead, which says: the best thing in the world is — orientation.

It is all the same, whether in communal leadership[?], in politics, or even in private life. Everywhere, if there is only a crumb of orientation, one is already a man of standing. The wind blows to the right — well then, one flies to the right; new birds come with new songs — one has to adapt and do[?] as the world does, for that is the kind of time it is today.

As facts for my words I could enumerate for you here quite a long list of various little people, both from Będzin and from the whole country, who, thanks to their orientation, are always on top and lead everyone by the nose. But since the first days of Passover are already over, I will leave our local "worthies"[?] in peace for now and rather tell you how I myself, on the first Seder night, was saved from a grave misfortune, thanks to my bit of orientation.

And the story went like this:

Passover, the first Seder night. The house is tidied up nicely, clean, festive, royal. On the table stands the finest and the best; my wife[?] — may she be well — in her new holiday clothes, like a true queen, no evil eye harm her, bustles at the table. My little ones[?] — the princes and the princesses — are meanwhile still standing in the corners chatting about something among themselves, probably about politics, as befits princes; and I myself busy myself at my throne. I make it up with cushions, with a backrest, so that it should be soft for ruling the kingdom, both sitting and reclining; and when everything is ready, I order everyone to take his place and to imitate every movement of His Majesty the King — that is, me.

I say it once, a second time, and nobody listens and nobody obeys; one only looks at the other sulkily, sternly, and "jak by nic" [as if nothing], as though I were no king at all, and no father either.

"Folks, come to the table!" I now shout in my weekday voice. "If not, if not..."

Here my little Tsitsik runs up to me in his new buttoned trousers and tells me as follows:

"Daddy! Talmen[?], Yosl, Feyrl, Moshe and Shloyme say that there is no kaiser any more today, all the kaisers have been killed off all over the world!"

And before I even begin to understand what my little Tsitsik means, my elder boy[?] Kalmen comes out with it, the rest of the crowd helps him along, and from everyone's words I catch that things look bad for my dynasty and my throne. Simply — no more kaiser in our day! No more king!...

I even think that my crowd is "joking" at my expense, for — just between us — what sort of a kaiser, so to speak, am I? The whole day before the holiday I worked with my wife as hard as donkeys before we managed to coax Passover into the house, and even now my bills of exchange are still circulating all over town — so what sort of a king am I? But my Moyshele steps forward out of the whole company, takes me by the shoulder and turns to me in an oratorical[?] tone:

"Comrade Daddy! You are, after all, a person with a psychology not of a bourgeois nor of a bloodsucker, and you know how much marrow and how much blood the autocrats, the kings, the protectors of big capitalism have gnawed and sucked out of us! How much[?] blood the proletarian of the whole world shed in the World War, all because of the whims of individuals, of usurpers; but the proletarian, bathing in his own blood, finally cried out: Enough! And... the heads of the firmly-founded, solid emperors with their families flew, without a cock even crowing, and no one even said a Kaddish de-Rabbanan after them — and now you want, Daddy... you want..."

"Down with emperordom! Off the throne! Out with the dynasty!" a shout goes up in all voices from my crowd, and their little eyes sparkle, their little hands clench into fists, ready to put me to death, to tear me like a fish right here on the spot — and here I recall with terror the end of "Tsar Nikolka" with his household, and of "Kaiser Wilus" [Wilhelm II], and of others, and I already want to bid farewell to my life in good time.

"But my dear children!" I still try, nevertheless, to argue with them gently. "I am your father until a hundred and twenty, and you are my children, and I am no despot — after all, I allow you to ask as many as 4 whole questions; and if I am a king, then you are princes and princesses, one dynasty, so..."

"Spare us, spare us!" they all burst out in a shout and an uproar. "A disgrace for a father to be a king! What princes nowadays! Spare us your tsarist equality! Out! Down! Down with everything that smells of tsarism."

And my crowd goes straight for my royal throne, already wants to make a revolution and destroy, one-two, everything standing on the king's table, and later probably also to set about me, the king himself, and my wife the queen, poor thing. Here I feel that this is no longer any joke, and God alone knows what such a wild crowd is capable of — but soon my bit of orientation comes to my aid, and loudly, commandingly, I launch into this kind of "speech":

"Comrade children! If you speak of proletarian power, then who am I, I your father? Am I not myself also a proletarian? And tell me yourselves, what sort of proletarians would you, so to speak, have been, if I had really been a bourgeois, and you — bourgeois children? So it means you have me to thank for your happy proletarian name, life, psychology and methods of struggle? There![?] So, as the eldest of the proletarian household, I declare myself from now on as... as your dictator, you understand? I am no longer called king, because that is really not a fashionable word, and I crown myself, spo![?] That is, I extend my dictatorial power over you, and you must obey me as dictator, and all counter-revolutionaries I will punish with the greatest cruelty."

"Bravo, bravo! Long live our dictator!" my crowd jumps for joy, with my little Tsitsikl in the middle, and my wife, like a devoted mother, rejoices in the children's joy, and I go on speaking:

"Well then, comrade children! Now, when the situation has juridically changed with a new name and a new proletarian power rules, let us get down to factual and practical work and divide the dictatorial leadership in the following manner: you, Kalmen, become the commissar of 'Marorcom' and 'Charosetcom'; Feygl — of 'Winecom'; Yosl — of 'Afikomom'; Moshe — of 'Yachatzcom'; Shloyme — of 'Haggadahcom', and little Tsutsik — the commissar of 'Kushya-Question-com'. Well divided? Nobody wronged[?]? Well then, sit down now all of you at the table and get diligently down to work."

My crowd sat down at my laid Seder table, with the same Haggadah, the same kneidlach and the same "Chad Gadya", and the Seder was conducted with full splendour, like every year — only no more than that, except that I was veiled under a different, more modern name: dictator...

That is how I celebrated my "dictatorial" Seder — all thanks to my bit of orientation.

B. Mendilzon[?].
The Song of Songs

[Passover — Torah sayings and comments.] Torah sayings, remarks and light talk on the Song of Songs. Collected and styled by Yehuda Yafet.

a) The Song of Songs (1:1)
In the Zohar one finds on this verse the following incomprehensible sentence: "The Song of Songs — the sign is TTRV (1006)." What does the Zohar mean here?
The Vilna Gaon gave the following explanation: in Kings (I, 5:13) it is said that Solomon composed a thousand and 5 songs. And this is what "Song of Songs" means: a song above all the songs. So together with the Song of Songs Solomon made 1006 songs. That is why the Zohar gives a sign, TTRV = 1006, to indicate that the Song of Songs does not belong to the thousand and five, but that it is the thousand-and-sixth...
(Edut ha-Gershuni)

b) "Rightly do they love thee" (ibid. 4)
The Sages interpret the love of the Song of Songs as love of God, as piety. But piety must be "meisharim" — straight, human, not a hunchbacked and crooked one..
(Tseror ha-Mor)

c) "As the tents of Kedar [misprinted 'Seder'], as the curtains of Solomon" (ibid. 5)
The tents — the inside of our tents, our homes — "Kedar": they are black and melancholy. The curtains — our outward appearance — "Solomon": it gives the impression of Solomon's wealth. The eternal Jewish tragedy: inside, poverty and want, and outside, before the world, we make the impression of the richest nation...
(Mahaneh Levi)

d) "They made me keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept" (ibid. 6)
"They made me keeper of the vineyards" — all vineyards I have worked, industries I set up for strangers, countries I built up for strangers — "mine own vineyard have I not kept". Only for myself have I not cared, and everything I built with blood and sweat has been recognised as the property of others.
(Beit David)

* * *
"Poor is our honour among the nations, and they abhorred us like the impurity of a menstruant" —
If "our honour" — if we earn respect among the nations — it is "poor", meagre, inferior, and it is belittled as much as possible; whereas "they abhorred us" — if some Jew has sinned "like the impurity of a menstruant", the very smallest sin, it is proclaimed at the top of one's voice: Jews are this and that...
(Knesset Yisrael)

e) "I will rise now and go about the city, in the markets I will seek him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not" (3:2)
In the streets and the markets, there the Shekhinah finds no honesty, no piety, "him whom my soul loveth"; there everyone throws off the Torah and the commandments, which demand honesty and justice — all that is left behind in the beit midrash, in the synagogue...
(R' Yaakov of Lissa)

f) "I adjure you" (ibid. 5)
The Lubavitcher Rebbe once wrote a letter against Zionism, on the ground that God has made us swear not to hasten the End, as the Gemara infers from the said verse that God adjured the Jews "that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till it please" — that one should not wish to leave exile before the time; and the nations, in turn, God adjured not to work the Jews in exile beyond their strength. In short, Jews may not hasten the End.
A Zionist rabbi answered him in a pamphlet: the oath was, after all, a joint one for Jews and nations — the first, that they would not hasten the End, and the latter, that they would not enslave the Jews too much in exile. Well, do the nations keep their oath?.. Then we too may break our oath...

g) "Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet" (4:3)
The scarlet thread — says the Gemara in Yoma (fol. 67) — by it one could tell whether God had forgiven the sins, or whether they had remained sins. So too "thy lips": in a person's mouth one can recognise his sins...
(Siftei Tzaddikim)

*
"Rabbah examined by the tongue" (Hullin 17).
Rabbah analysed a person by his tongue, by his speech...
(Binat Yissachar)

h) "I am sick with love" (5:8)
All our sicknesses and troubles come only because we love our God. That is why we are hated...
(Sforno)

i) "Thy teeth are like a flock of ewes" (6:6)
"This ewe is wholly holiness: its wool for the blue thread, its flesh for a sacrifice, its horns for shofars, its legs for flutes, its innards for harps, its skin for a drum; but the wicked are likened to dogs, from which there is nothing for holiness." Rashi.
So from dogs nothing at all can be used for a holy purpose. That is why the Sages say "the face of the generation is like the face of a dog", because, unfortunately, from our present-day "faces" [leaders] too nothing can be had for a holy purpose...
(R' Yosef Shaul Nathanson)

j) "Sing from the top of Amana" (4:8)
The Gemara says: "Israel will in the future sing a song in the world to come." Jews sing a song about the world to come — about that which they do not see with their own eyes, but only believe... "Sing from the top of Amana [emunah, faith]": we sing for the good fortune that we have faith, that is, that what we are promised will come to be...
(Shelah)

Perished for the Sanctification of the Name (Kiddush Hashem)

[Serialized story — Ukraine, the pogroms of 1919.]
H. Aserman.

(A tragic story of a Jewish daughter at the time of the Ukrainian pogroms in 1919).

Hanna was their darling [lit. "the one trembled over"], and they were afraid to take their eyes off her. The Hornsteins [printed "Harnshteyn"] brought down the best teachers from other big cities for their only daughter. One teacher taught Hanna Russian and prepared her for a gymnasium education, and the second teacher taught Hanna Hebrew.

Chaim Hornstein came from a family of "connoisseurs", maskilim, Hebraists. So he wanted his child to know Hebrew well. Hanna had a good head, and in a couple of years she learned "the holy tongue" quite well. She knew the Bible [Tanakh] so well that even boys would not have needed to be ashamed of it. And the Hornsteins were very glad that their daughter was so accomplished [?] and so learned.

So several years went by. With her Russian teacher Hanna prepared for the examination for the full eight classes of gymnasium. She travelled to Proskurov [today Khmelnytskyi] and sat the examination there. She passed the examinations and came home to her parents a "graduate" with an "attestat" [matriculation certificate]. Her parents were glad. That their daughter had always been together with them, and that she had finished gymnasium. When Hanna brought her certificate home from Proskurov she was about seventeen years old. The Hornsteins, of course, wanted their only daughter to go on to a university and continue studying. But here the old story began once again. They did not want to send their daughter away — she was, after all, the apple of their eye — while Hanna did want to go to Kyiv and get into the "courses" [the Higher Women's Courses], and a difference of opinion broke out between the Hornsteins and their daughter over whether she should go to Kyiv or not.

But something happened such that the Hornsteins themselves had to persuade their only daughter to go away from them into foreign parts.

As already said, Hanna was very accomplished [?], sharp-witted [?], slender as a palm and with dreamy Jewish eyes. The squire [the local nobleman] had a young son who was almost always abroad. Once, when he came home and saw Hanna, she evidently went deep into his heart. With his lordly pride and his habit of always commanding, he thought that he need only tell Hanna that he liked her, and she would grab such good fortune with both hands, and he would be able to do with her whatever he alone wished.

But Shcherbatov [Szczerbatow] made a big mistake. When he once struck up a conversation with Hanna and began paying her compliments, she did not even answer them, and the second time she already avoided even meeting him. But it was hard for her to avoid him. Shcherbatov's manor lay a couple of miles from the forest that Hornstein held on lease. And Shcherbatov liked to ride out every day on horseback into the forest.

And every day he would already seek out some pretext to come to the Jew himself about "business". And here Hanna could not easily avoid him. He would draw her into conversations and speak seductive words to her. But she did not listen to him.

The first few times he told Chaim Hornstein, "just like that", out of the blue, that he had a very beautiful daughter. Shcherbatov talked to him this way about her once, twice, three times, and Reb Chaim Hornstein pretended not to know what the squire meant, until Shcherbatov once told him in plain, simple words that he liked Hanna very much and wanted to marry her.

Shcherbatov came several times uninvited to the Hornsteins' house and each time brought gifts for Hanna with him. Not to accept the presents from him would have been a great insult to him; to accept the presents — he would have taken it as encouragement. It was bad this way and bitter that way. And the Hornsteins decided that the best thing would be to take their daughter and send her away to another town, until the squire's "craze" passed.

But Shcherbatov did not let go. Once, when the squire asked [?] after Hanna and the other [her father] told him that she had gone away, he did not even ask to which town and what her address was; he pretended not to know. But through an official at the small-town post office he found out where the Hornsteins were sending letters and money to Hanna Hornstein. He found out that she was in Proskurov, and it did not take long before Shcherbatov was already in Proskurov, and he even put up at the same hotel.

When Hanna saw the squire at her hotel, her heart nearly leapt out of her from fright, and she told him openly that she was not his equal and that he should look for someone else to pay compliments to.

But now Shcherbatov did not merely pay her compliments. He demanded of her no more and no less than that she convert [from Judaism] and go with him to the "shlyub" [church wedding] (chuppah), and he promised her golden fortunes.

First, the forest for which Hanna's father pays him "lease" every year he would give her father as a gift forever; second, he would take her to Petrograd and present her as his wife to the greatest "heads" of Russia, and she would fare as well with him as a real princess.

What's New in Zagłębie? — A Boycott Week Proclaimed in Zagłębie

[Head of the local page; Zagłębie — anti-Hitler struggle, boycott.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Thursday, 20 / 20 Nisan 5694 — czwartek 5 kwietnia 1934 [Thursday, 5 April 1934].)
A Boycott Week Proclaimed in Zagłębie.
On Sunday the district conference of the anti-Hitler committees in Zagłębie took place in the premises of the Będzin „Merchants' Association“.
About 100 persons from Będzin had been invited to the conference; there came.. in all 20 (read: twenty). The „notables“ did not consider it important to take part in the deliberation; even prominent members of the committee did not come.
From Sosnowiec came 2 representatives and from Dąbrowa — 3.
The conference was opened by Mr. A. Liwer [?], who pointed to the importance of the anti-Hitler action and the necessity of strengthening the boycott action.
It was unanimously resolved to proclaim in Zagłębie a boycott week from the 3rd to the 10th of this month. During the week every town must organise protest meetings; in all minyanim, houses of prayer and synagogues there will be speeches about the sad situation of the German Jews and about strengthening the boycott of all German products.
Sunday, the 8th of this month, has been proclaimed a special protest day.
On that day public protest meetings will take place in all 3 towns: in Sosnowiec in the morning, in Będzin — in the afternoon, and in the evening — in Dąbrowa.
While this point was being considered it turned out that Sosnowiec still has no anti-Hitler committee up to now. The delegates from Sosnowiec openly declared that the Sosnowiec Jews do not show the slightest interest in the anti-Hitler action. This declaration provoked a real storm.
The storm grew even greater when it was established that some Sosnowiec merchants import and trade in German goods. After a stormy discussion the conference unanimously resolved to call upon the leaders of Sosnowiec Jewry to form an anti-Hitler committee immediately and to organise a protest meeting on the 8th of this month.
Mr. Wygodzki points out that during this year, since Hitler began his policy of plunder, various conferences have already taken place in Warsaw, Kraków and Katowice, at which Sosnowiec was not represented at all. Mrs. Ts. Szajn, Messrs. Goldsztajn, Rechnic and others also point out that the honour of the Sosnowiec Jews demands that this time [?] one must immediately begin to work energetically in the field of the struggle against the Hitler plague.
All organisations and parties must be drawn into the action, and those who will sabotage the work should simply be put in the pillory.
The women present — Ts. Szajn, Hojzner and Dr. Taraszewska [?] — also raise the question of activating the Jewish woman in the struggle against the use of German products in the household.
A project is put forward to call a special women's conference in Zagłębie. For this purpose a consultation of representatives of women's organisations will first of all be called. Parallel with the protest action the boycott action is also to be strengthened. All merchants are to be called upon not to trade in any German goods; in particular, women will be called upon not to buy any German merchandise, which is soaked with the tears and blood of the German Jews.
The conference also discussed the question of the „one-time levy“ (danina) for the refugees from Hitler's land — and resolved to call upon all the Jews of Zagłębie, without exception, poor or rich, to take part in the campaign, which must bear a popular character.
The conference also discussed the dangers of Hitlerism in other countries, and it was resolved to undertake concrete steps after coming to an understanding with the central office or with the delegate who will be staying in Zagłębie in the coming days.
———
In conclusion the presidium appeals to all present to work with the greatest energy in the committees, in order to help our unfortunate brothers and to convince the outside world that the Jewish people will in the end overcome the heirs of the barbarian Huns with their bloodthirsty leader: Attila — Hitler.
—o—
[Będzin — economy, Merchants' Association.]
General Meeting of the Będzin „Merchants' Association“
The wish of those assembled is that tram tickets and the telephone charge should become cheaper.
On Monday the annual general meeting of the Merchants' Association in Będzin took place in its own premises.
The president, Mr. Rubinlicht, opens the meeting with a short introductory speech, in which he recalls the loss [printed „avre“] of the former president, Mr. Salomon Gutman of blessed memory; those assembled honour the deceased by rising. On the proposal of those assembled Mr. Icchak Wygodzki takes the chair; Messrs. Herman Pinkus, Natan Goldsobel, Becalel Berkowicz and secretary L. Rechtman are invited to the presidium table.
The report on the activity to date is given by Mr. Rubinlicht, who points out that during the past year the board intervened with various authorities on behalf of the members and of Jewish merchants in general.
The treasurer's report shows that the expenditure and income of the association amount to 6079 zł. Then a discussion took place, in which the outcry of the merchants burst forth in connection with the new Industrial Law. Messrs. Jungster, Buchwejc, Sanduar [?], Leszman, Zelinger, Lewin, Goldfeld, Goler, Wygodzki and others took part in the discussion. The latter criticised the merchants for their indifferent attitude towards the association.
In the discussion the question was also raised of the terrible competition being waged among the merchants, which causes the ruin and downfall of Jewish commerce; the central office in Warsaw was also censured for having neglected its task with regard to the new Industrial Law.
Then advocate Tajtelbaum gives a lecture on the subject „The amendment (nowela) to the Industrial Law and the new Tax Ordinance“. The speaker touches on the most important points of the law and comes to the conclusion that the Industrial Law brings a change into the whole economic life of Poland, and that this is the new line of the government, that all associations and economic organisations must be under the influence of the government.
After fixing the budget for the current year at 8400 zł., the following proposals are adopted: 1) the Merchants' Association should intervene so that electric light, tram tickets and the telephone tariff become cheaper; 2) the express (courier) trains should stop at the Będzin station; 3) the head (naczelnik) of the tax office should extend the reception hours for the public; 4) every month lectures in the Yiddish language should take place in the Merchants' Association; 5) an appeal should be issued to the merchants not to engage in harmful competition; 6) to apply to the Magistrate [town hall] so that the fee for health certificates becomes cheaper.
The elections brought no change at all. The board consists of the existing members.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — health and charity.]
Report Meeting of the „Linat HaCholim“ Society in Sosnowiec.
The board of the „Linat HaCholim“ society, in order to publicise the activity of the society in general and of the out-patient clinic (ambulatorium) in particular, organised on Monday of Chol HaMoed a report meeting in the „Angielski Hall“.
Only „amcha“ came to the meeting — ordinary everyday Jews, who wanted to „have a good time“ where it costs no money; whereas the element the board [?] wanted to interest in the important achievement of the clinic — sat, as always, at home...
After the introduction by the president, Mr. Icchak Goldkorn, Dr. Broniecki reads a lecture on the activity of the clinic for the broad Jewish population. The speaker reports on the society's plans for the future, such as setting up an ambulance (karetka), opening a pharmacy and the like, and he appeals to the Jewish public to support this important institution.
Then the board members, Messrs. Bunem Szpiler, Czarnacha [?], Ajzenbach [?], Klajnman, Konopińska and Goldkorn, speak with bitterness about the indifference of the Jewish public, and especially about the activity of the similar little societies of the suburbs, which, under the cloak of „Linat HaCholim“, collect money in the town and cause material damage to the „Linat HaCholim“ of Sosnowiec. Sharp criticism is also heard directed at the gmina [municipal council], which has stopped giving medical aid and at the same time does not want to pay out the subsidy to the above-mentioned society.
The delegates of the suburban societies reply to the criticism and declare that they are ready to negotiate so that their activity to date in the field of collecting money should be regulated.

The Activity of the Women's Association in Sosnowiec.
For a number of years now a women's association has existed in Sosnowiec, which occupies itself with supporting the poorest strata of the Jewish population with money and also with foodstuffs. Despite the severe crisis, the board of the women's association has not grown tired, and under the hardest conditions it fulfils its tasks within the limits of its material means.
For this year's Passover the association bought a large quantity of potatoes and distributed it among needy respectable Jewish families, but the help is like a drop in the sea; day after day the board receives dozens of requests from the poorest women, who ask for help for themselves and for their children, but not all requests can be met because the necessary relief capital is lacking.
In this connection it has been decided that the pledges (nedarim) on Shvi'i and Acharon shel Pesach [the last days of Passover] belong to the women's association in Sosnowiec.
The board of the association appeals to those who will be called up to the Torah to pledge larger donations; the compassionate women of Sosnowiec are also called upon to remember their unfortunate, needy sisters and to enrol as members of the association.

At “Nowości” — “Only Yesterday”.
The main motif of the picture is the psychological conception of the notion of “love” in the modern man and woman. The man reacts to life and love quite differently from the woman: “For him it was one night”, — “but for me — a whole life”, says the heroine Mary in the picture. And here a deep psychological conflict must inevitably break out between the two sexes, where both, however, are right from their own standpoint, or better said, not guilty.
This very conflict is masterfully carried through in the picture “Only Yesterday”.
The whole centre of gravity of the action is concentrated on the heroine Margaret Sullavan, who plays well and convincingly. Her partner John Boles and the little 10-year-old actor (Jimmy Butler), who plays the role of their illegitimate son, are also excellent.
The content, which is highly topical for our youth, the direction, which aptly brings out the nuance of every psychological moment, and the acting of the performers all move and overwhelm the audience so that people wipe their eyes properly, and sobbing is heard throughout the hall.
A picture that speaks to the heart of the soul.

Będzin municipal budget adopted in the 3rd reading / and further news from Będzin, Sosnowiec and Katowice

Subsidy for the Gmilus-Khesed (interest-free loan) fund — struck out.
On Wednesday evening the Commissarial Council in Będzin held a session at which the budget for the year 1934/35 was adopted in the third reading.
The session looked like a seder... Around the table the councillors sit or stand, drink tea and smoke cigarettes. The rapporteur "says the Haggadah", and the budget, amounting to nearly 2 million złoty, "moves along" slowly but surely, until it is finished just "as the Rebbe wills"...
The most interesting "number" at the session was setting a subsidy for the Gmilus-Khesed fund in the amount of 2 thousand zł. Like a bone in the throat, like a knife in the back — as the commissioner called it — this item stood for the non-Jewish councillors. All budget items went through offhandedly, but when it came to the subsidy, everyone suddenly found their tongue, and the end was that the one who decided to strike the subsidy was the commissioner himself, in person.
In the second reading, after the factual arguments of councillors Gutenstein and Hampel, who demonstrated the benefit the fund brings to the impoverished Jewish population, the subsidy was adopted. But at the third reading the well-known Otseshimski[?] proposed striking the 2000 zł. for the G. Kh. fund; in the vote councillor Salski also voted against, and since the votes were split 4 to 4, the commissioner, after brief deliberation, declared that he too votes against...
At the general vote on the budget councillor Rechnitz declared that, since he is dissatisfied with a number of budget items, he abstains from voting for the budget.
The same declarations were made by Messrs. Gutenstein, Hampel and Szwajcer.

The Fate of the "Moshav Zkenim" in Sosnowiec
Depends on the Jewish Population and on the Kehilla in Particular

[Sosnowiec — welfare and kehilla.] Jews of Sosnowiec!
The economic situation of the society "Moshav Zkenim" [old-age home] in our town is at present a very painful one.
The society's income is minimal, so that there is no possibility of maintaining even the smallest number of old people who qualify for admission.
In spite of this there are today in the "Moshav Zkenim" 26 old men and women, who are cared for properly and find the longed-for rest in their old age in the premises of the above-mentioned institution.
Of the total number of persons, the Jewish kehilla in Sosnowiec undertook to maintain 141[?] old people, which amounts to 7,200 zł a year. The kehilla has used the quota with an even greater number, but its obligations are not being fulfilled at all.
How far the scandalous indifference on the part of the kehilla goes is shown by the following fact: from 1 January 1933 to 1 April 1934 the gmina [kehilla] owes the institution a sum of 9000 zł. Such a large sum of money is of colossal significance for the financial situation of the society.
Despite the repeated demands for the debts addressed to the kehilla, not only has nothing at all been paid on this account — the kehilla has not even deigned to give any answer whatsoever. The warnings that the "Moshav Zkenim" will be forced to discharge the 14 persons, because it is unable to keep maintaining them, remain a voice crying in the wilderness and are not heeded by our "communal workers".
Because of the situation created, we hold the Jewish kehilla in Sosnowiec and Jewish society responsible for the sad consequences regarding the fate of this important institution.
The Board of the society "Moshav Zkenim" in Sosnowiec.
Jewish Property of Dąbrowa Jews Is Sold for Pennies

[Dąbrowa — economy and taxes.] In the course of the last weeks we have been told of unheard-of distraint (execution) cases taking place in Dąbrowa.
As an illustration we bring the following fact, which was told to us by the town councillor Mr. B. Rechnik.
On the 3rd of this month — Mr. Rechnik relates — an auction was held at the Silbersztajn family on Fabryczna Street, which owes the Treasury (Skarb) a sum of 1,600 zł. To carry out the auction a bailiff came together with a Christian porter, and the two of them conducted the auction.
It is worth[?] noting that at the auction the bailiff let nobody into Silbersztajn's flat, not even the children, and therefore, undisturbed by anyone, all the household goods were sold for 5 (read: five) złoty...
This is one of dozens of such similar facts; families are being ruined despite the fact that this is against the law.
— What does the head (naczelnik) of the local tax office say to this? After all, he knows the circulars (okólniki) well, that where ruin threatens no distraints are to be carried out.
— The naczelnik — Mr. Rechnik explains to us — does not treat people properly; many a time he simply throws them out, and his answers are insults to Jews.
Having heard these scandalous facts, we ask the board of the "Merchants' Association" in Dąbrowa: Why are you silent? Why do you not defend the rights of your members?

Murder or suicide.
In Kochłowice the 64[?]-year-old jewellery dealer Lejzer Feinlicht lived as a sub-tenant with a Christian landlord; last Sunday he was found lying dead in his room, and next to him lay a revolver.
