The Tasks and the Representatives. — Our Crumbling Economic Institutions. — How Should They Be Reorganized So That They Bring Benefit?

At the general meetings of our economic-professional associations one could ascertain that we are both backward and helpless in the public sphere. We saw clearly that we neither have well-founded institutions nor even members for them.
It has already become the custom among us that a member comes into his association only when he wants something from it, and since it gives him nothing, his foot never crosses the threshold of his association. Unfortunately we have not yet matured to the point of giving the association something, so that later we can draw sustenance from it. This idea does not even occur to anyone, and that is our greatest shortcoming. Why should we not understand that an institution, a public association, is exactly like any private business? If one founds any enterprise whatever, one must first of all put in the necessary capital, and only then. When everything has been set up properly, one opens the business and shows that one has goods to sell.
The same ought really to apply to our institutions, which we must have. We must not say that an institution we need should be liquidated merely because it gives us nothing; on the contrary, measures must be taken so that it lives and works, lives and brings the proper public benefit. And that we need the professional public institutions is as clear as day; we need them now more urgently than ever before.
Life has become narrower and harder, drier and heavier. Existence has never been so strained and complicated as it is today, in a time of heavy breathing, in a time when new laws are created one after another and one law contradicts the next. And how can we, poor, helpless, middling citizens, find our way in the great flood of laws, which are liable to make the already strained, helpless Jewish situation even harder? How can we form any notion of the laws being created for us, when lawyers, sharp-witted jurists who are immersed in it, have to study them constantly and with all that still do not find their way in them properly? Not to mention that poor, ordinary people, who toil for their daily piece of bread, should be able to occupy themselves with the laws that have been made for them!
What, then, does one do here? How does one become versed in matters for which one has neither the head nor the understanding? And since they remain alien to the average citizen, he suffers and is quite often fined for not keeping to the regulations that have come into force.
Surely one cannot demand that people who toil hard and bitterly to bring in [printed "ארויסצוברעגגען", a misprint] their livelihood — and even so their livelihood barely reaches the threshold — that such people should keep their own lawyers to fulfil the legal mission; of course that is nonsense, a dream that can never be realized in life. But to go on leaving such cardinal questions, which change life and make it harder, hanging in the air is by no means just.
And therefore we would be of the opinion that this mission should be handed over to the proper institutions, but this should not be done merely to discharge an obligation, merely because there is no other way; that would once again mean spoiling what must be guarded like the apple of one's eye.
Just as every enterprise has a chief, a responsible body that decides and rules and is responsible for everything, so it must be in public institutions; on the contrary, there there must be much more responsibility, because it is a communal matter in which the members place their trust. And these institutions must have competent persons who will protect and serve the members in whatever they need.
The greater part of the Jewish population in Poland is divided into three bodies: industrialists and small manufacturing, merchants and traders, and artisans. And these institutions of theirs stand on chicken legs and are torn apart and splintered, so that their work consists of squabbling and conducting intrigues.
It is enough to point out that every town possesses several merchants' and artisans' associations, and one tries to overthrow the other, although none of them fulfils its tasks; incidentally, it is not even capable of doing so, because they have accounts to settle among themselves and old grudges [?] besides, and one wants to drown the other, surely, in a spoonful of water. So how can one have a head for productive deeds? Quite often one forgets which association one is in and what tasks one has taken upon oneself.
So it is no wonder that the members avoid their institutions; they have been misled by them several times and therefore have reason to look down on them. Thanks to their disregard for the community they could not survive, and therefore they have all lost their lustre in the Jewish street. Of course not all look the same; not all are equally underrated. One cannot compare the institutions whose leaders committed embezzlements with those that simply took the public work they had undertaken lightly; but trust has been lost in all of them, and that is no wonder — they have honestly earned it.
The present situation in Poland, however, is such that we cannot manage without institutions. The merchant as well as the small trader, the artisan as well as the small industrialist — all must be organized and must have the association that will be a lever [?] for them in the hard struggle for existence. The associations must be a school for them, where they will learn to calculate and to work and to run their enterprises on a basis and according to a proper system. After all, one must know that there is an aim to throw annihilation bullets ["פערניכטיגונגס-קוילן"] into our camps, which we, as citizens of free, independent Poland, must consciously repel.
Our institutions, the merchants', traders' and artisans' associations, must first of all be united, so that a town should have no more than one association of each type; and only then must there be useful and fully responsible people who will, with full responsibility, take it upon themselves to renew them, or [printed "ארער"] to reorganize them entirely, so that the member will see that his association gives him something.
The legal and tax branches must be very well staffed, so that the member can rely fully on his association, where he can settle all his affairs — not as with a "macher" [fixer], but as through his own representative, who will have the right to represent and defend him as a delegate sent by society.
It must incidentally also be stressed that, owing to our helplessness, owing to the pessimistic situation in which we find ourselves and sink ever deeper, we lose our proper balance and pay both what is due and what is not due.
Thus we know that it often happens that the bailiff ["עקזעקוטאר"] comes to make a distraint ["סעקוועסטער"] for taxes that were paid long ago; but since such a confused Jew does not have the receipts lying ready to confirm the sum paid, nobody helps him, and he must immediately pay the paid tax once again. And such a thing happens not once in a jubilee but literally every single day. So the question arises: why should one not intervene in such a matter? Why should money be wrung from people a second time for one and the same tax, only because he has not had the possibility of keeping the receipts for what he paid? Surely the government treasury did not foresee such incorrect revenues.
This department is one of the most important and most responsible, and must without doubt be run by authoritative legal persons. But one more branch ought to be created, which is of no less importance than the first, namely attending to the member, who must be schooled at every step: he must be taught to trade, to compete and to calculate and in general to develop, because the great majority do not find their way properly and know neither the way in nor the way out — this we see on every occasion.
This work could be done through lectures, of course popular ones in the Yiddish language. At the said associations small libraries should be created for this purpose, where one would be supplied with the reference books needed for this purpose, of which there is a quite limited number.
The evenings and Sundays should be properly used for this purpose. Above all, one must endeavour to transform the institutions, on the one hand, into a practical help-school, through which he will have the possibility both of learning to run his line of livelihood and of settling his civic tax obligations; and on the other hand his institution should become for him a place of rest and a home, where he can spend the evening over a glass of tea and some light entertainment.
It would be only right to dwell on this problem and to try to create from it something real and useful for the benefit of the Jewish masses, who find themselves in a very pessimistic state; possibly there he will learn something and thereby also be uplifted.
We must not lose our heads now; we must not stand aside and look on indifferently as the shingles fall one by one from the roof, which can and must be saved — if only we set our hand to it.
A duty and a sacred obligation lie upon us to guard and rescue our positions. We must not let the last morsel be torn from our mouths at a time when we fulfil all our duties as citizens and as human beings.
We have no other course but to reorganize the institutions, which can bring us benefit in the hard struggle for existence.
These are the tasks that lie upon our people's representatives.
R. Let.
The Participation of the Będzin Jews in the Polish Freedom Struggles

[Będzin — history.] Moshe Feinkind.
(On the 140th anniversary of Kościuszko's uprising.) (2
This could, after all, easily have been ascertained from the tombstone, which is said still to be found to this day in the old Będzin cemetery on the Schlossberg [Castle Hill] and is decorated with a Polish eagle on account of his patriotism toward Poland. One could also have found out when he died.
Without seeing the tombstone, and without having its inscription — about which I have already written my fingers off to my Będzin friends — I nevertheless hold that R' Yaakov Natan was not a rabbi in Będzin.
In the pinkas of the Będzin Chevra Kadisha (as my old friend, the teacher Warmund, writes to me) the rabbis are recorded up to the year 5559 (1799), and from that year there is dated the moreh tzedek R' Menachem Nachum, who headed the rabbinate for a long series of years. And it is, after all, known to all that where there is no mara de-atra [official town rabbi], a moreh tzedek stands in for him temporarily or permanently, whereas when there is a rabbi, [he] is called [?] the moreh hora'ah; and since he [R' Yaakov Natan] does not figure in the pinkas, one must come to the conclusion that R' Yaakov Natan was not a rabbi in the full sense and meaning of the word, but he must have been the rosh ha-kahal (senior) or the syndic, i.e. the plenipotentiary of the kehilla. Such a person was indeed also called and titled "the Rabbi". For at all times the heads of the kahal were no ignoramuses, but indeed learned men and men of wealth.
The seniors and syndics did indeed collect money for various purposes and represent the Jews before the authorities.
Because of his self-sacrifice for the Jewish people, miracles were also attributed to him, i.e. to R' Yaakov Natan, as often happens among Jews.
* * *
To the credit of the Będzin Jews must also be mentioned their financial participation in the later Polish uprisings.
In the secret reports, which were found in the archive of the Piotrków governor and were lost in a mysterious way, it was related that the Będzin Jewish merchants supplied the insurgents [powstańcy] with ammunition, "kases" [?] etc.
The late Salomon Gutman in Będzin told me a short time before his death that his forefathers had been the suppliers of ammunition, and that the Jews in Będzin also gave money, on account of which several were arrested. One of them was R' Yochanan (Joachim) Manszejn of Mandżew [?], who was then punished by the authorities with 3 years of strict police supervision for spreading revolutionary proclamations against the Russian authorities, as is noted in the archive files.
The Jews of Będzin, to their great glory, produced heroes in the ranks of Piłsudski's Legions, which carried a risk to life.
One of these heroes was Doctor Mateusz Frenkel, who took part in many front-line battles and was finally interned by the Germans in the concentration camp at Beniaminów for refusing to swear loyalty to the coalition.
Dr. Frenkel then broke out of the internment camp, came back to Będzin, and is now director of a Jewish gymnasium in Warsaw.
In Będzin the heroic doctor disarmed the Germans and was then appointed by the Polish authorities as vice-commandant of Będzin.
For his merits on the battlefield Frenkel was decorated with several orders.
But Będzin produced, among others, yet a second Jewish hero.
This was the seventeen-year-old pupil of the local secondary school, Shmuel Schweitzer.
At the outbreak of the World War the boy left the school bench and, joining the Legions, went through all the front-line battles and the torments of war, and in the end was also interned by the Germans at Szczypiorno. There the heroic child fell gravely ill from exhaustion and unfortunately died at home on 25 April 1922.
Shmuel Schweitzer was decorated after his death with a cross of the First Brigade.
With their blood the Jews of Poland in general, and of Będzin in particular, in former times sealed their love and loyalty to Poland's revival, independence and freedom — and especially in the last struggle for liberation, no worse and no less than Poland's other children.
(The end.)
Our Struggle Is Only Beginning (On the First Anniversary of the Proclamation of the Struggle against Hitlerism)

[Article — the fight against Hitler; anniversary of the Warsaw congress.] (Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", by Mark Turkow).
The first half of the year 1933 contains a series of dates that have been deeply engraved in the history of the Jewish people. These are sad dates, because they are bound up with the Hitlerite regime's seizure of Germany and with the robbing of German Jewry of its most elementary civic and human rights. It makes no difference whether it is the day of 31 January 1933, when Adolf Hitler came to power in Germany; the 5th of March, when the bloody Hitler regime legalised its power in the Reichstag elections; the 1st of April — when the German government officially proclaimed and carried out the day of shame of the anti-Jewish boycott, which was carried out with such baseness, with such hypocrisy and insolence by the brown barbarians throughout Germany; the 10th of May, when the National Socialists publicly burned, on pyres in the German university towns, books by Jewish and pacifist writers; but also the many different unofficial, but for that reason quite frequent days on which the Hitlerite rulers persecuted the defenceless Jews in Germany in a truly medieval manner. These are dates which cannot, and must not, be erased so quickly from our memory...
But at the same time we can also note a whole series of dates which we shall recall with joy for as long as it takes until the great date of our final victory over Hitlerism arrives.
And today we must indeed remind the Jewish community of the date of 23 April 1933, which will occupy an important place in the history of Polish Jewry, and above all in the history of the great struggle for our national and political rights.
In the great tragedy that the whole of world Jewry lived through with the victorious march of barbaric Hitlerism, it could have seemed that we were so crushed by the sad news that used to arrive from Germany that we would have no courage at all to undertake a struggle of self-defence. At the same time the German government, thanks to its well-organised apparatus, while persecuting Jews in the vilest manner, sent agents all over the world in order to decry the truths about the sufferings of our brethren in Germany as "atrocity propaganda".
Polish Jewry therefore had to take upon itself the responsible mission of awakening world Jewry from its apathy, of leading it out of its error about the actual situation in Germany, and of helping to organise the mighty anti-Hitlerite front, which gave Hitler-Germany such signs of our capacity for defence that the German government had to be thoroughly frightened by it.
The anti-German boycott, which was organised by world Jewry and which brought about the difficult economic and political situation in Germany, is one of the many proofs that fully confirm our assertion.
But for this to happen it was necessary to create the united front against Hitlerism, and the grandiose congress to protest against the persecutions of Jews in Germany, which took place on 23 April 1933 in Warsaw, was the most powerful factor in the struggle for our rights.
Yes, for our rights! For the right of the whole of Jewry to live as human beings equal with human beings, as citizens equal with citizens.
We said it last year at the congress in Warsaw, we said it at the international Jewish anti-Hitler congresses in London, Amsterdam and Geneva, we repeated it at every rally, at every meeting, and we say it again today: f i g h t i n g for the rights of our brethren in Germany, we are also fighting for our own rights in every country, in every community where we live.
We Polish Jews know well what a struggle for full equal rights means, and therefore we understood the great tragedy in Germany best of all, and therefore it was we who gave the signal for the struggle of defence.
We knew that the victory of Hitlerism over the Jews in Germany would be a victory of the antisemitic gangs in all countries — the defeat of Hitlerism will be a defeat of antisemitism in other countries too.
Therefore we must fight Hitlerism consistently if we want to defend our rights.
On 23 April 1933 we publicly demonstrated our feelings and our fighting capacity. We also moved [?] the Jews in other countries to this struggle.
Though torn into parties and party coteries, Polish Jewry proved that in a time of trouble it stands above petty party ambitions, and thanks to this the united anti-Hitlerite front of the whole of Polish Jewry was created, which was later extended to the whole of world Jewry.
It is a historic date in the hard moments we are now living through, but at the same time it is a reminder to us that our struggle against our greatest enemy is still far, far from finished.
Although the first year of our struggle has already brought us certain successes, we must nevertheless carry the struggle further.
Our struggle is in fact only beginning, and the final victory depends on ourselves alone.
We must intensify the struggle in all areas of the anti-Hitlerite action, and so that this can be conducted properly and systematically, we must all take an active part in the struggle by joining the ranks of the members of the United Anti-Hitlerite Committee.
Let us begin the second year of our struggle against our enemy with redoubled energy and self-sacrifice.
Let us remember that the struggle for our rights is only beginning!
Information on Social Insurance

[Social insurance — public information.]
Continuing the insurance.
Persons who were insured in a social insurance institution (Ubezpieczalnia) and have paid at least 20 weekly contributions in the course of the last 52 weeks may, as soon as they become unemployed, continue the insurance, but only in case of illness, if they apply about it within 3 weeks.
The specified 3-week period does not include the time for which the unemployed person receives benefit, nor the time of military service. It follows, then, that if an unemployed person wants to remain insured, he must notify the insurance institution of this within 3 weeks after he received his last benefit.
Likewise, if a worker held a post and was insured, and through being drafted into military service lost the post and his insurance also ceased — as soon as he wants, after being released from the army, to remain insured, although he does not have the post, he must apply about it immediately, within 3 weeks after his release.
The right to benefit from the continued insurance begins from the day on which the contribution was paid in; it ceases, on the other hand — after falling behind by 4 instalments or after a written resignation.
As regards the right to the other insurances, it belongs to persons who have gone through [?] at least 150 weeks of contributions under compulsory insurance, if they report about it within 13 weeks after losing the right to compulsory insurance. The right to the continued insurance is lost if, after the lapse of half a year, the contribution has not been paid for 20 weeks.
Our Panorama

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — satirical feuilleton: life in the prayer-houses and shtiblekh at Passover.] (Progress on all Jewish fronts. — "The Season of Our Freedom" has the floor. — A gabbai who preaches morals receives "gifts". — 2 cats in one sack. — The "Bride" got off safely. — A gabbai must not be an aesthete. — An Agudah missionary. — It smells of gunpowder.)
Jewish life moves forward, makes progress in every field — not to mention the cultural, political and economic fronts — but our homely petty squabbling ["gemoyzekhts"] also grows from day to day. For example, the accepted opinion has always been that Jewish fervour flares up on the holiday of "the Season of Our Rejoicing" [Sukkot/Simchat Torah], as at "Atah Hareta", the hakafot and the like, whereas all other holidays pass by quiet as can be. But as is said, to everything a season — times change, laws are altered, and in our squabbling too a change has come about: not only in "the Season of Our Rejoicing" but also in "the Season of Our Freedom" [Passover] the common folk ["amkho"] have their say...
Democratic circles interpret this to mean that spring has a great influence on freedom movements, on uprisings, on revolutionary upheavals; but be that as it may, it is a gratifying phenomenon that the people of "Thou hast chosen us" laughs at all the decrees and restrictions that pour down on our heads and does not give up a single hair of the "holy folk traditions"...
It is curious to note the self-sacrifice of the gabbai of the minyan "Beit Elimelech" in Będzin: like a true folk martyr he fell in order to sanctify the Name — so that no clean-shaven man should be found in the holy congregation of that minyan.
And the story went like this.
On the holiday the gabbai of "Beit Elimelech" received confidential information that the face of one of the worshippers had become "smoother". Well, well — the "wrath of the people" flared up in him, and he resolved to sanctify the Name. First of all he informed the wife of the "criminal" that immediately after the holiday she must summon her husband to the rabbi and demand of him the 12 lines [i.e. a bill of divorce]... Then he turned to the recalcitrant [printed "vudershpeniger"] himself and honoured him with a second lecture on how a Jew ought to behave.
— What did the "condemned man" say to that? When he became truly convinced that the gabbai was such a holy man, he helped him on to holiness and made him
— into a true "kadosh" [martyr]...
As the "experts" ["rzheshetshaznavtses", Polish rzeczoznawcy?] of the minyan explain, the pledges [printed "nrorim" for "nedorim"] of the whole holiday did not suffice to cover the medical expenses caused by the "gifts" the gabbai received as reward for his interventions...
—o—
The gabbai of the minyan "Adat Yeshurun" also found himself in a very threatened [?] situation: the air smelled of gunpowder, any moment the explosion would come — but thanks to the "democratic views" of some of the minyan's worshippers the affair was liquidated without the slightest sign of... blood, and the one single unpleasant "number" that did take place consisted in a split occurring during the prayers; it happened to be precisely the Seventh Day of Passover, so the split served as a symbol of the Parting of the Red Sea...
And truly it is worth recording the great "miracle" that occurred: for when the prayer-leader delegated by the gabbai stood at the lectern, and at the reading table — a second prayer-leader from the revolutionary side, and no blows were left over from it — is that a small "miracle"?...
—o—
Since we are speaking of "miracles" that happened on this past Seventh Day of Passover, we must also mention the "miracle" that befell the minyan of the society "Hachnasat Kalla" [dowering of brides].
The "miracle" happened before Musaf. Fists were already being dealt out, teeth gnashed, and people were on the point of calling out "droshe geshank" [the wedding call announcing gifts], but luckily the "Bride", thanks to her "merit of the fathers", got off safely, and
— the "Bride" has income again...
—o—
The finale of our holiday reports was played out in the Krimilov [Kromołów?] shtibl in Sosnowiec.
The events in that shtibl prove again and again that there is no justice in the present epoch: for if there were even a crumb of justice in the world, the gabbai of that shtibl would be literally carried shoulder-high, a living monument would be erected to him for his good deeds, for the comfort of his subjects...
On the contrary — show me another gabbai in Sosnowiec who would collect groszy by groszy to "fit out" for Passover the "shtibl" where he is gabbai!
No, a thousand [printed "toynt"] times no — you will not find, on the whole globe and especially in the "merry" [printed "frlikher"] town of Sosnowiec, such a gabbai as the Krimilov shtibl possessed. Day and night he pondered plans for beautifying the appearance of the "shtibl", and so that all his plans should be carried out properly, he locked the "shtibl" before Passover. Don't question a story — he was afraid, God forbid, of the evil eye; let the public see what he could do only on the eve of Passover. But (oh, the "but" is to blame...) "the gabbai plans and the public laughs" — there is no gratitude for serious work, there are no connoisseurs who appreciate a gabbai who simply sacrificed himself for his holy flock.
— What was the end? you ask. Simply a tragic event: in the middle of the work the lock of the shtibl was torn off, the public went in and made "chametz" of everything the gabbai had prepared.
The "vile deed" had an echo on the night of the first day of Passover. The "shtibl" split into two [printed "bvey"] camps: "aesthetes" and "lock-rippers". The "aesthetes" grouped around the gabbai and bloodily defended his postulates, whereas the "lock-breakers" stormed in with the anti-gabbai slogan:
— We want a new gabbai! Long live freedom!...
And as in all countries, victory remained with the Right, with the old government; the number of scratched [faces?] ["tsudrapete gen", unclear] has not yet been established, for there are rumours that the battle has not yet been liquidated and both sides are preparing to entrench themselves with new forces.
—o—
A spring offensive is being prepared in the young men's circles of the Radomsko Hasidim in Będzin. The attacks are to be made on the Agudah "missionary" R' Natkele G. (the letters "G" and "K" are often interchanged...). This R' Natkele is infected with great envy of the "Keter Torah" yeshivas, which are developing so well in all towns and townlets, Będzin included, and he has taken upon himself the mission of catching "souls": to tear out of those yeshivas the poor "boys led astray", bring them back to the right path and immerse them in the Agudah cauldron...
He carries out this work to perfection. He lies in wait for "strange souls" in all the streets [printed "nasn" for "gasn"], and his Agudist lust is stilled when he manages to catch a little Radomsko soul in his net.
The "danger" opened the eyes even of the neutral Radomsko Hasidim, and they spoke up:
— Come, let us deal wisely!... To sit with folded hands and dismiss it [?] with an "oh, what do I care" — that one must not do.
No sooner said than done: a crowd of several dozen Hasidim, among them also kehilla officials who are harnessed [?] to the Agudah wagon, went into the beit midrash while R' Natkele was studying, and there gave him the real "bedekns" [the bridal veiling ceremony]...
But the young generation, the boys of the above-mentioned yeshiva, are not satisfied with what their elders say. We live — they say — in this century, when "R' Justice" is already in the World of Truth... We will talk to him — in a modern language...
Yes, gentlemen, this spring is a very "hot" one; the air is saturated with gunpowder...
Ben Amotz [?].
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Tazria-Metzora)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Tazria-Metzora
The Portion
—o—
a) "When a man shall have in the skin of his flesh a rising or a scab.." (13:2)
Jewish scholars are divided over the reason why the Torah orders the leper to be isolated: whether it has a religious-mystical ground, or whether the matter of the leper's quarantine is actually of a sanitary character — to protect the population from a contagious disease.
The famous Jewish thinker Samuel David Luzzatto writes in his "Yesodei ha-Torah" (§44) that it is purely a religious-mystical matter, "because a change in skin colour was among the ancients a sign of God's punishment, and the leper was in their view one punished — one punished by God for some grave sin he had committed. And therefore people kept apart from him as from a man excommunicated by God". He cites the famous physician Johannes Petrus Frank [Johann Peter Frank], that leprosy is not contagious.
Of the same opinion is also Dr. I. M. Rabbinowicz in his French Talmud translation (in his translation of tractate Nega'im, Mishnah 1 and 2), that leprosy is not contagious.
Dr. Y. L. Katzenelson, however, proves in "Ha-Yekev" of 5654 [1894], in a wonderful article, that according to the medical discovery of Dr. Neisser [printed "Geisser"] (1879) it turns out that leprosy stems from Bacilles lepare [sic] — thus indeed a contagious disease, and therefore the Torah orders the leper to be isolated, because he is contagious.
* * *
The Sages say that leprosy comes for the sin of slander (lashon hara): "Whoever speaks slander, plagues come upon him" (Arakhin 15). The Alshich asks: so why do we not become lepers today according to the signs in the Torah? Do we then sin less with slander today?..
But the point is — answers the Alshich — how slander leads to leprosy: the man who is a slanderer — that is a sign that he has base blood in him, and the bad blood comes out on the outside in the form of leprosy. That was all so once, when people were inwardly pure, and when a little evil was found in a man, it grew out to the outside. Today, however, we are all impure through and through, so that the impurity does not come out at all, because there is no pure force within that would push it out...
* * *
And that is why the leper is brought to the priest (kohen), because mostly one sins with slander against the kohen, against the leader...
Imrei Chen.
* * *
In Midrash Rabbah (section 16) it is told that R' Alexander went about calling out: Who wants life? The whole world gathered around him and cried: "Give us life!" R' Alexander read them the verse: "What man is he that desireth life, and loveth days, that he may see good? Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile".
Having heard about life — that someone wants to hand out life — masses of people gathered around him. But hearing that it was about slander, they all went away, and he was left with one man and spoke to him in the singular...
Also the verse in Psalms begins "Come, ye children, hearken unto me" — in the plural, and ends "keep thy tongue from evil" — in the singular.
Because he who wants to guard himself against slander must remain an individual against the many, for the many, through our many sins, are full of slander through and through...
Le-Beit Yaakov.
* * *
R' Itzikl Hamburger was a fervent misnaged (opponent of Hasidism), and he said unspeakable things about the Baal Shem Tov. The Besht did nothing to foil R' Itzikl's slander, and even gave him more and more opportunities to speak about him. When he was asked why he acted so, he answered:
— R' Itzikl is a Torah scholar; he takes pleasure when he speaks against Hasidim. So what harm is there? "This one benefits and that one loses nothing" — let such a Jew, a scholar, delight himself with talking against Hasidim...
* * *
Rabbi Nachman of Bratslav, about whom many great men spoke slander, used to interpret:
"By this I know that Thou delightest in me, because mine enemy doth not triumph (yari'a) over me" — by this I know, Master of the Universe, that You love me: that my enemies are not wicked (re'im) but righteous men... If one is to be slandered at all, better that it be by Torah scholars...
—o—
b) "And the hair of his head shall go loose" (ibid., 45)
Because among the ancient peoples an uncovered head was a sign of disgrace. And to this day the man of the East regards covering the head as a sign of authority and an uncovered head as a sign of lowliness.
Kol Yehuda.
* * *
R' Zalman Poyzner [Posner] was an exceedingly rich man, a Jewish "squire", but he dressed modestly; only the shtreimel he wore on the Sabbath was a precious one and cost a great deal of money.
Once a nobleman asked him:
— You are not particular about your clothes, yet you wear on your head a shtreimel worth so much money?
R' Zalman answered him:
— With you gentiles the body is the main thing and the head secondary, therefore you go about bareheaded and make only the clothes on the body precious. With us the head is the main thing and the body is secondary, therefore we pay no attention to the clothes of the body, whereas the head [we] adorn "for you" [sic; read "we"] with precious things...
—o—
c) "Then shall he that is to be cleansed take two birds" (14:4)
There is an opinion in the Midrash that leprosy comes for stinginess (tzarut ayin), and the Gemara (in Sotah 38b) says that birds recognize the stingy...
Nefesh David.
* * *
The Gemara (Bava Batra, folio 9) says: "Greater is he who causes [charity] to be done than he who does it, as it is said: And the work of righteousness shall be peace".
Because the doer — he who gives the charity — mostly shames the recipient out of stinginess; from the charity a good angel is created and from the shaming a bad angel is created, and the two angels constantly quarrel... Whereas the one who causes it — he who moves others to give charity, through whom no shame at all comes to the recipient — from his good deed only a good angel is created, and "the work of righteousness shall be p-e-a-c-e": the angels do not quarrel...
Lachmei Toda.
—o—
Avot
"Which is the right path... that which is an honour to him who does it and brings him honour from men" (2:1)
What you hold to be good for people, you should hold to be good for yourself as well... Do not preach one thing to others and another to yourself...
R' Avraham, brother of the Vilna Gaon.
Forms, Questionnaires.

The date of the elections to the town councils is truly drawing near.
The questionnaire and the forms that will be sent out to the house-owners are a concrete beginning.
Soon conferences, meetings and closed consultations will begin, and there will no doubt be negotiating, mediating and diplomatising.
But all this will deny it —
all this will, after all, be devoted to the great problem of — mandates.
A small matter, mandates!
It is, after all, a question: I or he, we or they; and rather than him and not me — better me and not him...
But one must point out that the forms with the questionnaires are very closely connected with the mandates.
If there are no voters — that's the end of the mandates.
It turns out, however, that when it comes to such a "boring" thing as making sure that the Jew of Będzin, Sosnowiec or Dąbrowa has the right to vote, there is nobody who remembers it.
Not one of the parties and not one of the organisations, which are pushing hard behind the scenes and have already set their sights[?] on mandates — not one of them remembers that some t e c h n i c a l action must be undertaken to help the Jewish voter not to lose his right to vote.
It is indeed great wisdom to print election appeals, to hold meetings and to make a racket at opponents' meetings. But an even greater wisdom is to take care in good time that one is not [—] to the wall.
And this must be done a l r e a d y n o w. What is neglected now can by no means be repaired later; already now one must see to it that every tenant receives the necessary forms and that all Zagłębie Jews entitled to vote are entered in the voters' list.
One must get down to election work.
Otherwise the bear will run away, there will be no fur, and you will have nothing to divide.
A. Szwarcer.
Days of the Omer Count

By A. D. Egoz.
I do not like the days of the Sefirah. I do not like them because of the melancholy that lies upon them.
The loveliest, best and most pleasant time of the year — and in the middle of it, go and keep mourning!
This stretch of time between Passover and Shavuot should have been the happiest time of the year. One is rid of the gloomy, monotonous winter, the grasses grow, the trees burst into leaf, the air is mild, neither too hot nor cold; there is a fragrance, it seems, in every corner of the earth — and after all that one must be gloomy, in mourning. What is it? It is Sefirah!
People greet the spring, tell its praises, are greatly enthused by it and by the pleasures it brings to mankind — and we must walk about with lowered heads; we may not hold any weddings, any merry entertainments, as though the authors of our laws had done it out of spite, because they begrudged us any enjoyment of the world.
The blessing over counting the Omer is said to a mournful tune. The cantor or the rabbi who counts the Sefirah, as soon as he gets to it, says the blessing with such a tune that it truly cuts to the heart. Master of the Universe, we are, after all, saying a blessing: "who has sanctified us with His commandments"; we thank God for having sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to count the Sefirah — so why not perform a commandment in a cheerful mood? Why so sad, so wailing?
I once asked a rabbi about this, and he answered me jokingly as follows:
"I count the Sefirah to a gloomy tune because, while counting the Sefirah, I remember that this is the only thing the community, my householders, give me to count. If they paid me a decent salary and I had money to count, my heart might be merrier and I would count the Sefirah to a merry tune."
They tell of a great rabbi, famous as a sage, that two Jews came to him for a din Torah. When he had heard out both sides and issued his ruling, the litigants laid down a dollar for him as a ruling fee. The rabbi spoke up: "What, do you think, my dear Jews, that I am such a fool that I cannot count to two?" The Jews understood what the rabbi meant and added another dollar.
Yes, there are rabbis who can count, but the poor things have nothing to...
But what that rabbi answered me is, after all, nothing more than a joke, a jest; and what really is the reason that the Sefirah is counted to a gloomy tune? For the mourning in the Sefirah days there is a reason, since in the weeks between Passover and Shavuot Rabbi Akiva's disciples died out; but what is the commandment of Sefirah to blame for — why perform the commandment with a broken heart? On the contrary: a commandment must be done with joy, as the verse says, "Serve the Lord with gladness" — serve God with joy, with merriment, with cheerfulness.
The Sefirah has been wrapped in secrets, in Kabbalah. If I were a rabbi, a respected rabbi on whom people relied, I would have made it all simple. I would have said that while counting the Sefirah we must regret that we do not count Sefirah, that we do not live with a reckoning, with an account, all the days of the whole year. If we all always lived with an account, we would be much better off.
And melancholy falls upon us when, while counting the Sefirah, we remember how many of us do not count, do not reckon up where they stand in the world — and that is the worst, the very worst, as they say.
There are Jews — be it said to no one's discredit — who every day or every week count their big profits that they make in business; they count large dowries [for] their children; they count the estates they own, the interest they get on money that they lend out "as a free-loan charity", and so on and so forth — but the main count, the count that the whole of Israel counts of the years spent in exile, that they forget. They reckon, and still they live without an account.
And a Jew must reckon not only his own accounts but also the accounts of his people. It is not enough that he knows where he personally stands in the world; he must also know and reckon and remember where others stand in the world.
There are people who live without an account in other particulars. They raise their children without an account, marry off their children without an account and treat people without an account. If everyone always lived with a proper account, counting Sefirah in everything they do or do not do, in everything they say and think — it would have been a much better and more beautiful [world].
This, I want to say, is the reason we count the Sefirah in a broken mood. We are not, God forbid, showing dissatisfaction with the commandment of counting, but with the not-counting.
In the "Master of the Universe" prayer of the Omer count we say: "in order to purify us of our klipot" — in order to cleanse us of our husks. What does "klipot" mean? If I were asked, I would say that it has no connection with secrets, with Kabbalah, but quite simply: klipot, I would say, simply means human husks, human pests, of which, thank God, we have no shortage. We have them in schools, we have them in other institutions and establishments, we have them in good local and national movements, and wherever the klipot push their way in, they do not repair, they only spoil.
And why is that? Where do these klipot come from? Because they do not occupy themselves with Sefirah, with counting, with reckoning, with reflection. If they lived with an account, if they first carefully considered everything they want to do, say or think — considered it with reason and with a sense of integrity, truth and justice — they would not have been klipot, and they would not have disturbed any good undertaking, any good movement.
This, I think, is how the klipot are connected with the Sefirah, and that is why we pray when counting the Sefirah: Master of the Universe, cleanse us of the klipot.
What Is the Main Thing?

[Article — economy, taxes and the crisis.]
We have read in the press that the Ministry of Finance has sent out to all tax offices a circular on the manner in which smaller tax sums are to be collected. It happens very often — the circular says — that someone owes only a few złoty, and the sequestrator [bailiff] comes, makes a "zajęcie" [distraint], sets an auction, etc.[?], and the expenses the tax office incurs thereby are entirely out of proportion to the sum owed to the tax office.
For this reason the Ministry of Finance has explained that with small tax sums, before the taxpayer's belongings are taken, several "upomnienia" [reminders/warnings] should be sent, and only if that does not help should the whole enforcement procedure be carried out. Therefore it really is worth asking: what is the purpose of this, and in what have we actually become any wiser from this explanation? What novelty have we been told here, and what practical difference is there between the earlier and the present procedure?
So, plain words: formerly such a debtor received one "upomnienie", and now the circular surely meant "to ease matters", especially as it is admitted that the expenses the tax office incurs are entirely out of proportion to the sum owed to the tax office — the circular says that, to be on the safe side[?], several "upomnienia" are to be sent and the enforcement carried out anyway; and another thing: every recipient of an "upomnienie" (and who does not get "upomnienia" nowadays?) — from every "upomnienie" a handling fee of 1,50 zł. is charged. That means the enforcement costs have been increased still further, and that for the very poorest.
But if one reads such a circular between the lines, it takes on quite a different meaning. Quite simply: there is still a tendency that the public does not want to take its money out of the "shenik"[?]. And why is that so, and why should there be such a tendency? — a question about a plain fact.
The hard times make it impossible for the taxpayer, especially the small one, to pay his obligations. With the best will in the world he cannot do it, even if he were to give up his last. Must one first paint the situation in black colours? Must we first prove the actual situation with statistical figures? One can say quite boldly that thousands upon thousands of those who receive "upomnienia" go about worried and lost in the one thought: where to get a piece of bread to bring home to his hungry family.
It is clear that ordinances or circulars which the tax offices receive must be carried out by the offices. The only flaw is that the law is not adapted to life; no one considers whether the conditions of life correspond to it[?]. If one prescribes — so to speak — the remedy for the patient while looking in through the window, the medicine cannot be a radical one. And one more thing worth stressing: even from those who are the "latest authorities" on these questions you can quite often hear: yes, you have been complaining like this for the last several years, and nevertheless you are still alive, aren't you? It would take up too much space if we wished to discuss this in detail and answer the question, but between ourselves, what is there to talk about when people will on no account rub their eyes to see the real facts, or simply wish to look through rose-tinted glasses. It is already, as they say, "a secret for all of Brody" [an open secret] that Jews, especially of the poor and middle class, now live in worse economic conditions than others.
* * *
It may sound at first like a paradox when we say that the constant fear of the "upomnienia", of the sequestrator and of tomorrow in general, touches very deeply the roots of our youth[?].
The holder of a handful of such "upomnienia", which even with the best will he can no longer settle, cannot sleep a night through in peace. He is always wrapped in fear. At the slightest rustle he pictures the whole enforcement procedure with all its consequences, and thus the very edge of the abyss.
This is precisely the result: a fairly large number of those "who live nevertheless" are already suffering, or at best are already candidates for a cure. True, this is a separate chapter, and especially one for those who are researchers in this field. But we are, after all, the victims, and therefore we must criticise and thus point out which are the bad sides.
Our conclusion is: let these words we say here not remain hanging in the air: if the tax office did not sell off the last things out of the home, it would save thousands upon thousands of poor and weak livelihoods, save them from total ruin, from sinking to doles and alms, from losing their health and their human face — that is the main thing.
Lejb Prajs.
Let's Tell Each Other the Truth...

A story with a moral for men and for women.

Leon B. and Adela, his wife, had been an ideal couple ever since the wedding. For her he was the ideal of a man: clever, energetic, capable and a real mensch. Literally all women envied her. He, in turn, saw in her the embodiment of all feminine[?] virtues: beautiful, piquant, elegant and, on top of that, clever and intelligent. And since both of them never forgot to use every opportunity to show those around them how much they loved each other and how happy they were, it is no wonder that Leon and Adela were regarded[?] as the most exemplary and happiest couple in the world.

And suddenly — a sensation. Leon and Adela have separated. She on her own, he on his own, and they are getting ready to go to the rabbinate.

What happened?

Two years after the wedding Leon took it into his head to hold a strange conversation with his little wife; perhaps he had seen it at the cinema, perhaps he had read it in a book. The conversation went more or less like this:

— Do you love me, Adela?

— "Love" is a weak word, my dearest. There is no word in the lexicon that could express my feelings for you.

— I know it. I know that with every breath, with every thought you belong to me. Two bodies in one soul, and that is exactly why, you see, there must not be the slightest secret between us. Let us be as honest with each other as two kings [sic; probably "angels" was meant]. Tell me the truth, the whole truth. Have you ever betrayed me? Have you thought about others? Back then, when I was abroad for three months, did you have no one on your mind? Tell me, I will tell you too, and again we will feel towards each other like two innocent children, like back then when we first met.

— You say you will tell — that means you have some secret. Do tell, let me hear. But the whole, the pure truth, and then I won't stay in your debt either.

— Of course I'll tell you; after all we are grown-up, free and cultured people, we will surely understand each other well and, as two lovers, forgive everything.

— Tell me, don't wait a second, I am burning with curiosity.

— You see, Adela, when I was in Danzig for those three months, I got acquainted there with several women; one of them was very similar to you, and that is why I got close to her, and in this way saw you and felt you all the more vividly.

— Tell me, exactly, I want to know everything.

And Leon began to describe the details, omitting not the slightest thing; his tone at times even sounded boastful, as is the way of most [printed "srov"] men. Leon did not notice how the colours on Adela's face were changing, how her eyes grew sharp, filling with anger and fury.

— And now, my dearest, you tell too what happened with you here.

— The same as with you. Your colleague Artur always accompanied me, and you know that he is so similar to you — your character, your manners, a very noble, decent man — and you know that he had a liking for me since my girlhood[?]; and that is exactly why, to remember you better, I went walking with him, invited him to supper, and —

— Tell me! What happened? Did he stay the night with you?

And Adela did not spare[?] any details either.

— Yes, he stayed... sleepless nights.., his strong arms... He is better, stronger than you.

— How dare you!

— And how did you allow yourself to do it!

— You have shamefully betrayed me! You, Adela! You — doing such a thing!

— And you were allowed to!

— I am a man! I may [printed "megn mir"], it does me no harm. But you are a woman, you have covered my name with disgrace!

— Where does this privilege suddenly come from? Why may you do what you do not allow me?

— Quiet! Don't let me hear you any more!

— And I don't want to look at your face any more.

— Today it comes to an end!

— Today, without fail.

— Today we go to the rabbinate.

— Right now.

Good friends intervene, try to bring about peace, assure Leon that Adela fooled him: she made it all up so as not to remain in his debt. But Leon does not believe it; he knows that Adela does not tell lies, does not deceive... and if she told of betrayal, it is the truth.

Yet the couple still love each other deeply and will probably make up again. But the illusion of absolute love and faithfulness has been shattered forever.

———

Adam and Eve were driven out of the Garden of Eden because they tasted of the Tree of Knowledge. Leon and Adela lost their Garden of Eden because they tried to taste of the Tree of Truth.

Men and women, be careful with the truth!

Pik.
Perished for Kiddush Hashem (the Sanctification of the Name)

By H. Akerman.
(A tragic story of a Jewish daughter at the time of the Ukrainian pogroms in 1919.)
And in Bilavke[?] too the sky began to darken over the Jews' heads. Some four hundred and fifty Jewish souls lived in that shtetl. As if by some miracle, no Jewish victims fell in that shtetl. True, one gang turned the old synagogue into a ruin-heap, kept horses in it and left it a wrecked ruin. And rumours spread that the squire Shcherbatov was a really close "shmelke"[?] of the pogromists; all the gangs with their "batkos" that swept through the shtetl always used to spread their camp in Shcherbatov's manor and felt like quite "homely" guests in his courtyard.
And then, in 1919, an ataman of Petliura's turned up[?] in Bilavke; his name was Volasenko[?] and he had seven hundred soldiers with him. As that ataman used to conduct himself, Jewish blood poured into the gutters without end. And Volasenko's name cast great terror on all Jews. Volasenko raged through the whole Podolian gubernia, and there was hardly a single shtetl in Podolia where Volasenko and his pogromists did not wreak destruction.
A few days before Tisha b'Av Volasenko with his "khlopetses" [peasant lads] arrived "as guests" in Bilavke. Even in good, quiet times the small Jewish shtetls back home were shrouded in mourning on the eve of Tisha b'Av, and a kind of gnawing gloom was spread over everything and everyone; now imagine Bilavke a few days before the Kinot, when Volasenko is still standing around the shtetl!
The shtetl was wrapped in a silent mortal terror, and people were afraid of their own voices. The Jews of Bilavke expected a pogrom. The Jewish cellars were made ready for the Jews to hide in when the pogrom broke out, although each one knew in his heart that there was no hiding place.
Everyone's hands and feet trembled and their teeth chattered against each other. The Jews of Bilavke took Tisha b'Av upon themselves several days early, and a full two days before "Eikhah yashvah" they had already shut their shops and hidden, however they could. Their bit of property and their lives they handed over to God, that He should save them from the evil wolves lurking around the town.
Like all the pogromists who used to come to Bilavke, Volasenko and his gang stopped at Shcherbatov's on the estate.
They arrived riding on horses, and the shtetl was soon surrounded on all sides. The pogromists rode on horses, and a horde of men on foot — goyim, lads with girls from the surrounding shtetls — fell upon the Jewish shops with sticks and shovels. The windows began to crack and the doors began to break, and soon Jewish toil and drudgery of many years lay strewn about the streets. From the shops the frenzied[?] gang went back to where they had come from, and on the way they meanwhile smashed Jewish windowpanes and cursed the Jews with all kinds of curses. But there were no fatalities. Except for a few people who simply died of fright lying "hidden" in the cellars and hearing what was going on in the street.
That was, for the time being, only the prelude. The real pogrom was to unfold only on the morrow. The Jews expected it, and their souls fluttered.
But in truth Volasenko had other plans, and apparently Shcherbatov helped him in making the plans. Shcherbatov, who all the time had been full of murderous rage against the Hornsteins and their daughter Chana, because they had shamed him, now wanted to settle accounts with them. And not only with them alone, but with the whole shtetl of Jews. And he worked out the following plan: Volasenko would demand that Chaim Hornstein's daughter be delivered to him for one night at Shcherbatov's manor, and in return he would leave Bilavke with his "party" the next day and would no longer bother the shtetl; and if Hornstein would not send him his daughter, he would massacre the whole shtetl of Jews.
And on the eve of Tisha b'Av, in the morning, three mounted couriers rode up to the house of the Bilavke rabbi, Rabbi Nachum-Tzvi Rozman, handed him their ataman's order and told him that they were giving him twenty-four hours for an answer. If the answer was — no, then ataman Volasenko with his seven hundred soldiers would come down into the shtetl... and that meant the whole shtetl with all its souls would be slaughtered.
And the rabbi promised the couriers to give them an answer in due time.
Among the Jews of Bilavke the news about the riders who had stopped at the rabbi's house spread at once, and many Jews came to the rabbi to ask what the riders had wanted. But the rabbi did not want to tell them the truth, and told them that the riders had been looking for money in his house and nothing more.
But the Hornsteins the rabbi did have to tell the bitter truth. And he went to them and told the parents what it was about.

A stormy meeting of the kehilla board.

[Head of the local section; Będzin — kehilla.]
What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 5 Iyar 5694 — piątek 20 kwietnia 1934 [Friday, 20 April 1934].)
Będzin
A stormy meeting of the kehilla board.
On Monday evening, chaired by the president Mr Rubinlicht, a meeting of the kehilla board took place; on the agenda: technical changes in the budget for the year 1934.
The chairman reports on the amended items and proceeds to the vote.
Before the vote Mr Banhart reads, on behalf of the Agudah faction, the following declaration:
"We the undersigned declare that we take no part in the final vote on the budget for the year 1934, being[?] decided opponents of the entire composition of the budget. This declaration is to serve as a protest against the budget.
At the same time we consider it our duty to declare that we bear no responsibility for the activity of the present kehilla board, because: 1) the kehilla chairman and vice-chairman conduct an independent activity on their own hand [i.e. on their own initiative], without any agreement with the kehilla board. 2) We do not even have the possibility of exercising control over the activity of the president and vice-president, and 3) from the activity known to us we can bear witness to a series of deeds that contradict the kehilla regulations, such as spending various monies without a legal and statutory basis. For this reason we declare that we cast off from ourselves every responsibility for the consequences of such activity."
Shmuel Piekarski, Eli' Ber Werdiger, Simcha Bunem Banhart, Dawid Skacylas.
Then the vice-president Mr A. Liwer submits the following declaration:
"We establish that the gentlemen of the 'Agudah' have been carrying on, from the very first minute, ever since the present kehilla has existed, a work of ruin. All positive work by the kehilla is fought by the gentlemen Agudists in very low ways. It is enough to point out that the last Passover campaign conducted by the kehilla, which made it possible for 1000 families to be provided for with dignity for Passover, is fought and questioned by the gentlemen Agudists; all possible and impossible means are used, the Agudah people intrigue and spread false rumours. Such a case occurred with Mr Banhart, who permitted himself to make an intrigue against the president.
We put such ugly activity of kehilla representatives in the pillory — let the public brand such irresponsible work of so-called religious Jews."
During the discussion there was also a sharp exchange of words between the chairman and Mr Banhart.
The agenda item is put to the vote and the budget changes are adopted by 5 votes to 4.
The Agudah faction submitted a protest against the vote.
Later the decision was approved by the kehilla council. At the kehilla council meeting the parnas Kisner declared that a "national-religious and economic bloc" is being created, which will go hand in hand in all kehilla matters.
The starosta suspends Mr A. Liwer's activity as vice-president and member of the kehilla board.

[Będzin — kehilla.]
The starosta suspends Mr A. Liwer's activity as vice-president and member of the kehilla board.
On Tuesday morning the vice-president of the kehilla board, Mr A. Liwer, received from the starosta [district head] a notification which states that because Mr L. conducts politics in the kehilla work and pushes the Jewish religion down to second place, he is suspended. "Zawiesza" [suspends] as vice-president, and also as a member of the kehilla board, until the matter has been thoroughly investigated.
The decision naturally struck the national circles hard; by contrast, among the "Agudah", who apparently had known beforehand that this would happen, the joy was beyond measure.
As we are informed, a consultation is to be held in the coming days, at which the position of the national camp in connection with the decision will be discussed.
Hooligan attacks on young Jews out walking on Kościuszki Street.

[Będzin — attacks.]
Hooligan attacks on young Jews out walking on Kościuszki Street.
On Saturday evening, at about 10 p.m., Yurl Langfus, Leib Hamer and Bunem Cukierman were strolling on Kościuszki Street. As they came close to Lasker's mill they were attacked by several hooligans, who beat the young men cruelly [lit. "with a blow of cruelty"].
As we are told, the attacks have been repeated several times on that street.

The magistrates [municipal authorities] in Zagłębie have already received the decree on the city-council elections.

At the same time the nominations of the main and local election commissioners were received.
The vice-president of the district court in Sosnowiec, Mr Walski, has been nominated chairman of the main election commission, and Mrs Chalezicka[?] of Dąbrowa vice-chairwoman.

The kehilla budget for the year 1934 has been laid out for public inspection as of yesterday, Thursday.

On 1 May the Deadline for Filing Income Declarations Expires

[Będzin — taxes; short news.]
We once again draw attention to the fact that on 1 May of this year the deadline expires for submitting the income “zeznania” [declarations] for the tax year 1934.
The declarations must be filed by the set deadline at the appropriate tax office.
Persons who do not submit the “zeznania” will be fined and run the risk of not being properly assessed, since the fiscal authority will assess further income according to the material in its possession.

The Eviction Moratorium Extended
The latest “Dziennik Ustaw” [Journal of Laws] has published the decree of the President of the State on extending the housing moratorium for the unemployed over the summer months.
That means that the unemployed who occupy a dwelling of one or two rooms (a kitchen is not counted as a room) may not be evicted during the whole summer either, until 31 October (from 1 October until 1 April — the entire winter months — a permanent law against eviction is in force, and no special decree is needed for that).

The Voivode in Zagłębie
In recent days the Kielce voivode, Mr. Paciorkowski, stayed in Zagłębie, where he held a conference at which the question of organizing a campaign to employ the unemployed was discussed.

Income from a Badge Sale for the Fire Brigade
The badge sale held on Sunday the 15th of this month by the firemen in Będzin brought in 245 zł. 42 gr., for which the board thanks the donors.

The Kehilla Council Adopts the Budget en bloc

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.]
For the third time, last Sunday, the local kehilla council (the old one) assembled to deal with the kehilla budget for the current year.
Like the previous ones, the present session too aroused no interest, and the “speeches” were held in the absence of a “gallery” [public].
The chairman, Mr. Szwajcer, declares the session open; the discussion begins, or rather the “cosy chat” about the budget.
Councillor (parnas) Mr. Cycemski again speaks about a rational budget and proposes postponing the session and electing a budget commission to work out an “honest” budget.
Against the proposal are: Danziger, Braner, Kupferminc, Silberberg, Orman, Cyzajnghaft and board member (dozor) Weinsztok; the last declares that the board's budget commission has dealt seriously with every item in a rational manner.
After the talk, the proposal of parnas Mr. Kupferminc to adopt the budget en bloc is accepted.
Parnas Cycemski submits a vote of no confidence.
Then the item is discussed: setting the level of the etat [kehilla tax assessment].
Board member Braner is for raising the level of the etat up to 3000 zł., arguing that even in Dąbrowa the highest etat sum is 2000 zł., and in Sosnowiec there are such as can pay an etat of 3000 zł.
However, after the president's statement that since the budget is being set by the old council, the etat sum should also remain at the “old” level, i.e. the highest etat sum is 1,200 zł.
The Starost Calls the Kehilla Leaders to a Conference on the Neglect of Marriage Records by the Jewish Population

[Sosnowiec — kehilla, civil registration.]
Under the chairmanship of the city starost Mr. Heger[?], a conference was held on Monday with the participation of the kehilla president Mr. Wendel and secretary Mr. Lewenhof.
At the conference a number of kehilla matters were touched upon, above all the neglect by a large part of the Jewish population of the matters of chuppah [marriage] records, birth certificates (metryki), etc.
As is known, a heavy penalty threatens those who violate the law on putting chuppah records, metryki, etc. in order.
With the consent of the starost it was decided to call upon the Jewish population of Sosnowiec that 1 September of this year is the last deadline for putting in order the formal records of weddings or births; whoever violates the ordinance will be severely punished.
Among other things, a number of kehilla matters were also discussed, above all the system of paying the pensions of the shochtim [ritual slaughterers].
Regarding the latter, the starost ordered that the income from shechita [ritual slaughter] must go into the kehilla treasury and be distributed proportionally among all officials.
Tax Embezzlement at the Tax Office. The Sequestrator Collected Taxes for... Himself

[Sosnowiec — taxes, crime.]
At the Sosnowiec tax office tax embezzlements have been discovered, carried out by one of the sequestrators [bailiff-collectors], Henryk Grips.
Of the podatki [taxes] he collected, Grips paid part into the treasury and took the rest for himself.
This week the “distributor” stood before the district court, which sentenced him to a year in prison.
Zawiercie. — The Starost's Demand to the Kehilla President: He Must Repay the Subsidies

[Zawiercie — kehilla; Zionism; economy; crime.]
In the year 1933 the starost ordered the kehilla board not to pay out any subsidies. The president, however, did not comply with the order and paid out subsidies to the amount of 2.600 zł. This week the president received an ultimatum from the starost to return the sum in question to the kehilla treasury; otherwise he will be held legally responsible.

The local gmina has fined several bakers 100 zł. for bringing in outside flour for Passover. This caused great agitation among the bakers, who burst into the municipal beit midrash and with threats and insults attacked the councillors (parnassim) present, Cwajgel, P. Birenfrajd and P. Kachan.

Boycott Breakers
As we learn, the local Jewish haberdashery merchants are selling, instead of the D.M.C. silk[?], the firm J.S., which is stained with Jewish blood. We call upon the Jewish population to react to this criminal deed.

On Sunday a demonstration of the unemployed was to take place in the “Stella” theatre. Thanks to the strong guard of the police, the demonstration was dispersed.

Mr. Rozenberg, walking to the railway on Sunday, was hit by a bullet in the head. As it turned out, a student had been learning to shoot...

A Golden Rain.

[State lottery — winnings.] Having distributed smaller gifts on the first day of the State Lottery drawing, fate reserved the greatest of its favours for the second day. And indeed last Thursday a golden rain poured down on the heads of the lucky ones upon whom the capricious goddess deigned to cast her gracious glance.
And as usual the thick drops began to fall[?] first, that is, first of all 300,000 złoty, which fell in one of the Warsaw lottery offices (kolektury). The owners of the lucky ticket 74639, however, were residents of the provinces, namely: Mr. Y. G. of Drohobycz (a half ticket), Mrs. St. B. of Piotrków and Mr. S. R. of Olkusz (in quarters).
A somewhat smaller, but still a strong drop worth 100,000 złoty also fell in Warsaw on number 75359; half of this prize was won by Mr. A. S. of Brześć (Brisk), one quarter by an employee of a certain institution, and the other quarter by Mr. A., a resident of Szamotuły in Poznań county.
Two prizes of 50,000 złoty fate divided between Warsaw (number 141,365) and Silesia (number 154.468). The well-known lucky man, the owner of the confectionery on Midzhigane[?] Street, on whose ticket 300,000 złoty had already fallen in one of the previous lotteries, owns one quarter; the second was bought by Miss D., an office clerk, the third by the dentist Mr. L., the fourth by Mr. L., a merchant from Żelazna Street. In Silesia the 50,000 złoty will be shared by Messrs. A. H. of Siemianowice, Mr. B., an official of the tax office in Rybnik, Mrs. F. B. of Katowice and Mr. M. K. of Łagiewniki.
Thus the thick drops of Thursday's golden rain together made up half a million złoty. After them poured a golden lava[?] of smaller drops, and among them there were also bigger ones worth twenty, fifteen, ten, five and one thousand złoty. In the course of the two days of the drawing, two million złoty fell on six thousand prizes.

Tonight, Friday, Yosele Kolodny sings in Sosnowiec.
[Sosnowiec — culture, concert.] After a longer break Yosele Kolodny has again come to Zagłębie for several concerts. Yosele Kolodny is no new face here; with his first appearances he already made a name for himself and was stamped as a great talent of the living Yiddish word.
Kolodny possesses a baritone voice of no wide range, but with a very pleasant, ringing timbre.
With Kolodny it is not a matter of voice, but of the manner of interpreting a song, which he does in his own original way.
Kolodny is an individual artist; his singing is not stereotyped; it is not just some song sung off, but at the same time a performance by a first-class actor.
[Picture:] Yosele Kolodny (in caricature)
He has wonderful facial expression, his movements are masterly, he never falls into caricature (charge), and therefore he works directly through his subtle artistry.
Kolodny is not only a first-class song singer but also a talented reciter and monologist. One does not tire quickly of his songs and monologues, and one wants to hear him again and again.
It is superfluous to enumerate the individual numbers, because almost everything was performed masterfully.
It is certain that with his appearances in Zagłębie Kolodny has won an audience of devoted[?] listeners, and his success here is assured for the future.
The question arises: where were the connoisseurs who long so much for a true artistic word? How they shed crocodile tears over the vanished theatre — and when a true artist comes, one does not see them.
———
Tonight, Friday evening, Yosele Kolodny sings in the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre. On the programme — a treasure of folk songs, humoresques, monologues that refresh the listeners.
Incidentally, we point out that it was posted by mistake that two concerts would take place in Sosnowiec; in fact only one concert takes place.

"Queen Christina" at the "Eden" cinema.
[Cinema — film review.] After a longer break the greatest tragedienne of the screen, Greta Garbo, has again shown that she is without rival.
Now Greta Garbo appears in the historical film "Queen Christina" (printed "Kristinia").
Greta Garbo is the most cultured and subtle film actress; her face, her expression — that is a piece of film history. Dozens of volumes have already been written about her eyes, and the whole world has crowned her the queen of film.
Therefore the film is worth seeing; the director made it without fault, wonderful photography, splendid sets, and first-class acting by the performers.
Only John Gilbert (printed "Zhibert"[?]), the former favourite, is now somewhat pale; he is acting for the first time in a talking picture, and therefore does not feel entirely at ease. In general it is hard to succeed when one has as partner such an actress as Greta Garbo, for she puts everyone in the shade.
The film also has splendid music and very good technical photography.

Yesterday a complaint against the kehilla budget was lodged by the Rabbi of Będzin.
In the complaint the Rabbi turns to the authorities [asking] that the salaries („pensions“) for the young shochtim be provided for in the budget, and that the level of the salary be restored without the reduction.

Help, So That the Home for the Aged Is Finally Completed / The Kashoy Cantor Leads Sabbath Prayers in Będzin / Proposal to the Będzin Rabbinate to Permit a Shochet from the District to Slaughter Poultry / The Będzin Kehilla Board Now Agrees to Go to a Din Torah with the Shochtim

[Będzin — charity and institutions; followed by three short items: cantorial, shechita, kehilla.]
From the board of „Linat HaHolim“ in Będzin we have received an appeal to the Jewish public of Będzin.
The appeal draws attention to the fact that the new „Moshav Zekenim“ [old-age home] building is already about to be completed. There is, however, a large number of people who have not yet fulfilled their duty towards the twenty-odd old men and women and have not yet contributed for the benefit of the building, because of which a great number of old people are homeless and wandering („na-ve-nad“).
It is therefore to be hoped that the delegates of „Linat HaHolim“ will be received with a friendly face and will help with an open hand, so that the old people may as quickly as possible find their true home in the new building.

The Kashoy Cantor Leads Sabbath Prayers in Będzin
At the invitation of the Będzin synagogue committee, a telegraphic message arrived yesterday afternoon from the Kashoy cantor [Košice / Kassa?] that he is coming to Będzin today and will lead the prayers this Sabbath in the city synagogue („Shtot-shul“).

Proposal to the Będzin Rabbinate to Permit a Shochet from the District to Slaughter Poultry
In connection with the „behind-the-scenes politics“ being conducted around the young shochtim in Będzin, the kehilla board has turned to the rabbinate with a proposal to permit a shochet from the Będzin district to work in the slaughterhouse at poultry slaughtering.
—o—
The Będzin Kehilla Board Now Agrees to Go to a Din Torah with the Shochtim
On Wednesday a consultation of board and council members took place in the kehilla premises; at the consultation it was decided, after a stormy discussion, to go to a din Torah over the dispute with the shochtim.
On behalf of the board the Rabbi of Koziegłowy is to appear; but if the shochtim do not agree to this candidate, the shechita matter is to be dealt with by arbitration (borerut). And as arbitrator the kehilla puts forward Rabbi Blumenfeld of Königshütte [Chorzów].

To the Jewish Public of Będzin!

[Będzin — sport; appeal.] The Jewish gymnastics and sports association "Hakoach" turns to the Jewish public in Będzin with an appeal to join its ranks.
"Hakoach", which will soon celebrate the 20th jubilee of its existence, still has no stadium of its own to this day.
The Jewish Gymnastics and Sports Association "Hakoach" has already gone through and fought its way through various hard times, and now too we find ourselves in a very critical situation. It is superfluous to enumerate the financial difficulties in which the association finds itself today; let the single fact suffice that today we do not possess even a rented ground.
We are aware how hard it is, in the present crisis, which has struck all strata of the population, to come with a call to keep up the oldest and only non-partisan gymnastics and sports association in Zagłębie, which already has great merits in this field. It is a moral duty of the Jewish population of Będzin not to let such a useful society go under.
The newly elected board has set itself the task of creating a sports ground of its own. We therefore turn to the whole population: enrol as members of the association and thereby help "Hakoach" in its existence and its tasks.
With respect,
The Board of "Hakoach" Będzin.
The Famous "Ararat" in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — theatre.] It will surely be gladdening news for our readers and especially for theatre lovers that the only Jewish revue and kleinkunst theatre "Ararat", under the artistic direction of Moshe Broderzon, has reorganised itself anew, and after the stormy success of its month of guest performances in Łódź it is setting out on a large summer tour through the larger towns of the country and will also appear in Zagłębie.
The well-recommended "Ararat" ensemble now consists of the young artists: Dovid Birnbaum, Yoel Bergman, Maria Dalska, Shimon Dzigan, Rut Taru, Reyzl Levi-Borovska, Sheyne-Miriam, Yisroel Shumacher and others.
The tour repertoire of "Ararat" includes the hit programmes "Himl efn zikh" ("The Sky Opens") and "Nisht geshtoygn nisht gefloygn" ("Neither Here Nor There"), which were staged in Warsaw by the Ararat directors Dzigan and Shumacher and were played in the capital for half a year in a row to sold-out theatre halls.
How Does One Obtain, and to Whom Is Due, the Postponement of an Eviction?

[Housing — rent moratorium; the unemployed.] In connection with the fact that many unemployed, who are supposed to benefit from the recently published housing moratorium, still do not know how they must act in order to postpone an eviction from a one- or two-room flat, and also in connection with the inaccurate information in the press on this matter, we contacted the provincial chancellery of the Łódź district court, which gave us the following explanations.
The right to postpone an eviction is not due automatically, as many unemployed mistakenly believe; rather, one must obtain this right by legal means, by submitting individual petitions to the municipal court.
In order to obtain a moratorium one must present a certificate from the "PUP"[?] of the current month and a certificate of poverty, likewise of the current month.
To confirm all the particulars that make it possible to grant the moratorium one must name at least 2 witnesses.
It must be stressed that only persons who were unemployed at the time they did not pay the rent benefit from the moratorium.
If the fact of unemployment arose later, the moratorium will not be recognised for the occupant of a one- or two-room flat.

Last Deadline for Income Declarations.

The last deadline for submitting declarations (zeznania) on income (dochód) for the year 1933 is next Monday, before 1 May.
All merchants of the second and third category are obliged to submit income declarations.
Exempt are merchants of the third category who live in towns of the third and fourth patent-class.
Merchants who own houses in which there are more than 3 apartments must also submit declarations.
The declarations may be sent by post in a registered letter.
When handing in the declarations one must pay half of the income tax which one has calculated oneself.
