Two of Them Sat Together...

Specially for the "Zaglembier Cajtung", by Advocate M. A. Hartglas.
...Two friends from the same milieu: one thin, with a nervous face, a dishevelled forelock, dark glasses on a thin, elongated nose. The other well fed, with a smoothly shaven face, precisely pressed trousers, an elegant suit and a geometrically measured parting[?] in his hair.
Two friends from the same milieu, intelligent people, spoke the same language and... did not understand each other.
They talked about the struggle against Hitlerism: "I do not understand," said the elegant one, carefully laying his cigar on the little ashtray, "this whole boycott and all the fuss around it." Well, all right — at the first moment — a spontaneous reflex — that I understand, but it has been a year already. Can one go on endlessly following senseless mass outbursts? What are you politicians for, if not to rein in these spontaneous outbursts with reins, to give them the proper direction, to hold them back when they are aimless? What has the boycott given us? You speak of the shrinking of German exports? But is that the result of the boycott that Polish Jewry is conducting? That was done by America, Holland, England, and not by us. What percentage share does Poland take in German exports anyway? And the boycott was not a hundred-percent one either. In any case it was impossible to boycott a whole series of German goods, for lack of articles that could replace them. Simply[?], is it not cowardice that, instead of pursuing a realistic policy and explaining to the Jewish masses the whole aimlessness and ridiculousness of their Lilliputian boycott — which has caused a whole number of Jews to lose various sources of livelihood, thereby enriching further "Aryan" competitors, the noble Endeks [National Democrats], who not long before had proclaimed a holy crusade against the Germans — you give in to moods and justify the boycott. You are afraid of losing your popularity.
His friend, with a nervous movement of his lips, shifted his papirosa to the other corner of his mouth, tousled his unruly hair and said: "That is not right." The question is not whether our boycott has made itself strongly felt by the Hitlerites — for it is only they who are at issue, not the Germans in general. Against the Germans as a people and a state we have nothing — what concerns us is Hitlerism, and above all the inhuman and intolerable attitude towards us.
I do not deny that our aim is to weaken Germany through the boycott, in order thereby to demonstrate[?] the grave[?] consequences of zoological antisemitism, and to disillusion the unemployed German masses about the rightness of the demagogic slogans of the lesser and greater leaders, who feed them with Jewish blood and Jewish property instead of with rational economic methods and love for their neighbours. But that is not yet all, nor the most important thing. First of all we must care for our honour as human beings and as a people. We must convince them that we will not let ourselves be spat in the face with impunity, that we have the strength to defend ourselves and to bear sacrifices, even if the struggle were hard and looked hopeless. If the Germans trample us underfoot, we cannot, for the sake of passing profits, forget it, do business with them and shake the hands of those who have only just spat in our faces and whose hands are still to this day stained with the blood of our brothers and whose pockets have filled with looted Jewish property. What is at stake here is Jewish honour. We cannot and must not be like the Jews of Bialik's "Maasei Nimirin"[?] [apparently the scene in "In the City of Slaughter"], who, crawling out of their holes after watching their wives and daughters being violated, turned with questions to the rabbis whether they should perhaps divorce their wives because they had become impure. Even if the boycott does not succeed, even if it brings no real gains — it makes no difference: we must boycott, because as long as Germany does not treat us as human beings, so long must we have nothing in common with them. Thus we must answer all their flatteries (abroad) with contempt. It is not only about the practical results of the boycott, but about its moral significance. And this is precisely the most valuable thing: that the boycott broke out spontaneously, and while the politicians were thinking and wavering whether it was possible to begin the boycott struggle or not, the Jewish masses instinctively decided and resolved on the boycott, seeing in it the only dignified and national way of reacting to the Hitlerite barbarities — and only afterwards did they draw in also the over-thinking and over-weighing politicians. That alone already suffices to speak of a victory, because this spontaneity of the boycott has shown that the long-dominant "Ma Yafit" type [the fawning Jew] has already died out. Besides, you are mistaken in thinking that the boycott has not made itself strongly felt by the Hitlerites; perhaps not so strongly directly, since exports to Poland are not large in any case, but had it not been for Polish Jewry, neither English, Dutch nor American Jews would have undertaken the boycott action, which there has also embraced the non-Jewish world. This boycott the Germans already feel very well, and they speak of it quite loudly. If we stop the boycott today, tomorrow the Jews of those countries that take their cue from us in Jewish-national questions will do the same, and Hitlerite antisemitism will triumph all along the line, and we will once again prove that we cannot defend ourselves and that one may trample us underfoot with impunity. I assure you that then the Hitlerite methods will find their imitators in a whole series of countries which still refrain from these methods for fear of our boycott and our moral self-defence.
And how long do you intend to go on with the boycott? said the elegant one, drawing on his cigar — perhaps until the end of the world? If one goes to war, one must after all mark out for oneself the final aim. Do you intend in this way to bring about the partition of Germany, or at least to force them to reintroduce the parliamentary-democratic order?
That is not our purpose. It will be enough for us when Germany stops treating the Jews in a medieval manner and they stop the policy of extermination towards the Jews. We demand no harm whatever to the state or the people. The internal political order is their private affair; whoever wishes may sympathise with the democratic, parliamentary, communist or fascist order — none of that, however, constitutes the Jewish problem.
If so, said the elegant one, we are already on a good road. The Jewish merchants in Germany carry on their business without disturbances, and only from time to time do they have to take on Hitlerite partners; if here and there in the provinces anti-Jewish excesses still occur — well, that will pass, and in the end the lawyers who were not removed on account of their Jewishness will also be able to continue their practice in peace. And if there are no Jewish officials in Germany, no Jewish deputies, no Jewish doctors in the sick-funds and hospitals, no Jewish judges and no Jewish professors — none of that is so terrible; one can live without it too.
"First of all, even now it is not so good," replied the thin one, throwing away the smoked-out papirosa; it is so only in Berlin and perhaps in a few more large cities, and precisely because of our boycott, to calm us a little and lull us to sleep. Apart from that nothing has changed there. But we want the Jews to be given back their legal rights, which they already possessed. We cannot agree that our rights be taken from us merely because we belong to another race. We cannot permit ourselves to be treated as an inferior race, even if the whole of human culture did not owe its existence in great measure to us. And as long as the yellow patch is not lawfully[?] removed from us — we will not rest.
"Romanticism," the elegant one laughed, and walked away.
The thin one looked after him and said sadly: "Even Hitler has not yet made human beings of them"...
They spoke one language, but did not understand each other.
Protests or Informing (Mesirot)?

Mesirah (informing) — this terrible, abominable word is unfortunately heard ever more often in the Jewish street. This hideous thing, which every decent person condemns and turns away from in disgust, has regrettably penetrated our world and poisons the air to the point of suffocation.
But as long as the matter of informing was the programme of base creatures, of dark individuals who drew their sustenance from this pestilential [swamp?], in order to satisfy their greedy and sadistic inclinations, we could understand it; but when people come wrapped in silk and in tekhelet, people who demand to be respected as eminent householders, people who pretend to be leaders, people who want to be recognised as leaders, as spiritual leaders — and do such things, that is a tragedy!
And it is done in such a way that before the world one is in the right, and for oneself — certainly [?].
— One protests...
Certainly protesting is an entirely kosher means, accepted in the cultured world. Certainly, when someone is attacked [?] and he protests, he is ethically and morally fully in order; but it depends when, where, whom, before whom and about what.
When, in the struggle with an opponent, one writes protests to the decisive authorities full of lies and insinuations, when one writes slanders "where needed" over the heads of the Jewish masses and their representatives — that already goes beyond the framework of "protests"; here decency ends, here begins baseness, informing...
———
Let it be recorded; it is worthy of history.
The Będzin Jewish kehilla worked for months on the budget for 1934. All the currents that represent the population argued for a long time, debated, fought each according to his outlook, hotly defended their positions. Hardly a single figure passed without passionate disputes, until somehow an agreement was reached; naturally, on every question there must be a majority and a minority. But for God's sake! It cannot be otherwise — in which parliaments in the world, and which laws, pass by everyone's consent? The minority must after all be outvoted; that is an axiom!
But the minority of the Będzin Jewish community has a different slogan: for it, "follow the majority" (aharei rabim lehatot) is a zero. And it took up its old weapon... and inspired protests.
———
Three they are, three protests, which were submitted to the authorities, protesting against the activity of the kehilla board.
Their content and their argumentation differ, but from all of them there breathes a kind of aftertaste, plain lack of character.
Along comes such a householder as Mr. Boszykowski [?], a Jew, quite a calm, quiet one, known also as a handsome donor; fate willed it, and perhaps he was assessed a few hundred zł. more than he expected — and instead of appealing to the proper instance and arguing that the sum imposed on him was too high, he took it upon himself to protest to the authorities; to everyone's astonishment he writes no more and no less than:
"At a time when government institutions and communal institutions are reducing their budgets(!), Jewish communities come and raise their budgets — the authorities must not tolerate this"...
— So protests Mr. Boszykowski.
And further:
"Formerly 500 zł. a year (!) was enough for a cantor; now they have set a full 3000 zł. for a cantor. Formerly 2000 zł. was set for coal for the poor; now the board has put in 5000 zł. (truly a scandal!...). For kimcha [de-Pischa, Passover flour for the poor] 8000 was hitherto provided in the preliminary estimate, and in this budget it has been raised to 12000 zł."
— Do you hear the complaints?
And further:
"For the gemilut-hesed (free-loan) fund they raised the subsidy to 5000 zł. — what on earth, protests Mr. Boszykowski — the free-loan fund, which is supported so much by foreign and domestic capital"...
— So then, what is this to be called — a protest, or ...?
Over the few hundred złotys by which he feels wronged, Mr. Boszykowski cries out that a cantor in the Będzin town synagogue has enough with 500 zł. a year, i.e. 10 zł. a week... and coal for over a thousand Jewish families in the [winter?] — 2000 zł. a year, and 12000 zł. for kimcha — that is certainly, certainly too much! And above all the free-loan fund, which has other capital.
Had Mr. Boszykowski taken a little interest, he would have known that 1200 families in Będzin had nothing for Passover and took support from the community — and 12000 zł. was far too little to give each one something for the bread of affliction and for potatoes; he would have known how many hundreds of Jewish merchants and traders wait in the queue at the free-loan fund to be lent a few hundred zł., so that they may go on somehow sustaining their lamentable existence; had Mr. Boszykowski first given himself an account of what he was about to sign, he would have understood that to write to the authorities that the government is reducing taxes while the kehillot make themselves big budgets is simply irresponsibility!...
No, this is no protest; this is something else.
The second protest is from the rabbi.
The Rabbi of Będzin protests and invokes many, many laws, circulars (okólniki) and paragraphs — not, God forbid, from the Hoshen Mishpat, but from various [official ordinances?] — that his pension may not be touched. And further the rabbi does now invoke the ritual regulations, i.e. that according to halakha there must be 5 shochtim in Będzin... Well, one feels like asking the Rabbi of Będzin: do you know, Rabbi of Będzin, what poverty and want prevail among the Będzin population, and with which craftsman, merchant and manufacturer has income not fallen by seven and a half percent from last year to today? Did anyone intend to wrong you personally with the reduction? Have expenses not become much smaller from last year to today? Has not the government, as the command of the times, reduced the salaries of all officials by more than seven and a half percent?
— Why search, why rummage in the paragraphs? Why write such protests? Why cause so much bad blood, provoke so much opposition?
Now the chapter of the shochtim: but let us rather not speak of it; this matter is very, very painful [?], very drastic. Enough that the Będzin kehilla agreed to go to a rabbinical court (din) with the two young men who want to become Będzin shochtim — and the Rabbi of Będzin comes and writes to the authorities that he demands that these [?] young men be deprived of their position as shochtim. Where then is "there is justice in Israel"?..
— Who then is to respect that?..
And now comes the third; here lawlessness has broken the record! Lies, gossip, informing — you find everything in this protest, among whose signatures you find Jews of every kind.
In this "protest" one does not speak in hints; the vileness cries out openly:
"The present kehilla wants to draw money at the expense of the poor population and spend it on Zionism! They have reduced the rabbinate's [due?] pensions by as much as twenty percent (!...). All the subsidies will not be paid out anyway; everything will be given to the Zionist party; all these things are not needed at all, and the proof: until now, what was set in the budget they also handled at their own discretion; they gave nobody a groschen, only to the National Council, which is under the authority of the Zionist deputies!"...
And more and more such "iron" arguments are slipped to the decisive authorities.
"And let the public know what Jews are capable of —
— "Seven thousand zł. they are going to grab for the Keren Hayesod and the Keren Kayemet!.. Only they deliberately put it in under the name 'aid for emigration to Palestine', so that the authorities would not notice" — so they write, black on white!
— Well, the question arises!
Did the greater part of the signatories, that part which has not been drawn into the fire of hatred and strife, give themselves an account of what they were signing? Never mind the strife-mongers — they have a purpose in it, and "the end justifies the means"; but the greatest part, those who signed the "protest" — can they have a quiet conscience? Do they know what they have signed?
When Jews come and write to the government that 6000 zł. for "extraordinary aid" for the poor is too much, it surely means that they themselves are not so badly off!...
When one writes: they want [?] to take the poor's money for party purposes!
— What is that, a protest or informing?..
When one writes that preliminary-budget money is taken and sent to the "Żydowska Rada Narodowa" [Jewish National Council] and that one accepts "Zionist pali [?]"...
What is this? What does one aim at by it?
———
— — — The atmosphere in our narrow ghetto is poisoned.
— — — Let them sow hatred, whose fruits they will enjoy together with us. Let them lay stones under our feet — we shall all fall together...
L. Goldsztajn.
(Parnas of the Jewish kehilla in Będzin).
Avraham-Ber's Grievances Against the Almighty

(A story of our present time).
He was in despair, embittered against everyone and everything, and against the Almighty Himself. Everything He had taken away from him. Everything... First He had given it to him and then taken it back with bloody interest... God had toyed with him!
Like an evil storm the crisis had come, and broke and tore and left behind it terror and despair, want and misfortune...
Him too, old Avraham-Ber, it struck without mercy.
He had once been a poor trader; then, in the famous "good times", he began to deal and grew rich. He was a widower, and he married a young, pretty girl, who took him for his wealth... He had a daughter from his first wife; for her he got a husband — a doctor...
He wore a top hat. His long black beard, mixed with white threads, he wore trimmed[?] and combed with great care. His young wife he showered with diamonds for her favours. And he thanked God for "this world", and he gave charity and did good turns. In their hearts people begrudged him and cursed him, and with their lips they blessed him and paid[?] him honour...
The world was a beautiful spring for him, life — a paradise, his young wife — the bright sun in his paradise...
And suddenly the crisis came, and — paradise was over!..
The bank where his money lay closed its doors. Four houses he had owned in Germany [so printed: "in Daytshland"], and he lost them. First one, then a second, and the third he abandoned himself, because the tenants stopped paying rent. He was left with one more house. But when the taxes had to be paid he had nothing to pay them with, and then he had to beg his young wife to pawn her jewellery and save his last house — and she refused...
He began to demand it of her sternly and in anger: "Save me, I am burning, I am going under!" She answered him. That if he was burning, she would not crawl into the fire; she had first to save herself; to be left with at least[?] something for having married an old man whom she had never loved.
Then he threw himself on her wildly!
— The jewellery here, you wicked woman! It is mine! Mine!
And she ran away from him with the jewellery.
Then they took his last house away from him.
No more houses, no more wife, no more of this world...
His life now became a hell. Death would be much better! He began to think of taking his own life.
But he was a pious Jew and was afraid of losing the World to Come too.
And so, living and suffering with the burning feeling that his little wife, whom he had loved so much, had deceived him so foully, and with the bitter thought in his mind that he might now again have to go hungry to earn his living, his despair grew, and the fear that he might lose the World to Come too turned in him into a feeling of rancour, of hatred against everyone and above all against God.
He began to think that God had toyed with her[?], had made a joke of him... What for? What for?
And once, while he was praying with great devotion, as was his custom, he suddenly stopped: why does he thank Him? Why does he praise Him? He will not do it! — he said aloud with bitterness — he does not want to! He does not want to...
And he took off his tallit and tefillin.
And later, at night, when he sat alone in his house, which was no longer his, when he sat and thought about his yesterday and his today and his tomorrow, he suddenly jumped up with a wild fire in his eyes and began to bang on the table and shout:
— I have a just grievance against You! Answer! By what justice shall I lose the World to Come too?.. Why did You toy with me so? Who asked You to give me wealth? Had I stayed a hungry man, I would not have married that one either! Why did You make such a joke of me? Had You not raised me up so high before, I would not now have fallen so low.. Why did You laugh at me so? After all You are some sort of God, a merciful and gracious God. Where is Your justice, Your mercy? Why did You make such a mockery of me, why?!..
He sat down again at the table and made wild gestures with his eyes and his hands.
The room was half dark. Outside the rain poured and beat on the windows...
Then he jumped up again from his place, raised a threatening hand on high and again broke into shouting:
— And if You think You will make me a pauper again, I tell You plainly: no, no, no! I will not knock on "the doors again! I cannot, I cannot! But I do not want to suffer, do You hear — he spoke through teeth clenched with a kind of mad hatred — You cannot forbid me to die! I have a just grievance against You! Why, why? You must answer me!
— again he began to bang on the table — You must! I am not afraid to come before Your Throne of Glory...
Well. What can You answer me to that? What?.. But You will not wriggle out of it, do You hear, h-e-a-r...
And with wild eyes he went into the kitchen and shut the doors. Then he went up to the gas stove, attached a tube to the stove, pulled up a chair, sat down, took the tube into his mouth and turned the gas burner to which the tube was attached...
His eyes began to move, large, drunken, restless. For a while he swayed on the chair with his whole broad, heavy body like a drunkard. Then he remained frozen, his head thrown back against the back of the chair, the tube in his mouth, over his long, tangled[?] beard, which was now more white than black, and with staring, glassy eyes...
In the kitchen it was half dark and quiet. Outside the rain was still pouring, beating on the windows, and a wind was whistling...
L. Tamrin[?].
The Goy Is Not So Bad...

[Opinion — the municipal elections (27 May 1934) and the mood in the Jewish street.]
Something about the present moods in the Jewish street.

Do you remember the election campaigns of just a few years ago?
Excitement, activity, joy:
the Jewish street felt that it too was being called upon to perform an important act as a citizen.
Parties leafed through the books of programmes and theories, and those whose theories shone little and did not suffice to capture the street — they were ashamed to come out with a cheap [?] demagogy, but [used it] so subtly that the opponent should not catch them red-handed. The target was the city council, but along the way people talked about the future of the nation, about universal human ideals or about the Torah of Moses. And party leaders, or plain activists, knew and remembered that a day of judgement would come, that they would have to come before the voter, before the conscience of the masses, and one must come to them clean, whole, honest, because the masses are jealous, and the masses sometimes judge very ruthlessly. There reigned "eimata detzibura" [awe of the public].
A feeling of equality reigned: the Zawale [?] considered itself as noble as Kołłątaja Street, and the "Mandushever" [?] as Małachowskiego.
———
May 1934.
The town has already actively entered the period of an election campaign.
It is a matter of building a self-government on the basis of a new statute.
The Jewish population is being put to a new examination.
What is going on in the Jewish street? Where does such melancholy come from? With every day that we draw nearer to the 27th of May, the apathy grows ever greater!
I talk with an old Jewish activist, a man whose hair has turned grey in public work. Apart from idealistic joy he never had the slightest benefit from this work, and he complains to me:
— Dear friend, if only I could sleep through a few weeks and not have to take part, or even be merely a witness to the business now being carried on — not [?] to the self-abasement, baseness and lawlessness that have burst in at the very top. There is no strength to resist, not even the courage to bang one's fist on the table and shout: go to the devil!
And another apologises:
— I have worked for decades, gone through cold and heat, and wanted to lend a hand now too, but — impossible. One must run away, and in good time at that.
A third, a man of character, a man who cannot bend and cannot make peace with servility, refused right from the start:
— The air is stifling, one can come to harm...
———
When the smell of elections began to be felt in the air and the necessary preparations had only just begun, I happened to meet a leading personality, with whom I had a talk about holding a meeting of a small number of Jewish activists.
And with what respect and esteem he spoke about the Jewish street! In his imagination he pictured a united and conscious community, its activists full of responsibility, dignity, character and sense. An outstretched hand from equal to equal.
A few weeks have passed [?], and how quickly everything has changed, so deeply and so radically!
People no longer go to the Jews. Rather the Jews have become the goers, and once the Jews set off, people stopped going: they began to run, to crawl, to tug at coat-tails, in the office, at home, in the street. It is no longer possible to get rid of them; all the shopkeepers chase after one peasant, ready to sell for half nothing or to pay until the day comes [i.e. give endless credit].
And which of us, had he been in that man's place, would have acted otherwise?
Does he know the Jewish street, then? He knows who stands before him and hears what is said to him — a human being and not an angel.
Who were the first? What offers did they submit? What did they demand at all? Did the general Jewish need speak out of them? Did they bring Jewish demands, Jewish claims? Were these faithful emissaries of the public?
Perhaps one day we will be able to tell about this; for the time being we must content ourselves with establishing one truth: that little Jews ran. What they had in mind, God knows; "Klal Yisroel" [the Jewish people as a whole] turned into "Reb Yisroel", and each one thought this was the opportune moment, that the heavens had opened and one could beg every good thing for oneself.
Jewish postulates, Jewish demands? Negotiations, deliberations, agreements? — Yes, such things are possible between equals and equals. With crawlers one speaks from above, downwards; it is enough that one does not chase them away.
———
That, then, is the source of the melancholy in the Jewish street, of the lack of faith in our own strength, and that is why such a scramble behind the scenes and such a competition in crawling became possible.
Will there really be no one who will bang on the table and cry out: the Jewish street is not ownerless! We want to live, to exist and to breathe freely, as human beings, as citizens!
Let our own people stop making our life loathsome!
The goy is not at all so bad.
Little Jews spoil him, and of us [they make] — a ruin heap...
Y. N. — Vim.
Daniel in the Lions' Den (A Short Feuilleton)

Not Daniel the Righteous, who was thrown into a lions' den, but an entirely different Daniel, who went among the lions voluntarily and with joy, and they received him as one of their own.
Daniel Bachrach.
In Poland he was once a trainee (aspirant) in the investigation office. We knew it, and he was removed from there; afterwards we heard his name in connection with a series of criminal trials. But when things were no longer so cheerful in his pocket, he squeezed his way into a Warsaw Jewish newspaper, wrote spicy memoirs of his criminal practice and made a penny.
In writing he hinted more than once between the lines that he was all but a victim of his Jewishness; the Jewish paper told its readers in big letters that its contributor was a „Jewish aspirant“ — and kept silent about the fact that Daniel is an apostate.
People found this out only recently, in connection with a sensational report that Daniel had gone to Berlin and become a commissar in the Hitlerite police there.
An apostate indeed, but... still... as in the „Aryan paragraph“! And how did this „righteous man“ earn the privilege of a high post in the Hitlerite lions' den? After all, with his Jewish blood he could poison the milieu of the ideal Hitlerite policemen, and in general, who knows what such a Jew is capable of.
It turns out that Daniel is a chosen one of the chosen people: not only an apostate, but he has other merits too. In his time, while once holding a police post in Germany, he caused people as many troubles as one can only expect from an apostate, and surely [?] the Jews did not lick honey with him. It went so far that his victims passed a death sentence on him and he had to uproot himself from Germany.
Now Daniel has reminded [them] of his past merits, showed that he practised Hitlerism when Hitler had not yet dreamt of becoming ruler of Germany — and for such virtues the Hitlerites made room for him in their lions' den.
Daniel will be entrusted with Marxists and Jews... he will surely know how to „teach“ [?] them...
———
To be allowed to live in Petersburg, Jewish women students had to register as prostitutes; for decent Jewish daughters there was no room in Nicholas's residence city.
The Einsteins are a disgrace and a misfortune for today's Berlin; the Hitler-land can also allow itself a portion of Jews, even needs them. But — the Jews must be such as Daniel Bachrach.
„Heil Hitler“! A. Szwarcer.
Laws on Social Insurance. Payments.

Only the employer is responsible for the entire insurance contribution; he deducts the appropriate share from the worker's wages paid to him, but only for the period covered by the payment — so that if an employer did not deduct the amount of the insurance contribution at the first payment, that is already his loss; at the second payment the missing sum may no longer be deducted from the worker.
An insured person has the right to pay unpaid [?] insurance contributions himself for a period of at most 52 weeks and to reclaim the sum paid from the employer.
The insurance contribution amounts to:
In case of sickness and old age — for white-collar ("mental") workers 4.3/5 percent, for other categories 5 percent. Half of the contribution is paid by the insured.
For other branches of insurance — for all insured 5,1/5 percent; for workers in glassworks 5,4/5 percent.
Of this the insured pay 3,3/10 percent.
The relevant insurance contribution for accidents and occupational diseases is paid entirely by the employer.
For insured persons who receive no wages at all or receive only board, the employer pays the whole contribution. Likewise no insurance contribution is paid for those unable to work because of illness or childbirth, for the entire period, as long as they receive sickness, hospital, family or maternity benefit.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Emor)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Emor
The Portion
—o—
a) "Speak unto the priests the sons of Aaron" (Lev. 21:1)
"To admonish the adults concerning the minors." Rashi.
"To admonish the adults" — to warn the grown-ups that they should conduct themselves properly. "Concerning the minors" — so that the young should have someone from whom to learn... Be'er Mayim Chaim.
* * *
"To admonish the adults concerning the minors" — purity, spiritual cleanliness, must be instilled from childhood on. If from childhood the child's mind becomes defiled — "even when he is old he will not depart from it." That is why this is the only commandment about which it is said "to admonish concerning the minors." Siftei Da'at.
—o—
b) "Speak unto the children of Israel and say unto them: the appointed seasons of the Lord" (23:2)
"Dibbur" (speaking), according to the Sages, means "words as hard as sinews." On a festival the verse must warn sternly, because festivals are days on which work stands idle[?], people eat and drink and do not work — days on which it is easy to sin. That is why "dibbur" comes here — "words as hard as sinews." In the Tur, Orach Chaim, at the end of the Laws of Yom Tov, it is said that the court has a duty on a festival to keep watch over the gardens and places of amusement, where Satan dances, for our many sins... Dvash ve-Chalav.
—o—
c) "And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath" (ibid., 15)
The reason for the commandment of counting the Omer is explained by the "Abudarham": since after Passover the people were out in the fields with the harvest, the Torah commanded the Jewish farmer to count forty-nine days, so that he would know when to come up to Jerusalem on pilgrimage.
* * *
Why does one not say the "Shehecheyanu" blessing when counting the Omer? Because "Shehecheyanu" is said only over something that brings joy, and the counting of the Omer only reminds us of the time of the Temple [printed "zman chavit"], whereas today we cannot offer the Omer; therefore we do not say "Shehecheyanu" when we begin counting the Omer. Kol Bo.
* * *
For a time R' Yisrael (a son of R' Yosele Slutsker) used to travel to the Koidanover Rebbe. At first the son of the Misnagdic Gaon was carried away by Hasidism, but later he became disillusioned and became a Misnaged again.
Once the Koidanover Rebbe delivered a Torah discourse, speaking about the sefirot, about "Tiferet within Tiferet." The Hasidim did not understand the Rebbe's teaching and afterwards asked R' Yisrael, who had a fiery[?] mind, to explain the Rebbe's teaching and to make clear what the Rebbe had meant by the term[?] "Tiferet within Tiferet."
R' Yisrael, who by then was already mocking his Rebbe, says to the Hasidim:
— Good, I will explain "Tiferet within Tiferet" to you in a tangible way.
And he leads them to the window, points to a hole in the wall opposite and asks them:
— What do you see?
— A hole, an emptiness.
— And if I make another hole in the hole?
— There will be a hole in a hole. An emptiness within emptiness...
— No — smiles R' Yisrael — it will be "Tiferet within Tiferet"...
—o—
d) "And the son of an Israelite woman went out" (24:10)

Overheard at an election meeting.
The elections are still some way off, the commissioner still sits firmly in his chair, Jews love politics and are already dividing up the bear's skin.
"Nester"[?], "pifter"[?], a platform here, a platform there — the main thing, after all, is the seats.
Who has the greatest claim to the seats, behind whom do the Jewish masses stand?
That will become clear from the speeches delivered at the last meeting about the bloc.
A representative of the merchants — every Jew, whether he is a house-owner or a tenant, is after all engaged in trade and is a merchant, whom I have the great honour to represent. The mandates on the city council belong to the Merchants' Association.
A Zionist — all Jews are Zionists, after all one says three times a day "And a redeemer shall come to Zion"; Zionism is the only political party in the Jewish street, the mandates belong to us.
A Revisionist — who today does not want a Jewish state on both banks of the Jordan? All Jews side with Jabotinsky, the mandates on the city council belong to us.
A small trader — there are no big merchants at all nowadays; come into our association and you will see how thousands of people have nothing with which to buy out a trade licence (patent); all Jews are small traders, or plain paupers; the mandates on the city council belong to us.
A tenant — how many house-owners are there in town? Every Jew [printed "yur"] and person is after all a tenant; our association counts 10,000 members, we are a power, the mandates on the city council belong to us.
A craftsman — we are the true aristocracy; without us the Jewish people would have had no existence; we live, after all, by the toil of our hands; we will not let ourselves be terrorised by the party-fixers — the mandates on the city council belong to us.
An Agudist — thank God, in the Warsaw kehilla and in the Łódź kehilla we have a majority; in the Będzin city council, too, a majority is due to us.
From the "Club for the State Idea"[?] — which Jew is not a loyal citizen? We are looked upon kindly from the important windows; taxes will be reduced; when the government wants, it can do anything! The Jewish people will be saved — send our statists to the city council.
A house-owner — true, not every Jew is a house-owner, but in every Jewish home there is, after all, a housewife (balebuste), and the votes belong to us; we got many councillors elected at those elections, and now too the mandates belong to us.
Go and figure out a people — who is speaking in the name of the Jewish masses...
Yosef.

Perished for the Sanctification of the Name

[Serialized story — the Ukrainian pogroms of 1919; martyrdom.]
H. Akerman.

(A tragic story of a Jewish daughter at the time of the Ukrainian pogroms in 1919).

The next morning Kholostenko's messengers came to the rabbi for an answer. And the rabbi told them that Hanele would go, but he told them to ride back and bring gentile clothes for Hana.

The rabbi had the messengers bring gentile clothes because he wanted the whole matter to remain a secret from the entire shtetl; he wanted Hana to disguise herself as a shiksa (a gentile girl), so that she would not be recognised.

And now the terrible hour came; it is a dark evening. Hana and her parents are at the rabbi's, and when the messengers came with the clothes they already found her there.

Hana took leave of her parents, fell on her mother's neck and drenched her with tears, and after that she took leave of her father. And then of the rabbi, and she put on a gentile dress with a "serdyk" [a short Ukrainian coat] and with "salkes" (coral beads) on [printed "on on"] her neck, and rode off with the messengers to Kholostenko the ataman, at Shcherbatov's on the estate.

Father and mother went home; if the Hornsteins survived that night, it was by miracles. Both of them paced the house back and forth and wept. Their pain had no shore and their grief no limit. That night both of them aged by many years, and in the morning they did not recognise each other. So changed had they become.

The whole morning passed and Hana had still not come back.

The parents did not know at all what to think and what to ponder; all kinds of dark thoughts crept into their heads and gave them no rest. The morning passed, the day passed, and Hana was still gone. Only in the evening, when it was already dark, did she appear. Where had she been the whole terrible day?

She had wandered about in the field; she could not, in the bright light of day, step back onto the streets of her little town; she was ashamed before the earth, before the houses, and most of all before her father and mother; and only when the stars appeared in the sky did she then enter the shtetl.

She came in to her parents in the house and broke into bitter weeping, so that for hours they could not calm her. Looking at her, her parents wrung their hands and tore the hair from their heads: oh, how changed their daughter had become! The bright gleam of her eyes had been extinguished, and a thick darkness lay on her beautiful face. When she came to herself a little, she began to tell her parents about the great shame that had befallen her that night.

In a dead voice she told: when the three bandits brought her to Kholostenko he was very drunk; it did not take long before Prince Shcherbatov came into Kholostenko's room, and when he found Hana there he began to tease her and mock her, that at last he had her under his roof after all...

Kholostenko, drunk, began to tear the clothes off her, and he began to bite her on the cheeks, over the neck, on the breast... and Shcherbatov watched and giggled... Hana screamed in [?] voices [printed "betumene", doubtful] and wrestled with him, though she knew well that she would not be able to overpower him. She would have torn herself free and run, but on the other side of the door soldiers stood and kept guard.

And when Hana saw that nothing would help her anyway, she pretended to appeal to Kholostenko's "noble" [?] feelings, that he should keep the word he had sent to the rabbi through his messengers, and that he should give her a written document that in the morning he would ride out of Gilovka [?] with his band and would not come there. And when he had sworn it to her and when she began to grasp what was going on in him there, she decided to get herself drunk, to numb her feelings, so that at least she would not know what would be done with her. So she began to pour wine [?] and brandy, as much as she could take in, until she remained lying unconscious.

Thus, weeping, she told her parents a hundredth part of what had happened to her, but she could not look them in the eyes for shame, and she buried herself in the pillow and did not stop crying.

(Conclusion follows.)

In his two-hour
Paper, Dr. Berliner
the speaker illuminated from every side the new decrees, such as the industry law, the compulsory guilds, the education census, which are aimed at striking the Jewish merchant and pushing him out of his economic positions, which even until now were weak enough. Polish Merchants' Associations in Kraków and in Upper Silesia Are Satisfied with the Industry Law

[Trade — Economy.] On Sunday the general meeting of the Polish merchants' association in Kraków ("Konkurencja"[?]) took place. At this meeting the Christian merchants kept on praising the new industry law, which introduces the obligation of examinations and concessions in trade. They are highly satisfied with it, although the law may well hit them too. In a resolution the Christian merchants expressed their demand that the examinations be introduced as soon as possible, and that they will wage a struggle for this in Galicia.
Further, the same meeting resolved to turn to the government and to the Sejm so that a law be issued on freeing trade from private commercial debts. The important action of freeing agriculture from debts has caused colossal damage to trade. The merchants cannot obtain their debts from the farmers, and at the same time trade is losing its credit; therefore the government should issue a law under which they could prolong them and pay them off over a long period. For this purpose settlement commissions for merchants and manufacturers should be created.
On the same day a conference of the merchants of Upper Silesia also took place in Katowice, where the following resolutions were adopted:
1) unconditionally to prohibit peddling;
2) the tax offices should not be so strict in carrying out tax distraints for tax arrears, and should take into account the difficult material situation of the merchants;
3) because of the severe crisis, a number of towns belonging to the second patent class should be moved to a third class, so that the merchants in those towns obtain cheaper patents (trade licences).
4) in assessing the income tax (dochodowy), a list of average earnings of all branches should be compiled, which should be based on the true state of trade. The assessment of income tax should rely on it. Unfortunately the assessment of the dochodowy is made on the basis of such earnings as do not exist at all in trade.

Theatre Notes

[Theatre — Review.] ("The Forty-First", a play in 3 acts by Boris Lavrenyov).
A young girl from the Volga region joins — during the civil war in Russia — as a volunteer in a detachment of the Red Army.
This girl "specialises" in shooting White Guard officers. From her conversation with the Red Army men we learn that she has already shot 40 officers and is waiting impatiently for the 41st.
And then the moment comes: a White officer appears, and when Marjusza (that is the girl's name) shoots at him she misses the target, and the young officer is brought to the Red commissar.
Compromising material is found on the White Guardist, and the Red Army men want to shoot him at once, but the commissar orders him to be taken alive to the Red general staff.
A few Red Army men under Marjusza's command receive the order to carry out the mission. On the way all of them — except the girl and the officer — are drowned. The last two save themselves on a deserted island, where they feed on fish and wait for the fishermen to arrive.
The day comes when a sailing ship appears on the horizon, but instead of fishermen there are White Guardists on it. The officer is overjoyed and wants to run over to the Whites; at that moment the girl shoots him with her revolver. That is all — he is the 41st, the Tsarist officer.
That is, in short, the content of the play.
"The Forty-First" belongs to the kind of reportages in which there is no original idea whatsoever; it is stuffed with mass-meeting propaganda and with cheap, poster-shouting slogans, which today already seem like anachronisms.
The author of the play does not master the technique of writing for the stage. The third act is absolutely superfluous, because for the sake of waiting for the fishermen it was not worth making a whole act; this could also have happened in the 2nd act.
Jonas Turkow (the Tsarist officer) is a well-known brand. He is truly a talented, subtle actor with a fine artistic culture, but for lack of action he had nowhere to let himself go.
Miss Lerner in the role of Marjusza was too monotonous; her speech comes out as if hummed, without any nuance.
The other performers in the first act were satisfactory.
Sh. R.

Secure Your Right to Vote.

[Zagłębie — municipal elections.] The Jewish population of Zagłębie must not wait until somebody calls it, wakes it and reminds it.
The Jewish population must take its affairs[?] into its own hands.
The Jews of Zagłębie must already now seriously see to securing their right to vote. Every neglect in [printed "and"] these present days causes complications and difficulties. Instead of a little bit of effort to go to the electoral office, one later has to write complaints (reclamations) and go to commissions. The Jewish voter, however, gets into the "mood" only after a dozen election meetings and after he is brought into "ambition". First he neglects, and later he is at a loss.
