The Torah... (A True Story in Honour of Shavuot)

In years gone by my uncle Hersh-Leyb held the festival of Shavuot to be a whole world and all its fullness. He never said so out loud, because my uncle was altogether a silent Jew and all his days guarded himself against a superfluous word.
But it makes no difference that he kept silent! The main thing is that at Shavuot the Divine Presence truly rested on uncle Hersh-Leyb, and everyone knew that this very festival stood, in uncle's eye, on a very, very high level.
Aunt Kayle, however, could in no way agree with uncle, because she could not imagine how one could even compare Shavuot to „such a festival as Passover. A fine comparison! Passover lasts a whole week, and it begins right after Purim. At Passover one washes and scours and koshers and bakes matzah and sits down to the Seder and says the Haggadah, and in every little corner it is so clean then, and at Passover one dresses in a new garment and eats from new dishes, and — she could not restrain herself, aunt Kayle, and used to say every time:
— The most beautiful festival is still Passover!
Uncle Hersh-Leyb, however, almost never answered her on this in words. He would make a dissatisfied wave of his hand and keep silent, as is his nature. Only very rarely, when the older children joined in, and one son sided with mother, and a second agreed with father, and a third said it was all the same to him — then uncle Hersh-Leyb would rise from his place and, looking at the whole household, would ask very briefly:
— Do you know what Shavuot is?
— What should Shavuot be? aunt Kayle would answer: Shavuot is a festival!
— A festival, you say?
— What else? Of course a festival!
Here, however, one of the sons would join in, mostly the one to whom it was all the same, and would rule dismissively:
— A festival is a festival, what difference does it make!
Uncle Hersh-Leyb could no longer restrain himself then, and with few words would cut[?] the son short:
— Rather than talk idly into the air — it is much better to keep silent.
A little later, when uncle's anger had passed, he would again look good-naturedly at his wife and children, and at the same time he would speak as if to himself:
— One festival is not like another: on Shavuot, after all, we were given the Torah... Do you understand? The Torah.
The wife and children understood a little and did not understand a little, but then all their faces would become very serious, and none of the household said another word.
That is how uncle Hersh-Leyb lived for days and years, and Shavuot was always for him the best festival, the most beautiful festival and, above all — the holiest festival, until...
To this day uncle still thinks very highly of Shavuot, because in uncle's eye all festivals are very[?] important — even Hanukkah, even Shabbat Nachamu, even on the fifteenth [of Shevat] my uncle Hersh-Leyb puts on his festive frock-coat, all the more so on Shavuot, when the Torah was given...
But in recent years uncle Hersh-Leyb somehow became different, became a bit of another[?] uncle — somehow not quite at one with Shavuot..
At first aunt Kayle liked this very much, and she often thought to herself with pride that now he himself also understands that the best festival of all festivals is, after all, Passover!
But one Shavuot uncle Hersh-Leyb was sad.. that is, uncle would, God forbid, not spoil any festival, and — he even sang the zemirot as well. But already for several Shavuots, as aunt began to notice, — it is it and yet not it! Aunt Kayle began to grieve greatly why it is not so, and uncle — he only keeps silent and with him one never knows anything!
— Listen, Hersh — aunt tried last Shavuot to draw uncle into a conversation, — the further it goes the more I see that...
— What are you saying?
— Nothing.. I only say that Shavuot is really...
— I can't hear — speak louder.
— I'm saying it with regard to the festivals...
— Well?
— You were really right... Now I see that you were really right...
— It's... I mean...
— Shavuot really is a delightful festival, a treat, I tell you!
Uncle Hersh-Leyb, however, quietly ate the festive meal, silently looked into a little book and did not even raise his head.
— Hersh Leyb... aunt roused him as if from sleep: Hersh Leyb...
— Are you asking something, Kayle?
— It's a festival today, after all, it's Shavuot today, after all..
— Why are you saying this? Why? Of course it's a festival... A festival, what else?
— So why are you somehow so... Hersh Leyb, what's the matter with you, eh?
— Nothing...
— On a festival should a Jew sit so lost in thought and gloomy... It's a festival today, after all, it's Shavuot today, after all...
— We are eating, aren't we, I mean...
— The best festival, I say: on Shavuot the Torah was given, after all...
— The Torah?!! uncle growled: the Torah, you say, and where is it today, the Torah, eh? Who thinks now about the Torah, eh? Who keeps the Torah today, eh?
— The best festival, aunt stammered; the most beautiful festival...
Uncle shook his head!
— It was once... only once...
Don.
The Scroll of Ruth.

[Essay — Shavuot; the Scroll of Ruth.]
"The Scroll of Ruth contains neither impurity nor purity, neither prohibition nor permission. Why then was it written? To teach you how great is the reward of those who perform deeds of loving-kindness"!
(Midrash Ruth).
It is very characteristic that precisely on the festival of Shavuot, at "the time of the giving of our Torah", on the day of the receiving of the Torah — which consists of 613 positive commandments ("aseh") and 365 negative commandments ("lo ta'aseh") and countless fences and safeguards — precisely on this festival it is a mitzvah to read the Scroll of Ruth, in which not a single commandment of the Torah is mentioned. "Neither impurity nor purity, neither prohibition nor permission" — one must therefore admire the commentator of the Midrash [who says] that the Scroll of Ruth was written only so that we should understand the importance of loving-kindness (gemilut chasadim) and draw a moral lesson from it.
What, in fact, is depicted in the Scroll of Ruth?
Apart from the type of the principal heroine, the modest, humane, noble Ruth, who through a remarkable coincidence and various circumstances becomes the ancestress of the dynasty of King David, and the luminous figure of Naomi, and incidentally also of Orpah — the Scroll of Ruth depicts two heroes of opposite and different characters, the types of two Jewish patriarchs: Elimelech and Boaz.
Of Elimelech and his two sons the Sages say: "Elimelech and his sons were the great men of the generation and the providers of the generation", and again: "Elimelech was a very rich man and the provider of the generation". Nevertheless he had the character of a true bourgeois; he was a great egoist and thought that he need care only for himself and his family. And when a cataclysm occurred, a disaster — a famine broke out in his land of Judah, with all its consequences: crisis, unemployment, poverty and want — Elimelech, "the great man of the generation and provider of the generation", did not think long, and instead of sharing the misfortune of his people and organizing a broad relief action for those in need, he did exactly the opposite. As the Sages say: "And when the years of famine came, he said: now all Israel will crowd around my door, this one with his basket and that one with his basket; he arose and fled from them". He was afraid that he would be asked for support for his hungry brethren — so he took his whole family and fled with them from the hungry land of Judah into a foreign land, to a foreign people, to Moab.
In Moab Elimelech's house is severely punished: of all his great wealth only a ruin-heap is left; he is impoverished and, unable to bear the great suffering, he dies. Then his two sons, Mahlon and Chilion, also die, poor and lonely, among strangers and in a foreign land, and not only his great wealth but his whole house becomes a ruin-heap.
The Sages ask: "Why was Elimelech punished? Because he [caused] the heart of Israel [to fall] upon them"! Why was Elimelech punished so severely? Because by his flight he brought depression and despair into Jewish hearts, and that is the most dangerous thing for a people, since depression and despair bring ruin and destruction upon a people.
Boaz is the opposite type and character. Boaz is the expression of the deeply human and humane, the expression of compassion and mercy for every unfortunate and suffering person. Boaz too was a leader of Israel — "Boaz was a righteous man and the great man of the generation" — and when the famine broke out in the land of Judah, not only did he not flee from his starving people, but on the contrary: he stands on guard, organizes a broad relief action and distributes to the starving the produce of his rich estates and fields, does[?] loving-kindness to the right and to the left, and thereby strengthens hope and raises the spirit of the people so that it does not fall into depression and despair, and rescues the people from destruction.
Naomi, the patriarchal Naomi, is the expression of nobility and goodness — "and she was called Naomi because her deeds were pleasant". Naomi, the former aristocrat and lady of state — "at first she was clothed in garments of fine wool", "at first she rode in a covered wagon and now she walks barefoot" — this unfortunate woman and mother, who after the death of her husband and two sons was left poor, lonely and in despair among strangers in a foreign land, is now preparing to return to her homeland, Judah.
In the land of Moab, however, Naomi had acquired two gentile daughters-in-law, Ruth and Orpah, who had married into the lineage of the formerly rich, aristocratic Elimelech family. And these daughters-in-law loved their mother-in-law very much and decided to go with her. Naomi shows them and argues to them the pointlessness of their decision. And Orpah — although she loved her mother-in-law very much — nevertheless lets herself be persuaded, takes a passionate leave of Naomi, kisses her and weeps, and returns to her gentile parents.
Ruth — an opposite type and character was Ruth, the royal daughter of Eglon, King of Moab. Whereas Orpah had been bound to Elimelech's house only physically, and after the death of her husband all the threads of connection were torn, Ruth, on the contrary, after her husband's death bound herself to Naomi with even stronger and unbreakable threads, not only physically but also spiritually, and Ruth declares to Naomi her categorical decision: "For whither thou goest — I will go, and where thou lodgest — I will lodge, thy people — my people... only death shall part me and thee": wherever you go I too will go, wherever you spend the night I too will spend the night, your people is also my people, your God is also my God, where you die I too will die and be buried together; only death can part us.
After such a decided, categorical, dramatic answer, Naomi no longer had any moral right to turn Ruth back, and then the final decision falls to return together to the land of Judah.
And again the luminous figure of Boaz rises up. Ruth goes about Bethlehem, among the fields, to gather a little food from "gleanings, the forgotten sheaf and the corner of the field", so as to feed herself and her mother-in-law Naomi. Fate led her to the fields of the rich landowner Boaz. The modest, homely Boaz, who works together with his labourers in the field, noticing Ruth, tells the workers to give her to eat and to drink and also to give her food to take home. But afterwards, when he learns that this is Ruth, Naomi's daughter-in-law, who left her land, her people, her royal parental home and became a Jewess, he makes efforts on her behalf so that the closest relative in the family should fulfil the commandment of "levirate marriage" (yibbum) and take her as his wife. But that man declines. Then Boaz comes, as a close relative, and himself fulfils the commandment of "yibbum". He takes Ruth as his wife "to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance" — to restore the memory of Ruth's deceased husband.
With this last act of loving-kindness he attains the highest level of humanity, righteousness and nobility.
For this Boaz is rewarded, and through his union with Ruth he becomes the founding father of the dynasty of King David.
And that is why we read the "Scroll of Ruth" on Shavuot, for from this story one can learn a great deal, a very great deal...
J. Wygodzki.
Important clarifications for those liable to military service.

[Poland — military service.] Missing fingers.
The absence of 3 fingers on the right hand, 4 fingers on the left hand, 3 toes including the big toe and the one next to it, entitles one to category E. The absence of the thumb on the right hand, 3 fingers of the left hand, the big toe and 2 other toes entitles one to category D. The absence of the thumb on the left hand, 2 fingers of the right hand, the big toe and one more toe, or alternatively 3 ordinary toes — entitles one to cat. C.
The absence of 1 finger on the hand or of 1 ordinary toe does not disqualify one's fitness for service.
Exempt from military service.
Persons who live on the territory of Poland and hold proof that they are citizens of foreign states, or who acquired Polish citizenship when over 38 years of age, are exempt from active service in the Polish army.
Excluded from military service.
If one is sentenced for committing a crime to imprisonment for a term longer than 3 years, one is automatically excluded from Polish military service.
The exclusion remains in force for 10 years, counting from the day on which the sentence was served, or on which it lapsed by prescription or was pardoned.
Women, don't go with the men!..

[Będzin — humour; city council elections.] By J. Obrzanek [?]
(An election monologue by a Będzin Jewish woman.)
Who am I? What's my name? Zlate Kvitsh [Złata Kwicz] is my name! A "postępowa" [progressive] Jewish woman, that's me. A Jewish woman with a bang, who doesn't let anyone blow into her wig; I am "samodzielna" [independent], I go where I like, I do what I want, I don't reckon with the "opinia" [public opinion]. I laugh at the men, and basta!
Such big shots they are, the men, because they go about in trousers? And so they go about in trousers — so what? Because of that we women must let them lead us by the nose?
Everywhere they are the top of the heap [?], everywhere they are the pedigreed ones. Whom do they call up to the Torah? — Them, the men! Who gets maftir and shishi? — They, the men! Who leads the prayers before the lectern? — They, the men! Who blows the shofar? — They, the men! Who reads the Megillah? — They, the men! Who makes kiddush and havdalah? — They, the men! Who sits in the sukkah and who conducts the seder? — They, the men! Who travels to the rebbe? — They, the men! Who sits in the "gmina" [the Jewish community council]? — They, the men.
Everything is them, the men: cantors, beadles, wedding jesters, rabbinical judges — even circumcisers — everything is them, the men!
I ask you: why shouldn't we women get maftir and shishi? Why shouldn't we blow the shofar? Why shouldn't we make kiddush and havdalah? Why shouldn't we be gabbaiyot, beadles, she-jesters, she-judges and she-circumcisers? All because we go about in little dresses and they — in trousers! For that we must let ourselves be exploited by the nasty [paskudny] male sex?
No, and a thousand times no! At a time when everything goes "do góry nogami" [topsy-turvy], when any "lada pętak" [good-for-nothing] can become Reich Chancellor of Germany — at such a time we women must show the world that besides cooking, baking, darning "skarpetki" [socks], besides carrying, bearing, nursing and washing nappies, we can do something more — sit in the "Rada Miejska" [city council] and chatter away [lit. "chop a teakettle" [?]] on equal terms with them, with the men!
So then, sister-comrades, women, wives and Jewesses of the female sex: now the time has come for us to put an end to male rule; we must take the government away from the men. Long enough have we let ourselves be seduced by their sweet little speeches, by their sugary promises. We know them well, the windbags: they lie down like little lambs and get up like little lions; when they need our "łaska" [favour] they are soft as coconut butter, and an hour later they turn carpenters and make legs [i.e., take to their heels]...
Sister-comrades, women, wives and Jewesses of all strata and classes. It is high time you understood that we women have our own women's interests, which must be defended by ourselves. We must win our rights ourselves, and we have better means of struggle than the men. The men with fists, and we with our nine measures of talk; and if we just set our little mouths "w ruch" [in motion] in the city council, they, the men, will run off to where the black pepper grows; and once they run off, we women will do what we like... And should they be stubborn and not run off, we will take up our old, well-tried weapon: tears, fits [spasms]... And if all that doesn't help, we will take up our best methods: we will put on charms, make eyes, shower them with compliments — and our victory is assured...
Proceeding from this standpoint, I call on you, sister-women of all classes and strata, to tear yourselves away from the men and go to the city council elections independently, with a purely women's list, with purely women candidates, with a purely women's programme, with a purely women's platform — and above all, that in first place on the purely women's list should figure my name — Zlate Kvitsh.
When I, Zlate Kvitsh, am elected councilwoman of the city council, a different "porządek" [order] will be introduced. In the city council I will organise a women's "koło" [caucus], and we will fight until the final victory of womankind.
The women's caucus in the city council will put an end to male rule and will introduce new women's reforms. The women's reforms we will introduce in all fields.
"Przede wszystkim" [first of all] we will take up the hospital system: we will "skasować" [abolish] the hospital, and all that will remain is... the maternity clinic.
We will strengthen sanitary supervision; our sanitary inspectresses will carry out sanitary inspections... of the neighbour-women's pots; we will check all the hidden little corners to which we women have so far had no "dostęp" [access].
In the cultural field we will close all the schools — we already have enough lawyers [?] and doctors. We will leave only the dancing schools, where our daughters can now and then catch suitors "z miłości" [for love].
To introduce thrift, our women's caucus will abolish all the theatres; the only things played will be bridge, poker and mahjong. One will also be allowed to play: at love, at flirting, on the nerves, and other games.
In the cinemas there will always be on duty [dyżurować] an official of the civil registry office and a member of the rabbinate. Should they notice something "outside the programme", it will be possible to perform chuppah and kiddushin on the spot.
In the social field the women's caucus will take over all the philanthropic institutions; the only institutions that will go on existing will be: the society for marrying off bridegrooms, the "dowering of brides" [so printed] and the card clubs.
As regards the growth of the population, we will draft a compulsory marriage law, and "jednocześnie" [at the same time] we will set maximum prices for bachelors, widowers and divorcees. The "cennik" [price list] will be fixed by a special dowry commissioner, and bachelors who speculate, or try to charge "lichwa" [usurious] prices, will be brought to court; these speculators will be led at once under strict guard... beneath the chuppah poles. Thus an end will be put once and for all to the rampant [?] dowry speculation in the Jewish street.
The women's caucus will endeavour to beautify the town. At every house there will have to be a mirror where one can fix one's "fryzura" [hairdo]. On the street corners [rogi] special automats will be set up, where the female sex will be able to get, for a couple of groszy, powder, rouge, lipstick and other articles of prime necessity.
In short, if we women get the "władza" [power] in the city council, we will introduce new "porządki" [orders] and a whole series of women's reforms. We women will, besides carrying, bearing, nursing and washing nappies — have a say in the town.
So then, hear what Zlate Kvitsh tells you: tear yourselves away from the men, go to the elections independently with a purely women's list, with purely women candidates, with a purely women's programme, with a purely women's platform.
Women, don't go with the men!..
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bamidbar) and for Shavuot

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion and Shavuot.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bamidbar
The Portion
—o—
a) "By their families, by their fathers' houses" (Num. 1:2)
R' Eliyahu Chaim Meisel, the Rabbi of Łódź, took a great interest in the Łódź Talmud Torah and in its pupils, whom he looked after even when they had finished the Talmud Torah. One of the pupils was a great prodigy (illui), but he was the son of an unknown father... The young man was proposed as a match to a well-known great magnate of Łódź, who was looking for a prodigy as a bridegroom for his daughter. When the magnate learned that the young man did not know who his father had been, he immediately withdrew from the match.
So R' Eliyahu Chaim wrote a letter to the rich man, that he should take the young man as a bridegroom. And if it is lineage that concerns him, let him know that he, R' Eliyahu Chaim, is the young man's father... well, then he is already of distinguished lineage...
The letter made a tremendous impression on the rich man, and seeing how R' Eliyahu Chaim truly[?] humbled himself so, just to make the young man happy, he decided, regardless of the prodigy's doubtful descent, to make the match with him. This prodigy later became a famous Łódź scholar. Mi-Dor Dor.
—o—
b) "And the tribe of Zebulun" (Num. 2:7)
With all the tribes it says "u-matteh" ("and the tribe") with a vav; only with Zebulun does it say "matteh". But Zebulun was the tribe that itself engaged in commerce and supported the tribe of Issachar so that it could engage in Torah study. And because "the one who causes others to do is greater than the doer", it says "matteh" of him without the added vav, for he depended on no tribe at all and stood greater than all the tribes — even than the tribe of Issachar itself...
R' Shlomo Sluger [probably = Kluger].
—o—
c) "And the prince of the princes of the Levites" (ibid., 32)
"Said R' Yehoshua ben Levi: Elazar was a dukhna." Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, ch. 10.
In prayer, too, we say "the priests at their service and the Levites at their dukhan". What is the meaning of the word "be-dukhnam"?
Now in Bava Batra fol. 21 the Gemara says "we appoint a resh dukhna". Rashi explains: "he hears from the teacher and repeats it fluently to the children." So dukhna means a helper, a deputy (segan). And the Levites were, after all, deputies to the priests, vice-priests; so their office is called dukhna, and that is the meaning of "and the Levites at their dukhan". (Incidentally, the word levi also means deputyship: "that they may be joined unto thee and minister unto thee.") And this is also what the Jerusalem Talmud means: Elazar was a "dukh[?] dukhna", a chief of the deputies. Divrei Shaul.
—o—
d) "And they assembled all the congregation" (Num. 1:18)
Because here everyone declared his pedigree, recounting his lineage. And lest someone lie, the whole congregation was assembled, and if someone should have a blemish in his family — well, there would surely be someone who would not let him obtain his pedigree... Ahavat Yehonatan.
—o—
e) "And the children of Israel did according to all that the Lord commanded Moses" (ibid., 54)
They lined up according to the order only later, and yet the verse already calls it "doing", because the very fact that Jews heard how they were being divided into ranks, this one first and that one last, and they did not quarrel but agreed to Moses' arrangement — that is already such a great thing among Jews that for the consent of the heart alone the Torah already says "and they did"... Torat Moshe (Alshich).
—o—
f) "Number the children of Levi" (Num. 3:15)
The Levites were the fewest of all the tribes: "for they were fewer than all the tribes." Although they were counted from one month old, they were still the smallest in number: "for the Ark consumed them." In "Chronicles", on the other hand, we find that the Levites multiplied proportionately more than all the tribes. Why did such a change come about?
Because before the giving of the Torah the Levites were the scholars and the distinguished lineage, and every tribe sought to marry into them; so they were assimilated into the other tribes. After the giving of the Torah, on the other hand, when all were equal, the process stopped, and the Levites multiplied among themselves... R' Menachem Mendel Krengel.
—o—
g) "And thou shalt give the money unto Aaron and to his sons" (ibid., 48)
In Ostróg there lived a son of the famous rebbe R' Yeyvi. Once a little rebbe came to Ostróg who handed out blessings, as was customary, in return for pidyonot (ransom-gifts). It happened that a Jew received a blessing and had nothing to give as a pidyon. So the rebbe cursed him. Said R' Getzl to him:
— You are worse than Balaam. Balaam wanted "his house full of silver and gold" for cursing the Jews, and he blessed them for nothing. You, on the contrary, take silver and gold for blessings and hand out curses for nothing... Dor De'ah.

"Since the Temple was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the prophets and given to fools." Bava Batra 12.

Rabbi Samson Raphael [Hirsch] once met a Reform rabbi, who kept trying to convince him that the Torah must be reformed, that it is not suited to the present time. He answered him with an anecdote:
Once a carter and a timber merchant, who had hired him to haul timber, came to a rabbi for a din Torah. The carter wanted more than had been agreed, because the road had been snowbound and hard. But the rabbi ruled in favour of the merchant.
— Is that how the Torah rules? — asks the carter.
— Yes — answers the rabbi.
The carter thinks it over and suddenly asks:
— When was the Torah given, Rabbi?
— On Shavuot.
— Aha — the carter triumphs — you see, Rabbi? Back then the roads are clear, it is summer in the world, so the Torah rules for the merchant. But now it is winter and there was such a snowstorm on the road — had the Torah been given at such a time, you can be sure, Rabbi, it would have ruled in my favour...

Their Heads Don't Ache...

[Humorous feuilleton — Sosnowiec, summer lodgings.] Told by a Jew from Sosnowiec who travelled to Olkusz to rent a cheap flat.
— Berl!... — Berl!
In my sleep I recognized my wife's voice, and I woke up with a start:
— What, what is it?
— What's going to happen?
— What do you mean?
Aren't we going away?
— Where to?
— Why are you playing so dumb? You think I'll darken away[?] ["opkhoyshekhn", from Hebrew khoyshekh, darkness] a whole summer here? Not see[?] even a scrap of grass?
— You mean a dacha?
— No, I mean a noodle board...
— Nowadays[?], in such times, with such fine livelihoods we have?
— They say that in Olkusz you can get flats today at half price. Bad times, nobody is renting...
— Well, so you already know that nobody is renting?
— That's just my misfortune, poor me, that you're a shlimazl... you can never take advantage of the situation.. grab the other fellow just when his head aches...
Well, so I got dressed, ran quickly to the train and — off to Olkusz.
With me in the carriage sat three more Sosnowiec Jews: one with a beard, the second without a beard and the third — with half a beard.
At first they all sat quietly, as if each had a kehilla bench [a seat in the community synagogue] hidden in his mouth and couldn't let it out.
But the further the train travelled from Sosnowiec, the more the Jews opened their mouths and began to unburden their hearts.
— Akh!
— Akh-akh!
— Akh, akh-akh!
I sort of understood, and I answered:
— Akh, akh, akh-akh!
By that I wanted to tell them that I was no better off than they were and that I too have a wife who needs grass...
So, in chopped-up troubles, we travelled three quarters of an hour, until the conductor called out:
— O l k u s z !
I had barely managed to get out of the carriage and step over the threshold of the station, when a dozen hands grabbed me and every hand dragged me towards itself..
— Young man, a lovely flat! A fine flat! I have for you a gem, a bonbonnière ["bombonierka"]...
Luckily they soon came to terms among themselves. They handed me over to the chief commandant of the brokers, Reb Arele, and he promised to share the earnings with all of them.
— Do give me your hand five times — he says to me.
— What good is that to you?
— You understand? We are five of us and we have to share the earnings...
And right afterwards we wiped the sweat from our faces and I said:
— Bitter, eh?
— Very bitter.
— No livelihood?
— Where should it come from? Flats cost a lot and people are stripped bare.
— Flats expensive? God forbid... What do you mean... Two lovely rooms with a kitchen in the second "Szarga Góra"[?] you can get for three hundred gulden [= złoty]... The newspapers write that this year there will be strong heat waves; snap it up quickly, because later it will cost even more.
— For me it's expensive either way.
— I can give you a room with a kitchen for two hundred... listen, I have one for a hundred and fifty too, or maybe you want one without "wygody" [amenities]? I can give you one for a hundred gulden... Come, I'll show you... There are still several hundred flats here... You'll be able to choose; come, let a Jew earn something from you, I don't want to buy myself a stone tenement ["kamienica"] with it...
And the broker takes me first into the second, then into the third "dvoyalkes"[?], shows me a freshly painted flat, from which I got my kapote smeared[?], and in the end it was no lovely cheap flat at all. The worse flats were without salt and the prices peppered...
So I took my hands in my feet [ran for it], went off to the station and wanted to go home.
But here, in the blink of an eye, a second broker ran up, a short little Jew with a pair of big boots:
— Come with me..
— What?
— I mean, maybe you need a cheap boarding house?
— Excuse me [no thanks].
— Maybe a flat?
— At what price?
— From fifty to three hundred.
— For fifty, can you show me one?
— Everything, you know[?], show?
— Is it far?
— Half a minute's walk.
Within half an hour we were already "on the spot", where there is a flat for a hundred gulden.
The landlady, a young, strong peasant woman, takes me into a dark hut and opens a stable for me:
— This is the flat.
— Such a tiny little room and such a little kitchen?
The peasant woman raises her eyes, measures me up to see how big I am, and says:
— Not far from here there is Toybe's boarding house.
— Well, so what?
— You'll be able to graze there ["oyspashn", from Polish paść].
The peasant woman soon even softened. She was already ready to knock something off the price, but it still wasn't for me.
On the whole it became clear to me that even "out in the distance"[?] you can't snap up any bargains. Even though more than half the flats there are still not rented.
So I was left standing, desperate, helpless:
What does one do? How does one go home without a flat? What will my wife say?..
But never mind, there was no other choice; I went back to the train, and in my head my wife's complaints rang:
— You're a shlimazl.. you can't take advantage of the situation.. grab the other fellow just when his head aches.
And at once I justified myself to myself:
What am I to blame?..
If their heads don't ache..
Avihayil.

The Heavens Split Open...

(To be recited with great devotion to the tune of the Tikkun [the Shavuot night vigil].)
Thunder and lightning accompanied the days of the Giving of the Torah; the heavens split open and Moses our Teacher came down with the Tablets.
With the thunder and lightning of this week one might have thought the heavens were splitting again and a new Moses would come down with a new Torah — but as the heavens split, it happened to be right over Zagłębie, and the new Moses took a look down at the earth, quickly shut the heavens again and withdrew.
What did he see at that moment?
Instead of around a golden calf, Jews were dancing around a picture resembling a man, only of another race.
Then he saw how meetings were held under the open sky and speeches were made in seventy languages, with such „zagraniczne“ [foreign] words that even in heaven they couldn't understand them.
Further, in heaven they saw Jews in rabbinical dress and all kinds of old and new public figures running to the „urzędy“ [government offices] as if — to make the distinction — to Akdamut; in heaven they couldn't understand what all this running was about — perhaps new decrees against the Jews?
Suddenly an angel came and said: Moses! Moses! On earth elections are coming. The public figures are running to confer with the squires, and the little rabbis are running to get their pensions paid...
— And who are the Jews with the sacks? — asks Moses...
— They are collecting alms to pay the turnover tax...
The new Moses withdrew and shut the heavens.

The False Messiah

[Serialized historical tale — David Alroy, "the false messiah"; chapter "The Gaon's Daughter".]
Sh. Berg.

The Gaon's Daughter.

David Alroy is known in Jewish history as a false messiah. He wanted to redeem the Jews from exile, and he was the first and the last to organize a Jewish army in exile to conquer the Land of Israel. He lived in the twelfth century, and his native town was Amadiya, Persia. He was a great Talmudic scholar and also learned in the secular sciences. He was known as an adept of the secret teachings, and it was said of him that he was "one who sees and is not seen" — that he sees everyone and, if he wishes, no one can see him — and that he had "kefitzat ha-derekh" [the miraculous shortening of the way]: that in a single minute he could run hundreds of miles, not by sorcery but by holy "Names".

This was after the Crusades, when the Christians of Europe had taken Jerusalem from the Mohammedans. The crusaders then inflicted great troubles on the Mohammedans in Asia Minor and in Persia. The power of the sultans and of the caliph was weakened. So David Alroy found the time favourable to take the Land of Israel for the Jews.

He did not win. The Land of Israel he did not take, but he did capture many fortresses and towns in Persia, and he had a great Jewish army, which won many victories. He perished at a Jewish hand, but his movement shook up the exile, and later thousands of Jews from Europe, Africa and Asia travelled to settle in the Land of Israel. 300 rabbis from France and England, among them the greatest men, the "Ba'alei ha-Tosafot", went to the Land of Israel at that time. The "Nasi of Babylon" came too. Many took up working the land and raising sheep.

David Alroy came of the highest Jewish lineage. He descended from the Jewish royal family, from King David. His father was the "Rosh ha-Golah", the "Elder of the Exile", in Amadiya, Persia. He [David] was an only son and the heir to the title together with the office. But his father died young, when David Alroy was still a small child, so his uncle, his father's brother, became the "Rosh ha-Golah" and raised the young "crown prince".

The uncle gave him the best education. At the age of ten there was no longer any teacher for him in Amadga [sic, = Amadiya], and the uncle sent him to study in Baghdad.

Baghdad was the largest and richest royal city in the world. Through the middle of the city flows the river Hiddekel (Tigris); a great, wondrous bridge unites both parts of the city, which had, according to legend, eighty thousand streets, twelve thousand inns [?], twelve thousand mills and a thousand bath-houses.

The Jews of Baghdad had 28 synagogues and 10 yeshivas. The yeshiva of R. Shmuel Gaon was the largest.

When David Alroy came to Baghdad, he was, because of his great knowledge, immediately admitted to the highest yeshiva. He lived with his relative, the Nasi (prince) of Baghdad.

The caliph, the ruler of Baghdad, gave the Nasi of the Jews much power and honour. All the Jewish communities of Mesopotamia, Babylonia, Persia, Arabia and Yemen conducted themselves according to the will of the Nasi.

The Jews paid the Nasi dues from their property and businesses, and he, the Nasi, was very rich. He had many palaces, fields and gardens and his own soldiers. He rode through the street on a splendid white horse, and his horsemen rode ahead and cried out:
— Make way for our lord, the son of the House of David!

Whoever passed by had to bow to the Nasi of the Jews. That was the caliph's order.

The yeshiva was in a great palace, hung with the costliest curtains. The Gaon sat on a rare divan and the students on the floor around him. David Alroy was the youngest, but the best and the handsomest. He was so handsome that when he walked through the street, passers-by stopped and admired his beauty.
— A prince! A prince! — everyone said.

Soon David Alroy became the leader of his companions in the yeshiva. Many older young men.

Once the young men were talking among themselves about the greatness of the Nasi and his honour. David Alroy cut them short:
— He is a servant, the Nasi, a servant of a gentile! What is all his honour worth? The caliph can depose him, throw him into prison, cut off his head. He is the caliph's servant for collecting dues from the Jews. In exile there is no honour for Jews.

His companions knew that he was destined to become the "Rosh ha-Golah" in Amadiya. So they told him that he too would surely become a Nasi. He replied sharply:
— In exile I will not become a Nasi. I do not want to be a servant of a gentile and rule over the Jews. First one must become free of exile.
— Do you want to become the Messiah? — someone asked.
— If it be God's will — said David Alroy — I am, after all, an only son; I shall be Messiah son of David.

The diplomatic peace negotiations between the “Agudah” and the kehilla presidium have led to no result

[Będzin — Kehilla.] This week R' Yitzchak Meir Lewin, son of the Rabbi of Będzin [R' Tzvi Hanoch HaKohen Levin], stayed in Będzin. The visit was prompted by the Agudah leaders, who came to the president of the kehilla with a peace proposal.
The main conditions of the “peace” proposal were: to take on the young shochtim [ritual slaughterers] and to settle the debt of the rabbi's pension. As compensation, the Agudah undertakes to stop its opposition campaign against the present kehilla leadership.
On this, “diplomatic negotiations” were conducted. “Couriers” from both sides ran back and forth and brought it about that both sides should sit down at the “green table” and conduct the official negotiations.
The meeting place was the premises of the “Merchants' Association” [Sokhrim Fareyn]. Taking part were: President Mr. Rubinlicht, Vice-President Mr. Liwer, board member [dozór] Mr. Banhart, parnas Rinski and Mr. Lewin.

Finally the presidium declared that the question of engaging the young shochtim could not be settled, and because of this the “peace” conference was broken off.
———

She Found Her Runaway Husband in the Synagogue.

[Sosnowiec — family life.] Mrs. Sarah B.. has for several years been a living agunah [deserted wife]. Her husband, who had promised her golden fortunes, went off a short time after the wedding, and she did not know where his bones were to be found. She had already searched for him in a number of towns and shtetls, but without success.
One day she receives news from her friend that her husband is in Sosnowiec, where he has also married a second woman.
Having heard such tidings, the little wife came to Sosnowiec to find her vanished “bird”. Day in, day out she strolled the streets and kept watch, but she did not manage to meet the one she was looking for...
The wife had almost given up hope of finding out where her “destined one” was, but the family with whom she was temporarily staying comforted her, saying: “They’ll catch the fellow yet”...
— “I’ll give you a piece of advice,” another woman said to her, “go to the synagogue on Shabbat, perhaps he comes there to pray”.
The wife followed the advice, went to the synagogue on Shabbat, and looking out from the women’s gallery she let out a cry: “Oh, woe is me! Why, he’s praying in the synagogue, there he stands wrapped in a brand-new tallit...”
In haste she went out into the street, ran up to the first policeman she met and asked him to come with her into the synagogue, where her husband, whom she had been seeking for a long time, was.
At the moment when the congregation was singing “El Adon” with the cantor, a policeman entered the synagogue together with the wife and invited the “bridegroom” to the police station.
The next day a lively scene took place on Niemiecka Street between the stranger and the Sosnowiec wife over their husband.
The epilogue of the story is to take place at the Będzin rabbinate.

What We Shall Demand of the Future City Council (On the City Council Elections)

[Article — city council elections; the Jewish minority.] In our struggle for national justice we are still standing almost at the letter aleph, and precisely now we shall have to unfold the front with great energy.
Our representatives will have to demand that in the distribution of municipal works Jews shall not be wronged[?] under any pretext whatsoever. Our right to work must not be diminished.
An end must also be put to the process of de-Judaization ("entyudishung") in all kinds of municipal offices, whether directly in the city administration or indirectly in various municipal enterprises.
We are watching how this process goes on and develops with the fatal progression of a natural phenomenon. We do not wish to point to any particulars here. In the coming city council the Jewish minority will stand on guard, [lest] under the cloak of outward formality Jews be robbed of their elementary rights.
The same, and to an even greater degree, will have to be fought for with regard to the subsidies for Jewish institutions. The whole matter will have to be subjected to a deep and serious revision, which should bring about a fully just treatment of the Jewish minority.
It must on no account be allowed any longer that Jews should bear a double burden of taxes and that thereby the process of Jewish pauperization should be accelerated[?] and intensified.
Our future representatives in the city administrations will first of all have to fight for this: that it, the minority, shall not be ignored at all, that the majority shall be obliged to listen to its complaints and demands.
Moreover, our representation must be a strong one. Strong both in numbers and in quality. Hands alone are not enough; there must also be minds to go with them, which will direct the hands..
This last condition is especially important when one cannot prevail by means of the majority, but must exert influence by moral forces...

[Będzin — Anti-Hitler Committee; public appeal.] Once again we turn to you with an appeal and a call;
Help our unfortunate sisters and brothers from Germany!
The Hitlerite fire, far from having been extinguished, is on the contrary growing ever stronger, and our unfortunate brothers are constantly compelled to leave that hell-land and are dependent on our material help. Lately even the formerly wealthy and intellectual strata have been turning for help — people who until the last minute, not wishing to become dependent on the gifts of flesh and blood, sold off everything they had and now find themselves in a tragic and desperate situation.

"Fulfil your elementary duty towards your unfortunate sisters and brothers and help them out of their needs and sufferings! Let everyone help according to his means!

Receive our delegates, who will visit you in the coming days, with a friendly countenance.

I've Fallen in Love... (From the Local Tales)

[Będzin — feuilleton; humorous tale.] Two colleagues, two dear friends, both of them worked in jobs and lived in one room. One worked by day, and the other had the kind of occupation that he carried out at night. One room they had. They met only on the Sabbath. If they wanted or needed to come to an understanding, they left each other little notes on the table. The rest they talked over on the Sabbath.
Once Natan found such a note on the table:
"I've fallen in love... Details I'll tell you on the Sabbath. Selim."
Natan at once wrote back:
"You're a fool... Details on the Sabbath. Natan."
That same day Natan went strolling on the "Górka" [the hill in Będzin] and there got acquainted with a pretty girl. The lips painted even too heavily, but that has nothing to do with beauty. Natan began meeting with her.
The next morning Natan found a new note on the table:
"You're a fool yourself; I'm in love and I'm happy, my girl is an angel, I'm writing the tnoim [engagement contract]; on the Sabbath I'll tell you the rest. Selim."
This time Natan wrote back thus:
"My girl is a better one; I'm not writing any tnoim with her; on the Sabbath I'll tell you nothing at all. Natan."
Again Natan went off to a rendezvous and met his girl. She told him that she had a fiancé, a decent young man; that one works at night, and so she has time. Natan invited her to his home in order to show her his radio set. Meanwhile he again found a note on the table:
— "I don't give a hoot about you[?] [literally: 'I have you in the trak']... I love, I am loved. I'm already engaged, and on the Sabbath after Shavuot the wedding will be. Selim."
Natan sat a long time with his girl by his radio, and both were so absorbed that they did not notice how the night was running away and the day drawing near, and when they both[?] dozed off, they did not hear how the door opened and closed again, and suddenly Selim stood before their eyes:
— Natan, what is my bride doing at your place?...
— From where[?] does she know my address? When did she come? And what are you both doing?...
— And if I tell you that we are learning to swim here, will you believe me?
But the betrayed Selim had no patience for jokes and pranks. He did not vent his anger on his bride, who in any case had fallen into spasms, and Natan revived her. Selim turned the whole room into a heap of ruins and himself ran out in such a state that Natan and the bride thought he was running straight to the "Przemsza" [the river].
Now the "angel" demands that Natan become her fiancé.
A great mitzvah on his part.
Selim now lives alone in a room, and his aim is to change his occupation so that he can work by day and sleep at night; before that he will not become anybody's fiancé.
What's New in Upper Silesia? — A Large Meeting on Sabbath Observance in Katowice

[Upper Silesia — Katowice; Sabbath observance.]
A „Gdud Meginei Shabbat“ (Battalion of Sabbath Defenders) founded.
On the initiative of „Mizrachi“ in Katowice, a meeting was held on Sunday, the first day of Shavuot, in the kehilla hall in connection with the arrests of the Sabbath observers (shomrei Shabbat) in Tel Aviv.
The meeting aroused great interest in religious circles, except among the „Torah-true“ [Agudas Yisroel people], who did not deign to come to the meeting but contented themselves with sending a few „spies“. There is a conjecture that this happened because the initiative to strengthen Sabbath observance in Katowice had been taken up by the „free“ Mizrachists...
Before a packed hall the meeting is opened by the president of „Mizrachi“, Mr. Dawid Ehrlich, who explains the purpose of the gathering and gives the floor to Rabbi Dr. Vogelmann.
The rabbi gives a lengthy speech in which he dwells on the Sabbath rest and its religious and national significance for Jewry.
A speech rich in content is given by Rabbi Dr. Chameides; among other things he says that „if we had kept the Sabbath in the Diaspora, the desecration of the Sabbath in Tel Aviv would not have come about“; the Sabbath-desecrators — he says — are the element that we send there...
The speaker reproaches[?] the parents who send their children to school on the Sabbath, at a time when the government exempts them from it.
After the closing words of Mr. Ehrlich the following resolutions are adopted:
1) At the public meeting held in Katowice, in the presence of nearly 600 men and women, it is resolved to create an association under the name „Gdud Meginei HaShabbat“.
The Gdud undertakes to buy in the shops where the Sabbath is kept and to give employment to the craftsmen who do not work on the Sabbath.
2) The meeting declares its solidarity with those arrested in Tel Aviv and calls on them to continue their courageous work for Sabbath observance.
In an elevated mood the meeting is closed.

Go to the Ballot Boxes!

[Article — the city-council elections.] Well then, we stand on the eve of the city-council elections. Any moment now we shall hold the ballot papers and go to the ballot boxes. We are thus going to elect the municipal self-governments, and the procedure is far from being the same as before. We find ourselves now in different circumstances and under different conditions, which make the forming of the new city councils harder. And yet we must stand on guard and protect every position, every step. That is on the one side. On the other side we know only too well how the dangerous antisemitism is raging through the Jewish streets in all the towns and townlets, which is out, with every trick and every means of force, to tear out the Jewish citizens and to brand them as citizens of the second category, as burdensome and superfluous elements, of whom the country has no need.
It goes without saying that in such a time we need, more than ever, to stand on guard and protect our interests, our rights, as never before. And yet this has not been achieved. Apparently none of this was taken into account, and no unified blocs were created.
Chaos reigns in the Jewish street. All the trends and shades, from left to right, are split, so that nothing came of the meetings and consultations; it was not taken into account that unity is such a necessity, and the struggle of personalities and narrow-minded partyism did not allow the necessary unified platform to be realised.
It is interesting: when it comes to the voting procedure among us, people vote first and foremost for candidates for "seats". There come people of pedigree, "carp-heads", fine Jews, and simply respectable people one wants to do a favour, or such as have pretensions to public activity — although the whole year round they do not put their hands into cold water. And later a tearing and a boiling starts, as if the world stood on it. Everyone shouts "it is all mine", I must take the head of the table, the place at the eastern wall is mine by right.
Every candidate will want to "work on"[?] you in order to find himself in first place, which should secure him the "seat" for the whole term of office.
At the same time one must not forget one thing: there is quite a large number of the population who do not go to the elections at all, without a why and without a wherefore; they never in their lives give themselves an account of their deeds, and it does not even occur to them that there is anything here to think about.
Do people among us know what such a thing as self-government is? Do all average voters know the full significance of the word? Does everyone know how to assess the merits and shortcomings of this necessary communal institution? Do all know that a self-government is the pulse of the town? And that this institution has the possibility of bringing in and spending the town's money? A self-government can and must make the citizen's life easier, it can introduce normal and easy conditions of life for him — and the same can also be the other way round: a municipal self-government also has the possibility of making the situation of its householders harder, for in fact it is the one that sets the tone in the town, and it is able to steer the rudder as it pleases and as it understands.
Whom should we elect? Who should be the city fathers from our side? Were things normal, as in former years, one would really have had to point this out; but unfortunately there is such a split, such a chaos, that we are not [able][?] to have the desired and necessary complement of representatives, since for the most part the institutions do not put forward the people on whom we could have counted to give the town something.
It goes without saying that first of all we need intelligent people, people who command the language of the country and, most important of all, people who can find their way and know what economic problems, economic matters are. At the same time it would not be desirable to get such as would think that by their very person they are bestowing a joy upon us, and who would make light of the offices they have taken on. That would mean bartering away Jewish interests and dishonouring Jewish dignity.
If a town has a good economic self-government, it is a sign that the citizens have understood their task in regard to the choosing of their representatives. As soon as there are bad managers, and the town costs heavy sums and in return nothing is achieved, or only a minimum is achieved, it is a sign that its citizens do not understand their tasks and do not make use of the rights they have at their disposal.
In many parliamentary countries it is understood that every single person must turn out to vote, and all regard it as a sacred duty to cast their vote. Among us things have not yet come that far, and it is no wonder either, since quite a large part of the population does not know at all what connection it has with the self-government and what binds it to the communal institution, and consequently does not regard it as any misfortune if it does not cast its vote.
We know very well, after all, that a large number of the population do not go to the elections at all, without a why, and they never in their lives give themselves any account of their deeds; it does not even occur to them that there is anything here to think about.
In the first place, therefore, measures must be taken so that people go and vote; first of all we must win voters for ourselves, so that we can carry through as many councillors as possible. Among us the candidates are not as important as the voters themselves, who can save the day and bring in a larger number of mandates. All possibilities must therefore be applied so that nobody stays at home on election day, and besides, the public must be won over, for the simple, average person cannot grasp at all that he does someone harm as soon as he does not go to the elections. And such a contingent of non-voters we have very, very many.
It is therefore very, very important to make the broad strata of the population as a whole aware that they must not let their right to vote slip by, and that all must go as one man to the ballot boxes.
All means must be applied to make the citizen ready for the time when he has to exercise his civic right.
Let this therefore be well remembered now; let it not be forgotten that upon civic rights and upon casting one's vote depends the winning of the number of Jewish mandates.
R. Les.
Pintshe Drang Becomes a City Councillor!..

[Będzin — satirical feuilleton; the city-council elections.] By Y. Aberzhanes.
(Monologue of a candidate for the Będzin City Council).
You may wish me mazel tov — with luck I am becoming a city councillor in Israel!
How do I know I am becoming a councillor? What do you mean, how? I'm on the list, after all! And standing where? You think I just stand there somehow, like a number on the lottery prize table, from the bottom? Begging your pardon, you are mistaken — I stand at the very top, among the very biggest I stand, and if only luck plays along, I shall be a councillor.
And since I already figure officially on the list as a candidate for the Będzin City Council, I want to introduce myself to you: my name is Pintshe Drang, co-owner of the firm „Smolka Akcyna Bratsha Drang & Company“.
Who in Będzin does not know the well-known „public worker“ — Pintshe Drang? In the books of all the institutions you will find my name on the membership lists; whatever society's book you look into, you will find my name.
In the Talmud Torah you will find my name: „Member Pintshe Drang owes 5 years of membership dues“.
In the „Linas haCholim“ you will see in black and white: „Pintshe Drang does not pay a broken farthing“.
In the „Moshav Zkeinim“ (old-age home) you will find in the members' book a note: „Pintshe Drang threw the collector down all the stairs“...
In the „Beis Lechem“ my account is clean, nothing at all is written — not a single letter!..
As you see, I am a member of all the institutions. True, I don't pay any money, but a member I am! And do you know why I don't pay? Because I have, may it not befall you, a heart defect. I want to give money, but the heart won't let me...
A respectable Jew comes to me for a donation, I go at once for the purse, but the moment I open the pocket I get an „attack“ in the heart, the heart won't let me give — that's the kind of rotten heart I have!
And what a protector of animals' feelings I am! It's simply unbelievable! I have a little bit of a factory, and only gentiles work for me. You will surely ask: why? The excuse is compassion for living creatures — I cannot bear to see Jews toiling at machines, Jewish girls getting blackened and darkened and working hard. That's the kind of man I am, a Jew with a soft heart...
Now, since you already know what a gentle Jewish heart I have, I will acquaint you with my biography, from which you will be convinced that I have all the necessary qualifications a councillor must have.
When I was born, I came out with a great yell and made such a racket that the midwife got frightened and said to my mother: „This one is a ready-made bandit“!..
When I went to cheder, I stole the bagels from all my mates, and when once they caught me in the act, the rebbe said: „Oh, he's growing up to be somebody [reading uncertain]“!
At 15 I was already taking money out of the Rabbi Meir Baal haNes charity box, and whoever saw how cleverly I did it said: Ay, ay, ay, what a precious expert!..
Now, my public career: my public career I made step by step.
Years ago I was elected gabbai of the society „Pas Lishtos“ („Bread to Drink“). After it came out that they had „drunk up“ the pledge money, I was promptly elected president of the cooperative „Ozer Dalim“, and in one year I swallowed a wagon of flour. (Apart from „pentshkes“ [?], little hammers, „shitere“ [?] soap and other trifles).
From then on I grew higher and higher. I became a „fixer“ among merchants, a „provider“ for small traders, and above all — a Jew with money, and as the verse supposedly says: silver and gold purify, God save us...
Now that you have become acquainted with my biography, with my virtues, with my soft Jewish heart and with my qualifications, I ask you: do I not have the right to want to be a councillor in Israel? Do I not have the right to stand on the candidates' list for the Będzin City Council? It seems to me that I have every right and have everything a councillor needs, and I assure you that if I am elected councillor, I will do the same as all councillors have done until now:
First of all I will take on a shikse, and if a Jew comes about a favour, the shikse will answer him:
„Pan radny śpi“ (The councillor is asleep).
„Pan radny nie przyjmuje“ (The councillor is not receiving).
„Pan radny zajęty“ (The councillor is busy).
What else will I do when I am a councillor? I will not go to any sessions of the City Council, and if I do go to a session once, I will keep my mouth shut and not provoke the squires, and if it concerns a Jewish matter, I will fall sick with the flu.
When I become a councillor, I will order myself visiting cards:
Pintshe Drang
Radny Miasta Będzina (Councillor of the City of Będzin)
And when I have such a visiting card in my pocket, I will laugh at the world. Someone comes to demand a debt — I'll settle it [reading uncertain] with a visiting card.
The landlord comes to demand the rent — I'll show him the visiting card.
The butcher, the baker, the tailor, the shoemaker, the milk-woman come — I'll show them my visiting card „Pintshe Drang, Radny Miasta Będzina“, and no more talk!
Yes, all this will be when I am elected councillor. Now I have one more worry: in which district shall I be elected?
Shall I say on Zawale [?]? Ech, how does that fit? Pintshe Drang on Zawale! How does it suit my wife that her husband should mix with Zawale folk? Feh!
In the Old Market? No good either: on the Old Market live my creditors, who hold court judgments against me.
In short, I'm all set. I'm already on the electoral list, the necessary qualifications I have too. My only worry is just where my candidacy will be.
In sum, Jews, you may wish me mazel tov, I am becoming a councillor in Israel.
Yes, the main thing I quite forgot. Remember the name Pintshe Drang, the one and only, steadfast candidate for the Będzin City Council — I have finished!

“The Jews Make Poland Unhappy”

(From the local Polish press).
Our local organ of the “Nara” people [apparently a nickname for the nationalist camp], the Endek [National Democrat] “Kurier Zachodni”, well known to us, has lately become very arrogant, and there is hardly a day on which it does not look for sins on the part of the Jews. Last Sunday a certain Stefan Arnold (perhaps a candidate for “Führer”?) came out with an article in which he proves with signs and wonders how the Jews, poor things, make Poland unhappy, and above all what must be done in order to take their machinations away from the Jews.
Here is what he writes:
“In Poland there are two categories of foreign capital: the Jewish, and the German, English, French, Belgian etc. The first, i.e. the Jewish, has penetrated deep into our organism, so far that people of weak faith and weak strength simply cannot believe that we will ever be able to free ourselves of it. The second capital is concentrated in big industry, in the big joint-stock companies. Which is the more harmful? Obviously the first, because with the share of the first we have in our economic life not merely foreign capital, but we have 3 million industrialists, merchants, craftsmen, workers. The second, however, is calculated for the profit of a small group of people, and can be regarded, until we become richer, as a loan, which gives the possibility of providing a livelihood to the Polish worker.”
It has long been no secret that it does not pay the “K. Z.” to fall out with the second category of foreign capital, for were it not for that capital, such an Endek organ might never have seen the light of day. It is quite an understandable thing that it is easier to lash out at the “Jewish little horse” and to propagate the nationalization of Jewish property.
In the further part of the article “the awl comes out of the sack”, because: “A proper municipal self-government policy can ease the existence of the Polish craftsman, merchant and manufacturer.
Every honestly thinking Pole — says the author — must see to it that things come to the point where he feels that he is the master of his country, and therefore he must not let any opportunity pass. Clear and open. If only the “Nara” people get into the city council, they will know what to do.

“Polish Jews with Weapons in Hand”

A talk by Prof. Dr. Majer Bałaban on Polish Radio.
(For the 125th anniversary of the death of Berek Joselewicz).
On the 5th of May of this year it was 125 years since Colonel Berl Joselewicz, the creator of a Jewish regiment, fell a hero's death on the battlefield near Kock in the fight against the Austrian troops.
In order to honour the memory of one of the most honest figures in the history of Poland, Polish Radio has invited to speak before the microphone the great Jewish scholar and specialist in Jewish history in Poland, Prof. Dr. Majer Bałaban.
Countless legends already circulate about Berl Joselewicz, often contradicting one another. Some Polish historians, for example, who are hostile to Jews, doubt altogether that Berek Joselewicz succeeded in forming a regiment of Jews only, and do not believe that this regiment fought a bitter battle on the Praga ramparts against the Russian troops of Suvorov and perished there to the last man. It is therefore a very good thing that Polish Radio has invited Prof. Bałaban, who, on the basis of the newest archival documents, will acquaint the radio listener with the history of the formation of the Jewish regiment and with Joselewicz's famous appeal “to his brethren”.
On this occasion the lecturer will give, in brief words, a picture of the heroic struggles of the Polish Jews, which they waged during centuries of Poland's history, and together with the Poles more than once repulsed the common enemy. We will hear about the heroic struggles of the Jews in the days of Chmielnicki and learn how Jews defended Tulczyn, Połonne, Niemirów and Lwów (1648), about their bloody battles in the defence of Tarnopol, Husiatyn and Trembowla.
Then the lecturer will go over to the history of Kościuszko's uprising and dwell in detail on the figure of Berek Joselewicz and his era.
Dr. Bałaban will conclude the interesting lecture with the history of Jewish participation in the insurrectionary struggles of the years 1831 and 1863, and finally tell about the participation of Jews in the Legions of Commandant Piłsudski.
This sensational talk, which Dr. Bałaban will give on the radio on Saturday, 26 May, at 5:40 in the evening, will surely be listened to by the broadest masses of Jewish radio listeners, who will thereby pay honour to the memory of a great Polish-Jewish hero.

Two Grey Doves...

[Feuilleton — a literary sketch: an old couple remembers their youth.]
(A Picture)

He — seventy; she — sixty-eight.
Old, tired, broken.
Life has bent them, twisted them, made them a little deaf and a little blind.
They had twelve children, and no more than four are left.
Eight funerals they have had.
Eight times they have sat shiva.
They have wept out all their tears; now their eyes are dried out like dry graves.
Eight graves in the cemetery, eight small headstones; five of them already washed out by the rains and crumbled by the winds and storms —
They sit on a bench in Third of May Square [Plac 3 Maja], the two old people, the husband and the wife, and watch how the trees have blossomed and the flowers have opened, and the sun throws down, through the branches, golden coins onto the green grass.
They see how nature lives and spins out young, bright hours,
and a longing for something comes over them... for the young years, in that little town.
And between the old pair a conversation like this begins:
— Do you remember, Nekhe, back home in the shtetl, the valley behind the synagogue?
— Yes, I remember; we used to go walking there so that our parents wouldn't know.
— And do you remember how long ago that is now, eh?
— Wait. Just let me recall: it must be some... some sixty-three or sixty-four years.
— Hush, I'll tell you right away: I was about seventeen then, no more; if you take seventeen from seventy, how much is left? [?] After all, you can count a little [printed "ru" for "du", you].
— It seems that it adds up... fifty-three years have gone by since then.
— As if it had been only yesterday.
— You had a head of blond hair and blue eyes and a fine singing voice.
— I remember that very well [printed "ras" for "dos"].
— And what kind of hair and eyes did I have?
— You had black hair, shining like silk, and eyes black too.
— Upon my word, you have quite a good memory! You haven't forgotten yet, eh?
— Those days cannot be forgotten; they stay engraved in the heart forever.
— Do you remember how we became bride and groom, Nekhe?
— Do I remember!
— Who was our matchmaker?
— Leyzer, Moyshe Menashe's.
— Right!
— I even remember how my father wanted to give three years of kest [board for the young couple] and your father wanted four years.
— Right!
— And your father also wanted my father to sign half a house over to you.
— Right as gold!
— Just tell me, Nekhe, do you remember the river that ran not far from your uncle's house?
— Which uncle do you mean?
— Uncle Elye Meir.
— Of course I remember! By that river the women of the shtetl used to wash laundry: they would spread out [?] the wet laundry on a stone and beat it with a washing-paddle [pralnik].
— Yes, I remember that.
— I even remember how my grandmother Shifre-Mirl was at our engagement, and right the next day she died.
— Yes, that I remember too. She was no longer young. If I am not mistaken, she was 96 years old.
— And how lively she still danced at our engagement!
— And she needed no glasses and heard with both ears.
— People in olden times knew nothing of worry, so they lived long.
— Right! Worry cuts the years short and makes one old and grey before one's time.
— That is true. Just tell me, Nekhe, can you recall whether I ever gave you a kiss before the wedding?
— No, that I don't remember; it seems to me that I didn't; after all, they never left us alone.
— You see, that you no longer remember — I remember it.
— What do you remember?
— That I gave you a kiss before the wedding; I remember it as if it had been yesterday.
— Where was that?
— Try to recall.
Old Nekhe ponders and answers:
— I don't remember.
— If so, I will remind you: do you remember how once they left us alone in your uncle's house? There was a bar mitzvah there, so everyone went off to the synagogue, and they called me along too. Then I suddenly remembered that I had forgotten the khumesh at home. So I went back for the khumesh, and since nobody was at home but you, I gave you a kiss on the neck and ran straight out; for several days you were ashamed before me, and I — before you.
— Ah, yes... I do remember that Sabbath. It was, it seems, on a Sabbath after Shavuot.
— Yes, yes.
— And it had gone clean out of my memory.
— But not out of mine.
— You were already a crazy one back then, a wild one.
— But I kissed my bride, not, God forbid, some stranger...
— But it could have happened that the match fell through.
— I was sure we would not part; I had just such a feeling. And you see, I guessed right,
— We were children then.
— Yes, children, but with sense.
— Today's children are a lot cleverer than we were.
— Different times today.
A bird burst into song on a branch, and the old pair listened and sighed.
— Do you remember, Nekhe, that back then too we heard such a song: just such a one.
— Yes, the birds always sing the same songs; they don't adapt themselves to the new times... So they sang for our great-great-grandfathers, and so they will sing a thousand years from now. Birds remain birds.
— Listen, just listen! Exactly as then, fifty-three years ago, in our shtetl.
A breeze lifted a piece of newspaper and began to carry it on its wings high, high, pressed it against a bush of flowers and left it there.
— Do you see, Nekhe, what the wind did with the piece of paper? Life does the very same with a person: one flies high, high, one thinks to reach the sky, the sun, but one does not reach it... Life throws you back down, and you stay caught somewhere on a prickly thorn, until another wind comes along and tears you off and plays with you so long that you are torn apart, plucked to pieces.
Yes, a person too is no more than a scrap of paper, a plaything of all sorts of winds. And so it was before we were born, and so it will be after our death; life and death will never go under.
Both will outlive all eternities; we are no more than dust of dust.
Here a quiet snoring was heard... While he, the husband, had been talking and philosophizing, Nekhe, the old, tired Nekhe, had meanwhile fallen asleep. Over their heads, on a little tree, a little bird chirped, calling its beloved.
G. K-h.
Pesach Kaplan: We Must Have Strong Nerves.

[Essay — the Jewish people under persecution; Hitlerism.] (By Pesach Kaplan.) The old rule of war, that victory goes to whoever has the stronger nerves, can hold true also for the eternal war of the eternal people against the seventy wolves that encircle it and seek to destroy it. It is, it seems, no war at all: only assaults, beatings, killings, or persecutions and oppressions on one side, and clenched teeth with stubborn patience on the other; and nevertheless it is precisely this mute patience that is a force capable of wearing out the one who strikes.
An illustration of this is the familiar picture of a child who sometimes gets angry at a grown-up and starts hitting him on the knees with his tiny little feet; he keeps hitting so long that he himself grows exhausted and bursts into tears.
But the parable is not entirely apt, for although, compared with the many-thousand-year age of 'Israel the Grandfather', the newly revived nations are indeed only young chicks[?], their individuals nevertheless have quite strong fists, and in those fists hard sticks and stones, sometimes even knives, which can wound, bloody and even kill.
The main thing here is the strength of the nerves. Their attacks are, after all, in fact the result of a nervous irritability that reveals in them a childish lack of balance. We can respond to this only with iron calm, with a crushing endurance that will in the end wear out the childish attacker and bring him to tears!.
But endurance does not consist merely in clenching one's teeth; at the same time, while the senseless attacker wastes his time on his petty provocations, one must seriously consider what to do and how to come out of the trouble alive, healthy and honourable, without losing one's own dignity.
At times it seems that under the impact of the heavy blows we lose our balance, become nervously agitated and let ourselves be dragged by sentimentality and hysteria into neck-breaking leaps. Thus, for example, a sudden psychosis of emigration to America, or an outburst of Zionist-nationalist moods, or a death-leap of Jewish youth into the abysses of revolutionary movements, and the like.
But if one views all these phenomena from a certain perspective, when one can already weigh and measure their results, we must come to the conclusion that these are no accidents or passing enthusiasms, but parts of a planned historical action of the ancient Jewish people for its own preservation — an action whose wisdom can be grasped only from the proper distance of time and place.
This wisdom, which comes to each Jewish individual perhaps unconsciously, instinctively, impulsively, is what reveals the strong nerves of the entire Jewish community. Its mighty instinct of self-preservation and [sic] serves as a guarantee that it will endure everything and outlive everything.
The ancient biblical image: 'Some with chariots, some with horses, and we with the name of our God; they kneel and fall, and we stand and remain strong' [after Psalm 20:8–9] can hold true also figuratively, in the spiritual sense, regarding the contest between us and them: who will wear out whom, who will hold out longer in his stubbornness.
As regards Hitler, the distance is still too small and the perspective too weak to be able to see the picture from all sides already. But certain signs already show now that he is beginning to grow weary under the pressure of our obstinate endurance.
In other countries, which only later began to ape Hitler, one certainly cannot yet know the outcome, because the drama is only just beginning to unfold. The young, mischievous nations have not yet even had their fill of the fresh spectacle of blood.
But our old, settled reason and historical experience must teach us to look at these things from a bird's-eye view and to foresee that, just as they ended in one place and another, at one time and another, so surely will the present end be too, for 'the Jewish spiritual strength will not prove false' [an echo of 'the Eternal One of Israel will not lie', 1 Sam. 15:29].
Apparently it sometimes looks as though we are doing nothing, or that we are frittering ourselves away into small change, while the storm clouds threaten to destroy us. In truth, however, a whole is made up of small details, and our sense of self-preservation is what prompts us which detail to stress at given moments.
For example, in one place they want to fight us, to defeat us by weakening our numerical strength in order to diminish our influence. There we throw ourselves with all our ardour into an election campaign, use the maximum of energy, fight tooth and nail and in no way let ourselves be weakened.
In a second place they strike us economically, through declassing and pauperisation. We answer by strengthening economic and financial institutions and economic organisations, and in general with a policy of economic defence.
In a third place they want to weaken us spiritually and culturally, to block for us the sources of education and development so that we should remain backward in the struggle for existence — there we throw ourselves with enormous thirst upon Torah, science and art and in no way let ourselves be degraded.
Somewhere they try to weaken our power of resistance through assimilation, by erasing the Jewish image of God from our spirituality — there comes, as a living protest against this, the Jewish national or religious feeling, which holds together, as with clamps, Jewish distinctiveness and the capacity to resist.
Our work crumbles and scatters into all sorts of colours, so that it is sometimes hard to find the harmony among them, and sometimes they even look contradictory to one another; but in their very essence, according to historical logic, they complement one another — just like the functions of different parts of one organism.
Every act separately and all together prove our great vitality, the instinct to live and to defend life by all manner of stratagems. Here the strength of our nerves finds expression, which guarantees us victory in the struggles.
And precisely in this lies the harmony between the most diverse actions and plans for our deliverance.
