[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Naso
The Portion
—o—
a) "And those that were numbered of the families of the sons of Merari, according to their families" (Num. 4:42)
Only with the sons of Merari is the word "family" repeated many times: "families of", "according to their families" — because the sons of Merari were the poorest among the Levites, as their very name says: "sons of Merari" (the children of bitterness), and it is precisely among poor people that there are, no evil eye, large families with many members...
Tzror HaMor.
—o—
b) "If any man's wife go aside" (Num. 5:12)
Come and see: a married woman [who commits adultery] is sentenced to strangulation. A sotah, who after all only transgressed the prohibition of a married woman, suffers a far more shameful and uglier death ("and her belly shall swell, and her thigh shall fall away", etc.), because she sinned in secret, because she had previously wanted to pass herself off as honest and decent — so her punishment is harsher..
Commentary of the Shach on the Torah.
—o—
c) "And make atonement for him, for that he sinned by reason of the soul" (Num. 6:11)
"Against which soul did this one sin? Rather, that he caused himself suffering by abstaining from wine." Nedarim 10.
Rabbi Israel, the Maggid of Kozienice, used to say:
I prefer the Jew who eats in secret, fools the world and says that he is fasting, to the one who truly fasts and thereby fools himself...
* * *
Before his death the Chacham Tzvi asked to be handed a cup of wine. He wants to appease — he said — the body, which he had tormented his whole life, not granting it the slightest pleasure...
* * *
Rabbi Moshe of Kobryn could not stand the would-be fasters, and he said:
Better to abstain from foolishness than from eating and drinking...
* * *
The Nazirite brings the offering "for having caused himself suffering by abstaining from wine".
The question arises: if so, why does he not bring the offering as soon as he takes the Nazirite vow upon himself, but only when the days of his Naziriteship have already ended?
Because the harm of "causing himself suffering by abstaining from wine" does not lie in the thing itself; it can be determined only once the days of Naziriteship have already ended — then that is the main thing: how he relates to wine after the days of his Naziriteship. Whether he does not grab the bottle with a pent-up craving..
Even Moshe.
—o—
d) "On this wise ye shall bless the children of Israel" (ibid., 23)
The Lubavitcher Rebbe, Rabbi Israel Noah Schneersohn, once came to Bauska. The local rabbi, Rabbi Mordechai, the well-known Hovev Zion, came to him. On taking leave, the Rebbe says to the rabbi:
— Bless me.
— You bless me first — says the rabbi.
Rabbi Israel Noah takes the rabbi's hand in his own and says:
— May God bless you in material things and in spiritual things.
And he adds:
— Now you bless me.
— May God bless you in spiritual things — says Rabbi Mordechai.
— And why do you not bless me with material things too?
— the Rebbe asks him.
— Because — answers Rabbi Mordechai — all Jews take material things and make spiritual things out of them: from the money they earn they give charity and the like. We, on the other hand, rabbis and rebbes, make material things out of spiritual ones: out of our spirituality we make a trade, a business... with us spirituality is a means to material gain... Therefore I bless you with spirituality, because the more spirituality there is, the more material gain there will be, the more business...
Torat veHaTechiya HaLeumit.
* * *
A Jew, a village Jew, comes to Rabbi Hirsch of Rymanów and asks for a blessing. Rabbi Hirsch asks to be given a "forty" [a 40-groszy coin]. The village Jew says to him:
— Rebbe, it is written "On this wise (koh) ye shall bless" — just so, bless just so, without money...
Rabbi Hirsch smiles at the village Jew's "Torah" and says to him:
— If "On this wise ye shall bless", then "The Lord bless thee": may God bless you just so, without money — God needs no money, He can bless just so...
Daat Zekenim.
—o—
e) "The Lord lift up His countenance upon thee" (ibid., 26)
The Gemara in Berakhot (20b) says: the ministering angels said to God: In Your Torah it is written "who regardeth not persons [lit. lifts not the countenance]", and You show favour to the Jews? God answered them: [How should I not] show favour to the Jews? I said "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless", and they are strict with themselves to say the blessing even over an olive's bulk.
The question arises:
— Well, what has that answered? Is God therefore permitted to show favour to the Jews?
But if the Jews show favour, as it were, to Him, then He is surely obliged to repay them measure for measure, and so His showing favour is no favouritism at all but a binding recompense.
Yakar MiPaz (Rabbi Zisha of Płock).
—o—
f) "And give thee peace" (ibid.)
Because "The Lord lift up His countenance upon thee" is said, according to the Gemara mentioned, of those who say the blessing even over an olive's bulk when they have no more — and when there is no bread, one needs the blessing of peace.
Kohelet Yitzhak.
—o—
g) "Say unto them" (ibid., 23)
"Say unto them — face to face." Sifrei.
Between the priests and the people there must be "As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man", and unfortunately this is not so very often [?]; there is such a lack of openheartedness in the relationship between the priests and the people.
Tekhelet Mordechai.
—o—
h) "And they shall put My name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them" (ibid., 27)
"The priests bless in the Sanctuary, as it is said: And they shall put My name, etc. Whence [do we learn it] for the provinces? Scripture says: In every place where I cause My name to be mentioned, etc." Sifrei.
The Vilna Gaon interpreted the Sifrei thus:
In the Sanctuary, as is known, one was permitted to pronounce the Ineffable Name. In the provinces, outside the Temple, one may read the Name only with a substitute.
This is what the Sifrei means: "And they shall put My name" — the Ineffable Name the priests read only in the Sanctuary; but in the provinces there was only "where I cause My name to be mentioned" — a mention of the Name, a substitute.
Biur HaGra.
How good it would have been, if... — Nothing is too late yet

Nothing is too late yet.
Every time people begin to talk about some plan to rescue or help Jews, it seems to us that the plan is a little too late. In general we often have a habit of counting the days backwards.
Here, for example, when there is talk now of a territory, the immediate answer is: how good it would have been if 27 years ago we had accepted the English Uganda plan; who knows what an enormous settlement we would already have now — the problem might perhaps already have been solved altogether.
When Professor Hermann Schapira came out in "HaMelitz" more than forty years ago with his project to found a National Fund to redeem the land in Eretz Israel, he used this very argument at the time: if the Jews who were driven out of Spain had at that time deposited [?] in a bank one grosz each, the interest alone would by now have accumulated an enormous capital, enough to redeem the whole country.
In general the opinion prevails among us that once, in the Middle Ages, or in general earlier than now, there were still many different possibilities, which are now, however, already closed off, and that with every day things grow narrower and tighter, and whatever we do not snatch today we shall no longer be able to catch up with tomorrow.
This idea is fundamentally false. Here we see, for example, that the terrible troubles that have lately befallen our heads make life simply impossible for us and force us to save ourselves however we can and wherever we can. These troubles are quite exact copies of the medieval troubles; what is more, they also stem from one and the same source.
The begrudging envy of the Christian urban population towards the Jews is what brought about in Germany the terrible decrees of the Middle Ages. All the Crusades and massacres and expulsions — and the same begrudging envy is repeating itself today. If then it was kneaded with religious prejudices and today with national ones, the difference is surely not a great one.
In exactly the same way, too, the increased troubles and persecutions in other countries.
That means, then, that already in those days the same so-called overcrowding prevailed, and the same difficulty in finding a morsel of bread.
And when new continents opened up, America at their head, how many hundreds of thousands of different peoples, thrust out of their homes, sought a place of refuge there, because in the old homelands people were simply being suffocated by overcrowding and dying of hunger and poverty.
And our Jews, too, did not lag behind in this campaign: some five million of those thrust out did indeed settle in those new settlements, and they are now our greatest helpers and a bulwark [?] against want.
And the new technical achievements have brought a revolution in our various concepts: the development of communications has changed the concept of territory; the technical improvements in building have led to it that in a relatively small area like New York up to ten million people can live, trade and move about, who in the Middle Ages would have had to occupy a state as large as Germany and Poland together! The improvement of agriculture has led to it that cramped Germany can already almost support itself, and that in tiny Eretz Israel Zionists dream of settling millions of Jews by means of an intensive economy!
If people had only found the sense to divide the good of the world among the classes, nations and peoples, there would now in fact be more room than there was five hundred years ago, because people now know better how to make use of the space.
On the contrary: inasmuch as the human spirit still drives man to wander constantly and to take ever new corners of the world, there are still huge expanses in the American prairies and the Russian steppes where tens and hundreds of millions of people could still settle.
That means that the time lost can be made up quite easily, and still less need one lament the money lost. After we have already seen how quickly entire monetary systems in a state sometimes become a heap of ruins — such as the devaluations in France, Germany and Poland, and the latest wondrous action of President Roosevelt in America.
Fifty million pounds, they say, Jews have already invested in Eretz Israel. Has the Jewish people become poorer for it? Presumably the present Jewish wealth in Eretz Israel, also in America and other countries — even in those countries where Jews are tossed about like a superfluous thing, a portion of the Jews have in the meantime amassed enormous fortunes.
America, on the other hand, lost in one day of the stock-market crash, as was calculated at the time, 60 billion dollars, among which there was certainly a fair bit of Jewish money too.
The bottom line is that one must not count the days backwards; one must not lose heart through constant brooding over "if only I had, I would have" [?], but must always look ahead and not reject any means of help that is proposed.
After all, even the fortunate peoples living in their own homelands have not found the secret of how to live in peace and security: why should we, the people of exile, be in a better position?
P. K.
Self-Sacrifice for Art

[Będzin — art; interview with the painter Zuckerman.] P. K.
(A conversation with the painter Zuckerman)

The well-known painter Zuckerman, who is staying in Będzin with his picture exhibition, gave one of our staff, in an interview, some interesting details about the way he painted his works.

Among Zuckerman's pictures there are many that were created with real self-sacrifice. The outstanding artist, who has had art exhibitions in Paris, Berlin and Jerusalem, and about whom European and Jewish criticism responded with enthusiasm, literally sacrificed himself with a quiet, stubborn artistic fanaticism in order to be able to immortalize on canvas the colourfulness and fantastic quality of the oriental landscape of the Land of Israel.

"I often had to lie in the greatest heat," Zuckerman relates, "under the burning sun of the Land of Israel, which beats on your head like a hammer. In an unusual, almost tropical heat I painted many of my pictures, and I was so absorbed in my creating that I hardly felt the heat at all...

"On the terribly stifling days of the so-called hamsin, when people hide in the cool shade of the houses, I would lie somewhere among the rocks and paint and, with hardly any air to breathe, abstract the wonderful surrounding landscape, the mountains, the clouds, so as to bring it out later onto the canvas."

"The hardest thing," says Zuckerman, "was with the Arabs.

"Arabs often took me for a sorcerer when they saw how I paint. More than once Arabs attacked me with knives, thinking I was going to do them harm, that I had some hidden evil intentions... But I did not let myself be frightened. And I would force them to obey me, to pose for me. That, of course, came anything but easily. Every one of them was mortally afraid of being, God forbid, painted, and when they saw that my eye lingered longer on their red-orange turbans, which are so colourful and oriental, they would shout at me and shake their fists:

"'Haram, haram (a sin)!'

"When I set up my easel in the middle of the market in Jaffa, where the Arabs live, the whole of Jaffa would come running together to see the wonder [?]. People simply deafened me with wild voices and shouts. At every application of colour on the board the Arabs would fall into fright and at the same time into some kind of wild enthusiasm...

"When I painted the old Kabbalah town of Safed, I chose [?] a spot on the high, picturesque mountains of Canaan. From there I saw the Sea of Galilee (Kinneret), the mountains of Moab and the whole wonderfully beautiful natural panorama around, to a distance of 50 kilometres. I stood by a small garden gate and began to paint. Suddenly an Arab woman came running out. When she caught sight of me she quickly covered her face and wanted to run away. I showed her with my hands that I wanted to paint. But she ran away, and soon her husband came out, a tall, angry Arab. He looked at me with wild, glowing eyes and grabbed at his belt (in his belt the Arab carries a knife); behind me stood my wife. Seeing that there was also a woman with me, his face suddenly brightened into a friendly expression. He asked what we wanted. I answered him in Arabic 'Saaula' [?] — that is: I am a painter, I have come to paint. He then asked me to come into his garden. Though he still did not understand exactly what I was after, my cheerful [printed 'freydlikh'] appearance disarmed him. He saw that I was holding no knife in my hand — nothing more than a brush...

"The Arab's garden lay on the highest mountain peak, and I simply could not stop marvelling at the unusual beauty revealed before my eyes. I set up my easel in the garden and began to paint. The Arab attentively watched every movement of my brush over the canvas. Curiosity and surprise showed on his face. He began to shout, to shrug his shoulders, and suddenly he went into the house and came out with two women. To one he showed the picture; the other he ordered to bring out jugs of water for washing the hands and for drinking.

"When I later told my Safed Jewish acquaintances [printed 'rekante', probably for 'bekante'] how amiably the Arab had received me, they were very surprised: how could it be that an Arab would show his wives to a stranger and even order them to serve him? When I went home with the picture, the Arab ran after me for a stretch of the way and kept staring right into my mouth, as if I were some kind of god..."
The False Messiah (2)

[Serialized historical tale — David Alroy, the false messiah; installment 2.]
Sh. Berg.

Rabbi Shmuel Gaon had an only daughter, Menuha, and no son. So he wanted his daughter to inherit his Torah. And indeed she was great in learning. Every day she gave a "shiur" [lesson] for the young men; she was not, however, in the yeshiva but in an upper room, behind a curtain; through a window she studied with the young men.

The students of the yeshiva had never seen her face. Besides the fact that her face was covered, the Gaon let no one near her. He turned down the best matches; he did not want her to marry, but to devote herself to Torah.

Many young men dreamed of her. But they had no hope of ever seeing her. David Alroy [printed "Al-Rai"] also wanted to see her, and what no young man had dared even to conceive, David Alroy carried out.

Soon after his bar mitzvah, when he was already a man, he decided that he must see Menuha. She knows him, she knows who he is. She sees him every day, she hears his words in study. In her father's house she has surely also heard about him; he was sure that she liked him. And she him? He did not sleep at night because of her. Her figure always stood before his eyes, so beautiful, so wonderful. He must see her, he must tell her how he loves her.

One day he did not go into the yeshiva. Outside he waited in a hiding place, and as soon as he heard her voice from the upper room, when she began to give the "shiur," he went up to her in the upper room.

Menuha caught sight of David Alroy in her upper room, and her heart nearly leapt out of her for fright. For the first time a man had crossed her threshold. A scream almost tore wildly from her throat, but she steeled herself, clenched her teeth and held back the scream.

All this lasted a moment. David Alroy, tall and slender, came close to her and said quietly:

"Fairest of all daughters, show me your face, my bride. I love you; I see you by day and I do not stop seeing you at night. Bride, Menuha, show me your face."

Menuha stood mute, and even had she wanted to lift the veil from her face, she could not have done so. Her hands were as if taken from her, and David Alroy, like a prince, a ruler for whom no laws hold, lifted the veil and revealed her face, beautiful and radiant, delicate and pure, with eyes — a flame of fire.

Overjoyed, with burning enthusiasm, he murmured:

"I know you, bride, I recognize you. So I saw you in my dream, the fairest of all daughters. I love you, I long for you, bride."

Frightened and weakened as Menuha was, his words strengthened and fortified her, and she begged him to go away; she had to give the "shiur," after all. But he reassured her: the students think she is now pondering a hard passage of Gemara; they will suspect nothing. Pleading in a commanding way, he told her that in the evening he would wait for her by the Tigris [Hiddekel], a hundred feet from the bridge, and without an answer he went out.

Menuha tried to go on with the "shiur," but neither her head nor her heart was in it. She had had no say before her great, stern father. But her heart was pining for love. She wanted to marry. Many of her girlfriends had already married, and she was withering while still young. All her stifled desires David Alroy had now let loose, and they began to eat and gnaw at her heart. She somehow [?] finished the "shiur" and went off to her room, to her maidenly tent.

Alone she sat and tormented herself: he will be waiting for her by the Tigris, and she may not go to him. But when evening came she, as if led by a hidden hand, took her faithful maidservant and went to the "Arkel" [misprint, presumably for Hiddekel, the Tigris].

David Alroy was already waiting for her. He was not surprised when she came; he knew that she must come, that she was his bride. With the most wonderful words of love, as only the people of the East know how, he spoke to her, and he told her that he would soon speak with her father and ask him to give her to him as a wife.

"My father, Reb Shmuel Gaon," she said, and a heavy sigh tore from her heart, "will not give me to you. All the young men who wanted me he drove away."

"Me he will not drive away," David Alroy said firmly. "I am a son of David! And the time is not far off. I see it, when Rabbi Shmuel Gaon will boast of me, that I am to be his son-in-law."

Proudly David Alroy went in to Rabbi Shmuel Gaon and told him that he wanted his daughter as a wife. Rabbi Shmuel cut him off angrily:

"Not you will be Menuha's husband!"

"I am a son of David," David Alroy said. "Menuha is my destined one, and if you will not give her to me, I will take [?] her. I am your king, and if you do not obey my command now, the day is not far off when you will obey!"

Where Does One Vote in Będzin?

In the 8th electoral district, which elects 18 mandates, the Jewish voters are concentrated, apart from the few houses on Kołłątaja Street, which have been assigned to the electoral district of Krakowska Street.
The 8th district has 6 polling precincts. To the first polling precinct belong the streets: Czeladzka [?], Browarna (from number 1 to 13 inclusive), Stary Rynek (the Old Market), Plebańska, Zawadzie [?], Bóżnicza, Podzamcze (from number 2 to 8 inclusive), Zamkowa (from no. 1 to 5 incl. and from 2–12 incl.).
Second precinct: Modrzejowska (from 41 to 95 and from 42–84 incl.), Podjaże [?], Piłsudskiego, Jasna and Potockiego.
3rd precinct: Berka Joselewicza, Krótka, Św. Jana, Modrzejowska (from 15 to 39 and from 20–40), Podwale, Rybna, Rybny Rynek, Zaułek and Zawale.

How Should One Vote?

[Będzin — municipal elections.]
The ballot slip on which the names of the candidates are written or printed must absolutely be of white paper, otherwise the vote will be disqualified. All the candidates one wishes to elect must absolutely be from one electoral list. The voter may not write any names from different electoral lists. On the slip there must appear, besides the names of the candidates, the number of the list or the name of the list. No dots or other marks whatsoever may be made. Every voter may write one and the same name several times.
Every voter, when casting his vote, must have a personal document with him. Whoever does not have such a document can confirm his identity with 2 witnesses.
A Mentally Ill Jewish Woman Commits Suicide

[Będzin — suicide.]
On the second day of Shavuot the 39-year-old Urbach poisoned herself with vinegar essence. The suicide was a mentally ill woman, who had suffered from severe nervous attacks. She carried out the terrible deed outside the town. The suicide was taken to the municipal hospital, where she died on Wednesday.
Hitlerites Throw Stones at Jewish Visitors on the „Górka“

[Będzin — antisemitic attack.]
On Monday towards evening the Jewish visitors on the „Górka“ were pelted with stones and bricks. This was done by Hitler's comrades. The attack caused a terrible panic among the Jewish visitors.
Stopped the Train Because of a Hooligan Attack

[Zagórze — attack on a train.]
Mr. Aron Skacylas of Zagórze, travelling by train to Ząbkowice, was attacked in the carriage by Endek students, who began to beat Skacylas. Mr. S., wanting to save himself, stopped the train. For this a police report was drawn up against him.
A Warning to the Boycott-Breakers!

[Będzin — boycott of German goods.]
Now that various merchants in our town are breaking the boycott and trading in German goods, and thereby supporting the greatest enemy of the Jewish people, him who bathes in Jewish blood and strives to annihilate, God forbid, the entire Jewish people, we declare that we will fight those Jewish traitors with all the means we have in our hands.
In particular we turn with an ardent request to the Jewish consumers to be watchful when buying goods and not to buy any German goods, which are stained with Jewish blood.
Meanwhile we announce to the public that the iron merchant Jekel M. Gutman (3 Maja 7) and the paint merchant Bendet (Benie) Fiszel (Modrzejowska Street) bring in goods from Hitler's land.
Anti-Hitler Committee in Będzin.
New Code on Earnest Money

[Law — earnest money.]
If one of the parties does not carry out the obligation it has taken upon itself, the earnest money received is counted as compensation in favour of the other party. If [?] the party that received the earnest money withdraws, it must return the sum received — doubled.
These sanctions are applied only in the case where the agreements concluded do not provide for any compensation for non-performance of the agreed conditions. It goes without saying that what is meant here is a deliberate, in any case unjustified, one-sided non-performance. If [?] an agreement is not carried out through the fault of both parties, the earnest money given must unconditionally be returned.
Summer Colony of Fürstenberg's Gymnasium.

[Będzin — education.]
As every year, the management of Fürstenberg's Gymnasium is organizing a summer colony this year too. The colony will be located in “Mszana Dolna”.
As we are informed, the management is making every effort that this year's colony should be satisfactory in every respect. Besides all kinds of amenities, the colony has huge stretches of fields with gardens, where the children will have every opportunity to spend their time well. The prices too have been reduced this time.

Bloody Struggle in the Hall of the District Court Between a Prisoner and a Policeman.

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
On Tuesday, in the building of the local district court, a deadly struggle took place between a convicted prisoner and a policeman.
It happened under the following circumstances. While a policeman was leading a well-known thief out of the courtroom, the latter threw off his jacket (marynarka) and flung himself at the policeman with a razor blade (żyletka).
The policeman, wishing to avert the danger from the criminal, fired and seriously wounded him with a bullet.
19 Electoral Lists Disqualified.

[Sosnowiec — elections.]
At the session of the main electoral commission the submitted lists were examined, of which 19 lists were disqualified, among them also the lists of “Poale Zion” (Right and Left).
The “Activity” of the Anti-Hitlerite Boycott Committee.

[Sosnowiec — boycott of German goods.]
We have already pointed to the unheard-of matter that the anti-Hitlerite boycott committee in Sosnowiec has entirely ceased to exist; some Jewish merchants indeed felt that their hands were untied and began again to trade in German goods. All these merchants are noted down by us, but we have waited until the anti-Hitler committee would respond.
Some weeks ago a representative of the central anti-Hitlerite boycott committee in Warsaw stayed in Sosnowiec and conferred with a number of communal activists about reviving the activity of the anti-Hitlerite boycott committee in Sosnowiec.
But right after this conference the activity of the committee stopped — an activity that is an absolute necessity at the present moment.
On Withdrawing from Agreements.

[Law — contracts.]
When concluding an agreement, each party may reserve for itself the right to withdraw; if no time limit has been set, the interested party may set such a time limit; after the set time limit has expired, the agreed reservation of withdrawal loses its validity.
As regards the form of withdrawal, it is sufficient that the interested party notifies the other party. If the subject of the agreement amounts to more than a thousand złoty, the notification must be made in writing.
A Big Communist Trial.

On Monday the 28th of this month a big communist trial will take place in the local district court. In the dock will sit 45 defendants, among them members of the district committee.

[Dąbrowa — city council elections.]

Law on Agreed Compensation.
[Law — contracts.]
There are cases where parties undertake to pay the other party a specified sum of money as compensation for withdrawing from an agreement. The claimant then has the right to demand the agreed monetary compensation or to demand performance of the agreement.
If under the agreement the monetary compensation is to be paid merely for delay or for improper performance of the agreement, the interested party may, in the case where the agreement is not performed at all, claim both forms of compensation simultaneously, and even when the plaintiff has suffered no damage whatsoever.
Judith Berg / Registration of those wronged in the turnover-tax assessments / Appointment by the "Izba Skarbowa" / Brought to court for singing Jew-baiting songs / "Mother's Day" in Sosnowiec

[Będzin area — culture; dance review.] (From her dance concerts in Zagłębie).
Dance is as old as the human race has existed. It is the product of a deep inner need to express the most varied spiritual moods of an individual or of a mass. Joy and sorrow, ecstasy and depression, heroism[?] and submission, as well as in general every state of the soul in its thousandfold nuances, can find expression through dance.
From the most ancient times to the present day dance has not passed over any people or race.
The savage Bushman and the civilized European, the millionaire and the worker, the religious man and the freethinker — they all serve, each in his own way, the common "god of dance".
Among the savage tribes dance is used as a narcotic before a war; it creates a sexual mood in the salon, mystical ecstasy among believers, and can evoke refined artistic emotions in every person.
The very appearance of the dancer Judith Berg bears witness that she is as if created to be a priestess in the temple of the art of dance. There is something unearthly in her movements, her mimicry is full of splendid expression, the figures she creates look as if hewn by the hand of a great master.
Dance means chiefly the movements of the feet, but with Judith Berg it is mainly the hands that dance, creating wonderful symphonies of vibration.
Masterfully performed was the dance "Yudl with the Fiddle", in which the deeply human tragedy and the hopeless resignation of a perishing generation find expression.
The same can be said of the dances "Plovil"[?] and "Menakhem Mendl". No characterization of Sholem Aleichem's hero is able to present Menakhem Mendl as expressively as Judith Berg did with her dance. With the help of her artistic movements the dancer created an artistically stylized Menakhem Mendl, eternally restless and laden with schemes.
The costumes were well chosen for the various dances and contributed to the overall harmony.
The well-known composer H. Kon accompanied well.
Sh. R.

Communiqué of the Jewish National-Economic-Religious Bloc

[Będzin — city council elections; paid notice.] At the last moment, when the voter must already go to the ballot box and when almost the whole town is in agitation because the general bloc did not come about, we consider it necessary to declare the following:
From the very first minute we worked towards uniting all parties and groups, in order to increase our representation in the city council, which would have been a moral gain for us and would also have brought great benefit.
First of all the Agudah broke [unity]: it did not come at all — that is, it did not want at all to go together with all the Jews. All the other groupings reached an agreement after great trouble and effort. But at the last moment the candidate of the small traders did not want to abide by the agreement of his delegates and demanded third place instead of fourth. Naturally all the other organizations and groupings could not annul everyone's decision because of the ambitions of one single person, and because of this the whole bloc fell apart. The responsibility and accountability for breaking Jewish unity therefore falls not on us but on those who brought it about that because of them 5 to 6 mandates will be lost.
The voter will give the answer to this by casting his ballot not for those who broke unity among Jews, but for those who wanted to preserve it with all their strength.
In the name of the Jewish National-Economic-Religious Bloc:
"Merchants' Association", Zionist Organization, "Mizrachi", WIZO, Ha-Achdut, Revisionists, Torah ve-Avodah in Będzin.

The Defeat of Truth

[Będzin — city council elections; editorial.] (After the Będzin city council elections).
Our Dr. Weinzieher, who is without doubt the foremost Jewish citizen in the town, did not get into the Będzin city council.
People look for reasons, make excuses, each tries to throw the blame on the other; they say that this is a terrible moral slap in the face, which one cannot forgive oneself — how[?] could this have happened at a time when everyone regrets it, and everyone from right to left loves him and respects him and wanted to have him in the city council: some for the prestige and some for his wisdom; some wanted him as a teacher, as a guide, and some as a friend and adviser. But apparently fate willed that they should not be granted this honour, nor we. Jewish Będzin has been struck by it. And when, more than now, did we need to have him there? Precisely now we needed to hear a strong and mighty word that would burst forth from a truly Jewish heart. And who else could have shown that in so strong a form — both by his sharpness and by his beautiful Polish diction — as our doctor?
And if the new councillors have not had the privilege of sitting together with him, that is a terrible moral loss, which nobody can forgive himself; nobody can remain indifferent to this event.
But when we give ourselves a little account of all that has now happened, we must come to the conclusion that it could not have been otherwise. For how can there be a place for people who want the truth to win by itself, without lending a hand to it? At a time when demoralisation and enormous lawlessness have taken hold of every corner of our life, and they confuse and blur the Jewish street, so that one can by no means whatsoever see the truth.
So then, a slap in the face was received by all those who aimed to have in the city council representatives of the highest quality — representatives who would defend Jewish honour when it would be needed, without regard to anything or anyone, and stand on guard and protect the common economic interests, which[?] is the intention.
Unfortunately, and to our greatest shame, we have brought into the future city council, instead of representatives — seat-grabbers and careerists, who aim with the strength of the Jewish votes to do everything that will be in their own favour, without taking into account the interests of the Jewish people. Already now one can thus assess their future activity, having observed with what means and in what manner they grabbed their way in there.
Incidentally, we would like to be sincere and tell the truth: most representatives will not have the possibility of protecting Jewish interests — not because they will not want to, but because they will simply not be able to do it with the best will. There will after all be there the greatest number of mute judges, true extras.
The doctor was defeated because there is no place for truth, there is no place for the intellectual; otherwise such a thing would surely have been out of the question. If only because for everyone, without exception, he was a welcome and fitting representative, regardless of the not infrequently bitter words that would have been heard from his mouth. It goes without saying that his heart would not have been strengthened by it, and the shameful defeat is for his own good, for the sake of his health.
On the other hand, the defeat has been suffered by those who still operate with the truth, those who still rely on it and who were brought up on its foundations.
And therefore we must, with grief and pain, take amiss what has happened — admittedly unconsciously, but happened it has.
Our satisfaction towards the esteemed doctor will be this: that we shall show him even more love than until now, even more sympathy, even more devotion, even more respect.
His place, then, is in the institutions, where he works with devotion and cares for them with self-sacrifice and with love. Let us help him realise all his ideals, which are distinguished by true humanity and love, and let us, together with the doctor and with his esteemed wife, continue his important social activity, which occupies so respected a place in the town.
L. Szpigelman.
The City Council Elections in Czeladź

[Czeladź — city council elections.] In recent years we have had here only one Jewish councillor, Mr. Chaim Szwajcer, president of the local small traders' association. This is not the place to sum up his 30 years of useful activity for the benefit of the local Jewish population; from the fact that there is hardly a single Jewish inhabitant in Czeladź on whose behalf Mr. Szwajcer has not intervened with all the authorities, one must come to the conclusion that the success of his interventions is at a maximum.
Under the new electoral ordinance, by which artificial "ghettos" were created, the local Jewish population — which does not live in compact masses but scattered — had no chance of getting even a single Jewish councillor elected; so an approach was made to the representatives of the local BB [the Non-Partisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government], asking that they give one Jewish mandate, in return for which all Jewish voters would cast their votes for the BB. The representatives of the BB rejected this, arguing that the Czeladź Endeks are conducting a big antisemitic agitation and decry the BB as partners of the Jews, etc., and if a Jewish candidate figured on the official list of the BB, the Endeks would have even more material for their agitation against the BB.
Then the representatives of the BB put 2 alternatives before the Jewish population, namely: if the Jews do not give them their votes but put up a separate Jewish list, the BB will regard it as an acknowledgement that we are going against them, and the BB will understand it as "neither mine nor yours shall it be". For if the Jewish votes are weakened for them in relation to other parties, and if by a lucky chance we succeed in getting a Jewish mandate elected, their future councillors will fight him, and the remaining councillors, whose official programme is antisemitism, will certainly fight the one possible Jewish councillor. The 2nd promise was that the BB councillors would not only take our demands into account, but also that a Jew would be invited onto every committee.
On receiving the proposal, Mr. Szwajcer invited Messrs. Gelbard, Hire[?], and also the writer of these lines, A. A. After a lengthy discussion it was decided not to put up any Jewish list, but to give all the votes to the BB. And so indeed it was. All the Jews cast their votes for list 1, and the victory of the BB with the help of the Jewish votes is a colossal one: of 24 councillors, 20 BB, 3 leftists and 1 Endek were elected.
The future will show whether the BB councillors will keep their promise.
Abraham Epsztajn.
