The “Quick” Medical Aid of the Będzin Magistrate

[Będzin — health and municipality.]
Not just once have we pointed out that Zagłębie finds itself at a very low level where public medical aid is concerned — the aid the poor population has to make use of.
Several times already we have pointed out that Zagłębie has a wide scope: it possesses trams, automobiles, and its traffic is lively. Our pace is thus that of a big city, a European one. There is hardly a day on which accidents and catastrophes do not happen. Life here is therefore not as it was decades ago, or as it is today in a small provincial shtetl.
For these reasons we have several times demanded that our magistrates (municipalities) take into account the circumstances in which the population of Zagłębie lives, and that public medical aid be expanded and popularised. We said that a widely ramified "quick aid" (ambulance service) must be created which, as in all big cities, would be able to rescue at lightning speed not only the poor but also the well-off, whenever a person suffers an accident in which seconds decide a human life.
We have witnessed how, more than once, people had to pay with their lives — not because they could not afford to pay for a doctor's visit, but because the doctor could not be obtained in time. The facts thus prove how necessary it is to have in Zagłębie the so-called "doraźna" (emergency) aid.
But paper, it seems, has a great dose of patience. The pen writes, the typesetter sets, the machine prints and the reader reads it all with the greatest attention — and yet everything stays as it was, as though nothing had been said and no misfortune had happened.
And if our municipal institutions have time and are in no hurry to organise the "quick aid", if that branch is not yet topical for them, we at least understood that they would expand what they do possess, what has been concentrated with them for years.
We thought that the "Opieka Społeczna" (Social Welfare) would take a larger place in the life of the broad masses, and that at least the poor, those without means, those who cannot afford to call a doctor — would enjoy public medical aid.
But what do we see? We see that not only has the project of the quick aid been buried, the medical aid at the magistrates has not been strengthened; and more than that: not only has it not been strengthened — and it is enormously needed, since under present conditions more poor people are added week after week — but what we do have has also begun to limp, and unfortunately this limping is making giant strides. Thus about a year ago we had a death in Będzin only because the magistrate's doctor could not be obtained in time, and now we face a second incident, which has again cost the life of a young woman.
It must be established once and for all for whom the magistrate is obliged to provide medical aid and who is to decide these matters. What are the doctors there, what duties do they have, what is their mission, what must they do and what not, whom must they listen to and whom not? And the opiekunowie (welfare guardians) — what are they? What tasks and obligations do they have, both towards the magistrate and towards society?
It is unheard of: people are taken and made into guardians, they give away free of charge their best time for the common good — and with the doctors, who are employed at the magistrate and are paid for every visit, they have no say whatsoever. That is a terrible disregard which must not be tolerated.
What does it mean that a doctor allows himself to answer that the sick person "is not dying yet" when it is a matter of issuing a referral slip to a hospital? What kind of talk is that, and from whom does it come? What attitude towards the patient can one demand of the staff when the doctor himself, in person, expresses himself so "delicately"?
And now the very matter for whose sake it cost the life of a young person. What does it mean that the guardian requests urgent help for a patient, which is confirmed by a recognised doctor, a specialist — and all this is taken lightly and what the dangerously ill patient needs is not complied with? Is that called recognised public aid, maintained from the municipal taxes?
Can a magistrate really allow itself to engage doctors with caprices, who are to decide whom they must save and whom not? Surely the doctor must have one single task: to stand on guard and protect the life of the sick.
It must not be permitted that public doctors take patients lightly only because the unfortunate one is poor and cannot pay out of his own pocket. The doctor must remember — quite the reverse — that he holds a public office and the sick person is maintained by the municipal treasury; in this case the responsibility is unquestionably all the greater.
A city must not permit victims to fall only because of the carelessness of a doctor who wants to play the role of an autocrat, and perhaps a dictator, in his domain.
After all, this is not some question to be decided about, let us say, fashion items or luxury matters of some kind. It is a matter of nothing more and nothing less than human lives.
It is therefore important for us to know what position the magistrate will take here and in what way it will react to this merciless tactic. Such problems must not be passed over as if nothing at all had happened. If only there had been a proper reaction then, when the first misfortune occurred — perhaps the second victim would now have been avoided.
In any case, be that as it may, such lawlessness must not be permitted. It is bad enough that there is no "quick aid", which the inhabitants of Zagłębie need so badly; at least there should have been progress in the field of the existing public protection maintained by the magistrates.
R. Let.
The Trade in Charity Badges

[Zagłębie — charity and public institutions; opinion piece.] This or that institution often complains that it cannot keep going, that the public does not support it, that people do not know[?] how necessary it is and what benefit it brings. And often it indeed comes to appealing to the masses not to let any institution whatsoever go under.
And yet, how often does it happen that we do not want to "put our hand into cold water" [i.e. lift a finger], and that is because one is often disgusted ["s'eklt"] by many institutions which really ought to be removed altogether, because they bring no benefit, and on top of that they lie as a burden on the already sufficiently burdened Jewish population, which must above all take care of itself. One may boldly say that the institutions cost the Jewish population a heap[?] of money; no people in the world pays for as many social institutions as we Jews do; we have to give separately as citizens and separately as Jews, and in today's hard time of crisis that is certainly not one of the easy things.
This is said with regard to the badges ["aptseykhnungen" — charity tags sold in the street] that keep turning up here in Zagłębie. Every morning, as soon as one goes out into the street, one meets here a young lady and there a young man who will not let you pass[?]. You must buy yourself off, and then the way is free for you.
Granted, a Jew like me used to be curious to know for whom the money goes, for what purpose, and who the trustees over the cash box are. But all that was once upon a time, when one could still keep track, when such a badge collection happened once in a jubilee.
Lately, however, the badge collections have multiplied so much that not only can I no longer keep track of them, but they themselves, the "makhers" [operators], have already run out of names. It is enough that it should say[?] "for" this or that "fund", or even "for a cultural fund", and the matter is settled. One takes up the bags ["torbes"] and sets off on the hunt.
For what purpose the money goes, where it ends up, who is in charge of it? What do I know, whose business is it, and who should take an interest in such trifles. Since these are private matters, one might say. For when a Jew who has already done everything in the world, who has already lost all his positions and cannot show his face to anyone — when such a soul wants to go to Eretz Israel, a tag day ["tseykhn-tog"] is held for him — is that not a private affair? Or as soon as a few boys or girls of this or that party want to take a little trip to the Beskids [Beskidy], it is given the name of a "colony" [summer camp] and a tag day is held — is that not purely private? Is that not begging, merely with a different approach?
After all, we live in the present century, in the age of all sorts of combinations and bright ideas.
Can one be in favour of such "institutions" being supported? May the face of society be defiled in such a manner? Must "the trade" be allowed [to go on] openly and freely, while it is being done in the name of the community, in the name of society? These machinations must be cleared away from the Jewish street once and for all, so that people will know how to distinguish what ought to be supported and what ought to be avoided.
Selekt.
Two Marranos (2)

[Serialized story — Nazi Germany, diplomacy and the Jews; installment 2.]
Chaim Berg.
A story from Nazi Germany.

"The little hands of a prima donna," the German thought to himself.
"What is the proposal, Marquis?"
"Give us your Jewish professors and scientists, the Jewish industrialists and financiers, and Spain will receive them with great honour. We will take from you as many Jews as you took in Spanish Jews after the expulsion of 1492."
"Take them all! With pleasure, Marquis! Ha-ha-ha! We will even pay the freight, ha-ha-ha!"
The Marquis leaned over the table and shouted straight into the Baron's face:
"You are a damned liar, Baron!"
The Baron turned white, then red, and white again from the insult.
"You will not let the Jews out. You need to torment and torture them. If you get rid of the Jews and of the Jewish question, you will have no more breath to live as a party; you will be completely bankrupt, because your whole programme is nothing more than a great swindle. The people will later hang you and tear you to pieces... With your antisemitism you climbed up to power, and you must keep the ladder beside you."
Confounded, the Baron no longer knew how to use his diplomatic sword or what move to make: should he take offence, or swallow the coarse insult as it was.
"Marquis," the German burst out shouting, "who is to blame? Why did you take the damned Jew into your automobile when you knew the police were chasing him?"
"What then did you want? That I should leave the unfortunate man in the hands of his murderers?"
"A diplomat, an envoy of a state, does not get mixed up in a street brawl."
"A street brawl! You call it a street brawl? It was a hunt by wild beasts after peaceful and defenceless people. And because I am a diplomat, may I no longer have a spark of humanity in me? May I not stand up against the wild beast that has run riot in you Germans, so-called men of culture?"
At that moment, however, the door opened and the legation's footman came into the envoy's study:
"Hand the Baron his hat and cane," he ordered the footman, rose calmly from his seat, made a gesture of greeting[?] with his hand toward the Baron and left the study. In the doorway, however, he stopped again, turned back to the confounded Baron and said to him:
"I have a second surprise for you, Baron! I probably took the Jew under my protection because I myself descend from anusim, from those very ones whom the Christian Spaniards baptized by force. My great-great-grandfather conceived and carried out the unification of Spain, and not Isabella and Ferdinand. He built the Spanish empire for them and made them, from petty princes, into the greatest monarchs in the world. Out of gratitude they forced him to be baptized. That scoundrel Ferdinand could not manage without the Jewish statesman; the fact has always struck me as remarkable that in that same Ferdinand Jewish blood flowed[?]... His mother was a Jewish daughter. But from his father he got a hefty portion of Germanic blood, from your Goths or even Vandals, and that spoiled his Jewish blood to the very last degree."
"Enough!" the Baron struck the table.
"Yes, enough:" the Marquis shouted even louder. "Yesterday I cabled my government that I must leave Berlin; I demand my diplomatic passport."
After the "bath".
And so the Nazi diplomat came out of the diplomatic tournament with the Spanish Marquis like a plucked rooster, without feathers and bleeding... Not only did he fail to carry out the delicate mission the minister had given him — to apologize for the government for the "ugly incident with the police" and to give the Marquis the fullest possible satisfaction — but he even brought about a complete diplomatic break with a friendly republic, where Germany had great economic interests and had hoped in time to develop even greater ones...

Pirate Rule.

S. Rotenberg.
When the Hitlerites came to power they preached that the task of Nazism would be to create a new, pure Aryan type of German, a kind of superman, who would have to serve, physically as well as spiritually and morally, as a model for all mankind. They also tried to persuade people that National Socialism was the happiest synthesis for a social order, one that must satisfy both the nationalists and the socialists.
Further, they sermonized that with their coming to power unemployment would vanish and the renaissance of German trade and industry would begin. All the troubles that had befallen Germany they ascribed to the Jews and Marxists. The latter — so they argued — were the source of all evil and wrong, and the moment they were removed from public life the national and social redemption of the German people would come.
People with a political sense realized right from the start that Nazism was a dangerous hybrid (sha'atnez), a wild growth on the German national organism, for how is it possible that nationalism in its hyper-chauvinist form, which could at most serve as a point of attraction for big industrialists, landowners and Junkers, should mate with socialism? The whole Nazi theory stands here in glaring contradiction with itself. The first part of their programme absolutely excludes the second part, and vice versa. But demagogues do not reckon with any real facts; for them the main thing is to exploit a favourable conjuncture and, with the help of a dazzling phraseology, to stop up the eyes of the masses.
Naturally, Hitlerism could only realize the first part of its programme, nationalism. He Saved Himself.

M. Mandelzon.
(A humoresque).
His name was Lowa Dąb, and he was tall, strong, broad, a giant, a colossus, a Hercules — in short, a real strapping [?] man.
Now this Lowa Dąb, the giant, the colossus, with everything else besides, fell in love with Miss Chajele Sperber, who was thin, small, weak, a little kitten, a little sardine, "a dried fig of Rabbi Tzadok" — in short, a real little sparrow of a Chajele.
He fell gigantically in love with her and married her.
At first sight it is even a puzzle: how is it that such a giant, such a huge "figure" [?] as Lowa Dąb, should marry such a little kitten and little sardine as Chajele Sperber?
We have a couple of answers to that: first, as we all know, there is up on high a finger that points and an indicator that shows that the daughter of so-and-so belongs to so-and-so; and second, there is also, they say, a law of nature that brings contrasts together and joins [?] extremes.
But answers here, answers there, the main thing is: they got married and — may it be in good luck for us!
People even laughed up their sleeves [lit. "into their fists"] at such a "noodle-and-little-bean couple" and made merry [?] quite heartily at their expense, as jokers can.
But jokes here, jokes there, our young couple did not want to hear or know of anything, and right after the wedding set about celebrating [?] the honeymoon, as respectable people do.
All well and good — excellent!
But right in the middle of it, just after the first few honey-days of the first couple of honey-weeks, Chajele, the little wife, cast a glance with lawful, chuppah-and-kiddushin eyes at her athletic husband and — her little heart gave a start of fright.
She began to fear that he, the solidly built, iron-healthy and massive husband of hers, would outlive her. Surely outlive her.
He will outlive a hundred like her.
She begrudged him this and could not help begrudging it.
And out of begrudging, out of nervousness [?] and out of hysteria her little mouth would let loose so, that Lowa Dąb would each time start up gigantically and look for a place to bury himself for shame and heartache.
So once, so ten times, so countless times.
She loved him, loved him dearly, but it irritated her, and she could not bear his firm stride, his strong appetite, his healthy breathing and snoring.
If only he had been ill just once, if only something had hurt him just once!
But he is healthy as an oak, he is always healthy — iron, and she, she is so weak. She has no strength to look at it.
So she would lie down in bed, her little head bound with a wet towel, and from the bed she would nag him, devour him like a zhasher [?], scream, wail that she was done for, that he had made a broken vessel of her, that any moment she would die and he would — be able to take himself a fresh wife.
So once, so ten times, so countless times.
And after every time she came back to life fresh, went on screaming and nagged him again.
When Lowa Dąb saw that there was no end to the business, that his Chajele would with her rusty little mouth rust right through his heart, he went for advice — not to the rebbe's, nor to any lawyer, but to a doctor he knew.
And the next day, when Chajele's little mouth let loose again, as was her way, Lowa Dąb, the colossus, the mastiff [?], the giant, suddenly collapsed with heart-stabbing, belly-gripes, head-splitting and limb-breaking, and began to groan and toss so pitifully and so "mortally" [?] that his little wife Chajele was frightened to death and rushed straight off for the doctor.
The doctor examined, felt and tapped the "patient" on all sides, and the harder Chajele looked into the doctor's eyes, the more sadly, the more despairingly and hopelessly he shook his head, until he said, very sadly:
"It's bad with him... quite nasty... another attack like this he won't survive... your husband has a very weak heart... his strength and massiveness are not worth a groschen... it's only for show... he needs a lot of 'watching' [?]... he must not be upset... excitement is deadly poison for him... he must have quiet... 'complete rest'... he must take the prescription 'constantly'..."
When the doctor had gone, Chajele, the little wife, looked at her sick husband, poor thing, and with heart-rending weeping gave herself her word: from now on to watch over her husband like the apple of her eye, and never again to let a word be heard from her mouth.
On the Death of Chaim Nachman Bialik. — "We Have Become Orphans"...

"My heavy tear will not soon cease —
my tear I drew from the depths of my soul"...
(Bialik).
Our spiritual father Bialik has died. The Jewish people has been orphaned — "we have become orphans"!
Deeply shaken and faint [?] with grief over the sudden tragic calamity, the Jewish people stands before the mystery of death, before the coffin of the great departed, of the spiritual father and leader Chaim Nachman Bialik, of blessed memory.
At a moment when we are under so heavy and sorrowful an impression of the great national calamity that has struck us at so desperate a moment, when human language is too weak and powerless to describe the great national loss, to express our feelings, the "grief of the nation" — there can come only the despairing "cry of woe" from the depths of the heart, which bursts out spontaneously and instinctively from the unhappy, suddenly orphaned orphans — "we have become orphans"! And woe to the orphan!
The Jewish people has lost its teacher, its leader, its spiritual father. As a teacher he was the creator of a sea of old and new Jewish literature and poetry; he created inestimable literary treasures.
As a leader he was at once awakener, organiser, builder and defender of Jewish national honour and pride. As a father he was at once chastiser and comforter: on the one hand he showed tender, fatherly love, and on the other he stormed with prophetic words of rebuke, and he possessed a remarkable quality — both the love and the rebuke acted like a divine prophecy upon our spirit and psyche and like a balm upon our body; they healed and strengthened, encouraged and invigorated our spirit, so that we would continue our struggle for national liberation and for the realisation of the age-old dream of the Return to Zion. And with his works he wrote a glorious page in Jewish history and in the national renaissance.
But it is a mistake to think that Bialik was only a modern teacher and leader. No! He was also the great master in the field of the ancient and Talmudic literature, and in that field he created whole worlds. He was the true genius, "sharp-witted and erudite", a "Sinai and uprooter of mountains". He was universal, and only the true prophet, the "prince of the nation", can rise to such heavenly heights and concentrate in himself all these qualities and virtues.
And this mighty giant has suddenly been torn away from us, in the midst of his rich creative work. — "We have become orphans"!
And as we mourn the great departed and lament our national calamity, a bitter question bursts unbidden from our aching heart: whom must we lament and mourn — the great departed, the mighty spiritual giant, the authority whom we have lost, or our national calamity, because we have been left without a spiritual leader and guide? Whose tragedy is greater? And we must answer: "Weep not for the dead!" It is not the deceased who must be mourned, for every person must die, as the Sages say, "those who are born are destined to die"; whether leader or creator, to the dead it is all the same. On the contrary, the dead man himself is already better off: he no longer needs anything, no longer wants anything and no longer knows anything — especially since a person's life is worth little in so unhappy and tragic a time as the one we live in now, when all of life is nothing but death-throes, "the pangs of death", and as our great master Bialik teaches us:
"Instead of your death, a thousand deaths a day, moment by moment" —
"Die but once, fade out suddenly, rest in peace and silence!"
Instead, we must weep and lament for the Jewish people, which has been orphaned and wrapped in deep mourning; "weep sore for him that goeth away" — mourn the unhappy orphan, the Jewish people, which has lost its spiritual father.
Alas, such is our fate in exile: we are eternal orphans, and hardly does a bright star appear out of the exile before it is soon extinguished. We are very rich in great losses even in the most recent time. The tears for the Zionist leader Leo Motzkin have not yet dried; we are still mourning the great tragic victim Dr. Arlosoroff — and already, like heavy thunder, we have once again been shattered by the sad loss of our national pride and ornament, Chaim Nachman Bialik!
"Our breach is great like the sea; who can heal us!"
One consolation we have, and that is to fulfil his wish, his testament, which we had the privilege of hearing from his own mouth when he was with us 3 years ago, and which rang out like a mighty divine prophecy. He stormed and thundered: "Cast away your groundless hatred", "Show deeds" and "Back to the cheder"!...
J. Wygodzki.
Bialik Is Dead...

[Poetry — elegy for Hayim Nahman Bialik.]
"There was a man — and lo: he is no more,
before [printed 'kum', for 'kodem'] his time this man died"... (Bialik)
I wipe my eyes, I want to grasp what is happening here:
a name that shone, that sparkled generation after generation,
that awakened a whole people, inspired it and gave it heart,
so bright a star — blackened with a mourning frame!
"Bialik is dead" — how terrible it sounds, how strange!
The heart resists, is pressed tight in despair;
can he too die, who reached as far as eternity,
can the flame of the sun too be put out forever?
And I still thought that I would find in the paper
an echo of Bialik's word, a sound of Bialik's deed;
the darkness around was not yet quite so forlorn
while Bialik's lion-roar thundered out to us.
And now, how painfully clear the dreadful truth becomes:
the star that shone so bright
has already gone out.
Gone is "Israel's greatest singer", gone his pride and glory,
his wondrous harp is broken and mute...
The Poet and the Builder

[Eulogy — H. N. Bialik and the Jewish National Fund; on KKL's 25th anniversary.]
Before the coffin of the great departed stand his own words, which he so often uttered [?] in his prophetic inspiration — the only ones one can repeat after him without fear of underrating his greatness. The builder of the Jewish spirit and renewer of the original ancient Jewish culture constantly and unceasingly urged and roused people to acquire the national soil and to build up the Jewish home; he was the man who turned his word into deed. The lamenter and mourner of Jewish sorrow and pain, of inquisitions and pogroms — at the same time roused and called to resistance and self-liberation; from the historic striving for liberation he passed on to the song of rebuilding and redemption. The verses [?] of his poems he turned, through his personal deeds, into actions for the Jewish people and land.
One of his most beloved and devoted ideals was always the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael [Jewish National Fund].
It often happened to me in personal conversations to see how much [?] the progress of land purchase "through the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael" constantly interested him, and how often he was thrilled when he anticipated a possibility that the Jewish national land treasury in Eretz Israel would be enriched. I had the impression that he wished thereby [printed 'radurkh' for 'dadurkh'] to cast off from himself and from all of Klal Yisrael the disgrace of landlessness, which he sings of so lyrically in his poem "Ba-sadeh" ["In the Field"].
For the 25th anniversary of the "Keren Kayemet LeIsrael" the Jerusalem head office organised a grand celebration in Jerusalem in the "Eden" hall. It was announced that Bialik would speak. Bialik appeared in public in Eretz Israel not infrequently, but this time too, as always, everyone's expectation was very great. And when he rose that evening and spoke about the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael, one truly felt that the greatest spirit of our generation, speaking here of the greatest popular achievement of our time, surpassed himself. His words were no longer the rhetorical phrases of a speaker honouring some celebration, but flaming rocks [?], hurled by a giant into the roaring sea, in order to set down in the middle of the sea a firm base for the aimless [?] ships driven by the storm-wind. Thus he greeted the creation of the "Keren Kayemet LeIsrael" up to that time and argued the urgent necessity of an intensive, rapid continuation of the redemption of the land [ge'ulat ha-karka] by the Jewish people. At that time there was not yet any restriction on land purchase in Eretz Israel, but in his menacing demand one could feel the call: "Jewish people, remember that you must not miss the opportunity of redeeming your land."
And when he exclaimed: "Every individual must have four cubits of land for himself, and every people must have land according to its stature" [printed 'shiur kima'], the listeners in the "Eden" hall at the assembly for the 25th anniversary of the "Keren Kayemet LeIsrael" saw palpably as though a revelation had appeared before them, and many, many, under the impression of the poet's chastising and calming words, recognised their deep truth.
At this present moment, standing bowed before the coffin of the great departed, his words — which serve at the same time as the finest monument to his greatness — must unite the whole people to realise his great ideals and, first and foremost, to care for the acquisition of national land in Eretz Israel, so that on this soil the splendid edifice of the liberated Jewish people may rise.
Moshe Manela
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Matot-Masei)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Matot-Masei
The Portion
—o—
a) "If a man vow a vow unto the Lord" (Num. 30:3)
"This is what is written: For man also knoweth not his time." Midrash Pli'ah.
The Gemara, Nedarim 10b, says that in a vow one should say "a vow unto the Lord" and not "unto the Lord a vow". The reason: lest he utter the word "unto the Lord", some misfortune happen, and he be unable to finish the word "vow" — he would then have taken the Name of Heaven in vain.
This is the meaning of Midrash Pli'ah: "If a man vow a vow unto the Lord" — in a vow one says "a vow unto the Lord" and not "unto the Lord a vow", because "man knoweth not his time": a person does not know his hour, and something may happen to him in the middle of pronouncing the vow... Hida.
—o—
b) "Avenge the children of Israel of the Midianites" (Num. 31:2)
Taking up the wrong done to Jews is a higher level than avenging the vengeance of God... That is why Moses said (verse 3) "to execute the Lord's vengeance on Midian": because he was humble, he ascribed to himself a lesser level... Marganita de-R"B.
—o—
c) "And Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys" (Num. 33:2)
It is the way of nature that when someone sets out to wander about the world, he comes back worse than when he left, above all in matters of piety... That is why Moses wrote "their goings out according to their journeys... and these are their journeys according to their goings out": both their "goings out" — the departure from the places — and their "journeys" — the return from the wanderings — were the same; they had not changed... Ma'adanei Melech.
—o—
d) "Then ye shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you" (ibid. 52)
Drive the gentile ways out of your faces, so that a Jewish face may be recognised in you... Devarim Nehmadim.
—o—
We cry to God "Hear our voice": recognise us by our voice and listen to us, for by our faces you will no longer recognise us... We have become very different; there is no longer a Jewish mark on our faces. But by our voice, by the "voice of Jacob" — recognise us; we still cry out as we used to... Zivhei Ratzon.
• •
"The early ones, whose sin was revealed — their end was revealed; the later ones, whose sin was not revealed — their end was not revealed."
With the early ones it was "their sin was revealed": if a Jew sinned, it was recognised, because he dressed like a Jew, spoke like a Jew... Today it is "their sin was not revealed": one cannot tell whether a Jew has sinned, because it is hard to distinguish between a Jew and a gentile... Har Sinai.
—o—
e) "The land of Canaan according to the borders thereof" (Num. 34:2)
Our geniuses cannot understand at all what use there is in knowing the borders of the Land of Israel... R' Meir Eisenstadt in his book "Ketonet Or" explains that since the Gemara says in Horayot page 3 that the halakha is decided according to the practice of the majority of the inhabitants of the Land of Israel, and the Jews outside the Land are not counted, there is consequently a practical legal difference in knowing the borders of the Land of Israel...
The Hida in "Nahal Kedumim" explains again that since Tosafot (at the beginning of tractate Pesahim) write that the Jews outside the Land are exempt from bringing the pilgrimage offering, there is again a practical legal difference in knowing which Jews belong to the Diaspora and which to the Land of Israel.
That the borders of the Land of Israel are needed simply to know which piece of land belongs to the Jews — that our geniuses no longer understood...
—o—
f) "Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh" (Num. 34:19)
With all the tribes it says "of the tribe of the children of...", except with Judah and Benjamin, where it says only "of the tribe".
From the wording of the Midrash one infers that the younger generation of those who entered the Land is called "children"; and here we [see] that all the princes were new, not of those who came out of Egypt, so it says of them "of the tribe of the children of...". Only the prince of the tribe of Judah, Caleb son of Jephunneh, and the prince of the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad (that is Eldad, see Ba'al ha-Turim) — they were still of those who came out of Egypt, and so "the children of" is not said of them... Binyan Ariel.
—o—
g) "And he shall abide in it unto the death of the high priest" (Num. 35:25)
Why precisely "unto the death of the high priest"? It appears that the high priest has some connection with it, because he did not teach the people how ugly murder is... Shalom Yosef.
—o—
h) "So shall not the inheritance remove" (Num. 36:7)
How many quarrels arise over inheritances! Of many heirs one may say in jest: "Let the days of mourning for my father be at hand, and I will slay my brother" — let only father die, and I'll already kill my brother over the inheritance... "Yerusha" also means becoming poor ("lest thou come to poverty", "the Lord maketh poor"), because one becomes poor from an inheritance sooner than one gets rich from it... R' Eliezer Reines.
The “Cooking Spoon” — Chatskele Kalbonik Goes on Vacation

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour and satire; feuilleton in folksy Polish-Jewish dialect.] Humour and satire. Compiled by Ben Amotz.

Chatskele Kalbonik goes on vacation
Listen, fellows [“yatn”], I’ll tell you a secret [?], and if you don’t like it — I have decided that I too have to go on vacation [“urlop”].! Say for yourselves, what, is my soul a raisin? Other nobodies [“pentakes”, Polish pętaki] may go on vacation and I not? Other nobodies may fry themselves [“smazhen”, smażyć] in the sun and I not? Well, so I decided that I am going too.
I’ll tell you the plain truth [“nivaris” — ?], that it is very painful [“pshikre”, przykro] for me to leave the Podzamcze lane [“Parzamtshe gesl” — Podzamcze, the Jewish quarter of Będzin below the castle], but I must [?] go. You think perhaps that I have no appetite for eating? If you think so, you are mistaken: I do have an appetite, only I have no [“tsub” ?] appetite — how can I eat, when everything [“khmalyen” ?] disappears around the mugs [“yapn”, japy ?] of the summer-colony people [“kolontaya”, kolonia]? Who gobbles up the strawberries [truskawki], the blueberries [jagody] and the bananas [“binanen” ?]? — The summer guests [“kolontayanikes”]. Who slurps up the sour cream [śmietana], who drinks soda water with juice [sok], who splurges [“puplt” ?] on all the ice creams [“lyadis”, lody]? — The summer guests.
But if I go on vacation, I’ll also have to do something about it. Oh, where will I get money from? — Nonsense! And all those who go — do they have it? They too have [“sgidukhes” ?]; one borrows from the other, they write promissory notes [“vaksn”, weksle], and when it comes to paying they wriggle out [“dreyen zey zikh os dem drashek” ?] and say [“yshakeygi” ?]! That’s how people live today.
Where am I going? That I can’t say yet; I’ll write to you — and you will find out.
Be well and strong — I am going on vacation.
I Swear to You, Oh No...

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour and satire; comic poem.] (A hymn to the straw widower [“shtroyener almen” — a husband whose wife is away at a resort] by X-Y [“Iks-Igrek”]).

O straw widower,
You widower of straw,
You’re well off now, aren’t you,
And so important [“vazhne”, ważne].

In Krynica, in Rajcza,
Or in Bystra
You now have somewhere to stick
Your “faithful” wife.

She sits there at the trough [“oyf pashe”, na paszy — eating her fill],
She burns in the sun,
In sheer paradise,
She is a “personage” there...

And faster and wider
She grows than a barrel [“tun”],
And the guests there
Enjoy it.

Your wife now lives as by day [?],
She doesn’t sleep — she stays awake,
With her girlfriends [“pshiatshulkes”, przyjaciółki]
She has fun and laughs.

So don’t think, O “widower”,
Don’t brood and don’t think,
She barely lives by day now —
So you live by night.

O straw widower,
Don’t be a sucker [“yold”],
You have paid for your peace now
Not too badly.

So have a good time
By electricity and steam,
And get ready in good time
For victory in the struggle.

Do exercises [“tshvitsheniyes”, ćwiczenia] now
With plenty of women,
And just do it properly —
Get down to the business.

Remember that your so-and-so,
Who has a thousand charms,
Is not writing tefillin there [i.e. is not doing holy work there] —
I swear to you — oh no!

They Keep the Rabbinical Court’s Ruling

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour and satire; Będzin.] She doesn’t drink, she only sucks; he doesn’t beat, he only pinches

Walking along Gzichowska street [“Gushikhovska”, Będzin], a “Nara”-dowiec [narodowiec, Polish nationalist, alluding to the ONR] comes towards me and, noticing that nobody is looking, he gives me a jab [“dushukh” ?] in the side and walks on as if nothing had happened. So I walk on and recall that divorce.
A married couple came to the rabbi to get divorced. The rabbi asks the reason for the divorce.
— I can’t live with her — the husband pleads — where has it ever been heard of, that a Jewish woman should drink; all day long she keeps knocking back little glasses.
— And he — the Jewish woman lashes out — keeps on beating. We have lived together so long already and in his old age he has actually taken to beating.
The rabbi issues a ruling that she should stop drinking and he should no longer beat.
Both accepted the ruling: she stopped drinking and he stopped beating.
After a while she craved a little glass, and he had a strong urge for [beating] the Jewish woman. To keep the ruling, they thought it over and came up with this plan: she brought home the vodka, poured it into a little bottle with a teat [“mamke”] and sucked it out — she didn’t drink, she only sucked... And he gives her from time to time a pinch, a tweak — that surely isn’t called beating. And so it went on. They obeyed the rabbi: not drinking, only sucking. Not beating — only pinching...
Reles.
A Letter from a Sosnowiec Litvak

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour and satire; Sosnowiec; comic letter in “Litvak” dialect.] To his wife at the “dacha”.

We bring here a letter from a Litvak [Lithuanian Jew], who speaks in the plural, with “we”, to his wife at the “dacha” [summer house].

Dear woman [“zensine”, Russian zhenshchina in Litvak pronunciation]!
You surely want [“kerst” — misprint for kenst?] to know how your husband [“muzh”] is getting on [“pozhivayet”] all alone in town. So we can write to you that we are living not badly [“nis kase” = nishkoshe]. All day long one has to deal with the business, because the dollar doesn’t stand in one place, but rises and falls like a black year. But on the other hand, when the evening [“vetsher”, vecher] comes it is a delight to the soul. [“Vapne-veykh” ?] we go for a little stroll [“gulyayen”], then [“potom”] we go to the cinema, and finally [“nakonets”] — home [“domoy”]. We make our bed, we straight away lay out the featherbeds [“perines” ?], we get undressed and we lie down to sleep, so that it is a delight to the soul.
I thought that without you it would be nasty [“paskudne”], but you know, after all, that one finds a way.
The Messiah in Krynica.

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour and satire; Krynica, spa town.] All of Krynica is buzzing [“kokht” — boiling] with the story: in a little bottle of wine somebody found some sort of written little letter.
When people ran over to the rabbi so he would read it, he answered that it looks like the Messiah’s handwriting, and the wine — that is the yayin ha-meshumar [the wine preserved for the righteous].
And the proof: it says explicitly in the little letter that the Messiah comes only when: “I will come to you when everything is asleep” — so it is written in the Messiah’s kvitl [note].
So they called a meeting and resolved that at night everyone must [printed “muv” for “muz”] really sleep, and then the Messiah will surely come.
At night, around 2 o’clock, they did indeed see someone in white stop in front of a villa in which lives a pretty young wife whose husband went away yesterday.

A Jewish Woman with an Appetite.
Doctor: — What is wrong with you?
Sick woman: — I don’t know, panie doktorze [Polish: doctor, sir], I have, “nie dla pana powiedziawszy” [Polish: begging your pardon] (may it not happen to you), a weak, a very weak appetite for food.
Husband (from behind the door): Don’t believe it, doctor, she has a quite decent appetite — she eats me up with great relish.

Among Men.
— You know, I consider my wife an angel!
— You know what I’ll tell you? I would also like to send mine to heaven.
Polish Women Who Sacrificed Themselves for the Jewish Faith

[Serialized history — Christians who embraced Judaism; Kraków, 16th century.]
M. Starkman.

(An interesting historical tale that happened 200 years ago).

The history of Jewish martyrs who sacrificed their lives for their faith is a long and a sad one, and it means telling of thousands who perished for the sanctification of the Name [kiddush ha-Shem]. But there are also non-Jews, born Christians, who perished at the stake for their love of the oppressed people and its faith. Here we shall tell of four such Christians, three Polish women and a Russian naval officer, who bound their fate to the Jewish people and went joyfully to their death, just so that they could remain Jews.
One of them is Katarzyna Malcherowa Weigel Zakewowska [?] [Katarzyna Weiglowa], whose husband was a member of the magistrate [city council] in Kraków. She herself came from the very most honourable families in Poland. The most distinguished aristocrats of the city used to frequent Katarzyna Malcherowa's house. She herself, however, did not belong to that type of rich Polish women of the 16th century, i.e. 400 years ago, who occupied themselves with balls, amusements and hunting; on the contrary, she was a very serious and deeply religious woman. In her free time she used to occupy herself with reading pious Christian books and philosophized about various religious problems.
When Katarzyna Malcherowa Weigel had grown old, about 70 years of age, there was a great stir in Poland around the Christian sect of the "Unitarians", who denied the Catholic dogma of a divine "Trinity": God the Father, God the Son and the "Holy Ghost". This sect also rejected a whole series of fundamental principles of Catholicism. The "Unitarians", in contrast to the fanatical Catholics, related sympathetically to the Jews and took much more interest in the writings of the Tanakh than in the New Testament, the Christian addition to the Bible. The leaders of the "Unitarian" movement were a number of Polish professors, and a good many Polish intellectuals and aristocrats joined them.
Unitarianism also attracted the attention of the religious-philosophical Katarzyna Malcherowa. While also studying the fundamental principles of the new sect, she meanwhile became acquainted with the tenets of the Jewish religion, and little by little she came to the conviction that the Jewish faith is the only right one, and she told this to her friends.
The news of Katarzyna's religious conviction reached the Kraków bishop Gamrat, a fiery antisemite and fanatical fighter against all Christian "heretics" [apikorsim]. So in August 1530 he forced her to appear before the church tribunal and to answer the charge of denying Catholicism. Being found guilty would have meant being burned at the stake. Katarzyna Malcherowa, however, was no simple Christian woman but a Polish aristocrat, and moreover a lady of advanced age, so the bishop decided to spare her if she would retract her denial of the "Trinity" and become a believing Christian again.
Katarzyna's relatives, too, moved heaven and earth to save her, and in the end they prevailed upon the old woman to declare publicly that she regretted her step. The old woman gave in to their demand and saved her body from the red tongues of the stake.
Deep in her heart, however, Katarzyna held to her belief in the Jewish religion just as before. And with time her conscience began to torment her, because she had not had the proper courage to pay with her life for her religious convictions. She went to church ["kloyster"] very seldom. She lived quietly and in retirement. Only the Jewish doctor Moshe Fishel was her friend at that time, and taking advantage of his frequent visits as her house physician, she held long conversations with him about the Jewish faith, and from him she also learned all the commandments that a pious Jewish woman must observe.
When Katarzyna approached the age of 80, she understood that she would probably not live much longer, and she therefore decided to disregard all dangers and publicly declare her belonging to the Jewish faith — and so she indeed did. Bishop Gamrat, who for nine whole years had nursed a grudge over her un-Christian conduct, at once seized the opportunity and again dragged the old woman before the church tribunal.
The Polish chronicler Łukasz Górnicki, who was present at that trial, tells of it in his memoirs:
"The priest Gamrat, bishop of Kraków, called together all the priests in order to examine her regarding her principles of faith. When she was asked whether she believes in the almighty God, the creator of heaven and earth, she answered:
— I believe in the God who created everything, what we see and what we do not see; in the God who cannot be grasped by plain human reason; in the God who protects all people and all things in the world.
— The almighty God has no wife and no son. He does not need that. Only those who die need children, but God himself is eternal, and since the Creator was not born, it is therefore impossible that he will die; we are all counted as his children when we walk in God's ways.

Będzin: General Meeting of the Jewish Charity Society

[Będzin — welfare; orphanage.] In the hall of the "Merchants' Association" the annual general meeting of the charity society of our town was held on Monday evening.
About 8 days ago a meeting of the Discount Bank was supposed to take place in the same hall. That meeting, at which "interesting" questions were on the agenda, was indeed attended by so great a number of members that, because of the great crush, the meeting was dissolved; on the other hand, the meeting of "Dobroczynność" ['Charity'], where one gives a report on the upbringing of orphans, relief actions and other such "nonsense", aroused interest — apart from the board (and not all of it either) — in 5 (read: five) members...
Dr. Weinziher opens the meeting with "grateful" words for the great "interest" shown by Jewish society in the meeting, and hands the chair to Mr. Rubinlicht, who invites into the presidium Mrs. Hutner and Messrs. Y. Gelbart, N. Landner and Lewkowicz.
The board's report is given by Dr. Weinziher, who points out that during the past year the board succeeded in putting the institution back on its feet and placing its economic situation on sound foundations. The greatest share of credit for the work must be ascribed to Mr. S. Potok, who reorganized the administration and set it up in the proper way.
The treasurer's report is given by Mr. S. Potok. From the report we see that the institution owes about 25 thousand złoty for provisions etc.
Mrs. Ts. Szajn, in her report on the orphans' home, tells of the development and upbringing of the 74 children who are being brought up in this institution as Jews and as human beings.
Mr. Wygodzki dwells on the educational side of the children of the orphans' home and on the great progress the children have made during the past year, and proposes protesting against the women's part of the local Jewish population and against the rabbinate in general for their indifference in the field of orphan education.
After the budget for the coming year is read out, Mr. A. Liher[?] takes the floor and says that in the present distress in the Jewish street there is not one single institution that would be the so-called "pogotowie" ['emergency service'] to help with a couple of złoty, and he calls on the board of Dobroczynność to undertake an action in this field.
A discussion developed around the proposal, in which Messrs. Potok, Boruszykowski[?], Lewin, Wygodzki and Dr. Weinziher took part. The last gave a historical survey of the origins of "Dobroczynność", which was founded 35 years ago by the late Będzin rabbi Graubart and embraced all branches of philanthropic work. Today — says Dr. W. — there exists a whole series of small societies that advertise their activity for the purpose of their own benefit and create a mood for themselves in the town, but the work in the orphanage is quiet and modest; the children — he says — tell no one, and they have no vote either...
The result of the discussion is the adopted proposal of Mr. Wygodzki that a special section be founded at Dobroczynność, which is to recruit new members and work out a plan of income to be used for urgent relief.
Then elections were held for 2 representatives on the board. Elected were Mrs. Hutner and Mr. Sh. Lewkowicz.
At half past twelve the meeting was closed.
Departure of the Second Group of Children to the Municipal Colony in Sławków

Human Bones Found During Sewer Works on Zawale Street

[Będzin — municipal; respect for the dead.] Sewer-construction work has begun on Zawale Street. While digging, human bones were found there, lying scattered around the excavations. Only thanks to the local neighbours were the bones gathered together and afterwards brought to burial.
In connection with this we have received an open letter to the rabbinate and to the kehilla leaders, who did not take care beforehand that the human bones should promptly receive their due honour and not lie about in the street.
Echo of Bialik's Death in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — mourning; Bialik.] The terrible news that the great poet Hayim Nahman Bialik has died aroused a shattering grief in the Jewish circles of Zagłębie.
Immediately after the cruel tidings were received, a mourning session took place in the kehilla in Będzin under the chairmanship of President Mr. Rubinlicht, with the participation of members of the board and council.
After short mourning speeches by Messrs. G. Landner and M. Manela it was resolved to send a telegram of sympathy to the Va'ad Leumi in Jerusalem and to announce the great loss by a black-bordered notice (klepsydra).
The committee of the Będzin "Tarbut" likewise lamented, in a klepsydra, the most painful loss of the great poet.
———
This Sabbath a memorial service for the great departed will be held in the Będzin synagogue.
———
On the Sabbath a mourning academy dedicated to the memory of the unforgettable Hayim Nahman Bialik was held at the Będzin "Gordonia".
In a very depressed mood the academy is opened by Mr. Shlomo Zimmerman, and after honouring the name of the great poet and singing "Tehezakna", the floor is given to Mr. Yehuda Anulowicz[?], who depicts the greatness of the unforgettable prince of the nation and the inconsolable sorrow that has befallen the Jewish people.
At the end it is resolved to name a gdud [unit] after Bialik and to take part in the 30-day mourning proclaimed by the Central Committee of "Tarbut" in Poland. It was also resolved to send letters of condolence to the Central Committee of "Tarbut" in Poland and to the supreme leadership of "Gordonia". With the singing of "Hatikvah" and "Tehezakna" the academy was closed.
The "Season Supervisors" Already Have "Hazakah" Claims Too

[Będzin — shechita and kashrut.] Some weeks ago — as our readers know — on the initiative of a group of Hasidic Jews, 2 butcher shops were opened with their own supervisors (ne'emanim), who supervised the meat sold in the shops.
The butchers, seeing that the business was not a success, removed the supervisors. This greatly vexed the initiators, and they called a meeting in the "Talmud Torah". At the meeting, held on the Sabbath, the assembled Hasidic public spoke with bitterness about the prevailing lawlessness in the field of shechita, and of kashrut in particular, thanks to the petty shochtim who want to force their way in as Będzin shochtim.
On the proposal of the parnas Chaim Wellner it was resolved that a new Va'ad ha-Kashrut be created, which together with the rabbinate is to begin a fight against the clandestine slaughter in our town.

General Meeting of the Butchers' Guild

[Będzin — butchers' guild; economy and shechita.] Last Sunday, under the chairmanship of Mr. Noach Ojzer [?], an extraordinary general meeting of the local Jewish butchers' guild took place.
The meeting was called in connection with the vote of no confidence that the guild had expressed a few weeks ago in its president, Mr. G. Saks.

After the reports on the activity and on the treasury, a board was elected consisting of: Noach Ojzer [?] (president), Hirsz Ber Goldblum, Wolf Paumantir [?], Gerszon Saks (vice), Icze Majer Pszerachski [?] (treasurer), P. Warsz (secretary), Patasz [?], Zingdorf [?] (audit committee), Jankel Mandelbaum, Icchak Szwarcberg, Aba Strubel and Aba Ruszyniek [?].
Sosnowiec — Strict Orders from the Starosta to the Kehilla Board and Council

[Sosnowiec — kehilla; government supervision.] The finances are neglected. — Secret shechita. — Demand for the overdue etat [kehilla tax] debts. — Issuing of etat receipts abolished.
From 5 to 19 June [czerwiec] of this year an inspection [lustracja] of the local Jewish community was carried out under the supervision of the starosta [district head].
The result of the inspection are the orders which the starosta sent this week to the kehilla board and council.
First of all the starosta points out the neglect of the kehilla's finances by the board and council: not only do the kehilla officials make no effort to create revenues for the community, but they neglect the collection of the etat. Also — the report says — secret shechita has spread on a wide scale, unauthorized promissory-note [weksel] operations are being carried out, there is no registration of the Jewish population in Sosnowiec, kehilla officials dispose of kehilla funds without the consent of the board, etc., etc.
In connection with this it is ordered: by the 15th of this month the enforcement measures against those owing etat for the years 1926 to 1933 (inclusive) are to be intensified.
Measures are to be taken so that secret shechita stops; otherwise the most far-reaching penalties will be applied against the guilty, even dismissal from their posts.
Real-estate matters may be handled only by members of the kehilla board, without any mediation by private persons.
No promissory notes are to be issued, and private persons may not collect the etat under the system used until now (private receipts).
The kehilla collectors must submit an account every day and hand over the sums collected.
By the month of November [listopad] of this year the kehilla must carry out a registration of the permanent Jewish residents.
The vital-records books [metryki] must be kept by the rabbi; but considering that the present acting rabbi does not command the Polish language, the books are to continue to be kept at the community office according to the instructions of the one who acts as rabbi.
At Sunday's meeting of the kehilla board it was decided to inform the starosta that the board and council take note of the orders sent by the starosta.
Wife of a Court Trainee Commits Suicide

[Sosnowiec — suicide.] On Tuesday morning, in the “Bałkan” houses on Jagiellońska Street, the 30-year-old Mrs. Man(n), wife of an aplikant [legal trainee] at the Katowice district court, hanged herself.
Before carrying out the deed she sent her 6-year-old child out into the courtyard, and then hanged herself from the lamp. That same day her husband had taken leave from his work so as to be at home with his wife, who suffered from a heart condition. On coming home he already saw the terrible sight. The doctor from the sick fund, whom he had telephoned for help, came only an hour and a half later.
A Beggar Who... Discounts Promissory Notes

[Sosnowiec — police and crime.] The local police have launched a campaign against street begging. Among others, a Christian beggar was also detained, and a search was carried out on him.
The search produced a surprising result: 25 blank promissory notes for 3,413 zł., which he was to collect from various people, were found on the beggar.
The beggar has been brought to court for begging and for engaging in usury.
She him, or he her?...

[Katowice — Court.]
A sensational trial was held in the district court in Katowice against the official Augustyn of Neu-Beuthen (Nowy Bytom). He was accused of taking from a certain Helena L. a ring worth 700 złoty. The whole affair appears very complicated.
According to the statements of the injured party, she was accosted in the street by some unknown man, who invited her to a restaurant. Since the gentleman took her fancy, Helena agreed to meet him a second time the next day.
That person then noticed a valuable ring on her hand and declared that he would like to find out how much the ring was worth. Suspecting nothing, Helena took the ring off her hand and gave it to her acquaintance, who went off with it to a jeweller.
About an hour later he came back and told a story that the jeweller was not at home, and that he would therefore bring her the ring the next day. When Helena demanded the ring back and wanted to go to the jeweller, the man implored her not to compromise him, because he had told the jeweller that the ring was his.
The injured woman believed him. But he never came back. About three days later she went to the jeweller, where, however, she received no information at all. Only when she reported to the police did she learn the address of the vanished person.
The accused presents the matter entirely differently. As he declares, it was in fact he who was accosted in the street by Helena. She complained to him that she was in great need, had no coat, and offered to sell him a ring.
They then both went to the jeweller, who valued the ring at 700 złoty; and since the girl wanted 300 zł. from him for the ring and he had no more than 150 zł., he gave her that sum for the time being and told her to come to his home afterwards for the rest. But instead of coming for the money, she reported to the police.
The court proceedings were also rich in piquant scenes, and therefore the trial was partly held behind closed doors. The plaintiff fainted while giving her statements.
Because of the absence of a witness, the piquant trial was adjourned.

The new regulation on auctions.
[Law.] On the basis of the new Commercial Code, a regulation on auctions (licytacje) has been published in the "Dziennik Ustaw".
According to this regulation an auction must take place no later than 15 days after the judgment is lodged with the bailiff (komornik).
The auction must begin at the appointed hour — if that is impossible, one may wait at most two hours. If only one single bidder is present, the auction may not take place.
The following may not appear as bidders: the debtor, his wife and children, the bailiff and the official assistants.
Whoever has bought an auctioned object must pay the amount immediately on the spot in cash. If the sum exceeds 5,000 zł., he has the right to pay one third and pay the rest the next day by 12 noon. The third paid in, however, cannot be less than 5,000 zł.; thus, for example, when the sum amounts to 10 thousand zł., one must pay a full 5 thousand zł. on the spot, and when the sum is higher than 15 thousand zł., one must pay as much as makes up one third.

[Sport — Zagłębie.] "Unia" champion of Zagłębie.
"Unia" — "CKS" 1:4 (1:0)
On the 8th of this month, the final between Sosnowiec's "Unia" and Czeladź's "CKS" for the championship of Zagłębie took place in Częstochowa on the sports ground of "Brygada". The above-mentioned match aroused great interest in all sports circles of Zagłębie. Already early in the morning a special popular train arrived in Częstochowa, bringing with it the supporters of "Unia", and several buses from Czeladź. Besides that, a great many cyclists came from all over Zagłębie, and also quite a few pedestrians.
5000 spectators attended the match, of whom about 1500 were from Zagłębie. The match ended in a significant victory for "Unia", which thanks to it took the championship of Zagłębie and will take part in the championships of the Kielce voivodeship. Both teams appeared in this match in their best line-ups.
The course of the match was as follows: CKS kicks off and in the first half carries out very sharp attacks on the "Unia" goal, and twice the CKS forwards even hit the post. CKS has a great superiority in the field; in the 34th minute the referee awards an eleven-metre kick to "Unia" [i.e. against it — so in the original], from which Boguski [?] scores the first goal for CKS. Despite the very energetic efforts of the "Unia" forwards, the result remains unchanged until half-time. Meanwhile rain began to fall, because of which the ground became impossible to play on. CKS, which plays short [?], had to fail. "Unia" adopted a very good tactic and strongly pushed the wings, which very easily got to the opponents' goal. This tactic led to the "Unia" forward line taking over the whole initiative in the second half and scoring four goals. Referee Dr. Rumpler of Kraków — . A Heavy Thunderstorm with Human Casualties in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — storm and floods; Sosnowiec, Niwka, Zagórze.]
On Wednesday afternoon a heavy thunderstorm passed over Zagłębie, which caused considerable damage in the gardens and in the fields. The streets in the suburbs of Zagłębie were also flooded.
On First of May Street in Sosnowiec the water tore away a wall of a small building; the tenants, a Jewish and a Christian family, managed to save themselves in time.
Tram traffic was halted during the storm because the line was flooded.
There were also fatal accidents caused by lightning. In Niwka lightning struck a hut in which five workers were present; they suffered concussion.
In „Yenuar“[?] [probably Jeżor] lightning struck the flat of the Najda family; as the 5-year-old Najda boy was about to close the door, the child fell dead on the spot.
Several lightning accidents occurred in Zagórze.
27 Young People Set Out on Foot for Eretz Israel / Reassuring News from the Rescue Committee at the Kraków Voivodeship About the Summer Colony in Mszana Dolna

[Będzin — Zionism and aliyah; the Revisionists.]
A visit to the editorial office by Commandant Mr Silver.
Yesterday the group of walkers — 27 young Revisionists, among them 4 women — who are setting out on foot for Eretz Israel stayed in Będzin.
The group is led under the direction of Commandant Mr Silver, a refugee from Germany, who is one of the men of the Jewish Legion. Mr Silver visited our editorial office and gave details about the undertaking.
Among the walkers there are 10 who are victims of the Hitlerite regime. Everywhere the group is received as befits it by all strata of the Jewish population.
From Będzin the group went on to Katowice and from there to the Czech border.
The route is: Czechoslovakia, Austria, Switzerland, France, Spain, Gibraltar, and from there they travel by ship to Morocco; from Morocco the group goes on to „Soyta“[?] [Ceuta?], Tangier, Tripoli, Syria, Beirut, etc.
The group covers the travel expenses from the postcards („cards“) it sells.
—o—
[Będzin — the gymnasium and the flood.]
Reassuring News from the Rescue Committee at the Kraków Voivodeship About the Summer Colony in Mszana Dolna
On Wednesday evening a representative of the Fürstenberg gymnasium in Będzin got in touch by telephone with the rescue committee of the Kraków voivodeship. The head of the rescue committee reported that the summer colony at Mszana Dolna is out of any danger and the children are in the best of order. On that occasion the head of the rescue committee reported that the water is receding and communication is already being restored with all the places that suffered from the flood.
Yesterday the administrator of the above-mentioned gymnasium, Eng. Mr Żmudzki[?], left for Mszana Dolna.

[Sosnowiec — transport.]
Because of the sewerage works on Modrzejowska and „Zayale“[?] streets, tram traffic to Czeladź will be suspended from next Tuesday, the 24th of this month.

[Sosnowiec — kehilla and taxes; followed by: Będzin — education.]
As we have already written, the supervisory authority, which carried out the inspection (lustration) of the Sosnowiec kehilla, censured the neglect of the overdue (zaległe) kehilla-tax (etat) debts from the years 1926 to the year 1933 (inclusive); at the same time the starosta [district head] ordered that the community („gmina“) proceed to an energetic collection of the etat debts without any consideration.
In this connection we draw attention to the fact that the etat debtors should not make light of the order, because later the matter of collection will be under the supervision of the supervisory authority, which will lead to considerable enforcement (execution) costs.

Notes of the Week

[Notes of the week — abroad, Palestine and Poland; followed by news from Dąbrowa, Wolbrom, Zawiercie, Bystra and Upper Silesia.]
Hitler's chief commissar in Austria has been shot dead in Vienna.
—o—
A terrible flood occurred in Galicia, causing enormous devastation. Dozens of people drowned.
—o—
In Jerusalem the appeal trial against Abraham Stavsky has begun.
—o—
On Monday the funeral of Hayim Nahman Bialik took place in Tel Aviv with the participation of tens of thousands of people.
—o—
In a suburb of Berlin an organisation was uncovered that wanted to kill Hitler, Göring [—] and Goebbels.
—o—
In India a fire broke out in a church during a prayer service; 30 people were burned to death, 40 are struggling with death.
—o—
The anti-Jewish terror in Germany has intensified. After 9 in the evening Jews are forbidden to go out into the street.
—o—
The activity of the kehilla president in Dąbrowa suspended.
Several weeks ago the supervisory authority carried out an inspection (lustration) of the activity of the Dąbrowa kehilla. During the inspection it was established that the president, Mr A. Neufeld, had paid out subsidies (this concerns the support for the „Talmud Torah" and „Beit Yaakov") and had violated the [?] regulations concerning the payment of the pensions for the religious functionaries (klei kodesh).
This week Mr Neufeld received a notice from the starosta that, because of the above, he is suspended as kehilla president pending a further resolution [?].
At the same time the starosta ordered that the functions of the president be carried out by the vice-president, Mr L. Rechnitz.
—o—
Conductors chase a „blind" passenger.
On the way from Wolbrom to Miechów the conductor came upon a passenger who was travelling „na gapę" [without a ticket]. The blind passenger, wishing to escape from the conductor's hands, climbed — while the train was at full speed — onto the roof of the carriage and jumped from one carriage to the next. Other railway officials came to the conductor's aid, and they succeeded in catching the „blind" passenger.
—o—
On tourism to Palestine.
Our previous groups have arrived safely in Eretz Israel; the remaining tourists registered with us are already leaving in the coming days. Having fresh possibilities to send out a larger number of persons in the shortest time, we announce that candidates who still register with us at the office by the 27th of this month will still have the possibility of leaving within the next 3—4 weeks.
The price is now 1650 zł. Members of organisations can receive a discount. The above sum covers: handling of all departure formalities (foreign passport). All necessary visas, travel expenses to Eretz Israel, „the stay on board the ship and the disembarkation in the Land).
Note: besides an advance on expenses of 150 zł. (account at P.K.O. 15913, holders: Dr Bernard Jaz [?] and Leon Pszytomsker [?]) the following documents must also be sent by registered letter to the address of the tourist department, Warsaw, Leszno 8 apt. 37: 1) a Polish passport with a certificate of citizenship, 2) 8 photographs, one of which must be certified on the reverse side. 3) a certificate of last place of residence (from the magistrate or the gmina), 4) a certificate of loyalty from whichever organisation [one belongs to], and 5) for men, the military booklet.
Tourist Dept. of the Revisionist Org. in Warsaw.
—o—
Murder and suicide near Zawiercie.
In the village of Skała [?] near Zawiercie two sisters-in-law did not live in peace. This week they met, and one of them treated the other to a drink. The one who drank the „drink" soon got severe stomach pains and died a few hours later.
The one who had treated her to the drink, afraid of the punishment awaiting her, also took a glass of the „drink", from which she too died.
—o—
Fire alarm in Bystra.
The summer guests („letniki") in Bystra were frightened on Saturday night at about 11 p.m. by a fire alarm. People came running to the scene of the fire from all sides: those startled out of their sleep, those who were in the middle of „bridge", and also those who had barely snatched the first dance at the dancings — everyone ran.
It turned out that the fright was for nothing: a little dried wood was burning in a field.
—o—
Smaller merchants must deregister from the commercial register.
It is important to point out that merchants and manufacturers whom the new law has exempted from registering in the commercial register should have themselves removed from the register if they were entered in it on the basis of the earlier law.
One must know, namely, that if one is registered in the commercial register one must bear all the obligations incumbent on registered merchants. The obligation, for example, to keep commercial books lies on merchants who are registered, even when they hold a third-category patent [trade licence], because once one is registered one is therefore called a „registered merchant".
It is therefore advisable that merchants of the third category, and also small merchants of the second category whose turnover does not exceed 100,000 zł. a year, submit notifications to the court, to the commercial register, so that their businesses be removed from the commercial register; one must apply in writing to the commercial-register department of the court and rely on the Kodeks handlowy [Commercial Code], part 7, art. 26, paragraph 2.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
Upper Silesian Rabbis in Defence of Avraham Stavsky.
The Association of Rabbis of the Silesian Voivodeship has sent the following appeal to the Government of Eretz Israel:
"Deeply shaken by the fate of the condemned Avraham Stavsky, the Silesian rabbis join the appeal of the Chief Rabbi Kook in Jerusalem and of the Vienna rabbinate, and express the hope that an all-round[?] examination of the whole affair will demonstrate Stavsky's innocence and will lead to a revision of the trial."
The Silesian rabbis have also sent a copy of the appeal to the Polish Consulate in Jerusalem, with the request that it concern itself with the fate of Avraham Stavsky.
—o—
Died of Fright.
Sixty-year-old Markes was walking along Piłsudski Street in Katowice; at that moment a car passed[?], whose driver gave so loud a signal that Markes died of fright.
—o—
A Fight at the Station.
On Monday the young man Yosef Rybsztajn of Będzin was attacked at the Katowice railway station by a young hooligan, who began to beat Rybsztajn. Rybsztajn for his part "honoured" him with a "gift of the hand", and the policeman on duty took both to the police station, where the attacker was arrested; Rybsztajn paid 2 zł. for disturbing the public peace.
—o—
Banknote Forgers in Court.
On the 28th of this month a trial against[?] banknote forgers will take place before the District Court in Chorzów. In the dock will sit 8 defendants, among them officials, who circulated counterfeit banknotes in the Upper Silesian and Zagłębie area.
The trial has aroused enormous interest.
—o—
Japanese Guests in Katowice.
On Sunday a group of Japanese professors, who have come on a visit to Poland, arrived in Katowice. The guests visited several educational institutions. From Katowice they travelled on the next day to Kraków.
—o—
Suicide of a Jewish Woman.
In her own flat on Piłsudski Street in Katowice Mrs. Chana Rozenblum hanged herself on Sunday evening. The suicide had suffered from severe nervous attacks.
—o—
Fires Caused by Thunder.
On Saturday a violent rainstorm accompanied by thunder passed over Rybnik and its surroundings; the thunder[bolts] set off fires in several places.
—o—
Because of the Flood.
This week a large group of children was to travel from Katowice to Rabka. Because of the flood in Galicia the children's departure has been held back.
—o—
Attack on a Tram Conductor.
On a tram in Chorzów[?] a certain Brynda was riding who did not want to buy a ticket. When the conductor wanted to remove Brynda from the tram, the passenger "honoured" him with hefty blows.
—o—
The Tragic Death of Two Schoolboys.
On the Puck [Bay][?] beyond[?] Wielka Wieś the kayak capsized and two schoolboys from Katowice were drowned.
—o—
A Dangerous Bandit Escaped from Prison.
On Sunday night the dangerous bandit Lis managed, by breaking through the iron bars, to escape from the prison in Tarnowskie Góry.
—o—
Memorial for Ch. N. Bialik in Katowice.
On Monday a memorial service for Ch. N. Bialik took place in the synagogue in Katowice. Rabbi Chamides spoke with an address rich in content.
Which Businesses Count as "Large" and Must Keep Commercial Books

[Zagłębie — economy and trade; legislation.]
Great Confusion in Merchant Circles.
As is already known, the Ministry of Commerce has issued a clarification as to which enterprises are to be recognised as "large", that is, those which according to the Code must keep commercial books.
Such enterprises include: commercial enterprises of the 1st and 2nd category — of the 2nd category only such businesses as have a turnover of more than 100,000 zł. in the course of the year.
In industry, the enterprises of the 1st to the 5th category must keep books, as well as those craftsmen of the 6th to the 8th category who sell their own products.
The ordinance also states that all industrial categories must keep books, provided only that the owners sell their own products.
It thus turns out that even smaller manufacturers and craftsmen who hold special patents [licences] for selling their products will have to keep books.
This reform has therefore aroused great confusion in local merchant and manufacturers' circles, because they are not yet prepared for it, and[?] failure to carry out the ordinance carries a penalty of up to 6 months' imprisonment.
It is also not clear from when the official books must be introduced. The ordinance comes into force on 10 July, but one surely cannot introduce new bookkeeping books in the middle of a month, so people are debating whether to begin from 1 July or from 1 August.
As is reported, a delegation of the economic circles in Zagłębie is about to intervene at the Ministry so that the introduction of the books may begin from 1 January 1935.
