Twenty Years Later

[Lead article — on the 20th anniversary of the outbreak of the World War.] By L. Szpigelman.
Twenty Years Later.
(On the 20th anniversary of the outbreak of the World War.)

A few years ago the alarm was raised in the press and at meetings that the population of Poland was becoming impoverished, that everything was going downhill, and that those who live and have something to live on are still living off what was saved during the "seven good years". But now — so people cried out [?] at the time — one earns nothing and there is nothing to make a living from.

In the authoritative circles the pessimists were hardly believed, and nobody wanted to adapt themselves to their conditions [?]. There we constantly heard optimistic talk that "the devil is not as terrible as he is painted"; and by the way it was said that the wailing was merely superficial, whereas in reality everything was in the best of order and there was nothing at all to complain about.

Life, reality, conditions — none of these let themselves be fooled; they did their work. Several years went by, and the naked face revealed itself in its terrible form. For those who had neither the possibility nor the will to take a deeper view — before them there suddenly, quite unexpectedly [?], grew up a giant of poverty, which wrought destruction in the economic field. We suddenly saw well-established industrialists, rock-solid capitalists, around whom tens of thousands of people had lived — as poor, helpless creatures who themselves had begun to feel the taste of want and hunger, at a time when they would never in their lives have imagined anything of the kind. After all, these had been absolute rulers over thousands upon thousands of working hands, which were clamped body and soul to the will or caprice of this or that charlatan, as their capital decided. It may be that these are the convulsions of a dying rule and the birth pangs of a new order. It may be that this is how capital and labour sway [?]. It may be that our generation finds itself between the hammer and the anvil, and then our lot, and perhaps also that of our children, is a very bitter one, because we find ourselves between day and night: it is neither dark nor does it grow light. And if the twilight lasts long and stretches into deep infinity, it is certainly not easy to bear, and it therefore takes countless victims.

We certainly live in a very interesting era, and it is certainly well worth living through such a period, in order to see with one's own eyes how it hatches, how it crystallizes. After all, history has waited hundreds and sometimes thousands of years for such colossal transformations.

In truth we do not know how to assess what kind of era we are living in. And if we say that we live in the present [?] era, we are greatly mistaken, because in reality we are living through whole eras. Our decades amount, taken together, to hundreds of years and perhaps whole thousands.

Let us leaf back, for example, no more and no less than a total [?] of two decades, that is, to the time when the World War broke out. Are we really able to consider conscientiously and calmly, and to penetrate with our minds into the great historic twenty years that have flowed past? Are we really in a position to consider them from all sides — and not merely to consider them, but to form a notion of them, to picture to ourselves the losses and the gains that humanity has gone through in this period?

Humanity is conscious that during this time we have had only losses; and therefore it must be stressed that whenever [?] one speaks of losses, it must definitely be said that the medal [printed "merdal"] also has a second side. It must also be mentioned that thanks to the victims who perished, lands and peoples rose again as if from the dead, technology progressed enormously, and tremendous inventions came to the surface thanks to the war — inventions which we already use in everyday life, and to which we have grown so accustomed that we do not remember at all that they were only just created.

But the truth must be told: the world does not accept the new inventions with love, because the ruins outweigh them. The bad outweighs the good, and because the circumstances of life have become harder and more burdened with responsibility, one cannot enjoy what was prepared for the welfare and pleasure of humanity.

Certainly one can never go backwards, and it would not be bearable either. It smacks of obsolescence and fanaticism, and it goes without saying that nobody among all the people of the whole world wants to be backward, fanatical and not modern. And yet, when one casts a glance twenty years back, when one tries to draw a parallel between today and the year 1914, before the outbreak of the World War, a gleam comes into one's eyes, which spreads into a flame of pleasure and boundless joy. When one remembers how people lived before the war — poor, perhaps, but calm and modest, with a light conscience and an honest heart. People without means were terribly poor; people starved for a groschen, in the literal sense of the word, but humanity was decent, hearts were crystal-pure. Besides, the burden was not so great, needs were minimal, and if one had enough to get through the day, one was content with that. People were not money-greedy at all, and every kind of luxury was an article for the highest court aristocracy.

Before the outbreak of the war, philosophers and thinkers prophesied that things would be bad and hard only until the fire was stopped; but as soon as — so they said then — the white flag of peace was raised, humanity all over the world would revive, and the verse "the wolf shall dwell with the lamb" would simply be fulfilled.

So it is no wonder that humanity has remained so disappointed, since twenty years after the outbreak of the world conflagration things are not only no better than before the war, but on the contrary — people would gladly climb back up to that level. People would gladly begin to live with such a calm conscience, with as small a burden as there was then, when one did not yet use the radio and television, flying over land and sea, and all sorts of other newest inventions.

The war itself, granted, people would somehow have forgotten by now; willingly or unwillingly they would have made peace with the great number of victims, who were torn from their nearest and dearest — but the trouble is that the after-pains are unbearable; the further we move away from those dreadful battles, the harder the situation becomes for the welfare of existence — that is what is most tragic.

No one imagined that, after so much innocent blood had been shed, black spirits would still be able to play their roles and all sorts of individuals would have the possibility to storm and to stir up a world. No one expected that the underworld and all sorts of fringe elements [Yid. "periferies"] would still have the power to smash with blunt fists the finest and best that had been given to the world with pride.

It is painful and sad that twenty years later we have still not come out into the light, which should flood the whole world with its wondrous rays, which were meant to bring happiness to the world.

May this be a twilight after which, in a short time, the dawn will appear, and bright wondrous rays will adorn the children of men with the beauty of dew?
— Perhaps; would that it were so!
Two Marranos (3)

[Serialized story — Nazi Germany; installment 3.]
Chaim Berg.
A story from Nazi Germany.

The rupture itself, however, and its consequences for the new Nazi regime, did not at first seem to him as terrible as the terrible, unforgettable insults that the fatherland and the German people had received from the Jew... The Spanish Jew had simply thrown him out — him, the German baron, son of one of the most distinguished noble families; he had run out of the legation and leapt down the stairs, not at all like the proud, dignified diplomat and Prussian Junker who had walked in there half an hour earlier.
Wiener's first thought, when he got into his automobile, was a "duel". Only blood can wash away the terrible insult to his personal honour and to the honour of the fatherland. But that thought was quickly extinguished by another: since the marquis had himself declared, and with such pride, that he was a Jew, he was not worthy of honour for that. To fight a duel with a Jew? He, the Baron von So-and-so? That is simply unthinkable, impossible!
Yet to receive such an insult from a Jew was even worse... And so the feeling of insult flared up in the baron all the more and raged in his blood, in every limb; he cursed with every German "Donnerwetter" and oath and threw himself into the car like a wounded bear, drawing frightened glances over the shoulder from the chauffeur.
But the thought that, in fact, this had not been a diplomatic tournament according to the accepted rules of fencing — that he had used the finest fencing sword, "verdammter Jude" ("damned Jew"), while the other had struck as if with a cudgel, boorish and coarse, so that in fact it was not he who had lost the diplomatic tournament but the marquis — this thought calmed him a little.
After this thought, the whole slender figure of the marquis rose before his eyes, with his two small, white, womanly hands, the classic profile of an Assyrian prince, and a tremor of desire ran through his body again, as it had there, in the marquis's office... "Whom does he resemble?" the baron thought. "Where have I seen such a handsome face before?..." Donnerwetter, what a temperament the Spaniard has! The temperament of a spoiled woman and a prima donna. He recalls Lassalle — a remarkable resemblance! Possibly there is a blood relationship between him and Lassalle... Who knows! Perhaps the Lassalle family came from Spain with the expulsion of 1892 [sic; read 1492] and was [?] related by blood to the marquis? Did his Jewish great-great-grandfather really play so great a role in Spanish history? That must be researched!
Taking such a direction, the baron's thoughts gradually began to calm down. The pain of the insult and the burning sense of shame grew milder and milder. After all, the police had in fact grabbed the marquis by the collar,
The thought of a duel suddenly turned into an impossibility, an absurdity. The diplomat and the diplomatic schooling of the young baron came back to him, to full command of the diplomatic art, and that art soon began to argue with him that the best and wisest thing would be not to tell his minister what had happened between him and the marquis in his office. At least not to pass on the compliments that Nazi Germany had received from the Spanish diplomat. If the Nazi hotheads in his ministry learned of the insults, they would become as enraged as bloodhounds and make a "pancake" [i.e., a big to-do] of the diplomatic incident.
At this point his thoughts leapt entirely to the Nazis, who had seized the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as well. Though himself an ardent Nazi, the baron was against the Hitlerites running the foreign policy of the Third Reich. On this point he was more diplomat than Nazi. "What dreadful diplomats they are!" the baron reflected. "Hotheads exactly like the marquis."
"And in what light will he himself appear when he tells his chief everything that happened between him and the marquis?!... He will look like a whipped boy. No! That is impossible; the diplomatic incident must be smoothed over in some other way [garbled in print]; he must apply all his diplomatic art to it" — an art of which he himself had a high opinion.
When the baron reached his office, his first act was to prepare a memorandum for his chief on the Jewish descent of the marquis's family. For this purpose he mobilized on his desk a heap of Spanish and Jewish history.

„The State, Which Earns... and the Citizens, Who Lose"

[Poland — economy; etatism (state-run economy).]
An interesting voice on etatism in Poland.
In the Sunday „I.K.C." [Ilustrowany Kuryer Codzienny, Kraków] a sharp article was published under the heading „The State which earns and... the citizens who lose". The whole article is one great indictment of etatism in the economy. It should also be stressed that this is already the second statement against etatism in that newspaper.
We bring here some of the arguments of this very interesting article.
History teaches that etatism is a misfortune for nations, that it weakens private initiative, dries up the sources of taxes, that it is — a source of immorality in the economy to a greater degree than private capitalism, because it breeds [?] protectionism, the system of concessions and subsidies.
And what does our practice say? Together with etatism go centralism, monopolism, bureaucratism and fiscalism. This whole row of wild growths hold together and feed on one another. Etatism creates central offices [„centrale"], purchasing and selling centrals, companies for regulation, organisation and control. The seat [?] of all these centrals is in the capital; the entire economic life of the provincial industrial centres depends on the decisions of the central authorities; even the purchase of writing materials for various institutions, printed matter and various other materials is done through the Warsaw centrals — at higher prices, of course, than locally. Whole economic centres are impoverished and ruined, while the central monopolist grows rich, having secured for himself, in one way or another, the exclusive supply to the central. Etatism is the source of the monopolisation of economic life. The etatist and the monopolist go hand in hand, understand each other well and support each other mutually.
Etatism means — creating offices in place of firms; instead of the work of „living people" and private enterprises come offices. The merchant, the industrialist, the farmer, the banker, the insurer are replaced by the official. The authority of this official is limited; about everything he must turn to Warsaw, to his superiors; he is subject to constant control and inspection, and the result is endless paperwork.
An etatist society creates the psychology not of a merchant, an industrialist — but of a bureaucratic official. This psychology becomes the main obstacle to the economic development of the country — it only makes it possible to eat up the wealth that has already been created. And what will happen when the wealth has been eaten up?
Etatism means bringing politics into the economy. When offices run the economy instead of private firms, the economy turns into politics. Where there is not, and must not be, any place for politics, political criteria suddenly arise.
The threatening competition of the state, of municipal and social institutions destroys the private economy; the etatist enterprises pay no taxes, and so the source of taxes dries up. The state, wishing to avoid a deficit, must tighten the tax screw harder; this lies as a heavy burden on the private enterprises, which are forced to go bankrupt, and the bankrupt enterprise is again taken over by the state — and thus a vicious circle arises.
That the government suffers losses is very easy to prove. The government takes part in every private enterprise, which yields income and even losses. A number of taxes are paid even when the enterprise brings losses. When the private enterprise has large incomes, the government takes 40 to 50 per cent of the income in the form of various taxes. Thus the government is a partner in every enterprise of a private character — and without risk, to boot.
The situation is different in the etatist enterprises. In theory the government takes the whole income. But usually there is no income at all, because the economy rests on other criteria and it cannot be so precise [?].
The etatist enterprise pays no taxes. And if such an [?] enterprise does bring an income, the income does not cover the normal taxes paid by private enterprises. On the other hand, if there are losses, the government must cover the losses.
All these arguments are as old as the world, and nevertheless on the political ground they unfortunately have the character of something new. One must discover them again and proclaim them constantly, because although in theory they are already recognised, in practice one sees [?] no retreat from etatism. It already has its own dangerous dynamics and keeps moving forward. The number of industrial enterprises taken over by the state is rising with surprising speed. The number of centrals holding exclusive rights is growing as well.
At the end of the article a survey is also quoted, carried out among the Wilno merchants about the places where the Wilno offices and institutions make their purchases. It turns out that all purchases are made in Warsaw, and so the question arises: what is the local merchant class still needed for under such conditions? Small shops, soda-water kiosks, trade in fruit and sweets are enough! Warsaw will take care of everything else.
From the quoted survey in Wilno — and probably things are no better elsewhere — it turns out that the sick fund, Bank Rolny, Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego, „R.O.K. III" [probably D.O.K. III — Corps District Command III], all offices subordinate to the Ministry of the Interior, the courts and prisons, all offices subordinate to the Ministry of Finance, the P.K.O. directorate, the Post and Telegraph directorate, the State Forests directorate, „ZUS" [Social Insurance Institution], etc. — all offices and institutions without exception buy practically nothing in Wilno; everything they need they receive from their centrals in Warsaw.
This survey has a threatening significance and must not remain without an echo.
My Prayer for Rain

[Humour — feuilleton; summer and dachas.]
(A short feuilleton.)
Jews! I'm fine, I'm well off. The One who may not be mentioned has heard my prayer for rain, and as you see, hardly a day goes by without it pouring.
It already pours even a bit too much, by day and by night, in the morning and in the evening: if the sun ever peeps out on one side, a downpour comes right away from the other.
But no harm done — the more rain, the more content my wife, the safer the livelihood...
She opened the attack on me right after Passover, as is the way of all women — a dacha!
But I know my own accounts, I still feel the after-pains of last year's dacha — so how does one crawl into a new one?
So I quietly set about praying, and the prayer helped.
First of all there began a business with the „Nara" people [ONR — the National-Radical Camp] — they are attacking the dacha-folk! And when my missus heard that it was coming to blows, she...
That is to say, she is quite a creature [?] and isn't afraid even of the devil — but when is that true? When the devil appears in the shape of her own husband; but when she sees a strange devil, she hides in the innermost rooms...
But afterwards, when the „Nara" people had been put away [„eyngepravet"] and the wives set off to emigrate — one to Rabka, one to Bystra and one even to Olkusz [?] — my missus again began to wag her tongue.
What is one to do? I was left with no other way out but to ask the Old One for help — Give rain!...
And the result of this prayer you can see — it rains and it rains.
My missus has become a completely different person. She looks through the window at how it rains, and licks her lips.
— You are a clever man, my husband — she argues — for not taking a dacha. A fine time they are having there now at the dachas, when it keeps raining nonstop. They can't even put a foot outside, the poor things...
And the more my wife pities the dacha-folk, the more she enjoys herself — better than at the best dacha...
And when the wife enjoys herself, it is so good for the husband; I keep my eyes raised on high all the time and thank Him:
— Father in Heaven! Keep the business going, and as You have started to pour, pour on! Don't spare [„zhalueve nisht"] the water — just imagine You are a Jewish writer...

[Essay — for Shabbat Hazon; the boycott of German goods.] By Ben Amotz.
(In honour of Shabbat Hazon.)

1.
"...The Jews have rebelled against you" [Aramaic "mardu bakh Yehudai"; misprinted "Yehudahi"].
The Gemara tells us a story of a Kamtsa and a Bar Kamtsa, who wanted to take revenge because he had not been allowed to be at the feast; so he ran to the authorities and said:
"The Jews are rebels" — they rebel against your laws, they make use of false declarations [Polish "zeznania"], so that the tax assessments should be much smaller than what they actually ought to pay; there are also among the Jews — said Bar Kamtsa — very many merchants who trade without licences ["patents"], and with the money they ought to bring into the state treasury (today this is called the "urząd skarbowy" [tax office]...) they let themselves live well, these "Żydzi"; they spend the summer months at the spas and in dachas; very large [?] sums of Jewish capital are taken out abroad; the sons of well-to-do Jews get themselves exempted from military service; the greater part of the Jewish youth is communist-minded
— the Jews have rebelled against you...
So spoke Kamtsa two thousand years ago, at the time of the destruction of the Second Temple, when baseless hatred among brothers reigned in the Jewish street, when Jewish unity was crumbled and splintered, when lawlessness and hooliganism reigned everywhere, and the most "serious" [?] impudent ones occupied the seat of honour, gave opinions and decided the most burning questions of Jewish life...
— And today?
— Today the situation is much better.
True, the roots of the Bar Kamtsa of old are still firmly enough established, but the content of "mardu bakh Yehudai" has changed; it is not the same as it once was. A present-day Bar Kamtsa will not run to the authorities because he was not invited to the feast; rather, he makes use of the "mardu bakh" when higher matters are at stake — for instance, when the rabbi's pension is not paid regularly, when a kehilla board member "degrades" the Jewish religion, when his opponent has been elected town councillor ["Ratmann"], or when a rival organisation wants to hold a protest meeting against the "aliyah decrees". It also happens that Bar Kamtsa's methods are applied in rabbinical elections, but not every town merits that; there are only a handful of kehillot in Poland where the rabbinate affair requires the help of the authorities... There indeed reigns a blazing hatred; each wants to drown the other in a spoonful of water, and all the energy is used so that Reuben may uproot Simeon root and branch; the offices ["urzędy" [?]] are simply flooded with denunciations, in which the Bar Kamtsas of the 20th century tell the authorities that —
— the Jews have rebelled against you..

2.
History repeats itself.
In the 15th century [sic], at the time when Don Joseph Nasi proclaimed a boycott of the "Greek" [sic] products, the boycott had good results and things were on the point of the Pope capitulating to the Jewish economic revenge; but a Jewish hand exerted its influence, "so that the Jewish victory should not come about.
500 years later there arose a Hitler, may his name and memory be blotted out, and poisoned the air in all the countries and places where Jews are found.
The new Haman has written on his swastika banner not only to destroy, to slay and to annihilate the Jews in his own state, but in the whole world.
We have, after all, no army, no stratagems of war with which we, like all other nations, could send ultimatums, declare war, break off friendly state relations; we have one single means:
— to cry out and to appeal to the world's justice, to the world's conscience, that we should not be persecuted so.
But who listens to our call, to our protests?
So we began calling to our own, to those very people who are persecuted at every step and turn, to our brethren the children of Israel, to whom we called:
— Do not buy any Hitlerite goods, have no dealings whatsoever with them, with the Hitler gangs; "thou shalt utterly detest it and thou shalt utterly abhor it"...
To this call the people answered:
— We will do and we will obey!
And some time later the wild beasts in human form ran even wilder, gnashing their wolfish teeth in anger at the Jewish chutzpah that wants to ruin their mighty industry, to reduce exports and, what is more, to disgrace the name of the nation which over long generations has acquired an eminent name in the cultured world.
— Don't be upset — an evil spirit soothes them — don't be frightened of this boycott proclaimed by the Jews; you need not even take measures to fight the boycott, for that will be done by others...
— By whom? — you ask — who will they be, the boycott-breakers?
— The Jews themselves, only they; if you do not know them, the Jews, just leaf through Jewish history and you will find there very [?] many who in every epoch performed deeds in order to break any Jewish influence whatsoever.
— And something else you will find there: that precisely the arms-bearers, the "chosen" of the people — brought the greatest troubles upon the community of Israel... The same [?] will happen in the present century: there will come to you (quietly, it is true...) "fine" Jews, gabbaim of Hasidic shtiblekh, also preachers of nationalism, of Zionism, who want to establish trade relations with you; they want to be the buyers of your products — not only new ones, but also used goods, junk, old clothes. Even when the articles will have been plundered from the Jewish families who were first ruined and later driven out... everything they will buy, these "Leute" [German in the original: "Leute kaufen"]...
— Over this the prophet laments:
— "All her people sigh"; the whole people sighs and weeps over the misfortune that has befallen it, but there are such as do not want to see "the breach of the daughter of my people", the people's grief, the people's ruin; these are the ones who "seek bread", the betrayers of the Jewish people, the birds of prey flying over the battlefields to sate their gluttonous lusts, those who roll their eyes up to heaven and pray that the wagon of goods from Germany may arrive here in peace... In the street people say that "one really must boycott German goods"; to discharge their duty they donate a few gilden for the refugees from Germany, but in silence, quietly, they count the profits from the goods that are stained with Jewish blood;
— "One speaketh peaceably to his neighbour with his mouth, but in his heart he layeth his wait"...
— History repeats itself.

Parashat Devarim
The Portion
—o—
a) “These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel” (1:1)
“Because they are words of rebuke… therefore he spoke the matters obscurely and mentioned them only by allusion, out of respect for Israel.” Rashi.
Moses went to rebuke all the Jews, “unto all Israel” — so why did he speak in allusions, “between Tophel and Laban and Hazeroth and Di-zahab”? Such hints could, after all, be understood only by learned Jews.
The point is precisely that those who need rebuking, chastising, are only these learned ones, the “fine Jews”… The common folk does not need so much rebuke at all. Me'irat Einayim.
—o—
b) “To expound this Torah” (ibid. 5)
“He expounded it to them in seventy languages.” Rashi.
Because He knew, as it were, that Jews would speak in seventy languages, He expounded the Torah right away in all seventy languages… Imrei Hen.
—o—
c) “And it came to pass in the fortieth year” (ibid. 3)
“This teaches that he rebuked them only close to his death… and for four reasons one rebukes a person only close to death: so that he should not rebuke him and then rebuke him again…” Rashi.
One may rebuke a fellow and preach morals to him only close to death, when one is already sure that one will not oneself commit the very sin for which one rebukes the other… But not close to death — preach morals to nobody, for you do not know whether you yourself will not stumble into that sin, “so that he should not rebuke him and then rebuke him again” — so that the other should not one day rebuke you in turn for the very sin for which you rebuke him… Mizrahi.
—o—
d) “May He make you a thousand times as many as you are” (ibid. 11)
The Midrash on Ecclesiastes (section 7, §28) says: “One man among a thousand have I found — this is Moses, who was equal to a thousand generations.” Therefore Moses could bless the Jews with “a thousand times as many” [printed “ככה”, for “ככם”].. (“This is my own [blessing]” — Rashi). Afrot Zahav.
—o—
e) “And bless you as He has promised you. How can I myself alone bear your cumbrance” (ibid. 12)
As soon as things begin to go a little well for the Jews, as soon as there is just “and bless you” — their life is at once embittered by “your cumbrance, and your burden, and your strife”, by quarrels and baseless hatred.. Tuv Ta'am.
—o—
f) “And I will make them heads over you” (ibid. 13)
“Va-asimem” — if the heads are guilty (ashemim — see Rashi) “over you”, it is surely your own fault, for having chosen such heads and leaders… R' Menahem ha-Bavli.
—o—
g) “Hear the causes between your brethren, and judge righteously” (ibid. 16)
To the rabbis it was said: “Hear between your brethren” — listen to what your brothers say, to what the people says. Do not say “accept my opinion”; no rabbi may do anything that is against the will of the community. It is the rabbi's duty: “hear between your brethren”, to listen to the opinion of the community, and then — “judge righteously”…
R' Tsvi Hirsch Kalischer.
—o—
h) “You shall not be afraid of the face of any man” (ibid. 17)
Of rabbis who flatter all sides, the Rabbi of Nitra, R' Avraham Katz, said:
“If the rabbi is like an angel of the Lord of Hosts, let them seek Torah from his mouth; and if not, let them not seek Torah from his mouth.” An angel is created for one mission only: “no angel performs two missions.” A rabbi too must be like an angel and take upon himself only one mission… If the rabbi is not like an angel and fulfils many missions at once, flattering all sides — let them not seek Torah from his mouth… Melitsei Esh.
* * *
In Berakhot (28a) the Gemara relates: “A certain heretic said to R' Yehuda: your face resembles either that of usurers or that of pig-breeders.”
When the heretic saw that R' Yehuda had a well-fed face, he wondered: how does this come to a rabbi? A rabbi ought always to be worn out and gloomy from quarrels and from being pulled every which way. So it is one of the two: either you are a pig-breeder — you flatter all the communal swine.. or you are a usurer — you simply lend them money and they depend on you… Milei de-Shmaya.
—o—
Between the Straits (Bein ha-Metsarim).
i) — R' Yechezkele of Kuzmir [Kazimierz Dolny] once decided to come out against a certain powerful man, and he ordered his moreh-hora'ah to proclaim something. But the latter was a coward and hesitated:
— Eh, what will people say?
Says R' Yechezkele to him:
— Because of this “what will people say?” the Temple was destroyed. As the Gemara relates in Gittin (26a [sic]), the Temple was destroyed because of the humility of R' Zechariah ben Ankilus [sic, for Avkulas], for he was always afraid: “they will say” — people will say..
—o—
j) — R' Yitzhak of Radzivilov [Radziwiłłów; reading uncertain], hearing about R' Avrahamle the Angel, once made a special journey to see him. R' Yitzhak arrived at the “Angel's” on the eve of Tisha be-Av. The two of them went to the synagogue to say the kinot. When the congregation had sat down on the ground and the cantor stepped up to the lectern to say Eikha and began the mournful tune — he had barely uttered the first word when the “Angel” let out a bitter cry: “Eikha!” and threw his head between his knees and lamented quietly: “Eikha, eikha!” The cantor finished the kinot, the whole congregation dispersed, and the Angel still sat in the same posture with his head between his knees, weeping: “Eikha”. R' Itzikl waited until after midnight and went home to rest a little; coming to the synagogue in the morning, R' Itzikl found the “Angel” in the same posture: his head between his knees, lamenting: “Eikha”.
“Not for nothing does the world call him the Angel,” R' Itzikl exclaimed, “he is truly an angel of the Lord of Hosts.”
What Can One Still Sell Today?

[Economy — export and trade; list of lines by country.] (Compiled by our correspondent.)
In order to give Jewish merchants the possibility of still selling something in today's hard times, we have compiled a list of trade lines. Everywhere we have noted in which countries the articles are sought. One need only correspond with whoever it may be who lives in the countries mentioned, and we are confident that connections can be made which will surely bring a livelihood in the present critical time.
Surgical and medical articles: in particular, various dressing materials are needed in Italy and in Sweden. In all countries various medicaments against external cosmetic diseases are sought. All kinds of glassware for surgical purposes are needed in the Dutch East Indies. Medical apparatus for irradiation, high-frequency, radium. Dental instruments and apparatus are sought in Italy. All kinds of thermometers (Norway and Denmark). Surgical rubber articles, tubes, dental plates are needed in Denmark, Sweden and Italy.
Electric lamps: all kinds of lamps, ceiling and wall lighting, lampshades of paper and fabric are sought in the Dutch East Indies, in Bulgaria and in Finland.
Cutlery: spoons, forks and knives of stainless steel, especially little spoons for ice cream ("lody" — frozen treats) of wood or aluminium, are sought in Sweden, Norway and Denmark. Chrome-plated and nickel-plated cutlery is also needed there.
Jewellery: imitation, of glass; articles of bronze, metal, artificial amber, little candlesticks, pocket trays [?], writing sets and the like are needed in Switzerland, Holland, Norway and Sweden.
Office articles: all kinds of novelties for offices, pen-holders, pencils, signal tabs for card indexes, fountain pens, all kinds of apparatus, folders, portable typewriters (used), stencils and the like are sought in Holland, Sweden, Switzerland, Hungary, Italy, Holland, Yugoslavia and Palestine (Eretz Israel).
Chemical articles: all kinds of paints, oils, essences, fire-retardant coatings. Anti-frost coatings, wax, impregnating products, silk flock [?], cloth flock, cold glue, leather cement, adhesive and office glue are needed in Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Holland, Hungary, Austria, Italy and Palestine.
Fancy goods: powder compacts, cigarette cases (Holland and Italy), little bottles of crystal and fine glass (Yugoslavia and Bulgaria), porcelain jars with labels for pharmacies, hospitals, sanatoria, drugstores (Italy, all the Nordic states and all the Balkan countries).
Household articles: all kinds of wooden items needed for the house can be sold in South Africa, India, China, Egypt and Turkey. Salt and pepper mills, can openers, corkscrews, nutcrackers, little bowls of all kinds, candlesticks, brass trays, orange peelers, all kinds of aluminium ware (Denmark, Switzerland, Holland, Sweden and Norway).
This list has been compiled on the basis of reports that have arrived in recent days from the countries mentioned.
We shall bring a second article on this subject.
Z. Haber (Vienna).
Regulations on Setting Off Debts Against Debts

[Law — law of obligations; set-off.] Without the creditor's consent a debtor may not set off his claims if the matter concerns the return of items that were handed over to him for safekeeping or for use, or that he took without right; concerning alimony, or concerning a debt that cannot be attached; or concerning remuneration for work (wages).
A guarantor (surety, "good-sayer") may set off what the creditor owes the principal debtor. The principal debtor, however, may not set off what the creditor owes the guarantor.
A debtor may set off against one of the joint (solidary) creditors what another jointly-and-severally liable creditor owes him.
Dacha Pictures

[Feuilleton — summer life; Zagłębie holidaymakers at their dachas.] Friday on the Train
If you think that we Zaglembiers don't have as good a "linia" [holiday rail line] as the Warsaw people do, then just pop over to the station on a Friday morning[?] and you will be convinced that we too have nothing to be ashamed of. It is just as [word unclear: "geharbet"] to hear on the "kolej" [railway] that sets off on Friday to the Beskids as on the Warsaw "kolejka" [holiday train], which takes the passengers to Naczałkowice[?], Bystra, Rajcza or Ustroń. The same voices, the same shouting; Jews drag parcels, dead slaughtered fish; some carry big challahs and even slaughtered fowl. The zealous run to the train 2 hours early, so as to snatch a ticket in good time and so that later, because of some mishap, God forbid, they do not end up stuck outside for the Sabbath. From there on everything goes "po warszawsku" [Warsaw-style][?]. People are shaken about; one squeezes the other, poor things, [word unclear] the few dried-out bones, and truly feels that one is travelling to [?] ["Zh'eyb" — perhaps Żywiec] to the dacha. In a word, it is "layehudim" [the Jews had light — Esther 8:16], lively, and more than that one does not need — if only a couple of Endeks [Polish nationalists] happened to fall into this "Judaized" train, they would have had something "to sing and to tell" for weeks.
The Rain "Rages"
But what comes of the whole "letnik" [summer holiday] when lately it has been pouring without a break? It is really "winter". The crowd goes about, poor things, with gloomy faces, hunched up against the cold, and whoever took a warm garment along puts it on, poor soul, and parades about in it. If for a minute it has stopped raining, the dacha folk come out "pomalinke" [slowly, little by little] from their burrows and keep looking up into the sky to see whether it is clearing up. Until — the sky bursts into tears again and chases all the sky-gazers back into the village lodgings; then one searches all through the meteorological section for what the weather will be at least tomorrow, people run from house to house wherever there is a radio, and wait for some little bit of weather news, and when at last they manage to catch a happy tiding that any day now [lada dzień] it should get finer, they still remain as sceptical as heretics and have no trust even in the radio reports. Thus this week the rain kept on "raging" and did not let the dacha folk enjoy the forest, the fresh air and other, other pleasant summer delights.
People Play Cards.
Weather or no weather, the card season is in full blaze. People go visiting neighbours, relatives and acquaintances, and they bang away until the smoke rises. Young wives play, and even old ones too. People sit in the little rooms, on the verandas, in the forest and wherever it is possible. And every circle plays "po swojemu" [in its own way]. Ordinary Jews play a "selefan"[?] [a card game — unclear], and meanwhile they hum fine "pieces" from Rosenblatt's records [the cantor Yossele Rosenblatt]; the intelligentsia play "bridge" together with the wives, who, smoking cigarettes, forget about their husbands, children and even about eating. Besides that, the "amkho" [common folk] also gets together for a game of cards. Quite often it gets really hot among these fellows, and when it goes well, fiery slaps fly too and they curse each other with the bitterest curses. In short, as you see, the best article at the dacha is simply cards. And they do play cards with a bang.
Madame "X".
Madame "X" is a big-city lady. She is beautiful, slender, and from sunbathing on the "plaża" [beach] her skin has become like the lapels ["klapes"] of her brown pyjamas... She knows that she is beautiful, Madame "X", and if she ever forgets it, the cavaliers and dandies by whom she is surrounded remind her of it.
All day long she reigns in the forest. Her "throne" is the "hammock", and from there she sends out her orders: "Pogie[?] Mańku, hand me a cigarette, a light..." — and "Pan Maniek" hands her everything she demands and more besides...
When night comes, she begins to "królować" [reign] on the veranda, and her admirer, "Pan Czesiek", runs, poor fellow, every time on another errand.
She does not yet have any special serious admirer. After all, she is not just anybody, and until she finds a man from her "towarzystwo" [social circle][?], an engineer or at the very least a law trainee [aplikant], it must take a while; but she is patient, because such a one will surely be found at the dacha.
Madame "X" lives in perfect peace with the Zaglembier "chłopcy" [lads]; she smiles and meanwhile shows her pearly little teeth, saying: "Oni wcale nie są głupi" [They are not at all stupid]! But how she got to know the "chłopcy", and how our townsmen "bawią się" [amuse themselves] at the dacha — that we shall write about another time.
Luks.
Grievances Against the Young Generation

[Article — family, education and the young generation.] A painful question that no one talks about. When children do not understand their parents and treat them with contempt.
In the New York "Forverts" a writer touches on an important question, one that affects very many Jewish homes, not only in America but here too. For this reason we consider it necessary to reprint the article, in part, here as well.
In all times there is a struggle between parents and the young generation, between fathers and children. Our present generation of parents still remembers very well the struggle it waged against its own parents. It was a struggle between two worlds, a bitter struggle, often with tragedies.
The parents a generation ago had grievances against their progressive children: "You want to remake the world? The Emperor doesn't suit you? You are casting off Jewishness and becoming shkotzim, good-for-nothing youths!" The youth of that time tore itself away from the narrow, closed ghetto life toward the wide world of light and progress. The parents could not understand the children, but when they saw the idealism, the earnestness and the self-sacrifice of the children, they felt a deep respect for them. And the children pitied their parents, but they also deeply respected them.
Quite different, however, is the case with the present young Jewish generation. People write about it, unfortunately, very little. It is dismissed with a few words. But this is a painful question for the greatest number of Jewish families; it is surely worth dwelling on it, making a moral reckoning (cheshbon ha-nefesh) of the past 30—40 years. In the life of a people that is perhaps a short time, but in the life of an individual it is the greatest and most important part.
We have in our families a situation that is very tragic, and we are helpless and do not know how to help ourselves. But the first thing is that we must see the situation clearly as it is.
How do we stand here with our young generation? Do we also have with it the same quarrels that our parents had with us? What grievances do we have here against our sons and daughters? What do we demand of them?
It is enough for a few people to get talking with one another about their personal affairs, and they soon come round to their children. Hearts open, people pour out their hearts, and such a[?] conversation usually goes roughly like this:
— Oh, yes, my children are quite fine. My son finished university two years ago already. No, for the time being he isn't doing anything yet. And my Oskar is going into his second year at university. Yes, my daughter is the youngest, she is still at secondary school this year.
— Well, then you're a lucky father! All your children turned out well!
— Yes, but — and a heavy sigh breaks out of the aching heart — life has become so hard, unbearably hard; imagine, out of a little shop one has to knock out enough to support a large family of grown-up children, whom one has to provide with everything from a pair of trousers to a few groszy for the cinema. Not one of my children brings a grosz into the house. Yes, I understand, there is a crisis in the country. There is no work, nowhere to earn. I can understand all that. But what I cannot understand and can in no way make peace with is the thought that parents, who sacrifice themselves for their children, do not receive the slightest recognition and devotion, which it is natural to expect from grown-up children for whom one does everything beyond one's strength.
"The cold indifference of the young generation toward their own parents gives the impression that feelings of gratitude and loyalty are entirely lacking in today's Jewish generation. We see in our youth a narrow egoism, which makes itself felt at every step; indifference, impudence bordering on chutzpah, is a common phenomenon in our homes."
The writer of the article goes on to cite a few facts which characterize the attitude of American children toward their parents. Not all the facts fit our local conditions. But some of them do. For instance, the up-to-date, modern-world children being ashamed of their old-fashioned, old-world parents; being ashamed to speak Yiddish; laughing at the parents' pierogi, etc.
These facts, unfortunately, are not absent among us either. Moreover, of course, they are helped along by the tendencies toward assimilation on the part of the young generation, which the parents themselves implant in it from childhood on, educating the child in a foreign language, in a foreign school and in a foreign spirit. So what wonder is it that children later begin to be ashamed of their own parents?
Let Jewish parents reflect on this; only then will they understand that respect can be expected from children only when one does not, with one's own hands, distance them from their own source, but on the contrary draws them close by means of Jewish education in a Jewish school, in the Jewish language and in the Jewish spirit.
A. Y.
Father, When at Last...?

[Feuilleton — a mood piece (Shtimung).]
"...and amid the mighty blasts of the shofar there will come riding to you on a white donkey the Messiah son of David, who will bring the true redemption to the people of Israel and to the tormented humanity of the whole world"...
So the legend tells, and so my father used to tell me when I was still a small child!
When I used to ask him: Father! When will he come, the Messiah? — he would answer me somewhat crossly: He will come, he will come. In time, the Messiah; before the good time nothing can come.
When I had grown a little older and began pestering my father more often[?] to tell me at last when the good time would be, so that the Messiah could come, he explained to me with a deep sigh: The good time, my child, will be when the whole world is either entirely righteous or entirely guilty, and then, only then, will the Messiah come...
Years have gone by, my father is long no longer among the living, I am a father myself, and when I contemplate the present world order, I see and feel with all my senses that the supreme "good time" has already come, the true days of the Messiah.. The whole world is now entirely guilty — it is full of robbers, killers, murderers, bandits and... Hitlerites; race hatred is poured out openly and brothers are murdered openly, hard-earned property is robbed openly and holy things are desecrated openly; besides, the world's granaries are full of grain while millions of human stomachs are empty, the world's warehouses are full of clothing while millions of human bodies go about naked — well, are these not the days of the Messiah? And yet the world is flooded with false messiahs, and the true Messiah son of David is still not here...
If my father were alive now, I would let out a cry: — Father, well, it is all entirely guilty now, where is he, the Messiah, our redeemer? Why does he not come?
But unfortunately my father died long ago, and all that remains for me is to cry out to the Father in heaven:
— Father! When will the Messiah come at last? When at last?...
Sh—n.

Polish Women Who Sacrificed Themselves for the Jewish Faith (2)

[Serialized historical tale — Christian women converted to Judaism and burned in Poland: Kraków 1539, Dubno 1716; installment 2.]
M. Starkman.
(An interesting historical tale that happened 200 years ago).
"When the priests heard this," Górnicki goes on to relate, "they shouted at her:
— Your words are blasphemous, you sinful creature! Consider yourself! Are the prophecies not true, that God will send His only son into the world so that he be crucified for our sins, and that we, who have been rebellious since the time of Adam, the first man, shall be reunited with God the Father?
"Many other questions were put to the heretical woman by the learned priests, but the more they talked [?], the more obstinate she became in her assertion that God was not born as a human creature. When they realised that it was impossible to free her from her Jewish religious notions, it was decided to condemn her for blasphemy against God. Right afterwards she was taken to the town prison, and a few days later she was burned. She went to her death without the slightest fear."
Katarzyna Melchiorowa [?] Weigel was burned at the stake on 19 August 1539, but with that the tragedy was not yet over. According to Polish law, which in this respect imitated the laws of the other Christian countries, the death penalty applied not only to the Christian who had gone over to the Jewish faith, but also to whoever had talked him into it. Since Gamrat, the bishop, had investigated everything connected with Katarzyna's "blasphemy against Christ," he also found out that the Jewish doctor Moshe Fishel had been a frequent guest at her house. From this he concluded that it was under his influence that she had drawn closer "to Judaism. The tribunal then tried him separately and pronounced the same sentence: to be burned at the stake, and the sentence was carried out very quickly. The greasy [?] bishop rubbed his hands with joy and thanked the Son of God for having sent him two victims to "sanctify" His name.
In the Volhynian town of Dubno, in the year 1716, a wedding took place. A young man of Dubno stood under the chuppah, ready to put the betrothal ring on his destined one, the bride, who had come there from a distant foreign town. The in-laws surrounded the young couple and, with pounding hearts and tear-filled eyes, watched the ceremony in which two young people make a covenant for their whole life. Suddenly several soldiers arrived and in rough voices ordered the ceremony stopped, and all the in-laws, bride and groom included, were immediately led off to the town jail. The arrested were bewildered, Dubno was in an uproar [?], and the entire Jewish population was thrown into desperate fear. Everyone was sure that this was most likely the result of a new blood libel. But it did not take long, and to everyone's amazement it became known that it had all come about because of the bride, a former Christian who had secretly converted to Judaism. For this she was charged with "blasphemy against Christ," and her in-laws with having talked her into this step.
A short time later the bride, whose Christian name was Maryna Wojciechowa, was put on trial. Together with her, a second woman was charged with the same crime: the widow Maria Dawidowa [?].
The proceedings revealed that the widow Maria Dawidowa was the daughter of a priest. Her father himself had studied the holy books with her. She too had begun to study the religious scriptures seriously, and in this way she came to the conviction that the only true faith is the Jewish one. After her husband's death she converted and went off to Dubno, where nobody had known her before, to live as a true daughter of Israel. Maria was put on the torture machine. They twisted and stretched her limbs and broke the bones of her body, but she remained obstinate and would not return to the faith of her parents, and at the same time she also refused to tell who had helped her become a Jewess, and when and where this had happened. The judges and torturers grew even more enraged when Maria proudly declared that she was ready to pay with her life for her faith and to give up her soul to the one God in heaven, who watches over the world and protects His children, the Jewish people.
Having finished with her, they turned to the bride, Maryna Wojciechowa. On the torture machine, where she was tortured in the same way as Dawidowa, she related that she had come to Dubno from abroad. She had previously been a servant in a Jewish house, where she became closely acquainted with the Jewish way of life and with the Jewish religion. She too had decided that the Jewish religion is the only right one; therefore she converted and came to Dubno to bind herself for her whole life to the Jewish people.
Since the two women themselves confessed their crime, the trial was quickly concluded. The sentence was: death by burning.
Maria Dawidowa, the widow, who had behaved very impudently at the trial, the judges did not want to let die so easily for that. Before she was tied to the stake in the middle of the pyre, her flesh was torn with red-hot tongs, and only afterwards were the flames allowed to finish the rest. Maryna Wojciechowa had more "luck": her head was first chopped off, and then her dead body was thrown into the fire.
This trial, too, had its painful aftermath for the Jews. The Dubno priests were not yet fully sated with blood and roasted flesh; they lusted [?] for more victims. They searched among Maryna Wojciechowa's in-laws for people who were supposed to have talked her into converting. But however hard the priests tried, they did not manage to obtain such proof, although the accused were tortured with the greatest mercilessness. But to let the Jews go entirely free — that would have been too much.
So the in-laws were sentenced to a hundred lashes each, and on top of that the Dubno kehilla had to pay a large sum as a fine. The money went [?] to the Catholic Church, which had so attentively protected its holy [?] little sheep from the influence of the Jewish religion.

[Będzin — accident; followed by seven local news items: ritual slaughter, burial society, cheder, trade, artisans, industry, charity.]
An accident with a Jew from Wolbrom.
On Tuesday afternoon the 40-year-old Josel Zielonka of Wolbrom was riding on a cart along Małachowskiego Street. Suddenly it began to rain heavily, and Zielonka jumped down from the cart and wanted to run into a neighbouring gateway. At that moment a tram came by, and Zielonka fell under it. Several Jewish passers-by carried the bleeding Jew to the hospital, where he received first aid. Zielonka was saved from certain death; he received only light wounds to the head.
As is reported, the motorman, while Zielonka was lying under the tram, wanted to drive on, but under the pressure of several young Jewish men he did not do so.
—o—
R' Shlomo the Shochet Can Get Leave if the Kehilla Takes On the Young Shochtim in His Place
Such is the will of the Rabbi of Będzin.
Last week R' Shlomo the shochet (ritual slaughterer) turned to the kehilla board with a request to grant him a month's leave because of his weak state of health.
The kehilla board, wishing to comply with R' Shlomo's request, turned to the rabbinate with a proposal that during the leave one of the shochtim of the Będzin district, for example from Grodziec or Czeladź, should work in his slaughterhouse.
To this proposal the rabbinate replied that on this question they must consult [?] the Rabbi, who is staying in Marienbad.
On Wednesday the rabbinate informed the kehilla board that the Rabbi's answer is that the leave for R' Shlomo the shochet can be granted on condition that the kehilla puts the young shochtim in the slaughterhouse in his place..
—o—
Sharp Conflict Between the Kehilla Board and the Committee of the Chevra Kadisha
This week a conflict broke out between the kehilla board and the committee of the Chevra Kadisha (burial society). The conflict, which may even lead to the Chevra Kadisha resigning, consists of the following.
A certain Sindorf [?] approached the board with a proposal: he will give 300 zł. for being allowed to do the „malas“ [?] during the days of the month of Elul.
The kehilla board, and especially the chairman, is in favour of abolishing the „chazaka concession“ [?] and accepting the offer of the 300 zł. But the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha are categorically against it and demand that the existing status quo be preserved.
In connection with this, the committee of the Chevra Kadisha has turned to the board with a proposal that the offer of the 300 zł. be rejected; if not, they will draw the appropriate consequences.
—o—
Stormy Parents' Meeting at the Cheder „Yesodei Torah“
The situation of the melamdim (teachers) at the cheder „Yesodei Torah“ is very tragic. They receive no tuition fees and have been reduced [?] to hunger and want. Their situation became even worse when the committee resigned and they had no one to turn to.
In connection with this the melamdim went on strike and lessons were interrupted.
Because of this, on Sunday evening, under the chairmanship of Mr S. Fridler, a parents' meeting took place which had a very stormy course. The melamdim poured out all their anger on the members of the committee, which ignores them and does not pay them the „starvation pensions“.
The task of repelling the „attacks“ fell to committee member Herzberg, who declared that he had been determined to call the police to disperse the illegal parents' meeting, but did not do so because of pressure from the headmaster.
After Mr Herzberg's speech of defence, the melamed Werdiger took the floor and said: „When our colleague Herzberg speaks about the finances we agree with him, but not when he is against our interests“.
The storm ended with the resolution that several persons be co-opted onto the committee.
—o—
To the Address of the Merchants' Organisations
Once again we have to touch in the columns of our newspaper on the painful question which brings great damage to the trade of our town.
The question is this: customers who come from Upper Silesia get robbed, or they lose their money at „three cards“, which has still not been uprooted in our town.
It is therefore the duty of the representatives of the economic organisations to hold a conference with the authorities in order to put an end to this plague, which brings damage to Jewish trade in Będzin.

Conference on Legalising Jewish Artisans' Workshops
The United Committee for Jewish Crafts Affairs invited communal artisan activists from 60 towns in Poland in order to work out instructions for legalising the existing artisans' workshops.
The conference, which took place on Sunday at the Academic House in Warsaw, lasted until Thursday. After the papers delivered by Messrs Dir. Giterman, Sag. [?] Pojering [?], Dir. Zajdeman, Eng. Szaszkes (Warsaw), Chairman Mr Kruk (Wilno), Eng. Rogowski (Białystok) and others, appropriate resolutions were adopted.
Będzin was represented by the chairman of the Artisans' Union, Mr H. L. Goldsztajn, and the secretary, Miss Brojner, who will give a report in the coming days.

Sosnowiec — Posed as a German Refugee and Thus Swindled 50 Złoty out of the Anti-Hitler Committee / A Policeman Shoots His Wife and Then Himself / The Terrible Revenge of a Deceived Woman / Memorial Services for H. N. Bialik in Zagłębie / The Economic Bridge Between Poland and the Land of Israel

[Sosnowiec — fraud; followed by four items: murder and suicide in Pogoń, an acid revenge, memorial services for Bialik, and a piece on the P.K.O. bank (probably promotional).] About 2 weeks ago a young man came to the plenipotentiary of the local Anti-Hitler Committee, Mr. B. Tencer, and, presenting himself as a German refugee, asked Mr. Tencer for support that would give him the possibility of settling in Sosnowiec. The "refugee" presented his documents and certificates as a craftsman making travel bags.
On the strength of the documents Mr. Tencer gave him a few złoty and promised to go on helping him. A few days later the young man came to Mr. Tencer again and told him that he had already found a flat as a sub-tenant, only he had to pay 10 zł. for the lodging; later he again received more money to buy goods, etc. In the end, however, it turned out that the "refugee" is a professional swindler, and having obtained more than 50 zł. he vanished from Sosnowiec.
—o—
A Policeman Shoots His Wife and Then Himself
On Monday at midday a terrible family tragedy took place on Racławicka Street in Pogoń, which cost the lives of two people.
On that street lived the senior constable (starszy) Rozenberg. Coming home for lunch, a sharp exchange of words broke out between him and his wife; at a certain moment Rozenberg pulled out his revolver and fired several times at his wife, who fell dead on the spot; then he shot himself and was mortally wounded.
—o—
The Terrible Revenge of a Deceived Woman
She Doused Her Husband with Hydrochloric Acid
In a beer tavern on 1 Maja Street in Sosnowiec several Christians were sitting and enjoying themselves. At a certain moment a woman came in and doused one of the merry company, a certain Gracz, with hydrochloric acid. As has been established, the woman did this out of revenge on her husband, who had abandoned her.
Gracz is seriously injured and is in danger of remaining crippled in both eyes.
—o—
Memorial Services for H. N. Bialik in Zagłębie
In the Będzin synagogue, on the Sabbath after the Torah reading, a memorial service for H. N. Bialik of blessed memory took place. The service was held in a very serious mood, which is a rarity in the local synagogue. Mr. G.[?] Landner spoke about the great loss; then the cantor Mr. Baum with the choir performed the appropriate prayers.
— On Monday evening a memorial service took place in the Sosnowiec synagogue. Even at this solemn moment, when it is a matter of honouring the name of the great departed H. N. Bialik, there could be no peace among the Jewish organizations, among those who preach national work. The issue was that a collection was to be taken at the service for the Keren Kayemet (K.K.L.). The Revisionists would not agree to this, and the other organizations would not give in. Finally Rabbi Hager succeeded in making peace, in the sense that the collection is held for the Bialik Fund...
Before a packed synagogue the proper memorial service is held, and the speakers are: Rabbi Hager and G. Stawski, who speaks about the profound content of Bialik's poems.
With Her Beautiful Eyes... / Lightning Strikes a Horse and Wagon / A Flat Burgled

[Sosnowiec — fraud; followed by two short items: lightning strikes a wagon, a flat burgled.] Mr. G., a young householder, a mere year and a half after the wedding sent his wife off to a summer cottage, and he himself remained a "straw widower".
G., who likes to "live it up" a little, decided to make use of the freedom he had gained.
Already a few days after his wife's departure from Sosnowiec he made the acquaintance of a young woman, who at once "conquered" the heart of the straw widower.
They began to meet day after day. Leon[?] G. flared up for the beautiful lady with a hot feeling of love, but the lady remained cold to his hot declarations of love.
"In Sosnowiec it is impossible for us to meet," she kept insisting. "You must know that I have a husband. But if you could send me off to a summer resort and come to me there, we would spend a few happy days."
At this the lady gave him such an enchanting look that the straw widower felt he was literally burning up.
The next day he brought her 200 gulden.
"Go off to Kamińsk, and I will come to you the day after tomorrow."
On Friday night the young man, full of the best hopes, arrived in Kamińsk. He went to the address he had been given, but — there an unpleasant surprise awaited him:
the enchanting lady was not there.
For a whole day the straw widower wandered about Kamińsk, visited all the boarding houses, and finally convinced himself that the lady of his dreams was not there at all.
Only on returning to Sosnowiec did the young man understand that he had fallen victim to a swindler, who had cheated him out of the 200 gulden and made off.
As it turns out, Leon[?] G. is not the only victim of the beautiful lady, who has "specialized" in swindling straw widowers.

From Sporting Life.

[Sport — Zagłębie.] „Brygada“ (Częstochowa) — „Unia“ 3:2.
On Sunday the first match for the championship of the Kielce voivodeship took place on the „Unia“ sports ground, between the champion of Częstochowa, „Brygada“, and the champion of Zagłębie, „Unia“. About 4000 people attended the match. „Brygada“ proved to be a very tough[?] team, whose strongest point was its goalkeeper. „Unia“, on the other hand, got into superfluous combinations and, despite its superiority, could not exploit a great many brilliant situations. Only thanks to good organisation and the not-bad shooting ability of the centre-forward Słota did „Unia“ win the match. Referee Mr. Schneider — very good.
„Hakoach“ (Będzin) — „Hakoach“ (Bielsko) 3:1 (0:0).
On Sunday the Będzin „Hakoach“ played a return match in Bielsko for the championship of the „Maccabi“ federation in Poland. The match aroused great interest, and several lorries full of people went to Bielsko. Besides that, a great many people could be seen on the sports ground in Bielitz who had come from the surrounding summer-resort places, so that the „Będzin“ colony was very richly represented. Right at the start the Bielitz side carry out[?] a couple of fine attacks on the Będzin goal; the Będzin players do not feel particularly at home on the grass. But very quickly they get used to the pitch and the play takes on a normal character. The first half passes with very fine chances on both sides, which neither team exploits. But one can see that the referee is very subjective. In the second half the Będzin team take over the initiative. And already in the first minutes Hampel, despite the goalkeeper's „Robinsonade“ [diving save], shoots a splendid goal. This apparently does not please the referee Mr. Szwer, who begins to award eleven-metre kicks [penalties] against the Będzin side. It came to the point that as soon as a Będzin player approached the ball the referee stopped play. In this way the referee awarded 3 eleven-metre kicks which should never have been given at all. The atmosphere became very heated and people began to run onto the pitch. The Będzin players, very unnerved, played on, but when the referee awarded a fourth eleven-metre kick although the ball was not in play, and moreover sent Szywek[?] off the pitch because he had asked him why he was awarding an eleven-metre kick, their patience snapped [lit. „the bladder burst“] and the Będzin players refused to play on. Meanwhile many people came onto the pitch, and the sadly-famous referee Mr. Szwer abandoned the match. Mr. Szwer gave the Bielitz referees' board a great deal of joy [ironic].
Immediately after the match a meeting of the „Maccabi“ executive took place in Bielitz. The meeting was held in a very depressed mood, because all the delegates were under the impression of the painful match. The speakers very sharply criticised the referees' board and the management of „Hakoach“ Bielitz, which had allowed such a referee[?] to conduct this match. It was resolved to annul the match and to fix a second match on neutral ground, most probably in Kraków or Katowice.
Debe.

[Zagłębie — TOZ.] The second group of children at the „TOZ“ summer colony.
The Zagłębie branch of „TOZ“ [Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jewish Population], which revived a year ago and set about fulfilling its tasks with fresh energy, can now record a new success in its activity[?].
Last Monday a group of 96 boys left for summer colonies; together with the group of girls sent out earlier, „TOZ“ has thus sent out 107 children this summer, who for a month enjoy a free and healthy life in fresh air and under special medical supervision. When one further takes into account that these children were selected from among the neediest in Sosnowiec, Będzin, Dąbrowa and Czeladź, one must recognise how important the „TOZ“ activity is, thanks to which this society[?] has taken its place among the most useful in Zagłębie.
It is worth noting that last year over 60 children used the „TOZ“ summer colony and this year already 107, i.e. almost double the number — and this is only one branch of „TOZ“ activity. In addition, the children of various Jewish schools which do not enjoy municipal (magistrate) support, above all religious schools, are under the medical supervision of „TOZ“. During the school year a feeding campaign for schoolchildren is also conducted, as well as broad hygiene propaganda among the Jewish population, etc.
All this, however, is not sufficient for such a Jewish centre as Zagłębie. Therefore at the last „TOZ“ conference in Warsaw — where, incidentally, the esteemed chairman of the Zagłębie branch, Dr. Weinzieher, was elected to the main council — a resolution was also adopted to organise in Zagłębie, where there are many consumptives, a tuberculosis dispensary.
The realisation of these tasks depends to a great extent on the support of the Jewish population, which already understands today that the existence and activity of „TOZ“ is a great achievement in the grey social life of Jewish Zagłębie.

[Bystra — memorial.] Mourning assembly for H. N. Bialik in Bystra
The K.K.L. [Jewish National Fund] committee in Bystra held on Tuesday evening, in the hall of Mr. Twarda[?], a mourning „academy“ devoted to the passing of the great poet H. N. Bialik.
The assembly was well attended and left an unforgettable impression on the hundreds of visitors. The hall was splendidly decorated with pictures of Herzl and Bialik, the latter draped in black crêpe.
After the opening by the chairman of the committee, R' Shlomo Frenkel, „El male rachamim“ was recited by Mr. Kaszycki (Erets Israel), and the choir of the local kibbutz of „Hanoar Hatsioni“ sang „Techezakna“.
Then Dr. Silberstein spoke on the topic of the day, delivering a brilliant speech on the life and work of the great Jew, national fighter and divine poet.
The speaker quoted several poems, which he translated into Polish.
The pupil Chana Borensztajn (Będzin) recited very successfully the poem „Acharei moti“ [„After my death“].
The closing speech was given by Mr. S. Frenkel, and with „Hatikvah“ the mourning assembly was closed.

Support the action for the victims of the flood!

„Jewish merchants avoid giving to state funds“.
Such scandalous words were heard in the Sosnowiec magistracy.
On Tuesday an organising meeting took place in the Sosnowiec city council to set up a committee that is to conduct the relief action for the families who suffered in the flood.
Not a single Jewish communal or merchant activist was invited to the session, nor any organisations, but that did not prevent a grave accusation from being hurled at the Jewish community at the meeting.
This was permitted to herself by the wife of Dr. Chalewicki[?], president of the local B.B. [BBWR] committee, who said that „the Jews dodged giving to the Sea Fund, and it may well be that in this action too they will do the same“.
The unheard-of accusation was snatched up like a delicacy by the „Jew-friendly“ sheets „Kurjer“ and „Express“, which appear in Sosnowiec — the very ones whose columns are always full of advertisements of Jewish firms — and they told their readers (the Jewish ones too) that the words of Mrs. Chalewicka had made a moving impression and that Polish society will surely start a counter-action against those „who can and will not give“..
In connection with this, on the initiative of Mr. J. Safer, an urgent meeting was held on Wednesday afternoon in the premises of the kehilla with the participation of representatives of: the kehilla, the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association, the Small Traders' Association, the house-owners, the Jewish commercial judges, the Zionist Org., „Agudat Israel“, the Charity Society, the Jewish Hospital, „Maccabi“, „TOZ“ and others, who resolved to send the above-mentioned editorial offices a protest against the accusation that had been hurled.
The protest at the same time stresses the readiness of the Jews to make sacrifices at every call for the good of the country and for the entire population.
A copy of the protest resolution was also sent to the starosta [district head].
“If You Won’t Help Me, I’ll Commit Suicide” / The Sosnowiec Merchants’ Association for the Flood Victims.

[Dąbrowa — relief; a carter in distress. Followed by: Sosnowiec — merchants, aid for the flood victims.] So cries out a poor Jewish carter.
Reuben Silberstein [Silbersztajn], who lives in Gagaushe[?], beyond Dąbrowa, drew the livelihood for his family from his poor nag [“klyatshe”, a worn-out old horse].
Last week Silberstein drove off to fetch zharik[?]. On the way the horse lay down and “stretched out its hooves” [died].
The poor carter, left without a livelihood, began knocking on the doors of communal workers; he shouted, he wept — but who today has another’s suffering in mind?
On Wednesday morning Silberstein went into the Zagórze beit midrash, found several worshippers there, and, holding little bottles of vinegar essence, said to them:
— “If you won’t help me, I’ll drink up this vinegar before your eyes.”
The experiment worked a little, and Messrs. Moshe Grünwald, Shmelke Zajdler, Mendel Najman and Getsl Ehrenfried went to the Dąbrowa kehilla to ask for support for the helpless Jewish carter.
But the intervention did not help at all; the present president, Mr. L. Rechnic, answered the delegation:
— “We can do nothing, there is no money.”
After the president’s answer the delegation came to us at the editorial office and asked us to appeal to the Dąbrowa kehilla that they take an interest in the Jewish carter.

Help the Unfortunate Victims of the Flood!

A terrible catastrophe has struck a large area of Poland; nature in its fury has killed dozens of people, destroyed enormous sums of hard human labour, taken away the livelihood of thousands of people, and taken the roof from over the heads of dozens of Jewish and non-Jewish families.
Whole camps of homeless people, thousands of unfortunate children, are now looking for a piece of bread, a place to lay their heads, and are exposed to the danger of infectious diseases and perhaps of death by starvation.
The population of Poland, all 3 million Jews, must as one man strain all their forces to help the stricken; no one may refuse, even with the smallest donation, to help our fellow citizens, our brother Jews.
We know the situation of the Jewish population, the severe crisis that oppresses it, but that is in no way an excuse — quite the opposite: the Jewish population must and will once again convince the gentiles of the land that the misfortune of its fellow citizens is not foreign to it, and with the greatest effort raise the sums needed to help our unfortunates, at least in a minimal way.
A local committee has been formed, which appeals through our newspaper for help for the victims of the flood, and we are sure that our readers, friends and the whole Jewish population will fully pass this examination of compassion and self-sacrifice!
A Marble Plaque in Memory of H. N. Bialik

Esteemed Editors!
We ask you to print in your esteemed newspaper the following appeal to the Jewish population of Sosnowiec.
At the meeting in the Zionist premises, where it was intended to found a joint committee to honour the untimely death of our greatest poet H. N. Bialik, the following proposal was put forward in the name of the Hatzohar [Revisionist Zionists] in Sosnowiec concerning the perpetuation of the memory of the late poet and prophet H. N. Bialik. The proposal reads: since the town of Sosnowiec is the only town in Poland where Hayim Nahman Bialik lived and worked, in the years 1897—1899, before he left for Odessa, a marble stone with a fitting inscription should be set into the house at Targowa no. 11. Unfortunately the proposal was rejected by the majority of the Zionist representatives. We therefore turn, through the esteemed newspaper, to the Jewish community of Sosnowiec to contribute voluntarily and help to buy the above-mentioned stone.
The house-to-house collection will take place next Sunday, by authorised members of Brit HaChayal.
The setting of the stone will take place according to a special programme on the day of the shloshim [thirtieth day after the death].
In the conviction that Jewish Sosnowiec will help us, we sign
With the blessing of the Kingdom of Israel,
The Command of „Brit HaChayal“
in Sosnowiec.

The Tax Reliefs for Merchant House-Owners

The Finance Ministry has sent out a new circular on granting reliefs to merchants who owe arrears of taxes from before 1 October 1931.
Merchants who own houses can also enjoy the bonification [rebate] of 25 per cent of their[?] tax debt, if they pay the tax debt at once, or over three years in 12 quarterly instalments.
Merchants who do not own houses can also receive the bonification of 25 per cent without any need to submit an application, if they voluntarily declare that they wish to pay the tax arrears at once.
The circular bears the number L. D. V. 34—1—7376.
