The Landlord and the Tenant.
(The prevailing situation. — Can there be a way to make rent cheaper?)

People have already grown used to the crisis and no longer notice [?] that it is an abnormal [?] phenomenon, which, the further it goes, leaves behind ever more painful and deeper wounds that perhaps cannot be radically healed.
This time it concerns the tenants' question. Somehow people persuaded themselves [?] that the question was topical only during the war, and that with the end of the war the tenants' associations, too, ought to have been liquidated. True, officially these institutions exist all over Poland, but in fact they have died off, and at best they do not fulfil their tasks; they do not stand at the proper level, if only because they are not active in life. Calling a meeting or sending a delegate to a convention does not by any means mean that the institution exists and is active in life. Even if it were not as it actually is — that many of them sleep for a whole year, and the board has even altogether forgotten what mission it bears — so that it happens to remember this only on some occasion, at an opportune moment.
Well, it is self-evident that the institutions do indeed exist, but only on paper, and we remember them only when we walk past the premises and see that the signboard is still hanging.
We do not know what the general opinion is — that the tenants' associations are no longer needed, at a time when they are an urgent necessity, and not only now during the crisis, but always [?]. In our opinion the institutions must exist as long as there are tenants.
We would go even further; we would venture [?] to say that perhaps the tenants' associations were never such a necessity as now, in the time of the prevailing crisis, because during the war paying rent was not such a hard matter: one had barely held the house-owner off with the money for a while, and the debt had already lost its value, and the tenant paid it off easily. Quite different is it nowadays. Today, the longer one does not pay, the harder it becomes to pay, and one becomes ever more liable for the accumulated debts, from which one can no longer crawl out, and the landlord's chances of obtaining an eviction grow ever stronger.
Do the tenants or their professional associations take account of what nasty situation they are being dragged into this way? It is quite certain that the situation then becomes very, very hard for the tenants, and almost without a way out for those without means, who will no longer be able to get out of it the straight way, because they will not be able to cover the accumulated debt.
Then yet another question arises, which becomes more and more topical. The tenants demand reductions, justifying this by the bad times. The landlord does not want to hear of it, because he for his part claims that his administration expenses have not only not decreased but, on the contrary, are increasing.
The landlord proves to you that his local conditions are getting harder, because the municipal authority demands more order, both hygienic and technical, which drags in more expenses. The same is with the state: it too does not want to hear of anything, and not only does it not want to reduce the taxes, it even raises them.
These are all reasons that have substance, and indeed on the basis of these very reasons the house-owners' associations are lobbying the government to allow them to raise rents.
That is how the situation looks. It is not only that the tenants demand a reduction and the landlords do not allow it; they demand an increase at the same time. And just as the tenants justify the demanded reduction by the bad times, so exactly do the house-owners justify their demand by the heavy taxes imposed on them, which the government can also fix.
Granted, in larger or new houses with "well-paying" tenants the properties can still bear proper income. Quite different, however, is it with smaller houses with tenants who are not first-class, and which are moreover encumbered as well. It is self-evident that their owners must lose money on the houses.
We are not out here to defend the interests of the house-owners, who can, by the way [?], stand up for their cause [?] themselves. On the other hand one must absolutely look the truth in the face: if one wants to achieve anything for the benefit of the popular masses, this problem must be dealt with clearly and plainly, honestly and sincerely. If this is not done by the tenants, the owners of the houses will do it — which they perhaps do anyway — and then it will certainly not be more favourable for us tenants. We must therefore have the courage to show the competent authorities how the situation presents itself in the light of truth and reality.
If one really wants to improve the tenant's condition, such a method must be adopted that can lead to our not deceiving ourselves and not going about with mere illusions, which for the most part are not realised.
And we regard the question as too serious, and would not want it to be treated just like this, for form's sake, with nothing at all coming of it. It is certainly not right to spend either public money or energy on such "spectacles".
That the question has already now taken on serious consequences can be seen from the fact that lately there is not a week in which clashes do not occur between tenants and landlords, ending in serious brawls, shootings, murders and evictions.
In general a kind of disregard has set in concerning the payment of rent. Certainly this has to do with the hard situation the masses find themselves in, but one must not forget that this must not be allowed to happen, because the landlord will exploit it to his advantage and the tenant will certainly suffer badly from it.
Had we tenants' associations standing at the proper height, they would have had to warn their members not to let things come to such a state from which the tenants would have to suffer. It must be said once and for all that rent must be paid, and one cannot rely on every newspaper canard and think that thereby one will be freed from the heavy yoke.
We therefore think that a bridge must be built between the tenants' and the house-owners' associations, which should together endeavour to ease this painful question.
It may be that to many this proposal will look ridiculous — that one should enlist the house-owners' help in order to reduce rent — but it is not so. We know, for instance, that even now many house-owners reduce the rent of their own free will and only wish that everyone would pay, certainly less, but for real — and this at a time when they could legally demand more, and they pay heavy taxes.
We think that together something could be achieved in this field, and if it is to be achieved, one would have to begin at the root.
We see that the government does not want to meet the masses' demand to reduce rent, and that is because it knows that the landlord is burdened enough with taxes; therefore it is important first of all to demand that the government reduce the taxes on houses, and that this be done for the benefit of the tenants.
The central house-owners' association will certainly take note of this and accept this proposal, since the landlord has no benefit at all from the heavy taxes, whereas it is considerably easier and more convenient for him when the tenant has to pay less and will thus be able to keep up with paying the rent.
These two associations must therefore launch a joint action aimed at making house rents cheaper.
Before the government this can easily be justified already by the fact that everything in the country has become cheaper, and this has gone so far that even the government itself has cut the prices of its monopoly products. The railway, the post etc. have also become cheaper, whereas the rent of flats stands at the same height as in the most brilliant time in the country.
One must therefore begin to work intensively so that the rent of flats be made cheaper, and this must absolutely be done both by the tenants and by the landlords.
R. Let.

The history books, however, gave him no material for his memorandum; so he called to his aid a professor of Jewish history at the Rabbinical Seminary.
The Jew was, naturally, frightened to death by the telephone call from the Foreign Ministry. The baron sensed it from his trembling voice and applied all his diplomatic courtesy to calm the Jew and to convince him that he had nothing to be afraid of. The Nazi baron was, at the same time, himself proud of his skill. And the professor, in a most grateful and most obsequious[?] voice, told him over the telephone that the marquises and dukes Coronel descend from Abraham Senior, Isabella's finance minister and the Spanish Bismarck of that time; but into the blood of the Coronels a good deal of the blood of the Habsburgs and of the Albas had been mixed — of the cruel Alba, who trampled the Netherlanders[?] underfoot and flooded the land with rivers of blood in the period of the Reformation.
Incidentally, said the professor, he was not so sure about the admixture of Alba blood in the Coronels. But he would investigate the great matter more closely and submit[?] to the ministry a detailed report in a few days.

The marquis and his friend, the prima donna.

The Foreign Minister listened to the baron's own invented report on his diplomatic mission to the Spanish legation, and to the memorandum on the Jewish descent of the marquis.
He approved his order to the police to have the Spanish diplomat watched by detectives, so that he would be protected from further similar street incidents, and expressed his full satisfaction with the way he had acted in general. It was further decided not to return to the marquis his diplomatic passport and, for the time being, to ignore the breach — in the hope that the marquis would be ashamed to bring before the public and before the diplomatic corps the fact that the police had broken his bones before it learned of his rank[?], that he is the deputy of the Spanish envoy.
The press, naturally, printed not a word about the incident, and the diplomatic corps could not know about the incident unless the marquis himself were to tell of it... That, however, German diplomacy considered psychologically impossible.
German diplomacy, however, made a great mistake. The marquis did indeed decide to keep silent about the ugly incident for the time being. But not out of shame that two policemen had beaten him, the Spanish grandee, in the street when he stood up for a tormented Jew — rather because he had resolved to provoke an even greater and even uglier diplomatic incident, one that would stir up the whole diplomatic world.
His plan was to conceal his identity and, with his original Jewish appearance, to provoke the Nazis into some street incident, so that he would be dragged into one of their inquisition cellars, undergo there a full "Nazi cure", and at the right psychological moment reveal his identity.
It would take us too long to describe the feelings of the marquis and to be able to show how such a wild, fantastic and dangerous plan could be born in the diplomat's mind; for that one would need a long walk through the dark labyrinth of the Marrano's soul, to tell the long story of this romantic [printed "ramandisher"] personality, which played a great role in the last revolution, which drove out the Bourbon dynasty and brought with it a republic — a revolution that was against the interests of the Spanish aristocracy, i.e. of his own class. By taking the side of the revolution the marquis quarrelled with his family and his class, who turned away from him in horror as from a traitor.
Hitler's land[?] with its persecutions of the Jews, to which he had been sent, awakened in him thoughts and feelings about the medieval Inquisition and about the expulsion of the Jews in 1492 — the mystical, incomprehensible feelings that used to awaken in the Marranos after three and four generations of Catholic faith, rousing them as if from a long, hundred-year lethargic sleep and driving them like sleepwalkers into exile, where they would become Jews again.
(To be continued).
Mountains

Y. Segal.
The selfsame nature, as it has been described ever since the first fool or sage who dared to sing praise in its honour. I look around from a narrow house-porch, across the great chain of mountains opposite, and there come to my mind the hundreds and thousands of pictures and images with which a world of paper has been filled, and I think of the diligence, the effort and – the talent that has been laid out on it. Which writer, which poet has not given half of his work to painting nature, to conveying its beauty and majesty? What would literature have been without the descriptions of nature? And surely [?] it would be a joy for the city person to read the beautiful pictures of mountain and stream, valley and grove.
A practical generation, a generation of enormous matter-of-factness [?], a generation that has lost every sense for play and beauty; the seriousness of the hidden, perfect stomach-functions, which has crept into the brain of this generation and seeks to push out the shadowiness, the dark web of mystery from between the folds of the brain. A generation that has suddenly seen through and spied out the surface of world and time, which has been mathematically measured out, and it wants to fill this surface with a certain few appetites. What use to it are all those far-running, galloping illusions? It wants only the illusion that has already become real and that it "can make use of". The illusion that has already outlived its childish periods of beauty and play, of idea [?], and has sat itself down, quite corpulent and fat, on the real earth and eats its three good meals a day, recalling, for a change, while passing from one dish to the next, that once, in the times of "backwardness", their grandfathers [?] sang songs and praises while eating – they said grace.
Nevertheless, however far we may be from rapture over nature, when the mood is still "better tuned" and the day is fine and one picks out a path somewhere where no one walks, and one is alone with oneself on the way – a different kind of stillness creeps into the "soul" of even the most urban of men, and something of what one could call the work of Creation one begins to feel in the breadth and freedom of nature, however amazed we may be at technical achievements. With nature we live through something eternal in our rapture; we ourselves grow greater, and that, I believe, is why we feel so – because we love nature's greatness and freedom, we love it with that inexplicable love which we feel for the growing and moving of the children who come out of our body. In nature we can still lose ourselves in play; we can feel like children who have above them a mighty, great father on whom to rely.
What is a tree? For the tired person from the city a tree is the god of calm. In the hiding-places of the mountains the Baal Shem Tov sat and made whole and calmed within himself the great love and the great goodness towards man. He himself first had to fill himself with godliness and festivity, and only afterwards come among people, so that from his face this calm and goodness would shine down upon them and raise and uplift them above all the pettinesses that had dragged their lives down into a mire of worry. Into a sand of desolate wilderness and lostness.
It is hard for the city person, who is not whole and not beautiful within, to be able to accept the calm of nature, somehow as if he felt himself unclean before it. As if he could not look it in the eyes. He comes to the mountains and frets, gets nervous with all sorts of foolish gestures, and feels bored and monotonous. When he wants to give himself an honest answer, he knows that nature does not accept him. It must tear out of him a great deal more. Tear out and destroy much impurity, and little by little open his eyes and his heart to it; it settles accounts with him in silence, he "pours himself out" before it, and it becomes ever nearer and more understandable to him.
Great and luminous stand the mountains under the broad, deep afternoon sky; little, quiet silver pieces – clouds – lie still over the warm clarity of the high day. The house where I live here now is the only one on a not-high mountain, and behind the [?] pine forests I hear people bathing in the river. It is quiet and peaceful.
And from me, I feel, like a heavy weight, the painfulness slowly and gradually evaporates [?]. Days earlier it was harder for me, something unbearable; the reasons cannot be told, nor need they be. Perhaps because at bottom the reason is not worth the pain – always, perhaps, and with everyone and in all cases. It is good that we have been given the fine feeling of shame. With me too, silently and without words, nature has settled accounts. I told it everything, and it listened to me without words and, it seems, consented to heal me of pettiness and narrow feeling.
Like the sun of the broad noon, like the shadows of a pure and quiet dusk, I want to spread my spirit over the heights and slopes of the mountains. From a small window in a wooden hut here I look out and across the wooded ridges and feel that I understand so vaguely and so little. Though I know the names of all the things that encircle me, I do not understand, for understanding, it seems to me, is an abstract concept. No one can say anything with certainty about his understanding; our only truth is feeling, and through feeling we can murmur that – we understand too.
Who Goes to a Dacha Nowadays?

(From a conversation on the New Market.)
Last Saturday towards evening the Jews refreshed themselves and savoured [?] the refreshing scents of the flowers in the "square" on the New Market.
But there has to be a "but".. There was nowhere to sit. The town administration has put up a handful of benches, and one needs special luck to get a bit of room there.
I go up to a bench. One Jew says to the other – "move over half a bit" and makes [?] a bit of room for me to squeeze in...
I look around at my neighbours, 2 Jews who, from their talk, are evidently long-settled Będziners. They know everyone, know at once whose son-in-law each person is and what kind of business he does.
A conversation develops about today's livelihoods.
– I assure you, – says one, – that in Będzin barely 5 percent of the shopkeepers earn a living. Here I live on the Market – there only a handful make a living, the rest don't have enough for Sabbath.
– It's not so bad yet, – the other cuts in, – after all, so many people are sitting at dachas, Bystra, Rajcza, and everywhere is packed, and precisely with business people.
– Ah, then I'll tell you a story.
– At the beit midrash where I am gabbai, a month ago a local tailor I know came up to me and said: it's bitter, everything is finished, there is simply nothing for Sabbath.
A couple of weeks later I learn that the tailor has actually gone off to a dacha.
So I ask him – what is this?
– I couldn't do otherwise; here the shopkeeper woman won't give credit any more, so for a room in the village I gave a promissory note for 40 zł. And the shopkeepers give the people at dachas credit too, "on the book".
– I have yet another story to tell about a dacha, – the Jew continues his talk. – A local young man I know went off to a boarding house in Bystra. In the great bustle the owner didn't notice, and the young man sat it out like that, everything provided, for 40 days. When the boarding-house keeper asked him for money, the young man took out a twenty [-złoty note].
– But you owe me 200 zł., – the boarding-house owner got angry.
What did the young man do? He packed up and left.
These are today's "rich men" at the dachas...
Yud Reysh.
—o—
Registration of automobiles.
An automobile must be registered in the name of the person to whom it belongs at the given moment. The authorities have no right to go into inquiries as to whether the full purchase price has been paid for the automobile or not. Consequently the seller's reservation that the car will become the buyer's property only after the purchase price has been paid has no significance whatsoever for the administrative authorities [?] at registration.
Hanna Pesa — the German Woman!...

[Humorous feuilleton — summer life at the dacha; Nazi Germany.] By J. Oberżanek.

Troubles of a summer holidaymaker [letnik].

I've told you once already that all troubles, all misfortunes come from the dacha [summer cottage]. At the dacha the men get acquainted with new female neighbours and the wives with new male neighbours. The men look askance at the new neighbours, and the wives "squabble" ["pshemvyen zikh", from Polish; reading and sense uncertain] with the new female neighbours. When you come back to town, a whole series of invitations begins: "I invite you to cards" ["mzaprashem[?] na karty", zapraszam na karty], "to tea" [na herbatkę], "to the radio" [na radio], and with the "birthday parties" [urodzinki] begins a business with "receptions" [przyjęcia]. Each one wants to outdo the other. One gives a "sugar reception" ["tsukrove pshyentshe"], the other gives a "sugar reception" with canapés [kanapki], and on whose head does it all land? — On the men's! Every Saturday night other drinking parties [bibki], other celebrations, other dances [zabawa], and what do wives do at these parties? They chat. And what do wives chat about coming back from the dacha? — About winter!...
And perhaps you think they chat about coal for the winter? About paying the winter rent? About providing[?] for the household, about something practical? — God forbid! They talk about winter... dances!
One asks a young wife: Where are you going for the winter, madam? [Polish: dokąd pani jedzie na zimę?]
— I'm off to Zakopane [ja do Zakopanego] — answers the other.
— Oh, madam!
— To Krynica [do Krynicy].
— Oh, madam!
— To Otwock [do Otwocka].
I sit at the table and listen to the conversations, and the blood rushes to my head, and I think to myself:
If only I could now give these wives a shout:
— Silly goats, ducks! What are you babbling about? You've only just come from the meadows [łąki], where you fattened up your double chins, you've only just roasted yourselves in the sun like brown cholent potatoes! You haven't even managed[?] to take off your bathing trunks [majtki kąpielowe] — and you're already talking about Zakopane and snow?
But go and talk to wives. They have nine measures of talk, and however much you try to convince them, you'll be the loser [przegrana]...
Yes, all troubles, all misfortunes come from the dacha, but such a misfortune as befell my wife this year I never expected.
— What happened? A terrible thing! A strange occurrence — my missus ["yudene"] Hanna Pesa has gone mad! She went off healthy and fresh and went mad!
And what, do you think, does her madness consist of? You think she smashes windowpanes? That she talks nonsense? God forbid! In that respect she is quite normal. She talks sense, answers sensibly, dolls herself up and dresses up [stroić się], paints her lips and blackens her eyebrows, stands for whole hours at the mirror dressed in her see-through pyjamas, like all Jewish women...
So what does her madness consist of?
— She has become a German woman.
What? You don't understand? If you don't understand, I'll tell you the story in detail [podrobnie]:
As soon as my Hanna Pesl went off to the dacha, a dybbuk entered her, may it not befall us, a German dybbuk, and she keeps on speaking "German", and for two weeks now she has become a complete German woman, a "pure Aryan", and should you say a bad word about the Germans, she is ready to murder you.
The first Saturday I come to the dacha and say as always:
— "Good morning, Hanna Pesa."
My missus doesn't answer.
— Why don't you answer me? — I wondered.
— Because that's not how one says it — she answered.
— How does one say it, then?
— First you kiss the hand and you say: "Guten Mojen [mock German, 'Guten Morgen' in Berlin dialect], my treasure" — she answered.
— Guten Mojen, my treasure Hanna Pesl — I said in jest.
Since then she keeps on speaking "German". I ask her: is lunch ready? She answers:
— "Bizt nisht khole[?] tsu vartn" [garbled German; probably: can't you wait?].
I ask her: have you eaten anything yet today? She answers:
— "Das ist nicht deine Sache!" [That's none of your business!]
I say to her: Hanna Pesa, why on earth have you started speaking Hitler's language just now?
She gets angry and shouts: "Lass man hier"[?]! "Donnerwetter noch einmal!"...
So I started arguing with her, explaining what the Germans are, what dreadful troubles Jews have had and still have to this day from the Germans — so why has she taken to German just now?
And what do you think she answered me? She answered that everything I tell her is exaggerated, that it is "atrocity propaganda" [Greuelpropaganda], that she has nothing against the German, that I am not worthy to stand next to the German — a "pure Aryan" has my Hanna Pesa become...
But all this is still nothing compared to what I went through with her last Saturday.
I come to the dacha, go into the house, and everything goes dark before my eyes — a shaygets [gentile lad], no less!
I ask her: Hanna Pesa, what is this?
— What is this? The milk-woman — she answered.
— A milk-woman with a moustache [wąsy]? — It's the first time I've seen a milk-woman with such a moustache!
So I made a scene:
— What is this shaygets doing here with you? Who is this shaygets?
— This is the son of the German village head [sołtys], a dear German, a golden German, he guards me like the apple of his eye — she answered.
— Well, and what business does he have with you?
— He gives me German lessons — she answered.
— Aha, so that's the story! Now I understand why you suddenly started speaking German! Now I understand who taught you that when you come in you must first kiss the hand and say "Guten Mojen", my treasure! Now I understand why you won't let anyone say a bad word about the German and why I'm not worthy to stand next to a German — now that I've had the honour of meeting your teacher ["rebbe"], I understand where your German madness came from.
Jews, I tell you once more: all troubles, all misfortunes come from the dachas, but such a misfortune — that my Hanna Pesl should become such a dyed-in-the-wool Aryan — that I never expected!
May fire, I tell you, come upon all the dachas, so that not a trace of them remains!...
What Must Parents Know?

(On the margin of the school year just ended).

And once again a school year has ended. Thousands of Jewish children have now finished the elementary [public] schools; whole camps of Jewish school-leavers have come out of the secondary schools with the long-dreamed-of matura certificate in their pocket. Not small, either, is the number of Jewish university students who will now leave the universities with diplomas in their hands. But not a single "cheerful" face is to be seen among any of them. All of them are permeated with heavy worry, and in everyone's mind the sad thought keeps hammering:
— And what next?
There were times when an intellectual profession provided, if not a luxurious, then a secure and respectable existence. The Jewish father used to pull the load beyond his strength, toil and pay the highest prices to educate his child, knowing that thereby he was providing him with a purpose, with a goal in life. And he too, the Jewish pupil, used to study with diligence and zeal, always pinning his hopes on the thought, the awareness, that once he finished, with luck, he would be provided for.
— How does it look today?
The doors of the government secondary school do not open easily for Jews; getting into the private secondary school is also hard for most because of the tuition fee, which by today's earnings is a fortune; and now there is in addition a general tendency to degrade the private secondary schools by taking away their government rights [accreditation]. Well, and if a lucky one does get in there, into the gymnasium, and holds out through more sleepless nights and underfed days until he gets the matura, only then does the real worry begin: what does one do with the matura? A cloud of gloom rises over the spirit of the young pupil and makes him prematurely aged and full of care.
And let us go further still. What if one even finishes the university? Only then is one left completely helpless, because there is not the slightest possibility of practising the profession for which one struggled so many years.
For lately so many difficulties and restrictions have been added that they make every intellectual profession impossible for our children. The legal profession is already almost entirely closed. A Jewish engineer has nothing at all to do, since prospects of government posts are absolutely nil. What, then, is left for the Jewish intellectual?
There are no emigration possibilities for the Jewish intellectual, and the prospect of settling in here is not even to be thought of; we are, after all, witnesses that for a post paying a few dozen złoty a month one receives offers from dozens of matura-holders and students. What, then, is left for the young Jewish man other than to join a hakhshara kibbutz and wait for a certificate, thanks to which he gets the possibility of earning his livelihood by hard physical labour?
Was it for this that people had to give their best strength and years to studies, to education? Would they not have done much better had they learned a trade from the outset?
And here we come to the main idea, which must take first place with parents who think about a purpose for their children, and also with the youth who think about a goal in life:
One must turn to vocational training!
A question that has already been touched upon a thousand and one times and to which one must return once again.
The highest time has come for Jewish parents to think more carefully and understand that, in light of the present Jewish situation all over the world, they must bring up their children quite differently. The average Jewish person, whose own existence is a shaky one, even if he still earns a living today, must nevertheless provide his child with a trade.
He must be practical and sober.
Unfortunately, the lack of vocational training among us looks very lamentable. We stand before the decline of craftsmanship among Jews. A whole series of laws has come out that aim to hamper the path of practical craft training; it is precisely for that reason that the urgent task of the day is to make sure that the Jewish child is given the possibility of enjoying education and at the same time also of learning a trade, which will later give him a future in life.
This the parents must now take well to heart.
Sh. K.
Palestine and Czechoslovakia.

(From our correspondent Z. Haber, Prague.)
A few days ago the Czechoslovak society for distributing Czech products in Palestine and for importing products from Palestine into Czechoslovakia was founded. This society is quite different from all the societies founded so far in various countries, because it is the first time that such a society has been set up officially by the highest authorities of a country. The Prague society was founded with the help of the Czech government, and the president of the society is the Czech Minister of Trade, Engineer Dostálek.
The society includes the biggest industrialists of Czechoslovakia, the most important politicians of the country, and all the Jewish and non-Jewish personalities who have an interest in exchanging goods between Czechoslovakia and Palestine.
The writer of these lines, who was present at the founding of the society as the representative of the largest Czech newspaper concern, had a conversation with the Czech Minister of Trade about the economic possibilities between the two countries mentioned.
"The greatest credit for the growth of relations between Palestine and Czechoslovakia," says Minister Dostálek, "belongs to the last Zionist Congress in Prague. The Prague fair was being held just then, and we sold more to Palestine at that time than we sometimes sold in the whole year before. To give you a few figures: in 1932 we sold 13 million crowns' worth to Palestine, and in the half-year 1933, from the Prague fair to the end, we sold 26 million crowns' worth.
And in 1934 we sold large quantities at the fair in Tel Aviv, and we also made purchases for ourselves, because we saw that we can always maintain a good connection between the two countries.
We founded the society because we know that we are able to supply everything Palestine needs, and Czechoslovakia also needs products that grow in Palestine. Our goods are the best that can be manufactured, and we set prices with which no country in the world can compete.
Unfortunately we lack figures on Jewish trade in Czech goods in other countries, because we cannot know which firms are Jewish and which are not; but we are sure that all over the world Jews buy with great eagerness the goods that bear the stamp 'Made in Czechoslovakia'.
The newly founded society will do everything possible to strengthen the relations between the two countries, which are very important both for us and for Palestine."
Big railway discounts for travel to Warsaw during the "Festival of the Capital".

From the 4th to the 18th of August of this year the "Festival of the Capital City of Warsaw" will be celebrated for the first time. During these two weeks large railway discounts (from 60 to 70 percent of the normal price) will be valid for all provincials who come to Warsaw at that time. The discounts will be individual and will be valid both for the journey to Warsaw and for the return, to any railway station whatsoever.
Besides the railway discount, every provincial who comes to Warsaw during the two weeks mentioned will, after buying the proper festival card, enjoy enormous privileges, such as: breakfast, lunch and supper entirely free (for Jews — in a kosher restaurant). On the other days he will receive a large discount in certain restaurants and cafés, free rides on the trams, discount tickets in the Jewish theatres (50 percent), free visits to all museums and art exhibitions, and a free visit to the Wilanów Palace. In addition everyone receives free a plan of the city of Warsaw, a travel plan, etc.
Countless attractions and entertainments are being prepared for the visitors from the provinces.
Anyone who has no relatives in Warsaw and wishes to obtain cheap lodgings will have to apply to the "Association for Tourist Propaganda" (Wierzbowa 8), which, in the order in which applications arrive, will provide everyone with cheap private lodgings.
It is therefore very important for every provincial to visit Warsaw in the days from the 4th to the 18th of August of this year, because such discounts and privileges are truly a rarity.
The festival cards mentioned can be obtained at the bookstalls at all railway stations.
Don't throw fruit stones!

Our readers have drawn our attention to the following phenomenon:
Every year, when the season of cherries, plums and other fruit begins, the public is in the habit of eating in the street and throwing the stones onto the pavement. This is a very ugly and harmful habit, because many people slip, fall, tear their shoes, and so on.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Va'etchanan)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Va'etchanan
The Portion
—o—
a) "And I besought the Lord at that time" (Deut. 3:24 [sic])
"This is one of the three places where Moses said before the Omnipresent: I will not let You go until You let me know whether You will grant my request or not." Rashi.
The commentators ask: in Parashat Beha'alotcha (12:13) Rashi himself writes: "In four places Moses asked of the Holy One, blessed be He, whether He would grant his requests or not." So in four cases Moses demanded of God that He answer him whether He would fulfil his request or not — and here Rashi says it happened in only three cases. Truly a difficult contradiction!
But Rashi is being precise here and changes the wording from that in Parashat Beha'alotcha. Here Rashi says "that Moses said before the Omnipresent: I will not let You go until etc." — that is, Moses importuned God, pleaded with Him at length, said to Him: "I will not let You go until You tell me whether You will fulfil my request or not" — and that happened in only three cases; for in Parashat Beha'alotcha Rashi says there that Moses prayed a short prayer, so "I will not let You go" does not apply there... Ponder it.
Torat Yekutiel.
—o—
b) "Righteous statutes and judgments" (4:8)
For there are also abominable statutes ("that ye commit not any one of these abominable customs" — Parashat Acharei); there are sins that are in the category of statutes, which one does even though there is no reason or sense in them... sins for the sake of sinning... If statutes are things whose meaning one does not know, then better already: "righteous statutes and judgments" — better already statutes that are commandments...
R. Amram Blum.
—o—
c) "But ye that did cleave unto the Lord your God are alive every one of you this day."
Be with God while you are still living, while you are still young, and do not leave your piety for old age... "Alive every one of you this day" — while you are still alive...
Devarim Nehmadim.
—o—
d) "As the Lord thy God commanded thee" (5:15–16)
Only regarding the Sabbath and honouring one's father is it said "as the Lord thy God commanded thee," because the Sabbath and honouring one's father are rational commandments. The Sabbath — one day a week one must rest from work; honouring one's father — your parents raise you, give you food — so you must honour them, says the Torah. Yet even these two commandments you should perform only because "the Lord thy God commanded thee," purely for the sake of the commandment; and that is why Rashi remarks: "As He commanded thee — at Marah." For at Marah there was already manna, so one did not need to work six days a week, and children did not need to "depend" on their parents for bread, since the manna fell for everyone — and it was then that honouring one's father and the Sabbath were commanded...
Ktav Sofer.
—o—
e) "Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently... and make them known unto thy children and thy children's children" (4:9)
Most parents want their children to be pious, although they themselves are not pious. This has a bad effect on the children. "Take heed to thyself" — the Torah warns — "and keep thy soul diligently" — guard yourself against being sinful, and only afterwards — "make them known unto thy children and thy children's children"...
Tiferet Shlomo.
—o—
f) "And these words shall be upon thy heart" (6:6)
The words should be upon the heart; the words should reach straight to the heart; there should not be between the words and the heart even a little coarseness and vulgarity...
Imrei No'am.
—o—
g) "And there ye shall serve gods, the work of men's hands" (4:26 [?])
A high official once arrived in Łódź. A reception was arranged for him. At the station he was awaited by representatives of the city, clergy and others [?]. On one side stood two priests, an Orthodox and a Polish [Catholic] one, and only after them was placed, as was customary, the rabbi, R. Eliyahu Chaim Meisel. After the reception the city president asks R. Eliyahu Chaim:
"Does it not offend you that you, a representative of the oldest faith, stood below the priests?"
"Heaven forbid, it does not offend me," replies R. Eliyahu Chaim. "The Jewish faith is, after all, the mother of all the other religions — and is a mother jealous of her children?..."

“Der Kokh-lefl” [The Ladle] — A Word of Consolation

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl” (The Ladle); summer resorts, Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa.] [Page banner:] “Der Kokh-lefl”. — In honour of Shabbat Nachamu. — Compiled by Amutslo.

A Word of Consolation.

I come with a word of consolation for all oppressed intellectuals, idlers, or respectable paupers of great lineage.

You, brothers, [—] are well off in the world [printed “ח די וועלט”]; you sit in town and spare yourselves the taste of the concentration camp called a dacha.

What is lacking in town? A “nasz brat” [Polish: “one of ours”]? First thing in the morning you go and watch how the sewerage works are getting on, and you can pass the time counting the “priobes”[?] stones [perhaps the paving stones].

In the evening you pop into a cinema. For 25 groszy they give you as many as [“azh”, Polish aż] 2 pictures, with a “dodatek” [supplement] from behind and from the front.

But just try going to a dacha — you’ll see what it smells of! Here they tell of Rajcza that, because of the great crowding, people sleep under the beds at night, and in the morning they take mud baths in the peasants’ mikvehs...

In short, oppressed intellectuals, idlers or plain paupers, be consoled, don’t envy the dacha-goers; you are well off, you sit in town.

Let the vice-president of the Będzin kehilla be consoled. Elsewhere things are even worse. Why, in Dąbrowa they actually “hanged out” the kehilla president...

Diet

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; poem.] By A. L. Wolfson.

Once I had teeth
Like a wolf,
I could with them
Chew up [?] nails [“tshvekes”];
And had I only
Had the means then,
I could have
Eaten for three.
I was then
A lad, a “chwat” [Polish: a dashing fellow],
I had perhaps ten appetites;
For eating
I had no time,
And yet
I rode
On principles.
I used to sound the “trwoga” [alarm]
And call to battle!
In the heat of the call
I quite forgot
That somewhere there is
A stomach that begs,
That demands:
Give, little brother, food!
And when I did hear
That call at times,
I would [?]
Not listen to it at all;
I was busy
Feeding the spirit
And about the stomach
I did not think.
The end was —
Not as anyone [?] thought.
I fell in love
And got tied;
And soon
The practical hand
Of the times flayed,
Like a glossy skin,
The dream.
I saw dreams
Melt away in foam,
Dreams smashed into
Shards:
Need drove me:
Go, brother, earn!
Make dollars,
Make “rendlekh” [gold coins],
Make “kerblekh” [roubles].
And God helped,
Freed me from worry.
Entirely
I forgot my troubles.
I make, as they call it,
A fine living,
I lack, thank God,
No food any more,
But here’s the trouble:
Now I am already old,
Gone are the curly
Little hairs.
The nose — bespectacled,
The mouth without teeth,
The “lippers”
Move
With difficulty.
Now I can treat myself
Fully in Viennese style [?]
And live
As God commanded,
But my stomach
Has gone out on strike
And everything I love
Is forbidden.

Polish Women Who Sacrificed Themselves for the Jewish Faith.

M. Starkman.
(An interesting historical tale that took place 200 years ago). (3
Just like Catholic Poland, Orthodox Russia too feared the influence of the Jewish population on its "right-believing children", and therefore would not at all allow the "Christ-killers" to live on the "holy" Russian soil. The great "pious lady" Catherine the First signed a decree in 1727 that all Jews be driven out of Russia; their property in gold and silver they would not be allowed to take with them, but must exchange it for copper coins. Every Jew who still owed money to his non-Jewish neighbours was permitted to stay a little longer in order to pay off the debts. But if an Orthodox Russian had to pay a debt to a Jew, the Jew had to forget about it. The ban concerning Jews continued under the other tsarinas as well, who, together with the whole Orthodox Church, believed that the Jews were sorcerers who by witchcraft lured people to their "accursed" faith.
Russian commerce, however, began to suffer badly from the expulsion of the Jews, so at the request of a number of "kuptsy" [merchants] the Jews were allowed to enter the country solely for trading purposes, and only for a short time.
Among the Jews who were staying in Russia at that time was one Baruch Leibov, of the village of Zverovichi in Smolensk province, where he had earlier built a synagogue at his own expense. Baruch was a well-to-do Jew, and besides travelling about various towns on business, he also earned a good deal from holding the lease on the liquor levy of the village tavern.
On one of his business journeys Baruch Leibov became acquainted with a retired officer of the Russian navy — Alexander Voznitsyn. As happens not seldom between people of different nations, the two became good friends and quite often held discussions on religious questions; each of the two tried to prove that his faith was the right one and the best. Since Voznitsyn was no simple soldier but a true lover of knowledge, he listened with great attention to his friend Baruch's arguments. Baruch, for his part, was a learned Jew and no fool, and it did not take long before Voznitsyn realised that in many details the Jew was right and that his faith held the true position on this or that question of religious belief. After his conversations with Baruch, Voznitsyn would ponder the arguments the Jew had put to him. He spent restless, sleepless nights over it and then waited impatiently for the next conversations with his Jewish friend.
The discussions went on like this for a good while, until Voznitsyn admitted to Baruch that he had convinced him of the full truth of the Jewish faith. The retired officer was a man of iron principles, and once he had acknowledged a certain truth he had to accept it; Voznitsyn therefore asked Baruch to help him become a true Jew.
The officer's wife, however, remained a truly pious Orthodox woman. She knew very well about the change that had taken place in her husband. He no longer went to church [tserkov], he looked at the holy icons with contempt, and when she said her prayers he looked at her with a mocking expression. But she did not give up hope that he would become a true believer again. She knew his whims; she knew that he was a man of moods, and so she thought that with him this was only a passing thing.
Voznitsyn, however, acted otherwise. He talked over with Baruch his decision to become a Jew, and Baruch arranged for his friend to travel to his relatives on the other side of the border. There he was secretly circumcised and became a full-fledged Jew.

The Commercial Register and the Obligation to Keep Commercial Books.

[Sosnowiec — economy and trade; lecture.]
Lecture by Adv. A. Kahn at the premises of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association in Sosnowiec.
(S.) In connection with the entry into force of the Commercial Code on the 1st of July this year, a lecture by Adv. A. Kahn on the subject „The commercial register and the obligation to keep books“ was held on the initiative of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association.
The chairman Józef Safer opened the meeting and gave the floor to Adv. Kahn, who delivered an interesting two-hour talk.
Under Art. 280 of the Commercial Code — Adv. Kahn began — one can be punished with 6 months' arrest for not keeping books. The question then arises: who must keep books under the new law? Registered merchants are obliged to keep books. Until now almost all merchants were registered. From the 1st of July a change takes effect, so that not everyone who — as was the practice until now — bought a patent [trade licence] counts as a merchant. Today the matter looks different: only the merchant who runs large businesses will have to register. The supplementary regulations, which have only just appeared, say that larger businesses means those whose turnover exceeds one hundred thousand zł. a year. The smaller merchants need not register.
But the merchants who are registered must keep proper commercial books. The law provides that books must be kept by trade categories one and two (in the second, if the turnover exceeds one hundred thousand zł.) and by industry of categories 1 to 5. While a large part of the merchants (small traders) are exempt from registering, all kinds of partnership businesses must nevertheless be registered. The court can also compel registration, and that with sanctions (a fine of up to 500 zł.). The registration will also be different from before. Until today a booklet was kept in which the firms were noted; now there will be a book and files in which everything that takes place in the business will have to be found. Every year the balance sheet with the inventory will have to be added to the files. But every business has its secrets; the business[?] [probably: the law] foresees this, and not everyone will be able to access the files.
A great change has also come about regarding marriage settlements (intercyza): today, if a registered merchant does not report a marriage settlement, the merchant's wife may do so, and at any time.
We also find an interesting thing in the new Commercial Code, among others: nowhere is it mentioned that the books must be laced [and sealed]. For merchants who keep commercial books this is a very important matter, because until now the tax offices, in order to stamp the books, held them back for several days.
Responsibility for the books is borne jointly by the merchant and the bookkeeper. The bookkeeper must sign the balance sheet and the inventory. The books must be kept in the Polish language; an exception can also be made, but in any case it must be in Latin script.
The books with the documents (letters, invoices, etc.) must be kept for ten years.
Adv. Kahn also spoke about the technical side of how to register, as well as the advantages that registration can bring the merchant, and advised every merchant, in order to become better acquainted with the new commercial law, to obtain the „Dz. Ustaw“ [Dziennik Ustaw, the law gazette] nos. 57, 59 and 60, where the whole law is published.
The numerous assembled merchants applauded the esteemed speaker for his interesting exposition, and the chairman, city councillor Mr.[?] J. Safer, closed the meeting.
Radio Corner.

[Radio.]
Some remarks and instructions on how to install an aerial correctly.
The most important component of every set, and especially of a detector [crystal] set, is the aerial and the earthing. The radio listener must pay close attention to these two things in case one begins to hear worse in the earphones[?]. In that case one must first of all check whether the aerial or the „earth“ is in order. It is therefore advisable, when installing a new aerial, to keep to the following rules:
1) The aerial must be installed as high as possible.
2) The aerial must not touch any objects on its way, such as the roof, chimney, gutter, a tree or another aerial.
3) For each type of set the length of the aerial must be different. For detector sets the aerial must be 40—50 metres long (including the lead-in wire); two- and three-valve sets require a somewhat shorter aerial of 30 to 40 metres, and multi-valve sets — only a short one, no more than a 15—10-metre aerial.
4) The ends of the aerial must be well insulated with the help of the so-called porcelain eggs. These insulators must not be strung with wire, only with rope.
5) The lead-in wire of the aerial must, at the place where it passes[?] through the window, be well insulated with the help of a rubber-ebonite[?], porcelain or glass tube. The lead-in wire must be as short as possible; the wires connecting the set with the aerial must also be short.
6) If wires of the electric network, telephone or telegraph are not far from the aerial, one must try to keep the aerial as far as possible from these wires and at a cross [perpendicular] direction. In any case not parallel.
7) After the end of the radio broadcast one must not forget to disconnect the aerial.
The danger of lightning.
Day in, day out we hear at the end of the broadcast the announcer's words: „After the end of the broadcast the aerial must be earthed.“ But[?] not all radio listeners want to comply with this instruction, and most of the time people go to sleep forgetting to disconnect the aerial. This is, however, certainly[?] a mistake that can sometimes have the most fatal consequences.
There have already been cases where lightning struck an aerial, causing a fire; therefore many people have little trust in roof aerials, and others, still greater cowards, prefer to give up listening to the radio altogether rather than be exposed to the danger of lightning.
This standpoint, however, is entirely wrong. It is superfluous now to point out the great advantages that a roof aerial has for good radio reception. We would rather show what must be done to prevent the roof aerial from leading the lightning into the house.
The reader is probably already familiar with the task and function of lightning conductors. Copper or iron rods ending in a point are set up on the roofs of houses. The other end of the rod is connected to the earth by means of a thick wire.
The great masses of electricity that gather in the air, especially during a storm, constantly seek a way to unite with the electricity of the earth. Such a lightning conductor therefore makes it possible for the lightning to have the easiest and shortest way to the earth; this is precisely what protects the house from lightning.
The roof aerial fulfils the same task as a lightning conductor, but much better and more safely, since the aerial consists of a long wire, and the electric charges found in the air can easily „float down“ to the earth. The aerial does not allow many electric charges to accumulate above it at all, since they are conducted through it without pause to the earth. But this can only happen when the aerial is connected to the earth. That is why it is so important that during a storm the aerial be connected to the earth. Therefore one must do the same before going to sleep, since a storm may break out at night. If we keep exactly to this rule, one can be sure that the lightning will avoid the house and that no danger whatsoever will threaten from the roof aerial.

Greetings via the „Zeppelin“

[Zagłębie — personalities; aviation.]
As we have already written, President Fürstenberg travelled on business on the airship „Zeppelin“ to Brazil and Argentina.
Because of the great interest the journey[?] aroused among the inhabitants of Zagłębie, we found it necessary to inform ourselves about the outcome and course of the air journey.
From the information we received from Mrs. President Fürstenberg we learn a number of interesting details of the journey. In the letter which the „Zeppelin“ sent from Brazil to Friedrichshafen, Mr. Fürstenberg gives brief details of the great technical wonder that the human mind has created. The „Zeppelin“ carries 24 passengers, among them 3 women. The crew consists of 45 persons; the Zeppelin is 236 metres long.
The return of President Mr. Fürstenberg is expected around the 14th of this month.

A Time to Keep Silent, and a Time to Speak...

[Letter to the editor — Zagłębie; the press.] (A letter to the editors).
A large part of the Jews of Zagłębie have probably read the praises and seen the gallery of pictures in the illustrated supplement of the "Nasz Przegląd" number devoted especially to Zagłębie, about the life and work of a series of personalities who have built and created for Zagłębie, and for us Jews in particular.
The "Zagłębie number", however, aroused bitterness in the writer of these lines, and also in hundreds of people among the inhabitants of Zagłębie (so I believe): how can it be that the editors of a supposedly serious newspaper allow themselves to publish photographs of people who are not at all worthy of it, of "lo amar klum" [nobodies] people, whose only "merits" consist in having money and being able to pay for the honour... This is simply a base impudence, for a large part of the photographs are, for us Jews of Zagłębie, a compromising embarrassment and a loss of dignity before the outside world; one's face turns red with shame when one sees that among [printed "tsayshn"] exceptional people who truly earned it there are people who have created nothing and, what is more, stand far from Jewish public life. It is a scandal crying to heaven, what the above-mentioned editors have permitted themselves — for where are the founders and leaders of the charitable associations, the kehilla heads, representatives of numerous Będzin and Sosnowiec public activists, the veteran Zionist workers, the pioneers of the Jewish public and national life of Zagłębie?
Then a second scandal and a plain desecration of God's name: if the editors wished to immortalise also those who dwell in the dust, why then did they profane the honour of such proud and influential Jews, Torah scholars, as R' Berish Preger[?], R' Yeshaya Hendl Erlich, R' Ber Halpson, R' Leibish Dimant and the like, who are dear to all of us; and instead of them, the true notables of Zagłębie, they sold themselves to "idolatry" and for pennies put before the outside world such people as are known for their wickedness and cruelty, far from Jewish life and alien to the Jewish community.
Let the esteemed readers of the newspaper not suspect me of having some personal stake in this matter... (by the way, those who know me will not do so...) for I express my indignation, and also that of many hundreds of people, the present residents of Bystra, who turned to me as one who has always had, and still has, the warmest interest in Jewish life in Zagłębie. [We] have the courage to come out against the disgrace that the editors of "Nasz Przegląd" have caused the Jewry of Zagłębie with the 47 photographs.
— A time to keep silent and a time to speak!
Respectfully,
Shloyme Frenkel.
A Priest Comes to the Częstochowa Rabbi to Study a Chapter of Mishnah

[Częstochowa — Jews and Christians.] On Tuesday during the day the priest of the parish of Rushetshkovitse[?] [perhaps Rększowice], near Wieluń, came to the home of the Częstochowa rabbi with the request that he explain to him a number of laws that were binding on the service in the Temple on the festival of Sukkot. On this occasion the priest explained that he understands Hebrew and wishes to become acquainted with the original text of these laws in the Mishnah, which he needs for a work he is writing.
Since the rabbi is staying at his summer residence, the rabbi's son, "adt."[?] Leib Asch, took out a Mishnah, a Gemara with commentaries, and together with the priest became immersed in the laws of the water libation and of the Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing (Simchat Beit HaSho'eva).
The priest thereby displayed a sufficient expertise regarding Jewish laws and customs in the time of the Second Temple.
On leaving, the priest thanked him and expressed himself in Hebrew: "From all my teachers I have gained understanding" [Psalms 119:99].
Zagłębie Has Won a Victory..

[Bystra — summer resort; dance contest.] At the dance contest in Bystra...
Last Saturday night a "dancing" [dance evening] took place at Szarewski's[?] "Gan Eden Vinkl" ["Paradise Corner"] in Bystra. Naturally, when the guests from Zagłębie heard the good news, they ran there like pious women to the first Selichot. Everyone hurried ahead and wanted to grab a "little table" at the great celebration.
And to tell the truth, it is no wonder the dancing "drew" so much: this time the dancing was not an ordinary one, as on all the days "of the whole year" — this night[?] a dance contest took place at the dancing...
Several "panienki" [young ladies] from Zagłębie and also professional dancers entered the contest.
And when the jury declared that the contest should be won by a Sosnowiec girl, a "va-yitz'aku" [great outcry] began that the contest belonged to a professional dancer.
In connection with this, two "fronts" were formed, one of amateur dancers and the other of professionals.
The "battle" was a passionate one, because some of the Zagłębie guests were not "neutral" in this matter and secretly supported the side of the professional dancers, who are not residents of Zagłębie. It was little short of a fratricidal war breaking out between the guests from Będzin, Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa, but thanks to the energetic stance of the committee the conflict was settled; what is more, the side of the amateur dancers won a victory, and the dance prizes were taken by Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — Lipiny; attempted suicide.]
Out of Despair She Jumped from the First Floor.
On Tuesday a Jewish woman jumped from the first floor of a flat in Lipiny and was injured.
As we are informed, the woman wanted to commit suicide because of the following circumstances: a year ago the would-be suicide was taken on as a servant by a certain family. After a year's time the servant was due to become a mother. For that purpose she was admitted to the local clinic, where she gave birth to a child.
After leaving the clinic she came with the child to her employers, asking for support from her "breadgiver" [employer], whom she suspects of being a bit of an "in-law" to the child [i.e. its father]. But for this "audacity"[?] the young mother was set upon by the accused party, who started to beat her. Finding herself then in a desperate situation, she ran to the window and jumped down onto the pavement. The unfortunate woman was then taken to hospital and the child was given to a nursemaid.

A Jewish community with a Christian "mikveh-keeper"..

Not far from Strzemieszyce there is a Jewish settlement in Niemce. The local community consists of 35 Jewish families in all. And since a community needs a mikveh, an arrangement was made with a local Christian, who made.. a mikveh in his house, which was leased out to a Jewish shoemaker.
And it came to pass one day that the shoemaker takes leather on credit from Mr. R. and does not want to pay. The merchant argues: how can this be? Why don't you pay me the debt? The mikveh-keeper answers: money I have none, but I allow you and your family to go into the mikveh until the debt is amortized. And so it was: the leather merchant used the mikveh and the debt grew ever smaller.
Last Friday the "mikveh agreement" broke down and at the same time brought harm to all the Jews of Niemce. It happened because the leather merchant "engaged" his whole family into the mikveh, to which the mikveh-keeper did not agree. You may go — argues the debtor — but not your father-in-law and brothers-in-law. From words they passed to deeds, until the landlord came and locked up the mikveh.
In the shtetl darkness reigns. How can a community be without a mikveh? So a series of interventions began with the rabbi, and also, to make the distinction, with the Christian landlord, but without success. The rabbi is powerless against the forcefulness of the "revolutionaries", and the Christian threatens with... blows.
Fell asleep off the cart and was killed

The fruit dealer Paliwoda of Pilica was travelling to Będzin together with a peasant from the village of Sława. On the way both the Jew and the peasant who was driving the horses fell asleep — and while asleep the carter fell off the cart and was killed.
The Jew went on sleeping and the horses walked on without a driver. By chance peasants who were working in the field saw it and woke the Jew from his sleep; he ran back and found the carter lying dead on the road.
