"We Owe God Our Soul" — On the scandalous accusations by the Sosnowiec antisemites at the founding of the relief committee for the flood victims

It is, upon my life, a cheek with our little Jews — health to their little bones! How many times do we storm, rouse and plead that this or that necessary institution is on the verge of collapse, that this or that society, which does so much for the benefit of the broad strata, must close because the budget[?] is exhausted. But who listens to these "trifles", who stops to think about what the "fantasists" are saying there — and precisely because of this "intensity" we suffer constant ruin in the social-philanthropic field.
Yes, that is how it is when we speak to our brothers, when Jews come to Jews and show that we must save[?] what we still have and what is of use to us.
Quite different, however, is when people talk about us in the non-Jewish camp. Oh, then we jump out of our skin and beg with supplications that, for God's sake, they should accept[?] us and not have any bad opinion of us.
Last week a meeting was held in Sosnowiec at the Magistrate [town hall] on organising a local committee to help the victims of the floods. But it is an old rule that where it comes to deeds, one cannot manage without Jews. So voices were immediately heard: where, pray, are the Jews? Where is their representation? Why do they not show up? And a woman immediately began to preach that this was no wonder, because just as they give no money to the Fund for defence against the sea, just so they want to wriggle out here too.
Naturally it became "cosy"[?] in the hall. A trifle? Such a fat bone — and let it slip by as if it were nothing? Lively discussions took place, and it was resolved to adopt the strictest measures against us.
These reports were promptly worked up as they deserved — first by "our liberal" "Express", then by the "Kurier Zachodni" — as a tasty dish for their dear readers: see what little Jews these are, that whatever one says about them is still too little.
The Jewish public as well as its representation learned of the organising meeting precisely from those same newspapers. So nobody had been invited, and Jewish Sosnowiec knew nothing of the committee's creation.
But one is frightened of the squire. At once there was a storm among us; a large meeting was called in which all organisations took part, and it was unanimously resolved to declare to the editorial offices that they, that is we Jews, "owe God our soul". We would gladly take part in the necessary public campaign, and[?] that we did not come to the meeting is no fault of ours, because we knew nothing about anything.
So it came out as though one were swearing by beard and sidelocks and striving to prove that everything one says is truth and justice, and that, for God's sake, they should accept[?] and believe that it is as one says and that there were no bad intentions whatsoever.
That is how one defended oneself before those who seek at every opportunity to incite and provoke and to arouse hatred and bitterness between Jew and non-Jew. Further[?] than that, apparently, there was neither the courage nor the understanding to go. That is how one gets frightened, how one loses one's head when the squire speaks.
After all, we know that we fulfil all our duties beyond our strength. It is a rule that we take part in all campaigns as soon as they are launched. The latest flood catastrophe can serve as proof: before anyone even knew how great the disaster was, appeals were already appearing in the columns of our paper that we should donate money for the unfortunate families — that is, even before the local Polish newspapers had managed to do so, and even before the local committees were set up.
This proves, then, how great our feelings of compassion for the unfortunate are. Regarding the suffering, the poor and the unfortunate, we Jews do not know how to distinguish to which nationality they belong, and we do not want to know it at all. For us it is enough that a person has met with misfortune to rescue him.
And if people come who want to satisfy their antisemitic instincts with the help of the unfortunate and impoverished, we must have the courage to throw the lie in their faces and show them that they are not out here to fulfil the duty of human humanity. One can tell them that the strings[?] of suffering have not yet touched their hearts, since straight away in the sequel[?] antisemitism is already on their agenda, and they come along with the old, threadbare phrases that Jews always wriggle out of taking part in money campaigns.
Of course it would not have been necessary[?] to prove that we do take part in everything, because that is noticeable at every step. We pay taxes[?] whether we can or not; we fulfil our civic obligations beyond our strength. Honest, upright people who stand at the helm see that perfectly well.
What really hurts us is that when a meeting takes place in the City Council hall under the chairmanship of the municipal vice-commissioner, who is surely aware of our participation as citizens, this personage does not react to reproaches that ought to have no place there. It means that those others have grounds to preach the antisemitism they need even at such a time, when we are being shunned, and when time had not yet shown that we refuse to take part in the necessary campaign.
The Jewish citizens of Sosnowiec rightly feel hurt when they see that groundless reproaches are being made at their address and there is no one to defend them and stand up for their honour, at a time when we were not given the possibility of being represented there.
Thus we see[?], for example, that at the same time such a committee was also set up in neighbouring Będzin, and since the Jews were not avoided there, a joint, peaceful work began at once.
There is a clique of Jew-eaters who will themselves never give anything. They will wriggle out at every opportunity. On the other hand they understand perfectly how to raise a storm so that people forget about them[?]; and to be left in peace one needs no fatter bone than antisemitism, which is at all times topical and modern.
And if at such a time one resorts to this means, and has the courage to accuse us and to incite against us just when we are being shunned, we must react to it and not prove that "we owe God our soul".
If we know that we fulfil our civic duties, take part in everything the country and the state need, stand on guard and protect the necessary interests, then we must also have the courage not to allow hatred and poison to be sown in the Polish ranks.
And if people come along who preach openly that we now want to wriggle out, just as we did at the time of the Maritime Defence Fund, we must react properly to such incitements.
Words that are spoken and popularised in public, over there[?] in a city council, take on a public character. Moreover, by the next day they are worked up in the Polish press in such a way that they certainly bring us neither honour nor benefit. To such deeds we must absolutely react as is proper.
Of course we are used to all sorts of chicanery and libels, to which we do not react; it often does not even occur to the Jewish public to take the lies seriously. We have suffered and toiled too much in our long history of exile to take to heart every chicanery hurled at Jewish heads. Yet one must know when and where to react, and when and where to pass by the provokers and inciters and proceed to our general order of the day.
Now, when it is a matter of a national catastrophe which has unfortunately flooded a part of the country, which we feel together with all the citizens of the country, and at such a moment accusations are thrown at us that we want to hide, etc., we must throw back the bullets aimed at our camp with the sole intention of provoking frictions and libels between us and our neighbours.
Jewish Sosnowiec must lodge the strongest protest against such incitements, and our communal workers must call the "sayers" to account, so that they know that we are not fair game for anyone who wishes to degrade our prestige and the honour of the Jewish people.
Dr. Papuri.
Two Marranos (5)

[Serialized story — Nazi Germany; installment 5.]
Chaim Berg.
A story from Nazi Germany.
5)

These very feelings had long since awakened in the great-great-grandson of Abraham Senior; the Hitler inquisition of the year 1933 gave them the last mighty push, and from that push there was born in the marquis the passionate urge to taste it, to live through the pain and the state of mind of a Marrano in the cellars of Torquemada's Inquisition.
The first taste the marquis felt under the rubber whip with the lead knob at its end, with which the policeman in the brown shirt had set about tormenting his body. When he brought the bloodied and stunned[?] Jew with the plucked-out beard into his car — how sweet, though, were the blows of the whip that had cut into his body! Not for nothing had he kept silent!... He had wanted to take in as many of them as possible, to sate himself with the sweet pain... And when the Jew, in his car, with bitter weeping threw himself at his hands to kiss them, he embraced him, pressed him to his breast like a brother and wept together with him, with the tears of a mother who has rescued her son from the murderous hands of a Torquemada...
Yes, German diplomacy made a great mistake when it believed that the guard of detectives would protect the Spanish diplomat from similar incidents in the future. In his present state of mind the marquis needed martyrdom at the hands of the Nazis as a balm for his soul.
And he did not have to look for it long in Hitler-land. Before the assigned detectives had had time to take up their watch, the marquis was already on the way to his adventures. The plan of voluntary martyrdom quickly took concrete form[?]. That night a famous opera singer, a good friend of his, whom he had met on a sea voyage, was to appear at a charity concert.
The singer was of Jewish descent. On the day before the incident with the brown fellows[?] he had had supper with her in one of the famous Berlin hotels and warned her not to appear at the concert, because the Nazis would surely whistle her down, if not pelt her with rotten eggs. The prima donna, however, laughed at his warnings.
She... she laughed: why[?] Ha-ha-ha! She will open her mouth, let out a few nightingale trills, and even the Nazis will be bewitched by her singing and applaud her! Has she sung only once at their charity concerts? Ha-ha-ha! Besides, what kind of Jewess is she? Her mother a Christian, the daughter of a German general and former wife of a German baron; her father, the second husband of her Christian mother, is indeed of Jewish descent, but long since a Christian, and on top of that a professor of chemistry with a Nobel Prize, who distinguished himself in the war and made so many sacrifices for the fatherland. 2 sons, her brothers, fell on the battlefield, and with his scientific inventions her father helped the fatherland in the war more than a whole army. Besides, she is in full accord with the Nazis, and some of the leaders, her personal and best friends, know it..
But when the marquis, after the [—] visit, read in the evening papers that her father, the [world-famous?] professor and Nobel laureate, had resigned from his post, and when he read the comments of the Nazi press on the resignation, he recalled, with a broken-off word, the confidence of the singer with the Nazi sympathies... Now, even more than back when he had warned her, he was certain that the Nazis would drive her off the stage with an ugly scandal, that she needed his protection and that he must be present at the concert.
The marquis did not even change into theatre clothes — too little time was left him for that; he left the legation in great haste, but deliberately took a taxi and not his own car, which could have been recognised by the police, and went off to the theatre where the concert was to be given.

The Mysterious Laboratory
When the marquis drove up to the theatre it was already too late... The scandal had played out very quickly, at the first moment when the curtain rose and the prima donna appeared before the Nazi audience. The taxi in which the marquis came could no longer stop in front of the theatre door; the whole street between the door and the taxi was blocked by a large crowd. At the moment he jumped out of the taxi he saw from afar how the theatre's uniformed attendants[?] were leading a woman's figure down the steps by the arms — they were carrying her more than leading her... A second woman followed and wept hysterically. Her weeping was drowned in the caterwauling with which the Nazis in the crowd pursued the two women, hidden by the crowd, which recalled a wild mob of human beasts in a Roman circus watching[?] wild animals tear living people apart. The marquis could not see[?] who the second woman was, the prima donna's mother or her maid. All the blood rushed to his brain and his face at the wild, barbaric scene. He began to push with both elbows and make his way towards the two women through the packed crowd, but the crowd jostled him and pushed him back, and before he reached the car into which the half-fainting prima donna had been carried, policemen shut the car door and, standing on the running boards on both sides, led it out of the wild human crush.
The marquis ran to the taxi and ordered the driver to follow and not lose the car; to make a quick way through the crowd was impossible; the taxi had to turn round and take a detour, and in the time he lost on the detour the car vanished...
The marquis gave the driver the address of the prima donna's flat. The taxi arrived there ahead of the car. But the car never arrived there that night.
Professor H., the prima donna's father, did not live in Berlin all year round, but on his estate, which lay about 50 kilometres from Berlin. To his lectures he used to drive every day by car and stay at the university only as long as his lectures lasted.
The Leaders Pay with Their Lives

[World — politics; article.]
Viewing from afar the latest wild events in Central Europe, it seems as if before our eyes the titanic struggle between Gog and Magog had begun to flare up — the struggle that is to serve as a harbinger of the final redemption of the world; but the fighting sides are not some [?] two giant empires: one side is the popular masses of the countries, and the other side — the leaders of those very same countries. It looks as if before our eyes a decisive, final battle had begun to unfold between the peoples and their leaders — over the power that should and can bring the world the true peace of complete rest, tranquillity and plenty.
We are living now in a time of neither war nor peace, which in certain respects is even worse than war. In war the masses make enormous efforts, under the rod of the military drivers, in expectation of a speedy peace and victory. Here, however, there are supposedly no drivers, no bloodshed; the masses look as if bathed in comfortable peacefulness — but there is no peace, no security, no calm and... no bread to eat.
In the great World War there was one side that won [?] in all nations and countries — the broad popular masses, who everywhere drove out or killed the crowned rulers and chose from among themselves, believing that by holding the reins in their own hands, in the hands of their own chosen ones, it would be possible to restore the longed-for peace and secure for everyone a quiet piece of bread. For greater security the great empires were broken up into small countries, so that the self-determination of the peoples might find sharper expression — peoples who are once again supposed to secure for the common man everywhere his quiet livelihood.
But when this did not happen, when gradually one country after another began to be convinced that the peoples themselves, through the strength of their representatives, are not capable of disentangling themselves from the hard problems of war and peace and of securing for themselves the longed-for perfect rest, there appeared in every country heroic leaders, who took upon themselves the mission of dictating to the people its conduct, showing it the right way and forcing it to walk the straight path for its own happiness and well-being; the peoples, feeling their hopeless [?] situation, renounced their political freedoms and submitted to the power of the dictators, who wanted [?] to bring them salvation.
But year after year goes by and the problem does not begin to untangle itself; on the contrary, it seems to grow ever more entangled. Who here has the ill will that strives precisely once again to drown the world in a sea of human blood? It is hard to give an objective answer to that. Most of all to blame is the system of leadership, which still — despite the dictatorship — is built on demagogy, on deceiving and inciting the masses; talking them round and turning their heads, in order to divert the popular anger against [?] those who have undertaken [the task] and are unable to create in the world an atmosphere of calm and peacefulness, secured for a longer time.
And so one sees how lately, here and there, bloody attempts are made to tear the reins by force out of the leaders' hands. The direct causes may be different everywhere, according to the particular circumstances in the particular countries — but taken in general and in essence the cause is one and the same: to remove the incapable leaders from the helm and to give the people, on a better path, the longed-for life of tranquillity and livelihood.
It comes out as though the masses were saying [?] to the leaders: you toil in vain and cannot create any real peace for us; the end of your leadership will be that you will drag us into a war again and drown us in our own blood — so we had better remove you and try to take over the reins ourselves, and if you will not go by fair means, we will clear you away by force.
It need not everywhere be the masses themselves, or their beloved, faithful representatives, who settle accounts in blood with the present leaders; but everywhere the bloody struggle for leadership goes on and the blood of the leaders is shed, as if there were somewhere a higher power that has decided that rather than millions being slaughtered on the battlefields, it is better to bring the individuals as sacrifices; perhaps there will yet come such as will be able to protect the world from the horrible bloodshed.
Whether it will really succeed — to protect the world — no one can foretell, but in the bloody events one can see this deep meaning of history.
P. K.
Floods. (A Little Feuilleton).

[Będzin — feuilleton.] Nothing else but that the Almighty has grown angry at our little world, which somehow does not behave in order, and to frighten folk a little He opened a small window in heaven and sent down upon the world a flood in miniature, as a trial...
Not a day passes without a downpour. Without hail drumming, without poor cellar dwellings being flooded.
The grain in the fields is rotting.
Peasants look at the black clouds and cross themselves — they fear a famine. Foolish shopkeepers, men and women, look sweetly content [?]; they dream of high prices, when they [?] will be able to pull off a "pasek" [profiteering] and get rich — and we become ever more flooded and drenched.
The misfortune is great, because a water flood is no toy; it is a natural catastrophe, and that is what we least expected. Besides, we are not used to it.
Until now we were used to other kinds of floods.
We were flooded with brand-new "benefactors" and "public workers"...
We were swamped by a new wave of party people of every kind, who display hundred-percent idealism, want to do Jewry a great favour and sacrifice themselves to go to the Land of Israel with a certificate. And meanwhile make a good match and actually live in Tel Aviv...
Here it flooded so much that we were flooded by a wave of "philanthropists" and Zagłębie bigwigs, "representatives", "intelligentsia" and who knows what other plagues sent by His dear Name, who brought into our little world a "tohu-vavohu", a chaos without a way out.
True, we are indeed sinful, but it seems that with the flood of uninvited "benefactors" and such [?] "intellectuals" we have already been punished enough for our sins, and the flood of rains and storms may well stop now...
———
My neighbour Reb Berish is a pious Jew, and he understands the cause of the floods in his own way:
— The world — says Reb Berish — is sinful, and it becomes especially sinful in summer, when bathing season comes and women and men lie on the beaches naked as Adam; the evil inclination runs wild [?] there and does [?] all kinds of evil...
That is precisely why the rains, floods and storms broke out exactly in beach season, so that the "naked crowd" should know that the world is not lawless... And the proof
— Reb Berish adds — only those areas have been flooded where there are dachas and beaches: Krynica, Szczawnica, Świder; and where there are no lakes [?] and beaches, it is dry and nobody splashes in water...
So says Reb Berish; he sees in the floods "the finger of God" — God's punishment, and therefore he prays day and night that our Zagłębie be spared a flood, because in [—?] many "fine deeds" would float up to the surface, of which we know nothing to this day.
But he need not fear, Reb Berish, for there will be no floods on the Będzin hill.. Będzin is altogether an extraordinary town — on the contrary, what do you think?
Ha-Tsofe.

Heard and Seen.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

The verse has come true...
The saying — "Money answers all things" — has always been incomprehensible to me. These words sound somehow strange, for is the rule not enough:
— "Silver and gold purify bastards"? Why did King Solomon pack [?] almost the same thought into the words that "money excuses everything"? It is, after all, almost one and the same? Either way: if bastards are purified by silver and gold, whom else does the verse mean by "all"?
This constant question has been clearly answered for me, thanks to the editors of the Jewish-Polish newspaper
"Nasz Przegląd"...
The gentlemen of that editorial board did not want to shame the Zagłębie readers of their paper, and presented them with a gift that will also be immortalised in history: they published a special issue devoted to Zagłębie.
What is more, since the eyes of all Jews, and of Zagłębie too, are now turned towards the Land of Israel, the editors "united" Zagłębie with Eretz Israel and gave the "gift" the name:
"Zagłębie-Palestine".
The "juxtaposition of passages" [?] of this is probably known only to the great men of the aforementioned paper, but to us simple flesh-and-blood it is incomprehensible, just like the saying.
— "Money answers all things"...
We mention this only in passing. Our only aim [?] is to give a hearty yishar koach to the aforementioned editors for the untiring effort and work (which truly lasted many weeks...) around the historical materials, such as monographs, autobiographies, so as to have a clear picture of who were, and who still are, the builders of Zagłębie, the meritorious people in the field of philanthropy, art, industry, each with his photograph, (there are also man and wife...) only the exception was made for the very great "donors", i.e. the well-known magnates of Zagłębie with open hands...). Let the great wide world indeed see what Zagłębie possesses and who its representatives are. We are firmly convinced that thanks to the "historic" issue of "Nasz Przegląd" the opinion held until now abroad will be changed — that Zagłębie possesses nothing but coal, coke, ironworks and the like — rather, that Zagłębie possesses a series of interesting personalities whom nobody knew and of whose merits for Jewish society nobody had heard; and above all, through this revelation we have only now understood the true meaning of "Money answers all things".
Yes, gentlemen.
— The verse has come true...

"Atah-bechartanu-niks"... [a mocking Slavic-style plural from "Thou hast chosen us"]
In the latest issue of "Ba-Derekh" [?] we read an article by the Hebrew writer Zvi Rumld [?]. In the article the author brings a few "little flowers" which you will not find [?] among any nation or tongue, only among our brethren the Children of Israel. Among other things he relates that in Zakopane the Jewish guesthouses stand empty, whereas the guesthouses famous for their antisemitism, those that welcomed Hitlerite guests with swastika flags — are overflowing with Jewish guests...
Such a "little flower", only of a different colour, I happened to see in Bystra.
Schoolgirls of a private gymnasium in Warsaw came to Bystra. With the large number of schoolgirls, daughters of Israel only, came also their educators — after all, one cannot leave Jewish girls, grown-up ones, without proper supervision, especially in a strange environment.
— Do you know who the educators of the Jewish daughters are? — a resident of Bystra asks me.
— Probably someone from the school's management — is my answer.
— True, from the management, the director himself, the supervisor over the Jewish daughters, is a guardian; and for greater force, so that the education be complete, the Mrs. Director is a born Christian.
Well, show me, if you please, another such nation or tongue that would be so "loyal" to its neighbours, that would push itself where it is not wanted, where it is laughed at, and that would entrust the education of its children to those who hate it, persecute it and invent the most terrible blood libels. No, you will not see this among any people, only among those who were crowned with the title:
— Atah-bechartanu-niks...

Not of today's world...
In a youthful company — more precisely, a modern company — the young ladies with cigarettes in their painted little mouths were discussing topical summer-house [?] problems: for example, at which dancing the music is better, what the most modern pyjamas should look like, and about the "exercises" [?] of the "...-boys" [?] in the pool.
The young men, for their part, argued about sports matters, which sports "club" will take the championship of Zagłębie; others ventured to tell about "...s" [?], about some "..." [?] and also "..." [?] etc. etc. [?]
In the modern youth company there were also two [?] young men, one studying medicine and the other philology.
— "We beg your pardon," the young men said to the modern youth company, "we must break off for a short time, because
— we must pray Mincha"...
— "Co takiego?!" [What?!] — asked one of the ladies' set, a dressed-up [?] "panienka" [young lady] — "Kto to jest ten Mincha?!" [Who is this Mincha?!]
Soon she and her girlfriends too realised "who this Mincha is"?!, for the two young men had gone to stand in a corner and were praying.
One by one the merry company dragged itself out of the room. They deeply regretted that they, who belong to the modern youth, had spent several hours in the "towarzystwo" [?] [company] of such "fanatical" young men, who, not only do they have no idea about the tango or décolleté pyjamas, can hardly whistle a modern hit, dance — know nothing at all about a "goal" — and then suddenly they go and stand by the wall and
— "modlą się" [pray]...
— "Słuszna racja" [quite right] — modern "culture" has not yet penetrated the "ludność żydowska" [Jewish population]. Among the youth, too, there is still a large part that is not conscious.
— Not of today's world.
Jewish Crafts and the Jewish Craftsman

It is clear to everyone that there can be no Jewish crafts without a Jewish craftsman. If Jewish society has lately been sounding the alarm about the danger facing Jewish crafts, it follows as a matter of course that the Jewish craftsman, too, is in great peril.
Nevertheless, we must keep apart these two notions: the danger threatening Jewish crafts with ruin, and the situation of the Jewish craftsman.
Saving Jewish crafts in general can and must be the task of the whole of Jewish society, because the existence of us Jews depends to the greatest degree on a healthy economic structure of the Jewish population, and the healthy economic factor has been until now, and will remain for many, many years to come — Jewish crafts.
On the other hand, dealing with the extraordinarily difficult, truly tragic situation of the Jewish craftsman must be left exclusively to the craftsmen's central organisation with all its agencies, such as: Jewish craftsmen's associations, guilds, craftsmen's co-operatives, banks, etc.
The government, together with society as a whole, is interested in and obliged to care for the state of health of the entire country; yet every doctor, pharmacist, feldsher and the like must himself take care of his own personal, day-to-day livelihood.
A whole series of Jewish public organisations and activists have come to the conclusion that unless extraordinary measures are taken, Jewish crafts will perish within 10—20 years. To prevent this, one must make the widest possible use of the right that the amended law grants craftsmen, namely that until 1 January 1935 they may register their workshops, which would otherwise be recognised as not legal.
It seems a simple matter and truly a vital necessity for Jews in general. Keeping a non-legalised workshop will mean the same as trading illegally on Sunday nowadays, no more — with the sad difference that the craftsman's "Sunday" will last from Sunday morning until Saturday night, and this will apply to tens of thousands of Jewish craftsmen.
In a number of towns some consultations on this matter have taken place, and naturally the craftsmen's activists are in favour of legalising the workshops that are not legal today. But at the same time they have put forward a proviso that only the workshops that existed up to the year 1927 can be legalised — but what are those from the later years to do? On the contrary, give them work in your own workshops, and they will liquidate their workshops with great pleasure.
But our craftsmen do not want to reckon with the fact that these new workshops are precisely a consequence of their having themselves dismissed their old journeymen from the workshops for lack of work, and now they count on getting rid, in this way, of unwanted young competitors. Perhaps from a purely personal craftsman's standpoint this is good, but for the Jewish community as a whole it is a misfortune, and here precisely one must place the point of rescue — the craft — above the interests of the craftsman.
But we can, with a clear conscience, reassure the craftsmen that their situation is hard not because there are too many workshops, but because the living standard of the population has fallen, and consequently our craftsmen cannot be given as much work as they could do, nor the prices they ought to receive. That is the source of the craftsman's sad situation, and by no means the so-called "non-legal workshops".
* * *
Certainly we are interested in improving the living conditions of our craftsmen; certainly they must be helped in every way in their bitter struggle for a crust of bread. But first of all Jewish society as a whole faces the task of saving Jewish crafts as such, and if this should "at certain moments" lead to "delicate" conflicts with the craftsmen's activists, they will have to forgive, and what must be done will be done without any hesitation in order to save Jewish crafts from ruin.
Mag. M. Balberyszski.
How the Japanese Are Flooding the World

Decades have passed since Europe was suddenly flooded by thousands upon thousands of little Japanese, all with a sugar-sweet little smile on their faces; in all the large European cities they were to be seen at every step, and nobody knew what they had actually come for, what they were doing and what they wanted. It was said: they are studying. But what they were studying nobody knew, and nobody took them seriously either. They were regarded as inferior.
Only now does one realise what they have done. They spied in all the European industries, pushed their way in everywhere and obtained what they wanted, and at home they slowly, slowly began to work out everything they had seen in the European world.
And since the Japanese have no needs whatsoever, neither cultural ones nor as regards food, they make all our industrial goods almost for nothing, and they spread all their articles so cheaply that the whole world stands at a loss what to do. It is enough if we give a few examples:
The most expensive books of world literature, in all the languages of the world, they have photographed, and they spread these same books so cheaply that the publisher himself has to charge ten times as much for them.
Electric bulbs are sold for one American cent apiece, while all the factories in the whole world cannot sell the same bulbs for less than fifteen cents apiece.
Rubber coats for gentlemen or ladies they sell at fifty American cents, while other factories cannot sell them, from the same material, for less than three to four dollars.
Silk fabric they already sell at twenty American cents a metre. The great silk factories of Lyon cannot supply the fabric in the same quality for less than a dollar.
Toothbrushes cost about three cents apiece. The same quality costs anywhere else at least ten times as much.
Thus they spread one article after another so cheaply that the whole commercial world is raising an outcry about the catastrophe with which the entire world economy is threatened by the little Japanese, who for decades spied out everything among us — how we make it — in order now to ruin Europe economically and to strangle it.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
"Holidays" (Yamim Tovim).

Grey, humdrum and monotonous is our present life.
But I must admit and confess that these words still fall far short of expressing what you and I think of today's wretched life — unless [?] we perhaps make use of such a rich vocabulary as: hell-ridden, gnawed-away, despairing, tormented, darkened, worry-laden and nightmarish is our life; it presents a trampled, crushed [?], rotten [?], abysmal [?], foolishly petty episode [?] in its entire height, length and breadth.
Well, now the essence of our modern life is clear to you?
It was therefore a stroke of genius to gladden the citizens' hearts from time to time with newly created "holidays," which refresh and distract them, so that one forgets a little the hard times that weigh so mercilessly on the spirit.
Thus we have had a "Sea Day" [Święto Morza], now we have a "Warsaw holiday," a "Mountain holiday," and so on.
These "holidays" are warmly welcomed by everyone, and hearts fill with deep gratitude to their initiators. One need only extend them and adapt them more closely to the vital needs of today's sorely tried and exhausted people. In that way there is still room for many, many useful holidays, namely:
A "Taxes Holiday" [podatki]. The tax office exempts all merchants and manufacturers from all sorts of taxes for four weeks. During this holiday the bailiffs are sent off to rest somewhere in the mountains or on a distant island; the "wagons" [used for seizures] are sent to the blacksmiths to be repaired. For four weeks there will be no assessments, no appeals to file; for four weeks no interest and penalties will accrue on overdue instalments and forgotten "reminders" [upomnienia]!
Just imagine what joy that would be — a true, heartfelt joy for hundreds of thousands of citizens. Their overwound and frayed [?] nerves would rest a little, and they would gather strength to keep dragging the yoke for a whole year. Why not faithfully arrange such a holiday for them — they fully deserve it...
A "Livelihood Holiday"
For so-and-so many weeks every citizen is provided with an abundant livelihood. You will [ask] how to do this — that is a somewhat more complicated question, which I do not undertake to answer; but surely the world does not lack brilliant minds, great economists; they would already devise something. The main thing is only to find the initiators, and the holiday would be created. And the citizens? Well, my pen is too poor to describe their feelings...
A "Land of Israel Holiday"
The British government, seeing the tremendous pressure of the Jewish people to go to the Land of Israel, declares such a holiday for a period of half a year. During this time it places its entire merchant and even naval fleet at the disposal of the Jewish people. Every Jew who has the least desire is carried over to Eretz Israel free of charge and without certificates, visas and other troubles, in great pomp. Half a year and no more. What harm would it do them, the gentlemen [?] English, if they granted us such a holiday? We have long since earned it. After such gigantic, superhuman efforts we are owed a bit of justice.
Who is against? Y. Tur.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Eikev)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Eikev
The Portion
—o—
a) "Thou shalt be blessed above all peoples" (Deut. 7:14)
"Above all peoples" — looking around at how bad other nations are, "thou shalt be blessed" — you may already count yourself blessed. With all our Jewish shortcomings we are still better than other nations... Noam Megadim.
* * *
"And Thy people Israel shall need neither one another nor any other people." — When a Jew comes before the heavenly court and is reproached for his sins, the angel Michael brings against him another Jew, a worse one. And when there is no worse one left, he brings against him a gentile, compared with whom even the worst Jew is still better...
But woe when one has to resort to that — when one has no good deeds of one's own at all and one only needs to show that there are worse ones still. "And Thy people Israel shall need neither one another nor any other people"... may they not need to resort to proving, by means of a gentile, that compared with a gentile they are still better... Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev.
—o—
b) "And He afflicted thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna" (8:3)
"From here [we learn] that women light the Sabbath candle."
A Midrash Peli'ah.
R' Chaim Yosef David Azulai (the Chida) explains this Midrash Peli'ah in his book "Birkei Yosef" in a witty way:
On the face of it the verse makes no sense: "And He afflicted thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna" — He tormented you, starved you and gave you the manna to eat. If they ate manna, then surely they were no longer hungry? But[?] "a blind man is never sated" — a blind man does not feel full. If one does not see with one's eye what one eats, one does not become full. And because they saw nothing at all in the manna, for its appearance was "like coriander seed, white" — they were hungry even though they ate it.
Therefore "from here [we learn] that women light the candle on the Sabbath": that is why on the Sabbath many candles are lit at the meal, so as to feel the abundance of the Sabbath meal, since light also has an effect on taste[?]...
—o—
[c)] "Thy raiment waxed not old upon thee" (ibid., 4)
In Berakhot (folio 6) the Gemara says: "The clothes of the Rabbis wear out — it is from their [the demons'] rubbing." The commentators explain: that is why the clothes of the Torah scholars are worn and torn, because it comes from the demons, who are envious of the scholars. And that is why the clothes of the scholars of former times were torn and tattered.
Nowadays, however, Torah scholars dress elegantly and nobody tears their clothes, because, as the Gemara says: "Why are the Torah scholars of Babylonia distinguished (in their dress)? — Because they are not [true] sons of Torah"; since the scholars of "Babylonia", like our scholars, were not sons of Torah, the demons are not envious of them and do not tear their clothes...
R' Tzvi Hirsch Veliger[?].
—o—
e) "Ye have been rebellious with the Lord" (9:24)
One can be a rebel "with the Name of God" — with God's name on one's lips. Supposedly one carries God's name on one's lips, and with that very name, under the mask of zeal for God, one does every kind of evil... Ma'adanei Melekh.
—o—
e) "What doth the Lord thy God require of thee" (as printed: 9:22; actually 10:12)
"'What doth the Lord thy God require of thee, but to fear' — is fear [of God] then a small thing? — Yes, for Moses it is a small thing"... Berakhot 33.
"For Moses" — in the generation of Moses, said Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev, when Jews openly saw so many miracles, the fear of God was indeed a small thing, a trifle; but today, when one sees no miracles — [—] You must forgive, Master of the Universe, when Jews are not such God-fearing people...
—o—
f) "And to serve Him with all your heart" (11:13)
"Service that is in the heart — that is prayer." Rashi.
The Chatam Sofer used to pray at great length. Once one of his pupils said to him:
Rabbi, in the time that you pray so long, you lose meanwhile a few folios of Gemara with Tosafot that you would have studied in that time.
The Chatam Sofer answered him:
The Gemara says: "He who prolongs his prayer, his days and years are prolonged." So I shall live longer because of praying at length. In the added days and years I shall manage to make up the folios of Gemara with Tosafot...
* * *
Rabbi Pinchas of Korets used to pray at daybreak. He used to say: I pray at dawn, before the world has yet been filled with follies...
—o—
g) "With all your heart and with all your soul" (ibid.)
Why does it not say "and with all your might", as it says in the first paragraph of the Shema?
But the first paragraph speaks of accepting the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, and for that a Jew must give up all his might, his entire fortune. Here it speaks only of a commandment, and for a commandment the law is that one is not obliged to spend more than a fifth of one's fortune on a commandment; that is why "and with all your might" is not said here... R' Yisraeltshe of Ruzhin.
—o—
h) "That your days may be multiplied" (ibid., 21)
Two things bring long life: Torah — "For by me thy days shall be multiplied" — and he who forgoes his grievances (see Chagigah 4[?]).
But the difference is this: long life through forgoing one's grievances can be reached only through quarrels (if one quarrels, then forgoing one's grievances becomes possible), whereas long life through Torah can come even when there is peace...
That is what the verse says: "My son, forget not my law... for length of days, and years of life, and p e a c e, shall they add to thee." Through Torah you can attain long life even in peace...
The Polish Jews in the Upbuilding of Eretz Israel

[Article — Eretz Israel, immigration and settlement; Polish Jews.]
By Dr. D. Cel-Cyjon (Tel Aviv).
On the activity of the new institution "Hashgacha".
(Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".)
The Polish Jews in Eretz Israel have for many years been taking a very active part in the upbuilding of Eretz Israel; thanks to the initiative of the Fourth Aliyah (1925—1926), which consisted mainly of Polish Jews, the work in Eretz Israel moved forward quickly and strongly, and the small part of the Yishuv that until then still believed that the national funds (KKL, Keren Hayesod) were the only and surest means of building became convinced, after the "experiment" of the year 1925—26, that the private capital and energy of individuals, united with an ideal of partnership, are far stronger and more direct [?] than national capital: after all, everyone has already realised that private initiative is a source of life and creativity, brings tempo and ambition into the work and opens new horizons for building and development.
The catastrophe that befell the Fourth Aliyah forced hundreds of Jews to leave Eretz Israel in haste, abandoning their goods and possessions. This catastrophe brought with it an even greater misfortune. The leaving of houses, plots, orange groves (pardesim), etc. without supervision in Eretz Israel created a "grab" system in the country, and whoever could, grabbed other people's property and lorded it over it as if it were his own; the property of those who for various reasons could not remain in Eretz Israel and look after their holdings themselves was literally robbed. It is not hard to compile a long list of hundreds of Jews who bought something in Eretz Israel, paid the necessary money for it, even received contracts and other "secure" documents, but [?] since the buyer remained in Poland while the seller and the land are in Eretz Israel, all the transactions ended in misfortune for the Polish Jews. The system of robbing private property has driven many Polish Jews away from the upbuilding of Eretz Israel and has robbed them of the desire to invest their capital in Eretz Israel enterprises, although in truth these bring very good and secure income; the "grab" system has rooted the conviction that in Eretz Israel injustice and lawlessness reign and that private property stands outside all law and protection.
The organisation of Polish Jews that exists in Eretz Israel, with its headquarters in Tel Aviv, saw in the "grab" phenomenon a great danger to the upbuilding of Eretz Israel, and for the purpose of combating it a special institution was created under the name "Hashgacha" ("Supervision"). At the head of the organisation of Polish Jews stands the well-known Zionist public figure, head of the Zionist Organisation in Warsaw, Mr. M. Y. Frajd, and this gives us still more confidence in the work.
Thus was created the important institution "Hashgacha", with the task of administering and supervising the goods and possessions of the Polish Jews in [printed "and"] Eretz Israel, combating lawlessness and thereby strengthening confidence in the country. The initiators set about their work with great energy, and within a short time they have already managed to accomplish a great deal. Thus an institution has been created that guides and teaches the new immigrant, protects him from mistakes, often rescues him from the hands of irresponsible brokers who lie in wait for him, think always only of their own profit and income, and often lead the "greenhorn" into bad deals; an institution has been created, of Polish Jews for Polish Jews, which guards his property like its own. "Hashgacha" is under the management of experts [?], under the supervision of the organisation of Polish Jews. The new immigrants, who until now went to Eretz Israel without any plan or order and often settled in places that were not at all suited for it, have now got in "Hashgacha" a guide and instructor. "Hashgacha" is also the only institution in Eretz Israel that regards the whole problem as a social one, and as such it has a great future and still more important tasks before it.
The founding of "Hashgacha" was received in Eretz Israel with great joy, and the hundreds of inquiries coming from every corner of Poland show even more how important the new society is, and what a painful problem and what serious questions "Hashgacha" has to solve. Let us hope that its work will succeed.
Let the organisation of Polish Jews in Eretz Israel create several more such institutions, and it will earn itself everlasting renown and will find itself among the honoured organisations that have generously and honestly helped to build our new land.
Tel Aviv, July 1934.
From the Book Table

[Book review — Jewish history: the Cantonists in Tsarist Russia.]
"Kantonistn" ["Cantonists"] by A. Lewin. On the Jewish military conscription ["rekrutchina"] in Russia in the times of Nicholas the First (1827—1856). Warsaw 1934, 359 pages.

A book about a cruel period. A document of a dark epoch in the former Tsarist Russia, which cut with horror and dread into Jewish life in the first three decades of the last century [sic] and wrought an indescribable destruction that lasted a full 29 years in a row. Above all among the poor Jewish popular masses. All the torments ["enuyim"] that the Jewish people has endured on its long martyr's path pale beside the murders, the cruelty and the killings that were endured at that time by the weakest of the weak, the tender 9—10-year-old children, boys, upon whose tender and tormented little bodies all the wrath of that time was poured out. And as we read through the book, we are thoroughly [?] shaken [?] and pained, and we ask ourselves: how could such child-murders take place, how could such cruelties be done to children, and nobody reacted to it?

What does A. Lewin tell us in his work?

It is the tragic history of Jewish life in the former Tsarist Russia at the beginning of the last century, when the cruel Tsar Nicholas the First — the one through whom thousands of Jewish children were tortured to death and all of Russia was transformed into a dark prison — issued in the year 1827 an order that Jewish children, 9—10 years old, would be taken by force as soldiers of the Russian army; they had to serve [?] a full 25 years without a break under the most horrible conditions, and were sent off to the most distant Asiatic regions, so that only a small part of them survived it. The discipline in the barracks was so terrible that for the slightest trifle the children would be beaten on all parts of the body, and flogging until blood flowed on the naked body was a normal, everyday occurrence. And very often the children were flogged to death.

There was one way for the unfortunate children that could ease their sufferings a little: that was apostasy. The cruel Tsar expressly wanted all the Jewish children to convert, and indeed thousands of them did not hold out and converted. Statistics show us that in the years from 1837 [?] to 1897, 58,582 Jews were converted in Russia, and in the course of the 19th century 69,400 Jews converted in Russia, and all this was done through the coercive means of the Tsarist satraps.

This, in brief strokes, is the cruel life-path of the child-Cantonists, which has no equal in any martyr's history.

How has A. Lewin depicted and conveyed the above-mentioned period?

It is the first thorough work in the new Yiddish literature on the subject, and it is conveyed conscientiously and with devotion [?]. The author of "Kantonistn" collected the great material and through the book made us acquainted with it.

Reading the book "Kantonistn", a large section of Jewish life of the last century passes before us, a life that was so rich in tragic events, happenings and dreadful experiences, which until now have not found expression in the new Yiddish literature.

A quite special place in the book is taken up by the folk songs and the memoirs of the Cantonists. Through the former we become acquainted with the moods and the sad state of mind of the Jewish masses of that time, and through the memoirs we become acquainted directly with the life of that time and with all the cruelties that the participants themselves tell us about.

Certainly the book is not free of faults, especially in the narrative-belletristic sense, since there is not [?] the unified larger narrative that we encounter, for example, in Yehuda Steinberg's larger work on Cantonist life entitled "In Those Days"; but A. Lewin was concerned not with making fine literature but with bringing back to life for us a tragic epoch in Jewish life that has long been forgotten among us. And in this the author has succeeded. The language — fluent enough, and the book itself reads with great suspense. Yiddish literature has gained a serious and interesting book that deserves to be read.

N. Sternberg, Warsaw
Important Decisions of the Supreme Court

[Law — Supreme Court rulings: taxes, bookkeeping and rent.]
Costs in fiscal ["skarbowe"] penalties.
Only in those cases when no confiscation of the seized goods is ordered [?] must the convicted person also refund all costs connected with storing, or possibly with selling, the goods in question. In any case, once the goods are stored in a government warehouse, no fee whatsoever may be charged for the storage.

Simple bookkeeping.
Enterprises that are allowed to keep simplified commercial books do not have to draw up balance sheets; they are only obliged, at the beginning of their business activity and at the end of each year, to make an inventory of their entire assets and debts.

Stamp-duty penalties.
A double penalty for stamp-duty offences is imposed only in those cases where the tax office knew nothing at all about the concluded deed but discovered it only by chance.
But if it did know about the deed, and only the party concerned ["felsher" — doubtful reading] did not pay, or did not want to pay, the proper stamp duty, only penalty interest may be claimed, but not a double penalty.

Securing rent debts.
A landlord can obtain from the court security for a rent debt without proof [?]. The provisional attachment (tymczasowe zajęcie, "zashandrovenie" [?], zabezpieczenie) may, however, be laid only on the goods located in that same dwelling, but not in another house.
Polish Women Who Sacrificed Themselves for the Jewish Faith (4)

[History — Jews in Russia, the Voznitsyn and Baruch Leibov affair; serial, installment 4 and conclusion.]
M. Starkman.

(An interesting historical tale of what happened 200 years ago.) (4

When Voznitsyn [printed "Vasniezhin"(?)] returned, his wife no longer wanted to live with him; for now she was already deeply convinced that he had been bewitched by the Jews into going over to their faith, and that the chief culprit in this was the Jew Baruch Leibov, her husband's friend. But Voznitsyn's wife was not satisfied with leaving him. After all, she was a faithful daughter of the Orthodox Church. So she went off to the priest and told him the whole story. The priest did not wait long and submitted a report about it to the Russian church Synod.

An order was then issued to arrest both of them: Voznitsyn and his "seducer" Baruch. They were seized, put in chains and thrown into prison.

In Russia, too, the same laws prevailed as in the other countries concerning "blasphemy" and concerning Jews who persuade Christians to adopt the Jewish faith. The church Synod suddenly caught the scent of human blood and roasted human flesh — and set about trying the two accused.

The trial took place at the end of June 1738. The chief witness for the prosecution was Voznitsyn's wife, who told the court how the change in her husband had come about, and how he had later begun to defile the Orthodox religion and to blaspheme the name of "Jesus Christ". The judges listened in wrath to the accusations against this stray sheep of their holy flock.

Then they turned to Baruch; against him other charges were also brought, besides the one that he had led the officer astray. Witnesses were found who related that when Baruch Leibov was still living in Smolensk, he had constantly held religious conversations there with the peasants and agitated them to cast off the Orthodox faith. But even that was not enough for him. The servant girl who served in his house — he raped her.

Both of them, Voznitsyn as well as Baruch, saw that their fate was sealed. The judges and the witnesses were blinded by religious fanaticism. When [?] could they pass a judgment of true justice?

And indeed the two accused were not mistaken. The verdict was that both should be burned.

This trial aroused enormous interest throughout Russia. Tsarina Anna ordered that a full record of the proceedings be delivered to her every day, and on the 3rd of June 1738 [as printed] she herself signed the verdict: that Voznitsyn, who had blasphemed the Redeemer Jesus, and Baruch Leibov should both be burned, so that all Orthodox heretics, and the Jews who bewitch the "true believers" into adopting their accursed religion, should take a lesson from them.

On the 15th of July 1738, at daybreak, the two condemned men were led through the streets of Petersburg to the stake. The whole city ran to attend the carrying-out of the sentence, in order to take a lesson — as the Tsarina's order had prescribed.

Both victims were tied to posts and surrounded with dry wood, which later began to smoke and enveloped the bound men; and from amid the smoke the fiery tongues soon began to leap. Two Jews breathed out their souls in agony with "Shema Yisrael" on their lips.

(The End).
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Accident in Wiener's Courtyard

What's new in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 22 Av 5694 — piątek 3 sierpnia 1934 [Friday, 3 August 1934].)
Będzin
Accident in Wiener's courtyard.
On Monday Silberberg's son, together with a Christian worker, opened a collection point of a sewer pit. Silberberg was holding a light in his hand; just as he had removed the cover, an extraordinary force of gas burst out with a blow and threw the worker several metres away. And on Silberberg, who was holding the light, his clothes began to burn. Thanks to the quick rescue Silberberg was saved from great danger; he received only a few wounds on his body. Nisan Silberberg, too, was lightly injured while rescuing his son.
Commercial Register by 15 August

[Będzin — trade.]
The Merchants' Association points out that every merchant was obliged to report to the starostwo (district office) on conducting trade of whatever kind. The question is now of great importance in connection with the amendment to the commercial law, which provides[?] for restricting the right to trade.
The amendment comes into force on the 15th of this month. Therefore every merchant should, in his own interest, check whether he is registered; if not, he should immediately file a supplementary notification about it at the starostwo.
The registration is carried out by the secretariat at the Merchants' Association.
Jewish Merchants Are Called On to Support the Flood Victims

[Będzin — trade; flood relief.]
At Sunday's meeting of the board of the Merchants' Association it was decided to issue an appeal to the Jewish merchants to support the victims of the flood. The minimum is 5 per cent of the price of the [trade] patent.
From Craftsmen's Life

[Będzin — craftsmen.]
On Sunday an extraordinary general meeting took place at the Craftsmen's Association (Porgórska[?] 4 [Podgórska?]), devoted specially to the new Industrial Law, which comes into force on the 15th of this month.
With a large number of craftsmen of all trades present, the chairman Mr. Grossman opens the meeting and gives the floor to the manager of the association, Mr. Efraim Klejman, who delivers a lecture on the amended Industrial Law. Mr. K. explains to those assembled the main points that are of interest at the present moment to the Jewish craftsman. For example, Art. 147 says that all those who in the year 1927 ran an independent workshop can, until the 15th of this month, obtain from the magistrate a certificate on the basis of which the craftsman will be able to receive a craftsman's card. After that deadline such certificates will already be issued by the Chambers of Crafts, which will involve difficulties and great costs. The speaker then moves on to the commercial code [printed 'Karex'], which provides that craftsmen who sell their products for resale will have to keep commercial books. As it turns out, this will be a great difficulty for those whose workshops are not adapted to it.
In conclusion the speaker calls on all craftsmen in Będzin to provide themselves with craftsmen's cards, in order to save the Jewish artisan from ruin.
Mr. A. L. Grünwald points to the great task that the society to help poor Jewish craftsmen in Poland, 'CEKABE', has taken upon itself: it will endeavour, through the aid and the interest-free loan (gemilut chesed) funds in every town, to help obtain a card for every poor craftsman, so as not to miss the deadline. He asks that all craftsmen see to obtaining cards. For those who have no financial means, the local committee of 'CEKABE' will cover all expenses.
After the explanations, those assembled express their thanks to the board for its tireless work for the benefit of the Jewish craftsmen at the present moment.

By 15 August It Is Time to Legalise Craft Workshops

[Będzin — craftsmen.]
Report meeting of the Craftsmen's Association.
On Sunday a report meeting took place in the premises of the Craftsmen's Union, at which the chairman Mr. Goldsztajn described the activity of the committee that was created in Warsaw with the aim of rousing the Jewish craftsmen to legalise their workshops by 15 August of this year, and he presented the actual situation of the Jewish craftsmen. Mr. G. reproaches the Jewish intelligentsia, which cares for Yiddish and Hebrew schools, but for Jewish craftsmanship nobody cares. Even more terrible is that those concerned treat this important question so apathetically. As a fact it is enough to point out that of about 1000 apprentice boys and girls in our town barely one per cent are registered; the journeymen spend their evenings in the organisations and do not see to it that they will have the possibility of becoming independent masters.
There are also — says Mr. G. — over a hundred ladies' ready-made clothing workshops, which are indifferent to the decree; but later, when the workshops are closed down, no requests and entreaties whatsoever will help any more.

Sosnowiec — 16-Year-Old Boy Wanders the Length and Breadth of Europe

[Sosnowiec — wanderers; Palestine.]
The policeman on duty on 3 Maja Street in Sosnowiec last Monday noticed a ragged, barefoot boy wandering along the street and stopping at almost every shop window.
Asked who he was, the boy answered: I am an international... Because of this unclear answer the boy was taken to the police station, and from there to the investigation office.
During the investigation it emerged that the young wanderer is 16-year-old Meir Gottesdiener, born in Lubartów[?], who owns and holds a foreign passport bearing the stamps of the consulates of all the European states.
For two years the young wanderer has already been in Germany, France, Belgium, Italy, Austria, Romania, Greece, and even in Turkey, from where he decided to get into Palestine; but in Constantinople he was arrested and sent back to Constanța. There the Romanian authorities kept him locked up under arrest for several weeks and then transported him to the Polish border, from where he came to Sosnowiec.
— For what purpose did you come here? — the investigator asks him.
— From Sosnowiec I am heading — says Gottesdiener — to Upper Silesia, and from there to carry on with my plan of getting into Palestine by way of Morocco.
Gottesdiener has command of several languages; in every country he came to he passed himself off as a local citizen.
Several local Jewish families are taking an interest in the fate of the 16-year-old wanderer.

“A Victim of the Flood” / Catastrophic Collision of a Car With a Train. / A Grass Widower Who Will Have to Eat Grass.

[Sosnowiec — swindle; followed by two short news items: accident, crime.]
He begs for suits and packs them into a sack.
When Mr. Sz—s was standing in his room on Friday morning, getting dressed, the door opened and in came a young man of dreadful appearance: his face overgrown, rags and scraps of a patched jacket hanging over his torn shirt, his trousers full of holes. Bare toes stuck out of his patched shoes.
In a weeping voice the young man said:
— I am from the Kraków district, a flood victim. Here the committee that was set up has taken me in; it gives me food and a corner to lay my head; but the committee has no clothing, and from shame I feel I am close to doing something to myself.
The young man had an intelligent look and spoke so persuasively that Mr. Sz—s was touched to the heart. Without a word he went to the wardrobe, took out a good suit of his own and handed it to him.
The other rushed to kiss his hand, but Sz., of course, did not allow it, saying:
— No one is safe from a catastrophe; take it and wear it in good health.
The stranger at once threw the jacket on, covered his shame, took the trousers under his arm and went out of the room thanking him.
A moment later Sz—s's sister came up from the street, and her brother told her what had just happened.
— But he's a swindler! — the sister exclaimed. — I saw him downstairs, in the gateway, take the jacket off and hand it to a woman who was standing there and who packed the things into a sack, together with more clothes! —
Sz., furious, ran down to look for the fellow, meaning to teach him a lesson, but he was nowhere to be seen any more.
Only later did he realise that the stranger had actually spoken with a Lithuanian accent and had even slipped in a Russian word, “polozhenie”. How could he have believed him to be a Galician?
So at least let others know of it and not be caught on the hook[?] of this cheat!

A Grass Widower Who Will Have to Eat Grass.
At the police station in Sielce one Bytomski[?] reported that thieves had got into his flat and stolen 800 złoty in cash.
The police, to whom the matter seemed suspicious, opened an inquiry, which produced an interesting result. It turned out that the official, who is a grass widower, wanted to have a good time in his wife's absence. To that end he travelled to his wife, who is at a summer resort, and took 800 złoty from her, telling her that with the money he would buy a small plot of land. But fearing that he would later meet a black end at his wife's hands because he had squandered the money, he went to the police and reported that the money had been stolen.
The police, however, found the money hidden in the stove, and he is being brought to court for misleading the police.
What Every Craftsman Must Already Know.

[Poland — Craftsmen; the new Industrial Law.]
In two weeks' time the new industrial law comes into force, and it is very important that every craftsman should know the new laws and obligations that are being imposed on him. From now on the crafts will not be open to everyone; taking up a craft and carrying out the work will be under constant control and will from now on be bound up with various formalities.
One will be able to run a craft workshop only if one holds a craftsman's card (karta rzemieślnicza), which will be issued by the industry department at every starostwo (district office). Such a craftsman's card will be granted only if one proves professional knowledge of the trade. If a legal person — that is, a kind of company (spółka) or a firm of a group of partners — wishes to run a workshop, it will have to have an authorised representative who holds a craftsman's card, and the management of the company will have to include two members who hold craftsman's cards.
An independent master craftsman may be one who has completed his apprenticeship in the craft and passed an examination after completing his training as a journeyman (czeladnik) and after having been a "czeladnik" in that trade for at least three years; likewise one who has completed a craft school and has afterwards worked three years as a journeyman.
The industry department at the starostwo may exempt from the examination and from the trade certificates if the Chamber of Crafts recommends it, i.e. that the person can prove in another way that he knows the trade well.
A person who enters a master craftsman's service to learn the trade must make an agreement with the master. The agreement must be sent to the Chamber of Crafts within 14 days.
It is forbidden to employ apprentices in the crafts without pay. It is also forbidden for masters and owners of workshops to take payment for teaching the craft.
If one wishes to obtain a certificate of an independent craftsman, one must submit an application to the Chamber of Crafts and enclose the following documents: a certificate that one was apprenticed for three years and passed a journeyman's examination; a craftsman's card with a certificate that one has worked six consecutive years as a craftsman; [or] a certificate that one has completed a vocational school.
All craftsmen who already exist now as independent craftsmen will not need the above-mentioned documents in order to be allowed to continue practising their trade, if before 1 September 1935 they report to the industry department at the starostwo and prove that they have already been practising their trade before. They will have to submit for this a certificate from the Chamber of Crafts that they practise the craft. These craftsmen will receive craftsman's cards on the basis of having practised the craft before the new industrial law came into force.
All craftsmen in the towns and shtetls must already now see to it that they legalise themselves and obtain craftsman's cards; otherwise, after 1 September 1935 they will not be able to carry on their craft.
A. M.

The match ended in a deserved victory for "Unia", 4:2, with 1:1 at half-time. In the first minutes both teams played very chaotically, but soon the guests take the initiative and score a goal. On Saturday and Sunday a football tournament took place in Będzin in which four Jewish workers' clubs took part: Kraft, Gwiazda, Jutrznia and R.K.S. Będzin. On the first day there met
Kraft · R.K.S. 2:4 (1:1).

The sensation of the day was the victory of "Jutrznia" over "Gwiazda", which could have been even higher. The goals were scored by Szywek [?] and Wiczysła [?]; for "Gwiazda": Lindenbaum. It is worth adding that the match was very rough, and individual players of "Gwiazda" even played brutally.

The Polemic and the Reply

[Zagłębie — transport; the tramway.] Concerning the abolition of the monthly tickets on the tram.
As is known, the tramway management has introduced a change in the tariff, which has already been in force since 1 August. And it was supposed to mean that the prices of tram tickets in Zagłębie would become cheaper — meanwhile exactly the opposite has come out. Those who suffer most from it are the officials among the inhabitants of the suburbs, who used to buy monthly tickets and could ride as many times as they liked. After the latest change, however, they have to limit themselves, because the monthly tickets have been abolished and subscription booklets introduced in their place. It goes without saying that this provoked a great storm among the category of travellers, and the protests do not leave the columns of the Polish press. On this occasion the Endek "Kurier Zachodni" (No. 214) allows itself to make a little merry[?] at the expense of the Jew... Here is what it writes:
"About the monthly tickets it is not even worth talking, because formerly the holder of a monthly ticket for two sections, which cost 11.— zł., could ride without limit, whereas now he must buy a booklet of 50 tickets, which barely suffices him for two weeks, and must pay 7.50 zł. for it. That is what the cheapening of the tram tickets really looks like. Surely a golden head thought up these tickets, for not only are they dearer than before, but people trade in them and make combinations to the detriment of the tramways. The value of the booklet tickets was quickly appreciated by the Jews, the main buyers of the tickets: since a two-section 'ride' costs 20 groszy and a booklet ticket costs only 15 gr., one saves — or, as the Jews say, one earns — 5 gr.
On certain busier sections the Jews arrange matters in such a way that they pass tickets from their booklets to their co-religionists at the normal price, i.e. at 20 gr., thanks to which the holder of the booklet, after selling 3 tickets, has a free ride."
Where the "K. Z." got the idea that one can pass on tickets at a time when the conductor tears the ticket out of the ticket pad, and above all what sort of business the buyer makes paying the normal price — remains its secret. For us it is no secret at all any more: when one needs to take a ride on the Jewish horse, it is worth writing even such nonsense.
Interesting too is the reply of the tramway management to all the protests.
"The greatest agitation among the passengers — writes the management — was caused by the change and the issuing of the subscription tickets. We agree that for those who used to ride 4 times or more a day the travel costs will increase; in return, however, we give them great conveniences, etc.:
1) The new subscriptions (booklets of fifty tickets) are not tied to any restrictions whatever. Anyone may use them, even several people at once. (So it is not, after all, as the "K. Z." writes, that this is a Jewish combination. Sh.)
The subscriptions have no restrictions whatever as to time or persons. They can be bought at any time without formalities and without photographs.
3) In case of illness, leave, etc. the passenger loses nothing. With the tickets used until now he lost the unused time.
4) The former monthly tickets entitled one to ride on certain stretches, whereas with the new subscriptions the passenger can ride along the whole line — of course on one ticket only as far as the subscription provides.
5) Several persons can ride together on a subscription by cancelling the appropriate number of tickets. Unchanged remain the school tickets, monthly, workers' tickets, weekly and four-weekly tickets for state and municipal officials."
As we see, the tramway management seeks its own benefit more than the benefit of the passengers, and according to the rumours circulating, it will not stop at this change.
Sh. Szach.

A Letter to the Editor

[Będzin — letter to the editor; press.] Reading in the last number of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" the letter of the esteemed Będzin citizen Mr. Shlomo Frenkel, and also the critical remark of the editor Ben Amotz, I would consider it my duty to express solidarity with the opinions voiced about the "famous photographs" of Zagłębie personalities and philanthropists that were revealed in the year 1934 by the editors of "Nasz Przegląd".
The good deeds of these editors are already well enough known to Jewish society. I, as a reader of the paper, have more than once wanted to express my protest by ceasing to read the paper, but I am also one of the parents whose children study at the local Jewish gymnasium, for whose education the children must have a Jewish-Polish newspaper, which is unfortunately still the only one on the Jewish street.
In recent years we have become used to a series of "surprises" which have brought no excess of honour to the Jewish press in Poland, but the photographs affair, which we in Zagłębie had awaited with trust, has finally shown that the main thing for these editors consists of only one thing — money. And it goes without saying that this has unmasked the articles hitherto about morality, ethics and the like.
One thing only is surprising: that the paper's representative, incidentally a very capable and intelligent young man, has also been dragged onto the "Nasz Przegląd" wagon and has lent his hands[?] to that which has aroused great bitterness in Zagłębie.
