Antisemitism in the Country (On the Propaganda Incitement of "Piast")

[Politics — Antisemitism in Poland; commentary.] Observing the antisemitic propaganda that the organ of Witos's party, "Piast", has lately been conducting, I was reminded of a private conversation with one of the leaders of the peasant party. The leader from "Piast" threatened the Jews that his party would soon begin to pursue the worst antisemitic policy. One might have thought he would name the sins of which "Piast" accuses the Jews, but this he did not do. On the contrary, in his words he admitted that the Jews in Poland live in terrible want, that the poverty of the Jewish population in the small towns is such that even among the village population it is rare to find. The peasant, for instance, has by now freed himself of his debts, whereas the Jew today lies under a bigger mountain of debts than ever before; he himself knows of cases where peasants lend Jews a little potatoes and grain, because otherwise the peasant and his family could not afford to have a piece of meat in the house now and then. And with all that, the said peasant deputy declared that he and his party would launch a terrible incitement against the Jews, because the Jews support the present regime in Poland.
Last week one could read in the organ of the peasant party, in "Piast", an article about Jewish "leeches", about the Judaization of trade, about cartels, which are nothing but a Jewish contrivance, about Jewish artisans who persecute Polish craftsmen. The author of the article strove by every means to prove that the question of the Jews in Poland — this is a question of security in the country for the state.
In this connection I recalled that the article was written by one of the Piast deputies who had declared in the Sejm that the May coup had been a Jewish affair and that the Jews would have to pay for it. The same author strove to prove that the land in Poland must belong to the Poles; about the Jews he wrote that on that account the Poles need not have a headache.
One could recall that in a private conversation in the Sejm the same author of the said article spoke somewhat differently. To the question whether he did not realize that antisemitism in Poland would destroy the Jews, but at the same time would undermine the existence not only of the village but also of the entire state, he tried to avoid an open answer. One had to explain to the gentleman that the Jews are, after all, the buyers of the village's produce; that if the village's consumer is impoverished, the first to suffer from it will be the peasant; that the antisemitic agitation will, true, ruin the Jews in the first place, but at the same time the agitation will also lay waste the peasants.
The peasant deputy was asked whether his conscience allowed him to take upon himself the possible economic catastrophe of the peasant because of the anti-Jewish policy. Did he not, as a Polish patriot, realize what loss the state would suffer when the storm against the Jews is unleashed [?] in the country; and if the antisemitic agitation ruins the Jews, then the state will have no taxes from them. The present system of taxes has been able to hold out until now only because the largest share of the taxes was thrown onto the Jews. But if the Jewish population is completely ruined, then no distraints and no auctions will help, and since the state must have revenues, the taxes will be laid on the peasants.
Here the peasant deputy said: that is exactly what I am striving for. It is high time that tax revenues shrink so much that the deficits grow more and more every day. Only that will put an end to the present regime. The fear that in such a case they will start extracting taxes from the peasants too does not deter the said peasant activist. On the contrary, he longs for the time when the peasant will begin to groan under the taxes. That will surely bring about the catastrophe of the present regime.
Such and similar motives have their influence on antisemitism in Poland. Better not to quote the further statements of the said peasant leader. Whoever looks objectively at what is happening in the country sees clearly that the struggle is not about how the country should be governed, but about who should rule in the country.
Three parties have entered the struggle for power in Poland. Apart from the Socialists (one cannot speak of the Communists now), the Nationalists [Narodowcy, the Endeks] and the peasant parties are defenders of the present order. They fight the excessive interference of the state, they are against etatism and for private property. Only in relation to the Jews are they for confiscating private fortunes and for the most far-reaching etatist policy. If a government wished even to carry out in practice their policy regarding the Jews, it would consequently have to introduce the same policy in the country in general, because the assault on private property cannot stop at the Jews.
But in their blindness, in the struggle for power, they do not see that their whole antisemitism contradicts their own demands. Every member of the peasant parties knows this perfectly well. And in spite of this they have launched a huge anti-Jewish campaign which, in its consequences, is bound to ruin them themselves.
Important Decisions of the Supreme Court

[Poland — law; Supreme Court rulings: social insurance, labour, mortgages, surnames, trade.]
Insurance with the Insurance Institution.
An employer who gives out work to "chałupnicy" [home workers] is obliged to insure not only the chałupnicy but even the journeymen employed by those same chałupnicy.

Unemployment insurance.
Employers who employ at least 5 workers are obliged to insure them against unemployment. Although in this case the insurance right applies exclusively to manual workers, intellectual (white-collar) workers are also counted in the stated number.
As regards the insurance of intellectual workers, the employer's duty to insure does not depend on the number of hired people he employs, so that even if he employs only 1 clerk, he must already insure him.

Right to holidays.
The rule that only enterprises employing at least 5 workers are obliged to give their staff holidays applies only to craftsmen's workshops, but not to enterprises of a different character.

Mortgage moratorium.
Since by not paying interest for 3 months, beginning from 1 April 1933, one loses the right to the mortgage moratorium, the legislator compensates the debtor for the hardship of this sanction with the concession that he may demand that the sum paid on account of interest must be credited to the said period, even though the debtor also owes interest for the earlier period.

Changing ugly surnames.
The law giving those Polish citizens who have ugly surnames the possibility of changing these names to nicer ones is valid for 10 years, i.e. until the year 1939.

Trading hours in inns.
Inns may use the extended trading hours to sell food articles only for consumption on the premises, unless the articles in question were prepared in the same inn. Such food articles the inns may sell for taking away even during the extended trading hours (from 8 in the evening).
Two Marranos — A Story from Nazi Germany (6)

[Serialized story — Nazi Germany; installment 6.]
Chaim Berg.

Even the management of the chemical laboratory had passed to his assistant professors, and he devoted very little time to the laboratory. For his private chemical research he had his own richly equipped laboratory on the estate.
About the private laboratory on his estate, which was equipped with [?] of the best sorts that he himself had specially cultivated, whole legends circulated in academic circles. The legends had psychological causes. After the lost war the world-famous chemist and creator of the dangerous gases had withdrawn entirely from public life in academic circles and spent all his time on his estate and in his private laboratory with two Jewish assistants.
The very fact that the professor did not work in the university laboratory but created a private one of his own was bound to create such legends.
One legend said that the professor was working in his old field and had already created a gas which, with a single drop from an aeroplane, could kill a whole army in the trenches.
This legend the professor solemnly denied several times in the press, assuring the world that it was nothing but a lie, that he had given up this branch entirely for humanitarian reasons and would never return to it again — according to the professor's declarations in interviews...
But precisely the solemn tone of the correspondence in the foreign press only helped to spread the legend. Truly, with what else would the famous professor occupy himself in his private laboratory, located somewhere on an estate in the middle of a dense forest, to which only two of his assistants were admitted, if not with plans for a war of revenge and with new gases that would give Germany victory in a war? The rumours, and the old interviews that correspondents of foreign newspapers had demanded of him because of the rumours, brought the professor to the point of inviting the very international commission that supervised Germany's disarmament to make an inspection of his laboratory and convince itself of the groundlessness of the legend.
The commission declined the invitation with polite [?] thanks, but the German patriots laughed up their sleeves [lit. "in their fists"] at the professor's clever move and became still more confirmed in their belief that the professor was fooling Germany's enemies and preparing for the great day of judgment that would give Germany the great victory and the great revenge.
A second legend went round that the brilliant chemist had now devoted himself to agricultural chemistry, and especially to dairy farming, that he was on the way to great discoveries, to synthetic food products, which would make the whole of mankind partly or entirely independent of the soil.
But this legend too was sharpened with the supposition that all this meant revenge, and it became interwoven with the revanchist dreams of every German. The explanation was that the inventions would make Germany independent of the import of grain and food products and give her endless [?] staying power in the next war, so that Germany could no longer be defeated by any blockade of her ports, as had been the case in the last war.
And thus the professor, in his mysterious laboratory on his estate, became the centre of the German dreams of revenge and passionate hopes, which live like glowing sparks under the supposedly cold ash of national humiliation in the soul of every German, whatever party he may belong to. Remarkable is the fact that until the Nazis came to power, every German completely ignored the descent of the brilliant chemist.
Was there a drop of truth and reality in the legends that circulated about the professor's work in his mysterious laboratory, even though the professor sought to convince the world that his laboratory neither possessed nor worked on any secrets unknown to other scientists?
This question the Marquis now asked himself, driving late at night to the professor's estate, and he at once answered the question with a confident "No"!
"If there were a drop of truth in the legends," the Marquis thought, sitting in the fast-moving taxi, "the government would not have accepted his resignation. It would not have let go a man with such a brilliant head and dangerous plans, a head that had helped Germany sustain a war against the whole world for four whole years." The Marquis still knew the Nazis little.

The same question — "What does the Marquis know about these legends?" — was asked by the espionage service of the German War Ministry, which spied on all the legations and military attachés.
The Marquis's acquaintance with the professor's daughter was well known to them.
Nevertheless the Marquis's late-night visit to the professor's estate remained unnoticed.

The remarkable encounter.
The professor's estate lay a mile from a small town near a railway station.
With a large bouquet of flowers in one hand, which he had still been carrying for the prima donna to the theatre, the Marquis with his other hand pulled for a long time at the iron handle by the great gate that led to the estate owner's residence, which lay deep within the fenced-in tract of land by the highway.
But the bell did not ring, as though someone had torn it off, and nobody came to open for him. The estate lay in the bright moonlight of a spring night as if empty and abandoned; not even dogs barked, and the Marquis began to regard his late visit as a failure. Having decided to himself that the professor and his family had surely already fled abroad, leaving the estate and the laboratory to the mercy of God and Hitler, the Marquis set off back to the station in order to return to Berlin by the first train.

But not far from the town he noticed a small human figure under a black broad-brimmed hat, and ahead of it two large St Bernard dogs were striding phlegmatically. In the bright moonlight the three figures cast long, trembling shadows.

In one hand the professor carried a wrapped bottle and in the other a thick, long bamboo stick. The dogs stopped and began to sniff at the Marquis with phlegmatic German punctiliousness. The Marquis was sure that he had met the professor.

It Smells of Gunpowder

[World — Austria, Germany and Italy; commentary.]
In the atmosphere, above all in that of the editorial offices, one smells the gunpowder-scent of war, very much like the hot days after the Sarajevo shot in 1914.
Just as then, Austria now again stands at the centre of events — no longer the great Habsburg empire of Austria-Hungary, but the tiny little state, one of the smallest in Europe. And indeed, exactly as then, the bloody events in Austria are merely a cause, a pretext, for the war turmoil that is felt everywhere. And Italy, which was then a fifth wheel on the wagon and which only after the outbreak of the war decided, shamefully, to betray its allies, the Central Powers, and to join the Coalition. This same Italy now plays first fiddle, was the first to bring its mobilised forces to the border, and does not stop rattling the sword. Germany, on the other hand, which is supposed to be the main cause of this mood, which is supposed to have thrown the spark into the barrel of dynamite. Which is supposed to have sent its emissaries to carry out the upheaval in Austria — now stands as quiet as a "trushesl" [?], holding its breath like a thief at work. It does everything it can to prove its innocence.
The situation is clear.
That Hitler wants a war is beyond doubt. He knows very well that without a war he has no hope whatsoever of redressing the Versailles "krzywda" [wrong]. But the time has not yet come — not only because he is not yet well armed, because every new month makes his army stronger, but above all because the German population itself must still be greatly enlarged. All territories around Germany must be thoroughly Hitlerised, permeated with the Nazi spirit, and wherever there is a German-speaking group, it must either be officially united with the German Reich or become its spiritual sister.
Thus Danzig has long been a special branch of Berlin Hitlerism. The Saar territory is, any day now, to pass into Hitler's hands through the plebiscite. In Austria 80 per cent of the population is already Nazi-minded; this was helped by Berlin radio, and also by Hitler himself, who every Monday and Thursday [i.e. constantly] makes speeches in the border towns near Austria before tens of thousands of Austrians, who cross the border freely in order to hear "the rebbe's Torah". In Schleswig [?] and in Alsace-Lorraine, too, agitation is carried on on a very large scale, and even the German-speaking areas of Italy are not spared — not to speak of a whole series of former Hungarian and Austrian provinces.
All in all, it is reasonable [to expect] that in some ten or twelve years Germany will hold in its power and under its command over 30 million more people added to its present population, and then, being such an enormous power in the very middle of Europe, it could truly dictate to the world the future borders in Europe and also, in other parts of the world, take back its colonies.
This tactic of Hitler's is quite well known to the world, but nothing is done [?] to take measures to oppose it. The European politicians, it seems, live from day to day, are quite content that they have managed at least until now to protect the world from a bloodbath, and do not feel able to take care of us for later as well.
There is talk of a European démarche ["remarsh", ?] in Berlin against the Hitlerite incitement in Vienna, but such an action could look like mockery. Hitler will surely receive the European representatives in a friendly way and will swear to them by solemn oath that he has not even had it in mind [?] to meddle in others' affairs — the proof being that he is recalling the ambassador, and he can also give every possible satisfaction. But if Austria itself, of its own good will, adopts the Nazi teaching, just as Danzig did, then surely no one will have anything against it...
Therefore Europe itself does not believe in the power of such an action and for the time being holds back.
Italy, however, does not want to keep silent about it. It is hard to know whether it merely wants to guard itself against a German invasion of the territories of its spheres of influence, or whether it really wants to fish in troubled waters and meanwhile, in the tumult, strengthen its own influence, as is the way of things.
No one, of course, will believe that the sudden patriotic upsurge in Italy came spontaneously, that the demonstrations in the cinemas and in the squares were not organised by Mussolini's intimates.
The other European nations are certainly in solidarity with Italy in its immense hatred of the Hitlerite aspirations, but whether they agree with the Italian tactic and whether they will help it — of that there is great doubt.
Because in Europe today, just as in the past, there is no unity; everyone wants to interpret the verse in his own favour. If a unified line could be created, Hitler could be ground up like a pinch of snuff. But with unity no war would be needed at all; merely through treaties at the writing desk Hitler could be made harmless to the whole world.
Only a single feeling, the feeling of panic terror at the possible dreadful slaughter, holds the world's leaders back from war. And it is hard to believe that anyone at all would be found — even Mussolini, even Hitler himself — who would master this fear and take upon himself, before history, the responsibility for a war.
May this very fear protect us from the danger hovering over Europe's head.
P. K.
"Al d'atefet atfukh" — Because You Drowned Others, You Were Drowned

[Article — international politics; Austria and Nazi Germany.] By Leo Senig.

Hillel saw a skull floating on the water and said to it: "Al d'atefet atfukh" — because you drowned someone, you were drowned, and in the end those who drowned you will be drowned too. The latest terrorist events in Central Europe, and especially in Germany and Austria, unwillingly bring to mind this figurative saying of our old Hillel.
On the bloody and muddy political waters float "heads." Heads of those who only yesterday themselves made heads fall, and the heads of today's fighters will most likely "tomorrow" be cut off too.
A bloody nightmare-play that surpasses even the epoch of the tyrant-dictators who undermined and destroyed the old Roman civilization. And there can now, it seems, be no doubt that today's European civilization will also go under if this bloody game with dictatorship continues and spreads to other European countries as well.
We have reached a stage where every exalted mediocrity can persuade himself that "he is the highest court and the conscience of his people," and that he may therefore, on his own responsibility, chop off heads to the left and to the right.
We live in a time when a couple of young Junkers, who in the "good old days" could at most break mirrors in brothels, can conspire with a couple of financiers and, out of the blue, make a bloody revolution.
We live in a time when thought and level-headedness are utterly discredited and "deeds" have become the highest and most ideal slogans.
And the wilder and more barbaric the "actions," the more they are praised before the tormented masses and peoples, in whom one seeks to kill every will to think and to work actively and independently.
We live in a time when, compared with certain statesmen and their "good deeds," such "gangsters" as Al Capone and Dillinger look like decent, upright citizens.
Heads are falling, and these are not the last heads.
—
Will Europe — or more precisely: the little that is European that still remains in Europe — finally wake up and put an end to the bloody Nazi nightmare, which overshadows the darkest epochs of human history,
or, driven by narrow-hearted momentary interests, will Europe go on flirting with dictatorship until the various dictators and petty dictators destroy her completely?
When Dollfuss crushed the Austrian socialists with a strong hand, "Europe" kept silent and even applauded him for his courage and iron will.
One must [?] not, however, forget the "al d'atefet," and who knows whether one would not now be applauding (in other countries and circles) the Austrian Nazis as well, had their latest bloody, barbaric acts succeeded.
The game with dictators is a game for the devil. Maniacs and tyrants, who can persuade themselves and their millions of immature admirers that they are "the conscience and the highest court of the peoples," can very easily lose the game and flood the world with blood.
This is what the latest bloody events in Austria have so tragically shown us.
But the bloody game in Austria is not over yet.
And the "actors" there are still dictators and would-be dictators. "The foul business (in which Dollfuss was murdered) has made the name Nazi stink in the nostrils of the world" — the London "Times" wrote these days in a leading article.
If only that were true. Europe would then have cleansed the moral stench [?].
And the Owl Laughed.

(A dramatic play in one act, but with a lot of scenery.)

CHARACTERS:
HE — a man.
SHE — a woman.

The scene that is about to unfold here and to "make young and old shudder" takes place somewhere in the Beskid mountains [Beskidy]. A hot evening. The air is full of the sounds of poker games. Somewhere two birds are singing. All around there is a great racket: crickets are reciting the Shema, mosquitoes are singing, girls are squealing. From time to time something like the slap of a wet rag is heard. That is a kiss. Human voices are heard too. One hears a man saying: "The economic situation of the peasant is..." Then a girl: "Let it be as you say about the peasant, but only without hands".. Then yet another girl: "If my mother knew about this"..

But none of this has anything to do with the dramatic scene that is about to unfold here. The scene takes place a few hundred paces further on. On a large stone at the edge of a stream sit two persons, whom we shall call "Herr" and "Frau"; for various reasons their faces cannot be made out, but that is not important, there is nothing to see. What is important is what they say. She says: "But my husband.. he might still turn up"... He says: "Your husband does not interest me"... She says: "Me neither, but after all I am his wife"...

Above them, in the old trees, the leaves are rustling [?]. Among these leaves — on a branch, hiding — sits a laughing owl. She laughs, but whether she is laughing at the "Herr" or at the "Frau", or at both of them — is not known; it is a secret, nature is full of secrets.

We now come to the stream, beside which the dramatic scene that will make young and old shudder is about to unfold.

The stream is blue — that is how streams are.

Millions of stars are mirrored in the stream. As many stars as there are in the sky are mirrored in this stream. The stream is wonderful; it has only one flaw: it does not babble. That is probably because the water in the stream does not flow [?], and why the water does not flow [?] is not known. It is very possible that it does not flow [?] because the water is standing water; it is also possible that the stream is no stream at all. But that is a mere trifle.

On the bank of this stream lies, as has been said, a large stone. On this stone sit two people. When the mist that envelops the stream drifts apart, one sees who these two people are. One of them is a man; the other — a woman or a girl — can one tell nowadays?
(Let it be a girl.)

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Re'eh)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Re'eh
The Portion
—o—
a) "And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you put your hand to" (Deut. 12:18)
"In all that you put your hand to" [literally: "all your hand sends forth"] means what you send away, what you give away out of "all with which the Lord has blessed you"; by sharing your food with poor people — with that you shall rejoice before the Lord your God... Kli Hemda.
—o—
b) "Then you shall slaughter of your herd and of your flock" (Deut. 12:21)
The Rebbe R' Barukh of Medzhybizh [Międzybóż] had an old shochet [ritual slaughterer]. Once the Rav (R' Shneur Zalman of Liadi) came to him as a guest. The Rav would not eat of the slaughtering of R' Barukh's shochet, because he was old and his hands trembled. This annoyed the Rebbe R' Barukh, and he exclaimed sharply, as was his way:
— When my shochet goes [?] to slaughter, the angel Michael comes and slaughters...
— If so — says the Rav — then one certainly may not eat of his slaughtering. The slaughtering of an angel is, after all, invalid according to the law: just as the slaughtering of a gentile is invalid, because he himself is not obliged to slaughter his animals and he is not subject to the law of slaughtering, and so his slaughtering is invalid — the same applies to an angel. He too is not obliged in slaughtering, so his slaughtering is invalid...
• • •
In a certain community a group of Hasidim spoke out against a shochet of a different Hasidic court, saying that some suspicion had been heard about him. They demanded that another shochet from their own shtibl be added alongside him, because they did not trust that shochet alone.
The matter reached R' Yehoshuale of Kutno, who undertook to investigate and inquire where the suspicion against the shochet came from, and it turned out that the suspicion rested only on the testimony of a single witness.
Said R' Yehoshuale of Kutno to those Hasidim:
— "He that slaughters an ox is as if he slew a man" (Isaiah 66:3) — let the shochet not be worse in your eyes than the ox. If to slaughter the ox you will not trust the one shochet and you must have a second one, then why, to "slaughter" the shochet, did you believe only one person, one testimony?..
• • •
When the "Hafla'ah" came to the Rebbe R' Ber in Medzhybizh, he would not eat of the slaughtering of the Rebbe's shochet until he had seen his khalef [slaughtering knife]. The Rebbe R' Ber said to him: Now I understand what the Gemara says in Bava Batra, folio 74, that God took the wild ox [shor ha-bar] and hid it away alive for the righteous in the world to come. It must be because the righteous would not want to believe even the Holy One, blessed be He, that the knife of His shochet was in accordance with the law; so He hid the wild ox away alive, so that in the world to come all the righteous will stand by at the slaughtering and examine the knife themselves..
• • •
R' Mordechai of Chernobyl [Czarnobyl] would not eat of the slaughtering of a shochet from whose mouth he had once heard a lie. He said: the Gemara says "Rabbah examined it with his tongue" — which means that Rabbah examined a shochet by his tongue, whether he was not a liar... Melitzei Esh.
• • •
Doctor Dembo was known as a fighter for permitting ritual slaughter in Switzerland. When he came to the First Zionist Congress in Basel, he was asked what he was doing there.
— I want — he answered jokingly — to prepare myself in good time, in the future Jewish state in the Land of Israel, for the fight to permit ritual slaughter there...
—o—
c) "And this is the manner of the release" (Deut. 15:2)
The Vilna Gaon [Wilno] was asked: how will a bankrupt be judged in the world to come? We know how grave robbery is. Robbery is forbidden even for less than a perutah's worth. Neither Yom Kippur nor the day of death atones for robbery. "He who robs his fellow of a single perutah must carry it back to him even as far as Media." Because of robbery a flood comes upon the world — so what measure can be applied to a bankrupt?
The Vilna Gaon answered:
In Avot it is said: R' Yohanan ben Zakkai asked his disciples: what is the good way that a man should choose for himself? R' Eliezer answered: a good eye, etc. R' Shimon said: one who foresees the outcome. And when he asked them: what is the bad way? — they all answered with the reverse formulas of their earlier answers. Rabbi Eliezer answered: an evil eye, etc.; R' Shimon answered: one who borrows and does not repay.
One may ask: what opposition is there between "one who borrows and does not repay" and "one who foresees the outcome"?
But there is a connection between them, and that is exactly what R' Shimon means to say. If someone foresaw the outcome — he knew that he would go bankrupt and nevertheless borrowed money from his fellow — he is the true "one who borrows and does not repay", the true wicked man. If his bankruptcy could not be foreseen and when borrowing the money he had no evil intentions, he cannot be counted as a robber...
—o—
d) "You shall surely give him" (Deut. 15:10)
"Whoever averts his eyes from charity is as though he worships idols." Ketubot, 68.
Because "poverty makes a man transgress the will of his Maker", and with charity one makes peace again between God and the poor man. He who averts his eyes from charity brings it about that the poor man is at odds with God. So he is like an idol worshipper... Devarim Yekarim.
• • •
Of certain donors it has been said: "The secret things (he who gives charity in secret) belong to the Lord our God (he means it seriously, for God's sake), but the revealed things (and he who gives charity only when people see) belong to us and to our children" (he only means that people should see...)
• • •
Why is it called tzedakah?
Tzedakah means: justice, and what we give the poor man is not a donation but justice, because it is due to the poor man — for why should we have money and he not?... It is merely an act of justice and not a donation... R' Joseph ibn Kaspi.
• • •
"He looked for justice, but behold oppression; for righteousness [tzedakah], but behold a cry [tze'akah]" (Isaiah 5:7) — you come to the rich man for charity — and behold, a cry: he even shouts that he is a poor man and that one should at least give [?] him something more... "The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great": if the Sodomites cry out that they are poor, it is a sign that someone wants a donation from them; "and their sin is very grievous" — that they do not want to give any charity, so they even cry that they are paupers... Hinukh Beit Yitzhak.
• • •
"Happy are they that keep justice, that do righteousness at all times" (Psalms 106) — because happy are those who give charity at all times, and not only when they fall ill... Siah Yitzhak.
—o—
e) "And it be sin in you" (ibid., 9)
"Redeem your sins by charity" — and if you do not give any charity, you remain with your sins... Maharsha Teomim.
Well Bought and Badly Eaten...

(A dacha story.)
A faithful husband, whose honest, faithful little wife is, poor thing, sitting out the hot weeks in Olkusz, wanted to give his wife a surprise. So on Wednesday he searched the market and found a fat hen. He carried the hen around with him a whole day, until he finally got an opportunity — someone with whom to send the chicken — and he wrote a warm little letter to his wife in these words:
"My dear, beloved little wife Tsipele!
I know that it is hard for you to buy a good piece of poultry among the dacha gluttons, and I also know that you are a connoisseur of a good fat little chicken. So I took no account of any shame; I crawled about a whole day among all the poultry dealers until I finally grabbed this good fat little hen, a bargain into the bargain. I send it to you with joy — eat it in good health together with our little 'primet' [?], only don't forget that I, your faithful husband Yosef Chaim, am to come to you for the Sabbath, so I would like you to leave me a share"...
In his hurry he wrote on the envelope only his wife's name: "To be delivered to my dear Tsipele."
The messenger found in Olkusz the first woman who was called Tsipe and handed her the letter with the fat chicken. She was very pleased with the chicken and took great delight in the kind letter. She had a true Oneg Shabbat.
The husband, our faithful Yosef Chaim, could hardly wait. On Friday towards evening he dressed himself up "in vinegar and honey" [to the nines], as befits such a capable husband, and travelled with joy and pride to Olkusz.
When he arrived, his wife was just setting the table, and she placed before him a plate of potatoes with sour milk.
He goggled a pair of eyes and asked: Tsipele! Tell me, where is the fat chicken I sent you by an opportunity?
The wife looks at him in astonishment.
— What are you talking about, Yosef Chaimshi? What chicken?
— What do you mean? I did send you, by an opportunity, a good fat chicken.
But when the wife assured him once again that she had not received any chicken at all, only then did he realise that a mistake had happened, and he began to eat the potatoes with the sour milk.

England will be in a festive mood. On the second day after Hitler's downfall she will proclaim Transjordan a Jewish home, will suppress every outbreak by Arabs, and will make peace with the Revisionists.
In Africa the Kaffirs will proclaim themselves the lost ten tribes, and in Canada all Christian patients will be driven out of the hospitals to make room for Jews.
But I will tell you the truth, my Sabbath Jews: my heart trembles when I think of that great moment. I am afraid that with the downfall of antisemitism the Jewish people too will go under, God forbid. For what good, so to speak, is all of Jewishness if there is no one to hate us.
Love is perhaps a good thing, but only for a little while. Sooner or later love must lead to suicide.
So that is my proposal...
Z. H. Rubinstein.
“Der Kokh-lefl” [The Cooking Ladle]. — Elul

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; poem; the month of Elul and the High Holidays.] Humour and satire. — Compiled by Amutslu [the column editor's pen name].

Elul.

The month of Elul
is a pious one.
He comes to spoil
our summer.
He comes to us
to drive away the sins,
so that nothing at all
should remain of summer.

He bursts
into our camp
like a tear-stained
“Bobe Yakhne” [Yiddish byword for a loud, gossiping old woman].
He leaps in
with sickly voices
into our merry
revel [“hulyanke”, Pol. hulanka].

We want to run,
to jump, to race,
and he tells us
to recite Psalms.
We want to frolic
like a “runner”,
and he — he tells us
to blow the shofar.

In the month of Elul
life itself
is the greatest sin
there can be.
He wants us to stop
everything
and only
beat our hearts [as in the “Al Het” confession].

“Wicked ones!” — he shouts
at the “sinners”
who play about
like children.
“Repent!” — he growls,
not at all gently,
at every lad
who kisses a girl.

You may not sing
and may not laugh,
and nothing may
make you merry.
You may not yearn
and may not covet —
you may only weep,
groan and cough.

You may not, my friend,
sometimes even sleep;
he threatens
the harshest punishments.
“Get up for Selichot!”
he wakes you,
and tears off us
the blankets.

That is Elul —
dry, sober,
a true
joy-destroyer [?].
His loveliest song
is tekiah, shevarim,
his pastime
is measuring graves [the custom of measuring the cemetery with wicks for High Holiday candles].

Luckily, my friend,
this month
is no gabbai and
no parnas.
He cannot, friend,
arrest you
if you go on
romancing.
A Galitsianer [a Galician Jew].
How to Quarrel with Your Wife

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; feuilleton; married life.] (A free summer lesson).

Introduction.
Quarrelling with your wife is a great Torah.
One has to learn it.
Not everyone is capable and able to conduct, as they call it, a decent little dispute...
Many men start a quarrel quite respectably, but at the very first attack from the other side they run out of ammunition and retreat.
Much more capable and nimble in the field of family warfare are the wives, and that is precisely [?] why my lessons are intended for men only.
To continue, then:
Do you know, gentlemen, that quarrelling with your wife is a pleasure? One of the few pleasures a married man possesses?
If, God forbid, husband and wife lived in peace all the time and never quarrelled, family life would be an even far greater failure than it is!...
Quarrelling with your wife has in itself many virtues, which can be divided as follows:
Virtue number 1: improvement of language.
Virtue number 2: strengthening of memory.
Virtue number 3: economics.
Virtue number 4: ancestry.
The language virtue consists in this: during a quarrel you sharpen your tongue, find new words, improve your diction and simply enrich your vocabulary.
A virtue for memory: it strengthens your memory. Quarrelling with your wife, you and your wife stir up chapters of your life that would otherwise have sunk into the sea of oblivion. Long-dead pictures and scenes rise from the dead and all the old disputes are refreshed. You recall how you bantered back and forth while you were still “going out” as bride and groom. And when the quarrel flares up, your shrew reminds you of a sin from thirty years ago, and the good of it is that meanwhile you remember that you were once a young man.
The ancestry virtue: in the middle of a dispute your wife throws your pedigree at you.. and you remind her where she comes from... If there happens to be a carter or a cobbler in your family, you learn about him. And in general you leaf through your book of lineage, and that is surely good for every person, because a person ought to know where he comes from and what his origins are.
The economic virtue: during a quarrel you always draw up an account of your economic situation and add up the total.
Your wife says, for example: Such great happiness I have with you!
You answer: What, I don't give you enough for expenses, what!
Your wife shouts: A joke, what you give me! The miserable [?] thirty złoty a week for expenses!
You shout back: But that's only for food! And who pays the school fees!
She rages: You pay me no more than [?] one pays a maid.
You rage back — — —
But the rest you will learn from the following lessons.
Get ready...
An Educated Lady

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; jokes; the nouveaux riches.] The new rich lady, Madame Zuckerbraten [“Sugar-roast”], has returned from a pleasure trip around Europe.
— Did you see the Dardanelles?
— a neighbour asked her.
— The Dardanelles? — Madame Zuckerbraten was slightly flustered, — oh, certainly! We met them in Paris.
— And did you see the Pyramids?
— the neighbour asked with a faint smile.
— No, the Py... Pyramids we didn't catch. Just when we arrived, they had left.
—o—
They say —
that Hitler has already bought a brush and polish. He wants to go back to his old trade — shining shoes...
—o—
Says a philosopher:
A strange thing about women: those who have the finest clothes go about naked, and those who have no dress on their body would, of all things, like to put something on...
Hitler and Mussolini

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; satirical poem; Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy, the persecution of the Jews.] (An unheard-of conversation. Reported word for word).

Hitler:
Mussy, brother,
tell me, how are you?
Do you feel fine
in Noodle-Land [Yiddish nickname for Italy]?
Do your
black-shirted men
still patiently
bear their shame?

Do you feel secure
in your saddle?
Do your spurs
still jingle?
Are your
subjects
not yet tired
of the heavy yoke?

Mussy:
For the time being, thank
God, brother,
business is going
like clockwork [lit. greased],
and my
noodle-gobblers
go wherever
my hand leads them.

They raise their hands
and salute,
they dance according to
my dictatorship;
from all the
paths of freedom
I have wiped out
every trace.

I have armoured my fist
in steel,
everything goes
as I dictate!
Now, little brother,
tell me,
what's new
over there with you?

Hitler:
Nothing cheerful,
brother Mussy,
somehow things are going
downhill for me.
Often I feel
my hair
standing up
on my head.

You're lucky,
you have no Jews
who scream
when they are beaten.
Me, God has punished
with six hundred
thousand screamers.

When a Jew
is tortured under me,
the whole world
storms up,
and I, as a savage,
am at once
put in the pillory
of shame.

Like a plague,
Jews there,
that is already
an old rule.
Even today
the ideas
of the Jews
Marx, Lassalle still threaten.

If the God-
damned Jews
didn't make
all this racket,
my “brown”
Hitler regime
would have been shaped
after your pattern.
A. L. Wolfson.
500 zł. Reward

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; mock notice (parody of a lost-person advertisement).] I hereby announce that my husband Henekh Umglik [“Henekh Misfortune”] has gone missing. His distinguishing marks:
Not capable of anything at all, has a red-blue nose, a large bald patch [“lysine”, Pol. łysina]; on the left side of his head he has 21 hairs, on the right side — 19 hairs.
He eats little, drinks a lot; when he is drunk he cries. When he is sober he is ill, when he sleeps he snores, when he talks he sprays with his mouth.
Whoever brings him back alive will receive 50 zł. Whoever brings him back dead will receive 500 zł.
Granny Zlate's Ready Tongue.

[Humorous feuilleton — monologue; card-playing and the summer holiday.]
(Monologues of a good-natured Jewish woman)
Rendered by Ba Gad.

About Card-Playing.

A good morning to you. The "bkhmelekh" [?] are back from pasture already? Why so quick to be done with the dacha [?]? Missed your little husbands?

You did well, children; a wife should not be away from her husband for long. A husband, you should know, dear wives, is a delicate creature, who must not be left alone. Leave a man to his own devices, and he may yet, God forbid, turn into a lawless lad; he may fall in with bad friends, but [sic; perhaps "or"] with "good" girlfriends — and no good comes of it. There are, sisters, many crooked paths, and once a man gets entangled in them, it is hard to bring him back to the right road.

You trust your husbands, you say? Very nice of you. I am not saying, God forbid, that your husbands are the kind one must not trust; but you should know, dear wives, that not all men are such "muzhelekh" [?] as one thinks. There are some who, when they have troubles before their eyes, each would [?] be busy with his own trouble; but if they have none, they go looking for new troubles — and one must give them no opportunity for that.

I am already, my dearest, an old "higer-feserke" [?], as they say; I have heard and seen plenty of such things: sometimes the husband goes bad without the wife, and sometimes — forgive me, all of you, I don't mean you, I mean the wall — the wife gets "geshtrakhlt" [?] without the husband. So it really is always better not to leave it long "in the bank". You went, had a little rest, had a bit of pleasure, and back again — why take risks? It is always better to walk on an iron bridge. May the little bit of dacha do you good, and may we live to go again next year and beyond.

No evil eye, may no evil eye befall you — you have grazed yourselves quite nicely in these few weeks, you have all filled out [?] nicely. How much, my dears, did you win or put on at the dacha?

One won nothing, you say, because one didn't play, and one put on nothing, because there was nothing to put on from? Bless you, joy to you — now that is what I call a clever answer! When I see your husband, I'll tell him to give you an "addition to the ketubbah" for it.

And you really didn't play cards at all? If so, I love you — as surely as you see me a Jewish daughter — and you have much more favour with me than the lady card-players. May blessing and success come upon your little heads, amen selah.

In former years I too used to go out to a dacha in summer with mine, may he be well. And my gall, sisters, would boil [?] watching people sit whole days and even whole nights playing cards. They supposedly came to rest, and only there did they work hard and bitterly. They would often get so lost in the cards that they couldn't get up. And more than one woman — [printed "vert ir", perhaps "you hear"] — would gamble away the money she had and even her things, and come home "with the whip" [empty-handed], not having paid even at the guesthouse, or ["arer", misprint for "or"] the rent; no doubt it's the same today. So I ask you: really now, is it nice? Is it decent?

Letting oneself go at cards is no better and no nicer than letting oneself go at drink; especially for for a woman it is not fitting "beitim" [?] [sic] at all.

And here too there are, thank God, "kartovnitses" [?] [card-mad women] who spend day and night at the card table and haven't even the time, as they say, to cook the barley soup. May they live long and play — what I wish them, may it happen to me; but needs be — it needn't be so.

You think, dear wives, that I am an ignoramus and know nothing of what's in the cards? Just as you see me, I understand all kinds of card games: you want poker — poker it is; you want "pishe-pishe" or dominoes — I can do that too, and even the very biggest game — bridge — I understand quite well too. There is, my dearest, nothing to boast about; after all it's not such an important Torah; but I assure you that in this I can compare myself with the greatest players, men and women.

And perhaps you think, dears, that I am such a saint or pious woman as never takes a card in hand? On the contrary, I too serve this idolatry. You know, after all, my old man and I are "dziad z babą" [Polish: old man and old woman]; it happens sometimes that there's nothing to do and one's heart feels somehow gloomy ["kalemutne"], so the two of us have a little game of cards. The years of courting ["lyubken zikh"] — of carrying on "kutseniu-mutseniu" [billing and cooing] — have long since passed us by, thank God, so we fool around a little with a poker, a sixty-six. [Printed "ir volt", for "ir zolt":] may you all live to my age together with your husbands, and play with them as I do with my old man.

And I go to the "club" too. Not, God forbid, to carouse [?], but sometimes for a good deed's sake. If you belong to a society, you surely know that benefits are held — say theatre or balls — and when such a thing comes along, Zlate is there too.

About the "charity cards" I have, children, something to say; but I have no time now, and we'll put it off for another time.

Good day

We share the sorrow of the men whose

Collection of Linen, Shoes and Foodstuffs for the Victims of the Flood

[Będzin — relief.] On Tuesday a meeting of the committee for carrying out the relief action for the victims of the flood took place at the Magistrat [town hall]. It was decided to organise a broad collection of clothing, mainly linen and shoes, flour, kasha [buckwheat], beans, rice and other products of prime necessity.
The collection, which will be conducted in every house, begins next Wednesday, the 15th of this month.
— Let no one refuse to take part in the action; let each, as far as he is able, help to ease the sad plight of the thousands of families who have been stricken and impoverished by the flood catastrophe.
“We Don’t Slaughter in Secret” — Declare the Young Shochtim

[Będzin — kehilla; shechita.] On the basis of an application by the Gmina [Jewish community] to the proper authority, the “dollar shochtim” [?] were questioned about the secret slaughtering that they carry on. But the young shochtim did not deny what they are accused of; rather, they declared explicitly: “We don’t slaughter in secret, but openly”...
— That is how far lawlessness in the field of shechita in our town has already gone.
He Came to the Orphanage Looking for a “Professor”

[Będzin — crime.] Last Tuesday the children of the “Orphans’ Home” noticed an unknown person walking about on the third floor. To the question “whom is he looking for here?” the person answered: “I am looking for a professor here”...
When the caretaker [?] had the “fellow” arrested, he went into the bedroom and hid under a bed; the police who were called in detained him and took him to the commissariat. As it turned out, the “professor-seeker” had come to the orphanage looking for “tsalakhes” [slang: loot, a good haul — ?].
Former Mayor Michel Sentenced to 2 Weeks’ Arrest

[Będzin — courts; politics.] This week, for the second time, the trial took place of the former Będzin mayor (prezydent), Mr. Michel, who was accused of having called, at a meeting of the Endeks [National Democrats] in Dąbrowa, for resistance against the police. Mr. Michel was sentenced to two weeks’ arrest. The sentence is suspended for 2 years.
Terrible Windstorm over Upper Silesia and Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — weather; resorts.] On Saturday night a terrible windstorm swept over Upper Silesia and Zagłębie, causing great damage. Dozens of trees were torn out by the roots and some roofs were ripped off.
In Będzin the electric light was cut off, so that the whole town was wrapped in darkness for about an hour.
On the 3rd of May Square several trees were broken.
———
The windstorm also — as we are written from Bystra — wrecked the whole programme of the “Venetian Night” for which the summer-cottage guests had been preparing.
And it really is a “tragic” occurrence. Let us just imagine: an entertainment under the open sky, just as in Venice itself, the music plays, couples dance, the light is — as the “rule” requires — put out... hearts begin to pound, and suddenly
— a whirlwind, thunder, lightning and a downpour...
Well, no wonder the public had willy-nilly to leave that “Garden of Eden” and go back into the peasant buildings!
Interesting, however, was the behaviour of a Sosnowiec public figure: with self-sacrifice he fought with... the wind and did not stop dancing. Wags say it was a pity for him to part from his partner, but be that as it may, we have become convinced that for a “mitzvah” the Sosnowiec public figures dare to sacrifice themselves...
The Cantor Question — Not Topical

[Będzin — kehilla; cantorate.] Mr. L. Bauszykowski [?] has received a letter from a Vilna cantor, Mr. Weinstein [?], who wishes to put forward his candidacy for the local cantorate.
Mr. Bauszykowski submitted the offer to the kehilla president, who declared that the cantor question is not topical, because no salary for a cantor is provided in the budget.
A Jewish Representative in the Chamber of Crafts in Kielce

[Zagłębie — artisans.] As is known, 3 councillors of the Chamber of Crafts in Kielce were allotted for the 3 districts (powiaty) of Będzin, Olkusz and Zawiercie as well as Sosnowiec — 2 Christians and 1 Jew — from the following trades: a mason, a locksmith and a cholewkarz [boot-upper maker], as well as deputies from these same trades. The mason from Będzin and the locksmith from Zawiercie went to the Christians; the Jewish artisans received the gaiter-stitcher in the person of Mr. Daniel Kilsztak [?], a board member of the branch of the Central Artisans’ Union.
This week Mr. Kilsztak received the confirmation of the Kielce voivode as councillor, and Mr. Tejchner [?] of Sosnowiec as deputy.
At the end of this month the first constituent meeting of the newly elected councillors is to take place; they must elect a board from among themselves.
It is to be hoped that Zagłębie will no longer be treated in stepmotherly fashion, as it has been until now.
General Meeting of the Talmud Torah

[Będzin — Talmud Torah.] Next Sunday an extraordinary general meeting of the Talmud Torah will take place in its own premises.
At the meeting a new board must be elected that will be capable of maintaining the institution, which, thanks to the management so far, has been brought to a catastrophic state.
If R' Shlomo the Shochet Gets Leave, Only the Young Shochtim Must Work — So Declares the Rabbinate

[Będzin — kehilla; shechita.] As we have already written, R' Shlomo the shochet (ritual slaughterer) applied to the kehilla administration with a request that, because of his weak state of health, he be granted a month's leave.
Over this matter there are conferences, consultations, correspondence. The kehilla writes to the rabbinate, the rabbinate to the rabbi, and so on continually back and forth, because "here the creditor has found a way to collect his debt" — here is the opportunity for the young shochtim ("shochtimlech") to get into the slaughterhouse in a "legal" way.
This week the "truth" was finally revealed. The kehilla administration received a letter from the rabbinate in which they declare that the leave for R' Shlomo the shochet can be granted on condition that the young shochtim work in his place.
Sosnowiec — Reckless Motorcyclist — Rides Onto the Pavement and Injures Several Children

[Sosnowiec — accident.] On Sunday at midday a certain Kasperczyk [?] from Czeladź was riding a motorcycle at great speed on Dżewicza [?] Street in Sosnowiec. The motorcyclist, wishing to show off his skills, performed various stunts while riding in order to draw the admiration of passers-by. At a certain moment the reckless motorcyclist rode up onto the pavement by house No. 5, where several children were playing. The result was that 4 children were injured; one child is in a very serious condition.
Explosion at the "Huta Katarzyna" — Five Workers Injured
[Sosnowiec — industrial accident.] On Tuesday morning, at the "Huta Katarzyna" ironworks, an artillery shell exploded while scrap iron was being smelted. Five workers were injured.
Because of the "Kingdom of Israel" the Jews of Sławków Lived Through Mortal Terror

[Sławków — Revisionist Zionism; incident.] Last Sunday the Jews of Sławków lived through minutes of mortal terror. On that day, in the afternoon, when a fine rain was drizzling from the sky, a "Jewish army" suddenly appeared in the shtetl.
The news spread lightning-fast through the shtetl, and men, women and children ran to see with their own eyes what people were telling.
And indeed they saw real Jews in military uniforms. Not just ordinary soldiers, but commandants, lieutenants and the like.
The joy was even greater when the public learned that the high-ranking military men were passing through from Dąbrowa and would regale them with lectures on the "Kingdom of Israel" on both sides of the Jordan.
At the appointed evening hour the beit midrash was packed with young and old, who thirstily swallowed the words of the commandants, who called for a branch of "Brit HaHayal" named after Ze'ev Jabotinsky to be founded in Sławków as in other towns.
Everything would have gone off properly, [but] in the beit midrash there were young fellows from the opposing parties, who disturbed the speakers. The mood in the beit midrash turned quarrelsome. It had already almost come to blows, but when one of the "Brit HaHayal" men showed the attackers something one shoots with, the crowd fled in great haste.
Soon the news spread through the shtetl that "they are shooting in the beit midrash". Well, well — a stampede began; the frightened fathers and mothers cried out, wringing their hands:
— "Where are my children?"
Later it turned out that the fear was groundless. The guests had only been threatening, in order to protect themselves from the attacks of the opposing parties. Meanwhile, however, the Jews of Sławków had lived through mortal terror.
The Sosnowiec "Romeo and Juliet" — A Merry Summer-Holiday Story with a "Tragic" Ending

[Sosnowiec — gossip; romance.] The young man P. from Sosnowiec got acquainted in Ustroń with a certain [young?] C., the daughter of a well-to-do Jewish family.
Between the two a passionate romance was struck up.
P. began to visit their house, but immediately after the first visit it became clear that the young man had not found favour with her parents, [that is, her father,] who apparently sensed beforehand that nothing good would come of it.
And he was not mistaken: the father forbade her [?] to meet P. That, of course, did not separate the couple. The meetings took place in secret.
At night the Sosnowiec "Romeo" would jump over a high fence surrounding his beloved's villa and knock at the window of his "Juliet"; the window would open and the lovers would fall into each other's arms.
So days and nights went by. The idyll lasted on, until there came, as they write in novels, the fatal night.
The happy lover, as always, stole into his beloved's room.
The couple did not notice how the time ran, and went on cuddling each other.
On Saturday evening, however, the idyll was disturbed — by the sudden appearance of her father.
Seeing a stranger, and moreover in such an intimate phase with his daughter, the father ran up to the lover and honoured him with a fiery slap.
This P. could no longer bear, and he answered his beloved's father with a slap and began to beat him.
After this scandal the combative "Romeo" left the flat, this time already for real [?] — through the door...
Interestingly, the frivolous "Juliet" took her father's side entirely.
— How could I now marry a man who beat up my father? Can one love such a man?... — she declared to her acquaintances.
—o—
Will Sosnowiec Have New Kehilla Elections?
[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] As is known, complaints were lodged at the time against the kehilla elections. The complaints — as we are informed — have been sent to the public prosecutor's office, which is conducting an investigation into the matter.
—o—
Appeal by the Chamber of Commerce to Timber Merchants, Brickworks and Cement Factories.
[Sosnowiec — economy; relief.] We have received from the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec an appeal addressed to the merchants of the timber trade and the owners of brickworks and cement factories to donate in kind in order to rebuild the bridges destroyed by the flood in Galicia.
—o—
4,200 Zł. Stolen from an Iron Safe.
[Sosnowiec — crime.] In the night from Friday to Saturday the wall of the dairy on 3 Maja Street was broken through. The burglars broke open the iron safe, from which they took 2,400 zł.
—o—
Died on His Way Home from the Mikveh
[Sosnowiec — death.] On Friday towards evening the 63-year-old Yudl Kreplboim was walking home from the mikveh. Coming along Piłsudskiego Street he felt unwell; at his call he was taken into the gateway at Piłsudskiego 12, where he died.
—o—
For the Victims of the World War.
[Sosnowiec — events.] In connection with the 20th anniversary of the World War, a service for the victims of the war was held in the Orthodox church in Sosnowiec.
—o—
Inspections on the Buses — Sosnowiec–Kielce.
[Sosnowiec — transport.] In recent days inspections were carried out on the buses running on the Sosnowiec–Kielce line, during which many letters and parcels that should have been sent by post were taken from the drivers and conductors.
—o—
A Woman Under the Tram.
[Dąbrowa — accident.] On Królowej Jadwigi Street in Dąbrowa the 53-year-old Sobaszek fell under the tram and was seriously injured.
—o—
A Fire in Wolbrom.
[Wolbrom — fire.] In the night from Thursday to Friday a fire broke out from an unknown cause on Ligocka [?] Street in Wolbrom. 7 buildings went up in smoke. 3 Jewish families are among those affected by the fire.
From Sporting Life.

The championships of the Kielce Voivodeship
On Sunday two further matches were played for the championship of the Kielce Voivodeship. The results of the two matches are as follows:
“Brygada” — “Unja” 0:1 (0:0).
This match took place in Częstochowa in [very] unfavourable weather. In the first half the play is very boring, but in the second half the teams set a strong pace and the play becomes interesting. At times “Unja” even had the upper hand, but it did not take advantage of it. The defence of “Brygada” played excellently, breaking up all the attacks of the “Unja” forward line. In the 30th minute “Brygada” carries out an attack on the left wing and scores a goal through no fault of the “Unja” goalkeeper. Despite all the efforts of the “Unja” forwards the result remains unchanged. Referee Mr. Gryszka of Mysłowice — good.
W.K.S. (Kielce) — R.K.S. (Radom) 2:2.
In Kielce the second match of the series was played between the local W.K.S. and R.K.S. of Radom. The match was a very sharp one and ended in a draw, 2:2. The Radom players played very brutally, and because of this it came to scandals. The referee, Mr. Zalewski, allowed impermissible clashes on the part of the players and was neither energetic nor decisive. Only thanks to the board members of W.K.S. did he get home safely.
After the latest matches the table looks like this:
“Brygada” 5 games 8 points.
“Unja” 4 games 6 points.
“W.K.S.” 3 games 1 point.
“R.K.S.” 4 games 1 point.
“Płomień” in the Zagłębie “A” class.
In Dąbrowa the return match for promotion to the Zagłębie “A” class was played between “Płomień” and “Dąbrówka”. After a very dogged struggle the match was won by “Płomień” by 1:2 (1:0). Thanks to this victory “Płomień” has qualified for the “A” class. Referee Mr. Grajcer — very good.
Opening of the “Zagłębianka” ground in Będzin.
On Sunday, with the participation of all “Zagłębianka” members, invited delegations and guests, the ceremonial opening of the club’s own ground took place. Attention, Craftsmen!

(Appeal).
In connection with the latest regulations of the industrial and guild law, all craft workshops not legalised so far (which do not yet have craft cards) must be registered at the industrial office of the starostwo [district administration] by the 15th of this month (August 1934) at the latest.
Craftsmen who prove that their workshops were founded before 15 December 1927 and register them by the 15th of this month will receive a craft card without a confirmation from the Chamber of Crafts (Izba Rzemieślnicza).
After the 15th of this month such craftsmen, whose workshops were founded before 15 December 1927, will no longer receive a craft card without the confirmation of the Chamber of Crafts.
The following is particularly important: until the 15th of this month a craftsman can [freely] open a workshop or register an already existing workshop and at the same time enclose his certificate of professional qualification.
Even if the industrial authority does not recognise it as sufficient, the craftsman concerned can defend himself through administrative channels, even up to the Supreme Administrative Tribunal, and meanwhile run his workshop.
After the 15th of this month every newly registered workshop, even if it has already existed for a long time, will be regarded as newly opened.
If the administrative authority refuses to register it, it may be closed.
Because the deadline is so short and the matters concerned so important, since they affect thousands of livelihoods, the “United Committee for the Affairs of Jewish Crafts” in Będzin appeals to all Jewish craftsmen in Będzin and the vicinity who have not yet registered their workshops to carry out the necessary formalities in their own interest within the next few days.
No one may miss the stated deadline of 15 August 1934.
Craftsmen! If you miss the above-mentioned deadline, you face the danger of losing the legal possibility of work and livelihood.
Exact information on how to carry out the formalities can be obtained by every interested craftsman at the premises of:
the Central Craftsmen’s Union, Będzin, Kołłątaja 45,
the Gemilut Chesed (interest-free loan) Fund, ditto, 24,

The content of the interpellations submitted gives a clear picture of the galloping[?] of the faction that stops at nothing to carry its „victory“ through to the end. Thus, for example, the interpellation submitted by Dr. Spielberg revealed that the board member (parnas) Berishel Liberman and his gang had applied to the supervisory authority with the request that „Paragraph 20“ be applied against the board members Neufeld and Birnbaum...
During the discussion of the matter the president, Mr. Rechnic, was censured for having sent the „request“ to the starostwo (district office) without the knowledge of the board.
The chairman[?], unable to control the situation, dissolved the meeting.

A Boarding House at the Trade School in Piotrków

[Piotrków — vocational education.] The Piotrków trade school of the Society for the Spreading of Crafts and Agricultural Work among Jews [ORT] — licensed by the Ministry of Education — is holding a new enrolment for its departments of mechanical locksmithing and furniture joinery. The course in each trade lasts 3 years.
Boys aged 14 to 17 are accepted.
Attached to the trade school there is a boarding house for out-of-town pupils, where for a modest sum — at the level of cost price — they receive full daily board and lodging, and are under the supervision of the school doctor.
In the current school year the boarding house held pupils from a whole series of towns, such as Warsaw, Poznań, Kielce, Będzin, Włocławek and others.
Applications for admission to the new school year 1933/25 [sic] must be accompanied by a birth certificate (metryka) and a school certificate. After finishing the school and passing [?] the examinations, the graduates receive “journeyman's papers” (papiery czeladnicze).
More detailed information can be obtained at the school office: Piotrków Tryb., Leonarda 12, upon sending a postage stamp.
The Sad End of a Summer Holidaymaker, a Card Player

[Beskids — summer resort.] At one of the summer-resort places in the Beskids, people are now buzzing with the story of a young wife who gambled away her jewellery at cards.
The story goes like this:
A certain merchant sent his young, pretty wife to a dacha to recuperate. The wife always liked to amuse herself playing cards. She had great “powodzenie” [popularity/success] there. For that very reason she had no luck at cards; she always lost.
To her husband — although he did not begrudge her money — she told that she was winning and earning, and was even contributing toward their livelihood.
The neighbours, however, noticed that the matter was assuming great proportions, that the wife was losing all the time, and they talked to the husband, asking why he allowed his wife to get so deeply into cards.

New Changes

[State Lottery — economy; lottery communiqué (likely an advertorial).]
For the benefit of the players of the State Lottery.
On 16 August of this year a conference took place at which the director of the State Lottery, Mr. Colonel Stanisław Markus, acquainted the press representatives with the new principles of the 31st Class Lottery. The said plan constitutes an important stage of the reforms that Director Markus is carrying out, and thanks to which the public's interest in the lottery has grown. These reforms meet the wishes of thousands of players, who are interested first of all in winning, while the size of the prize interests them less.
It is worth drawing attention to the fact that the number of prizes has been considerably increased, both in absolute figures and relatively.
The following table clearly illustrates the differences in this respect between the 30th and the 31st Class Lottery:
30th lottery | 31st lottery
1st class: 12,080 | 16,000
2nd class: 9,100 | 10,000
3rd class: 6,140 | 10,000
4th class: 49,209 | 68,039
Total: 76,529 | 104,039
Bearing in mind that the number of tickets issued amounts to 180,000, the 104,039 alone make up more than half the number of tickets, which considerably increases the players' chances.
It has proved possible to increase the players' chances without harming the interests of the State Treasury, which, as is known, concern all citizens, thanks to certain changes in the size of individual prizes.
A great many lottery followers speak out for abolishing the very large prizes in the various classes and for fixing in their place a greater number of smaller prizes. They start from the assumption that for the player the improved chances of winning, say, 100,000 zł matter more than the doubtful[?] chances of a prize of 300,000 zł. It is therefore more desirable to fix 3 prizes of 100,000 zł each and not 1 prize of 300,000 zł.
The above-mentioned assumption has been taken into account in the new plan of the 31st lottery. In the 1st class (as also in the following ones) the prizes of 15,000 zł have been abolished. In return, the number of prizes of 5,000 zł has been increased by 5, the prizes of 500 zł also by 5, those of 400 zł by 10. In the second class the prize of 200,000 zł has been divided into 2 prizes of 100,000 zł, and the number of prizes has been increased: of 15,000 — by 5, of 5 thousand — by 2, of 1,000 — by 5, of 250 — by 30. In the third class, too, the prize of 300,000 zł has been divided into 3 prizes of 100,000 zł, and the number of prizes has been increased: of 50,000[?] zł — by 1, 20,000 — by 3[?], 10,000 — by 7, 5,000 — by 5, of 3,000[?] — by 5, of 500 — by 10.
In the 4th class the wishes of the followers of the big prize have been taken into account by leaving the big prize that has such drawing power — the million zł. On the other hand the prizes of 250 thousand zł and 150 thousand zł have been abolished, and in their place the number of prizes has been increased: of 100,000 zł — by 3, of 50,000 zł — by 5, of 10,000 — by 30, of 5,000 — by 20, and of 500 — by 200.
A completely new thing is the introduction in all classes of prizes of 50 zł, which, after deduction of the due percentages, will have the value of a ticket in the following class.
Until now, when someone won the stake and wanted to go on playing, he had to buy a new ticket and pay for the previous classes; but from the 20th[?] lottery on one can go on playing by paying only 10 zł for a quarter [ticket], thanks to the fact that the tickets go into the wheel. This system has been retained, but in addition a new type of prize has been introduced, which gives the possibility of playing free of charge in the following class.
The 50-zł prizes will be drawn normally in the first 3 classes, whereas in the 4th class they will be drawn in the last 6 days, i.e. from the 12th day of the drawing on. These prizes have no influence on the drawing of the million złotys, which will belong to the number on which, on the last day of the 4th-class drawing, the first prize of 200 zł falls.
The consolation prizes of 500 and 2,500 zł in the 4th class will fall only on the numbers on which no prize at all fell in the previous classes.
In conclusion Dir. Markus once again stressed that the collectors [authorised ticket agents] may not demand any surcharge on the normal ticket prices, except postage, insofar as the ticket was sent to the player at his request. Nor may any sum be taken apart from the statutory 20 per cent of the prize. The collector receives his remuneration from the General Directorate of the State Lottery and must be content with it.
The Jewish School System in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — education and schools; opinion piece.]
[Boxed:] To the attention of parents who are interested in the upbringing of children.
One of the most important problems in our life today is without doubt the upbringing of children. This matter concerns everyone who has children, whether he wants it or not, whether he is poor or rich, uneducated or an intellectual. In any case parents must seek a future for their growing children.
It is a rule that in order to make a human being of a child, he must first of all receive an upbringing both at home and at school, where he spends a large part of his life. The school is nowadays the institution of upbringing, where the child tastes his sorrows and joys and where he has the possibility of growing up as a person who will bring benefit both to himself and to society.
And therefore the question arises whether our schools stand at the proper level, so that they have the possibility of re-forming the children into accomplished human beings who will bring benefit both to themselves and to the people. This big question mark is easily answered: no, the schools are far from fulfilling their tasks, and the obligation towards the children is not what it ought to be, what perhaps it also could be.
The notion of "schools", however, is varied. There are several types of schools with us in Poland. First come the elementary schools, the so-called "powszechne", which are maintained by the government; then come the Mizrachi and Agudah cheders; then we have the gymnasiums, which must be maintained by the children's parents — although we would like these, too, to be maintained by the government, because citizens ought to receive the kind of schools they need. There are also elementary schools and gymnasiums with Yiddish [or: Jewish] instruction, but since to this day we have none of these in Zagłębie, we do not dwell on them at the present moment.
So the government gives us only the general schools, and whichever citizen does not want to send his children there should maintain his own school, one that pleases him and is suited to his views and his ideals.
It goes without saying that parents who send their children to paid schools have the right to demand that the school or the cheder be run according to the spirit and outlook of the parents, and that they stand at a proper height.
It became customary that a Jew who still wants to raise his children traditionally, who wants to give them a larger dose of sacred studies, sends the children to the Agudah cheders. Later, however, he is disappointed, seeing that the cheder gives him nothing. It is no better with the Mizrachi cheders — neither a cheder nor a school. In these types of supposedly modernised cheders more politics is practised than learning; everyone who takes his place in the management is a kind of autocrat, and nobody has any right to tell him or them an opinion, or to want to point out tactless mistakes that must not be tolerated [?].
It is enough to say that these leaders have led the institutions astray, without taking into account that the institutions were created for society and that, as such, they should have been safeguarded.
Then we have in Zagłębie two Jewish co-educational gymnasiums, which for the time being stand at a respectable [?] level, but not at the p r o p e r one. We say f o r t h e t i m e b e i n g, because we see that they too are beginning to totter and the lustre is growing paler, and therefore we warn that one must [?] stand on guard and safeguard the integrity of these necessary institutions.
Maintaining the said institutions grows harder from year to year, the deficits keep growing larger and larger, and one must reflect on the situation already now, as long as it is not too late, as long as one can still somehow rescue it. One must take stock of the state of affairs. One must not forget in this connection that the number of pupils there is shrinking, and that is certainly no cause for satisfaction, because however it may be, the relatively average Jew, from whom the children in the gymnasiums are recruited, wants to keep the child in school, and he barely has to take him out of there — it truly reaches the utmost degree.
One must not forget that the whole school system, as well as the gymnasiums of which we are now speaking, belong to society, and as such society must concern itself with them. One must safeguard the integrity of these institutions, and if a danger threatens them, one should not regard it as a trifle; one should become acquainted with the defects and with [?] the dangers, so that the proper measures can be taken that will rescue the situation.
One must not allow large deficits, because they ruin every healthy institution as soon as one does not see to it in good time.
And therefore we consider it a duty to tell the Będzin and Sosnowiec heads of the gymnasiums that they should take up the question seriously already now, as long as — possibly — it is not yet too late.
About the problem of upbringing itself there is also a great deal to say, and incidentally not merely to talk but really to create something substantial, because upbringing does not stand at the proper height. One must absolutely concern oneself more with the children, devote oneself to them more than has been done until now.
After all, it must not be forgotten that here one has to do with different children's characters, which it should be in the teachers' interest to improve, and paying no attention to them can lead to the most fatal results.
But about such similar [?] problems one can talk when everything is in the best order. First of all the schools as such must be rescued, and then, when the basis is firmer, when we need not fear that the ice is cracking under our feet, we will have the courage and strength to take up problems of lesser value, although they too are important and also urgent.
But, as said, first of all we must rescue the institutions, and that is at the present moment our duty, our sacred obligation, from which we must not turn away.
R. Let.
From the Village to the Town.

[Feuilleton — children back in town at summer's end.]
(A few lines to our little children.)

And it became brighter, and the sun somehow began to shine differently — warmer, more blossoming.

When one went out into the street one could find no place for oneself; the streets were so gloomy, so melancholy, so orphaned, that they drove one out of them, frightened one like something not good.

And now — it is a sheer delight to go out into the street: everything lives and laughs and winks and echoes and calls to life and to mischief.

What has happened? Why, all of a sudden, such joy? It seems that nothing at all has improved in life. Making a living is still an insoluble question; how to earn a loaf of bread — impossible, no way out to be found — and yet something has become different, at home as well as in the street.

What has happened? Nothing, absolutely N-O-T-H-I-N-G; nothing at all has happened, no more than that the little children have come back. And as soon as they came, everything began to glow and shine and bloom and live.

It seems they get in the way at every step; wherever you don't sow them, they sprout up; they wreck everything; they are under our feet everywhere — and yet, as soon as they appeared, as soon as they came into town, everything began to come alive, and it is a pleasure to go out into the street.

With their innocent dew of youth they adorn the stones and enliven the streets.

Without the little children the streets are empty, just as life is empty without them. Without them we have no content in life.

And here we see them again in the street and at home; everywhere they fill the air with their voices and squeals — and yet, and perhaps for that very reason, they are dear and precious and devoted to us.

Yes, the little Moshes and Shlomos and Sarahs and Sheyndls are already back in town, again among us and with us, and — may health go into their little bones!
