A story from Nazi Germany.
7)

"The dogs won't do you any harm," the professor reassured him from a distance, and greeted him with a cordial "Good evening, my dear sir."
"Good evening, Herr Professor! Here I come [?] to you, Professor; I have come to pay you a visit. I have the honour —" he bowed crookedly before the professor — "it is even an unusual, one may say an extraordinary hour for visits... isn't it so, Herr Professor? Ha-ha-ha!"
And his laughter echoed far into the warm night air.
"Yes, extraordinary! Especially with that bouquet of flowers. I hope the bouquet is not meant for me, as an expression of sympathy for my resignation."
"Oh no, Professor! But for a member of your family."
"For my daughter, is it not?"
"Yes, you have guessed it, Professor!"
"That was not hard to guess."
"Does he already know what has happened to his daughter?" — the thought flashed through the marquis's mind and made him cautious with the bad news he was carrying.
"My daughter will soon be at the Czechoslovak border," said the professor, as if he had guessed his thought and the reason for his late visit with the bouquet in his hand. "A few more hours and she will shake the dust of the fatherland from her feet for ever...
She telephoned me from the road, and so I went to the station to wire her. You probably mourned the beautiful concert? What?" — and the professor's thin, clean-shaven lips lit up with a good-natured little smile —
"On my way to the telegraph station I already took care, in passing, of this cognac" — and the professor raised the bottle before the marquis's face — "as if my heart had told me I would have a guest, heh-heh-heh!"
The marquis looked into the professor's face with a kindly, cheerful smile, with a wooden [?] gaze of mute astonishment, the gaze of a man who does not believe his own eyes...
"And your daughter is accompanied by her mother?" the marquis brought himself, after a long pause, to ask the question.
"Oh no!" the professor answered in still higher spirits, almost merrily. "The German Ruth has left her Boaz and her family and is returning to her Nazi people" — and at these words he burst into loud laughter, and suddenly bent down to the dogs and began to talk to them in a serious tone: "Enough sniffing and feeling, you stupid doggish heads that you are! Don't you see that the gentleman is a friend [printed 'freygt'] and no enemy of mine? This is Prince Caranel, the Spanish envoy and a personal friend of our common friend Lore [?]... Well, greet the marquis! Marquis, I have the honour to introduce to you the members of my family who have not yet abandoned me. This is Viktor! Viktor, give the marquis your hand! That's it!.. And this is Siegfried! Two canine symbols of revenge... Siegfried! Shake the marquis's hand. My 'loyalty' to my friends means loyalty to me, and now we can go, Marquis! You are welcome to me, I assure you!" And taking the stick under his left arm, in whose hand he carried the bottle of cognac, he warmly pressed the marquis's hand with his freed hand, then took the guest by the arm — the guest, who had gone through the whole ceremony of being introduced to the professor's dogs mutely and automatically, as if in a [—?], and let himself wander with him along the broad, empty-lying highway. For a while they walked without exchanging a word between them, as though each were sunk in his own thoughts; Viktor and Siegfried went ahead of them, but likewise straight and close to each other, like two soldiers, just as the professor walked with his guest.
"How do you know, Professor, that I am the Marquis de Caranel?" the marquis asked him, trembling in his whole body, as if he had woken from a dream. "After all, you have never seen my face before."
"No! I have indeed never seen your face before, Marquis. But I have thought a great deal about you, and especially tonight, so that your visit is no surprise to me. As if my thoughts had brought you down here. When I caught sight of you with the bouquet in your hand, I understood at once — or, better said, I felt — that this could be none other than the Marquis de Caranel, the great-great-grandson of the Spanish Bismarck, Abraham Senior."
"Oh, you know that too?" the marquis marvelled.
At these words the marquis stopped and looked the professor straight in the face.
"What made you think about me, Professor?" the marquis asked him, almost breathlessly.
"It is no miracle of telepathy, but a perfectly natural psychological phenomenon," the naturalist explained to him. "My daughter acquainted me with your life story and your spiritual wanderings, which are extraordinarily romantic, though also natural in your circumstances. She wrote to me in her letters about the nights you spent in intimate conversations on the long voyage aboard the ship where you got to know each other. She even told me about your wanderings in the Orient to find the branches of your family tree, which the expulsion of 1492 scattered over the whole world. Perhaps she ought not to have told anyone such an intimate affair of yours, but you must forgive my daughter; between her and me there exists such a close comradeship that we cannot hide any secrets from each other — they float to the surface..."
"Certainly! Certainly!" remarked the marquis. "I am only flattered by your interest, Professor."
"At such a moment in my life as the present one, which is so similar to the fate of your great-great-grandfather, Abraham Senior, an association of ideas in which you would be the centre is very natural... And that explains everything to you, Marquis! No riddle! A natural, psychic fact, is it not?" the professor concluded, taking out the key of the courtyard by which they were standing.

A New Storm Cloud Is Coming Upon Us

[Editorial — Poland, economy and policy; the Jews of Poland.]
Once again a storm cloud is gathering over us. The reins of our government are passing, as it seems, into more progressive hands. On the one hand this is an advantage for us, for the progressive leaders of the state will surely energetically suppress the chauvinist-antisemitic movement, which only not so long ago made itself felt so tangibly; at the same time, however, the economic programme of these progressives is a deadly poison for Jews, for it contains elements of socialization that are capable of ruining Jewish economic life in Poland still further. Jews can say of themselves the verse: "The ploughers ploughed upon my back" — and they keep making their time [?] ever longer.
The new President of Warsaw announced in his exposé a policy of etatism, which will certainly serve as a model for all municipal administrations, and the new Premier, for his part, announced a policy of cooperatives, which — as he put it — will be carried out by himself in the most remote little towns and villages of the Polish Republic.
These reforms are all chains on the hands of free initiative, in which Jewish creative energy moves, and the meaning of this is the mass declassing and pauperization of the Jewish population in Poland.
This storm cloud does not come on a summer's day. Our horizon is already heavily overcast anyway by the consistent policy of eliminating the Jew, which is carried out in all state and public spheres and on every occasion where private initiative used to collide with regulation by the governing authority.
One can say, conversely, that were it not for the constant line of avoiding the Jew, we would not feel the new socializing system so painfully. We Jews are not at all so keen to cling to the horns of the altar of economic conservatism, into which a history of hundreds of years has thrown us. On the contrary, we do have a sense of evolution and progress, and we are very eager to adapt ourselves to the new conditions of life.
But what does adapting oneself mean? It means gradually setting our life to the same norms that the newly created circumstances demand: learning the new trades, knowing them, loving them and beginning to seek our livelihood in them. And that is just the trouble: those thrown out of the old livelihoods are not allowed to approach the new ones; for those there are preferred candidates. That is precisely why we fear every innovation that breaks up our old fortresses, while we are not able to build new ones.
How will the etatist tendency of the cities express itself in our life? We already have one example of it. Formerly the municipal councils used to hand public works over to private contractors, among whom there were not a few Jews, and when, for example, the streets had to be paved, Jewish pavers played a considerable part in it. Today it is handed over to the Labour Fund, and Jewish work is finished ("kaput").
The same will happen on all fronts, wherever etatism penetrates and drives out private initiative.
And the cooperative movement aims, after all, to destroy completely the small town with its market days and its petty trade. True, we can be sure that precisely in this field not much will be achieved, for practice has already shown that the cooperative in Poland costs more and serves the consumer worse than Jewish private trade. Let theory say what it likes — life is stronger and more convincing. But one may fear that precisely because the transition to cooperatives creates many posts for thousands of Polish graduates of the intelligentsia, it will perhaps be considered right even to overlook its unprofitability, as is being done until now as well...
In any case, even if it should proceed at a slow tempo, it will still inflict great troubles upon us, which it will be very hard for us to bear.
But the serious thing in all this is our own despair. The "ofhentigkeyt" [?] (helplessness / dependence [?]) of our leaders.
We have two Jewish bodies from which we could have expected some kind of organized action against the misfortune. One body is the political representation and the other — the economic organization. Well, the head of the Jewish Sejm Club (Koło), Dr. Y. Thon, has explicitly declared that in Poland we have nothing more to do and the struggle is a pity. After such a declaration it is superfluous to wait for any advice or help from that side. The economic strata are crumbled into various cliques, and they are all occupied only with saving what can be saved of the status quo. But they do not lift a finger with regard to adapting themselves to the new circumstances. They do not even have it in mind, and we can have absolutely no complaints against them as to why they do not occupy themselves with matters for which they are not called.
And the new organization, which should watch over and encompass the modern economic problems of our life, is not being created; its midwives strangle it while it is still in its mother's womb.
That is why the newly approaching storm cloud is very dangerous for us, and no remedy whatsoever is to be seen against it.
P. K.
A Little Feuilleton. A Bad Week.

[Satirical feuilleton — small trade and livelihood worries.] A Bad Week.
My uncle Natan is angry this week; he simply scalds people.
It began with the trip to Warsaw.
Uncle Natan, a Jew, may it not befall you, who is barely breathing, suffers from whatever illness you like: sugar, kidneys, gallstones, liver, rheumatism, heart, lungs — so he wanted to pop over to Warsaw, to seek advice on what to start treating first, to get a diet, or perhaps an operation.
He has been getting ready for years, only he, poor man, is always harried by worries about making a living. By the way, we are among our own — the few dozen złoty simply aren't there.
Now he had finally decided, come what may, for a meagre few gulden one must pop over to Warsaw.
And here a real bomb burst: one has to buy a holiday ticket for 20 gulden. True, they promise[?] mountains and hills: free theatres, museums, antiquities — but Uncle Natan is travelling for an "intimate" matter after all, what does he need the operas for?
So Uncle Natan stays sitting where he is, — and here's a fresh trouble for you — trade books.
Go on, write it into a book and tear out a coupon when you sell 2 lots of pepper with cinnamon — Uncle Natan grumbles[?] again.
About this there is still a dispute going on between the Small Traders' Association and the Merchants' Association. One says pepper must indeed be entered in the book; another says one need not keep any books at all — and meanwhile not a single Jewish woman, not even for a cure, will come to buy the bit of pepper.
And as Rashi says: the stomach demands a little piece of fowl, a piece of kurczak [chicken]. That too we have nearly sinned away[?]; from abroad they have even come to wrest from us the bit of poultry.
It would be better if an exporter came for gabbaim and parnasim — those[?] they leave to us, while the quiet fowl they rob from us.
On top of all this there had to come a flood; a little Galician bill of exchange already comes back with a "płachta"[?], and one has to take a few złoty out of one's pocket for the flood victims — so Uncle Natan ended, angrily.
Yosef.
Important Decisions of the Supreme Court.

[Law — Supreme Court decisions; social insurance and trade.]
Right to unemployment benefit.
If a worker has been removed from his post because of a theft he committed, he thereby also loses the right to unemployment benefit.
Moratorium on overdue social-insurance debts.
The moratorium on overdue social-insurance debts is applied obligatorily in the cases provided for, and not only with regard to debts to the Sickness Fund, but also with regard to debts to the Insurance Institution for Mental [white-collar] Workers.
True, the moratorium on debts in favour of the Insurance Institution is narrower than that in favour of the Sickness Fund. The first moratorium covers only the actual debts and not the penalty interest, whereas the other (Sickness Fund) also extends to penalty interest.
A marriage-settlement deed (intercyza) and its value with regard to the husband's creditors.
A merchant's wife can protect her property (furniture, clothing, etc.) from her husband's creditors on the strength of a marriage-settlement deed (intercyza), if it was registered in the commercial register at the moment when the debt in question arose, unless the wife married only afterwards.
At a Joyful Mitzvah Celebration... (Instead of a Report on the JNF Evening in Bystra)

(Instead of a report on the K.K.L. [Jewish National Fund] evening in Bystra.)
Conveyed by Sh. Libas-Zon.

...All of us, almost all the Jews of Zagłębie, ought to send our thanks to the Ministry of Education for the fact that the school holidays were not extended and the summer-resort season (more accurately, the rain season) is already drawing to its end.
Special praise is due to Będzin, the town which this year's summer season "occupied" the Beskids in general and Bystra in particular. For apart from the fact that the town was represented by its "beauties", who paraded in the many colourful pyjamas, and apart from the merits of the resort ladies in the "cultural" field, Bystra this year set a record in the field of national work — solely thanks to the energy and effort of the Będzin youth.
That same Bystra, where a gentile was the supervisor over kosher meat, where a Yiddish word, a Jewish letter, was treyf — has, thanks to the Jewish guests from Zagłębie, become so "Judaized" that very many of the local Christian lads are ready to convert to Judaism...
But we have mentioned this here only in passing, by the way. We do not mean the Haggadah but the knaidlach. Just as a resort lady appears in Eve's clothes — she too means nothing by it, God forbid; she only wants to "skorzystać" [take advantage] of the "słońce" [sun]...
And so, in the very heat of the past summer season, for the first time in the history of Jewish Bystra, a committee was formed to collect money for the Keren Kayemet. "How much longer," cried R' Shlomo Frenkel, "will Bielitz [Bielsko] be our guardian! After all, we are Będziners; let us form a committee and show the Bielitzers what we Będziners can achieve even abroad" (the jesters of the generation even say that the Będziners are always more capable abroad than at home...).
And no sooner said than done — they went and did it. Sleeves were rolled up and — a committee was formed.
At the time when in Będzin a wrangle was going on among the parties as to which party should organize the Bialik evening (the dispute, incidentally, has not been settled to this day...), the committee in Bystra showed that the late great poet could be honoured within the bounds of what was possible.
The committee was not content with that, because collecting a few dozen złoty does not discharge one's duty — that suits Będzin rather, but not Bystra — and so a dance evening in aid of the K.K.L. was organized.
The preparations for the event were feverish; dozens of couples (from Będzin in particular) threw themselves into the work and "worked on" the Jewish resort guests, not passing over even extreme Beys Yaakov girls and Marxist women... So that every mortal in whom the spark of Jewishness still flows had to give a "terumah" [contribution].
And when the day of redemption [sic] came, the enthusiasm rose from hour to hour; several of the active young helpers were immersed in the work heart and soul, forgot their own "I" and only worked, so that the Jewish festival should turn out in pride and glory.
—
Around the building where the evening takes place it looks like a wedding in a small shtetl. Everyone's eyes are enviously turned toward the entrance to the celebration; among those standing outside are also the parents, whose desire to snatch a little dance has already cooled — they have sent the children, so as to train them in mitzvot...
Once — I think to myself — parents waited late at night for their children to come home from the beys-medresh, but today, in the "cultural" epoch, 13–14-year-old children spend their time at dance evenings.
Right by the entrance stand a few young men, modern types; one of them is the chief spokesman [printed "rosh ha-moverim"], and he expounds to them the "problem" of "going alone or with a young lady". To a ball one should not take a partner, because one must — he says — "support" her. It is better to go alone, and better still to bring food with you.
—
Entering the tastefully decorated hall and watching the dancing couples, I had a "complaint" to the Almighty: why is His people Israel so persecuted and tormented? Does one see among the well-fed nations of the world such youth, with such self-sacrifice, toiling in 40-degree heat just to bring in a few more guilders for the Keren Kayemet...
The chief in-law [i.e. host], R' Shlomo Frenkel, is pleased with the successful event; every złoty that flows into the Keren Kayemet's cash box revives him.
In the hall — a crush; getting a "table" is no easy matter. Just like a certificate from the Mandatory power...
From the eastern wall the letters cry out: "If you will it, it is no legend" — an old, familiar, discarded slogan, yet always new: "if only we would want it", no force would defeat us, if we spent our strength on our aims, for our culture, for our schools.
—
A "hora" is danced which sweeps everyone along; even the guests of the neighbouring restaurant pause their eating and drinking, the billiard players put down their cues and stare open-mouthed at how the "żydowski taniec" [Jewish dance] goes. One of the gentile heads, however, cannot grasp how so many "Zhidkes" [Jews] dance so enthusiastically, and how they have not yet drunk a single little bottle of vodka.. "Such a people this is," he says — "it dances sober."
The mood is elevated, and when comrade Durek of Sosnowiec appears with the "Chaim-Bloyen" rooster, the hall rocks with laughter.
At the distribution of the "prizes" of the beauty contest, too, it did not come to any serious frictions that might lead to a world war. — Sosnowiec received the first and Bielitz the second prize.
On the whole the evening was a brilliant success. The public enjoyed itself well and the Keren Kayemet cash box was enriched by 120 zł. (would that all events brought such an income...), and therefore the initiators from Będzin, Sosnowiec and Bielitz, and in particular the Cygo [?] family, deserve a warm "yasher koyech" for their devotion.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shoftim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shoftim
The Portion
—o—
a) "And thou shalt not take a bribe" (Deut. 16:19)
"Every judge who takes a bribe does not depart from the world until he rules justly by his ruling." Yalkut.
The meaning of this wondrous "Yalkut" is: every judge who takes bribes, at the beginning still knows that he is ruling falsely, but in the end he becomes so accustomed to it, "until he rules justly by his ruling", that he already believes he is ruling truthfully, even though he takes bribes; he already believes he is truly a righteous judge... Karnei Re'em.
• • •
"Once a man has committed a sin and repeated it, it becomes to him as if permitted" — a person commits a sin, "and repeats it", and he is moreover a Torah scholar and studies his way into it ("shanah" = to study), "it becomes to him as if permitted" — he already finds a permission for it, an explicit[?] ruling, that he may commit the sin, that it is actually permitted... The "Chozeh"[?].
—o—
b) "Thou shalt not plant thee an Asherah" (ibid., 21)
"Whoever appoints an unworthy judge is as if he planted an Asherah beside the altar."
R' Zvi Hirsch Kalischer writes about today's leaders and rabbis:
"For lo, Thine enemies are in an uproar, and they that hate Thee have lifted up the head" — once, Master of the World, You had to look for Your enemies among the masses ("Thine enemies are in an uproar"); today — "and they that hate Thee have lifted up the head": today look for "those that hate Thee", Your haters who "have lifted up the head", among the rabbis and the heads of the community...
• • •
R' Moshe Itshl of Ponevezh[?] used to say:
There are four kinds of rabbis: some possess Torah together with derekh eretz (good manners); others possess Torah without derekh eretz; yet others possess derekh eretz without Torah; and there are also those who possess neither Torah nor derekh eretz...
—o—
c) "Thou shalt in any wise set him king over thee" (17:15)
"One from among thy brethren shalt thou set king over thee; thou mayest not put a foreigner over thee." Of a Jew it says "set" ("tasim"), which means by force, and of a foreigner it says "put" ("latet"), which means of good will — for only a foreigner, a non-Jew, who does not know this stiff-necked people, would agree of his own good will to be king over Jews... RY"Ch Sofer.
• • •
"Thou shalt in any wise set over thee" — "that his awe be upon thee" —
that the fear of him be upon you, and not as it is, for our many sins, that the leader is afraid of the people and not the other way round... Or Chadash.
—o—
d) "That his heart be not lifted up" (ibid., 20)
The Gemara says: "Why is it not common for Torah scholars to have sons who are Torah scholars? Because they call the unlearned man a beast, and because they step over the heads of the holy people."
And therefore, if "that his heart be not lifted up" — if the king will not trample on the heads of the people, "and that he may learn to fear" — if he will not call the unlearned "beasts" but will teach them — then "that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he and his children": his children too will be like him... R' Yaakov Meir Yeshurin.
—o—
e) "Neither shall he multiply to himself..." (ibid., 17)
All these warnings to the king are said in the future tense: "Only he shall not multiply horses to himself", "Neither shall he multiply wives to himself". For at the beginning there is no fear that the king will do evil deeds; at the beginning he will surely behave well and piously. The fear is only for the future, when he is already sitting firmly on the throne; then he may begin to behave as he pleases... Tekhelet Mordechai.
—o—
f) "Who is fearful and fainthearted" (20:8)
"He who is afraid because of the sins in his hand." Rashi.
That does not mean — said Rebbe Mendele of Kotzk — the one who is a sinner, but the one who trembles because of his sins, "who is afraid because of the sins in his hand", who broods over them and cannot rid himself of them...
—o—
g) "So shalt thou put away the innocent blood from among you, when thou shalt do that which is right in the eyes of the Lord" (21:9)
By doing that which is right in the eyes of the Lord you will put away[?] the innocent blood; you will merit that no innocent blood will be shed, you will be spared from bringing heifers whose necks are broken and from crying "Our hands have not shed this blood", because then no innocent blood at all will be shed...
Torat Moshe (Alshich).
Radio Corner

[Radio — world.]
More playing and less talking.
Autumn is already approaching. For the radio this means the arrival of the so-called high season, during which the radio will work at full steam.
The radio management has already worked out a precise plan and programme for the winter season, which will begin on 2 September and last until 1 March 1935.
The new winter plan is distinguished by the fact that the percentage of music will be increased this winter even more than hitherto. It is planned that the music broadcasts will make up 66 per cent of the whole programme.
The whole daily programme will consist of three segments: morning, midday and evening. The first time segment will last from 6.45 to 8 a.m., the second from 11.57 to 13.30 and the last from 15.30 to 23.00. By dividing the day into such time segments the radio will be able to satisfy the demands of all its subscribers, who belong to various spheres and circles — both the inhabitants of the towns and the rural population.
On the whole the radio will be active on weekdays a scant 11 hours, and on Sunday a full 15 hours.
The winter radio programme provides for a mass of new, original ideas in every field, which will surely arouse interest among the broad masses of radio listeners.
—o—
14 hectares of land for one franc.
The city council of the great port city of Marseille has leased out for 99 years a huge plot of 14 hectares. The rent was set at a symbolic franc, which amounts to about 35 groszy a year.
On this huge plot the French radio company will erect a new, powerful radio station, thanks to which the whole French Riviera will be able to hear the programmes on a crystal (detector) set.
—o—
Psychological experiments through the radio.
The great Danish radio station has approached scholars in the field of experimental psychology with a proposal that it place its radio station at their service and wishes to collaborate with them. The first experiment consisted in the radio listeners having to describe how they imagine the character and appearance of the speaker they hear.
This original experiment, which was conducted under the slogan "By the voice you shall know them", took place in Copenhagen.
—o—
A gigantic radio report.
The annual radio report of the cyclists' race around France [the Tour de France] is one of the greatest in radio history. This year's race began on 3 July over a distance of 3,000 kilometres and lasted three weeks. Throughout the whole time French radio organised 100 reports from the route. These reports were broadcast every day in the early morning, the forenoon and the afternoon. The last transmission of the daily race was broadcast in the evening. The report was led by the famous French writer Tristan Bernard.
During the whole race the radio reporters followed the cyclists in cars and were able immediately to convey to the radio listeners their impressions of the individual stages.
These radio reports were a real sensation and won much acclaim.
—o—
Japanese radio dumping.
Japanese industry competes in all branches with the industry of Europe and floods the market with goods at much cheaper prices. As was recently reported, the Japanese radio-set factories have released on the New Zealand market new five-valve sets which fully meet the requirements of the New Zealand Ministry of Trade and Industry. Moreover the price of the sets is ridiculously cheap — about 70 zł.
In the circles of the Polish radio industry the problem of popular and cheap radio sets and devices has been discussed for quite some time, and probably as early as this coming autumn a new type of people's set will be released on the home market, which by its quality and price will be accessible to the broadest masses.
—o—
Radio news from all over the world.
Moscow is building a radio palace. The Commissar of Posts and Telegraphs has published a competition for the design of a radio palace, which is to be erected in the near future in Moscow. 8 prizes have been set, for a total sum of 38 thousand roubles.
—o—
Some explanations concerning auctions and seizures.
[Law — seizures and enforcement.]
Joining seizures.
According to Article 6 of the instruction for bailiffs (komorniks), the bailiff himself is obliged, before he proceeds to carry out a seizure, to check in his files whether the debtor's given belongings are not already under an earlier seizure, and if so, he joins the new claim to the earlier seizures.
Night executions.
As is known, in exceptional cases, by order of the local court, a seizure may be carried out also at night.
In such a case the time from 8 in the evening to 7 in the morning is regarded as night hours.
Treasury executions.
If the bailiff has to direct the execution against belongings on which a seizure has already been placed by the tax office, the bailiff must request the relevant enforcement files from the tax office concerned.
Bridegrooms, Shoes and Worm-Eaten Peas. (A Jew Talks, So He Talks).

[Humorous feuilleton — matchmaking and family.] (A Jew talks, so he talks).
...I don't know how y o u r daughter behaves, but m i n e behaves very oddly indeed. I don't mean, God forbid, in a bad way; not that; she is a clever girl and she knows the way in and the way out; she has sense and open eyes. What I mean is the "laws of choosing a bridegroom". That's what I mean. There is not a week, not a month, in which she, my daughter, does not bring home another young man. I'll tell you the plain truth, I marvel at her strong memory. She remembers every young man's name; you surely think she writes their names down in a little notebook? You are mistaken! So once I ask her: "Gitele, why must you drag yourself around every Monday and Thursday with a different pest, with a different schlemiel ["lapitute"]? Pick out one proper, decent one, marry him and get off the market! It will take a burden[?] ["toyker"] off our shoulders.
It seems to me that I am not talking nonsense, and yet she laughs at me, my daughter, the biggest laugh;
"Father," she says, and she laughs, "Father, when you go to buy yourself a pair of shoes in a shoe shop, what do you do? You have them fit you with ten pairs until you pick out one pair. Why? Because one is too wide, a second — too long, a third — too tight and a fourth — too short; you're afraid of corns, so you're afraid: that's why you pick out one pair out of ten. And if you still don't hit on the right pair, you throw them away and buy yourself others. The most you can lose is six or seven złoty. But a husband can't be thrown away so quickly... That's why one must choose and choose and choose again. True, it happens very often that the choosing doesn't help: the young fellows sometimes wear masks of angels and under the masks there are devils, they are playing theatre! The young men pass themselves off as kosher, as refined, as respectable, but meanwhile one keeps searching.
I look at young men as at shoes... with both one sinks into the mud... That's why I choose; that's why I search; that's why I go around every week with another one, until I hit upon one trouble that will be smaller than the other troubles."
"So it means," I say, "that you are not looking for a bridegroom but for a trouble?"
"Yes, Father, every bridegroom is no more than a trouble, a trouble for the bride, a trouble for the bride's parents and a trouble for himself as well..."
And at once she sets about proving to me that all her girlfriends do the very same; they too go around every Monday and Thursday with different young men; they pick through them as if they were worm-eaten peas...
Sometimes one young man goes around with all her girlfriends before he drops in on her, on my daughter. Or the other way round: the pauper my daughter dragged herself around with is now dragging himself around with a girlfriend of hers.
What the end will be, I don't know, and she, my daughter, doesn't know either; neither does she know, nor does she want to know!
Meanwhile all sorts of pests and bores[?] ["gudnikes"] pass through my house, tall and thin as planks; short and fat as little barrels, clever and foolish, dark and blond, Litvaks and Galicianers. Now, that is to say, this week, she is already going around with a cross-eyed young man; he is so cross-eyed that when he wants to look at me, he looks at my wife; when he wants to give my daughter a kiss, he kisses me.. That's the sort of person she's going around with now. What? He earns well and is thrifty, he has five thousand zł. in cash and a little business of his own: he deals in housewares...
Besides the five thousand złoty he is also a quiet person, a calm one, a sensible one; he doesn't drink, he doesn't gamble, he doesn't smoke, he doesn't take snuff — nothing! Sometimes, she says, such a one can make a good husband...
— The fact that he is cross-eyed is nonsense, it's still better than being blind, or dumb, or, God forbid, sick. When I want him to look at me, I'll tell him to look at others, and he'll look at me anyway. So says my daughter.
If at least she would stay with the cross-eyed young man, I wouldn't mind, let him be cross-eyed — as long as she's off the market — but she will soon show him the door as well and bring along another plague to drag around with...
My heart tells me that she will yet go around with a lame one, with a deaf one and with one who has a whistling in his ear...
With her you can see it through... Hardly does a girl look at young men the way one looks at shoes and at worm-eaten peas. It simply isn't proper!
Meanwhile the young men eat lunch and supper at my place, they smoke up my cigarettes ["papirosn"] and take up all my time.
The only thing the fellows save me is electricity. As soon as they stay in the evening at home alone with my daughter, they immediately switch off the electricity — they hate light, how they hate it!..
B. K-r.
The Future of Jewish Craftsmanship.

Exact instructions for those who wish to learn a trade.

In the last issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" an appeal was printed by the Committee for Jewish Crafts in Będzin, concerning registration. But the campaign must not be conducted only in the direction of legalizing the Jewish craft workshops not yet registered; it is also a matter of the "great problem of the future of Jewish craftsmanship, which depends first of all on the number of "legal" Jewish apprentices; by legal we mean such Jewish apprentices as are subject to all the regulations under the Industrial Law.

What must a boy know who goes to apprentice with a craftsman?

The Polish Industrial Law of 1927 regulated the life of craftsmen, including [?] a series of regulations with which the interested public has not properly acquainted itself. First of all, this concerns the regulations on apprentices, since parents very often hand their children over to craftsmen who have no right whatsoever to train apprentices [terminanci]. The general opinion is that every self-employed craftsman has the right to take on apprentices and to train them — and that view is a mistake.

The right to take on apprentices.

For apprenticeship — only persons who hold a master's diploma, or who have an academic technical education covering the trade in question (engineers), [have the right].

When entering an apprenticeship one must bear this well in mind, so as not to waste one's time in vain.

So we now know who may take on apprentices; and who may enter an apprenticeship?

Anyone may enter an apprenticeship who has completed 15 years of age and has fulfilled compulsory schooling. Compulsory schooling consists in completing an elementary school existing in the place where the apprentice is learning

The period of apprenticeship must amount to three years

and may not exceed 4 years.

On entering the apprenticeship one must conclude an agreement with the certified master, which must be registered with the guild; if the master is not a member of the guild, the agreement must be registered directly with the Chamber of Crafts. The agreement must be written on a special form issued by the Chamber of Crafts, and it must without fail be registered.

Beginning to learn a trade

entails the simultaneous obligation to study at a public vocational continuation school. The school course lasts 3 years. Holding a certificate of completion of the continuation school is required, together with a certificate of completion of the apprenticeship, in order to be admitted to the journeyman's examination. An exception exists only when there is no vocational continuation school in the place where the apprentice serves his apprenticeship.

After completing the apprenticeship and the vocational school one must proceed

to the journeyman's examination

For this purpose one must apply to the Chamber of Crafts with a request to be admitted to the journeyman's examination. To the request one must attach:

1) a curriculum vitae written in one's own hand, 2) a birth certificate, 3) the master's certificate concerning the apprenticeship, 4) a certificate from the guild that the apprenticeship has been completed (if the master is not a member of the guild, the master's certificate must be confirmed by the gmina office), 5) a certificate of completion of the vocational continuation school, 6) a copy of the apprenticeship agreement, 7) a fee of 32 złoty 50 groszy.

In all matters that raise any doubt one must apply for information to the guilds at every craftsmen's organization.
The Bloody Hero.

Y. Adler.

Hitler!
Down his hot marble stairs
there rolled in blood
the hacked-off heads
of his comrades in gilded buttons;
with fire and blood he
rewarded
those who had crowned him
their Führer!
Hitler!
The dreadful charlatan,
the black ataman
of the great German Reich,
has dipped his friends
in a bloody river;
with his rifle and sword
he has made the German soil red;
killed those who helped him
to victory;
who played and sang
his dark tune!
Hitler!
The prince of all murderers,
the lord of all robbers,
he has destroyed all that is beautiful,
that is pure, that is clean,
all that is new and free!
The finest and greatest
minds
of his land he drove out,
the most luminous books that deep thinkers
and poets have written,
he burned
with his bloody hands!

But the red flames
then, in the deep night,
inscribed in glowing words —
his downfall, his end,
his punishment!
And when of his dreadful rule
nothing at all will remain,
and extinguished forever will be
his black power,
and the darkness of
the night will vanish,
those flames from the
books
will still live on,
and weave a new age...
And a new day will rise,
a new sun, a new dream,
an age of peace...

Hitler!
It is coming, a new world is coming,
forgotten then will be the
bloody hero,
the dark maniac —
then his head too
will lie beneath the axe...
His great punishment is coming,
his dreadful end is coming!
Regulation Concerning “Flower Days”

[Poland — regulations and laws.] On the 15th of this month the Interior Minister's regulation on the control of public money collections came into force.
Public money collections may take place only with the permission of the administrative authorities. Collecting money in state and municipal offices, on the premises of schools or of military institutions is forbidden. Only in exceptional cases may collections be permitted on the premises of the said offices and institutions.
Children and young people up to 18 years of age may not take part in public money collections, nor may school youth, except for students of institutions of higher learning. Everyone who conducts a street collection must be provided with a credential from the institution that organizes the collection. The credential must be approved by the administrative authorities. The credential must contain the surname, first name and address of the person, a serial number, and the fixed period and place in which the person may conduct the money collection.
The institution conducting the collection is obliged to keep a register of the course of the collection campaign and its result. The register must be kept for six months from the day on which the collection campaign was concluded.
After the collection is completed, a report must be published in the press on the sum of the donations collected, the expenses incurred in conducting the collection, and the distribution of the net proceeds to the appropriate purposes.
Napoleon's Wife

[Serialized historical tale — Martinique, Joséphine and the fortune-teller; no installment number printed.]
H. Abramson.

The little hut where the witch lived was hidden among the dense trees of the shining, warm island of Martinique, which lies in the French West Indies. Seldom did anyone show up in the middle of the day at the little earthen hut where the black, shaggy, wild woman lived in solitude. Only in the evenings would the Negroes who had been freed from the hard [?] work come to visit her, so that she might divine what the future had in store for them. The witch had no other customers. People avoided her; grown-ups were afraid of her, [as were] the little children, whom the mothers frightened with her when they, the little ones, did not want to go to sleep at the appointed hour.

That is why the wild woman was so greatly astonished when, in the very middle of a bright day, she heard the voices of two young girls close by her hut. She peered out through a crack in the door and saw: one, a little black girl in a long white shift; the other, a white girl with pitch-black curly hair and a radiant, lovely little face; she was dressed cleanly, elegantly.

The witch saw how the white child was dragging her black companion by force and how the latter was trying to tear herself away from her.

"But come, I'll stand up for you, don't be afraid," the white girl cried in her thin, ringing little voice, which carried over the grove, "come, we'll see whether she will guess my fortune."

"Go by yourself, I'll wait here," said the black child, looking at the ground with her big round [?] eyes and pouting her lips, which were big as well.

"All right, I'll go by myself. Just wait here a while until I come back."

At that moment, as the white child drew near the little hut, the door opened and the gaunt figure, wrapped in rags, came out [approximately; the printed sentence is garbled]; her long hair hung over her eyes; this gave her a frightful look, and the child cast a frightened glance into the distance, to where her companion stood. Having made sure that the other was waiting for her, she grew bolder. She took a few steps closer to the wild creature.

"Come here, tiny little girl... hee-hee-hee, come here, give me your little hand and I'll tell you what awaits you in life... come, sit [?] down beside me," she said in a hoarse voice.

The old woman lowered herself onto a stone that served as a bench and made room beside her for the girl. The girl sat down next to her not very boldly and again turned her face in the direction where her black companion stood.

"Do you have a father, a mother?" the witch asked, looking into the child's eyes.

"No, I have no mother and no father," the child said quietly. "I..."

"Ah, let me guess: you live with your aunt, Madame Ragadin [so printed; presumably Renaudin], have I guessed right?"

The child looked into the half-extinguished eyes of the old woman and said:

"You guessed right, I live with my aunt."

"Did your mother have such blue eyes, or did you inherit them from your father?" asked the witch, looking deep into the child's blue eyes.

"I don't know, I don't remember what my mother looked like; she died when I was this little," and she pointed with her little hand toward the ground.

"Are you well off at your aunt's, doesn't she beat you?" the witch asked.

At this the child seemed to remember something and stood up to go. But the old woman sat her back down beside her, almost by force, and said in a changed tone:

"Do you want me to tell your fortune? Give me your hand and I'll read from it what I see."

The child held out her hand, but first she glanced in the direction where her friend was still standing.

The old woman looked for a while at the creases of the child's hand, then she gave a start, as though she had seen something terrible there.

"What did you see there?" the child asked in wonder.

"A terrible misfortune I see there, but what is this? Happiness, much happiness I see; you will be famous throughout the whole world; but, woe, woe, there is misfortune again, and death. Well, is that enough for you?" asked the old woman.

"No, more, speak, tell me, what awaits me in the future? Tell me everything!"

The child's little face was white as chalk, her blue eyes were wide open with terror; yet it was not this woman she was afraid of — no, she trusted her, she believed her; what frightened her was what the white [so printed; perhaps "distant"] future held in store for her and what was so clear to the one sitting beside her.

"You will marry, but you will not live happily with your husband. He will die, and then you will become the queen of France. People will fall at your feet, but then you will sink into the abyss. You will die in loneliness, in a hospital."

For a little while there was silence. The child wanted to ask the witch something more, but when she looked, she saw that she was alone on the stone in front of the little earthen hut; the witch had vanished.

She looked into the distance and saw the white shift of her black friend peeping out from among the trees. She ran quickly to her.

"Well, Josephine, did she guess your fortune?" her companion asked her with great interest, and added, "Oh, I was so afraid she would swallow you up.."

Josephine did not answer. She walked beside her friend with her head bowed. In her ears rang the words of the witch: "marriage, queen, hospital." This was incomprehensible to her. And when she was lying on her bed, her thoughts began to tangle. Now she saw herself with a golden crown on her head, now in terrible poverty, in rags like the witch. And so she sank into a restless doze.

The old witch had guessed almost everything. The child whose hand she had read later became the wife of Napoleon the First, and she was idolized by millions of people. But in the end she was driven out of the imperial palace and died in solitude — though not in a hospital, but in the wonderful palace of [M]almaison [printed "Almazan"], which Napoleon had given her as a gift when he divorced her in order to marry an Austrian princess.

But the young woman was fated to go through a great deal before she became the Emperor's wife. Many a time she looked death in the eye. Yet it was written there that she would reach the highest rung a human being can reach in this world.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Dr. Bielnik Does Not Recognize the Notes of Private Doctors

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 6 Elul 5694 — piątek 17 sierpnia 1934 [Friday, 17 August 1934].)
Będzin
Dr. Bielnik Does Not Recognize the Notes of Private Doctors
One more "little flower" of the "quick" aid through the Magistrat.
A few weeks ago we reported in our paper several outrageous facts about the so-called "quick" aid that is given through the Magistrat (municipal office) thanks to the rule of Dr. Bielnik.
Now we are obliged once again to touch on this painful question, which is becoming more serious from day to day.
On Wawala[?] Street a poor Jew, a certain Weigreich, fell seriously ill. Dr. Bren, who treated the patient, declared that he qualified for a hospital, but without Dr. Bielnik's consent the matter could not be settled.
Well, a series of interventions began. The guardians (opiekunowie) Balimaski and Berenblat intervened, and when they could achieve nothing, the Charity Society took upon itself the mission of settling it, and for that purpose delegated Mr. M. Lewin, who turned to Dr. Bielnik with the request that the sick Jew be sent to a hospital, adding that well-known private doctors had established that the patient qualified only for a hospital.
After a lengthy conversation Mr. Lewin finally achieved that Dr. Bren should examine the patient once more, because "perhaps he has already recovered"...
Dr. Bren's confirmation "that the patient has not yet recovered" still did not satisfy Dr. Bielnik, and he demanded a confirmation from the Magistrat that the patient was indeed poor... But when Mr. Lewin had also taken care of these formalities and demanded the long-awaited document for the hospital, Dr. Bielnik then declared that he had no financial means for it, because of the 30 thousand zł. provided in the preliminary budget there remained to him no more than barely 2 thousand..
This unexpected answer naturally angered Mr. Lewin, who censured the doctor's conduct toward a poor patient. For this "impudence" Dr. Bielnik showed Mr. Lewin the door...
At Tuesday's meeting of the board of the Charity Society it was decided, after Mr. Lewin's report, to react to Dr. Bielnik's scandalous conduct and to demand a proper explanation from the president[?].
Irresponsibility..

As is known, in connection with the new law on legalizing workshops, an appeal was issued in our paper and also by means of posters, in which the craftsmen were called to come for information on the above-mentioned question. Among the designated information points was also the premises of the Jewish kehilla.
In response to this call, dozens of craftsmen did indeed come into the Jewish community (gmina), but there was nobody there to give the proper information.
We regard this as an irresponsible step on the part of the committee created for Jewish crafts.
Appeal of the Rabbinate to Help the Victims of the Flood.
Appeals of the Rabbinate have been posted throughout the town, calling on the Jewish population to support the victims of the flood with an open hand.
General Meeting of the Talmud Torah.

Under the chairmanship of Mr. M. Dafner, an extraordinary general meeting took place last Sunday in connection with the fact that the board had tendered its resignation. Mr. Dafner, in his report on the sad state of the Talmud Torah, points out the causes that led to it.
The main cause is that in the year 1933/34 the subsidies from the gmina (kehilla) and the Magistrat amounted to barely 1425 zł., whereas in the years 1929 to '32 the subsidies reached up to 27.000 zł.
After the discussion a new board was elected. The new board held a meeting on Wednesday, at which the presidium was constituted, consisting of: Abraham Najmark, Chaim Fiszel Fridman and Hirszel Stapnicki[?]; deputies: Ozer Pergricht, Chaim Strachlitz and Israelke Fiszel.
The new board appeals to the Jewish population, when buying baked goods or bread, not to refuse the one-grosz "bread stamp" for the institution in which hundreds of children from the poorest strata study.
A Wife's Devilish Plans Against Her Own Husband. She Gives a Thief 400 zł. to Shoot Her Husband.

[Strzemieszyce — crime.] The 33-year-old Jurszykowa [?], owner of a grocery ("colonial goods") shop in Strzemieszyce [?], wanted at all costs to be rid of her husband; to that end she hired a certain thief to bring her poison, or alternatively to shoot her husband dead.
For this "deal" she agreed with the thief on 400 zł. The thief consented, but instead of poison he brought her some liquid, telling her to pour a few drops into coffee or soup, and within a few days the husband would die. The "faithful" wife used the remedy as the thief had told her, but without success.. Out of curiosity she poured the "poison" into the cat's food, and then she was convinced that the thief had fooled her. She did not, however, give up her criminal plan, and paying him dearly for the job, she gave the thief a loaded revolver with which he was to shoot her husband while she was away from home; to wipe away every trace, she managed to get from her husband a note on which it was written that he had committed suicide...
The thief, however, did not want to carry out the plan and told the husband the whole story.
After an investigation the police arrested the "faithful" little wife and the thief.
Sosnowiec — A Fake Groom Was Put Up to Obtain a Release...

[Sosnowiec — community life; matches and the rabbinate.] The prologue of the story takes place in 1927 in the shtetl of Pilica. The "heroes" are Miss W. and the young man Mr. L., who fell in love and by the moon and stars "swore" faithfulness for the whole journey of life.
Years went by, new times came, and also the crisis. That's the crisis for you! It makes a ruin of everything; even the hot love of the faithful couple it weakened, the crisis, because when the bride "realised" that her groom's material situation had once been different from what it is today — she began a "sulking dance", and at first she began looking elsewhere... But later the "bubble" burst and the groom saw that "happiness" had slipped out of his hand — she claims: regret..
Good friends intervened: how can it be? They loved each other for some 8 years, it is already 3 years since the official engagement contract (tenoim) was celebrated, and here suddenly such an upheaval?
But arguments do not help; "she" shouts: "I don't want the match", and that's that.
So both sides went to the Pilica rabbi, who issued a ruling that if the bride pays 500 zł., she will receive her release (p'turin).
But since the bride wants to get the release without the 500 zł., she took counsel with her relatives on how to manage it.
And "seek and ye shall find". In the bride's family there is someone who gave the following advice: to put up a "fake" groom, go with him to some back-street rabbinical decisor (moreh hora'ah), and so obtain the release...
To carry out the "brilliant" plan the bride travelled to Sosnowiec with her brother, with whom she went in to the moreh tzedek Halberstam in Old Sosnowiec.
— What do you request? — asks the moreh tzedek.
— "I want to break off the match with this groom here.
— Why? Perhaps a reconciliation can still be reached?
— No, rabbi — says the bride — "I must break off the match; it is already three years since he disappeared; I was told he was sitting somewhere in prison as a communist, and since a miracle [?] helped me, I sent him packing [?]. In Sosnowiec I'm doing well now, I want by all means to break off the match."
— And you, young man, do you want to break off the match?
The "groom" does not answer at first; he mumbles unclear words, but finally he declares:
— "If she doesn't want to, then no"...
And since both sides do not want it, for the moreh tzedek everything is already "in order", and they agreed to pay 20 gulden for issuing the release...
The "deal", however, was not carried through to the end. The real groom, on receiving word that something was being planned behind his back, went to the moreh hora'ah and unmasked the whole plan of his "faithful" bride.
Important Explanations by the Merchants' Association

[Sosnowiec — merchants; commercial legislation.]
In connection with the coming into force of the new Commercial Code („Handels-Kodeks“) of 1 July, as well as the industry law of the 15th of this month, the Sosnowiec Merchants' and Industrialists' Association, at whose head now stands town councillor („Ratman“) Józef Safer [?], undertook a campaign to inform the merchants about the content of the new laws as well as the possible penalties for not complying with them. Thus a lecture was given by Adv. A. Kohn [?], about which we have already written at length, and by Adv. H. Fuks [?], who in a rich and finely constructed lecture explained the new commercial law. Among other things, the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association also issued a bulletin, which deserves to be welcomed for this reason alone: that the Association was the first in Zagłębie to understand the importance of the matter and did not content itself merely with lectures — which, by the way, stood at a high level — but also used the written word to inform the merchants about their vital interests. We shall quote some items from the bulletin which we consider important for the Jewish merchant.
The obligation to register commercial enterprises.
On the 15th of this month the amendment („Novelle“) to the industry law came into force, under which every merchant must immediately register his commercial enterprise. Those merchants who hold industry cards from previous years need not register. Registration is a very [?] important matter. For not being registered the amendment provides severe (monetary) penalties, not excluding the compulsory closing of the commercial enterprises.
The obligation to keep commercial books and the obligation to register at the commercial court.
The regulations on these matters are found in „Dziennik Ustaw“ No. 57, item („poz.“) 502 of 30 June 1934. R. H. [?] in the „Kodeks Handlowy“ [Commercial Code], and came into force on 1 July of this year. According to the regulations, every merchant (under the concept „merchant“ the new law includes: merchant, industrialist, craftsman, commercial agent, hotel owners, forwarding agents etc.) who runs a profit-making enterprise on a larger scale is a registered merchant, that is, he is obliged 1) to enter himself in the commercial register, 2) to keep proper commercial books. For non-compliance, penal sanctions threaten, as provided in Art. 280 of the Commercial Code. Until now the sanctions had no actual legal force, because the provisions of the commercial law regulated the obligation to keep commercial books in an unclear way. Only the law of the Minister of Industry and Commerce of 10 July of this year (Dz. Ustaw No. 60, item 515) established precisely which enterprises are to be counted among those „which are conducted on a larger scale“. From the above-mentioned ordinance it follows that the obligation to register and to keep books applies to:
1) Industrial enterprises of the first 5 categories and, in some exceptional cases, of the 6th to the 5th [sic; probably the 8th].
2) Commercial enterprises of the 1st category without exception.
3) Commercial enterprises of the 2nd category only if the last already-assessed annual turnover exceeds 100 thousand zł.
The above applies only to one-person firms; in partnerships (spółki) of all kinds, on the other hand (that is, general partnerships, limited partnerships, limited-liability companies, joint-stock companies), the enterprise must be registered and must keep proper commercial books regardless of the trade patent and of the turnover for the year 1933.
———
Entry in the commercial register takes place — in principle — on the basis of a written application to the commercial court which keeps the commercial register; the signatures on the application must be certified by a notary. All documents must be enclosed with the application, i.e.: a one-person firm encloses the patent of the 1st or 2nd category, or a copy of the last „nakaz płatniczy“ [payment order] for turnover tax, or an industrial patent of categories 1—5. In the case of a partnership, on the other hand, one must enclose: 1) the patent, 2) the partnership agreement, and in both cases legalised by a „de-yens“ [?] [unclear word] — the manner of signing in the name of the firm. The required documents may be in the original or in a certified copy.
The commercial books kept on the basis of paragraph 2 of the above-mentioned law of 13 April 1932 are exempt from cording („Schnürung“) and stamp duty.
Accounts may be kept only in Polish currency.
We have thus extracted the very important items from the bulletin which interest the Jewish merchants, and we hope that the board of the local Merchants' and Industrialists' Association, headed by town councillor Józef Safer, will continue to exert itself for the good of its members.
Registration Deadline Extended

[Zagłębie — merchants; registration.]
As is known, merchants not yet registered had to register by the 15th of this month.
Following the intervention of a delegation of the Retailers' Union („Detalisten-Farband“) in our town with the starosta [district head], the registration deadline has been extended until next Monday.
Information about the registration is given at the secretariat of the above-mentioned association.
The Jewish Gymnasium in Sosnowiec for the New School Year.

[Sosnowiec — education.] With the start of the new school year the Sosnowiec Jewish co-educational gymnasium enters a new epoch in its development.
The main aim that the founders of the gymnasium set themselves was to give its pupils, on the basis of thorough Jewish knowledge, a Jewish-national education. If this did not fully succeed, the fault[?] lay with Jewish society, which had very little understanding for the above-mentioned aim. Times, however, have changed greatly, and so have the views of Jewish society regarding the aims of education.
At the present moment, when the Jewish co-educational gymnasium in Sosnowiec is housed in suitable premises, when pupil attendance is fully adequate, and when Jewish society already shows the proper understanding for the aims and purposes of a Jewish educational institution, this is the right moment to carry out in the broadest sense the programme of Jewish studies.
The teaching staff for Jewish studies has been enlarged to such an extent that it will be possible to ensure[?] that all Jewish learning, such as religion, Bible (Tanakh), Jewish history and the Hebrew language, is concentrated in the school.
Parents will be strictly warned to stop having the boys taught Jewish studies at home, because, firstly, it does more harm than good, and secondly, it will be unnecessary, since the school's programme will be broad enough.
With the help of Jewish society the school management plans to realise this plan and to raise the school, as regards Jewish studies and education, to a high[?] level, which will certainly satisfy the wishes of the parents.

has lately been showing lively activity. In the summer months three educational colonies [camps] took place, organised together with the other "kinim" [branches] of Zagłębie, as well as an instructors' colony (in Brenna near Ustroń), in which the member of the Supreme Leadership (Hanhagah Rashit) Aharon Fuks (Warsaw) took part.

For the Fight against Hitlerism and Antisemitism.
The executive of the United Committee to Combat the Persecution of Jews in Germany has resolved to call on Polish Jewry to unite in a solemn protest. First of all it was resolved to hold memorial services[?] for the Jews who fell in Algiers[?] [printed: "Alushir"] and to devote all the pledges (nedarim) of this Sabbath to the fight against Hitlerism and antisemitism.
General Meeting of the Discount Bank.

[Będzin — economy and institutions.] This coming Sunday a general meeting of the "Discount Bank" will take place in the hall of "Piast" in Będzin. The meeting was supposed to take place several weeks ago in the hall of the Merchants' Association. But because of the great crush, and even more because of the heated atmosphere that prevailed in the hall, the meeting was broken off.
It is to be hoped, however, that the meeting, at which the fate of the institution for the future is to be decided, will be conducted in a direction that will bring the institution to its proper level.

Appeal of the Będzin Mayor to Help the Flood Victims.
[Będzin — flood relief.] The mayor (prezydent) of Będzin, who is the chairman of the committee to help the victims of the flood, has issued the [following] appeal in the Jewish language [Yiddish].
Citizens! The hungry and homeless who have suffered from the flood ask for your help.
On 16 and 17 August (Thursday and Friday) of this year a collection will take place for the benefit of the victims: clothing, linen, bedding, shoes, hard and soft leather, fabrics, food products, flour, groats (kasha), rice, peas, beans, soap, candles, cooking utensils.
Prepare parcels for the collectors!
The collectors carry identity papers bearing the stamp of the Magistrate [municipality].
Chairman of the Committee
(—) Br. Rzeczkowski[?]
Acting Mayor of Będzin.
A Gang of Counterfeiters before the District Court in Sosnowiec.

[Sosnowiec — courts.] Next week a sensational trial against a gang (szajka) of counterfeiters opens at the Sosnowiec District Court.
In winter[?] time Zagłębie was flooded with counterfeit 5-złoty coins. The police, who began energetically to keep watch, picked up the trail and discovered the "factory", which was located with a peasant family in the Olkusz district (powiat).
The trial has aroused great interest.

[Dąbrowa — the unemployed.]
A demonstration of the unemployed in Dąbrowa.

On the Guest Performances of the „Yidishe Bande“ in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — theatre.]
The news that the famous Warsaw cabaret (kleynkunst) theatre „Di Yidishe Bande“ [„The Jewish Troupe“] is coming to Zagłębie has aroused sincere joy among all lovers of a better Yiddish theatre.
Wherever „Di Yidishe Bande“ comes, they bring joy, encouragement and cheerfulness, and above all: sold-out halls...
As we now see[?] from the whole Jewish and Polish press.
In Lwów „Di Yidishe Bande“ played 2 programmes for seven whole weeks to sold-out houses, and the entire Lwów press described the performances as highly artistic and amusing.
The same now in Kraków.
„Di Yidishe Bande“ is now in its entire large ensemble, enriched with the best artistic forces, such as we have not yet seen. With the „Bande“ there now come the stars of the Yiddish revue theatre in Poland: Chana Grosberg, Lili Liliana, Malwina Rapel, Dawid Lederman, Leon Liebgold, Herman Fenigstein, Zishe Kac, Ajzyk Rotman and the composer Dawid Bejgelman.
The brilliant Bande programmes „Oyf tish un oyf bank“ [„On the Table and on the Benches“] and „Mitn rebns koyekh“ [„By the Rebbe's Power“]... are composed of sparkling[?] pearl-numbers by the famous writers: I. L. Peretz, Itzik Manger, M. Broderzon, Mark Arnsztajn, Tunkeler, Berisik[?], M. Nadir, Pinkhes Kats, „Lustiker Pesimist“, J. Naushik[?], Broyde[?] and Nazitski[?], such as had never been seen in any Yiddish revue theatre until the founding of the „Bande“.
Word, song, music, dance and rhythm — all of this raised to the highest level of artistry.
„Di Yidishe Bande“ plays no more than 2 times in Będzin and 2 times in Sosnowiec. Tomorrow, Saturday, at 3,30 in the afternoon, at the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre — „Oyf tish un oyf bank“; Sunday evening — „Mitn rebns koyekh“.
In Będzin the „Bande“ plays the same two programmes — Monday and Tuesday at the „Nowość“[?] theatre.
Today and tomorrow night — in Katowice.

A Little Clarity! (A Letter to the Editors)

[Będzin — Education; letter to the editors.]
Honoured Editors.
Last week there appeared in the columns of your esteemed newspaper an article by Mr. R. Les under the heading: "The Jewish School System in Zagłębie", in which the author deals with the school question for the new school year.
We do not intend here to enter into a polemic about the painful question of the school system among us, because this is not the place to discuss a question that is for us so vital, which we call "religious-national education". In general, everyone here has his own opinion about education, and we do not intend to polemicise about it.
It is different, however, when the honoured author condemns and publicly voices an opinion about an educational institution about which he is, as it seems, not properly informed.
The "Yavneh" school of the Będzin "Mizrachi", which has already existed for 15 years and has already brought forth hundreds of well-educated religious-national pupils — and if you, Mr. Les, complain that the school has no public supervision over it, then you are unfortunately mistaken, for in our board of trustees (kuratorium) there take part not only Mizrachi people, but also those who have an understanding for a religious-national educational institution. As an example we can point out to you that your fellow editor Mr. Lewkowicz was for a long time a member of the board of trustees.
As regards your opinion about the education in our school, it will suffice if we quote to you the words of our recently deceased great poet and educator Chaim Nachman Bialik, of blessed memory, when 3 years ago he stayed in our town and visited our school; and these were his golden, pearl-like words from the depths of his heart: "How long yet shall our Torah lie in a corner — when will the time come at last when our great cultural values will be taught in large, bright halls, as other secular subjects are taught"!
And how great was his joy then, when he asked the little children in which language he should speak to them, and they all answered with one voice — Hebrew! A small pupil also greeted him in Hebrew, about which he said out of great delight:
I smell here the fragrance of the Torah.
So said Bialik, and we believe that in the field of education you yourself will admit that Bialik was an authority. Only — do you know what else he asked? Where are the patrons who should support and foster the institution?
If you truly have in mind the good of the schoolchildren (tinokot shel beit rabban), then help together with us to build, inwardly and outwardly, the great edifice called "religious-national education" for our children.
The Board of Trustees of the religious-national school "Yavneh" in Będzin.

Not Only Registered Unemployed, but in General: Anyone Who Does Not Earn Cannot Be Evicted.

[Law — tenant protection.]
According to the law introduced on the basis of the decree of the President of the Republic, no eviction may be issued against tenants who are unemployed, even when they do not pay rent. The law applies to such tenants as occupy flats of 1 and 2 rooms.
In such cases the courts usually demand confirmations from the State Labour Exchange that the tenant is really unemployed; one therefore had to produce the unemployment card.
It thus came about that only registered unemployed benefited from the decree, whereas[?] those who are not registered at the State Labour Exchange, although they too are unemployed and earn nothing, were indeed sentenced to be evicted from their flats.
Now the Ministry of Justice has issued a circular which introduces changes in this field. According to the circular, not only registered unemployed holding cards of the State Labour Exchange are to benefit from the decree on the housing moratorium, but in general anyone who can furnish the court with proof that he is unemployed and earns no livelihood.
When considering eviction cases of people who claim that they do not earn and therefore have no possibility of paying rent, the courts must demand that they produce some documents or proofs that their claims are well-founded, and in that case not issue an eviction order against them.
To prove that one is unemployed and cannot pay rent, a confirmation from the magistrate [municipality], the police commissariat, the Chamber of Crafts, or from the Chamber of Industry and Commerce is sufficient.
If a tenant presents the judge with a confirmation from one of the above-mentioned offices that he earns no livelihood, the court may not issue an eviction order against him.
