Compulsory Administration over the Estates of the Count of Pszczyna.
On the motion of the Prosecutor-General in Katowice, the court has decided to appoint a compulsory administration over the property of the Count of Pszczyna [Pless]. As is known, the Count owes the State Treasury 11 million zł. in tax arrears.
—o—
Several Cases of „Rarytas“ Cigarettes That Were to Be Sent to Kielce Confiscated.
At the railway station in Mikołów the police detained several cases of „Rarytas“ cigarettes that someone had wanted to dispatch to Kielce. Because no name of an addressee was indicated on the cases, the cigarettes were confiscated, and a further investigation is being conducted.
As is known, it is forbidden to take „Rarytas“ cigarettes out of Upper Silesia.
—o—
Thousands of Re-emigrants from France.
On Sunday a special train arrived in Katowice with 1000 re-emigrants, workers who had been sent away from French coal mines.
In the coming days another 2000 families are due to arrive from France.

Hitlerite Agitation among Schoolchildren.
In the Rybnik district Hitlerite pamphlets, among others the „Oberschlesische Heimat-Fibel“ [Upper Silesian Homeland Primer], are being distributed among schoolchildren.

Tragic Death of a 9-Year-Old Girl.
On Kościelna Street in Chorzów a cart loaded with hay was driving along. While it was moving, a little hay fell off the wagon, and 9-year-old Lucja Łaśniak [?] wanted to pick it up. At that moment a car passed by at speed and ran over the child, who died of her severe injuries.

Last Friday a performance of the „Jüdische Bande“ [„Jewish Troupe“] was to have taken place in the Municipal Theatre in Katowice; the performance did not take place, however, because of a ban by the local authorities.

An unknown young Christian woman came into the flat at 22 Poniatowska Street in Katowice and asked to be taken on as a maid. But during the short time she was in the flat she stole three rings worth 200 zł.

„Unia“ Champion of the Kielce Voivodeship.

Remarks of the Times: Should the Boycott Committee Resign? / Craftsmen's Centres, You Have the Floor! / School Self-Help

[Zagłębie — boycott of German goods; remarks of the week.] Should the Boycott Committee Resign?
The state of the implementation of the boycott here in Zagłębie — the importing of German goods acts not only decisively against the entire local boycott action, but it also acts in a demoralising and contagious way. The boycott committees, first and foremost in Będzin, have invested a little effort and energy in the fight against the import of German articles, and if their toil has to this day not been crowned with full success, one sees[?] the cause of it in the great[?] indifference and passivity of the Jewish population of Zagłębie in general towards the boycott action; and phenomena that the boycott committees note with regret force us to look with despair at the future of the Zagłębie boycott undertaking.
The boycott committees do not possess the necessary means to render harmless the „stray[?] sheep“ of the Jewish flock. The means needed for that, physical as well as moral, are partly in the hands of the organised associations and partly in the great power of public opinion. When the committees see that both „committees“ [sic; presumably: both these factors] react weakly and do not use for the boycott action the means they possess, nothing is left to it [the committee], foreseeing the tragic results that such conduct will bring and which it is not able to prevent, but to withdraw in good time and take the responsibility off itself.
The question arises: should the boycott committees resign? And we say, unfortunately — yes! For the effect of the boycott on the economic situation in Hitler's land is today clear and tangible to everyone. Every party that wishes to know and see it, sees it [?; the rest of this sentence is garbled in print] — in the Jew in whom the Jewish spark has gone out, you will not bring it back to life[?], even if you point at him with your fingers every day. Such Jews must, like lepers, be expelled from Jewish society; the associations must expel them as members of their organisations; they must be removed in disgrace from the offices they hold in public activity; in the batei-midrash they must be treated like lepers; the Jewish banks must be closed to them with seven locks; every Jew must, as far as possible, avoid having any dealings with them, and in the street one must point at them with one's finger.
Of those who separate themselves from the ways of the community (read: boycott-breakers) the Talmud says: „Gehenna is locked before them and they are judged in it for all generations; Sheol comes to an end, but they do not come to an end“ (Tosefta, Sanhedrin 4, 13). One could have expected that the more prominently and clearly the results of the boycott favourable to us showed themselves, the more the action would strengthen and broaden each time. In reality the opposite happened in Zagłębie: the boycott committees look on with open eyes and see what they can expect in the situation that has arisen. The committees did not take their task upon themselves — society placed the task in their hands, and if that same society refuses to give them the necessary help, they are compelled to hand the task they received back into the hands of society.
A. T.

[Zagłębie — craftsmen; craftsman's cards.] Craftsmen's Centres, You Have the Floor!
On the 15th of August the first deadline ended, by which the old craftsmen had the possibility of obtaining craftsman's cards (karta rzemieślnicza) for themselves under a facilitated system. According to the information received from the various craftsmen's organisations, it can be seen that far from all craftsmen made use of their right.
Now we are already entering the second phase of the work, in which every craftsman who ran a workshop up to the year 1927 can obtain a craftsman's card, but the procedure will now be a difficult one, because the opinion of the Chamber of Crafts (Izba Rzemieślnicza) will now be required. We wish to hope that the Chambers of Crafts will not create any special difficulties, proceeding from the standpoint that it is better to legalise every craftsman who applies about this than to have to deal later with a whole army of „non-legalised craftsmen and workshops“, against whom it will be no easy thing to fight. On this occasion I would like to draw the attention of the management of the Chamber of Crafts to the abnormal state of affairs in which a colossal number of applications pile up there and are not dealt with. In any case one must hope that on the part of the Chamber of Crafts there will be no difficulties, if only because the elections and nominations to that institution have already been completed and, as one can reckon, the apparatus will begin to function normally in the nearest future, and then the Jewish councillors (ratmenes) will have the possibility of energetically dealing with the matters connected with obtaining the craftsman's cards.
And now about what must already be done in order to provide the Jewish craftsmen with craftsman's cards. First of all, the Committee for Saving Jewish Crafts keeps too modest and conducts too modest a work. The committee has limited its work to „giving advice“ — does the committee not know that Jews are well supplied with „advice“? The committee has not even managed to create for itself the means to maintain a permanent secretariat for the few months, which would immediately, on the spot, practically and actually deal with the numerous visitors.
The craftsmen's centres too have thrown off themselves the duty of doing the „black work“ of obtaining a card and left it to the individual guilds and associations — which would have been quite natural, understandable and logical, if our craftsmen's activists had understood what it is all about. But when an association demands of a craftsman who applies about making a craftsman's card 10 zł. registration fee and 12 zł. membership dues for 6 months, i.e. a sum of 22 zł., no more than for the association, one must interpret this to mean that either the craftsmen's leaders of the individual guilds do not want the craftsman's cards to be made at all, or they do not understand the seriousness of the moment. Every association must indeed exist and must have money, but now is not the moment for wanting to „exploit the situation“.
Before people look around, the few months will run away and thousands of Jewish craftsmen will be left without ground under their feet and without a possibility of existing formally. Because of the seriousness of the moment the tactics must be changed. Not to be content with the „advice“ of the committee and not to rely on the good-heartedness of the guild activists, but the Jewish craftsmen's centres must themselves immediately set about, on a broad scale, the work of individually providing every craftsman with a craftsman's card for the smallest, most minimal fee. Incidentally, the costs and formalities of obtaining the cards are colossal. Could an intervention not be carried out, so that both the costs be reduced and all the formalities, which last several months before one gets the card, be shortened?
Craftsmen's centres, you have the floor.
Mag. M. B.
—o—
[Schools — self-help for poor pupils.] School Self-Help
The school year has begun, the lessons are already in full swing, and joy and happiness are poured over the children's little faces.
But for a very great part this joy will not last long. One already has to buy school books and writing materials. Soon one will have to come to school full and fed, soon it will turn cold and one will have to come warmly dressed. And how many parents cannot even think of making a warm garment for their children, do not even know how to give their children who are at school enough to eat.
How many tears the small innocent little children will shed, how ashamed they will be when for a long time they cannot have the books, when they come to school hungry and in rags.
For this there is one remedy — self-help. The parents of every elementary school and secondary school, each separately, must already organise themselves for a self-help action for the poor children of their school. The matter must not be delayed even by one day. One must agitate among the better-situated parents and among the children themselves that they give their last year's school books to their younger and poorer schoolmates; the book action must and has to be carried out at once. A fund for writing materials must be created. Further, one must already begin organising the feeding of children — a roll with milk. Every child has a right to a warm soup. The parents of every school, with good will and a little bit of organisation, could carry out such a feeding action, and that without too great exertions.
After the book action and after organising the feeding action there must also come an action to clothe the very poor children.
Let us not rob the innocent, cheerful children of their joy; let us not allow any tears of the poor children. Let us, school parents and school children, organise for self-help. This will be not only the joy of the children, but also our own satisfaction.
Let us not delay.
D.
Two Marranos (9)

[Serial story — Nazi Germany; chapter 9.]
Chaim Berg.
A story from Nazi Germany.
9)

I am not doing it simply out of revenge on the Nazis, but out of a sense of duty towards humanity. And my life is too small a sacrifice in comparison with the great debt. Germany must not possess my invention; with it she will destroy the world. But to make my words and their meaning clear and simple to you, so that you can grasp all the psychological motives for my actions, I must first show you my invention.
And looking up[?] with the same expression of love and trust of a father towards a son, he took the marquis by the arm and invited him to go with him. The marquis, however, could not move from the spot, as if turned to stone with surprise at the secret revealed, at the unexpected turn that his vision had suddenly taken.
"Don't be afraid," the professor reassured him. "Whatever may happen tonight or tomorrow with me and with my invention, the bloodhounds will not dare to touch you. You are, after all, an envoy of a great power, and the whole diplomatic corps will defend you with their heads. Come!"
"Ah, I am not afraid, absolutely not afraid of the bloodhounds! Besides, this is an adventure. It is worth any price."
— And the marquis drew himself up at this like a brave fighter facing danger.
The professor led the marquis out into a second, still larger room, which lay several steps lower than the first, switched on the electric light, and the bright light revealed to the marquis the great and terrible invention. The marquis began to contemplate it silently, with the enraptured interest of a military man and diplomat. His face expressed rapture and terror.
The professor did not interrupt him for long: then he began, in a sort of lecture, to explain the machine, which had the appearance of an ordinary torpedo.
"You have probably heard of experiments with a rocket flying[?] machine, which is driven and carried through the air by the force of an internal explosion. The invention is mine, although, for certain reasons, it deliberately bears a stranger's name as inventor. On the same principle of rockets this torpedo is built; it differs from ordinary torpedoes in that it is lifted high into the air by the force of its own first gas explosion. In addition it has at its side this radio-magnetic apparatus, which gives it direction and distance and does not let it deviate from the direction and range[?] that you give it. By setting this sight of the apparatus you can give the torpedo a distance of as many miles as you like, and a direction — let us say to London, Paris or Moscow. The radio-magnetic apparatus will then bring it to the desired place with greater precision than an aeroplane. In this way you do not need to drop the torpedo from aeroplanes or ships and risk human lives. You can set it in motion from Berlin, from my estate, from a forest. The force of the explosion carries the torpedo high under the clouds for a distance of a hundred miles. When the torpedo has covered the distance of a hundred miles, it is heated enough to create a second explosion. Then a third, and so on, until it reaches its appointed place — London, for example, Paris, etc. Then[?] it must fall down from exhaustion[?] of the exploding energy that carried it. When it falls to the ground it must be shattered by the impact. It contains enough deadly gas to annihilate the whole of London."

The Professor's Revenge

After the theoretical part of the lecture, in which the professor described the principles of chemistry, physics and mathematics on which the "devilish machine" had been built, the professor addressed the marquis:
"Have you convinced yourself that all the rumours that were connected with my name were not legends and old wives' tales?" — the professor ended his lecture with a melancholy-sad smile on his face.
The marquis, a captain of artillery and himself an expert in ammunition, had listened to the whole lecture with the enraptured eyes of a good pupil.
"Yes, the rumours were not old wives' tales!" he remarked pensively, trembling with his whole body, as if he had woken from a terrible nightmare of a dream.
"And what are you going to do with the devilish invention?"
"I am going to liquidate it."
"Liquidate? That is, destroy?"
The professor made no reply to this. He again led him into [—] fatherly love and tenderness for a dear son from whom he had been separated for long years, took him by the arm and remarked with the same melancholy little smile:
"Come, let us have a bite to eat; we shall have the last supper together."
Deep in his thoughts about the devilish invention which this good-natured man had invented for the destruction of humanity and its civilisation, he did not notice the tragic meaning that lay hidden in the words "the last supper", taken from the story of Christ.
The professor led him into a room by the laboratory; there the marquis saw a table laid with cold dishes for three persons. He set down on the table a bottle of cognac, which he had earlier had in the laboratory and had now taken along in passing, and showed the guest where to sit.
"I see a table laid for three," remarked the marquis.
"Yes, this was to have been the 'last supper' for three — for me and my two assistants..."
"Ah, I have heard of your assistants... They too figured in the legend. What do you mean by the words 'the last supper'? They sound so dramatic!"

[Article — the struggle against Hitlerism; the Central Anti-Hitlerite Committee.]
(On anti-Hitlerite activity. Sent in by the Central Anti-Hitlerite Committee)
One of the abnormal and clumsy phenomena occurring in Jewish social life is also the short memory.
Jews react to troubles and national misfortunes perhaps more strongly than all other peoples. Among no other nation and tongue do misfortunes make such an impression, or arouse such bitter feelings and experiences, as among Jews. Perhaps this is because they are "practised in trials"; they know how deeply painful and terrible the misfortunes that befall them are. Be that as it may, Jews react exceptionally to every trouble — may it never come. But they have one shortcoming: the reaction is not long-lasting; the feelings of bitterness and the power of resistance against plagues and enemies very quickly become dulled, weakened. One quickly cools down and forgets, or one gets used to the lowly state, even to a catastrophe. One agrees to, or makes peace with, reality and goes on living, until a new trouble comes and calls forth a new storm.
Most strikingly is this conduct borne out in the Hitlerite catastrophe, which struck the whole Community of Israel throughout the world so horrifyingly, which has already caused so much suffering and done so much damage to the whole of Jewry.
At the beginning of the Hitlerite cloudburst the Jewish world shuddered; the grief and anger were immense, the bitterness — beyond measure, the insult — enormous, and the feeling that this was an extraordinarily great national plague was rooted in every Jewish heart. The sense of resistance as well, the awareness that one must stand up against and wage war with courage on the great camps of enemies and angels of destruction arising in Germany, seized the whole Jewish public.
Compassion and the simple feeling of pity for the unfortunate brethren, the German Jews, also took hold of the whole of Jewry, which was ready for sacrifices. But unfortunately the whole tidal wave, the whole storm-wind, gradually subsided. The angel in charge of oblivion did his work, and the whole psyche of the people changed from one extreme to the other: over with grief and anger, over with the reckoning. Meanwhile black clouds keep moving from the Hitlerite inferno onto the Jewish horizon.
That antisemitism is being implanted in millions of hearts like some religious psychosis, that shedding Jewish blood is becoming almost a divine service, a worship, a mitzvah.
People have forgotten that we are dealing with a fearsome hydra, with an evil beast. People have forgotten that the anti-Jewish deadly poison is being spread over the whole globe and tens of millions of people are organising themselves, broadening and strengthening the anti-Jewish front.
And all this people began gradually to forget, and in truth almost came to terms with the situation.
It was forgotten by the "best of the nations" [sic; meaning the best of the people], the leaders of the people, the politicians, the communal activists, and as a result indifference penetrated the masses, the street, the simple Jew, who is preoccupied with his own personal troubles.
And as is the way of things, when a popular mood changes, one already finds excuses and self-persuasions, delusions, etc.
People persuade themselves that Hitlerism is falling, going under, and that very soon, very quickly, the enemy will be removed.
The consequence of this is that the anti-Hitler action is being weakened in all fields, both in the field of the boycott and in the relief action, etc.
This is undoubtedly an abnormal phenomenon, a self-deception, a crime against ourselves. Such horrifying moments must not be [removed] so quickly from the agenda, and the struggle against them must not be halted in mid-course because of weakness and short memory.
Instead of forgetting, one must remember:
1) that Hitlerism in general is strong enough; the greatest oppressor of the Jews since Torquemada's times will not yet so quickly give up his rule. He will still hold on for a long time, and during the time of his wicked reign he will still cause enough suffering to German and world Jewry.
2) that even when he falls, the seed he has sown all over the world will still bear fruit.
3) that in Germany the Jewish situation has not only not become better, but even worse. They have already spent a year and a half of suffering and persecution there, have been weakened and broken, but the decrees against them are not only not getting weaker, but even harsher and more cruel.
4) that the sufferings of the German Jews must not be regarded as simply ordinary Jewish poverty, but as the product of a sudden national catastrophe that has had no equal since the Middle Ages; that they are wretched, broken and stricken, and abandoning them to their fate is a sin and a disgrace. Our enemies will have a great revenge on us, watching how those they have thrust out and driven out go to ruin and the Community of Israel does not help them. Many of the enemies in other countries will want to imitate this, knowing that driving Jews out of a country means: throwing them into the sea, because even their own people will not help them.
5) and finally: every weakening of ours in the struggle against Hitlerism strengthens the enemy, and we thereby cause his longevity.
Remember this, Jews, and become braver and stronger in the anti-Hitlerite activity, which is for us a question of to be or, God forbid, not to be.
S. Kalker.
Around the Third World Jewish Conference in Geneva

[Geneva — World Jewish Conference; letter from our correspondent.] The daily papers have already carried detailed reports from the J.T.A.[?] and from their correspondents in Geneva on the agenda, the speeches, the debates and the resolutions of the Third World Jewish Conference. In this present letter to the readers of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" I shall therefore content myself with describing the behind-the-scenes politics before, during and after the Conference, which was perhaps richer and more dramatic in high political moments than the three-day congress itself.
First of all, the German government. It, the German government — or, as an important part of the world press calls it, "the gangster-and-Dillinger government" — did not at all relish the idea that Jews would gather in the city of the League of Nations and there, before the eyes of the whole world, confer and debate the shameful persecutions and insults of the Hitlerites against the Jews in Germany and against the entire Jewish people.
The Hitler government holds very firmly to the rule: "I may do anything — even kill, rob and beat the Jews with concentration camps; he, however, the plucked one, the tormented one, may do nothing, not even let out a peep, but must accept everything with love and acknowledge the 'chivalry' of the Hitlerites; hence, so far 'not even a hair on the Jews' heads has been harmed.'"
And since in Germany itself they succeed in everything, their appetite indeed grows with the eating, and they would very much like to achieve the same success abroad as well, or in the whole world.
In short, the first chapter began with "Vayishlach" ("and he sent"): emissaries were sent, Jews with long beards and without beards, from Germany to Paris, London, New York, etc. Their task was to "convince" the Jewish leaders abroad to renounce the boycott against Germany, thereby doing the Jews in Germany the greatest favour.
When that did not help at all, the "laws of diplomacy" began. The English ambassador let the Jewish leaders of the "Board of Deputies" know that if the Jewish boycott against Germany stopped, the Jewish situation in Germany would "probably" improve.
Finally, when the German politicians had really become convinced that the Jews are an old, stiff-necked people, Dr. Schacht, Germany's present economic dictator, was handed the mission of teaching the Jews a verse with a stick in the laws of economics. And Dr. Schacht pondered, investigated[?], and in the end — seek and ye shall find — he seized upon a great bargain, namely: the sadly famous "Transfer Agreement". As is well known, the opposition to it in the Jewish street is so great that the whole affair has almost smacked of "scandal", "betrayal", etc. At the closed session of the present World Conference the matter of the "Transfer Agreement" did indeed come onto the agenda. Sholem Asch, Dr. Stephen Wise and others could not find enough words to brand the agreement as a disgrace, a vile act, etc.
The chairman, Dr. Goldmann, then finally came out with open words and said: Honoured Conference! The Transfer Agreement will not last long in any case; the German economic dictator has let us know that "either we withdraw the boycott — or ... he will cancel the Transfer Agreement"...
Sholem Asch would not calm down and called out an interjection: "We must wait until the Hitlerites teach us what 'Jewish honour and dignity' means."
It is superfluous to say that the intensity and the activity of the boycott against Hitler-Germany is even stronger than a year ago, and, as the reports of the various delegations at the Conference show, we Jews can be proud of the result achieved so far: German exports have fallen in some countries by as much as 60–70 percent.
Shloyme Frohman, Zurich.
Geneva, 21/7 1934.
Heard and Seen

Heard and Seen. By Ben Amotz.
The first clappers...
At the cinema.
On the screen — a film filled with all sorts of goings-on, air disasters, surprises and — love betrayal...
The first rows in the hall are full of children of various ages. Among them there are even some who have, it seems, said the blessing "Shehecheyanu" — this is their first outing — today, to the cinema.
The children's looks are agitated[?]. Apparently the drastic scenes, perhaps precisely the scenes of false love, have had an effect on them; but soon their expressions change, a little smile of contentment appears on their innocent little faces — the curtain will soon rise and they will see "live stuff"...
And indeed it does not take long before the live numbers of the "after-programme" [nadprogram] begin. One "number" is stronger than the next. The children are "enthusiastic" and applaud very warmly; they are almost the first "clappers", they do not stint on applause for the half-naked dancing couple, their eyes feast on the "elastic" movements during the dance and — bravo, bravo...
And I looked around the hall and searched for the "modern" fathers and mothers, who deny their children nothing, not even films with love tragedies, with half-naked dancers...
I also searched for the modern educators of today's generation, the teachers with the headmasters, who show more interest in their monthly salaries than in questions of education...
But my search was in vain. The little bravo-clappers apparently no longer need any guardians, any supervisors; they are already mature people, independent connoisseurs of "cultural" productions... And it is no wonder: today's children are, after all, a product of the present time, of our chaotic life. Our whole life is, after all, without control: with Jewish money antisemitic rags are kept going, we send our children to antisemitic schools, we give to the right and to the left, we serve all idolatries, we ape what is foreign to us; the disease of so-called "modernism" eats away at our body, our soul, licentiousness along the whole front — and like the underage little children in the cinema, we are everywhere — the first clappers...
Informers...
The Polish rags that appear in the area of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia are bathing in an abundance of reports on Jewish life in Zagłębie — more correctly said, on our kehilla "gemoyrekhts"[?] [muddle].
Most distinguished in this field are the Chadecja [Christian Democrat] rags that come out of Korfanty's "cheder" in Katowice. From these very rags one learns which rabbis, who lay claim to the Sosnowiec rabbinical seat, have concluded "secret" agreements among themselves on how to "grab" the kehilla money, which kehilla president has committed abuses, etc.
And after the reports come explanations from the heads of the kehilla, who make clear to the readers of the above-mentioned rags, and give Korfanty's "hasidim" to understand, that the whole kehilla struggle is connected with the rabbinate question, that these or those hasidim do not want this or that candidate... All this is illuminated in such detail so that the readers should be precisely informed of what goes on in the Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa kehillas.
And they, the informers, deserve a "yasher koach" for their work. For a number of years now our great men in Warsaw have been seeking the way to a Polish-Jewish understanding, and to this day the question stands at a dead point. But what Warsaw has not managed to do is being realised in Zagłębie; the moment is not far off when the Polish press in Zagłębie will inform its readers about all Jewish matters, for example, which rabbi trades in shmura flour and does not pay any income tax [dochodowy], how much money Jews spend on etrogim, on Hanukkah candles, and so on and so on.
Of one thing I am "afraid": that the Warsaw "Jew-friendly" press should not snatch the informers away for itself; it will surely envy the fact that the rags in Zagłębie have in their service such a large staff of "tellers"... that in Zagłębie there is such a crush for — "informers"...
A lasting bond..
In a short notice in the chronicle of the previous issue it was reported that both associations, "the Merchants' and the Small Traders' Associations in Będzin, have decided jointly to carry out the campaign for the benefit of the flood victims".
The news item, hardly interesting — aroused in me a hotchpotch of thoughts, a confusion of minds, and I did not believe what my eyes saw — "united"...
How much ink (perhaps tears too...) has already been spilled so that these two merchant organisations should be united into one body; so that the two quarrelling "souls" should be transformed into one strong body!...
Once, in the times of "prosperity", when "angels walked in heaven and people on earth" — there were everywhere — in Będzin too — big and small merchants; so naturally one had to found separate little shops [kremlekh] as well, for the big "lions" and for the little lambs. But now that these elements have almost vanished[?] — not only the big ones, but, alas, there are soon no small merchants left either; when on the "Pietrikover" [street] in Będzin one can count the open shops on one's fingers — so what good is the fragmentation?
Therefore it aroused in me (probably in many readers too) satisfaction that the idea of unification is beginning to ripen, that the decisive factors are beginning to understand that unification is an urgent command of the hour, in order to rescue the remnant, the small handful who have to scrape a living from a cheap glass of soda water or a lunch of 4 dishes for 1 zł...
And we truly wish that the real unification of the two merchants' associations should come as quickly as possible, that a strong body should be created, which would act jointly not [only] when a relief campaign has to be carried out after a flood catastrophe, but should be[?] — a lasting bond...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ki Tavo)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Ki Tavo
The Portion
—o—
a) "And it shall be, when thou art come in unto the land" (Deut. 26:1)
"Vehaya" ("and it shall be") is an expression of joy. This indicates that a Jew should rejoice in nothing else but in living in the Land of Israel, as it is said: "Then was our mouth filled with laughter"... Or ha-Chaim.
—o—
b) "An Aramean would have destroyed my father, and he went down into Egypt" (ibid., 5)
"Arami oved avi" — the only words in the verse spoken in the present tense, because this is a permanent thing: Laban always wants to annihilate Jacob... R' Zvi Hirsch Kalischer.
* *
"An Aramean would destroy my father — Laban sought to uproot everything when he pursued Jacob; and because he intended to do it, the Omnipresent reckoned it to him as if he had done it, for with the idol-worshipping nations the Holy One, blessed be He, reckons the thought as the deed." Rashi.
Why should it be so, that with a gentile God reckons an evil thought as a deed, and with a Jew not? Is there then any partiality in the matter?
But the meaning is this: God joins the thought to the deed that the person will carry out; for when a gentile has an evil thought he carries it out, he turns it into a deed... He who knows all knows that he will indeed carry it out, and so He joins it to the deed. A Jew, however, even when he has an evil thought, will not carry it out; but if he does in fact carry it out, he is no better than the gentile... Likewise, when the gentile does not carry out the evil thought, it is not reckoned against him either... Leket Shoshanim.
—o—
c) "Nor given aught thereof for the dead" (ibid., 14)
When you talk to a rich man about charity, he says: to today's poor it is no mitzvah to give; the poor of old were pious, and it was a mitzvah to support them. This is what the verse says: "Nor have I given aught thereof for the dead" — don't make yourself out to be so good-hearted, as though you would have given to the departed; had they been alive, you would not have given to them either, you would have found a flaw in them too. R' Yaakov Meir Yeshurin.
—o—
d) "This day the Lord thy God commandeth thee" (ibid., 16)
"Every day they shall be in your eyes as new, as though you had been commanded concerning them that very day." Rashi.
The halakhic authorities ask why one does not say the Shehecheyanu blessing over a mitzvah that one performs for the first time in one's life?.. (see Shakh, Yoreh De'ah §28; Pri Chadash, ibid.; Responsa Chavot Yair §260; Mor u-Ketziah 222).
But this is the reason: with a mitzvah there is no such thing as a "first mitzvah"; every mitzvah a person performs is the first one — "every day they shall be in your eyes as new"... Yetiv Lev.
* * *
The Rabbi of Biała, R' Moshe Michel, was always a merry man and a wit. When he lay on his deathbed, he had vodka brought, drank "l'chaim" with the Hasidim, and even made a joke:
"Really one ought to say Shehecheyanu over dying, since a person dies only once in his life... But the law is that over a thing for which one says 'who creates the fruit of the ground' one does not say Shehecheyanu, because it is not an important blessing — and dying, it seems, also belongs to 'the fruit of the ground'..."
—o—
e) "Also every plague which is not written in the book of this law" (28:61)
The Written Torah laid down the foundations of Judaism, the Oral Torah interprets them. But among Jews there is never any peace. What one permits, the other forbids, and no small number of quarrels have already arisen among Jews because of it. That "which is not written in the book of this law" — the fact that not everything is written out, giving the rabbis the opportunity to quarrel, one saying that the slaughterer may slaughter and the other that the slaughterer may not slaughter — that is "a plague which is not written"... R' Shlomo Kluger.
—o—
f) "Because thou servedst not the Lord thy God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart" (ibid., 47)
You served Him only when things were bad for you — then you cried out and prayed to Him. But when you were in joy and gladness of heart, you already forgot God...
Divrei Shaul.
—o—
g) "And thou shalt become an astonishment, a proverb, and a byword among all nations" (ibid., 37)
Every nation has its own term of abuse. With one nation, for instance, "communist" is a term of abuse; with another nation "bourgeois" is an insult. The Jews, however, all nations will revile — both as communists and as bourgeois: "a proverb and a byword among all nations"; all will find in the Jew what they hate... Imrei Chen.
Radio Corner

[Radio corner — broadcasts.] A sensational broadcast by Polish Radio for the Jews in America.
Reports have appeared in the press about the sensational broadcast by Polish Radio for the Jews in America, during which the chief cantor Gershon Sirota will perform "Unetaneh Tokef" and "Atah Nigleita".
The broadcast of this religious concert has now been definitively fixed for Saturday evening, the 8th of September, at 11.46 at night. The late hour was chosen because in America that is then the best time for listening to the radio (6 in the evening).
Also taking part in this concert is the great choir of the Nożyk Synagogue under the direction of the well-known conductor Mr. Dawidowicz.
So that the Jewish radio listeners in Poland too may enjoy Sirota's splendid singing, his concert will also be broadcast on all radio stations in Poland.
In America 90 radio stations will relay the concert; thus the Jews of all America, from New York and Chicago to San Francisco and Hollywood, will be able to hear the broadcast of Polish Radio in honour of our New Year.
—o—
The fight against the "radio hares" in Egypt.
The radio stations in Egypt simply could not cope with the huge number of so-called "radio hares" [unlicensed listeners]. The Arabs listened to the radio quite gladly, but they did not think much of paying for the pleasure.
The Egyptian law says that whoever wishes to listen to the radio must pay the appropriate fee; on the other hand, the law says nothing at all about the owners of radio sets. The Arabs indeed interpreted it that way and declared to the radio officials that for having a radio set at home one is not obliged to pay the radio fee.
So the Egyptian authorities played a "Turkish" trick on their Arabs... A strict ordinance was issued to register the radio sets. It was stated that the registration of the set was being done for statistical reasons and would not entail any fee.
Already in the first week more than 3000 Arabs registered their radio sets. When the whole registration had been carried out, the Egyptian Postmaster General announced to his citizens that from now on one would have to pay for listening to the radio, and first of all those who had registered their sets, since it is not possible to have a radio at home and not use it.
Similar fights against the "radio hares", or "black listeners" as they are called, are now taking place in Belgium, France and Italy. The penalties are very severe: people are even punished with imprisonment and confiscation of the set.
In Poland too the fight against the "radio hares" is being waged energetically; they face a penalty of up to 3 months' imprisonment and a fine of 3 thousand złoty.
Looking for a “Shtot” [a Synagogue Seat].

[Humorous feuilleton — the High Holidays; a monologue.] By Y. Oberzhanek [J. Oberżanek?].
(A monologue of a married man)

Hard, very hard it is to be a married man. What do you know, all you wifeless men, of what troubles, what harsh torments, what calamities and sufferings a man must endure who has been punished with having a wife in his possession — especially a wife who laughs at "and he shall rule over her" [after Genesis 3:16]. God guard and shield you, you hear, from being blessed with such a piece of goods, one who says that a wife must be for God and for people — and just such a one is my Jewess; she is for God and for people... What is for God, she says, is for God, and what is for people is for people. And she really keeps her word: eleven months a year she is for "people" and one month she is for God, and do you know which month she is for God? — The month of Elul! That is why, when the month of Elul comes, I tremble like a fish in water; when I remember that Elul is coming into the land, my skin crawls.
The whole year, all eleven months, that is, I am already used to the "people" troubles; I am already used to the winter masked balls; I am already indifferent to the long winter nights when my wife dances whole nights for the public good while I lie at home in chopped-up wounds [?] and nurse the children. To the times when my wife is for "people" I am already accustomed.
Bad is the month when mine is for God. And God-fearing she always becomes when she comes back from the spa...
It was last year: a whole summer she immersed herself in Krynica. Three whole months she purified her sinful soul; soaked through by the baths, burnt by the sun and roasted like a citron [Hebrew hadar], she came back home in those days, and as soon as she had read the welcome on the door — she had not yet managed to read through the "Serdecznie witam!" [Polish, "A hearty welcome!"], and before she even asked me how my health was, how the children were, how business was going — the very first thing she asked was:
"Getzele, what's heard about the shtot?" [shtot — a regular synagogue seat; the word also means "town"]
"In town?" — the whole matter had gone clean out of my mind. "Not bad," I say, "as always at this time."
Up jumps mine like one scalded: "As always! Shlimazl! Cat-head [?]! I don't want it as always, you hear, I don't want it!"
"What do you mean," I say, "you don't want it? Is it up to you, then?"
"Up to whom, then?" — mine is already flaring up, and her roasted little cheeks begin to blaze with anger — "Maybe up to you? If I say no, it will be no, don't you annoy me!" — and the guest [sic, "der gast"] began banging on the table — "I took 'selianki' [probably solanki — brine baths] in Krynica!..."
"It seems to me," I say to her, "that you would sooner have needed a hydropathic cure. You really are talking nonsense."
"I'm telling you, Getzl," — she had already taken a lower tone — "that this year I won't take a shtot there as always. This year I want an 'urozmaicenie' [Polish, a change, some variety]."
Only then did I grasp what my roasted one meant, and I began to calm her:
"What, you mean a shtot for praying? Of course [printed "mehikha tita"], with the greatest pleasure — you want to change the seat — bitte sehr [German, please]."
And who would have imagined that because of a seat I would have so much to sing and say with my Jewess; who could have imagined that over such a "drobnostka" [Polish, trifle] I would have to put aside all my business for a whole month's time and be torn to pieces — would it have occurred to you, such a thing? And if you, too, have a wife who roasts herself three months in Krynica and takes selianki with hydropathies, if you, too, have a wife who is eleven months for people and one month for God, if you, too, have such a "treasure" — you may listen to the story, so that you may draw a moral from it:
It was, as I have already told you, a year ago today, at the beginning of Elul. I and my wife — off we go to rent a shtot.
Where does one go? — When the whole town is nothing but "shtet" [prayer places]: in every window stands a different cantor; wherever there is a house there is a minyan; before every gate there is another "to hearken unto the song"; wherever a heder, wherever a school, wherever a dance hall, wherever a factory premises — benches stand with white slips nailed onto them; whoever has a spare kitchen cupboard makes a Holy Ark of it; whoever has a reserve plush tablecloth makes a parokhet [Ark curtain] of it; wherever there is an empty coal box, they make a bimah of it; wherever there is a cripple, he becomes a "famous" cantor; all the boys who shout "Bagels!" the whole year round become little sopranos and little altos. Go be a sage and know where to go first.
So I and my wife really began climbing up the floors: into one house, out of another, getting acquainted with the strategic niches [?] of every minyan; I inquired about the cantor — who he is, whether he is a melodist, whether he prays with a choir, whether he is an observant Jew, and so on.
My wife, too, did not stand idle and kept gathering information: Is the cantor still a young man? A brunet or a blond? Does he have a wife? Can he break a heart? Will she have a good [printed "dobrane"?] "stanowisko" [Polish, position, place]? Who will be her neighbours — not, heaven forbid, a couple of old yentas? Is there at least a "lufcik" [Polish, small ventilation window] to the "men's shul"? Is there a special hole "dla pań" [Polish, for ladies]? And other information...
So we went day after day, measured out half the town; everywhere I laid out my questions and my wife — her questions, so long and so wide, until at last we rented a shtot at the "Raitshes" [?].
On the first day of Rosh Hashanah in the morning, I am already standing ready, the tallis bag in my hand; mine is not yet finished, she is still doing her toilette. At last, after a two-hour "remont" [Polish, renovation], mine appears in her synagogue toilette.
"What is this?" — I go dead. — "Are you going to a masked ball or to a five o'clock? In such a 'semd' [?] one goes into shul? In such a 'holekh' [?] you go to stand before the Master of the Universe? For this you needed two hours to dress — so that you'd be undressed?... If there are three such 'dressed' women there as you, they won't be able to drive away Satan even with cannons..."
"Idiot! Fool! Simpleton!" — that is my wife's answer for the New Year. — "Maybe you want the Rosenkranzes or the Steinbergs to 'reign' there [Polish królować]? They won't live to see it!"
In short, why should I go on at length: I said mine and mine did hers. Whitened, rouged, half-dressed, with golden masquerade-style "letshlekh" [?], her ears and her fingers hung with "little stones" and pearls and other "świecidełka" [Polish, glittering trinkets], with the little holiday prayer book in her hand — off we went to the "German shul" — "to pray"...
Now, when I remember that my Jewess is coming back from Krynica and that — as last year at this time — I will start climbing up the floors, that we will start putting the cantors to the test, I in my way and my wife in hers; when I remember how my Jewess will dress for two hours on the first day of Rosh Hashanah and in the end go off to shul undressed — when I remember this, a cold sweat runs through my bones; when I remember that now is the month when my wife is for God and not for people — I tremble like a fish in water.
Hard, very hard, I tell you, it is to be a married man, especially with a wife who laughs at "and he shall rule over her", and especially with such a wife, who is eleven months for "people" and one month for God...
Yes, I've talked myself away and quite forgotten that I have to look for a shtot for my wife — and a "wygodne" [?; Polish, comfortable] shtot at that...

To Selichot

Shammes, knock no more for Selichot,
the public has long been getting ready;
for long, long times already
"selichot" one upon the other...

Yes, the secret of Selichot is known
even to our kehilla,
and it can't hurt you women either:
you too should ask — forgiveness...

A Letter from Krynica
(written on a mountain)
By Sz. Bursztyn.

My dear husband Shimon, my life!
Don't be annoyed that I'm not writing to you. Firstly, I have no time, and secondly, I didn't go to the spa to become a writer here. I work here so hard[?] — without any writing.
We go to eat breakfast — I have to get dressed; right after breakfast I have to undress again, and before you know it "lunch" arrives, and I have to dress up again in style; when we're done with lunch, I have to undress again. Well, the undressing wouldn't bother me, but the dressing — it should never have been born... Every woman here wants to show what she owns — so they walk around here in clothes the like of which you have never seen in your life. One wants just to poke out the other's eyes and to convince all the guests that she is a who-knows-who and a who-knows-what...
In short, if you were here instead of me, you would surely forget me fast. You would surely be so busy here looking at the women and girls — I mean, at their clothes — that the days would be like minutes to you, so fast would they fly.
I want to write you now one more thing that will make your ears stand up like a hare's; you may as well hear it:
Yesterday I got acquainted here with a couple of men; supposedly they came here to rest from their hard work — and do you know what? — it's a bluff! They bluffed their wives at home and here they bluff even more! I have heard bluffs before, for instance from you yourself, sackfuls[?]... but bluffs like the ones they tell here I have never heard! One man, a red-haired one, with a pale face, tells us that he gives his wife [her way] in everything, just as she stands and goes. If she wants — she gives him "snuff to smell" [i.e. gives him hell]; if she doesn't want to — she doesn't! That's fine too! He takes everything in good part, and his wife, he says, has never yet said a loud or crooked word to him...
What do you say to that — how is it possible? How can one be a faithful wife to a husband and not give him at least once in four weeks a couple of "round" [juicy] curses?!
Take me, for example, I told him: I am to my husband, may he live and be well, a faithful wife, as faithful as one can possibly be, and nevertheless not a single month goes by without my having to throw something [a jab] at my husband... Whether I have to or not — a woman's nature demands it. One must show a husband what one can do. God forbid not — he'd fly off from home like a free bird.
All the women agreed that I was right.
Be greeted by me and send me money, but more than that week, because I need a few złoty for this, a few złoty for that; in short, I need more money.
Your Gitl.
The Vacation Is Over.

[Humour and satire — "Der Kokh-lefl": a poem on the end of the vacation.]
Our vacation
is already over,
with its hotels
and blintzes and meats,
with banaosh[?] and little rucksacks
and all sorts
of chic [szykowne] "little men".

We sat
with all sorts
of gabbaim, cantors,
and Jewish sportsmen,
we danced
and we sang,
but to feel merry —
that we did not manage.

We tore through
some thirty pairs of socks
measuring the promenade [deptak];
the sea roared
with its eternal murmur,
it still hums in our heads
from its murmur.

Even higher than the sea
and its waves
romped
the boys and girls,
the Stefans and the Elas
and the musicians
of various bands [kapele].

Oh, how we drummed, brothers,
and danced!
Yet our nerves
did not burst after all.
For we, you understand,
before our trip
ordered from a blacksmith
nerves of iron.

We diligently
basked in the sun
(a red wound now
is our shoulder from it).
We also swam
(five kilometres from shore) —
the captain had
no fear on our account.

We also tried
to think a little
on our vacation
in the cool evenings.
We tormented
our tired brain
to think at least one thought
about Hitler and the Jews.

But in a little world
of bare feet
thoughts have
no great interest.
Sun, squealing,
and in every second villa
a radio and music.

But now it's all over
with vacation and with everything,
and all that we have gained
is three pounds of fat.
Now we sit and think
and seek advice:
how does one get rid, Father,
of the burn on our shoulder!

At the open grave of her rich old husband stands a young woman, weeping. The bookkeeper, who had cast an eye on the young widow, began to comfort her: "If you will agree, gracious lady, I can take your husband's place.
Good, the woman answered, I have nothing against it; you only need to arrange it with the gravediggers..
A woman in a mourning shawl is looking for her husband's grave. Coming up to the grave, she notices an unknown woman wiping her eyes.
Who lies here? the widow asks the unknown woman?
Here lies my best, my dearest friend [przyjaciel], the woman answered.
The widow grows agitated and, turning to the grave, says angrily: Your luck, Motl, that you're dead — otherwise you'd have met a black end.

Napoleon's Wife (3)

[Serialized historical tale — Joséphine, Napoleon's wife; part 3.] By H. Abramson.
As soon as Joséphine had settled in her rich palace, the Englishman Williams appeared on the scene. He was now a grown man, highly educated, and on learning that Joséphine was in Paris he came to see her, for she was, after all, the one who had wanted to be his wife and who had exchanged him, for no reason at all, for another. It may be that in her simplicity and naivety she showed too much love, too much joy towards the handsome Englishman, who was now also very rich. From their conversations it emerged that the letters they had written to each other had been intercepted by someone. For a long time the two spent in conversation, recalling the days on the splendid island. And there were evil tongues who told Joséphine's husband unfounded stories. The end was that the husband forbade Williams to come into his house, and when Joséphine protested against this, it was for him the best proof that the stories being told about her and the Englishman were true.
Joséphine's husband sought out other women and would have nothing more to do with her.
By the time Joséphine and her husband had become estranged, she had two children by him, a girl and a boy, and they became her only consolation. With them she spent her days. And although she lacked nothing, since even now her husband kept her richly, in luxury, as befitted so distinguished a man as he was, she nevertheless felt unhappy. The only person to whom she could pour out her heart was Williams, and to him she turned. She wrote him letters, describing to him what she was having to live through. But these letters were intercepted by intriguers, and instead of Williams it was her husband who read them. Now he was sure that his wife was meeting her lover in secret, and it came to a [?] scandal. Beauharnais, knowing how much his wife loved her children, used this to punish her. He took her son away from Joséphine; she was not allowed to see her child. And, as said, he did it only because he knew that he would thereby strike her deep in the heart, for she loved her boy more than anything in the world. Joséphine tried to suppress her pain [?] and obtained from her husband a meeting with him. He used it to abuse and insult her in the worst manner, with nothing at all of the aristocrat about him, and although it was plain to see that he still loved the woman and longed for her greatly, he nevertheless filed for a divorce. As the reason he gave that she, Joséphine, had been unfaithful to him. Nothing was now left to Joséphine but to defend herself, to prove publicly that her husband was slandering her, that he wanted to blacken her name in the eyes of the world and of her children too. To avoid evil tongues she settled with her daughter Hortense in a convent, where she spent a few months in complete quiet, awaiting the judges' verdict.
But in France it was then the eve of the Revolution, and the mood was quite different from that of the old times. People had now begun to look on the woman not as the husband's slave but as a free human being. The judges recognised that Joséphine's husband was not in the right; that instead of accusing her, the woman, of improper conduct, he himself had behaved in such a way as to provoke a protest in the circles where the old aristocracy was not much loved. The result was that Joséphine's husband was refused a divorce.
And Joséphine now became even more popular than before. She won the sympathy of the broad public, because she was the wronged, the insulted mother. From all sides people came to congratulate her on her victory. Even the Queen found it necessary to invite Joséphine to her and congratulated her publicly on her victory.
For three years Joséphine was separated from her husband and her son Eugène [printed "Yudoshin"?]. These were three years of loneliness and gloom on the island of Martinique, despite the fact that her aunt was as good to her as to her own child, and that all her caprices [?] were indulged; but the whole time she was melancholy. She missed Paris, the bustling life, the attention she had enjoyed, the admiration and the esteem. Her only joy was her little daughter, Hortense, whose little voice was always carried on the air, and just as she herself had been when she was a small child, so now Hortense too was beloved by the Black people, who carried her about in their arms.
But quite unexpectedly an order arrived from her husband that she should come back to France, and the man who brought this order was to [?] accompany her with the child all the way home.
Joséphine received this news with great joy. Within a day she was ready to set out on the road, although her relatives begged her to remain with them for good. Now there was no power that could hold her back, and she set out on her way. The thought that soon she would be able to press her child to her heart made her happy.
But Joséphine arrived in France at a turbulent time. It was after the fall of the Bastille, and the Jacobin party had begun to take shape, which set about undermining the aristocracy. The struggle had flared up between the various groups that sought to seize power into their hands. Beauharnais was attached to the moderates; he was in favour of leaving the King in peace, but of introducing reforms. And when Joséphine met him, she almost [?] did not recognise him. He was a new man to her; no trace was left of that playboy and of the jealous man of former days.

What's Happening in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Bans on Praying, Torah Reading and Shofar...

[Będzin — Community; Religion.]
What's Happening in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 20 Elul 5694 — piątek 31 sierpnia 1934 / Friday 31 August 1934.)
Będzin
Bans on Praying, Torah Reading and Shofar...
A few weeks ago a committee was formed which took upon itself the task of completing the "historic" mikveh building in our town.
The committee, which by the way consists of energetic people and experts, appealed at its founding to the Jewish population for support, but the appeal did not bring the proper result and the necessary sum, sufficient to complete the building, was not collected.
Because of this the rabbinate issued a ban on praying, reading the Torah and blowing the shofar in those minyanim and shtiblekh that have not yet fulfilled their obligations regarding the mikveh.
The ban, which took effect from last Sabbath, provoked a bit of a "commotion" among the shtibl crowd. The upshot is that a large number declared that they would go out collecting money for the building campaign.
———
The writer of these lines visited the new mikveh building these days (or, as R' Mendel Rozenwast[?] calls it, the "bath establishment"). From the information we received from the building committee it emerges that for the complete finishing of the establishment a sum of about 25 thousand zł. is still needed. During the short time the building committee has been active, very important investments have been carried out. The machines — by the way, of the newest system — are being installed, the sewerage has been carried out "ar"g"[?], so that as soon as the interior work is finished, the establishment, which is being built according to the newest technical requirements, will be able to start operating and bring the kehilla treasury considerable income. If, on the other hand, the attitude of the townspeople is indifferent and the necessary sum is not collected, the enormous sum that the building has already swallowed up to now will go to waste. It is therefore to be hoped that the collection campaign will find a broad echo among the whole Jewish population and that everyone will help according to his means, so that Będzin should finally have a modern and hygienic bath establishment.
Mr. Dawid Zmigród Undertakes to Build the First Floor of the "Orphans' Home"

[Będzin — Charity.]
The board of the "Orphans' Home" is under the impression of the sensational proposal received from Mr. D. Zmigród and his wife concerning the building of the "Orphans' Home". In the proposal Mr. Zmigród declares that, in connection with the 25th anniversary of his wedding, which falls next year, he has decided to complete the first floor of the front building of the "Orphans' Home".
On the basis of this proposal Mr. Zmigród was invited to Tuesday's board meeting of the charity society. At the meeting Mr. Zmigród supplemented his proposal, adding that he is ready to give the undertaking in notarial form ("rejentalne") and that he will shortly set about fulfilling his promise, so that this should be an example for other wealthy men in the town.
The board accepted the proposal with satisfaction, expressing the wish that Mr. Zmigród carry out the fine promise as quickly as possible.
Tax Office Officials Will Carry Out an Inspection in the Town

[Będzin — Taxes and Trade.]
The local tax office has sent the Merchants' Association a communiqué with the following content:
The annual inspection (lustracja) carried out in Będzin this year established very many cases that are contrary to the binding regulations. For example, merchants who hold patents (trade licences) of a lower category, or trade entirely without patents, or run workshops; signboards are missing, the patents are not located in any designated place, registration cards are missing for the separate storehouses (składy).
In connection with this, the tax office is proceeding to a new inspection in Będzin. Delegates of the tax office have received an order to draw up reports (protocols) against those who will transgress the above-mentioned.
The Starosta Disregards the Petition of the Young Shochtim.

[Będzin — community; ritual slaughter.]
As we have already written, the gmina [Jewish community] has begun a campaign to combat the secret slaughtering carried on by the young "little shochtim" Radoszycki and Gerlic, and also by Yechezkele Heitzman [?]. When the police caught the shochtim "in the act", they took them to the police station (komisariat), where reports were drawn up against them.
The shochtim Radoszycki and Gerlic have — as it appears — still not given up their lawless deeds, and have turned with a petition to the starosta [district head].
In the petition they demand that the authorities permit them to practise shechita because: 1) they hold a semicha [ordination] from the local rabbi, and 2) in 1926 the Supreme Court issued a ruling that shochtim who hold semicha have the right to practise shechita even without the permission of the kehilla.
The shochtim, however, forgot that there is a law which says that all income from shechita must go into the kehilla treasury.
On the basis of this law the shochtim received the answer that their petition is not being taken into consideration.
How a Woman Fooled a "Kozak" of the Czeladź Magistrate.

[Czeladź — crime.]
The woźny [municipal usher] of the Czeladź magistrate's office, Mr. Kozak, received an order to take a certain woman to the municipal jail. When the woźny entered the woman's flat and told her the purpose of his visit, the woman showed no resistance whatsoever, but asked the woźny to allow her to step out for a few minutes, to which the woźny agreed. When several hours had passed and the woman had not come back, only then did it occur to the woźny that he ought to go and take a look where she was. Only then did he discover that the woman had "led him into the cheder" [had taken him in] — that the flat was locked up tight. At first he began calling for help. But seeing that his cries did not reach the street, he jumped out through the window onto a neighbouring roof, from where he managed to get out onto the street...

As 50-year-old Sara Szniorowska [?] was passing Trapojer's [?] house on 3 Maja Street on Thursday, a piece of wall fell from the house and struck the woman on the head.

Investigation dropped against the doctor accused of poisoning two children by mistake.

This week the prosecutor of the local district court informed the Doctors' Association in Zagłębie that "the investigation is being dropped because no crime whatsoever has been established".

The district committee of the National Loan appeals to all subscribers to pay, from today until the 5th of this month, the overdue instalments of the declared sum. Whoever does not pay within this deadline will lose the instalments paid so far.

Annual general meeting of “Gordonia”

Last Saturday the 9th annual meeting of the Będzin “Gordonia” took place.

A Jewish boy is struck by a tram.

Yesterday at midday the 9-year-old Szwajcer was walking back from People's School („Folks-shule“) no. 2 in Będzin. On Kołłątaja[?] Street he ran quickly out of a house into the street; at that moment a tram was passing, which struck the boy, and from this he fell unconscious. [—] Mr. Y. Rotenberg[?] carried him in his arms to the hospital, where it was established that the boy was injured in the head.
Reb Yisroel Moshe the shoykhet is active again.

Last Tuesday the kehilla board in Będzin held a meeting at which the question of shechita was brought up in connection with the coming holidays, when the shechita output is greater. And it was decided to reinstate Reb Yisroel Moshe in the slaughtering of poultry. The rabbinate also consented to this decision, and from Motzaei Shabbat on Reb Yisroel Moshe is active again...
The Rabbi's health has improved.

The Rabbi of Będzin, may he live long and well [R' Tzvi Hanoch HaKohen Levin], who came back this week from Marienbad, fell seriously ill. Yesterday his condition improved and the patient feels better.

Because of renovation the hospital in Będzin refuses to admit a sick Jew.

Passers-by on Małachowskiego Street in Będzin saw the following scene last Wednesday: in front of the hospital a sick Jew, a certain Fuks, was left standing outside, whom the hospital did not want to admit.
To the intervention of the secretary of the Jewish kehilla the answer was that „because of the renovation there is no room for the sick man“.
Hundreds of people watched this living „spectacle“. Finally the sick man was taken to the Sosnowiec Jewish hospital at the expense of the Będzin kehilla.
I have a child for sale...

— I have a child for sale, a child of a year and a half, a little boy.
With these words a woman addresses us who came to the editorial office, and before we had even managed to ask the woman anything, she went on talking:
Some 3 years ago she married and had this little boy, whom she wants to sell, because the husband thought it over and decided that he needs neither a wife nor a child, and left her.
The woman and the child find themselves in a situation with no way out; there is not even a dry piece of bread, and she cannot go out to earn either, because she has to stay with the child — so she decided, plain and simple, to sell the child.
— And you must know, the naive woman goes on, that I have no papers [„aktn“] with my husband, so that I will be able to sell the child outright. Whoever buys the child will have true joy of him. Write about it in the paper, I beg you.
— And how much do you want for your child? — we ask the woman.
— I would like 2000 zł. But if a suitable buyer turns up, one can bargain. One has to look at the „goods“.
— What did we want to answer this woman? Sad are the circumstances, sad is life, and sadder still today's notions of life. For this woman it is quite simple: she wants to sell the fine and good goods which she possesses, and if a buyer turns up, there will be bargaining. She sees a threefold benefit in it: she will be rid of a burden, she will have money, and finally the child will also be better off.
— Only let it be a good buyer, says the woman, not understanding why we do not answer her.
And what, indeed, did we want to answer this woman? It is sad — but true.

From Sport

[Sport — Zagłębie.] A disastrous start to the Class „A“ autumn championships.
On Sunday the autumn championships of the Class „A“ in Zagłębie began. Because of heavy rain, however, the matches did not take place; of the five scheduled matches only the match between the following took place:
„Płomień“ — „Policja“ 3:1 (0:0)
[It was played] on the police ground in Sosnowiec and ended with a victory for „Policja“ by 3:1. Until half-time the „Płomień“ players walled up their goal, and the police team, despite its great superiority, could not score a single goal. Only after half-time did the police team change its tactics, as a result of which it scored three goals. For „Płomień“ — an own goal. The „Płomień“ team proved to be a very weak side. Referee: Mr. Okularczyk.
„Cracovia“ (Kraków) — „Unia“ 0:1
On the sports stadium of „Unia“ a friendly match was played with the league team „Cracovia“ of Kraków. The guests played well despite all the difficulties caused by the weather. „Unia“ played with great ambition. The match was broken off in the 35th minute because of a downpour. The goal for „Cracovia“ was scored by Wieliński. Referee: Mr. Grajcer [?] of Częstochowa — good.
