The Year 5694. (Reflections for Rosh Hashana).

[Article — the year in review; Rosh Hashana.] By Moshe Feinkind.
The year 5694 has inscribed itself in the martyrology of the Jewish exile in black letters, to everlasting abhorrence...
Every page that tells us of the events and sufferings of the Jewish people in the past year is soaked with tears and blood.
Before our eyes the tragedy of the German Jews has played out, and is playing out still: they had to abandon their goods and possessions, take the wanderer's staff in hand and the rucksack on their shoulders, and leave their home — in which the bones of their holy forefathers "of generations upon generations" rest — and wander wherever their eyes carry them.
With the ringing of church bells, in many German localities the people were told that they would no longer have any dealings with Jews, that Jews may not set foot on the "holy" Hitlerite soil, that they must immediately [?] leave the place they occupy, etc.
When the Huguenots were driven out of France, the nations that took them under their arms and protection welcomed them with the ringing of bells and church singing and received them ceremoniously; whereas when tens of thousands of Jews had to flee Hitler's hell, or were expelled, there were barely a few countries, which one can count on one's fingers, that — looking away [?] — let in [?] the wandering, homeless Jews, in a fixed number.
Among these few, counted countries, Poland and the Land of Israel stand in the first rank.
Poland, which already has an old tradition of opening its gates to tormented and persecuted Jews — Poland, which hospitably received the Jews who immigrated in the times of the Crusades — this time too opened its gates to the refugees from Germany, giving them asylum and protection.
Poland was one of the first to defend the interests of the German refugees at the sessions of the League of Nations and at the meetings of its commissions. Poland also supported with all its authority the Jews of Upper Silesia, who submitted a petition to the League of Nations complaining of the chicanery practised by Hitler's regime against the Jewish minority — and as a result the Hitlerite beast had to withdraw all the decrees against the Jews there.
Poland also, through its diplomatic representative at the forum of the League of Nations, demanded free immigration for Jews into the Land of Israel, declaring that the Land of Israel must give an answer to the thousand-year-old longing of the Jewish people for the Land of Israel.
The Jews of Poland, furthermore, who feel the exile on their own skin, created a relief committee for the exiles from Germany, and at the same time this committee is conducting, on a large scale, a diligent economic boycott campaign against everything that may originate in Hitler's state, may his name be blotted out [printed "י"ש"]; and against all who break the boycott, sparing none and showing favour to no single Jew.
All of world Jewry supports this boycott in its full extent. The solidarity of the Jews in this field proves that in unity lies the strength of the wandering Jewish people.
And as long as we have not broken the obstinacy of Hitler's regime towards the Jews, the boycott campaign is the only weapon of self-defence and dignity. Let them know!...
*
"But the Land of Israel must also give an answer to the thousand-year longing of the Jewish people for the Land of Israel," said Poland at the session of the League of Nations in the year 5694.
Such an answer, unfortunately, the Land of Israel did not give in the past year.
Thanks to [i.e. owing to] the restriction and obstruction of Jewish immigration by the British authority as mandatory of the country, the Arab has meanwhile seized Jewish work; the purchase of land there by Jews has also been restricted and obstructed by the colonial authority, and no large new purchases have been made.
The "Keren Kayemet", apart from the land for "Kfar Ussishkin", has also barely bought any new land, because of the unheard-of boycott of the [national] funds on the part of certain Zionist circles.
To all demands and petitions the English authority is deaf and dumb, which gives the impression that England supports an Arab land and not a Hebrew land.
But England does not spare compliments addressed to the Zionists, who build the desolate land with their sweat and blood, repeating solemnly each time — at the opening of Haifa port, at the Palestine debates held in the past year in the English Parliament, and on other occasions as well — that the authority will abide by the Balfour Declaration.
In fact, however, this is mere [?] lip service, of which England is a skilled master, knowing the art of "one thing in the mouth and another in the heart."
The Balfour Declaration is violated with regard to the Jews at every step by the very same authority that preaches so beautifully in its name, so that soon almost nothing of it will be left.
* *
The fire of quarrels that has caught hold of our own ranks because of — let us say it openly — hegemony, has also done much to weaken our front and position in our land, for which every Jew now longs so strongly.
On the other hand, it has also weakened the prestige of the Zionist camp towards the outside.
The quarrels among the Jews, when they still sat on their own soil, each man under his vine and under his fig tree, always caused the destruction of the Land of Israel.
The enemy exploited the favourable moment of the disunity of the Jewish people, ruled over it and grew strong.
The same sad scene is unfortunately repeating itself before our eyes too.
The Zionist Organisation, which in its 35 years grew into a world power that must be reckoned with, willy-nilly, is broken, divided and crumbled into pieces.
It has turned into little parties and little groups that fight one another in the dirtiest way — from which the common enemy alone draws benefit for himself, entrenching himself with Jewish money on the land, seizing Jewish work, Jewish positions, etc.
God's curse — they are struck with blindness: they are blind, or do not want to see, what danger the "blind" tearing-apart within the Zionist camp poses to the existence of the General Zionist movement; and when the General Zionists from the whole world, those not yet seized by party egoism and wickedness, gathered in Kraków and stretched out a hand for peace, the Warsaw General Zionist conference rejected the hand of peace of their own flesh and blood with indignation and contempt.
One must say that what plays the role here is egoism more than principle, misleadership more than leadership.
And so the incitement continues to be carried on by a few irresponsible disturbers of the peace, who nonetheless sit firmly on their chairs, across the whole Zionist front.
In our year's balance sheet, which has shown so many liabilities in the history of Jewish suffering, the account also closes with the liability of the absence of peace in the Zionist ranks.
And that is the saddest thing with which the year 5694 closes.
Perhaps the new year will bring us the longed-for peace — that is what we wish.
The Kehilla Economy and Its Assets

(To the attention of those who wish to complete the mikveh building.)
When we look at how our economy appears — our kehilla "nemoyuekhts" [?] [probably: property/buildings], the system by which it is managed — it truly begins to nauseate. At such a moment one would like to spit and run far, far away and no longer look at the rotten, disgusting mould which is still in use to this very day.
It is, upon my life, quite a story, how the state of affairs looks today, what condition our kehilla economy is in. After all, the "Jewish local parliament" has made enormous progress in recent years: it has modernised itself, it consists of a council and a board, so that one body can do nothing without the other. It is not, after all, like once upon a time, when a town like, for example, Będzin had all in all three "dozores" [members of the old kehilla board, the dozór] and they ran the whole town as they pleased, [—?]. Today it is no longer so; those times are long past and will never return. Today the Jewish kehilla is a whole "urząd" [government office], so that every trifle must be brought to a meeting, and a decision is not made so easily and quickly — when one is talking about an urząd, that is simply out of the question.
But if there is a Jewish proverb, "Where there are many servants the house is not swept," it fits best of all this kehilla economy of ours. The state of the kehilla [property/buildings] has never stood at such a low level as we see today. In the worst times and under the hardest conditions the town had a cantor, and today the synagogue is orphaned, without a cantor and without any order whatsoever. There is no one there to show respect for, and reverence for a holy place has long since vanished. On the contrary, when one needs to quarrel and settle accounts, it has become almost a tradition to come to the synagogue for it. And whoever does not look at how the town beit midrash appears — [will see] that sweeping it out would be like carrying out a renovation; on top of that the beit midrash has become a sort of city of refuge for beggars, and if one does not catch a disease after such a "visit," one must truly recite the blessing of deliverance (gomel)...
The same is true of the mikveh. Formerly, before there were kehilla councillors, the town somehow had a mikveh, and today the matter has become a legend, a fantasy, a thing that apparently will never be realised. True, people set about completing [?] the construction of this useful municipal institution, but somehow everyone regards it all with apathy, for two reasons: first, the times are hard and bitter, so that even with the best will one looks for a pretext not to give; and second — we would like to be honest and tell the truth — people refrain from giving simply because there is no certainty that all the money will be used for the purpose appealed for [?]. After all, money has already been collected for the mikveh so many times that the building could already have been completed. Those who collected the money gave the town no account, and therefore it is no wonder that people are indifferent to the matter.
The use of coercive measures — closing the shtiblekh and forbidding prayer [there] — makes a downright ridiculous impression. Practice has already shown that nothing will be achieved by coercion; on the contrary, it only inflames tempers and the division grows still stronger. So, if one wants to halt an activity, if one wants to paralyse a campaign, let one adopt coercive measures — and then one can be sure that the campaign undertaken is doomed to fail.
We hold that, for all the defects and mistakes made until now, it must not be allowed that the mikveh building should go on standing at a dead point. One must not forget that the undertaking has already swallowed a large fortune — some 60–70 thousand zł. are already sunk in it. So one must reckon that in all only about 25 thousand zł. are still needed, and we shall have a modern mikveh, which will bring benefit to the town and to the kehilla — profits.
And let it not be forgotten that Będzin is a town which, even under the worst conditions, is accustomed to give, and collecting in the town the necessary twenty-five thousand zł. is no great matter, and they will certainly be found — but never with such [—] [?] and with coercive measures.
We have already said that today we live in very hard economic conditions, where every grosz plays a role, and without full certainty that the money will be used entirely for its proper purpose people will by no means give. Jewish Będzin must give, wants to give and will indeed give the necessary sum to complete the mikveh building, but one must not forget that this can only happen when there are people who will remain responsible for the campaign undertaken.
As we hear, there is a committee consisting of respected citizens of the town — so let these people take upon themselves the full responsibility, both for the money collected and for completing the building.
If one truly wants to complete the mikveh as quickly as possible, one must first of all create sympathy in the town, and that can only happen when we see that we have before us responsible people and that they take upon themselves the full responsibility for the completion campaign.
For this purpose it is necessary that the town should know to whom it is entrusting the money; it is therefore desirable that the committee issue an appeal in which it proclaims that it is responsible for everything, and to it are entrusted the collected, hard-earned pennies of the people — and then the money will without doubt be collected, and thereby the town will give the building committee the possibility of finishing the necessary work.
R. Let.
Let Sosnowiec Remove the Stain

[Sosnowiec — kehilla; the municipal Talmud Torah; opinion piece.]
How many times have we already spoken about this outrage, and today we must once again touch on the question which, were it not for us in Sosnowiec, would perhaps have had no place in any town in Poland.
Unfortunately we must once again talk about the gentile of the municipal Talmud Torah.
It is truly a disgrace and a pain that a newspaper has to touch so many times on such a trifle, such an absurdity; unfortunately, unfortunately, and to our regret we must speak about it so many times, and that only because Jewish Sosnowiec is so frozen towards both big and small matters.
Sosnowiec is a town that has a Talmud Torah building such as there are not many in Poland, and yet with its quarrels and squabbling it has brought matters to the point that the watchman (stróż), the [overseer?], is to be entitled to a pension of [one] thousand five hundred zł. And since they did not want to pay it to him, he went onto the mortgage of the Talmud Torah for a sum of no less than five thousand zł. From this alone we see how the Jewish community leaders took care of this debt, so that 1500 zł. became no less than 5,000 zł.
Now that the gentile already stands with such a tidy sum on the first mortgage, he wants to crawl further, so that around him a gang has gathered which has taken a liking to the building, and they want nothing more and nothing less than to put the building up for auction and buy up the Talmud Torah.
It goes without saying that in no town would such "miracles" have happened, but Sosnowiec has long been a town of surprises, so that it has presented us with such a pretty little flower as well.
And the question arises: could the smallest and poorest shtetl in Poland have shown us such little flowers? Certainly not; and if such an incident had happened in whatever way, people would have tried to hush it up, and before the news reached the public it would have been settled, so as to wipe out the disgrace that had arisen as quickly as possible.
To our shame and pain, however, Jewish Sosnowiec is still not mature enough to understand that this is a disgrace, and it remains indifferent to everything, as if nothing had happened.
Only now, when it has already cut them to the seventh rib [i.e. to the quick], have people begun to rub their eyes, as if they had woken from a lethargic sleep and seen how great and terrible the disgrace is.
And so it was decided to try at any price to throw off the shame and to remove the gentile from the mortgage.
For this purpose people came together, and at a meeting it was unanimously decided to raise the necessary sum, so that the mortgage can be cancelled.
The town may well be ashamed that with its apathy it has brought about such a shame; but now the time has come when the stain must be wiped away; therefore a redemption campaign should now be carried out at a vigorous pace, and we shall free ourselves of the disgraceful stain.
Dr. Papuri.
Chaim Berg — Two Marranos. A Story of Nazi Germany (10)

[Serial fiction — literature; Nazi Germany.] Chaim Berg. "Two Marranos". A story of Nazi Germany. (10)
— Don't you remember Leonardo da Vinci's picture of Jesus' last supper before the crucifixion? — asked the professor, pulling the cork out of the bottle.
— Who is going to be crucified? — the marquis was already frightened.
— They meant to crucify three Jews, Germany's greatest patriots, but two have already escaped, marquis, marquis! — He handed the marquis a glass of the liquor and raised his own.
— You frighten me, professor! What do you mean?
— What do you have to be afraid of? Am I afraid? I have never been as calm as I am now, before my crucifixion. Drink, marquis!
The marquis automatically poured the cognac into his mouth; his thoughts were concentrated on the tragic words "the last supper", "crucifixion".
— You have given me so much confidence, professor — the marquis spoke up — can you not explain to me? Have your assistants abandoned and betrayed you?
— Oh, no!... — I myself forced them to leave Germany. When I told you I was going to telegraph my daughter, it was not entirely the truth. I was also waiting for, and received, a telegraphic message from my assistants that they had already crossed the Czechoslovak border, thank God! They have freed my hands.
— So the tragic "supper for three" did not take place, and two Jews were saved from the cross; hopefully nothing will happen to the third either, eh?
At this the professor suddenly burst out laughing, began to choke with laughter and became hysterical. The transition from tragedy to laughter was so unexpected that the marquis was frightened to death:
"Has he gone out of his mind? Perhaps the devilish[?] invention and the whole séance in the middle of the night are nothing more than the product of a mad head, a phantom of the brain?"
— What is the matter with you, professor? — he rose from his chair, alarmed.
— Sit! Sit in your place and don't be frightened — the professor calmed him with a commanding movement of the hand — I have not yet gone out of my mind.
— For God's sake! — muttered the marquis, and could no longer calm himself.
— The War Ministry, then, did know about your private scientific work?
— What else did you think? That abroad should know and the German government should not? I invited the commission myself. One of my assistants, the greatest mechanical engineer the world has possessed (he also invented and designed "Big Bertha", which shelled as far as Paris!), is a very nervous creature, as befits a true genius; he has a habit of tearing paper, chewing it and swallowing it. This habit of his is known even to his students. So I arranged with him that in the presence of the bloodhounds, who would come to rummage and take from us all the drawings and formulas and afterwards remove all three of us from the world, he should not forget his habit just then and should swallow some scrap of paper — and that is how it happened. The commission raised an outcry that the Jew had swallowed an important formula, a tremendous military secret. As we had agreed between ourselves beforehand, I at once took the side of the commission and did not allow my assistant to be defended, stamped my feet at him and ordered a large portion of castor oil to be poured into him, so as to get the secret out of him. The result of this farce was that the commission waited a long time until the Jew relieved himself[?], and his stool was examined in the most thorough manner...
— Ah, yes! A colossal trick[?]!
— But this chapter is not yet closed; the revenge will not end with the Jew's stomach — only tomorrow at ten[?] o'clock the commission must come again for a demonstration of the revenge-tragedy. I asked for two days' time in order to give my assistants and my brothers and nearest relatives an opportunity to pack themselves off out of the country!... I used as a pretext the need to perfect something in the machine, and then the commission together with the inventor... — and the professor rose and made a movement of the hand that described how the laboratory, with each and every thing in it, would fly into the air and be destroyed...
The two Marranos looked at each other long and silently, like two great conspirators...
Now the marquis grasped the meaning of the tragic words, "the last supper".
Looking into the professor's suddenly frozen face, with his two bulging[?] eyes lit up with youthful hatred, he understood that no power in the world would be able to talk the professor out of his murderous and self-destroying plan, to tear out of his hands the revenge in Hitler-land... But he envied him, and began to think what role he himself could play in the great tragedy.
(The End.)

From Year to Year.

[Zagłębie — year in review; Sosnowiec and Będzin: kehilla, rabbinate, elections, institutions.] A small balance sheet of Jewish public life in the year 5694.
By S. Lewkowicz.

The past year 5694 was poor and pale for us in Zagłębie. There are no cheerful items to record in the annual balance sheet; everything has congealed, even on the "fronts" of the seven-year war over the

Sosnowiec rabbinic seat

no change at all has taken place. The forces expended were used only to guard the "strategic positions" on the "battlefield"... which spins like a witch's wheel around the Sosnowiec kehilla, sinking [?] ever deeper into the abyss. Years go, years come, the battle goes on, and the whole of Jewish public life falls victim to it.
The whole world groans under the heavy crisis; especially sad is the situation of the Jews all over the world. But the Jews of Sosnowiec, besides the crisis, poverty and other economic calamities, again went through a new misfortune this year —

Kehilla elections.

In the month of January kehilla elections took place in Sosnowiec. A hellish fire flared up around the elections. Sosnowiec had the privilege that the "world press" took an interest in the elections, to which the heaviest calibres were brought out. Jewish Sosnowiec was steeped in... election sermons and election leaflets, but today, when we already stand on the threshold of a new year, the fate of the new kehilla is still not clear... for in Sosnowiec they hold little [?] by the rule that "on Rosh Hashanah it is written" — there they write all year round... Appeals ("rekursy") and denunciations fly to Będzin and to Kielce from all sides, and so the little wheel turns back and forth.
And the sum total — chaos, a jumble; the whole of Jewish public life is paralysed and broken, destructive forces rage, the authority of the kehilla keeps falling, thanks to the fact that the organs of power limit the activity of the kehilla to a minimum.
A living example of this state of utter chaos is the Sosnowiec

Talmud Torah.

An institution which, with normal kehilla activity, ought to be a model for other towns. The large building with its proper grounds could surely have been a corner of paradise for the hundreds of poor children. But who cares about an institution from which one cannot make any party capital, which cannot be used for the vile behind-the-scenes politics? And so the institution has indeed been neglected, has become no-man's property, until the caretaker-woman [?] of the courtyard "took over" [?] and became the real mistress of the house...
The situation in other institutions looks no better. One completely forgets the institutions that struggle with all their strength for their existence, such as the Jewish hospital, the old-age home, the interest-free loan fund (Gemilut Chesed) and Linat HaCholim. The administration of the "GNE." [?] has created an important branch: an out-patient clinic (ambulatorium) has been opened, which is today the only panacea [?] for the poor Jewish population, for those who wander about like a passing shadow and have nothing with which to get through the day.
In other areas of public life in Sosnowiec, too, we have more liabilities than assets to record. As in all towns and townlets, in Sosnowiec too an

Anti-Hitler Committee

was created, which was not granted long life. For a few months after its "birth" the committee was properly active, but the "ardour" gradually cooled off, the body shrank so much that of the Anti-Hitler Committee there remained only — "Hitler", i.e. once again the merchants who sell their souls to the devil and grow rich on Jewish ruin became active...
The asset on the account of the past year is the victory of the Jewish lists at the

City council elections.

The opinion of the greatest optimists was that the Jewish population would be represented by at most six councillors — but the power of peace [unity] worked wonders and a "miracle" happened: a minyan [ten] of Jewish councillors were elected; for the sake of peace the Jews gave up one, and there remained — 9...
A tremendous apathy reigns among the merchants and craftsmen because of the new trade, industry and guilds law; at meetings reproaches are levelled at the central associations, which did not hold any protest rally [?] ("wiecyk") before the laws came into force. However justified [?] the reproaches may be, the greatest reproach must be levelled at the members themselves, because they have lost every interest even in their own institutions, lost the sense for public life and organisation.
— A sad balance.

* * *

No better did Jewish life look in Będzin, which in recent years had shown much life, energy and creative power in the Jewish social-economic field — it has almost nothing positive to record, such as ought to be created in the course of a year in such a Jewish community.

The new kehilla administration,

which people had hoped for years to see at the helm of the kehilla and which did indeed show signs of life, has, after a few months of its existence, remained standing at a dead point and become incapable. The reason is supposedly that not only has the new kehilla failed to tear out by the roots the weeds that had grown on the body of the Jewish kehilla, but it has allowed the wildness and lawlessness to spread even more and seize every detail of kehilla life.
The stumbling block of the kehilla are the illegal little shochtim who cause colossal damage through the

Secret slaughter.

"All may slaughter" has become "the fashion": whoever has a rabbinic licence (smicha) in his bosom and a slaughtering knife (chalaf) in his pocket — becomes a shochet in Będzin...
The shechita question, which was left as an inheritance by the previous leaders, is the main wheel of the kehilla wagon. During the last months the matter has not left the agenda; all sorts of suitable and also unsuitable means have already been used, but "the ice does not budge" — the little shochtim do their work and the kehilla till grows poorer from day to day...
A sad chapter in the history of Jewish Będzin will be taken up by the result of the city council elections. A few weeks before the elections the slogan of unity, of uniting all groupings, rang out — and the upshot was that the "unification" remained on paper and everyone "made his own Sabbath"... When the result became clear a protest rally [?] ("wiecyk") was held, people protested, negotiations were conducted about mandates to be ceded, but little by little the "storm in a glass of water" grew quieter and the mandates remained with the seat-grabbers.
A weak movement was also felt in the political organisations. The only work consisted of holding badge sales for summer camps and for so-called [?] "cultural" purposes...
Of cultural work there is of course no talk; in today's times it has become a luxury "article"...
The only plus in this field is the

"Hazamir" library,

where quiet, modest work is carried on, the newest books are bought, and around the library gathers the youth that still reads a Yiddish book.
The philanthropic societies are in a moribund state and consequently do not have the means to fulfil their tasks towards the large number of needy. One single "GNE." [?] had, despite the prevailing crisis, the energy to undertake a meritorious action — that is the "Moshav Zkenim" (old-age home), which was enlarged by several new rooms thanks to the help of the Jewish public.
The general balance is meagre, poor both in the economic and material sense and in the spiritual and cultural sense.
May the new year 5695 be a better one, a happier one in Jewish life in general and in the Jewish life of Zagłębie in particular.
— Would that it be so.
The “Widzew Manufaktura” — the Crown [?] of Polish Industry.

[Łódź — industry; descriptive report (possibly a PR piece).] The “Widzew Manufaktura” [Widzewska Manufaktura, Łódź] or, as one usually says in Yiddish, “Asher Kohn’s piece of linen” [Oskar Kon]: it is hard to give the reader in words an idea of how a piece of linen is created in “Widzew”, and harder still to picture for him, even in general outline, what this enterprise is — this mighty mechanical colossus that bears the name “Widzew Manufaktura”. The “Widzew Manufaktura” occupies an area of 340 morgs of land, on which there are more than 340 buildings, and in every building the most wondrous and varied machines; every machine serves a different purpose, and around all these machines turn no fewer than 7,500 workers. “Widzew” — it is a whole town, it is a town within a town, or more correctly, it is Łódź itself, that which gives it the right to the name “the Polish Manchester”. We visit the “Widzew Manufaktura”. We enter the factory building that is the foundation of the other buildings, the combing room, where the raw cotton that comes to “Widzew” from Egypt and America is cleaned and prepared [?] for spinning. In three such large halls the cotton is cleaned and refined until it becomes an ideal spinning material, and then it passes into the spinning mill. The long rows [?] of machines of the “Widzew” spinning mills move at such speed that the eye cannot catch it.
More than 300,000 spindles are found in these spinning mills; the full bobbins and the spun yarn are carried out on an aerial railway that runs high in the air, and one spinning mill is also connected with the next by an underground canal, through which a railway goes to the large weaving sheds. These gigantic weaving sheds are driven by 22 electric motors. Here 3500 looms of the newest construction are at work, turning out tens of thousands of metres of goods daily. From the weaving sheds the finished goods pass into the bleaching works, dye works, printing works and finishing works [appretura]. The “Widzew Manufaktura” holds to the principle of self-sufficiency [?]: all materials, machines and goods needed for the gigantic plant are made in the factories of the “Widzew Manufaktura” itself. Here the Widzew linens and fabrics are made, and especially the brilliant kind of linen O. K., which has won a name in the wide commercial world. The eye is dazzled by everything one sees [?] in the “Widzew Manufaktura”. One feels like the wanderer in an enchanted castle from a fairy tale; awe seizes one before the greatness of the human spirit, of organisation and creative power. The “Widzew Manufaktura”, the life’s work of Asher Kohn, is the wonder of “the Polish Manchester”, the pride of Polish industry.
Towards the New Year...

[Sosnowiec and Zagłębie — satirical New Year feuilleton; kehilla.] The first tremor, the great shudder that my soul feels before the approaching New Year, begins right from the first Selichot. As soon as the cantor cries out: Yi—t—g—d—l, I already stand there completely shaken [?]. And in every sleepless night such ghosts appear before my eyes — a mere trifle: they are going to audit us. Not, God forbid, to seize by force the stale “paratkes” [?] with the help of the local sequestrators of the “Urząd Skarbowy” [tax office]. Oh no! Here they take out the account books of a whole year’s deeds and set them before the “U-netaneh tokef”. Help, help, they are going to stage a new “Sosnowiec affair” [sprawa], and what that smells of, we already know ourselves...
Meanwhile over there, in the “heavenly district” [niebieski rewir], it is cosy: the “gre-bendige” [?] angels run with “shturkatsn” [?] in their hands; they carry in the thick-bound [?] gmina books with the “Sosnowiec lawsuits” (elections are not taken into account here), and finally the vital-records books and the whole “rabbinate agreement”... Flaming angels with heavenly knights also bring to the judges’ table the “secret memoranda” of the “sherem groshi” [?], sensations and gossip [plotki] with “shmek-broyt” [?] about all sorts of things, so that the story sets one trembling... Oy, oy — I think to myself — who knows how the affair may end.
At the side of the “poczekalnia” [waiting room] stands the litigant himself. Our melancholy-stricken 5694, wrapped in torn garments, desperate and grieved, lets scalding tears fall from his eyes and at the same time is seized by a violent trembling: Oh, Father in Heaven! Do you know what went on in the Sosnowiec kehilla office during my term [kadencja]? People did not sleep, did not eat, and we may both, dear Father, reckon [?] what the business has already cost (and how much more it will cost).
On the other side, again, a whole gallery of people sit in the “poczekalnia” on a big bench — all familiar faces. There he is, the whole “macher” [fixer] of the elections. Now he is waiting to give his testimony. He works with his hands and his voice reaches right into the courtroom. And the others — all familiar Jews — meanwhile peer into the “patiefkes” [?] and shake their heads ruefully: may it be said of stones [i.e. may it not befall us], that such a calamity had to happen...
In an adjoining room of the waiting room cheerful, merry voices are heard; there I see — sitting in wide armchairs, the modern young people of Zagłębie with all their “pitshevkes” [?]; they romp and flirt with girls until the whole little room shakes with youthful courage; they smoke papirosy, they whistle the modern hits “Skrawiane serce” [?], “Santa Lucia”, “Za tyle pięknych dni” [?]...
By the door stands, especially cheerful, the henpecked [“pantofel”] husband Andrek, who all summer long licked honey at his wife’s and smacked his lips: “Kiziu, my kitten, let’s be merry”... From minute to minute he runs over to the little wives Sheyndil and Yentil and cheers them up: Don’t worry, kittens, the redeeming angel is a good brother of mine. The dancings, dachas and masquerades he will not cancel [skasować].
And suddenly an alarm [trwoga] is heard — trrrrrr... brrrr. Shrapnel bursts and the whole crowd falls silent. What happened? — the crowd rises to its feet:
— Here he comes, the kind-hearted angel Michael with a pair of scales in his hand; tearful girls run up and kiss his hands: Panie Szanowny [Dear Sir], help us! Be our advocate! Act there in the court so that for the New Year “good inscriptions” may be written for us... We shall always remember you.
At that moment I cautiously approach and hand him my protest card.
The angel Michael sighs and answers me that the Sosnowiec affair will actually be heard behind closed doors.
A great hammer blow breaks off the dialogue, and the angel Michael quickly runs into the court with the scales.
And again strong, thunderous voices are heard: here enters, grown tall and in good spirits, the “contrahent” [the opposing party] — “Tav-Resh-Tsadi-He” [5695], and standing thus before the court entrance his lips whisper: Almighty Creator, ah, sweetest Father, no secret is hidden from You; tell me then whether in my term too the Zagłębie kehilla parliaments will look like the luckless League of Nations. Ah. Ah, “far be it from You to do such a thing”. Accept the prayer of our “advocate”. Ah, Father in Heaven, “as a father has compassion on his children”, inscribe for us a “good inscription and sealing” for the newly elected [?] kehilla for the New Year — — — — — — —
For it is written somewhere [?]: “On Rosh Hashanah they are inscribed” —
Avichayil.
Prayers

[Essay — the High Holidays; prayer and faith.]

"One does not stand up to pray out of sadness nor out of laziness, etc., but out of the joy of a commandment."
(Berakhot 31).

Prayers have existed among the Jewish people since the most ancient times. Already in the Torah we find how the Patriarchs prayed — for example, how Abraham our father prayed to save the city of Sodom from destruction, and that the house of Abimelech should be healed. Isaac prayed that Rebecca should bear children; Jacob prayed when he was about to meet Esau, and again when he sent Benjamin down to Egypt, etc. Moses, Joshua, Samuel, Hannah, David, Solomon, etc. All these, however, were so to speak distinctive, occasional prayers, which each person composed for himself according to the demand of the moment. The fixed daily prayers, on the other hand, which are binding on every Jew, begin, according to Maimonides, with Moses our teacher. From Moses to Ezra the Scribe there already existed a single fixed prayer which every Jew had to pray at least once a day; Ezra, in turn, together with the "Men of the Great Assembly", already composed three fixed daily prayers and arranged the "Shemoneh Esreh", which became sanctified among the Jewish people and remain binding to this day.

What do the prayers of the whole year consist of?

The prayers of the whole year consist of roughly three parts: a) songs of praise to the Almighty, b) on the Redemption, and c) on personal needs and wants.

The prayers of the whole year, however, do not awaken in the average Jew the proper ecstasy and stirring of the soul; he says them more out of habit than out of rapture, than out of spiritual elevation. That is because the hunted and tormented Jew of the whole year, with his day-to-day troubles and worries, is simply unable to pay proper attention to the prayers he utters and to grasp the beauty, the warmth and the sublimity of the words.

A quite different impression is made upon the Jew by the prayers of the "Days of Awe". The very fact that the religious Jew believes that in these days his fate is sealed, his "verdict" — "On Rosh Hashanah it is written and on the fast day of Yom Kippur it is sealed" — this alone, the dread of the "Day of Judgment", already acts upon his psychological and spiritual state, and a mystical mood comes over him. He forgets his day-to-day troubles and worries and rises out of the atmosphere of despair, from the world of chaos into the upper worlds, where no envy, hatred, strife or hypocrisy reign; he forgets his workaday, lamenting life, his shop and his workshop. In that sublime moment he is not interested in his personal problems, nor in any general problems, and instead of a wretched, broken, enslaved soul, he rises to the rank of "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" and is transformed into a proud member of the "Thou-hast-chosen-us people".

A certain influence on the psychological change and spiritual elevation of the Jew during the Days of Awe is also exercised by the morally sweet melodies, steeped in deep sorrow, in which the Jew finds consolation and sympathy for his spiritual and physical sufferings.

But the chief and absolute influence on the rapture and elevation of the Jewish spirit in the Days of Awe comes from the heartfelt, deeply moral prayers, which express on the one hand the greatness of the Creator, the universal, great wonder of creation and the cosmos, and on the other hand the pettiness, the nothingness, the vanity of vanities of human existence, down to the absolute annulment of being, and the longing for something unclear, mystical, fantastic — spirituality.

The religious Jew reaches the highest degree of rapture and ecstasy in the Days of Awe in the Musaf prayer, when in his fantasy and dream he flies across to the ancient holy "Mount Sinai", when he "hears" the "thunders and lightnings", and when he "beholds", out of the dark "thick cloud", the great divine light...

And then suddenly the prayers carry him over into the distant future, after "all wickedness shall vanish like smoke", when an idyll will reign over the whole world, and not only the Jews but all mankind of the entire world will acknowledge the One Creator, and all will love and praise Him, and He will reign over all, and there will be no more envy, no hatred, no war and no evil whatsoever of one man toward another, "for Thou wilt remove the dominion of arrogance from the earth". Instead, only love and purity, truth and holiness will reign in the world, and heaven and earth will rejoice and together with all mankind sing a song of praise.

In that sublime moment the true religious Jew really feels himself "the chosen of creation", is happy in his Jewishness and is ready to sacrifice himself for "the sanctification of the Name".

In this way we also understand the saying quoted above: for only one who is in good spirits and finds himself in an optimistic mood can be sincerely inspired, i.e. "but out of the joy of a commandment".

In the present tragic transitional epoch which the Jewish people is living through, at a time when so many heavy, dense and dark clouds cover more and more the horizons of the Jewish sky and the ground burns under our feet, when whole countries and nations have been poisoned with the venom of antisemitism and persecute us with the greatest cruelty — may the heartfelt, sweet prayers be for us a consolation and a hope for a better future; may the prayers speak to our bleeding heart, strengthen our sorrowful spirit and instil in us fresh strength to continue our existence in exile and the upbuilding of the Land of Israel. We must not fall into despair, for we Jews are a people of optimists, and this is indeed what the author of the saying means:
"One does not stand up to pray, etc., but out of the joy of a commandment."

Y. Wygodzki [?].

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Nitzavim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion and Rosh Hashana.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Nitzavim
The Portion
—o—
a) "You are standing" (Deut. 29:9)
"Why was the portion 'You are standing' said next to the Rebuke (Tochacha)? Because when the Jews heard ninety-eight curses, besides the forty-nine in the book of Leviticus, their faces turned green and they said: who will be able to withstand this? So[?] Moses began to appease them: 'You are standing this day.' Much have you already angered God, and He has not finished you off[?], and you exist before Him like the day, which exists forever and shines; so has He (God) shone for you, and He will shine for you in the world to come, and the sufferings set you up before Him — and make you endure"...
Yalkut.
• • •
And why did their faces not turn green when the curses of the book of Leviticus were read before them?
Because there the curses were said in the plural, and a trouble shared by many is half a consolation; therefore they were not so frightened. "Every trouble that is of an individual is a trouble, and every trouble that is of the many is no trouble" — says the Midrash. But here the curses were said in the singular, and every individual thought that the curses would strike him alone; that is why their faces turned so green... R' Gershon Ashkenazi.
—o—
b) "Your heads, your tribes" (ibid.)
"Your heads for your tribes" — Rashi.
What is Rashi adding to the verse?
Rather, Rashi means: your heads for your tribes — the heads according to the tribes; as you are worth, such heads you have.. a leader according to the generation... R' Elazar Fleckeles.
• • •
"The face of the generation is like the face of a dog" —
A householder buys himself a dog, feeds[?] it, raises it, so that it will bark at strangers; but if the dog barks at its own master, he drives it out of the house... Today's "faces of the generation" have such a face with their own householders too: they are paid to preach rebuke — but only to others... Should the rabbi rebuke his own people — they drive him out...
Tiferet Tzvi.
—o—
c) "And it shall come to pass, when all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse" (Deut. 30:1)
Here, after all, it speaks only of curses — how does a "blessing" come in here?!
Rather, the very fact that Jews survive even though all these curses come upon them — that itself is a special blessing from God... And therefore "and you shall take it to heart among all the nations whither the Lord your God has driven you" — you will see that they survive among all the peoples, encircled by such curses, and still go on existing — that is a blessing... Ktav Sofer.
—o—
d) "It is not in heaven" (Deut. 30:12)
The Torah is not found among the "heaven-Jews", among those who always climb only into heaven...
Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk.
—o—
e) "For the thing is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it" (ibid. 14)
"That you may do it" — repentance, outwardly — that is "very near", that is not hard; what is hard is not merely to "do" repentance, but to return to God with the heart...
R' Shlomo Kluger.
—o—
Rosh Hashana.
f) "Exalt the horn of Your servants."
Before the shofar blasts R' Shlomo Leib of Łęczna (Lentshner) pleaded with God: "Exalt the horn of Your servants" — Master of the Universe! When a Jew drops his tefillin, he quickly picks them up, kisses them and fasts a whole day, because Your name is in the tefillin; You, Master of the Universe, also wear tefillin, and in them is written the name of the Jews: "And who is like Your people Israel, one nation" — and these tefillin (that is, the Jews) lie on the ground, wallowing in the dirt, and You do not pick them up?!... Exalt the horn of Your servants!...
—o—
g) "Where she is" [sic: for "where he is"]
On Rosh Hashana one reads the portion of Hagar and Ishm[ael]; what has that to do with Rosh Hashana?
Rather, in that portion it is said: "where he is" [printed garbled] — that God judged Ishmael according to what he was then; although God knew that he is a wicked one, He heard his present weeping, and now, as a child, he was after all righteous... So too we stand on Rosh Hashana and weep. After Rosh Hashana we will surely[?] go on sinning... but God listens to our prayers — "where she is"... Now, on Rosh Hashana, every Jew is pious and is worthy of being heard...
Likutim Chrashim [sic; probably "Likutim Chadashim"].
—o—
h) "Your going after Me in the wilderness"
We remind God what kindness He has kept for us from when we followed Him in the wilderness, in the wasteland among wild beasts. And if so — then today it is on our part an even greater wonder that we follow God among wild beasts in a wilderness — which the whole world is for us today... Are today's beasts in human form any less dangerous than those wilderness beasts?!...
Likutei Shoshanim.

[Humour and satire — the "Kach-lefl" page; New Year poem.] (Humour and satire in honour of the New Year). Compiled by Amocło.

A Good Year to You!

1
May you be inscribed for a good year —
Here it is already, the year 5695!
Perhaps an end will now come
To the eternal plague and plaguing...

2
Perhaps it will, perhaps, perhaps,
Who can know, who can see?
Anything can happen in our darkness,
Anything, anything can happen!

3
Jewish life — one great "perhaps",
Forever perhaps, perhaps only!
Perhaps a miracle will happen —
And so from year to year...

4
Perhaps by the New Year there will come
Our redemption, as a people;
Or perhaps, dear Jews, there will be
In our camp at last some sense?...

5
Perhaps the tearing-apart will stop at last,
At every step and stride.
This one says: "kosher", that one — "treyf", even,
This one says: "Congress", that one — no.

6
And perhaps the world will be disarmed,
Really, at last, in truth;
Perhaps in the year 5695, even,
Our situation will become clear?

7
May you be inscribed for a good year —
Years — our "inventory",
Years — filled with hope,
Years — filled to the brim with sorrow.

8
A people we are, quite an old one,
Stuffed with many years,
Years — wheels — years turning,
Our old mill of exile.

9
Wheels of years — years turning,
The mill grinds nimbly, fast,
But the flour from the mill is carried off by strangers,
To us remains the whistling of the wind...

10
May you be inscribed for a good year —
Certainly, surely, dear Jew!
An old merchant sets out
For the old fair of time.

11
An old merchant, he sets out,
Without a penny in his hand;
To beg [?] favours of heaven
Is an old trade — well known.

12
May you be inscribed for a good year [misprinted] —
Give me, God, a happy year!
I will pay You for it
With good deeds, no less.

13
I will pay You for it
With prayers white [?] and long;
Hear then, Creator, our cries,
Our sorrowful song...

14
God, You surely know that we need
A good year, and soon indeed.
Bolted in all round stands the "scattered lamb"
Among wolves in the wild forest.

15
May you be inscribed for a good year —
Who is equal to our people?
A people that stands, for generations on generations,
Up to its neck in the deep river.

16
In the angry waves they dance,
There — swallowed up — without end!
Last year was a disaster,
The year 5694 — one giant terror.

17
Without livelihood and without standing,
Here boycotts, there persecutions;
And the world — it is shut,
Every land and place bolted.

18
So let the year 5695 come already,
Perhaps at last it will bring rest!
Ah, inscribe us, God, for life,
Ah, come now, write already, Father, You!...
The Politics of the Year.

[Humour and satire — "Kach-lefl"; world politics.] (A review).
No great events were to be recorded in the political world in the past year.
The year's politics began with people starting to talk about war, and the year also ended with the fear of war.
It was, one may say, almost a war year.
Germany is in fact constantly waging war with the world, i.e. with the present opinion-makers of world politics. The war that began in the year 1914 has not yet ended; there has only been a pause in the shooting — one does not hear shooting, but war is war.
We enter the New Year, too, in a war mood — there is war-making going on in the world.
Some world it is — how do you like our little world? — we mean our political little world, of course — some little world indeed. It would not hurt to have, for the New Year, a slightly better little world.
In the name of all world politicians, we wish a good political year.
New Year's Greetings

[Humour and satire — "Kach-lefl"; taxes and housing.]
1.
From a merchant to the Urząd [tax office]
From the bottom of my heart I wish you to be helped with better payers than me.
Whether the situation gets better or even worse, may they give you money — whole mountains!
May you flay the skin anew for podatki [taxes], until the payers are left with a pair of torn underpants.
The well-wisher,
A merchant.

2.
From the Urząd to the merchant
That you should grow rich — that is my whole aspiration, so that you have money to hand over to me.
May every merchant be able to have his business in his own name and not, when buying a patent [trade licence], put it down as one of the ten sons of Haman.
Should it be necessary to carry out a zajęcie [distraint] for not paying an instalment, may there at least be something to take — a pair of trousers without a patch.
The well-wisher,
The Urząd.

3.
From a tenant to his landlord.
May the rent rise by a whole two hundred per cent, may people pay two thousand dollars of key-money for the barest four walls.
May the President of the State also issue a manifesto that evictions can be carried out in winter too, in the greatest frosts.

The well-wisher,
A tenant.
The Merchant's 'Unetaneh Tokef'

[Humour — "Der Kokh-lefl"; a parody of the "Unetaneh Tokef" prayer about taxes; followed by four short humorous pieces.]
"And He writes and seals": at the "urząd" [the (tax) office] they write and they seal.
"And He remembers all things forgotten": they remember the overdue taxes.
"And He opens the book of records": the tax book is always open.
"And it reads itself": and they read out whom to send "upomnienia" [payment reminders].
"And every man's hand signs it": every person is registered there.
"And the angels hasten": and the sequestrators [bailiffs] run quickly to dun.
"And trembling and dread seize them": and fear and trembling seize the merchant when he sees them.
"And they say, behold the Day of Judgement": this, indeed, is the merchant's Day of Judgement!
Leib Sztabinski.
—o—
Important Paragraphs of the New Commercial Law.

Napoleon's Wife (4) — H. Abramson

[Historical serial — Josephine, Napoleon's wife; part 4.]
At their first meeting he begged her forgiveness for his behaviour and for the disgrace he had caused her some years before. Her son Eugène, too, was now in her arms. He was no longer a young boy, but a grown lad, handsome and proud. There was no happier woman than she in the first few months after her return from Martinique. She was surrounded by her good friends, and once again a round of balls and banquets began. In that circle the storm that was gathering over France was not felt at all.
And then one fine day it became known that King Louis XVI had been arrested, and that he and his wife Marie Antoinette were to be tried. A hunt began for those who had been connected with the imperial [sic] court. The days came when the guillotine started working...
Once a man came to the Beauharnais house with a pack of goods containing all sorts of household articles. When Josephine did not want to receive this man, he winked at her as a sign that he had to tell her something important, and she at once took him into her boudoir.
— Madame, I have come to inform you that in a few hours they will come to your home and arrest your husband, and it is certain that he will be punished with death. My advice is that he get away as quickly as possible. He must not lose a single minute.
— Who are you? — asked the frightened woman.
I am a member of the Revolutionary Committee, but I know your husband personally and it would grieve me if they chopped off his head. My name I cannot tell you, because you know what would happen to me if it were found out that I had warned you.
Meanwhile Beauharnais came into the house. Josephine took him into a side room, told him what the man had said to her, and began begging him to flee as quickly as possible.
For a short while the aristocrat reflected, and then said, calming Josephine and pressing her to his heart[?]:
— I cannot flee; I have committed no crime whatsoever. The only one towards whom I felt guilty was you, but you have forgiven me. That is enough for me. I am sure that they will realise that I am a friend of the people, and they will let me go home to my wife and children.
Josephine began begging her husband to hide, for he could see what had been done to the king and the queen. It was certain that they would not spare him, the friend of the royal family. But it did not help. Beauharnais did not want to leave his beloved fatherland, as others, the die-hard monarchists, had done, and he sat down calmly to wait for them to come for him.
It did not take long before a loud knocking was heard at the door. A crowd of people, ragged, unwashed, but angry, came in and declared that they wanted to see the master of the house, Citizen Beauharnais. With head held high, proudly, the aristocrat came in and asked what they wanted of him.
— We have come to take you to the Revolutionary Tribunal, where you will have to answer for yourself — said one of the crowd.
Josephine shuddered. In this man she recognised the one who a few hours earlier had been with her and warned her.
— Let me take leave of my wife and children — said the arrested man — after all, I know that you will hold me a long time, until it turns out that I am innocent.
The gang let husband and wife take leave of each other. At that moment Josephine felt that she truly loved her husband, that he was dearer to her than anything in the world. But she did not weep, did not cry out; she only looked into the eyes of the man who was the father of her children and, pressing a hot kiss on his lips, quickly left the room.
The second time Josephine saw her husband was when she came to visit him in prison, where he was held with hundreds of other aristocrats whom she knew. Her husband kept calm and assured her that no harm would be done to him, because he was innocent. But Josephine saw that he himself did not believe it.
When Josephine came to see her husband, a man with a rifle in his hand met her and said that she was wanted at the tribunal. When she explained that she had left her children at home and had to look after them, it did not help. He had an order to bring Citizeness Beauharnais before the tribunal.
In a dark room, together with other women, Josephine was locked up.
Only on that same day she received a short letter from her husband.

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
Masked bandits force their victims to lie down on the floor.

While Mr. Wodzisławski with his wife, Mr. Abraham Lipszyc of Będzin and two out-of-town merchants were in the shop, three masked bandits came in and, with revolvers in their hands, forced everyone in the shop to keep quiet and lie down on the floor. [Radio — Polish Radio listeners' plebiscite.] Radio Corner.
A Plebiscite of the Polish Radio.
(10 questions for radio listeners)
As is known, the Polish Radio has a special "Study Bureau" [Biuro Studiów]. Its task consists in becoming acquainted with the demands and wishes of the radio listeners.
It goes without saying that the "Study Bureau" of the Polish Radio will only be able to fulfil its task when it is in contact with the radio listeners.
In order to be precisely informed about the opinions of the radio listeners concerning the programmes and problems that are touched upon in it[?], the "Study Bureau" is organising a plebiscite among radio listeners, asking them to express themselves on the following questions:
Should radio programmes touch upon such problems as, for example: success or bad fortune in our everyday life? It is a very broad subject, embracing many questions which we come up against in life.
And perhaps the radio listeners would actually be interested in the problem of practical philosophy of life?
In a series of talks and lectures it should be shown how [to reach] a correct attitude, by which one attains true calm and faith in one's own powers.
Now comes a chapter for women.
This concerns a series of broadcasts [audycje] that should interest mainly women, for example: the culture of everyday life, thrifty housekeeping, guidance for young mothers, hygiene, women's social work, their rights, etc.
Which of the radio listeners is specially interested in social problems?
Those who are interested in hearing talks on technology and natural science should also respond.
The sixth topic would be devoted to practical medicine and hygiene. Every one of us is unwell from time to time. Should the radio talk about practical medicine?
Many of us love, and are interested in, the life of animals.
Now something different. Many radio listeners demand that lectures on regional and geographical knowledge be held on the radio. Others again demand as many lectures as possible on historical subjects.
In 10th place comes the question of the French and German languages. Whoever of the radio listeners wants to benefit from these radio lessons is asked to put the heading "Lessons" in first place in the answer he will send to the Polish Radio.
Listeners are asked to list the 10 above-mentioned topics in order according to the interest they arouse in each individual radio listener. The answers should be sent to the address of the Polish Radio, Warsaw, Kredytowa 1.

The Jewish Merchants Face a Hard Test

[Zagłębie — economy; Chamber of Commerce elections.] On the question of the elections to the Chamber of Commerce.
There is no doubt that the Jewish merchants and artisans face a hard test.
The reductions of Jewish representation in the general economic organisations, which began at the time of the last elections to the Chambers of Crafts, are now being carried over into the field of the Chambers of Commerce as well.
Jewish merchant circles are already aware that every Jewish mandate in the Chamber of Commerce will have to be fought for hard.
The elections to the Chambers of Commerce have been called. The relevant ordinance has already been published in the „Monitor Polski", preparations are already being made, the Chambers of Commerce have already chosen their electoral commissions, which are to conduct the elections, and everywhere the tendency is to push out the Jewish merchant community. Efforts are made to keep Jewish representation as small as possible, so that as few Jews as possible will be found in the governing bodies.
According to the number of trade licences (patents) purchased and the number of persons entitled to vote, the Jews ought to receive from 50 to 60 per cent of the councillors. As is reported, efforts are being made not to let it come to an electoral contest at all, but to a single unified list, conceding the Jews a certain percentage of councillors and thereby, of course, also reducing their influence to a minimum.
Therefore it must be borne in mind that great tasks face the Jewish merchant community: not to let itself be pushed out of trade altogether.
Will there now also be found such people as will come to haggle over a tenner down and a tenner up and will trade away Jewish interests? The Jewish merchants, especially the small traders, face a hard test; they must not, however, break down, but proudly demand their rights.

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — crime.] The „Editor" of the „Katowitzer Journal" Arrested.
Months ago a certain Rosenman was „active" in Upper Silesia; he swindled a number of firms by buying goods from them „on instalments". When that business ran out, he became the publisher of the „Katowitzer Journal", with whose help he carried out a series of swindles.

Last Tuesday he was handed over to the custody of the Investigation Office in Katowice.
He Does Not Know Whether He Got Married

[Silesia — court.] The court in Gleiwitz heard a case against a certain K., who was charged with forging documents and perjury.
Some time ago the accused registered with the civil registry office the birth of a child of his. At the office they soon realised that K. was not officially married, and he was called to account for deceiving the civil registry office.
K. defended himself before the court, saying that he was indeed a married man, and even put forward a series of proofs.
But the investigation established that K. is not married. The accused then presented to the court a letter from a waitress[?] confirming that K. is a married man... K. thus[?] categorically demanded that this letter be attached to the court files as proof that he is a married man... In addition he also showed a document with a forged stamp, which was supposed[?] to testify that the newborn child is his. It turned out that the stamp had been given to him by a nephew of his so-called wife.
In the course of the court proceedings it emerged that K., a very[?] limited person, in fact did not understand his situation and does not know clearly whether he got married or not. At one time he had already once had an alimony[?] suit, and since then he has regarded himself as married.
The court acquitted the accused K.

The peasant Paweł Brudek of Łąka, Pszczyna county, tried to murder his 49-year-old wife. At the same time he asked her to go into his house, and he himself went off, and nobody knows where he is. The alarmed neighbours, however, became convinced that this was Brudek's handiwork. Where Are These Paths Leading Us? — On the Latest Denunciations of Rabbi Hager by the Sosnowiec Kehilla Representatives

[Sosnowiec — Kehilla; opinion.] So, should anyone say that things are not good for us, should anyone say that the Jewish situation is not all that rosy [?] — that has surely been spread by begrudgers, people who cannot bear to watch how well, how quietly and pleasantly Jews live. And by the way, that is no wonder either. For enemies of Israel are never lacking, and nowadays — at a time when antisemitism is breaking records all over the world — certainly not.
Just such an opinion people from another country could have held about Polish Jewry when they stay [?] in one of our towns and shtetls. And indeed one cannot make out [?] the situation otherwise than that we are well and comfortable and have nothing at all to worry about.
For let us take, for example, and consider in what manner the denunciations against Rabbi Hager in Sosnowiec are being conducted — in which, God forbid, it is not some outcast of society who engages, as one was used to seeing in the old days. No. Not that. Today it is not done shoddily, just so, to discharge a duty. It has become the fashion that this is quite a pleasant occupation, worth taking up, and apparently. that this "work" is called holy, communal, so that it has even become an honour to engage in it.
Thus a denunciation arrived at the local starostwo [county office], which reads no more and no less than that "a certain Hager occupies the place of the rabbi in the town synagogue, where he comes out with Zionist-political sermons which demoralise the town's worshippers".
The initiators of the denunciation therefore demand of the Starosta that "this Hager should step down from the synagogue".
Well, one cannot say — the wording is even a nice one, a decent one, a gentlemanly one. So that if one merely reads it through in one go [?], one gains more respect and reverence for the "ancient chosen" Jewish people. Let no one think that the above-mentioned text was signed by chance people off the street who were asked for a "favour", since it costs no money and it is an old rule that the children of Israel like to do such favours. No, the "paper" was signed by people who hold a position in public life, hence responsible to the Jewish community at large, and they are no more and no less than members of the Sosnowiec Jewish Kehilla. We are dealing here, then, with our own emissaries, whom the Jewish public sent there to administer, and these "chiefs of the shtibl" [?] demand of the Starosta that he decree [?] on what does not belong to him but precisely to themselves — and the best proof of it is that the Starosta himself forwarded the complaint to the Jewish Kehilla board, which ought rather to deal with internal Jewish affairs.
And therefore we do say that if people from abroad were to come here to us, people who do not know the rotten and mouldy order in which, for a pot [?] of lentils, one sells both all the Jewishness for which one supposedly sacrifices oneself and the honour of the people — and if they were to watch this game, this agitation, they would then have to spread the opinion that we are well off and have taken care of everything; nothing more remains but trifles, defects, and since one cannot tolerate even small defects having a place in Jewish life, they must therefore be uprooted at any price.
Thus and not otherwise can the stranger think, he who does not know our life, he who does not know how sad and painful the Jewish situation is.
But why do we need people from abroad when we have here the Polish press — and let us watch how often they mock us and at every opportunity prove how fine our life is, and meanwhile our representatives, the religious as well as the national ones, are ridiculed. Often for weeks on end people make fun of those for whom they would have had respect, had we ourselves respected ourselves.
Well, when we laugh at ourselves within our homely little world, it is still somehow bearable — we must, like our unforgettable Sholem Aleichem, laugh with bitterness and "with lizards" [Yiddish idiom for bitter laughter]. But as soon as our shame is carried out before the outside world, we disgrace ourselves, and that we cannot forgive ourselves.
Often we cannot cope with our enemies, who want to exterminate us; but why should we want to swallow ourselves up in this case? What work will be left for the antisemites? After all, we must see to it that they too are not left without a stitch of work...
Must we, then, over every trifle, over every absurdity, approach the high windows and pester them, while not wanting to hear or know with how much ridicule people look at us after such an "action"? How much humiliation do we bring upon ourselves after carrying out such "undertakings"?
Does one give oneself an account of all this? Does one then remain clear-headed? Certainly not, for had they not been "sick" at the time, they would not have brought the situation to such absurdities, to such desecrations [?].
Have we really fallen so low that we cannot manage our internal questions, our purely Jewish matters, by ourselves? Do we not thereby demonstrate our degradation, our weakness? Is not the general opinion thus created that we are capable of nothing and that nothing can be entrusted to us? Do we still not see where this weakness leads? Have the lessons given to us so far taught us nothing at all? Has the entire Jewish community been punished with so short a memory that nothing is engraved in the old Jewish brain?
Upon my life, it would be high time, in these present "awesome" days, to ask a question about this and to draw the conclusions — where we will be dragged along these paths.
R. Les.
To the Heads of the Children's Educators.

[Zagłębie — education; opinion.]
Year after year we hear from parents that they are unable to provide their children with the expenses they need at school. There are[?] expenses besides the necessary books and writing materials, which they must as a rule[?] have and without which the child cannot manage at school.
But it is not a matter of the necessary items, but precisely of those one can do without. We know very well that the order of the teacher, male or female, is for the child the holiest commandment, so that hardly have they uttered a word in class[?] and the children will give their parents no rest at home until they get money for this or that item, for this or that event.
It seems that we all feel on our shoulders the grave situation into which the so-called crisis, which has already entered the phase of a chronic illness, has dragged us with all its force; and therefore it is only right that this year, more than until now, all this be taken into account and that one see to it that the schools do not lead the children into unnecessary expenses.
Without any excuse one must reckon with the hard times, which grow from day to day worse and more strained. The child is, after all, no more than an innocent little bird, so that it does not reckon, nor can it reckon, with the parents' means or lack of means; as soon as something is ordered at school, be it in the feeblest form, every child wants to be among the first to carry out the order. Therefore it is desirable to reckon with every trifle and not to lead the parents into unnecessary expenses.
After all, this year the Ministry of Education issued instructions to the teachers that even with school books they should be considerate and not lead the children into superfluous expenses; surely there is no doubt that before the Ministry issued the appropriate instructions everything was weighed precisely and from all sides, so that it was recognised that the teachers can make certain economies.
We know that year after year various events are held both in the public (elementary) schools and in the gymnasiums, and these very events swallow a great deal of the parents' money. This year one must without doubt reckon with all this, and one must not allow oneself, at the population's expense, to make outlays that are not of first-class importance.
Let the heads of the schools in Zagłębie bear this well in mind on every occasion.
Eles.
Let Us Ask One Another's Forgiveness.

(Thoughts for the Ten Days of Repentance).
By Pini Baal-Loshn.
I don't know how it is with others, but for me the day of Yom Kippur eve is always a dear day, a good day, a beautiful day — even if it happens to be a cloudy and rainy day.
Yom Kippur itself is somehow full of awe, but Yom Kippur eve is full of love.
And by nature I prefer to be a "mensch" out of "love" rather than out of "fear".
And do you know where my feeling of love for the eve of Yom Kippur comes from? — Only from the ceremony of asking one another's forgiveness!
And truly, I am very much in love [printed "feliebt"] with all our ceremonies and customs, because customs and ceremonies have something [?] of a charm in them. They speak to the feelings, to the heart, and not to the brain.
The brain, in general, regards everything as too dry, and people cannot live on bare dry "sukharki" [rusks]...
If the world, God forbid, were always guided only by the brain and never by the heart, it would be impossible to live in the world.
The brain, the intellect, can mock, laugh, criticise ceremonies and customs as foolish, as fanatical, as relics of primitive savages; — but the heart, the feelings need them and depend on them, like life itself.
Ceremonies and customs are the juice that sweetens the bitterness of everyday routine. They turn the weekday drabness of human life into a holiday.
There were, it seems, no greater mockers of customs and ceremonies among us than the maskilim. And yet they themselves had to keep up the ceremonies, for themselves and for further generations to come. Nothing more: they merely dressed them up a little in white "gloves" and black "frock coats"...
And that is why I have a great deal of respect for ceremonies in general, and as a Jew I am very much in love with our own Jewish ceremonies.
I am almost certain that customs and ceremonies have had the greatest share in the life of Judaism until now, and it will go on living as long as the customs hold out and are not forgotten — even if they are dressed up and modernised with time.
And our "secular Jews" [printed "yurn"], who think that one must precisely tear out by the roots and purge all our old customs and ceremonies and create new ones, are making a mistake from the start [?].
Firstly, it is hard to create new customs; and secondly, why toil in vain when there are ready, beautiful ones, and one can make them even more beautiful...
So, as I said, I am in love with our Jewish ceremonies.
Take, for instance, the ceremonies of Yom Kippur eve:
Well, with the custom of eating honey cake and meat kreplach, and simply the mitzvah of eating as much as possible — with this custom, I believe, even the greatest deniers [?] and radicals are content!
But take even the ceremony of kapores.
Despite the fact that many great rabbis were even against the ceremony of kapores, it is nevertheless a beautiful ceremony.
And let the enlightened ones not talk our ears off with pity for the poor innocent fowl that perish for our sins.
Firstly, it is far more fitting to have pity on people than on fowl and cattle. The vegetarians are indeed quite fine people, but I have even seen a compassionate vegetarian beat a man bloody — precisely out of compassion. So, we say, let us first reach the level of compassion for people, and afterwards we will be able to give some thought to compassion for fowl and cattle too...
Well, and the ceremony of the malkes lashes is truly splendid.
One takes people whom one would never have dared [?] [to strike], and they lie down by themselves, and one whips them — true, not dangerously, true, not hard; better, harder, hotter lashes would be needed, but this too is good, as they say...
But the ceremony of asking forgiveness is more beautiful still than all the ceremonies.
Asking one another's forgiveness!
How beautiful and good and fine and truly humane and deeply moral it is when a people sets a day for asking forgiveness of one another, so that no anger remains, no grudges [?], no hatred. To forgive and forget, to give up one's own honour and one's own egoistic feelings, and to make peace.
And not only with those who live in the world, but even with those who have long been citizens of the World of Truth — one must ask their forgiveness too.
Is there then any other such beautiful, heartfelt ceremony among another people of the nations? — I know of none!
And what is more: Yom Kippur, the day of asking forgiveness of the "Father in Heaven", cannot forgive the sins committed against the "children on earth".
Man with man, you know, have their own accounts, and they must make good among themselves the wrongs committed.
And the prophet said it even more sharply: that all the fasting and self-offering to "God" is not worth a sprig of parsley if one does not give a small sacrifice of one's own pleasure also for the sake of "man"...
I remember to this day the beauty and the loftiness of that moment when the whole shtetl used to go about on Yom Kippur eve, one to another, to ask forgiveness.
People who had been on bad terms, quarrelling, enemies a whole year — and when Yom Kippur eve came, in the morning, they asked each other's forgiveness, fell on each other's necks, kissed and wept for joy, and drank "l'chaim" and warmly wished each other all the best...
———
And therefore, my dear communal activists, I must ask your forgiveness too!
After all, I "butt" you a whole year round, I do not spare you, I poke you in the ribs, I rub mugs, I tear strips off you — with a little smile, as much as my strength can bear and as much as the editor permits.
And therefore I want to ask your forgiveness and make peace, and I promise you that...
That what? — That next year, "God willing", we will "butt heads" again and again ask each other's forgiveness!...
