The Value of Sincerity.

Where sincerity is lacking, a standstill must come in the energy of life, because the fear of sincerity is the fear of the dynamism and creativity of life, of its rawness and hardness and of its stormy beauty.
Worn-out, old and weak individuals. Or whole strata, are understandably afraid of sincerity, and they instinctively hide under the umbrellas of tradition, of philosophical mysticism and of false idealisation.
They themselves do speak in the name of sincerity, but every bold and understanding person must perceive that in the smoothness, the prettified affectation and the sweetishness in which their ideologies, words and deeds are wrapped, there must in truth lurk a false pretence, lies and hypocrisy, which hypocritically cover themselves with the mantle of sincerity; for "sincerity" can never be found in glazed, staring eyes, in a sugary smile and in moist [i.e. slippery] speech. Sincerity is hard and firm like the truth, and stormy like life.
Therefore only bold people with a strong will-power can be sincere.
The harmful forces, inferior and faulty traits, can be combated only with the help of true sincerity.
Cowards, the faint-hearted and weaklings, who cannot wage a bold struggle, cannot be sincere. At best they restrict this value to petty and superficial tasks, such as "telling the truth" or "taking care not to tell a lie" (but even that is impossible to carry out when courage and boldness are lacking). To look deep into themselves and contemplate the abysses that lie in their own soul — of that they are afraid, and they do not want to see the filth that is hidden in every person.
They cannot master the disgust and pain bound up with the process of dragging out, cleansing and changing. They do not presume much; they do not touch the foundations of falsehood, the lies which are thousands of years old and which embrace millions of people...
Both in the widest sense of the word and in the smallest tasks, sincerity, just like every value, must be administered consciously; otherwise the value begins to deny itself and goes against its own aspirations, and instead of combating the filth, the worthlessness and the disturbances, it enlarges them still further.
But every struggle must also have a tactic.
Conscious administration demands that every spiritual means of struggle be used with a certain tactic, so that it brings the necessary benefit, and that the means itself be refined and developed. The tactic of sincerity must consist in pointing out only that which can be improved. One should fight only against what one can change. Thus it is very tactless to point out physical shortcomings, outward faults and a certain spiritual inferiority.
It is unconscionable to tell a person who is outwardly not handsome that he is ugly; it is not humane to call a foolish person "a fool", etc., because such sincerity brings no benefit whatsoever and only discourages the person. But even traits that can indeed be improved must be pointed out only slowly, cautiously and pedagogically. We must first educate and encourage a person's spirit and only later point out his shortcomings to him, so that he can look them straight in the face and correct them.
We must not keep repeating and pointing out the faults, because then it can lead to the person becoming discouraged and thereby sinking even deeper into his shortcomings.
When one wants to point out bad traits to another, one must above all be humane, look without contempt at the other's imperfection, and at the same time have the courage to make the necessary reproaches to oneself and to set oneself the same demands — on the contrary, pretended sincerity points to the pettiness of the person who bears its name with [?] doggedness and in truth uses it merely to show off, to humiliate the other and to raise himself up on the other's shoulders.
Such sincerity cannot awaken any love — neither for the person who speaks in its name, nor for this spiritual value as such.
Most convincing of all is pointing out deeds that are not done properly. In the case of existing abuses, one must point out their harmfulness and keep repeating it until they are changed.
Where the concept of sincerity takes on a social scale, it must be merciless in its struggle against the deep disturbances and the neglect of human development.
Sincerity often goes as far as coarseness. The stronger the enemies of social justice and progress are, the coarser and more cynical sincerity must be, the stronger and bolder the struggle must be, and the more harshly the tactic must be applied, in order to uproot the evil more deeply.
Hitler Keeps His Word...

[Politics — Nazi Germany; satirical feuilleton.] (A short feuilleton).
In Hitler-land things are not going badly.
Ever since Hitler and his adjutant Göring set about liberating Germany from the "radical" storm-troop leaders, several hundred heads have already been chopped off and are rolling about in the sand.
He, Hitler, promised his people that when he came to power, heads would roll in the sand — and he keeps his word.
True, Hitler also made other promises. He promised to take Alsace-Lorraine from France; he promised to take the "Corridor" and Upper Silesia from Poland; he would also unite Austria with Germany and take back the colonies Germany had before the war. Then again, with all that already in hand, the Germans under Hitler's leadership were to fulfil the old German "Drang nach Osten" and take Ukraine, Lithuania, Latvia, besides all sorts of other countries lying close at hand.
All this he solemnly promised, and this he has not exactly carried out
Instead of taking the Polish Corridor and Upper Silesia, he even had to give Poland a pledge that he renounces the former German territories that belong to Poland. Instead of seizing Alsace-Lorraine, he actually had to send envoys to France to establish good relations. Instead of conquering the world, one must still beg the world for mercy — to lend a little raw material and to forgive the debts that cannot be paid out of the empty German treasury.
For all these promises Germany has to wait a little, but one promise he has kept, Hitler: he promised that heads would roll in the sand, and roll they do, the heads.
True, all these bloodhounds, who distinguished themselves by their sadistic cruelties against socialists, Jews, workers, liberals and all other people, deserved more righteous bullets than Nazi ones, but it makes no difference. Jews say: "Let it come from a Cossack, as long as it is for life." Let it come from a Nazi, as long as it is for death!
And perhaps it really is better that the right and useful work of exterminating the Nazis is being done by the Nazis themselves. First, the hangmen know the craft of chopping heads well; they have bloody practice in it, and one can rely on them to do it well. Second, why should decent people be compelled to take up so useful but so disgusting an occupation as exterminating Nazi scum[?] — better let Hitler and Göring do it. They are the right men in the right place.
But every dog has its day — says the world.
If Hitler holds the sword now, tomorrow or the day after his opponents will hold it — the hundreds of thousands of his parasites whom he fattened on blood, murder and robbery and has now muzzled — they will not keep silent and will take revenge; just as the heads of Röhm, Strasser, Heines and hundreds of others, who were the rulers of the land and the terror of the masses, now roll in the German sands to the joy of their murderers, so unexpectedly the heads of the Hitlers, Görings and Goebbelses may be chopped off by the revenge-thirsty Nazis and roll about in the sands.
That is where things are heading in Germany. Hitler's promise about chopping heads is being fulfilled.
The worms will devour the worms and choke on their own bite.
So, bravo, Hitler, Göring and Goebbels! — keep up the good work.
"When Nazi blood spurts from the knife, then things go twice as well."
G. Kuper.
What Does One Wish You for the New Year?

[Humour — feuilleton for Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur; verse and prose.] By Graf Kali ["Count Kali", a pen name].
What does one wish you — pick it yourselves,
Reb Berl, Shmerl, Reb Elyokum.
Ah, Jews are, after all, through and through
A people of utterly pampered folk —
A delicate people — go guess today
How everyone can be satisfied...
I have no means for it —
What does one wish you, dear Jews?
I have a poor widow I know, and she begs me:
— Panie [Mr.] Graf Kali, since you are a poet, and a poet is closer to heaven than to earth, that means a closer in-law of the Master of the Universe — do me a favour and pray to God for a good year for me. Above all a mild [?] winter, so that one won't need so much coal and wood, and my little children won't go about with frozen little hands...
— Good, I say — I will certainly keep you in mind. So, that means, you ask for a mild winter...
But I also have a furrier I know; he meets me a while ago in the street and stops me: Hallo, Graf Kali! How's it going?
— Thanks, I say — not bad, not so cheerful [?], but compared with [—] [?] a bit easier for me; I'm not yet asking for "nadzór" [supervision]...
— Przyjacielu kochany [dear friend], he says, and starts twisting my button — since Yom Kippur is approaching, and as a poet you are close to God [?], therefore I should ask you to intercede for me and beg a good year from the Master of the Universe.
— Very good, I say — why not? In any case, I say, I already have an order from a poor widow I know, so I'll ask for you too in the same go...
— For a poor widow? he asks me, and keeps twisting the top button of my jacket [marynarka] — what does she want, then, the poor widow, from the Master of the Universe?
— A trifle, I say, she asks. She wants no more and no less than a warm winter, so that her little chicks [?], God forbid, won't freeze.
— God forbid! he cries out — don't you dare ask for a warm winter. Because a warm winter is deadly poison for him [sic], a misfortune... a real catastrophe; on the contrary, I should ask the Master of the Universe to give a winter with great Siberian frosts, with lots of snow and blizzards [zawierucha], and people should simply freeze...
— And what will you get out of it if people freeze?
— Robber! [sic: "goylen"] he answers, and the top button is already in his hand — what do you mean what will I get out of it? When it's cold, people will buy furs and warm fur collars, otter [wydry] and monkey fur [małpy]; you know what I deal in.
— Yes, I say — but what will the poor widow do, who can't buy herself any fur?
— What do I care, he says, about the poor widow; for all I care she can freeze, I'll be warm... I have to think only of myself.
— Well, all right, I say — I'll pray for a cold winter.
Walking away from the furrier, I am met by a grain merchant I know, and he calls me aside.
— Panie Graf Kali? he asks — where will you pray this Yom Kippur?
— Where should I pray? I answer — I already have my "shtibl" where I pray every year...
— So, listen, Panie Graf, would you like to earn a decent sum [?] for the holiday?
— Ah, I say — why shouldn't I want to? You know I have a wife and children who hold strongly by the verse "and they ate", only without [—] [?]...
— So, listen, Panie Grafie, when you are busy praying to the Master of the Universe for a good year and a good inscription and sealing, then in the same go ask that oats should become dearer..
— Why on earth, I ask, should oats become dearer? Surely it's better when oats are cheap — I play the innocent, and meanwhile I feel the fellow is nearly getting apoplexy.
— No, he says — for me it's better if oats become dearer this year. You know, he says, and begins to shake me — that I deal in grain, and this very year I've accumulated large stocks of oats, and since nowadays Jews have many horses, which push in everywhere, where they aren't needed [?], and which you find even in many public institutions — and horses, as is well known, need oats, so you understand..
— What do I care, he says, about the poor carters; for all I care they can croak together with their horses. I have to see that things are good for me...
Walking away from the grain merchant, I meet a Jewish woman I know, who is lugging a can of milk from [?] Groytse [perhaps Grodziec].
— How are you, I ask, Dvoyre Zisele, haven't seen you for a long time; you're still lugging the milk cans?
— What can one do? she answers, panting heavily — such is my lot in the world, that I must only carry and carry, but never mind, I'm used to it already. The main thing is that God should not send a hard winter, so the rivers won't freeze.
— What do you care, Dvoyre Zisele, if the rivers freeze? I ask in surprise — do you have ships on the river?
— No, she says, blushing a little — ships I really don't have, but you know my line of business [branża]... it calls for a little water...
— Aha, I say — now I know; but what will the poor carters say, the poor things?
God, that the river should not freeze... [sic; words seem to be missing here.] But tell me, dear Dvoyre Zisele, what will the poor Jews do, the poor things, who draw their livelihood from cutting the ice? What will they live on with their wives and little children if the rivers don't freeze?...
So, gentlemen, it seems the world was created such that one must live at the expense of another.. What is good and fine for Berl is a real misfortune for Khatskl... Now imagine how hard it is to be God to the people of Israel, who must listen to everyone's requests and must be gracious and merciful to all..
But nevertheless, dear Jews, don't worry. The Almighty has many ways — God will find a way to satisfy everyone... that is, after all, why He is God... and above all let us pray to Him:
Bless, Master of the Universe, bless,
With every [?] kapores-swinging,

Yom Kippur among the Jews of Yemen

[Yemen — Yom Kippur; customs.] Sarah Osnat HaLevi.
The preparations for Yom Kippur. — Little sticks topped with eggshells instead of tombstones — in the small Yemenite house of study in the capital, Sana'a — "Kol Nidre" among the Jews of Yemen. — The worshippers sit on the ground for 24 hours on end. — During Yom Kippur it is strictly forbidden to speak with women. — Yemenite Jews do not sleep the whole Yom Kippur night. — The great shofar blast. — At the close of Yom Kippur the parents lie down to sleep with the children in one bed, in their holiday clothes.
—o—
It is an old custom among the Jews of Yemen to visit the cemetery two days before Yom Kippur. The custom of going to the graves of one's forefathers during the "Days of Repentance" is widespread in all the countries where Jews live. In Yemen, however, this custom is bound up with a very interesting ceremony which is, it seems, entirely unknown to the Ashkenazi Jews. The Jews of the capital, Sana'a, take with them to the "house of life" long sticks and... eggshells.
Everyone who comes to pray at the grave of his relatives sticks a long stick into the grave, and on the tip of the stick he places an eggshell, which has been pierced specially so that it slips easily onto the tip of the stick. On this eggshell the visitor writes the date on which his relative died and the day on which the eggshell was set on the stick. These eggshells on the sticks are meant to serve as tombstones. Since the Yemenite Jews are very poor and cannot afford to put up a tombstone on a relative's grave, they are accustomed, year in, year out, two days before Yom Kippur, to set such things on the graves of their near ones "in place of tombstones".
The Jewish cemetery in the capital of Yemen presents an interesting picture on the eve of Yom Kippur — "from afar" one's eye is struck by rows of sticks with little white heads — these are the eggshells guarding the dead gloom of the cemetery...
The main preparations for the great holy day come, of course, on the eve of Yom Kippur, when the Yemenite Jews finish their work at twelve noon and at once prepare for the fast. For the final meal before the fast the best dishes are prepared, ones a Yemenite does not set eyes on all year. After the meal, great and small put on long white shirts and set off, prayer books under their arms, to the single small house of study of the city of Sana'a.
Out of the little houses of wood and clay come short, dark little Jews with pious faces and long curled sidelocks; a deep earnestness is poured over their faces, their movements are permeated with a holy trembling, and from their gleaming black sparkling eyes a deep sorrow looks out.
The Jews of Yemen go to "Kol Nidre".
The Yemenite synagogue is very small, and the worshippers sit literally one on top of the other — on the carpets spread out on the ground the simple-hearted Jews sit in a circle, having come to spend a night and a day in the small dark house of study. Yes, not only cramped and stifling but also dark is the Yemenite minyan, which has no windows at all; the superstitious Yemenites hold that one must be shut up within the four cubits of the house of study and absorb all the holiness into oneself — so they have avoided making a window in the synagogue, lest the holiness, God forbid, fly out...
The wicks flame in bowls of oil and light up the gaunt, brown-skinned Yemenite Jews, who know nothing of cantors or choirs. An old, dignified Jew takes his place at the reader's desk and begins in a hoarse voice to draw out the notes of "Kol Nidre" to a Yemenite melody... All the worshippers, young and old, help the cantor along; all shout and sing in different voices, make all kinds of grimaces, and believe with perfect faith that their prayers are the first to reach the Throne of Glory. Are they not, after all, the most tormented, the most humiliated and the most oppressed of all Jews...
Old and young sway with their gaunt bodies and shout, each louder than the next, just as if they wanted to outdo one another — the Yemenite Jews do indeed hold that when one shouts louder the prayer reaches the Throne of Glory sooner, and "whoever shouts the more, is praiseworthy"... Yet out of the old voices break the heartfelt tones that penetrate into the depths of the wandering Jewish soul.
So one sits the whole night on the ground, legs tucked back, saying Psalms; it is strictly forbidden to rise from the ground, let alone go home and lie down to sleep — no one would dare commit so grave a sin... Even the little children lie the whole twenty-four hours on the ground at the feet of their fathers and mothers. As soon as night draws on, the children begin to doze, but the older ones strain with all their strength to spend the whole night saying various prayers — it is not a good sign to fall asleep on the holy night, when one must beg forgiveness and pardon for all sins.
In the morning the worshippers are worn out and tired after a sleepless night. But they stay sitting on the ground and gather their last strength for the service of the Creator. The greatest pity is for the hungry, exhausted little children, who spend a whole night and a whole day in the cramped, small, dark house of study, where the air is heavy and stifling. The mothers pity the hungry children, but at the same time they must also show their cruelty — no mother, after all, will give her child food on Yom Kippur; so the children lie all day beside their mothers, under the apron, and suffer...
The Yemenite women, for their part, cannot even ask their husbands for advice, because the men are strictly forbidden to speak on Yom Kippur even with their own wives.
Thus one sits for 24 hours on end in dread of the holy day. — The heart trembles and a feeling of fear seizes everyone; but now the sun is setting and night is coming; in the small dark house of study it grows darker still, and suddenly the sound of the shofar is heard, the great blast, announcing that the fast is over. The worshippers barely rise from their places, and in a bolder, braver but very hoarse voice the prayers are finished; the tired and hungry Yemenites take wife and child and hurry off to drink a glass of tea.
After the glass of tea the Yemenite Jews dance for a few hours, and only then do they sit down to the meal. They eat and drink until they literally drop from exhaustion. Afterwards the parents bless the children and praise the Almighty that the little ones have got through the fast and did not bring them to any sin.
After the meal everyone goes to bed. The parents with the children sleep in one bed. The men and the women do not take off their white holiday clothes, and fully dressed they all tumble into one bed and sleep soundly until well into the day. It is the custom among the Yemenite Jews not to take off the Yom Kippur shirts, because they hold that there is a certain holiness in the clothes too, and therefore one must not take them off until one again begins to lead the grey everyday routine of life.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayelech)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion (Vayelech); Yom Kippur.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayelech
The Portion.
—o—
a) "At the end of seven years... gather the people together" (31:11–12)
In a Sabbatical year, when the fields are ownerless for all, when there is no difference between rich and poor, between people of lineage and simple folk — then it is good to gather the people together and to study Torah with them; for at other times the wealthy persuade themselves that the Torah does not mean them, that it means only the poor... Olelot Efraim.
—o—
b) "The men and the women and the little ones" (ibid.)
"The men come to learn, the women come to hear — why do the little ones come? To give reward to those who bring them. He said to them: You had a precious pearl in your hands and you wished to make me lose it?" Hagigah, 60 [?].
Every child is like that stone of which one does not know whether it is a precious diamond or a plain stone. A child may become a diamond, and it may remain a stone. The father does not know whom he is raising. But the father too receives a reward for giving the child a good upbringing. And that is already a precious pearl, whatever may become of it later... Arono shel Yosef.
—o—
c) "For thou shalt go with this people unto the land" (31:7)
"Moses said to Joshua: The elders of the generation shall be with you; everything according to their opinion and their counsel. But the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Joshua: 'For thou shalt bring the children of Israel into the land which I swore unto them' (further on, 33 [?]) — bring them even against their will. Everything depends on you. Take a stick and strike them on the head. One leader for a generation and not two leaders for a generation"... Sanhedrin, 8.
Moses did not advise Joshua to deal harshly with the people. He had seen what had happened to himself — "and they gazed after Moses". So he advised him: better live with them in peace, "everything according to their opinion and their counsel"; do not fall out with them, for they did not spare even me.. Beit Yaakov.
—o—
d) "And their children, who have not known, may hear and learn to fear" (ibid., 13)
See to it that you teach your children to be pious "who have not known" — before they know anything yet.. Later they will no longer let themselves be taught... Leket Shoshanim.
—o—
e) "And they will say in that day: Is it not because our God is not among us" (31:17)
"And they will say" — they will merely say it and nothing more; in that alone will their repentance consist... Therefore: "And I will surely hide My face." Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
• • •
"Because our God is not among us" —
And yet this is said of idol-worshippers. And still they know that they lack a God. That is Jews for you! They serve idols and long for the Jewish God... Hegyonot el Ami.
—o—
f) "Take this book of the law and put it by the side of the ark of the covenant of the Lord" (ibid., 21 [?])
The Torah was placed in the Holy of Holies, which no one was permitted to enter. Were it not for that — it would have been altered right at the start: one would have erased and another would have added... Devarim Nehmadim.
• • •
"And observe to do... all the days that ye live on the land."
The Torah does not make itself dependent on a particular time... it obliges all the days.. Melekhet Mahshevet.
• • •
"Also every plague which is not written in the book of this law."
The curses are directed against those who transgress the Torah. But those who invent commandments that are not in the Torah — upon them come curses that are not in the Torah... Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
—o—
Yom Kippur.
g) The commandment of eating on the eve of Yom Kippur.
"Whoever eats and drinks on the ninth is regarded as if he had fasted on the ninth and the tenth." Rosh Hashanah 19 [?].
But this refers only to one for whom eating is an affliction... who wants to fast and eats only for the sake of the commandment... Siftei Tzaddikim.
—o—
h) "Bring us back in perfect repentance before Thee."
Repentance with the mouth is only half a repentance... "Bring us back in perfect repentance before Thee" — with the heart too... Imrei Hen.
• • •
The Vilna Gaon said: The Kabbalists compare repentance to the burning of the leaven. Just as one burns the leaven, so one must nullify the evil inclination... But just as Jews employ all kinds of ruses with the removal of the leaven, selling it supposedly to a gentile, as a kind of joke — so they treat repentance too: as a joke; they do not mean it seriously...
• • •
"Thou turnest man to contrition, and sayest: Return, ye children of men" — people do repentance "to contrition": they torment themselves, they fast. But that, after all, is not the essence. The essence is: repentance — "and sayest: Return, ye children of men"... Kiflayim le-Tushiyah.

What do we need roosters, what do we need hens,
kapores too — oh and woe!
We possess something “better”,
something cheaper than them!

These fowl here, all of them,
are after all worth nothing
compared with the kapores
that the earth is waiting for...

For the Jews, for all of them,
for the great and for the small,
may they become a ransom —
may they go as a kapore...

There is no need to swing them over our heads,
as it stands in our law —
better that they themselves
get their heads well twisted...

There will be enough [startshen, starczyć] for all the Jews,
for the Jews near and far —
there will be no shortage of kapores:
the millions of Hitler-folk...

Since it's soon Yom Kipper, I, Khatskele, come to beg of you, [“to-vens”?] public, forgiveness.

H. Abramson: Napoleon's Wife (5)

“A good man has promised me that I shall see you once more before the worst happens. Be ready, my dear Joséphine: today they will take me to court to hear my sentence, and tomorrow morning they will execute me. I die knowing that I have done nothing that should cast a shadow on my name or for which my children should have to be ashamed of me. My only wish is to see you one more time. I would very much [?] have liked to see our children too, but that must not happen. I do not want a drop of poison to fall into their young, pure souls. Let them not know now what has happened to their father. And I hope that when they grow up they will understand that I died for my convictions.
“Only you, my dear, whom I have wronged, do I wish now, in these last moments, to press to my heart.”
The meeting took place.
The next day, when the sun had already begun to set and was sending its last rays through the bars of the prison, Joséphine knew for certain that her husband was no longer among the living.
The days went by, and the nights too; night in, night out, dozens of women were taken to the square where the guillotine stood, to have their heads chopped off at dawn.
Once a friend turned to her with the following words:
Joséphine, let us say goodbye, for I know that tomorrow morning they will send you to the guillotine and after that it will be my turn; only be brave, as you have been all along — we must show the gang that we can die just as heroically as the men.
Joséphine thought for a moment and said:
— No, my dear, a voice whispers to me that I shall not part from the world so quickly, that something will happen. Now I will tell you the secret. At home, in Martinique, a witch once told me that I would be the queen of France, and a voice whispers to me that it will indeed happen so. Don't laugh at me; I know it is foolish to believe in it now, when the blade hangs over my head. But so it will be, and I assure you that if it happens, I will not forget you.
Her friend was sure that the poor woman was talking out of fever, that her thoughts were confused, and she did not want to talk about it any more.
In the middle of the night a voice began [?] to carry:
— Robespierre has fallen! The tyrant is no more!
The doors of the prisons were opened, and the tens of thousands who had been locked up [were freed]. Joséphine returned to her home.
And she began to live as in the old days, meeting her good friends, and then one evening, at a friend's, she met a young man who made a deep impression on her at first sight.
His name was Napoleon Bonaparte, and at that time he was a general in the French army. It was known that this man had for a while been quite friendly with Robespierre and that he had belonged to the Jacobin club, but being constantly occupied on the battlefields, he now had no time to busy himself with politics, and he had grown distant from his civilian friends. Now, after the death of Robespierre, when the latter had lost his head on the guillotine, when the whole course had changed, Napoleon became a regular visitor in the rich salons where the highest aristocracy, now returned from exile, gathered [?].
Soon a love developed between the two young people. Joséphine was now more beautiful than she had been before. The sufferings she had gone through had added to her charm, and it did not take long before the two married and embarked on their stormy career. Napoleon soon rose to be First Consul, whereupon he had himself crowned as king, and there began the epoch that put an end to the Revolution and its aims.
But it is a historical fact that it was Joséphine who fought with all her strength against Napoleon becoming the ruler of France. It is known that she worked for the Bourbons, who had been driven out during the Revolution, to get back the throne, but Napoleon was too ambitious and did not listen to her.

A Terrible Catastrophe with Human Victims in Będzin

A balcony with people on it collapsed. — 2 dead, 10 injured. — Mourning in the town.
The entire Jewish population of Będzin is still under the impression of the horrific catastrophe that occurred on Monday, the first day of Rosh Hashanah, in Będzin, in the Hambel[?] house („Hambels hoyz“) on Plac 3 Maja.
It happened at around half past three in the afternoon. The Kamiński and Broner[?] families, who live in the rear wing (oficyna) on the second floor of the said house, had already finished the holiday meal and were chatting comfortably. Suddenly they heard voices coming from a neighbouring courtyard, and everyone rushed out onto the balcony; at that moment the balcony, on which 11 people were standing, broke away and fell onto the pavement. The weight of the balcony also tore down half of a balcony on the first floor, where Mrs. Zysla Tenenbaum was sitting at the time.
The scene of the catastrophe presented a horrific picture: behind the pieces of iron and boards lay some of the children, unconscious and covered in blood. The lightly injured, among them several children, ran to the hospital without anyone's help. Twelve-year-old Lejbl Pankowski was left hanging on the first floor.
In a very serious condition were 58-year-old Rywka Kamińska and 5-year-old Sarale Poznański. All rescue measures were of no avail, and both
died in hospital.
Mrs. Kamińska died a short time after she was taken to the hospital; the child died during the night from Monday to Tuesday.
Sarale, who perished so tragically, had come a few weeks earlier to her grandfather, R' Israel Lejb Eisenman, who lives in that courtyard. At the critical moment she was playing in the courtyard, and the balcony with its mass of people fell upon her.
The terrible news spread through the whole town with lightning speed, and from every corner people streamed to the scene of the catastrophe. The square in front of the hospital, too, was full of people mourning the tragic victims.
Thieves took advantage of the opportunity: during the rescue in the courtyard a diamond was stolen from Mrs. Tenenbaum and 2 wristwatches from Mr. Hejsbert.
A commission headed by the police commissioner came to the scene of the accident and ordered the arrest of the owners of the house as responsible for the accident.
The arrested were sent to the public prosecutor in Sosnowiec for questioning. The tenants of the house were also questioned.
The child's funeral took place on Wednesday at 1 p.m., and at 4 o'clock — the funeral of Mrs. Kamińska. A crowd of a thousand people from all strata of the population took part in the funeral.
At the cemetery there were
heart-rending scenes
of the family and the mourners. The bitter wailing of the family, friends and mourners was indescribable; the town is wrapped in mourning.
——
Fresh victims again. The grave of the victim of a similar catastrophe that happened a few months ago in Winer's house is still fresh, and already we stand before the fresh graves of Rywka Kamińska and little Sarale, who perished so tragically. This is the sad consequence of the neglected state in which most of the houses in our town find themselves.
— We hope that this latest catastrophe will at last serve as an example, so that the authorities take more interest in the condition of the houses, and of the balconies in particular.

In January Zagłębie was stirred by the sensational trial that took place before the municipal court in Będzin.
In the dock at that time sat the president of the Będzin National Socialists, a certain Nawiński, who had said at a meeting in Będzin that the lawyer Kozielski of Sosnowiec had conducted negotiations with Hitler.

A Whole Family Poisoned by Goose Meat
On the past holiday the whole Goldberg family in Będzin was poisoned. The doctor established that they had been poisoned by goose meat.
The Warsaw Train „Whistled Past“ the Będzin Passengers — A Chełm-Style Tale That Happened at the Będzin Station

[Będzin — railways; a „Chełm“ story.]
Last Saturday night the following characteristic scene was played out at the Będzin railway station:
The station is full of people who have to leave for Warsaw by the 11.58 train. Among the passengers are also the artists of Grenach's [?] ensemble.
— „Strona Warszawa“ (Warsaw direction) — the ticket man calls out, and everyone hurries onto the platform, waiting for the train in the direction of Warsaw. At the appointed time the train came, but... did not stop at the Będzin station... it whistled and went on further.
It is easy to imagine the commotion among the passengers, especially among the artists, who urgently had to be in Warsaw on Sunday morning. An intervention was therefore made with the station master, who demanded [?] of the Katowice railway directorate that a carriage be sent to Ząbkowice, with which the passengers only then travelled on with the Kraków—Warsaw express („courier“) train.
Also characteristic is the fact that when the train stopped at Dąbrowa, reports were drawn up against the passengers who had tickets to Będzin.
Polish Bakers' Guild Demands That Street Trade in Baked Goods Not Be Permitted

[Zagłębie — artisans; petty trade.]
In Sosnowiec a congress of the Polish artisans of Zagłębie took place. After the greetings and lectures, each guild stated its demands.
The bakers' guild declared that street trade in baked goods should not be permitted and that baked goods should be sold only in the bakery shops.
— Next Sunday a congress of the Jewish artisans' associations of Zagłębie will take place in Będzin.
Strict Order on Putting the Balconies in Order

[Będzin — municipality; building safety; the balcony disaster.]
In connection with the terrible catastrophe that occurred on Rosh Hashana in Będzin, the city president, Mr. Ruszczkowski [?], has issued an order to the landlords that all balconies be inspected at once as to whether they can bear a weight of 900 kilos.
The order forbids putting up sukkot on the unsafe balconies.
Conference of Polish Craftsmen in Sosnowiec.

On Sunday a conference of the representations of the districts (powiats) of Olkusz, Zawiercie and Będzin took place in Sosnowiec. Present at the conference were the starosta, the commissioner and all seven councillors of the Chamber of Crafts from the 3 districts — 5 Christians[?] and 2 Jews, Goldsztajn and Kilsztak[?] of Będzin.
The starosta, Mr. Heinar[?], and the commissioner, Mr. Alemsztet[?], gave warm words of welcome and promised to support the crafts in Sosnowiec. Commissioner Alemsztet reports that the six-year plan of the Sosnowiec municipality (Magistrat) contains 600,000 zł. [for] supporting the crafts in Sosnowiec, and the Sosnowiec Craftsmen's Association will have a say in how the money is to be distributed.
A very heartfelt speech was delivered by Director Maur[?], councillor of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts. "Although I am no craftsman," he said, "the craftsmen's woes are very well known to me. The situation in which the artisans in Poland find themselves is unbearable. In the Western countries the craftsman, after work, meets in the café (konditorei) and the like with the greatest of noblemen[?]. There is no difference between the shoemaker or master joiner and the engineer or doctor; they spend time together as equals among equals — while here people are ashamed of the craftsman. But this must be fought; we must," he said, "raise the condition of the crafts and of craftsmanship in Zagłębie."
On courses for apprentices, Director Kruszyskowicz[?] and Manager Piotrowski reported. Mr. Piotrowski proposes that the time at which apprentices attend the evening courses be changed[?]: instead of 2–3 hours every evening, they should be one day a week, a full day.
After the reports a lively discussion developed. The representatives of the guilds spoke out against the law that requires masters to send their apprentices to school, to pay for them into the health-insurance fund (ubezpieczalnia) and not to take payment for the training. Apprenticeship with a master should not be treated worse than the schools. They therefore call for the law to be amended to this effect: that a boy be accepted as an apprentice in a trade only after he has completed 6 grades of elementary school and 2 years of vocational school as preparation for that same trade.
Then the following trades submitted their demands (postulates) to the Chamber of Crafts:
Tinsmiths: against illegal competition.
Joiners: furniture should not be distrained until it has been paid for.
Master builders: a house should not be sellable until the craftsmen who built it have been paid for their work.
Hairdressers: demand a long-term loan for fitting out their workshops in modern fashion and for combating[?] illegal competition.
Bakers: against the fact that Jewish bakers work 7 days a week.
Butchers: against illegal competition, which harms the legal butchers as well as the Treasury (skarb), and against the excessive fees at the slaughterhouse.
Then the councillors spoke. Mr. Kucki[?] (Dąbrowa) spoke out against the employment of juveniles, for instance by boot-upper makers, which makes the existence of craftsmen who work alone or with journeymen impossible.
He submits a proposal that every craftsman or merchant be obliged to stamp his goods.
Mr. Goldsztajn: the situation of the craftsmen is much sadder than it has been presented here. There are trades in which 90 percent work for the shops (magazyn), for example tailors, shoemakers and joiners; the craftsmen are treated by their big employers worse than slaves once were. The craftsmen work 3–4 months a year, and during the time they work they barely earn a meagre living; and because they cannot keep any journeyman, since they are not in a position to pay a journeyman properly, more illegal workshops of juveniles arise, who content themselves with a minimum, and thereby the price of labour is pushed down. The task of the new Chamber of Crafts will therefore be to find a way out of this bad situation.
— At the conference to be held on Sunday in the premises of the Central Craftsmen's Union in Będzin, the councillors of the Chamber of Crafts will also be represented, and the members of the presidium, Messrs. Szyluszek[?] and Goldsztajn, will give a report.
The Jewish craftsmen of the 3 districts must this time show their maturity and be represented in great numbers at this conference. Then let the voice of the Jewish craftsman be heard.
And Cast into the Depths of the Sea...

Caught at the main transport station of the "Przemsza".
On the first day of Rosh Hashana, in the afternoon, the banks of the "Przemsza" [the river at Będzin] were overflowing with men and women — many more women than men. Are our women really more sinful[?], and especially the women[?] with the wigs, with wrinkled faces and bent shoulders?
And because the women run first to Tashlich, they grab the best spots, the head of the place, and feel truly splendid. Among themselves there is no shame; and whatever each Jewish woman may be thinking privately at that moment, and whatever she may be weeping and praying about, and whatever sins she may be shaking out into the river — they all say the same "Yehi Ratzon".
And so camp after camp relieve one another on the bank, women and men, younger and older; they shake out their pockets and pour out sins, and — forbidden[?] if anyone is threatened[?] by a flood.
Christians pass by and become envious. With them, poor things, the "confessions"[?] take place individually. In secret. In a corner — retail; with us, however — a delight! — the sins are transported wholesale. And feeling how good we have it, how pleasant and fine it is to be a Jew — the true taste of "Thou hast chosen us" — the voices of the Tashlich-sayers, men and women, rise ever higher, all in one voice and with the same intention: a long life, a life of goodness, a life of good livelihood...
A young Hasidic wife edges slowly toward the bank. Dressed up in the latest fashion. All year long she can stroll[?] on Małachowskiego Street like a "progressive" [postępowa] lady. The clothes; the face rouged, the lips painted, the eyebrows plucked, the lashes blackened; and even if there is a little wig on her head, it is so fashionably[?] frizzed and pushed over the forehead, with a hat on top, that by no means will you make out her Hasidism. But when Tashlich comes, a real hell is made for her: the mother on one side, the mother-in-law on the other — and go shake yourself out...
And so, year in, year out, the banks of the "Przemsza" look at Tashlich.
A. Szwarcer.
From the "Darkei Noam" Heder.

Last week the first general examination took place at the Sosnowiec heder "Darkei Noam", and it made a good impression on those assembled. It was a joy to see how the very young children spoke at length in their learning and, with composure, answered at length the questions put by the local geniuses and scholars.
At the end of the examination the examiners expressed their satisfaction and wished [the heder] further fruitful activity in the field of Jewish acumen and learning.
327
A Piece of the Reality of the Hitler Regime.

From Granach's production of "The Yellow Patch".
Granach's longing, as we know, has always been to play Yiddish theatre.
This is what he strove for; and our German calamity gave him the opportunity and the push to take the first step.
He was needed by us; the Yiddish stage has been enriched by an actor who possesses cultivated gesture, human speech and a surging, youthful temperament.
The poverty that cries to heaven cries out, and one felt[?] that it was he who was crying...
In the reportage-play "The Yellow Patch" Granach gave the true type of the Jewish professor, who is ready to sacrifice himself and his children for the fatherland, and in the end he falls victim, is mocked and spat upon by his own students, who are infected with the plague of the Hitlerite regime.
The whole ensemble contributed to the success. Brilliant in their roles were the journalist (Simcha Natan), Ruth (Miss Natan), the Nazi commissar (Krelman).
The performances stood at a high artistic level and will long remain in the memory of the Yiddish theatre lovers of Zagłębie.

The Ninth Plague in the Katowice and Zagłębie Area / A Passenger Train Pelted with Stones / To "Kosher-Certify" a Sukkah One Must Pay 8 Złoty / Arrests at the Funeral of a Communist / Synagogue Worshippers Demand a Competition / Holiday Campaign of the Będzin "Beit Lechem" / Exhibition on Gas and Air Defence

The Ninth Plague in the Katowice and Zagłębie Area
On Thursday at 10 in the evening[?], in accordance with the relevant demand of the administrative authorities, a drill of extinguishing the lights and of protecting oneself against a gas attack from the air was carried out in the Katowice and Zagłębie area.
At the appointed hour the lights in all houses were put out, the windows were closed, and it became truly dark.
The trams ran with very weak light and covered windows. Police patrols kept watch in the streets. Reports were drawn up against those who had not carried out the order properly.
The darkness lasted an hour.
—o—
A Passenger Train Pelted with Stones
One passenger injured.
On Thursday morning the train that leaves at 7 a.m. from Kazimierz for Sosnowiec was pelted with stones. One of the passengers was hit on the head by a stone and had to seek medical help.
—o—
To "Kosher-Certify" a Sukkah One Must Pay 8 Złoty
In connection with the recent balcony disaster in Będzin, the local authorities have forbidden building sukkot on balconies without the approval of the building commission at the Magistrate (town hall). For this "hechsher" one must pay 8 zł. in advance. It happened[?], however, that owners of sturdy balconies protested against the charge — and from them only... 3 zł. was taken.
—o—
Arrests at the Funeral of a Communist
On Tuesday the funeral of a communist took place in Będzin. When the procession reached Czeladzka Street, red wreaths with anti-state inscriptions suddenly appeared. The police intervened at once and arrested several persons.
—o—
Synagogue Worshippers Demand a Competition
Since the cantor question in Będzin has become "topical", a large number of the synagogue's worshippers have turned to the kehilla administration with a demand that a competition be announced and that until then no cantor be engaged.
—o—
Holiday Campaign of the Będzin "Beit Lechem"
In honour of Sukkot the society[?] "Beit Lechem" gave out provisions to about 150 families. Meat, sugar, flour, beans, butter and candles were distributed.
—o—
Exhibition on Gas and Air Defence
Until 5 October an exhibition of products for air and gas defence will take place in Katowice.
The aims of the exhibition are:
1) To inform the public in every respect about the work of the L.O.P.P. [Liga Obrony Powietrznej i Przeciwgazowej — Air and Anti-Gas Defence League] to date and in the future.
2) To acquaint the broad masses with the methods and means of protecting oneself against gases from the air.
3) To acquaint the public with domestic products that relate to gas and air defence, and to point out where to buy them.
Who is organising the exhibition and who is taking part?
The exhibition was organised by the Upper Silesian branch of the L.O.P.P. through a special committee headed by Dr. Rogal[?], with the assistance of representatives of the military authorities, the Red Cross and other public institutions.
What will be exhibited?
Exhibits will be shown — defence devices of domestic manufacture. Very interesting is the sanitary section, which is equipped with the newest alarm sirens and a radio station.
The planned events
Today, Sunday, at 12 noon — a review (parade) in front of the Polish Theatre in Katowice with the participation of several[?] sports[?] and sanitary squads (drużyny).
On the 25th, 26th, 27th, 28th, 29th and 30th of this month and from the 2nd to the 6th of October (październik) model drills will be shown by the rescue squads, firemen, the technical emergency service (pogotowie) etc.
On 6 October the diplomas will be distributed, and with that the exhibition will be closed.
The exhibition is located on the former market square (Targ-plac) in Katowice.

Craftsmen's Conference of 3 Districts in Będzin.

[Będzin — craftsmen; regional conference.]
On Sunday, in the premises of the Central Craftsmen's Union in Będzin, a conference was held of the starsi [guild elders] and the boards of all the guilds from the 3 powiats [districts] that formed the third electoral district (okręg wyborczy) for the elections to the Kielce Chamber of Crafts.
Taking part in the conference, besides the boards of the guilds, were representatives of the starostwo [district administration], the town president, the director of the vocational continuation school, town councillors and board members of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts.
The conference was opened by the president of the association, Mr. H. L. Goldsztajn. After being elected chairman he invited to the presidium the starsi of Sosnowiec, Messrs.: Altman of the photographers' guild, Szejer (tailors' guild), Dawidowicz (butchers' guild), Goldkorn (jewellers' guild), Rotensztajn (carpenters' guild), Cymberknop (painters' guild), Nachemia (metal guild), Finkelsztajn, president of the craftsmen's association in Żarki [?], and Gliksztajn, president of the craftsmen's association in Olkusz. As secretary — Mr. Magister Baruszykowski. Mr. Goldsztajn greeted the representatives of the authorities, of the magistrate [town hall], of the school system and of the Chamber of Crafts, as well as the numerous representatives of Jewish and Polish craftsmen from the 3 powiats.
The floor for greetings was given to the town president, Mr. Eng. Ruszeczkowski, who declared that he had come to the conference because craftsmen's questions interest him. In the whole of Europe — he said — great attention is now being paid to the craft trades; Poland is doing the same, as proven by the amendment to the industrial law in favour of the craftsmen's interests. The craft trades should look to the future optimistically.
Councillor Szyluszek: The craft trades are now entering a new phase of work. Zagłębie received 7 of the 25 mandates in the Kielce Chamber of Crafts; that is a success, and it proves that the authorities reckon with the craftsmen of Zagłębie. The Jewish craftsmen, in order to improve their situation, must work hand in hand with the Christian craftsmen.
After the warm greeting of Councillor Kicki, Mr. Goldsztajn reported on the present situation of the craftsmen and of the school system. He said that the councillors are aware of the hard work awaiting them; the councillors' opinions differ on the ways leading to an improvement of the bad situation, for example on the question of who should receive a craftsman's card on the basis of a diploma [?]. Some say that such a [?] card should be given to a craftsman not younger than 30, arguing that a 30-year-old craftsman is mature, bears the burden of earning a living, and will therefore not engage in unfair competition. Another holds that those who are at least [?] 25 years old, have already practised the trade for 12 years and already run independent workshops must be legalised, because otherwise thousands of craftsmen will lose their bread, since there are no such workshops that could employ them.
Mr. G. said among other things that today's conference must state its position on the question of legalising workshops, because the councillors will certainly reckon with the craftsmen's opinion.
The starsi spoke: Messrs. Ferstenfeld, who pointed to the bad situation of the barbers' trade, because there is a large number of illegal workshops; besides, the barbershop at the station is a serious nuisance, being favoured to the detriment of the town barbers. He appealed to the councillors to make efforts to have the present unbearable situation changed.
Mr. Goldkorn spoke about the competition from the Upper Silesian jewellers.
Mr. Altman complained that the photographic trade has declined greatly because non-professionals engage in it. He proposed that amateurs pay a tax on cameras as well as on the accessories they buy.
After Messrs. Nachemia, Sz. Metal, Szejer, Sz. Sznajder, Sztern, J. Rotensztajn, Macner, Bojm and Rarenter [?] had spoken, the floor was taken by the naczelnik [department head] of the starostwo, Mr. Saszka, who promised active cooperation in raising the craft trades to the level befitting them.
On the school system, the director of the continuation school, Mr. Oczeszyński [?], reported. He spoke about the need for education for craftsmen, and also reproached the masters who do not send their apprentices to school at the appointed time.
Mr. Goldsztajn: The Będzin continuation school is far from satisfying the needs; Będzin — he said — is treated like a stepchild in comparison with Sosnowiec, where there is a broadly branched network of craftsmen's schools for various trades.
Further speakers were President Mr. Ruszeczkowski, Mr. Kicki and Mr. Szuluszek, and the postulates of various trades were presented. In conclusion Mr. Goldsztajn thanked the representatives of the authorities for showing so much interest in craftsmen's questions.
Healthy and Fresh Is „Menora“ Margarine. — A Special Train Exhibition.

[Poland — economy and domestic produce; likely a promotional piece („Menora“ margarine).]
(Sh) The Central Society for the Support of Domestic Production has recently introduced a truly modern economic propaganda. In the month of September it set in motion a special train exhibition, which reaches the most remote places in the country. So far the train has already been in about 60 places in the regions of Poznań, Pomerania and Upper Silesia. The train exhibition draws on such foreign undertakings (imprezy) as have given the best results.
The Polish train exhibition, whose task is to acquaint the broad public with Polish production, consists of 3 carriages, which take up 30 splendid salons. In the train are the newest technical installations. There is a cinema, telephone apparatus, radio, and also a short-wave radio station.
Not only economic circles, but also the broad public have taken a strong interest in the new undertaking of the Central Society, which, besides its practical purpose (the spreading of domestic products on the domestic market), has also shown a social-educational character.

The “Bikur Cholim” Society in Dąbrowa Opened an Out-patient Clinic.

In the first days of the new year 5695 an out-patient clinic (ambulatorium) was opened in Dąbrowa through the initiative of the board and the workers of “Bikur Cholim”.
The opening was organised with great “pomp”. The celebration was held not in its own premises but in the former hall of the “Wenus” cinema. At the entrance — uniformed Brit HaChayal men (who, however, had no hard work, since the few dozen bewildered Jews who came behaved quietly before the military guards...). From the decorated stage a transparency “shouts” out: one should support the “Jewish” clinic. (Apparently the stewards were afraid that “the common folk” might fall into the error of thinking that this was the opening of a “gentile” clinic.) Care was also taken[?] that the ceremony be conducted in perfect sanctity — men separately, women separately; only when it comes to “money matters” does one become modern for a while and honour precisely a woman with cutting the ribbon...
The opening was supposed to take place at 2 o’clock, but since it was already 2 hours past the appointed time and the “notables” had not appeared, the thing began “punctually”... at 4 o’clock, in the form of a theatre performance: first — the bell, then a stir in the “gallery”, and —
the curtain rises.
The chairman of “Bikur Cholim”, Mr. Farsal[?], opens, and delegates, the kehilla board and council, and representatives of all the social, philanthropic and political organisations are invited to the presidium.
Mr. Farsal gives a short survey of its founding and points out the reasons that led to the clinic being opened as quickly as possible.
Then comes a “series” of greetings: on behalf of the Sosnowiec “Linat HaCholim” — chairman Goldkorn and Kleinman; from the Będzin “Linat HaCholim” — L. Rozenblum; on behalf of the Jewish town councillors, the Gemilut Chesed fund and the synagogue worshippers — L. Futerko; from Agudat Israel — Ch. M. Eizenman; from Betar — Jakubowicz; from the Revisionists — A. Szczegowski; they point out the importance of the institution for the broad Jewish masses and call on the Jewish population of Dąbrowa to support and help, so that the newly created clinic, which will be the so-called “pogotowie” [first-aid service], may develop properly.
Further speakers are Messrs. Zylbersztejn, Mittelman and Farsal, and for the honour of cutting the ribbon Mrs. Lea Wajnsztejn is invited, who is received with stormy applause...
At the end the Revisionists and the Brit HaChayal men wanted to sing “HaTikva”, but the chairman, who was afraid of “partisanship”, did not permit it, and at his call “the public dispersed quietly”...

Professional Public Life — The urgent renewal of our merchants' and artisans' organizations

(The urgent renewal of our merchants' and artisans' organizations.)
A few years ago, when people watched how the economic situation was beginning [?] to grow ever harder and harder, authoritative circles wondered why these questions were being treated with such rare indifference, why these vital questions were being left to the last item and dealt with only once all other matters had supposedly been taken care of. People wondered — and remained wondering.
The press, the leadership, the representative bodies — everyone had time and room for everything in the world, only not for the most painful questions, which were as necessary as life itself, as existence, as the continued survival of all strata of our Jewish masses in Poland.
And meanwhile, meanwhile the pit that had been dug for us grew deeper and more dangerous, until it was impossible to save oneself, to crawl out of it. The abyss became infinitely [?] deep, almost bottomless, and now, when we already face an accomplished fact, people begin — as if after a long lethargic sleep — to look around and see where in the world they are, and then they see the dangerous situation in all its magnitude and horror. The economic condition of the average masses stands at the lowest level, so that no way out can be seen.
True, now something has somehow begun to be done in the face of [?] the bitter need, but this "something" is far too little; far too weak against the terrible impoverishment, and one can only hope an improvement will be found. If only some relief could be found, since the neglect has already taken such deep root.
For everything we always had time, and even today it is the same. Over the smallest absurdity people polemicized [?] for days and weeks and gave up their best time. Foolish quarrels take first place among us at all times, and the best energy is used up on them. Meanwhile the most important, the most burning matter — what ought to be the most topical and the most urgent — stands at the last item of the agenda.
At the lowest level among us stand the professional and economic institutions, although at all times they had the best chances to take first place, and then they could have accomplished a great deal, a very great deal, in the present impoverishment.
Let us take, for example, one branch: finance. How long ago was it that we had well-established public banks? How much benefit they brought the community, and how many strengthening drops they could have poured into today's sick body, if we still had them! Why did they disappear so quickly, even though they were well situated? We know: the accursed crisis came, which first of all began to visit there often; yet despite all this the consequences would not have been so tragic had it not been for the rot, the disorder, the system of favouritism, the internal frictions and the tripping-up of one another. This frivolity, this irresponsibility, this unheard-of lawlessness is what turns us into a heap of ruins.
The same is true of all our other institutions. Responsibility is lacking, a sense of honour is lacking, respect and common decency are lacking. Everyone pushes into the other's face; no one wants to acknowledge the other. "Who says I must show you respect?" — we hear quite often — and there lie the reasons why our public institutions collapse like houses of cards.
Yet to this day we still have merchants' and artisans' associations, which, it is true, have also already declined considerably. But we must not let them set up tombstones, for otherwise those who ought to be their members will be buried along with them.
It is no longer a secret to anyone that the institutions mentioned have already done the community much harm, and that the members have more than once been exploited by many of their "servants" and "creator of servants" [a liturgical pun]; but this by no means implies that because of all these defects the institutions must disappear from the Jewish street — no! For these very reasons we demand r e s p o n s i b l e representative bodies.
We must now take a clear accounting; we must remember in what situation we find ourselves. We hold that never before has the Jewish population needed professional public help as much as now. Now the artisan finds out that he is no artisan at all; the same goes for the small industrialist, the merchant and the shopkeeper.
The slightest negligence, missing a deadline — of which, incidentally, he knew nothing — is enough [?] for him to lose his livelihood and existence; such harsh regulations have never existed before. It turns out that every ordinary citizen ought to have a house lawyer at his disposal, so that instead of being engrossed [?] in his business and seeing how to earn a living for himself and his household, he should rather be occupied with the "laws of paragraphs", which multiply from day to day and which the ordinary citizen certainly cannot carry out.
The Jewish citizens in Poland consist for the most part of merchants and artisans; [and] the government has now begun to introduce new regulations in these fields which severely restrict the continuation and development of these trades.
We must therefore raise the professional institutions to the proper level, for the population needs them like life itself. At the same time it must not be forgotten that we may by no means keep the institutions on paper only, merely to fulfil an obligation. Nowadays we must have professional associations that will be equal to their tasks. They must be both information bureaus and advice centres for their members. At the same time they must bear full responsibility towards everyone, for they must be reliable both for the authorities and for their members.
If we want professional institutions with full responsibility — and such we must have — we must use all possibilities and means so that each town in Zagłębie has no more than one artisans' association and one merchants' association, because splintering them makes them weaker and of lesser worth, both in the eyes of the authorities and for our internal affairs.
Let us keep to the formula: better fewer institutions with more responsibility and more members than the other way round.
Let us now, during the free days of Chol HaMoed, use the time to make our public institutions healthier and more mature — institutions which the masses need simply as they need life itself.
So let us not regard the present public obligation as a trifle, for every smallest mistake causes great harm to the people. Artisans as well as merchants must, in the prevailing situation, have their own public tribunes, before which both the members and the associations must mutually bear the fullest public responsibility.
R. Let.
"The Festival of Booths" — "The Festival of Ingathering"

[Essay — festivals; Sukkot.] Followed by: [Law and administration — new circulars.]
Said R. Yohanan: What is the "festival of ingathering"? etc. — rather, a festival that comes at the time of ingathering (Hagigah 18a).
The festival of Sukkot is "the season of our rejoicing", the festival when it is a commandment to be joyful, more than at all the other festivals. Sukkot is the only festival that bears, so to speak, a popular, folk character; it is a mixture of the spiritual and the material, of holiness and the everyday[?], of religious and social elements[?], while the other festivals bear a purely religious character. Take, for example, Passover, which we celebrate in remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt: although it falls in the month of Aviv, in spring, at the time when nature awakens to a new, fresh life, when everything blossoms and sprouts, grows[?] and calls to joyfulness, to festivity — nevertheless Passover did not become bound up with nature, but remained a purely religious festival. Or take Shavuot: although Shavuot is also celebrated as the "festival of the first fruits", when in ancient times, while the Jews were still a free people in their "own" land, they brought the first ripe wheat[?] and barley[?] to the Temple and offered them as a symbol that the Jews are an agrarian people bound to the cultivation of the soil — it has nevertheless remained only the festival of "the season of the giving of our Torah", a purely religious festival. Quite different is the festival of Sukkot. Although the festival must remind us of the Exodus — "for I made [the children of Israel] dwell in booths" etc. — it is at the same time also bound up with folk life, with the economic, with the "festival of ingathering", with the celebration of clearing the fields and gardens, of gathering the harvest: "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered in the produce of the land, you shall keep [the feast]" etc. And further: "and you shall rejoice before the Lord seven days" — you shall rejoice for seven days; and the Jewish people has indeed kept sacredly the tradition of rejoicing and being enthused on Sukkot. This phenomenon already took place in ancient times in the Land of Israel, when Sukkot was the symbol of joy, of enthusiasm and ecstasy, when Jewish daughters held folk dances with song in the fields and gardens — "and the daughters of Israel made dances in the vineyards" — and the number of "pilgrims" from the whole country reached into the millions.
On Sukkot there also took place, as is known, the great festivities of the so-called "Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing", when the joy reached the highest degree of ecstasy, and about which the Talmud says: "Whoever has not seen this rejoicing has never seen rejoicing in his life."
What did the sukkah once symbolise?
The sukkah of old reminded us of the past, when Jews were enslaved in Egypt, when they had to build foreign cities, Pithom and Raamses, and when they were redeemed from the Egyptian exile they had to wander in the desolate deserts, suffer hunger and want, without a roof over their heads. But at the same time the festival of ingathering reminded them of the happy and splendid present, when they dwell in their own land, work their own soil as a fully free and independent people, and enjoy with a full hand the fruit of their labour and freedom. And it was this that gave the impetus to extraordinary joy and enthusiasm.
What does our present-day sukkah symbolise?
Our present-day sukkah symbolises the "temporary dwelling" — life for the time being, not being secure either of today or of tomorrow. Today's sukkah symbolises exile life, which is threatened every minute, which is exposed at every moment to the danger of being destroyed, of collapsing like the sukkah when a strong wind blows; [it symbolises] that our whole exile life is put together only of thin, weak boards, hastily and haphazardly, without plan and without harmony, and that all evil winds and all black spirits lie in wait for our existence and our life, to break us and to annihilate us.
And the question arises: "of rejoicing, what does it accomplish?" — what reason do we have to be joyful today, when our skies are covered with black clouds, when our existence is threatened by danger, when our enemies compete among themselves in their antisemitic deeds and in a policy of extermination towards us — does not today's "season of our rejoicing" sound like an irony, like a paradox?
But one can answer that we do have, precisely, a reason to rejoice in today's Sukkot, because once again the "festival of ingathering" comes to life before our eyes in our former free Jewish home; once again we sense the smell of field and garden, which are ploughed and sown, reaped and gathered by Jewish hands, by the labour of our sisters and brothers, and which give us hope for a brilliant and bright future.
And because we now live in such a terrible epoch, in a time of oppression and persecution in every sphere — the ray of light and hope that shines out to us from the dark exile life, from the reviving Land of Israel, must awaken in us joy of life and energy for great and strong deeds. Schopenhauer says that only after strong, shattering experiences can a person feel true happiness and joy of life; and only because we Jews find ourselves in such a condition are we able to feel "the season of our rejoicing", the "festival of Sukkot" — the "festival of ingathering".
Y. Wygodzki.

[Law and administration — new circulars.] New Circulars
What to do when one loses a "karta powołania" together with the railway ticket.
In the event that a person liable for military service loses his call-up card (karta powołania) with the enclosed railway ticket and is unable, owing to poverty, to buy another ticket with his own money, the local municipal administration (magistrat) must, upon his application, buy him another railway ticket.
The sum laid out is later refunded to the municipal administration by the military authorities.
Housing moratorium for the unemployed.
The Ministry of Justice explains in a circular (No. 1334/I C./34) that if an unemployed person wishes to benefit from the housing moratorium — i.e. that the carrying out of an ordered eviction be suspended — and he must prove his critical material situation, he may present a corresponding certificate not only from the Labour Exchange that he is a registered unemployed person, but in general from any public-law institution of economic self-government, for example: from the Chamber of Crafts, the Chamber of Physicians, the Bar Council, the Chamber of Commerce and Industry, etc.
In general one must remember that the said moratorium applies not only to the unemployed — hired workers — but in general to persons left without employment.
