People have stopped understanding one another (Reflections on the history of the whole past)

(Reflections on the history of the whole past.)
By L. Szpigelman.
If a curse has been poured out over the whole world, that one man wants to swallow the other alive, and thanks to this very curse it is growing narrower and narrower, it is simply becoming harder, and often impossible, to breathe — then this is thanks to the fact that one does not want to understand the other, one does not want to take the other into account; in the present period the course being followed is one of annihilation, of rooting out everything that should and can have a right to exist.
During the terrible World War people knew that the catastrophe was a dreadful one, and they kept hoping that the end would come; and when they saw that no end was in sight, they grew impatient and began to doubt whether an end would ever come at all — so choked [?] were they with longing to see the finish, the way out. Older people hoped only to live to see the end of the interesting, mysterious, thrilling drama.
An acquaintance of mine, an elderly man, told me at that time that he wished for nothing more than to live to see the peace and to see how the world would be shaped, how the earth and the countries and mankind would look on peaceful ground, and then — so he put it — I will be able to close my eyes with a quiet conscience.
People were certain that after the war the world would be purified and everything would be so bright [?] and clean and clear and crystallised that it would be a delight to live in the renewed world, where the prospects were surely splendid, for not in vain had mankind shed so much blood. It seemed that through the spilled blood the world would be purified, and the coming generations would enjoy life with full buckets of sap, which would flow like springs — the more one took, the more there would be.
That, roughly, was how people imagined and glorified the future.
It never occurred to anyone at all that after the war the world would begin to wander astray anew and would be unable to find a place of rest. People knew that the old, quiet world would not come back to us; on the other hand they were sure that we would enter the palace of life full of freshness and encouragement, and that our children would enjoy the world, which would arise for them in a brand-new edition that would ease, beautify and glorify the conditions of life.
Great hope was placed in the technology of the future and in all kinds of modernisations, whose prospects were painted in such bright colours that it seemed it had been worth bringing so many sacrifices all over the world, and that the spilled blood would bear its fruit, and the moral of it all would be a beautiful, quiet, peaceful and modernised world on entirely different foundations, which would free man from the heavy yoke, and every human creature would be free as a bird — free in spirit, free in thought, free under the yoke [?].
That, roughly, is how people dreamed about the whole future, and it did not look like a fantasy far from being realised either; on the contrary, there was every reason to dream so, for it was known that the technology that had been applied against mankind during the war would afterwards give a huge push to progress in the peaceful, renewed world, so that there were grounds to think and to argue that everything would beautify, ease and glorify the conditions of human life.
On the other hand it occurred to no one that things could get even worse, and that the world would be constantly so warlike in mood, and that all inventions would be exploited not for the good of mankind but, on the contrary, to the harm of the free, independent human being.
Mankind was disappointed thanks to the "surprises" that arose, and people kept reckoning that the after-pains of the terrible war would vanish and the contagious war-sickness would heal. But nobody could calculate that, as time went on, it would cling ever more firmly to the mind of mankind.
The consequences of the war are constantly warlike, the train of thought is warlike, youth, the coming generation, on whom we place so much hope and courage, is being brought up warlike in the full sense of the word and its meaning. And so it goes on constantly in all the folds and nuances of human life.
What more is needed? It is no longer a secret to anyone, it has become an everyday, understandable phenomenon, that in one place people go hungry and perish for a piece of bread, yes, literally for a piece of dry bread, while in another place the grain is burned or thrown into the sea because the harvest is too big and faces a catastrophe on account of low prices. Well, does one need more disharmony? Does one need more disappointments — that everything is tuned to war, that everything is studied on warlike foundations, that the glasses through which one looks are warlike? And that is the reason why everything finds itself in a war psychosis — in the psychosis of making the right to exist harder.
After the war the world slipped, it went off the rails and cannot, or no longer wants to, come to itself; and perhaps it is not allowed to by such individuals as are never [alive] when it is light, and come to life only in the dark depths? Perhaps they are governed by such a huge, incomprehensible force that no one can touch them? Perhaps it is some kind of secret, mysterious sorcery, whose bacilli one does not seek [?] and of which one does not even know that it hovers over our horizon?
Were it not some secret force, the world would not have become infected on such a scale, which must lead simply to madness.
We, whom the prevailing catastrophic situation has struck hardest, think in our camp that only we are suffering, whereas de facto this is far from so. True, we suffer, but only because we are the weakest and most helpless, and as such it is easiest, first of all, to attack the weak one, the one who does not draw the world's attention; for after all it is generally known that we are the most enduring; despite our age we are still like a young sapling, which in the strongest wind bends to every side and does not break, as often happens to a thick tree that is broken during a strong storm-wind.
We are the most beaten of the beaten, and as such we have grown used to bearing all kinds of suffering, and we are therefore also more enduring than all other peoples.
At the same time one thing must not be forgotten: that the antisemites, both our own and those all over the world, are too short-sighted in thinking that the rod that strikes us strikes no further. True, they aim only at us, but the echo resounds much further and leaves its deadly marks all over the world.
A strange thing: there are countries and peoples where no one lets another come near, each one puffs himself up, and one is a stranger to the other. A stranger from afar — one guards against him, lest he poison the air, lest he eat the local bread; and in this, it seems to them, lies salvation, and closing the gates will radically help the local native. But had the world, the whole world, been open to the whole of mankind, every person could, like a free bird, have filled [?] the whole world; he would have had the right, like every flying creature, to be in all the wild forests and fields — and then it would not have been too narrow. Then [?] people would have founded settlements and built palaces in deserts where no living creature had yet set foot, and new worlds would have been discovered.
People have talked themselves into believing that there are too many people in the world and that the world — the great, broad and beautiful world — cannot bear mankind, and that therefore it is too narrow and impossible to catch one's breath. But this is a false view. For we know that before the war the gates to America were open to the whole world, and from all sides people streamed in without stop and without end, and yet the country flourished at that time and developed enormously. In all corners and parts of the country unceasing wonders were created.
But then came the post-war period, when people stopped understanding one another and were simply turned into beasts; they stopped understanding the concept of love of mankind, and then fear and estrangement arose between man and man, and this led to the closing of the gates of the gigantic countries, which became afraid of the small, helpless human being.
The aim was to shut oneself up within one's own four cubits and not to allow an influx of people into the countries, reckoning in this way to improve the situation.
But what do we see? What have these experiments shown us? Before our eyes everything has been turned upside down. We have seen that not only has the material situation not remained standing firmly founded [?], as was intended, but on the contrary the huge crashes have wrought ruins everywhere — and this happened precisely at a time when foreign, harmful elements, consisting of two-legged human creatures, may not set foot on the soil.
And when people in America began to look around and see to what catastrophic level the country had come, the project arose to open the gates of the country to the whole world and to let an influx of people from all parts of the world begin again — it is possible that this will rescue the difficult situation, and things will be good again, just as in the time when an influx streamed in before the war.
The world has gone off the rails, mankind is wandering astray, a solution is sought, and often it seems to us that it is so near, so simple, so primitive — and yet one cannot reach it.
What is this — a sorcery or a curse?
We Are a Chosen People After All.

„National nationalism [so printed; probably: National Socialism] will exist for another thousand years.“
In short, we are a chosen people after all! For more than a year now Germany has „awakened“, and the new awakened land still revolves around the Jewish question.
Who talks about bread for the hungry? Who talks about work for the unemployed? These are all trifles that an inspired[?] land can do without, especially when the leaders are such „idealists“ who have in mind no crude, material needs of the people. The German people needs no bread; the German people can make a fine living out of hatred of Jews.
At first the Nazis took offence when they were pushed against the wall and asked: Gentlemen Jew-devourers, what news about your attitude to the Jewish question? The whole Hitlerite gang would pull a sour face[?] at such a question. How so — the foreigners think that Hitlerism has only one task: to hate Jews. Oh, the obstinate Nazis would argue, Hitlerism, they would say, is, begging your pardon, such a lofty matter, such a higher substance and such a supra-rational „philosophy“, that the Jewish question is merely a drop in the great sea of „sublime“ Hitlerism. So spoke the Nazi hooligans whenever the Jewish question was mentioned to them. Abroad, they fumed, people think that Hitlerism stands only for antisemitism, but in truth it is a revolution.
They spun around on the spot[?] for so long, until the Nazi revolution turned into a „river“[?], and then the revolution drained away entirely, and all that remained was Haman's old-new policy „to destroy and to annihilate“, with Haman's mouldy claims, not a hair missing! When one reads through the Hitlerite barkings, it seems that this is Haman's voice from the Megillah, and one feels like taking a grogger and drowning it out, because such banalities cannot be answered with any arguments — there is[?] only one logical answer: the grogger.
And when the Nazis saw that the whole Nazi programme had burst, they threw off their last pair of trousers and were left standing stark naked before the world. The last bit of shame they threw off and declared that nothing is left of Nazism but antisemitic hooliganism.
When a gentile is merely an antisemite, I can quite coolly send him to the devil and scarcely[?] eat my heart out over it. But Nazism is no longer some „liberal“ antisemitism; it is simply cannibalism — and yet, and yet, the world has listened indifferently to the bloody appeals, and none of the world's leaders has lost patience; the diplomats listen to the Reich Chancellor, and from no one has a thundering cry burst out:
— Degenerates! Bloody hangmen! Where are you leading the world?
No! Nobody cried out; only a few newspapers in England had the courage to mock with gall the wild, bestial speeches of Germany's premier.
And why does the world take Hitler seriously? Because he found a slogan: „Blood and Soil“ — the devil knows, though, how „blood and soil“ attaches itself to Christian civilisation. We Jews are too sceptical to fight for abstract soil, this very soil over which German students duel until blood flows, blood wipes[?] down the soil. Blood! Blood! Blood! Pfui: it stinks of such a civilisation, which can never wash itself enough in blood. The fields of Flanders and [—] have not yet rinsed the parched soil of the nations with enough blood. Pour them more blood!
And Hitler marches and drills the young, first-born little Nazis, and the cow-mothers sizzle with pleasure that they have supplied fresh blood for the soil. Ask no questions — whose soil, why so much blood? We Jews are a lowly people and cannot understand it. Therefore it befits us to rest[?]; but the great civilised nations understand at a wink when Hitler barks about blood and soil, because they, the other nations, also have blood and also soil, and the battlefields stand ready to answer all questions.
But until the question is settled on the battlefield — and that day is perhaps nearer than we can imagine — Hitlerism must be fought out on our battlefield. Hitler has declared war on us and we cannot hide; we must answer the call. It is not our fault that we are always the persecuted, and if we protest, it is not our fault that we are always the righteous. And righteousness is a weapon on our Jewish, bloodless battlefield. Our soil is justice; on our battlefield no blood is shed, but whole kingdoms and lands sink and vanish, so that of them there remains a fly-speck on the old book — history.
We, the helpless, the swordless, the defenceless, have taken up the fight with the accursed state, which has always been the „merciful“ mother of Jew-hatred. See how Hitler has swallowed a bone with the Jewish question! Hear how he chokes and gags, and in great despair he crawls on and drags Germany ever deeper into the mud.
Herem and boycott against the accursed land! On our battlefield you must lose. Do you not hear, [Hit]ler, Goebbels and snake company, how behind you the clocks of your own downfall are already laughing, giggling and grinning?
Hamans! We will drown you out with groggers!
Itskur[?]
Where Is the Woman?..

[Opinion — the threat of war, women and peace.] The newspapers of the whole world are again sounding the alarm with screaming headlines, that the air smells of gunpowder, that any moment a war will break out again with all its horrifying consequences!...
Although one has almost grown used to this constant war alarm — still it truly shakes every person to hear that it is merely a matter of a postponement of no more than counted minutes until the terrible explosion of the gigantic powder keg that all of Europe represents today. As well as until the release into the open of all sorts of bacilli, which must receive their due so that their creators shall not be put to shame — those who, poor things, strained their brains so much until they bestowed [?] upon humanity such precious "gifts"..
Besides that — these "saviours" of humanity must, on top of their large fee, also receive the Nobel Prize for their "cultural-humane" work... And if, God forbid, this "very useful" creation of the chosen of creatures should remain motionless and begin to rust, i.e. not do humanity its due — kill them with all the strange deaths not written in the Rebuke [Tochacha] — then their great labour would, poor things, go to waste, and for that reason alone it is already worth starting the war...
But if one were to ask humanity itself, it would surely answer that it would be far more proper for all these scholars to use their sciences better to abolish all evil in the world, to give humanity a crown of peace, so that in this way the dream of those immortal spirits might be fulfilled, who wanted to see all of humanity as one big family, in which "love thy neighbour as thyself" reigns far and wide...
But unfortunately, it has not yet come to that, and the plague of war is still murderously cruel on all sides! Yet the world says that for every plague there is a cure. One need only find the root from which the plague grows. And the root is, after all, also there — the blond beast of the West and the black little Japanese [yapanchik] of the East. On this everyone is already unanimous today, that these are the corners of all evil from which the epidemic of war develops; and if the world only wanted to, it could isolate these corners like a plague, and the world would be saved!...
But the world itself is also infected with the same plague; and the world does not want to be healed — on the contrary: it lets this plague develop into full-blown gangrene!
Yet a worldly saying is like a dogma, and if the world says that "for every plague there is a cure" — it must be true...
I think that the cure for this cruel plague called war lies in — the woman...
Where is the woman?
The woman could, after all, with her initiative have eradicated this plague in the full sense of the word; for all the scholars of the world are convinced and unanimous that the principal of all principles, the axis around which all human life turns, is the woman; all events that have shaken the world, for good and for bad, are owed to the woman.
The Bible tells of famous women who took a substantial part in the political life of their time and also achieved much in this field; it also tells there that when one wanted to make a strong impression on a ruler, or on the people, one always put forward "wise women", and success was assured...
And if in those times, when woman was enslaved, she could achieve so much in political life — how useful could she make herself in this field today? Woman has, after all, today completely torn the chains of slavery and occupies the place of honour in all areas of human life; she is, as many scholars would have it, the definite though uncrowned queen — so she surely might have turned to the warmongers and said: No! We no longer agree to give up our dear ones, husbands and children, as cannon fodder... Too expensive an article for you!... And especially since "the appetite comes with eating".. the more the cannons swallow, the hungrier they are...
No! We are simply disgusted and sickened by this game that a handful of enraged madmen are playing at our expense... Your quarrels, which you have among yourselves, you can settle like human beings, as is customary everywhere in society, but such a luxury — settling quarrels through a world slaughter that falls entirely on our shoulders — this we can no longer permit!...
And it is more than certain that if the women of all parts of the world organised and held congresses with the sole aim of preventing wars — they would achieve their goal. And without shedding a single drop of blood in the process...
Women have always decided over the life and death of nations — therefore the wonder is very great that woman takes no stand toward the spectre of war that poisons and darkens the world... Woman — she is [printed "in"] the immovable protective wall against which all possible weapons are powerless and cannot break through...
Our sages said long ago that the Creator gave woman more understanding than man, and with understanding one can turn even tigers or lions into calm little lambs.
And so woman could, with her understanding, turn all the enraged, combative men into calm, good-natured people, who would recast their weapons [printed "pli-zayin"] into useful tools of labour.. All the sages would then have had to sharpen their inventive brains on rooting out the sick and the evil from among humanity, and thus the world would have been healed of the terrible plague called war that is burning humanity up. The floor is the woman's.
Where is the woman?..
D. Z.
A Little Feuilleton.

[Będzin and Zagłębie — satirical feuilleton, kehilla.] Such a "Head".
I looked for a little head [heading] for my little feuilleton today and could not find one.
The reason is a simple one; it is hard to write about things that symbolise a headless creature.
I think you have already guessed whom this is about.
About our Jewish kehilla.
The kehilla goes about without a head; more precisely — it sits without a head, because walking it has long been unable to do: its feet have been chopped off. The masses, on whom a kehilla usually rests, have lost their trust in its capacity to work, and the masses are, after all, in the nature of feet, the foundation for such an institution as a kehilla.
So I looked for a topic for our Zagłębie kehillas, a topic with a "head", and could not find one.
I looked for some merit for them that would justify their existence, and unfortunately did not find any.
True, a sworn defender would surely say that thanks to the inactivity of the kehillas they have become popular among the population, because people have begun to talk about the kehillas.
But it is clear that from such a defence one comes out with a tooth and an eye [i.e. the loser].
The only defence is: these are creatures without heads, which must either be killed off entirely, or be brought back from the dead.
*
I have been going about these last days without a head.
The Far East worries me. That is to say, I have other worries besides the Japanese–Chinese interests, but what can one do against sentiments? And the Japanese have had such a reputation [printed "kol"? — probably "kol", voice/repute] for many years that people relate to them with sympathy; people talked themselves into believing that they are small, insignificant and helpless, and therefore everyone pitied them.
Lately, however, these tiny and insignificant little Japanese [yapanchiklekh] have turned out to be very big creatures indeed. So that it becomes truly sad at heart reading the news from the Far Eastern front.
Yes, people go about without a head now, each in his own way.
Rebus.
Yellow No. 1 and Yellow No. 2...

By J. Oberżanek.
(A Sukkot tale. Told, in fact, by a „yellow“ [red-haired] man.)
As you see, I am a „yellow one“ [a redhead]. A born yellow one. Not like today's women, who turn overnight from brunette to yellow — but a genuine yellow one, written down in my passport explicitly as „rudy“ [Polish: red-haired] — yellow!
The yellow colour I inherited — my father was a forest clerk for a yellow squire, and on top of that he dealt in etrogs...
Just as I am a genuine yellow one, so my wife is a genuine black-haired one, so I really have two „maszczy“ [Polish maści: coat colours]: six black boys like Negroes and six yellow girls, as if they had been smeared with yellow wax.
So there is indeed an eternal war in the house between the two „races“ — a race struggle between the black ones and the yellow ones: my wife shouts „my black boys!“ and I lament over my yellow girls...
One piece of luck I do have — that I am a well-to-do Jew, a rich yellow one; what would I do if, God forbid, I were a yellow one and a pauper besides — a fine face a yellow pauper has, like my neighbour, yellow Henech!
Oh, listen, the troubles I have from my neighbour, that yellow Henech, the wretched pauper! Nothing else would suit him — he had to move into the same house as me, and the yellow fellow is blackening my years...
[—], two yellow ones in one house, both with one name: he is called Henech and I am called Henech; whatever is meant for me goes to him, and whatever is meant for him comes to me. They look for me — they end up at his place; they look for him — they end up at mine.
A bridegroom comes to „view“ my daughter, asks in the building for yellow Henech, falls in on yellow Henech number 2 — and „views“ that yellow Henech's „piękność“ [Polish: beauty]...
A creditor comes to yellow Henech, the pauper, with a protested bill, and bursts in on me with cries of gevalt and shouting: „Anutser[?], bankrupt! Glutton and drunkard, yellow coward [tkhoyzh — Polish tchórz; doubtful reading] — off my toil you'll guzzle and swill — my money!“...
I try to explain to him that I am not the right yellow one, that he means the other yellow one, who is also called Henech — but it doesn't help at all: the man shouts and raises a gevalt, curses and abuses me and drags me through the mud as well; because of that yellow one they make me a „black Sabbath“...
They send me Purim shalach-manot — they carry the cakes with the bottles of wine in to that yellow Henech, and that yellow one asks no questions and has himself a holiday treat.
A messenger[?] [posłaniec] brings a pink love letter for that yellow Henech's little wife, asks a neighbour woman where yellow Henech lives — and the letter falls into my hands.
So of course I start wailing [„yelos“, prob. for „yelolos“] and keening over my wife like a yellow one — such an old shoe-polish tin with [—] [„lubtshes“, meaning unclear]! Such an old „supper“ [?], who has six yellow daughters to lead to the wedding canopy! Pink letters, no less!
I get angry (like a yellow one...), raise a gevalt, suspect my wife for nothing — for the pink love letter was, after all, for that yellow Henech's wife, not for mine...
Whatever is meant for me goes to him, and whatever is meant for him comes to me; they look for me — they end up at his place, and they look for him — they end up at mine.
But all this I would still have put up with. Nothing else would suit him, that yellow pauper, but to move into the same house as me — a second yellow one with one and the same name — two yellow Henechs under one roof...
I would have put up with all of it, were it not for the business with the sukkah:
As you know, I have a year-round sukkah [a permanent sukkah] — only called a sukkah: a „palace“, a „skyscraper“ — a building with all „modern conveniences“.
And it is already a custom with me that all the neighbours of the building eat in my year-round sukkah — rich and poor, from Reb Hertske the shochet to the shoemaker — all eat together in the sukkah.
So it happens, a year ago today: my wife, right on the eve of Sukkot, goes and lies down in childbed, and before I can turn around — mazel tov! — there is a sixth yellow girl...
Well, lost and gone, as you say — a punishment from God; but it has nothing to do with Sukkot.
On the first day of Sukkot, as always, I sat down together with Reb Hertske the shochet at the head of the table, and the neighbours along the sides — and here my downfall begins, and because of whom? Again because of the second yellow Henech:
First the shikse [gentile maid] brings, for kiddush — for that yellow Henech — on a silver tray a bottle of Carmel wine, fladen and egg cookies. The shikse hands it to that yellow Henech, and he accepts it, makes kiddush, and the fladen with the egg cookies „burn up“ [?] under his hands...
I sit and wait, and they send me down for kiddush — a dry tail of a herring with a piece of honey cake, like a dried-out brick.
A minute later the same shikse brings down the head of a live [fresh] carp as if from the Leviathan, with genuine yellow challahs, and that yellow Henech goes at the „little head“ and „works it over“ so that only the bare bones remain on the plate.
To me they send down two soft, soaked fishbones from a swooning tench.
To that yellow Henech the shikse brings down the real plate of noodles with a yellow broth with fat „eyes“, and to me — a little bowl of „sandpapered“ potatoes with beet borscht; that yellow Henech gulps down the noodles with the fat eyes and I chew the hard potatoes.
To that yellow Henech they serve half a chicken, so that it simply wobbled with fat, with carrots, with horseradish, with pickled cucumbers, and to me they serve — a dry, soaked cutlet that one could only make out on the plate through a lorgnette, and over that cutlet one had to say „ha-motzi“, because there was more bread in it than meat...
After the meat they brought that yellow Henech a compote of apples and pears. He chomped away with all his molars and washed it down with Carmel wine, and I looked on and „burst“ with heartache.
You want to know what it was? How come that yellow Henech was suddenly so blessed, and why I had such a meagre meal?
Quite simple: since my wife was lying in childbed, she had taken on a new maid, and instructed her to carry the food down [„abaptrogn“, prob. a misprint for „aroptrogn“] into the sukkah for the „pan“ [the master]. And she added that the master is a yellow one — and since that yellow Henech was sitting by the door, she served it to that yellow Henech.
Such a downfall I had last year at Sukkot, and all because of whom? — because of my neighbour, the second yellow Henech...
That's how it is, when two yellow Henechs live under one roof...

The Mamzer [The Bastard]. A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy.

[Literature — serialized novel; Konin.] By Adw. Sh. Gieliszkowski ["Adw." — probably adwokat, lawyer].
In the kitchens of the rich timber merchant Avraham Langnau things were happening.
Since daybreak there had been frying and greasing [?].
The maids were absorbed [?] in cooking, baking and frying. In big pots large pieces of beef and veal were cooking for the poor beggars who would come from every end of town to the grand, wealthy wedding of the Konin timber merchant Avraham Langnau. In the big pans fat, fattened geese and ducks were frying and roasting for the honoured guests who had been invited to the wedding.
Everyone was worked off their feet and busy preparing refreshments for the guests. Even from the forest they had brought down the workers, who chopped wood and carried it into the kitchen, hauled water and poured it into the barrels made ready, plucked the feathers off fat hens, cleaned kishkes, grated horseradish, and meanwhile, from the sharp smell of the horseradish, tears ran from their sore eyes down their sunken, gaunt cheeks.
The cooks, older and younger girls, dishevelled, with big breasts that dangled and shook with fat and from time to time pushed out of their blouses, as if they wanted to take a look at what was going on in the kitchen.
With fat, dirty, bare forearms the maids kneaded the various doughs, ran to the pots, tasted the dishes, spat on the floor and cursed the shkotzim [gentile lads] who carried wood and water.
— Janek! May fire take you; blow up the fire! Carry out the bucket of dirty water — they shouted at the shkotzim, already thoroughly worn out, who had worked from dawn till late into the night.
Everyone was in a commotion and worked off their feet with cooking and baking, preparing for the great wedding of Chanele, the only daughter of R' Avraham Langnau, with the yeshiva student Binyamin, whom the Sochaczewer [the Rebbe of Sochaczew] himself, long may he live, had chosen for her as a bridegroom.
R' Avraham did nothing without his Rebbe. If forest had to be bought, he travelled to the Rebbe; if forest had to be sold or felled, R' Avraham first asked the Rebbe about everything, and as the Rebbe, long may he live, ordered, so R' Avraham did. All the more so as the Sochaczewer himself was a partner in all those forests.
True, the Rebbe put no money into the partnership, but who needs his money? R' Avraham Langnau? R' Avraham the Koniner has enough money of his own to buy forests; he only needs the Rebbe as a partner for luck. And who else can have such favour with the Master of the Universe as the Sochaczewer tzaddik, may he be healthy [printed "געזוגט", misprint for "געזונט"] and strong? So what wonder is it that over every trifle R' Avraham the Koniner travels to ask the Rebbe for good advice, all the more so in a matter as important as making a match, and with his only little daughter Chanele, who is his very soul and the apple of his eye, for whom he is ready to do anything in the world.
The idea of marrying off his daughter had come to him not at home. No, at home there is no time [?] to think about a match for a daughter, even for so dear a daughter as his [?] Chanele. The idea came to him while travelling to the Rebbe for the Days of Awe. Then, as he rode in his carriage, harnessed to four horses "na szpic", to the Rebbe, and set in order in his mind everything he needed to ask the tzaddik, it occurred to him to consult the Rebbe about a match for his daughter, whom the Rebbe himself, long may he live, had blessed when, travelling to the "Fardembitzer" [?; perhaps the Rebbe of Dembitz/Dębica], he had stopped at his house overnight.
And indeed, right after Yom Kippur, while still at the Rebbe's and doing the accounts of the profit on the forest that had been sold, he asked about a match.
— I have a match for you, Avremele, as surely as I hope for a good year.
Hearing such words from the Rebbe — that the Rebbe himself, may he be healthy, was the matchmaker for his daughter — R' Avraham was filled with joy, and within an hour the whole court was ringing with the news that the Rebbe himself had chosen as a bridegroom for R' Avraham's daughter none other than Binyaminke the sharp-witted, the fine learner, the great singer, who stirs the world with his melodies at the Rebbe's table.
— You have good favour with the Rebbe, may he be healthy — whispered Itzik the gabbai to him, meaning by it nothing more than a few roubles for the holiday.
— Just imagine, R' Avraham, that the Rebbe himself, long may he live, took the trouble to think about a match for your little daughter.
Itzikl the gabbai is a tall, stout, fleshy Jew; he knows how to make a few roubles for the holiday from such rich men as R' Avraham the Koniner. All the more so since he, Itzig, is the strongman of the court; he runs things himself as he pleases, he lets people in to the Rebbe when he wants and whom he wants. He seats the Hasidim around the table, he distributes the Rebbe's shirayim. He knows, Itzikl, that R' Avraham must be seated [?] right next to the Rebbe on the left side, opposite the Rebbe's son-in-law; he knows that the first shirayim from the Rebbe he must bring to R' Avraham, and not later, when all the Hasidim crawl with their dirty hands into the plates and snatch the Rebbe's leftovers, pushing and cursing one another like drunken peasants. Yes, he knows everything and knows his job well. — You have merit with the Master of the Universe, R' Avraham, that the Rebbe, may he be healthy, has given you such a jewel, pf, pf, pf. Do you even have an idea who this Binyamindl is? As surely as I hope for a good year, what a silken young man he is — Itzikl said to him when he came out from the Rebbe pleased that the Rebbe had given him such a fine match for his Chanele; that widened his heart, and for that he handed Itzikl a twenty-five note.
And when R' Avraham came home from the Rebbe, he called out contentedly as he entered the house:
— Mazel tov! Mazel tov to you, Sore, bless you, mazel tov to you, Chanele! You've become a bride, and the wedding date is Lag BaOmer. May I have nachas and joy from you, amen, selah.
Sorele said nothing. Sorele was always silent and never meddled in her husband's affairs; he did as he wanted and what he wanted, and all the more so when she heard who the matchmaker was.
Not very pleased with it, however, was Chanele herself, quiet, good Chanele, who was lower than grass and quieter than a dove; all the little goodness and gentleness the world possesses was lodged in the good eighteen-year-old Chanele, who was as beautiful as the world.
Just like her mother, Chanele too was tall and slender as a pine. She had big black eyes, from which a warm gentleness sparkled.
Her face was white as alabaster. Her hands as if carved from snow-white marble. Like her hair, her eyebrows too were black and long, and looked like little black frames around her eyes. Her chiselled little nose had even more charm when she laughed. When she opened her mouth with its pearly teeth, nobody could say that all girls are blessed with such a mouthful of teeth.
— There goes beautiful Chanele! — everyone used to say when Chanele walked in the street on the Sabbath with her mother. — "Piękna Chana" [beautiful Chana] — the Christians would point their fingers at Chanele when she strolled with her girlfriends on the bridge that spans the river "Warta" in Konin.
Good and warm-hearted was Chanele. Never did one hear a bad word from her, never did she get angry; she was always a cheerful and good friend, obeyed her father and mother, whose command was holy and dear to her.
And yet, hearing from her father that she had become a bride, despite the strong love that burned in her young heart for the bookkeeper of her father's business, Naum Rozen — a slight shiver ran over her body, and without saying no or yes she left the big dining room.
The very next day, meeting Rozen, she said to him:
— Dear Naum, I love you, yes, I love you, but I will not go against my father — and she went away.
And when the beautiful spring arrived in Konin, when it came wholly full [?] like a ripe apple and cleared away the snow left over from the long winter, R' Avraham's house began to prepare for the wedding.
The hour struck, and the day of Chanele's wedding came; they began to receive the guests, who were to arrive from various ends of the country.
The whole town was full of the wedding. In-laws were getting ready [printed "גענרייט", misprint for "געגרייט"], invited and uninvited. All the poor people got up very early and could hardly wait for twelve o'clock, the hour set for the feast.

Ushpizin

[Literature — a verse tale for Sukkot.] By L. Malach.
(A Little Tale)

Reb Binyomin was
the one and only rich man in the shtetl,
all the others — paupers,
who served him:
in the forests — measuring timber,
in the "gorzelnie" [distilleries] — distilling liquor,
in the "browarnie" [breweries] — turning "pelen"[?],
all of them drew
their bit of bread from Binyomin
and Binyomin lorded it
over everyone and everything.
He[?] came to shul last
and was the first to leave.

Reb Binyomin was
a "philanthropist" — but woe and bitter
was it for the one
who needed, God forbid,
to turn to Binyomin.
When he gave charity
he did it in public,
so that the whole town should know,
all the Jews should see:
— I, Binyomin, rich man of the shtetl,
donate a whole half-ruble
to the great Torah scholar!

Every day of the month of Elul
Binyomin used to hand out charity,
poor folk used to gather,
abase themselves before him,
bow and turn and bend,
as one bows before a "tulip"[?],
and he used to throw the alms
right into the man's face,
so that he would wash himself in blood.

No one but Binyomin
dared to give alms,
as though he alone
held a "monopoly" —
and charity — that was his established right,
no one else has a licence for it...

That he takes the fat aliyot?
Well, nothing can be done about it.
That he keeps the town in fear?
Well, nothing can be said.
But how can he forbid
a Jew to have a mitzvah,
and once in a while give a slice of bread?
That is no longer bearable.

Once Reb Binyomin
found out: a Jew of the shtetl
had given a poor man
something to eat — and a place to sleep;
at once he summoned the Jew
and said: "If you can
allow yourself to hand out charity,
it is surely a good sign:
you covet[?] all my wealth,
you are robbing me entirely...
You can no longer serve me
and I dismiss you from the post."

And the Jew — the charitable one
was[?] left high and dry.
And here comes the holiday of Sukkot,
and here the winter draws near:
he himself will yet, God forbid,
have to turn to people.

And here is the holiday of Sukkot.

No one's sukkah may be
finer than Binyomin's sukkah,
and Binyomin's sukkah is indeed
like a palace of a king.
All the costly divans
brought here from Turkey,
all the costly vases
from the Land of Israel.
And the silver candelabra
and the sparkling goblets
and the handsome household,
adorned in gold and diamonds,
dressed in silk and satin,
sit in the fine sukkah
and from the whole region around
guests come to Binyomin,
sit with him in the sukkah.
And he boasts and brags,
he is sure that the guests
will carry out into the world
how great his wealth is...

— — — — — — — —

And at the other end of the shtetl,
where the Jew lives, the one
whom Binyomin ordered
thrown out of his livelihood,
a sukkah stands there too —
a few rotten little boards,
instead of schach — a few little twigs.
Instead of wine for kiddush — water,
instead of holiday dishes —
a few boiled potatoes.
And a bit of bread to fulfil the duty.

And his household, poor things,
wrapped in old rags,
darkened by worries,
choke on silent tears.

Suddenly, something stirs in the shtetl:
a covered wagon has come into the market.
And in the wagon sit Jews.
Broad beards and white foreheads,
eyes sparkling with love.
They stop at the beit midrash.
One jumps down and cries out:
"Praised be the One above us,
we have arrived in time"!
A commotion arises in the shtetl:
merchants have arrived,
and must keep the holiday in the shtetl,
here among strangers, poor things,
because the road to their home
they lost on the way.
But since Jews are
everywhere, thank God, still Jews,
the wealthy Reb Binyomin
took the trouble himself
(they are surely no paupers
but most likely real rich men...)
and went to their wagon,
wishing to invite them to his home.
But Binyomin is left in astonishment
and with him everyone is amazed,
when the Jews in the wagon,
with such dignified faces,
ask the way to the little Jew,
to that pauper who has not even
an olive's bulk for his festive meal,
that very one whom Binyomin
threw out of his post,
because he once gave
alms to a beggar..

— — — — — — — — — —

At Binyomin's the holiday
was, but was spoiled,
anger was kindled in him,
pride flared in him.

* * *

But in the shtetl people told
wonders about the guests.
How they had brought
costly gifts, great ones,
how they had with them
the finest and the very best.
How the whole holiday long
they would not stir outside,
only shared out and only gave.
They themselves were a minyan,
among them was a cantor,
they only prayed and only sang,
and they had a Torah scroll with them.
And the sukkah of that Jew
became so large,
became so beautiful.

Only when[?], after Simchat Torah,
the guests had gone their ways,
did the Jew see: they had forgotten
a great fortune,
gold and silver, precious stones..
The Jew was grieved,
for he does not know who they are
or where to send it.
So he thought it over
and travelled to the Rebbe,
to take counsel with him.

Having heard the whole story,
the Rebbe answered quietly:
"Go, make use of it, it is your wealth!
You have had a great privilege;
there appeared to you
not guests, but the Ush[pizin]:"
The Lulav (in place of “The Cooking Ladle”) — humour and satire in honour of Sukkot, by Amotsli

[Humour and satire — “Der Lulav” (in place of “Der Kokh-Lefl”), Sukkot.]
Politics of the Week.
So here we are again at Sukkot.
All year long we build politics. We play the diplomat, we become [?] real big shots, we politicians; we build and destroy worlds. A mere trifle — politics, and in the end one looks around and finds that in politics we have actually arrived at Sukkot.
Built and built, and at long last built — a sukkah.
All of politics is knocked together like a little shack: a few poles and a couple of boards woven together, barely, barely nailed together, and every little breeze can knock it over.
The League of Nations sits and holds conferences, works out plans, resolves and thinks that's it, it is done with everyone and everything. Along comes a Japanese, or even a Hitler, and the League-of-Nations sukkah is already knocked over.
Our politics in the world is once again at Sukkot.
Sukkot politics.
A Good Yom-Tov, Jew!

[Humour and satire — “Der Lulav” (Sukkot); poem.]
By Anim Zmiros.

We sit in the sukkah,
the cold makes us shiver...
A sukkah for us is —
the whole world.

It is so simple
and yet symbolic:
the sukkah — the exile —
they have the same essence.

One essence and one form,
the very same thing:
just look at the “building” —
with its roof of straw!

We sit in the sukkah,
built on one foot;
a structure that holds up
supposedly by merit [?]...

We sit in the sukkah
and it drips from the sekhakh;
thus the world has given us
a roof forever...

A sukkah — a little booth.
A plaything for the wind;
and close by there bark
the wolves and the dogs.

We have the sukkah,
they have the barn;
we shiver with the cold,
they sit by the fire.

Our “life” — it stands
on chicken legs;
a patched-up building,
a bit of everything...

They have buildings
on solid foundations;
of our condition
the sukkah is a witness...
* * *
You ponder and you wonder,
you rack your brains:
where in the sukkah,
the small one, lies the strength?

That despite all winds,
despite all storms,
it stands and laughs
at walls and towers.

The strength, dear Jews,
lies right up here:
the strength of the sukkah,
the strength of faith.

Our eternal faith
in the victory of the weak...
and also our not believing
in blood and in revenge...
* * *
I say “Ushpizin”
and nobody [?] hears me;
to behave like this
only a Jew can...

There stands his sukkah
in the middle of a forest...
and the winds — they shriek,
they storm with violence.

They tear and they pluck
at the little booth's hands [=walls?];
they tear and they pluck
with robbers' hands.

And the rain — it lashes,
and it drips from the roof quite nicely;
but inside sits
the Jew all alone...

And makes himself at home there,
like a bird in its nest,
makes his Kiddush
and invites [?] more guests...

He says “Ushpizin”
and hears nothing more [?],
to invite guests like this —
only a Jew can...
A Peasant with an Etrog

[Humour and satire — “Der Lulav” (Sukkot); anecdote.]
Some years ago a local etrog dealer sold an etrog to a minyan in a nearby village.
A few days before Sukkot a peasant from that village came to the dealer with a note from the buyer, asking that the etrog be handed to the peasant.
The etrog merchant put the etrog in a little box and, handing the box to the peasant, pointed out to him the etrog's “pitom” — he should guard it well...
When the peasant brought the etrog to the gabbai of the village minyan, it was without a “pitom”.
The gabbai flew into a rage: how could they ruin the etrog!.. But the peasant broke into a smile and said: “Don't be scared, Moshke! The Jew from town told me to guard the ‘knob’ (pitom) well, and I, afraid I would lose it, broke it off and put it right here in my pocket.”
And taking out the pitom, the peasant said with rapture: “Here you have, Moshke, the ‘knob’, and don't think Franciszek is a fool..”

Quo Vadis, Judaea?

[Opinion — the situation of the Jewish people worldwide; article.] By Shlomo Frohmann [?], Zürich.
"The situation on the Eretz Israel front", "General Minorities Conference", — "The enlarged Jewish Agency", — "Jewish resistance against Germany", — "The Jewish question at the session of the League of Nations in Geneva". — "Jewish World Conference". — "The resurrection of the Territorialist movement on the Jewish street". — Under these headings the future historian will describe the history of the public life of the Jewish people in the two decades after the World War, and, in contrast to the eloquent headlines, it will turn out that never yet in Jewish history were Jewish need and Jewish poverty so great and, above all, so tragic as in these years; that never yet were Jewish pauperization and the declassed masses so numerous and so desperate as precisely in these years, when Jewish parliamentarians and Jewish diplomats were able, and had the opportunity, to represent Jewish suffering and Jewish demands and to give them expression before national parliaments and international bodies.
A hundred and even thirty years ago, when residence, civic rights or the right of domicile for Jews became restricted in this or that country, or merely bound up with unpleasantness, because of religious or economic persecutions — then the Jew still always had his old, tried way out and remedy: "And Jacob went out — and went!" He took up the staff and went to seek a place of rest for himself and his children: a land of refuge, which still called the Jews and said to them: come to us, with us you will have all freedoms, equal rights and every good thing.
Today, however, in the age of all kinds of inventions and discoveries, the world has put man into a prison from which he cannot stir, and he must be loyal to it under duress, because no other country lets him in. And from every general deterioration it is the Jew who suffers most.
True, one cannot hold the Jewish politicians responsible for the results and the "great successes" of their work for Klal Yisrael; but the moral, the "what follows for us from this", one can and should draw from it and press home [?], and it reads: in the field of productive work for the Jewish people we are only at the very beginning of "beginning alef"; all tasks still lie — upon us and before us; nothing, however — behind us.
With the help of modern technology one could easily observe how, almost simultaneously, at the very same moment, Jews, Jewish women and Jewish men in Warsaw, Będzin, Nuremberg, Berlin, Strasbourg, Salonika, Czernowitz, Constantinople, Yemen and Bombay are talking to themselves and asking: "What are we, poor things, to do?" — how does one find a way out? — where shall we run to earn at l-e-a-s-t a dry piece of bread?; all these questions concentrate, cling together and melt into one body, a national question that blazes and flickers in the words of its best sons: "Whither, Jewish people?" "It cannot go on like this any longer!"
In his speech at the opening session of the Third Jewish World Conference in Geneva, Sholem Asch said among other things: "I have come here to make my voice heard and to cry aloud: Jewish people, awake! Your greatest enemy in the world is you yourself, your criminal indifference to your vital interests. Upon our generation falls the decision of destiny: to live or to die. Jewish people, give your answer!"
It is interesting to make a short, schematic analysis of the Jewish situation in the most important countries where Jews live, and in doing so to see how far the already known remedies suffice and can help, and how far one will have to seek entirely new solutions and go entirely new ways.
Poland: the chief misfortune of the Jewish masses is lack of livelihood. Jews with outstretched hands waiting to emigrate number here at least a million.
Russia: alongside productivization there is also a process of declassing of the Jewish masses. Emigration — impossible for the time being. Biro-Bidzhan — very problematic.
Germany: wild, intensified antisemitism. A dignified life for a Jew — impossible.
Romania: antisemitism and lack of livelihood among a large part of the Jews, chiefly in southern Romania. Readiness to emigrate.
France: contrast. Prosperity among the "French" Jews and, mostly, poverty among the Jews who immigrated from the Eastern countries.
North and South Africa, Asia Minor (Persia, Syria, Mesopotamia) and the Arab states: forced assimilation.
North and South America: from time to time — antisemitic agitation, national persecutions.
As one sees, then, the general picture, with the exception of a few countries with a small number of Jews, such as Switzerland, Holland, Yugoslavia and Italy, is — not cheerful [?]. And in all there are at least five million Jews who would, not tomorrow but already today, have taken their "goods and chattels" with them — and even without them — and emigrated, if only they were given a piece of land with prospects of a livelihood.
For the time being there are two remedies: Eretz Israel and occupational restructuring ["Umschichtung"]. As regards Eretz Israel there are two differing opinions on the Jewish street. Eretz Israel will be able to absorb at most one million Jews — some think; no: three, four, even five and eight [million] Eretz Israel will be able to absorb; but everyone agrees that we do not yet have full knowledge [?], and for the time being one will still have to wait, and a good many years will still pass before there are in Eretz Israel even one million Jews.
As regards restructuring, people on the Jewish street like to exaggerate its importance. Certainly one should support and propagate the restructuring of the Jewish masses, and chiefly of Jewish youth. But one should not believe that if, for example, the Polish Jews were tomorrow in their great majority craftsmen and industrial workers, they would already be helped; for with restructuring into craftsmen and industrial workers the Jewish question is not yet solved, the hunger of the Jewish masses is not yet stilled, nothing at all has yet been done for the five million Jews who sit against their will in their present places of residence and for whom an entirely new way must be sought.

Quo vadis, Judaea?

Napoleon's Wife (6)

[Serialized historical tale — Napoleon and Empress Joséphine; installment 6, final.]
H. Abramson.

When he came to the coronation, he did not wait for the Pope, who had come for that very purpose, to put the crown on his head. Well known are the words he spoke on that occasion:
— Woe to him who touches the crown which I have won with my own strength.
On that occasion Joséphine [Yozefin] knelt down, laid her hands upon her heart, and her husband placed on her the crown which he had held for a moment on his own head. It made a tremendous impression; later painters immortalized it in a picture. We see Joséphine kneeling with the crown on her head, but the pictures do not show that her heart was heavy, and the reason was quite clear to "fil" [sic; read: to her].
Several years had passed since the couple had been living together, but no children had come. Earlier this had not troubled Napoleon, but now that he had become a ruler he wanted his children to inherit his throne, so that the dynasty would continue from generation to generation.
Meanwhile the world bowed before the new queen; it had never yet seen before it so beautiful and so proud a woman as this one, who had grown up and been raised on an island. There was something wonderful in her personality that made kings kneel before her.
Napoleon took her along on all his journeys. When he went to Italy to have himself crowned king, Joséphine was with him, and once again the same story repeated itself: tens of thousands of people saw the emperor placing the crown on her head, and they saw how he adored her.
A plan was decided upon to unite the two families, Napoleon's and the Beauharnais [printed "Biuhararis"]. Hortense, who had now turned seventeen, was betrothed to Napoleon's brother Louis. Hortense was an exceptionally beautiful girl, clever and of strong character. It was even said that Joséphine's [husband], that is, the emperor, was not indifferent to her daughter, that he had relations with her; but that was[?] gossip, and Joséphine would not hear of it.
When Hortense gave birth to her first child, there was no limit to Joséphine's joy, for Napoleon had assured her that if it was a boy he would make him his heir. And so a child was born who would in time take over the throne.
Joséphine's only hope was her grandson, her daughter's boy, whom her husband the emperor had agreed to adopt and make heir to his throne. After all, he was the son of his brother Louis, whom he loved so dearly, and the son of Hortense, whom he loved like his own child. Now Joséphine again began to live calmly and contentedly; the fear that her husband would divorce her vanished.
But then came the great misfortune, the greatest of her life: she was told that the child had died, and in this she read her sentence. Now she knew for certain that she would not long remain Queen of France, that she would be sent away somewhere so that her husband could marry another woman.
When the news of the child's death reached Napoleon he was on the battlefield among his soldiers. When the tidings were brought to him he remained sitting as if paralyzed; his face was white as chalk, so that those close to him took fright. It took a long time before he came to himself, but he was still under the heavy impression of the news and muttered something under his breath that nobody understood.
When Napoleon met his wife in Paris, a coldness was noticeable between them; both felt that the worst had come. It was different from his returns after a great victory, as was now the case in his campaign against the Austrians.
She slept little; whole nights she wept, for she knew her sentence, that catastrophe awaited her.
Once, when she was left alone with her husband, he suddenly began to speak about their first meeting; he remembered every detail, and when Joséphine expressed her wonder he said:
— My dear, I know that you gave me the happiest moments of my life, but what can one do — the interests of France stand above everything in the world, and I must submit to the will of my people: they demand an heir.
When Napoleon had uttered these words, he saw Joséphine lying in a faint at his feet.
Napoleon began to ring; one of his closest people took [printed "gegumen" = genumen] the fainted woman and carried her into her boudoir.
All night Napoleon paced about his study sunk in thought. It was immensely hard for him to part from the woman who had given him so much happiness and freedom. In the palace it was so quiet the whole time that people were afraid to utter a word, for all knew that in secret everything was being prepared so that the divorce [get] procedure should take place as quickly as possible.
On 15 December 1809 all members of the "family" assembled in one of the halls of the royal palace; Napoleon stood all alone, and the divorce was quietly carried out.
* * *
Years went by. Napoleon married the daughter of the Austrian king. She bore him a son; all France rejoiced, cannons thundered, the streets were full of people, there was singing and dancing. But in a palace far outside Paris Joséphine sat all alone, listening for something. Every moment she went to the window and looked out. It was already past midday; she grew restless and muttered something to herself. Then the hoofbeats of a galloping horse were heard; a man entered the room and, bowing deeply, handed the queen a note. She opened it with trembling hands, and having read it she broke into sobs, falling onto the sofa — but it did not last long. These were tears of joy: her former husband had now become a father, he has his own child — how happy she is [sic; a line seems to be missing].
And on the day Napoleon was to be exiled to the island of Elba, Joséphine lay on her deathbed; she did not live to hear the terrible news about the man whom she had loved more than anything in the world.

(The End.)

Shops with Baked Goods, Fish and Meat May Be Open from 7 to 10
The Będzin Small Traders' Association once again draws attention to the fact that today, Sunday, bakery shops, fish halls and butcher shops may be open from 7 to 10 in the morning.

Because Bernsztajn Held the Ticket, He Tried to Say "It's All Mine"... — An Interesting Dispute Between 2 Lottery Winners in Sosnowiec
The shoemaker Horowicz bought a quarter lottery ticket at Kaptal's lottery agency in Katowice and took his friend Bernsztajn as a partner. The ticket was kept by Bernsztajn, but at the agency Horowicz was on record. And it came to pass, on the second day of Rosh Hashana, that the number came out with a prize of 100,000 zł. Bernsztajn pretends to know nothing towards his partner, runs to Katowice and, with the help of his witnesses that he is called Horowicz, manages to obtain 5000 zł. in cash and, for the rest of the sum, an assignation (money order).
The same day in the evening Horowicz receives a telegraphic notice about the prize from Kaptal's agency. On receiving such good tidings Horowicz quickly went to his partner in order to bring him the good news as well. But the latter declared that he already knew about it, and that there were several more partners to the ticket whom he had taken in. When Horowicz heard this he went to the police station and reported it. The police indeed took an interest in the matter, and thanks to this the dispute was settled as follows: Horowicz received 8 thousand zł. and Bernsztajn with his partners 12 thousand zł.
—o—
The Sosnowiec Kehilla Has Already Received Its Budget — The Subsidy Debts Struck Out
This week the kehilla board in Sosnowiec received its budget, which was approved by the authorities without any change. All the subsidies of the past year were struck out; an exception was made for the Jewish hospital, for which 9 thousand zł. was approved instead of 15 thousand zł.

A Serious Accident to a Jewish Resident of Dąbrowa
A grave impression was made on the entire Jewish population of Dąbrowa by the accident that happened on the eve of Yom Kippur to the local resident and coal merchant, Mr. Meir Szpigelman, respected by all.
Szpigelman, travelling to Sławków to visit his ancestors' graves, fell under the wheels while getting off the car and was seriously injured. Mr. S. received first aid at the Sławków outpatient clinic; afterwards he was taken, in a very serious condition, to the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec.

Kippers Come from Hitler-Land
The Anti-Hitler Committee draws the attention of the Jewish population of Zagłębie to the fact that after a thorough investigation it has been established that kippers (smoked herring) come from Germany, and therefore they must not be eaten.

At Ne'ila the Cantor Said: "Nie pojadę" (I Won't Go)...
The cantor of the Będzin beit midrash, Mr. Piotrkowski, felt wronged this year by the kehilla president Mr. Rubinlicht, who had ordered that the above-mentioned cantor should not officiate at the cemetery during the month of Elul. In connection with this Mr. Piotrkowski decided to take "revenge" and to declare a strike at Ne'ila.
The time for the Ne'ila prayer approaches, and the congregation is already heard:
— Well, cantor, it's time to pray Ne'ila.
— I will not pray — answers the cantor — "let Rubinlicht pray Ne'ila"...
— How can it be — argue the gabbaim, and also Reb Yehoshuale the dayan — to sulk before Ne'ila?
— That's how it is, "nie pojadę" ("I won't go"), and stop.
What worked, however, were the "strong hands" of several worshippers, who declared: "If you, Reb Cantor, do not go up to the lectern, you may as well say goodbye to the cantorate"...
Only after such words was the cantor appeased, and he prayed.

Radio Corner

[Radio — science and technology.] A brilliant invention by a Jewish scientist.
The American Jewish scientist Jacob Buchman has, after ten years of unceasing trials and experiments, finally succeeded in inventing an apparatus which he has named "The Talking Book".
This apparatus performs real wonders. It plays from sheet music and reads printed words. In a word: this apparatus fulfils all the functions which until now only the human brain carried out.
The most important part of this apparatus consists of the "electric eye", which reacts to light and shadow, and of a film strip on which the alphabet is found.
Reading by the apparatus comes about thanks to the fact that at each corresponding letter the electric current is switched off.
The way in which the switching-off of the electric current takes place at each letter remains the inventor's secret. Let us imagine that the apparatus has to read the last letter of the alphabet — Tav. In that case the strip, on which all the letters are printed in order, has to wind right to the very end, until the letter of the book covers the letter of the book [sic] of the film strip. At that moment the "electric eye", which checks the letters, reacts at once and immediately switches off the current. At that same moment the loudspeaker pronounces the required letter, just as in a sound film.
Will the "Talking Book" replace the gramophone record, on which the living human voice has been engraved? That is to be doubted. What the new invention of the Jewish scientist gives us is, however, nothing more than an automatic reading of a letter or word without any accent or expression. On the gramophone record, by contrast, the living word has been engraved with all its accents, nuances and feeling.
A gramophone record, however, is no more than a means of fixing the human voice or sound. But when it is a matter of a machine that can itself read out the printed word, one must admit that the Jewish scientist's apparatus is a true wonder of our generation.
—o—
[Abroad — England.] The 24-hour clock in England.
England is the last state in Europe to have introduced the 24-hour clock system.
Almost all European states have already been using this clock for several years. The railways, post, telephone, telegraph and radio constantly use the 24-hour clock.
It was hardest of all, however, with the English. This conservative people, which still cultivates the customs and traditions of centuries, could by no means bring themselves to throw out the old, faithful[?] clock of their great-grandfathers, who divided the hours of the day into "a.m." and "p.m.".
At last, however, the English gave in, and they too have reformed the clock to a 24-hour one.
From now on all English radio stations will announce the time according to the new formula, for example: twenty-two o'clock, etc.
—o—
[Economy and law — debts and currency.] How is a debt in złoty paid according to the American dollar rate?
In connection with the dollar rate, a great many doubts arise as to how one must pay debts that are secured in foreign currencies.
There are many kinds of dollar-loan agreements, and each different form raises different doubts. Among the various types of agreements on dollar loans, a very widespread type is the agreement for loans to be repaid in złoty according to a dollar rate. This dollar clause is fully valid even now, and the debt can be claimed according to the dollar rate that was stipulated.
For example: the loan document says to pay a thousand zł. at a rate of 8.90 zł. to the dollar.
Or to pay a thousand zł. at the dollar rate on the day of 15 July 1932.
These agreements are valid under Art. 8 of the dollar law; [in the first case] one must pay the thousand zł. not in paper dollars, but in a thousand zł. Or, according to the second example, one must pay the thousand zł. at the dollar rate of 15 July 1932, or at the rate of another date that was stipulated[?].

From tomorrow postal, telephone and telegraph rates become cheaper.

From tomorrow, Monday the 1st of October, the postal tariff becomes cheaper by 20 percent on average.
An inland letter will cost 25 gr. instead of 30 gr., and a postcard — 15 gr. instead of 20 gr.
Foreign letters also become cheaper by 5 gr. and will cost only 55 gr. instead of 60 gr.; postcards — 30 gr. instead of 35 gr.; to Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Romania — 45 gr. instead of 50 gr., and postcards 25 gr. instead of 30.
Just as registration (polecone) of inland letters has become cheaper, registration of foreign letters now also becomes cheaper, from 60 gr. to 45 gr.
The tariff for parcels becomes cheaper by 10 percent on average. The fee for parcels with food becomes much cheaper still.
Delivery of parcels, for which one has to pay from 30 to 80 gr., also becomes cheaper.
The tariff for money orders is reduced quite significantly. Until now one could send up to 2.000 zł. on one money order; now one can send up to 5 thousand zł. Until now the fee amounted to between 20 gr. and 3,55; now it will amount to at most two zł.
The fee for delivering money orders is abolished altogether.
For subscribing to newspapers at the post office no fee whatsoever is paid.
When sending value letters the handling fee of 20 gr. to 40 is abolished; the fee for delivering such letters, which amounted to 10 gr. for every złoty, is also abolished.
The telephone tariff becomes cheaper by 10 percent on average, both for the subscription and for calls.
Intercity calls over short distances have been introduced: up to 10 kilometres — 20 gr., up to 15 km. — 30 gr. and up to 20 km. — 40 gr.
The tariff for telegrams is: the basic fee is 25 gr.; a telegram of 10 words will cost 1,75 instead of 2 zł.
Congratulatory and condolence telegrams will cost only 5 gr. a word instead of 15 gr.
—o—

A library named after M. Winer.

The Będzin „Brit HaChayal“ is founding a library named after the tragically deceased Matek Winer of blessed memory.
On Tuesday, the 2nd day of Sukkot, the founding meeting of the library took place in the premises of the „Brit HaChayal“.
The meeting is opened by Commander Glirman, who speaks about the importance of a library at the „Brit HaChayal“ in Będzin, and in order to perpetuate the memory of the unforgettable comrade M. Winer he proposes that the library should bear the name of the deceased comrade. All present agree, and at once about 100 books are collected on the spot, and Mr. Yakov Winer, who was present, immediately pledges a splendid bookcase for the library.
Then a committee is elected consisting of: Y. Winer, Y. Langnus, A. Tenenbaum and A. Diamant.
The Sosnowiec kehilla mess before the District Court. Englard–Markowicz trial — postponed again.

On Thursday of Chol HaMoed the „dirty laundry“ of the local kehilla mess was heard for the first time before the Sosnowiec District Court.
In the dock sat Mr. Alter Markowicz, who is accused of having issued, during the kehilla elections in the year 1931, a leaflet against Rabbi Englard, in which it is said that „in August 1922 Englard sat in the Vienna[?] prison, where he ate the local dishes“. The accusation was confirmed by a certain Rozencwajg, who was also in the above-mentioned prison at that time.
Because the main witness Rozencwajg did not appear, the trial was postponed at the request of Englard's defence counsel.

[Będzin — electricity and Sukkot.] “The failed ‘żydowska afera’ [Jewish affair] at Sukkot”...
The frequent complaints and grievances against the municipal electric works — that it does not punctually fulfil its obligations, that it often takes several days until a disconnected supply is put back in order (many a time the cutting off of the light happens by mistake...) — we never accepted as correct, for we always had the hundred-percent “certainty” that the functionaries of the institution perform their duties to perfection.
This past Erev Sukkot a large number of the Jewish population became convinced that our opinion is a just one.
The following circumstances brought about this conviction: into some of the sukkot, as always, electric current had been led. This “audacity”, however, was not tolerated by the electric works, and on Sukkot in the daytime an inspection was carried out, the “secret wires” were cut, and reports were drawn up against the “insolent” Jews.
— Just so that nobody says [?] that the officials of the electric works are not punctual.
We believe that if the local Polish rags find out about it, the “sensation” will be reported under the heading “The failed żydowska afera at Sukkot”...

[Sosnowiec — municipality.] Session of the Council of Commissioners in Sosnowiec.
In the new magistrate building the first session of the Council of Commissioners took place on Wednesday evening.
At the session a series of tax statutes was adopted at the same level as last year.
A longer discussion was provoked by the question of granting concessions to build kiosks (“budki”) in the streets. The councillors sharply criticised the building department of the magistrate for the large number of concessions granted for setting up kiosks. It was resolved that permits be granted only to those who will build newspaper kiosks on the model of the Warsaw ones.
The question of reopening the market halls on 1 Maja Street, which is by the way a very urgent one, was postponed to the next session.

A Meeting on the Rabbinate Question in Dąbrowa.

[Dąbrowa — rabbinate; kehilla.]
In connection with the fact that the rabbinate question in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] is becoming topical, and with the fear that the majority of the parnasim [kehilla board members] will vote for the candidacy of Mr. Baruch Epsztajn (son-in-law of the late rabbi, of blessed memory), the committee fighting this candidacy has girded its loins and gone out to battle.
The first "bomb" released by the committee was the publication "Unzer Vort" ["Our Word"], in which the leaders of "Agudat [Israel]" as well as the "progressive" [postępowi] activists in Dąbrowa took part; in a series of articles they pointed out the unfitness of the above-mentioned candidate as rabbi of the Dąbrowa kehilla (incidentally, expressions were used that left a strong aftertaste...). Besides this, a meeting was organised on Wednesday evening in the "Venus" hall. The meeting had been advertised for 7 in the evening, but only half an hour later the hall, which could have held many more people, was closed. (As the writer of these lines was informed, the early "Ne'ila" [closing] took place because of the fear of the group that supports the candidacy of the rabbi's son-in-law.)
On the presidium — besides the committee members, also the local police commissioner. Speeches were given by Messrs. councilman B.[?] Rechnic, councilman L. Puterka, Agudah president Ch. M. Ajzenman, K. Epsztajn and Szlomo Winer, who sharply criticised the activity of the present kehilla leaders, and especially the plan to push through the candidacy of Mr. Baruch Epsztajn as rabbi of Dąbrowa.
At the end the following resolutions were adopted:
1) The mass meeting, held on Wednesday at the "Venus" with the participation of 800 (!) people, having heard the speeches about the wasteful and harmful activity of the Jewish kehilla, resolves to turn to the proper government bodies so that the Jewish kehilla be dissolved as quickly as possible and a commissioner be appointed until the new elections.
2) The mass meeting protests against Mr. Baruch Epsztajn, who, not possessing the least qualifications to occupy the rabbinical seat, nevertheless wants to seize it by force, and who also prevents our town from getting a suitable and able candidate. We therefore demand that the government strike out the candidacy.
3) The mass meeting expresses its thanks to the vice-president Mr. L. Rechnic, who uncovered (?) the irregularities in the Jewish kehilla, as well as to Messrs. L. Puterka and Hercel Liberman for their help in exposing the kehilla irregularities.
After the resolutions Mr. Jakub Mittelman addressed the presidium with the questions: 1) why no chairman of the meeting was elected, and 2) why the hall was closed to a large number of town taxpayers?
To the second question Mr. Rechnic answered that this was done at the demand of the police representatives.
After this explanation the meeting is closed.
New Laws on Turnover and Income Tax.

[Poland — taxes.]
The Ministry of Finance has already completely finished the work on the text of the implementing regulation to the tax ordinance [ordynacja podatkowa], and any day now the implementing regulation will be printed in the Dziennik Ustaw [Journal of Laws].
The implementing provisions contain 120 paragraphs and contain very important clarifications to the tax ordinance.
The new implementing provisions of the Minister of Finance introduce entirely new deadlines for tax payment.
The assessment of the income tax [podatek dochodowy] will now take place from the 15th of sierpień [August] to the 15th of wrzesień [September].
After this deadline every taxpayer will already receive the payment order [nakaz zapłaty]. This year the payment orders for income tax will be received only during the month of październik [October].
The assessment of the turnover tax will take place every year in the month of May.
During the year merchants will have to pay "zaliczki" [advance payments] on account of income and turnover tax. The tax authorities will now take great care that the advances are paid on time without fail.

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
An Expensive Flirt...
A resident of Wełnowiec came to Katowice to "catch" a flirt. He sat down in the "Ferdinand" park in the company of a "lady", with whom he spent several hours. On coming home the flirt-man noticed that his wallet with 3,800 zł had vanished.
—o—
Directors of the Discount Bank in Chorzów Arrested.
On the order of the prosecutor's office the directors of the Upper Silesian "Discount Bank" [Bank Dyskontowy] in Chorzów were arrested. The arrests are connected with the audit of the bank's books.
—o—
Diphtheria in Katowice.
Diphtheria has spread among the schoolchildren in Katowice. In this connection the school authorities have ordered the closing of the public elementary school [szkoła powszechna] named after Konopnicka.
—o—
Collision Between a Cart and a Tram.
In Siemianowice a cart collided with a tram. Both the cart and the tram were badly damaged. None of the passengers was hurt.
—o—
Instead of Wine — Ordinary Water.
Before the Rybnik court the trial began against a Kraków wine firm accused of having supplied ordinary water instead of wine. For formal reasons the sensational trial was postponed.
—o—
Booklets About Hitler Confiscated.
These days the booklets entitled "The Truth About Hitler and About the Jews" were confiscated.
The confiscation took place because of insulting Hitler, who is depicted beating a Jew...
—o—
A Big Smuggling Affair Uncovered.
In Upper Silesia a well-organised smuggling gang [szajka] was uncovered, which was engaged in smuggling flints for lighters [zapalniczki].
The leaders of the gang were put in Katowice prison.
—o—
The Same Yente, Only Differently Veiled.
As is known, the authorities dissolved the organisations of the "home-grown" Hitlerites in Upper Silesia. But these people have not given up their anti-Jewish agitation and have organised themselves under a new name, "Radykalny Ruch Odrodzenia" [Radical Movement of Revival]. Instead of "Błyskawica" they now publish a new rag called "Front Polski", which is full of poisonous articles against Jewry.
It is desirable that the Jewish community in Katowice bring the "editors" of this little sheet to legal account, and that they be punished just like the editor of the "Błyskawica".
—o—
Jews for the L.O.P.P.
The Jewish L.O.P.P. [Air and Anti-Gas Defence League] committee in Katowice, in which representatives of the kehilla, merchants, and small traders' and artisans' organisations are represented, is working very actively for the L.O.P.P. There are already 800 declared members.
—o—
Terrible Disaster at the "Wolfgang" Coal Mine.
At the "Wolfgang" coal mine in Ruda a terrible disaster occurred, in which 8 workers were killed and 44 injured.
