Pupil Shot the Teacher.
In Tarnowskie Góry a pupil of the local seminary fell in love with a teacher. She, however, did not return his love; on Sunday[?] he came to her home and wanted to have a short talk with her. On leaving, the pupil pulled out a revolver and fired several shots at the teacher. Luckily none of the bullets hit, and the teacher was not wounded. The lovesick pupil then tried to shoot himself, but this too did not succeed: the revolver was snatched from his hand and he was taken to the police station.
Bloody Brawl in the “Szmejka” Colony

[Zagłębie — crime.] In the “Szmejka” colony in Kazimierz [Górniczy], the Adamik brothers are known as dangerous ruffians.
This week the ruffians attacked a local resident and beat him murderously. On the alarm the police came in order to put an end to the fight. But the Adamiks began throwing stones at the police, and the mother of the sons scalded one of the policemen with hot water.
To defend themselves against the attack the police used their weapons, and the bullets wounded the attackers, one of whom died.

Final matches of the Maccabi Federation in Łódź.
As we have already reported, the final matches of the Maccabi Federation, which lasted 3 days, took place in Łódź. Taking part were: Hasmonea (Lwów), Maccabi (Kraków), Hakoach (Będzin), Maccabi (Łuck), Maccabi (Grodno) and Maccabi (Łódź). Unfortunately Maccabi (Grodno) did not turn up for the tournament, and because of this the whole event was somewhat disturbed, since it turned out that one club had to rest on the first day and afterwards came to the semi-final with fresh strength. And the one “favoured by the lot” was Maccabi Łódź.
On the first day, then, the following played:
Maccabi (Łuck) — Maccabi (Kraków) 6:0
The Kraków side had a very great superiority and did with their opponents whatever they wanted.
Hasmonea (Lwów) — Hakoach (Będzin) 1:0 (1:0).
This match was the most interesting of the whole tournament. The Lwów side is a very good team; both physically and technically it stands at a good level. Coming to Łódź as favourites, they could not at all imagine that they would meet any resistance there at all, and especially from Będzin's Hakoach. Our Hakoach players have shown that if they make an effort they can play after all; it is a fact, and this must be stressed, that the Lwów side is a much better team and had a great superiority.
But the Hakoach players played with such ambition and such a will to win that the Lwów side had to capitulate with clenched teeth. Especially outstanding were Gunberg[?] and Hönig (who now plays for Hakoach, Będzin), thanks to whom it was possible to achieve such a brilliant victory. The one and only goal was scored by Hönig from a splendid free kick from barely 30 metres!
On the second [day] Hakoach played Maccabi Łódź. The Hakoach players, who still had the hard match with Hasmonea in their legs, went out onto the field over-confident and unfortunately did not hold out. Already in the twenty-odd minute of play Helberg scores a very nice goal; afterwards Szywek[?] hits the post with a splendid shot. Over-fatigue is felt among the Hakoach players, whereas the Maccabi players, who had not played the day before, feel fresh and lively and keep up the tempo better; as a result Hakoach lost 3:1.
The final, which took place on Monday between Maccabi (Kraków) and Maccabi (Łódź), brought a deserved victory to the much better team of Maccabi (Kraków), which beat the Łódź side 3:1, thereby winning the Maccabi championship of Poland.
Internal championships of the tennis section at “Hakoach”.
On the courts of “Hakoach” internal tennis championships took place. The matches were very interesting and stood at a high level. It could be noticed that the Będzin tennis players have made great progress. If Jews Were to Be Angels...

What do the Endeks [Endecja, the Polish National Democrats] want? It is not about their goal that we ask, but about the content of their claims. If Jews engage in trade — the Endek press [says] that Jews engage in unproductive professions. If Jews settle on the land — they are reproached for grabbing Polish soil. If Jews emigrate abroad — the Endek newspapers rejoice that pogroms break out in Algiers [?], that the Arabs will not let the Jews in, that Hitler drives them out, and Nowaczyński [Adolf Nowaczyński] searches, as if with a candle, every little corner of the globe to find little pogroms there, antisemitism, and serves it up with joy to his readers.
So what do they want, the Endeks
This claim has lately often been raised not only by the Jewish press, [but [?]] also by some Polish newspapers, which posed the same question; and, feeling pressed against the wall, the Endeks' chief organ, the "Gaz. Warsz." [Gazeta Warszawska], has finally come out in plain words and writes as follows:
— "We declare that in principle the question of what Jews in Poland occupy themselves with is a matter of indifference to us — whether they are productive or unproductive, whether they deal in brokerage, in speculation, or even in crimes and swindles. Even whole groups of Jews may take up very productive work, they may even build a Tel Aviv, they may work in the fields in bitter sweat — all this will not change in the least the fact that Jewry as a collective is a parasitic element. The several hundred thousand Jewish peasants who work the land in Poland, in Russia, in Palestine and in other countries may grow to several million; besides that, as many Jews again may take up other productive work such as handicrafts, serious scholarship and the like — and then it will still essentially be those millions of Jewish capitalists, money men, speculators and 'intellectualists' of a suspect type who decide the Jewish question; they will always be the ones setting the tone in Jewry. If a group of creative Jews appears, it only strengthens the political and economic power of parasitic Jewry. If, for instance, we learn that in the Stanisławów voivodeship alone there are 25 thousand Jewish peasants and 180 [?] Jewish landowners, this does not please us; on the contrary, this Jewish expansion pains us. Jews have [?] brought into agriculture, too, the same dishonest elements as into trade, the legal profession, etc. [?], and even if Jews were to be nothing but angels, we would be just as dissatisfied with them as we are today. It is not a question of whether Jews will be productive or not productive; we would feel exactly the same if instead of 4 million Jews we had 4 million hard-toiling Chinese. We want only one thing — that the Jews should take themselves off out of Poland, because today's Jewish emigration has no significance. Far more Jews come into Poland. And it is also true that the growth of antisemitism in the world worries us little. We do not at all believe that the Jewish question can be solved by shifting the Jews from one country to another. Jewish parasitism must be removed everywhere. The caste which Jews create everywhere today must altogether be wiped off the face of the earth, and therefore we rejoice at the growth of antisemitism in all other countries, for otherwise antisemitism would not have had any success [here] either."
The Endek organ is even very good-natured, full of grace, and would regard with sympathy the colonisation of Jews in Palestine, Birobidzhan and Manchuria; but, out of honesty of course, it cannot tolerate a new nest of Jewish speculation, a new Nalewki [the Jewish commercial street of Warsaw], growing up in Tel Aviv.
That is how insolently, how brutally, how man-devouringly the Endecja in Poland thinks, speaks and writes. Certain and well-founded is its joy over the growth of antisemitism in the world: had such a hurricane of reaction and fascism not now been sweeping across the world, the black power in Poland too would not have dared to raise its head. When the servants of Nicholas II organised pogroms against Jews in Russia, Roman Dmowski's disciples in Poland too tried to do the same. Other times came, new and free ones, and the Endecja too fell silent. Fascism marched up in Germany — and the Endecja in Poland too tries to show its black and bloody claws.
It is raining — it is raining everywhere, and when the sun shines out again its rays will warm the Polish soil too, and the evil demons will go back to their rest.
— "Even if Jews were angels, we Endeks would be no different."
But Jews are not angels — they are human beings, of flesh and blood, with dignity, with a firm will to live and exist and with the ability to endure, to hold out and under all circumstances to wage a struggle and fight for their demands; and since, as always and like everyone, we have no intention whatsoever of letting ourselves be exterminated and wiped off the face of the earth, we shall have, having no choice, not as angels but as human beings, to continue our stubborn struggle in the places where we were born, where we live and want [to live], and where we will also build our future.
Y. Nissenbaum.

An application for deferment [odroczenie] of military service as sole breadwinner may be submitted even when the person liable to military service concerned is already serving in the army. In such a case, however, the military authority is entitled not to release such a person at once, but only after he has served the prescribed 5 months.
Citizenship and military service
Citizenship may be withdrawn for failing to report for, or evading, military service only when the place of residence of the person liable to service concerned is known to the authority; as long as the authority does not know where he has gone, there can be no question of withdrawing citizenship.
In any case the decision to withdraw citizenship must be communicated to the person liable to military service himself or to his parents.
Zagłębie in the Dark...

[Będzin — feuilleton; the blackout and air-defence exercise.]
Seen and heard in the dark hour.
By Y. Oberżanek.
All day Thursday I prepared myself for the attack on Zagłębie. I wanted to see how Będzin would look in the dark, what kind of face our „Little America“ would wear during the „ninth plague“.
As soon as I heard the first „blast of the shofar“ — the first factory siren, that is — I set out into town to welcome the plague.
I shall relate to our readers what I saw and heard in that dark hour.
Będzin just like Żarnowiec
On Małachowskiego Street two provincial Jews are walking from the railway station. They walk and grope with their sticks, and one says to the other:
— Oy! A dark town — may I not sin with my words. Such darkness that one could get killed! How is this Będzin any better than Żarnowiec? I would have sworn that here, too, the „kaves“ [?] walk about on the roofs — such darkness.
— Do you know what occurred to me? — said the second.
— What occurred to you?
— It occurred to me that instead of travelling to Będzin we actually travelled to Szczekociny.
Walking like this, the Jews were stopped by a policeman:
— „Skąd panowie?“ [Where are you from, gentlemen?]
— „Ja... ja jadę z Żarnowca“ [I... I am coming from Żarnowiec] — answered one of the Jews.
— „A pan skąd?“ [And you, sir, where from?] — he asked the second Jew.
— „Me?“ „Dlaczego [why] pan komendant khrume [?] for instance szpycza [?]“? — the second Jew asked.
— „Bo zaraz będzie atak“ [Because there will be an attack any moment] — the policeman answered.
— An attack?... Do you hear, Berl, what this fellow says? He's talking something about an attack.
— „Co za atak?“ [What attack?] — the Jew asked back: an attack of gallstones or of the blind gut [appendix]?..
What was the end? The end was that both Jews ran into a gateway, muttering:
— A dark town, Będzin; how is Będzin any better than Żarnowiec?..
The Jew's Revenge
When the lights were put out, a little Jew with a short goatee stands rubbing his hands with joy:
— Oh, good!... Oh, good!... Only a pity that the darkness lasts just one hour... If I had my say, I would give them such a „proszek“ [?] every week.
— Why are you so glad? What is the great occasion for you? — he was asked.
— I've got my revenge on the power station — the Jew answered, well pleased.
„My wife is going to the child“
On Kołłątaja Street a Jew is running with a little lantern in his hand.
— „Dokąd?“ [Where to?] — a policeman stops him.
— „Nie mam czasu“ [I have no time], the Jew answers and runs on.
— „Ale dokąd pan leci?“ [But where are you running, sir?] — the policeman holds him back by the sleeve.
— „Bo moja żona idzie do dziecka“ (my wife is going to the „siner“ [?]) — the Jew answered.
— „Nie rozumiem, co to panu obchodzi, że żona idzie do dziecka“ [I don't understand what it matters to you, sir, that your wife is going to the child] — the policeman did not understand the excuse.
— „Pan nie rozumie? Moja żona stęka (my wife is in labour), to ja lecę po drożdże (so I'm running for the yeast) — pan rozumie?“
The policeman did not understand the whole story. Does one need yeast to leaven [?] a cake, or yeast for the wife's groaning? And in general, what does one need yeast for when it is dark?
Since the policeman did not understand the whole story, he let the „suspicious“ person run on after the „drożdże“ [yeast]...
A Rare „Occasion“
It seemed very suspicious to me that just when it grew dark, in many local Jewish philanthropic and social institutions the windows were curtained with dark covers — why just now, of all times? Just in the darkness the proceedings became so „pilne“ [diligent, urgent]!
The question was answered for me. In one institution they „made“ the „balance sheet“ for the general meeting in the dark... and in a second institution they counted, by half a candle, the money from the last flag day.
Our „communal workers“ took advantage of the „occasion“, because they hold by the saying: „In the dark it is good“...
The Baker's Dream
On Mandżer [Modrzejowska?] Street a little „circle“ is standing and gazing up at the sky.
— What? Are you blessing the new moon? — I ask the Jew.
— What moon? Why a moon? — the Jew answered with a smile — Don't you see?
— What is there to see? — I asked.
— „It's happening“ — the Jew answered.
— What is happening?
— A little war! Don't you hear that „aeroplanes“ are already „roaring“? They're already throwing „reflectors“ [searchlights]; darkness is already here. „Przepustki“ [passes] to walk in the street will soon be needed too... Just one shot, and the little war [?] is ready...
— If only, sweet Father! — the other three Jews answered.
As I later found out, the three Jews were — bakers.
That is all I saw and heard in the dark hour in Będzin.

[Humour page — "Der Kokh-Lefl"; satirical feuilleton, community and associations.] (Urgent meeting of beaten hoshanas).
Right after "Kol Mevaser", when the hoshanas had been duly "beaten" [pasok?] and carted off onto the Holy Ark, they felt deeply insulted and decided to put an end to their enslavement... Every class has its association, its "związek" [union]; so we too must stand up for our interests: why is the cheap[?], heavy lulav untouchable, and the etrog too is fussed over and cuddled like a child — therefore we hoshanas must organise too, cries out in an iron voice a badly beaten hoshana, and no sooner said than done: an emergency ["lyarmove", from Polish alarmowe] general meeting is called at once, at which the oldest hoshana is unanimously elected chairwoman and the youngest secretary. After all the hoshanas that perished this year have been honoured by standing, the chairwoman delivers the following speech: Gone [printed "suenen", a misprint] are the years of oppression, when we let ourselves be beaten for so long by every single one. Any little nobody ["a lyade mentshele", from Polish lada] trampled on our heads... Therefore, comrade hoshanas, let us secure our future through a united front. The floor is given to a second wounded hoshana (bandaged with a lulav bandage). We can no longer let ourselves be beaten by whatever "Dovar"[?] [probably "Dozór", the community board] it may be, since it, together with the kehilla budget, is already a beaten hoshana too... The Jewish councillors in the city council are by law exempt from beating hoshanas as well, since they have long since "beaten" their voters[?]... And likewise with the rest, such as the "Craftsmen's Association" (welkherz[?]), the Householders' Association, the Office Clerks' Association [biuraliści], the "Dramatic Society" — they have long been like the beaten hoshanas... As for the merchants and small traders, it is superfluous even to mention them: with them the tax office says "Kol Mevaser" all year round... This last speech, delivered in an inspired tone, made a strong impression on the large number of assembled hoshanas... and they proceeded at once to concrete matters, drew up a statute according to the "Dziennik Ustaw" [Journal of Laws]. After electing a board and an audit committee, all the assembled hoshanas, amid great enthusiasm, united together and created a mighty, strong broom of beaten hoshanas...

In Reb Avraham's large garden long tables had been set out with white tablecloths, on which stood plates, and on each of them lay a large portion of fish and beside it a large braided challah. Nor was wine missing from the table.
— Put out bigger portions — Sarahle said to the waiter — let them, too, bless my Chanale with good luck, let them eat their fill, on this very day when my child goes under the chuppah; and in the merit of their gladdening the bride and groom, God will help them too.
In his room, in the leather armchair, sat Reb Avraham, arguing with the bookkeeper Nachum [printed "Naaim"] Rozen.
— Why today of all days, precisely today, Panie Rozen, are you running away from us? Are you, God forbid, an enemy of ours, that you don't want to be at Chanale's wedding?
— She is, after all, your Chanale; have you perhaps forgotten how six years ago she sat on your knees and you played with her? I don't understand it either — do you want to spoil my celebration?
— I am truly sorry that I am leaving for home today; I have received a letter from my father that I must come home at once — the bookkeeper Nachum Rozen answers him, his head sunk to the ground, while a terrible murderous hatred burns in him against Reb Avraham, because he is tearing Chanale away from him, whom he loves like his own life.
— That is not right of you, Panie Rozen; you are like one of our household after all; travel tomorrow, what's the fuss?
— Reb Avraham — says Rozen — what do you think of honouring one's father? I believe you would not want your Chanale to disobey you.
— Well, certainly, certainly, honouring one's father is a great thing.
— There, you see, and you are keeping me from obeying my father's command.
— Well, here, do as you see fit.
He goes over to the iron safe, takes two hundred roubles out of it and hands them to Rozen, saying as he does so:
— I am giving you eighty roubles more, but I will deduct it from you later; perhaps you will need money at home?
— No, Reb Avraham. I thank you for it, but I cannot take the eighty roubles, because I am going home and will not come back.
Avraham Langnas knits his brow, looks at Rozen and says:
— What does that mean?
But Rozen gives no answer, gives Avraham his hand and says:
— Be well — and walks out of the room.
— You don't want to say goodbye at all to Sarahle, to Chanale?
But Rozen no longer heard the words. Like a madman, agitated, he ran out of the room as if from a fire. In the corridor he stopped for a moment and, raising two fingers into the air, said:
— Chanale, I swear to you that I will take revenge on you for having broken your word. — And he went out into the street.
On that same day, when everyone ran to the highway to meet Chanale's bridegroom, Rozen too was there, waiting for his arrival.
— I must see him, I must see what he looks like — he said to himself, and pushed his way to Reb Avraham's carriage, which stood waiting for the bridegroom.

Chapter 2.

For seven whole days there was dancing and revelry in the house of Reb Avraham Langnas.
Other Hasidim, together with the Aleksander Hasidim, forgot their Hasidic quarrels and went off into a dance in honour of the bride and groom. Older Hasidim sat and listened to Torah.
Reb Avraham, too, sat with closed eyes among all the side-locked and bearded Hasidim, drinking in every word that came from his son-in-law's mouth, and reaping joy.
Pure, pearly words flowed from the bridegroom Binyomindl, who displayed his sharp wit and his good head before the whole company.
And when Binyomindl had finished his discourse, they said grace after meals and, wishing one another all the best, everyone went their way.
In Reb Avraham's house, too, they went to bed. The waiters and the maidservants, tired from the great labour, decided to leave the clearing of the dishes for the morning and went off to rest from the whole day's work.
In the middle of the night, when the whole town was wrapped in a thick fog and everyone was sunk in sweet sleep, there was heard in all the streets the ringing of the fire bells and the whistling of the night watchmen.
— Fire, fire — people shouted and raised an alarm.
To help came the winds, which began to howl and bark most terribly.
Through the streets the firemen run in every direction, sleepy, worn out from their day-in, day-out work. People pack things, utensils, pillows; they carry out everything there is in the house. Sleepy, terrified mothers carry their naked, crying children and run with them to the bank of the river.
— Where is the fire? Whose house is burning? — one asked another. Everyone was talking, everyone was shouting, and no one knew where and at whose place the fire was.
And suddenly the cry is heard of Vigdle [?], the waitress, who screamed in a voice not her own:
— Jews, why are you standing there? Don't you know that it is burning at Reb Avraham's? Jews, run and rescue, Jews, have pity, run and rescue.
And in a rush [?] they all made for Reb Avraham's big house, which was already entirely in flames. From all the windows and doors great, long tongues of fire burst out into the street, licking the walls and setting them alight as well.
Terrified, in his underwear, Avraham Langnas ran round and round the house and, wringing his hands, shouted and wept: rescue, rescue, have pity, Jews, rescue.
But it was not possible to save anything from the house, because the fire was too strong and too big for anyone to be able to get into the house.
Binyomindl, too, half naked, ran with Chanale and with Sarahle to Reb Shimon the timber merchant, holding in his hand his tallis and tefillin bag.

What's New in Zagłębie? — The First Two Days of Sukkot in Zagłębie

[Head of the local page; Zagłębie — Sukkot.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Sunday, 21 / 21 Tishrei 5695 — niedziela 30 września 1934 [Sunday, 30 September 1934].)
The first two days of Sukkot in Zagłębie.
The greatest virtue of the first 2 days of Sukkot was the weather. Everyone delighted in the sunny weather; Jews felt excellent in the sukkah. No rain, no wind. The same for the young people, who still managed to take leave of their summer strolls. Incidentally, one could still wear summer clothes, and that was a double blessing for those who are still not ready for winter today.
Those who suffered from it were the craftsmen — the tailors and the furriers, whose season the weather spoiled.
Etrogim and lulavim sold very little, even less than in the last crisis years. Only a few individuals allowed themselves to buy an etrog.
The local authority's ban on putting up sukkot on balconies was enforced with full severity. Those who thought that „nobody will know about them“ and put up sukkot on balconies had to „wander“ to other courtyard sukkot, and administrative penalties await them.
As every year, the „Beit Lechem“ in Będzin carried out a broad relief campaign and distributed various foodstuffs to about 160 families.
In this field Jewish Sosnowiec ought to be ashamed: it has no philanthropic institution at all that would organize a relief campaign for the poor.
On the cultural front — hush, quiet, not a peep...

We Boycott German Mineral Waters

[Zagłębie — boycott of German goods.]
We boycott German mineral waters.
Great indignation has been aroused among the broad masses of the Jewish population by the fact that, despite the proclaimed ruthless boycott of all products originating in Hitlerite Germany, some Jewish wholesale merchants are still bringing large shipments of mineral waters from Germany, such as „Ems“, „Wildungen“, „Wiesbaden“, „Selters“, „Kissingen“ etc.
This can happen simply because the broader masses of the Jewish population do not know exactly where the waters come from.
In accordance with the principle „We boycott everything that can strengthen Hitlerite Germany“, we appeal to all Jewish doctors not to prescribe German mineral waters to their patients; these can be replaced with good results by Polish waters, or else by French, Czechoslovak and Hungarian ones.
We believe that the Jewish population, which has declared itself for an unconditional boycott of all goods originating in Germany, will not wish — by buying German mineral waters — to support directly the Hitlerite regime in Germany, which has condemned tens of thousands of our brothers to a terrible death by starvation and degraded them to second-class citizens.

Sosnowiec. What happened to a Jewish girl who dreamed of becoming a film star...

[Sosnowiec — fraud.] Miss P., 23 years old, the daughter of a well-known Sosnowiec landlord, has now fallen victim to a crafty swindle.
While still sitting on the school bench, young P. dreamed of the career of a film star.
She would constantly buy various film magazines, occupy herself with film literature, collect pictures of film artists and so on. She also took part in a series of "photogenic" contests and was even awarded a prize twice, which only awakened her hope of becoming a film actress.
A few days ago, sitting in a Katowice cinema, she happened to strike up a conversation with a young man of thirty-something, whose looks reminded her of the well-known film actor "Douglas Fairbanks". The naive girl told him so and little by little told him of her fantastic plans to become a film star.
They left the cinema together and the stranger saw her to the train. Before parting, he gave her to understand that he was indeed the famous film star Douglas Fairbanks.
She believed him. For the next day she arranged a date (randka) with him. The young man promised to place her with a film company and help make her career.
Little by little he gave her to understand that she needed to have at least 1,000 dollars with her. The end was that the future "star" stole the sum from her father's cash box and handed it over to "Douglas Fairbanks". She arranged to meet him the same day at the railway station. But she never saw him again.
"Douglas Fairbanks", who had persuaded her that he was travelling through Europe incognito, did not show up again. Only now did she understand that the young man was a plain swindler.

On the Annual Session of the League of Nations

[Politics — League of Nations; Geneva.] (Special for the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“)
Geneva is today the modern Zion of the world, the centre of all important events in the life of the nations, and even of those states which like to spit in the face of the whole world and insist on being „the exception to the rule“ and „the one who does not know how to ask“ — of whom one part did not want to be represented in the Geneva family of nations at all, and the other part acted forcefully, slammed the door and said: „Don't want it [?] — the in-law relationship is over“, — „I can run my little town myself“; and yet precisely these grandees are „behind the back“ — or, diplomatically speaking: unofficially — more and more strongly represented in Genf [Geneva] through all sorts of plain world politicians, journalists and spies, so that their government chancelleries in the capitals should not miss [?] any significance, mood and change of mood in the League of Nations, which they have just left in the hope that any moment now the whole edifice will crash and fall apart.
As regards the League of Nations itself, opinions are divided: some of the great ones already want to sing lamentations and dirges over it, because, they say, the League of Nations is a living „bar-minan“ [as good as dead]; it has achieved nothing yet, and despite its existence 2 members in South America are waging a war against each other with all the trimmings, while the security politicians point to clear proofs that were it not for the League of Nations all calamities and plagues would long since have come upon us, and a war would long since have been raging over the whole world.
The truth lies in the middle, on the golden path. The League of Nations is still today a power factor in international politics, but its real significance and strength lie only on the horizon of the great powers, i.e. only in those countries in which the interests of the great powers and of their natural and artificial allies intersect, — here the League of Nations is still an instrument of power, not only of words and speeches but also of political and military sanctions, in order to maintain the „status quo“, the equilibrium of the present world order and consequently also peace in the greatest part of the world. It is, however, powerless and almost meaningless for the political development far, far away in the East or among the „dew and rain“ [petty] states of South America, because neither France, nor England, nor any of the main power groups has any practical interest there, and we have not yet come to the point where the great powers would get involved for the sake of an ideal or even for the sake of truth — indeed they say: let the „smurim“ [?] there behind the mountains of darkness tear each other's noses off and bang their heads against the wall, what has that to do with us?
We Jews, on the other hand, view the League of Nations from an entirely different standpoint. We have a great, almost a vital interest in the existence of a body where the voice of the weaker may also sometimes be heard, where we can concentrate all our work in order to influence the world's public opinion for our cause and for our future. And since our only weapons, our only arms, consist for the time being only of „the voice is the voice of Jacob“, the fact that the League of Nations will not or cannot at all times make its voice heard as final arbiter and say: „Listen here, my dear peace-breaker, if you do not stop and make peace at once with your war opponents, — then you will have to deal with our cannons. You have time this week to convince yourself, within 2 hours, 50 minutes and 25 seconds. Basta!“... plays no great role for us.
At the current session of the League of Nations three points of the agenda mainly dominate: the Saar plebiscite, the Polish proposal to generalise minority protection, and the entry of Soviet Russia into the League of Nations family.
All 3 points interest us Jews extraordinarily, and in any case more than its regular members, let us say Liberia and Ecuador.
The Saar plebiscite is to decide, on the model of the Upper Silesian plebiscite, to whom the small but economically very important territory of the Saar district and its surroundings shall belong: to Germany, to France, or whether it shall remain under the present League of Nations rule.
In the Saar territory, however, there also live several thousand Jews who do not want to suffer the same fate as their brethren in Germany under Hitler's rule. Therefore representatives of the Jews of the Saar territory are now present in Geneva, who are lobbying the various state delegations that in the future constitution of the Saar territory all Jewish rights, such as economic, political and religious equality with all other citizens, be publicly guaranteed [?] and protected.
As a minority, which we Jews constitute in all countries, we are also interested in the Polish proposal to extend minority protection to all countries. According to the latest reports this proposal has been referred to a study commission [printed „shtudir-misye“].
The entry of Soviet Russia into the League of Nations also awakens some hopes among us Jews. It is very probable that Soviet Russia will now at long last agree to enter into direct negotiations with Jewish representatives, who demand only that Russia finally stop the groundless persecutions against our religious and national interests. Russia is now in need of, and is seeking in all corners of the world, good friends, and therefore has no great reason to make world Jewry into a mortal enemy for nothing.
This is how the general and the Jewish picture looks in the Geneva world of politics, and „what comes out of it for us“ reads:
— „Not enthusiastic — but not despairing either“.
Geneva, 23 September. Shlomo Frohman, Zürich.

[Będzin — kehilla; budget; followed by eleven short news items: Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa, Zagłębie.]
All social subsidies struck out, except the Agudah ones.
In today's chronicle we bring a notice about the Będzin kehilla budget, in which the supervisory authority made many changes, above all in the sections of subsidies for social and philanthropic institutions.
In the notice we report that the subsidy for the gymnasium was reduced to 2,000 zł. As it turns out, we made a mistake: not 2,000 but 1,000 zł... Well, one should not have great complaints either, since[?] the subsidy for the „Beit Yaakov Gymnasium“ amounts to no more than 500 zł.
Then further: all subsidies for national and social institutions — struck out entirely; untouched remained only the subsidies for „world organisations“ such as „Bnos Agudath Israel“ and „Poalei Agudath Israel“.
Of the subsidies for the yeshivas only... the „Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin“ came out unscathed.
Attached to the budget is also a protocol containing a series of decisions, among them also the order that, on the basis of a resolution of the kehilla board in the year 1932, the little shochtim Radoszycki and Gerlic are to be engaged with pensions of 2,500 zł a year... (These are the „famous little shochtim“ who introduced demoralisation into the field of shechita.)
In short, Jews of Będzin, open your purses, for the community („gmina“) needs a lot of money for the clergy (kley kodesh), for the half-dozen shochtim, and above all for the Agudah „little shops“...
—o—
Week for the Elementary Schools
Throughout the country a fund-raising campaign is being carried out to build elementary schools („szkoły powszechne“).
In this connection a meeting took place under the chairmanship of the Starosta, Mr. Baksa[?], at which the district committee that is to carry out the collection was organised.
Next Sunday a sale of badges will take place throughout Zagłębie in aid of the above-mentioned purpose.
—o—
Dąbrowa Takes Another Loan of 100 Thousand Zł.
At the last session of the town council in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] it was decided to borrow a sum of 100 thousand zł from the Labour Fund.
At the session a series of tax statutes for the coming year was also adopted.
—o—
150 Thousand Zł. for the Victims of the Flood
The public in Zagłębie gave cash and produce to the sum of 150,000 zł for the victims of the flood.
—o—
One of the Burglars of the Sosnowiec Free-Loan Fund Caught
This week the Sosnowiec police caught one of those who carried out the burglary at the office of the Sosnowiec Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) fund.
—o—
On Night Transport Between Katowice and Sosnowiec
The Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec has approached the tramway management with a proposal that night trams should run between Katowice and Sosnowiec.
As we are informed, the management agrees to the proposal, and night transport is to be introduced soon.
—o—
Taking Photographs on the Railways Forbidden
The railway management has issued an order according to which it is forbidden to take photographs at railway stations, station buildings and railway installations.
If anyone takes photographs without permission from the railway management, the guilty will be treated as spies.
An exception can be made only for groups who are photographed on the platforms or in the carriages standing in the stations.
—o—

We have received the following communiqué:
1) On Friday, 2 November („listopad“), elections to the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec will take place.
All merchants who took out trade licences (patents) for the year 1934 and are on the voters' lists are entitled to take part in the elections.
All merchants must check whether their names are properly entered in the voters' lists.
2) On Sunday the 7th of this month a lecture by advocate[?] Mr. Teitelbaum will take place at the premises of the Merchants' Association, on the subject „The Register of Firms of [—?] and the Obligation to Keep Commercial Books“.

Dr. S. Kalker, plenipotentiary of the Central Committee for the Defence of Jewish Rights in Germany, is staying in Zagłębie. In connection with his mission Dr. Kalker held conferences with the local anti-Hitler committees in Zagłębie.

From the 1st of this month the interest rate on tax arrears has been reduced. Instead of 15 per cent a year one will now pay only 12 per cent, that is 1 per cent a year [sic; read: a month].

The New Tax Ordinance

[Poland — taxes.] On the 1st of October of this year the new tax ordinance came into force. Put simply, from the 1st of this month a new tax law on income, turnover [?], capital, houses, apartments etc. begins to be binding on the territory of the Polish state.
Under the said tax ordinance the so-called civic assessment commissions, which conducted the assessments together with the competent organs of the tax offices, will be abolished. From now on the assessments will take place without the help of commission members, solely by the officials of the tax offices. Already in the assessment of taxes for the year 1934 (tax year 1935) no assessment commissions will be active.
As for medium-sized and smaller industrialists, craftsmen and merchants, we do not know whether the changes will in any way harm their economic interests; we do not want to believe that because of the changes the taxes will be raised, or that [?] an unjust assessment or distribution of them will occur. Nor do we want to admit the thought that such a thing should be made possible. That would mean further burdening and weighing down the taxpayer. But we must state that the liberal character of assessing and apportioning taxes has been completely lost.
It seems that not long ago it was planned and projected that the sessions of the assessment commissions should be public, as is the practice in a parliament or a town council; the upshot of all this has been a change in the opposite direction.
Although an activity of a civic and state character, subject to the citizen's control, is much closer and dearer to us, we must come to the conclusion that the new tax ordinance is the result of the privileged, and in many cases tendentious, conduct of the commission members in a number of towns and townlets.
It remains for us only to make peace with the new tax law, and in that case to take all organisational means to stand on guard in order to defend the interests of the average taxpayer, who struggles with all his strength for his bit of existence.
From practice we know that the officials of the tax offices do not know and do not understand the living conditions of the smaller craftsman and trader. In no way [?] do they believe that 3–4 złoty a day is a matter of livelihood for such [?] little people. Therefore it is the task of the economic organisations, of their central bodies and of the competent chambers to take proper steps so that no fatal or official “errors” should be permissible...
The greatest attention must be paid to having sub-commissions or opinion commissions created at the tax offices, which the competent assessment organs should take into account; the experts (rzeczoznawcy) must be expanded and at the same time concentrated on the eve of the tax assessments. Every trade must without fail be represented by responsible persons as experts, delegated by organisations and accepted by the central bodies and chambers; these experts or opinion commissions should be regarded as advisers, who however will have to consist of honest people who know the circumstances of the taxpayers and — the main thing — are responsible and suited to the new task; likewise the persons of the appeal commissions.
G. L.
A Fight over a Place in the Sukkah

[Sosnowiec — daily life.] The story happened on Ch[?]--ka Street in Sosnowiec.
Two neighbours, who live with each other in peace all year round, put up a sukkah jointly for Sukkot.
One contributed a shutter, the other a door. Together they found a noodle board somewhere, bought a little skhakh [roofing greens] and “built” a sukkah — at least for the sake of Heaven.
But Satan, may his name be blotted out, could not bear that Jews should live in peace with each other, so he instigated a quarrel between the housewives over the “little place” in the sukkah.
The quarrel broke out on the second day of the holiday. Both neighbours came straight from the shtiblekh [prayer rooms], and since the little sukkah is so small that one can barely squeeze into it, the housewives began to quarrel, because each wanted her husband to be the first and the other to wait.
The housewives started it, but the quarrel was finished by the husbands, who mutually “honoured” each other with slaps.
Neighbours came running together and made peace. One of them, a pious neighbour who pleads the merit of Jews, came to the editorial office and told the story. “Let the world know,” he says, “that Jews still come to blows even today over a mitzvah”...
We do him the favour and describe it. We withhold the names of the neighbours, because they are respectable householders and will surely forgo this “honour”...

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
A Bandit Attack in Broad Daylight.
Near Niedobczyce, Rybnik county, a girl who had 15 zł. on her was attacked. The bandit struck the girl on the head with a blunt object, from which she fell unconscious; then the bandit covered her head with sand and carried out the robbery.

The Revenge of a Laid-Off Worker.
In [?] Zgoda [?], Świętochłowice county, the Steiger [mine overseer] of the coal group „Fakja“ [?] was wounded by a laid-off worker, who afterwards threw him into a river.

„Tseirei Mizrachi“ in Katowice Wages a Campaign against Corfu Etrogim.
In the „Mizrachi“ minyan in Katowice a strict warning was issued this year not to buy any etrogim from Corfu. There were, however, a couple of „fine“ Jews who laughed at the warning and came to pray with the Greek etrogim in their hands.

The Events in Częstochowa

[Częstochowa — politics; Endek disturbances. Followed by: Sosnowiec — labour.]
(From our correspondent).
On Sunday, Hoshana Rabbah, a congress of the Association of Hallerites [Związek Hallerczyków — veterans of General Haller's army] took place in Częstochowa with the permission of the authorities. On the day of the congress a group of Endek [National Democrat] youth came to the Cathedral Square wearing the insignia of the dissolved „Obon“ [?] [perhaps „Obóz“, a right-wing camp], trying to push into the ranks of the Hallerites. Since the participation of the young Endeks had not been foreseen in the programme of the congress, the police called on the arrivals to disperse, which the latter promptly did.
An hour later a group of young Endeks again tried to form a demonstration, which, however, was dispersed at the demand of the police.
After the church service, when the Hallerites were getting ready for the march-past, the young Endeks again tried to join the procession of the Hallerites. Upon the police's demand to disperse, the young Endek group pelted the police with stones and also with iron balls, which were hurled from slings; at the same time several shots were fired at the police from the ranks of the young Endeks.
As a result of the events, which were quickly liquidated by the police without the use of weapons, several policemen were battered with stones; one of them has a serious head wound. On the spot a young Endek was detained with a weapon in his hand at the moment when he was about to shoot at the police sergeant [przodownik].
Apart from that, up to some twenty persons were detained for attacking the police with stones and balls. Full order was immediately restored. The events themselves, which did not last even a full 10 minutes, had no influence whatsoever on the further peaceful course of the Hallerites' celebration.
—o—
A Meeting of Jewish Commercial Employees Broken Up.
At Targowa 14 [?] in Sosnowiec a general meeting of office and commercial employees took place. During the speech of Comrade S. Warszawski the meeting was broken up by the police.

Small remarks on big matters

[Article — Będzin and Zagłębie, municipal affairs.] The houses and the safety of the tenants.
After balconies began to collapse in Będzin, and together with them human victims also perished — it has already cost lives — the municipal authority came to its senses and began inspecting the balconies in town. Apparently, earlier, as long as this had not become a "mass article", the "work" was taken lightly. In order to inspect the condition of the balconies, they first had to fall down and cost human victims; otherwise it was not understood that such an inspection must be carried out — which is not at all one of the very great things, since this inspection does not involve so many costs. But let us say that even if it did, one should still have allowed oneself the expense, since it is a vital necessity.
But that is not yet all. Let no one think that as soon as a balcony is inspected and found to be dilapidated, one orders a second one [?] to be made or the balcony to be sealed off, and thereby one has already done one's duty. A. [?] The question has far from been settled by such a solution, for one must not forget that the balconies are not everything: there are houses in various parts of the town in a terrible state, and not necessarily the balconies, which catch the eye — it is dangerous to walk up the stairs, and the ceilings are sunken [?]; many of them hang almost in the air — and this not necessarily, as many would think, in old, small houses, but precisely in modern two-, three- and four-storey buildings.
One must therefore set about energetically inspecting the condition of the houses all round, from outside and from inside, for several times already the catastrophes have happened with the balconies, and another time the same can happen with the stairs or ceilings, or above all with a wall.
And no wonder, for many houses have been badly neglected, and during the war no serious repairs were made, so that it is self-evident that the neglected houses have become complete ruins. Now, moreover, the house-owner is not in a good enough position to allow himself a larger repair, so that there is every chance the houses will go to ruin even more. And here the question arises: can this simply be left to God's mercy [?], and what will come of it? The question must not be let pass, for this is not a matter of individuals — it concerns the whole community, and so it must be dealt with more broadly and must absolutely be considered from all sides.
Incidentally, this concerns not only Będzin but the whole of Zagłębie. In Sosnowiec the situation is one and the same, and in the surrounding area it is much worse still.
And therefore a sacred duty lies first of all on the building commissions attached to the Zagłębie magistrates (town councils) to carry out the proper inspection of houses; and afterwards, when the whole material is available and one sees how matters stand, the appropriate resolutions will have to be adopted, which will make it possible to carry out the necessary undertaking-repairs [?].
The question is extremely topical today, and it must be properly considered — the sooner the better — for every delay can cause human victims, about which the past has already sought [?] to give us a good lesson.
This is the duty that lies today on the Zagłębie town councils, and which they must discharge most urgently, for the good of the economy and for the good of the community.
Będzin and the express trains.
In the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce the question was recently considered of the express ("courier") trains once again stopping in Będzin, as they used to. The said institution is to take up the question in order to achieve the desired result.
We wish to hope that with good will and strenuous work it will be possible to bring it about that Będzin citizens too will have the right and the possibility to use the express trains, which until now has become impossible for them.
But we would not wish to rely entirely on the Chamber of Commerce, which, incidentally, is not located in Będzin and has no possibility of feeling the enormous defect for a town when it is deprived of a European necessity that it was always [?] accustomed to use. The inhabitants of Będzin feel it quite differently, for they are on the spot and feel the deficiency on their own shoulders every time.
We mean to say that it is still far from enough that the Chamber of Commerce is occupied with the matter; all the other Będzin institutions too must take it up as they should.
Będzin as a county (powiat) town, Będzin as the oldest town in Zagłębie, Będzin as a commercial centre has the right and the grounds to demand that it not be deprived of the right that is due to it and that it always had.
All economic institutions and the commercial and financial organisations must also simultaneously adopt measures that will make it possible to realise the matter. It [the Chamber] must also enlist the help of the local official and semi-official institutions, which certainly have great influence in the Railway Ministry and with whom one must reckon without any excuse. At the same time one must not forget that the town has the right to demand this from the proper authorities for two reasons: first, as citizens who suffer enormously from it, not only because of the inconvenience but even more materially; and second, the authorities themselves also suffer very much from it on every occasion.
Let the local public figures not take the question lightly, but start an energetic campaign in this field.
One must see to drawing into the interventions [?] all those who need the express trains to stop in Będzin.
One can argue that more passengers get on and off in Będzin than, for example, at a small Upper Silesian station where the express does stop, regardless of the fact that the cashier sells not a single ticket.
No doubt it can be achieved that the expresses continue to stop in Będzin; but since this has already grown somewhat too old — for which the town is to blame — a sacred duty therefore lies on those who represent the town to deal properly with the question and see [?] that the matter is realised, for it is an urgent necessity for all inhabitants of Będzin.
Reducing telephone prices and service to subscribers.
Two more matters were dealt with in the Chamber of Commerce that are worth dwelling on. There was talk of reducing the telephone fee, and of the fact that the service at the exchange is bad.
Of course both demands are justified. That the subscription price must be reduced is self-evident, since a great many monopoly articles and enterprises have become cheaper. And that a cheaper telephone was necessary [?] can be seen from the fact that, owing to the sticking to the price, a very large number of firms have given up their telephones. Had the price reduction come in time, most firms would not have given up the telephones already installed, to which they were already accustomed.
Now, on the other hand, many firms are entertaining the idea of removing their telephones if no reduction comes. Of course, if it should come to that, it will certainly do no good; therefore it is desirable that the reduction come as soon as possible, so that those who are of a mind to give up the telephone refrain from it — so that this may save the situation of the telephone owners now [?] running away.
At the same time one must not forget that the fewer telephone subscribers there are, the less use the telephone owner has of his telephone — so that this too must be taken into consideration today.
The reduction is therefore necessary in order to preserve the popular telephone network; otherwise the telephone will remain a rarity in an average house or at a medium-sized firm — and this is what one must reckon with at the present moment.
Now about the poor service of the telephone staff. The off-handedness of the "young ladies" [operators] exceeds every limit. It happens often enough [?] that one holds the receiver [?] for a few minutes and the exchange does not answer. Just dare to say a word to her, and as a protest she will not answer you at all for a couple of hours, or she will make a point [?] of telling you that the number you ask for is constantly engaged or that it is out of order. That is how she will settle accounts with you, so that a second and a tenth time you will swear off saying a word to her.
Why should the management not react to such awful treatment? Why should the young lady go about with the attitude that she is doing you a favour when she serves you? And the service is like this at a time when the telephone network is not being enlarged — at a time, then, when the employees are not swamped with too much work.
One must therefore make efforts so that the management reacts properly to this defect as well, for after all the subscriber pays for the service, so that he has the right to demand to be treated decently and promptly.
Selekt.
Bankrupt (A Story)

[Serialized story; chapter 1.] By Meir Herz [Meir Herc].
(A story)

1.
People stand in the street and wonder:
— Oh-wah, oh-wah, Reb Simcha Szlamowicz bankrupt too already? Is it really true? How did it happen?
Over the huge display windows, which stretch along half a street, the roller shutters have been let down from inside, and from the other side, outside, they are blocked with the iron bars [?] ("rik-lerns" [?]) with palisade spikes jutting outward.
So they stand, armour-plated, by day and by night, for almost a week now.
On the first day, when the shop was not opened, a rumour spread in town that someone had died at the Szlamowiczes'; people could not imagine it otherwise, for lately they had heard it told that Mrs. Sarale Szlamowicz was not in the best of health, that she lay in bed half-days at a time and did not leave the house. She had always been the mainspring of the business, and not a single transaction was made without her shrewd merchant's calculation and without her reckoning on paper [?]. Reb Simcha used to travel to Łódź, where he was highly respected by the manufacturers; his [?] word was as good as given, and one could discount it for cash. Not to mention when he had signed a bill of exchange — people simply fussed over it and carried it about in their hands like a gold coin. For they knew that to the minute, to the second, and quite possibly even a day or two before the appointed date, the bill would be redeemed.
The Łódź manufacturers had known Reb Simcha Szlamowicz for many years, had done a world of business with him and held him in very high esteem. It was enough for Reb Simcha to write a little letter saying he wanted such-and-such goods, and the goods were sent out no sooner said than done, and sometimes nobody even asked for any security.
The goods that arrived could hardly be unpacked [?] in time, and such an abundance poured into the shop that the dozens of shop assistants simply did not have enough hands and did not know which of the swarm of customers to serve first. From the whole surrounding province, from countless little towns, the merchants came to buy at Reb Simcha Szlamowicz's huge wholesale warehouse.
The takings rose as if on yeast, and already by the next morning the post [?] carried heavy thousands to Łódź, to the manufacturers, who simply could not stop marvelling at such honesty, at such punctuality.
Later, when times grew harder and Reb Simcha himself realized that taking goods on open account obliges one to more punctuality and to earlier payment than buying on bills, he began to travel to Łódź himself more often, and for the most part bought precisely on bills.
It was Sarale, the clever businesswoman, who had opened his eyes to this. She was the whole sales force, and when she grasped that the small-town merchants were short of ready cash and were starting to write bills, she said to her husband:
— Simcha, I don't like this business. Jews are beginning to lose their money, things are getting bad, we are starting to walk on a paper bridge. The merchants pay with bills, and you deal with the Łódź manufacturers on your word, and that is no good; to me a word is stronger than a bill, because one has to pay at once. So it is better that you, too, should trade on bills. I want to see the customers' bills fall due before yours, and so we will be able to remain honest people.
Reb Simcha obeyed, and the trade went over to bills. But Sarale Szlamowicz realized afterwards that she had made a mistake. That was after protests [of unpaid bills] began to come in from the provincial merchants, and from the other side a flood of taxes came down; the well-known, reliable and solid firm of Szlamowicz began to feel how an invisible hand was pulling a strong rope, and little by little, little by little, the noose draws closer to the throat and grows ever tighter, until one begins to run short of air.
One day, when tall lorries ("autobuses"), laden with goods, stood before the wide-open doors, when the great consignments were being carried in on the shoulders of dozens of porters into Szlamowicz's giant [?] warehouse, Sarale stood by the counter ("buffet") near the cash desk, her lovely, refined face turned to the wall, and wiped the tears from her eyes with a white handkerchief.
In the shop there was a tremendous din, a clamour; all the rooms were full of merchants from places near and far, devouring with sparkling eyes the splendid goods unpacked on display, and each of them had already chosen in his mind such-and-such a pattern. Each one was quietly reckoning to himself which goods to take and for how many roubles [?]. The shop assistants stood on the tables or on tall ladders, making room for the goods. Everyone was toiling, and hardly anyone noticed whether the great capable woman, the clever businesswoman Sarale Szlamowicz, was in the shop at all.
