The Jews in the Provinces

Do you know Szczekociny? And perhaps you have been in Żarnowiec[?], Pilica, Skała, and in Siewierz on the market square — you haven't been there either? A pity: one can see many things there that deserve attention, admiration and even sympathy. Of course, whoever is impressed by the big-city tumult, the café life and the hooting of the automobiles — let him go on dragging himself along the pavements forever, smelling the petrol and the rumble of the buses, because there, in the provinces, life is a little different. How many inhabitants? — a thousand, two thousand; to the county (powiat) town it is a long way, an hour by bus; quiet, small houses, with and without fences, a sleep as if of decades. On the market square a little group[?] of people. The shops empty, the shopkeeper downcast. What do people live on? To earn one złoty a day, 100 groszy — that is a fantasy. One box of matches is sold to several peasants, 8 matches for a grosz. And on such a "turnover" one still has to pay taxes. Yet the Jew manages to keep himself going in the hardest conditions, and that is no longer a miracle, but simply a habit: one lives with hope, one believes in tomorrow.
There are also "rich men": one has a wooden house on the market square, another deals in horses and owns over a hundred złoty in cash and — eight hundred zł. of debts; the third has a cousin in the county town who married the daughter of a deceased merchant, and a brother of that merchant had a brother-in-law whose uncle owned two houses in Warsaw before the war. That is what the Jewish "estates" (majątki) look like — mere legends, but quite often one has to pay taxes on these legends too.
Spring: the orchards begin to blossom, and then Jews go out for months on end into the orchards they leased back in January, and there they sleep in the huts.
Quiet are the provincial nights.
———
There, where the antisemitic agitation does not reach, Jews and Poles live in peace and even in friendship, and help one another. The Jew buys from the peasant and at the same time gives him advice in his farming and even family matters. The peasant listens comfortably as the Jew pours his heart out to him, shakes his head with pity; they confer about their common poverty. Illnesses[.] They weep together in misfortune, invite each other to celebrations, respect each other's holidays and feel no hatred whatsoever toward each other. But there, where an Endek agitator appears, where the Christian shopkeeper subscribes to an Endek rag in which people are incited to all kinds of vileness and in which every infamy and crime concerning Jews is believed — there hatred seizes old and young. Some towns are enormously[?] steeped in "politics" and already have parties; regarding antisemitism there is unanimity among them: some favour an open, pogrom antisemitism, others like a quiet, discreet, but no less effective antisemitism. These towns are mostly in the neighbourhood of large cities, where the anti-Jewish agitation finds support or friendly neutrality. Small-town folk are more naive and readily believe the assurances that the Jews are to blame for the crisis, to blame that grain is cheap and for the hardship in general. One can easily persuade them that Jews are to blame for the flood.
———
One need not be too surprised at the success of antisemitism in the provinces, where people blindly believe all sorts of "arguments", if even in the circles of the Jewish intelligentsia it is considered "good form" to speak a little ill of the Jew. To such an intellectual the Jewish kapota looks less aesthetic than a peasant's sukmana (sermięga) or bekesza. That is a matter of taste. One need only add that the long kapota was actually worn in the Middle Ages by the Polish "mieszczanin" (townsman).
This does not prevent Polish writers of Jewish origin from coming out, of all times today, with abuse and mockery aimed at the long kapotas and at their poor knowledge of the Polish language. The latter is already somewhat exaggerated. The Polish elementary school has existed for only eighteen years, and yet how nicely Jewish children, the Jewish youth, already speak Polish, even when they attend their own Jewish schools; and the older merchants? Where would they know this beautiful but difficult language so excellently from? After all, they attended Russian schools, where no Polish was taught!
I have strayed somewhat from the subject, because in speaking about the provinces, and also about the provincial towns in the vicinity of Zagłębie which I recently visited, I wanted to stress their truly extraordinary cultural development. The spiritual awakening of the Jewish youth — the big-city libraries cannot compare with the libraries in the small towns; there people simply devour books, newspapers wander from hand to hand throughout the whole town. There are cultural and educational associations, literary societies.
It would be worthwhile to work out a geography of the Polish provinces, worthwhile to take a closer interest in the small towns. True, these towns have no radio stations, but what one hears from them in the silence, without language and without words, is worth listening to, in order to learn from it.
M. B.
A Procession of Holidays.

[Holidays — feuilleton.] (A short feuilleton).
The holiday of mosaic is gone: not "of one piece" [?], but every day a different content and a different name.
Last Sunday, first — "Hoshana Rabbah". That is already the greatest effort, like a national loan. After the ordinary hoshanot, like the ordinary taxes, do not help, one turns to the real hoshana, with the twig, one thrashes [?] and whips it at "Kol mevaser", and then one throws it under the bench; and if God helps later and one already gets the [—?] ["sarpingn"] note, one puts on a show as if [?] one had got it not by squeezing the hoshana but for one's own good deeds...
The next day came Shemini Atzeret, and that is a somewhat strange holiday. In essence a continuation of what came before: the same "Hallel", even with the two middle pieces, the same sukkah, the same "season of our rejoicing", only the name is new. Lest someone get sick of too long a procession of Sukkot days.
And the prayers were refreshed with a bit of "Geshem" [the prayer for rain], which one weaves and trills [?] in the gloomy melody of the Days of Awe, as if to say: you think that, having already snatched a little note, you are done and need carry no yoke on your head any more? You are mistaken, little Jew! The note is only a general one, like today's constitutions, in which all that is good may be written, but which have no practical, meaningful value; only now must you still pray for "rain", for simple matters of livelihood, for a piece of bread, for a potato, a roll.. The main thing, you understand me, is the interpretation of the constitution, its realization.
And if you like, it is the same story with the League of Nations in Geneva: you may whine out the finest resolution there, and afterwards you must only begin to beg and fight for every crumb of bread separately.
That is "Shemini Atzeret".
And then comes Simchat Torah. The only Jewish holiday of joy. Here is the question: why does one rejoice with the Torah now and not at Shavuot, when it was given? To this Rabbenu Bahya answers that the main joy is not that the Torah is given, but that it is kept — again the same story with the constitution on paper and in life...
Other commentators say that at Shavuot, in spring, when there are other joys, one can then go out into the woods, roll about in the greenery and the fragrances, bathe in invigorating air; but now, in autumn, when everything is damp ["fervilgatsht", from Polish wilgotny] and the air is soaked through with raindrops, is the most fitting time to rejoice with the Torah...
And the Simchat Torah service is full of mosaic that catches the eye. You get the hakafah, with the real "Ozer dalim" [Helper of the poor]. What is meant here is no longer a loan ["pozhitshke", pożyczka], only a little credit. Tomorrow, for your business, you will get no credit even if you strip yourself naked; a Torah scroll, on the other hand, you get on credit: somebody lends it to you so that [?] you may turn around with it a little, dance around, and he is sure that you will not slip it into your pocket — that is exactly why he entrusts you with the Torah...
Today, Hatan Torah and Hatan Bereshit... Well, for a bridegroom to come to "Bereshit" [a beginning] is a rarity nowadays; but for a bridegroom to make his way to a chair [?] ["kat"] of Torah at a university is also very hard — that is why they sit, the graduates, at home and practise small-town politics instead of sitting in a place of Torah and creasing the bench...
Soon after that comes again the plain Shabbat Bereshit: if you like, the holiday is already over, and if you like, it is a double-eightfold holiday — no small matter, the true Sabbath of the Creation of the world, the Sabbath of Sabbaths, which hides all the holidays up its sleeve, and so one must go on eating fish and meat and kugel and broth and tzimmes, and for everything one must have money, and everything I must [?] prepare today, on the eve of the holiday, and that is the real "af grey" [?]...
And when you have already holidayed yourselves for four days, fattened the soul together with the body, emptied the pocket, there comes again a day with the name "Isru Hag!" — don't ask me, on pain of ban, what it means; I only know that I must hang about by the shop and once again [—?] ["lustshen"] the pocket emptied by the long procession of holidays...
What Zagłębie Chimneys Tell

[Sosnowiec — poetry.]
Chimneys stand upon the roofs,
threatening fists, swollen [?],
chimneys tell each other stories,
they know many still untold...

"Comrades, it's bitter, it's not good!
A chimney spits out sparks,
like a consumptive spitting blood —
that will one day sink away.

Let world and man be equal now!
Let there be no poor, no rich,
for how long is the measure...
to look on at pain and suffering? — we ask

— — In the basement, four by four,
lives a family of eight;
the weakened father, the porter,
lies in bed,
a loaf of bread is seldom brought home.

The mother washes linen in people's houses;
the children, rickety, skin and bone,
tubercular, scrofulous, cry and beg:
'Daddy, we're faint for food, give us bread, bread'!

And how long is the measure
to look on at pain and suffering, tell me,
faithful comrades all over the world,
why the poor man suffers so?.."

"You argue, and I still cannot understand,
objects a sooty bakery chimney —
day after day, night after night, they bake nothing but bread,
and you come along and tell of want"!..

"You idiot of a bakery chimney —
a chimney among red roof tiles speaks up —
with that bread bourgeois stomachs stuff themselves,
they gobble it at the cost of your bread, and not only bread"!..

Breaking in, spitting black pillars of smoke,
a threatening red factory chimney:
"Pah! What good is telling you stories,
may one fire sweep away all of theirs"!

— — — — — — — — — —

Chimneys stand upon the roofs,
threatening fists, swollen [?],
chimneys tell each other stories,
they know many still untold...
Sosnowiec, 1934.
Lejzer Szykman.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bereshit)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bereshit
The Portion.
—o—
a) "And God blessed the seventh day" (Gen. 2:3)
"The blessing of the Lord, it maketh rich, and He addeth no sorrow with it" — this is the Sabbath, as it is said: "And God blessed the seventh day."
A blessing without sorrow is actually impossible, because the more blessing, the more worry: "He who increases possessions increases worry", "He who has a hundred wants two hundred." Only the blessing of the Sabbath, of which it is said: "Whoever honours the Sabbath is given an inheritance without bounds" — that is, an inexhaustible wealth — can already be free of the accompanying sorrow, for with infinite riches "he who has a hundred wants two hundred" simply does not apply...
Tzintzenet ha-Man.
—o—
b) "And He took one of his ribs" (Gen. 2:21)
Woman was not created from man's hand, nor from his foot, nor from another limb, but from the side, from a limb that one does not use — to show that the woman too must take such a role in man's life... Unhappy is the man to whom the woman must bring a livelihood, for whom she must be a useful limb...
Arono shel Yosef.
—o—
c) "And behold, it was very good" (Gen. 1:31)
"Very good — this is the evil inclination." Midrash.
"Very good": everything that is too good, that is too pious — this is the evil inclination, this is the work of the evil inclination...
Sama de-Hayei.
—o—
d) "Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife... cursed is the ground" (Gen. 3:17)
So it is a sin to listen to one's wife's advice. Adam [printed "Aram"] was cursed for it: "because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife"; and thus the Gemara says in Bava Metzia, folio 84 [?]: in matters of piety one should indeed consult one's wife, but in other matters one should not follow her advice...
Pri ha-Tzvi [?].
—o—
e) "And Adam called his wife's name Eve" (Gen. 3:20)
Rashi remarks that the verse belongs far higher up, by "And Adam gave names to every living thing" [so printed], so why indeed is the verse said only now?
Because to praise [?] Eve, that she is "the mother of all living", and therefore to call her — as the verse says — Eve, Adam could only do once he had been told about death: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." As long as Adam did not know about death, he did not know how to appreciate life...
Sihat Hullin.
—o—
f) [printed "r)"] "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground" (Gen. 3:19)
For so long you will toil in the sweat of your brow. You will rush about and work for a living, with toil and sweat you will want to win something for yourself in life — till you return unto the ground, until life will be no more...
Mashal u-Melitza.
—o—
g) "And the Lord said unto him: Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold" (Gen. 4:15)
"...Cattle, beasts and fowl gathered to demand the blood of Abel. He said to them: Therefore I say, whoever kills Cain shall be killed. Rabbi Levi said: The primordial serpent came to demand the blood of Abel. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: Therefore I say, whoever kills Cain shall be killed."
Midrash Rabba.
Everything depends on luck, even a commandment. There is one commandment that everybody wants to fulfil: the commandment "so shalt thou put away the evil from the midst of thee"... Even the primordial serpent is suddenly a relative and comes to take up the cause of Abel's blood... All the cattle, beasts and fowl came to demand his blood... The good fortune of a commandment!... Even of Nebuzaradan the Gemara relates (Gittin 54b [?]) that he took up the cause of the blood of Zechariah and slaughtered thousands of Jews for it. Anything to take up the cause of whoever has been wronged...
Hegyonot el Ami.
End-of-Harvest Celebration

[Palestine — feuilleton; the end-of-harvest festival in a kvutza in the Jezreel Valley.] (Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".) By the beloved Eretz-Israel poet Yizraeli.
At daybreak the bustle began. Even before the sun came out from behind the Gilboa hills, people were already up for their work. Each to his corner, to his task, alone or together with others. At the bell's command everyone streams out of the houses and the barracks, disperses and spreads far, far out over the fields, vineyards and orange groves, for there is truly a great deal of work here, and besides, this year is a bumper year, a blessed year — after years of want and troubles, of natural mishaps and disasters. It is harvest time; the vineyards are laden with fruit and the fields gleam with plenty. The ears bend under full, thick grains and beg to be cut. The vegetable garden has dressed itself in red; it catches the eye and entices. The tomatoes have clambered up the wires of the fences that stretch along its length, have branched out and stayed hanging in the air. They are redder than red and bursting with ripeness. The kvutza lies under the yoke of its burden, so people rise at dawn and come back late — so that the hand should not tire of gathering and collecting the good fortune with which the earth has overflowed [?] and blessed the labour with abundance.
But something unusual was felt that early morning; a special feeling accompanied those who went out to work, a good, pleasant and heart-refreshing feeling accompanied those who went out to work. "Today is the end of the harvest," one quietly said to another, and from the hillock spread out the reaped, bald-shorn fields, small and large heaps of straw scattered far and wide, to east and west, on all sides — all finished. Only one small patch of field still stands stubbornly and looks around stiffly and haughtily, because the reapers chose it for the closing of the harvest. "Today is the end of the harvest," the grape pickers tease the grain cutters. "We still have work for days and weeks, and with you, 'shearers', it's already over." And the grain cutters answer with a dismissive smile those who are only now starting from "Bereshit". Out went the tractors with clattering laughter, and after them the winged machine, serious and fully responsible; they rose carefully and with powerful strides, they went out to pronounce the blessing over the completion. All day long eyes followed from the hillock the combine that showed itself on the horizon. Today is the end of the harvest. In that feeling there was something of release from a yoke, relief from the everyday anxiety, and above all the bumper crop, the loaded wagons, the full granaries and storehouses. Here in the middle of the yard there is no barn of straw and no heaps of dry branches, but little hills of sacks laid out in rows, each kind in its own rows. Wheat and barley, full, plump grains, reddish and ringing like little sparkling drops of gold. The eye is sated and the heart is glad, for the village has seen good fortune in its toil; the earth has come forward to meet its owners.
At midday, when the members sat around the tables waiting for lunch, the dining hall buzzed with arguments, because opinions were divided about the time of the celebration. Some demanded that it be postponed to Friday night, and with a just argument: tomorrow is Shabbat, a day of rest, so it would be a double celebration. But in the end the view prevailed that no celebration should be put off: this very day they would dance, this very day they would sing, this very day they would celebrate the wonderful event — there was no strength to wait. Someone taps on a plate — the sign of a public announcement: Comrades, today is the end of the harvest; this evening we will celebrate our holiday, the holiday of the harvest. The members received the news with jubilation, for the soul was seeking an outlet. The eyes bore witness to it; the faces expressed joy.
The bell rang: gan, gan, tsil-tsil-tsil, gan, gan, tsil-tsil-tsil. The celebration begins. The members are not in their rooms, because that evening after supper they did not go home as always; they gathered in the yard, made plans, worked at decorating the dining hall with greenery, flowers and sheaves of grain, gave advice and made up inventions — this one one thing, the other another — how and in what order the evening would be celebrated. A merry group of children mingled with the grown-ups, pushing and jostling as they pleased, making noise and laughing, and filled the space with laughter and joy. The yard roared with people. Everyone gathered outdoors, chatting and joking freely and proudly. Mules and wagons, horses and riders, machines, tractors and all kinds of work tools — everything suddenly appeared, sprang up in a single moment. Even the two donkeys that stood in the sheep pen were troubled from their bedding and led out to the square where people and beasts had gathered. They pierced the air and deafened the ears with their unrestrained, sky-rending braying. The foals sensed that their mothers were gone and came out of the stable at a gallop, running and leaping with a loud, unbridled [?] cry of joy, nostrils flared, tails raised high, running and whirling. Over the Gilboa hills stood a half moon, wondering and gazing down from above at the valley. Its light kept moving, and now it propped itself on the mountain top like a broken and ridiculous horn. Darkness descended on the village and wrapped the yard. On the tower of the dining hall a torch was lit, and trumpets sounded. "Move to the patch of field near the village" — an order was heard. And the whole group moved off with noise and tumult. People and beasts mingled, all striding, all walking; nobody asks what for or where to.
When the kvutza reached the field, silence reigned. Faces became serious and silent. Everyone was seized by the smell of the earth, the smell of grain. Here is the patch of field of the completion. Here the hope of years sprouted; from here the joy too will sprout. All lined up in rows — children and grown-ups. Parents and children go out in a procession, bringing home the blessing of the field.
The torch was raised on the village tower. The trumpets sounded — a signal for the procession; dozens of torches were lit; at the head the riders with torches in their hands, after them the grain cutters carrying sheaves of grain, ploughs, sowing machines, the combine with its wings and on it sacks of grain; on the balcony stood all who can sing, with torches in their hands; rows of children singing, and after them all the people of the kibbutz from great to small — not one was missing. When the procession reached the gate of the yard, a song burst from every throat.
The heavy seriousness vanished from the faces; they became light and liberated, young and naive as children. "If not now, when?", "If I am not for myself, who will be for me?" rang out again and again. The words encourage and the melody refreshes. [?] They make hakafot around the buildings, cheer in honour of the horse stable, cheer in honour of the cowshed. "Hurrah" for the sheep and "hurrah" for the cattle. Every yoke has been thrown off. Light is the body and glad the heart, seeing what has been created: from a hill of desolation to a hill of plenty, from a small band to a permanent settlement. Hurrah! Hurrah!
In the dining hall the ceremony began. On a small, beautifully decorated platform the eldest of the members received the grain the procession had brought, and spoke before it in warm, moving words: We have gone through long years of effort until we reached this. Drought, a plague of mice, lack of rain and all kinds of bad mishaps that nature brought upon us to test us on the spot. Not easily did the earth come to meet us. It is stubborn and it subjugates very harshly. But our will conquered it; it submitted to our strength and bestowed on us with a generous hand. Great is the harvest and great is the blessing. The earth has shown its strength.
One of the members began to sing:
Your time too, reaper, has now come,
Listen closely, hear the good tidings,
Full is the barn, full is the row,
The head of the ear is golden from suns.
And after him all joined in:
Those who sow in tears shall reap with song.
Long they went on singing, long they went on dancing. Forgotten the toil of the day, vanished the weariness, the feet are light and light is the soul. The faces flush, the eyes burn:
Light and good, light and good,
Be merry, lad, beat the drum.
It is already two past midnight and the line dances still roar on. Circle after circle. Dances of enthusiasm and exaltation of the soul, joined, interwoven and bound together with the bond of comradeship, with the bond of toil and with the bond of creation.
The valley is sunk in darkness, the light extinguished; a little more and day will begin to break, the sun will burst out of the east over the furrows. Over all the scattered hillocks — the settlement points of the valley. Whole blocks of soil, firm and strong as if forged foundations, watchful in their place. There are dozens of them here in the Jezreel Valley, settlement points founded by Keren Hayesod; they fought the mishaps of nature and time, and this year they saw blessing from their toil — the earth has given its fruit. Yesterday everyone celebrated the holiday of its harvest.
Character — Our Poverty

[Essay — Jewish society and culture; the Yiddish theatre.] Poverty, people say, is no disgrace, but it is not true: poverty is indeed a great disgrace. Of nothing is one so ashamed as of poverty; except when one makes a living out of poverty — then one dresses it up, so as to look as poor as possible, and carries it out into the street, so that everyone can see it as well as possible. But when one does not make a living out of poverty, one hides it in the innermost chambers, so that no one should notice it, as though being poor were not merely a great disgrace but a great crime. And that is precisely why the saying "poverty is no disgrace" was later amended. The words "but no ornament either" were added to it. But that is too weak; I would rather say short and sharp that poverty is a great swinishness.
I know it is not a nice word, but where does one take a nicer word to [?] say it — to say that poverty is bad, ugly, vile is not enough. One needs a stronger word, and I can find no other word than swinishness. The Germans say that poverty is no disgrace, but — a "Lumperei" [a shabby business]. But that too is too delicate. They should rather have said that poverty is a "Schweinerei" [a swinishness]. But it makes no difference to me what word one uses for it; the main thing for me here is to say that poverty is a very, very shabby, vile thing, and that is why one is so ashamed of it.
And it is not only a matter of personal poverty. About personal poverty even the Gemara already said that it is a great ugliness. Beautiful are Jewish daughters, says the Gemara, only their [?] poverty makes them ugly. But the Gemara, which [?] knows so well what ugliness is for the individual Jew, is precisely [?] of the opinion that for the whole Jewish people poverty is very becoming. Poverty, says the Gemara, is becoming to the people of Israel and suits it like a red bridle [?] on a white horse. And with exactly this I do not agree. I say that poverty is a great ugliness too, not only for Reb Yisroel but also for the people of Israel. And if material poverty is a great swinishness, cultural poverty is an even greater one.
If it were only a matter of the material poverty of the Jewish people, it could still somehow be endured. There is a view that materially Jews are not so poor at all. There are opinions that Jews are materially rich. But that is a lie. There are rich Jews, but the Jewish people in general is a pauper. True, not as great a pauper as people often try to present it, but a rich man it certainly is not. Much worse is the case with our cultural poverty. Here we are enormous paupers, and want whistles through every corner.
I know that in certain circles people will take offence at me for my words. It is still a duty nowadays to shout in all the streets that culturally we are great rich men, and when I say that there is want, I have insulted Jewish national honour; my Jewish national duty is to say that Jewish literature is rich and great, that Jewish art has reached a high level, and that Jewish culture in general has grown wonderfully.
But I cannot help myself. Sometimes one feels like putting the "national duty" aside and telling the truth, and the truth is that culturally we are still great paupers.
And the worst thing about a pauper is that not only must others always take pity on him, but he himself must look upon himself with pity; this very self-pity brings us to the point that we quite often have to say that something is beautiful when it is ugly, and that it is a success when it is good for nothing.
And when one is a pauper, every little rag is a whole fortune that has to be guarded. Yes, one may not even say that it is a rag, but that it is a piece of silk.
Let me take, for example, our Yiddish theatre. I take it because the Yiddish theatre is right now on the agenda. There is, namely, a crisis in the Yiddish theatre — so we are told. And if one cannot do away with the crisis, it is at least a good subject to talk and write about. So people talk and write.
Theatre is a part of human culture, and the Yiddish theatre is a part of Jewish culture. If theatre were merely a business, people would not have talked and written so much about the theatre crisis. The crisis in tailoring and in shoemaking is certainly no smaller now than the crisis in the theatre, and yet people talk and write about the crisis in tailoring and shoemaking much less, incomparably less than about the crisis in the theatre.
And not only in the theatre do we have beggary and want; the same is true of Yiddish literature, of the Yiddish book market, of Jewish cultural institutions and of Jewish enterprises — everywhere the pauper. Everywhere want, and one must always have pity, and one must always be careful lest it do harm, and so one can rarely say a full-blooded word of truth.
I know that I was not supposed to say this; it is an insult, one person will reproach me; it is harmful, another will tell me. And I will not defend myself. I have touched a sore point. I have touched our poverty, and poverty is a great disgrace. And worse than everything is that it is a great pity.

The Bastard (Der Mamzer), 3 — a gripping tragic novel by an Ilui

Adv. S. Geliszkowski[?].
The Bastard (Der Mamzer). (3
A gripping tragic novel by an "Ilui".
And when it was already broad daylight and nothing was left that could burn, the fire went out with the help of the firemen.
Everyone dispersed; the night watchman whistled his last six whistles and went off to rest after the sleepless night.
Only Reb Avrom remained, alone, searching and rummaging among the ruins, but evidently not finding what he was looking for.
"Panie Langnas," he hears a voice behind him.
He turns round and sees beside him the starszy strażnik [senior constable] with two more...
"Where is your son-in-law?" asks the starszy.
"My son-in-law? What do you need him for."
"That we will tell you later; you tell us for now where he is."
A shudder runs through Reb Avrom's body. All sorts of thoughts begin to tangle in his head.
"But surely you can tell me what you need him for," he says to the senior constable.
"We have to arrest him; we already know that this is his doing."
"What doing? What do you know?" asks a trembling Avrom.
"He set fire to the house; we even know at what hour; there is a witness."
On hearing such a thing Avrom stepped closer to them and began to prove to them that their suspicion was groundless.
But Reb Avrom's arguments did not help. "We must arrest him," the elder one kept insisting.
Long, very long did Avrom Langnas argue with them, and he obtained that his son-in-law would not be arrested before nightfall.
Like a thunderclap the terrible news fell upon everyone.
"How can it be, how can it be!" everyone cried and said. "Where has such a thing ever been heard of? Such a false accusation, such a false accusation!"
Khanele wept and wrung her hands, looking at her broken father and mother. Everyone wept with them. Reb Avrom borrowed money together for Beniminidl's expenses, packed up his remaining things and in great haste took him to the German border, which he had to cross illegally that very night in order to escape from there to America. Father-in-law, mother-in-law and Khanele rode along with him to the border, as far as the Słupca forest. The father and mother lamented and wept over the dark fate of their only daughter. Khanele did not weep: she saw in it God's punishment for having broken her word, which she had given — if only in jest — to Pan Naum Rozen.
Gloomy, utterly broken, Beniminidl took leave of his father-in-law and mother-in-law and of his seven-day-old little wife, promising to write to her immediately as soon as[?] he reached America.
"Czas nie stoi [time does not stand still]," said the peasant, who for a three-ruble fee had undertaken to smuggle Beniminidl across the border, "make it quicker, for they may still seize us."
Beniminidl gives the last kiss on Khanele's forehead and says the last "Stay well."
The peasant cracks the whip, the horses leap from their place and vanish into the dense Słupca forest, which leads to the German border.
The night was very dark. Not a single star showed in the sky. On such a night one is sure not to fall into the hands of the border guard. One grows bolder. One can even smoke a papirosa. And without thinking long the peasant takes from his pocket his pouch of makhorka, rolls a thick cigar to last half an hour, and...
"Stój! [Halt!]" they hear someone give an order.
Both tremble and quiver with fright and fear; the peasant trembles lest he lose his horse and wagon — and Beniminidl?
"Don't be afraid," they hear someone say, coming closer to the wagon, "I am no snatcher, no. I have been waiting here for you a long time. I knew you would have to[?] be here, so I decided to wait until you drove up, so as to catch a ride with you. I am tired already and have no strength to walk any further. What, perhaps you are not pleased?" he says, climbing into the wagon. "Wojtek, drive!" he shouts, giving the driver a slap on the shoulder. "What, don't you recognise me? A devil in your father's father!"
The peasant cracks the whip and peers into the stranger's face.
"Ah, Jesus!" he cries. "Why, it's Pan Roz..."
"Shut up and drive," the other orders him, not letting him finish his surname.
"You know, I am driving Pan Avrom's son-in-law, who married his daughter a week ago?"
"So, so," says the stranger, "very pleased."
"So you are Reb Avrom Langnas's son-in-law?"
"Yes," answers Beniminidl, still frightened, and very pleased that the stranger knows his father-in-law.
"You are smuggling yourself across the border and I am smuggling myself across too," says the stranger with a sarcastic laugh, "so we are colleagues po fachu [in the same trade], ha-ha ha!"
"Yes, yes," says Beniminidl with a foolish smile, still frightened.
"If so," says the stranger, "we must join hands, and from this day on we shall wander together. You are going to America, aren't you?"
"Yes, I am going to America," answers Beniminidl.
"And so am I; so we'll travel together, all right?"
"Excellent. I am very glad that the Holy One, blessed be He, has brought us together. Everything is from Heaven, everything comes from above."
"Right, right, quite right, everything comes from above..."
"You can get down now," says the driver, stopping the horses.
"Where are we?" asks the stranger.
"Here, on the highway to Strzałkowo," says the driver, pointing in the dark to the right.
"Right, that's it," says the stranger and jumps down from the wagon.
Beniminidl too gets down from the wagon, taking the little valise with him.
The stranger takes a ruble out of his pocket, hands it to the peasant and says, "Here, that's for your trouble."
"Thank you, Panie Rozen — oh, excuse me, I forgot that I mustn't call out your name."
"Jazda, drive on!" says the stranger, who was none other than Naum Rozen, Reb Avrom Langnas's bookkeeper.
Chapter 3.
How does Rozen come to be here? the driver racked his brains. Could he too have taken part in setting fire to Pan Avrom's house? In town they somehow say that the new son-in-law did it; they wanted to arrest him — but how does Pan Rozen come to be here? Why is he fleeing abroad?
And the driver did not know, Reb Avrom did not know, and Khanele did not know either — nobody knew — that the sudden fire during the last of the Sheva Brachot had come about by none other than Rozen's hand.
He had done it, having sworn to take revenge on Khanele: he hired two thugs, who for a good sum set fire to Reb Avrom Langnas's house. And not only set it on fire, but also went to report where one has to that they had seen with their own eyes how Reb Avrom Langnas's new son-in-law set fire to the house in order to collect the large fire-insurance money.
And Rozen knew that Reb Avrom would not let his son-in-law be locked up; he knew that for a good sum they would buy the son-in-law off and send him away across the German border, because the matter smelled of prison.
He knew everything, this Rozen, and like a good conductor he directed with his baton the base operation, which was bound to force the son-in-law to leave Poland and at the same time Khanele as well — whom he loves dearly and will give to no one.
And like all villains, the base Rozen too succeeded: his plan was to separate Khanele from Beniminidl by every possible means, so as to marry her himself later.

The "Cooking Ladle" — The Holiday Is Over!... / In the Six Days of Creation

[Humour and satire — the "Der Kokh-Lefl" (Cooking Ladle) page; poems.] The "Cooking Ladle". Humour and satire in honour of Shabbat Bereshit. By Amotsl.
The Holiday Is Over!...
1.
The holiday is over.. it's windy.., the birds have fallen silent,
the sechach is scattered, the sukkah taken apart...
Dead lie the great willows,
the lulav will expire, like the Sejm — a man condemned to death..
The quiet "Hoshana" — a goat is already chewing it,
it will go out, poor thing, like a premier's ecstasy...
2.
The field is desolate, the leaf is yellow,
the forest — it stands bare,
oh dear, a town councillor is preparing
a report for the voters..
Who knows, ah, whether the report
will not betray its maker,
whether on his tram ticket
he will not make protests...
G. K.
—o—
In the Six Days of Creation
In honour of Shabbat Bereshit
When God had created the earth and the heavens,
and was already longing[?] to squeeze in a nap,
He suddenly remembers — a wife is still needed,
to be created for Adam, of blood and of body.
A trifle[?]! "A woman must be born at once!"
And here Shabbat is approaching, soon it won't be permitted
to create and to work, to do any melacha,
for Shabbat is holy through Kiddush and blessing.
So God at once ordered His angels
to grab hold of Adam and give him a jab,
(that is, to inject him with such a substance
from which a person falls into a sleep),
and carefully "take" a rib from his side
and create a woman — for God and for people.
* *
Quickly snatching the seal of the Ineffable Name,
the angels at once spread their wings
and carried out the operation in full;
they create a little woman — a true grace;
only one small flaw — her gullet is empty[?],
she is missing, poor thing, in her little mouth — the tongue!
In their haste they had simply forgotten
that one needs a tongue to speak and to eat.
And when the angels said: "May it be Thy will
that such-and-such limbs sprout from the rib"!
the tongue they just failed to mention,
because it lies hidden in the mouth, concealed.
But never mind! A tongue can be created separately,
and indeed they at once performed the wonder.
The situation, however, remained quite pitiful:
for the tongue to grow on — that is impossible,
for from a person's birth until his grave
a new limb can never grow on him.
So they remain standing with the tongue in their hands
and look for a means, a new patent.
They stand and don't know what to do,
how does one fasten [—?] the tongue on to her?
And now it is getting late. Any moment night will fall,
they think and have thought up nothing,
until, God helped, the devil flies by
and gives them some advice — let it be on a little screw...
From the Torah Portion.

[Humour and satire — the "Der Kokh-Lefl" page; parody on Parshat Bereshit.] Interpreted by Socrates.
"And the earth was without form and void" — proof that the crisis was created before everything else, for who brings chaos into the world if not the crisis?
"And darkness was upon the face of the deep" — a hint that when business goes under, the face darkens.
"The land of Havilah, where there is gold" — proof that money is only "chwilowe" [Polish: temporary]... it will not [last] forever.
"That compasses the whole land of Cush" — a hint that the "kush" [Yiddish: kiss] ("let him kiss me") is a very marketable article in the world.
"In the Garden of Eden, to till it and to keep it" — that if you work energetically and have a złoty, you can have the Garden of Eden in this world.
"And a deep sleep fell upon the man and He created the woman" — so that man should not see from what poisonous substances woman is made...
"And He took one of his ribs" — why precisely from the sides? It is a hint that because of her he will have to work with his sides...
"This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh" — proof that she will break his bones and tear off pieces of his flesh.
"And Cain was a tiller of the ground" — proof that the farmer [rolnik] has something to chew.
"And Abel was a keeper of sheep" — that if the wife hammers at his teeth [nags him] and he "grazes" her, then he really is a hevel, a nothing.
"Where is Abel thy brother? And he said: I know not" — that when the poor brother, the hevel, the nothing, cries "oy", the rich brother says: "I know not, I don't know you at all."
"The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, the mighty men of renown" — proof that already in ancient times the currencies of the strong states caught the falling sickness [epilepsy].
"Noah was a righteous man" — because he did not make any speculations when letting [creatures] into the ark...
After Bereshit comes the portion of Noah, because only the beginning is hard; afterwards it gets easier [noach = easy].
"And the door of the ark shalt thou set in its side" — a hint that when you do someone a favour, you must leave yourself a little door to crawl out of the evil he will repay you with for the favour.
We Are Still at Bereshit...

[Humour and satire — the "Der Kokh-Lefl" page; Zagłębie kehillas.] The Sosnowiec "Mizrachi" shouts that the kehilla elections have already been confirmed, while Englard's side is only — at Bereshit.
With some of the parnassim in Dąbrowa the "rabbi" is already in their pocket, but the opposition comes and argues: we are only — at Bereshit.
In many kehillas they are already thinking about how to draw up the kehilla budget for 1935, and in the Będzin and Sosnowiec kehillas they are — at Bereshit.
The building of the Będzin [printed "Bendinger"] mikveh has been going on for 10 years. But when the present building commission set to work, it saw that one must begin — from Bereshit.
For weeks the Zionist camp was abuzz that peace was drawing near. It turned out, however, that every party is still only — at Bereshit.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Meeting of the General Zionists in Będzin

[Będzin — Zionism.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 26 Tishrei 5695 — piątek 5 października 1934 [Friday, 5 October 1934].)
Meeting of the General Zionists in Będzin.
On 27 September a general meeting of the Zionist organization took place in its own premises.
Mr. Wygodzki opens the meeting and honours the memory of the Zionist dead, especially the great loss of H. N. Bialik.
Mr. M. Preger was elected chairman; as assessors: Dr. Steiger, Tintpulwer; as secretaries: Seger[?], Gärtner and Moshe Warszawicz[?].
The report on the year's activity is given by Mr. Wygodzki, who declares that many opportunities were not exploited. There are few active members, but despite all the difficulties and obstructions the organization has fulfilled its task. "We have now come together," says Mr. Wygodzki, "at a hard time for Jewry, both in the economic and in the political field. Jewish rights are being restricted; as glaring proof one may point to the facts — the systematic[?] chicanery against the 'Tarbut' schools and the dismissal of Jewish teachers from their posts. Now every Jew can already see that the only solution to the Jewish question is in Eretz Israel."
The report of the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael is given by Mr. Suszczek[?]. It emerges that in the course of the year 5694 a sum of 6,639 zł. 54 gr. was raised. The main income comes from the collection boxes ("pushkes"), which are distributed to the number of 420. Among the Mizrachists — says the reporter — who have actively joined the work, there are still very many who do not want to support the Keren Kayemet.
The report on the activity of the Keren Hayesod and on the kehilla activity is given by Mr. Nute Landner. "Three years ago," says Mr. Landner, "when we went into the kehilla elections, we won a victory, but we soon became convinced that our effort had been in vain; the Agudah began fighting us with various machinations and all kinds of combinations. When we put up our deserving comrade Yitzhak Wygodzki as kehilla president, the authorities confirmed his brother-in-law as president and afterwards pushed Mr. Wygodzki out. We made a big mistake in appointing Mr. Rubinlicht, a non-Zionist, to the office of president; and when we turned to practical work, we realized that we have no possibility whatsoever of working. We fixed the budget (etat) at a sum of 120 thousand zł., and the Zionists pay 75 per cent. According to a circular of the authorities no expenditure at all may be made in the kehilla until[?] the pensions of the religious functionaries have been paid. When Mr. Liwer, while carrying out the kimcha [de-pischa] campaign, wanted to withhold a certain sum from their pensions, an informer's denunciation was lodged against him, and for that Mr. Liwer was indeed suspended from his activity." In conclusion Mr. Landner declares that the Zionist faction should leave the kehilla, because it in fact has nothing to do there.
After Mr. Wygodzki's report on the 11th national Zionist conference, discussions take place, in which Messrs. Gelbard, Herszlewicz, Wygodzki, Eng. Żmudzki and Herzberg take part.
Finally the motion of Mgr. Mr. Gärtner is adopted to elect a new committee that is to work out a plan for further work. The chairman's motion to grant a vote of discharge (absolutorium) to the outgoing committee is also adopted.
The new board consists of:
Y. Wygodzki, N. Landner, A. Liwer, M. Preger, N. Tenenberg, Pelc, Herszlewicz, Adv. Steiger, Gelbard, Dr. Löwenstein, Eng. Ingwald[?], Mgr. Gärtner, Naomi Urbach, Yechezkel Kerner and Moshe Suszek.
With the singing of "Hatikvah" the meeting is closed.
American Jew Comes to His Relatives for the Holiday and Dies Suddenly in the Street

[Będzin — Sudden death.]
As we already reported in the previous issue (owing to technical reasons the item did not get into part of the copies), on Friday evening there died in the street the 62-year-old Moshe Mordechai Lugerner of America, who had come for the holiday to his relatives in Będzin.
The suddenly deceased Lugerner had lived for many years in Łódź and was engaged in trade. 7 years ago, when the crisis years began, he left for America, leaving his wife in Łódź. Some years later he brought his wife over, but she did not feel well in America and for that reason came back to Łódź.
Then the question of a get (religious divorce) arose, about which negotiations were conducted for a long time. Lugerner, realizing that the get would not come about by letter, decided to come to Łódź in order to carry out the get.
A month ago Lugerner came to Łódź for this purpose, but the get question again met with difficulties on his wife's part, because she demanded that he give her 1000 dollars and he wanted to give her only 500 dollars.
In the meantime Lugerner decided to travel to Będzin in order to see his family, whom he had not seen for over twenty years.
He arrived in Będzin on Friday and stayed with his close relative Mr. Yekutiel Hampel on the Old Market (Stary Rynek).
On Friday evening after the meal Lugerner went out for a walk accompanied by several relatives. Coming onto Jana[?] Street he said "I don't feel well" and collapsed. All means of rescue proved futile. The doctor established that Lugerner had died of a heart attack.
On the deceased were found 12 dollars, 20 zł. and also a little notebook in which are written down a series of names of people who had sent money through him to their relatives in Poland.
His wife and children in Łódź, who were informed of the terrible news by telegraph, came to the funeral.
The Passengers from Zagłębie Were Saved from the Disaster at Krzeszowice

[Zagłębie — railway disaster.]
As is known, on Tuesday morning a terrible railway disaster occurred at Krzeszowice station, in which 10 people lost their lives and dozens were injured.
On that train several passengers from Zagłębie were travelling from Gdynia, among them the head (naczelnik) of the telephone office in Sosnowiec, Mr. Brarawski [?], and they were saved from the disaster.
The “Wife” Is Coming!..

[Czeladź — humorous incident.]
In the restaurant on Milowicka Street in Czeladź a group of Christians sat setting out bottles. Among the company was one who had a fairly large sum of money on him and indeed did not grudge any money on the “bitter drop”. At a certain moment, however, he took a great fright on hearing the tidings that the wife was coming. So he went out through a back door, but the “woman of valour” ran after him. Seeing [?] that he was about to fall into the hands of his “angel of death”, he threw off his boots, thanks to which he ran faster and escaped from “the enemy's hands”...
Session of the Będzin Commissioners' Council

[Będzin — municipality.]
On Friday afternoon the Commissioners' Council in Będzin held a session at which the dispute between the magistrate [municipality] and the military authorities concerning the rent money [?] for the barracks was discussed. No final resolution on the question has yet been adopted.
Meeting Concerning the Ryczałt Tax

[Będzin — small trade, taxes.]
This coming Sunday a meeting of the various sections will take place at the Będzin Small Traders' Association. On the agenda is the consideration of the question of the ryczałt [lump-sum] tax in the future.
—o—
Pitlings Come from Hitler-Land
[Zagłębie — boycott of German goods.]
We once again call on the Jewish population of Zagłębie not to use any Pitlings, because the product comes from the land where Jewish life is outlawed [hefker].
—o—
A Secret Distillery in a Peasant Hut
[Sławków — crime.]
In a village hut in Okradzionów, near Sławków, an apparatus for refining spirits was discovered. The whole installation, as well as several litres of spirit, was confiscated, and the “manufacturer” was handed over for judicial proceedings.
After the Proper “Operation” the Będzin Kehilla Budget Has Been Approved

[Będzin — kehilla.]
On Isru Chag the administration of the kehilla in Będzin received an official notice from the voivodeship that the kehilla budget and the staff establishment (etat-rozkład) had been approved and sent to the starostwo in Będzin.
As we are informed, a severe “operation” was performed on the budget: for example, of the 23 000 zł. projected for the school and cultural purposes barely 5,300 remained. The subsidy of 6000 zł. for the Jewish gymnasium was reduced to 2.000 zł., and the subsidies for charitable purposes were also reduced to a minimum. The salaries (pensions) of the clergy, officials and the like were left untouched.
The debt of 87 thousand zł. which the gmina [municipality] owes the kehilla officials was also restored.
Stones Thrown into the Minyan of the Sosnowiec Talmud Torah

[Sosnowiec — Talmud Torah, attack.]
On Monday, during prayers, stones were thrown into the minyan of the Talmud Torah in Sosnowiec. The attack caused indescribable panic among the worshippers.
An Unusual Storm over Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — weather.]
On Monday evening an unusual storm passed over Zagłębie, accompanied by terrible lightning and thunder. From the heavy downpour the low-lying parts of the town were flooded, and the water also got into many cellars on Mandżewer [Modrzejowska?] Street and on Third of May Square in Będzin.
Owing to the heavy thunder the electric wires on Sienkiewicz Street were torn down.
“A Gentile's Error Is Permitted”...

[Zagłębie — press, antisemitism.]
In the Sunday issue of “Kurier Zachodni” there is an “alarming” note that “the Jews throw peelings out of the sukkahs, which fall on the passers-by”. The note ends with an appeal to the authorities to intervene over this “impudence” [?], so that it should not be repeated on the second days of Sukkot...
Workers' delegation from Zagłębie at the Ministry of Social Welfare.
The Vice-Minister of Social Welfare, Mr. Jastrzębski, received a delegation of Zagłębie workers. The delegation intervened concerning the changes in the law on social welfare for the working class.
Elections to the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec.

The Main Electoral Commission for the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec is conducting intensive work in connection with the elections to the Chamber of Commerce.
It has been published where the electoral districts are located, the office hours and the regulations concerning the elections.
The main electoral lists will be displayed until the 10th of this month in the local electoral districts. The Main Commission holds office every day from 11 to 14 in the building of the Chamber of Commerce at 3 Maja Street 22.
The offices of the electoral districts are located:
In Sosnowiec — in the Chamber of Commerce.
In Będzin — "Bank Loradze" [?], Kołłątaja 23.
In Częstochowa — the Polish Merchants' Association.
In Olkusz — in the Magistrate (town hall).
We point out that everyone who holds a patent (trade licence) has the right to check the voters' lists and to file an appeal if he has not been entered in the voters' list or has not been entered correctly.
In general, the merchants' organisations in Zagłębie have a duty to inform their members about the current elections to the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec.
A new "związek" — the "Hefker Khevre"..

In the Będzin beth midrash there exists a "secret" organisation by the name of "Hefker Khevre" (the Lawless Gang). This brand-new society, which began its "activity" during the holidays, has sent a letter to the gabbai, Reb Moshe Szwajcer, that he should no longer boss things around with the aliyot; if he does, he will get "hakafot" (i.e. a beating)...
The letter is signed by the "Hefker Khevre"...
Help, bandits...

On Sunday at around 11 in the evening [?] unknown persons knocked at the flat of the dentist Fiszel on Kołłątaja Street in Będzin. In the flat there was only the housemaid, who, to her question "Who is knocking?", received the answer that it was an acquaintance suffering from a severe toothache. The girl, however, recognised from the answer that these were bandits, went out onto the balcony and raised an alarm. The police came and found no one.

Bloody incidents between police and rowdies
One killed and three wounded.

Last Sunday, during an outing in the Grodków woods, a brawl broke out among the visitors. The intervening policeman was met with abuse, and then they threw themselves at him and tried to disarm him.
The attacked policeman, after warning the assailants to disperse, fired and wounded one of the rowdies, who died the next morning in hospital.
A similar incident occurred in Groyce [?] on Limanowskiego Street, when the policeman on duty ordered a group of rowdies to disperse; they threw themselves at him and began to beat him, whereupon the policeman fired and wounded three of them.
From Sporting Life.

[Sport — Zagłębie; football and tennis.] Further championship matches of Class „A“.
On Sunday further matches of the championship series took place. The results of the matches are as follows:
Sarmacja — Policyjni 0:1 (0:1) [i.e. 1:0 to Sarmacja].
A very sensational and brilliant victory was won by „Sarmacja“, defeating in Sosnowiec the quite strong police team. Which had been the favourite of the match. The match took place in a very tense atmosphere, which was caused by the indecisive and weak referee, Mr Okularczyk. Much of the blame for this lies with the supporters of „Sarmacja“, who by their shouting got on the referee's nerves. Only thanks to the energetic attitude of the police team and of the stewards was it possible to avoid a brawl. The one and only goal was scored in the first half by Michalik.
Zagłębianka — C.K.S. 1:1 (1:1).
On its own sports ground „Zagłębianka“ „defeated“ [?] the guests from Czeladź. For C.K.S. Stauszycki [?] appeared after a rather long absence. Zagłębianka scored its goal from an eleven-metre kick [penalty]; C.K.S. scored a goal through Bogucki. Referee Mr Grabowski — good.
Płomień — Solvay [?] 0:1 (0:0) [i.e. 1:0 to Płomień].
„Płomień“ gave its supporters a very pleasant surprise by beating the quite strong „Solvay“. Płomień owes the victory in great measure to its goalkeeper, who was in very good form that day.
Brynica — Ruch 1:4 (1:1) [i.e. 4:1 to Brynica].
In Czeladź „Brynica“ won against the weak „Ruch“ by 4:1. After half-time the Czeladź side took over the initiative and did with the opponent whatever they wanted.
Garbarnia — Unia 0:7 (1:0) [i.e. 7:0 to Garbarnia].
On its own sports stadium „Unia“ lost in compromising fashion to the Kraków league team „Garbarnia“. Up to half-time the result was a near-draw. After half-time Unia does not get a word in at all, and Garbarnia scores another 6 goals. At the end of the match the public applauded the guests very warmly. Referee Mr Grajcar [?] — good.
Hakoach — 06 Mysłowice 3:5 [i.e. 5:3 to Hakoach].
As we have already reported, the very lively tennis section of the Będzin „Hakoach“ invited the strong team from Mysłowice. The match ended with an unexpected victory for the Będzin players. The technical results were as follows; men: Hanak—Paradistal 6:1 6:2, Łuczyk—Barenblat 6:2, 6:0, Szyński—Helberg 3:6, 6:3, 6:3, Prus—Buchweitz 6:4, 6:4, Nigan [?]—Hanach (06) — Mrs Grundman—Einhold (H) 7:5, 6:3.
Doubles: Hanach—Szyński (06) — Barenblat—Buchweitz (H) 5:7, 7:5 3:6, Łuczyk—Prus (06) — Helberg — Einhold (H) 5:8 [?] 6:2, 7:5.
The overall result 5:3 in favour of „Hakoach“. After the match the prizes for the club championship were distributed; they were taken by Mrs Landa and Barenblat.
„Ruch“ (Hajduki) — „Hakoach“ (Będzin) 0:4 (0:2) [i.e. 4:0 to Ruch]
The appearance in Będzin of the Polish football champion „Ruch“ Wielkie Hajduki aroused very great interest in all of Zagłębie. „Ruch“ came to Będzin in full line-up, without Wodarz [? printed „Wladawsz“], and showed very fine play. Our Hakoach men held up very well; the forward line played well enough in the field, and there were even situations from which goals could have been scored. But that is already an old trouble. Particularly good were both backs, Dan [?] in the half-back line and Szywek [?] in the forward line. The match was a very fine one, stood at the proper level and was very well received by all present. The result of the match is for „Hakoach“ not a defeat but rather a victory. The match was conducted by one of the best Polish and German international referees, Mr Schneider of Kraków, whom „Hakoach“ had specially invited. Spectators: about 2,000. Order — exemplary.
Debe.
The Name Fits.

[Advertisement — advertorial; „Biały Jeleń“ soap.] The best example of this principle is the Schicht soap „Biały Jeleń“ [„White Stag“]. Its appearance fits the name; it is white, snow-white, and so too is the laundry washed with the soap „Biały Jeleń“. Not a single stain remains on it, all the dirt disappears. Besides that, the soap „Biały Jeleń“ protects the laundry, which lasts many years.

How much turnover tax will be paid in 1935? / A mentally ill woman attacks a doctor in Sosnowiec. / Why should the gates be closed at 10 in the evening? / Which children are admitted to the Medem Sanatorium in Miedzeszyn (near Warsaw) / Thieves pose as peddlers and do their "work".

[Taxes — turnover tax; followed by four news items: Sosnowiec, house gates, the Medem Sanatorium, thieves.]
Under the new tax ordinance, which came into force on the 1st of this month, we present here the most important changes, so that every merchant, manufacturer and artisan should know how much he will have to pay.
Merchants in wholesale, retail and petty trade, as well as those who keep commercial books and those who keep no books, will go on paying the same percentage as until now.
As until now, wholesale merchants with books, retail merchants with books, and retail and wholesale merchants without books also pay [the same].
"Skup" [buying-up] merchants of the fourth category without books, with a turnover of up to 20 thousand zł., pay only half a percent.
Independent agencies[?] ("zastaves") with books pay half a percent; without books, 1 percent.
Industrial enterprises of all kinds holding industrial licences of the first to fourth category pay 0.895 percent of this year's turnover.
Mills and oil-presses that keep books will pay 1 percent in the coming years; but when mills of the first four categories sell flour to bakers, they pay like industrial enterprises that sell their goods to other industrial enterprises.
Industrial enterprises of the first four categories that keep no commercial books will pay 1 percent in the coming years when they sell their goods to industrial enterprises.
Industrial enterprises, manufacturers, holding licences of the 5th to 8th category who sell the goods to factories, pay 0 87.5 [=0.875] percent for the present year.
All other manufacturers and industrial enterprises of the 5th to 8th category without books pay 1.75 percent of this year's turnover, 1.50 percent of the turnover in 1935, 1.25 percent of the turnover in 1936, and from the turnover in 1937 the manufacturers and industrial enterprises will pay 1 percent.
The same also applies to mills and oil-presses of the 5th to 8th category that keep no books.
Mills and oil-presses holding licences of the 5th to 8th category that keep commercial books pay 1 percent.
Workshops and artisans holding artisan cards who sell the goods to other factories and artisans pay 0 87 5 [=0.875] percent of this year's turnover, 0.75 percent from 1935, 0.62.5 [=0.625] percent from 1936, and half a percent from 1937.
All workshops and artisans who sell their goods to anyone will pay 1 percent in the following years.
Commercial intermediaries pay 4 percent turnover tax in all the following years.
—o—
A mentally ill woman attacks a doctor in Sosnowiec.
On Tuesday evening, as Dr. Branicki was walking along 3 Maja Street in Sosnowiec, he was attacked by a mentally ill woman, who started beating and abusing the doctor; only thanks to the help of the police was the victim rescued from the mentally ill woman.
—o—
Why should the gates be closed at 10 in the evening?
From the 1st of this month the gates are closed at 10 in the evening.
It smells of a summery autumn, yet with the caretakers it is already deep winter. Closing the gates so early has only one advantage — that the caretakers can collect "opening money" from the tenants; but for that very reason it is a hindrance to the economic and cultural life of the town.
It is desirable that the administrative authority should order that the gates not be closed so early.
—o—
Which children are admitted to the Medem Sanatorium in Miedzeszyn (near Warsaw)
(Sent in by the "Children's Sanatorium" society in Miedzeszyn.)
In the provinces little is known about which children are and which are not admitted to the Medem Sanatorium.
It happens quite often that parents from the provinces come with their children straight to Miedzeszyn, to the sanatorium, without medical certificates, and must go back to Warsaw and spend days there to obtain the necessary medical certificates and X-ray examinations, without which the children cannot be admitted to the sanatorium.
The Medem Sanatorium admits weak children, children whose lungs are at risk, convalescents and others who are not contagious to those around them. In the sanatorium there is also a large number of perfectly healthy children, who are sent there for purely educational reasons.
It is best for parents who want to send their children to the Medem Sanatorium to apply first to the sanatorium's office in Warsaw (Leszno 28 m. 17, tel. 11-94 04) for information, and in this way save time, health and money.
—o—
Thieves pose as peddlers and do their "work".
As is well known, door-to-door peddling is very widespread in Zagłębie: people of various ages, poorly and richly dressed, go from house to house selling all sorts of goods such as shoelaces, shoe polish, needles, buttons and the like. Unfortunately criminal elements have also exploited this trade, going about supposedly to trade and committing various thefts along the way.

The Starosta Imposes a Fine on the Members of the Kehilla Board

These days the members of the kehilla board in Sosnowiec were fined by the local starosta [district head] a sum of 7.332 zł. and 32 groszy, i.e. every dozor [board member] must pay back into the community („gmina“) treasury a sum of 723 zł. and 23 gr.
The fine was imposed because more was spent on administrative expenses than had been provided (preliminarily) in the budget. For example, more was paid for lighting in the synagogue, for medicines and doctors, for burial needs; tefillin and prayer-books were bought for the children of the orphanage, etc., etc.
The Tangle Around the Sosnowiec Rabbinical Seat Grows / The Meeting of the Będzin Kehilla Council Called Off

A new candidate for the rabbinical seat...
The kehilla board has received a letter from the „Agudat HaRabbanim“ [Union of Rabbis], in which it is reported that Mr. Yona Sztencel, son of the former moreh-tzedek [rabbinical judge] in Sosnowiec, is summoning the Sosnowiec kehilla to a din torah [rabbinical court case] over his right to the Sosnowiec rabbinical seat.
—o—
The Meeting of the Będzin Kehilla Council Called Off.
In connection with the changes in the Będzin kehilla budget, a meeting of the kehilla council on the budget question was to have taken place on Sunday evening.
Before the invitations were sent out, the meeting was called off by the chairman of the council.

Rabbi Frommer Has Taken Over the Leadership of the „Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin“ / The Meeting of the Zionist Faction Did Not Take Place / The „Noble“ Deed of a Landlady / Report of the Mikveh Committee / The Chadek Rally Dissolved / They Stole the Treasure Together With the Pot

As is known, negotiations were held with Rabbi Frommer about taking over the leadership of the „Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin“. After long negotiations Rabbi Frommer agreed to take over the spiritual leadership of the yeshiva, but only temporarily, i.e. for the current term (zman).
Already next Sunday Rabbi Frommer leaves for Lublin.
—o—
The Meeting of the Zionist Faction Did Not Take Place.
On Wednesday evening a meeting of the Zionist faction in the Będzin kehilla was to have taken place. On the agenda was the faction's position on the „operated“ budget.
However, no more than two members came, and for that reason the meeting did not take place.
—o—
The „Noble“ Deed of a Landlady.
At Modrzejowska Street no. 56 in Będzin lives the Futersznit family, against whom the landlord has claims over rent. A misfortune strikes the family: Mrs. Futersznit dies on Hoshana Rabbah. The landlady used this opportunity to take revenge and actually shut off the water, so that the water for the tahara [ritual washing of the dead] had to be brought from another courtyard...
This scandalous fact is confirmed to us, apart from the family concerned, also by other tenants of the house.
—o—
Report of the Mikveh Committee.
On Sunday a report meeting of the committee dealing with the mikveh building will take place in the town[?] beit midrash in Będzin. The donors so far, and those who want the building to be completed, are asked to come to the meeting.
—o—
The Chadek Rally Dissolved.
On Sunday a rally of Chadeks [Christian Democrats] was to have taken place in Sosnowiec in connection with the unveiling of their banner. The leader Korfanty also took part in the rally. But during his speech the rally was dissolved.
—o—
They Stole the Treasure Together With the Pot...
On Perl Street in Sosnowiec lives a Christian woman, a certain Danach[?], who for years saved the bite from her mouth and over years accumulated a capital of 1275 zł. Wanting to keep it safe, she put the money into a pot and placed it in a corner of the room. But a „stranger's eye“ noticed this and stole the treasure together with the pot.

Towards the 31st Class Lottery

[Lottery — promotional piece.]
Our lottery has become useful to the greatest part of the population, just like the railway, the post and the telegraph; it is simply a necessity. In present times hope has grown stronger than ever, because without hope life is impossible. The lottery awakens hope, it shapes people into optimists and reawakens the vanished joy of mankind, and to the persevering players it gives wealth and happiness.
The results have been such that the population already knows how to appreciate this most popular state institution. Almost every citizen has come to the conviction that he must sacrifice a small sum of his monthly income to buy a ticket, and so takes a direct part in winning the million; people have come to the conviction that the class lottery has become a people's lottery. Formerly a handful of well-situated people used to play, whereas today everyone would play were it not for the crisis, [lack of] earnings and unemployment. There are, after all, known cases in which one ticket is bought by several, and even several dozen, poor people.
The majority understand that one should play in all classes; in this way the maximum chances are ensured of winning in the first 3 classes too, in which the sum reaches over 5 million zł. It goes without saying that the last class has the most chances, since it comprises about 77 per cent of the winnings of the whole lottery. Besides the main prize of a million in the last class there are further prizes totalling 16 million zł. The golden rain flows into the pockets of our lucky players three times in the course of the year. And experience proves that the millions fall first of all to the persevering players.
Brawls in the Beit Midrash in Modrzejów

[Modrzejów — the beit midrash.]
Mandzhev [Modrzejów?], a place "as big as dew and rain", can compare itself to the Balkan states in the field of quarrels and squabbles. Only a short while ago the rabbinate fight there was liquidated, and already a fire has flared up in the local beit midrash that seizes ever more new "positions".
The fight broke out over the question of the gabbaim. The attack came from "Brit HaChayal", which wants to take over the power in the beit midrash. Partly they succeeded: they threw out the gabbaim whom the community [gmina] had nominated and began to rule with the aliyot [the Torah honours]. When the old dozór members tried to put up resistance, one of them, a certain Hochzeit, got a slap.
Then the dozór members went to the starosta and reported to him the events that had taken place in the beit midrash. The starosta then ordered that the old gabbaim should take over the government again.
60,000 Cigarettes in the Forest beyond Maczki

[Maczki — crime.]
Last Sabbath, in the forest beyond Maczki, 2 sacks of "Płaskie" cigarettes, 60 thousand pieces in number, were found buried in the earth.
As it turned out, the cigarettes come from the theft carried out a day earlier at the tobacco wholesale store in Myszków.
What Is Happening in Upper Silesia?

[Katowice — education and Sabbath observance.]
The Sabbath question at the vocational school in Katowice.
Intervention of Rabbi Dr. Chameides.
As we have already written, the Jewish girl pupils who study at the vocational school in Katowice are forced to attend school on the Sabbath; if not, the pupils are removed from the school.
In this connection Rabbi Dr. Chameides intervened with the school's management, and also with the curator of the voivodeship, with whom Dr. Chameides conferred, and endeavoured to bring it about that the decree be withdrawn for the Jewish children who do not want to desecrate the Sabbath.
As Dr. Chameides informs us, he received the promise of the above-mentioned that the matter will be considered, in order to find a way out that would solve the question.
It is interesting to add the following: at the meeting with the headmistress, the latter wondered why the Jewish public in Zagłębie does not create a vocational school for Jewish children.
— Truly a hard question...

Beaten Bloody for "Dzień dobry"

[Upper Silesia — Hitlerites.]
A Polish boy worked for a Hitlerite [Hitlerowiec]. Once in the morning the boy greeted his employer with "Dzień dobry" [Good morning, in Polish]. For this "impudence" he beat the boy bloody and dismissed him from work.

Dr. Kalker's visit to Zagłębie

As we have already written, Dr. S. Kalker is staying in Zagłębie on a mission of the Central Anti-Hitler Committee in Warsaw.
In connection with this, on Sunday, under the chairmanship of Dr. Weinzieher, a conference took place in the premises of the Jewish kehilla.
The opening address was given by Dr. Weinzieher, who said that we must do whatever is possible in order to strengthen the anti-Hitlerite campaign.
Dr. Kalker, in his detailed lecture, pointed out the dangers of Hitlerism for the future and appealed for the creation of the necessary front, so as not to lose the struggle with our enemies.
Dr. Weinzieher spoke about the levy at the rate of 25 per cent according to the budget (etat) sums and proposed that the names of those who have not yet fulfilled their pledge be published.
Mr. Wygodzki [?], in his report on the levy campaign, declared that the Orthodox had given nothing at all for this purpose.
It was decided to visit those who have not yet given. For this purpose Messrs. Wygodzki, Gelbart, Y. Gutman, Herciger, Pinkus and others volunteered.
—o—
On Sunday, in Dąbrowa, in the hall of "Maccabi", a meeting took place devoted to the boycott campaign against German goods as well as to aid for the refugees.
The meeting was opened by Mr. Yitzchak Bukowski, who, welcoming the guest Dr. Kalker from Warsaw, gave an opening address, criticising Poalei Zion and HeChalutz for not joining the committee, as well as the incomprehensible passive attitude of the "Pni" [?].
Then the delegate of the C.C. from Warsaw, Dr. S. Kalker, gave a rich and instructive lecture on the situation of Jewry in the world.
The lecture was listened to by the assembled with the greatest attention, and the speaker was rewarded with long applause.
Mr. Bukowski thanked the esteemed guest for his brilliant lecture and, appealing to those assembled to assist the committee in all its undertakings, closed the meeting.
