Będzin Is Shrinking — Let This Not Be Permitted by the Jewish Public

Let this not be permitted by the Jewish public.
It is a rule that people who see each other often do not notice that they change — whether for the better or, God forbid, for the worse. It seems to them that it is always the same face, the same appearance, the same qualities.
It is quite different, however, when people come together who have not seen each other for a number of years. These people see quite differently; they look at one another with quite different eyes and see different faces too, and then one hears opinions voiced [?]: this one has blossomed and become a quite different person; another, on the contrary, has grown old and grey before his time, and a backwardness can be noticed in him; his character too has changed entirely — no matter whether for the better or the worse, that plays no role at the given moment. We are only out to show here that those who are always together do not see in one another the systematic changes that occur in the everyday process of human life, which is, incidentally, quite understandable and normal — whereas the one who comes together with them only now and then does see, and in very sharp outlines, and has the opportunity to put forward an all-round discussion that changes the situation.
Yes, so it is in human life: we change, we grow old and fall behind, and we ourselves do not notice it; strangers who have not seen us for a number of years must first come and tell us so.
Why has this come up — why are we talking now, in today's workaday [?] time, about spiritual matters [?]? Simply [?] because this very parable can be applied to our Będzin.
It seems to be well known that our town has always been a town with heart, with conscience and with feeling, so much so that one cannot complain: to this very day people here respond warmly to every campaign, every cry and appeal finds ears that listen, and no one here is ever wronged — though of course it is not what it used to be. Still, we have a sense and understanding for everything, and that says a great deal.
Just as people who are always together cannot see the systematic change taking place in the human spirit, in the human physiognomy, so we Będziners, the town's permanent residents, do not see what is becoming of us.
True, everyone complains all the time that today things are not as they once were, that the further it goes the worse and worse it gets. But each one thinks that he has it bad and the other fellow has it better. We do not see, and we cannot form any idea at all of how bad the general situation in the whole town is. We live together, we are together, and the change for the worse comes bit by bit; so we get used to it, until we no longer see the colossal change.
It is quite different, though, when a guest comes to us who knows the town and the people and the businesses and the surroundings. Such a guest, when he comes — as the saying goes — "for a while, sees for a mile."
Not long ago we had guests here who know the town, who lived in it and were, like a mother with her children, bound and knotted together with one another — and these "mothers" were left astonished, and they keep asking with regret: What has become of the town? Where has the great bustle gone? Where are the lively businesses and the broad scope of the population, which held within it so much beauty [?] and grandeur and tradition? They cry out — where has all this gone? Why do you not see how all this is going to ruin, and why do you allow it?
The "guests for a while," however, say that they are [sic; read: see] for a mile — at a time when we see nothing, thanks to our being worn out with toil [?] and harried, preoccupied with earning our daily piece of bread.
Yes, so it is: we do not see; thanks to our rush we have no chance to see what is being lost, and at the same time we do not see how impoverished the town has become. And when people come who know the town and note the tragic poverty, only then do we begin to understand how terrible our situation is and how poor and naked we are. Then we understand that the whole town is impoverished and that each one thinks the other is better off.
Of course individuals do not come into consideration here, for if there are some whose situation is good, the community is far from helped by it. We are speaking of the general situation, which is so grave that we are not in a position to take stock of it; and when strangers come and draw our attention to the impoverishment, only then do we see how terribly we are sinking and how far we have fallen together with the town where we have drawn our nourishment since childhood.
And willy-nilly the question arises: may we remain indifferent to all this? Are we not sinning when we do not look around on all sides and do not seek a remedy for this terrible plague, thanks to which we are being degraded down to the deepest abyss?
After all, Będzin is not some forsaken little town in a remote corner from which the government gets nothing. Therefore a sacred duty lies upon our economic and professional institutions to make efforts with the proper authorities that the prestige of the town be raised; for the loss of its lustre has come about both thanks to the prevailing crisis and, even more, thanks to the deliberate aims of certain influential circles, which were interested in having the town of Będzin, because it has a large number of Jewish inhabitants, become poorer, smaller and more inferior.
We Będziners, however, must not allow this. We must demand our rights, for we all pay taxes at the highest rate, just like the citizens in the big cities.
We must therefore be watchful and guard our interests, for both the honour of the citizen and the honour of the Jew demand it of us.
We must not allow Będzin, which was always the pride and the heart of Zagłębie and the centre of commerce, suddenly to be turned into an inferior little town — and only because the greater part of its population is Jewish.
R. Let.
What Every Radio Listener Needs to Know

When moving to another flat or changing one's address?
If the radio listener moves to another flat that lies within the district of the post office which issued the radio licence, the post office must be notified within 7 days of the change of address, so that the change can be entered in the papers there.
If the radio listener moves to a flat that belongs to another postal district, one must report this to the post office where one was registered and request that the registration card be sent on to the new post office. On that basis the new post office will issue a fresh radio licence and cancel the old one. In doing so the radio listener must pay a fee of 1 zł.
At the same time the radio listener is obliged to dismantle in his former flat all the radio installations, such as the aerial, the earthing and all the wires — unless the radio listener continues to pay the due radio fee for the old flat as usual.
If the radio listener moves away only for a short time (no longer than 4 months), for example to a summer residence, on holiday or for a cure, the radio fee must be paid at the same post office as always.
If the radio listener gives up the radio and no longer wishes to pay the monthly fee, he is obliged to notify the post office of this in writing, to return his licence and at the same time to dismantle the entire radio installation in his flat.
The radio licence is strictly personal. A subtenant, for example, who has a radio set in his room, cannot rely on the radio licence of the main tenant. He must register the radio set in his own name and pay the due monthly fee.
A radio licence is valid for one flat only.
The permit to install an aerial and to use a radio set applies only to the address of the radio installation stated in the licence.
On the basis of one licence one may not keep two or three radio installations at the same time in different premises or places; whoever therefore has two flats in the same town or in different towns must accordingly hold two licences and pay separately for each flat.
In one and the same flat one has the right to keep several radio installations only for one's own use.
The Fiftieth Jubilee of the "Kattowitz Conference"

[Katowice — Zionism; history.]
Mosze Fajnkind.
A year ago we already described in detail in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" the "Kattowitz Conference" of the "Hovevei Zion", which took place on 18 Cheshvan 5645[?] (6 November 1881).
On the coming 18 Cheshvan the Zionist camp is due to celebrate the fiftieth jubilee of this historic conference, on liberated Polish soil.
Fifty years ago it was more than audacity to convene such a conference of Jews who did not conceal their strong will to rebuild the Jewish Land of Israel, upon which all of Europe, all of Christendom, had looked out with open eyes, to rule it.
Neither Europe nor the Jews were then imbued with the Jewish national idea, and yet some twenty "fantasists", as the Jewish foreign-language press used to call them mockingly in those days, dared to proclaim this historic idea publicly — the idea that had never ceased to occupy[?] the Jewish mind, to dream year in, year out of the liberation of the Jewish land by Jews.
In the "Concordia" B'nai B'rith lodge the very most prominent fighters for the so-called Zionist idea in the second half of the twentieth [sic; read: nineteenth] century came together.
We see there in the front row the author of "Autoemancipation", Dr. Leon Pinsker, Rabbi Shmuel Mohilever, the editors Alexander Zederbaum (HaMelitz), David Gordon (HaMagid) [?], and Pinchas Rabinowitz (Shefer), and others, all of whom are already in the World of Truth. It was they who in Kattowitz laid the foundation of Zionism and carried out into the street the slogan of consolidating and strengthening the national ideal among the Jews.
In Kattowitz the Zionist bridge was laid that led to Basel, where Zionism received hand and marrow, vital force, and the hope for a Jewish Land of Israel, which had been dormant among the Jews, awoke everywhere and revived among all of Israel.
With this conference the young German town of Kattowitz inscribed a fine page in the history of the Jewish revival, and national Jewry looks upon this town with reverence to this very day.
* * *
In Kattowitz the first Jewish national organization was created, which in time embraced the entire Jewish world and became a factor in Jewish and in general political life, with which people, willy-nilly, began in time — and indeed were forced — to reckon.
The Kattowitz Conference was the first step on the road to realizing the Zionist programme.
One sees from the debates and from the resolutions so presented[?], which took place and were adopted at this historic conference, that it grasped its task clearly and distinctly from the very first moment.
The second point of the resolutions was the colonization of Eretz Israel by Jews, which was the quintessence of the whole gathering[?].
And when Herzl convened the first Congress in Basel, the same initiators of the Kattowitz congress were there, which had placed on the agenda the demand to proceed at once to colonize Eretz Israel with Jews.
And like a red thread that demand ran through all the Zionist Congresses — a demand that was in fact an echo of the Kattowitz Conference. It greatly influenced the course of the Zionist Congresses, which were also strongly influenced by it.
And indeed, when Kattowitz celebrated the twenty-five-year jubilee of the "Hovevei Zion Conference" (Sunday, 7 November 1909), all the speakers, from Sokolow to Dr. Thon, from Adolf Stand to Dr. Klausner, stressed and underlined the same thing: that Kattowitz led Zionism to Basel, and that thanks to Kattowitz the Zionist ideal began to develop and to inspire the masses.
* * *
Now we stand on the threshold of the fifty-year jubilee of the "Kattowitz Conference", so beloved by national Jews.
Jewish Katowice today is no longer the same as fifty years ago, nor as twenty-five years ago, when the Jewish delegates were received there with suspicion and coldly, for fear of "what will people say"...
Today Katowice is freed from the inveterate "hupia"[?] assimilation. Polish Jewry has brought there and spread national consciousness and Jewish life.
And since Katowice today no longer [bears] the German standard, Katowice must therefore prepare in good time to celebrate the 50-year jubilee festival of the first Zionist conference, which took place within it[?], and with great splendour, as the festival has deserved.
May this festival be a great manifestation for political Zionism, for the Zionist postulates and — at this time, now so critical for the Jews throughout the world — a festival of the revival of the Jewish Land of Israel and for free emigration to the Jewish national home.
May our Zionists of all shades, who gather under the blue-white flag, on this blue-white festival reach out their hands to one another in "Shalom".
Under the sign of peace this Zionist festival must be celebrated by all of us.
That is the commandment of the day.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Noah)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Noah
The Portion.
—o—
a) "These are the generations of Noah" (Gen. 6:9)
Once a rich man from Kraków came to Radomsko, to the "Tiferet Shlomo"; he had an open hand and always gave the Hasidim money for a "tikkun", for drink. Whenever he came, the Hasidim rejoiced in him, knowing that there would be no shortage of brandy. And even the Rebbe drew him close for it. This once annoyed another rich man, who was a greater Torah scholar and whom the Rebbe's court cost more — only he did not care for drinking. To him neither the Hasidim nor even the Rebbe showed any closeness. So he once asked the Rebbe: How can it be? Why is such a fuss made over the Kraków rich man? Is he more pious than I? Can he study better?
The Rebbe answered him with a "chalbat" [?]:
We have in the Torah two portions that both open with the same words: "These are the generations of Noah" and "And these are the generations of Isaac". Why is the first portion called Parashat Noah, after Noah, while the second portion is not called Parashat Isaac, after Isaac? Was Isaac any less righteous than Noah?
But Noah was the first to plant [?] a vineyard — "and he planted a vineyard" — and he took a glass of drink into his mouth, and really did get drunk too. And surely he once also invited his companions for a glass of drink, to drink "l'chaim" — for such a man a special portion is made... Everyone crowds [?] around him, because one benefits from him. Isaac, on the other hand, was indeed a great tzaddik and a rich man too; he worked the land, but he planted [?] no vineyard, and nobody ever got a glass of wine from him — for such a man no special portion is made...
—o—
b) "He was blameless in his generations; Noah walked with God" (ibid.)
"Noah walked with God" — he did not preach morals to people, he went his way with God, and therefore — "he was blameless in his generations": that is why people loved him and did not quarrel with him, for who cared that Noah was pious there for himself?.. Ktav Sofer.
* * *
"He was blameless in his generations" —
This is a special praise: to live in two generations ("in his generations") and to be counted a tzaddik by both. For as a rule, whoever is called a tzaddik by one generation is held a villain by the next, and vice versa. The views of the generations change. And Noah, because he was blameless, was counted a tzaddik by both generations... Leket Amarim.
—o—
c) "Noah walked with God."
"And Noah begot three sons" (ibid. 10)
"Noah walked with God" — he simply walked with God and preached morals to no one, because "Noah begot three sons", and since he had children of his own, he left the world in peace... "When you have children in the cradle"... as the folk saying goes.
R. Asherl of Rymanów.
—o—
d) "For the earth is filled with violence through them" (ibid. 13)
"Through them" — they themselves cry out about the violence. To other sins they do not confess, but about robbery they themselves cry out: each one cries that his fellow robs him. Though when he does it to another, he says it is no robbery..
Kiflayim le-Tushiya.
* * *
And therefore the Gemara says in Bava Metzia: "He who exacted payment from the men of the generation of the Flood... will exact payment from one who does not stand by his word." For the generation of the Flood "did not stand by its word": when one robbed his fellow, he cried that it was a bankruptcy, but God forbid not a robbery. Yet when the other did the same to him, he cried "gevalt". That is "they do not stand by their word": regarding others they call it bankruptcy and the like, but when it is done to them, they call it robbery...
Pninim Yekarim.
—o—
e) "Three hundred cubits the length of the ark" (ibid. 15)
A homily says that the ark was therefore three hundred cubits long, fifty wide and sixty [so printed; the Torah has thirty] high, so that it could hold six hundred thousand (shishim ribo), which is the number of the Jews. Everyone wonders at this homily.
To this the Ostrowiec Rebbe offered a wondrous calculation.
In Eruvin folio 53 the Gemara says that four disciples of R. Oshaya stood in a space one cubit wide. And in Eruvin folio 48 the Gemara says that the height of a person is three cubits; so a space three cubits high and one cubit wide holds the room of four people. It follows that for six hundred thousand, for 600,000 people, one needs some four hundred and fifty thousand cubits by one cubit... Multiply the width by the length and the width [sic] and the length of the ark, and you will get exactly the number four hundred and fifty thousand by one...
—o—
f) "For you have I seen righteous before Me in this generation" (7:1)
"And it does not say 'a blameless tzaddik'"... Rashi.
But "blameless", says the Sforno, means "in the heart". Well, earlier, when the Torah praises Noah before the world, "blameless" had to be added — that he is not pious only outwardly, but in his heart too he is pious. But here, when God speaks to him, He need not add that he is pious in his heart as well, for God surely knows what goes on in a person's heart, and if He says "pious" He means of course also pious in the heart, since outward piety does not exist at all before God.
R. Avraham Shmuel Binyamin Sofer.
—o—
g) "And he sent forth the raven" (8:7) [printed "או" for "את"]
Why did Noah first send out the raven and only afterwards the dove?
Because the raven is a bad bird, and in order to see whether the Flood had already stopped, whether the world had already been cleansed, he first had to send the raven; and if the bad bird could survive in the world, only then could he try with the good bird...
Mashal u-Melitza.
Legal remedies against irregular enforcement proceedings

[Law — enforcement; followed by a notice: treasury — revenue stamps.] Court decisions on complaints against bailiffs (komornicy) cannot, in principle, be appealed. Nevertheless the Enforcement Ordinance (ordynacja egzekucyjna) does provide for certain cases in which such decisions may after all be appealed.
The following situations come into consideration:
1) When it concerns demands for payment and enforcement costs.
2) When it concerns furnishing a court judgment, settlement, decision or other act with a so-called enforcement title ("tytuł wykonawczy").
3) When it concerns the release of a security deposited in the files as provided by law.
4) When it concerns suspending or annulling the entire enforcement procedure for a given claim.
5) When it concerns the limiting of enforcement.
6) When it concerns the release of moneys on which an attachment (zajęcie) was laid.
7) When it concerns recognising the purchase right of a given participant in an auction (licytacja).
8) When it concerns compelling a debtor to disclose his property and take an oath.
9) When it concerns applying a custodial [?] coercive measure against a debtor who refuses to swear.
In all the cases listed, the interested parties may appeal the court's decisions insofar as they feel wronged by them.
J. Einfeld [?].

What Will the Gentiles Say...

[Satirical feuilleton — Zagłębie; Dąbrowa, Sosnowiec; assimilation and the fear of "what will the gentiles say".] Topical remarks by Ben Amotz.

...And so[?] we thought that the Hitlerite plague, which has spread from Berlin to Afghanistan, would be for us Jews, the "Thou hast chosen us" people, the answer to the age-old question that humiliates us utterly, namely the
— "What will the gentiles say"...
The "What will they say", which on every occasion has been the strongest scare-weapon for our brethren the Children of Israel, would perhaps no longer have the same content as until now. So we thought, but unfortunately we were greatly mistaken. On the contrary, the "What will they say" is taking root ever deeper in the Jewish camp and assuming new forms in Jewish life.

Story number one:
In a well-to-do Jewish family in Dąbrowa a male child was born, and the father, who possesses more money than "present-day modernism"[?], went off to the Jewish kehilla and registered his only son under the name — Herszel.
— Have you registered our little son already? — his wife asks him.
— Yes, my little dove.
— How did you enter him in the metryka [birth register]?
— What kind of question is that? Herszel is his name.
— "Co takiego?!"[?] [What?!] My child is to be called Herszel? Just as they call Herszel the shopkeeper, Herszel the milkman. Oh, "szlag mnie trafi" [I'll have a stroke]... Oh, "dajcie mi trochę wody" [give me some water]...
— "Kochana moja" [my darling] — the husband pleads with her — "uspokój się" [calm down], it's really not so terrible. Calm yourself, I didn't know that Herszel would seem so "brzydliwe"[?] [disgusting] to you. I didn't mean to cause you grief. Quite simply, I gave a name after my grandfather; he was a fine, decent Jew.
— "Milcz!" [Be quiet!] What tales are you telling me about that grandfather of yours, a Jew from "starożytne" [ancient] times? We are living in today's "wiek" [century], after all. So how will I be able to show myself in front of people with my son? Exile will stare me in the face when someone in my "towarzystwo" [social circle] shouts:
— "Chodź no[?], Herszlik" [come here, Herszlik]...
And "w ogóle" [anyway] — what will the gentiles say?
So recounted the compassionate "Pensulek"[?] in the kehilla office, telling how he had managed to bring it about that the correction be made:
— Instead of Herszel — "Jerzy"...
— "Dzięki Bogu" [thank God] — the modern lady heaved a heavy sigh — a stone has fallen from my heart and a disgrace from my child.
— Jerzy is now his name...
———
Story number two:
One of the most Jew-hating newspapers appearing in Zagłębie celebrated its 10th anniversary a few days ago. Although it is no more than 10 years since the rag began to appear, its merits towards its co-religionists are considerable[?]: throughout the whole time it has faithfully fulfilled its tasks, especially in the field of anti-Jewish incitement. It has let slip no opportunity when it was necessary to pour pitch and brimstone on the "Żydzi" — upon my life, no worse than the "Dwa Grosze" in the capital of Poland.
But as the saying goes: "The Jew is treyf, his money is kosher." So the jubilarians of the paper indeed absolved themselves of their constant slogan "swój do swego" [each to his own, i.e. the anti-Jewish boycott] and turned to a number of Jewish firms — to those from whom one can milk[?] handsome guldens — with a proposal to place advertisements in the jubilee issue.
And do you perhaps think the Jewish firms refused? Then, begging your pardon, you are greatly mistaken. Jews can refuse to place advertisements in Jewish newspapers, refuse to pay for important institutions, turn away Jewish workers — but, God forbid, not want to give advertisements to antisemitic rags? Heaven forbid the thought[?], is such a thing possible? One simply can't do otherwise — "what will they say?"
— What will the gentiles say?...
———
Story number three:
— Make way! Clear the road, "civilisation" is on the march! — so, last Saturday, hundreds of children being educated in the "Jewish" public elementary schools in Sosnowiec wanted to "shout"...
Throughout the country — as everyone knows — collection drives are being carried out in Zagłębie on behalf of building elementary schools. In Będzin the collection began last Sunday, and in Sosnowiec — on the Sabbath... precisely on that Sabbath when one begins "Bereshit" anew... Because once an order was given, our "kierownicy" and "kierowniczki" [headmasters and headmistresses] in Sosnowiec would surely have nothing else to say but "przecież[?] nie możliwe" [it's surely not possible]...
— What will the gentiles say?...
On Friday at twilight the "rozkaz" [order] was issued to the Jewish children — to come on the Sabbath morning to the assembly points, where the "pochód" [procession] would be formed...
And when Pan Kierownik or Pani Kierowniczka orders you to come, is there any other choice?
— So Jewish children did indeed come to the schools on Sabbath morning, from where[?] they were to march under the command of the "szanowne nauczycielstwo" [honoured teaching staff], who also wished to take part in the work of presenting passers-by with "znaczki" [badges] — and why not? One must be loyal, after all; otherwise there is again the same old question — "what will the gentiles say"?...
Unfortunately the hyper-patriotism of the headmasters was disrupted. Heaven prevented it: the Sabbath "pochód" was held back from on high, for, as the devil would have it, it began to rain, the little children ran back home, into the "shtiblekh" [Hasidic prayer rooms] to their fathers, and the "loyal występ" [loyal performance], poor thing, never came off.
— And where were the children's parents? — you ask — why did they not react to such a public desecration of the Sabbath by their children?
— Their minds were entirely elsewhere. The reason — a simple one. That Sabbath the Jews of Sosnowiec were immersed in pure holiness: a gathering of rebbes and rabbis from all the Diaspora of Israel. So who was interested in such "nonsense"; who would have imagined that the educators of the so-called "szabasówki" [state schools for Jewish children, closed on Saturdays] would organise a "pochód" in honour of the Sabbath?
And to tell the truth, from the standpoint of being "consistent", one must "justify", indeed vindicate, the "gest" [gesture] of the headmasters and headmistresses of the "powszechne" [public elementary] schools in Sosnowiec. For after all, their souls are in exile, and that is why they tremble so before the
— What will the gentiles say..
Jews, Think It Over...

S. Salker.
(For the fund-raising campaign for the German refugees.)
The most tragic and the worst thing to be seen in Jewish life today is that people have stopped thinking, stopped reflecting on their own fate; a kind of lethargic sleep and a terrible apathy reign in the Jewish street. Let the storm winds rage, let the volcanoes pour fire on the heads of millions of Jews, let the danger already be close to one's own "little soul" — as long as it has not yet come, as long as there is still some possibility, however it may be, of living through the troubles, I am at peace; it is not my business what goes on around me; I don't want to know about the perhaps, God forbid, terrible tomorrow; what interests me is today; "future", "further on", "later" — these are concepts that have nothing to do with me.
That is the mood of the great majority of the Jewish people.
And it is a degenerating phenomenon, a sleepiness — there is no doubt of that; it is anaemia, bloodlessness and enfeeblement of the national organism after a terrible struggle lasting many years.
For conscious people and nations do not stop for a single minute reflecting, understanding and grasping[?] the present, the here and now, the whole sum of historical situations and circumstances into which fate has thrown them; and the "instinct of survival" compels them under all circumstances to seek means of securing tomorrow, to save what can be saved, to protect themselves from hostile destructive forces, to create, build and strengthen the possibilities of existence.
Must I repeat once more what has already been said hundreds of times from many sides and by myself, and also the bitter, so obvious truth that every Jew feels?
1) That we live in an age of "danger to our existence", of threats to the further Jewish existence, or at the very least of terrible enfeeblement for generations to come.
2) That our "being" is being fought — and very actively and intensively — by a large part of present-day humanity.
3) That a great movement, or movements, of savage antisemitism and of uprooting the Jews root and branch have arisen, and spread and deepen ever further over the whole globe.
4) That all the world upheavals, which bring new social orders with them, first of all overturn the Jewish "order of the world" and make the Community of Israel ownerless prey.
5) That the struggle against our political rights and our acquired[?] economic positions simply takes on terrible forms.
6) That a large part of the Jews in various countries have already fallen in the battle, and the rest are threatened by the same fate.
7) That loneliness, want, pain and hopelessness have reached the highest degree, such as Satan himself could not have imagined.
Does all this still need proving?
No, I think. Only madmen, blind people, will not know[?] this any longer. Is the "wise and understanding people" not mad, [if it does not see] that we have no one to lean on, that from nowhere except ourselves can or will salvation come, that none of the nations of the world, not even the best of them, is interested in the "Eternity of Israel", in the existence of a Jewish nation on our planet, and will not lift a finger to save that existence? Has the experience of the two decades of post-war years not shown us this clearly? Especially the war of the German people against the Jews in the last 2 years. How all the sympathy, the compassion, the speeches in all the parliaments, in the League of Nations, by all the great and the powerful, came to nothing — a soap bubble, a cinema show and no more; and no one has yet wiped away a single tear from a Jewish eye, and every day we become lonelier, more forsaken and more abandoned. And if, after all, we manage, even partly, to hold back the cloudburst, to save the situation here and there, to overcome the elemental force, to hold on to Jewish positions and still, somehow, to keep body and soul together — it is thanks to our own strength, our own struggle and our own effort.
The watchword "If I am not for myself, who will be for me" has never been so bloodily true as today. In whatever form it is fulfilled — whether in the fight against the Third Reich by boycott, or in rescuing German refugees, or in settling Jews in the Land of Israel, supporting the stricken through world organisations, the emigration of small parts of the Jews to new countries, political noise and clamour[?], awakening the conscience of the world, averting evil decrees and the like — by whom has even a hair's breadth of it been done, if not by ourselves?
And when the situation is so, how does that square with apathy, with silence, with despair, with indifference to the community and with incomprehension of the rescue struggle in all fields of the rescue campaign?
Astonishing — a wonder of the Creator.
After all it is no secret that the German offensive is no passing phenomenon; it is a "weeping for generations"; nor is it a purely territorial or German-state matter. It is a world campaign; the persecutors and antisemitic ideologues in Germany say so explicitly, and more than saying it they do it: that the majority of the 100 million German people in the whole world have taken upon themselves a mission to wipe out the Jewish race, to fulfil Laban's mission of "uprooting everything". And the serpent sows and spreads its venom among all human settlements.
Various historical causes have called forth the plague; one must go deep into them and perhaps learn a moral from them: that we are dealing with a world force and power which has gone seriously mad over a "Jew-disease" and has dug its deep, bloody nails into the Jewish national organism everywhere it is to be found. The German people suffers from some kind of Jew-persecution mania. (This is a mass movement and not merely the will of individuals.) It thinks that Jews and "Jewry" stand in the way of its historical flowering, and strives to clear them out of the way entirely — not only at home.
This is proved by the world sweep and international scale of German antisemitism and by the world apparatus through which it is spread, rooted and realised. Realised literally, for in many places the shoots have already borne fruit.
—
And so, dear Jews, is it worth thinking about all this? Giving it a thought? Looking around? Upon my life, it is not merely worthwhile but a duty, a commandment of the hour, an unconditional necessity dictated by the primitive will to live. And I am convinced that you will think it over, and then you will respond more to an outstretched hand asking for help — help that will help you yourselves.
Sitting Ten Days (An Overheard Conversation)

[Humour — a conversation overheard in the editorial office; prison, fines and amnesty.]
(An overheard conversation).

A Hasidic Jew comes into the editorial office and asks:
— Is it true that a week from now there will be an amnesty?
— No, they say five weeks from now.
— That long? There is no strength left to wait.
— What is the matter?
— I have to sit [in jail] ten days.
— So you drag it out a little.
— I have already been dragging it out like this for a year and a half.
— Why do you have to sit?
— What do I know? A trifle: I kept a yeshiva boy as a boarder ["on stantsye", with board] and did not register him [with the police].
— And for that a whole ten days?
— The starosta [district head] sentenced me to 50 gulden [colloquial for złoty], or 3 days. We were [?] clever, filed an appeal — and the court increased it to ten days.
— You can't appeal any further?
— I'm afraid they might add on up to a whole month.
— Well then, never mind, you go and sit it out.
— What are you saying? All in all we are, thank God [?], eight souls, and we live on ten gulden a week.
— From what do you earn it?
— I no longer earn anything; my eldest girl earns it in a factory.
— So how do you get by?
— That is just the point: when I am here, I have steady work — borrowing interest-free loans [gmiles-khesed] and paying them back, and on that we live [?]. But if I go and sit for 10 days, my family — may it befall the enemies of Israel — could die of hunger.
— But then you will save one eater...
— We have thought of that too: but here is the trouble — nowadays the state board [in prison] is no longer free; afterwards one must pay a gulden a day for lodging with food at the prison [?] "windows" [?] — so again it doesn't pay.
— You are quite right, better to sit at home. But how did you manage to wriggle out of it for a year and a half?
— God helped me. At first they did not summon people so strictly. Apparently there was no free place. Later a przodownik [police sergeant] began coming after me [lit. "after my head"]. But when do they find me at home? Twice a day I sit in the shtibl for a couple of hours, several hours I spend in the street with the interest-free loans that I take and give, and when I come home for a while to eat, someone stands at the window "on the lookout" ["batshnashtsh", Polish baczność], and when they spot the blue coat, they tell me, and I — out through the back door. And at night, the few hours when I sleep, he has to sleep too — at night he doesn't come...
— The reckoning adds up exactly —
— Wait! But there is a time when I sleep and he doesn't — that is Shabbat after the cholent, and there a real miracle from heaven happened to me.
— What happened?
— Not long ago, I am lying like that on a holiday after the meal, snoring away happily in bed under the feather quilt, and there was not even a guard at the window; suddenly the door opens and the przodownik is here. My wife, a Cossack of a Jewish woman, had the nerve to say that I was not at home. But he did not believe her and went to search. Meanwhile I overheard the conversation and burrowed deeper into the feather quilt. The przodownik went straight to the bed and my wife after him. Both lifted the under-bedding with the pillow, gave it a shake and let it drop, and my wife even pretended to be angry:
— So the gentleman [pan] didn't believe me!
— That was the last time, — the Jew concluded — since then he has not come again, and I have no more strength to wait. I was told there would be an amnesty, so I came to ask, and you say it will drag on another five weeks or so. Oh, Master of the Universe! — — —
Avi-Her.
Bankrupt (A Story)

[Serialized story — "Bankrupt"; installment 2.]
Meir Hertz.

2.

Sarah'le could not keep herself from looking around at the merchandise. Before her eyes there now floated a terrible picture: it seemed to her as if a funeral were now taking place in her shop — the business is dying, no goods are brought in, but on the contrary, the goods are only carried out... In her imagination the small-town merchants mingled with bailiffs, protested bills with auctions; how everything stretches out into a sea of walls [?], and of all her goods and property, of her labour of so many years, a heap of ruins is made, and all the big cupboards become empty, full of holes [?].
She could not drive away the sad thoughts. A wild fear pressed upon her heart; in her head ran one picture blacker than the other; she saw how her rich house is broken up, everything is sold off from there, and she and the children have to set out into the world with beggars' sacks.
At this thought she began to tremble. She stepped away [?] from the sideboard, wiped her eyes so that no one would notice that a tear had stood there; something raised her from her place, and without her strength or will an elemental force led her into the last room, where the iron safe stood. From there she sent for her husband, and when both were there alone, she shut the door, and her tears, stifled until now, broke out in a spasmodic weeping:
— Simcha, we are unfortunate, we are done for. This very minute order the goods to be packed back, and let the buses take the goods back to Łódź, to the manufacturers. The goods that have not yet been unpacked — let no one touch them, let them stay on the buses. My heart foretells me nothing good; I'm afraid I will trade no more — enough! The debts we owe we may still be able to pay; we will sell the house — if something remains for us from it, good; if not, at least we will remain honest poor people. Simcha, have mercy on yourself, take pity on yourself, on me and on our children. Drive out the merchants, send away the buses, and let there be an end to it.
Reb Simcha stood there bewildered [?]. He did not understand what his wife was saying to him; he gave her to understand that her fear was groundless: what does it mean — so many years a merchant, having played such a role, and here suddenly go, grab [?] and nail shut such a business with hobnails! How would that look and what would the world say? People would be astonished and take us for madmen.
Reb Simcha tried to calm her and to show her [?] that this is the way of commerce; there had been worse times already, and nevertheless God had helped and they had dug themselves out; it is nothing terrible [?], and God will help further, and they will live out the rest of their years in wealth and honour.
— The whole world behaves like this, after all. Must we of all people be the exception and fall in [?]! — Reb Simcha now objected, taking an angry tone with his wife; but he soon made it up with her and implored her to go back into the shop and enter everything in the book — which goods had come in — and set about running the trade with the provincial merchants and taking in the money from them.
Sarah'le the wholesaler ["hurtovnitshke", Polish hurtowniczka] — that is what they called her — would by no means give in. She no longer went into the shop, but went from there straight up to her own place, to the rich apartment, threw herself down on the ottoman and did not get up from it for whole days.
She wept and lamented and became from day to day ever more melancholy.
Everyone in the house was frightened of her; the children took the father's side and tried to influence their mother, and kept trying to win her over with all sorts of kind words.
Sarah'le was silent, with a pair of big eyes, and to everything she had only one answer:
— We are going under, remember, let us save ourselves, perhaps there is still time. —
In the shop there was still bustle: merchants in, bailiffs [?] out; but Reb Simcha Szlamowicz was a Jew full of trust in God, and so he took heart that he would get over everything and still stay on his feet; the children thought the same, and the husband and the children began to worry that Sarah'le was not quite all there, and who knows whether her nerves had not been shaken by so much straining of her head over business.

They did not want to give her to me with good — they will give her to me with evil. Yes, with evil — he said to himself.
He had waited for him on the way and begun to befriend him. He strove to win his trust and at the same time taught him how to be conspiratorial in America, where, God forbid, they might catch him and send him back to Poland for such a piece of work.
— The first thing — he tells him — you must not write them a single letter. Not one dip of the pen may they have from you. Everything you will need, I will arrange for you, and since I have a good friend in Knin [?], I will send him your letters and he will answer you.
— You must understand, after all, that you may not lead them into danger.
— I understand, I understand — said Binyamindl, and tears appeared in his eyes — I only thank the Master of the Universe for sending me such a good guide.
For that very reason, however, the good guide acted so that, as long as Binyamindl was in New York, he would not receive a single letter from his father-in-law and his wife. — One mustn't, after all, God forbid, there is danger; he will write for him, answer, everything — he, Rosen; what a good man he is, this Rosen — Binyamindl kept saying to himself.
And the second part of the plan too will apparently succeed — Rosen thinks to himself, and of this he is sure.
The whole way he guarded him like the apple of his eye. And when they sailed on the ship, when Binyamindl fell ill with seasickness, he sat a whole day and a whole night by his bed and poured lemon with water into him.
— Why do I deserve this! In whose merit! — asked Binyamindl, lying in bed.
— In the Rebbe's merit, may he live long — Rosen answered sarcastically.
When they arrived in New York, Rosen again ran about and looked for a room for himself and for Binyamindl, a kosher kitchen, everything — he did everything only to win Binyamindl's trust.
They became like two brothers of one father and mother. Rosen wrote one letter and then a second to the father-in-law, but no more.
The other letters, which Binyamindl wrote in his own hand, no longer reached Poland — [?] Rosen had already seen to that. Rosen also saw to it that from Poland terrible, frightening letters should arrive, letters that would make him shudder and tremble.
More than that, he began to weave a plan to stop writing letters to the father-in-law altogether — the father-in-law, who through him must end up in prison, and Chanele!... Chanele must die of grief, yes, die. Then there will be an end. Then the second part of his vile plan will be complete.
Binyamindl believed, believed everything Rosen used to tell him. And how could one not believe such a man as Rosen, who had done him so many favours, who runs about and sees to getting him a post as a cantor or a ritual slaughterer.
And both were pleased with themselves: Binyamindl was pleased to have such a faithful [?] friend, and Rosen was pleased that the second part of his vile plan was succeeding.

Chapter 4.

Hard days full of pain, unrest and despair began for Chanele in her father's house.
All day long she sat at the window and heard only her father's lamenting over her dark luck. The lamenting had so sickened her that she would have run wherever her eyes might carry her.
It is already deep into winter. Reb Avraham has given up all his businesses and lives only on the rent from his four houses, which he owns on the market square in Knin [?].
In the whole eight months there had been barely two letters from Binyamin. He wrote that he had not yet settled into anything.
He told that on the way he had made the acquaintance of a certain Rosen, who helps him and does a great deal for him, but beyond that not one dip of the pen had come from him.
The last letter had come after Sukkot, and now it is already Hanukkah, and still no letter has come.
Hard, very hard it was for Chanele to see the grief of her father and mother, who wept over her bitter fate.
So the dull, senseless days dragged on for Chanele, full of the gloom of grief. Not cheerful were the nights. The long winter nights.
Whole nights she lay with open eyes, not closing them for a single minute; she wept, sobbed and longed intensely for Rosen, who is far, very far from her.
Only now, when he was no longer there, did she begin to remember him, to summon up in her thoughts his face, his beautiful chiselled body; she [printed "ni"] saw him so clearly that she embraced the pillow and began to stroke it as she used to do with the beautiful curly hair of his head.
Her husband had, after all, not given her even one thought — what is he to her anyway? A stranger, yes, a stranger. Altogether they had known each other seven days; she had not been a wife to him, because she had been unclean.
Rosen she has known so long, so long — six years, six whole years. How good it had been for her with him; he taught her Polish books, told her stories, walked with her into the depths of the old pine [?] forest. And there! There [he] kissed her so, kissed her so sweetly. At this she begins to bite the pillow and bursts into tears.
God has punished me for shedding his blood, for causing him so much suffering; yes, this is God's punishment — she said to herself in the quiet; how good it would be if he came now. They were nights of waiting; she would listen to every rustle that came out of the stillness, to every sound with which the nights are so full. She knew that the one she was waiting for would not come, that he was far, very far, and yet she lay with open eyes. They were nights, nights of anger at her father, at the Rebbe, for having torn her away from Rosen, for having thrust upon her a man whom she does not know and knows nothing of. A stranger. A wildly strange man. She was angry at all her acquaintances, even at Rosen, because he does not feel her longing and does not come running. In anger she tore from the wall the old clock, which irritated her with its tedious tick-tock, and between one of whose strokes and the next [printed "tsion", probably "bizn"] there passes not an hour but an eternity.
Quite often she would open the window and, in nothing but her shift, with bare arms, sit on the open window and with her large eyes gaze at the deep-heaped snow lying lit by the clear white moon. I want to catch cold and die — she said, and leaned out with her whole body.
And sometimes a great pity would seize her. Pity for her young body; then she would undress completely naked, sit down opposite the mirror and begin to stroke and caress her slender legs, her shoulders, her young, firm, still small breasts, and meanwhile tears would pour from her eyes.

Men

[Humoresque — short story.] By Shmuel Rubinshteyn.
(A humoresque. What girls should not read)

Moritz Blumental sat a long while in his room, thinking. He had a lot to think about. That evening he had to write a letter to a girl with whom he had been going out for two years, and in his letter he finally had to propose to her that they marry.
He paced about the room and from time to time cast a glance at the table, where an opened letter lay, and next to it writing paper and an envelope.
A young woman with a laughing face appeared in the doorway. Her hair a little dishevelled and her neck bare, in the manner of a coquette. This was his landlady, with whom he lodged.
She stood in the doorway and with both hands began to draw in her waist.
Blumental smiled when he saw her.
"Is your husband here?" he asked.
"He has only just gone out and will be away a couple of hours."
Blumental went up to her, put his arm around her waist and gave her a kiss.
"Come into the garden and drink tea," the woman said.
"No, I can't now," Blumental said in a soft voice, in which one could feel that he was struggling with himself.
"I must write an important letter."
"A love letter?"
"Yes!"
"Faithless man! You'll marry a girl and forget me! There is no faithfulness in the world!"
The woman gave him a light push on the shoulder and went out.
Blumental sat down at the table and began to read the letter he had received today from his Brantshe. She writes to him:
"It is already two years that we have been friends, and from your last conversation one can see that you love me. If so, why don't you tell me so plainly? After all, I did not understand your words, but after you left me and I thought your words over, I understood in them words that I have not heard from you until now."
How sweet and pleasant his Brantshe's words were to Blumental. He must answer her at once. He took the pen in his hand and began to write:
"Dearest Brantshe!
"You ask whether I love you? Yes, I love you with all the fire of my heart, I love you with all the strength of my youth, with the first flame of my love, for until I came to know you I had never loved any woman; more precisely — I always avoided them — — — —
Here he stopped. His [?] lips twisted into a strange smile: why does he need to tell a lie? Who is asking him to tell her that this is his first love? But — too late, he has already written it, and he doesn't feel like rewriting it. So he writes on:
"Never in my life have I embraced a woman, never kissed one, except perhaps my late mother"...
Here his hand trembled: why must he also "drag" the name of his dead mother into such a foolish lie? He laid the pen aside for a while and began to think again, to recall his past life. More than once he had sworn eternal love to Berta and confirmed his oaths with hot, fiery kisses. Berta, however, was a prettier girl, a cleverer and a richer one. He abandoned Berta, and she, with her broken heart, suffered [?] in silence and said not a word to anyone.
He went on writing:
"Dearest Brantshe! If you knew what a shy man I am, you would laugh. Many times I wanted to tell you that I love you, but I was afraid you might refuse me. You were even very friendly to me, but I was afraid that perhaps it was no more than the friendship of a sister for a brother. Yes, I am a very shy man."
"Liar!" a voice cried out behind Blumental's shoulder.
He had been so absorbed in his writing that he had not felt his landlady standing behind him and reading his letter.
Blumental took fright, but he soon recovered, looked into his landlady's eyes with a sly smile and tugged her by the hand. She was dressed in a light coat and a hat. She was getting ready to go into town.
"Let me go. I have to leave," she said. "I want to ask you something: my friend is due to come to me soon; I arranged with her that we would go together to the milliner, but she didn't come at the appointed time and I can't wait for her any longer. If she comes soon, tell her that I'll be at her place tomorrow. But don't you flirt with her — she's a great coquette."
"A hundred thousand ladies and girls are not worth your littlest fingernail!" Blumental cried, set his landlady on his lap and began to cover her face and neck with hot kisses.
"Let me go! Let me go! You'll crumple my hat and my dress. Let me go! I must go! We'll see each other again!"
The woman left. Blumental began to write again, but very slowly:
"Brantshe! You have opened a new world for me. Until I met you I did not yet know what such happiness is. I am sure that had I not met you, I would never have loved any other woman"...
There was a knock at the kitchen door. Blumental went out to open the door and at once came back in with a short woman, plump and blonde like a German, with a turned-up little nose.
"My landlady has just gone out," Blumental said. "She couldn't wait for you; she'll be at your place tomorrow."
"I'm very sorry," says the woman, going up to the mirror and putting her toilette in order. As she did so, a handkerchief fell out of her hand.
Blumental, like a cavalier, quickly picked up the handkerchief and handed it to her.
"Thank you," the woman said. "You men are lucky people. You have so many pockets and lose nothing. I have only one pocket."
"Where?" Blumental asked.
"You're curious to know? Well, guess — find my pocket yourself."
Blumental did not need to be asked twice.
"Right here!" he exclaimed, laying his hand on one side of her dress.
"No!"
"Right here!"
"No!"
"Right here!"
"You want to guess with both hands? Let me go! Do you put your arms around your landlady too?"
"No, I have no desire for her," Blumental said somewhat heatedly. "I liked you very much at first sight. Only I never had the opportunity to talk things over with you alone. Tell me, could you perhaps drive out of town with me tomorrow?"
"Not tomorrow. On Sunday I can."
"Very good, I'll wait for you at 2 o'clock in the afternoon by the bridge. Meanwhile — a kiss!"
"Enough! You've already had more than 20," the woman said. "Let that be enough, someone might still come..."
"My sweet life! My dearest! I am so happy!"
"Oh, you're bluffing!" the woman said. "All men bluff. But never mind, I'll go with you. Tomorrow [sic] by the bridge at 2 o'clock in the afternoon I'll expect you. Don't let slip a word to your landlady; it wouldn't suit me for her to know."
"To my landlady? I have no dealings with her; she looks like a monkey compared with you. Goodbye, my dear!"
When the woman had gone, Blumental sat down to finish his letter:
"The sun here is so glorious; I am very sorry that I cannot allow myself such a luxury as driving out of town with you; just today I have an important piece of business that I must not break off"...
Then Blumental sealed the great lie in an envelope, wrote the address, stuck on a stamp and hurried off to the post box...
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Premises of Zionist Organisations to Be Closed

In one of Mr. Zmigród's houses on Kołłątaja Street are the premises of the organisations of the General Zionists, "Hitachdut", "Hapoel" and "Svue"[?].

The great celebration at the Radomsko Rebbe's.

[Sosnowiec — Hasidim and rebbes.] Sosnowiec.
The Rebbe's only daughter has given birth to a baby boy. — Dozens of rebbes and rabbis at the circumcision. — Demonstration by Agudah youth against the Munkács Rebbe.
Last Friday a circumcision celebration on a grand scale was held at the Radomsko Rebbe's. The Rebbe's one and only daughter gave birth to a baby boy eight days earlier.
The joyful news spread through the Hasidic world, and throughout the Jewish diaspora people prepared to come to Sosnowiec for the feast.
From early in the morning groups of Hasidim, rebbes and rabbis from Poland and Galicia arrived with every train. It gave the impression that a national Hasidic congress was taking place.
At 9 o'clock there is suddenly a rush on the "Mandushever Besl"[?] [doubtful reading — perhaps the name of a square or street]; people hurry from all sides of the town. It becomes clear that the Munkács Rebbe has arrived.
For everyone really wants to see the Rebbe, who is so famous for his bans and curses against all parties, the Agudah among them. When the Rebbe came to Targowa[?] Street (he stayed with Mr Józef Abramczyk), the crush at the "sholem" [the handshake with the Rebbe] was enormous; pickpocket-specialists did indeed use the opportunity and
performed a "miracle"
— pulling a gold watch out of the Rebbe's pocket...
The Munkács Rebbe's participation in the celebration was due to a promise made by the child's father at a meeting with the Munkács Rebbe, that if a boy were born the Rebbe would be honoured with performing the circumcision.
In honour of the celebration there also came the rebbes and rabbis of Amshinov [Mszczonów] (Radomsko), Zawiercie (Srimilov[?] — probably Krimilov), Rawa, Krasne, Szydłów, Pilica, Warta, and many hundreds of Hasidim.
In the streets it looked as it once did on the eve of Kol Nidrei in a small shtetl. Hasidim in satin and silk zhupitses [long coats], with and without shtreimels on their heads, marched back and forth. The very strong ones even allowed themselves to strike up a merry tune and dance a little round.
The honours
were distributed among the following rebbes: sandek — the Krimilov Rebbe; kvater — the Radomsko Rebbe; and mohel — the Munkács Rebbe. Many dozens of mohels had hoped to earn the mitzvah, but the Munkács Rebbe "barred" their access and they were left without a stroke of work...
The newborn was named[?] with 4 names: Avraham, Yechezkel, Elimelech and Aharon. The first three are the names of the grandfathers, and the fourth name was added because the child was born on the day of the ushpizin of Aaron the Priest..
After the feast.
At around 3 in the afternoon, when a large part were already tipsy, the big courtyard of the Rebbe's house was packed full of Hasidim and they launched into a round dance. Everyone danced, young and old; with heads thrown back they shouted "mazel tov" loudly as they danced, so that it would reach the Rebbe, who was still in his daughter's apartment.
One of the dancers, a strapping young Hasid from Chmielnik, got carried away and performed various "acrobatic numbers"; among other things he led a "popularny pociąg" [people's train] that would not stop at the stations of Aleksandrów, Sochaczew, not even at Ger, but only at the station of Radomsko... Then the Hasidic engine-driver shouted "wysiadać" [all off!] and his passengers obeyed and steeped themselves in delight...
On Friday evening the Radomsko Rebbe came to the Munkács Rebbe's "tish". To avoid a crush, a strong guard was posted in front of the gate of Abramczyk's house in the persons of the stróż [caretaker] and his helpers, who made sure that no "outsider" slipped in.
The guard carried out his mission perfectly; for instance, when older Hasidim wanted to enter, he — the stróż, that is — received them with "Zhidushi[?] do Palestyny" [Polish: "Jew-boys, to Palestine!"].
The young men, on the other hand, received a "gift of the hand" [a blow]..
The celebration at the third Sabbath meal (shalosh seudos) was disturbed by a demonstration of the Agudah youth against the Munkács Rebbe.
As is well known, a certain hatred of the Munkács Rebbe prevails among the Ger Hasidim, for he often allows himself to insult the Agudah and the Rebbe of Ger in particular, and "here the creditor found the chance to collect his debt". On this occasion the young Ger yeshiva boys decided to take revenge and cause the Munkács Rebbe distress.
They did it in the following manner: after the Torah discourse at shalosh seudos, in which the Munkács Rebbe again called on people to keep away from the treyf organisations regardless of party, suddenly shouts were heard: "Long live Agudath Israel", "Long live the Agudah", "Long live the Keren HaYishuv", and at the same time Agudah leaflets were thrown at the Rebbe.
The outburst caused great agitation among the Radomsko Hasidim, and it was immediately reported to the Radomsko Rebbe. Soon "Radomsko" boys arrived and began to drive the attackers away. As a result a brawl broke out between the two sides, which was, however, quickly ended. (The correspondent of "Unzer Ekspres" saw with his own eyes how blood flowed like water...)
Soon after the events there appeared in the streets a
Declaration by the Agudah,
stating that they are not responsible for what took place. The Ts"R [Tseirei Agudath Israel], who were out to insult the Munkács Rebbe, were not content with the demonstration and exploited the mistake that the Munkács Rebbe made when blessing the new month: instead of Tuesday and Wednesday he said Monday and Tuesday..
The mistake was a fat bone for those who were out to compromise the Rebbe, and they issued an "extra edition" with the following content:
"To all Jews in Sosnowiec.
To prevent a stumbling block! Jews! Know that Rosh Chodesh Marcheshvan 5695 falls on Tuesday and Wednesday, not, as the Munkács Rebbe holds, on Monday and Tuesday. No one need be frightened by his cry of 'ignoramuses' (God save us), for he is a lone individual against the whole world."
On Monday at 12 noon the Munkács Rebbe departed. To make the most of it, as an answer to the insults from the Agudah, a very large crowd of Radomsko Hasidim came to take leave of him. The Radomsko Rebbe himself, in person, accompanied him right into the train.
The Munkács Rebbe paid a visit to the "Dąbrowa" Rebbe on Deckerta Street. In honour of the guest a splendid banquet was held at the Rebbe's, at which the Munkács Rebbe spoke about Hasidism and told sayings of tzaddikim.
District Conference of Keren Tel Chai in Zagłębie

On Sunday the first district conference of Keren Tel Chai in the Zagłębie region took place here, attended by representatives of the following towns: Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa, Zawiercie, Olkusz, Wolbrom, Ząbkowice, Strzemieszyce, Żarki, Myszków, "Magdushów" [?], Czeladź, "Krimilów" [probably Kromołów] and Königshütte, numbering 36 delegates and many guests.
At 12 o'clock a festive academy and a public meeting devoted to the sad situation of the Jews in the Saar territory took place in the "Ida" hall.
The academy was opened by Mr. Dov Jasny, who welcomed the guests from the Central Committee and the delegates.
On behalf of the Artisans' Association Mr. Ekstein gave greetings.
Then the president of Brit HaTzohar in Poland, Dr. Wdowiński (Warsaw), gave a lengthy lecture on the subject "Our attitude to the present situation in Zionism", and also spoke about the action of the Revisionist Executive to ease the fate of the Jewish population in the Saar territory after the plebiscite that is soon to take place there.
Finally the director of Keren Tel Chai in Poland, Mr. Z. Lerner (Warsaw), gave a lecture on the subject "In the struggle for the building of the Jewish state".
In the afternoon the district conference took place in the premises of "Brit HaChayal".
The representatives of the various towns delivered reports and discussions followed, during which various wishes were expressed as to how to improve the work and the methods of collecting.
After the lectures of Mr. Jasny on the subject "The educational problems of Keren Tel Chai" and of Director Z. Lerer on the subject "The new methods of Keren Tel Chai", a regional secretariat was elected, consisting of:
Dov Jasny (chairman), Jaskierowicz (vice-chairman), Kruk (secretary), Grinfeld (treasurer), Chmielnicki [?] and Strzegowski.
A resolution was adopted to protest against the round-ups of illegal "tourists" and to call upon the League of Nations to secure the rights of the Jews in the Saar territory in the event that it is united with Germany.
“TOZ” begins [?] its activity.

[Będzin — health and welfare.] Last week the board of “TOZ” [Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jews] held its first meeting after the summer holidays.
Before proceeding to discuss the plan of further work, Dr. Liberman gave a detailed report on the colony [summer camp] that “TOZ” ran last summer. The report shows that this time 105 children were sent to the colony free of charge, children who come from the poorest strata of the Jewish population. The children sent mostly attend the religious schools, such as Talmud-Torah etc. The hygienic conditions and the food at the colony were exceptionally good, as is shown by the fact that on average each child gained about 2½ kilos on the scale. Expenses for the colony amounted to 2,643.50 zł and income to 2,327.53. The deficit is thus over 300 zł.
Next, the question of organizing an out-patient clinic for consumptives was discussed, which Zagłębie greatly needs because of the large number of Jewish tuberculosis patients in Zagłębie; but from the present income from membership dues this is impossible. It was therefore decided to organize a broader campaign to recruit members for the society and to turn with an appeal to the Jewish population.
It is to be hoped that the Jewish public will show understanding for the necessity of the “TOZ” work and will support it as it deserves.

[Zagłębie — economy.] Who has the loss and who has the livelihood
An article whose price has risen fourfold because of the warm weather.
The broad public regards the prolonged summer with the fine weather as a nice gift and is quite pleased with it, but for the merchants of the various winter articles it is a real curse — they stocked up on goods, bills must be paid, and of takings there is nothing to speak.
From this trouble many artisans suffer too, especially the furriers — always at this time their season is in full swing, and this year they sit with folded hands.
If it goes on like this a few more weeks — they complain — they can altogether forget about working this year, because their season is a short one — until the New Year.
But there is one article whose price has risen sharply because of the warm weather, and that is...
The Zagłębie soda-water manufacturers and ice dealers did not reckon on such a summer and stocked up on ice as usual. But now this commodity is badly lacking, and the price has risen from 30 gr. a pood including delivery to 1 zł.
Most soda-water kiosks therefore use no ice at all, and explain to their customers that cold soda water is harmful to health.
Why one wants a divorce

[Będzin — local life.] (Caught in the rabbinical court)
For 30 years Leib T. lived with his wife, had half a dozen children with her and has even already married them all off in peace — and now, at the threshold of the 31st year of their life together, Leib runs to the rabbi in an uproar: Holy Rabbi! I can no longer bear it with my shrew [?], and see to it that I get rid of her.
What is the story? — the rabbi asks the party concerned.
What do you mean? She is a slattern, a slob — where has it ever been heard of, Rabbi, our crown, that a Jewish woman should not know how to run a household, but only lie whole days and nights at the neighbours’ and gossip [?] about the whole world.
Women, after all, cannot keep a secret; at once it is carried to them [?] that my wife has talked about them, and they too are no angels — quarrels break out and quite often even fights. All year long my wife goes about with blackened eyes and a bandaged face.
My wife is a dogged, stubborn creature, a real snake. After every attack there begins a series of doctors, examinations, [?], trials, police reports, witnesses — and the other side does not sleep either. In short, a quarter of my hard-earned toil crawls away into barber-surgeons, doctors, pharmacies, courts, lawyers and fines. So tell me yourself, Rabbi: is it possible to stay even one minute longer in such a hell?
— Well, why have you only made up your mind so late?
— Holy Rabbi, I knew my misfortune right away on stepping [?] from under the wedding-canopy poles — that the shrew was good only for the eve of Yom Kippur [i.e. for kapores]; but I reckoned that in time, when she had a child and had something to keep her busy, she would stay [?] at home and leave the world alone; but it turns out that I was mistaken. She dumped half a dozen children on me and remained the same snake as before.
— Oh, Rabbi, you will probably wonder why I did not “swing kapores” with my shrew straight after the birth of the first children? The excuse is indeed [?] the children. For children a father makes the greatest sacrifices. So I too sacrificed my young life for the children. Now, thank God, I have already raised all my children to the wedding canopy and good deeds — so why should I not know a little bit of life in my last few years?
The moreh hora’ah [rabbinical judge] tried to bring the elderly couple to domestic peace. The attempts did not succeed, and the divorce will take place soon.

A Driver from Dąbrowa and a Student from Warsaw as Swindlers

[Dąbrowa — crime.] The head (naczelnik) of the post office in Dąbrowa has recently received many complaints from families of deceased persons in Warsaw that they had been swindled.
The swindle consisted in this: a few days after a member of the family had died, a parcel from Dąbrowa arrived in the deceased's name, cash on delivery. The family, naturally, paid for and took the parcel and then saw that they had been swindled: the parcel contained rags, newspapers and other such "valuables".
After careful observation at the Dąbrowa post office it became clear that the one sending the "parcels" is a Dąbrowa driver, and his partner in the swindles is a student from Warsaw; the latter informed his Dąbrowa friend of the names of the deceased and their exact addresses, to which the driver sent the "parcels".
Explosion of an Infernal Machine in Klimontów. A Woman Is Torn to Pieces

[Klimontów — crime.] A certain Tabisz, a resident of Klimontów, received a notice that a parcel sent from Miechów was waiting for him at the post office.
When Tabisz brought the parcel home, his wife was curious and began to unpack it. Suddenly a powerful explosion was heard and the woman was torn to pieces. Tabisz, who was standing some distance away, was seriously injured.
As it turned out, the parcel contained a constructed infernal machine (bomb), which exploded when the parcel was unpacked. The police are conducting an energetic investigation. There is a supposition that this was an act of revenge.
Mysterious Murder of a Jewish Merchant in Zawiercie

[Zawiercie — crime.] On Tuesday at 8 in the evening the Jewish population of Zawiercie was shaken by the terrible news that the 33-year-old S. Majzels had been found dead in his own small grocery shop on Piłsudski Street.
It was established that Majzels had been shot dead.
The police are conducting an energetic investigation. There is a supposition that Majzels fell victim to a robbery attack.
A Fire in Żarnowiec
[Żarnowiec — fire.] On Saturday night a fire broke out in the town of Żarnowiec. Several houses went up in smoke. Most of those affected are Jewish tenants.

The purpose of his visit is to mobilise all forces for constructive Zionist work in Będzin and in the whole of Zagłębie. It is to be hoped that the Jewish population will receive the distinguished guest warmly and come out to meet him.

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — building disaster; Katowice.]
A Terrible Catastrophe with Many Workers' Victims in Katowice.
About 100 workers fell from a scaffold. — 70 seriously injured, 30 lightly.
On Monday a terrible building catastrophe occurred in Katowice on the site where the cathedral is being built.
At about 9 o'clock in the morning a group of unemployed men, 100 in number, came to the building site; they had volunteered for the work and first wanted to acquaint themselves with the state of the work done so far. When the workers were standing on a scaffold, the boards and beams, soaked by the recent rains, could not bear the weight of the large number of people, and the scaffold collapsed. The results were fatal. All the workers, together with the building foreman and a priest, fell from a height of one and a half storeys. The doctors who were called gave help on the spot to several dozen seriously and lightly injured. The seriously injured were taken to hospital.
A building commission arrived at the scene of the catastrophe and established that the scaffold, which had even been made of new boards and beams, could nevertheless not bear the weight of 100 people.
Third-Year Schoolgirls Exempted from Desecrating the Sabbath

[Upper Silesia — education and the Sabbath; Katowice.]
As our readers know, the management of the vocational school in Katowice informed the Jewish schoolgirls from Zagłębie that they may study at the school on condition that they also come to the lessons on the Sabbath.
The decree hit hardest the girls of the third year, because throughout all three years they had not attended school on the Sabbath. In this connection the schoolgirls swore an oath that they would not agree to any compromises whatsoever, ready [?] rather to resign from the school altogether, as long as they would not desecrate the Sabbath.
The school management, seeing the stubbornness of the third-year girls, informed them that they may come to the school under the previous conditions.
