Concerning a Crafts School for Zagłębie / (With the Help of Society the Institution Can Be Realised)

[Zagłębie — vocational education; article.]
From the article by the esteemed Katowice rabbi Dr. Chameides, printed alongside, our readers learn that the said rabbi intervened with the management of the Katowice vocational school so that the children from Zagłębie should, as until now, not have to attend the school on the Sabbath in future either.
As we see, exempting the pupils from attending school on the Sabbath is not one of the easy things, and the rabbi therefore advises the Jews of Zagłębie to create a school of their own, that is, a Jewish one, so that the Jewish population should not be dependent on anyone's favours and could do as is convenient for us, as is good for us.
The heads of the said school, too, cannot stop wondering why Zagłębie Jewry should have to depend on foreign hands and not be able to keep the Sabbath for itself. The question is indeed a hard one. Strangers cannot understand it.
Founding a crafts school for Jewish children would really not have been one of the very great things; palaces [?] certainly need not be built for it — and yet, how many times have we already touched on the question in the columns of our newspaper, and how many times have we thought that any moment now the institution would be realised; and yet all of it has come to nothing [literally: "turned out an attic"], and we have remained with mere talk. Besides, talk about the school serves as a slogan for every party at town-council or kehilla elections. Every time we hear how one party reproaches the other for why the school has not been realised, and the other, the opposing party, promises to carry it out; and the end is that, despite the competition of mouths, neither of the two, God forbid, took fright, and no one put a hand into cold water. Evidently all the professional speakers know, in the heat of the moment [?], with what to win over the crowd, and that from saying to doing is quite a long way, and the one has nothing whatever to do with the other. One can say whatever one likes and whatever is nicer and impresses the matter, and later it concerns nobody.
If there was once talk of the necessity of vocational schools, today they are not only a necessity but at the same time an urgency.
The rush to obtain the matura diploma has gone bankrupt on the Jewish front for two reasons: first, the population in Poland has become greatly impoverished in recent years and there is no longer the means to keep the children either in the secondary schools or in the higher schools, to which, incidentally, access is almost closed to us; and secondly, after the parents have broken their backs and their child has already graduated from a university somewhere abroad, he can achieve nothing here anew, gets no employment and is admitted to nothing at all.
These very circumstances have led the Jewish population to throw itself into trades. Today, whoever you talk to, everyone wants to learn something, and with it — one would like to hope — will reach a goal in life and at the same time also be a useful citizen, wherever one may find oneself.
But it is only easy to say "learn a trade" when one does not have the possibility of carrying it out properly. Where, in fact, are we to send our children, when we have not prepared the necessary vocational schools for them?
Yes, as said, there has already been very much talk about this matter, but further than that, God forbid, nobody has gone. "A good word does the mouth no harm," says a Jewish proverb; in this case, however, it does harm. Why speak empty words if nothing comes of them? On the contrary, they do harm, because the public is misled thereby into thinking that in the end we will get the necessary schools.
There was even once a case when it was thought that now the plan would be realised. Zagłębie communal workers met at the time and decided to open vocational schools; but since not every town in Zagłębie could undertake to maintain such an institution, a concept was then created that Zagłębie should for the time being have one school — and then they could not agree [?] among themselves where the school should be, and it is supposed that this was the reason why the school was not founded then.
Since that time a few years have passed, and today we believe that one would not stop at such trifles. It goes without saying that at the given moment there would be wavering between Będzin and Sosnowiec, but it would not be worth tearing ourselves apart over such a thing, because communication is exceptionally good: we have a good railway connection and a tram every few minutes. Let us imagine that we live in one of the great European cities, where one literally travels from one quarter to another. Besides, a way out can be found for this too: whichever town outdoes the other in cash will earn the right to have the meritorious institution in its midst, to which the whole Jewish population belongs [?].
It is therefore important first of all to meet for a consultation on this very important question. There is no more time for dragging out and neglecting this matter. We see, after all, what we look like thanks to our apathy. Katowice citizens, after all, cannot understand how such a Jewish community as exists in Zagłębie should not possess one single vocational school.
And this apathetic attitude is truly to be wondered at and regretted. From now on, therefore, we must no longer be so cold; one must, without any excuse, take up earnestly, sincerely and energetically the realisation of the necessary institution.
And therefore one should first of all meet, one should try to confer, the first proposals should be made.
First of all the Będzin and Sosnowiec communal workers must come together. They must bring the question forward and make it topical. The will always has much to say, and in the given case certainly, certainly.
We hope, we want to hope, that the call of the Katowice rabbi Dr. Chameides and our words too will not be a voice crying in the wilderness, but that the Zagłębie leadership will understand its obligation at the present moment and will endeavour to realise the institution, which is today an urgent necessity.
R. Let.
Create a Jewish Vocational School in Zagłębie!

[Zagłębie — vocational education; Sabbath; article.] By the Rabbi of Katowice, Dr. Chameides.
In recent weeks Jewish parents from the Zagłębie region have turned to me with the request that I intervene with the Katowice school authorities so that their children should not be compelled to attend the vocational school in Katowice on the Sabbath. The talks I held on the matter with the headmistress, with the teaching staff and, last but not least, with the school curator in person, convinced me clearly of the difficulties the Jewish youth — and in the given case, the Jewish daughter — must struggle with when she does not want to commit a betrayal of the Jewish religion and will on no account give up the Sabbath. There is simply no understanding for our demands, and according to "dina de-malkhuta" [the law of the land] we do not even have the right to demand that Jewish pupils be exempted from lessons on the Sabbath, because the school administration relies on the law, which knows no exceptions and no consideration.
It is therefore necessary to draw the attention of the Jewish population in Zagłębie to the fact that, despite the greatest effort and exertion on my part, there is unfortunately only faint hope that the Sabbath question can be solved here by an intervention or by "protection" [string-pulling] with the authorities. And as I have heard, the vocational schools in Zagłębie, too, are making difficulties and will not agree to exempt Jewish girl pupils from lessons on the Sabbath.
The time has therefore come for the Jews of Zagłębie to begin thinking about a Jewish vocational school of their own. For "if I am not for myself, who will be for me!" Jewish vocational schools already exist in Kraków and Lwów, and they stand at a high level. Why should it not be possible in time to build a vocational school of our own in Zagłębie as well? Need one prove, in today's hard times, what significance such a school would have for our young Jewish daughters?
I speak specifically of a vocational school for Jewish girls, because the school in Katowice is a girls' school, and secondly, because in the field of girls' education there are still many mistakes to put right. Hard is the situation of the young Jewish man, who stands before life's road helpless and desperate, and from day to day the prospect grows darker and gloomier... Harder still and more dangerous is the situation of the Jewish daughters, who have no employment and also lack the necessary dollars to reach the desired goal soon... "Idleness leads to dullness of mind": the hopelessness of their situation leads them onto dangerous paths — family tragedies, which unfortunately become known often enough and which arose only because the Jewish daughter saw no purpose and no aim in life before her.
The Jews of Zagłębie must collect grosz by grosz and set up a vocational school of their own, so that their children should not, God forbid, be compelled to desecrate the Sabbath. Today in the Land of Israel we need good, qualified workers in all fields; a craft does not only "sustain its master", it does not only provide a livelihood — it educates the person first and foremost and teaches him to be useful and productive for his surroundings.
The economic crisis must not hold us back from starting the work at once. It would be worthwhile for all the fruitless party quarrels to stop for a short time, and for all the Jews of Zagłębie, regardless of party and tendency, to join together and carry out the plan. What is at stake here is the future of your children; it is a question that concerns you yourselves.
I hope that my appeal will awaken the men of action in Zagłębie to take up the question, and I am sure that their efforts will be crowned with success, for "nothing stands in the way of the will".
Meir Herc: Bankrupt (a story) — 3

[Literature — serialized story; part 3.] By Meir Herc.
3.
So they called doctors, and they shook their heads along, saying it might indeed be so, and so it remained.
The doctors advised taking her to fresh air, to a boarding house or a sanatorium, somewhere in a spa town. Reb Simcha Szlamowicz was a devoted husband; he wanted to do everything for her health, and he begged her with tears in his eyes:
— Sorele, Sorashi, have pity on yourself and go, I don't begrudge you any money, my right hand, look, save yourself, you are still a young woman, and after all we have not yet married off even one child.
The children too came up to her and begged her to do it for father's sake,
but Sorele shook her head:
— No, I mustn't, I can't and I don't need to; no, Simcha, you are mistaken, you have nothing left any more, you mustn't send me away on other people's money; do the accounts and you'll see that you are behind. Besides, I am healthy, you are all sick; I am the best doctor and my cure is: shut down the business and stop being merchants!..
Seeing there was nothing to be done, Reb Simcha and the children began to take less interest in her; it became clear to everyone that mother was not in her right mind, that something had got mixed up in her head.
So they went on running the business, and Sorele lay all the time on the sofa, put wet cloths on her head and groaned.
The merchants, acquaintances, good friends — when they did not see Sorele the "hurtowniczka" [the wholesaler] in the shop for so many days, and her place now taken by the eldest daughter, the beautiful Rusza, they soon guessed that Sorele was probably not quite all there. And indeed they were told later that the clever businesswoman was seriously ill, and the merchants pitied her and wished her a full recovery — yet at the same time they had the opposite in mind: quietly, in their hearts, they wished that the too-clever businesswoman, Sorele the wholesaler, would take longer to recover; if only — it would be easier for them to get parcels [goods on credit] from Reb Simcha; with Sorele, the seasoned, shrewd businesswoman, it had not come so easily. She knew each one exactly, through and through — how far he could be trusted and from whom one must have proper security.
She read in the faces of the small-town merchants what they had in mind and were thinking in their hearts: would they pay or not? Would they let the bills of exchange be protested or not? She already had special signs: she looked them well into the eyes, how they sparkled as they spoke, and even more into the mouth, how the words shot out of it.
It was hard to fool her, and yet sometimes she was fooled; that is why the merchants were now pleased that she was no longer in the business. But they did not wish her any harm. To look forward to her death — certainly not; she was, after all, a fine, clever woman; only to have a little more to do with herself and no time for the business — that they were glad to grant her.
There were others too who were pleased that the beautiful Rusza was taking her sick mother's place. These were young petty merchants, commercial travellers, sequestrators, bailiffs, who would have let an eye be put out for the beautiful Rusza and were happy to snatch a little flirt with her in the shop when the father was looking somewhere else or was sometimes not in the shop.
Ever since the picture-pretty girl Rusza had appeared in Reb Simcha Szlamowicz's shop, the finest of the Polish intelligentsia suddenly began coming in to buy — officials of various institutions, bank employees, even directors: when, strolling along the pavement, they caught sight of the splendid alabaster face and the finely carved figure of Reb Simcha Szlamowicz's daughter shining through the shop window, they found all sorts of pretexts and came into the shop with the sole intention of getting acquainted with her and snatching a look and a chat with her.
Reb Simcha Szlamowicz in truth had a wholesale business, but because of the distinction of the respectable non-Jewish customers it would not have been fitting, and so everything was sold to them retail.

The General and the Particular

[Essay — the general and the particular; fundraising, charity and national funds.] By S. Salcer.
I.
No nation or tongue in the world is so burdened with obligations and monetary levies, both with regard to the particular — that is, the community, the settlement where the Jew lives — and with regard to Klal Yisrael [the Jewish people as a whole] — that is, the campaigns ["actions"] that have a general, all-Jewish significance.
The Jewish domain is impoverished; the greater part of the population is destitute[?]; over everything and everyone hovers poverty; there is no livelihood; schools for the youth, institutions for the sick, orphanages, feeding — there is nothing. And when there is, after all, something here and there, it is simply like a drop in the ocean compared with the great need.
Besides need of a personal nature, there are the burdens of the communal requirements, the religious personnel of rabbis, slaughterers, etc. In short, the "needs of Thy people Israel" are not only "many" — they are "awesome," frightful, truly extraordinary.
And when one comes to a session of a Jewish kehilla council or a town council and listens to a draft budget for the coming year, which must cover, if only in the smallest measure, the needs of the Jewish community, both in private life and in the needs of the town, one immediately asks: "Where shall all this go in" [ana yikanes hashetan hazeh, a Talmudic quip] — truly, where does one get it, who can be the provider for such a large, needy family burdened with so many straits?
On the other side — the need of "Klal Yisrael." For Jews everywhere are "one entity": persecuted politically and economically, uniform socially, living almost everywhere from one and the same occupations — trade and handicraft — from which they are systematically pushed out, while the nations and states care little about creating new sources of existence. Besides that, they are constantly threatened by antisemitic outbreaks, pogroms, destruction, etc. So that always, at almost any time, there is a necessity of outside help, of rescue — people from people, somewhere in other countries — as happened recently with the German, Algerian and Turkish Jews.
The negative situation of the Jews over almost the whole globe has also historically created the great renaissance movement of upbuilding, which strives for independence, freedom in all fields, up to its own state forms of life. The movement has already struck such deep roots in the people's soul, has already borne so much fruit, created so much that is positive "there." But the growth of the Jewish centre swallows, and will go on swallowing for many years, perhaps generations, treasures of material means which the Jewish world public gives and collects among itself.
The one together with the other. The need of the whole thus also becomes a mighty factor in quantity — in the sum of monetary means — and in "quality," in the "unconditionality" of the "must," in the categorical imperative. Out of all these necessities the specifically Jewish situation (for no other people is so scattered and dispersed over the whole world) has created a conflict, a kind of disproportion, even a competition between the general and the particular. The local need demands, shouts, calls out and always stresses that it has the better claim, because it is local, close, and therefore prior — "the poor of your own town come first"; the collective need argues that it is greater, deeper, more "historic," because its permanence concerns millions of people, and not for the moment, momentarily, but for generations, for the Congregation of Israel, and it embraces[?] a great space and time.
And so the two concepts of general and particular wrestle with each other and raise the eternal question of "who comes before whom?"
At times it is simply painful to watch the competition, the race between an emissary of Keren Hayesod or of an anti-Hitler centre and the dozens of "dunners and demanders" for local needs — over the giver, who regrettably is always one and the same: the small well-to-do minority amid the great poor majority. [The giver] becomes confused out of sheer[?] perplexity, struggles with himself, does not know to whom to give precedence.
II.
And therefore it is very important to make the matter clear once and for all, to untangle the knot. And simply to educate the decisive strata in the spirit of harmony between the two popular needs, popular levies, as the one complements the other; the one is tied and bound up with the other, and it is impossible to switch off one at the expense of the other. For it is not true that between the general and the particular lies an abyss, that these are separate institutions which have no connection with each other.
In our time general causes are also an answer to the questions and needs of masses of poor individuals. In the great chain of Jewish need the links between the individual and the many close together. Take, for example, the institutions for the upbuilding of Eretz Israel: they decide questions of thousands of families from every place, every shtetl, from which pioneer immigrants [olim-halutzim] emigrate to Eretz Israel, or which partly receive support from relatives settled there; so that the general cause is already a deed not for someone else, but for oneself. It is almost hard to find a donor to the funds who would not be interested — directly, himself, or indirectly, for his relatives — in the ongoing, day-to-day growth of the Eretz-Israel Yishuv.
The same is true of the anti-Hitlerite and anti-antisemitic world struggle, which concerns every individual, because he is simply threatened with becoming a victim, with suffering personally, whether physically or economically, from the world plague that penetrates all human settlements — a plague that can certainly be fought, or at least made less harmful, if on our side it runs up against resistance and self-defence.
On the other hand, local mutual help for the destitute is also a general cause, because the stronger the particular — the single individual — is, even if only temporarily rescued, the stronger and firmer is the general, the common collective, and vice versa.
"All is one, and one is all" — says Spinoza.
The upshot is that everyone who is always in the ranks of the defenders and fighters, who takes part and makes sacrifices (be they material — that is very important), should always consciously recognise the naturalness, the necessity and the equal social justice of both concepts, general and particular, and give equal standing to the readiness for sacrifice on both fronts.
It Is an Art to Satisfy Everyone...

— We often think, when we encounter criticism, that in life one rarely possesses this art. Yet there are exceptions. One of the fields of life in the household, and of the range belonging to it, is washing. And washing is indeed the exception. There is no doubt whatsoever about it, because there is, after all, Radion — a universal means for washing. It removes every kind of dirt, and at the same time it is suitable for washing the finest fabrics. Radion washes thoroughly and spares the laundry.
Where Does the Road Lead?

[Article — craftsmen, the guild law.] In the Warsaw Jewish press, as well as in the local press, there have appeared in recent months a series of articles, explanations, appeals and even warnings about the danger approaching the Jewish craftsman in connection with the coming into force of the guild law and the industrial law as early as the beginning of 1935. The craftsmen are therefore warned and called upon to register in the craftsmen's organizations, which alone and exclusively are able to defend the economic existence of the Jewish craftsmen.
[?] the main question[?], directed first of all to the craftsmen themselves: why do they not register, and still more, why are they at best indifferent?
There are even some article-writers who come to the conclusion that there exists among the craftsmen a trend recruited from young former workers and labour activists, who hold that the whole guild law was invented by Rasner [Rosner?] and his colleagues, and therefore they do not recognize such laws.
That we do not agree with the above-mentioned conclusion goes without saying, if only for the simple reason that we hold that Rasner and his colleagues are not capable of inventing laws. But what we must indeed establish and stamp with complete categoricalness is this: that Rasner and his colleagues contributed a great deal to the adoption and implementation of the guild law (which in its consequences will destroy thousands of Jewish craftsmen's livelihoods). That is a fact which nobody can deny any longer. Let at least that side (the Rasnerite one) not weep bitter tears over the fate of the Jewish craftsman. So they decided it, and so they want to have it in future too.
It is indeed the "leaders" who are to blame that the broad public avoids the craftsmen's organizations like a stench. Not for nothing does a saying go around among the masses: "To say a few words that don't suit the 'leaders' costs a hundred in taxes"... It is therefore no wonder that the appeals fall on stopped-up ears.
To confirm and also to explain what has been said above, we want to go back a few years, when the craftsmen's organizations flourished, ran their own banks, were honourably represented in all public institutions, and everywhere had a considerable and often even a decisive influence, as for instance in the municipal self-governments and also in the Jewish kehillot. What did the work and help for the benefit of the craftsmen look like then? Was there even any substantial work carried out by the craftsmen's chairmen, the ławnicy (lay assessors) and even the [?] vice-presidents, apart from the beggarly work of a free doctor or perhaps rotten potatoes? Or in the kehillot, where they contributed large sums to the budget (etat), in order afterwards to beg it back and in this way show the world what great doers they are and what great power they have? Hence begin the quarrels among the chairmen, quarrels of half-baked fine fellows... The same happened in the banks: the creation of personal followers necessarily caused the main goals to be avoided and not even thought about. So it is also with the law on crafts.
Among the membership of the craftsmen's organizations there are adherents of various political tendencies. One part always and every time came out against the new measures which in their consequences will make still heavier the already embittered life of the Jewish craftsmen. We have always pointed out that restrictions, however necessary[?] they may be, will (under present conditions) always hit the bad sides of the Jewish craftsmen's mass. Therefore we must [—?] oppose every restriction until we ourselves shape and regulate our organizational and consequently also economic existence.
Already since the year 1927 dates the trade in diplomas, craftsman's cards and examinations, which had a broad field for wheeling and dealing. As a result new easy livelihoods were created for irresponsible wheeler-dealers, once again to the detriment of the craftsmen; for already now, at the second session of the newly created Chamber of Crafts, the agenda includes the question of revision and control of diplomas and craftsman's cards. What such control and revision smells of — one surely need not hint...
Further: we have always pointed out that the craftsmen's mass is the only scattered stratum among Jews which, however, with goodwill, patience and perseverance, could become a great social-political force, both by its numbers and by its inner strength. That, however, demands effort, serious and above all honest inner work.
In a similar sense (but with a different conclusion), we further argued, the government spheres too understand[?] it, and through the amendment (nowela) to the guild law they therefore want to kill two birds with one stone: on the one hand the so-called "not legal" workshops will be choked[?], and on the other side they will have, hooped in, half-coerced consenters.
Nevertheless the decisive factors still had doubts, and again and again demanded from the craftsmen's organizations that they hold meetings, poll the members and pass on not only adopted resolutions but also the moods among the craftsmen's masses.
It is characteristic and noteworthy that, apart from a handful of individuals, the overwhelming majority of craftsmen were unanimous with the decree.
The question arises: how is this consent to be explained?
It is explained, first: by the fact that with the "craftsmen's leaders" everything goes, so to speak, "poufnie" (confidentially). The "leaders" kept it hidden from the members; when from above they want to know the mood of the masses, they described only the good sides of the compulsory guild law and added that this is what is wished from above. Well — thinks the public — worse than bad it can't be anyway; when the government wants something there is nothing to say — and they voted..
But why did the leaders keep it hidden like that? Again a simple reason:
The craftsmen's organizations at their founding were oriented towards the so-called "Folks-Partei" (Folkists), and one could expect that in their further development they would become a pillar and a force in the Jewish community, which, according to their needs and psychological characteristics, would help shape and rebuild at least their own economic and political life. Unfortunately elements got in who began to exploit this powerful (by its numbers) movement for personal purposes. And the leaders made it their motto: we are fine, we have no principles, we are bound by nothing and no one, we do what we want and we ally ourselves with whomever we want.
Hence also the fact that the craftsmen to this day have no backbone, no position on any social or political question, in Jewish as in non-Jewish life; everything therefore depends on this or that "craftsmen's activist", on how "he" understands and puts the question, or agrees to vote. And so it became a matter of chair-grabbing and wheeling and dealing, and with it a matter of greater or smaller personal gain. Hence too the gorging over craftsmen's candidate lists at public elections.
The ugly bacchanalia with the most vital life-interests of the Jewish craftsmen caused the splits in the craftsmen's organizations and consequently the outflow of members. No appeals and warnings help any more; nobody will let himself be caught by "talk", and so the "last resort" became compulsory guilds: there one will be able to rule with the help of the strażnik (policeman). And what is more: when they command, one will also have to obey.
To confirm my words still further, I want to add a few more words that concern many towns in Poland.
Almost everywhere parallel Jewish guilds and associations have been created. The question arises: what differences of principle divide them, that even in the face of the great danger it is impossible for them to unite? Both guilds and associations call on people to register — which of them should we really go to? Which is the true one? Or is it all swindle and personal ambition! Shed no tears and don't fool the public; don't wait for any medals for demoralizing the broad Jewish craftsmen's mass!
M. W.[?] Kamiński.

The Mamzer (5) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Geliszkowski[?]

[Literature — serialized novel "The Mamzer"; instalment 5: summary of the previous chapters, end of the previous chapter and "Chapter 5".]
Adv. S. Geliszkowski [?].
The Mamzer. (5)
A gripping tragic novel of a prodigy.
Summary of the previous chapters:
In the home of the timber merchant Avraham Langnas they are preparing for the grand wedding of the beautiful Chanale, the only daughter of Reb Avraham Langnas, to the yeshiva student Binyomin. All the household, especially the bride's side, are beside themselves with joy that their daughter is marrying the groom whom the Rebbe matched. But Chanale's alabaster face is sad; in her young heart burns a love for the bookkeeper of her father's business, Rozen.
In Reb Avraham's large garden the wedding feast for the poor takes place. The groom is due to arrive soon, but Reb Avraham is busy in a conversation with Rozen, who does not want to attend the wedding, with the excuse that he must travel home to his father. Rozen takes his leave and, on going out, swears an oath to take revenge on Chanale.
In the middle of the night the town was alarmed: Reb Avraham's house is burning. After the fire a second misfortune struck Reb Avraham: his son-in-law Binyomin was accused of being the arsonist. Quickly his things were packed and he was sent off to the border, to flee from there to America. On the way he met Rozen (the real arsonist and avenger against Chanale), who travelled together with him to America and there directs his base scheme of how to separate Binyomin from Chanale. In this too Rozen succeeded, and he worked on Binyomin to stop writing letters to his Chanale.
And now read on:
So days and weeks and months ran by, until spring arrived, the beautiful spring.
From the houses[?] people began to carry out the bedding with the straw mattresses [sheynikes, Polish siennik; doubtful reading] full of crushed straw.
Everything became new, fresh and lively, but nothing became different, with the coming of spring, in the longing heart of Chanale, who could no longer bear the sighing and groaning of father and mother over Binyomin's silence.
"You may yet, God forbid, remain an agunah," her father would nag at her [printed "egbern dem moyekh"; doubtful reading], "what will happen then, what?"
"Go ask the Rebbe," Chanale would answer her father, and leave the house.
She was glad that there was no letter from her husband. If only he were dea[d]... she took fright at her own terrible thought.
Chapter 5.
On the eighth floor on Colling[?] Street in New York live the two friends who smuggled themselves across the border together, Binyomin and Rozen.
Binyomin, who is already called Benoit[?] Davidson, is no longer as hirsute as he once was. The small pointed little beard, with shaven cheeks, the tiny moustache, which can barely be noticed and looks like a thin black stripe under the nose, give him a different appearance than in the yeshiva.
Now he sits in his room, on Colling Street, and waits for his friend[?] Rozen, who is to bring him an answer from the synagogue member concerning his candidacy as cantor at the Russian synagogue, in which he had led the prayers this Sabbath on trial.
Impatiently he walks about the fairly large room, in which stand two beautiful beds made up with bedding. In the middle of the room stands a not large round table, surrounded by six beautiful chairs, and in a corner not far from the window, on a beautiful red divan, stands a not large square red little table with three not large stools of the same colour.
The clock says three and Rozen still does not come. Something must have happened, Benoit Davidson says to himself, pacing the room.
He already wants to put on his coat and go out into the street, but he holds back because of the footsteps he hears from the corridor, and which he recognises as Rozen's.
The door opens and into the room comes a cheerful, laughing Rozen, who calls out: "Mazel tov, Mr. Cantor, mazel tov."
"What news?" Benoit Davidson runs to meet him.
"It's good, you have been accepted as cantor of the Russian synagogue with a salary of two thousand dollars a year." And taking a paper out of his pocket he hands it to him.
Binyomin, or as he is now called, Benoit Davidson, opens the paper, but beyond the figure 2 thousand he understands nothing. Absently he folds the paper back up, which is called a contract.
"Good, all right," he says, "and now, what news do you have from Poland, from my father-in-law?"
Rozen lowers his head to the ground and is silent.
"What is it! Has something bad happened?" Benoit asks him, frightened.
"Benoit, I would not want to give you such bad news, but what can one do? You remember, you always used to say everything is from Heaven, everything comes from above. Take comfort like a man."
"But what has happened? What has happened?" the frightened Benoit asks once more.
"Sit shiva, Benoit: your wife Chanale has died of the troubles over her father getting six years in prison. Here, here is the letter, read it."
With trembling hands Benoit takes the letter and reads.
Much beloved friend Reb Binyomin!
It pains me that I must inform you of such terrible news, but who more than you should know that one must not question the Master of the Universe, and about everything one must say "this too is for the good" and "Blessed be the true Judge". Yes, dear friend, know that your wife Mrs. Chana daughter of Reb Avraham died in Nisan h"y[?]. May she be a good intercessor for you and for all of us. Amen, and amen.
Also about your father-in-law I must write to you that he has been sentenced to 6 years in prison; God knows whether he will endure it.
I beg you very, very much, do not write any letter to us, because if, God forbid, a little letter of yours were intercepted, they could give me prison. Also, for heaven's sake, do not write to the Rebbe, may he live long, because it is a great danger. Be well and strong, from me your friend
Moshe Kat.
Having read the letter that Rozen had brought him, Benoit rent his garment (kriah) and sat shiva for his wife Chanale.
Of the great misfortune that had befallen their cantor Benoit Davidson all the rich men and wardens of the synagogue learned at once, and they hastened to comfort their cantor in mourning and wished him that from now on he be spared all sorrow.
And when the thirty days (shloshim) had ended, a great parade took place on Sixth Avenue, where the great Russian synagogue stands.
All the worshippers gathered. The new cantor recited the proper chapters of Psalms and was led into his new apartment, which is on the first floor of the big building next to the synagogue.
Rozen too stayed together with Davidson, without whom he could not manage. And indeed, it was thanks to Rozen that Benoit Davidson had been engaged as cantor at the great Russian synagogue, and so it is no wonder that Rozen, the "pipiker"[?] Rozen, remained the private secretary of Benoit Davidson, who became ever more famous as a phenomenal master of voice not only in New York but in all America. Rozen had already seen to that, and he licked a bone from it himself.
"Will you ever travel to Poland again?" Rozen once asks him thus.
"What do I have to do there?" Davidson answers. "My father-in-law sits in prison, my wife is dead, and of my parents too, after all, no one is left to me. So I doubt that I shall ever go there."
A sarcastic smile appears on Rozen's lips and, contented, he begins to pace the room, humming under his nose a melody from an unknown operetta.
"You know?" says Rozen. "You need to get married."
Benoit Davidson raises his eyes to him and says:
"Not so fast, my friend, will that happen. If I did not succeed the first time, I will not do it myself the second time."
"Tell me, Benoit, was Chanale, may she rest in peace, a wife to you?" Rozen asked him.
"No..."
"And thank God that she was not. Pure as an angel she will come to the Throne of Glory and stand before the Ruler of the world," he answers, and heaves a heavy sigh.
And Benoit did not notice how a contented, sweet smile spread over Rozen's face.
(To be continued.)
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Lech Lecha)

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parshat Lech Lecha
The portion.
—o—
a) “Say, I pray thee, thou art my sister” (12:13)
The evil inclination talks a person into nothing but sin. As soon as the Egyptians learn that Sarah is a married woman, they will lust after her; she will look many times more beautiful in their eyes, and they will kill Abraham in order to get her. But if they think she is only his sister and has no husband, she will no longer have such allure in their eyes.. For that is how the evil inclination works in man: the unattainable, what is forbidden — that is what looks far more enticing... Kiflayim le-Tushiya.
—o—
b) “And he went on his journeys” (13:3)
“On his return he paid his debts” — Rashi.
It turns out that the Torah tells it as praise that Abraham paid his debts; that even for a righteous man like Abraham it is also to his credit that he repaid the debts as soon as he got money... Leket Amarim.
—o—
The Gemara says that when a person is brought to judgment in the world to come, he is asked: “Did you deal in faith (nasata ve-natata be-emuna)?” — Why do the Sages express the notion of trade with the phrase “nasata ve-natata”?
But the merchant is asked, after a hundred and twenty years: “Did you deal in faith?” — Did you faithfully also give back what you took? Did you pay (“natata”, you gave) what you borrowed (“nasata”, you took)?... That is what “massa u-mattan” means: one must give back (mattan) what one has taken (massa) on loan. That is the first thing asked at the judgment in the world to come. Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
—o—
R' Efraim Zalman Margaliot was a very rich man who ran businesses and, as was the custom, also gave credit. When he began conducting his trade, he declared his entire fortune ownerless before a rabbinical court. “Let no Jew stumble through me — he said — into the prohibition of theft, should a ‘creditor’ [i.e. one who took credit from me] go bankrupt on me...”
—o—
A Jew came to R' Moshe Aharon Kutner [of Kutno] who was trying to become a ne'eman[?] [kashrut supervisor] in Kutno. R' Moshe Aharon took the man for a dishonest person and began talking him out of the post:
— Better become a rabbi — he says to him.
— But I can't study — the man answers.
— Then become a merchant.
— But I have no money.
— One trades on credit.
— Nobody will want to trust me...
— So you want the community to trust you?... People won't entrust you with money — so they should entrust you with kashrut, which can also sometimes be sold for money?..
—o—
c) “Let there be no strife, I pray thee” (ibid., 8)
For that is how it goes. From “and there was a strife”, a small dispute, comes a quarrel, a bigger dispute... In Sanhedrin, folio 7, the Gemara likens disputes to a stream of water which, if not stopped at once, grows ever wider and stormier... Shelah.
—o—
f) “Let there be no strife... for we are brethren” (ibid.)
From the fact that “we are brethren” — just let no dispute come out of that... Abraham's herdsmen shouted nothing but “we are brethren”: we are brothers, we must make peace; and with those cries of “peace”, “after all, we are all brothers”, it was precisely then that they incited and kindled the greatest fires of dispute.. Devarim Nehmadim.
—o—
g) “And ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin” (17:11)
At a circumcision one says: “Just as he entered the covenant, so may he enter into Torah, the wedding canopy and good deeds”, because circumcision is the only commandment that a person surely fulfils without any personal motive, without any evil thought... Therefore: just as he entered the covenant — just as he was brought to the covenant when he certainly had no ulterior motive — so may he enter into Torah, the canopy and good deeds; so should he perform all the other good deeds too..
R' Shmuel Kaminker.

“Der Kokh-Lefl” (The Cooking Ladle) — How Does One Become a Doctor?

[Humour — the “Der Kokh-Lefl” (“The Cooking Ladle”) column; Sosnowiec — satire on the kehilla elections.] “Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour and satire. Compiled by Amotz.
In connection with the rumours that have spread that the kehilla elections in Sosnowiec have been confirmed, we present the following treatise by our contributor from the scientific department:
A doctor.
What sort of creature is that? What talent must one have in order to be a doctor?
What must one know?
What must one demonstrate?
Must one be a writer? A diplomat? A philosopher?
No! A thousand and ten thousand times no and no!
— Who can be a doctor?
I will answer you: every person living in the world can be a doctor. He need only demonstrate something that not every plain Jew demonstrates. As soon as he demonstrates that “something”, he can already be a doctor.
What, then, is the “something” that the doctor must demonstrate?
We will explain it to you:
When a Jew wants to become a melamed, he must know how to teach children, deal out a smack now and then, have a healthy heart, and he must also know how to go hungry.
Such a Jew can in time become the greatest melamed in the world.
The same goes for other professions.
A watchmaker[?] must know how to poke about in the little wheels. A tailor must have a stomach that demands no food, that can strike and take blows, and have a wife with seven children.
A cantor must have a voice, get paid, and not give a hoot about his gabbaim!
A poet must demonstrate a rich imagination; a writer must have a rich handwriting and must know how to copy from other people's little books.
An orator must demonstrate a mouth for shouting like a Jewish housewife, and he must know when to stop.
In stopping lies great wisdom. There are orators among us who talk — the audience sleeps and he talks, the audience snores louder and he talks louder.
Such an orator ought to be shot, simply shot!
The sooner the better for the listeners, and the healthier for himself.
Before a person is born, an angel comes flying and gives him a kiss. If the angel kisses him on the head — he is a man with a head; if he kisses him on the throat — he grows up a singer; if the angel kisses him on the hand, he becomes a fiddler or a communal worker with “long fingers”; and if the angel kisses him on the place one needs for sitting — he grows up a doctor...
Hasidic Sport.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-Lefl”; satire on Agudas Yisroel and sport.] As we learn, the following was resolved at the last meeting of the Central Committee (Ts. K.) of the Aguda [Agudas Yisroel]:
Since they have already “out-eaten”[?] the Zionists [i.e. copied them] with schools, newspapers and congresses of their own, Hasidic matches should also be organised.
The Aguda football team [“drushine”, drużyna] will be called “The whole Torah on one foot”.
The matches will take place every Fast of Gedaliah on the square by every beis-medresh.
Each side will consist not of eleven men but — of a minyan.
Matches will be played only against teams of our own, namely: the Gerers against the Aleksanderers, the Radomskers against the Munkatchers, and so on.
Before the match one must pray Minchah on the sports ground, and only then does one go and play.
The match is conducted by a beis-din. Where there is no beis-din, a referee [“sendushe”, sędzia] is enough.
No women may be present on the sports ground, so that the referee should not come to sinful thoughts...
When a player needs to relieve himself, the match must be interrupted until after the “Asher Yatzar” blessing.
When a goal goes in, the crowd must recite “Shekocho u-gvuraso male olam” [“whose power and might fill the world”].
Care must be taken that the ball [“pyalke”, piłka] is not shatnez.
A mezuzah must be nailed onto the “gate” [goal].
When a player falls and smashes his “Asher Yatzar” [i.e. his body], the referee must ask his “forgiveness”...
During play the players may not interrupt...
The referee must give signals with a shofar and finish with a tekiah.
Should one side see[?] that it cannot by any means score in the “bramke” [bramka, goal], it must cry out: “Open the gate for us at the time of the closing of the gate, for the day is waning”...
Why I Must Smoke.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-Lefl”; satirical monologue on smoking.] The doctor told me that smoking is harmful to my health.
My wife insisted to me that the cigarettes [“papirosn”] are harmful to my pocket.
My employer gave me to understand that smoking is harmful to my work.
My creditors are of the opinion that it is simply harmful to my memory.
So I agree with all of them and say: yes, it is true that smoking harms me in all the things listed, but stop smoking I cannot by any means. Firstly, I have a great many partners in my cigarettes, and I cannot just go and throw smoking away without asking them a word. I believe their opinion must be heard too; after all they too are somewhat concerned in the matter, and one must hold a survey [“ankete”] among them and hear out their opinion as well.
Secondly, I ask you: when one has such a good client, who takes cigarettes from you day in day out, how can one stop smoking? What if, God forbid, that fellow runs out of cigarettes, or what if he even takes offence at me over it — how can I suddenly, in the middle of it all, be left without good friends?
So I must smoke!
Legal Advice — Not by Adv. Dr. Rechtman.

[Humour — “Der Kokh-Lefl”; satirical “legal advice”, followed by two jokes: “Oh, the Doctors” and “No Consolation for Him”.] Not by Advocate Dr. Rechtman.
A young man who goes to look over prospective brides and everywhere grabs something into his mouth — if he gets “found out”[?] [“fershit”] and nobody lets him in anywhere any more, he may submit an application to the Unemployment Fund stating that he has been left without means of subsistence, and should demand “zasiłki” [benefits].
• • •
If an old man has a young wife and holds a bris, he has the right to demand of his neighbour (or of the sub-tenant [“sublokator”]) that the latter cover the costs.
• • •
If a merchant walks along Gzichowska[?] Street and “takes in” [“leyzt” — pun: both ‘takes in receipts’ and ‘relieves himself’] from afar, he need not pay any turnover tax [“obrotowe”] on it.
—o—
Oh, the Doctors
A patient with swollen tonsils comes in to the doctor.
— It's nothing, says the doctor, I'll cut out your tonsils and you'll be well.
Some time later the patient comes again with a pain in his side.
— It's nothing, says the doctor, I'll cut out your back and you'll be well.
Some time later the doctor meets the patient and asks him:
— What's the matter, that one doesn't see you any more?
— This time, says the patient, I'm afraid to come to you, because I suffer from headaches...
—o—
No Consolation for Him
Mrs Górka has returned from Krynica.
— For three months I left my dear husband alone in town — Mrs Górka said to the maid with a feeling of pity — he surely felt sad and lonely because I wasn't there. Yes?
— Not the whole time did he feel like that — says the maid — only the last few days did he go about like a sad man, almost a desperate one...
Chronicle

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — satire, “Der Kokh-Lefl”; kehilla and rabbinate.]
A place for the refugees.
The Będzin Anti-Hitler Committee, which has merits in its field, managed in recent weeks to carry out a thing of the first order: for instance, as we are informed, the committee prevailed upon the rabbi to allow all the refugees from the Będzin “shtiblekh” [Hasidic prayer rooms] to have access to the rabbi's minyan.
An important decision.
As is known, all subsidies in the Będzin kehilla budget have been struck out, except the subventions for “Bnos” and “Poalei Agudas Yisroel”.
In connection with this, a joint consultation of the women members and members of the above-mentioned organizations took place, and it was decided that matchmakers and their [?] matches must belong only to the B. B. club.
The Sosnowiec rabbinical chair sits “shiva”...
In connection with the new candidate for the Sosnowiec rabbinate, the rabbinical chair must already sit “shiva”... (because there are already seven candidates).
A good sign.
At the academic ball in Sosnowiec a little scene “from all the gentiles” took place... This is a sign for the future that the academics will have gentile success...
Decision of the kehilla administration.
Because the dozors [kehilla board members] in Sosnowiec must pay back into the gmina [municipal] treasury for increased economic expenses, the kehilla administration held a meeting at which it was decided to issue an appeal to the poor Jewish population that they should stop dying, falling ill and having babies...
The “Japanchiks” Are Crushing Us

[Economy and trade — world; report.] From our correspondent Z. Haber, Vienna [?].
Day by day Japanese competition throughout the world grows ever stronger. Day by day they spring up with new articles, which they dump at such prices that not only do they push all foreign suppliers out of the most important markets in the world, but they even kill off [?] the manufacturers of those countries themselves.
In Poland, for example, they sell rubber wheels at a price of a little over one złoty. The wheels are made of the best rubber qualities. In Poland itself rubber wheels are manufactured. But the worst quality costs, in the country itself, more than three times as much as the Japanese rubber wheels.
If one wants to get an idea of how strongly the Japanese have built up their industry lately, it is enough to take a look at a few figures on the money they have put in recent years into various industrial enterprises in their country.
In the year 1932 various factories were founded in Japan with a capital of three hundred million dollars. — In the year 1933 various factories were again founded with a capital of no less than three thousand million dollars. That means that in the last year they invested ten times as much money in newer industries as a year before. And the figure for the year 1934 will be much greater than in the year 1933.
In this they work with various means that in Europe one would never have thought of. Thus, for example, they concentrated the entire beer production in one village, to which they gave the name Pilsen. Naturally they sell all over the world “genuine Pilsner beer”, which costs a trifle and is indeed as good as the Pilsner beer from Czechoslovakia.
Likewise they have a village, in which they concentrated the entire steel production, which they named Solingen, and they sell “genuine Solingen steel” at about five hundred percent cheaper than Solingen steel from Germany. It goes without saying that the quality and the workmanship are matched exactly to the German Solingen goods.
Now they are planning to call a village Gablonz, so as to be able to sell the world-famous Gablonz goods all over the world as “genuine Gablonz”.
When they need it, they will give a village the name Jerusalem, so as to be able to sell tefillin, tallitot and ritual objects “kosher from Jerusalem”.
The main place for deliveries to Europe lies in Fiume; almost the whole city lives from Japanese goods that arrive in and depart from Fiume. Gold watches they sell at five dollars apiece. Non-gold watches of the finest makes cost a dollar, and ordinary watches, for which they give a written guarantee for a year, they sell by weight... A nice nickel watch comes to about ten American cents (half a złoty).
The finest pencils they sell at a grosz apiece. With cheap fabrics, at forty groszy a metre, they flood [?], for example, the entire Balkans.
It has gone so far that Sweden, which dominated all the match monopolies almost throughout the world, has now had to come to terms with the Japanese and join hands with them, in order to supply the whole world with matches in partnership. The Japanese had threatened that they would break the entire Swedish trust.
In South America they have penetrated almost all the countries. In every larger place there they found their own Japanese banks, so that it should be easier for them to collect their debts.
In China they compete very strongly with “genuine Chinese porcelains”, which are made exactly as well as the genuine Chinese ones and cost a pittance [?]. In Norway, Portugal and other countries that live from the export of fish preserves, they sell the same preserves so cheaply that it does not pay the local manufacture to work at all.
The big canning factories of Portugal buy up their preserves from them, which are already labelled with Portuguese banderoles, and they are sold as genuine Portuguese fish and sardines.
As it turns out, it will not take very long before Europe, too, shuts down its entire industry and leaves all the markets to the Japanese competition, by which we are already being crushed now.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Sharp Stand by the National Councillors against the Agudah Faction of the Kehilla Board

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Kehilla.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 10 Cheshvan 5695 — piątek 19 października 1934 [Friday, 19 October 1934].)
Będzin
Sharp stand by the national councillors against the Agudah faction of the kehilla board.
Under the chairmanship of President Mr. Y. M. Kurland, a meeting of the kehilla council took place on Saturday night. Taking part in the meeting were the Agudah board members (dozors) Banhart, Werdiger, Skoczylas and Piekarski.
The meeting was called in connection with the fact that in the kehilla budget almost all subsidies for cultural, national and social institutions had been struck out, whereas the subventions for the Agudah organisations — for the "Bnos" and the "Poalim" [Bnos Agudath Israel and Poalei Agudath Israel] — had been increased.
After Mr. Kurland opens the meeting, Mr. N. Landner turns to Mr. Rubinlicht asking him to give an explanation about the budget changes. To this Mr. Rubinlicht answers that the question has not yet been considered by the board and therefore he cannot give the requested explanation.
The floor on the substance of the matter goes to Mr. Landner, who gives a historical survey of the great influence of the Jewish kehillas of old, as the spiritual centre of Jewish life, in comparison with the present time, when there lies before us — he says — a budget in which all cultural and national subventions have been struck out except those of the Agudah. The pain is all the greater because 75 per cent of[?] the etat [kehilla tax] flows in from the national strata; moreover, several etat payers voluntarily assessed themselves at higher etat sums so that the national needs of the kehilla would be met. But when such a budget lies before us, we must — says Mr. Landner — face up to the fact that the only thing to do as a protest is
to lay down our mandates
and leave the gmina [community] in Agudah hands. Enough of playing the comedy of making budgets which are afterwards turned into a heap of ruins. The national councillors are, after all, ashamed to show themselves in the street for disgrace, when subsidies for the "Bnos" and "Poalim" are approved and the subsidy for emigration to Eretz Israel is struck out...
Councillor Herszlewicz[?] speaks out against the proposal to lay down the mandates. We should have — he says — laid down the mandates when our best comrade Wigodzki was removed and in his place the Agudah brought into the gmina a man who is no longer capable of public work. Mr. Herszlewicz reproaches the board for not having protested when the vice-president Mr. Liwer, who had worked in the gmina with self-sacrifice, was removed.
President Rubinlicht: We should not have too many grievances against the authorities, who struck out the most important items. This happened on the basis of
this bundle of denunciations
which was handed in about the budget. When we provisionally set a sum of 6000 zł. for urgent aid for Jewish want and suffering, Shlomo Yitzchak Dinski came along with Nute Kater and the rabbi's secretary, a certain Herzberg, and sent off a little denunciation to the authorities saying that 6000 zł. is too much; 1000 zł. — they wrote — will also be enough. Well, the authorities granted their request and approved 1000 zł... But these stumbling blocks must not deter us; we must go on pulling the heavy cart loaded with stones and uproot the wild growths in the gmina.
Councillor Kornfeld turns to the Agudah dozors with the question: why do you fight us over every budget item at a time when you, gentlemen of the "Agudah", know clearly that the items you do not like will be struck out? Mr. Kornfeld also censures the Zionist councillors for not having protested against the removal of Mr. Liwer. In the name of the Left Poalei Zion faction Mr. Kornfeld declares that he will vote against Landner's proposal.
Councillor Rawinker[?] also speaks out against Landner's proposal. We must go on fighting — he says — until victory.
Speaking for Mr. Landner's proposal is Councillor L. Goldsztajn. He speaks with great pathos and says that not only the council but also the board must lay down its mandates. We must not be — cries Mr. Goldsztajn — any
executors for the clergy.
Let the "Agudah" take over the whole gmina; our work is futile anyway. When "editor" Lipman Berkowicz needed support, when he wanted to go to Eretz Israel, they came to the Zionist dozors for help, and now the very same Agudah people strike out the item for emigration to Eretz Israel.
Mr. Landner puts his proposal again, and incidentally speaks about the denunciations which will remain — he says — an everlasting disgrace.
Dozor D. Skoczylas takes the floor on the question. The voivode — he says — struck out the items not on the basis of the accusations but for the sake of economy; the "Agudah" sent accusations because we are against a large budget. You want to run away because you cannot accomplish anything at all...
Mr. Skoczylas's "defence" throws off balance even the calm and not extreme-partisan[?] chairman Mr. Kurland, who orders the denunciations about the budget to be read out.
And "woe to the ears that hear such things" — woe to the ears when one hears it — a denunciation by "Agudath Israel" in Będzin, signed by the president and present city councillor Avraham Leib Grünwald and by the secretary Moshe Chaiml Kaminer (the "little editor" of the "mikveh leaflet", who collects many guilders every month, of all people from Zionists...). In the denunciation they point to the invalidity[?] of every subvention; they go so far as to relate that the items are partisan and were put in under false names in order to "blind the eyes" of the authorities. The above-mentioned "communal workers", who are anxious that the authorities should not be misled, also propose that half be struck out of the sum provisionally set for
coal for poor people.
This disgraceful denunciation arouses bitterness among the councillors and dozors of the national camp who are present.
Dozor Piekarski: I do not want to speak about the question itself, I only want to tell you that you, the national representatives, brought into the gmina the "we" and "they"; you threw the Agudah dozors off balance, especially when you reduced the rabbi's salary (pension) by 7½ per cent...
At these words a storm breaks out again on the part of the opponents of the Agudah; Messrs. Rubinlicht and Kurland shout: for the sake of a few złotys you write denunciations? Destroyers! One's face turns red with shame. That such a thing should happen in the Będzin kehilla — where is Jewish honour?
After the "storm" it is resolved: 1) the board and the council shall jointly lodge an appeal (rekurs) against the struck-out items, and 2) the denunciations shall be published in the press.
At 11.30 the meeting is closed.

Motl Tenenbaum, of Blessed Memory.

At the age of 48, Mr. Motl Tenenbaum, of blessed memory, was torn away this week. The grievous, untimely loss struck like thunder all strata of the Jewish population of Będzin, among whom the deceased was so beloved and respected.
Despite the bad rain, thousands of people came to pay him their last respects. At the cemetery the cantor Mr. Klingswald sang "Yoshev beseter" [Psalm 91], and Mr. Rubinlicht, as a close friend, pointed out in a short speech the great virtues of the esteemed deceased. Mr. A. Barlenski [?] also spoke.
With broken hearts the large crowd leaves the cemetery, casting last glances at the fresh grave of the unforgettable, dear Motl Tenenbaum, of blessed memory.
May the earth lie lightly on him!
At the Grave of My Friend Motl Tenenbaum.

"Chaver" [friend, comrade] was his word of greeting. The word "chaver" characterized him entirely. And rightly could he use that word, for everyone who had had any dealings with him remained his friend; he enjoyed extraordinary trust among all strata. It will be no exaggeration to say that whenever any matters arose, even the least important, whether private or public, everyone sought advice from him, from the great man of wisdom. He was always an honest public worker who did not like cheap titles, but devoted himself, heart and soul, to the cause that interested him. Not shrinking [?] from work, more than once he had occasion to argue with the most offensive argument — with the truth, for which he did not endear himself to the patented public figures. Every mission entrusted to him he carried out perfectly; with him there was no half-done or amateurish work. Everything was thought through precisely and weightily, and he defended his standpoint with dignity. At the same time a modest man, who hated drum-beating. His modesty holds me back from speaking about him any further.
Comrade Motl Tenenbaum has died. Long will the mourning last among his devoted friends.
Matek Gold.
Association of Będziners in Eretz Israel.

This week Mr. Abraham Liwer returned from Eretz Israel and gives us interesting details about the well-being of the Będzin olim [immigrants] in Eretz Israel. Almost all of them live in "Neve Sha'anan", and all of them are doing fine and well.
In honour of Mr. Liwer a banquet took place [?] in Sternfeld's restaurant, attended by about 100 guests, Będziners only, men and women. The banquet was opened by Mr. A. Hampel, and the chair was handed over to the first chalutz [pioneer] from Będzin, Mr. Steinfeld. Speeches were given by: Metal, Meir Jungste [?], Yosef Tsinat [?] Reich, Shabtai Liwer and Kakotek. Afterwards Mr. Liwer reported on the situation in the Diaspora in general and in Będzin in particular, and called on those assembled to organize themselves into an association and undertake a relief action for the benefit of the destitute olim [prospective emigrants to Palestine] in Będzin.
The proposal was accepted, and a committee was elected consisting of: Metal, Liwer, Steinfeld, Mordechai Yosef Tenenbaum, Reich and Hampel.
The committee held a meeting in Mr. Steinfeld's apartment, and it was decided to carry out a registration of all Będziners living in Eretz Israel.
Scaffolding Collapses and Injures a Worker.
On Wednesday at midday, in the courtyard at Kołłątaja 48, the scaffolding of the second floor collapsed. A worker who was working at the balcony fell down and was seriously injured.
One Grosz for the "Talmud Torah".

On Tuesday a meeting took place in the rabbinate house with the aim of renewing the grosz campaign for the benefit of the Talmud Torah. The moreh tzedek [rabbinical judge] Reb Henech David and the Rebbe Shapira undertook to organize the bakers, so that they should uphold [?] the campaign.
It is the duty of every single person who wants the Talmud Torah to go on existing to remind his family not to forget, when buying a loaf of bread, to give one grosz for the Talmud Torah.

On Thursday at about 11, Messrs. Rubinlicht, A. L. Grunwald, A. D. Balimazski [?] and Bauszykowski [?] were strolling along Kołłątaja Street. Sosnowiec — Supplementary Elections to the City Councils in Zagłębie.

The Voivodeship Department in Kielce has considered the protests lodged against the city council elections in a number of towns of the Kielce Voivodeship. As a result, several protests were recognized as justified, and therefore supplementary elections will take place in 2 districts in Sosnowiec, in Będzin in 2 districts, in Dąbrowa in 3 districts and in Zawiercie in 1 district.
The elections will take place next month. Because of this the new city councils will convene only in January or later.
A small factory of 5- and 10-złoty coins discovered

The fine [?] 'manufacturer' is the watchman of the local 'Moshav Zekenim' [old-age home].
The local investigation office received confidential information that in the flat of Jan Miszczyk, watchman of the 'Moshav Zekenim' on Chmielna Street, a small factory of silver [?] coins had been set up.
A search was ordered at once, and it produced a sensational result.
In the yard a pot [?] was found buried in the ground with 100 counterfeit 10-zł. coins, several dozen 5-złoty coins, and in the dog's kennel the factory itself was found.
The watchman with his whole family, and also a certain [?] Fritz from Lemberg [Lwów], were arrested. After questioning, only the watchman's wife with the minor children was released.
Our Tribune. (A Foreword to Our Readers).

[Kielce — editorial; the „Kielcer Tsaytung“ renewed as the Kielce section.] (A foreword to our readers).
Any address or foreword is, properly speaking, superfluous. We know the Jewish public of Kielce — our countless friends and acquaintances — far too well to need to doubt the genuine satisfaction and joy that the renewal of the „Kielcer Tsaytung“ will arouse in them. After all, we have more than once had occasion to convince ourselves of the loyalty and devotion of sensible Jewish Kielce to our work and achievements in the field of the local Jewish press.
Work and achievements! The virtue of modesty demands a more restrained tone when telling of one's own merits and efforts. But it will be no self-praise at all if we mention our pioneering work in the field of the Jewish local press in Kielce. We were the first who, years ago already, created for Kielce a Jewish platform of the word of its own, later made an attempt at a daily newspaper of its own, and finally, under difficult material and technical conditions, consolidated the existence of a local organ which honestly and faithfully served the national interests of the Jewish public in our town.
Being ourselves strongly engaged in the day-to-day national and communal work, we reacted without the slightest interruption to every event and objectively shed light on every phenomenon in public life, went through [?] together a piece of the history of a Jewish community of 20 thousand souls and — without exaggeration — contributed, directly or indirectly, to its development.
On this path — often not a very easy one — we were always accompanied by the sympathy and recognition of a wide circle of readers and friends who knew how to appreciate the role of a Jewish organ. That was a great satisfaction for our work and toil.
This sympathy showed itself especially at another, rather unpleasant moment, when the prestige of the printed word had fallen sharply and the standing of a local organ was put under a question mark. This was done in a petty [?], ugly manner. We could not respond to the constant vilenesses, just as a self-respecting person cannot respond to wanton scrawls somewhere on a fence on the edge of town. We would have considered it beneath our dignity, at the present renewal of our newspaper, to devote space to polemics with unworthy people. No provocations, nor attempts to force a reply, will help here. We shall no longer concern ourselves with such things.
It is enough for us that the reading public reacted to all this, and only for its sake did we spare no effort, until we finally succeeded in joining with the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“, which is the largest Jewish weekly in Poland, has been appearing for 24 years already and is known for its rich journalistic and informative content, which stands at a high journalistic level.
It is clear to us that our newspaper will now be received with joy by the whole Jewish public of Kielce, which will know how to appreciate the importance of a serious organ rich in content. Besides the permanent, enlarged section of Kielce articles, feuilletons and chronicle, readers will find in every issue many articles, feuilletons, stories and essays of a general character, as well as the latest news from the whole voivodeship.
The „Kielcer Tsaytung“ now becomes the only Jewish organ of the Kielce voivodeship. Without doubt it will have the widest support of the Jewish public in this area, whose interests it will faithfully serve.
Life in Kielce

[Kielce and district — short news items.] Head of the Security Department of the Kielce Voivodeship Transferred to Poznań.
The head of the security department at the Kielce voivodeship office, Mr. Zwirski, has been transferred to the same post in the Poznań voivodeship. Who will be appointed in Mr. Zwirski's place is for the time being not yet known.

An Alarm in the Rabbinate over a Cholent of… „Squealing Meat“ [i.e. pork].
Last Saturday morning one of the Hasidic residents of Sienkiewicza Street alarmed the rabbinate that, according to information he had received from the owner of the Hotel „Francuski“, Mr. Moshe Rozenberg, among the Sabbath cholents that had been placed at the baker Mr. Brajtman's on Friday towards evening there was also a cholent of… „squealing meat“. The treyf cholent came — as Mr. Rozenberg reported — from a Jewish bar on the said street.
The rabbinate at once delegated one of its members, who, in the presence of dozens of women, men, children and plain onlookers, opened all the cholents and subjected them to „a thorough inspection“. Some „specialists“, „connoisseurs“ of kishkes, „confirmed“ that the smell of the cholent marked with the sign of „the bar“ was not of any squealing meat, and that it was a „kosher“ cholent like all the other cholents. Only after this „finding“ and a further examination lasting several hours did the rabbinate's representative declare the cholents kosher, and the Jews breathed more freely.
But since the cholents had been opened for the rabbinate's inspection, it was afterwards hard to recognise to whom each cholent belonged, and a great commotion broke out among the women present, which very nearly led to [—?] rows and brawls. The situation was saved by the baker Mr. Brajtman, who politely calmed the agitated women and showed each one her proper cholent — and that indeed worked.
